item.title: Seth Meyers mocks Trump’s cognitive abilities after bizarre claim
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Seth Meyers mocked President Donald Trump after Trump told reporters, following early voting in Florida on an unspecified Saturday, that his uncle John G. Trump “invented radar.” The article says John G. Trump was a respected MIT professor who worked on radar during World War II but did not invent it. Meyers used the false claim to ridicule Trump’s repeated boasts about passing cognitive tests.

Meyers also targeted two campaign spectacles described by AlterNet: Republican congressional candidate Joe Mitchell presenting Trump with a self-created “Man of the Century” award in Iowa, and Trump proposing at a Florida rally that New Mexico be renamed “New America.” The article says these appearances renewed questions about Trump’s mental fitness, but it supplies no medical evidence or expert assessment establishing cognitive impairment.

The power is not on late-night television

Meyers has a platform, an audience and a joke writer’s ability to puncture vanity. Trump has presidential authority. That distinction matters more than the monologue.

The consequential fact is not that a comedian found the remarks absurd. It is that a president made a plainly false historical claim while speaking publicly, then continued through a campaign environment built to applaud him. Institutional power belongs to Trump and to the political apparatus that promotes, excuses or launders his statements—not to the host describing the performance.

Flattery as political infrastructure

The invented award is more revealing than its cheap appearance. According to AlterNet, Mitchell created it and then bestowed it on Trump. That makes the episode an act of political ingratiation, not an achievement being recognized.

Mitchell exercised agency: he manufactured a distinction and presented it to the most powerful figure in his party’s orbit. Trump accepted the spectacle. The exchange shows how political subordinates can convert deference into campaign theater, supplying the leader with symbolic triumphs when reality does not cooperate.

Diagnosis is a distraction

AlterNet frames the remarks as evidence renewing concern about Trump’s cognitive fitness and adds speculation about his physical appearance. But the article offers neither a diagnosis nor evidence connecting appearance to incapacity. That framing is weak because it turns observable conduct into amateur medicine.

No diagnosis is necessary to assess what happened. Trump made a false claim about his uncle. A Republican candidate fabricated an award for him. Trump floated an incoherent renaming of New Mexico. Those are political facts involving judgment, truthfulness and a culture of sycophancy. Treating them principally as symptoms risks converting accountable behavior into an involuntary condition—and lets the officials enabling it disappear from view.

The permission structure

The larger pattern is an ecosystem in which falsehood and flattery carry little internal cost. A president can invent family history, while an allied candidate invents an honor for the president. One fiction magnifies personal genius; the other manufactures public acclaim. Both move in the same direction: power receives affirmation instead of correction.

Late-night ridicule can expose the absurdity, but it cannot impose institutional consequences. The sharper question is not whether Trump can pass a test he boasts about passing. It is why people seeking power through him have an incentive to reward his claims, stage his validation and leave correction to comedians.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Seth Meyers mocks Trump’s cognitive abilities after bizarre claim

item.title: Five-alarm fire for Republicans as Fox News ratings take massive 'plunge’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News was on track for its lowest-rated month since December 2023. Nielsen data obtained by Status showed the network averaging 1.1 million total-day viewers in October 2026, down 27 percent from October 2025, while its audience among adults ages 25–54 fell 32 percent to 98,000—its lowest monthly average in that demographic in 25 years.

Status reporter Oliver Darcy called Fox an anomaly because CNN and MS NOW were expected to report year-over-year gains before the November 2026 midterms. Fox nevertheless remained the dominant cable network in total-day viewership, even surpassing ESPN, according to the report.

The evidence establishes a severe ratings decline, not the cause of that decline or an impending Republican “wipeout.” Status and media commentators suggested that Fox’s audience may track conservative enthusiasm, while AlterNet connected the numbers to Donald Trump’s low approval ratings. The article supplied no polling or electoral data demonstrating that Fox viewership caused—or reliably predicted—Republican losses.

The signal is real, the forecast is not

A 27 percent contraction in total viewership and a 32 percent fall in the commercially prized demographic are consequential. They suggest that fewer people are choosing Fox’s political programming during a period when election coverage would ordinarily attract attention.

But television ratings are not ballots. Viewers can abandon cable without abandoning a party, move to other platforms, or disengage temporarily. AlterNet turns a plausible indicator into a near-certain electoral prophecy. “Five-alarm fire” and “impending wipeout” are conclusions the reported figures cannot carry by themselves.

Power does not disappear with the audience

Fox still dominated cable television. That detail punctures the article’s preferred storyline: this is not a collapsed institution but a powerful one suffering a sharp decline.

Its power also cannot be reduced to a monthly Nielsen average. A network shapes which conflicts receive attention, which politicians gain legitimacy, and which explanations become routine. Even a shrinking audience can remain large, disciplined, and politically useful. Decline may weaken Fox’s reach without ending its capacity to set the conservative agenda.

Disengagement is not resistance

The article casts reduced viewing as evidence that Republican voters are losing enthusiasm. That may be true, but the data do not establish whether viewers rejected Trump, tired of election coverage, migrated elsewhere, or simply stopped watching cable news.

That distinction matters. Tuning out is not the same as changing allegiance, opposing a policy, or refusing to vote. Treating audience fatigue as political conversion mistakes absence for agency. It also shifts attention away from the institutions that actually control nominations, campaign spending, legislation, and election administration.

The convenient horse race

The headline directs blame and consequence toward Republican electoral fortunes, making the party appear endangered by forces emerging from below. Yet viewers did not create the political environment described in the report. Party leaders, officeholders, donors, campaigns, and media executives hold the institutional power to choose candidates, distribute resources, and define political messages.

By centering whether Republicans will suffer at the polls, AlterNet converts a media-power story into another horse-race omen. The stronger question is what Fox and Republican leaders produced that audiences may no longer find compelling—and whether declining attention changes their conduct. The article offers no evidence on either point.

A shrinking machine can still govern the conversation

The broader pattern is not simply conservative decline. It is the tendency to confuse weakening media consumption with weakening political power. Ratings measure attention within one medium; they do not measure control over institutions.

Fox’s plunge may be an early warning for Republicans, or it may reflect a fragmented media system in which political audiences have scattered. The reporting cannot decide between those possibilities. What it does show is narrower and still important: a dominant partisan broadcaster lost a substantial share of its audience at a politically consequential moment. Calling that a guaranteed electoral reckoning substitutes wishful arithmetic for analysis.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Five-alarm fire for Republicans as Fox News ratings take massive ‘plunge’

item.title: CNN tries to pretend its MAGA scandal 'never happened': report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Hasan Piker sued CNN contributor Scott Jennings in federal court in Washington, D.C., alleging defamation and seeking $72.5 million in damages. The complaint concerns an August broadcast on Jennings’s Salem radio show, where Jennings said Piker was “calling for Black voters to be lynched.”

According to the lawsuit, the underlying clip combined excerpts from three streams and removed context showing that Piker was describing and mocking someone else’s remark. AlterNet says the clip circulated through the National Republican Senatorial Committee before Jennings’s program used it. These remain allegations in a pending civil case; the report supplies no ruling on whether Jennings defamed Piker.

Journalist Colby Hall argued that CNN had responded conspicuously: 64 words aggregating Variety in its Reliable Sources newsletter and, at the time of his writing, no on-air coverage. Hall said CNN did not answer his request for comment.

The power is institutional

Piker can sue, deny the accusation and show the omitted context. But Jennings, Salem, CNN and the NRSC occupy the institutions that can convert a manipulated social-media clip into a nationally distributed political claim.

That hierarchy matters. CNN pays Jennings and repeatedly places him inside its news product. Hall’s point is not merely that Jennings appears on the network; it is that CNN has made him a central conservative voice across debates, conventions and major speeches. The network supplies reach, prestige and an implicit judgment that his commentary belongs within legitimate political discussion.

The decisions have names

The lawsuit alleges that Jennings broadcast a grave accusation based on a deceptively edited clip. Salem aired it. The NRSC reportedly circulated the clip. CNN did not make the disputed statement, but it chose to build programming around Jennings and then, according to Hall, largely avoided covering the resulting lawsuit.

Those are separate decisions with different degrees of responsibility. CNN is not automatically liable for what a contributor says on another company’s program. But editorial responsibility is broader than legal liability. A network cannot make a pundit valuable through constant exposure, benefit from his provocations and then treat scrutiny of his conduct as somebody else’s departmental problem.

The scapegoat machine

The political function of the disputed clip was straightforward: turn a left-wing streamer into evidence that Democratic politics harbors extremism. AlterNet describes Republicans using Piker as a boogeyman against Democratic midterm candidates. If the complaint’s account of the editing is accurate, the maneuver was not criticism of what Piker said. It was the manufacture of a more useful thing for him to have said.

That is how scapegoating works in modern campaign media. A weaker actor’s words are stripped of context, recirculated by a party committee and repeated by a credentialed commentator. The accusation then becomes the story, while the institutions that produced and amplified it fade into the background.

Silence is also framing

CNN’s scant treatment, as described by Hall, redirects attention away from its own role. The issue is not that the network must declare Jennings guilty before adjudication. It can report the complaint, describe the allegation, seek responses and state clearly that the case is unresolved. That is routine journalism.

Ignoring the case on air instead creates an asymmetry. Piker can be extensively covered as a political liability for Democrats, while a serious allegation against the CNN personality helping construct that image receives minimal institutional scrutiny. The network’s apparent standard is therefore not simply newsworthiness. It is newsworthiness constrained by self-interest.

The pundit loophole

The larger pattern is a media business model built to harvest provocation while dispersing accountability. Networks hire personalities whose value comes from conflict across television, radio and social platforms. When those personalities generate attention, the network claims the energy. When their outside conduct becomes damaging, it invokes the corporate boundary.

That boundary may matter in court. Politically, it is a loophole. Institutions manufacture authority through repetition and visibility, then pretend that authority disappears whenever responsibility arrives. The result is a system in which inflammatory claims travel at full institutional speed, while corrections, context and accountability are forced to proceed one lawsuit—and one conveniently neglected story—at a time.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: CNN tries to pretend its MAGA scandal ‘never happened’: report

item.title: 'Saw' director: Hollywood is shy about Trump content — and that's scary
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that director Kevin Greutert believes studios and financiers avoid explicit Trump-era political stories because they fear alienating “half of the American body politic.” He said that concern killed The Endorsement, a proposed horror film about a small-town journalist threatened by a politically motivated serial killer after persuading her newspaper to endorse Hillary Clinton in 2016.

Greutert also said a planned version of Saw XI involving two mayoral candidates and an election-themed trap was abandoned when “a different approach was selected,” though he did not say political pressure caused that decision. He contrasted those experiences with Saw VI, whose attack on health-insurance power reached theaters in 2009 partly, he suggested, because producers had not anticipated how politically charged healthcare reform would become.

In the interview, Greutert condemned the killing attributed to Luigi Mangione and rejected political violence. He also argued that horror can expose abusive power through stories of captivity, exploitation and helplessness, even when filmmakers avoid naming contemporary politicians directly.

The veto belongs to capital

The decisive actors here are not moviegoers imagined as two equally sized, permanently offended camps. They are studio executives, producers and financiers who control which scripts receive money, distribution and an audience.

According to Greutert, those gatekeepers rejected The Endorsement because explicit political content might repel part of the market. That is not public censorship, and the interview does not establish government coercion behind the decision. It is private capital exercising cultural power through risk avoidance.

The distinction matters. “Hollywood is shy” turns an institutional choice into a personality trait, as though an industry became bashful. Executives made—or declined to make—specific investments. Their caution protects revenue and access; its consequence is a narrower political imagination on screen.

Neutrality for sale

The demand not to “offend half” sounds like fairness only if every political subject is treated as an interchangeable consumer preference. A story about intimidation following a newspaper endorsement is not merely partisan branding. It concerns whether threats can punish political speech.

Yet the financing logic Greutert describes converts that conflict into market segmentation. The aggressor, the target and the institution capable of protecting expression disappear into a spreadsheet labeled “controversy.” This is how commercial neutrality launders power: the powerful retain their capacity to intimidate, while artists are told that naming the conflict would itself be divisive.

Ambiguity can produce excellent art. Greutert points to Invasion of the Body Snatchers and The Twilight Zone as works that used genre to approach politics indirectly. But creative indirection and compulsory evasiveness are not the same thing. One expands meaning; the other limits what can be financed.

Where the interview overreaches

AlterNet’s strongest evidence concerns Greutert’s own projects and what he says financiers told his team. Its broader claims are considerably less secure. The interviewer asserts that Trump allies are purchasing media companies and that the government has tried to stifle critical comedians, but the supplied article does not substantiate those claims.

Greutert also speculates that Trump, given the opportunity, would treat political opponents as Augusto Pinochet’s regime did. That is an opinion and a hypothetical, not a reported act or established plan. Presenting it alongside concrete accounts of rejected film projects risks substituting analogy for evidence.

The article’s political framing is therefore uneven. It identifies a real gatekeeping mechanism, then dilutes that finding with claims it does not document. Scathing conclusions require stronger sourcing, not louder comparisons.

Horror knows who controls the room

Greutert’s most useful observation is simpler: horror is often organized around unequal power. Someone controls the basement, the trap, the institution or the terms of escape. Someone else bears the pain. That structure can illuminate politics because politics also determines who may impose costs and who is forced to absorb them.

But the language of universal helplessness can blur responsibility. Greutert says audiences are implicated in systems from which they benefit, yet shared participation does not mean equal agency. A consumer, a filmmaker and a studio executive do not possess the same ability to decide what gets produced. Nor does a patient denied coverage wield the power of the executive administering the policy.

The sharper political horror story is not that everyone is trapped. It is that identifiable institutions build the trap, authorized decision-makers maintain it, and weaker people are then blamed for failing to escape.

The system prefers a monster without a name

This episode reveals how cultural institutions domesticate political art. They may tolerate injustice as metaphor, corruption as atmosphere and authoritarianism as an unnamed monster. What alarms them is specificity: a recognizable election, an identifiable movement, a conflict whose beneficiaries cannot pretend the story concerns somebody else.

No censor needs to issue an order when concentrated financing already rewards ambiguity and penalizes confrontation. The result is not silence, exactly. It is an industry permitted to depict terror while remaining coy about who holds the keys.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Saw’ director: Hollywood is shy about Trump content — and that’s scary

item.title: It's not about golf: Trump's latest defiance exposes an 'extraordinary' assault
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump said his administration would proceed with the planned Nov. 15 closure of Washington’s East Potomac Golf Course despite a federal judge’s order restricting further development. Judge Ana C. Reyes extended an injunction and required the government to provide 10 days’ notice before making irreversible changes to the federally owned park.

The dispute followed the removal of more than 400 trees. Reyes wrote that conflicting accounts from Trump, government employees, and Justice Department attorneys had forced the court to examine whether officials had complied with her earlier orders. Residents and a preservation group brought the lawsuit seeking to preserve the park and its existing public course.

Trump attacked Reyes’s knowledge of golf and claimed she lacked constitutional authority to require notice. AlterNet’s central claim is that the confrontation is not fundamentally about course design: it is about whether the executive branch will accept judicial supervision when pursuing the president’s preferred project.

The power is federal

The residents challenging the redevelopment can sue, and Reyes can issue orders, but the machinery capable of transforming the land belongs to the executive branch. The Interior Department controls the project. Justice Department lawyers represent the government. Federal employees and contractors can close the course, deploy equipment, alter pathways, and remove trees.

That imbalance matters. The preservation plaintiffs did not produce the confrontation by objecting. They invoked the legal mechanism available to people facing an administration with control over public land and the resources to change it irreversibly.

The decision has an owner

Trump publicly claimed the redevelopment as his project and declared that the closure would proceed. Interior officials and government lawyers are therefore not incidental characters. They are the people positioned to execute, enable, explain, or restrain that decision.

Reyes’s order reflects the practical problem: judicial review becomes meaningless if officials complete irreversible work before challengers or the court can respond. Her notice requirement does not design a golf course. It preserves the court’s ability to adjudicate the dispute before the government destroys the subject of it.

Golf is the diversion

Trump’s focus on Reyes’s golf expertise shifts attention from the question she actually confronted: whether the government obeyed court orders and gave accurate accounts of its conduct. A judge does not need to know how to shape a putting green to determine whether executive officials complied with an injunction.

AlterNet is right to reject that diversion, but its own rhetoric occasionally outruns its evidence. The reporting establishes conflicting sworn accounts, sharp judicial criticism, and an announced intention to proceed with the closure. It does not establish what happened after the article was published, whether Trump ultimately violated the extended order, or whether any contempt finding followed.

Defiance depends on enablers

Personalizing the episode around Trump captures who demanded the project, but it can obscure how presidential defiance becomes government action. A social-media declaration cannot fell a tree. Agencies, attorneys, employees, and contractors must translate it into physical and legal reality.

The larger institutional failure begins when those actors treat loyalty to a presidential preference as superior to candor before a court. Reyes described “different accounts,” not a settled finding that every official deliberately deceived her. Even so, a government whose representations cannot be reliably reconciled with its conduct forces judges to supervise routine compliance as though anticipating an ambush.

The systemic error

The golf course is politically revealing precisely because the stakes are smaller than in disputes over detention, health, or civil rights. No emergency rationale is required here. The pattern is executive power pursuing a personal priority, dismissing legal restraint as illegitimate inconvenience, and daring other institutions to stop irreversible action in time.

Courts possess authority, but executive agencies possess the equipment, personnel, and capacity to create facts on the ground. When an administration exploits that gap, law becomes a race against demolition. The trees are not merely scenery in that contest. They demonstrate the consequence of power acting first and treating accountability as paperwork to be argued over afterward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: It’s not about golf: Trump’s latest defiance exposes an ‘extraordinary’ assault

item.title: Trump lives in a world of 'total delusion' to fill his 'limitless void’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Michael A. Cohen, director of the International Affairs Program at The New School, described President Donald Trump’s rallies as an “ego-stroking exercise” meant to fill what Cohen called a “limitless void.” That is Cohen’s psychological interpretation, not a fact established by the reporting.

Six days before the midterm election, Trump traveled to heavily Republican Texas as his popularity reportedly slipped. On Tuesday, he portrayed the war in Iran as an economic windfall and discussed naming the Strait of Hormuz after himself. On Wednesday’s “Daily Blast” podcast, Cohen and host Greg Sargent argued that these remarks showed a president mistaking affirmation from loyal rally audiences for broader public approval.

AlterNet says Cohen characterized the trip as Republican electoral “triage” and faulted Trump for focusing on personal projects, grievances, and rivals instead of issues affecting voters. The article provides no response from Trump or the White House and no polling, economic data, or audience research substantiating its larger conclusions.

The power is presidential

The consequential fact is not whether Trump feels empty. It is that a president can direct the executive branch, shape war policy, command public attention, and use the office’s machinery to turn personal fixations into national business.

That power makes the reported remarks more than rally eccentricity. Trump was presenting a war as proof of prosperity and proposing his own name for a strategic waterway. Even if neither claim became policy, the presidency gave both an institutional platform while Republicans reportedly deployed him to protect their electoral position.

Psychology obscures responsibility

Cohen’s “limitless void” diagnosis is vivid but unverifiable. It also shrinks a political problem into a personality profile. No outsider needs access to Trump’s soul to evaluate the conduct AlterNet describes.

The observable choices are sufficient: Trump chose self-celebration, territorial symbolism, political retaliation, and branding. Republican officials, meanwhile, continued treating his rallies as campaign assets. The relevant agency lies in those decisions—not in speculative explanations about an inner emptiness the article cannot prove.

Loyalty as a feedback system

Sargent’s stronger point concerns the structure surrounding Trump. A rally assembled from committed supporters is not a representative sample of the country. Treating applause there as national consent creates a closed loop: loyalists validate the leader, and the leader cites their validation as evidence of success.

But the loop is not self-sustaining. Party strategists schedule the appearances. Officials repeat the claims. Friendly audiences supply the spectacle. Political institutions convert affirmation into authority. Trump holds the greatest power in that arrangement, while Republican actors enable the system because they expect electoral benefit from it—even when, as Cohen argued, the campaign has been reduced to shoring up a narrowing base.

The missing ledger

AlterNet’s framing leaves the most important claims underdeveloped. If Trump said the Iran war was making Americans rich, the political question is what evidence supported that assertion and who bore the war’s costs. The article supplies neither an economic accounting nor details about the conflict’s consequences.

A weak claim should be tested against material results, not answered mainly with amateur psychoanalysis. By centering Trump’s alleged delusion, the story risks making governance look like one man’s confusion rather than a chain of choices enabled by advisers, party officials, and institutions with the capacity to resist or amplify him.

A system built around the leader

The larger pattern is personalization of public power. Policy becomes autobiography, geography becomes branding, war becomes a campaign testimonial, and the presidency becomes a stage on which loyalty substitutes for evidence.

That system does not require proving Trump’s private motives. It requires powerful people deciding that his desires deserve institutional expression and that their own interests are served by indulging them. The void that matters politically is not inside one man. It is the absence of restraint among those empowered to say no.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump lives in a world of ‘total delusion’ to fill his ‘limitless void’

item.title: Trump’s 'limitless money' is useless against what’s coming: biographer
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff predicted Democrats would win the House, the Senate, and a contested Texas Senate race in the midterm elections the following week. His answer to the headline’s premise was that Republican money would be overwhelmed by voter contempt for President Donald Trump. These were Wolff’s predictions, not reported election results.

On a Daily Beast podcast, Wolff argued that ultrawealthy donors had given Trump and the Republican Party effectively “limitless money.” He specifically claimed Elon Musk had poured more than $250 million into Texas and praised Democrat James Talarico’s message that Musk was trying to buy the election.

Co-host Joanna Coles disputed Wolff’s Senate forecast. She expected a substantial Democratic House majority but said the Senate remained uncertain, citing Musk-funded turnout efforts and extensive Republican field operations. AlterNet supplied no independent support for the spending figures or either speaker’s electoral projections.

Power is more than money

The article’s strongest political fact is buried beneath its horse-race excitement: wealthy donors can finance turnout machinery at a scale ordinary voters cannot approach. Wolff and Coles disagree about whether that advantage will work, but neither disputes that concentrated private wealth is shaping the contest.

Trump also holds presidential power. Republicans are not merely a campaign struggling against hostile sentiment; they are the party aligned with the incumbent president and backed, according to the discussion, by enormous donor resources. Treating the election primarily as a referendum on Trump’s popularity understates the institutional and financial machinery operating on his side.

Prediction dressed as momentum

AlterNet’s “wipeout” framing runs ahead of its evidence. The story establishes that Wolff expects sweeping Democratic victories. It does not establish that those victories are coming, that contempt for Trump will determine them, or that money has become politically useless.

Even Coles’s more restrained forecast remains speculation. Her references to turnout spending and ground operations identify mechanisms that could matter, but the article provides no polling, expenditure records, race-by-race evidence, or election results. Confidence is not analysis, even when delivered by a prominent biographer.

The billionaire becomes the villain

Talarico’s reported pivot toward running against Musk gives Democrats a clear antagonist: a billionaire allegedly using extraordinary wealth to influence a Senate election. That framing correctly directs attention upward, toward concentrated power rather than toward voters subjected to its messaging.

But Wolff’s account also turns Musk into a convenient explanation for a broader system. One donor can spend heavily only because campaign-finance structures permit wealthy people to acquire disproportionate political reach. Personalizing that structure may be effective messaging, but it risks reducing an institutional design to the misconduct or vanity of a single billionaire.

Contempt is not a governing program

Wolff treats hostility toward Trump as an electoral force powerful enough to defeat money. It may be. The reporting offers no evidence that it will be, and even a Democratic sweep would not prove money irrelevant. It would show only that spending failed to secure particular outcomes under particular conditions.

More importantly, opposition organized around contempt remains dependent on Trump. It tells voters whom to reject, not what governing coalition will replace him or how that coalition would constrain billionaire influence after winning office.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is a political press increasingly comfortable presenting elections as collisions between personality and money: Trump’s unpopularity against Musk’s fortune, with democracy reduced to forecasting which force has greater “velocity.”

Actual power is less cinematic. Presidents wield state authority. Parties control legislative agendas. Billionaires finance political infrastructure. Candidates choose whether to challenge that arrangement or merely exploit resentment against its most visible beneficiaries. AlterNet’s framing makes a dramatic prediction the story when the more consequential fact is the system everyone in the conversation appears to accept: public power is contested through machinery that private fortunes can purchase.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘limitless money’ is useless against what’s coming: biographer

item.title: Trump’s obituary already has a grim opening line: historian
item.description:
What happened

Historian Allan Lichtman argued that the first line of Donald Trump’s obituary should record what Lichtman considers Trump’s defining legacy: persuading Americans that elections are dishonestly counted. AlterNet reported that Lichtman made the argument in a Salon column published Wednesday, October 28, ahead of the November 3 midterms.

Citing an October 18 60 Minutes report, Lichtman said Trump had made more than 150 claims about election rigging during the first 21 months of his second term. He identified a July 16 White House address as the centerpiece of that campaign, saying Trump presented heavily redacted documents that election officials and security experts said did not demonstrate rigging.

Lichtman predicted that Trump would answer Republican defeats with lawsuits and pressure on Republican legislators and election officials to alter results, as he did following the 2020 election. That was a forecast, not a reported outcome; the article was published before the midterm votes were counted and certified.

Power without accountability

Trump is not presented here as an outsider complaining about an institution he cannot influence. He is the president. His party controls both chambers of Congress. He commands the executive branch and speaks from the White House. Those facts make the grievance politically useful precisely because it is institutionally dishonest: the person at the center of federal power depicts himself as the helpless victim of the system that put him there.

That posture changes the function of an unsupported rigging claim. It is not merely an opinion about election administration. Coming from a president, it can establish a permission structure for officials and supporters to treat valid results as provisional whenever those results become inconvenient.

The decisive actors are therefore not limited to Trump. Republican legislators and election officials possess their own legal authority. If they validate unsupported accusations, obstruct certification, or entertain pressure to change legitimate results, they are making choices—not being swept along by “controversy.”

The conditional concession

According to Lichtman, Trump’s promise to accept results if they are “honest” effectively means accepting them if Republicans win. The formulation is designed to sound procedural while reserving unilateral authority to declare defeat fraudulent.

That is the trap. Evidence no longer determines whether the result is legitimate; the preferred outcome does. A victory retroactively proves the system worked. A loss supposedly proves corruption. No election administration can satisfy a standard built to move with one politician’s fortunes.

Lichtman distinguishes this from legitimate disputes over election rules and partisan redistricting. That distinction matters. Criticizing identifiable laws or district maps invites evidence and remedies. Indiscriminately attacking ballot counting makes verification itself suspect and leaves partisan loyalty as the only remaining test.

The headline shrinks the offense

AlterNet packages the story around a “grim opening line” in a future obituary. That hook turns an argument about presidential power into a piece of historical scorekeeping. The central question is not how posterity will phrase its verdict. It is what current officeholders may do with claims that the reporting describes as unsupported.

The obituary framing also makes Lichtman’s condemnation the event. It is not. The consequential conduct described in the article is a sitting president repeatedly alleging electoral corruption while benefiting from the same electoral order, and doing so before votes are counted.

A historian’s insult carries no institutional force. A president’s accusations do. Coverage that centers the clever epitaph risks substituting rhetorical spectacle for an examination of who can pressure officials, mobilize supporters, and weaken acceptance of certified results.

The machinery of preemptive delegitimization

The larger pattern is preemptive delegitimization: attack the process before the outcome exists, then use the attack to explain any unfavorable result. Repetition does the work. More than 150 claims, as Lichtman cited from 60 Minutes, need not prove fraud to create a political environment in which fraud is presumed.

The foreseeable consequence is broader than one disputed contest. Election workers face suspicion. Republican officials face pressure to choose between their duties and their party leader. Voters are trained to regard defeat as evidence of theft rather than a possible judgment against their candidates.

This is how institutional damage becomes self-reinforcing. Unsupported claims create distrust; that distrust is then presented as proof that the system lacks legitimacy. The official who cultivated the suspicion points to its existence as vindication.

The system behind the man

Lichtman locates responsibility in Trump’s conduct, but the system described here requires more than one man. It requires legislators willing to indulge the claims, officials vulnerable to partisan pressure, media outlets drawn to the provocation, and a governing party that benefits from keeping its voters convinced that only its victories can be real.

The historical verdict is less urgent than the institutional one. Presidents can speak falsely about elections; they cannot convert those claims into governmental action alone. The lasting question is which people with actual authority refuse the premise—and which decide that public distrust is an acceptable price for retaining power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s obituary already has a grim opening line: historian

item.title: Bush lawyer sees a corruption problem '1,000 times worse' for Trump family
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Richard Painter, George W. Bush’s former chief White House ethics lawyer, called the Trump family’s business activity “1,000 times worse” than Hunter Biden’s. He was responding to a Financial Times investigation that documented at least 18 meetings between Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump and foreign politicians or officials since January 2025, alongside an expansion of Trump family business interests during President Donald Trump’s second term.

Neither Trump son holds a government position. Donald Trump Jr.’s spokesperson said he tells foreign officials that he acts as a private citizen, while the Trump Organization said its business remains separate from the White House and complies with applicable ethics laws. The reporting did not establish that official favors were exchanged for business benefits, and Painter said the contents of the brothers’ conversations are unknown.

The Financial Times reported that Trump’s fortune grew by more than $2 billion last year, including more than $500 million from token sales by World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture his sons co-founded. Since Trump returned to office, his private business has announced 15 overseas projects, with five more listed in presidential ethics disclosures; foreign licensing, development and management revenue rose 40 percent, to $63 million, between 2024 and 2025.

The power is in the presidency

The central issue is not that two presidential relatives have businesses. It is that their father controls the executive branch while those businesses operate in sectors—including cryptocurrency, prediction markets and critical minerals—that can depend on federal regulation or government contracts.

Foreign officials do not need Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump to carry diplomatic credentials to understand the family relationship. They can see access to the president’s sons as potentially valuable even if the sons explicitly identify themselves as private citizens. That disclaimer addresses formal status; it does not erase proximity to presidential power.

The Trump Organization’s claim of separation also leaves the underlying conflict intact. A privately owned business can be organizationally distinct from the White House while its owner exercises presidential authority. The relevant question is not whether the entities share an office. It is whether presidential decisions can affect the financial interests of the president and his family.

The comparison conceals the imbalance

Painter’s comparison with Hunter Biden is politically revealing because he supported scrutiny of Hunter Biden’s conduct. But the phrase “1,000 times worse” is his judgment, not a measurable finding established by the reporting.

The more defensible distinction is institutional. Hunter Biden’s business activity drew investigations and denials of wrongdoing from both him and Joe Biden. Here, the person at the center of the family fortune is also the president, and the reported business expansion is occurring during his administration. The presidency is not incidental context; it is the source of the conflict’s scale.

Treating this merely as another story about presidential relatives would misdirect attention from the officeholder with actual authority. Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump conduct the meetings and manage business interests. President Trump holds the governmental power that makes access to his family potentially valuable.

Private labels do not neutralize public leverage

The family’s branding makes the relationship difficult to dismiss as accidental. Painter pointed to Donald Trump Jr.’s venture-capital firm, 1789 Capital, and a members’ club called Executive Branch. Those names do not prove an exchange of favors. They do, however, market political association as part of the product.

That is the structural danger documented here: influence can be sold without anyone issuing an explicit promise. A foreign official, investor or applicant for regulatory approval may reasonably believe that cultivating the president’s family could matter. The reporting does not show that such expectations produced official action, but the arrangement invites them while denying the public access to the conversations needed to evaluate them.

This is how opacity serves power. The absence of proof of a bargain becomes a defense, even though the president’s ownership interests, his sons’ foreign meetings and the government’s authority over relevant industries create the conditions under which an undisclosed bargain would be hardest to detect.

Corruption thrives before the receipt appears

The article is strongest when it refuses to claim more than the evidence supports: it does not establish a trade of government favors for business benefits. Its weakness is allowing the unanswered quid-pro-quo question to dominate the frame.

Public corruption is not only a completed transaction that investigators can reconstruct afterward. It also includes institutions designed so that private gain and public authority repeatedly converge without meaningful transparency. By the time a receipt appears—if one ever does—the conflict has already shaped who seeks access, what they believe access can buy and whether the public can trust decisions affecting countries where the presidential family does business.

The larger pattern is not confusion about where business ends and government begins. It is a governing arrangement that preserves formal deniability while leaving the president’s private financial interests exposed to people and governments affected by his administration’s choices. The public is asked to accept separation on assertion alone, while the family retains the money, the access and the presidency.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Bush lawyer sees a corruption problem ‘1,000 times worse’ for Trump family

item.title: 'Absolute immunity’ under fire as new plan hatches to hold Trump accountable
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former deputy U.S. solicitor general Philip Allen Lacovara condemned the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling as constitutionally unsound and argued that it gives President Donald Trump “a virtual get-out-of-jail card.” He told New York Times contributor Thomas B. Edsall that the decision’s supposed exceptions for some official acts and all unofficial conduct are largely unusable while the Court’s current majority remains intact.

The report does not identify a new plan to hold Trump accountable. It presents Lacovara’s legal criticism and historian Luke Nichter’s broader argument that presidential policymaking, judicial intervention, and congressional passivity have scrambled the constitutional roles of the three branches. AlterNet also connects Trump’s interest in rehabilitating Richard Nixon to supporters’ portrayal of the Watergate prosecution as partisan “lawfare.”

The headline promises more than the reporting delivers

The headline advertises an emerging accountability mechanism. The article supplies none: no legislation, lawsuit, prosecutorial strategy, constitutional amendment, or pending institutional action. Lacovara describes why accountability may be exceptionally difficult; he does not unveil a way around the ruling.

That distinction matters. Turning a severe institutional barrier into the suggestion that some corrective plan is already “hatching” substitutes suspense for substance. The reporting’s actual conclusion is harsher: the institutions empowered to constrain presidential abuse have either fortified executive immunity or declined to exercise their own authority.

Power sits with the Court and the presidency

Trump holds the executive power at issue, but the Supreme Court’s majority established the legal protection surrounding its use. According to Lacovara, the 2024 ruling created an extraordinarily high barrier to prosecuting a president for official conduct and sharply limited the practical value of its nominal exceptions.

Congress also retains substantial constitutional authority. Nichter’s account depicts it surrendering initiative—holding hearings and talking while the president governs through executive action and courts increasingly determine the permissible boundaries. That is not institutional confusion. It is a distribution of choices: executive expansion, judicial permission and legislative retreat.

Accountability cannot survive as a slogan

Lacovara warns that the ruling may obstruct prosecution even where evidence appears to show presidential favors exchanged for financial benefits. His list of potentially insulated abuses includes corruption, election interference, pardon-selling and federal contracts awarded to donors. These are his legal conclusions, not findings that Trump committed each listed act.

The political consequence is nevertheless concrete. A legal system that recognizes presidential criminal liability in theory while making prosecution nearly impossible in practice preserves the language of accountability after draining it of force. “Absolute immunity” need not be formally declared if the evidentiary and procedural barriers produce nearly the same result.

Nixon’s rehabilitation serves executive power

The effort to recast Nixon’s prosecution as Democratic “lawfare” does more than polish one disgraced president’s reputation. It attacks the legitimacy of the historical precedent showing that presidential power can encounter criminal investigation and forced political accountability.

That revision serves the present. If Watergate becomes persecution rather than evidence of executive abuse, then investigation itself can be portrayed as illegitimate whenever it reaches a president. The stronger office becomes the aggrieved party; prosecutors, courts, legislators, and critics become the alleged aggressors. Power is rewritten as victimhood.

A system can fail through permission

The larger pattern is not simply an ambitious president overwhelming helpless institutions. AlterNet’s own evidence describes institutions with agency: Supreme Court justices made the immunity ruling, presidents choose executive action, and members of Congress choose whether to legislate, investigate effectively, or accept marginalization.

Constitutional breakdown rarely requires every formal safeguard to disappear. It can proceed through doctrines that preserve exceptions too narrow to use, hearings that replace consequences, and headlines that imply remedies the reporting cannot identify. The system still performs accountability rhetorically while its most powerful actors make accountability materially harder.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Absolute immunity’ under fire as new plan hatches to hold Trump accountable

item.title: Life-saving disaster relief sabotaged by right-wing trolls
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet’s publication of Grist’s reporting shows how false disaster claims obstructed relief after the 2023 Maui wildfires and Hurricane Helene in 2024. Right-wing influencers and other social-media accounts spread unsupported allegations about energy weapons, government land seizures, withheld aid, and FEMA interference. During Helene, a reported armed threat forced FEMA to suspend North Carolina field operations for several hours; anonymous callers also prompted police SWAT deployments at the homes of FEMA leaders.

The reporting traces one supposed image of a Maui “laser” to a 2018 refinery flare in Ohio. Although the account that misidentified it later apologized, another account’s video repeating the falsehood received 432,000 views—more than 40 times the apology’s audience. Elon Musk’s unsupported accusation that FEMA blocked his aid flights drew almost 30 million views; his walk-back drew about 1 million.

The precise human toll cannot be calculated from the reporting. Former FEMA administrator Deanne Criswell said there is no way to know how many Maui residents avoided assistance because of the rumors. But disrupted fieldwork, diverted emergency resources, and fear of applying for aid created obvious risks for people who needed shelter and support.

The saboteurs had names

“Misinformation” is too bloodless when prominent accounts use institutional distrust as engagement bait. End Wokeness accused President Biden of starving North Carolina of aid without evidence. Musk broadcast his FEMA allegation to an enormous audience before retreating from it. Charlie Kirk and other right-wing personalities amplified Maui conspiracy claims. These were choices made by people with platforms, not weather-generated confusion.

The reporting does not establish that every person sharing a falsehood knew it was false. Some apparently believed what they circulated, and accounts linked to China also promoted Maui rumors. That distinction matters when judging intent. It does not erase agency: influential publishers chose to broadcast extraordinary accusations without adequate verification, and their reach magnified the foreseeable damage.

Platforms hold the machinery

Individual trolls supplied the content, but social-media companies supplied the distribution system. Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and X possess the institutional power to rank, recommend, label, and restrict posts. According to the reporting, major platforms have retreated from serious fact-checking and moderation while verified accounts produce much of the conspiracy material.

That structure rewards accusation over correction. The false claim reaches millions while the retraction limps behind it. Treating this as an unfortunate feature of human psychology misdirects attention from companies that design and govern the amplification machinery. Users press “share”; platforms decide how far the result travels.

Distrust is being weaponized

Fear of government does not arise from one source. Native Hawaiians carry legitimate historical memories of colonization, while undocumented residents may reasonably fear state scrutiny. Disaster propagandists exploit those vulnerabilities by attaching invented plots to real institutional trauma—such as the false warning that FEMA would seize Maui applicants’ homes.

That is not skepticism serving accountability. It redirects scrutiny away from documented failures and toward fantasies that make public assistance itself appear dangerous. The result benefits political actors seeking to portray government as inherently predatory, even when government workers are delivering shelter, benefits, and emergency information.

The article’s broad language about a fragmented “information landscape” risks blurring that asymmetry. Confusion is the environment; powerful accounts and permissive platforms are the actors exploiting it.

A weakened state pays twice

Emergency agencies must now perform two jobs at once: respond to the disaster and defend the legitimacy of responding. Every hour spent rebutting laser stories, investigating threats, or suspending field operations is capacity unavailable for relief. Staffing reductions described in the reporting make that burden heavier.

FEMA’s partnerships with a Native Hawaiian employee, caregivers, and other locally trusted messengers were a practical response. But community trust cannot substitute for platform accountability or sufficient public staffing. Forcing emergency workers to out-organize viral falsehoods one relationship at a time leaves the state permanently on the defensive.

Disaster politics by attrition

The larger pattern is institutional sabotage without the need to abolish an institution. Flood the public sphere with claims that FEMA steals land, blocks aid, or serves a secret plot; provoke threats and operational delays; then point to strained relief as proof that government cannot function.

The reporting cannot quantify every lost application, delayed placement, or endangered resident. It establishes something more basic: false claims consumed attention, interrupted operations, and made assistance harder to trust. In an era of worsening climate disasters, that machinery does not merely degrade debate. It turns political propaganda and platform incentives into additional hazards for people already trying to survive.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Life-saving disaster relief sabotaged by right-wing trolls

item.title: Trump's unusually small venue stuns veteran reporter
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that NBC News correspondent Garrett Haake was surprised by the unusually small venue chosen for Donald Trump’s Wednesday rally in Chillicothe, Ohio. Haake said the Ohio University athletic facility might hold about 1,000 people—smaller than any Trump rally space he could recall after covering “dozens if not hundreds” of them.

The event was presented as an effort to boost Republican candidates Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy ahead of the following week’s midterm elections. Citing Mediaite and Axios, AlterNet reported that Ramaswamy had fallen further behind Democrat Amy Acton in internal polling after an attack ad involving Acton’s estranged mother drew bipartisan criticism. The supplied reporting was published before the rally and does not establish its final attendance or effect.

The room is not the power

A smaller arena may indicate lowered expectations, tactical caution, local constraints, or weakening enthusiasm. The reporting does not establish which explanation is correct. Treating venue capacity alone as proof of Trump’s political decline would turn a suggestive detail into an unsupported conclusion.

Trump’s institutional importance here comes from his ability to direct attention, activate partisan media, and confer standing on Republican candidates. A 1,000-person room does not erase that leverage. The operative fact is that candidates in statewide races were still being positioned to receive his endorsement and audience.

Republicans made the choices

Husted and Ramaswamy were not passive objects caught in Trump’s gravitational field. Their campaigns—and the Republican organizations supporting them—made strategic choices about candidates, messages, and alliances.

The clearest reported electoral damage concerns Ramaswamy’s own campaign. According to Axios, Republicans feared that his personal attack involving Acton’s estranged mother could cost them the governor’s race, while internal polling reportedly showed Acton widening her lead. That is agency, not confusion: a campaign selected an attack, aired it, and then confronted a backlash.

Spectacle displaces accountability

The venue provides an irresistible visual shorthand: the former stadium act reduced to something critics compared to a school gym. But crowd-size mockery can misdirect attention from the people exercising power and the decisions shaping the races.

Even Trump’s reported comments about examining Husted’s body—crude remarks that Mediaite said he had repeated—risk becoming another piece of spectacle detached from consequence. The political question is not whether the performance is dignified. It is why Republican candidates continue treating the performer as a valuable campaign asset despite the degradation and distraction he brings with him.

The shrinking-stage trap

Political journalism often substitutes optics for measurement. Room size is easy to photograph; organizational control, donor influence, party discipline, and candidate dependence are harder to compress into a post. The result is coverage that can mistake a diminished stage for diminished power.

The larger pattern is a party ecosystem organized around attention rather than accountability. Candidates seek Trump’s imprimatur, journalists track the scale of his crowds, and campaign decisions disappear behind the traveling show. The venue may have been unusually small. The machinery that made him central to these Ohio races was not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s unusually small venue stuns veteran reporter

item.title: Jeanine Pirro threw FBI director under the bus in new case he demanded
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt testified at a Tuesday hearing that FBI Director Kash Patel personally directed an investigation of agents Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides. Witt said the July assignment, routed through the Kansas City field office, was unlike any tasking he had received from an FBI director during his career.

Defense questioning also exposed serious weaknesses in the resulting case. Witt acknowledged that neither agent had been sworn to tell the truth, despite his affidavit saying they were, and that House Judiciary Committee counsel Steve Castor was absent from the interviews in which the alleged false statements were made. Witt had spoken with Castor only the day before the hearing, and the Justice Department declined to disclose Castor’s knowledge, citing the Speech or Debate Clause.

The headline’s claim that Jeanine Pirro “threw” Patel under the bus is not established by the reporting. The damaging attribution came from Witt’s testimony: Patel ordered the investigation. Pirro’s role, as presented by AlterNet through national security writer Marcy Wheeler’s analysis, was in pursuing charges that gave defense lawyers an opportunity to expose how the case originated.

Power ordered the case

Floris and Benavides did not choose this confrontation. Patel held the institutional power to initiate an extraordinary investigation from the top of the FBI, and Witt carried out the assignment through the chain of command. The unusual feature was not merely bureaucratic untidiness. It was the director’s direct intervention in a case targeting agents whose 2020 work included resisting foreign election interference.

That distinction matters because “the FBI investigated” conceals agency. According to the testimony AlterNet recounts, Patel directed it. Career personnel then inherited the legal and professional risk created by that decision.

The case weakened under examination

The government’s theory depended on alleged false statements to a congressional committee. Yet its investigating agent lacked direct knowledge of what the committee’s counsel considered material, had only just spoken with Castor, and admitted a basic factual error in his own affidavit about whether Floris and Benavides testified under oath.

An inaccurate affidavit does not by itself prove intentional deception. It does, however, expose a glaring asymmetry: officials were attempting to criminalize alleged inaccuracies by the defendants while presenting their own inaccurate description to the court. A prosecution built around truthfulness cannot treat precision as optional when the government supplies it.

The headline obscures the chain of command

Casting this as Pirro betraying Patel turns an institutional abuse story into palace intrigue. The consequential fact is not that one Trump official embarrassed another. It is that the FBI director allegedly initiated an unusual investigation, prosecutors advanced a defective complaint, and the Justice Department invoked a constitutional protection that limited scrutiny of a congressional staff member central to its theory.

That framing redirects attention from state power toward personality conflict. Floris and Benavides face the coercive machinery of federal prosecution; Patel, Pirro, and senior Justice Department officials control that machinery. Those positions are not interchangeable, and the reporting should not flatten them into a spectacle of allies “throwing” one another around.

Criminalization as discipline

Wheeler argues that the case sought to make rejecting frivolous election-fraud claims legally dangerous inside the FBI. The hearing does not independently prove that motive, but the reported sequence supports scrutiny of it: Patel personally ordered an unusual inquiry into agents associated with protecting the 2020 election, and the resulting case faltered when tested against its own evidence.

The foreseeable message to other agents is plain. Professional judgment can become personal exposure when it conflicts with the political leadership’s preferred account. Even a weak case can punish through legal fees, reputational damage and the threat of prosecution.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of law enforcement hierarchy into a channel for political retaliation, followed by procedural language that disguises who exercised power. Orders become “taskings.” Political choices become ordinary casework. Evidentiary defects become confusion.

This hearing disrupted that laundering process. It placed the director’s instruction, the investigators’ omissions and the prosecutors’ choices into the same record. The scandal is not that the officials involved failed to coordinate their stories cleanly. It is that federal authority was reportedly mobilized against agents tied to election-protection work—and that the case’s internal weaknesses emerged only after the targets had already been forced to defend themselves.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Jeanine Pirro threw FBI director under the bus in new case he demanded

item.title: The 8 enablers shaking up the DOJ to do Trump's dirty work
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting by Devlin Barrett, identifies eight federal prosecutors who allegedly used Justice Department power to pursue President Donald Trump’s grievances against critics, protesters and officials. The reported targets included Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, former FBI Director James Comey, former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell and people protesting immigration enforcement.

According to the account, Daniel Rosen, John Sarcone III, Dan Bishop, Bill Essayli, Jason Reding Quiñones, Jeanine Pirro, W. Ellis Boyle and Andrew Boutros advanced investigations or charges that repeatedly met resistance from judges, grand jurors and career prosecutors. Some cases collapsed or were dismissed; a judge found Sarcone was not lawfully serving as acting U.S. attorney; and three of the eight reportedly ran their offices without Senate confirmation.

The reporting also says prosecutors who concluded that charges were unwarranted were pushed out, while weak cases consumed federal resources and damaged careers inside the department. Those claims rest here on AlterNet’s account of Barrett’s reporting, court rulings and unnamed people familiar with certain events.

The power runs downward

Trump held the decisive political power described in this story. He publicly or privately identified enemies, demanded action and placed loyal appointees in institutions capable of searching homes, seizing ballots, issuing subpoenas and bringing criminal charges.

The prosecutors still had agency. A presidential demand is not a self-executing indictment. Lawyers chose whether to test evidence, resist pressure or convert a grievance into a federal proceeding. The reported removal of prosecutors who found no basis for charges shows how the system disciplined restraint and rewarded persistence.

Failure is not the same as harmlessness

The record presented by AlterNet is full of failed prosecutions: protest cases collapsing, charges dismissed and subpoenas rejected. That can create the comforting impression that judicial review worked and the danger passed.

But prosecution itself imposes punishment. A target can face a search, legal costs, reputational damage and years of uncertainty before a judge finally says the government lacked evidence. The state does not need to win every case to make opposition expensive.

Thin evidence, heavy machinery

The sharpest example is not merely that judges rejected cases. It is that officials allegedly pressed forward after internal objections or visible evidentiary defects. AlterNet reports that Essayli insisted on charging a man who supplied face shields to anti-ICE protesters despite staff resistance. It also reports that Pirro’s office pursued David Hearn after learning of a significant weakness, according to filings by Hearn’s lawyers.

Those details matter because they strip away the language of bureaucratic confusion. The account describes identifiable officials making discretionary decisions. Where evidence was thin, institutional power remained immense.

The framing understates the system

Calling these officials “enablers” is accurate but incomplete. It can make them sound like secondary characters indulging one man’s impulses. They were reportedly officeholders exercising delegated federal authority, and some did so without the legitimacy ordinarily supplied by Senate confirmation.

The deeper scandal is an incentive structure: loyalty appears to open doors, evidentiary restraint can end careers, and courtroom defeat arrives only after the government has imposed the process. The stronger actors create the pressure; weaker targets absorb the cost. Blaming only Trump’s temperament would conceal the lawyers and institutions that translated it into action.

Personalized justice is still state policy

This story reveals how retaliatory government becomes routine. It does not require every accusation to produce a conviction. It requires officials willing to launch proceedings, supervisors willing to punish resistance and institutions slow enough that eventual dismissal cannot undo the damage.

The systemic error is treating collapsed cases as proof of resilience. They are also evidence that extraordinary coercive power was activated on weak grounds. When professional independence becomes a liability and personal loyalty becomes a qualification, the Justice Department’s failures stop looking accidental. They become the foreseeable output of how power has been organized.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The 8 enablers shaking up the DOJ to do Trump’s dirty work

item.title: FBI agents 'worried' about being tools in Trump's power grab: report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing MS NOW, reports that current and former FBI officials fear the Trump administration could use the bureau to seize voting machines, ballots, or other election materials through legally questionable investigations. The officials pointed to prior seizures of state voting records and equipment, including ballots in Fulton County, Georgia, as grounds for concern.

According to the report, two Atlanta-based FBI intelligence analysts were fired in July after refusing to work on an administration investigation into the 2020 election. Former FBI supervisor Rob D’Amico said agents worry the bureau could be used to obtain warrants based on questionable probable cause. Election advocates are reportedly preparing legal and professional support for agents ordered to perform work they consider illegal or unethical.

The power is at the top

The central actors are not anxious rank-and-file agents. Institutional power belongs to the president, Justice Department officials, U.S. attorneys, and FBI leaders who can open investigations, seek warrants, assign personnel, and punish refusal.

That distinction matters. Agents may execute a seizure, but senior officials create the conditions for it: selecting allegations, authorizing investigations, presenting applications to judges, and directing armed federal personnel. The reported firing of two analysts shows why private concern is an inadequate safeguard. An employee who refuses can lose a career; an official issuing the order retains the machinery of the state.

Anxiety is not resistance

The article frames FBI agents as “worried,” but worry neither blocks an improper order nor protects an election. The decisive question is whether officials will refuse legally unsupported assignments, document pressure, alert oversight bodies, or challenge retaliation.

The reported preparations by election advocates recognize this imbalance. Legal assistance can lower the personal cost of refusal, but it cannot substitute for institutional controls. If preventing abuse depends on individual agents risking dismissal after political appointees have already mobilized federal power, the system is relying on conscience at the final stage of a process designed above their heads.

The seizure can become the sabotage

The danger described by officials is concrete even without proving that a future operation has already been planned. Removing ballots or machines can obstruct voting or counting and disturb the chain of custody used to establish that election materials were not altered.

That disruption can then manufacture the uncertainty invoked to justify it. Federal authorities act on unsupported fraud claims; their intervention compromises ordinary election procedures; the resulting disorder becomes material for further suspicion. The government does not need to prove fraud to damage confidence. It can create a procedural mess and point to the mess.

The framing understates responsibility

Calling this a fear that agents might become “tools” risks making the bureau sound like an inert object caught in somebody else’s scheme. Institutions act through people. A U.S. attorney who advances baseless allegations, an FBI official who approves a dubious operation, or an agent who knowingly executes an improper seizure each exercises agency at a different level of power.

The reporting itself supplies the sharper frame: officials fear that at least some federal personnel would cooperate. Conservative agents and progressive legal groups may now share an interest in preventing election interference, but that unusual alignment is not the main political fact. The main fact is that internal compliance can convert partisan election denial into state action.

The systemic error

Election subversion does not require every official to embrace it. It requires political leaders willing to apply pressure, enough institutional gatekeepers willing to comply, and a bureaucracy that makes refusal personally costly.

That is the larger pattern exposed here. False claims can acquire coercive force when prosecutors, warrants, armed agents, and disciplinary authority are placed behind them. The system fails long before ballots are physically removed: it fails when obedience is rewarded, resistance is punished, and officials treat the deliberate use of public power against election administration as merely an ethical dilemma for individual employees.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: FBI agents ‘worried’ about being tools in Trump’s power grab: report

item.title: GOP knives out after internal polling shows major 'backlash' against OH ad
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy fell eight percentage points behind Democrat Amy Acton in a private poll commissioned by a Republican group. Acton had led by two points less than 10 days earlier, before Ramaswamy’s attack ad began airing on October 19. The article does not provide the poll’s methodology, field dates, or year, so its findings establish Republican concern—not a settled electoral outcome.

The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar. The public then learned, according to the reporting, that the mother had left decades earlier with Acton’s sexually abusive stepfather. Republicans had warned Ramaswamy against the attack, but President Donald Trump endorsed it as “hitting pay dirt,” while Vice President JD Vance told critics to “stop whining.”

The reported backlash has Republicans worried about damage beyond the governor’s race, particularly to Senator Jon Husted’s reelection bid and potentially Senate control. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine called the ad wrong and urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it; Trump attacked DeWine in response. Campaign figures are now blaming Ramaswamy for insisting that the ad run.

The power was never mysterious

Ramaswamy reportedly pushed for the ad. His campaign aired it. Trump and Vance used their authority inside the Republican Party to defend it after its cruelty became apparent. Those are decisions made by powerful political actors, not an unfortunate communications mishap produced by nobody in particular.

DeWine objected, but his objection also clarifies the hierarchy. A sitting Republican governor could call the attack wrong; Trump could answer by accusing him of wanting a Democrat to win. The message was blunt: loyalty to the party’s dominant figure outranks judgment, restraint, and even protection of the broader ticket.

Polling changed the moral calculus

The Republican alarm described here is not principally about what the ad did to Acton. It is about what the ad might do to Republicans.

Before the poll, some party figures warned that exploiting a painful family history crossed a line. After the poll showed an eight-point deficit, insiders began emphasizing who demanded the ad and who opposed it. The conduct remained the same. What changed was its apparent electoral price.

That is damage control masquerading as accountability. “Vivek got what he wanted” shifts responsibility onto one candidate while leaving intact the political culture that rewards personal degradation when strategists believe it works.

The backlash did not create the offense

Coverage built around GOP “knives” and internal panic risks making Republican infighting the central event. It is not. The central event is that a campaign weaponized an estranged relative and a history involving alleged sexual abuse, then received public encouragement from the president and vice president.

Calling the result “backlash” can also obscure agency. Voters did not mysteriously become upset; the campaign supplied a reason. Nor did the ad merely “cross a line,” as if political boundaries enforce themselves. Named officials chose to air it, defend it, or oppose it.

The private poll may suggest a reaction, but without methodological details it cannot prove that the ad alone caused the six-point movement in Acton’s reported margin. The attached memo’s conclusion that the ad was having a significant effect remains the assessment of the Republican group behind the survey.

Cruelty as a party test

Trump’s response to DeWine turned a dispute over campaign conduct into a loyalty test. Rather than address whether the ad was defensible, he questioned DeWine’s partisan allegiance and praised the attack’s tactical value. Vance likewise treated criticism as weakness.

That pattern matters more than the consultants’ finger-pointing. When leaders define any usable wound as legitimate ammunition, cruelty becomes evidence of commitment. Objections are recast as sabotage; restraint becomes assistance to the enemy.

The predictable consequence is institutional cowardice. Party operatives may recognize the harm, but many speak clearly only when polling suggests that the harm could cost them power.

The system rewards remorse on a delay

This episode reveals a political apparatus with abundant agency and highly selective responsibility. Candidates authorize attacks. Party leaders validate them. Operatives distribute them. Then, if voters recoil, the same structure describes itself as “reeling,” as though it were struck by an external force.

The deeper failure is not that one attack ad may have backfired. It is that the party’s internal mechanism for rejecting the attack appears weaker than its mechanism for measuring the electoral damage afterward. In that system, conscience arrives only after the polling memo.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP knives out after internal polling shows major ‘backlash’ against OH ad
