item.title: 'Grow a spine': Mark Kelly on The View rips 'pathetic' Republican senators
item.description:
What happened

Sen. Mark Kelly told The View that Republican senators refuse to challenge President Donald Trump because they fear losing their seats. Appearing Tuesday, Kelly called that behavior “pathetic” and suggested Republicans might “grow a spine” if the midterm elections alter the balance of power.

Asked whether a Democratic House should investigate the Trump administration or focus on affordability, Kelly rejected the choice as too narrow. He argued that elected officials must address healthcare costs and food insecurity while confronting what he described as serious damage inside the Justice Department.

Kelly further alleged that the administration had purged DOJ leaders it considered insufficiently loyal and fired Black employees and women. AlterNet’s account provides no administration response or independent evidence substantiating those allegations.

The power is already visible

Republican senators are not helpless spectators waiting for courage to arrive. They hold votes, committee authority, confirmation power, investigative tools, and public platforms. Trump may influence their political survival, but they decide whether fear of that influence overrides their institutional obligations.

Kelly’s diagnosis is therefore sharper than his proposed cure. The problem is not missing vertebrae. It is a functioning incentive system in which senators calculate that submission is safer than independence. Calling that cowardice is fair; treating it as a personality defect understates the institutional choice.

Job security is an explanation, not an excuse

Kelly attributes Republican compliance to career preservation. If his account is correct, these senators are protecting positions of power by declining to use the power those positions provide.

That distinction matters. “They are afraid of Trump” can misdirect responsibility toward the dominant figure and away from the officials enabling him. Political pressure does not cast Senate votes, approve nominees, abandon oversight, or remain silent. Senators do those things.

The false choice on accountability

The television question set investigations against affordability, as though governing requires choosing between institutional accountability and material relief. That framing serves officials who want scrutiny portrayed as a distraction and economic policy reduced to a campaign slogan.

Congress can investigate executive conduct and legislate on costs. Whether it does either depends on priorities, votes, and the willingness to confront concentrated wealth and executive power. The scarcity here is not congressional capacity. It is political commitment.

Serious allegations require serious scrutiny

Kelly’s claims about the Justice Department are the most consequential part of the appearance and the least developed in AlterNet’s report. A purge based on loyalty, race, or gender would implicate both institutional integrity and unlawful discrimination. Those allegations require documentation, affected officials’ accounts, and a response from the administration.

Instead, the article largely packages Kelly’s condemnation as a satisfying clash. That is weak framing. The relevant question is not whether his language was forceful enough for daytime television, but what decisions were made at DOJ, who authorized them, and what mechanisms Congress has used—or refused to use—to establish the facts.

The system rewards obedience

The larger pattern is political submission disguised as personal timidity. Trump’s leverage matters because senators have careers, party structures, donors, and electorates they value more than confrontation. Their compliance is not confusion; it is an allocation of loyalty under pressure.

“Grow a spine” is memorable, but the systemic error is more durable: institutions cannot restrain concentrated power when their occupants benefit from surrendering to it. Courage may change individual conduct. Only consequences change the incentives that make cowardice rational.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Grow a spine’: Mark Kelly on The View rips ‘pathetic’ Republican senators

item.title: Trump's tanning makeup mistake raises new questions about his health
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump appeared with a visible contrast between his tanned face and paler neck while traveling from Joint Base Andrews, and that makeup on his bruised hands was also noticeable. The reporting does not establish that the makeup error revealed a health problem.

The Daily Beast attributed the facial contrast to Trump’s use of tanning products, bronzer, or makeup. It reported that makeup has also covered bruising on his hands, while noting expert speculation that such bruises could result from blood draws, medication, or intravenous hydration. No diagnosis, medical record, or confirmed treatment was provided.

AlterNet then connected these observations to earlier comments from mental-health professionals about Trump’s conduct. Psychiatrist Henry Abraham described him as displaying nighttime mania, while forensic psychologist Alan Blotcky argued that narcissism could explain behavior others interpret as illness. Neither assessment resolves the cause of the bruising or the makeup.

Power is not a complexion

The president holds executive power. His makeup artist, his critics, and spectators studying the boundary between bronzer and bare skin do not. Any serious health story should therefore ask whether Trump can perform his duties, whether a condition affects official decisions, and whether the White House is withholding material information.

This article supplies evidence for none of those propositions. A poorly blended cosmetic may reveal vanity or carelessness. It is not a medical test. Bruising can warrant legitimate questions, but listing possible causes without evidence connecting any of them to Trump turns uncertainty into insinuation.

The headline outruns the evidence

The framing converts an appearance mishap into “new questions” about presidential health, then answers those questions with conjecture. That is not accountability reporting. It is a chain of associations: visible makeup, concealed bruises, hypothetical treatments, late-night posting, psychiatric commentary.

The distinction matters. Abraham offered a stark characterization and said Congress should invoke the 25th Amendment. Blotcky disputed the illness-based interpretation and described Trump’s behavior as manipulative narcissism. AlterNet reports both opinions, but it provides no clinical examination establishing either account. Remote commentary—however credentialed—cannot substitute for disclosed medical evidence.

Gossip displaces scrutiny

Trump’s appearance is politically relevant only when it bears on deception, fitness, or the management of public information. The article never establishes that link. Instead, it devotes attention to bronzer, scalp speculation, and cosmetic concealment while leaving the institutional question underdeveloped: what health information has the administration released, who controls it, and is it adequate?

That omission misdirects scrutiny away from the actors with power to disclose or conceal consequential facts. The public cannot compel candor by inspecting photographs. The president and his administration decide what medical evidence to release; journalists decide whether to investigate that record or decorate a rumor with expert possibilities.

The spectacle serves the powerful

Appearance-based speculation gives Trump an easy escape from substantive examination. He can dismiss the coverage as mockery, while supporters can treat legitimate concerns about transparency or fitness as merely another sneer about his face. Weak reporting contaminates stronger scrutiny.

The larger pattern is a political press repeatedly mistaking visible oddity for evidence and spectacle for accountability. When coverage cannot distinguish an observed bruise from a diagnosed condition, it does not expose presidential power. It trivializes the question of how that power is exercised—and lets the institution controlling the relevant facts remain comfortably offstage.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s tanning makeup mistake raises new questions about his health

item.title: Trump's 'creaking' brain reveals a disturbing GOP calculation: analyst
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that New Republic editor Michael Tomasky interpreted President Donald Trump’s remarks at a Saturday rally in Perry, Georgia, as evidence that Trump may see political advantage in Republican midterm losses. That is Tomasky’s theory, not an established fact about Trump’s intentions.

At the rally, Trump acknowledged higher fuel costs while claiming the United States was making “a frickin’ fortune” from the war in Iran. AlterNet says Tomasky disputed that claim, citing reports that Persian Gulf oil exports had exceeded prewar levels while higher tanker costs had sharply reduced Asian orders for American crude.

Tomasky offered three possible incentives for Trump: indifference when he is not on the ballot, an opportunity to claim Republicans cannot win without him, and the prospect of using a defeat to generate investigations, conflict, and fraud allegations. He cited a Justice Department lawsuit concerning certification of Alaska’s Senate race, but the article does not establish that Trump wants Republicans to lose or that the administration will obstruct certification.

Power is not a personality quiz

Trump holds the presidency. His administration controls executive agencies, including the Justice Department. Republican candidates, by contrast, can distance themselves from him, but they cannot neutralize presidential power or prevent federal institutions from being used in election litigation.

That distinction matters more than Tomasky’s speculation about an “aging, creaking” mind. Insults about cognition substitute amateur diagnosis for institutional analysis. The relevant question is not whether Trump’s remarks reveal decay. It is what a president says, what his administration does, and which officials are positioned to impose consequences.

The decision-makers are visible

Trump chose to boast about supposed wartime profits while acknowledging that advisers wanted him to avoid the subject because people were paying more at the pump. Whatever his motive, the reported statement shows a deliberate communications choice: he understood the obvious political liability and spoke anyway.

The Justice Department, according to the cited analysis, chose to sue over possible certification of Alaska’s Senate result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan lost to Democrat Mary Peltola. The administration said a second Republican candidate with the same name could confuse voters. That stated rationale must be preserved; so must the harder fact that federal litigation aimed at certification carries consequences far beyond campaign messaging.

Speculation obscures the machinery

The article’s central claim—that Trump secretly wants a Republican wipeout—is provocative but unproven. It converts observable conduct into a psychological mystery and makes Trump’s appetite for conflict the organizing explanation. That framing risks misdirection.

Republican candidates are not merely victims of one man’s erratic rhetoric. Those who support him make a political choice; those who retreat only when he becomes electorally costly are managing exposure, not surrendering power. Nor should a Justice Department lawsuit be reduced to evidence of Trump’s emotional needs. It is an exercise of state authority and should be examined on its legal basis, timing, and requested remedy.

Conflict can be politically useful

Tomasky’s strongest point is structural, even if his claim about intent outruns the evidence. A congressional defeat could furnish Trump with antagonists, investigations, and grievances. Those conditions may be politically useful to a leader who portrays scrutiny as persecution.

But usefulness after a defeat does not prove a desire to lose beforehand. The grounded conclusion is narrower: Trump’s political method can convert setbacks into loyalty tests and institutional confrontation. That leaves allies carrying electoral risk while he retains the starring role whether they win or lose.

The system rewards the spectacle

The larger pattern is a politics organized around personal dominance rather than collective governance. Candidates are valuable when they validate the leader, expendable when they fail, and useful again when their defeat can be blamed on disloyalty or fraud.

Coverage weakens that analysis when it dwells on a politician’s allegedly “mildewed” brain. The consequential story is not mental deterioration inferred from a rally performance. It is concentrated executive power, party dependence, and the possibility that election administration becomes another arena for presidential grievance. Personality supplies the spectacle; institutions determine who pays for it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘creaking’ brain reveals a disturbing GOP calculation: analyst

item.title: 'Death of the Republic': Top analyst fears GOP wipeout is only the beginning
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that University of Virginia political analyst Larry Sabato forecast major Republican losses in the November 3 midterms: Democrats winning at least 224 House seats and the Senate reaching at least a 50-50 split. His Crystal Ball rated Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans’ Virginia Beach seat as leaning Democratic and Rep. Rob Wittman’s race against Shannon Taylor as a toss-up. These are projections, not results.

Sabato’s larger fear was that electoral defeat would not settle the country’s political crisis. He said it was possible to trace how the republic could decline and die, citing the collapse of meaningful discussion about the public good. AlterNet connects that warning to President Donald Trump’s attacks on election administration, pressure for mid-decade Republican redistricting and threats of prosecution against local officials over voter rolls.

The article also attributes Republican vulnerability to public dissatisfaction with Trump administration policies, including tariffs, cuts to Medicaid and food assistance, immigration enforcement and the reported economic effects of war with Iran. It notes that Virginia officials had sued to block armed federal agents from polling places and that the Supreme Court had rejected an administration effort involving Postal Service screening of mail ballots.

Power is not evenly distributed

The decisive actors here are not voters being “nasty” to one another. They are the president, his administration, Congress, state legislatures, federal agencies and courts. They possess the authority to draw districts, reduce benefits, deploy officers, administer elections and determine which executive actions survive legal review.

Republicans held the congressional majorities described by AlterNet and approved the reported cuts. Trump demanded new maps from Republican-controlled states and used the presidency to pressure election officials. Democratic-controlled states answered with partisan mapmaking of their own, including an effort in Virginia that voters narrowly approved before the state Supreme Court overturned it. The institutions differ in reach, but the operative choice was the same: manipulate district lines for partisan advantage.

Civility is a decoy

Sabato’s concern about public nastiness may be sincere, but it is a poor diagnosis of institutional decay. Rude political speech does not redraw a congressional district, cut Medicaid or place armed federal personnel near polling locations. Officials with legal authority do those things.

Framing the crisis as a collective loss of civility spreads responsibility across the population and obscures the hierarchy of power. The relevant distinction is not between polite and impolite Americans. It is between people arguing about government and officials using government to entrench themselves, punish vulnerable groups or raise the cost of administering an election.

Defeat does not erase the machinery

The article’s strongest point is buried beneath its electoral forecast: a Republican wipeout, if it occurs, would be a consequence rather than a cure. Seats can change hands while the incentives that produced partisan redistricting, attacks on voting systems and retaliatory threats remain intact.

Trump’s claims about election security, as characterized by AlterNet, also serve a practical function regardless of whether they persuade a majority. They prepare supporters to treat an unfavorable outcome as illegitimate. That converts ordinary electoral accountability into another pretext for institutional pressure. The Supreme Court’s intervention and Arlington County’s lawsuit show other institutions resisting, but resistance after escalation is not evidence that the system is healthy.

Cruelty has a constituency in government

AlterNet describes policies whose burdens fall primarily on people with less institutional leverage: low-income recipients of Medicaid and food assistance, immigrants facing detention or deportation, and even very young children in immigration proceedings. Calling the resulting anger a “national funk” sanitizes the relationship between policy and suffering.

The reported harm was not produced by national mood alone. Congress authorized benefit cuts. Executive agencies conducted enforcement. The administration pursued tariffs and war policy. Whatever electoral judgment follows, the chain of agency should remain visible: powerful officials made choices, and people with fewer means absorbed the consequences.

The systemic error

American political coverage often treats elections as both diagnosis and treatment: unpopular governance produces a wave, the wave changes control, and the system corrects itself. This story contains evidence against that comforting sequence. The same actors anticipating punishment can use public power to alter districts, intimidate administrators and discredit the vote before it is counted.

The larger pattern is institutional self-protection disguised as political conflict. When coverage emphasizes polarization, incivility or generalized despair, it turns exercises of state power into a shared cultural failure. The sharper account identifies who controlled the machinery, what they chose to do with it and who was forced to bear the cost.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Death of the Republic’: Top analyst fears GOP wipeout is only the beginning

item.title: 'He's going to explode': White House 'moles' claim Trump on the brink
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Labor Secretary Robert Reich said two unnamed White House sources described President Donald Trump as increasingly isolated, agitated, and “on the verge of exploding.” Reich made the claim during a podcast discussion with Heather Lofthouse about Trump’s standing and the coming midterm elections.

According to Reich, his sources believe Trump recognizes that his crowds are smaller, his polling is weak, and Republicans could suffer major losses. The report provides no independent corroboration, names no White House officials, and does not establish what “explode” means or whether any specific action is imminent.

The claim outruns the evidence

The headline’s alarming language comes from Reich’s characterization of what anonymous intermediaries supposedly told him. There is no documented incident, identified witness, or concrete decision behind it. The story therefore cannot answer its own teaser beyond this: Reich says unnamed people around Trump are anxious about his mood.

That may be politically interesting, but it is not firm evidence of an impending event. “He’s going to explode” could describe anything from an angry outburst to a political counterattack. Treating that ambiguity as revelation converts gossip into apparent diagnosis.

Power matters more than temperament

Trump’s emotional condition is relevant only because he holds presidential power. The consequential question is not whether he is “steaming,” but what orders he issues, which officials execute them, and what institutional restraints remain operative.

By concentrating on private agitation, the coverage personalizes a structural problem. A president does not act alone. Advisers shape options, appointees carry out directives, congressional allies protect the administration, and party leaders decide whether political cost matters more than institutional responsibility. Anonymous anxiety inside the White House is not resistance.

The convenient psychology of decline

Reich and Lofthouse present a tidy political arc: MAGA mistook reelection for a mandate, voters are discovering the material costs of Republican governance, and Trump senses that public support is slipping away. But the AlterNet report supplies no polling figures, election data, crowd counts, or evidence connecting voter attitudes to particular policies.

That does not make the argument false. It makes it unproved by this story. The article substitutes Trump’s alleged private awareness for public evidence of political decline, allowing readers to experience anticipated Republican defeat as though insiders had already confirmed it.

Anonymous sources are not accountability

Unnamed sources can expose facts that powerful institutions would otherwise suppress. Here, however, they disclose no policy, document, order, or misconduct. They offer an impression of Trump’s mood while remaining protected from scrutiny.

The result flatters insiders without forcing them to act. White House personnel get cast as worried observers even though some may possess formal authority, access, or the ability to resign and speak publicly. The reporting does not identify their roles, so it cannot establish whether they are constrained witnesses, passive enablers, or merely secondhand voices.

Spectacle conceals the machinery

The larger pattern is political coverage that turns government into court drama: a volatile ruler, nervous aides, shrinking crowds, and whispers of collapse. That frame is vivid, but it directs attention toward personality and prophecy instead of decisions and consequences.

Trump holds the institutional power. His administration and political allies enable its exercise. If that power is being used harmfully, the evidence will be found in policies, orders, enforcement, budgets, and the conduct of officials—not in an unverifiable promise that the man at the center is about to lose his temper.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘He’s going to explode’: White House ‘moles’ claim Trump on the brink

item.title: GOP's new 'small business' scheme is a scam
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump administration officials expanded the Small Business Administration’s definition of a “small” business, raising a cited annual-sales threshold from less than $25 million by roughly 1,000 percent. The change allows some companies with billion-dollar operations to qualify for benefits carrying the small-business label.

According to the outlet, those benefits include federal grants and contracts intended to support smaller firms. The practical result is that large companies—with greater access to capital, lobbyists, and lawyers—can compete against genuine small businesses for the same public resources.

The rulemakers hold the power

Main Street businesses did not redefine themselves. Federal officials changed the eligibility rules governing access to public money.

That distinction matters. This is not primarily a story about large companies behaving aggressively in a competitive marketplace. The government widened the gate. Corporations may exploit the opening, but officials created it and bear responsibility for its foreseeable consequences.

A label becomes a subsidy

“Small business” is not merely a flattering description. In federal policy, it determines who can claim preferential access to contracts, grants, and other assistance.

Once billion-dollar enterprises can enter that category, the designation stops distinguishing firms by economic power. It becomes administrative camouflage: the language of helping small competitors attached to a policy that exposes them to stronger rivals.

Competition rigged from above

Large businesses already possess advantages that smaller firms cannot easily reproduce: financing, specialized legal counsel, lobbying capacity, and the staff needed to navigate government procurement. Allowing those firms into programs designed for weaker competitors does not create a neutral contest. It imports an existing power imbalance into a space meant to counteract it.

The predictable consequence is concentration. Public support nominally reserved for independent businesses can instead reinforce companies already positioned to dominate markets and absorb compliance costs.

The misdirection is the sales pitch

The policy is presented as an expansion of the small-business universe. But changing a definition does not create a single new enterprise. It changes who qualifies for government benefits.

That rhetorical substitution—reclassification presented as growth—directs attention toward a larger number on paper while obscuring the transfer of opportunity underneath it. The article’s central accusation is persuasive on that point: officials can claim to support more “small businesses” precisely because they have stripped the term of economic meaning.

The system protects scale

This episode reveals a familiar governing pattern: retain the language of economic pluralism while rewriting policy for concentrated power. The small-business brand remains politically valuable because it evokes independence, local ownership, and competition. The beneficiaries need not embody any of those things.

When government definitions ignore actual disparities in wealth and influence, formally equal eligibility becomes a mechanism for unequal extraction. The scam is not simply that big companies receive a smaller label. It is that institutional power converts that label into public money—and calls the result support for the businesses most likely to be displaced.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP’s new ‘small business’ scheme is a scam

item.title: Morning Joe panel howls at GOP's 'desperate' Cheesecake Factory meltdown
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republicans attacked former President Barack Obama over a campaign joke comparing President Donald Trump’s ornate White House décor to Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory. Obama’s target was Trump’s gold-plated aesthetic and governing priorities, but Republican critics recast the remark as contempt for Americans who eat at the restaurant chain.

On MSNBC’s “Morning Joe,” Joe Scarborough and Jonathan Lemire ridiculed that interpretation as a bad-faith diversion. The discussion also covered Obama’s criticism of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his Ohio remarks linking Trump and Vice President JD Vance to Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign tactics.

AlterNet further reports that Ramaswamy ran an advertisement featuring Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling Acton a liar. Acton and her brother had accused their stepfather of abuse; he was indicted, and the children were removed from their mother. Bloomberg’s David Drucker said the ad intensified some Republicans’ existing discomfort with Ramaswamy and made opposition to him—and possibly Senator Jon Husted—more politically acceptable.

The outrage required a false target

Obama mocked Trump’s conspicuous display of wealth and power. Republican critics answered by pretending he had mocked restaurant customers. That inversion shifted scrutiny from a president’s priorities to an imagined insult against ordinary people.

This is class resentment manufactured on behalf of the powerful. Trump controls the presidency and the White House. Obama made a joke. Yet the response cast Trump’s camp as defender of the insulted masses while removing Trump’s use of public office from view.

Power sits above the punch line

The institutional hierarchy is not difficult to identify. Trump holds executive power. Hegseth directs the Defense Department. Vance holds the vice presidency. Ramaswamy and Husted seek or hold political authority. Obama, Scarborough, and the panel possess influence, but they did not make the governing decisions under discussion.

That distinction matters because the Cheesecake Factory dispute is political insulation disguised as cultural grievance. A trivial semantic controversy consumes attention that could otherwise remain on how officeholders use state power, what they prioritize, and whom their campaigns are willing to harm.

The uglier tactic was elsewhere

The panel’s laughter is the easiest material to package, but the consequential allegation concerns Ramaswamy’s advertisement. According to AlterNet’s account, the ad enlisted Acton’s mother to attack her credibility despite the reported history involving allegations against Acton’s stepfather, his indictment, and the children’s removal.

That is not merely abrasive campaigning. On the facts presented, it turns a family trauma into electoral ammunition while stripping away the context needed to understand the mother’s accusation. Drucker’s reporting suggests the tactic unsettled Republicans who were already wary of Ramaswamy. The article does not establish what electoral effect followed, only that some party figures reportedly saw new political permission to oppose him.

Mockery is not analysis

Scarborough and Lemire correctly identified the distortion described by AlterNet: the Republican response substituted a fictional insult for Obama’s actual target. But televised hilarity can become its own evasion. Calling propaganda stupid does not explain why it is deployed.

The maneuver offers partisan media an emotionally efficient story: powerful Republicans become victims of liberal elitism, their supporters become the supposedly despised public, and criticism of presidential excess disappears. Its usefulness does not depend on logical coherence. It depends on repetition outrunning context.

Manufactured offense protects real authority

The larger pattern is grievance laundering. Political actors take criticism aimed upward, rewrite it as contempt aimed downward, and then claim solidarity with the people whose attention they are redirecting.

AlterNet’s framing captures the bad faith but leans heavily on the panel’s amusement. The sharper point is institutional: contrived cultural offense shields officeholders and candidates from scrutiny, while personal pain can be converted into campaign content. The joke was never the exercise of power. The decisions protected by the uproar were.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Morning Joe panel howls at GOP’s ‘desperate’ Cheesecake Factory meltdown

item.title: History repeating: What Nixon's secret tapes reveal about Trump
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet asked what Richard Nixon’s secret recordings reveal about concerns over Donald Trump’s fitness for office. Historian Luke Nichter’s answer was limited: Nixon’s tapes do not establish the alcoholism, violent rages, or alleged abuse described in the interview, and they provide no direct evidence about Trump’s health.

Nichter said the roughly 3,400 hours of recordings capture much of Nixon’s working life from 1971 until the taping system ended in July 1973. He acknowledged gaps—including Nixon’s final 13 or 14 months in office—but said the available audio contains little evidence that Nixon was routinely out of control.

The tapes do document something more concrete. According to Nichter, White House press secretary Ron Ziegler and doctors discussed how to describe Nixon’s temperature during his 1973 hospitalization for viral pneumonia: serious enough to justify hospitalization, but not so severe that the public might fear his death. Nichter suggested that administrations routinely manage presidential health disclosures, while stressing that he does not know the truth about Trump’s condition.

The headline outruns the evidence

The reporting begins with speculation about whether two presidents were “crazy,” then produces an expert who rejects the evidentiary premise about Nixon and declines to assess Trump. The secret tapes reveal no diagnosis of Trump, no verified parallel between the two men, and no reliable basis for remote medical judgment.

That does not make the interview useless. It makes the stated comparison the wrong story. The strongest evidence concerns information control inside the presidency—not mental illness. By organizing the piece around personal instability, AlterNet risks turning a documented exercise of institutional message management into an argument about individual psychology that its own interview cannot substantiate.

Power sits inside the disclosure machine

A president’s health is not merely private when it affects the exercise of executive authority. The presidency commands the armed forces, directs the executive branch, and can move markets through a single disclosure. That gives White House officials and presidential physicians extraordinary power over what the public learns and when.

Nichter’s account shows that Ziegler and the doctors were not passive observers struggling to describe Nixon’s pneumonia. They reportedly negotiated the presentation of his condition. The institutional advantage belonged to the people controlling the records, the medical access, and the briefing room—not to citizens or reporters trying to evaluate the president’s capacity from outside.

Speculation protects the gatekeepers

Debating whether a president is “crazy” invites sensational claims that are difficult to prove and easy for officials to dismiss. It also misdirects attention from conduct that can be documented: who released information, who withheld it, who shaped the official account, and whether those choices concealed facts relevant to presidential duties.

The interview’s unverified allegations about Nixon illustrate the problem. Nichter did not prove that misconduct never occurred; he said the extensive recordings he studied do not support the characterization presented to him, while acknowledging periods and places the tapes did not capture. The responsible conclusion is evidentiary restraint—not vindication, diagnosis, or analogy by insinuation.

The presidency grades its own condition

Nichter’s broader claim is that administrations build and defend narratives about presidential health. The Nixon example gives that claim a concrete mechanism: officials with privileged information calibrating a public statement to manage political and economic reactions.

That is the larger pattern. The executive branch possesses the facts, selects the messengers, defines the acceptable disclosure, and invokes privacy around the person whose condition may affect public power. The public then receives a curated account and is pushed toward guessing about symptoms instead of examining the officials who designed the information gap.

The lesson from Nixon’s tapes is therefore narrower—and more consequential—than the headline promises. They do not decode Trump. They show how presidential institutions can convert a matter of public capacity into a controlled communications problem, leaving outsiders to argue over rumors while insiders decide how much reality the country is permitted to see.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: History repeating: What Nixon’s secret tapes reveal about Trump

item.title: The 'reckoning': Trump capitulators spooked as blowback looms
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing reporting from The Washington Post, says technology, defense, manufacturing, and mining companies with close Trump administration ties are preparing for congressional investigations if Democrats win House and Senate majorities in the midterm elections. The investigations remain prospective: the supplied reporting establishes neither Democratic control of Congress nor any resulting findings.

According to the Post, possible targets include firms connected to Donald Trump Jr. that received Pentagon funding; companies tied to Elon Musk and the U.S. DOGE Service; and military contractors awarded noncompetitive contracts or equity investments. Congressional staffers reportedly want to examine whether some firms benefited financially from government information or relationships, but the article supplies no adjudicated findings of wrongdoing.

Jamie Bair, a congressional-investigations lawyer, predicted that Democrats would move faster than they did after the 2018 midterms. Staffers also reportedly see the proposed inquiries as a way to develop policy arguments and political messaging for the 2028 elections.

The power was never in the apology

The companies described here were not helpless institutions swept along by Washington weather. They possessed money, technical infrastructure, government access, and—in some cases—valuable federal contracts. The Trump administration possessed the greater coercive prize: control over procurement, regulation, executive agencies, and privileged information.

“Capitulation” can obscure that exchange. The relevant question is not whether executives acted cravenly in public. It is whether government decisions steered public money, access, or competitive advantage toward politically connected firms. Corporate flattery is embarrassing; the use of state power for favored relationships would be the consequential issue. That is what subpoenas, records, and sworn testimony would need to establish.

Suspicion is not a verdict

AlterNet calls the second term’s dealings corrupt, but the evidence summarized here does not prove that conclusion. It identifies investigative priorities and alleged risk areas: Pentagon funding, noncompetitive awards, military equity stakes, DOGE access, and possible private benefit from government relationships.

Those are legitimate subjects for oversight precisely because they involve concentrated public power. But a target list is not a set of findings. Donald Trump Jr.’s or Elon Musk’s connection to a company may justify examining how an award was made; it does not, standing alone, establish that the award was improper. Serious accountability requires more than reversing the partisan direction of insinuation.

Congress chose delay before

Bair’s account exposes an institutional failure with consequences. After Democrats took the House in 2018, he said, investigations lost time to “polite” protocols. Courtesy was not an external constraint. Congressional leaders chose procedures and pacing while the executive branch retained every incentive to resist scrutiny.

If Democrats gain subpoena and committee power, speed will matter—but speed is not the same as rigor. Hearings designed chiefly for viral confrontation can produce spectacle without durable findings. Investigators would need to trace contracts, communications, access, recusals, and financial gains. The test is whether Congress can convert suspicion into a documented public record.

Accountability or campaign production

The reported link to 2028 messaging is politically revealing. Oversight can inform legislation and expose misconduct. It can also become opposition research conducted with public authority. The difference lies in the work product: verified findings, enforceable reforms, procurement safeguards, and consequences where evidence supports them.

Companies are reportedly “bracing” because congressional control determines whether relationships with the executive branch receive serious examination. That is itself an indictment of episodic oversight. Public contracting should not become transparent only when the opposition wins an election.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a government in which access, contracts, and scrutiny can all turn on partisan control. Executives cultivate the administration holding procurement power; the opposition promises investigation if it later captures Congress; both accountability and impunity become electoral contingencies.

The alleged “reckoning” therefore remains conditional and incomplete. The systemic failure is not that powerful firms may finally face uncomfortable hearings. It is that institutions allowed politically connected companies to operate amid unresolved conflicts until a possible change in congressional power made examination plausible. A functioning oversight system would inspect those arrangements when they occur—not save accountability for the next campaign cycle.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The ‘reckoning’: Trump capitulators spooked as blowback looms

item.title: Trump's revenge campaign backfires as scorned Republicans hit back
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that several outgoing Republican lawmakers are withholding support from candidates endorsed by President Donald Trump after clashing with him or losing influence within the party. Their refusals could weaken Republican campaigns in Texas, North Carolina, and Nevada, but the reporting does not establish that Trump’s endorsement campaign has already “backfired” at the ballot box.

In Texas, Sen. John Cornyn has declined to assist Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated him in the Republican primary with Trump’s endorsement, while continuing to raise money for other Republican candidates and organizers. In North Carolina, retiring Sen. Thom Tillis reportedly has not delivered donor support to Trump-backed Michael Whatley. In Nevada, retiring Rep. Mark Amodei said he voted for a third-party candidate instead of Trump-backed David Flippo.

The immediate result is a Republican coalition with visible fractures. Trump allies are demanding obedience, while the sidelined lawmakers are using the leverage they still possess—money, donor relationships, endorsements and public criticism—to deny his chosen candidates a unified party apparatus.

Trump holds the power

The central actor is Trump, not the lawmakers portrayed as suddenly “turning their backs” on him. He used presidential influence and control over the Republican base to promote preferred candidates, including Paxton, Whatley and Flippo. Those endorsements helped determine who received legitimacy, money and attention inside the party.

Cornyn, Tillis and Amodei retain institutional connections, but each is leaving office or has already been pushed aside. Their resistance matters precisely because Trump holds more power: he can shape primaries and nominees, while they can mainly refuse to repair the damage afterward.

Loyalty cannot replace capacity

The candidates described by AlterNet do not merely face wounded feelings from establishment Republicans. Cornyn continues supporting other Republicans but says his primary criticism of Paxton remains true. An unnamed source described Whatley as a weak candidate who had relied on being Trump’s “guy” instead of building an independent political identity. Amodei said Trump received “awful advice” about Flippo and pointed to questions surrounding Flippo’s military record, residency and campaign finances.

Those assessments are partisan and, in two instances, partly sourced to unnamed figures. They are not proof that the candidates will lose. But they expose the risk in a system that treats personal loyalty as the chief qualification for nomination: an endorsement can defeat an internal critic without producing a candidate capable of holding the resulting coalition together.

The enforcement mechanism

Club for Growth President David McIntosh’s response makes the expectation explicit. Rather than address the candidates’ reported vulnerabilities, he accused Cornyn and Amodei of posturing for television contracts and ordered them, in effect, to support the nominees.

That is discipline through insinuation. The demand is not that former rivals reconsider the candidates on their merits; it is that they “get on board.” Under this model, loyalty flows upward to Trump, while responsibility for weak nominees flows downward to anyone who refuses to pretend they are strong.

A misleading rebellion

Calling this a “rebellion” flatters politicians who supported Republican power until Trump’s machinery threatened or displaced them personally. AlterNet reports that Cornyn is still raising substantial money for other Republicans, including more than $1.1 million in the previous month. Tillis’s alleged failure is that he did not sufficiently mobilize donors for one candidate. This is selective noncooperation, not a wholesale break with the party.

The revenge framing also risks confusing cause and consequence. Trump backed challengers or successors aligned with him; the politicians who lost influence then withheld resources. Their resentment may be real, but the politically significant fact is that a party organized around one leader has weakened the ordinary expectation that defeated factions will reunite behind the nominee.

The cost of personal rule

A personalist party can punish dissent quickly. It is less capable of preserving institutional knowledge, donor networks and local alliances after the purge. The very officials Trump could sideline still control assets his endorsements cannot automatically reproduce.

AlterNet’s broader claims about Trump’s approval, foreign policy and living costs are asserted without supporting figures in the supplied report. The evidence here establishes something narrower but consequential: Trump can impose candidates, yet he cannot compel every displaced Republican to supply the relationships needed to elect them. When a party substitutes obedience for coalition management, retaliation does not eliminate internal conflict. It merely postpones the conflict until the general election, when the cost becomes harder to contain.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s revenge campaign backfires as scorned Republicans hit back

item.title: John Oliver has an idea for how to fix Donald Trump's broken brain
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that John Oliver’s “idea” was a joke: after Donald Trump made an unexplained guttural sound during a South Carolina rally, Oliver said Trump needed to be unplugged and plugged back in. The report offers no medical evidence about Trump’s cognition and does not establish what caused the sound.

Oliver then shifted to Republican candidates and appointees associated with Nazi imagery or rhetoric. AlterNet cites congressional candidate Peter Oberacker’s Veterans Day photo of his grandfather in a Wehrmacht uniform; a 2022 video in which Texas congressional candidate Brandon Herrera discussed an MP-40 before footage of goose-stepping to a Nazi marching song; and leaked messages attributed to Paul Ingrassia, who reportedly withdrew his nomination to the Office of Special Counsel after writing that he sometimes had a “Nazi streak.”

The article itself contains serious apparent errors, describing a rally for “Darline Graham,” calling her the sister of the “late” Sen. Lindsey Graham, and identifying Trump as president without supplying a date that would clarify the timeline. Those defects leave basic circumstances unresolved and weaken confidence in the presentation.

The headline sells a diagnosis it cannot support

A strange vocalization is not evidence of a “broken brain.” Oliver’s reboot line was comedy, not a diagnosis, yet AlterNet turns it into medicalized clickbait. That framing invites readers to speculate about Trump’s health while providing neither clinical assessment nor even an explanation of what happened.

This is weak political journalism because it replaces a question of conduct with a question of presumed impairment. Trump’s public words and decisions can be assessed directly. Inventing a neurological conclusion adds heat while surrendering precision.

The real story is institutional permission

The politically consequential material comes later. According to AlterNet, Oliver highlighted Republican candidates and a Trump nominee whose reported conduct invoked Nazi uniforms, language, weapons, music, or gestures. The people with institutional power are not comedians or online spectators. They are party officials, nominators, donors, and primary voters who decide which conduct remains compatible with public office.

The report says Ingrassia withdrew only after attributed private messages became public. It does not establish who knew what beforehand or why Republican institutions supported any individual candidate. But the examples raise a concrete question the article barely develops: what screening, standards, and enforcement mechanisms exist, and who chooses not to use them?

Spectacle misdirects accountability

The bodily-noise clip makes Trump the object of ridicule and viewers the judges of whether he seems normal. That is politically easier than tracing responsibility through nomination systems, party endorsements, and candidate recruitment.

It also muddies agency. If Trump’s conduct is presented as the product of a malfunctioning mind, responsibility begins to dissolve into confusion. If candidates repeatedly circulate Nazi references, treating each episode as merely weird or tasteless similarly avoids the institutional decision at issue: whether those actions carry any meaningful political cost.

Comedy identified what reporting obscured

Oliver’s segment, as AlterNet recounts it, joined a presidential spectacle to a warning about Republican tolerance for Nazi-adjacent material. AlterNet preserved the jokes but did not adequately separate documented conduct from inference, comedy from medical fact, or candidate behavior from party authorization.

The strongest criticism does not require exaggeration. A Wehrmacht photograph may have family context; the report does not supply Oberacker’s explanation. Herrera’s cited video can be described without pretending the article proves his beliefs. Ingrassia’s reported message is more explicit, but it remains an attributed leaked remark. Precision does not soften scrutiny. It directs scrutiny toward what can actually be established.

The system rewards distraction

This story reveals a familiar political economy: spectacle attracts the headline, while gatekeeping decisions disappear into the background. A strange noise becomes a diagnosis; comedy becomes evidence; and the officials who control access to power escape sustained examination.

That is the systemic error. The issue is not whether politicians appear odd enough to mock. It is whether institutions repeatedly absorb extremist imagery and rhetoric without enforcing boundaries—and whether political coverage will name the people empowered to enforce them. Here, AlterNet’s sloppy framing turns an accountability story into a gawking session, leaving the machinery of permission largely untouched.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: John Oliver has an idea for how to fix Donald Trump’s broken brain

item.title: Psychologist exposes the grim mission driving Trump’s ultimate endgame
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist Alan D. Blotcky believes Donald Trump’s “ultimate” objective is to dominate a world destabilized around him—to become, in Blotcky’s words, “the last standing hero.” That is Blotcky’s interpretation of Trump’s public conduct, not a clinical diagnosis or an established fact.

Blotcky argues that Trump is neither psychotic nor unable to distinguish truth from falsehood. In his view, Trump knowingly repeats false claims because repetition, presidential authority and ideological alignment can make supporters accept them. He likens Trump’s public behavior to that of a con man who treats every unstopped abuse as permission for the next one.

Blotcky also acknowledges a decisive limitation: he has never interviewed or evaluated Trump. His assessment rests on public statements and recorded behavior. The interview therefore establishes what Blotcky thinks Trump is doing; it cannot establish Trump’s private mental state or prove the sweeping motive attributed to him.

Power is not a personality trait

The article’s psychological frame is vivid, but institutional power is the operative fact. Trump occupies the presidency. Congress controls legislation, spending and oversight. Media owners, university administrators, law-firm leaders and other executives control institutions capable of resisting government pressure. Their choices determine whether presidential demands remain provocations or become policy.

Blotcky identifies congressional Republicans as crucial enablers, arguing that their refusal to push back has expanded Trump’s freedom of action. He and interviewer Matthew Rozsa also describe powerful institutions capitulating because their leaders fear lawsuits, lost federal money or financial damage. Whether that account explains every cited institution is not demonstrated here, but it correctly directs attention toward people with actual authority.

Millions of followers may reward Trump’s conduct. They do not possess Congress’s votes, the executive branch’s machinery or corporate management’s control over major institutions. Treating mass devotion as the primary engine risks obscuring the officials and executives who can say no—and choose not to.

Diagnosis can become misdirection

Calling Trump a “malignant narcissist” offers a compact explanation for otherwise disparate conduct. It can also shrink a political system into one man’s pathology. Annexation rhetoric, institutional branding and attacks on marginalized groups matter because officeholders and organizations give them reach, not because a psychological label makes them legible.

Blotcky is unusually explicit about the boundary: he has not examined Trump, and Trump’s private self could differ from his public persona. The article nevertheless builds its central claim around a confident account of Trump’s inner mission. That exceeds what the interview can establish.

The firmer case is behavioral. According to the reporting, Trump repeatedly advances falsehoods, personalizes public institutions and uses presidential power in ways that produce compliance. Those actions can be assessed without converting political analysis into remote diagnosis.

The permission structure

The strongest insight in the interview is not about Trump’s mind. It is Blotcky’s description of a con man’s governing logic: if nobody stops the act, the absence of resistance becomes retroactive permission.

That logic thrives when gatekeepers calculate that surrender is cheaper than conflict. Congress declines confrontation. Institutional leaders protect revenue and access. News organizations soften coverage or fail to sustain attention. Each retreat teaches the executive that the next demand may also go unanswered.

This is agency, not confusion. The article sometimes presents capitulation as something that simply spreads through frightened institutions. But institutions do not feel fear; their leaders make decisions. They weigh public obligations against private exposure and choose which one to protect.

Followers are leverage, not the sovereign

Rozsa argues that Trump’s supporters accept claims that flatter existing racism, xenophobia or transphobia. Blotcky agrees, saying ideological agreement can outweigh concern about dishonesty or misconduct. That interpretation may explain part of Trump’s durable support, but the interview supplies no polling or other evidence establishing supporters’ motives as a whole.

What the account does show is how a committed constituency can become leverage. Its loyalty raises the cost of dissent for Republican lawmakers and gives institutional leaders a ready excuse for submission. The crowd matters, but chiefly because powerful actors treat it as a veto over their own responsibilities.

Blaming followers alone would be convenient for elites. It would turn calculated accommodation by lawmakers and executives into an unavoidable response to public passion. The institutional record described by Blotcky points in the opposite direction: elite surrender magnifies the faction’s power.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is personalization reinforced by institutional cowardice. A president makes public power serve personal image and grievance; supporters normalize the demand; officials and executives decide resistance is too costly; each concession enlarges the next one.

AlterNet packages that pattern as a revelation about one man’s grim endgame. The more consequential revelation is about everyone positioned between impulse and consequence. A leader’s appetite does not implement itself. It requires votes, administrators, money, publicity and repeated decisions by people who retain agency while pretending they have none.

The system fails most predictably when those with the power to impose limits describe their own surrender as inevitability. Trump’s psychology may remain disputed. The permission structure surrounding him is visible in the conduct the article describes.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist exposes the grim mission driving Trump’s ultimate endgame

item.title: Republicans are furious — and 'Trump’s apocalyptic screw-up' is to blame
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet attributes worsening farm finances and rising Republican anger in rural states to policies under President Donald Trump’s second administration. The outlet reports that fuel costs surged after the United States entered the Iran war, agricultural trade with China deteriorated, and cuts to Medicaid and food assistance increased pressure on rural households. It says farm bankruptcy filings have risen roughly 85 percent since Trump’s reelection, though the article does not define the filing category or comparison period.

The report cites polling suggesting Republican Senate candidates could lose in Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska, and Texas after Trump carried those states in 2024. Farmers describe steep increases in fuel and fertilizer expenses, while Nebraska Farmers Union president John Hansen calls the situation the worst agricultural crisis since the 1980s.

AlterNet reports that Trump responded by announcing $8 billion in emergency farm aid at a Kansas rally under the name Harvest Fuel Relief Program. The article presents that payment as an attempt to recover rural support before the midterms, but it does not establish that any of the cited states have actually shifted to Democrats.

Power made the damage scalable

Farmers did not set foreign policy, impose tariffs, reduce federal benefits, or design the resulting bailout. The administration and its congressional allies held the institutional power to make those choices. Rural households were left to absorb the consequences through operating costs, lost markets, weaker health coverage, and reduced food assistance.

That distinction matters because “rural America is turning blue” turns a story about government decisions into an electoral curiosity. The politically significant fact is not that Republican voters are angry. It is that officials used federal power in ways the reporting says materially injured a constituency whose loyalty they had treated as dependable.

The bailout conceals the sequence

Emergency aid does not erase responsibility for creating an emergency. According to AlterNet, American suppliers’ share of Chinese soybean imports fell to 23 percent while Brazil’s rose above 60 percent and Argentina’s reached 10 percent. The article links that deterioration to Trump’s trade wars and reports an annual loss of $10 billion in U.S. soybean exports.

If that account is accurate, the $8 billion program is not a substitute for stable markets. It is a public payment offered after policy disrupted farmers’ income. Washington first exercises concentrated power; farmers bear the dispersed losses; then the administration presents compensation financed by taxpayers as rescue. The state is made to pay for damage attributed to the people controlling the state.

Anger is not accountability

The article’s color-change framing gives rural voters more agency than they possess while granting policymakers less than they exercised. Voters can punish candidates at the next election. They cannot unilaterally reopen export markets, reverse benefit cuts, or reduce the price of running farm machinery.

Nor do suggestive polls prove a partisan realignment. AlterNet supplies no results, margins, or methodology. “Seemingly turning blue” is therefore stronger than the evidence presented. Electoral vulnerability is plausible within the article’s account; a durable transformation of rural politics is not established.

The reporting also notes that rural voters backed Trump after promises to lower costs and avoid unnecessary overseas wars. Their continued support in 2024 is politically relevant, but it does not transfer responsibility for federal decisions from officeholders to the people now paying for them.

Material harm outruns campaign branding

The reported consequences extend beyond farm balance sheets. AlterNet says cuts in Trump’s major tax-and-spending legislation are estimated to leave 1.8 million rural Americans without health insurance and make food harder to afford. That estimate is not a completed outcome, but it identifies who is exposed when national policy treats rural services as expendable.

The administration’s branding cannot alter that allocation of risk. “Harvest Fuel Relief” describes the remedy while omitting the decisions AlterNet says made relief necessary. That is political misdirection in its most efficient form: isolate the benefit, blur the cause, and ask recipients to thank the same authority the reporting holds responsible for their losses.

A constituency is not a captive asset

This story reveals a broader pattern of one-party dominance. When leaders assume a constituency has nowhere else to go, loyalty becomes something to extract rather than repay. Policy costs can be pushed downward, emergency checks can be sent later, and electoral identity can be invoked to suppress the connection between decision and consequence.

The real test is not whether several red states change color in one election. It is whether rural voters identify where power actually sat: with the officials who chose the tariffs, war policy, benefit cuts, and bailout—not with the farmers forced to calculate how much of the resulting damage they could survive.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republicans are furious — and ‘Trump’s apocalyptic screw-up’ is to blame

item.title: Psychotherapist says Trump supporter’s bizarre claim reveals a deeper chasm
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychotherapist Elliott Connie highlighted a video in which a Trump supporter endorsed $8 billion in aid to farmers harmed after retaliatory tariffs, yet repeatedly rejected the same intervention when interviewer Davram Stiefler described it as “socialism.” The man supported helping farmers in need but insisted socialist policies and subsidies were bad.

Connie argued that repetition can make politically loaded words feel true or dangerous regardless of whether listeners understand them. He attributed the contradiction to messaging that teaches voters to fear labels such as “socialism” while leaving them free to support policies carrying those labels when presented without them.

The article also cites JD Vance’s answer when asked to define socialism: he referred to replacing American workers with foreign workers and allowing boys to compete in girls’ sports. Connie characterized such messaging as a deliberate strategy for exploiting confusion and fear, though the report supplies his interpretation rather than independent evidence establishing a coordinated plan.

The contradiction is real, but the label is imprecise

The interview captures a genuine political contradiction: the supporter approves of government assistance when the beneficiaries are farmers, then condemns the abstract category into which the interviewer places that assistance. His judgment changes with the vocabulary, not the material policy.

But calling one subsidy a “socialist program” does more rhetorical work than analytical work. Governments operating within capitalist economies routinely subsidize industries. The sharper point is not that the man secretly favors an entire economic system. It is that partisan branding has displaced any consistent standard for deciding when public assistance is legitimate.

Power created the loss and selected the rescue

The supporter is not the principal holder of power in this story. Trump imposed the tariffs described by AlterNet; foreign retaliation reportedly damaged farmers; the administration then directed billions in aid toward those farmers. Executive policy produced the injury and government spending softened it.

That sequence matters. The subsidy was not merely spontaneous generosity toward people facing bad luck. According to the account, it compensated a politically important constituency for losses arising from the administration’s own trade policy. The governing institution could impose the costs, choose whom to reimburse and market the reimbursement as help.

“Confusion” can hide political agency

Connie’s psychological explanation illuminates how repetition works, but it risks making propaganda sound like a defect inside an individual voter’s brain. The supporter did not invent the political language surrounding him. Powerful actors supplied a vocabulary in which assistance to favored constituencies is help, while assistance associated with ideological opponents becomes socialism.

Vance’s quoted response is instructive because it did not define an economic doctrine. It attached the label to immigration and transgender participation in sports—separate culture-war targets. Whether that answer reflected confusion or calculated rhetoric is not established here. Its effect, however, is plain: policy analysis disappears, and an elastic enemy-word takes its place.

The weaker actor becomes the spectacle

The Good Liars clip makes one supporter’s inconsistency the punchline. That is entertaining, but institutionally backward. A voter repeating contradictory slogans has less power than the officials and political organizations that manufacture, circulate and benefit from those slogans.

AlterNet partially recognizes this structure, yet still builds the story around a “bizarre claim” by an ordinary man. The more consequential contradiction belongs to leaders who condemn public intervention in the abstract while using it to contain damage from their own decisions. Focusing on the supporter’s ignorance can let the architects of that arrangement recede from view.

The system rewards selective government

This is not simply a story about hypocrisy or inadequate political education. It shows how ideological labels can ration public sympathy. State assistance remains acceptable when it protects a favored group, repairs a politically dangerous loss or arrives under an approved leader. The same governing instrument becomes disqualifying when attached to a stigmatized word or an opposing coalition.

That asymmetry is politically useful. It allows officials to exercise expansive government power without defending a coherent principle for its use. Citizens are left arguing over a label while those in office decide who absorbs the damage, who receives compensation and whose hardship will be described as undeserving.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychotherapist says Trump supporter’s bizarre claim reveals a deeper chasm

item.title: Judge nails glaring omission in brutal ruling against Trump DOJ
item.description:
What happened

A federal judge ruled that President Donald Trump’s Justice Department illegally fired career prosecutor Maurene Comey in July 2025. AlterNet reports that U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman ordered her retroactively reinstated through December 20, 2025—the period before she accepted another job—and awarded back pay.

Comey received no advance notice, opportunity to respond, or explanation tied to her conduct. The government conceded that neither performance nor cause prompted her dismissal. Furman found that the removal violated the Civil Service Reform Act, separation-of-powers principles, and Comey’s Fifth Amendment due-process rights. But the glaring omission remained: the record did not establish who in Washington actually made the decision. The ruling also did not find that Comey was fired in retaliation for her father, former FBI Director James Comey.

Power without a name

The institutional power here belonged to Justice Department leadership. Furman held that the attorney general may remove assistant U.S. attorneys, but must exercise that authority within federal employment law. The administration instead claimed that presidential power under Article II displaced those protections—a position Furman said contradicted nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.

Yet the individual decisionmaker disappeared behind the institution. Manhattan officials reportedly told Comey only that the order came from Washington, while the complaint itself named no responsible official. That absence matters because obscured authorship makes accountability harder even when a court can identify the unlawful act.

A firing in search of a justification

Comey had spent nearly a decade as a career prosecutor, and Furman noted that supervisors and colleagues had consistently praised her work. The dismissal email cited constitutional authority but supplied no performance failure, misconduct, or other cause.

That does not prove the retaliatory explanation Comey alleged. Trump supporters had publicly demanded her removal, and her family connection made the firing politically conspicuous, but Furman did not determine that retaliation was the reason. What the record does establish is narrower and damning enough: officials exercised coercive personnel power without the process the law required and without identifying a lawful basis.

The misdirection of executive supremacy

The Justice Department tried to turn a concrete employment violation into a sweeping constitutional entitlement. That framing shifts attention from what officials did to what they claimed the president could theoretically do.

The weaker actor was a career employee denied notice and a chance to respond. The stronger actor was an executive department invoking presidential authority to escape statutory restraints. Presenting that clash as uncertainty about the boundaries of Article II sanitizes the conduct. Furman’s ruling says the relevant boundary was already written into law.

Accountability stops at the institution

The remedy corrected part of the material harm: back pay and retroactive reinstatement for the period before Comey found other employment. It did not reveal who ordered the firing, why that person did so, or whether anyone inside the department resisted an action the court later found unlawful.

That gap is politically useful to officials. Institutions can act through emails, chains of command, and unnamed Washington authorities while personal responsibility dissolves into bureaucracy. A court may reverse the result, but anonymity protects the decision-making structure that produced it.

The larger pattern

This case shows how executive overreach can operate without dramatic declarations. An administration removes a protected employee, withholds a reason, denies ordinary process, and then argues that presidential power places the act beyond Congress’s limits.

The danger in that structure is not confined to one prosecutor. Career protections exist to prevent public institutions from becoming instruments of personal or factional retaliation. The ruling blocked one unlawful dismissal. The concealed decisionmaker and the maximalist claim of presidential authority reveal the deeper systemic error: power was asserted expansively, responsibility was assigned nowhere, and the burden of enforcing the law fell on the person the government had already harmed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Judge nails glaring omission in brutal ruling against Trump DOJ

item.title: Fox News offers explanation for Trump’s Bill Maher meltdown
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump posted a roughly 1,300-word attack on Bill Maher after Maher’s HBO program aired with former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt as a guest. Trump insulted Maher, disputed the length and value of their earlier White House dinner, accused him of dishonesty, and declared that he would never watch the show again.

Fox News guest Tim Young, a comedian and Heritage Foundation media fellow, offered a speculative explanation: Trump may have watched a full episode because Leavitt appeared and only then grasped how routinely Maher criticizes him. The reporting supplies no confirmation that this was Trump’s motive.

The power is at the White House

The central political fact is not that two entertainers traded judgments. Trump is the president, with the authority and attention of the executive branch behind his speech. Maher hosts a television program. Their platforms are substantial, but their power is not comparable.

Trump chose to turn presidential attention toward punishing a media personality rhetorically for criticism. His post did not rebut Maher’s claims in detail; Trump explicitly said he would not spend time fact-checking him. Instead, he attacked Maher’s ratings, appearance, alleged substance use, courage and professional standing.

Access was mistaken for approval

Before the broadcast, Trump described his dinner with Maher as “very informative.” Afterward, he called it a waste of time and told Maher not to call again. The reversal makes the transaction plain: cordial access was acceptable while it could be presented as validation, but criticism triggered public degradation.

That does not prove Trump misunderstood Maher’s politics until watching the episode. Young’s theory is conjecture. What the reported sequence does establish is that Trump’s assessment of the dinner changed publicly after Maher’s program aired.

Fox supplied a flattering excuse

The “explanation” was not a reported finding from Fox News. It was one guest’s guess that Trump had simply never watched enough of Maher to understand the criticism. Framed that way, a president’s extended personal broadside becomes a comic misunderstanding—a belated discovery of what a television host says about him.

That framing misdirects attention from agency. Trump wrote and published the attack. Nobody forced him to answer criticism with insults or to invoke White House timestamps while revising his account of a private dinner. Treating that choice as bewilderment launders conduct into temperament and power into celebrity gossip.

The loyalty test keeps expanding

Trump’s complaint was not merely that Maher was inaccurate. He accused Maher of cowardice for failing to tell viewers how well the country was running and how badly Democrats had performed. In that formulation, favorable coverage is “truth,” while criticism is “FAKE NEWS.”

The larger pattern is the conversion of political approval into an evidentiary standard. A media figure may dine at the White House, speak pleasantly in private and still be cast as fraudulent once he declines to provide public affirmation. Access becomes conditional, disagreement becomes betrayal, and presidential communication becomes a tool for personal reprisal.

A spectacle that conceals the institution

The insults are gaudy enough to dominate coverage, which is precisely why the institutional meaning can disappear beneath them. The consequential actor here is not an HBO host making jokes. It is a president using the stature of his office to announce that critics are illegitimate, dishonest and unworthy of access.

The systemic error is covering that exercise of power as a mystery about what “set him off.” The relevant question is not why Trump became upset. It is why presidential retaliation against routine criticism is repeatedly processed as entertainment—and why media institutions keep supplying psychological excuses for a decision the president plainly made himself.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox News offers explanation for Trump’s Bill Maher meltdown
