item.title: I'm exhausted by Melania and Donald Trump's stupidity
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the Trump White House demands acceptance of claims that collapse under basic scrutiny. Its lead example is the administration’s assertion that Melania Trump initiated talks for a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine. The report says neither the Russian nor Ukrainian government immediately confirmed that account.

The article also describes Donald Trump defending a Republican attack ad against Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton. The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar, despite the reported history behind their estrangement: Acton said her stepfather repeatedly raped her beginning at age 12; her mother disputed her account, lost custody, and later left the state with the stepfather after he was charged.

When an NBC reporter raised that history, Trump said he knew nothing about the stepfather, ordered the reporter to be quiet, attacked her and her network, and declared the ad “fair game.” The article does not report a resolution of the ceasefire claim or the Ohio campaign dispute.

Power decides what counts

The institutional power here belongs to the president, the White House communications apparatus, and the campaigns capable of purchasing and amplifying political advertising. Amy Acton’s estranged mother can speak, but she does not control how her words are packaged or why they are broadcast. Trump and the campaign supporting Vivek Ramaswamy possess the machinery that turns a damaged family relationship into statewide propaganda.

Trump’s defense was not a detached comment on somebody else’s tactic. He endorsed the exploitation directly. Presented with the alleged abuse that made the mother-daughter rupture politically relevant, he dismissed it as ancient and unrelated. That is the decision: preserve the usefulness of the accusation by stripping away the facts that undermine its credibility.

The cruelty is functional

The ad’s force depends on presenting “a mother says her daughter lies” as self-authenticating evidence. The reported abuse history makes that framing grotesquely incomplete. According to AlterNet, Acton’s mother sided with the man Acton accused, lost custody, and accompanied him when he fled prosecution. Those facts do not automatically prove every later claim about Acton false, but they plainly destroy the premise that motherhood alone confers impartial authority.

Trump’s response demonstrates how political cruelty operates when truth is inconvenient. He did not rebut the reporter’s account. He announced that he did not know it, interrupted efforts to explain it, and then insisted it had nothing to do with the ad. Ignorance became a license to keep endorsing the attack.

The foreseeable consequence extends beyond one election. Survivors watching powerful officials weaponize estranged relatives learn that disclosing abuse may later furnish raw material for campaign advertising—and that the people using it can simply refuse the context.

Confusion as a press product

The Melania Trump episode reveals a softer version of the same power arrangement. The White House makes an extraordinary diplomatic claim; a news organization reports the claim alongside an absence of confirmation; the administration still receives the headline-sized benefit of having said it.

Attribution is necessary, but it is not adjudication. “The White House says” protects accuracy at the sentence level while potentially laundering nonsense at the story level. If neither government participating in the war confirmed the supposed ceasefire diplomacy, then the central fact was not Melania Trump’s achievement. It was the administration’s unsupported assertion of one.

The article is strongest when it identifies that asymmetry. Officials can manufacture an event by announcing it, while journalists often treat the lack of evidence as a secondary caveat. The public is left to sort a state-backed claim from the conspicuous absence of corroboration.

Spectacle protects authority

AlterNet’s broader polemic sprawls into claims about Trump’s health, family, religion, masculinity, foreign policy, and popularity, several of which it asserts without supplying enough evidence here to sustain them. That excess weakens the argument. A critique of propaganda should not imitate propaganda’s habit of piling assertion upon assertion.

The documented exchange with the NBC reporter is damning without embellishment. Trump redirected scrutiny from the ad to the reporter, from the abuse allegations to her employer, and from Acton’s history to praise of his own mother. Each diversion served the same purpose: avoid the evidence while preserving the attack.

Calling this “stupidity” risks obscuring the structure. Whatever the speaker’s intellectual discipline, the political method is legible. Authority asserts, insults, interrupts, and moves on. The chaos is not an alternative to power; it is one way power evades accountability.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is an information system that grants powerful actors endless opportunities to introduce claims while placing the burden of correction on people with less reach. A White House assertion becomes news before it becomes fact. An estranged parent’s accusation becomes an attack ad after the history explaining the estrangement has been cut away. A reporter who restores that history becomes the target.

The damage is not merely public exhaustion. Exhaustion is politically useful when it lowers the cost of lying, cruelty, and evasion. The systemic failure occurs when institutions describe the resulting confusion without naming who produced it, who benefits from it, and whose suffering was edited out to make the message work.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: I’m exhausted by Melania and Donald Trump’s stupidity

item.title: Trump just threatened to start another war
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump told a Friday rally in Fort Myers, Florida, that the United States would “take Cuba on our way back from Iran.” He described American ships stopping off Cuba and Secretary of State Marco Rubio “finish[ing] up the thing.” The remark invoked military force but, as reported, was not accompanied by a formal policy announcement or operational plan.

The comments came amid an oil blockade that AlterNet says has caused widespread harm in Cuba and an ongoing U.S.-Iran war associated with higher fuel prices. Trump claimed oil prices were falling substantially; the Wall Street Journal reporting cited by AlterNet said they had instead reached successive five-month highs as markets feared further escalation and attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.

The power is in Washington

Cuba does not control the blockade, the American fleet or the prospect of military escalation. The Trump administration does. Trump commands the armed forces; Rubio runs the State Department and, according to a longtime acquaintance quoted by the Guardian, has wanted greater authority to pursue Cuba for years.

That distribution of power matters. Trump was not describing a dispute between comparable actors. He was publicly imagining how the world’s most heavily equipped military might force the submission of a neighboring country already under severe economic pressure.

A threat disguised as banter

The rally performance makes coercion sound effortless: ships pass by, one stops offshore, Cuban officials surrender, and Rubio closes the deal. That is not a serious account of warfare. It is domination repackaged as an amusing detour.

The unserious delivery does not erase the institutional authority behind it. But the reporting establishes rhetoric, not an adopted invasion plan. The responsible conclusion is that Trump publicly normalized the prospect of attacking Cuba while leaving the policy status unclear—not that an operation was definitively ordered.

Rubio is an actor, not a prop

Trump cast Rubio as the official who would “finish up” Cuba. The Guardian quotation supplied by AlterNet portrays Cuba as a longstanding Rubio priority and says he finally possesses authority to pursue it. That makes Rubio part of the administration’s power structure, not merely the ethnic symbol Trump’s performance made of him.

Still, the quoted acquaintance’s characterization is evidence of perceived ambition, not proof that Rubio designed a military plan. The established fact is narrower: he holds substantial institutional power inside an administration already imposing material pressure on Cuba, and Trump publicly assigned him a role in the fantasy of capitulation.

War abroad, denial at home

Trump also claimed oil prices were dropping while the cited market reporting showed them rising. The political maneuver is plain even without inferring motive: celebrate military supremacy, promise another easy victory and contradict the economic evidence confronting voters.

The costs disappear from that script. Cuban civilians become leverage. American consumers encounter higher fuel prices. Regional infrastructure faces further attacks. Yet power is presented as spectacle while foreseeable consequences are treated as irrelevant—or simply denied.

The imperial shortcut

The larger pattern is government by coercive fantasy: economic punishment softens a target, military force is advertised as quick and clean, and surrender is assumed before anyone accounts for the human or economic damage.

That framing protects the officials making the decisions. It converts deliberate exercises of state power into casual improvisation and shifts attention from blockade, escalation and price shocks to Trump’s performance style. The systemic error is not merely that a president speaks recklessly. It is that enormous coercive authority can be discussed as a joke while the people exposed to its consequences are written out of the scene.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump just threatened to start another war

item.title: WSJ analyst: Time to 'take away gramp's phone’
item.description:
What happened

Wall Street Journal columnist Holman W. Jenkins Jr. said it would be time to “take away gramps’s phone” if President Donald Trump accepted Vladimir Putin’s supposed promise that surrendering additional Ukrainian cities in the Donbas could earn Trump a Nobel Prize. As AlterNet reports it, Jenkins was mocking what he sees as Trump’s susceptibility to flattery, not describing a documented proposal from Putin.

Jenkins argued that Trump was pressuring Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries while offering Russia incentives without meaningful coercion. He characterized Trump’s approach—including an inadequately explained “diesel deal”—as strategically empty and driven by a desire for lower fuel prices.

The column also warned that continued accommodation of Russia could alienate congressional Republicans and expose Trump to investigations or abandonment by his own party. That is Jenkins’s forecast, not an outcome established by AlterNet’s report.

The president holds the leverage

Trump is not a bystander being confused by a difficult war. As president, he controls immense diplomatic, economic, and military leverage. Decisions to pressure Kyiv, accommodate Moscow, or treat Ukrainian territory as bargaining material are exercises of state power with consequences for people who have no seat at his negotiating table.

Putin has power as the leader prosecuting Russia’s invasion. Ukraine bears the immediate cost. Treating this arrangement primarily as a test of whether Trump appears sufficiently sharp risks shrinking a struggle over sovereignty into palace gossip about one man’s faculties.

Senility is not an explanation

Jenkins’s “gramps” language gives the criticism bite, but it also supplies Trump with an alibi. The reported conduct does not require a medical explanation. Jenkins himself offers a political one: Trump pursues whatever he believes will benefit him in the next five minutes.

That describes agency, however reckless the calculation may be. A president who privileges personal acclaim, fuel prices, or favorable attention over Ukraine’s position is making choices. Calling those choices evidence of senility can obscure responsibility and turns a dispute over policy into speculation about cognition that AlterNet does not substantiate.

Flattery as foreign-policy leverage

The imagined Nobel Prize pitch matters because Jenkins presents Trump’s vanity as an exploitable weakness. If personal praise can influence the use of American power, then access to the president becomes a strategic asset for foreign leaders.

The institutional failure would extend beyond Trump. Advisers, cabinet officials, congressional Republicans, and allied policymakers all possess varying means to challenge or enable presidential decisions. Jenkins predicts that Republicans may eventually turn on Trump, but delayed self-preservation is not oversight. Until power becomes politically costly, party loyalty can function as permission.

The weaker party gets pressured

AlterNet’s account says Trump urged Kyiv to stop attacks on Russian refineries while offering Russia carrots without an effective stick. If that description is accurate, the asymmetry is stark: the invaded country is pressed to surrender leverage, while the invading power is courted in pursuit of an agreement.

That is not neutral dealmaking. It shifts the burden of ending the war toward the party resisting invasion. The framing of “improving relations” can sanitize that transfer of pressure, making accommodation sound prudent while leaving the territorial and security costs to Ukraine.

The system rewards the five-minute presidency

The larger pattern is government organized around one leader’s immediate political appetite, reinforced by officials who act only when his choices threaten them personally. Foreign policy then becomes transactional in the narrowest sense: praise, prices, spectacle, and short-term advantage displace durable strategy.

Jenkins’s sharpest point is therefore not the joke about confiscating a phone. It is his claim that Trump’s conduct follows a consistent incentive: whatever appears useful to Trump right now. The systemic error is allowing personal impulse to command institutional power—and allowing enablers to rename the consequences strategy until the damage reaches them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: WSJ analyst: Time to ‘take away gramp’s phone’

item.title: Trump admin fights back after judge rejects $400M settlement
item.description:
What happened

The Trump Justice Department is appealing U.S. District Judge George Wu’s refusal to approve a proposed settlement with TikTok. As AlterNet reports, the agreement would resolve a 2024 children’s-privacy complaint while vacating a 2019 Federal Trade Commission consent order requiring TikTok to pay $5 million and comply with continuing safeguards.

Wu ruled in the Central District of California that the government had not shown why the earlier order should be discarded. The Justice Department argued that its conditions were no longer necessary because they arose from conduct by TikTok predecessor Musical.ly. Wu found that neither changes in the platform nor new ownership altered TikTok’s obligations under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.

After Wu permitted the government to amend and refile its request, the administration declined. In papers filed Thursday, it said it would appeal on the existing record. The supplied reporting does not establish the $400 million figure featured in the headline.

The administration chose retreat

The central actor is not TikTok alone. The Justice Department used federal enforcement power to ask a court to remove an existing child-privacy order. That was an affirmative policy choice, not administrative confusion.

The 2024 complaint alleged that children 12 and younger could evade TikTok’s more restrictive Kids Mode, allowing data collection. Against that allegation, the government sought to eliminate safeguards it called unnecessary. Wu’s ruling exposes the weakness in that position: a corporate transformation does not itself prove that legal protections have accomplished their purpose.

Ownership is not compliance

The government’s distinction between Musical.ly and TikTok substitutes corporate lineage for evidence. A platform can change its name, structure or owners without satisfying the obligations imposed on it.

Wu kept the relevant question in view: whether the consent order’s objectives had been achieved and whether enforcement remained necessary. According to his ruling, the ownership change established neither. The administration’s argument would make restructuring an escape hatch from regulatory obligations.

Power sits on both sides of the bench

The Justice Department controls whether the federal government defends, weakens or abandons an enforcement position. Wu controls whether the parties may use his court to erase an existing order without an adequate legal showing.

His rejection did not permanently settle the dispute. It blocked the proposed arrangement and invited a better-supported filing. The administration instead chose appeal, shifting its effort from proving the order unnecessary to challenging the judge who demanded that proof.

That distinction matters. The court did not create the government’s predicament. The Justice Department selected the settlement, defended the proposed rollback and refused the opportunity to supplement its case.

The article muddies its strongest case

AlterNet introduces speculation that ByteDance may have improved its White House position through a sale involving Oracle and Trump ally Larry Ellison. It also relays critics’ claims about Ellison’s media ambitions. But the supplied reporting does not establish that those relationships caused the Justice Department’s settlement position.

That material distracts from the documented exercise of power. No speculative quid pro quo is needed to scrutinize an administration asking to discard child-privacy safeguards while a new complaint alleges that young users remained exposed to data collection. The decision itself warrants examination; unsupported insinuation only gives officials an easier argument to attack.

Enforcement becomes negotiable

This dispute reveals a familiar regulatory pattern: protections imposed after misconduct become vulnerable once corporate form and political circumstances change. The regulated company gains another chance to shed constraints, while the public must rely on a judge to ask why those constraints should disappear.

Consent orders have little deterrent value if the government treats them as disposable after rebranding or ownership changes. Wu’s ruling preserved the basic burden where it belongs: on the institutions seeking weaker enforcement, not on children and families to prove again why the law should still apply.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump admin fights back after judge rejects $400M settlement

item.title: GOP insiders tear apart Todd Blanche for evaporating DOJ
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Republican communications officials Doug Heye and Tara Setmayer condemned Attorney General Todd Blanche and congressional Republicans after President Donald Trump said he had directed the Justice Department to intervene in Alaska elections if Republicans lose. The report says Blanche signaled no objection to serving that political purpose, but it does not provide his exact remarks.

Appearing Friday on CNN’s OutFront, Heye argued that Republican senators knew they were confirming a politicized Justice Department when they voted for Blanche. Setmayer warned that Trump allies had spent years preparing ways to strain election systems and now occupied positions capable of carrying them out.

Neither commentator established that election interference had already occurred. Their immediate claim was that Trump had announced a conditional use of federal law-enforcement power and that Blanche had failed to defend the department’s independence.

The power is federal

The central actors are not local election workers, Democratic strategists, or voters. They are the president, the attorney general, and the Republican senators who placed Blanche in office.

A president can issue directives. An attorney general controls formidable investigative and prosecutorial machinery. Senators decide whether a nominee receives that authority. Whatever happens in Alaska, those officials hold the institutional power described in this story.

Confirmation was the decision

Heye’s steak-dinner anecdote identifies the decisive moment more clearly than the article’s overheated framing. Republican senators, including Thom Tillis, Bill Cassidy, and John Cornyn, reportedly had concerns about Blanche and voted to confirm him anyway.

That was agency, not capitulation in the abstract. Senators possessed a constitutional check and declined to use it. Their private discomfort, if accurately described, does not mitigate the vote; it establishes that concern and compliance coexisted comfortably.

Independence cannot simply evaporate

The headline’s suggestion that Blanche is “evaporating” the Justice Department obscures how institutional capture works. Departments do not vanish. Their legal authority, personnel, and coercive capacity remain—and can become more dangerous when redirected toward a president’s partisan interests.

Nor is Blanche solely responsible. According to AlterNet, Trump issued the directive, Blanche accepted the role, and Republican senators enabled his appointment. Reducing that chain of decisions to one attorney general’s failure lets the officials who supplied both the command and the confirmation recede from view.

The warning and its limits

Setmayer connected the episode to January 6, Project 2025, legal organizations aligned with the MAGA movement, and preparations to “stress test” election systems. Those are her stated conclusions and warnings; this report does not independently document the alleged planning or establish that the feared interference occurred.

Still, the conduct AlterNet does describe carries a plain political meaning. Conditioning Justice Department involvement on whether the president’s party loses would replace a neutral enforcement principle with a partisan trigger. Announcing that posture in advance could also help discredit an unwanted result before evidence of wrongdoing exists.

The system rewards willing enablers

The larger pattern is not a solitary official forgetting a Watergate lesson. It is a governing party treating institutional restraint as optional while preserving plausible distance through expressions of private concern.

Power was distributed across the chain, and responsibility follows it: Trump reportedly gave the direction, Blanche reportedly accepted the premise, and Republican senators knowingly supplied the confirmation. When officials retain the machinery of law while abandoning neutral limits on its use, the institution has not disappeared. It has been repurposed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP insiders tear apart Todd Blanche for evaporating DOJ

item.title: Trump fumes at Don Jr. behind closed doors over Russian wedding gift
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump privately complained that Donald Trump Jr. showed poor judgment by allowing Russian businessman Umar Kremlev to pay for a post-wedding celebration in the Bahamas, according to reporting cited by AlterNet from The Wall Street Journal. Trump said his son repaid Kremlev, but the supplied reporting provides no details about when, how, or in what amount.

AlterNet also reports tension over the conflict with Iran. A person close to Trump Jr. told The Atlantic that he privately opposed his father’s approach but would not publicly break with him; Trump Jr. declined to comment. Separately, AlterNet connected a proposed Alaska infrastructure venture to Russian energy company Novatek and Gentry Beach, a longtime Trump Jr. friend, but the article does not establish that Trump Jr. controlled or participated in the venture.

A complaint is not accountability

The president holds the institutional power here. He commands the executive branch, benefits from the authority of his office and can impose ethical discipline within his political operation. According to the reporting, he instead complained privately about his son’s judgment.

That distinction matters. Displeasure manages embarrassment; accountability establishes what Kremlev paid for, whether repayment occurred and whether the arrangement created access or obligations. The reported assurance of repayment answers none of those questions without records or dates.

The family is the power structure

Trump Jr. is not described here as a government official. His importance comes from proximity to the president and membership in a family that operates simultaneously as a political organization, business network and source of influence.

That structure invites transactions whose value cannot be measured only by the cost of an island party. When wealthy foreign-connected figures finance benefits for a president’s immediate family, the central issue is access to power and the appearance—or possibility—of indebtedness. A private family reprimand cannot resolve that public concern.

Loyalty overrides disagreement

The Iran dispute exposes the same hierarchy. Trump Jr. publicly celebrated his father’s supposed restraint in April 2024, yet a person close to him now says he objects privately and refuses to break publicly.

If that account is accurate, Trump Jr. still has agency. He is choosing loyalty and continued standing inside the family operation over an open argument about presidential policy. AlterNet’s language about “ranting and raving” personalizes the conflict, but the consequential issue is silence: a prominent ally allegedly withholding his criticism while the White House publicly claims Iran has been “decimated” and predicts the conflict will soon end.

The reporting outruns its proof

AlterNet repeatedly treats association as cumulative evidence: a Russian businessman financed the celebration; a Trump Jr. friend was associated with an Alaska venture reportedly backed through a UAE company by Novatek; therefore these are presented as more Trump-Russia connections.

Some connections are reported. The stronger insinuation is not established. The article supplies no evidence that the wedding payment bought influence, that Trump Jr. participated in the Alaska project, or that the separate events were coordinated. Invoking the earlier investigation into the Trump campaign does not fill those evidentiary gaps.

That loose framing also misdirects attention from the strongest documented problem. Readers do not need an all-purpose Russia narrative to recognize the danger of undisclosed largesse around a presidential family. The concrete questions—payment, repayment, access and disclosure—are more serious than the article’s pileup of suggestive associations.

Proximity becomes currency

The larger pattern is a political system in which family access is valuable, private discipline substitutes for transparent standards and public loyalty conceals reported internal disagreement. The president has the power to demand disclosure and establish boundaries. The account describes irritation instead.

That leaves consequences without resolution. Foreign-connected wealth can circulate around the presidential family, allies can leverage proximity, and the public receives assurances rather than documentation. The systemic error is not merely that powerful people exercise poor judgment. It is that personal networks absorb public power while accountability remains a private conversation.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump fumes at Don Jr. behind closed doors over Russian wedding gift

item.title: MAGA bank collapse traps Trump allies
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing New York Times reporting, says Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy invested in GloriFi, a MAGA-branded financial company that filed for bankruptcy months after launching its website. Its backers included right-wing billionaires Peter Thiel, Ken Griffin and Jeff Sprecher.

Jackson later invested millions more in the remains of GloriFi and now controls decisions about whom the bankrupt company sues, according to the Times. Former White House ethics counsel Norm Eisen warned that, if Jackson became governor, creditors could appear vulnerable to pressure from an official controlling litigation against them. Jackson’s campaign would not say whether he would relinquish that role if elected. Ramaswamy’s campaign did not answer the Times’ questions.

GloriFi marketed itself to consumers supposedly neglected by “liberal Wall Street,” with pitches built around faith, freedom and culture-war symbolism—including plans for credit cards made from metal used in shell casings. Its collapse left investors and Republican megadonors fighting through bankruptcy litigation.

The power sits with Jackson

The central political issue is not that two candidates made a bad investment. Investors lose money. The consequential fact is that Jackson reportedly acquired decision-making power over litigation involving wealthy creditors while seeking control of Georgia’s executive branch.

That arrangement would give the same person political authority and leverage in a private legal conflict. Eisen’s proposed remedy—an independent trustee and complete separation—is therefore not decorative ethics advice. It addresses the obvious danger created when a prospective governor retains the power to pursue or spare financially and politically connected people.

Jackson’s refusal, through his campaign, to say whether he would surrender that control leaves the conflict unresolved. Silence does not establish misconduct, but it withholds the most basic assurance that public office would be insulated from his private financial campaign.

A grievance brand met financial reality

GloriFi sold political identity as if it were a banking model. Its appeal rested on the claim that conservative consumers had been abandoned by liberal financial institutions. Candace Owens helped pitch the company; Republican donors and Trump allies supplied money and connections.

The company’s rapid bankruptcy matters because it exposes the hollowness of that proposition. Cultural resentment may attract customers and billionaire investors, but it does not substitute for a durable business. The shell-casing card was not merely a gimmick. It captured the enterprise’s priorities: partisan signaling presented as institutional competence.

The failure did not eliminate the underlying power network. It converted a culture-war venture into a contest among rich Republican actors over losses, lawsuits and control.

“Trapped” hides agency

The headline’s suggestion that the collapse “traps” Trump allies is too forgiving. Ramaswamy and Jackson were not powerless customers ensnared by an impersonal disaster. The Times identifies them as investors, and Jackson reportedly chose to commit millions more after the company had already failed.

That distinction is essential. Ramaswamy’s precise role beyond his investment is not established in the supplied reporting, and his campaign’s nonresponse does not prove wrongdoing. Jackson, however, reportedly pursued an additional strategy that placed him at the center of the litigation. He did not merely remain caught in the wreckage; he sought influence over how the wreckage would be divided.

Framing powerful investors as victims shifts attention from their choices to their discomfort. The weaker parties are the creditors subject to decisions made by someone who may soon wield state power.

The unanswered question is the story

Neither candidate’s campaign supplied the transparency the circumstances warranted. Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond. Jackson’s campaign declined to say whether he would reduce or abandon his litigation role if elected.

Those omissions do not answer whether any legal or ethical violation occurred. They do show that the candidates were unwilling to resolve foreseeable concerns created by their private interests. The relevant standard is not whether allies promise they can manage overlapping loyalties. It is whether the overlap is removed before public authority makes it dangerous.

Politics as a private asset

GloriFi reflects a larger pattern in which partisan identity becomes a commercial product, wealthy political networks finance it, and public ambition follows the money into the aftermath. When the venture succeeds, its promoters sell grievance. When it fails, the same network battles over control—and candidates ask voters to treat those battles as irrelevant to governing.

They are not irrelevant. A governor commands appointments, enforcement priorities and access to state power. A candidate who simultaneously controls litigation involving politically connected creditors carries a private web of incentives toward public office. The systemic error is allowing that entanglement to be treated as colorful campaign baggage rather than a problem of institutional power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: MAGA bank collapse traps Trump allies

item.title: Cult expert tries to deprogram MAGA mom
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that cultism expert Dr. Steven Hassan joined Chad Kultgen, Haley Popp, and their mother, Mary Lou Kultgen, on their podcast to discuss her continued support for Donald Trump despite policy views that clash with the Republican agenda. She opposed ICE’s conduct in communities, supported universal healthcare, and wanted the United States out of the war in Iran, yet said the issue of boys competing in girls’ sports was pulling her toward the GOP.

Hassan compared political identification with other consuming group identities and urged people estranged from Trump-supporting relatives to rebuild contact through apology, affection, and reciprocal discussion. AlterNet says he also led Mary Lou toward accepting that the reported assassination attempt against Trump could have been staged. The article supplies no evidence for that possibility.

The power is political, not familial

The Kultgen family has agency over its relationships, but it does not control immigration enforcement, healthcare policy, war, or the national machinery that turns cultural grievance into votes. Political parties, officeholders, wealthy donors, and media institutions hold that power.

Mary Lou’s preferences expose the asymmetry. Several concern policies with enormous material consequences; one concerns a highly charged dispute over school sports. Yet the cultural dispute appears capable of overriding the rest. That is what disciplined political messaging accomplishes: it concentrates fear on a narrowly defined target until symbolic allegiance outweighs broader interests.

Scapegoating does the work

The article identifies transgender participation in sports as the issue moving Mary Lou toward the GOP, but it does not examine who elevated that issue, what policies were actually proposed, or whose lives would be affected. Without those details, “boys playing in girls’ sports” passes through the story as a neutral description rather than a political formulation aimed at defining transgender people out of legitimacy.

That omission matters. A scapegoat is politically useful precisely because the targeted group has less institutional power than the people exploiting hostility toward it. The resulting debate directs scrutiny downward—toward young athletes—while politicians seeking authority escape comparable examination of their records on healthcare, immigration, and war.

“Deprogramming” hides a contradiction

AlterNet’s framing treats Mary Lou as the person who must be decoded. But the more revealing subject is the system capable of making one fear-laden issue dominate several stated policy commitments.

Calling this “deprogramming” also grants Hassan more authority than the reported exchange earns. His advice about restoring family contact may offer a way to resume conversation. It does not establish that he changed Mary Lou’s politics, and her observation that she is “in a thing” is not proof that she belongs to an authoritarian cult.

The headline promises an intervention. The reporting provides a mediated family discussion, a checklist of influence, and a claim that truth will eventually prevail. Those are not the same thing.

Reality testing cannot excuse speculation

The sharpest failure comes when Hassan’s stated commitment to reality testing collides with his handling of the assassination attempt. According to AlterNet, he moved Mary Lou toward believing it could have been staged. Possibility alone is cheap; evidence is the discipline that separates inquiry from insinuation.

A method supposedly designed to loosen propaganda cannot responsibly replace one unsupported narrative with another. Encouraging skepticism toward powerful actors is legitimate. Teaching that any event may be staged without supplying evidence reproduces the conspiratorial habit under a therapeutic label.

The system behind the error

This story’s larger pattern is not simply that families are divided or voters are confused. Organized political power selects emotionally potent targets, media repetition enlarges them, and personal relationships are then asked to absorb the damage.

AlterNet partially recognizes that structure but retreats into the safer drama of a mother and her children. The family becomes the site of repair while the institutions manufacturing the conflict remain indistinct. Reconciliation may reopen a conversation. It cannot substitute for naming who converts fear into political power, which policies that power enables, and who bears the consequences.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Cult expert tries to deprogram MAGA mom

item.title: The 11 words that should have ended Trump’s career
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Robert Mueller’s May 29, 2019 statement—“If we had had confidence that the president clearly did not commit a crime, we would have said so”—should have destroyed Donald Trump’s political career. Mueller did not accuse Trump of a crime. He said his office could not clear him and explained that Justice Department policy barred charging a sitting president.

The commentary says Attorney General William Barr’s earlier presentation of Mueller’s findings helped Trump portray the Russia investigation as a hoax. It then connects that episode to Trump’s conduct after the 2020 election and to his posture toward Vladimir Putin and Ukraine, arguing that Republican protection and institutional hesitation repeatedly insulated him from consequences.

AlterNet further alleges that Trump has aided Putin by lifting sanctions, disrupting satellite support used by Ukraine, and pressing Ukraine to surrender. The supplied article does not document those assertions in enough detail to evaluate them independently, and its claims of treason go beyond any legal finding established in the text.

Mueller’s actual message

Mueller’s statement was narrower—and more damning—than either Trump’s declaration of vindication or AlterNet’s demand for immediate imprisonment. His office had not exonerated the president, while department policy foreclosed the ordinary prosecutorial decision that might otherwise have followed.

That policy transferred responsibility to Congress. Mueller’s caution did not erase congressional power to investigate, impeach, or publicly assess the evidence. Yet institutional language designed for legal precision entered a political system that rewards repetition, certainty, and speed. Barr and Trump supplied all three.

Barr seized the narrative

Barr held the decisive executive-branch power at the crucial moment. As attorney general, he described Mueller’s work before the public absorbed the report itself. Mueller later objected that Barr’s account did not fully capture his findings.

Calling this merely a messaging failure obscures agency. Barr made the interpretive intervention; Trump exploited it; Republican officials reinforced it. News organizations that reduced the dispute to competing partisan claims helped a politically useful summary outrun the underlying record.

The weakness in AlterNet’s framing is that it treats one sentence as though sentences end careers. They do not. Parties, prosecutors, legislators, donors, and media institutions impose consequences—or decline to. Trump survived because powerful actors continued to make choices that preserved his viability.

Accountability was a decision

The article’s anger is aimed heavily at Mueller and later at Attorney General Merrick Garland. But institutional caution was not an autonomous force. Officials chose timelines, priorities, legal theories, and standards of acceptable risk. Congress chose how aggressively to use its own powers. Republican leaders chose continued alliance with Trump.

Voters were not the only or even the first line of accountability. The people best positioned to constrain presidential misconduct repeatedly passed responsibility elsewhere: prosecutors to Congress, legislators to elections, party leaders to voters, and media organizations to an imagined neutral audience. Each transfer weakened the chance of timely consequences.

That is not confusion. It is a political system distributing responsibility so widely that no institution must admit it decided not to act.

Russia as loyalty test

AlterNet presents Trump’s deference to Putin—from his 2018 Helsinki remarks to his description of Putin’s invasion strategy as “genius” and “savvy”—as part of a continuous pattern. Those statements are politically significant without converting them into an unproven legal charge of treason.

The central power question is simpler: Republican officials retained the capacity to withdraw support, deny nominations, conduct oversight, or make alignment with Putin politically costly. According to the article’s account, they instead continued protecting Trump. That choice made foreign-policy conduct subordinate to domestic partisan control.

The misdirection comes when the story is reduced to Trump’s personality or presumed private motives. Why he admires or accommodates Putin remains inferential here. What Republican institutions did in response is visible: they kept treating Trump’s retention of power as more important than enforcing their professed standards.

The system protects through delay

The larger pattern is not that Mueller failed to utter a magical phrase. It is that American institutions repeatedly convert urgent questions of power into slow disputes over wording, procedure, and personal intent. Delay then becomes protection. By the time one process ends, the next election, appeal, investigation, or crisis has begun.

AlterNet weakens its case when it substitutes unsupported criminal verdicts and personal abuse for demonstrated institutional analysis. The stronger indictment lies in the documented allocation of power: Barr shaped the initial public account, Congress possessed constitutional remedies, prosecutors controlled charging decisions, Republican leaders controlled their party, and each institution’s choices affected whether Trump faced consequences.

Careful language is indispensable in law. In politics, however, caution can become an alibi when officials use it to avoid decisions only they have the authority to make. The systemic error was not public failure to memorize Mueller’s sentence. It was powerful institutions hearing what he said and arranging for responsibility to belong to someone else.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The 11 words that should have ended Trump’s career

item.title: Todd Blanche is infinitely more sinister than his boss
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Attorney General Todd Blanche refused on NBC’s August 16, 2026, broadcast of “Meet the Press” to pledge independence from the White House, arguing that no attorney general should do so. The article’s central claim is that Blanche is more dangerous than President Donald Trump because he is converting Trump’s demands into Justice Department policy and legal action.

According to AlterNet, Blanche became acting attorney general after Trump fired Pam Bondi on April 1, secured a new indictment of former FBI Director James Comey before the end of that month, and won Senate confirmation as Bondi’s permanent replacement on August 8 by a 50–49 vote. The outlet also reports ethics complaints, a judicial referral concerning Blanche’s conduct, and repeated criticism from federal judges. The article does not report the final resolution of those matters.

Power belongs to the office

Trump holds presidential power and, as described here, supplies the targets and demands. Blanche controls the institution capable of turning those demands into subpoenas, searches, prosecutions and lawsuits backed by the United States government.

That distinction matters. Trump’s grievance politics may establish the objective, but an attorney general decides whether the Justice Department will resist political pressure or operationalize it. Blanche’s refusal to promise independence is therefore not an abstract dispute over constitutional theory. It is a declaration about how he understands his office: presidential loyalty first, institutional restraint second.

The machinery has an operator

The reported sequence strips away any pretense that these outcomes simply emerged from an unruly bureaucracy. Career prosecutors reportedly found insufficient evidence to charge Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Trump pushed Bondi to act anyway. Lindsay Halligan obtained indictments, but a federal court dismissed them after finding her appointment unlawful; a later grand jury reportedly refused to indict James again.

Blanche then obtained Comey’s re-indictment after becoming acting attorney general. AlterNet further reports that he signed an agreement shielding Trump and his family from IRS investigations, despite an earlier recusal pledge, and participated in removing more than 200 prosecutors and FBI agents connected to Trump-related cases. Those are decisions by officials with names, offices and authority—not institutional weather.

Election interference dressed as enforcement

The most consequential allegations concern the 2026 midterms. AlterNet reports that Blanche’s department continued litigation seeking state voter rolls despite losses in 26 federal courts, sued California after demanding the removal of 20,000 voters using a disputed federal database, and searched Representative Ilhan Omar’s home 22 days before an election in which she was a candidate.

The article argues that these actions support Trump’s effort to discredit the election in advance. That motive remains the outlet’s interpretation, but the foreseeable effect is plain: federal law enforcement actions close to voting can stigmatize candidates, threaten eligible voters and furnish partisan claims that election systems are corrupt.

Blanche also reportedly campaigned for Republicans after relaxing Justice Department restrictions on political participation by presidential appointees. The problem is not “confusion” about departmental norms. The reported conduct collapses the boundary between enforcing federal law and advancing the governing party’s electoral interests.

The framing lets Trump off too easily

Calling Blanche “more sinister” personalizes what is fundamentally a structure of shared responsibility. Blanche may be the disciplined executor, but Trump reportedly selected the targets, demanded action and appointed the officials who complied. The Senate then confirmed Blanche by one vote after this record was already substantially visible.

The power structure is therefore broader than one ambitious lawyer. The president directs. The attorney general implements. Senators legitimize. Political appointees execute. When coverage turns that system into a contest over which individual is more malevolent, it risks making institutional capture look like a character defect rather than a governing project.

Personalized rule becomes policy

Watergate-era restraints were never self-enforcing. They depended on officials accepting that the Justice Department’s coercive power could not become a president’s private instrument. Blanche’s reported position rejects that premise at the top of the department.

The larger pattern is authoritarian administration through ordinary offices: personnel purges, selective enforcement, partisan legal theories and election-related interventions presented as routine governance. The durable harm is not merely that one president seeks retribution. It is that officials with institutional power are constructing a Justice Department in which presidential grievance can pass for federal purpose—and partisan loyalty can be exercised with the force of law.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Todd Blanche is infinitely more sinister than his boss

item.title: Insider fears 'movement of sociopaths' following massive GOP defeat
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative writer Nick Catoggio fears a major Republican electoral defeat would not moderate the party but drive it toward even more extreme candidates. The article does not establish that the “massive GOP defeat” in its headline has occurred; Catoggio is discussing what Republicans might do after a prospective November drubbing.

Catoggio cites former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie’s condemnation of a Republican attack ad in Ohio and Vice President J.D. Vance’s defense of it, though AlterNet does not describe the ad’s contents. He also points to a Wednesday Truth Social post in which, according to AlterNet, Donald Trump called Democrat Amy Acton a liar over her account of childhood sexual abuse. The outlet reports that her stepfather was indicted by a grand jury in connection with the alleged crime and later fled.

Catoggio predicts that Republican activists would explain electoral losses as a failure of turnout or ideological purity, then promote Vance-style isolationists and similarly aligned congressional candidates. That forecast—not a documented party decision—is the basis for his description of postliberalism as a “movement of sociopaths.”

Power is not an infection

Christie says the Republican Party has been “infected” by a corrupted moral center. That metaphor conceals agency. A party does not contract attack ads, smears, or political cruelty like a virus. Candidates authorize them. Officials defend them. Influential media figures rationalize them. Voters and donors reward them.

The institutional power here belongs to Trump, Vance, party officials, major funders, and the media personalities capable of defining Republican orthodoxy. Christie can diagnose the decay, but he no longer controls the organization. His objection illustrates the balance of power precisely because the people he condemns possess the offices, audience, and machinery that he lacks.

Cruelty with a distribution network

Trump’s reported attack on Acton matters beyond one social-media post. Calling a political opponent a liar about alleged childhood sexual abuse turns personal trauma into campaign ammunition. The foreseeable effect is to punish disclosure and signal that no vulnerability is protected from partisan exploitation.

But precision matters. AlterNet supplies no evidence that every postliberal conservative shares one motive or psychological condition. “Sociopaths” is Catoggio’s condemnation, not a clinical finding. The substantiated political point is narrower and stronger: prominent Republicans are willing to use or defend degrading attacks, and their movement’s power structure provides mechanisms for amplifying them.

The alibi of irrational voters

Catoggio places considerable weight on what the right-wing base may do after defeat. That risks shifting responsibility downward. Ordinary voters influence primaries, but they do not independently manufacture candidate fields, finance campaigns, commission advertising, or give commentators national platforms.

Party elites may claim that “real Trumpism has never been tried” or blame an unreliable working-class electorate. If they do, those explanations will serve an institutional purpose: protecting the people who selected the strategy from accountability for its consequences. An electoral loss does not compel leaders to learn. It merely creates a struggle over which faction gets to define the lesson.

Defeat is not reform

The comforting theory is that sufficient electoral punishment forces a party back toward restraint. Catoggio’s forecast exposes the missing mechanism. Losing can weaken officeholders without dislodging the donors, propagandists, primary incentives, and safe districts that reward escalation.

In heavily Republican seats, ideological actors can nominate harsher candidates while facing limited danger from the opposing party. That structure allows national rejection and internal radicalization to occur simultaneously. A smaller caucus can become more extreme because defeat removes marginal members while leaving the safest—and often least accountable—political terrain intact.

The system reproduces the conduct

This story is ultimately not about whether Republicans can “regain their soul.” That language turns organized choices into spiritual weather. The relevant question is whether cruelty continues to bring attention, loyalty, money, nominations, and protection from consequences.

AlterNet’s thin description of the Ohio ad leaves an important evidentiary gap, and its headline overstates a defeat the article presents as prospective. Yet the structural warning survives that weak framing: elections can remove officials, but they do not automatically dismantle the machinery that selected them. When humiliation is rewarded and accountability is redirected toward weaker actors, electoral defeat can become fuel for the next round rather than a cure.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Insider fears ‘movement of sociopaths’ following massive GOP defeat

item.title: Trump's 'pay dirt' blows up in the heart of MAGA land
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy spent $4 million promoting an attack ad in which Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton’s estranged mother accused her of lying about her childhood trauma. Acton responded with court records showing that her stepfather was indicted in 1978 for raping her when she was 12 and that her mother had accused her of lying; the stepfather fled Ohio and died in 2004.

The ad drew condemnation from the Columbus Dispatch and prominent Ohio Republicans. Governor Mike DeWine called it “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged Ramaswamy to remove it, but did not withdraw his endorsement. Vice President JD Vance defended Ramaswamy’s attack, while President Donald Trump praised the ad as “hitting pay dirt.”

The cruelty was a campaign decision

This was not an accidental lapse in judgment. According to AlterNet, Ramaswamy invested millions in circulating the ad after it had already generated outrage. Whatever his campaign’s initial role may have appeared to be, that expenditure made his agency unmistakable.

The relevant power lies with the candidate who financed the distribution, the national figures who legitimized it and the party officials who can confer or withdraw support. Acton’s estranged mother supplied the accusation, but Ramaswamy turned it into campaign material. Vance reinforced it from the stump. Trump publicly rewarded the tactic.

Condemnation without consequence

Ohio Republicans described the ad as appalling while largely preserving the political arrangement that made it useful. DeWine’s response is the clearest example: he urged Ramaswamy to remove the ad but retained his endorsement.

That is institutional cowardice dressed as disapproval. A request to improve campaign decorum costs little. Withdrawing material support would impose a price. When party leaders condemn conduct while continuing to back its beneficiary, they teach candidates that cruelty remains acceptable so long as it is followed by a sufficiently grave press statement.

The misdirection is deliberate

Vance redirected attention from the substance of the attack to Democrats’ supposed danger to the country. His complaint was not that the reporting about Acton was wrong; it was that Republicans were objecting too loudly when they should have been focused on defeating the opposing party.

That maneuver converts an exercise of power into a test of partisan loyalty. The people objecting to the exploitation become “whiners,” while the campaign that paid to amplify it escapes scrutiny. The weaker actor—a candidate forced to disclose records concerning her childhood rape—is put on trial again, this time for failing to absorb the attack silently.

Trump’s approval explains the incentive

Trump’s “pay dirt” remark identified the governing standard: an attack is good if it wounds an opponent and useful if the press condemns it. The backlash becomes proof of potency. Ethical limits become evidence of weakness.

AlterNet argues that Vance’s defense reflects his ambition and dependence on Trump’s coalition. The reported facts establish the political alignment, though not Vance’s private motives: Ramaswamy deployed the ad, Vance defended the attack after controversy erupted, and Trump praised it. Each man showed the next one what conduct receives protection inside their hierarchy.

A system that rewards degradation

The larger pattern is not merely that political rhetoric has become ugly. It is that powerful actors can weaponize private trauma, demand party discipline when challenged and rely on allies to separate moral condemnation from political consequence.

The backlash in Ohio may indicate that this tactic has limits, but outrage alone does not establish lasting rejection. The decisive question is whether institutions impose costs. When endorsements, money and party standing remain intact, disgust becomes another disposable stage in the news cycle—and degradation remains a rational campaign strategy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘pay dirt’ blows up in the heart of MAGA land

item.title: Top Republicans declare war on Trump's favorite new congressman
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, a Trump favorite, was being considered for expulsion from the House Freedom Caucus. According to Axios reporting cited by AlterNet, caucus members accused Gill of benefiting from introductions to the group’s donors while failing to support colleagues financially or participate sufficiently in difficult votes.

Gill nevertheless retained powerful allies. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer praised him as “the future of our party,” while Gill pursued leadership of an influential House committee. AlterNet also recounts Gill’s 2025 promotion of anti-immigrant claims, territorial expansionism and accusations that federally supported children’s programming advanced “far left ideologies.”

The dispute is about patronage

The Freedom Caucus criticism is not presented as a repudiation of Gill’s politics. Its members reportedly object to his conduct inside the party’s machinery: he received access, they say, without adequately returning money, labor or loyalty.

That distinction matters. Gill’s reported rhetoric about immigrants, mass deportation, Greenland and children’s television did not trigger the threatened punishment described here. The alleged offense was failing to pay his institutional dues while climbing toward greater power.

Power protects its prospect

Gill is a first-term congressman, but the institutional balance described by AlterNet favors him. He has support in Trump’s orbit, praise from Republican leadership and ambitions to control a powerful committee. The Freedom Caucus can threaten his membership; party leaders can help determine whether his career accelerates.

Emmer’s endorsement is especially revealing. His emphasis on Gill being “out front” and possessing strong communication skills treats politics as message delivery. What Gill communicates becomes secondary to his usefulness as a disciplined and visible partisan operator.

The headline oversells a factional quarrel

Calling this a Republican “war” invites readers to mistake competition within the ruling coalition for opposition to its agenda. The reporting establishes a dispute over Gill’s participation and support for colleagues, not a broad conservative revolt against his record.

That framing misdirects attention from the people with actual power. Gill’s critics are not weaker outsiders suffering the consequences of his politics; they are lawmakers contesting access, money and advancement within the same party structure. The people targeted by anti-immigrant agitation or anti-trans rhetoric remain largely outside the article’s conflict altogether.

Extremism as a résumé

The larger pattern is political selection. Jared Holt, quoted by AlterNet, described Gill as part of a rising Republican generation equipped with wealthy backing, social-media skill and an appetite for the movement’s most inflammatory ideas. Gill’s ascent, as reported, suggests that provocation can function as evidence of talent when party leaders prize reach and loyalty.

The consequence is not merely worse discourse. When institutional advancement rewards conspiratorial claims, territorial bravado and attacks on marginalized groups, those messages gain congressional authority. The caucus dispute shows the limit of internal discipline: Republican factions may police who shares resources and endures difficult votes while leaving the underlying politics untouched.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Top Republicans declare war on Trump’s favorite new congressman

item.title: Trump may be preparing to throw another top official under the bus: insider
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Republican strategist Sarah Longwell believes President Donald Trump may eventually push Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth out to absorb public anger over the Iran war. She named Hegseth as the likeliest “sacrificial lamb,” while warning that voters would not accept him as the person ultimately responsible.

Longwell based her assessment on focus groups with people who voted for Trump in 2024. According to her, those voters increasingly connect the continuing war, military deaths, higher gas prices, and rising household costs directly to Trump—who had promised lower prices, fewer foreign entanglements, and a quick end to the fighting.

AlterNet does not establish that Trump has decided to dismiss Hegseth. The story reports Longwell’s prediction, not an announced personnel move.

The power is in the Oval Office

Hegseth runs the Defense Department, but the political authority at issue belongs to Trump. Longwell’s account says the war and tariffs are unusually difficult for the administration to redirect onto its predecessor because voters recognize them as Trump’s decisions.

That distinction matters. A defense secretary may advocate, administer, and publicly celebrate a war. He does not convert the president into a spectator. Firing Hegseth could change the face at the Pentagon; it could not retroactively transfer presidential responsibility for the policy.

Hegseth is an enabler, not an explanation

Longwell portrays Hegseth as an enthusiastic cheerleader whose leadership includes inflammatory language and performative fixations. That makes him politically expendable, not politically innocent. He holds enormous institutional power and, by Klein’s account, has eagerly claimed ownership of the war.

But reducing the failure to Hegseth’s conduct would confuse a willing instrument with the source of authority. His apparent usefulness is precisely that he can promote the policy when it is popular and personify its failures when it is not.

The scapegoat has limits

The reported possibility of sacrificing Hegseth is less a change of policy than a familiar method of blame management: remove a subordinate, dramatize accountability, and preserve the decision-maker. Longwell’s crucial point is that voters may reject the substitution.

The material consequences make the maneuver harder. According to her focus groups, discontent is tied not merely to tone or staffing but to military personnel dying, an open-ended conflict, and costs reaching household budgets. A personnel shuffle cannot make those consequences belong to someone else.

Promises met policy

The sharper political fracture runs through Trump’s own coalition. Longwell says some supporters expected an operation resembling the administration’s reported intervention in Venezuela: quick, decisive, and without casualties. Instead, they encountered continuing fighting after repeated assurances that it would end quickly.

That gap exposes the weakness of personality-based politics. “America First” voters opposed foreign wars and expected economic relief, yet loyalty to Trump asked them to excuse policies they had been promised he would reject. Figures including Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene, Longwell says, have broken with him over Iran and other White House decisions. The split is not an outside critique imposed on the movement. It is a collision between its stated commitments and the president who commands it.

Responsibility does not resign

AlterNet’s framing invites speculation about who may be thrown under the bus. The more important fact is who is driving it. Trump possesses the authority, made the promises, and remains the actor whom Longwell’s focus-group participants connect to the results.

The larger pattern is executive power attempting to preserve itself through disposable subordinates. That tactic works when political coverage treats staffing drama as accountability. It fails when the public follows the chain of command from the spokesman and administrator back to the president who chose the policy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump may be preparing to throw another top official under the bus: insider

item.title: Trump’s manufacturing 'boom' is busting badly —and leaving MAGA behind
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the manufacturing “boom” is narrowly concentrated in advanced industries tied to AI and energy investment, not broadly shared across the traditional factory economy Donald Trump promised to revive. In September, factory output rose 0.3 percent even as auto production fell 3 percent, while the Institute for Supply Management recorded a ninth consecutive month of expansion.

Employment tells a weaker story. According to figures cited by Axios, manufacturers added a net 40,000 jobs over the previous 12 months: advanced manufacturing gained 56,000, while all other manufacturing industries collectively lost 16,000. Employment outside advanced manufacturing remained only slightly above its 2016 level.

AlterNet presents that split as a broken political promise to blue-collar Trump voters. But it supplies no polling, interviews, or other evidence for its claim that many of those voters are now questioning Trump’s commitment to them. It also cites claims about federal debt without establishing a causal connection between those figures and the manufacturing results.

A boom built for capital

The headline numbers reward aggregation. Put computer equipment, chemicals, machinery and transportation equipment beside the rest of manufacturing, and the gains can be advertised as a national revival. Separate them, and the supposed boom becomes a concentrated surge in sectors serving two capital-intensive buildouts.

That distinction matters politically. Rising orders and output do not automatically produce broad employment gains, especially when investment flows toward industries capable of expanding without hiring on the scale associated with older factory production. A sector can grow while the workers invoked in campaign speeches see little of that growth.

Calling this a manufacturing comeback without identifying its beneficiaries turns an uneven allocation of investment into a comforting national statistic.

The promise and the power

Trump courted blue-collar workers by promising a thriving manufacturing economy. As president, he holds substantial institutional power to shape trade, taxation, spending and industrial policy. The outcomes reported here therefore belong in an assessment of his governing record, not merely in a discussion of impersonal “market trends.”

But the supplied reporting does not identify a particular Trump policy that produced the 56,000 advanced-manufacturing jobs or the 16,000 losses elsewhere. It establishes a mismatch between his broad promise and the reported labor market, not a complete causal account.

That gap should sharpen the criticism, not weaken it. Political promises are designed to claim credit for prosperity. They must also create accountability when the promised beneficiaries are excluded.

The worker as campaign scenery

The familiar maneuver is to treat “manufacturing” as a cultural symbol rather than a distributional question. Politicians praise the factory worker, companies announce investment, analysts celebrate output, and almost nobody asks which industries hired, where the jobs appeared, what they paid or whether displaced workers could obtain them.

Trump’s rhetoric made traditional manufacturing workers central to his economic appeal. The reported gains, however, came entirely from advanced manufacturing. Workers outside those industries were not merely receiving a smaller share of the expansion; their industries lost jobs on net over the measured period.

That is the consequence hidden by the boom narrative: the constituency used to sell the policy story is not necessarily the constituency receiving its benefits.

Misdirection in the coverage

AlterNet correctly emphasizes the divide between output and employment, but then weakens its own case with unsupported claims about what Trump voters supposedly think. Without evidence, “many” workers wondering whether he cares is political narration, not reporting.

The debt material is similarly underdeveloped. AlterNet says Trump added $2 trillion to the 2026 deficit and that debt reached $40 trillion, but the article does not show how those figures affected manufacturing employment. Dropping them into the story creates an indictment by accumulation instead of tracing power through specific decisions and consequences.

The strongest evidence needs no embellishment: broad promises were followed by narrow gains, while most manufacturing industries combined lost employment.

The politics of selective prosperity

This is a recurring structure of American economic politics. Leaders announce success through national totals; concentrated industries capture investment; and workers outside the favored sectors are told that growth somewhere constitutes recovery everywhere.

The central failure is not that every factory industry failed to expand at once. It is that political rhetoric erased the difference between a technologically concentrated investment cycle and a broad revival of blue-collar employment. When government celebrates the first as proof of the second, statistics become camouflage for unequal power.

A manufacturing strategy should be judged by who gains bargaining power, stable work and durable income—not by whether politicians can place a flattering headline over an economy leaving much of its advertised constituency behind.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s manufacturing ‘boom’ is busting badly —and leaving MAGA behind

item.title: Trump attacks judge who keeps handing him wins
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump attacked federal Judge Ana Reyes after she criticized his administration for failing to provide advance notice of major work at the East Potomac Park golf course. After Trump called her a “crazed lunatic,” Reyes said she received death threats; Trump then claimed she was “freaking out” over them.

The article’s central point is that Reyes, a Biden appointee portrayed by Trump as an enemy, has repeatedly delivered outcomes favorable to his administration. She declined or was unable to grant relief in disputes involving civil-liberties offices, fired inspectors general, alleged sharing of Iranian asylum applicants’ information, tenant-eviction notices, and the removal of National Mediation Board member Deirdre Hamilton.

In the inspectors-general case, Reyes reportedly found that Trump had violated the law but concluded she lacked authority to reinstate those fired. Other challenges stalled when agencies withdrew or delayed policies, while Hamilton’s case was paused pending a Supreme Court ruling that ultimately accepted Trump’s position on presidential removal power.

Power does not require gratitude

Trump holds executive power. His administration controls the agencies making the disputed decisions, the government lawyers defending them, and—within legal limits—the ability to withdraw or postpone policies before courts can rule. Reyes can review particular cases, but she neither commands the executive branch nor controls Supreme Court doctrine.

That imbalance makes Trump’s attack more revealing. Reyes did not need to oppose him consistently to become a target. She merely exercised judicial scrutiny and publicly objected when his administration disregarded her demand for notice. In this political model, favorable rulings purchase no independence. Any resistance, however narrow, can trigger personal vilification.

The accusation replaces the record

Calling Reyes a Trump hater is not an argument about her decisions. The record summarized by AlterNet cuts against that label: she withheld injunctions, declined intervention, found herself unable to provide a remedy, or waited for controlling Supreme Court guidance.

The insult therefore serves as misdirection. It moves attention away from the administration’s conduct—especially its handling of the golf-course dispute—and toward the supposed temperament or allegiance of the judge examining it. A legal disagreement becomes a loyalty test, and a public official’s criticism becomes evidence of personal instability.

The machinery of consequence-free illegality

The inspectors-general case exposes the deeper institutional problem. According to the reporting, Reyes concluded that Trump violated the law by firing inspectors general without the required notice to Congress, yet also concluded that she could not restore them to office. Trump lost on legality and won on consequence.

That is not merely a judicial technicality. A rule that can be violated without an available remedy is a weak restraint on an executive willing to absorb criticism. Courts may describe the breach accurately while leaving the resulting transfer of power intact.

The other cases show additional routes around accountability. An agency can reverse course before an injunction, call a policy only a proposal, delay it indefinitely, or withdraw the contested action. Those moves may resolve the immediate legal dispute, but they can also prevent courts from reaching broader questions about executive authority.

Intimidation is part of the environment

The reporting does not establish who sent the death threats or that Trump directed anyone to send them. It does establish the sequence AlterNet describes: Trump branded a federal judge a “crazed lunatic,” Reyes reported receiving threats, and Trump mocked her reaction.

That response treats intimidation not as a danger to judicial work but as another weapon for humiliating the target. The foreseeable effect is larger than one judge: officials learn that even limited resistance may bring presidential denunciation and threats from unidentified actors, while prior rulings favorable to the administration offer no protection.

The loyalty state beneath the courtroom drama

This story is not fundamentally about an ungrateful politician attacking a judge who helped him. It is about an executive conception of power in which institutions are legitimate only while they comply. Judges are recast as partisan enemies when they impose friction; adverse facts are replaced by insults; and legal victories are accepted without accepting the authority of the court that delivered them.

The systemic failure lies in the combination: concentrated executive power, procedural escape routes, remedies too weak to reverse unlawful conduct, and personal attacks that raise the cost of oversight. The administration can prevail in court, evade a ruling, or violate a requirement without reversal—and still present itself as the victim of the official tasked with reviewing its actions.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump attacks judge who keeps handing him wins
