item.title: The real reason Trump keeps defending one of history's most infamous scandals
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet asks why President Donald Trump keeps defending Richard Nixon and recasting Watergate as persecution by a “deep state.” But the article never establishes Trump’s actual reason. Its interview with historian Luke Nichter offers context and analogy, not evidence of Trump’s motives.

Nichter rejects the idea that Watergate was merely a liberal coup. Nixon had powerful enemies, including Republicans on his right, but he also made himself vulnerable. Five men tied to Nixon’s reelection operation were arrested after breaking into Democratic National Committee headquarters, and Nixon ultimately lacked the partisan protection later presidents cultivated during impeachment crises.

The interview then shifts to Trump’s reported decline in support. Nichter argues that Iran, gas prices, inflation and corruption may have worsened it, but says the larger cause is the familiar erosion of power during presidential second terms: Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028, so Republicans are already preparing for a post-Trump political order.

The headline promises more than the reporting proves

The supposed “real reason” is never demonstrated. AlterNet begins with Trump’s identification with Nixon, then asks a historian to interpret Nixon’s enemies, Watergate and second-term decline. It supplies no Trump statement explaining why he defends the scandal and no evidence tracing that defense to a particular strategy.

The most supportable inference is political utility. The Nixon-as-victim narrative turns misconduct into persecution and institutions of accountability into partisan attackers. That is useful to any president seeking to make loyalty, rather than evidence, the test of legitimacy. But usefulness is not proof of motive, and the article should not market interpretation as revelation.

Power was in the White House

Watergate was not fundamentally a story about an embattled politician besieged by cultural elites. It involved men connected to the president’s reelection operation breaking into the opposition party’s headquarters. Nixon was president. His political organization possessed money, access and executive power; the DNC was the target.

Nichter is right that Nixon accumulated enemies and that some Republicans wanted him gone. Those facts may help explain how his coalition collapsed. They do not redistribute responsibility for the conduct that created the crisis. Hostility toward a powerful official is not evidence that accountability for his administration was persecution.

Partisan protection is the institutional lesson

The interview’s sharpest point is that later presidents understood something Nixon did not: survival in an impeachment crisis depends on controlling Senate votes. That is not a defense of innocence. It is a description of power.

When legislators treat oversight as a party-containment problem, constitutional accountability becomes arithmetic. The decisive question shifts from what occurred to whether enough senators fear their own voters, donors or party apparatus more than they fear enabling presidential abuse. Nixon’s failure to retain Republican protection made removal plausible. Later presidents’ stronger partisan defenses made comparable political jeopardy harder to sustain.

Decline is not accountability

Nichter’s account of second-term decay also exposes a dangerous substitution. A president losing relevance because he cannot run again is not the same as institutions restraining him. Supporters drifting toward the next candidate may weaken a leader’s command over the party, but electoral attention is not oversight, adjudication or removal.

Nor do falling approval numbers answer the specific allegations AlterNet’s interviewer lists. The article attributes to Nichter the view that Iran, prices, inflation and corruption worsened Trump’s decline while his lame-duck status mattered more. That may explain political disengagement. It does not determine the truth or consequence of any alleged abuse.

Scandal becomes persecution when parties abandon judgment

The larger pattern is not that history mechanically repeats itself. It is that partisan institutions learn. Watergate taught political operators that presidential misconduct becomes survivable when a party can keep its coalition disciplined and persuade supporters that investigation itself is the offense.

That is why rehabilitating Nixon has contemporary value even when the evidence does not reveal Trump’s private reason for doing it. The story converts an abuse-of-power scandal into a grievance myth, shifts attention from those who wielded state power to those who challenged it, and recasts institutional restraint as sabotage. The central political struggle is no longer over what officials did. It is over whether their followers can be trained to regard consequences as illegitimate.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The real reason Trump keeps defending one of history’s most infamous scandals

item.title: Trump raises eyebrows with 'Hail Mary' pass to save Collins' hide
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Wall Street Journal reporting, says the Trump administration was expected to remove 50 percent tariffs from certain Canadian agricultural and forestry products after Senator Susan Collins requested relief for Maine industries and consumers. The proclamation could have arrived as early as that Friday, but its timing and scope remained unsettled; officials were reportedly considering higher levies on other Canadian goods to offset the reductions.

The proposed change came just over a week before Election Day, with Collins tied in polling against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, who had made the trade conflict central to his campaign. Trump had imposed the tariffs in late August on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods—about 5 percent of Canada’s exports to the United States—and Canada retaliated. The Journal’s reporting also suggested the adjustment could aid Republican candidates in Michigan and New Hampshire.

The power sits in the White House

Collins could request relief. She could criticize the tariffs and advertise previous exemptions. She could not remove them. Trump imposed the levies, escalated the dispute and retained the authority his administration claimed to revise them.

That distinction matters because the reported intervention was not an act of economic weather correction. It was the White House considering relief from damage produced by its own policy, with politically vulnerable Republicans positioned to claim the rescue.

Collins wants credit without ownership

Collins broke with Trump only after the tariffs became a liability in a state deeply dependent on Canadian trade. She had already taken campaign credit when the administration exempted road salt and cement. Jackson’s reply—that Mainers “can’t eat road salt”—cut through the performance: a narrow exemption does not erase the broader costs of the policy.

Collins had agency as a senator and as a member of Trump’s party, but the article establishes only that she requested relief, not that she designed or imposed the tariffs. Her political maneuver was simpler: separate herself from the harm while presenting access to its author as evidence of effectiveness.

Selective relief is political leverage

The timing described by the Journal makes the institutional purpose difficult to ignore. The administration was reportedly preparing targeted tariff reductions as Collins faced a tied race, while other Republican candidates who had supported or tolerated Trump’s policy scrambled to distance themselves from it.

That does not prove every economic consideration was pretextual. But the reported electoral context shows how arbitrary trade power can become campaign machinery. The executive creates broad disruption, then distributes exceptions where Republican candidates need protection. If tariffs on some goods fall while levies on others rise, the policy does not necessarily become less punitive; the burden merely moves to different industries and consumers.

The framing understates the choice

Calling the move a “Hail Mary” captures Collins’s electoral desperation but risks making the episode sound like clever campaign improvisation. The more important story is the concentration of power that made such improvisation possible.

Trump’s administration invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, an authority the Journal described as never previously used, to impose the 50 percent tariffs. A New Jersey food importer challenged that action as exceeding presidential authority. The reporting does not establish how that lawsuit would be resolved, but it identifies the underlying institutional conflict: the administration claimed sweeping power to impose economic penalties, then contemplated tailoring relief around electoral pressure.

Manufactured harm, rationed relief

This episode reveals a durable political pattern: officials turn preventable damage into a demonstration of patronage. Industries absorb the costs, consumers become angry, endangered allies petition the leader, and partial relief is marketed as constituent service.

The consequence is larger than one Maine Senate contest. When economic rules can be tightened, loosened or shifted according to the governing party’s electoral needs, policy stops functioning as a stable public framework. It becomes leverage—imposed broadly from the center, then selectively withdrawn for those with the right political access.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump raises eyebrows with ‘Hail Mary’ pass to save Collins’ hide

item.title: Trump’s wild 250-foot statue plan 'doesn't pass the laugh test': historian
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration is arguing a 1925 law already authorizes a proposed 250-foot arch near the Potomac River, despite more recent language requiring congressional approval for new monuments in Washington. The administration says the project fulfills an unrealized Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission plan for two columns at the bridge’s western end.

David Maloney, the District of Columbia’s state historic preservation officer, rejected that historical rationale during a recorded National Park Service meeting in September, saying it “doesn’t pass the laugh test.” The reported design includes gilded eagles, a winged figure, an observation deck and a plaza near Arlington National Cemetery. Veteran groups, preservationists and local organizations oppose the proposed scale, location or both.

The reporting does not establish that the monument has received every approval needed for construction. It instead describes an unresolved dispute over whether the 1925 authorization is sufficient and whether Congress must act again.

Power disguised as interpretation

This is not chiefly an argument among historians. It is a struggle over whether the executive branch can convert an abandoned concept from the 1920s into permission for a radically different project a century later.

Congress holds the legislative power at issue. The administration is trying to narrow Congress’s present role by claiming Congress already acted in 1925. That interpretation would let the project’s sponsors treat modern approval as an unnecessary repetition rather than a current safeguard.

A monument to executive appetite

The mismatch is the story. The old commission contemplated two tall, narrow columns. The reported proposal is a 250-foot arch with gilded ornaments, an observation deck and an extensive surrounding development. Calling the latter a completion of the former does not settle the legal question; it launders a new political choice through an obsolete design history.

Trump and his allies are not passive beneficiaries of bureaucratic confusion. They are advancing the project and its legal justification. Mark Paoletta’s declaration that the existing traffic circle is a “disgrace” recasts resistance to the administration’s preferred monument as disrespect for veterans. That is rhetoric, not evidence that the 1925 law authorized this particular structure.

Veterans as political cover

The proposed site near Arlington National Cemetery gives the project borrowed solemnity. It also makes opposition easier to caricature. Paoletta invokes veterans to defend the monument even though AlterNet reports that veteran groups are among those opposing its location or scale.

That is a familiar misdirection: attach executive ambition to a revered constituency, then imply that objections insult the constituency rather than challenge the ambition. The weaker actors here—local advocates, preservation officials and veterans’ organizations—can object, but the administration controls the machinery pushing the proposal and the interpretation used to justify it.

The framing falls short

AlterNet presents the controversy as a “fundamental constitutional question,” but the supplied reporting does not provide enough statutory language or legal analysis to resolve that question. It establishes the administration’s argument, the critics’ rejection and the existence of more recent approval language. It does not establish which interpretation would prevail.

The “laugh test” remark is vivid, but ridicule cannot substitute for institutional scrutiny. The consequential issue is whether an administration may stretch a century-old authorization until it covers a contemporary project built around presidential grandeur.

The systemic error

Personalist politics does not always arrive through an openly declared seizure of power. Sometimes it advances through tendentious legal readings, patriotic branding and a bureaucracy asked to treat a leader’s vanity as inherited national purpose.

The larger pattern is the attempted conversion of public space into executive self-mythology. The arch’s extravagance makes that ambition unusually visible. The deeper danger lies in the method: declare an old law sufficient, portray fresh consent as needless and use national symbols to discipline opposition. The monument remains disputed, but the governing impulse behind it is already clear.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s wild 250-foot statue plan ‘doesn’t pass the laugh test’: historian

item.title: Military boards have been quietly defying Trump’s orders
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that military review boards in the Army, Navy, and Marine Corps have allowed some transgender service members to remain despite a Trump administration policy intended to remove them. Citing New York Times reporting, AlterNet says nine of 12 service members brought before the boards were retained. The Air Force, by contrast, was reportedly discharging transgender personnel more quickly.

The proceedings were closed, spouses were excluded, and the Pentagon would not disclose the total number of hearings or removals. One Marine staff sergeant won his case in August; his lawyer said early proceedings had produced dismissals before outcomes began to shift. Another service member, discharged after 18 years, was told that her commendable record was not the issue before the panel.

AlterNet describes these decisions as quiet defiance. But the reporting does not establish that board members disobeyed a specific lawful order. It shows that some panels, operating within an administrative process created by the Pentagon, declined to produce the result the administration apparently expected.

Power wrote the policy

The decisive institutional power belongs to President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon. The administration set the exclusionary policy, defined transgender troops as a burden, and created review proceedings whose instructions reportedly made removal the expected outcome.

Individual board members possess narrower authority: they can decide cases placed before them. Their retention votes matter enormously to the people involved, but they do not reverse the policy, open the secret proceedings, restore those already forced out, or protect future service members. Calling their choices “defiance” risks mistaking limited discretion for control.

The process was built to deliver removals

According to the reporting, the Pentagon established boards with parameters that heavily favored expulsion. Former Air Force lawyer Rachel VanLandingham characterized the process as an attempt to obtain a predetermined rubber stamp. The nine retention decisions suggest that some panel members refused to supply it.

That resistance exposes the policy’s weakness on its own terms. The administration invoked fitness and military effectiveness, yet the policy drove out doctors, lawyers, pilots, and nuclear technicians. Those were not abstract culture-war symbols. They were trained personnel whose qualifications had already been demonstrated through service.

Secrecy protects the institution

Closed hearings and undisclosed totals prevent the public from measuring the policy’s full operation. The Pentagon’s refusal to say how many boards convened or how many troops were removed leaves scattered victories more visible than the system-wide damage.

That asymmetry matters. A successful appeal can be presented as evidence that the process works, while discharged personnel, delayed careers, and months of uncertainty remain difficult to count. Secrecy does not prove illicit intent, but it plainly shields decision-makers from comprehensive scrutiny.

“Defiance” is the wrong center of gravity

AlterNet’s framing gives the most dramatic role to lower-level military panels. The more consequential act came from above: political leaders imposed a category-wide presumption against roughly 4,250 transgender troops, about 0.1 percent of the military, then required individuals to fight for careers they had already earned.

The reported board decisions are significant, but they are not the policy. Nor does the evidence show a coordinated revolt across the armed forces. The sharply different Air Force outcomes demonstrate that institutional implementation remains uneven—and that a service member’s future may depend less on performance than on which branch administers the exclusion.

Bureaucratic resistance cannot substitute for accountability

This episode reveals a recurring structure of discriminatory government: senior officials establish the harm, opaque machinery distributes it, and isolated acts of decency by subordinate officials are celebrated as resistance. The people targeted still absorb the cost through discharge, delay, legal expense, lost expertise, and prolonged uncertainty.

A system should not require anonymous board members to quietly frustrate its leaders before qualified people receive individualized treatment. The reported retention votes show that some officials retained agency. The larger fact is that presidential and Pentagon power forced them to use it against a process designed to turn political exclusion into routine administration.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Military boards have been quietly defying Trump’s orders

item.title: Pope Leo is using a Cold War playbook to fight MAGA
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that writer Christopher Hale casts Pope Leo XIV’s defense of immigrants as a modern version of Pope John Paul II’s resistance to communist rule. Hale argues that Leo, the first American pope, is using the papacy’s moral authority to oppose President Donald Trump’s treatment of migrants and MAGA politics more broadly.

The contrast rests on specific public choices. In a June letter, Leo said defending life includes “welcoming, protecting and assisting immigrants.” While Trump used a Mount Rushmore speech to allege a communist resurgence involving newcomers, Leo declined the symbolic value of appearing at America 250 events and instead visited migrants on Lampedusa. AlterNet also reports that the Pentagon invited Cardinal Christophe Pierre to discuss papal language some regarded as anti-Trump.

The power is not evenly divided

Leo possesses an influential pulpit, but Trump controls the executive branch and the coercive machinery behind immigration policy. The pope can define a moral conflict; the administration can determine who is targeted, detained or excluded.

That distinction matters because the “two leaders clash” frame can flatten the actual power structure. This is not merely a contest between rival messages. One side offers pastoral teaching and symbolic solidarity. The other commands institutions capable of converting political rhetoric into government action.

The red scare has a target

Trump’s warning about a communist menace “including from newcomers” does political work beyond condemning communism. It attaches ideological suspicion to immigrants as a category. The allegation supplies a grand enemy, then places people with far less power inside its silhouette.

Leo’s language breaks that maneuver apart by beginning with migrants as human beings rather than ideological instruments. His Lampedusa remarks invoked people “stripped of everything” and the obligation to approach them before imposing an intellectual or political scheme. That is precisely what scapegoating cannot tolerate: attention to the person hidden beneath the label.

A strained historical analogy

Hale’s Cold War comparison identifies a real continuity in papal rhetoric about human dignity, but AlterNet presents the analogy too cleanly. It says the Berlin Wall fell “a little over a year” after John Paul II’s 1979 visit to Poland, although the article supplies no chronology or evidence sufficient to support that compressed causal story.

Nor does the reporting establish that Leo is consciously deploying a coordinated “Cold War playbook.” What it establishes is a pattern of statements and symbolic decisions that Hale interprets as resistance. The distinction is important: forceful commentary does not require turning analogy into demonstrated strategy.

Access is the leverage

The administration reportedly wanted Leo at America 250 events. His decision to spend that time with migrants denied Trump the legitimizing image of an American pope participating in a presidential spectacle. That refusal mattered because political access is valuable only when it does not purchase silence.

The Pentagon appearance by Cardinal Pierre also shows the struggle moving inside state institutions, although AlterNet gives too little detail to establish who arranged it, what was said or what effect it had. Calling it a “lecture” and noting that some viewed the pope’s language as anti-Trump gestures toward conflict without fully reporting the event.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of vulnerable people into evidence for an invented national emergency. Powerful officials name a menace, associate it with outsiders and then present state aggression as public defense. The people carrying the accusation bear little of its cost; migrants bear nearly all of it.

Leo’s intervention cannot itself restrain executive power. It can, however, deny that power an uncontested moral vocabulary. The political significance lies there: an institution Trump sought as ceremonial validation instead supplied a public argument against treating suspicion as patriotism and cruelty as strength.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Pope Leo is using a Cold War playbook to fight MAGA

item.title: Psychologist reveals new signs of Trump’s manic 'neurological dysfunction’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist and body-language commentator John Garrison interpreted Donald Trump’s conduct at Wednesday rallies as evidence of possible neurological dysfunction. Garrison pointed to an abrupt vocalization, facial and arm movements, a brief interruption in speech, repetition, and apparent trouble recalling names.

Garrison suggested several possible explanations, including a focal aware seizure, but the report supplies no examination, diagnosis, medical records, or corroborating clinical assessment. It does document verbal errors: Trump apparently referred to “Lake America,” could not clearly name the lake he was discussing, and substituted the Pulitzer Prize for the Nobel Peace Prize. Garrison characterized Trump’s subsequent behavior as unusually uninhibited, grandiose, and “almost manic,” and predicted further deterioration.

The diagnosis outruns the evidence

The observable facts are limited: Trump made an unusual sound, moved oddly, hesitated, repeated himself, and confused prominent names. Those incidents can legitimately prompt questions about his fitness. They do not, by themselves, establish a neurological disorder, seizure, mania, or progressive decline.

Garrison repeatedly moves from describing behavior to assigning clinical significance without direct evaluation. Even his most specific explanation is presented as one possibility among several. Yet AlterNet’s headline compresses that uncertainty into a psychologist “revealing” new signs of dysfunction. Nothing was revealed in the medical sense. A commentator watched clips and offered an interpretation.

That distinction matters because weak evidence does not become stronger when attached to technical vocabulary. “Motor dysfunction,” “vocal dysfunction,” and “disinhibition” sound diagnostic, but the article provides no clinical basis for determining their cause.

The presidency is the power center

Trump holds the institutional power in this story. A president can direct the executive branch, shape foreign policy, command the military, appoint officials, and dominate the national agenda. Any credible evidence that a president cannot reliably perform those duties deserves serious scrutiny.

But the report does not examine how presidential capacity is actually monitored. It identifies no assessment by a treating physician, no formal review, no disclosure decision by White House officials, and no action by officials empowered to respond to incapacity. The people around a president control access, information, scheduling, and much of the public account of his health. They are largely absent here.

That omission leaves a structural question unanswered: not whether a remote commentator can label a video clip, but whether institutions responsible for evaluating presidential fitness are providing reliable evidence to the public.

Spectacle replaces accountability

The article’s framing invites readers to treat Trump’s strangest moments as a diagnostic puzzle. That is a form of misdirection. Trump’s confusion over names and his boasts about power are politically relevant without requiring a speculative neurological explanation.

When coverage medicalizes public conduct, it can blur agency. False statements, reckless decisions, authoritarian rhetoric, and abuses of office must be assessed as actions by a powerful political actor unless evidence establishes that incapacity caused them. An unsupported diagnosis can inadvertently turn responsibility into pathology: the problem becomes what may be happening inside Trump’s brain rather than what he does with presidential authority.

It also gives defenders an easy escape. They can dismiss the amateur diagnosis and pretend that the documented behavior—and the legitimate question of fitness—disappears with it.

Evidence must match the stakes

The larger pattern is a degraded system of presidential accountability. Official health disclosures are often managed political products, while partisan media fill the resulting vacuum with certainty they have not earned. One side minimizes visible problems; the other converts clips into diagnoses. Neither practice supplies the public with a trustworthy mechanism for judging capacity.

A president’s health is not gossip because presidential power is not symbolic. But the answer to institutional opacity is evidence, not remote clinical theater. AlterNet had material for a defensible story about unusual public behavior and unanswered questions. By presenting speculation as revelation, it weakened the very scrutiny that concentrated power requires.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist reveals new signs of Trump’s manic ‘neurological dysfunction’

item.title: GOP pollster tears apart how low the 'toxic' GOP has sunk
item.description:
What happened

Former Republican consultant and pollster Frank Luntz condemned a Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad targeting Ohio gubernatorial rival Amy Acton, calling it a “horrible example” of how toxic American politics has become. AlterNet reports that critics accused the ad of exploiting Acton’s estrangement from her mother without explaining that authorities had removed Acton from the home after sexual abuse by her mother’s then-husband.

Luntz argued on X that modern electioneering increasingly misleads and destroys rather than informs. He predicted the ad would influence voters but said it crossed a line beyond the ordinary ugliness he analyzes professionally. AlterNet also reports that President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance did not oppose the ad.

The story does not establish the ad’s effect on voters, provide a response from Ramaswamy or detail Trump’s and Vance’s reasoning. It establishes Luntz’s denunciation, the criticism surrounding the ad and the political permission structure in which it circulated.

Power chose the weapon

Ramaswamy’s campaign held the operative power here. It selected the material, shaped the accusation and placed it before voters. Acton’s childhood trauma was not an autonomous campaign issue that simply appeared; political professionals converted it into electoral ammunition.

That distinction matters because coverage of degrading politics often dissolves responsibility into phrases such as “backlash,” “drama” and “how low we have sunk.” Politics did not lower itself. A campaign made a decision, and powerful Republican figures reportedly declined to oppose it.

The victim becomes the suspect

According to the account presented by AlterNet, the ad’s force depended on stripping an estranged family relationship of its defining context. If authorities removed Acton from her mother’s care after abuse by her mother’s then-husband, presenting the estrangement as evidence against Acton redirects scrutiny from the reported abuse toward the child who endured it.

That is more than an “ugly tone.” It is scapegoating through omission: take evidence of a person’s vulnerability, sever it from the circumstances that explain it and repackage the resulting distortion as a character indictment. The weaker actor is forced to answer for what was done to her while the campaign responsible for the attack sets the terms of discussion.

A belated diagnosis

Luntz’s objection is notable because he spent years inside the profession he now condemns. His assessment is also narrower than the problem he describes. Saying campaign tools are used to deceive identifies the mechanism, but lamenting the condition of “our election process” risks turning accountable choices into a system-wide fog.

Jessica Riedl’s claim that voters should assume campaign portrayals are false captures the collapse of trust, but her “90%” figure is presented as commentary, not documented evidence. The stronger point requires no invented statistic: when campaigns face few penalties for distortion, deception becomes a rational tactic.

Permission is political power

Silence from dominant figures is not equivalent to authorship, and the reporting does not establish that Trump or Vance created the ad. But leaders possess more options than spectators. They can condemn an attack, deny it legitimacy or signal that it remains acceptable within the coalition.

The absence of opposition therefore matters as an exercise of institutional power, even if the article leaves the precise reasons unstated. Standards inside political parties are enforced by people with the authority to impose costs. When they decline to do so, outrage from consultants and commentators arrives after the incentive structure has already delivered its verdict.

Cruelty with a campaign budget

The larger pattern is not merely that politics has become rude. It is that organized power can mine personal trauma, erase the facts that make it intelligible and force the target to relive it as campaign rebuttal. The ensuing controversy then centers on whether the tactic was tasteful rather than on who financed, approved and tolerated it.

Luntz predicts the ad will be remembered as a marker of political toxicity. Its more durable lesson is about incentives: if exploitation works and party leaders impose no cost, moral condemnation becomes commentary on the machinery rather than resistance to it. The degradation is systemic because the people with power can choose it, benefit from it and leave everyone else debating the tone.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP pollster tears apart how low the ‘toxic’ GOP has sunk

item.title: Ex-Trump Air Force chaplain issues eye-popping warning on 'religious tyranny’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Air Force Reserve chaplain candidate Leigh Larson warned that the Trump administration’s reduction of Defense Department faith codes amounts to “religious tyranny.” She argues that narrowing more than 200 classifications to 31 allows the government to blur religious differences and weaken the administrative recognition needed for accommodations, spiritual care, holy-day guidance and burial practices.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth oversaw the consolidation earlier this year. Christian denominations with substantial theological differences were grouped together, while Wiccan, Unitarian Universalist and Humanist identities were placed under “Other Religions,” and atheists under no religion. Service members may still state their faith on dog tags, but Larson says the paperwork used to advocate for their religious needs is now less specific.

The government’s classifications also proved politically malleable. After the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints initially received a category separate from “Christian,” Republican Senator Mike Lee publicly demanded that Hegseth reverse the decision. The Pentagon changed the list the next day.

The Pentagon holds the power

The decisive actor is not an abstract bureaucracy. Hegseth’s Defense Department controls the classification system, and commanders rely on that system when administering religious accommodations and chaplain services. The department chose to compress the categories; affected service members did not choose to become administratively interchangeable.

A faith code is not a theological verdict by itself. But when the institution controlling military life uses crude religious categories to route care and evaluate accommodation requests, its taxonomy has material consequences. The state may call the exercise recordkeeping, yet it is still deciding which distinctions remain visible to the machinery of government.

Political pressure exposed the fiction

Lee’s intervention punctured any claim that the new categories were merely neutral housekeeping. He objected to the treatment of Latter-day Saints, ordered the Pentagon in public language to “get rid of it,” and obtained a revision the following day.

The reporting does not establish who internally authorized that reversal or why officials acted so quickly. It does establish unequal responsiveness: a politically connected senator could force reconsideration of one classification, while dozens of other identities remained compressed. That is discretionary power responding to influence, not a self-executing administrative principle.

“Consolidation” conceals the choice

Calling the change consolidation shifts attention from the officials who imposed it to the supposed untidiness of religious diversity. More than 200 categories did not disappear through natural decay. The Defense Department reduced them to 31.

Larson’s strongest point is therefore institutional, not rhetorical. A government capable of recognizing distinctions is also capable of withdrawing that recognition by memo. The immediate issue is narrower paperwork, not a formal ban on belief. But narrowing the official channels through which service members seek accommodations makes their needs easier to overlook and harder to document.

Recognition follows access to power

The danger revealed here is selective legibility. Religious identity becomes visible when an influential politician insists upon it and collapses into “other” when nobody with comparable leverage intervenes.

Larson proposes congressional oversight through the National Defense Authorization Act, accurate auditing of beliefs across the force and policies reflecting actual service-member needs. Those remedies target the proper institution: the government that created the categories and can change them, rather than the minorities forced to navigate whatever labels remain.

Bureaucracy is where hierarchy becomes policy

This episode shows how religious preference can enter government without an explicit declaration of an official faith. It can arrive through classification, administrative simplification and selective correction—procedures that appear technical while determining whose differences receive institutional respect.

The larger pattern is not confusion. It is concentrated discretion with uneven accountability. When officials erase distinctions wholesale but restore one after pressure from a powerful ally, the lesson is blunt: under such a system, religious recognition depends less on freedom of conscience than on proximity to political power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Ex-Trump Air Force chaplain issues eye-popping warning on ‘religious tyranny’

item.title: Trump's own spy chief just secretly delivered a warning to Putin :report
item.description:
What happened

According to AlterNet’s account of The Atlantic’s reporting, CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow in August 2026 and warned Russian security officials that neither Russia nor Ukraine was winning the war. He reportedly said Russia had made no meaningful gains while Ukraine had been unable to expel Russian forces from occupied territory. Ratcliffe did not meet Vladimir Putin; Russian intelligence officials documented the message for him through a private back channel.

U.S. officials reportedly hoped the assessment would persuade Putin to negotiate, believing his advisers were misleading him. Ratcliffe later discussed the trip with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a September refueling stop in Ireland.

The report also describes a contradiction inside the Trump administration. The CIA was reportedly helping Ukraine identify Russian energy targets even as Trump condemned Ukraine’s refinery strikes, blamed Zelensky for obstructing peace, and called him harder to deal with than Putin. Ukraine’s defenses later faced Starlink restrictions that disrupted defensive-drone operations, though the article does not establish who imposed those restrictions or why.

Power is not evenly distributed

Putin holds the power to stop Russia’s war. Trump controls the public posture of the United States and commands an administration reportedly supplying Ukraine with targeting intelligence. Zelensky governs the country defending itself from Russian occupation. Treating these three men as comparably positioned “parties” obscures the basic structure of the conflict.

Ratcliffe’s reported mission recognized that structure only indirectly. Washington did not send him to Kyiv to persuade Ukraine that occupation was tolerable. It sent him to Moscow because the Kremlin controls the Russian forces holding Ukrainian territory and therefore controls the central decision prolonging the war.

The contradiction belongs to Trump

Trump’s rhetoric, as reported, conflicts with his own intelligence chief’s assessment. Ratcliffe reportedly told Russian officials that Moscow had achieved no meaningful gains. Trump publicly targeted Zelensky as the obstacle, denounced Ukrainian attacks on the infrastructure supporting Russia’s war economy, and portrayed Putin as the easier partner.

That is not merely a messaging inconsistency. Presidential statements shape diplomatic leverage. When Trump publicly pressures the invaded government while his CIA privately urges the invading government to recognize its failure, he weakens the warning Ratcliffe was sent to deliver.

The administration’s conduct is even more incoherent if The Atlantic’s account is accurate: U.S. intelligence was helping Ukraine identify Russian energy targets while Trump attacked Ukraine for striking them. A government can revise its strategy. What it cannot honestly do is facilitate a campaign in private and then publicly scold the recipient for carrying it out.

The convenient myth of a misinformed Putin

The claim that Putin is being misled by advisers deserves scrutiny. The reporting attributes that belief to U.S. officials but supplies no evidence establishing what Putin knows. It may explain why Washington chose an intelligence channel; it does not absolve the Russian president of responsibility for decisions made by the state he controls.

Framing the problem as bad information reaching the Kremlin risks converting agency into confusion. Putin is not a passive consumer of battlefield briefings. He presides over the government conducting the war. Even if subordinates distort facts, the system that rewards distortion is his system, and the military policy sustained through it remains Russia’s policy.

Pressure aimed at the weaker party

AlterNet reports that Ukrainian attacks substantially reduced Russian refinery throughput and fuel production, citing International Energy Agency analysis. Those attacks imposed costs on the state occupying Ukrainian territory. Trump nevertheless condemned them and blamed them for higher global fuel prices, while the article says most experts attributed the increase primarily to the Iran war.

The political effect of that framing is clear regardless of motive: Russian aggression becomes background scenery, while Ukrainian resistance becomes the disruptive act requiring discipline. Russia retains occupied territory; Ukraine is instructed to choose less effective targets. That is not neutral peacemaking. It shifts pressure from the actor able to end the invasion to the actor being asked to endure it more quietly.

A policy built from incompatible realities

This episode reveals an administration operating with two accounts of the same war. In private, its intelligence chief reportedly told Moscow that Russian forces had failed to achieve meaningful gains. In public, its president attacked Ukraine’s leadership and one of its more consequential pressure campaigns.

The larger pattern is institutional power without coherent accountability. Intelligence agencies can deliver unwelcome facts and quietly support battlefield operations, but the president determines which actor receives public blame and which costs become politically unacceptable. When those choices consistently burden the weaker party, the contradiction itself has consequences: Moscow hears that Washington understands Russia’s failure, but may lack the resolve to make that failure matter.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s own spy chief just secretly delivered a warning to Putin :report

item.title: Lifelong southern Republican unleashes stunning defection from the GOP
item.description:
What happened

South Carolina real estate developer Warren Norman, a lifelong Republican, said he was leaning toward voting for Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews rather than Donald Trump-backed Republican Darline Graham. AlterNet reports that Norman objected to Graham’s campaign tactics, allegiance to Trump and perceived unwillingness to confront corruption.

Norman said millions were being spent on attacks designed to frighten voters while offering little explanation of what Graham would do for South Carolina. Although he still supported several Republicans and disagreed with Andrews on many issues, he said their shared interest in fighting corruption could lead him to cast his first vote for a Democrat in a partisan election.

The report does not establish that Norman had formally changed parties, despite presenting his decision as a “defection.” It describes one Republican voter rejecting one Republican candidate.

A vote is not a defection

AlterNet inflates a dissenting ballot into a partisan rupture. Norman explicitly still called himself a conservative, endorsed the Republican platform and planned to support other GOP candidates. His refusal to vote for Graham is politically notable precisely because it is limited: he is withholding support without abandoning his political identity.

Calling that a “stunning defection” converts a specific judgment into electoral spectacle. The stronger story is that party loyalty has limits even for a voter with deep Republican ties—and that Norman believed Graham had crossed his.

Power belongs to the candidate and her patrons

Norman can cast one vote and use whatever public standing he has as a developer and member of a political family. Graham, by contrast, is the party nominee described as carrying Trump’s endorsement and benefiting from millions of dollars in campaign spending. Those are not equivalent forms of agency.

According to Norman, Graham and the interests financing her campaign chose fear-heavy attacks over a substantive account of how she would govern. His central question was whether she could resist the people funding and promoting her. That is the institutional issue: not whether one Republican feels alienated, but whether a prospective senator would exercise independent judgment after powerful patrons helped place her on the ballot.

The evidence has limits

Norman accused the campaign of fear tactics, falsehoods and insufficient attention to policy. AlterNet reports those claims but supplies no examples of the advertisements, identifies no specific false statement and does not name the funders behind the spending. His account is evidence of his reasoning, not proof of every allegation embedded in it.

The outlet weakens its own case further by declaring Trump “synonymous with corruption” as though an editorial characterization were an established fact. It also invokes a Fox News poll without providing its date, wording, sample or scope. Scathing language cannot substitute for documentation.

Fear is a governing strategy

Norman’s sharper observation is that campaign fear does not reduce insurance costs, address affordability or eliminate corruption. Attack advertising can make an opponent culturally menacing while allowing the favored candidate to remain programmatically vague. The public is instructed whom to dread, not told who will exercise power, for whose benefit or under what constraints.

That strategy is useful to candidates backed by an established partisan apparatus. It turns scrutiny away from donors, endorsements and prospective conduct in office, then relocates politics into the emotional reactions of voters. The powerful choose the message; the audience is blamed for being polarized by it.

The systemic error

This story is not primarily about a heroic partisan conversion. It is about the cost of treating party affiliation as a substitute for oversight. Norman’s break matters because he applied a test that partisan politics routinely suppresses: whether a candidate will resist the coalition that financed and elevated her.

But AlterNet partially buries that question beneath click-driven drama and unsupported certainty. The systemic pattern runs through both the campaign and its coverage: political institutions obscure accountability with fear, while media outlets obscure power with personality. One voter’s refusal is worth reporting. The machinery that made refusal necessary is the real subject.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Lifelong southern Republican unleashes stunning defection from the GOP

item.title: Trump gets chilling prison warning after president’s coup backfired
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Nation analysis by Paul Loeb and South Korean activist Jungmin Choi warned that any attempt by President Donald Trump or his administration to overturn or obstruct the 2026 midterm results could provoke resistance and eventually carry severe legal consequences. The “prison warning” was the authors’ comparison to former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol—not a reported charge, prosecution, or sentence facing Trump.

According to AlterNet, Yoon declared martial law on December 3, 2024, banned political activity and deployed troops to the National Assembly. Lawmakers pushed past military forces and overturned the decree while protests rapidly expanded. Yoon was impeached, removed from office and, the outlet reports, sentenced to life imprisonment for insurrection in February 2026; he has appealed.

Loeb and Choi argue that protecting an election requires more than voting. They call for local protection of polling and counting sites, resistance to illegal military orders, litigation and immediate mass nonviolent protest if an administration obstructs the electoral process.

The warning is conditional

The headline manufactures immediacy that the underlying account does not support. Trump did not “receive” a judicial warning, and AlterNet reports no pending prison sentence tied to the midterms. Two writers drew a cautionary comparison and urged Americans to prepare for a hypothetical attempt at election interference.

That distinction matters. A dramatic headline can turn political analysis into the appearance of breaking legal news. It also reverses the real sequence of accountability: Yoon was not imprisoned because critics issued a warning. According to the account, state institutions prosecuted him after an overt deployment of armed force against the legislature, a conviction and a sentence that remain under appeal.

Power sits in the executive

The relevant power is not evenly distributed among protesters, poll workers and the president. Citizens can demonstrate, monitor elections and pressure institutions. A president commands the executive branch and exercises influence over federal law enforcement, election-related litigation and the military chain of command.

That imbalance is why Loeb and Choi emphasize refusal of illegal orders. An authoritarian project does not advance through one person’s will alone. It requires officials, commanders, lawyers and political allies to convert an unlawful objective into operational decisions. The decisive question is not merely whether the public recognizes misconduct, but whether people holding institutional authority carry it out, resist it or hide behind procedure.

Resistance cannot replace institutions

The South Korean comparison highlights public agency, but romanticizing protest would miss the machinery that made resistance effective. Demonstrators surrounded the National Assembly, yet lawmakers still had to enter, vote and exercise constitutional power. Impeachment, removal, prosecution and sentencing required institutions to act after the immediate crisis.

The same applies to an American election dispute. Local officials certify results. Courts adjudicate claims. Police protect—or fail to protect—polling and counting sites. Military personnel obey or refuse orders. Mass protest can raise the cost of abuse, but it cannot substitute for officials performing duties that only their offices empower them to perform.

The pardon problem

AlterNet closes by linking fears about future election interference to the January 6 attack and Trump’s subsequent pardons of participants. That is the sharper political fact in the story because clemency is an exercised presidential power, not a speculative future scenario.

Pardons can alter incentives even when they do not prove what anyone will do next. If political allies see participation in anti-democratic violence followed by presidential clemency, accountability becomes less predictable and loyalty to a leader can appear safer. The consequence is institutional: deterrence weakens while the burden shifts toward officials and citizens who may have to confront the next abuse in real time.

Accountability is a chain

The larger pattern is staged consolidation of power. Election subversion does not begin and end with discarded ballots or soldiers outside a legislature. It develops through escalating demands, permissive legal theories, compliant subordinates and institutions waiting for someone else to intervene.

AlterNet’s sensational framing blurs that lesson by selling a hypothetical prison fate for one powerful man. The more useful conclusion is less cinematic: consequences become possible only when lawmakers, judges, civil servants, commanders and local authorities use the power they already possess. Public resistance can force the issue into view. Institutional actors still decide whether the law constrains executive power or merely records its victory.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump gets chilling prison warning after president’s coup backfired

item.title: Trump's latest NC factory announcement completely backfires
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced a North Carolina manufacturing plant tied to Sibelco, but the company did not confirm the project. As AlterNet reported, citing The News & Observer, Sibelco said only that it knew of public comments about a “potential project” and was awaiting official communication from the federal government.

The proposed plant was presented as support for western North Carolina’s high-purity quartz industry, which The News & Observer said supplies 70% to 90% of the global market for a material used in semiconductors and solar panels. The reporting provides no confirmed project details, groundbreaking date, investment figure, or employment estimate.

AlterNet calls the announcement a political setback, but does not document a measurable backlash or establish that the project is dead. What it does establish is narrower and still damaging: federal officials promoted a factory before the company identified as its operator was prepared to verify it.

Power made the announcement

Trump and Lutnick held the institutional power here. They controlled the federal megaphone, attached presidential authority to the proposal and turned a potential private-sector project into a public claim of economic delivery.

Sibelco’s statement did not create the confusion. It exposed it. The company was left explaining that it lacked official communication while the president and commerce secretary were already claiming progress. Responsibility therefore belongs with the officials who announced more than the available confirmation supported.

A factory as campaign scenery

AlterNet places the announcement amid Republican electoral pressure and Trump’s effort to sell his record to voters. The article does not prove that electoral anxiety caused the premature announcement, so motive should not be declared as fact. But the political utility is obvious: a factory offers an easy image of jobs, industrial strength and presidential action.

That symbolism matters because the article also cites Fortune business editor Nick Lichtenberg’s account of a manufacturing sector moving in the opposite direction. According to figures quoted by AlterNet, manufacturing and construction recorded roughly 150,000 net job losses on an annual basis as of March, while manufacturing alone shed 108,000 jobs during Trump’s first year back in office. An unconfirmed plant cannot carry the weight of a claimed renaissance.

The misdirection is the “setback”

Calling this merely a setback softens the central failure. A setback is something that happens to an administration. This was an announcement the administration chose to make without public confirmation from the named company.

The headline’s claim that the announcement “completely backfires” also outruns the evidence presented. AlterNet documents contradiction, not complete political reversal. That exaggeration distracts from the stronger, supportable indictment: powerful officials used the credibility of the presidency to market an outcome that the company itself would describe only as potential.

Promises without an accounting

The same gap appears in the fiscal claims AlterNet includes. Trump campaigned on eliminating the national debt in one term without cutting Social Security or Medicare, invoking growth, cryptocurrency and tariffs. AlterNet cites Atlantic columnist David Frum’s estimates that Trump’s tax cuts would reduce revenue by $4.5 trillion over a decade, while food-stamp and Medicaid cuts would reduce spending by $1.1 trillion and budget plans would produce $3.4 trillion in direct costs, rising to $4.1 trillion with debt-service costs.

Those estimates do not independently prove what will happen, and they should not be confused with current totals. They do show the scale of the contradiction described by the article: expansive promises are advertised immediately, while costs, missing details and adverse results are pushed elsewhere in the frame.

Government by premature victory lap

The larger pattern is political power substituting announcements for completed outcomes. A president can command attention long before workers are hired, construction begins or a company commits publicly. By the time caveats arrive, the desired image has already circulated.

That is not confusion created by a cautious corporate spokesperson or skeptical coverage. It is an accountability failure produced at the top: officials claimed credit before establishing what existed. The systemic error is a political information structure that rewards the victory lap immediately and treats verification as an inconvenient correction afterward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s latest NC factory announcement completely backfires

item.title: Anderson Cooper struggles to keep straight face thru Trump obsession supercut
item.description:
What happened

Anderson Cooper kept his composure while presenting a CNN supercut of President Donald Trump repeatedly praising the looks and physiques of male politicians and athletes, AlterNet reported. The segment centered on Trump’s comments about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, whose body Trump said he had closely examined, before compiling similar remarks about Republican candidates, senators and sports figures.

Cooper aired the segment Wednesday night after Trump had spoken in North Carolina. He paired the clips with jokes about Trump’s insistence that admiring men is “not my thing” and noted a CNN poll placing Trump’s approval rating at 32 percent. AlterNet also reported Cooper’s claim that Trump’s preferred Senate candidate in North Carolina was trailing badly enough for the Senate Republican campaign arm to cancel most or all remaining spending there.

The article says Cooper “barely blinked”; it does not describe an actual loss of composure. Its headline turns a carefully written comedy segment into a tease about whether the anchor could keep a straight face.

The joke replaces the politics

Trump’s remarks are strange, repetitive and easy to mock. CNN chose the easiest frame available: assemble the innuendo, emphasize his disclaimers and let the contrast carry the segment.

That produces television, but little scrutiny. The politically significant fact is not that a president publicly appraises men’s bodies. It is that he is using presidential attention to promote favored Republican candidates while the party’s campaign apparatus decides where to deploy money and where to retreat. AlterNet mentions that machinery only in passing, then returns to locker-room jokes.

Power sits with the endorser

Trump holds the institutional power in this story. He has the presidency, a national platform and influence over Republican voters. The candidates he praises receive attention from the most powerful figure in their party; those deemed politically uncompetitive can lose support from the Senate GOP’s campaign arm.

Trump made the remarks. CNN’s editors chose to package them as a supercut, and Cooper delivered the ridicule. Those are distinct exercises of agency: one advances allies through presidential spectacle, while the other converts that spectacle into an entertainment segment.

The candidates are mostly props in both performances. Their appearance becomes shorthand for strength, desirability and political worth, while their records and the offices they seek largely disappear.

Identity bait obscures accountability

The segment’s running suggestion that Trump’s comments sound gay is a weak analytical frame. Cooper’s sexuality, which AlterNet explicitly notes, does not make that framing more politically revealing. Nor does Trump’s insistence that such admiration is “not my thing” explain what his rhetoric accomplishes.

The relevant pattern is Trump’s fixation on dominance-coded imagery: bodies, strength, “central casting” and the presentation of allies as physically imposing men. The supplied reporting establishes the repetition of that language. It does not establish Trump’s private motives, sexuality or mental condition.

AlterNet nevertheless gestures toward critics who say comparable remarks would have destroyed a Democratic politician and toward others who connect Trump’s profanity to mental deterioration. It supplies no evidence sufficient to establish either proposition. Those claims add insinuation without accountability.

The asymmetry is institutional

Trump “getting away with it” is not merely a story about hypocrisy. It reflects an ecosystem in which conduct that might once have triggered sustained questions becomes another clip, another joke and another fleeting outrage. Republican candidates still seek Trump’s favor. Party organizations still allocate resources around electoral calculations. Television still benefits from making his behavior compulsively watchable.

That arrangement does not require anyone to misunderstand what Trump is doing. It requires institutions to treat the spectacle as more valuable than the decisions surrounding it.

Spectacle is the governing shield

The broader pattern is not that Trump says things no other politician could say. It is that his political power repeatedly survives by turning scrutiny into content. Provocation attracts coverage; coverage concentrates on the provocation; the machinery of endorsement, money and party control recedes behind the punchline.

AlterNet’s framing participates in that displacement. The story offers an extended inventory of suggestive remarks, but only a glancing account of presidential influence and Republican campaign strategy. The result is abundant mockery with little pressure on power—the precise bargain political spectacle is built to secure.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Anderson Cooper struggles to keep straight face thru Trump obsession supercut

item.title: Haberman exposes psychology behind Trump’s radical power grab to Morning Joe
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that MSNBC host Joe Scarborough attributed Donald Trump’s conduct to a theory he had discussed with New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman: Trump repeatedly pushes institutional boundaries to discover how much Republicans, the press, and the courts will permit. That—not a clinical diagnosis—was the “psychology” offered behind the headline’s power grab.

Scarborough argued that Trump and Stephen Miller squandered political support by extending immigration enforcement beyond the violent offenders voters had been promised would be the priority. MSNBC’s Jonathan Lemire similarly described Trump as focused on immediate attention and advantage rather than durable political gains, citing Iran, deportations, and unsuccessful rally appearances.

The segment also dwelled on Trump’s unusual rally remarks about male politicians’ appearances. AlterNet provides the hosts’ assessments but no polling figures, immigration data, or direct response from Trump, Miller, or the White House.

Permission is the instrument

The strongest point in Haberman’s reported formulation is not psychological. It is institutional. A president can test limits only because other institutions possess limits they may enforce—or abandon.

Trump holds executive power. Miller, as described in the segment, helps shape its immigration use. Republican officials can resist or facilitate it. Courts can impose legal constraints. News organizations decide whether to scrutinize the exercise of power or convert it into spectacle. “What can he get away with?” is therefore also a question about what these actors choose to allow.

Policy is not a personality quirk

Scarborough’s account identifies a concrete political decision: an enforcement agenda sold as targeting “the worst of the worst” was, he said, applied to many people without criminal histories. If accurate, that is not merely evidence of bad electoral calculation. It is state power imposed on people who lack anything resembling the president’s institutional protection.

Reducing that choice to Trump’s appetite for boundary-testing risks turning responsibility into temperament. The relevant issue is not whether Trump behaves strangely. It is who authorized the policy, who implemented it, who was subjected to it, and which officials declined to stop it.

The spectacle redirects attention

The rally remarks are politically revealing only to a point. They may demonstrate indiscipline, but extended mockery of them gives television an easier subject than deportation authority, military action, or judicial constraint.

Scarborough’s jokes about Republicans performing Guys and Dolls reproduce the very diversion his analysis should expose. The president’s comments become entertainment; the machinery acting under presidential direction recedes. That framing directs attention toward embarrassment rather than accountability and toward cultural ridicule rather than material consequence.

Electoral damage is not the public damage

The segment measures failure largely through lost political capital, deteriorating issue ratings, and damage to Republican candidates. Those consequences matter, but they center the fortunes of powerful people.

The more consequential question is what happens before voters impose any penalty. People without criminal records can still become enforcement targets. Executive boundaries can shift. Officials can learn that temporary outrage carries little institutional cost. An unpopular abuse of power remains an abuse of power; falling poll numbers do not reverse it.

The system being tested

This story reveals a governing pattern built less on strategic brilliance than repeated permission. Trump pushes; allies enable; institutions hesitate; television fixates on the latest provocation. Commentators then describe the resulting damage as squandered opportunity, as though the central tragedy were inefficient politics.

The sharper conclusion is structural: personal appetite becomes public power when parties, courts, administrators, and media organizations repeatedly treat enforcement as optional. The test succeeds whenever those institutions discuss the boundary more energetically than they defend it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Haberman exposes psychology behind Trump’s radical power grab to Morning Joe

item.title: Trump’s Epstein scandal comes roaring back to haunt his GOP allies
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s handling of the Epstein files has become a campaign liability for Republican candidates. Citing Washington Post reporting based on AdImpact data, it says Democrats have spent $53 million on advertisements mentioning Epstein in competitive races, compared with $3 million spent by Republicans.

The Democratic ads target Republicans who initially opposed releasing the files or accepted contributions from people associated with Epstein. They include Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall. Hinson denied having links to Epstein after Democrats highlighted donations from Epstein-linked contributors; Marshall had called the disclosure effort a “political stunt.” Republicans have answered by emphasizing their eventual votes for release and accusing Democrats of exploiting the scandal.

AlterNet also reports that protesters appeared at Trump and JD Vance events and that Democratic groups displayed documents in battleground states. Trump resisted demands for disclosure for months before signing off on a release that Congress overwhelmingly approved. The article does not establish electoral results caused by the campaign, though it cites public protests and one former Trump supporter’s defection as evidence of political damage.

The power was inside the government

The decisive actors were not protesters, donors or campaign strategists. Trump controlled the executive branch’s response, while members of Congress possessed legislative power to force disclosure. The central institutional fact is that Trump resisted release and some Republican lawmakers initially supported that resistance, minimized the demand or delayed joining it.

Congress ultimately approved disclosure overwhelmingly. That sequence matters: lawmakers who later voted for release did so after sustained pressure made continued obstruction politically expensive. A final vote does not erase the earlier exercise of power. It records where officials landed once the cost of resistance changed.

Association is not responsibility

Some Democratic advertising described here leans on contributions from people associated with Epstein. That may be politically potent, but association is not evidence that Hinson, Husted or any other recipient participated in Epstein’s crimes. Les Wexner’s reported employment of Epstein as a financial manager is relevant context; it does not make every recipient of Wexner’s political money responsible for Epstein’s conduct.

The stronger case concerns official action. Marshall’s initial opposition to releasing the files—and his dismissal of the effort as a stunt—is a decision voters can assess directly. When campaigns substitute donor proximity for documented conduct, they risk weakening a legitimate accountability argument with guilt by association.

The defensive pivot

Republicans’ response illustrates a familiar form of misdirection: answer scrutiny of their own conduct by pointing toward Democrats. Sen. Dan Sullivan cited his vote for disclosure and accused opponent Mary Peltola of accepting money from Epstein associates. The counterattack may expose comparable questions about campaign financing, but it does not explain Trump’s months of resistance or why Republican officials initially opposed release.

Nor does invoking family, as Hinson reportedly did in her advertisement, resolve the institutional issue. Personal indignation can rebut an insinuation of private affiliation. It cannot answer a record of official votes, public statements or participation in a governing coalition that controlled disclosure.

Pressure changed the calculation

The available evidence does not prove that the advertising changed votes or will determine an election. Protesters appearing at campaign events show salience, not causation. One supporter abandoning Trump shows an individual rupture, not the size of a broader movement.

What the reporting does establish is that sustained pressure altered the political environment around disclosure. Trump’s own supporters joined demands for release, Congress approved it overwhelmingly, and Republican candidates began scrambling to separate themselves from resistance to it. The consequence is not merely reputational discomfort. Officials who expected partisan loyalty to contain the controversy were forced to account for choices they had treated as politically survivable.

Accountability after obstruction

The larger pattern is retrospective compliance: powerful officials resist scrutiny, relent only after the resistance becomes costly, and then present eventual acquiescence as proof of transparency. Campaign coverage can assist that laundering when it fixates on tactical spending, donor networks and partisan advantage instead of the officials who possessed authority and how they used it.

Democratic ads deserve scrutiny when they blur documented decisions into insinuations about social or financial proximity. But that flaw should not obscure the power structure. Trump’s administration controlled the records, Trump resisted demands for their release, and Republican lawmakers had to decide whether to enable that resistance. The systemic error is allowing the last, politically compelled act of compliance to overwrite the obstruction that made pressure necessary.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s Epstein scandal comes roaring back to haunt his GOP allies

item.title: Psychologist sees 'dementia' signs in 3 'peculiar' Trump encounters
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist John Paul Garrison described three recorded encounters involving President Donald Trump as potentially consistent with neurological decline: Trump saluting or waving when no obvious recipient was visible, walking past his waiting limousine after an event in Dalton, Georgia, and reacting angrily during a clash with Independent reporter Andrew Feinberg. Garrison said such conduct can occur with dementia, but the reporting provides no diagnosis.

The evidence is more ambiguous than the headline suggests. Garrison acknowledged that construction workers or law-enforcement officers may have been outside the camera’s view and that several conditions could explain Trump’s behavior. The article supplies no examination, medical records, longitudinal assessment, or corroborating clinician.

A diagnosis the evidence cannot carry

Garrison’s interpretation may justify questions about Trump’s fitness, but it does not establish dementia. Short video clips cannot show whether Trump was confused, responding to someone off-camera, following mistaken directions, or simply behaving awkwardly. Anger is not a diagnosis, and walking past a vehicle does not identify a neurological disorder.

The article nevertheless packages these incidents as “signs” of dementia. That framing converts one psychologist’s remote speculation into a medical-sounding conclusion while leaving the decisive uncertainty below it. The weakness is not that Trump deserves polite treatment. It is that serious claims require serious evidence.

Power makes fitness relevant

Trump holds presidential authority. Confusion or cognitive impairment in a president would matter because the office controls executive agencies, military command, appointments, pardons, and immense public resources. Scrutiny of presidential capacity is therefore legitimate and necessary.

But institutional power also identifies who must do more than speculate. Senior officials, medical personnel with lawful access, congressional overseers, and political allies who observe the president directly possess information and mechanisms unavailable to a commentator reviewing clips. The article does not report that any of them assessed these incidents or concealed an established diagnosis.

The headline outruns the reporting

The central misdirection is epistemic: the presentation encourages readers to treat ambiguous conduct as clinical evidence. Garrison himself offered alternative explanations, yet the headline foregrounds “dementia” and counts three “encounters” as though repetition resolved the evidentiary gap.

That shortcut also weakens political accountability. A president’s documented decisions, public statements, and official conduct can be judged without assigning an unverified disease. Medical speculation can turn chosen behavior into pathology and shift attention from what an officeholder did to conjecture about why he did it.

Accountability without armchair medicine

If Trump wandered away from his vehicle, Secret Service agents had immediate responsibility for redirecting him, and AlterNet reports that they did. If his behavior raises broader concerns, officials with direct knowledge bear responsibility for addressing them through credible disclosure and lawful oversight.

Garrison made the interpretive claims; AlterNet chose to amplify them. Neither act proves the condition invoked. The defensible conclusion is narrow: the videos prompted one psychologist to suspect possible decline, while the supplied evidence leaves the cause unresolved.

The systemic error

Political media routinely substitutes provocative inference for institutional reporting. A clipped gesture and an expert label are easier to publish than sustained investigation into who has observed the president, what safeguards exist, and whether empowered officials are performing their duties.

That pattern serves power poorly. It gives audiences a dramatic diagnosis without establishing one, while the people with actual access and authority remain largely outside the frame. Rigorous scrutiny should make responsibility clearer. This framing makes certainty louder than evidence.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist sees ‘dementia’ signs in 3 ‘peculiar’ Trump encounters
