item.title: 'Can't take the heat': Judges fire back at Trump after he targets colleague
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that fellow federal judges and former colleagues defended U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes after President Donald Trump called her a “crazed lunatic” amid litigation over allegedly unlawful renovations at Washington’s East Potomac Golf Course. Retired federal judge Paul Grimm said that officials who object to judicial scrutiny should be prepared to “take the heat.”

Reyes rejected the administration’s effort to disqualify her for alleged bias, answering the accusation with the court record. She noted that she had repeatedly credited government lawyers’ representations, denied requests to restrain the government’s work, and publicly praised government counsel’s briefs and performance.

The reporting also describes Reyes as a direct, highly regarded former Williams & Connolly lawyer and notes that she keeps a Pac-Man machine in her chambers. That biographical color is memorable, but the consequential dispute concerns executive conduct, judicial oversight, and an attempt to remove the judge conducting it.

Where the power sits

Trump commands the executive branch. Reyes controls one federal courtroom and the proceedings before it. Those are substantial judicial powers, but they are not equivalent in reach to the presidency’s control over agencies, government lawyers, public communications, and the machinery carrying out the disputed project.

That imbalance matters. The president’s insult was aimed at a judge reviewing executive action. The administration then sought her disqualification. Whatever legal arguments accompanied that request, the reported sequence is clear: the government received adverse scrutiny, attacked the judge’s impartiality, and tried to remove her from the case.

The record defeats the caricature

The administration’s accusation of bias collides with Reyes’s documented treatment of its lawyers. According to her response, she repeatedly declined to restrain the government, credited its representations, and praised its counsel in unusually strong terms.

That does not by itself resolve the golf-course dispute or prove every criticism from the bench correct. It does expose how little the president’s personal caricature explains. “Crazed lunatic” is not a legal rebuttal. It converts a contest over evidence and government representations into a spectacle about a judge’s temperament.

The useful distraction

The Pac-Man detail humanizes Reyes, but it also risks shrinking an institutional confrontation into personality journalism: the blunt judge, her arcade machine, her admirers, and her sharp exchanges with Trump.

The harder question is why executive officials allegedly proceeded improperly with public property and why the administration responded to scrutiny by seeking the judge’s removal. The government’s conduct created the controversy. Reyes’s manner became the diversion.

Accountability recast as aggression

This is a familiar exercise in political misdirection. Officials with the power to act portray the person demanding an adequate explanation as the aggressor. A judge’s impatience with weak or inconsistent government conduct becomes “bias”; a president’s personal attack becomes merely another installment in an “exchange.”

That framing launders the power difference. Reyes can issue rulings subject to appeal. Trump can deploy the presidency’s public platform against an individual judge while his administration litigates before her. Calling that a mutual feud obscures who initiated the personal attack and who is answerable for the underlying executive action.

The larger pattern

The systemic issue is not whether a judge is congenial. It is whether institutional oversight can function when executive officials answer scrutiny by attacking the legitimacy of the official applying it.

Reyes’s response points toward the only useful standard: the record. When political power substitutes personal vilification for evidence and seeks to turn accountability into alleged persecution, the insult is not incidental. It is a tactic for moving public attention away from what the government did and onto the supposed defect of whoever demanded an explanation.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Can’t take the heat’: Judges fire back at Trump after he targets colleague

item.title: Wall Street can't wait for Trump to crash and burn: economist
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that economist and journalist Hamish McRae argued that major investors would welcome Republican losses in the approaching U.S. midterm elections because divided government could restrain President Donald Trump. His case was not that Wall Street wanted Trump “toppled,” but that markets historically tend to rise after midterms and businesses often prefer legislative gridlock.

McRae also contended that a weaker White House would leave the Federal Reserve better positioned to address inflation, which the article put at 3.7 percent. He attributed that inflation partly to higher fuel prices following Trump’s attacks on Iran and warned that rising rates, heavy government debt, weak manufacturing and an eventual correction in AI-related stocks remained serious risks.

The reporting does not cite investors, market data or financial institutions saying they want Trump to “crash and burn.” That inflammatory conclusion belongs to the headline; the evidence supplied is McRae’s analysis that financial markets could benefit from limits on presidential power.

The power is in Washington

The decisive actors are not vaguely defined traders “praying” for an electoral humiliation. Trump exercises presidential power, Republicans exercise congressional power, and the Federal Reserve controls monetary policy within its statutory independence. Voters can alter the congressional balance, but a midterm defeat does not remove a president.

McRae’s central institutional point is straightforward: unified partisan control enabled an assertive president because congressional Republicans declined to restrain him. Losing the House would break that arrangement by denying the White House an obedient legislative partner. “Gridlock” is therefore not an atmospheric market condition. It is the practical consequence of voters transferring power away from the president’s party.

Wall Street wants restraint, not justice

Business opposition to presidential volatility should not be confused with principled resistance. In McRae’s account, investors favor gridlock because it reduces the chance that government will disrupt profit-making. Their concern is predictability, not accountability.

That distinction matters. Capital can tolerate considerable public damage when the returns remain attractive. It becomes anxious when erratic decisions threaten prices, borrowing costs or asset values. If Wall Street prefers a weakened Trump, the article provides no basis for portraying that preference as moral clarity. It is institutional self-interest responding to instability.

The headline sells a fantasy

“Crash and burn” converts a narrow argument about congressional restraint into a melodrama about Trump’s downfall. It also gives Wall Street a voice the article never actually documents. McRae offers an interpretation of market incentives; AlterNet turns that interpretation into a collective declaration by “big money.”

The distortion obscures the more consequential story: Republican lawmakers enabled concentrated executive power, and an election could reduce that power without ending the presidency. By replacing this institutional account with gleeful speculation about Trump’s personal fate, the framing makes politics look like spectacle and markets look like political protagonists.

Markets are not a governing conscience

McRae’s broader warning undercuts the celebratory headline. A congressional setback for Trump would not erase inflation, high bond yields, public debt, weak manufacturing or an AI-driven market bubble. Nor would a stronger Federal Reserve painlessly resolve them. Higher rates can discipline prices while increasing borrowing costs and economic strain.

The systemic pattern is familiar: elected officials and powerful financial institutions create or tolerate instability, then describe market approval as evidence of political repair. A market rally after divided government would show that investors expect fewer disruptive decisions. It would not show that the underlying economy is healthy, that accountability has occurred or that the people absorbing higher prices and fiscal retrenchment have gained power.

Thanks to Alter Net

item.title: Top Trump officials’ finger pointing just blew up in their faces
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration blamed SpaceX for restrictions affecting Ukraine’s Starshield service, but Vice President JD Vance’s own explanation pointed back to the US government. Vance told Fox News that Elon Musk would need Washington to direct his company’s conduct in the war.

Reuters correspondent Erin Banco similarly said the Defense Department holds the Starshield contract and that SpaceX cannot act without a US government decision. The reporting does not identify the precise directive, official, or technical mechanism behind the reported degradation, so it does not conclusively establish who ordered it.

AlterNet says lawmakers are seeking investigations, while seven Republican senators have asked Musk to remove the restrictions. That request still places the public burden on Musk even as the reported contractual arrangement indicates that the Pentagon possesses the relevant authority.

The power sits in Washington

The central issue is not Musk’s personal disposition toward Ukraine. It is control.

If Banco’s description of the contract is accurate, the Defense Department is the institution with the power to direct Starshield’s operation. SpaceX may own the infrastructure and Musk may dominate the headlines, but the federal government holds the contract and sets policy. Vance effectively acknowledged that hierarchy when he recast the dispute as a question of US policy toward Ukraine and Russia.

That does not prove Vance personally ordered any restriction, nor does the article establish which official did. It does, however, make the administration’s attempt to assign responsibility solely to a contractor look untenable.

The contractor makes a useful shield

Musk is an unusually plausible decoy because he is powerful, politically entangled and publicly erratic. Those facts make it easy to frame every Starlink controversy as another billionaire’s unilateral intervention.

But notoriety is not the same as legal authority. When officials direct scrutiny toward Musk while withholding a clear account of the Pentagon’s decisions, they blur the distinction between the operator of a system and the government purchasing and directing its military service.

The unanswered question is therefore concrete: What instructions did the Defense Department issue, who approved them, and when? Calling for Musk to “remove” restrictions does not answer that question if SpaceX lacks contractual authority to do so independently.

Policy disguised as confusion

Vance’s remarks matter because they shift the dispute from corporate conduct to state policy. His formulation—what America’s policy toward Ukraine and Russia will be—treats the reported restriction not as a mysterious technical failure but as part of a government choice.

AlterNet goes further, characterizing the episode as active degradation of an ally’s military capacity. The material presented supports demanding an investigation into that possibility; it does not, by itself, prove sabotage, treason or an intent to aid Russia. Paul Krugman’s description of the conduct as “treason” is his judgment, not an established legal finding.

The administration’s refusal, as presented here, to identify the responsible decision-maker converts an accountable chain of command into fog. That fog protects officials while Ukraine bears the operational consequences.

Accountability follows authority

The larger pattern is government by deniable intermediary. Public power is exercised through contracts, platforms and private executives; when consequences become politically costly, officials point to the intermediary as though privatized delivery had also privatized responsibility.

It has not. A contractor can be scrutinized for its conduct, but elected and appointed officials remain answerable for the policy they authorize and the leverage they decline to use.

The Starshield dispute will remain unresolved until investigators establish the actual order and decision chain. But the political structure is already visible: Washington holds the institutional power, Ukraine absorbs the risk, and a famous contractor is positioned to take blame that may belong higher up.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Top Trump officials’ finger pointing just blew up in their faces

item.title: Trump’s lawyers fight to keep FBI agents quiet about buried Smith report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s lawyers asked U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon to preserve restrictions preventing FBI personnel from receiving advance clarification about what they may disclose from the classified-documents investigation. The agents argue that Cannon’s February 2026 order blocking release of former special counsel Jack Smith’s Volume II leaves them vulnerable to contempt sanctions if they answer questions about the investigation.

Trump’s legal team and the Justice Department oppose the agents’ request. The department called their concerns “fear-mongering” on October 16, while Trump’s lawyers argued in a Wednesday filing that loosening Cannon’s order could allow people familiar with the unreleased report to claim a right to discuss it.

Cannon, whom Trump appointed to the federal bench, dismissed the prosecution in July 2024 after ruling that Smith’s appointment was unlawful. The charges against Trump and two former co-defendants were therefore never tested at trial. Cannon has not yet ruled on the agents’ request for clarification.

Power is not evenly distributed

The agents do not control the report, the injunction, the investigation now aimed at their conduct, or the penalties they fear. Cannon controls the scope of her order. Trump’s Justice Department controls the questioning. Trump’s lawyers are defending the secrecy that constrains the witnesses.

That alignment matters. The sitting president’s administration wants information from agents who investigated him, while joining his private lawyers in opposing assurances about what those agents may safely say. Calling this a mere dispute over procedure obscures the institutional imbalance.

Secrecy with selective access

Trump’s lawyers defend Cannon’s restrictions as necessary to prevent people from claiming a right to speak about unreleased findings. But the agents are not asking the court to publish Smith’s report wholesale. According to AlterNet, they want to know whether they may answer investigators and discuss interviews conducted with their lawyers present without risking contempt.

The practical arrangement is stark: the government may demand testimony, yet the witnesses must guess whether providing it violates a court order. Their reported concern is not erased by immunity from prosecution because contempt sanctions are a separate risk. The Justice Department’s “fear-mongering” label dismisses that legal distinction instead of resolving it.

The buried merits

Cannon’s dismissal ended the prosecution before the allegations could be tested at trial. Her later order kept Smith’s account of the investigation from public view. Those facts do not establish Trump’s guilt, nor does Smith’s unreleased report constitute a verdict. They do mean that neither a trial nor public access to Volume II has supplied the scrutiny that competing claims require.

The vacuum is politically useful to the people with the greatest power over it. Officials can invoke an alleged conspiracy by investigators while the underlying investigative account remains sealed and the agents themselves seek guidance about speaking. The reporting does not establish that this arrangement was designed to suppress rebuttal, but suppression is its foreseeable effect.

Accountability turned downward

The institutional focus has shifted from the conduct Smith investigated to the officials who investigated it. Scrutinizing investigators can be legitimate. Doing so while defending rules that leave them uncertain about what they may disclose creates a structurally lopsided inquiry.

AlterNet’s story is strongest when its facts expose that contradiction. Its phrase “Trump’s Justice Department” captures political control, but the deeper issue is not branding. It is the executive branch using its authority to question subordinate or former personnel while resisting judicial clarification of the boundaries governing their answers.

The systemic error

This is how accountability is inverted without any formal declaration that accountability has ended. A prosecution is dismissed on appointment grounds before trial, the resulting report is sealed, investigators are summoned to answer allegations against themselves, and their request for clear speech rules is opposed by both the administration and the president’s lawyers.

The larger pattern is institutional power converting unresolved facts into controlled ambiguity. Powerful actors retain access, initiative, and legal representation; weaker actors inherit uncertainty and exposure. The public is then invited to treat the resulting silence as absence of evidence rather than the product of decisions made by identifiable officials.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s lawyers fight to keep FBI agents quiet about buried Smith report

item.title: Retired general thinks he knows who was moving the Eisenhower globe
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that retired Gen. Mark Hertling speculated that “a couple of lieutenant colonels” in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s outer office moved and damaged a World War II-era globe used by Dwight D. Eisenhower. Hertling offered no evidence identifying the people involved; his answer was explicitly a guess.

According to AlterNet’s account of Washington Post reporting, Hegseth decided in February that he wanted the globe displayed in his office. His staff allegedly moved it without waiting for trained curators, leaving a large hole in Antarctica. The report does not establish who physically handled the artifact or who gave the operational order beyond Hegseth’s decision to obtain it.

The power was in the office

The unidentified staff members may have carried the globe, but Hegseth held the institutional authority. He wanted a historic object brought into his office, and subordinates acted within a hierarchy built to satisfy the secretary of defense.

That distinction matters. Focusing on whichever lieutenant colonels may have lifted the globe risks converting a leadership failure into a story about clumsy underlings. The consequential decision was to treat a protected artifact as office décor and bypass the professionals responsible for preserving it.

Hertling’s guess is not evidence

Hertling sharpened the anecdote by suggesting the movers were staffers who spent their time posting attacks on X. AlterNet supplies no evidence connecting any such staffer to the damage. That flourish may express his view of Hegseth’s operation, but it does not identify the culprit.

The stronger criticism requires no speculation: personnel working for the defense secretary reportedly attempted a specialized move without the trained curators whose expertise existed for precisely this purpose. The documented institutional failure is more damning than the unsupported personnel theory.

History as a prop

The globe’s value came from its association with Eisenhower’s wartime command. In a responsible institution, that history imposes obligations: controlled handling, professional conservation and stewardship beyond the tenure of any officeholder.

Here, the artifact reportedly became an accessory for impressing visitors. Hertling described resisting a similar effort when an unnamed senior official wanted a desk associated with George Patton or Erwin Rommel moved from Europe into an office. His story exposes the recurring temptation: powerful officials mistake custody for ownership and public history for personal staging.

Professional systems were bypassed

Curators are not ornamental bureaucrats. Their procedures protect fragile objects from predictable damage. Ignoring them did not produce efficiency; it reportedly produced a hole in an artifact that had survived roughly eight decades at the Pentagon.

Calling this merely “careless” understates the structure of the failure. A senior official’s preference displaced institutional expertise, while subordinates apparently carried the practical risk. That is how hierarchy launders responsibility: the person with power expresses a desire, lower-ranking personnel execute it, and blame settles on the hands rather than the authority that set the action in motion.

The larger pattern

Hertling argued that military artifacts should embody standards, professionalism and constitutional service. The damaged globe instead illustrates what happens when an institution’s history is valued for its prestige but its custodians are treated as obstacles.

The systemic error is not simply that somebody mishandled an old object. It is that concentrated authority can turn expertise into inconvenience, public property into executive decoration and foreseeable damage into an anonymous staff mishap. The reporting cannot tell us who tore Antarctica. It tells us whose desire put the globe in danger.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Retired general thinks he knows who was moving the Eisenhower globe

item.title: A 60-year-old rule is keeping doctors from telling you if Trump is insane
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the American Psychiatric Association’s Goldwater Rule prevents its members from offering professional diagnoses of public figures they have not personally examined. The rule does not keep all doctors from discussing President Donald Trump’s conduct, and it does not prevent voters from judging whether he is fit for office. It restricts one association’s psychiatrists from presenting remote diagnosis as professional fact.

Bioethicist Jacob Appel told AlterNet that the rule is outdated and inconsistently restrictive because psychologists, neurologists, and psychiatrists outside the association may still diagnose public figures in public. But he also stressed that observers do not know whether Trump’s behavior reflects illness, calculated performance, or ordinary belligerence—and that cruelty, ignorance, and selfishness are not psychiatric diagnoses.

The practical safeguard is also weak. Appel argued that the 25th Amendment is extraordinarily difficult to use in a partisan government, while no independent medical body currently evaluates presidential candidates or officeholders.

The headline overpromises

The rule is not keeping “doctors” generally from telling the public that Trump is “insane.” It governs members of one professional association, and its purpose is to stop clinicians from converting distant observation into purported diagnosis. AlterNet’s framing turns a real dispute over professional ethics into a cleaner, more sensational story about suppressed expert knowledge.

Yet Appel repeatedly declines to supply the certainty that framing invites. He says the public does not know what is happening medically, that diagnosis is distinct from political judgment, and that visible misconduct may have no psychiatric cause. The interview’s most responsible conclusion therefore undercuts its premise: no professional label is required to evaluate conduct.

Power does not require a diagnosis

Trump holds presidential power. He and his administration make policy; Cabinet officials, political appointees, legislators, and allied institutions can enable or resist those decisions. If a trade conflict with Canada inflicts economic damage, the relevant questions concern who ordered it, who implemented it, who could have stopped it, and who benefited or suffered—not which disorder might explain it.

Psychiatric speculation can become an alibi. Calling destructive conduct “insane” relocates responsibility from political choice to private pathology. Appel explicitly raises the possibility that an appearance of instability can be cultivated to intimidate opponents or absolve a leader of responsibility, while also emphasizing that Trump’s actual condition is unknown. That uncertainty makes diagnosis a poor foundation for accountability.

The stronger misdirection

The story directs attention toward psychiatrists constrained by an ethics rule, but psychiatrists do not possess the constitutional authority at issue. The officials with that power are the vice president, Cabinet, and Congress. The public’s vulnerability comes less from professional silence than from institutions structured around loyalty, partisan incentives, and an exceptionally high removal threshold.

Appel’s account of the 25th Amendment identifies the central defect: a president may be surrounded by subordinates whose positions depend on him, while any attempt to declare incapacity can trigger an immediate legitimacy crisis. That is an institutional design problem. Turning it into a dispute about whether experts may diagnose a president from television obscures the officials who retain agency and choose whether to act.

Conduct is sufficient evidence

A medical diagnosis could explain behavior; it could not decide whether that behavior is acceptable. Nor would a clean bill of health excuse reckless policy, dishonesty, vindictiveness, or incompetence. As Appel notes, serious illness has coexisted with effective leadership, while physical health has never guaranteed sound judgment.

Citizens already have the evidence that properly belongs in political evaluation: public speech, official orders, policy results, personnel decisions, and the use of state power. Those acts can be documented and judged without stigmatizing mental illness or pretending that medicine can settle a constitutional conflict.

The system prefers an impossible threshold

The recurring pattern is institutional evasion through medicalization. When a president’s conduct becomes alarming, debate shifts from what he did to whether a clinician can prove what is “wrong” with him. That standard is both unavailable and unnecessary, which makes it useful to officials looking for a reason not to exercise their own authority.

A system that demands diagnosis before accountability has engineered paralysis. The decisive question is not whether Trump can be clinically explained from afar. It is whether powerful officials will accept responsibility for the decisions they make, implement, and permit.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: A 60-year-old rule is keeping doctors from telling you if Trump is insane

item.title: GOP mayor restrained after lunging at attendee during chaotic town hall
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini, a Republican, charged toward an attendee during a New Jersey council meeting after an exchange that the livestream did not clearly capture. The attendee raised his middle finger; Bianchini then left his seat behind the dais and approached him before several people restrained the mayor.

According to the account, Bianchini was removed from the room while yelling, “I’m going to get you.” The attendee said he had been threatened and called for Bianchini’s arrest. The reporting did not establish whether police arrested, charged, or otherwise acted against the mayor.

The confrontation occurred during public comment while recently fired township official Kenneth Gerber and his attorney were at the podium. The reporting does not establish Gerber’s connection to the dispute beyond his presence when it erupted.

Power left the dais

Bianchini was not merely another angry person in the room. He was the mayor, seated behind the governing body’s dais and confronting someone participating in a public meeting. That institutional difference matters more than the attendee’s rude gesture.

The attendee could insult the mayor. The mayor occupied an office backed by public authority, access, and status. When an officeholder physically advances on a constituent and must be restrained, the relevant failure is not a mutual decline in decorum. It is the officeholder’s inability—or refusal—to keep official power separate from personal rage.

Restraint was not accountability

Gerber and others reportedly stopped Bianchini in the moment. Council members told him to stop, and someone removed him from the room. Those actions prevented escalation, but they do not answer the institutional question created by the incident.

The mayor’s colleagues and local law enforcement now hold the meaningful agency. They determine whether the episode produces a formal response or is reduced to embarrassing footage. The article leaves that outcome unresolved. That uncertainty should not be disguised as proof of impunity, but it exposes the decisive next step: whether public institutions apply ordinary standards to the person who sits behind the dais.

The provocation is a distraction

The raised middle finger explains the sequence, not the mayor’s conduct. Giving that gesture equal analytical weight would transfer responsibility from the official who charged forward to the constituent whose expression offended him.

Public comment is often hostile because government decisions have consequences. Officials are not entitled to obedience, admiration, or emotional protection from the people they govern. The burden of restraint falls most heavily on the actor with institutional power.

The article outruns its evidence

AlterNet tries to turn the confrontation into a broader portrait of New Jersey Republicans, detouring through Representative Tom Kean Jr.’s public absence and the party’s embrace of MAGA messaging. The quoted reporting supports the claim that Republican candidates competed over Trump-aligned positioning. It does not establish that MAGA politics caused Bianchini’s behavior.

That connection may be politically suggestive, but suggestion is not proof. The sharper indictment requires no speculative partisan genealogy: a mayor responded to contempt from the public by leaving his official seat, advancing on an attendee, and shouting words the attendee understood as threatening.

Authority without discipline

The larger pattern is the conversion of public office into personal entitlement. A constituent’s hostility becomes an affront to be answered, while the official’s greater power is pushed out of frame as though everyone in the room arrived on equal terms.

They did not. One man had a gesture; the other had the mayoralty. A functioning institution recognizes that difference, imposes consequences proportionate to it, and refuses to let “chaos” become a euphemism that conceals who chose to escalate.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP mayor restrained after lunging at attendee during chaotic town hall

item.title: Biographer warns Trump’s 'aggression' just caught him in a trap
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s own $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC has exposed him to a deposition he sought to avoid. A federal judge ordered Trump to testify by December 11 or face sanctions; U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett warned his lawyers that continued noncompliance could result in dismissal.

Trump sued over a 2024 BBC documentary that combined separate portions of his speech concerning the march to the Capitol. The BBC apologized for the edit but maintains that it does not justify the lawsuit.

Biographer Michael Wolff argues that Trump created this predicament through reflexive aggression: he initiates conflicts, then confronts legal obligations produced by his own choices. Whether the deposition ultimately damages Trump before a jury remains speculative; the reporting establishes only the order, the deadline, and the possible sanctions.

The power belongs to the plaintiff—and the court

Trump was not dragged into this case by the BBC. He invoked federal judicial power and demanded $10 billion. That decision carries procedural consequences, including discovery and sworn questioning.

The court now holds the immediate institutional power. It can compel compliance, impose sanctions, or dismiss the case. Trump retains substantial agency because he chose the lawsuit and can comply with the order. Describing him merely as “caught” risks obscuring that he set the machinery in motion.

Aggression is not an explanation

Wolff presents Trump’s conduct as an inability to temper his aggression. That may describe a recurring style, but it can also make deliberate choices sound like uncontrollable impulses. Trump filed the lawsuit. His lawyers pursued it. Those were actions, not weather.

The relevant political question is not whether Trump enjoys conflict. It is how conflict serves him. Wolff’s account suggests that Trump casts institutions as enemies whenever they constrain him—even institutions shaped by his own appointments. That posture converts an adverse ruling from an ordinary limit into another performance of persecution.

The weaker target is not responsible

The BBC’s acknowledged editing decision is central to the dispute, but an apology does not establish Trump’s defamation claim, just as the broadcaster’s denial does not dispose of it. The court must address the legal merits.

The larger misdirection is Trump’s attempt, as described here, to make every institutional resistance appear like an attack on him and his supporters. That framing erases his authorship of the confrontation. The BBC made the contested edit; Trump chose a $10 billion lawsuit; the court imposed the deposition requirement. Those acts belong to different parties and should not be collapsed into a single grievance narrative.

Conflict as political insulation

Wolff says Trump portrays judges and other institutional actors as shared enemies while presenting himself as the supporter’s lone defender. The tactic does not require a coherent legal theory. It requires only a new antagonist whenever an institution refuses submission.

The consequence is political insulation from accountability. A favorable ruling validates power; an unfavorable one supposedly proves betrayal. Under that structure, no institution can legitimately constrain the leader because every constraint becomes evidence of disloyalty.

The system rewards the spectacle

This story reveals a broader pattern: powerful political actors can turn self-created legal exposure into another episode of grievance politics. Coverage that emphasizes personality—Trump’s aggression, appetite for conflict, or inability to restrain himself—can miss the institutional strategy and the agency behind it.

The deposition order is therefore more than an ironic trap. It is a test of whether ordinary legal obligations still attach to a president who initiated the case. The court has stated the consequence of defiance. What matters now is whether institutional power follows through, or whether another plainly assigned obligation dissolves into spectacle.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Biographer warns Trump’s ‘aggression’ just caught him in a trap

item.title: Beer-throwing Trump staffer filmed getting tossed out of NBA game: report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Britt McHenry, a State Department press adviser in President Donald Trump’s administration, was removed from the Washington Wizards’ home opener after a confrontation with other spectators. Video published by TMZ shows her throwing a drink toward a fan while leaving, arguing with a security guard, and exiting amid boos and objects thrown from the crowd.

People described by TMZ as sources close to McHenry said spectators behind her and her male guest had made misogynistic and inappropriate remarks, including comments about Winnie Harlow, and had thrown objects at McHenry. Those sources could not identify precisely what prompted her to throw the drink. The reporting provides no account from arena management, law enforcement, or the other spectators, and establishes no official consequence beyond her ejection.

AlterNet also recounts earlier controversies from McHenry’s media career, including her 2015 suspension from ESPN after she berated a towing-company employee. It notes separately that her sexual-harassment lawsuit against Fox News and George “Tyrus” Murdoch ended in a confidential settlement after both parties voluntarily dismissed it in 2021.

The power in the room

During the confrontation, arena security held the relevant institutional authority. Security personnel could remove McHenry, and the footage reportedly shows them doing so. Her federal title did not place her above the venue’s rules.

Beyond the arena, the State Department controls whether conduct by one of its press advisers warrants professional scrutiny. AlterNet reports that McHenry entered that role in September, but it does not say whether the department investigated the incident or imposed any employment consequence. That omission matters: public embarrassment is not institutional accountability.

Conduct is not context-free

Throwing a drink during an argument is conduct McHenry controlled. If spectators made misogynistic remarks or threw objects, they were responsible for those actions. One allegation does not erase the other, and the available reporting does not establish the full sequence.

The crowd’s reaction is not a verdict, either. Boos document hostility, not truth. Objects thrown at a person being escorted out would remain unacceptable regardless of what preceded them. The evidence supports a chaotic confrontation with competing claims, not a clean morality play.

The headline does political work

Calling McHenry a “Trump staffer” converts an arena ejection into a national political item. Her government position makes her judgment relevant, particularly because she works in public communications. But AlterNet supplies no evidence that she acted in an official capacity, invoked federal authority, or received protection because of her employment.

The framing therefore does two things at once: it identifies a legitimate public-interest connection, then leans on that connection harder than the facts permit. Trump’s name supplies political voltage, while the article offers little examination of the institution that employs McHenry, the standards governing her position, or who would decide whether the episode matters professionally.

Biography as borrowed proof

The account of McHenry berating a towing clerk is relevant as documented history, especially because she apologized and acknowledged losing control. Her unrelated sexual-harassment case is different. A lawsuit alleging that she was harassed and retaliated against does not establish a pattern of misconduct by her, and placing it beside the ejection risks turning victimization allegations into atmosphere for a character indictment.

That is a familiar editorial shortcut: assemble old controversies, flatten their moral distinctions, and let proximity imply guilt. It may make a subject look consistently scandalous, but it does not clarify responsibility for the event being reported.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is accountability reduced to spectacle. A politically connected public employee behaves badly on video; the audience punishes her socially; a publication attaches the president’s name; and the government institution with actual employment authority remains mostly absent from the story.

That arrangement rewards outrage without testing power. The useful political question is not whether McHenry was booed loudly enough. It is whether public institutions apply coherent standards to officials whose work depends on judgment and credibility—and whether political media will examine those standards instead of mistaking viral humiliation for accountability.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Beer-throwing Trump staffer filmed getting tossed out of NBA game: report

item.title: The truth behind Christiane Amanpour’s exit as CNN execs begged her to stay
item.description:
What happened

Christiane Amanpour decided to leave CNN after more than 43 years despite months of appeals from network chief Mark Thompson. AlterNet reports that concerns about CNN’s direction under David and Larry Ellison influenced her decision, while the recurrence of her ovarian cancer—described by Amanpour as “being very well managed”—also played a role.

CNN plans to reduce Amanpour to one weekly episode early in 2027, end the program in May, and conclude her tenure at the end of June. According to reporting cited by AlterNet, Thompson personally tried to keep the network’s leading international anchor from leaving but failed.

The departure follows the Ellisons’ expansion into major news properties. AlterNet points to reports of weakened editorial independence at CBS News and says Amanpour shared wider concerns that CNN could move away from fact-based journalism and toward friendlier coverage of President Donald Trump and other Republicans.

The owners hold the power

Amanpour controls whether she remains at CNN. She does not control what CNN becomes.

That authority belongs to the Ellisons and the executives who will translate ownership into editorial priorities, personnel decisions, and acceptable boundaries. Thompson could plead with Amanpour to stay, but the reporting provides no indication that he could give her the institutional guarantee that mattered: continued independence from owners with the power to reshape the network.

This is why the failed retention campaign is less reassuring than it sounds. Management recognized Amanpour’s value. Recognition without protection is merely an admission that the institution may lose what made it credible.

The warning came from CBS

AlterNet treats the Ellisons’ record at CBS News as relevant evidence, not background decoration. Insiders reportedly described declining newsroom independence after their August 2025 purchase, while Semafor reported that editor-in-chief Bari Weiss sent journalists after conspiracy theories about Texas Democrat James Talarico, including a claim involving a mental-health facility in Ohio.

That report does not by itself establish what the Ellisons will order CNN to do. It does establish why journalists might regard assurances about editorial autonomy as inadequate. Ownership patterns become politically meaningful when newsroom leaders respond to them by pursuing poorly grounded partisan narratives.

The danger is not confined to overt censorship. A newsroom can be bent through assignments, promotions, resource decisions, story selection, and the steady lesson that certain political suspicions deserve investigation while others do not.

The health explanation cannot carry the story

Amanpour’s cancer recurrence is material and should not be minimized. But presenting her exit primarily as a personal health decision would obscure the institutional conflict AlterNet describes.

Her condition helps explain why she might choose this moment to leave. It does not explain the reported concerns about ownership, Thompson’s months-long effort to retain her, or the political signals surrounding the takeover. Health is a factor; it is not a solvent that washes corporate power out of the account.

That distinction matters because powerful institutions routinely become invisible when consequential departures are narrated as individual life choices. The employee “moves on,” while the people changing the conditions of the workplace escape grammatical responsibility.

Political approval is not incidental

Trump publicly celebrated the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger after reporters told him on October 6, 2026, that it had closed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had likewise said the sooner David Ellison took over CNN, the better.

Those statements do not prove a bargain or establish direct editorial interference. They do reveal the political expectation surrounding the acquisition. Two senior Republican figures openly welcomed control of a network Trump has repeatedly denounced and sought to exclude from the White House press corps.

That approval should be analyzed as an expression of perceived advantage. Politicians hostile to independent scrutiny do not need to dictate every headline if owners and executives create a newsroom more attentive to their displeasure.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the concentration of editorial power in owners whose decisions can alter multiple major news institutions at once. Journalists retain personal agency, but owners determine the environment in which journalism is funded, rewarded, constrained, or abandoned.

Amanpour’s departure is therefore more than the loss of a prominent anchor. It is an early institutional consequence of uncertainty about who CNN will serve under its new ownership. Thompson could ask her to trust the network’s future. The reporting suggests he could not make that future trustworthy enough for her to stay.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The truth behind Christiane Amanpour’s exit as CNN execs begged her to stay

item.title: Trump humiliates Melania with stunning remark at her big White House moment
item.description:
What happened

According to AlterNet, President Donald Trump used a White House ceremony for Melania Trump’s women’s-health initiative to question publicly whether her signature “means anything.” After uncomfortable laughter, he added, “I think it does.” The first lady replied that his signature was “the most important.”

Melania Trump presented the directive as a major expansion of research and treatment for conditions disproportionately affecting women. The order instructs the Department of Health and Human Services to establish a Women’s Health Division within the National Institutes of Health and creates a White House task force led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and chief of staff Susie Wiles. AlterNet reports that it identifies no new funding.

The order also revokes a similar 2024 directive issued by President Joe Biden. During the ceremony, Trump shifted attention from the initiative to his signature, White House renovations, a proposed heliport and ballroom, and remarks about his wife being “not so easy.”

The signature was the power

Trump’s remark was revealing because it was institutionally accurate before it became personally insulting. Melania Trump could consult experts, campaign internally and lend the initiative her name, but the president controlled the executive authority. Her response acknowledged that hierarchy in real time: his signature mattered most.

Trump then made the imbalance into a joke at her expense. The officials’ laughter supplied the familiar choreography of concentrated power: the principal belittles someone, the room reacts, and the target smooths over the disruption. This was not merely an awkward marital exchange. It was a public demonstration of whose work counts and whose approval makes it count.

Ceremony without commitment

The administration advertised transformation while leaving the central material question unanswered. A new division and task force can rearrange responsibility charts, but AlterNet reports that the order specifies no new fund. Research capacity depends on grants, staff, laboratories and sustained appropriations—not ceremonial language.

That omission matters more than Trump’s manners. The presidency had the power to define the initiative, claim the achievement and determine what agencies must do. Yet the reporting establishes directives and organizational changes, not the resources required to produce the promised treatments or expanded access.

Rebranding is not a breakthrough

The order reportedly revokes Biden’s 2024 women’s-health directive while replacing it with an almost identical initiative. That makes the administration’s presentation of the policy as a new beginning deeply misleading. The operative political act is not simply creation; it is cancellation followed by rebranding.

Columnist Holly Baxter, writing in The Independent, further alleged that the administration had already damaged women’s-health research through grant scrutiny and withdrawn funding. AlterNet’s excerpt does not independently document the scale or specific cases behind that claim, so it should not be treated as established by this account alone. But it identifies the contradiction the ceremony needed to answer: whether the new structure restores capacity or merely repackages a field the administration has weakened.

The insult is not the whole story

AlterNet frames the episode around Trump humiliating his wife. The remark deserves scrutiny, but the tabloid framing pulls attention toward the weaker actor and the easier spectacle. Melania Trump’s reaction is not the consequential exercise of power here. The president’s order, the absence of specified funding and the erasure of his predecessor’s nearly identical policy are.

Focusing on whether the first lady was embarrassed converts governance into personality content. It also allows an administration to receive credit for announcing institutional machinery without demonstrating that the machinery can do anything.

Power prefers the unveiling

This episode exposes a durable political pattern: dismantle or rename an existing policy, stage its replacement as unprecedented, and let spectacle obscure continuity and capacity. The ceremony supplies images of action; the missing resources remain buried beneath the performance.

Trump’s remark made the hierarchy unusually plain. One person’s signature carried legal authority, everyone else supplied labor or applause, and the promised transformation remained dependent on decisions the event did not establish had been made. That is the systemic error: coverage fixates on the insult because the insult is vivid, while power operates through the order’s fine print—and through what the order conspicuously fails to provide.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump humiliates Melania with stunning remark at her big White House moment

item.title: 'Have their hands dirty': Billionaire GOP donor throws down on Trump policies
item.description:
What happened

Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of Citadel and a major Republican donor, said President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans made a serious fiscal error by extending tax cuts when the United States lacked the capacity to absorb the lost revenue. Speaking Tuesday at a New York conference, Griffin said Republicans “have their hands dirty” primarily because of the tax cuts, and called Trump’s tariff conflict with Europe “a fiasco,” according to AlterNet’s account of Bloomberg’s reporting.

Griffin’s criticism comes as federal debt has exceeded $40 trillion and the budget deficit reportedly rose from $1.78 trillion in fiscal 2025 to $1.99 trillion this fiscal year. The reporting links rising borrowing costs to investor anxiety over federal debt, persistent tariff-related inflation and an oil bottleneck associated with attacks on Iran.

Yet Griffin continues financing the officials and party responsible for the policies he condemns. Bloomberg reported that he gave $10 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, $5 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund and $10 million to support Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, plus $2.5 million each to Senators Dan Sullivan and Susan Collins.

The donor has agency

Griffin speaks as though he were auditing a government operated by strangers. He is not a spectator. He is spending tens of millions of dollars to strengthen the Republican Party’s electoral machinery and its candidates.

That does not make him personally responsible for every Republican vote or Trump decision. It does make his posture politically revealing: he wants credit for objecting to the consequences while continuing to subsidize the people producing them. His money is an exercise of power, not an expression of helpless concern.

Republicans made the choice

The central conflict is not between fiscal discipline and mysterious economic forces. Trump and Republican lawmakers chose further tax cuts despite the debt burden Griffin cites. They also chose tariffs that Griffin says are obstructing the growth he prescribes as the remedy.

“Grow the economy” is not an adequate answer when the same governing coalition is cutting revenue and imposing trade barriers. Growth is a desirable outcome, not a fiscal mechanism guaranteed to erase politically convenient arithmetic.

The deficit alibi

The article partly muddies responsibility by invoking military spending, safety-net programs and interest payments together. Those categories do not carry equal political meaning. Interest costs reflect accumulated obligations. Safety-net spending sustains people entitled to benefits. Tax cuts are discretionary decisions to collect less revenue.

Bundling them into one mass called “spending” helps powerful actors redirect scrutiny toward programs serving weaker constituencies. Griffin’s own emphasis cuts through that diversion: he blamed the recent tax cuts more than spending increases.

Dissent without withdrawal

Elite criticism often arrives in this carefully insulated form. A donor denounces selected policies, preserves his access and keeps funding the coalition. The complaint becomes evidence of independence while the checks remain evidence of allegiance.

The reporting does not establish why Griffin continues donating, and his motives should not be invented. The observable arrangement is enough: Republican leaders retain his financial support despite pursuing policies he describes as fiscally reckless and economically damaging. His criticism imposes no evident political penalty on them.

Power without accountability

This is the larger pattern: wealthy patrons can finance a governing project, recoil from its results and present themselves as outside experts diagnosing the damage. Ordinary borrowers encounter the consequences through mortgages, credit cards and auto loans; the donor retains influence over which politicians hold office.

Griffin is right to locate responsibility with Trump and Republican lawmakers. But responsibility does not stop with officeholders. A political system organized around enormous private donations gives benefactors power before the decision and plausible distance afterward. The money enables the policy; the interview launders the relationship.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Have their hands dirty’: Billionaire GOP donor throws down on Trump policies

item.title: 'Go to Trump University or die': The Supreme Court's new radical agenda
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that legal commentator Elie Mystal warned about activist Ed Blum’s proposal to require universities to disclose extensive applicant data—including test scores, grades, family income, Pell Grant eligibility and coursework—broken down by race and ethnicity. Mystal argues that such disclosure could deter Black and Latino students from applying.

The report connects Blum’s proposal to his successful campaign against race-conscious admissions in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, decided by the Supreme Court in 2023. But AlterNet identifies no pending Supreme Court case involving the disclosure proposal. The headline’s “Go to Trump University or die” language is Mystal’s hyperbolic description of an admissions ideology based on test-score ranking, not a statement by the Court, Blum or Donald Trump.

The power is institutional

Blum has influence because he organizes litigation capable of reaching a Supreme Court whose conservative majority has already accepted his central constitutional argument against affirmative action. He can recruit plaintiffs and advance legal theories; the justices possess the state power to turn those theories into binding law.

Universities retain control over admissions within the boundaries courts impose. Applicants have the least power. They must surrender information to institutions while absorbing the consequences of rules designed by litigants, judges and administrators.

A proposal is not a ruling

AlterNet weakens its own case by presenting speculation about future litigation as the Supreme Court’s “new radical agenda.” The reporting establishes that Blum proposed mandatory disclosure and that Mystal fears the Court could eventually endorse it. It does not establish that the justices have adopted the proposal, agreed to hear such a case or even been presented with one.

That distinction matters. A court powerful enough to reshape admissions does not need its conduct exaggerated. Conflating an activist’s demand with an existing judicial program gives defenders of the Court an easy way to dismiss legitimate scrutiny as alarmism.

Neutrality as leverage

The political strategy described here is more sophisticated than an open demand to exclude particular groups. It treats selected admissions metrics as naturally authoritative, then labels scrutiny of racial inequality as improper preference. After race-conscious admissions are prohibited, racial disclosure can be demanded in the name of proving that institutions are still cheating.

That is not ideological consistency. It is asymmetric control: universities may be forbidden to consider race when addressing exclusion, while outside activists seek race-specific data to challenge outcomes they dislike. “Colorblindness” becomes a restriction on remedial power, not an end to racial monitoring.

Privacy becomes pressure

The foreseeable consequence of publishing family income, Pell Grant eligibility and other sensitive applicant information is not merely administrative transparency. Even if records were aggregated or anonymized—a detail AlterNet does not clarify—the demand would expand outside surveillance of admissions and create another basis for litigation and political intimidation.

Mystal infers that deterrence is the point. The supplied reporting does not establish Blum’s motive, so that claim remains an interpretation. But deterrence is plainly a foreseeable risk when applying to college may expose or intensify scrutiny of a family’s finances, race and academic record.

The litigation pipeline

The larger pattern is organized minority rule through constitutional litigation. Advocacy groups develop claims, recruit cases and return to sympathetic courts after each victory, converting political preferences into nationwide restraints on institutions.

AlterNet is right to examine that pipeline, but wrong to collapse its stages. Blum’s proposal is not yet Supreme Court doctrine. The danger established by the story is more precise: a successful legal campaign has produced another demand, and the people advancing it know that six justices—not students, faculty or the broader public—can ultimately give it coercive force.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Go to Trump University or die’: The Supreme Court’s new radical agenda

item.title: WSJ warns of Trump threat to 'blow up US global credibility’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that The Wall Street Journal editorial board warned President Donald Trump against pursuing a grand bargain with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping that would divide Ukraine and other regions into great-power spheres of influence. The board argued that such an arrangement would destroy U.S. credibility with its allies while rewarding governments hostile to American interests.

According to AlterNet, the Journal said Trump could not compel Ukraine to capitulate and would bear responsibility for foreseeable carnage if he withdrew U.S. intelligence and targeting assistance. It also warned that Xi could exploit any opening to weaken the American position in the Pacific and advance China’s ambitions toward Taiwan.

The editorial predicted a serious Republican split if Trump effectively conceded Europe to Russia and the Pacific to China. It acknowledged that Congress and the courts have limited power to stop a determined president in foreign affairs, though lawmakers could impose political costs.

The power belongs to the president

The decisive actor here is not “America,” an unruly alliance system or some abstract postwar order. It is the president, who commands enormous authority over diplomacy, military assistance and intelligence cooperation.

That power gives Trump agency. Ending support for Ukraine, marginalizing European allies or bargaining over Taiwan would be presidential choices with identifiable beneficiaries and foreseeable consequences. Describing Trump as governed by “tactical impulse” may characterize his behavior, but it can also obscure responsibility. Erratic decisions remain decisions.

Allies are not bargaining chips

The proposed “Yalta 2” framing is revealing because it reduces sovereign countries to territory that larger states may allocate among themselves. Ukraine and Taiwan become objects of negotiation rather than political communities whose residents bear the costs.

Putin reportedly floated the three-power meeting. But only Trump could supply the American participation and concessions that would give such an arrangement weight. Putin’s proposal does not diminish Trump’s responsibility for entertaining it.

The Journal’s warning is therefore less about diplomatic style than about hierarchy: whether the United States would use its power to support allies or help stronger states dictate the futures of weaker ones.

Confusion is the wrong frame

The weakest element of the Journal’s argument is its opening suggestion that it is difficult to know what Trump is doing. The editorial itself supplies a more concrete record: hostility toward Ukraine and Europe, interest in deals with Putin and Xi, and openness to dividing influence among powerful states.

Treating that pattern chiefly as inscrutability risks converting policy into personality. It invites readers to study Trump’s impulses when the consequential questions are institutional: What assistance will he withdraw? What concessions will he offer? Which commitments will he abandon, and who will be exposed afterward?

Uncertainty about motive does not erase clarity about leverage or possible effects.

The conservative warning has limits

The Journal’s case rests heavily on American credibility, deterrence and strategic advantage. Those concerns are real within the reporting, but they also reveal the boundaries of the objection: allied countries matter partly because they strengthen U.S. power.

That framing can still miss the people underneath the chessboard. The Journal invokes potential carnage in Ukraine and the freedom of 23 million people in Taiwan, yet its governing vocabulary remains alliances, military positioning and political legacy. Human consequences appear as proof that a strategy is unsound, not as the central stakes of allowing powerful governments to dispose of smaller societies.

The system concentrates the danger

The broader pattern is an executive branch with enough unilateral foreign-policy power to destabilize alliances before other institutions can respond effectively. Congress may raise the political price, as the Journal says, but punishment after the decision is weaker than control over the decision itself.

That is the structural failure exposed here. A president can treat security commitments as personal negotiating assets, weaker countries as tradable terrain and mass suffering as leverage. The scandal is not merely that Trump may use that power recklessly. It is that the American system has placed so much of it within one person’s reach.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: WSJ warns of Trump threat to ‘blow up US global credibility’

item.title: Trump's major foreign endorsement reveals way more about his own ambitions
item.description:
What happened

Donald Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a seventh term ahead of an Oct. 27 election, presenting Netanyahu as the leader Israelis should retain. AlterNet argues that the endorsement is less likely to decide the close contest than to advertise Trump’s own preference for aggressive military policy, personal loyalty and dominant leaders.

The outlet reports that Netanyahu is campaigning primarily on security while facing a fragmented opposition, unresolved questions over the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and criminal cases before Israeli courts. It also describes escalating Israeli conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, including an occupation encompassing 70 percent of Gaza and attacks on Palestinians, diplomats and journalists; those claims are presented by AlterNet and are not independently established here.

AlterNet further portrays Trump as favoring Netanyahu’s military approach despite objections attributed to U.S. intelligence and diplomatic advisers. The endorsement, on that account, signals a political partnership centered on force and loyalty rather than accountability or a durable settlement.

The power is governmental

The decisive actors are not abstract “voters on both sides” or an amorphous cycle of Middle East violence. Netanyahu leads the Israeli government and commands the institutions prosecuting the war. Trump, as described by AlterNet, can supply political cover and align American weapons, money and diplomatic influence with that government’s choices.

Palestinians facing military occupation, destroyed homes or inadequate food and medical care do not possess comparable agency. Treating this as a quarrel among equally empowered communities would erase the state machinery determining who may move, build, fight and survive.

Loyalty replaces scrutiny

Trump’s endorsement asks voters to evaluate Netanyahu through Trump himself: Is Netanyahu loyal, forceful and useful to the political image Trump wants to project? Questions about warnings before Oct. 7, Netanyahu’s court cases and the conduct of Israeli forces become secondary.

That is the same personalization AlterNet identifies in Trump’s domestic endorsements. Institutions and policy consequences are reduced to whether a candidate wears the approved political brand. Governance becomes a loyalty franchise.

Security becomes an alibi

Israeli polling cited by AlterNet places security at the center of the election, and Netanyahu presents his coalition as its indispensable guarantor. But a leader invoking security also bears responsibility for answering how a catastrophic security failure occurred and what his policies have produced since.

The reporting’s essential tension is therefore not security versus naïveté. It is power without commensurate accountability. Military escalation can display control while postponing harder questions about civilian survival, political settlement and whether the strategy is making anyone safer.

The framing still slips

AlterNet correctly directs attention toward Trump and Netanyahu, but at points it retreats into phrases such as a world “in a mess” and a “constant cycle” of violence. Cycles do not bulldoze homes, approve attacks, supply weapons or decline to investigate failures. Officials and institutions do.

The sharper account identifies each decision and its author. If Israeli forces looked away during assaults, that conduct requires institutional scrutiny. If Trump overrode intelligence and diplomatic objections to Iran attack plans, the relevant fact is his exercise of presidential power—not a vague absence of “strategic thinking.”

The larger design

This endorsement reveals a model of politics in which force supplies legitimacy, loyalty displaces oversight and spectacle substitutes for strategy. Trump’s apparent attraction to a leader willing to project military dominance is politically useful at home even if his endorsement changes few Israeli votes.

The systemic danger lies in how easily alliance management becomes personal patronage. Once public institutions are treated as instruments of powerful men, civilian consequences become background material, dissent becomes disloyalty, and accountability is dismissed as interference with the leader’s freedom to act.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s major foreign endorsement reveals way more about his own ambitions

item.title: Power brokers exploit Trump’s dwindling attention span behind closed doors
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that access to President Donald Trump has become a source of power inside the administration as his attention span reportedly declines. Historian Zeb Larson identifies aide Natalie Harp as a power broker because she can reach Trump, though the article says her precise role is unclear and does not document particular decisions she made.

The article also cites Washington Post reporting that former and current national-security officials were advising state election officials about possible uses of federal power to influence an upcoming vote, including hypothetical deployments of troops or immigration agents near polling places. Those were reported concerns, not established actions.

Much of the piece consists of Larson’s predictions: that Trump may become less constrained as elections approach, that his coalition could fracture over succession and accountability, and that Democrats should prepare institutions to resist election interference while presenting concrete plans for governing afterward.

Access becomes authority

The presidency holds the institutional power. Trump possesses the formal authority to direct executive agencies, shape foreign policy and deploy federal personnel within legal limits. Officials, aides and allies exercise derivative power by controlling what reaches him and when.

That makes the article’s central observation important but incomplete. If Harp controls access, she may influence the president’s information environment. The reporting supplied here, however, does not establish that she ordered policy, engineered a particular outcome or displaced formal decision-makers. “Power broker” is Larson’s assessment, not a demonstrated chain of command.

The deeper failure belongs to a system that permits consequential government decisions to depend on proximity to one man. Gatekeeping becomes governance when cabinet processes, professional review and transparent records stop constraining presidential discretion.

Diagnosis is not accountability

AlterNet repeatedly labels Trump “demented,” while Larson describes “dementia” and cognitive deterioration. The supplied article provides no medical diagnosis. It offers Trump’s hostile response to a reporter and broader impressions of his behavior, neither of which establishes a clinical condition.

That framing misdirects responsibility. Speculation about incapacity can turn chosen conduct into pathology and make powerful enablers look like attendants managing an unraveling patient. Whatever Trump’s health, presidential acts remain acts of government. Officials who recommend, execute or legitimize them retain agency.

The article names dramatic outcomes—changes involving Russian oil sanctions, Ukraine and laws aimed at Vladimir Putin—but does not supply enough detail to establish what measures changed, under what authority or who implemented them. Those omissions weaken its attempt to map power.

The enablers have choices

Larson’s strongest point is political rather than medical: Republicans and administration officials should not be treated as powerless extensions of Trump. They occupy offices, command agencies, cast votes and decide whether to comply, object, resign or disclose misconduct.

Predictions that Trump might manipulate elections, punish critics or further damage the economy remain predictions in this text. Treating them as completed facts would be propaganda in reverse. But officials preparing for specified contingencies are responding to the extraordinary powers already concentrated in the executive branch, not merely to one personality.

Democrats also possess agency. Larson calls for plans addressing election interference, the Supreme Court and damage attributed to DOGE. Those are proposals from an interview subject, not evidence that the party has adopted them. An opposition that substitutes warnings for operational preparation would be choosing passivity.

Succession exposes the coalition

The reported fear of a post-Trump future reveals a coalition organized around personal access, protection and inheritance rather than durable public commitments. Larson predicts that succession pressures could produce infighting; former Trump official Anthony Scaramucci similarly offers his interpretation that Trump may sabotage the Republican Party. Neither prediction is yet an outcome.

Still, the incentive structure is plain. Potential successors want Trump’s voters without inheriting every liability. Officials seeking protection want continued power without permanent dependence. Those tensions can fracture a coalition, but fracture alone produces no accountability. Institutions must investigate conduct, preserve evidence and apply law to identifiable decisions.

The systemic error

The story’s weakest move is making an unsupported medical conclusion carry an argument that should rest on institutional evidence. The central problem described is not confusion in the Oval Office. It is discretionary presidential power, opaque access and a surrounding political class with reasons to indulge both.

Personal decline, if established, would intensify that danger; it would not create it. A government becomes vulnerable when informal courtiers can influence public power, formal officials can hide behind the leader, and an opposition mistakes forecasting collapse for preparing to govern. The future does not impose accountability by itself. Institutions and the people controlling them either do that work or choose not to.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Power brokers exploit Trump’s dwindling attention span behind closed doors

item.title: Republican accidentally admits Trump is toxic in embarrassing website slip
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Eric Pratt, the Republican candidate for Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, briefly published an apparent internal instruction on his campaign website: “The president is not popular,” so campaign messaging should emphasize local concerns. A screenshot circulated on X, and AlterNet says an archived version confirmed that the language had appeared in the site’s “Pratt Playbook” section. The campaign later removed it without publicly explaining how it was published.

Pratt is running against Democrat Matt Little for the seat being vacated by Rep. Angie Craig. Little has argued that Pratt offers Trump-aligned policies beneath a milder presentation. Pratt rejected that framing in remarks reported by the Minnesota Star Tribune in September, saying Little was running against Trump while he was running to represent the district.

The admission was strategic, not ideological

The deleted instruction did not establish that Pratt opposes Trump’s policies, conduct, or control of the Republican Party. It showed something narrower and politically revealing: his campaign believed that mentioning Trump could hurt Pratt with the voters he needed.

That is not a repudiation. It is brand management. The strategy was to separate the local candidate’s presentation from the national party leader without demonstrating any corresponding separation in policy. Pratt’s campaign wanted the electoral benefit of distance while avoiding the political cost of an open break.

Power sits above the ballot language

Trump holds the presidency and commands enormous influence within Republican politics. Pratt, as a congressional candidate, has far less institutional power. But Pratt still has agency over the campaign he runs, the positions he advances, and the alliances he accepts.

The website instruction matters because it exposes a familiar division of labor. National Republican power sets the party’s direction; candidates in competitive districts translate that project into safer language about prices, farmers, and families. Local concerns may be genuine, but emphasizing them can also keep voters from examining how a candidate would use federal power once elected.

The “accident” is not the real story

AlterNet frames the episode as an embarrassing slip and repeatedly calls Trump toxic. The publication error is amusing, but treating it as the central scandal risks reducing political strategy to campaign incompetence.

The consequential act was not posting the instruction. It was adopting it. Someone associated with the campaign apparently concluded that candor about the president was electorally dangerous and that disciplined omission was preferable. The accidental publication merely made that judgment visible.

Misdirection works in two directions

Pratt’s response shifts attention from the national stakes of a congressional election to the claim that Little is improperly running against Trump. But House members do not operate as municipal customer-service representatives. They vote on federal legislation, investigations, budgets, and the president’s agenda. Asking how a candidate relates to the sitting president is not a distraction from the office; it is part of evaluating it.

Little’s phrase “quiet extremism” is an accusation, not an established fact in AlterNet’s report. The article provides no detailed policy comparison sufficient to prove it. But Pratt’s apparent messaging directive does support a more limited conclusion: his campaign saw value in foregrounding local benefits while minimizing an association it considered unpopular.

The system rewards camouflage

Competitive districts do not necessarily moderate parties. They often teach candidates to disguise national commitments behind locally tailored language. The candidate need not confront the source of the liability if consultants can simply remove the name.

That is the larger pattern exposed here. Political accountability fails when voters are offered personality distance in place of policy distance. Pratt’s website did not accidentally prove what he believes. It revealed what his campaign apparently believed voters should be encouraged not to consider.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republican accidentally admits Trump is toxic in embarrassing website slip
