item.title: 'Trump is our bully': Why some Americans can't quit the president
item.description:
What happened

Some Americans remain loyal to President Donald Trump despite policies that hurt their communities because, sociologist Arlie Hochschild told AlterNet, he has tied their economic losses and wounded pride to a story of betrayal, scapegoats and promised retribution. Voters she interviewed acknowledged that Trump lies and bullies but described him as “our bully”—a powerful figure they believed would fight for people otherwise ignored.

AlterNet reports that, less than two weeks before the midterm elections, Trump’s approval stood at 31 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll and that analysts expected Republicans could lose the House and possibly the Senate. Hochschild said enthusiasm had faded in eastern Kentucky, but she observed depressive withdrawal rather than a decisive political realignment.

She attributed that endurance to decades of lost coal employment, opioid addiction, low wages and collapsing civic institutions. She also said Trump had not restored coal jobs or substantially addressed the opioid crisis, while Republican safety-net cuts had inflicted particular damage on food-insecure Appalachian communities.

The people with the power

The decisive actors are not hungry families in West Virginia or unemployed miners in Kentucky. Trump holds the presidency. Republican lawmakers exercised legislative power. Their administration and congressional majority chose the policies Hochschild describes as cutting food assistance and shifting resources upward.

Yet the story devotes most of its attention to why injured voters remain attached to the politician presiding over that injury. That is a legitimate question, but it can quietly relocate responsibility: policy becomes a puzzle of voter psychology rather than an exercise of governing power.

Residents may have helped elect these officials, but casting a ballot is not equivalent to drafting legislation, controlling agencies or allocating federal resources. Political responsibility is shared unevenly because institutional power is distributed unevenly.

Pain converted into permission

Hochschild’s “emotional capture” describes a recognizable political transaction. Trump acknowledges real humiliation, supplies weaker targets to blame and presents himself as the instrument of revenge. Economic decline caused by disappearing industries and institutional abandonment is redirected toward immigrants, journalists and government workers.

The pet-eating falsehood she cites illustrates the mechanism. An outrageous claim attracts condemnation; Trump then recasts that condemnation as persecution shared with his supporters. The lie becomes secondary to the emotional bond produced by defending him. Accountability is repackaged as elite contempt.

This is propaganda built from genuine injury. The hardship need not be invented when its cause can be falsified and its anger pointed sideways.

“Our bully” is not confusion

Calling Trump “our bully” suggests that at least some supporters understand his conduct and accept it as useful. Their allegiance is not simply a failure to receive correct information. It can also be a decision that domination is tolerable when the dominant figure appears to target disliked outsiders.

That does not make impoverished voters the authors of every policy imposed on them. It does mean hardship cannot automatically be treated as political innocence. People can be manipulated and still possess agency; they can recognize a lie and continue rewarding the liar.

Hochschild’s account also identifies a practical failure by Democrats. In a region where they have become culturally marginal, sporadic appeals cannot substitute for durable organization, credible economic policy and institutions that remain after an election ends.

Division pays upward

The central misdirection is lateral. Rural and urban workers, poor and middle-class people, and voters with different levels of formal education are encouraged to treat one another as the cause of decline. Meanwhile, according to Hochschild, money and resources move from poorer people toward richer ones.

Her account of a Kentucky discussion over food assistance shows what breaks through that diversion: wages of eight or nine dollars an hour, caregiving obligations, unreliable cars, fuel costs and the absence of sustaining jobs. These are material constraints, not cultural riddles. They expose the fraud in demanding work while tolerating an economy that does not supply viable work.

The system behind the loyalty

The larger pattern is not that rural voters inexplicably prefer suffering. It is that concentrated political power can exploit abandonment it did not repair, direct resentment toward weaker groups and then use the resulting loyalty to deepen material deprivation.

Trump’s strength in this account rests on more than personal magnetism. It depends on social isolation, collapsed local institutions, weak unions, an absent opposition and a political culture that substitutes recognition for provision. The bully remains valuable because the system offers many people humiliation, then lets the most powerful man in it pretend he is merely avenging them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Trump is our bully’: Why some Americans can’t quit the president

item.title: Biographer predicts Trump’s explosive tantrum after looming disaster
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff predicts President Donald Trump would respond to a Democratic midterm victory by mounting an aggressive campaign to reclaim public attention. Speaking on his Daily Beast podcast, Wolff argued that Trump would try immediately to convince the country that he still controlled the political stage.

Wolff did not identify a specific planned action. He speculated that Trump would “attack” rather than retreat and pursue increasingly “Trumpian” tactics, while saying he considered a repeat of the violence associated with the January 6 Capitol attack unlikely. The supposed Republican “wipeout” remains a forecast in AlterNet’s framing, not a reported election result.

Prediction presented as news

The central fact here is that a biographer made a prediction. AlterNet inflates that prediction twice: first by treating a Democratic takeover as impending, then by advertising Trump’s unspecified future conduct as an “explosive tantrum.”

Neither claim is established by the reporting. No election result exists in the article, and Wolff offers no concrete act that Trump has decided to take. His familiarity with Trump may inform his judgment, but access and experience do not turn conjecture into an event.

That weak framing matters. When coverage packages speculation as imminent drama, it encourages readers to confuse confidence with evidence. The article supplies a vivid psychological narrative where it should supply clearer distinctions between history, forecast and fact.

The power is presidential

Trump is not merely a celebrity competing for airtime. In the story’s own timeline, he is the president: an office with executive authority, a vast communications apparatus and the capacity to make political retaliation materially consequential.

Wolff’s attention thesis therefore understates the institutional stakes. A president seeking to erase the meaning of an electoral defeat is not simply nursing a wounded ego. He can use official statements, personnel decisions and the agenda-setting power of the presidency to dominate public life. The article establishes no particular misuse of those powers, but it also should not reduce presidential conduct to spectacle.

The relevant agency would remain Trump’s. If he chose escalation after voters rejected his party, that would be his decision—not an involuntary symptom of dwindling attention and not something Democrats caused by winning.

Personality obscures responsibility

Calling anticipated conduct a tantrum can sound condemnatory while functioning as an excuse. A tantrum is impulsive and childish. A sustained effort to deny opponents the political meaning of a legitimate victory would be strategic conduct by a powerful officeholder.

Wolff’s formulation—that Trump believes he never loses—offers a character explanation, not an accountability framework. It risks turning choices into personality destiny: Trump behaves this way because Trump is Trump. That may be compelling branding, but it blurs the people and institutions that would have to amplify, defend or operationalize any escalation.

Trump cannot monopolize the national stage alone. Party officials, administration personnel and media organizations retain agency over whether they validate unsupported claims, convert rhetoric into government action or reward provocation with saturation coverage. AlterNet barely examines that enabling structure.

The machinery of attention

The article warns that Trump will seize attention while helping him do exactly that. An unnamed future eruption becomes the story; a hypothetical Democratic victory becomes scenery; institutional consequences disappear behind personality theater.

This is the recurring bargain of Trump coverage. News organizations denounce his appetite for attention while treating every prediction of his next performance as inherently newsworthy. The result is a political system narrated around one man’s emotional state, even when the public has ostensibly voted to shift power elsewhere.

The larger pattern is not simply that Trump seeks dominance. It is that political media repeatedly converts power struggles into psychodrama, obscuring the decisions that make domination effective. The useful question is not how spectacularly Trump might react. It is who would possess the authority to act, who would enable him, and what concrete damage their choices could produce.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Biographer predicts Trump’s explosive tantrum after looming disaster

item.title: Insiders reveal the singular theory guiding Trump’s historic world blunder
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that three people close to President Donald Trump told The Atlantic he believes Ukraine is attacking Russian oil refineries partly to raise energy prices and damage Republicans in the 2026 midterms. That is the “singular theory”: Ukraine, in Trump’s view, is not merely pursuing its war against Russia but meddling in an American election to weaken him.

The reporting says Trump announced a ceasefire that neither Ukraine nor Russia had approved; Ukraine paused while Russia continued attacking, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to declare, “We’re done,” according to NBC News. As Ukraine concluded that striking Russian oil infrastructure remained militarily useful, some people around Trump reportedly proposed ending US intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

AlterNet also reports that Trump was open to meeting Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China to discuss Ukraine, while a Ukrainian official complained that decisions appeared to be unfolding without Ukraine. The article does not establish that Kyiv is conducting an electoral interference campaign. It establishes only that Trump reportedly believes it is.

The power is in Washington

Ukraine can choose its military targets, but Trump controls the institution capable of rewarding or punishing that choice. The United States can provide intelligence, withdraw it, shape negotiations and use its leverage to decide whether Ukraine enters talks as a participant or an object.

That distinction matters. Trump’s theory does not need to be proved before it produces consequences. If he acts on it, an allegation about Ukrainian motives becomes grounds for withholding assistance from a country under Russian attack. Presidential suspicion acquires the force of state policy.

The officials reportedly suggesting an intelligence cutoff would be enabling that transformation. They are not spectators trapped inside Trump’s worldview. They are offering a mechanism for imposing it.

A battlefield decision becomes an election conspiracy

Russia’s refineries support Russia’s war-making capacity. According to the reporting, Ukraine considers continued attacks on them to be in its military interest. Trump reportedly interprets those operations through a narrower concern: fuel prices before the midterms.

That reframing shifts attention away from the attacker bombing Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure and toward the country trying to impair the attacker’s resources. AlterNet says Trump minimized Russia’s conduct by remarking that it had not “been doing much,” after which Zelenskyy responded with photographs of children killed in a park.

This is not demonstrated Ukrainian election meddling. It is a claim about intent attributed to Trump’s private conviction. The article’s evidence does not bridge the gap between Ukrainian military strategy and a coordinated effort to defeat Republicans.

The stronger actor disappears from the indictment

The reporting describes Russia continuing its attacks after Ukraine paused, yet the political penalty under discussion would fall on Ukraine. Putin retains the capacity to bomb, negotiate and wait for Washington to pressure his opponent. Kyiv faces the possible loss of intelligence because its conduct allegedly complicates Trump’s domestic politics.

That is the central misdirection. Russia’s agency recedes while Ukraine is assigned responsibility not only for fighting the war but for protecting the electoral interests of the American president managing its support.

AlterNet further argues that broader disruption tied to the Iran war and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is driving energy pressure. If that account is correct, blaming Ukrainian refinery strikes substitutes a politically convenient target for the larger forces affecting oil prices. The story, however, does not quantify the contribution of each factor, so it cannot establish Ukraine’s precise effect on US fuel costs.

Peace without the invaded country

Trump’s promised settlement rests, in this account, on personal diplomacy among powerful leaders. The contemplated meeting with Putin and Xi fits a model in which major states discuss Ukraine’s future while Ukraine waits outside the room.

Calling that arrangement a peace process does not change its structure. A ceasefire announced without the combatants’ agreement is not a ceasefire. A negotiation about a country conducted without that country’s meaningful participation is a division of influence, not consent.

The reported fascination with American, Russian and Chinese spheres of influence makes the hierarchy unusually plain: powerful governments claim authority to arrange the security of weaker ones. Ukraine’s refusal to accommodate that arrangement can then be recast as obstruction—or, now, electoral sabotage.

Suspicion as foreign policy

The larger pattern is government by personalized grievance. A president reportedly interprets another country’s wartime strategy as an attack on his party, advisers propose using intelligence access as punishment, and an adversary gains room to operate while its victim is pressed to serve Washington’s electoral calculations.

The danger in this structure does not depend on proving Trump’s motive or accepting every inference in AlterNet’s framing. It lies in the documented asymmetry of power: an unsupported theory at the top can redirect US policy, impose costs on Ukraine and spare Russia pressure.

When state power is organized around a leader’s belief that foreign events are secretly about him, evidence becomes secondary. Policy turns into retaliation, allies become suspects, and the government’s immense institutional machinery is made to enforce one man’s political narrative.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Insiders reveal the singular theory guiding Trump’s historic world blunder

item.title: Trump loophole for 'limitless source of power' demolished by federal judges
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that federal judges rejected key parts of the Trump administration’s attempt to use the Constitution’s supremacy clause to expand federal authority over immigration enforcement and voting. In New York, U.S. District Judge Ramón Reyes dismissed a Justice Department challenge to New York City’s sanctuary policies on October 15, finding that the federal government lacked standing and could not force local officials to carry out federal immigration policy.

The administration also sued in California to prevent ballots from roughly 20,000 people it considers likely noncitizens from being counted, despite California already prohibiting noncitizen voting in federal elections. Separately, on October 1, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz dismissed the prosecution of a Jamaican-born woman who had unlawfully registered to vote, ruling that the federal provision was unconstitutional as applied to her. That decision neither invalidated the statute nationwide nor ended the California case.

Power without a legal foundation

The supremacy clause establishes that valid federal law prevails when it conflicts with state law. It does not manufacture powers the Constitution withholds from the federal government.

That distinction is fatal to the administration’s position as described here. New York City was not overriding federal immigration law; it was declining to provide local personnel and resources for federal enforcement. Reyes called the Justice Department’s preemption theory a “backdoor around the Tenth Amendment.” In plain terms, the administration tried to convert federal priority into federal command.

The federal government holds immense enforcement and litigation power. New York City did not create the underlying immigration regime, and local officials do not control the Justice Department. Casting their refusal to serve as federal auxiliaries as obstruction obscures who is demanding additional power from whom.

An election lawsuit looking for a conflict

The California case exposes an even thinner theory. The state already bans noncitizen voting in federal elections, so the conflict supposedly triggering federal supremacy is not apparent from AlterNet’s account.

What remains is an effort to stop the counting of ballots from about 20,000 people the administration labels likely noncitizens. “Likely” is doing dangerous work. The reporting does not establish that those people are noncitizens, that their ballots are unlawful, or that the government’s classification is accurate.

The proposed remedy therefore reaches beyond enforcing an agreed legal prohibition. It puts thousands of ballots at risk based on a federal allegation about voter eligibility. The foreseeable consequence is disenfranchisement if eligible voters are swept into the government’s category.

The courts blocked a strategy, not a tendency

These rulings matter, but “demolished” overstates the result. Reyes dismissed the New York suit, while Leibowitz’s Florida ruling applied to one prosecution and did not erase the statute nationwide or terminate the California litigation. The administration still has institutional resources to continue pressing its claims.

That asymmetry is part of the strategy’s power. Governments can lose individual cases while forcing cities, states, and defendants to spend time and money resisting theories that test the outer boundary of federal authority. A courtroom defeat constrains a claim; it does not undo the coercive effect of bringing it.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is executive expansion through deliberate constitutional inversion: a clause limiting state resistance to valid federal law is recast as an independent reservoir of federal power. The New Republic’s Matt Ford describes the administration as treating the clause as “nearly limitless.” The rulings reported by AlterNet show judges refusing that reading where other constitutional limits still control.

The misdirection is to portray local noncooperation or contested voter eligibility as the central abuse. The more consequential act is the Justice Department’s attempt to turn federal supremacy into authority to commandeer local government and interfere with ballot counting without an established conflict in state law. When constitutional boundaries are treated as obstacles to be litigated around, institutional restraint depends on judges repeatedly saying no—and on that refusal arriving before the government’s allegation becomes someone else’s lost vote or surrendered autonomy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump loophole for ‘limitless source of power’ demolished by federal judges

item.title: Trump official abruptly flees DC before 'avalanche' of investigations
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Bloomberg Law, reports that Patrick Davis, the Justice Department’s top congressional liaison, planned to resign at the end of October after roughly a year leading the Office of Legislative Affairs. The report placed his departure before the November elections and an anticipated increase in congressional investigations if Democrats won either chamber. It did not establish that those investigations caused his resignation, so the headline’s claim that he “fled” Washington goes beyond the evidence presented.

Davis had also considered seeking compensation from a proposed Trump administration “anti-weaponization” fund because officials had subpoenaed his communications during the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Politico reported that he raised the potential conflict and sought to recuse himself from matters involving the fund. The reporting did not establish whether he filed a claim or how much he might have sought.

Where the power sits

Davis was not an ordinary employee escaping an unpleasant assignment. As assistant attorney general for legislative affairs, he occupied the channel through which the Justice Department defended its agenda to Congress. His office’s institutional purpose was to manage scrutiny from lawmakers, including scrutiny of a fund that could potentially have benefited him.

The larger power remained above him. Trump appointed the officials shaping Justice Department policy. Department leadership advanced the proposed fund. Congress could approve funding, demand records and conduct oversight—but only if lawmakers chose to use those powers, and the predicted Democratic takeover remained conditional in the reporting.

The conflict was structural

Davis’s possible claim exposed a basic defect in the proposed fund: an official responsible for selling it to Congress believed he might personally qualify for its benefits. Recusal may address one person’s participation, but it does not resolve the underlying arrangement—a Justice Department program designed to compensate people aligned with the administration’s account of past government wrongdoing.

Two administration officials reportedly objected that recusal was unnecessary because the fund did not yet formally exist. That is bureaucratic evasion masquerading as ethics analysis. A conflict does not become meaningful only after money is appropriated. It matters while officials are designing the program and persuading Congress to authorize it.

The blame is aimed downward

The unnamed official who called Davis’s recusal a “cop-out” shifted attention from the proposed beneficiary relationship to Davis’s willingness to endure hostile questioning. In that telling, the problem was not that a senior liaison might seek money from a program he was expected to promote. The problem was that he would not help prepare acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to defend the matter on Capitol Hill.

That complaint reveals an institutional priority: message discipline over clean governance. Davis may have had self-interested reasons to leave, but the reporting does not establish them. What it does establish is that administration officials treated his absence as a communications failure rather than confronting the compromised design that prompted the recusal request.

Oversight as an electoral contingency

The promised “avalanche” of investigations depended on Democrats winning at least one chamber. That makes accountability sound like a weather event arriving from outside government, when congressional oversight is a constitutional power exercised—or neglected—by elected officials.

The framing also lets executive officials appear besieged rather than answerable. Hiring lawyers before possible investigations can be prudent and proves no wrongdoing. But a Justice Department preparing to resist scrutiny while its congressional liaison departs illustrates how oversight becomes partisan trench warfare: one party anticipates investigations, the other prepares containment, and the underlying conduct risks becoming secondary to the combat.

The system protects the decision-makers

This story is not proved evidence of a panicked escape. It is evidence of something more durable: officials can construct ethically fraught programs, assign subordinates to defend them, and then blame those subordinates when the arrangement becomes difficult to explain.

The proposed fund, Davis’s potential financial interest and the department’s irritation at his recusal all point to the same governing pattern. Power writes the policy; intermediaries absorb the scrutiny; unnamed officials police loyalty; and accountability remains dependent on an election changing who controls the subpoenas.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump official abruptly flees DC before ‘avalanche’ of investigations

item.title: Elon Musk just crossed a dangerous line
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Elon Musk was involved in limiting Starshield service during a major Russian attack on Ukraine. Citing reporting by The Wall Street Journal and CBS News, it says connection-speed caps made some Ukrainian offensive and interceptor drones nearly unusable. The precise chain of command remains disputed: Musk blamed the Trump administration, administration sources blamed Musk, and the Journal reported that Musk’s team coordinated its public messaging with the White House.

The article also describes broader reductions in US support, including the reported withholding of Patriot missile shipments. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused President Donald Trump of helping Vladimir Putin through decisions involving sanctions and military support. Democratic senators Chris Murphy and Elizabeth Warren warned that the administration’s conduct was weakening Ukraine and that Musk possessed extraordinary influence over US foreign policy.

The power was privatized

The central issue is not Musk’s personality. It is that a military dependency was placed under the effective control of a billionaire whose company operates critical communications infrastructure and relies heavily on the federal government.

Musk did not acquire that leverage through an election or a public mandate. He acquired it because US institutions allowed a private contractor to become operationally indispensable. If one executive can materially affect battlefield communications, the state has outsourced not merely a service but part of its sovereign decision-making capacity.

That arrangement protects officials from accountability. The White House can point toward Musk; Musk can point toward the White House. Ukraine experiences the consequence while Americans receive competing accounts of who touched the switch.

Ambiguity is not absolution

The reporting cited by AlterNet does not conclusively establish whether Musk, Trump, or another official issued the decisive instruction. It does establish, as presented, Musk’s involvement and coordination between his team and the White House over messaging.

That distinction matters. The evidentiary gap should prevent claims of a proven conspiracy, but it should not erase institutional responsibility. The administration controls foreign policy and the federal contracting apparatus. Musk controlled infrastructure Ukraine reportedly needed during an attack. Both possessed power unavailable to the Ukrainians whose defense was impaired.

Treating this as administrative confusion would misdirect attention from the actual structure: powerful actors made or enabled a consequential restriction, then publicly disputed ownership of it.

Ukraine bears the cost

Zelensky’s leverage is sharply limited. Ukraine depends on American weapons, intelligence and communications while its leaders must negotiate with the same US officials and contractors capable of withholding them.

That dependency explains why public humiliation and policy reversals carry more than symbolic weight. A delayed missile shipment or degraded satellite connection can alter defensive capacity. Senator Murphy’s claim that the administration is positioning Ukraine for capitulation is his assessment, not an established fact, but the reported actions give that concern concrete substance.

The weaker actor here is not the corporation facing possible consumer anger. It is the country fighting an invasion while foreign officials and executives retain discretion over essential systems.

Accountability deferred

AlterNet points to Democratic interest in investigating Musk’s government contracts, foreign relationships, artificial-intelligence ventures and tenure at the Department of Government Efficiency if the party regains subpoena power. Those are prospective political plans, not present accountability.

The article weakens its own case when it moves from documented questions about Starshield and contracting into unproven implications of criminal exposure. A filmmaker’s accusation about “stock pumping” does not establish illegal market manipulation, and Musk’s joke about a possible prison sentence is not an admission. Those flourishes distract from the stronger, supportable indictment: public institutions created a private concentration of strategic power and have not provided a clear account of how it was exercised.

The systemic error

This story reveals what happens when privatization reaches the machinery of war. Government officials gain deniability, contractors gain geopolitical leverage, and allied countries inherit risks they cannot govern.

The scandal is therefore larger than whether Musk personally crossed some rhetorical line. The durable failure is a state that made one wealthy contractor difficult to replace, permitted uncertainty over who controlled a military capability, and left the consequences to a country under attack. When public authority and private power overlap this completely, opacity is not an accident at the edges of the system. It is one of the system’s principal protections.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Elon Musk just crossed a dangerous line

item.title: 'Not going to happen': Fox News has bad news for Trump
item.description:
What happened

The “bad news” came from Kevin Mahn, chief investment officer at Hennion and Walsh—not from Fox News as an institution. Appearing on Fox on Wednesday, Mahn said investors should not expect oil prices to fall quickly after the midterm elections or assume the Strait of Hormuz will simply reopen. With oil trading above $100 a barrel, he warned that sustained energy inflation could pressure the Federal Reserve to consider raising interest rates.

AlterNet reported that oil had approached $110 a barrel, a five-month high. Citing Reuters, it attributed the surge to intensified conflict around the Strait of Hormuz, stalled negotiations with Iran and declining oil stocks after President Donald Trump ordered the release of 820,000 barrels from the national reserve. The report also cited at least 18 vessel attacks over two weeks and statements from Iranian officials rejecting dialogue under what they described as US blockade and threats.

The administration’s other reported responses have offered uncertain or limited relief. AlterNet said temporarily allowing restricted dyed diesel produced little benefit and could create tax complications for farmers; an announced $8 billion farmer bailout offered little per farm and lacked sufficient funding; and Trump removed sanctions to permit Russian diesel imports. Fox anchor Liz Claman added that households were already confronting sharply higher beef and grocery costs.

The headline hides the actor

Fox News did not collectively deliver a verdict against Trump. Mahn made a market assessment during a Fox appearance, and Claman supplied a blunt reminder about grocery prices. Converting that exchange into “Fox has bad news” turns a specific economic warning into palace intrigue: the supposedly loyal broadcaster is now disappointing the president.

That framing trivializes the substance. The important conflict is not between Trump and a television network. It is between presidential decisions, an escalating regional confrontation and the material limits of executive improvisation. Oil markets do not become obedient because friendly media maintain message discipline.

Power sits with governments

Trump holds the institutional power described in this story. He ordered the reserve release, altered diesel rules, announced agricultural assistance, removed sanctions affecting Russian diesel and, according to AlterNet’s characterization, initiated the war with Iran. Iranian officials and forces also exercise state power in the confrontation, while the Federal Reserve independently controls interest-rate policy.

Consumers, farmers and homebuyers hold none of those levers. They absorb the consequences through fuel bills, food prices, taxes and borrowing costs. Treating their hardship as an atmospheric “energy crisis” obscures the chain of authority between government decisions and household exposure.

Improvisation is not control

The reported policy sequence suggests an administration searching for short-term offsets after the damage became visible. A narrowly useful diesel waiver, an underfunded bailout, sanctioned fuel imports reversed under pressure and a modest reserve release do not resolve disrupted shipping or a military confrontation.

That does not prove every measure was adopted solely for political appearance. It does show that the government’s tools, as reported, were mismatched to the scale of the problem. The administration could announce relief, but it could not command lower oil prices—and each attempted workaround carried costs or limitations of its own.

The economic chain is political

Mahn’s warning identifies the broader transmission mechanism. Prolonged oil prices above $100 can raise transportation and production costs; persistent inflation could then influence the Federal Reserve’s rate decisions. Higher rates would deepen pressure on housing affordability already strained by borrowing costs.

This is how foreign policy reaches the grocery aisle and the mortgage application. Claman’s reference to beef prices matters because it punctures the effort to isolate energy policy from everyday life. Households do not experience fuel, food and housing as separate policy categories. They experience one shrinking budget.

Crisis without accountability

The larger pattern is executive power followed by dispersed consequences. Presidents can escalate conflicts, adjust sanctions and draw from national reserves. The resulting costs arrive through markets and independent institutions, allowing responsibility to dissolve into talk of investor assumptions, supply disruptions and Federal Reserve reactions.

AlterNet identifies Trump’s decisions but weakens its own case by packaging the story as embarrassing news delivered by Fox. The central fact is not that a friendly network aired an unwelcome forecast. It is that concentrated political power can create risks that no televised reassurance, temporary waiver or thinly funded bailout can make disappear.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Not going to happen’: Fox News has bad news for Trump

item.title: Cornered Trump demands miracles from agency he gutted
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration wants to pursue tax charges against people accused of profiting from fraud, even as its own staffing and budget decisions have weakened the agencies needed to bring those cases. Justice Department fraud official Colin McDonald said investigators had identified dozens of cases involving an alleged combined $490 million in attempted fraud against the government.

According to figures cited from The Wall Street Journal, the IRS Criminal Investigation division lost 331 staff members last year, including 101 special agents. Its capacity was further reduced when work equivalent to 170 full-time agents was redirected to immigration and street-crime enforcement between May 2025 and March 2026. The administration has also proposed another $1.4 billion IRS budget cut for 2027.

AlterNet further notes that nearly 7,000 probationary IRS employees began receiving dismissal letters in February 2025, before the agency struggled to reverse some firings during tax season. Former IRS official Carolyn Schenck told the Journal that criminal tax cases are labor-intensive and the new initiative would be difficult to execute with diminished resources.

The power sits in the White House

This is not an agency inexplicably failing to meet an abstract challenge. The Trump administration controls the executive branch’s enforcement priorities, proposed the additional IRS cut, sought to unwind the Biden-era staffing increase and redirected criminal-investigation capacity toward its preferred enforcement campaigns.

Those were choices. Now the same administration is announcing an antifraud ambition that depends on the personnel and expertise those choices depleted. The contradiction belongs to the officials who created it, not to career investigators being asked to manufacture capacity from a shrinking workforce.

Enforcement by slogan

McDonald’s basic premise is sound: illicit income can generate tax liability, and tax charges can strengthen fraud prosecutions. But a prosecutorial memo is not an enforcement apparatus. Criminal tax cases require investigators, financial analysis and sustained institutional attention.

The administration is treating specialized capacity as if it were interchangeable labor. It moved IRS criminal investigators into immigration and street-crime work, then turned around and demanded a stronger tax-fraud push. That is governance reduced to announcements: declare a priority, strip away its machinery and expect the bureaucracy to absorb the contradiction.

Scarcity creates selective justice

Sean O’Connell, a former prosecutor quoted in the reporting, warned that expanding tax charges in existing fraud cases could pull investigators away from complex corporate-tax work. That is the political consequence of engineered scarcity. When enforcement capacity contracts, officials do not merely do less; they decide which violations receive scrutiny and which sophisticated actors benefit from neglect.

The new approach appears designed to attach tax charges to cases already underway. That may produce prosecutions, but it is not a substitute for the painstaking investigations required to uncover complicated corporate tax misconduct. A government can advertise toughness against readily identifiable defendants while leaving harder, better-resourced targets comparatively insulated.

The framing obscures responsibility

Describing the initiative as “running up against” budget cuts makes an imposed constraint sound like weather. The administration is not encountering an unrelated shortage. Its staffing reductions, proposed budget cut and diversion of investigators helped produce the shortage.

Nor were thousands of dismissals merely an administrative mishap. Administration lawyers defended the mass terminations as lawful exercises of authority. The subsequent scramble to halt firings and rehire workers during tax season does not erase agency. It shows the predictable institutional damage caused when dismantling government is pursued first and operational consequences are considered later.

Sabotage followed by spectacle

The larger pattern is government by self-created emergency. Political leaders weaken an institution, redirect its expertise and then demand conspicuous results from what remains. When performance deteriorates, the bureaucracy can be portrayed as sluggish or inadequate, while the officials who removed its capacity present themselves as reformers.

The immediate cost may be fewer viable tax cases or investigators pulled from complex corporate enforcement. The systemic cost is deeper: public administration becomes a stage for commands that cannot be carried out at the promised scale. Power escapes accountability by blaming the institution for failing under burdens that power itself imposed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Cornered Trump demands miracles from agency he gutted

item.title: Trump White House rocked by 'no paper trail' scandal
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that CNN analyst Aaron Blake identified a cluster of alleged conflicts, financial entanglements, and possible influence trading around President Donald Trump’s administration. The “no paper trail” allegation concerns former ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle: according to text messages obtained by The Wall Street Journal, she repeatedly discouraged written records while seeking $100,000 for credit-card debt from a man she was helping lobby the administration. Her lawyers deny the allegations.

Blake also cited aircraft purchases by the Department of Homeland Security from a donor to an outgoing secretary, with current and former officials blaming each other; a Russian oligarch’s reported payment toward Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding festivities, later refunded; and a Justice Department adviser’s acceptance of a prospective $50 million job from a banker who subsequently received a pardon. The adviser denied participating in the pardon.

AlterNet connects those reports to polling showing overwhelming concern about government corruption. Gallup found 89 percent of Americans describing corruption as widespread in the federal government, while Fox News found 88 percent extremely or very concerned. The article says other surveys associate Trump with the problem but also show little confidence that Democrats would correct it.

Power is not a mood

The decisive actors here are not vaguely defined “elites.” They are people controlling the presidency, federal appointments, procurement, pardons, and access to executive officials. Donors, investors, relatives, and prospective employers may seek influence, but public officials decide whether government power becomes available to them.

That distinction matters. A businessman can offer money; only an administration can award access, approve a purchase, shape policy, or issue a pardon. The presidency concentrates those powers, and the officials serving under Trump are responsible for how they exercise them.

Allegations require answers, not atmosphere

AlterNet’s headline promises a singular scandal rocking the White House. Its evidence is instead an accumulation of separate reports, some contested and some only loosely connected to official decisions. The Guilfoyle allegation is specific and documented in reported texts, but denied. The DHS aircraft purchase raises a procurement question, yet the account supplies neither the purchase price nor the evidence establishing inflation. The adviser’s lucrative job offer and the banker’s pardon create an obvious conflict concern, but she denies involvement in that pardon.

Those distinctions do not exonerate anyone. They identify what investigators and reporters must establish: who authorized each decision, what normal procedures required, whether those procedures were bypassed, and what benefit followed. A scandal montage can generate heat while leaving the machinery of responsibility frustratingly obscure.

Blame travels downward

The officials’ reported finger-pointing over the DHS aircraft purchase illustrates a familiar defense: distribute responsibility until no one appears to possess it. But a federal procurement did not materialize spontaneously. Named officials had authority, civil servants processed the transaction, and records should show who requested, reviewed, justified, and approved it.

The same principle applies to executive clemency. The politically important question is not merely whether a beneficiary had wealthy connections. It is who recommended the pardon, what review occurred, and who granted it. Trump held the pardon power. Any coverage that dwells on the surrounding social network while softening the president’s institutional agency misplaces the center of gravity.

Distrust is an outcome

The polling does not prove that any individual allegation caused public distrust. It does show that suspicion of government corruption is pervasive. That distrust becomes politically useful to the officials who benefit from weak oversight: every new allegation can be absorbed into a generalized belief that everyone is corrupt and nothing can be established.

Democratic skepticism compounds the problem. If voters expect a change in party control to produce no meaningful accountability, corruption stops looking like punishable misconduct and starts looking like a permanent operating system. That is not absolution through equivalence. Trump and his appointees remain responsible for decisions made under their authority.

The system protects the blur

The larger pattern is the conversion of public power into a field of private financial opportunity, followed by denial, diffusion, and procedural fog. Some allegations in AlterNet’s account may ultimately be substantiated; others may not. The systemic failure lies in how difficult it is for the public to trace benefits back to identifiable official acts—and how readily officials can exploit that uncertainty.

“No paper trail” is therefore more than a lurid phrase attributed to one former ambassador. It describes the political advantage produced when access, money, and executive authority overlap without prompt disclosure or credible investigation. The blur protects those with power. The public is left with suspicion, while the people capable of producing the records control whether clarity arrives.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump White House rocked by ‘no paper trail’ scandal

item.title: What Trump said to Stephen A. Smith after intense White House insults
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump initially accused Stephen A. Smith of being “nasty and mean” to him during a White House dinner attended by Smith, Bill Maher, and Kid Rock. Smith said he then challenged Trump over policies he believes discourage private support for historically Black colleges and universities and diversity initiatives.

According to Smith, Trump replied that he had not considered that effect and would think about it. Smith said Trump called several days later and asked him to repeat his points because the president planned to discuss them with others. Trump publicly described the dinner as successful, while suggesting his guests only criticize him to maintain a “facade” for their audiences. Journalist Jemele Hill called Smith’s participation a “dummy mission.”

Power sat at the table

Trump was not merely another dinner guest exchanging views. He was the president, hosting critics inside the White House while his administration controlled the policies Smith wanted reconsidered. Smith could make an argument; Trump held the institutional authority to act on it.

That distinction matters because access can create the appearance of influence without producing any measurable change. The reporting establishes that Trump listened, called back, and said he would speak with people. It does not establish that he changed a policy, issued an order, protected HBCU funding, or altered his administration’s approach to DEI.

The insult was a loyalty test

Trump’s opening complaint, as Smith recounted it, converted policy criticism into a personal offense. Smith was not first confronted on the merits of what he had said. He was accused of being mean to the president.

That tactic recenters political debate around the powerful man’s treatment rather than the consequences of his government’s decisions. The critic must explain his tone and relationship before the officeholder answers for policy. Smith did manage to raise substantive concerns, but only after passing through Trump’s ritual of personal grievance.

Access is not accountability

Smith had agency: he accepted the invitation and says he used it to press concerns directly. That is a defensible account of why someone might enter a room controlled by a politician he criticizes. Hill’s dismissal reflects the opposite judgment—that the encounter offered Trump legitimacy without securing a concrete result.

The available reporting cannot settle that argument because it identifies no outcome beyond continued conversation. Smith’s access may prove useful, or it may remain a flattering anecdote for everyone involved. Treating the meeting itself as an achievement would confuse proximity to power with power over policy.

Trump rewrote the encounter

Trump’s public claim that the guests “like Trump” but perform a critical “facade” for their audiences did more than declare the dinner cordial. It attempted to discredit their public criticism as insincere.

That is the sharper political move in the story. Trump could absorb critics into his own narrative simply because they accepted his invitation: private friendliness became supposed proof that public opposition was theater. Smith entered hoping to influence the president; the president used the encounter to suggest that Smith and Maher were misleading their audiences.

The politics of the private audience

This episode reveals a familiar imbalance in personality-driven government. The officeholder controls policy, access, venue, and the public interpretation of the meeting. The invited critic receives a hearing and must later prove that attending was worth the political cost.

AlterNet’s emphasis on the insults risks making the exchange sound like celebrity friction. The consequential question is whether presidential power changed course after hearing about potential harm to HBCUs and DEI initiatives. On the evidence reported, there was attention but no demonstrated action. A phone call is not a policy result, and powerful officials benefit whenever those two things are treated as interchangeable.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: What Trump said to Stephen A. Smith after intense White House insults

item.title: An eye-popping number of Republicans now want Trump impeached
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Politico poll conducted October 16–19 found 54 percent of Americans—including 25 percent of Republican voters planning to participate in the midterms—said President Donald Trump had committed impeachable offenses. The article’s headline overstates that finding: believing conduct is impeachable is not necessarily the same as wanting Congress to impeach him.

Half of respondents supported impeaching Trump, while more than two-thirds expected Democrats to attempt it if they won the House. The poll also found widespread doubt that House impeachment would materially constrain the president. Among Democratic midterm voters, majorities favored impeaching Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Vice President JD Vance; 49 percent supported impeaching Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

AlterNet says the polling preceded bipartisan anger over reported concessions to Russia and allegations that the administration hindered Ukraine’s war effort. It also cites a Telegraph report predicting that Pentagon insiders would provide information in proceedings against Hegseth promoted by Republican Representative Thomas Massie. Those allegations and predictions are not established as fact in the supplied reporting.

The headline outruns the evidence

The remarkable number is real but narrower than advertised. One quarter of surveyed Republican midterm voters said Trump had committed impeachable offenses. AlterNet converts that judgment into a desire to see him impeached, even though the article does not provide a Republican-only figure for actual support.

That slippage matters. A poll can reveal erosion inside a president’s coalition without proving that those voters want removal, intend to defect, or will make impeachment decisive in November. AlterNet further suggests the result has “major implications” for the election, but the poll establishes an attitude—not its electoral effect.

Power sits with Congress

Voters can register disapproval. They cannot initiate impeachment proceedings, subpoena administration officials, or convict anyone. Those powers belong to Congress, and the reporting says more than two-thirds of Americans expect Democrats to try impeachment only if they capture the House.

Even then, the public described in the poll doubts that a House vote would meaningfully weaken Trump. That is less a contradiction than a diagnosis of institutional arithmetic: impeachment can document misconduct and impose political costs, but removal requires power beyond a House majority. The decisive question is therefore not whether outrage exists. It is whether lawmakers controlling the relevant committees and votes will act on it.

Accountability becomes campaign merchandise

The article treats Republican unease as evidence that Democrats might profit by campaigning on impeachment. That converts a constitutional accountability mechanism into message testing. The central issue becomes whether the word polls well, rather than what conduct Congress can substantiate and what remedy the evidence warrants.

Democratic voters’ appetite for impeaching several senior officials compounds the problem. Kennedy, Hegseth, Vance, and Rubio occupy different offices and would require distinct factual and legal cases. Bundling them into one roster of targets may measure hostility to an administration, but it does not establish grounds against any particular official.

Allegations are not findings

The reporting invokes accusations involving Russia, Ukraine, and Hegseth to intensify the poll’s significance. But it supplies no adjudicated finding that the administration illegally obstructed Ukraine’s war effort, and its account of prospective Pentagon disclosures comes from an unnamed source predicting future cooperation and embarrassment.

These claims may justify investigation. They do not justify writing as though the investigation has already proved the case. When coverage collapses allegations, polling, and partisan strategy into one impeachment narrative, it weakens the very accountability it claims to champion.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is an accountability system filtered through electoral theater. Voters identify potentially impeachable conduct, anticipate congressional action, and simultaneously expect that action to change little. Media coverage then markets the dissatisfaction as a startling campaign development.

That framing misdirects attention from the officials who possess institutional authority. Republican voters expressing disapproval are not the operative power center; members of Congress deciding whether to investigate, subpoena, impeach, or protect the administration are. The consequential story is not that a surprising fraction of Republicans answered a poll critically. It is whether Congress will convert evidence into a disciplined case—or reduce constitutional power to another slogan calibrated for November.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: An eye-popping number of Republicans now want Trump impeached

item.title: Trump admin triggers showdown with furious judge
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration asked a federal appeals panel to condemn U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino’s use of civil contempt against Justice Department attorney Matthew Isihara. In February, Provinzino ordered Isihara to pay $500 a day until the government returned identification documents taken from a Minnesota man, after federal officials repeatedly failed to comply with her order.

The government returned the documents before any fines accrued, purging the contempt. Justice Department lawyers nevertheless argued that Provinzino improperly tried to coerce an agency by imposing personal consequences on its attorney. The appellate judges questioned whether any live dispute remained, while court-appointed amicus Jeffrey Justman argued that the panel should either uphold the order or dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

Power ignored the ordinary order

The institutional power belongs first to the executive branch officials who controlled the seized documents and then to the courts charged with enforcing lawful orders. Isihara was the lawyer standing before the judge, but the Justice Department was the client that had failed to produce the property.

Provinzino reportedly tried requests before resorting to contempt. The government complied only after continued defiance acquired a personal financial consequence for its representative. That sequence matters: the extraordinary measure did not create the confrontation. Executive noncompliance did.

The lawyer became the pressure point

The Justice Department’s strongest argument is also an indictment of its own conduct. It says Isihara lacked the personal ability to return the documents and should not have been used to coerce his client. Yet the department had supplied the court with no effective mechanism for compelling the officials who did possess that ability.

The order placed an individual attorney in an untenable position. But the administration’s framing risks making his predicament the central injury while minimizing the government’s repeated failure to return a Minnesota man’s identification documents. The weaker actor was not the federal agency represented by an Army lawyer. It was the person deprived of his property while officials blamed staffing shortages “again, and again, and again,” as Provinzino put it.

Compliance without accountability

Once contempt carried a daily price, the supposedly difficult task was completed before a fine came due. That does not prove why the earlier delays occurred, but it does show that ordinary judicial demands had failed to produce the result that coercive pressure produced quickly.

The appeal seeks something beyond relief for an unpaid penalty: a precedent restricting how judges may respond when government lawyers cannot or do not secure compliance from their agencies. Because the contempt was already purged, the panel questioned whether it could redress any remaining injury at all. The administration is effectively asking the judiciary to rebuke the tool that worked after the underlying violation disappeared.

Hollowed-out government, concentrated impunity

AlterNet reports that the Justice Department lost thousands of experienced employees, including attorneys, and turned to temporary lawyers drawn from the military and elsewhere. Isihara was among those stopgap personnel. That staffing collapse helps explain administrative dysfunction, but it does not transfer responsibility to the people harmed by it or oblige judges to accept noncompliance indefinitely.

An institution can weaken its own capacity and still insist on the full deference owed to a competent one. The result is a convenient asymmetry: the executive cites its depleted workforce when it misses obligations, then invokes institutional principle when a judge imposes consequences.

The systemic error

This case exposes a broader governing pattern: executive power treats compliance as negotiable until resistance becomes costly, then portrays the cost rather than the defiance as the institutional offense. The visible lawyer becomes the aggrieved party, the judge becomes the aggressor, and the person whose documents were withheld nearly vanishes from view.

Courts cannot enforce orders through ritual disappointment. If agencies can evade compliance through diffuse responsibility—no individual able to act, no office willing to answer, no remedy permitted to bite—judicial authority becomes advisory whenever the executive decides to wait it out.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump admin triggers showdown with furious judge

item.title: Nicolle Wallace left stunned as former official lists Trump’s concessions
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former State Department official Ned Price disputed President Donald Trump’s claim that his administration gave Russia “nothing in return” for the release of Stephen Hubbard. Speaking with Nicolle Wallace on Wednesday, Price pointed to actions he characterized as concessions to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Price cited an announced diesel deal, waived sanctions and tariffs, Trump’s reported demand that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil and diesel refineries, and degraded intelligence or technology sharing that Ukraine used for defense. He also said Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to step down, aligning with a longstanding Russian demand. The article does not provide responses from Trump, Russia, or Ukraine to Price’s claims.

AlterNet also quotes conservative foreign-policy analyst Rebecca Heinrichs, who argued earlier in October that negotiations conducted with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping rather than alongside Ukraine and European allies would be a serious mistake. In her assessment, Russia is seeking to weaken US support for Zelenskyy.

The power is in Washington

Wallace’s reaction supplies the headline’s drama, but her surprise is politically irrelevant. Trump holds executive power over US diplomacy, sanctions policy, intelligence cooperation, and support for Ukraine. Price and Heinrichs can describe the consequences; they cannot impose them.

That distinction matters because “coziness” is an inadequate description of the conduct Price alleges. Personal warmth is gossip. Directing Ukraine to limit attacks, reducing capabilities used for its defense, and calling for its president’s removal are exercises of state power with strategic consequences.

“Nothing” is the misdirection

Trump’s reported phrase narrows the transaction to a crude prisoner-swap ledger: Hubbard was released, and Moscow supposedly received nothing at that moment. Price’s argument is that the relevant account is wider. Concessions need not be announced as payment for a particular release to benefit the same government.

The article does not establish that every action Price lists was exchanged for Hubbard’s freedom. It does establish that Price challenged Trump’s description by identifying recent policies and statements he says favored Putin’s objectives. Treating those two claims as interchangeable would overstate the evidence; ignoring the larger policy record would accept Trump’s framing on his terms.

Ukraine becomes an object

Heinrichs identifies the underlying power arrangement: major states discussing Ukraine while marginalizing Ukraine and its European partners. Her Yalta analogy is a warning about powerful governments deciding the fate of a smaller country without granting it equal agency.

Price’s most consequential allegation follows the same pattern. A US president calling for Zelenskyy’s departure does not merely criticize another leader. It uses the authority and reach of the United States to place additional pressure on the government Russia invaded. According to Price, that demand reproduces Putin’s preferred outcome.

The spectacle obscures the decision-maker

AlterNet packages the exchange around Wallace being “stunned.” That is cable-news framing: the presenter’s face becomes the event while executive decisions become items in a provocative list.

The stronger story is not that a television host reacted visibly. It is that Trump reportedly claimed there was no reciprocal benefit to Russia while a former US official identified multiple administration actions that, in his assessment, advanced Russian interests. The reaction shot personalizes what should be an examination of presidential power.

Foreign policy by denial

The broader pattern is governance through atomized claims. Each decision is presented alone, stripped of the sequence that gives it political meaning. A restriction is merely restraint, reduced assistance is an administrative adjustment, and pressure on an invaded country’s leader is treated as an isolated opinion. Then the administration declares that nothing was conceded.

Price’s case remains an attributed assessment, not proof of a secret bargain or motive. But the foreseeable distribution of power is clear within the reporting: Russia gains leverage, Ukraine faces tighter constraints, and the White House controls the policies producing that imbalance. The systemic error is allowing the government that made those choices to define “concession” so narrowly that consequences disappear from the ledger.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Nicolle Wallace left stunned as former official lists Trump’s concessions

item.title: From 'shopping cart' chaos to nuclear codes: Trump's psychological red flags
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that clinical psychologist Vincent Greenwood described President Donald Trump’s conduct as showing “ominous” traits—impulsivity, remorselessness and a drive to dominate—and argued that they justified considering the 25th Amendment. Greenwood warned that the danger could increase if Republicans suffered major losses in the then-upcoming midterm elections.

The article also cites an open letter signed in May by 36 medical experts warning Congress about Trump’s fitness for office. Its lead author, Henry Abraham, stressed that clinicians observing Trump publicly could identify warning signs but could not establish a diagnosis without a full examination and the subject’s cooperation.

The reporting therefore establishes professional alarm and a call for institutional scrutiny, not a confirmed psychiatric diagnosis. The supermarket “shopping cart” episode was Abraham’s metaphor for conspicuously abnormal behavior, not an event involving Trump.

Power is not a diagnosis

The central political fact is simpler than the clinical argument: Trump held presidential authority, including command over the military, while the officials empowered to restrain him retained their own choices. A president’s temperament matters because institutions place enormous coercive power in one person’s hands. But psychological terminology does not explain why that power remained available despite publicly expressed concerns.

Greenwood could recommend considering the 25th Amendment. He could not invoke it. That authority belonged principally to the vice president and a majority of the Cabinet, subject to congressional procedures if the president contested the declaration. Congress separately possessed oversight and impeachment powers. The decisive actors were not clinicians warning from outside government, but officeholders choosing what to do with those warnings.

The enablers disappear from view

By organizing the story around Trump’s possible condition, the framing risks turning a political arrangement into a medical mystery. The unanswered question is not merely what drove Trump’s behavior. It is why Republican officials continued entrusting presidential power to someone whom experts quoted by AlterNet considered dangerously impulsive.

That distinction matters. A diagnosis, even if one could responsibly be made, would not remove a president, limit his authority or absolve those who enabled him. Institutions act only when people use the powers attached to their offices. Treating the danger as one man’s pathology can quietly erase the agency of Cabinet members, legislators and party leaders who benefited from keeping him in place.

Alarm is not adjudication

The article acknowledges the central evidentiary limit: neither Greenwood’s characterization nor the doctors’ letter constitutes a clinical examination of Trump. Abraham explicitly said observers could recognize red flags without knowing their specific cause. That caveat should govern the entire argument.

The strongest case does not require converting public conduct into a definitive diagnosis. Officials can assess observable behavior, decision-making and fitness without pretending that political opposition is medical proof. When commentary outruns that boundary, it gives Trump’s defenders an easy diversion: debate psychiatric labels instead of answering for conduct and institutional consequences.

The system chose exposure

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as uncertainty. Experts raise alarms; journalists debate whether those alarms amount to diagnosis; empowered officials avoid acting while insisting that the evidence is somehow never conclusive enough. Responsibility dissolves into a discussion of symptoms.

Presidential systems become especially brittle when a governing party’s access to power depends on protecting its leader from scrutiny. The lasting issue is not whether one clinician selected the perfect label. It is that concentrated executive authority remained protected by people with the legal power to challenge it—and every incentive to look elsewhere.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: From ‘shopping cart’ chaos to nuclear codes: Trump’s psychological red flags

item.title: Trump’s 'freak show' rallies have a problem even Republicans can’t ignore
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves called President Donald Trump’s campaign rallies a “freak show at the carnival” and questioned whether Trump’s Monday appearance in Wichita would help Republican Sen. Roger Marshall win reelection. Graves argued that spectators may attend for Trump’s performance without becoming votes for Marshall—and that the rally could instead energize Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton’s supporters.

The intervention came as a New York Times poll cited by the outlet placed Marshall and Hamilton at 45 percent each. CNN reported that Hamilton raised $9 million from July through September, compared with roughly $800,000 for Marshall. The Cook Political Report nevertheless rated the contest “Likely Republican,” and Graves acknowledged that a Democratic victory in Kansas would remain difficult.

Trump praised Marshall and predicted his victory while dismissing unfavorable polls as fake. Graves, who has endorsed Hamilton, criticized Marshall’s record, cited higher prices and harm from agricultural tariffs, and portrayed the senator as unwilling to exercise judgment independent of Trump.

The power belongs to the incumbents

The powerful actors here are not rally spectators. Trump holds the presidency and commands the Republican Party’s most valuable political machinery. Marshall holds a Senate seat in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Their problem is not exclusion from power; it is that their use of power has produced a contest they expected to control.

That distinction matters. A close poll does not establish that Hamilton will win, but it does expose Republican vulnerability. Trump’s arrival in Wichita was an exercise of institutional and partisan power intended to protect an incumbent, not merely another stop by a touring entertainer.

Marshall chose dependence

Graves’s sharper accusation is not that Trump is distracting. It is that Marshall has subordinated his political identity to the president. Trump can provide the spectacle, but Marshall chose to rely on it.

That choice helps explain the rally’s uncertain value. Trump’s devoted audience is not automatically transferable to another candidate. If Marshall cannot offer voters an affirmative case for his own tenure, presidential praise becomes a substitute for accountability: loyalty is presented as qualification, and association with power stands in for a record worth defending.

Spectacle is the instrument

Calling the rally a carnival captures its appearance but risks understating its function. The performance is part of the governing method. Trump praises the loyalist, predicts victory and labels inconvenient polling fake. The rally asks supporters to treat his confidence as more authoritative than outside measurement.

Republican strategists cited in the reporting still consider these events useful for mobilizing voters who might otherwise stay home. That may be true. But the Kansas contest illustrates the limit: spectacle can intensify allegiance without repairing the policies, economic complaints or candidate weaknesses that made mobilization necessary.

The weaker actors are not the cause

Coverage of political rallies often fixates on the crowd—its appetite for entertainment, its devotion or its anger. That framing can misdirect responsibility downward. Attendees did not decide agricultural tariff policy, create Marshall’s record or direct Republican campaign strategy. Officeholders did.

Nor is the central conflict a mysterious disagreement over whether rallies “work.” Trump decided to intervene. Marshall accepted the intervention. Republican strategists hope presidential celebrity can compensate for an endangered incumbent. Hamilton’s fundraising and the reported dead heat show why that calculation was made, even if neither proves what voters will ultimately do.

A machine consuming its candidates

The larger pattern is a party built around one politician discovering that personal loyalty and electoral usefulness are not identical. Candidates are expected to embrace Trump to reach his base, then absorb the consequences of his unpopular policies and low approval ratings described in the reporting. Some hesitate, but the party’s structure leaves them few competing sources of authority.

Kansas makes that dependency unusually visible. A seat once presumed safe required presidential intervention; the president denied the unfavorable numbers while campaigning because of them. The rally may still help Marshall, and the Republican advantage may still hold. But when an incumbent’s strongest argument is the leader’s blessing, the party is no longer developing independent representatives. It is producing dependents and hoping the show can carry them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘freak show’ rallies have a problem even Republicans can’t ignore
