item.title: The trigger that finally cracked Trump's base
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that corruption—not a sudden conversion over Russia—finally fractured Donald Trump’s political base. The immediate triggers were his failure to deliver the complete Epstein files he had promised, worsening living costs, and growing suspicion that he was using the presidency for personal enrichment.

The outlet also reports a sharp turn toward Vladimir Putin: Trump lifted restrictions on Russian diesel, declined to enforce new sanctions approved by Congress, and held up Patriot missile shipments to Ukraine. It says Ukraine also lost access to Starshield during a major Russian missile attack, although the article does not establish who ordered that interruption.

AlterNet cites polls showing intense concern about corruption and increasing belief, including among Republican-leaning respondents, that Trump is enriching himself in office. Its conclusion—that his supporters are preparing to punish him and may reconsider his relationship with Putin—is an interpretation, not a demonstrated electoral outcome.

Material harm broke the spell

The reported trigger was not one revelation. It was the moment corruption stopped sounding like an ethical abstraction and became an explanation for betrayal, high prices and government decisions serving wealthy insiders.

That distinction matters. Trump’s supporters had long been offered evidence of misconduct and trained to dismiss it as enemy propaganda. But loyalty becomes harder to maintain when promised disclosures remain hidden, billionaires appear protected and economic pain reaches the grocery aisle and gas pump. AlterNet’s cited focus groups suggest some Republican voters now connect that pain to “corrupt politicians” and “billionaires.”

Whether that diagnosis is economically complete is not established here. Politically, however, it shows how legitimacy erodes: not when elites produce one more indictment of character, but when ordinary costs become attached to recognizable decisions and beneficiaries.

The power belongs to the presidency

Ukraine, voters and rank-and-file Republicans are not the principal actors in the decisions described. The institutional power sits in the White House: control over sanctions enforcement, military assistance and the diplomatic posture of the United States.

Trump therefore cannot be treated as a spectator to an inexplicable “pivot.” According to the reporting, his administration eased pressure on Russia, declined to implement congressionally approved sanctions and delayed defensive weapons for Ukraine. Those are exercises of state power with foreseeable advantages for Putin’s war effort.

The Starshield episode requires more caution because AlterNet itself leaves responsibility unresolved, speculating that Trump or Elon Musk may have acted. That gap should not be papered over. The other reported decisions are serious enough without converting uncertainty into accusation.

Russia is not the distraction

For years, “Russia” became a media shorthand that allowed the underlying power question to disappear beneath partisan theater. The relevant issue was never whether Trump looked personally disloyal in some dramatic, cinematic sense. It was whether presidential authority was being used in ways that benefited Putin while weakening Ukraine and the Western alliance.

The critics quoted by AlterNet make severe claims. The Atlantic’s Tom Nichols described the sanctions decision as abandonment of the Western security order. National Review’s Andrew McCarthy argued that Trump’s conduct could fit the Constitution’s language about giving an enemy “aid and comfort” and called for immediate congressional hearings. Those are their assessments, not legal findings of treason.

The article weakens its case when it leaps from reported policy choices to the categorical slogan that Trump is “Putin’s puppet.” The evidence supports scrutiny of concrete acts. The slogan substitutes certainty about motive and control that the reporting does not establish.

Congress cannot outsource responsibility

If Congress approved sanctions and the president refused to enforce them, congressional power did not end with the vote. Hearings, appropriations, oversight and political confrontation are available precisely because executive obstruction is foreseeable.

Calling Trump’s conduct shocking can become its own form of evasion. Legislators and political institutions have had years to understand his posture toward Putin. If they possess authority to impose consequences but settle for alarmed commentary, that is institutional cowardice—not confusion.

The same applies to a press corps now rediscovering Hillary Clinton’s 2016 warning. Jake Tapper’s repost may reflect a changing elite consensus, as AlterNet argues, but belated recognition does not erase the media incentives that previously reduced substantive questions about Russian influence to campaign spectacle.

Corruption is a governing system

The larger pattern is not that a loyal base suddenly learned one decisive fact. It is that patronage, secrecy and concentrated executive power became costly enough to penetrate an identity built around denial.

That does not guarantee a durable realignment. Polls measure opinion at a moment; focus groups reveal attitudes, not election results. Nor does dissatisfaction prove that voters have accepted every allegation about Trump and Russia.

But the political structure is plain. A president exercises enormous discretion, wealthy actors operate close to that power, Congress struggles or refuses to compel compliance, and the press often waits for opinion polls before treating documented decisions as significant. Corruption becomes politically dangerous to its beneficiaries only when people can trace private advantage and public suffering through the same chain of power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The trigger that finally cracked Trump’s base

item.title: Psychologist warns Trump’s confusion and seizures aren’t getting better
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist John Paul Garrison believes Donald Trump’s apparent confusion and “seizure-like episodes” are not improving. Garrison based that assessment on public footage, including a White House event on women’s health and a rally in Kentucky—not on a personal medical examination.

At the White House event, Garrison said he observed movements spreading across Trump’s arms, face and eyes, along with faster speech afterward and apparent “microsleeps.” He said the behavior appeared consistent with seizure activity but acknowledged that many conditions could produce such symptoms.

At the Kentucky rally, Trump described an alleged Joe Biden gaffe involving Maine, Florida and palm trees. Garrison said he could not find evidence that the incident occurred and interpreted Trump’s trailing, internally inconsistent account as another sign of confusion. AlterNet provides no medical records, examination results or independent clinical assessment establishing a diagnosis.

The diagnosis the evidence cannot carry

The headline turns one psychologist’s remote interpretation into a claim about Trump’s medical trajectory. But “aren’t getting better” presumes a documented condition and a reliable baseline against which improvement could be measured. The article establishes neither.

Garrison’s professional credentials may inform his observations, but they do not convert edited public appearances into a neurological examination. He explicitly says he has not evaluated Trump. His references to stroke effects and vascular dementia are examples of possible causes, not diagnoses. Blurring that distinction produces medical certainty the reporting does not possess.

Power sits in the presidency

The legitimate political issue is not amateur diagnosis. Trump holds presidential power, and the public has a concrete interest in whether he can exercise it competently. The White House has access to his physicians, schedule and health information. Trump and his administration therefore possess the institutional capacity to clarify credible concerns—or to leave the public dependent on video analysis and speculation.

That imbalance matters. A YouTube commentator cannot order testing, disclose results or determine presidential fitness. The officials surrounding Trump can provide evidence, invoke formal procedures if warranted, or continue managing appearances. Coverage should scrutinize those actors and mechanisms instead of treating an outside psychologist as the central authority.

The Biden story is a factual test

Trump’s account of a supposed Biden mistake is politically relevant without any neurological theory. According to Garrison, he could not locate the gaffe Trump described, and Trump’s reference to palm trees made the story internally incoherent. If the anecdote was false or badly mangled, the first journalistic task is to establish that plainly.

Replacing a factual question with speculation about cognition creates an escape hatch. A powerful politician who spreads an unsupported story can be held responsible for what he says regardless of why he said it. Confusion, fabrication and careless repetition are different explanations, and the supplied reporting cannot determine which applies.

Spectacle displaces accountability

AlterNet’s framing directs attention toward Trump’s body and Garrison’s interpretation of it. That is vivid material, but it weakens the stronger inquiry: what claims did the president make, were they true, and how are the White House and other officials responding to observable concerns about his performance?

The larger pattern is political journalism substituting diagnosis-by-clip for institutional reporting. It invites audiences to debate symptoms while the people with actual authority avoid harder questions about transparency, capacity and responsibility. The consequence is not clarity. It is a fog in which medical conjecture competes with partisan instinct and the presidency escapes sustained scrutiny.

The system rewards uncertainty

Presidential power does not become less consequential because the available evidence is inconclusive. It makes accurate reporting more necessary. Journalists should document observable behavior, verify public claims and press empowered officials for substantiated information. They should not promote a remote assessment into a medical finding.

When institutions withhold evidence, speculation predictably fills the vacuum. But speculation is not accountability. The systemic failure is a political and media structure that turns uncertainty into content while leaving those who hold the records, authority and constitutional responsibility at the edge of the frame.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist warns Trump’s confusion and seizures aren’t getting better

item.title: Delusional Truth Social rant proves Trump has finally lost the plot
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump blamed Republican strategist Karl Rove and Texas Sen. John Cornyn for making it harder for Trump-backed Ken Paxton to defeat Democrat James Talarico in a Texas Senate race. The article argues that Trump’s Truth Social post—especially his praise of Paxton as Texas’s greatest attorney general—exposed the weakness of his own judgment rather than establishing sabotage by Rove or Cornyn.

The outlet also describes Republican Senate campaigns in Georgia and North Carolina as faltering after Trump helped elevate Mike Collins and Michael Whatley, respectively. It says Republican leaders had canceled millions of dollars in advertising in those races, while incumbents in Ohio, Kansas, and Nebraska faced unexpectedly difficult contests.

None of the cited polling establishes who will win. AlterNet explicitly acknowledges that uncertainty and frames its case conditionally: if Trump-backed Republicans lose on November 3, the article argues, Trump’s interventions will be a central cause.

Power belongs to the president

Rove may retain influence, and Cornyn may retain a political network, but neither holds the power described here. Trump is the president, the dominant figure in his party, and the official whose endorsements helped shape Republican nominations.

That distinction matters because Trump’s accusation reverses the chain of responsibility. He promoted Paxton, attacked Cornyn, helped Collins secure the Georgia nomination, pressured Tillis before his retirement, and backed Whatley in North Carolina. According to AlterNet’s account, Trump exercised power repeatedly. Rove is being assigned blame after those choices produced political risk.

The scapegoat is the strategy

Trump offered no evidence in the reporting that Rove and Cornyn were “doing everything possible” to defeat Paxton. The accusation functions as preemptive blame allocation: if Paxton wins, Trump can claim vindication; if Paxton loses, designated traitors can absorb the failure.

Calling this mere confusion would miss the political utility. Trump’s post shifts attention from the candidate he endorsed and the intervention he made to figures with less control over the result. The rant is not proof that he has literally “lost the plot.” It is evidence of a familiar refusal to accept accountability.

Loyalty displaced competence

The article’s strongest case is not psychological but institutional. Trump used presidential and party power to favor candidates who pleased him personally, despite liabilities that could burden Republican campaigns.

AlterNet notes that Paxton narrowly survived an impeachment effort in the Texas Legislature and that former staff members had accused him of corruption. It describes Collins as under House Ethics Committee investigation and reports associations between his political operation and white supremacists. Those are allegations and unresolved concerns, not convictions. But they are plainly relevant electoral risks—and Trump’s praise does not erase them.

Whatley’s thin record and the reported criticism of North Carolina’s Hurricane Helene recovery present the same structural problem. A party organized around one leader’s approval rewards displays of loyalty while weakening its ability to screen candidates for competence, credibility, or broad appeal.

The framing overreaches

AlterNet is right to center Trump’s agency, but its headline substitutes armchair diagnosis for political analysis. A social-media tirade cannot prove delusion, and “lost the plot” explains less than the article’s own evidence does.

The observable conduct is sharper: a powerful official made consequential endorsements, dismissed candidates’ vulnerabilities, and then accused weaker actors of causing the resulting danger. That is not a medical judgment. It is an accountability judgment grounded in who possessed authority and how that authority was used.

The article also occasionally treats prospective losses as more settled than the evidence permits. Polling, canceled advertising, and negative approval ratings indicate danger; they do not establish election results or prove a single cause.

A party built to evade consequences

The larger pattern is personalist rule converting an institution into an alibi machine. Candidate selection becomes a loyalty contest. Electoral weakness becomes sabotage. The person with the greatest power presents himself as the person least responsible.

That arrangement damages more than campaign strategy. It trains officials to flatter upward, blame sideways, and conceal foreseeable consequences until voters impose them. Whether every named Republican wins or loses, the governing defect is already visible: power is concentrated around Trump, while responsibility is continually exported to everyone else.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Delusional Truth Social rant proves Trump has finally lost the plot

item.title: GOP insiders stunned as 'bamboozled' rural Americans blame the rich
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican operatives were surprised when rural voters in recent focus-group conversations blamed billionaires, corrupt politicians, and a rigged economic system for their financial distress. The reporting does not establish that these voters are moving to the Democratic Party, but it says some are receptive to populist economic arguments.

The article cites rural voters in Colorado and Arizona who expressed disappointment with President Donald Trump’s economic record, war decisions, and government spending. One Colorado farmer said he felt “bamboozled” and planned to sit out the coming election. A Fox News poll released the week before AlterNet’s report found that 60% of voters were extremely concerned about government corruption, compared with 58% about inflation and 50% about gas prices.

The surprise is the indictment

The remarkable fact is not that rural Americans recognize concentrated wealth and political corruption. It is that Republican professionals were reportedly astonished to hear them say so.

That reaction exposes the operating assumption beneath the party’s rural strategy: economic anger can be harvested indefinitely so long as voters are directed toward immigrants, cultural enemies, or distant bureaucrats instead of the wealthy interests financing political power. The voters did not suddenly discover hardship. They began naming beneficiaries.

Power belongs to the people writing the rules

Rural voters possess electoral power, but they do not set tariff policy, initiate military action, allocate federal spending, or decide whose money sustains national campaigns. Those powers belong to presidents, lawmakers, senior officials, and the donor networks with privileged access to them.

AlterNet reports that Elon Musk has directed at least $276 million since July to Republican groups and his own super PAC. That figure does not prove that any specific policy was purchased. It does, however, clarify the imbalance: voters supply legitimacy one ballot at a time, while billionaires can spend fortunes shaping which candidates, messages, and institutions reach those voters.

Trump named the rigging, then owned the result

Montana Democratic candidate Sam Forstag argues that Trump accurately identified a broken system but failed to repair it. That is a campaign rival’s interpretation, not an established explanation of every voter’s discontent. Yet the voters quoted by AlterNet describe the same basic rupture: they expected Trump and his team to fix material problems, and they now judge the results against that promise.

The responsibility cannot be dissolved into “the economy” as though it were weather. The administration chose its trade, military, and spending priorities. Republican lawmakers and allied organizations enabled or defended those choices. When the reported consequences reached rural communities, political professionals treated the resulting anger as an unexpected change in voter mood rather than a judgment on decisions made by people with power.

Disengagement still protects the powerful

The Colorado farmer who plans to sit out the election is not transferring his support to an alternative coalition. He is withdrawing it. That distinction matters.

Disillusionment does not automatically become organized opposition. It can instead remove dissatisfied voters from the contest while donors, party institutions, and committed blocs retain their influence. A person who concludes that politics is hopeless may be registering a rational response to repeated betrayal, but the institutional effect is brutally convenient for those already equipped to govern without meaningful accountability.

The scapegoat has an expiration date

The larger pattern is a collision between populist language and donor-dependent government. Political leaders can condemn elites while relying on immense private fortunes, promise economic rescue while imposing disruptive policies, and present public frustration as confusion rather than consequence.

But scapegoating works only while anger remains pointed away from power. Once voters connect their economic pain to billionaires, officeholders, and the policies those officeholders chose, the propaganda machinery develops a targeting problem. The danger for Republican strategists is not merely that rural voters are unhappy. It is that some are beginning to identify who had the authority to act—and who benefited while they waited.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP insiders stunned as ‘bamboozled’ rural Americans blame the rich

item.title: Robert Reich slams the NYT For 'dangerously fraudulent' coverage
item.description:
What happened

Robert Reich accused The New York Times of “dangerously fraudulent” coverage for presenting online reactions to a Michigan Senate debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as two roughly equivalent partisan narratives. As described by AlterNet, the Times analyzed more than 13,000 posts on X and contrasted what purportedly left- and right-leaning feeds showed users.

The Times reported that left-leaning accounts emphasized El-Sayed’s positions on war, affordability, and healthcare, while right-leaning accounts frequently attacked his Muslim faith, questioned his medical background, or praised Rogers’s demeanor. Reich argued that packaging those responses as symmetrical “dueling narratives” obscured differences in both substance and the candidates’ records.

The AlterNet article supplies Reich’s critique but not the underlying Times analysis, dataset, classification method, or responses from the Times, Rogers, or El-Sayed. Its claims about the candidates’ records and positions are therefore presented here as Reich’s assertions, not independently established facts.

The institution with power

The decisive power in this story does not belong to anonymous social-media users. It belongs to the Times, whose editors chose the analytical frame, selected the categories, and converted thousands of posts into a polished visual argument.

Calling one set of posts “left-leaning” and another “right-leaning” may describe audience alignment. It does not determine whether their claims are accurate, relevant, or equally abusive. A graph can measure volume and timing while laundering away those distinctions.

That is the central editorial failure Reich identifies: the Times did not merely observe polarization. It organized the evidence so polarization became the story.

Symmetry without equivalence

The reporting summarized by AlterNet undercuts the equivalence it constructs. One group discussed policy matters such as living costs, healthcare, and war. The other, according to the Times passages AlterNet cites, often directed personal attacks at El-Sayed, including criticism involving his Muslim beliefs.

Those are not interchangeable forms of partisan enthusiasm. Treating them as matching reactions shifts attention from what people said to which “side” said it. The result is numerical symmetry standing in for editorial judgment.

Even the note that El-Sayed earned a medical degree but never practiced medicine risks assisting that distortion when detached from the question at issue: whether skepticism about his background was factually grounded, politically relevant, or simply another vehicle for disparagement.

What the frame conceals

Reich argues that readers needed the candidates’ records and governing agendas, not a tour through algorithmically filtered reactions. He describes Rogers as aligned with Donald Trump and cites Rogers’s votes for the Patriot Act, the Iraq War, and surveillance legislation. He portrays El-Sayed as supporting single-payer healthcare, taxes on billionaire wealth, restrictions on corporate campaign money, regulation of AI and data centers, changes to the Supreme Court, and an end to US military aid to Israel.

Whether every characterization survives fuller scrutiny cannot be determined from AlterNet’s article alone. But Reich’s underlying standard is sound: political journalism should test records, proposals, and factual claims. It should not replace that work with a taxonomy of audience sentiment.

The Times may have intended to explain how algorithmic feeds produce divergent perceptions. As presented here, however, the analysis appears to reproduce the algorithm’s central trick: rewarding identity, conflict, and reaction while pushing material stakes out of view.

The systemic error

This is horse-race journalism adapted to the platform age. Instead of counting campaign stops or obsessing over tactical momentum, the newsroom counts posts and maps partisan affect. The method looks empirical because it contains thousands of data points. Its political emptiness remains.

The larger pattern is institutional evasion through format. Powerful news organizations can avoid adjudicating evidence by treating every conflict as a contest between rival perceptions. That posture protects the newsroom from accusations of partiality, but it leaves readers with less knowledge about who exercised power, what each candidate would do with it, and whose claims withstand examination.

A democracy does not suffer from disagreement alone. It suffers when institutions capable of clarifying consequential differences choose to aestheticize the disagreement instead.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Robert Reich slams the NYT For ‘dangerously fraudulent’ coverage

item.title: Top Trump ally reveals why Republicans could be 'dead as a party’
item.description:
What happened

Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno told Fox News that Republicans could be “dead as a party” if they lose working-class voters. As AlterNet reports, Moreno argued that Donald Trump rescued a party that had abandoned those voters, only for Republicans now to risk losing them over economic pressure and the war with Iran.

The warning came less than two weeks before the 2026 midterm elections. AlterNet reports that Moreno said working-class voters “hate” both the war and the resulting increase in gasoline prices, while expressing doubt that the administration’s justification for attacking Iran had persuaded enough people. He nevertheless defended the military campaign and prescribed better Republican messaging.

The electoral evidence cited is bleak for the GOP: an October 14 Fox News poll found that 60 percent of voters named the cost of living as their leading economic concern and put Trump’s job approval at 36 percent. A May Fox poll found 67 percent of white voters without college degrees disapproved of his handling of the economy.

The people with power

Working-class voters did not choose the administration’s economic or military policy. Trump and the Republican officials supporting him hold federal power. According to the report, Trump and Israel began the war with Iran on February 28, 2026; Moreno then defended the campaign even while acknowledging that his constituents disliked its consequences.

That distinction matters because Moreno speaks as though Republicans are spectators watching a difficult political environment develop. They are not. The party controls the decisions it is asking voters to endure—and controls the sales pitch meant to make those decisions tolerable.

A governing failure recast as messaging

Moreno’s proposed remedy is revealing: Republicans must explain the case for war more effectively. But if voters are paying more for gasoline and rejecting the conflict, the problem is not necessarily that they failed to understand the administration. They may understand the consequences perfectly well.

This is a familiar maneuver in political communication. When policy produces an unpopular result, officials redefine the failure as inadequate persuasion. Material harm becomes a branding defect; public opposition becomes a problem of “penetration.” The policy remains protected while voters are treated as an audience requiring better instruction.

Loyalty is not economic policy

Moreno describes working-class support as something Republicans must “hang on to,” language that reduces voters to a bloc the party possesses until mishandled. Yet the figures reported by AlterNet suggest that loyalty is colliding with lived conditions.

Trump campaigned in 2024 on restoring prosperity and lowering costs. Moreno now faces voters reportedly angered by high living expenses, gasoline prices, and war. A political identity can delay accountability, but it cannot indefinitely substitute for affordable necessities. Republicans built their recent coalition by claiming to represent people ignored by governing elites. Once in power, that claim is tested by outcomes rather than posture.

The coalition’s contradiction

The larger pattern is not simply that Republicans may lose an election. It is that a party can use working-class grievance to acquire power while governing in ways that intensify the insecurity behind that grievance.

Moreno’s warning exposes the contradiction without resolving it. He recognizes the economic pain, defends the decisions associated with it, and asks for a stronger explanation. That is not representation. It is an attempt to preserve allegiance while insulating power from the consequences of its own choices.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Top Trump ally reveals why Republicans could be ‘dead as a party’

item.title: Lindsey Graham was saved from a bribery investigation by Trump's FBI
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing ProPublica’s reporting, says an FBI public-corruption investigation examined allegations that Sen. Lindsey Graham traded official help for campaign contributions. Former Navatek CEO Martin Kao told agents that, at a private Washington dinner on March 3, 2020, Graham agreed to support roughly $10 million in federal work benefiting Navatek after requesting a total of $100,000 for his reelection campaign. Graham’s office denied any quid pro quo, and a lobbyist present at the dinner denied witnessing such an agreement.

Records reviewed by ProPublica reportedly showed that Graham’s staff helped direct $9.5 million approved by Congress toward a Navatek–University of South Carolina partnership, while company-linked donors supplied about $40,000 associated with the dinner. Kao also accused Reps. James Clyburn and Joe Wilson of similar arrangements; their representatives denied wrongdoing or rejected Kao’s account. No lawmaker was charged, and Kao—a convicted fraudster seeking a reduced sentence—presented obvious credibility problems, although investigators believed company records corroborated parts of his story.

The investigation ended after Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, according to the reporting. His administration dismantled specialized FBI and Justice Department public-corruption teams, removed the two agents pursuing the Navatek case, and barred the relevant DOJ section from filing new cases. That did not establish the bribery allegations as true. It ensured they would not be fully tested.

The power was congressional

Kao had money, lobbyists and a company built to chase federal contracts. The decisive power still belonged to lawmakers and their staffs. They could write narrowly tailored budget language, communicate with the Navy and turn an ostensibly competitive process into one with an obvious intended recipient.

That distinction matters because the easiest version of this story is about a crooked contractor buying influence. Kao pleaded guilty to illegal campaign donations and loan fraud and received an 87-month sentence. But his criminality does not explain why congressional access was reportedly priced in campaign commitments, why Navatek’s preferred language appeared in appropriations materials, or why Graham’s adviser contacted the Office of Naval Research to confirm the intended beneficiary.

The people holding public authority were not passive targets of Kao’s scheme. The reporting describes offices repeatedly exercising institutional power in ways that benefited his company. Whether prosecutors could have proved a criminal quid pro quo is unresolved; the official assistance itself is documented in the account.

The shutdown was a decision

Calling the case “dead” can obscure who killed it. According to ProPublica, Trump’s administration gutted the units capable of pursuing it, swept the assigned agents out in a purge and imposed restrictions that prompted the assisting career prosecutor to resign.

Those were governing choices, not bureaucratic weather. The foreseeable consequence was that unresolved allegations involving powerful members of Congress—including Republicans and a senior Democrat—would lose their investigators. The intervention protected a political class, even if the reporting does not establish that Graham’s case was individually targeted.

This is how impunity is manufactured without an acquittal. Officials need not disprove the evidence when they can disable the institution responsible for examining it.

The convenient villain

Kao is an exceptionally useful figure for everyone else implicated by his account: convicted, self-interested and demonstrably dishonest. Those facts justify skepticism. They do not justify pretending he was the only evidence.

The FBI reportedly compared his statements with seized company records, emails, contribution data and internal spreadsheets. A witness confirmed key circumstances surrounding the Graham dinner, though he denied hearing an explicit deal. Company documents identified Graham as a “key supporter,” while correspondence showed congressional staff helping move Navatek’s requests through the budget and contracting machinery.

The denials largely attack Kao’s character or insist that donations never influenced official conduct. That defense benefits from the investigation’s termination. A witness can be discredited in public; corroborating records are harder to dismiss, which is why functioning investigators test them.

Corruption by design

The larger scandal is not merely an alleged sentence spoken over dinner. It is a political financing system in which purchasing access is treated as routine, appropriations can be shaped for a particular contractor without naming it, and campaign money arrives close enough to official favors to create dependence while preserving legal ambiguity.

Recent Supreme Court rulings had already made corruption cases harder to prove, according to the reporting. The administration then weakened enforcement itself. Together, those conditions create a generous shelter for officials: conduct may look transactional, produce the requested result and reward the relevant campaigns, yet still escape adjudication because the legal standard is narrow and the investigators are gone.

The proper conclusion is not that every allegation was proved. It is that power prevented a determination. Kao went to prison for crimes the government pursued. The lawmakers and executives named in his account received denials without trial, unresolved evidence and, ultimately, an enforcement apparatus stripped of the people examining them. That is not exoneration. It is a system protecting its own uncertainty.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Lindsey Graham was saved from a bribery investigation by Trump’s FBI

item.title: Leaker drops new bombshell theory on Trump’s real agenda
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Department of Homeland Security chief of staff Miles Taylor believes Donald Trump opposed foreign election interference selectively: not as a matter of national sovereignty, but when he thought it could hurt him politically. Taylor bases that conclusion on his experience in Trump’s first administration, while presenting Trump’s underlying motive as his own interpretation.

Taylor says that in August 2018 he assembled leaders from the FBI, the intelligence community and DHS to warn Russia against interfering in that year’s midterms. According to Taylor, Trump called the press conference “terrible” and asked whether anyone had pressured the officials to hold it. Weeks later at the United Nations, Trump accused China of election interference while saying nothing about Russia, which Taylor says administration officials had identified as the actual concern.

Taylor writes that this discrepancy made Trump’s position “click” for him: foreign meddling appeared objectionable when it threatened Trump or his preferred candidates, but tolerable when it benefited them. AlterNet also recounts Taylor’s argument that this pattern worsened after the 2020 election, when Trump promoted baseless voter-fraud claims and attempted to prevent the transfer of power.

The theory is Taylor’s, but the conduct is concrete

The headline promises a “bombshell theory.” The less inflated story is more useful: a former senior official describes a president reacting with hostility when his own national-security apparatus publicly warned a foreign adversary against election interference.

Taylor cannot prove Trump’s private motive merely by recounting that reaction. He can, however, identify the contradiction he witnessed. Trump reportedly disparaged a warning aimed at Russia, then publicly redirected attention toward China. The theory belongs to Taylor; the selective public conduct belongs to Trump.

That distinction matters because careless commentary can weaken a strong case by overstating it. The evidence presented here does not establish every element of a secret agenda. It does support scrutiny of whether Trump treated election security as an instrument of personal politics rather than a consistent government obligation.

The president held the power

The institutional hierarchy is not complicated. Career officials and agency leaders could assess threats, coordinate warnings and present intelligence judgments. The president could amplify that work, undermine it or redirect the government’s attention.

Trump held the greater power. According to Taylor, officials warned about Russia, while Trump attacked their warning and publicly emphasized China instead. Whatever Trump privately intended, that response placed presidential authority against his own officials’ stated effort to deter interference.

Calling Taylor and his colleagues a “resistance group” risks distorting that hierarchy. They were executive-branch officials trying to perform an election-security function inside an administration led by a president who could overrule, marginalize or remove them. The consequential actor was not the subordinate attempting to preserve institutional practice. It was the president deciding how the government would speak about the threat.

The misdirection was the message

Taylor’s account describes more than inconsistency. It describes political misdirection: suppress attention to the reported threat and substitute an adversary more convenient to the president’s narrative.

That does not establish that every accusation against China was false, nor does the supplied reporting document the basis for Trump’s United Nations claim. It establishes a narrower and still damning point: Trump reportedly declined to foreground the country his own team had warned him about, then accused another country instead.

The consequence is predictable. Election security stops being a rule applied to all foreign powers and becomes a partisan sorting mechanism. Helpful interference is minimized; potentially harmful interference is dramatized. Intelligence is no longer used chiefly to inform the public. It becomes material to be filtered according to the leader’s interests.

The larger pattern is personalized government

Taylor connects the 2018 episode to Trump’s conduct after losing the 2020 election. The common feature is not confusion about election administration. It is the subordination of institutional legitimacy to one politician’s fortunes.

In that model, an election is trustworthy when it delivers the preferred outcome. Foreign influence is intolerable when it disadvantages the leader and negotiable when it does not. Officials are credible when they validate the political line and suspect when they contradict it.

The systemic error is treating this as a clash of personalities or a mystery about Trump’s “real feelings.” Feelings are secondary. Power is exercised through decisions: which threats receive presidential backing, which warnings are disparaged, and which unsupported claims are promoted after defeat. Taylor offers an interpretation of motive. The reported pattern of selective institutional support is the more important indictment.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Leaker drops new bombshell theory on Trump’s real agenda

item.title: Trump resorts to bizarre new strategy to force reporters to read his posts
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump had White House staff distribute printed copies of a recent Truth Social post to reporters waiting outside the Oval Office on Tuesday, according to AlterNet. The post claimed that Trump had spent or would spend more than $400 million on the midterm elections, including more than $300 million on advertising, voter contact, rallies, turnout programs, and what he called “election integrity.”

The handout did not literally force reporters to read the post; it placed Trump’s preferred message directly in the White House press pool’s hands. AlterNet, citing Time, reported that Republicans were spending heavily in races normally considered safe, including the Texas Senate contest involving state Attorney General Ken Paxton, while still trailing Democrats in polling. The supplied reporting does not independently verify Trump’s spending figures.

The headline overreaches

Calling the printout a strategy to “force” journalists to read Trump’s posts turns a publicity maneuver into a melodrama about delivery format. Reporters could ignore the paper just as they could ignore the online post. The real institutional advantage is not the printer. It is the presidency.

Trump controls access to the Oval Office, commands a vast communications apparatus, and can convert a personal social-media claim into an official White House press event. By centering the oddity of paper handouts, AlterNet makes the story smaller and sillier than the power dynamic warrants.

The message was money

Trump wanted coverage of one claim: that he was personally directing extraordinary resources toward Republican victories. The White House’s physical distribution of the post helped move that assertion from his own platform into mainstream reporting without requiring a formal briefing, documentary support, or sustained questioning.

The wording also blurred completed spending with promised spending. “Have spent, or will be spending” combines money already disbursed with money that may be spent later. Even Trump’s narrower claim—that more than $300 million had already been spent—was presented in the supplied article without records establishing who spent it, through which entities, or during what precise period.

Power hides behind spectacle

The strongest evidence in the story concerns presidential agenda-setting. Trump made a claim, White House personnel circulated it, and reporters photographed and amplified it. That sequence shows how official infrastructure can serve a political leader’s personal and partisan messaging.

The article instead devotes attention to the maneuver’s supposed bizarreness and repeats journalist Laura Rozen’s comparison to the isolation of Russia’s final czar. That analogy may be caustic, but the reporting supplies no evidence that the handout resulted from paranoia, internal silence, or the departure of press secretary Katie Zacharia. It is speculation layered over spectacle.

Spending is not strength

Trump framed the reported expenditure as proof of commitment and Republican resurgence. AlterNet offered the opposite interpretation: unusually large spending may indicate that Republicans must defend territory they would ordinarily expect to hold cheaply. OpenSecrets analyst Brendan Glavin supplied the necessary restraint, telling Time that outspending an opponent does not guarantee victory.

That distinction matters. Money measures resources deployed, not public approval, electoral momentum, or eventual results. Polls are snapshots, not outcomes. The defensible political conclusion is narrower: if Republicans are pouring exceptional sums into traditionally favorable contests, their strategists evidently consider those races worth expensive intervention.

The systemic error

Modern political coverage routinely mistakes eccentric presentation for the underlying abuse of advantage. A president handing reporters printouts is easy to mock. A president using the White House to inject an unverified campaign-spending boast into the news cycle is more consequential.

The governing pattern is not that journalists were compelled to read a piece of paper. It is that concentrated institutional power can manufacture attention, while coverage rewards the stunt and leaves the financing claim insufficiently examined. The paper was merely the prop. The presidency was the distribution system.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump resorts to bizarre new strategy to force reporters to read his posts

item.title: Republican’s 'despicable' attack ad with Dem’s mom backfires spectacularly
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign circulated an attack ad featuring Donna Arthur, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, accusing Acton of lying about her childhood. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said the campaign was exploiting family trauma involving alleged sexual abuse by Arthur’s husband.

The ad drew condemnation from Democratic commentators, political observers and at least one Republican activist, who questioned the campaign’s decision to put Arthur on camera given the family history described by Acton and her relatives. The reported “backfire,” however, is an online backlash—not evidence of changed votes or polling.

AlterNet says Ramaswamy was trailing Acton in polls despite Ohio’s Republican lean, while Politico’s Jonathan Martin cited a Marist poll placing Ramaswamy’s favorable and unfavorable ratings at 37 percent and 53 percent. The report does not establish whether the ad altered those numbers.

The campaign made this choice

Arthur appears in the ad, but the institutional power belongs to Ramaswamy’s campaign. Campaign professionals recruited or accepted her, recorded her accusations, packaged them as political content and paid to distribute them. Ramaswamy is the candidate whose organization authorized the result.

That chain of agency matters. Describing the episode merely as a mother attacking her daughter would conceal the political machinery that turned a damaged family relationship into campaign inventory. Arthur supplied the accusation; the campaign supplied the reach, purpose and electoral weaponization.

Desperation is not an excuse

Stearns called the ad a desperate attack, and the polling cited by AlterNet gives that interpretation context. But desperation does not produce an advertisement by itself. People make decisions, approve scripts and decide that a candidate’s possible advantage outweighs the foreseeable harm.

The ad’s premise is that estrangement creates credibility: a mother denouncing her daughter must know something the public does not. Yet the family history reported here makes that shortcut especially reckless. The campaign asks voters to treat biological proximity as proof while stripping away the circumstances that could bear directly on the witness’s reliability and relationship with Acton.

The backlash is not the whole story

AlterNet’s headline oversells what it can demonstrate. A collection of furious social-media posts establishes widespread condemnation among the people quoted. It does not establish a “spectacular” electoral reversal.

That framing also risks converting a serious exercise of campaign power into another story about who won the internet. The central fact is not that commentators found the ad repellent. It is that a gubernatorial campaign reportedly used an unresolved account of childhood abuse and family estrangement to attack a political opponent’s character.

Cruelty as campaign technique

This episode reflects a familiar political pattern: private vulnerability becomes public ammunition, while the operatives who manufacture the attack recede behind the person placed on camera. The weaker actors—the estranged relatives whose history is being exposed—absorb the scrutiny. The campaign controls the edit, the money and the audience.

Even some ideological allies condemned the tactic, according to AlterNet. That does not make the political system self-correcting. It shows only that this particular exploitation was conspicuous enough to breach partisan tolerance.

The system rewards the attempt

If the ad fails, consultants may call it a miscalculation. That language is too antiseptic. The foreseeable consequence was renewed public exposure of alleged childhood abuse and a family rupture, all in service of damaging Acton.

The larger pattern is a campaign economy that treats intimate suffering as usable material and recognizes restraint mainly when cruelty becomes electorally inconvenient. The scandal is not simply that the attack may have backfired. It is that professionals with institutional power believed it might work.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republican’s ‘despicable’ attack ad with Dem’s mom backfires spectacularly

item.title: Trump scrambling to keep damning 'on-point' evidence out of court: expert
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s lawyers are seeking to prevent the BBC from calling former special counsel Jack Smith as a witness in Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the broadcaster. Trump alleges that a BBC documentary misleadingly edited portions of his January 6, 2021, Ellipse speech to suggest that he directly called for violence at the Capitol. The BBC disputes his claim.

Legal analyst Lisa Rubin told MS NOW that Smith may possess evidence relevant to whether the documentary conveyed a materially false account of Trump’s conduct and intent. Rubin said Smith has publicly described evidence that Trump foresaw the violence, caused it nonetheless, and then used it in an effort to obstruct the vote count. But AlterNet does not identify the undisclosed evidence, and Smith had not testified in the proceeding as reported. Trump’s lawyers argue that grand-jury secrecy bars its disclosure; Rubin said another rule can permit such material to be discussed in judicial proceedings.

The plaintiff with presidential power

This is not merely a dispute between a public figure and a broadcaster. The plaintiff is the sitting president, wielding the resources and authority of the country’s most powerful office while pursuing a private defamation claim over coverage of his own political conduct.

That does not decide the lawsuit. It does expose the imbalance beneath it. The BBC must defend its editorial choices in court while the president’s lawyers attempt to restrict testimony from the former prosecutor who investigated the underlying events. The judge—not Trump, the BBC, Rubin, or Smith—will determine whether that testimony is relevant and legally available.

The legal fight is over access

Trump chose to sue. That decision made falsity central and opened the disputed portrayal to judicial examination. His lawyers are now invoking grand-jury restrictions to keep Smith from presenting information developed during the federal investigation.

Grand-jury secrecy is a legal protection, not proof of concealment. But the practical objective of Trump’s motion is clear: prevent the BBC from accessing evidence it says could support its defense. The institutional question is whether a plaintiff can challenge a portrayal as false while narrowing inquiry into the events and intent behind that portrayal.

The headline outruns the evidence

AlterNet calls Smith a “major surprise witness” with “damning” evidence. The reporting establishes neither that Smith will testify nor what his undisclosed evidence contains. “On point” is Rubin’s assessment of its possible relevance, not a judicial finding about admissibility, credibility, or what it proves.

That framing converts a contested evidentiary issue into a preview of presumed exposure. It may attract attention, but it blurs the distinction between evidence known to exist in general, evidence available to the BBC, and evidence a court will permit Smith to disclose. Sharp political reporting still has to respect those boundaries.

The broader tactic

The larger pattern is the use of litigation to contest how powerful officials are portrayed while simultaneously fighting over how much underlying evidence can be examined. A defamation claim can seek reputational repair, but it can also force a news organization to spend money and defend its account under legal pressure.

The central issue is therefore larger than one documentary edit. Trump is asking a court to treat the BBC’s presentation as defamatory; the BBC is arguing that the overall meaning was substantially grounded in Trump’s conduct and intent. Once political power enters court demanding vindication, the evidence cannot be reduced to whichever isolated clip best serves the plaintiff.

Power seeks a narrow record

This case shows how control over the evidentiary record can matter as much as control over the public narrative. Trump initiated the proceeding, the BBC must justify its publication, Smith may hold relevant investigative material, and the court controls whether any of it can be heard.

The systemic danger lies in allowing power to define the accusation broadly and the permissible inquiry narrowly. Whether that happens here remains unresolved. But the struggle itself is revealing: public accountability depends not only on what was broadcast, but on who can compel scrutiny, who can resist it, and which facts the legal system allows into the room.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump scrambling to keep damning ‘on-point’ evidence out of court: expert

item.title: Trump’s Fox News throw down proves 'the wheels are coming off' his regime
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump has intensified his public attacks on Fox News while promoting the pro-Trump Right Side Broadcasting Network. Conservative commentator Jim Geraghty argued that the dispute shows an increasingly strained relationship between Trump and the network as the midterms approach.

Trump praised RSBN’s coverage of a Kentucky appearance and accused Fox of alienating “MAGA” supporters by occasionally featuring Democrats. AlterNet also reports that he attacked Fox over its decision to fire Maria Bartiromo, who reportedly told the White House that anchors had been instructed to stop platforming his false claims.

Geraghty described Fox as more willing to criticize Trump after its $787 million settlement with Dominion Voting Systems over false claims about the 2020 election. He concluded that the relationship had become colder, though he did not establish that a complete break was imminent.

The power is still concentrated

Trump holds the presidency, controls the executive branch and commands a political movement whose attention can materially affect conservative media audiences. Fox controls a powerful distribution system capable of validating, minimizing or challenging what that administration says. RSBN offers Trump something narrower but more reliable: coverage without meaningful editorial friction.

This is not a fight between equal victims of misunderstanding. It is a struggle between a president seeking favorable treatment and media institutions deciding how much reputational and legal exposure they will accept in exchange for access, audience loyalty and political influence.

Fox helped build the expectation

Trump’s indignation makes sense within the system Fox helped create. Years of highly favorable coverage taught him that conservative media existed not merely to cover his movement, but to protect and amplify it. An occasional Democratic guest or critical segment can therefore be cast as betrayal rather than ordinary journalism.

That does not make Fox an independent counterweight. The shift described by AlterNet appears bounded and self-protective. The Dominion settlement gave the company a concrete financial reason to reconsider broadcasting election falsehoods. A corporation responding to a $787 million liability is managing risk, not necessarily recovering principle.

“Tantrum” is too small a frame

Geraghty’s language emphasizes Trump’s “whining” and “self-pity.” Those descriptions may capture his rhetoric, but they reduce an institutional pressure campaign to a personality defect.

The consequential act is not that Trump feels aggrieved. It is that a sitting president is publicly signaling which outlets deserve his movement’s loyalty according to how faithfully they serve him. Promoting RSBN while denouncing Fox pressures conservative media to compete on obedience. Calling that merely a tantrum obscures the leverage behind it.

Loyalty has a price

Fox’s reported distancing also exposes the transactional foundation of the relationship. Trump benefited from sympathetic coverage. Fox benefited from an audience organized around Trump. The arrangement became less attractive when carrying his false election claims produced enormous legal costs.

That incentive structure remains intact even if the participants change. A compliant outlet can gain attention by eliminating scrutiny; a political leader can reward it with promotion and access. The immediate consequence is a media market in which ideological loyalty is measured by willingness to repeat a leader’s preferred account of reality.

The system manufactures replacements

The larger pattern is not simply that Trump and Fox may be breaking up. It is that partisan media ecosystems can discard insufficiently compliant institutions and elevate more obedient ones. Fox need not become hostile to Trump for RSBN to benefit; it only needs to impose limits that Trump considers unacceptable.

Institutional power is visible in who can punish whom. Fox can withhold a platform, but Trump can direct supporters toward competitors and redefine routine scrutiny as treason. The result is not healthy media pluralism. It is a selection process that rewards outlets for surrendering editorial judgment before legal liability forces them to rediscover it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s Fox News throw down proves ‘the wheels are coming off’ his regime

item.title: One single Trump decision is the direct cause of your shrinking paycheck
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet attributes the renewed squeeze on US paychecks to President Donald Trump’s decision to attack Iran at the end of February. The outlet reports that Iran retaliated by blocking oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up energy, transportation, and fertilizer costs while wage growth slowed.

According to the article, year-over-year wholesale inflation reached 6.3 percent in September, while wage growth fell from 4.0 percent in 2023 and 2024 to 3.0 percent in the latest data. AlterNet argues that consumer prices are therefore likely to keep rising—not necessarily by 6.3 percent—as businesses pass along some of their higher costs.

The article also says inflation had already been pushed upward by purchases made in anticipation of Trump’s tariffs. Its central claim, however, is that the attack on Iran transformed that pressure into a broader inflationary shock, causing prices to outpace wages and reducing workers’ purchasing power.

The decision belongs to the president

The institutional power here sits with the president who chose military escalation. Consumers did not raise the price of oil. Workers did not obstruct a major shipping route. Businesses stocking imported goods ahead of tariffs were responding to policy, not creating it.

AlterNet says Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wanted the attack, while also arguing that its stated nuclear rationale was unsound. That judgment is the outlet’s. The concrete political point does not require speculation about motive: Trump authorized a military action, Iran retaliated, and the resulting oil disruption spread costs through an economy dependent on fuel-intensive production and transportation.

Inflation is being used to hide causation

Republican messaging benefits when inflation is treated as an atmospheric condition—something that simply descends on a country without identifiable decisions behind it. That framing erases agency. The reported sequence is not mysterious: anticipated tariffs altered purchasing and prices; military escalation disrupted oil supplies; higher energy costs moved into wholesale prices.

The comparison with the Biden-era inflation surge matters because it exposes a deliberate collapse of unlike events into one political slogan. AlterNet describes the earlier spike as part of a worldwide pandemic reopening, when production struggled to meet rapidly returning demand. It reports that US inflation peaked at 9.0 percent in June 2022, fell to 3.1 percent a year later, and reached 2.6 percent by the November 2024 election. Whatever criticism Biden’s recovery package warrants, that chronology does not absolve Trump of responsibility for later policies that reversed the decline.

Workers absorb the damage

A paycheck can rise in dollars and still shrink in value. If wages grow by 3.0 percent while the prices workers pay accelerate faster, real purchasing power falls. That is the mechanism behind the headline—not a literal reduction in every worker’s nominal pay.

The distributional consequence is political, not incidental. AlterNet reports that wage growth is not matching the new inflation and argues that higher prices are feeding profits rather than compensating labor. Workers bear the loss through groceries, fuel, and transported goods, while firms with pricing power can protect margins and asset owners remain better insulated.

Fertilizer costs extend the damage beyond the immediate energy shock. The article says Gulf countries account for substantial fertilizer production and warns that the larger effect on crops may arrive the following year. A military decision can therefore keep extracting money from households long after the first headlines disappear.

Risk is socialized, power is not

The administration held the authority to impose tariffs and initiate military action. Households received neither a vote on those decisions nor protection from their economic fallout. Yet they are expected to manage the consequences privately: drive less, buy less, accept smaller real wages, and treat deteriorating living standards as personal budgeting failures.

That is the larger pattern. Political leaders exercise concentrated power, donors and profitable firms are positioned to capture gains, and the public is handed diffuse costs disguised as an economic puzzle. The misdirection works only if policy choices are stripped of authorship.

The system protects the decision-maker

This story is ultimately about how executive power converts geopolitical choices into domestic hardship without requiring the decision-maker to bear the price. The attack may have occurred abroad, but the reported consequences arrive through every supply chain that uses oil, diesel, or fertilizer.

Calling the result “inflation” is economically accurate but politically incomplete. Inflation names the symptom. The relevant cause, according to AlterNet’s account, was a chain of identifiable decisions made by officials with the power to choose differently. When responsibility is obscured, workers are blamed for failing to endure costs imposed from above—and those who created the shock remain free to market themselves as its cure.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: One single Trump decision is the direct cause of your shrinking paycheck

item.title: Agents stunned as ex-Trump official’s 'catastrophic' flub exposed
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Homeland Security Investigations, the ICE branch responsible for criminal investigations, inadvertently switched internet providers in April of the previous year and lost its ability to conduct court-authorized wiretaps for months. During the outage, wiretaps reported by Department of Homeland Security investigators fell by more than 80 percent under then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem.

According to records obtained by PunchUp and reported by The Daily Beast, DHS warned that prolonged loss of the capability could cripple major investigations and create an unquantifiable risk to undercover agents and the public. Because HSI surveillance systems also support agencies including the FBI and DEA, the disruption may have extended beyond ICE.

Former federal agent Eric Balliet called the failure catastrophic and said recovery could take years. Former federal prosecutor Brandi Young said some high-value cases could stall or collapse permanently. The reporting does not establish which official approved the provider change, whether Noem knew about it, or what corrective work has since been completed.

Power without accountability

Noem held institutional authority over DHS when the failure occurred. That makes the breakdown part of her department’s record, but the available reporting does not show that she personally ordered the switch or managed the affected systems.

That distinction matters. Political accountability attaches to leadership; personal culpability requires evidence. A serious account should identify the officials who approved the change, the safeguards they bypassed or lacked, and the executives who allowed the outage to continue. This one cannot.

The decision disappeared

The provider switch is described as “inadvertent,” a word that converts an institutional act into something resembling weather. Internet providers do not change themselves. Someone initiated, approved, implemented, or failed to test the transition.

Calling the result a flub also trivializes the scale described in DHS’s own warning. This was not an embarrassing typo. It reportedly deprived investigators of a central surveillance capability for months and may have damaged cases beyond repair.

Shock is not oversight

The headline sells astonishment: agents were stunned, an ex-Trump official was exposed. But disbelief is not the central political fact. The real issue is that a federal law-enforcement system apparently lacked the technical controls, redundancy, and executive oversight needed to preserve a mission-critical capability.

Balliet’s reaction supplies urgency, not responsibility. By centering his shock and Noem’s name, the framing offers readers recognizable personalities while leaving the operational chain of command obscure. The weaker the accounting, the easier it becomes for every decision-maker below the secretary to vanish into bureaucracy.

The enforcement contradiction

DHS exercises enormous coercive power. Its agencies investigate trafficking, narcotics networks, and other serious crimes while placing undercover personnel in dangerous positions. An institution claiming that authority also assumes an obligation to maintain the infrastructure on which those operations depend.

The reported failure reveals a familiar imbalance: the government can demand secrecy, surveillance powers, and public trust, yet responsibility becomes diffuse when its own systems fail. Suspects, agents, partner agencies, and the public absorb the consequences. The officials responsible for the decision remain unnamed.

Failure as a system

The larger pattern is not merely incompetence under one secretary. It is concentrated power paired with fragmented accountability. Senior leaders control agencies and claim their successes; technical disasters are recast as inadvertent mishaps produced by no identifiable person.

Noem’s tenure is relevant because the outage happened under her authority. But attaching the entire story to her name without establishing her role risks substituting partisan branding for institutional scrutiny. The sharper indictment is the one the reporting only begins to expose: a powerful department reportedly lost a critical law-enforcement capability for months, warned that the damage could be profound, and still left the public without a clear account of who made the decision or who answered for it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Agents stunned as ex-Trump official’s ‘catastrophic’ flub exposed

item.title: Kristi Noem’s $464M jet fleet is sitting in a parking lot collecting dust
item.description:
What happened

Seven Boeing 737-700 jets acquired for the Department of Homeland Security as part of President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign were largely idle at Lake Charles Regional Airport in Louisiana, AlterNet reported, citing Bloomberg. Aircraft-tracking data indicated that each had flown fewer than five times since April 2026.

The aircraft were part of a reported $464 million purchase pursued under then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem. The department bought five additional jets from Daedalus Aviation on Noem’s final day in office in March, including three business aircraft. Bloomberg reported that DHS, now led by Markwayne Mullin, was searching for other uses for the planes while deportation flights continued through existing contractors.

AlterNet also reported that Daedalus’s chairman had donated to a political committee supporting Noem. That connection does not by itself establish favoritism, but it intensifies the need for scrutiny of a no-bid purchase whose stated operational rationale has not been borne out.

Power made the purchase

The stranded aircraft are not a story about bureaucracy mysteriously malfunctioning. Political appointees controlling DHS spending chose to buy them. Noem held the institutional authority, adviser Corey Lewandowski reportedly helped guide the department’s priorities, and the Trump administration supplied the deportation agenda used to justify the expense.

The central question is therefore not why the planes gathered dirt. It is why officials committed hundreds of millions of public dollars without demonstrating that aircraft availability was constraining deportations. Former acting ICE director John Sandweg told Bloomberg that it had not been a significant constraint. The government then increased deportation flights through existing contractors—the very arrangement the purchase was supposedly meant to supplement.

Spectacle was the governing method

The fleet fits a broader record described by Bloomberg: more than $200 million spent on a self-promotional advertising campaign featuring Noem, along with over $1 billion spent acquiring warehouses for detention centers under a plan that was largely abandoned. Some initiatives were canceled, but cancellation does not recover the political attention they purchased or erase the public costs already incurred.

These projects shared a governing logic. They translated coercive policy into visible symbols: branded advertisements, immense detention sites and a government-owned fleet. Operational necessity appears to have been secondary. The administration could already charter deportation flights, but owning aircraft offered a more tangible monument to its enforcement campaign.

Waste is not the whole scandal

Calling this merely “wasteful spending” softens what happened. Waste sounds accidental: a bad forecast, an unlucky procurement or ordinary administrative drift. Here, officials reportedly pursued expensive showcase projects despite an available contractor system and then left successors searching for missions for the equipment.

The no-bid structure and the contractor chairman’s political donation create a serious appearance problem, though the reporting does not establish an illegal exchange or corrupt bargain. That distinction matters. So does the institutional failure: a politically connected administration was permitted to make a vast purchase without the source article identifying any demonstrated operational need, competitive test or durable deployment plan.

Blame should travel upward

The idle planes may invite jokes about government incompetence, but generic ridicule misdirects responsibility. Government did not act by itself. Senior officials selected the project, approved the spending and attached it to a presidential priority. Taxpayers and career personnel inherit the maintenance, staffing and repurposing problems; the decision-makers received the spectacle while they held power.

Even the effort to assign aircraft to congressional travel exposes the inversion. A fleet sold as deportation infrastructure is now reportedly being evaluated for unrelated uses, including converting an 18-year-old 737 for congressional delegations. Repurposing may reduce future losses, but it cannot retroactively validate the original purchase.

Cruelty can be fiscally unserious

This episode reveals how authoritarian politics and profligacy can reinforce each other. A government campaign built around mass removal rewards dramatic demonstrations of force. That creates fertile ground for poorly justified contracts because officials can present spending itself as evidence of resolve.

The result is not simply seven underused planes. It is a procurement system subordinated to political theater: immense sums committed in the name of punishment, weak evidence of operational necessity, politically awkward contracting ties and public assets left searching for a purpose. When spectacle becomes the measure of strength, failure does not stop the spending. It becomes another bill handed to everyone outside the room where the decision was made.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Kristi Noem’s $464M jet fleet is sitting in a parking lot collecting dust

item.title: Trump behavior raises mental health questions during Obama rant
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump delivered a confused passage at a Monday political rally, invoking Barack Obama, “Mohammed,” Michigan, and an unspecified campaign appearance without clearly connecting them. The report does not identify whom Trump meant by “Mohammed,” establish what event Obama was supposedly attending, or explain whether Trump’s claims were accurate.

AlterNet also says Trump was filmed the following Tuesday waving and saluting for roughly 30 seconds on the White House helipad when no audience was visible. It presents both episodes alongside commentary from psychiatrist Henry Abraham and journalist Timothy Noah about Trump’s possible cognitive decline. Neither episode, as described, establishes a medical diagnosis.

The power is presidential

The central issue is not whether Trump sounded strange. It is that the person exhibiting the reported behavior holds presidential power. He commands the executive branch and occupies an office whose decisions can carry immediate domestic and international consequences.

That institutional fact makes scrutiny of his capacity legitimate. It also raises the evidentiary standard. Reporting on presidential fitness should be more rigorous than circulating an ugly quotation, attaching a clinical suspicion, and asking readers to complete the diagnosis.

A diagnosis the article cannot prove

AlterNet moves too quickly from observable conduct to implied mental unfitness. An incoherent rally passage is evidence of incoherence. Waving toward an apparently empty space is unusual conduct. Neither, without fuller context and direct medical evaluation, proves a particular impairment or explains its cause.

The cited experts add concern, not confirmation. Abraham offered an analogy and had signed a letter declaring Trump cognitively unfit. Noah summarized specialists’ comparisons of older and newer videos. Those judgments may justify investigation, but the article does not provide a clinical examination, a diagnosis, or enough contextual evidence to settle the question it raises.

Confusion as political method

Trump’s rhetoric still has political effects whether its disorder reflects decline, improvisation, or habitual demagoguery. The reported passage uses Obama’s full name as a hostile cue, calls him “rotten,” labels another unnamed man arrogant, claims ownership of Michigan through an electoral boast, and invokes “Michigan values” against an opponent the audience is expected to reject.

That is not policy argument. It is associative politics: names, resentments, dominance claims, and exclusion compressed into a performance. Focusing exclusively on mental fitness can obscure the agency in that performance. Confusion does not erase the contempt being communicated or the political use of an audience trained to respond to enemies rather than facts.

The accountability gap

The article identifies alarming behavior but says little about the institutions surrounding it. A president does not exercise power alone. Senior officials, advisers, party leaders, medical personnel, and lawmakers possess varying degrees of access and authority. If they have reliable evidence of incapacity, they bear responsibility for addressing it through legitimate institutional processes. If they do not, public diagnosis by insinuation becomes a substitute for evidence.

That omission misdirects attention from accountable decision-makers toward spectacle. The public is invited to inspect Trump’s gestures frame by frame while the people positioned to assess, constrain, or enable presidential conduct largely disappear from view.

Spectacle is not oversight

The larger pattern is an institutional failure disguised as personality coverage. Trump’s reported conduct merits scrutiny because presidential power magnifies the consequences of impairment, recklessness, and incoherence. But sharp scrutiny requires separating what was observed from what has merely been inferred.

A press corps that asks whether a president is mentally fit while leaving basic references unresolved—and while barely examining the officials who keep his authority intact—produces alarm without accountability. The systemic error is not noticing disturbing behavior. It is treating the behavior as a self-contained mystery when power is being exercised through an entire structure of enablers, incentives, and institutional choices.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump behavior raises mental health questions during Obama rant
