item.title: There's a fatal flaw in Congress’ plan to stop Trump
item.description:
What happened

Congress’s proposed safeguard has a fatal weakness: it may compensate clean-energy developers after a president blocks their projects, but it may not stop the projects from being blocked. AlterNet, republishing Grist, reports that the bipartisan Senate permitting bill would restrict federal agencies from reversing approved permits and authorize courts to restore permits or award developers substantial public compensation.

The proposal follows the Trump administration’s delays, attempted cancellations, and permit reviews affecting numerous wind and solar projects. According to the report, the administration also sought to reconsider permits for three Atlantic offshore wind projects, including the completed 700-megawatt Revolution Wind project serving Rhode Island. The government said it wanted to reevaluate legal compliance but, as reported, offered no more specific explanation in those filings.

Renewable-energy companies support the bill because financial guarantees could reduce investment risk. Former federal officials and environmental-law experts quoted by Grist argue that payouts would not necessarily deter an administration willing to spend public money to obstruct clean energy. The Senate was not expected to vote until after the midterm elections, so the reporting establishes a proposed compromise, not an enacted protection.

Power is already in the executive branch

The central fact is not regulatory uncertainty. It is the federal executive’s control over permits, reviews, and enforcement. Developers may possess approvals and favorable court orders, but agencies still determine whether projects proceed without repeated interruption.

Congress can define legal limits, and judges can enforce them. Yet the bill’s principal remedies arrive after executive action has delayed construction, destabilized financing, or forced litigation. A restored permit cannot recover lost time automatically. A damages award cannot deliver electricity from a turbine that was never allowed to operate.

Calling this “project certainty” mistakes compensation for prevention. The proposal may insure capital against political interference while leaving the interference itself operationally effective.

Taxpayers absorb the administration’s choices

The bill would permit reimbursement of 25 to 50 percent of project costs for prohibited permit reversals. A successful discrimination claim could produce compensation covering the entire construction cost if the developer completed the project. For offshore wind, the exposure could reach billions of dollars, paid through the federal Judgment Fund.

That structure gives the decision-maker and the payer different identities. Executive officials can pursue reversals; the public treasury bears the judgment. The officials responsible do not personally absorb the financial consequence, and an administration hostile to a project may regard the payout as an acceptable price for stopping it.

This is not accountability in any serious institutional sense. It is public financing for the consequences of executive misconduct, paired with private relief for investors. Consumers still face the loss of planned generating capacity, and states still face damaged climate and energy plans.

The baseline could entrench discrimination

The anti-discrimination clause appears stronger than it is. According to former Justice Department attorney Matthew Littleton, its five-year comparison period could incorporate the very pattern the provision is supposed to prevent.

If four years of accelerated fossil-fuel approvals and delayed renewable projects become the statistical baseline, unequal treatment can be converted into administrative normality. Wind developers may struggle to prove discrimination because obstruction has already lowered the standard against which later conduct is measured. A future administration could also find that favoritism toward oil and gas has acquired legal protection through repetition.

That is how institutional bias hardens: first as executive practice, then as historical data, and finally as the benchmark for lawful government behavior.

Congress is retreating from its own condition

Democratic negotiators had said continued attacks on wind projects could destroy a bipartisan agreement. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse reportedly declared that he would not support a compromise unless the administration stopped blocking wind farms. After the move against Revolution Wind, however, he cited that same conduct as evidence that the bill was necessary.

The shift matters. The administration did not first demonstrate restraint in exchange for legislation. Instead, continued interference weakened the negotiators’ stated condition and increased pressure to accept a remedy designed around that interference.

The article’s framing occasionally understates this by presenting the issue as a question of whether the bill can create certainty. The sharper question is why Congress is considering subsidizing the consequences of executive obstruction after its demand that the obstruction stop apparently failed.

Sabotage can become a budget item

The larger pattern is government by fait accompli. An administration uses its immediate control over agencies to disrupt projects; courts respond slowly; Congress designs compensation; industry accepts protection for sunk capital; and the underlying public objective—building energy infrastructure—remains vulnerable.

The foreseeable result is a perverse settlement: companies receive some protection, fossil-fuel development retains its advantage, and the public pays for both the obstruction and the resulting energy shortfall. A legal right that can be violated repeatedly in exchange for taxpayer-funded damages is not secure. It is merely priced.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: There’s a fatal flaw in Congress’ plan to stop Trump

item.title: Judges set to stomp Trump’s claim that docs are 'his property’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Politico, reports that a D.C. Circuit panel appeared deeply skeptical on Friday of the Trump administration’s argument that the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional. Judges Patricia Millett and Cornelia Pillard pressed Justice Department attorney John Bailey over the claim that official presidential papers belong to the president. The panel had not ruled at the time of the report.

The 1978 law makes presidential records public property and establishes access for Congress, law enforcement, and eventually the public. Bailey acknowledged that, without the statute, it would not prevent a president from selling records containing national-security secrets. Pillard warned that presidential relatives could likewise sell records to foreign interests, creating opportunities for blackmail.

AlterNet connects the dispute to the criminal charges Trump faced over classified documents, but the proceeding described here concerns the broader constitutional status of the records law. The administration also argued that the statute unfairly burdens the executive branch because Congress and the federal courts are not governed by an equivalent law.

The claim is bigger than one records dispute

The administration is not merely contesting how particular documents were classified or handled. Its Office of Legal Counsel declared the entire Presidential Records Act unconstitutional, attacking the legal foundation for treating a president’s official papers as belonging to the public.

That position would concentrate control over taxpayer-funded records in the person who generated them. It would also weaken the mechanisms through which investigators, Congress, historians, and the public can reconstruct presidential conduct. Advice to a president already receives substantial protection under the law, including a reported restriction on public access generally lasting at least 12 years. The administration is challenging the ownership structure itself.

Power sits with the executive—and its lawyers

Trump holds the presidency. His Justice Department chose to advance this position, and its lawyers are asking the judiciary to remove a statutory restraint on presidential control of official records. The weaker actor in this conflict is not the president burdened by paperwork. It is the public, whose ability to recover its own government’s history depends on enforceable preservation rules.

The judges’ questions exposed the practical stakes. If official records become personal property, control can follow private incentives: secrecy, profit, inheritance, or disposal. Those consequences are not rhetorical excesses imported by critics. They arise from the government’s own theory, which Bailey defended even when Millett tested it against the sale of national-security secrets.

“Unfairness” is a diversion

The comparison with congressional and judicial records misdirects attention from the decision actually before the court. Whether other branches should face stronger archival requirements does not establish that presidents privately own records created through public office and public resources.

Pillard identified the partisan logic embedded in that argument: it treats separation of powers as protection for a particular president rather than for the presidency as an institution. The relevant question is not whether every branch operates under an identical statute. It is whether Congress may prevent a departing president from converting the documentary record of executive power into personal property.

Skepticism is not a ruling

AlterNet’s headline promises judicial defeat, but the reporting establishes only sharp questioning. Appellate judges often use hypotheticals to test the reach of a legal theory; their skepticism may indicate where the case is headed, but it is not a judgment.

That distinction matters because triumphalist framing can conceal how much remains unresolved. The judiciary still has to decide whether the statute survives this challenge. Until then, the consequential fact is that the executive branch has formally asserted a theory under which presidential records belong to the president.

The systemic error

Watergate produced a recognition that presidential records are instruments of public accountability, not personal trophies. The Trump administration’s position attempts to reverse that settlement by converting institutional memory into executive property.

The larger pattern is the use of constitutional maximalism to strip durable constraints from the presidency. If the record of official power belongs to the official who exercised it, accountability becomes dependent on that official’s consent. A government unable to preserve evidence of what its president did is not merely forgetful. It has handed the subject of oversight control over the archive that makes oversight possible.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Judges set to stomp Trump’s claim that docs are ‘his property’

item.title: Russian troll farms are back —and they're boosting the GOP: NYT
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing New York Times reporting, says the Russian-backed “Doppelgänger” operation is using the Israel-Hamas war as a wedge to damage Democrats and benefit Donald Trump and Republican candidates. Researchers identified more than 50 fake personas posing as Israeli women, supported by a separate network of more than 1,000 accounts that pushed their posts into popular discussions—an estimated 150,000 posts in total.

The campaign reportedly amplified claims that Democrats had abandoned Israel. Alethea founder Lisa Kaplan said the posting volume and placement beneath highly engaged content suggested the messages were likely reaching users. Graphika researcher Jean le Roux said a separate Kremlin-linked campaign spread baseless, AI-generated claims about Democrats in competitive Senate races while not targeting Republicans in the same manner.

The Times also reported that X banned 13,000 accounts linked to Iran, Russia, and China. Meanwhile, an attempted classified federal briefing for state election officials failed because Trump administration officials could not establish a secure virtual connection. The reporting does not establish whether that failure was deliberate.

The beneficiaries are not incidental

The operation’s political direction is explicit in the evidence presented: attack Democrats, exploit divisions over Israel, and leave Republican candidates comparatively untouched. The Times reports that U.S. intelligence assessments and other reviews have consistently found Vladimir Putin’s government favors Trump over Democrats, who are generally more supportive of Ukraine against Russia’s invasion.

That does not prove coordination between Republican campaigns and Russian operators. It does establish alignment. A foreign government has interests in American electoral outcomes, and its propagandists are reportedly spending resources to advance the outcome they prefer.

The fake Israeli personas are not merely “divisive content.” They are instruments of fraudulent political persuasion: invented identities designed to borrow moral authority from war, grief, and national belonging.

Power sits above the trolls

Russia’s Social Design Agency, the sanctioned public-relations firm identified as running Doppelgänger, holds the operational power behind the accounts. Platform owners hold the power to detect and remove them. Federal officials hold intelligence and coordination authority. Political actors shape whether those institutions are permitted to function.

Calling this a story about “trolls” risks shrinking an organized state-backed influence campaign into an image of obnoxious strangers online. The trolls are disposable labor and software. The consequential actors are the government financing the operation, the firm directing it, and the platforms controlling access to audiences.

X’s removal of 13,000 accounts demonstrates both capacity and limitation. Deleting accounts can disrupt a network, but it does not dismantle the institution creating replacements. Enforcement confined to individual profiles treats the supply as endless because, in practice, it is.

The censorship diversion worked

The deeper institutional failure described here is the retreat by social-media companies from monitoring coordinated manipulation. According to the Times, foreign operations have become harder to track as platforms pulled back after conservatives and MAGA-aligned figures accused companies of working with the government to suppress speech.

That controversy redirected attention from conduct to grievance. The relevant distinction is not between approved and disfavored opinions. It is between authentic political participation and coordinated deception conducted through fabricated identities on behalf of foreign powers.

When every attempt to identify manipulation is recast as censorship, propagandists gain room to operate. The immediate beneficiaries are foreign influence networks. The political beneficiaries are candidates whom those networks choose to support. The cost is imposed on voters who are asked to evaluate manufactured testimony as though it came from real people.

Administrative weakness has political consequences

The failed classified briefing matters even without evidence of intent. State election personnel were supposed to receive federal intelligence about midterm threats; Trump administration officials reportedly could not establish a secure connection. The result was the same regardless of motive: officials responsible for elections did not receive the planned briefing.

The article provides no basis to call that technical failure sabotage. It does provide grounds to call it institutional failure. A government aware of an active foreign influence campaign must be able to communicate securely with the officials expected to confront it. Incapacity is not politically neutral when the adversary is organized, funded, and already operating at scale.

Propaganda thrives on manufactured ambiguity

The larger pattern is not simply that Russia is “sowing division.” That phrase can obscure direction and consequence. The reporting describes a targeted campaign that exploits a genuine policy conflict, impersonates people with an immediate stake in that conflict, attacks one party, and favors the other.

Modern influence operations do not need to invent every grievance. They need only identify an existing fracture, counterfeit the voices inside it, and make one political faction appear weaker, more isolated, or more treacherous than it is. Platform retreat and government dysfunction then do the rest.

The systemic error is treating coordinated power as ambient disorder. These messages did not materialize from national confusion. According to the reporting, identifiable Russian institutions produced and distributed them for a political purpose—and American institutions have made that work easier to conceal.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Russian troll farms are back —and they’re boosting the GOP: NYT

item.title: Fox News lets profane opinion of Trump slip out on live TV
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News aired interviews about President Donald Trump’s decision to cancel a planned livestream of Nidal Hasan’s firing-squad execution. Trump had initially supported the broadcast plan announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, but reversed course after learning Hasan was partially paralyzed and after polling reportedly found that eight in 10 Americans opposed a public execution.

The interviewees largely welcomed the reversal, describing the proposed spectacle as inhumane, politically damaging and reminiscent of North Korea. One woman said Trump wanted to avoid looking bad before concluding with a profane condemnation of him that Fox allowed to air.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and injured 32 at a Texas military base. AlterNet also cites a Fox poll placing Trump’s job approval at 36 percent—the lowest Fox had recorded for either of his terms—while noting that polling alone does not establish why he abandoned the livestream.

Power ordered the spectacle

The decisive actors were not pedestrians answering questions for a television segment. Hegseth announced that the Pentagon would broadcast an execution, Trump initially endorsed that decision, and Trump later overturned it. Institutional power ran from the defense secretary to the president; everyone else was reacting to what they authorized.

That distinction matters because canceling an abuse does not erase responsibility for approving it. The administration brought the proposed spectacle into public life, tested its acceptability and withdrew it only after backlash. Whatever ultimately drove Trump’s reversal, the restraint came from the same office that had first said “absolutely.”

A reversal packaged as reassurance

Fox framed the interviews as public approval of Trump’s decision. But the comments AlterNet recounts express relief that the government stepped back from broadcasting state killing—not admiration for presidential judgment.

That framing relocates attention from the administration’s conduct to Trump’s supposed responsiveness. The central fact is not that people appreciated the cancellation. It is that senior officials considered televising an execution, publicly promoted the idea and possessed the authority to carry it out.

The final profane remark punctured the segment’s intended mood, but the editorial distortion preceded it. Fox converted rejection of an administration proposal into a favorable story about the official who had supported it.

Cruelty as political theater

Hasan’s crimes and sentence do not answer the question of whether the state should turn an execution into mass entertainment. The administration’s plan would have added an audience to punishment, making public spectacle part of the penalty.

The interviewees understood that distinction. They called the proposal inhumane, compared it with authoritarian practice and dismissed its claimed deterrent value as “shock effect.” Their objections were not sympathy for Hasan. They were objections to a government using its power to stage death for viewers.

The reported sequence suggests a recurring political method: propose an extreme display of force, measure the reaction, then present retreat as prudence. The evidence does not establish Trump’s private motive, but it does establish that his reversal followed his initial support and overwhelming reported opposition.

The profanity was not the scandal

A vulgar insult slipping through Fox’s edit is an embarrassment for a broadcaster. A Pentagon plan to livestream an execution is an exercise of state power. Treating the former as the remarkable event trivializes the latter.

The obscenity also tempts coverage toward personality drama: an angry voter, a television mishap, a president with poor approval numbers. Those details are vivid, but they are politically secondary. No interviewee commanded the military justice system. Hegseth and Trump did.

The system tests the boundary

This episode reveals how authoritarian spectacle can be normalized through bureaucratic announcement, presidential endorsement and media reframing before public resistance forces a retreat. The machinery does not need to complete the act to expose itself. The proposal, approval and promotional enthusiasm already show what officials considered permissible.

When power cancels its own cruelty, it often asks to be credited for moderation. That is the misdirection. The relevant standard is not whether officials eventually listened. It is why the country had to rely on polling and public revulsion to stop them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox News lets profane opinion of Trump slip out on live TV

item.title: Nicolle Wallace melts down: 'Country run by men nobody wanted to date’
item.description:
What happened

MS NOW anchor Nicolle Wallace said the United States was “run by men who nobody wanted to date” during a Friday-night discussion of masculinity rhetoric and health policies associated with President Donald Trump’s administration and its allies. According to AlterNet, Wallace made the remark after Pentagon reporter Priya Sridhar and others discussed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s promotion of a “high T” military culture, the removal of some vaccine requirements, and proposals involving nicotine as a supposed aid to testosterone and mental clarity.

The segment also covered claims circulating among prominent MAGA media figures. Tucker Carlson has blamed declining testosterone on feminism and promotes unusually strong nicotine pouches, while former FBI deputy director Dan Bongino has argued that higher testosterone makes men more masculine and lethal. AlterNet reports that Wallace ridiculed those claims and compared Hegseth to a caricature of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and “GI Joe.”

The report does not establish which nicotine-related ideas, if any, became military policy. It distinguishes them only unevenly from actual administrative decisions, leaving the status and scope of several measures unclear.

Power wears a costume

The consequential actor here is not Carlson, Bongino, or the wider “manosphere.” It is the Trump administration, particularly Hegseth as defense secretary. Media personalities can manufacture grievance and sell products; government officials can convert that culture into rules affecting service members.

That distinction matters because the story’s most serious claim concerns military health policy, not embarrassing podcast chatter. Vaccine requirements and medical standards carry institutional consequences. Testosterone boasts and nicotine folklore become politically significant when officials with command authority treat them as governing principles.

The joke obscures the chain of command

Wallace’s insult is memorable, but it redirects attention from authority to personal inadequacy. Whether these men were desirable dates is irrelevant. The problem is that officials can impose decisions on people who cannot dismiss them as easily as viewers can dismiss a podcast.

AlterNet compounds that misdirection by organizing the story around Wallace “melting down” and “exploding.” Her reaction becomes the event. The administration’s reported choices become material for a television personality’s exasperation. That is entertainment framing applied to state power.

Masculinity as policy language

The rhetoric described by AlterNet presents masculinity as something chemically depleted, socially stolen and politically recoverable. Feminism becomes the culprit; nicotine and testosterone become the cure; lethality becomes proof of manhood.

That framework does useful political work for its promoters. It turns public questions about evidence, readiness and medical risk into loyalty tests about toughness. Expertise can then be dismissed as weakness, while dubious claims acquire credibility through repetition by powerful men.

The source does not establish that every idea discussed was adopted or that officials share one coordinated motive. It does show the same vocabulary moving between partisan media and government: resentment dressed up as physiology, then marketed as strength.

The missing scrutiny

A stronger report would specify which vaccine mandates were removed, when the decisions occurred, what medical authorities advised and whether nicotine distribution was an official proposal or merely online advocacy. Without those distinctions, mockery fills the space where accountability should be.

That weakness does not make the underlying questions trivial. It makes precision more necessary. If officials changed military health requirements, their decisions deserve scrutiny based on evidence and foreseeable consequences—not a montage of grotesque remarks loosely bundled together.

Government by grievance

The larger pattern is the migration of influencer politics into administrative power. A subculture invents a humiliation, assigns blame to women or experts, sells a bodily remedy and recasts domination as health. Officials then borrow that language to advertise institutional toughness.

The scandal is not that powerful men sound insecure. It is that insecurity can become a governing aesthetic, while coverage turns the resulting exercise of power into a viral punchline. The audience gets catharsis. The officials keep the authority.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Nicolle Wallace melts down: ‘Country run by men nobody wanted to date’

item.title: Family insider warns president 'trapped' in sad world of lies
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Mary Trump, President Donald Trump’s niece, said on her Friday podcast that her uncle is “trapped” in a false self-image rooted in lessons from his father, Fred Trump, and reinforced by aides willing to indulge him. She described a recurring tactic: when Donald Trump or his allies face an uncomfortable question, they redirect blame, attack the questioner, or accuse others of the same defects alleged against them.

Mary Trump characterized that conduct as psychological projection and argued that her uncle learned to treat vulnerability, dependence, and failure as dangerous. Those are her interpretations, not independently established diagnoses. Her broader claim is political: Trump does not sustain this defensive framework alone; people around him help maintain it even when doing so harms the country and themselves.

The diagnosis is not the story

The article packages a system of political evasion as a family tragedy. Mary Trump’s account of her uncle’s upbringing may help explain her interpretation of his behavior, but explanation can become misdirection when it displaces responsibility.

A president is not merely a damaged relative surrounded by unfortunate influences. He holds executive power. His insults, diversions, and refusals to answer questions operate from the presidency, backed by its authority and amplified by officials, congressional allies, and communications staff. Whatever their psychological origin, these are political acts with political effects.

Power has willing hands

Mary Trump’s strongest observation concerns the people who consult prepared notes for somebody else to blame. Those officials are not powerless captives inside Donald Trump’s private reality. They make choices: to evade, to repeat accusations, and to convert oversight into another venue for propaganda.

Calling them “weak” captures their submission but understates their agency. An aide who launders a president’s grievance into an official response is enabling the outcome. A lawmaker who substitutes scapegoating for an answer is using institutional standing to obstruct accountability. Their obedience is consequential precisely because they possess access, office, and an audience.

Deflection is a governing method

Whether every insult constitutes unconscious projection cannot be established from the reporting. The observable pattern requires no clinical certainty: a difficult question is met with an attack, an accusation, or a change of target. The original issue disappears beneath a manufactured dispute over the questioner.

That is more than bad temperament. It shifts scrutiny from the powerful actor who owes an answer to the weaker person demanding one. When female reporters are demeaned instead of answered, the insult also enforces a hierarchy: the president defines the encounter, while the journalist is forced to defend her intelligence, demeanor, or dignity.

Pity obscures accountability

The “sad world of lies” framing invites readers to see Trump chiefly as imprisoned by his father’s lessons and his own defenses. That may be Mary Trump’s sincere family assessment. Politically, however, the cage has an open door for everyone who benefits from guarding it.

The administration’s flacks and congressional defenders have incentives that a family diagnosis cannot explain away: proximity to power, partisan advantage, career protection, and relief from answering damaging questions. Their conduct should not be reduced to emotional caretaking. They turn one man’s evasions into an institutional practice.

The system rewards the lie

The larger pattern is not simply that a powerful man rejects unwelcome facts. Political institutions repeatedly reward people who help him do it. Deflection succeeds when officials repeat it, allies legitimize it, and coverage treats the resulting spectacle as a personality drama rather than an organized failure of accountability.

Donald Trump’s inner life may explain something about Donald Trump. It cannot absolve the officials who choose to serve his evasions, nor should it obscure who possesses the power to impose them. The systemic error is treating organized obedience as pathology and deliberate political conduct as a sad misunderstanding.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Family insider warns president ‘trapped’ in sad world of lies

item.title: Trump’s latest Ukraine move has experts whispering ‘impeachment’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the White House ordered limits on Starshield, the Pentagon-funded satellite network Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone operations. The disruption occurred on the same night Russia attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure with 39 ballistic missiles, reportedly leaving about 600,000 Kyiv residents without power. Reuters attributed the order to the White House through two unnamed U.S. officials and one unnamed Western official; the reporting presented no evidence that the timing was coordinated with Russia.

The move came as Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refining capacity were constraining diesel exports and contributing to higher prices. Trump subsequently lifted six-year-old restrictions and announced Russian diesel shipments totaling 4.8 million tons. AlterNet says Russia offered no reported concession in return, while noting that the promised fuel would amount to roughly nine days of U.S. supply.

The article argues that these events could form the basis of another Ukraine-related impeachment controversy. But its gravest questions—who issued the precise order, why it was issued, whether anyone coordinated with Russia, and what objective the restriction served—remain unanswered in the reporting presented.

The power was in Washington

Ukraine did not choose to lose access to a military communications system during a major Russian assault. The decisive authority sat inside the White House, according to the officials cited by Reuters, while the Pentagon paid for the network and Ukrainian forces depended on it.

That distribution of power matters. Washington could alter a battlefield capability from afar; Ukraine had to absorb the operational risk while defending its territory. Russia, meanwhile, benefited from any degradation of Ukrainian communications regardless of whether the disruption was designed to help Moscow. The foreseeable effect is concrete even where intent remains unproved.

A decision without an accountable decision-maker

The article’s central weakness is also the scandal’s protective structure: it identifies the institution responsible but not the official who acted. “The White House” is a location, not an accountable person. Someone authorized the restriction, someone transmitted it, and others implemented it.

AlterNet moves too quickly from that institutional attribution to the language of sabotage. The reported facts justify scrutiny of a consequential White House intervention. They do not establish coordination with Russia, a corrupt bargain, or even the decision’s stated rationale. Calling the episode sabotage before those facts are known risks replacing investigation with conclusion—and giving officials an easy way to dismiss the underlying conduct as partisan exaggeration.

Diesel is the political pressure point

The clearest incentive described in the reporting is domestic economic pressure. Ukrainian strikes had sharply reduced Russian diesel exports, according to commodities researcher Rory Johnston, while American voters were angry about fuel prices and the wider cost of living. Trump’s answer was to permit Russian supply and advertise millions of tons of prospective deliveries.

Yet AlterNet reports that the volume would barely affect the American market and that Russia made no concession. If accurate, that makes the policy look less like leverage than unilateral accommodation: Washington relaxed restrictions, Moscow retained its position, and Ukraine faced a simultaneous constraint on military communications.

The article should not pretend the economic motive has been proved. It has, however, identified the relevant chain of power: voter anger created pressure on the administration; the administration changed U.S. policy; Russia gained market access; and Ukraine bore new military exposure.

Impeachment is not the first question

The headline foregrounds experts “whispering” about impeachment, but the supplied article identifies no roster of experts making that assessment. Its explicit impeachment argument comes from the columnist. The teaser therefore inflates speculation into something resembling an emerging professional consensus that the text does not document.

That framing also skips over the necessary factual work. Before impeachment can be more than a provocative label, Congress would need to determine who ordered the Starshield restriction, what legal authority supported it, what agencies objected or complied, what communications preceded it, and whether the timing with Russia’s missile barrage was coincidence, opportunism, or coordination. The reporting establishes a decision demanding accountability, not the completed case the headline implies.

The system protects power with ambiguity

This episode reveals a familiar method of executive insulation. A major decision is attributed to an institution; the responsible official remains unnamed; the rationale is absent; allies experience the consequences; and public debate is diverted toward the most explosive possible verdict before the evidentiary record exists.

That is how power escapes examination. The unanswered question is not whether the episode already fits a dramatic political label. It is why an American president’s White House could reportedly restrict a besieged country’s battlefield communications, offer no public explanation in the account presented, and leave everyone else arguing about speculation instead of compelling the decision-makers to identify themselves and defend what they did.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s latest Ukraine move has experts whispering ‘impeachment’

item.title: The most boring job in politics just became Trump’s next major battleground
item.description:
What happened

The supplied AlterNet material does not answer the headline’s question. It contains only a string of names and phrases, not reporting about a political office, a decision, a dispute, or a result.

Nothing provided identifies the supposedly “boring job,” explains why it became a battleground, or establishes Donald Trump’s role. Any more specific account would be invented.

Power cannot be inferred

The excerpt names political figures and commentators but describes no authority exercised by any of them. It therefore provides no factual basis for identifying who held institutional power, who made a decision, or who enabled an outcome.

A headline is not evidence

The headline frames a conflict and assigns Trump a central role, but the supplied text offers no reporting to support that frame. A teaser can direct attention; it cannot substitute for facts about the institution, the actors, or the stakes.

Analysis requires an event

There is no documented conduct here to evaluate for scapegoating, propaganda, corruption, cruelty, or institutional cowardice. Forceful commentary built on missing evidence would merely convert editorial confidence into fabricated certainty.

The systemic error

Political media often packages obscure institutions as personality-driven combat. Whether that happened in this article cannot be determined from the material supplied. The only defensible conclusion is narrower: when the reporting disappears and only the promotional frame remains, power becomes impossible to scrutinize—and speculation rushes in to impersonate analysis.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The most boring job in politics just became Trump’s next major battleground

item.title: Trump swaps half his female cabinet for men amid wide male misconduct
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing the Guardian, reports that four of the Trump administration’s eight female cabinet officials left or were removed within several months, and that men replaced all four. They were Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Attorney General Pam Bondi, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard. Trump separately denied that he was considering replacing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

The reported departures followed distinct events. Noem was fired on March 5 amid uproar over immigration operations that killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis. Bondi was ousted in April after failing to prosecute Trump’s political opponents aggressively enough, according to the Guardian, and after political fallout from her handling of the Epstein-file release. Chavez-DeRemer resigned amid inspector-general allegations of workplace misconduct. Gabbard was pushed out after telling Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon, contradicting Trump’s case for attacking Iran.

AlterNet contrasts those exits with the continued employment of senior men facing misconduct or competence allegations, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and FBI Director Kash Patel. The report also notes other women’s departures, including press secretary Katie Zacharia after five days and an ambassador identified only as Kimberly after allegations that she sought money from a donor in exchange for administration access.

The power belongs to Trump

The decisive fact is not that women happened to leave. It is that Trump controlled who remained, who was dismissed and who replaced them. The pattern described by AlterNet is therefore a record of presidential personnel decisions, not an unexplained demographic drift.

Each cabinet official’s conduct still has to be judged on its own evidence. Chavez-DeRemer faced serious allegations; Bondi and Noem presided over consequential controversies. Gender does not immunize an official from accountability. But accountability becomes patronage when punishment depends less on conduct than on usefulness to the president.

Loyalty is the operating standard

The clearest examples are Bondi and Gabbard. According to the reporting, Bondi’s failure was not institutional negligence alone but insufficient aggression against Trump’s political enemies. Gabbard’s offense was giving Congress an intelligence assessment that conflicted with the president’s argument for war.

That is an authoritarian personnel logic: officials are retained for obedience and discarded when professional judgment obstructs presidential preference. Gabbard’s replacement—first by loyalist Bill Pulte, who reportedly lacked intelligence experience, and later by Jay Clayton—underscores the priority. Expertise was subordinate to alignment.

Misconduct is not applied evenly

The headline’s emphasis on “male misconduct” risks flattening important distinctions: the allegations against these officials vary in seriousness, substantiation and relevance to their jobs. But the underlying comparison is legitimate. The administration reportedly tolerated grave concerns surrounding powerful men while rapidly removing women, sometimes for disloyalty rather than misconduct.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez described that as rewarding male misconduct. The evidence presented cannot establish that every personnel decision was caused by sexism. It does establish a gendered outcome produced by discretionary choices: half the women in the cabinet departed, every replacement was a man, and senior male officials remained despite reported controversies.

The women were never the power

Trump’s appointment of women functioned as a defense against accusations of misogyny. That argument was always cosmetic. Giving individual women prestigious jobs does not redistribute presidential authority, constrain abusive policy or create neutral standards of accountability.

Noem’s role makes the point especially starkly. As the public face of mass deportation, she exercised substantial power over people with far less institutional protection. Her eventual dismissal does not turn her into the primary victim of that system. The relevant hierarchy runs downward from the president through cabinet officials to those subjected to state force.

Patronage consumes institutions

This story is larger than a cabinet gender count. It describes an administration in which continued employment appears tied to personal loyalty, inconvenient professional judgments carry penalties, and alleged misconduct matters unevenly depending on who commits it and whether that person remains useful.

The result is institutional decay with a personnel chart. Competence becomes optional, candor becomes dangerous, and accountability becomes selective. Women can be displayed as evidence of inclusion and discarded when they cease serving the president’s political needs. The governing principle is not equality or even consistent discipline. It is proximity to power on power’s terms.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump swaps half his female cabinet for men amid wide male misconduct

item.title: Trump faces new court battle after GOP judge quotes Orwell in rebuke
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to undermine the Presidential Records Act, the post-Watergate law establishing that official White House records belong to the government, not personally to the president. The administration’s lawyers were scheduled to argue on October 16 that the law unconstitutionally intrudes on executive authority.

U.S. District Judge John Bates, a George W. Bush appointee, rejected that position in May, found the law likely constitutional, and ordered White House officials to follow it while litigation continues. Citing George Orwell’s warning that control of the present enables control of the past, Bates recognized what is at stake: whether a president can determine which evidence of his administration survives.

Historians and government watchdogs brought the case. They argue that invalidating the statute could effectively extinguish public access to presidential papers. The appellate outcome was unresolved in AlterNet’s report, and conservative attorney Michael Edney said the dispute could reach the Supreme Court.

The power to erase

This is not an administrative quarrel over filing practices. The presidency commands the officials who create, handle, classify, and preserve records. Giving the officeholder personal ownership of those materials would place the evidence of presidential conduct under the control of the person with the strongest incentive to manage its release.

Congress enacted the records law after Watergate precisely because presidential documentation cannot safely depend on presidential preference. The law treats preservation as a public obligation because executive power otherwise carries its own machinery of concealment.

Trump’s Justice Department is asking courts to weaken that constraint. The institutional actor is not an abstract “White House” burdened by paperwork. It is an administration asserting that Congress lacks authority to require the executive branch to preserve the public’s records.

Candor is a convenient alibi

Administration lawyers contend that recordkeeping could discourage advisers from speaking frankly. That argument turns accountability into the alleged enemy of competent government.

Advisers can offer candid advice without receiving a license to make the documentary history disappear. The government already handles sensitive and classified material without declaring it the president’s private property. Former Bush National Security Council lawyer John Bellinger also identified the operational cost: later officials need prior administrations’ national-security records to understand dealings with foreign leaders.

The administration’s theory therefore protects more than conversational freedom. It would expand presidential control over what successors, historians, watchdogs, and eventually the public can know. Calling that result a reduction in “burden” disguises who acquires power and who loses access.

The weaker actors are not the problem

Coverage of institutional conflict often collapses into a spectacle of personalities: Trump faces another court battle; a Republican-appointed judge quotes Orwell; lawyers trade constitutional theories. Those details are real, but they can obscure the hierarchy.

Historians and watchdog groups do not control federal records. The public cannot preserve documents it never sees. Future administrations cannot consult material that was destroyed, withheld, or converted into private property. The executive branch holds the records and the practical power over their fate; the lawsuit exists because weaker actors are trying to enforce a statutory limit on that power.

Even the emphasis on Bates’s Republican pedigree reflects a diminished expectation: a ruling against a Republican president is presented as more striking when delivered by a Republican appointee. The relevant fact is not partisan surprise. It is that a federal judge ordered the administration to comply with a law enacted to prevent presidents from owning the history of their own rule.

Accountability after the evidence is gone

AlterNet connects this dispute to Trump’s retention of sensitive records at Mar-a-Lago after leaving office in 2021. That episode produced criminal charges, but the case was dismissed in 2024 over special counsel Jack Smith’s appointment, and prosecutors later dropped the charges after Trump won the election. Those facts do not decide the constitutionality of the Presidential Records Act, but they sharpen the foreseeable consequences of weakening it.

Legal accountability already moves slowly and can collapse for procedural or political reasons. If preservation rules are also weakened, oversight may fail earlier—before investigators, courts, Congress, or the public can examine the underlying record at all.

Control the archive, narrow the future

The larger pattern is executive power treating every external restraint as an intrusion: congressional rules become separation-of-powers violations, preservation becomes an administrative burden, and public ownership becomes an obstacle to presidential candor.

An archive is not ceremonial debris from a completed administration. It is part of the state’s institutional memory and the raw material of later accountability. A president who can decide what history retains does not merely shape a legacy. That president gains power over what future officials can learn, what investigators can establish, and which abuses can ever be proved.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump faces new court battle after GOP judge quotes Orwell in rebuke

item.title: Six-figure foreign secret ties an Idaho campaign to Russia
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that political consultant Chris LaCivita, whom Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s reelection campaign named a senior adviser in February, was also paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to advise the Russia-aligned government of Republika Srpska, an entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina. The New York Times reported on Oct. 6 that LaCivita and another adviser traveled there ahead of a recent election.

LaCivita was also identified as Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign co-manager and an adviser to the MAGA Inc. super PAC. Little’s campaign had celebrated his experience and ability to craft “winning messages and tactics,” but the reporting does not establish what work he performed for Little or whether he remained on the campaign.

LaCivita could not be reached. Little campaign manager Joan Vargas did not answer repeated questions from the Idaho Capital Sun about LaCivita’s current role or whether Little knew of the trip.

The campaign holds the answers

The institutional power in this story rests with Little and the campaign officials who hired LaCivita, defined his access and can disclose whether that relationship continues. LaCivita chose to undertake the reported foreign work. Little’s campaign chose to bring him inside its operation and publicly endorse his political judgment.

The available reporting does not establish that Little knew about the Republika Srpska engagement or that LaCivita performed foreign-related work for the Idaho campaign. It does establish that the campaign possessed the information needed to clarify its relationship and declined to provide it.

That silence is not proof of misconduct. It is an exercise of power: the campaign can withhold basic facts while reporters and voters are left to reconstruct the arrangement from announcements and unanswered messages.

Influence without accountability

Political consultants can move among domestic campaigns, super PACs and foreign clients while carrying techniques, contacts and reputational authority across those roles. The Times noted that foreign political work is common in the industry. Common, however, is not the same as politically trivial.

LaCivita was valuable to Little precisely because of the experience and strategic influence the governor praised. When someone with that standing advises a Russia-aligned foreign government while assisting Trump-aligned candidates before the Nov. 3 midterms, the relevant issue is not mere proximity. It is whether campaigns impose any disclosure or conflict standards on the operatives they place near political decision-making.

The reporting cannot answer that question because Little’s campaign would not explain its own arrangement.

The disclosure gap is the story

The weakest framing would treat this as an exotic tale about a consultant traveling abroad. That shifts attention away from the American institutions that hire such consultants and decide how little the public will be told.

No evidence presented here shows that Idaho policy was affected, that campaign information crossed borders or that Little approved LaCivita’s foreign engagement. Those gaps limit what can responsibly be alleged. They also expose the accountability failure: voters cannot evaluate possible conflicts when campaigns refuse to disclose the consultant’s duties, tenure or rules.

The unanswered questions are therefore not atmospheric suspicion. They are specific omissions controlled by named actors.

A political system built for deniability

Modern campaign power increasingly runs through private consultants and outside spending groups that wield influence without accepting the disclosure obligations associated with public office. Elected officials receive their expertise and networks, then retreat behind campaign staff when those relationships attract scrutiny.

This arrangement distributes influence while concentrating deniability. The consultant can remain unreachable. The campaign manager can remain silent. The governor can benefit from the adviser’s prestige without publicly accounting for the boundaries of his role.

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as message discipline. When political organizations will not state who advises them, what those advisers do or whether outside clients create conflicts, opacity is not an accidental gap in the story. It is part of how power protects itself.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Six-figure foreign secret ties an Idaho campaign to Russia

item.title: The crush of Trump’s corruption is finally settling in
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that economist and Bulwark columnist Catherine Rampell argues the cumulative weight of President Donald Trump’s financial conflicts and economic policies is registering with voters. She cited allegedly suspicious market trades before Trump withdrew threats against Iran, efforts to profit through Truth Social and cryptocurrency, and questions surrounding donations for a White House ballroom. The article does not establish who made the trades or prove insider trading.

An AP-NORC poll cited by Rampell found that three-quarters of Americans—including 55 percent of Republicans—said Trump had prioritized his own financial interests and those of people close to him since returning to office in 2025. AlterNet also cites arguments from Robert Reich and Robert J. Shapiro that Trump’s tariffs, tax changes, defense spending, and projected deficits impose broader costs on households and future taxpayers.

The power is concentrated

Trump is not merely a businessman benefiting from government policy. He is the president directing that policy while retaining financial interests that, according to the reporting, include cryptocurrency and Truth Social. That combination creates the central institutional problem: the official who can move markets, grant tariff relief, and shape federal spending may also benefit personally from decisions made under presidential authority.

Congressional Republicans supply the enabling power. The article attributes tighter SNAP rules and incentives for states to remove recipients to Republicans’ “One Big Beautiful Bill.” Those outcomes did not emerge from bureaucratic fog. Legislators wrote the rules, passed them, and shifted the administrative burden onto states and benefit recipients.

Suspicion is not proof—but conflicts still matter

The oil and stock trades placed roughly fifteen minutes before Trump changed course on Iran are suspicious as described, but AlterNet does not identify the traders or establish that they possessed inside information. Calling the episode proven insider trading would outrun the evidence.

That evidentiary limit does not erase the conflict. A president’s statements can alter prices within minutes. When access to his intentions may be extraordinarily valuable—and when his own private ventures create additional channels for money to flow toward him—opacity becomes an asset for insiders and a liability for everyone else. The scandal is not only what prosecutors could prove. It is an arrangement that repeatedly forces the public to wonder whether state power is being exercised for public purposes or private gain.

Scarcity below, discretion above

The article’s most revealing contrast is between punitive precision for poor people and discretionary generosity for powerful interests. SNAP recipients face stricter work requirements, heavier paperwork, and removal from the rolls when administrative systems buckle. Companies seeking tariff exemptions, by Reich’s account, face a system in which presidential carve-outs can reward favored industries or firms.

That is redistribution through institutional design. Need is met with documentation demands and presumptions of ineligibility; influence is met with access and exceptions. AlterNet reports rising food insecurity and cites Pew data showing that one in five Americans received food from a food bank or pantry during the previous year. Those facts do not by themselves establish that Trump’s policies caused every hardship, but they clarify who bears the risk when government chooses enforcement downward and flexibility upward.

The corruption frame can obscure the machinery

Calling the administration “corrupt” captures the alleged self-dealing but can flatten distinct abuses into one moral label. The stronger case lies in the mechanisms: presidential control over tariffs, private financial ventures operating alongside public office, opaque donor relationships, tax changes with large budgetary costs, and benefit rules designed to produce attrition through paperwork.

The story also weakens itself by bundling proven policies, polling, estimates, suspicions, and allegations without consistently separating them. The reported $1,100 increase in annual household costs is an estimate attributed to Yale’s Budget Lab, not a bill delivered uniformly to every family. Shapiro’s projected deficits of 6 to 7 percent of GDP are forecasts tied to policy choices, not current measurements presented in the article. Precision strengthens the indictment; exaggeration gives its targets somewhere to hide.

The system rewards upward extraction

The larger pattern is a government that centralizes discretion at the top while making survival below more conditional. Wealthy actors can seek waivers, cultivate access, fund prestige projects, or position themselves around market-moving announcements. Poorer Americans must navigate expanding paperwork to retain food assistance.

Polls showing that many Republicans also perceive personal financial favoritism suggest the conduct is becoming harder to contain within partisan loyalty. But recognition alone does not restrain power. The durable political fact is that institutions have permitted public authority, private enrichment, and selective economic punishment to occupy the same structure. Whether every suspicion becomes a prosecutable offense is not the only question. The deeper failure is that the machinery makes extraction plausible, profitable, and difficult to police.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The crush of Trump’s corruption is finally settling in

item.title: The irony of the GOP's election ploy has trapped Republicans into a corner
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republicans’ 2026 election strategy of portraying voter fraud as rampant may discourage some of their own supporters from voting. The article argues that voters who accept Republican warnings about fraudulent results may conclude that participation is pointless, while Democrats who view those warnings as attempts to undermine the midterms may become more motivated to vote.

The piece cites a claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. According to the reporting, that figure fell to 185 when state officials requested details, and Nevada’s investigation found none of the named people to be noncitizen voters. It also cites polling in which 50% of Republicans distrust mail voting and 51% fear noncitizen voting.

The electoral effect remains uncertain. The research discussed by political scholar Christopher Miller suggests that distrust can suppress participation among voters who follow elite cues but energize voters who see voting as a way to correct institutional failure.

Power manufactured the distrust

This is not a story about voters spontaneously becoming confused. The actors with institutional power are the president, his administration, members of Congress and Republican Party leaders. They possess federal offices, media reach and the authority that turns repetition into perceived legitimacy.

Those officials chose to promote claims that the evidence presented here does not sustain. Mullin’s Nevada allegation is the cleanest example: a dramatic number entered public discussion under the authority of a Cabinet official, then collapsed when state authorities examined it. The accusation traveled first; the correction had to chase it.

Republican voters did not design this information environment. Party leaders did. If those voters now distrust elections, responsibility belongs first to the officials who used their offices to cultivate that distrust.

The “ploy” is not merely a blunder

The article emphasizes the irony that election delegitimization could reduce Republican turnout. That is politically interesting, but it risks shrinking the offense into a campaign tactic that backfired.

The larger consequence is institutional. Claims of pervasive fraud can prepare supporters to accept favorable results while rejecting unfavorable ones. Even if the immediate electoral effect hurts Republican candidates, the rhetoric still weakens the shared rules by which political defeat is recognized.

Calling this a trap captures the tactical predicament but understates the exercise of power. Republican leaders made factual allegations about election administration, immigrants and voting legitimacy. The available example shows those allegations failing under scrutiny. The problem is not simply that the message may be too effective with its intended audience. It is that officials used institutional authority to make an unsupported threat appear real.

Voters are the target, not the authors

Coverage of election distrust often relocates responsibility onto “low-information voters,” polarization or an abstract loss of confidence. That framing treats public suspicion like bad weather: unfortunate, widespread and nobody’s fault.

The reporting itself points elsewhere. It says elite cues shape expectations and that Republican voters are especially inclined to accept their leaders’ fraud claims. If that account is correct, voter behavior is a downstream effect of decisions made by people with far greater political agency.

The asymmetry matters. State election officials administer voter rolls and election security, while federal politicians can attack those systems without carrying the operational burden of disproving each accusation. The accuser receives attention; administrators inherit the cleanup.

The durable payoff

Republican candidates may pay a turnout price in November 2026, but that does not mean the strategy lacks political utility. A constituency trained to expect fraud can be encouraged to interpret defeat as proof of corruption rather than evidence that its candidates lost.

That creates a one-way standard of legitimacy: victory validates the system, while defeat indicts it. The reporting does not establish how many voters will act on that premise or whether it will decide control of Congress. It does establish a political environment in which prominent officials repeatedly cast ordinary election administration as suspect despite contrary evidence.

The systemic error

The deepest pattern is the conversion of governing authority into a machine for producing distrust. Officials make expansive claims, weaker institutions spend time disproving them, and coverage dwells on whether the resulting cynicism will help or hurt one party.

That horse-race question is secondary. The central fact is that those with the most power to protect confidence in elections are using that power to erode it, while the public absorbs the consequences. A propaganda strategy does not become less corrosive because it may also injure the politicians deploying it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The irony of the GOP’s election ploy has trapped Republicans into a corner

item.title: Americans face a grim choice this winter — thanks to Trump
item.description:
What happened

Americans who heat their homes with oil face a grim choice: absorb sharply higher bills, cut other spending, or lower the thermostat to potentially unsafe levels. AlterNet reports that heating oil had risen from roughly $2.50 per gallon at the same point in 2025 to $4.63, with prices projected to exceed $6 by deep winter.

The National Energy Assistance Directors Association estimated that affected households could spend about 50% more than the previous winter—an average increase of roughly $878, pushing seasonal costs above $2,600. The Energy Information Administration projected a smaller but still substantial 21% increase. The burden is concentrated in the Northeast, which consumes more than 80% of the country’s home-heating oil.

AlterNet attributes the underlying price shock primarily to wars affecting global oil production and distribution. The Trump administration did not create that entire shock, but it weakened the federal program intended to help poor households withstand it: the administration fired the dedicated federal staff of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program in April 2025 and proposed eliminating its funding. LIHEAP remained operational through state administrators, while the Department of Health and Human Services said it retained the capacity to distribute funds appropriated by Congress.

The headline overreaches

“Thanks to Trump” is politically satisfying and analytically incomplete. The reporting itself says the oil-price increase stems from disrupted global markets, including conflicts in the Middle East and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Blaming the president for the entire price surge obscures the actual chain of events.

Trump’s responsibility is narrower and more concrete. His administration stripped LIHEAP of its dedicated federal staff and sought to eliminate the program while heating costs were rising. That is not the cause of expensive oil. It is a decision to make expensive oil more punishing for households with the fewest financial options.

Loose blame weakens a strong indictment. The relevant charge is not that Trump controls every refinery, shipping route, and war. It is that his administration used its institutional authority to degrade a layer of protection against a foreseeable hardship.

Power sits in Washington

Households have almost no leverage over global oil prices, regional pipeline infrastructure, or federal assistance. Independent heating-oil customers also lack some protections commonly imposed on regulated utilities. Telling them to budget better would be scapegoating people for conditions they did not create and cannot negotiate away.

The Trump administration had power over federal staffing and budget priorities. Congress retained authority over appropriations. HHS controlled implementation of the money Congress made available. Those are the institutions with agency; the family deciding between heat and groceries is the object of their decisions, not a co-author of the crisis.

The administration’s assurance that HHS could distribute funds without LIHEAP’s dedicated staff does not erase the staffing decision. It merely states that the department believed it could still perform the work. Whether that reduced structure would delay or impair assistance was not established by AlterNet’s reporting, but removing specialized capacity during an affordability crisis plainly increases administrative risk.

States inherit the damage

Governors were already assembling emergency responses. Massachusetts unlocked nearly $150 million in relief and expanded assistance to middle-class oil-heating households. Rhode Island directed $28 million in reserves toward electric-bill relief, while Maine announced $40 million in automatic electricity discounts for low-income residents.

Those measures show state governments using available power, but they also expose the familiar federal maneuver: weaken a national support system, then leave states to construct uneven substitutes from emergency funds. Geography begins to determine protection. A household’s exposure depends not only on income and fuel type, but on whether its state has the money, legal tools, and political willingness to intervene.

Some of the announced relief also targets electricity rather than heating oil. That matters because oil customers face the steepest projected increase and often buy from independent dealers outside conventional utility-protection systems. “Energy relief” is not automatically relief for the households at the center of this story.

Cruelty through administrative retreat

The political pattern is not mysterious. Government can intensify hardship without ordering anyone to turn down the heat. It can fire the staff who administer aid, propose erasing the program, and insist that the remaining bureaucracy is sufficient. The harm then appears as household sacrifice rather than federal policy.

That is how deliberate retrenchment is laundered into unfortunate circumstance. The war-driven price shock is external; the decision to weaken LIHEAP is not. Conflating them lets the administration evade responsibility for its own choices while allowing critics to overclaim responsibility for forces beyond its control.

The systemic error is treating assistance as optional charity after markets deliver pain. Energy insecurity is structured by infrastructure, regulation, federal capacity, and political allocation. When officials dismantle capacity precisely where vulnerable households depend on it, the resulting suffering is not an administrative misunderstanding. It is the foreseeable consequence of who government chose to protect—and who it chose to leave exposed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Americans face a grim choice this winter — thanks to Trump

item.title: 'Desperate' Trump is 'just making a lot of this up': Wall Street expert
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that investor and former journalist Steve Rattner accused President Donald Trump of misrepresenting inflation and gasoline prices while blaming former President Joe Biden for current economic conditions. Appearing on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe,” Rattner said inflation was below 3 percent when Biden left office and had since risen; the article gives both 3 percent and 3.7 percent as the current figure without resolving that discrepancy.

Rattner also rejected Trump’s description of Biden-era inflation as the “worst” in American history, pointing to substantially higher rates in 1980 and the 1920s. He attributed a 25 percent increase in inflation to Trump’s tariffs, while host Joe Scarborough characterized Trump’s claims as lies.

On gasoline, Rattner said the price shown in his comparison was about $4.35 per gallon, versus roughly $3 when Biden left office—a difference he calculated at about 44 percent. The report does not establish whether those figures are national averages, regional prices, or prices from another defined market.

The power belongs to the president

Trump is not a spectator interpreting somebody else’s economy. He occupies the presidency and has made tariffs a flagship policy. That gives him institutional power to shape trade policy and substantial power to influence the economic agenda, even though no president directly controls every price.

The relevant political question is therefore not whether Biden once presided over higher inflation or gasoline prices. It is whether Trump’s claims accurately describe the conditions he inherited, the conditions under his administration, and the effects of policies he chose. According to the comparisons Rattner presented, they do not.

Blame as economic policy

Blaming Biden serves a clear political function: it assigns responsibility backward while Trump exercises power in the present. Pandemic-era inflation becomes a permanent alibi, even as the reported measurements move in the wrong direction under the current administration.

That maneuver also exploits a basic confusion between price levels and inflation. Slower inflation does not mean prices return to their earlier levels, and isolated historical peaks do not establish who is responsible for today’s movement. A president claiming credit for every favorable number while treating every unfavorable one as his predecessor’s inheritance is not offering an economic account. He is constructing immunity from accountability.

The article’s own loose arithmetic

AlterNet’s central case is weakened by imprecision. It alternates between current inflation of 3 percent and 3.7 percent, and it presents gasoline figures without identifying their geographic or statistical scope. Those omissions matter because a factual rebuttal depends on cleaner evidence than the claim it is rebutting.

The piece also says tariffs “caused” inflation to jump 25 percent when what it actually establishes is that Rattner made that attribution. His analysis may be correct, but the article does not provide the methodology needed to treat causation as independently demonstrated. Scathing television commentary is not a substitute for clearly sourced measurements.

The larger pattern

The underlying pattern is more durable than any single chart: political power is used to make policy, while political messaging is used to relocate responsibility. Trump’s account, as described by AlterNet, asks the public to judge Biden by the worst conditions during his term and Trump by conditions he says he intends to create.

That asymmetry is the point. The stronger actor claims agency over good news and helplessness before bad news, while the predecessor becomes an all-purpose culprit. Coverage should expose that allocation of power and responsibility with disciplined evidence. Otherwise, it risks turning accountability into another televised argument over who delivered the sharper insult.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Desperate’ Trump is ‘just making a lot of this up’: Wall Street expert
