item.title: 'A wake-up call': How Canada plans to insulate itself from volatile US politics
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Canada is responding to President Donald Trump’s trade war and repeated disparagement by seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States. McMaster University political scientist Don Abelson said Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is working more closely with European, Asian, and Latin American partners, while assessing which sectors require greater “strategic sovereignty.” The interview provides no specific agreements, targets, or timetable for that effort.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are intended to make American consumers feel the cost of their government’s policy, Abelson said. He argued that tariffs affecting Canadian lumber, energy, auto parts, aluminum, and steel would raise US consumer costs and could pressure members of Congress, governors, and the administration.

Abelson described Trump’s hostility as a rupture with the countries’ historically cooperative relationship, though he also noted that President Joe Biden’s “Buy American” policy caused friction with Ottawa. His central conclusion was that Canada can no longer base its economic security on the expectation of stable US policy after any one president leaves office.

Washington holds the leverage

The power imbalance is not obscure. The United States has roughly ten times Canada’s population and an economy Canada cannot match, as Abelson emphasized. Washington can impose enormous costs on its neighbor through presidential trade policy, while Ottawa’s available response is to retaliate, lobby governors and Congress, and begin the slow work of finding other markets.

Trump’s administration made the decision to wield that leverage against Canada. Ordinary Americans did not set the tariffs, and Canadian consumers did not choose the confrontation. Yet households and businesses on both sides of the border absorb the resulting costs.

That distinction matters because the interview repeatedly turns toward what consumers and civil society can do. They can complain, organize, and pressure officials. They cannot revoke presidential policy themselves. Institutional authority remains in Washington; public frustration is merely one possible constraint on it.

Retaliation is pressure, not symmetry

Canada’s tariffs are not equivalent evidence of two governments stumbling into a mutual dispute. In Abelson’s account, Ottawa imposed them in response to US tariffs and designed them to produce political pressure inside the United States. That still means deliberately imposing costs on people who did not personally make the decision. But sequence and power cannot be erased without distorting responsibility.

The article’s suggestion that Canadians are “taking it out on American consumers” performs exactly that distortion. It recasts a weaker state’s retaliatory instrument as popular vengeance, although Abelson explicitly describes a government strategy aimed at changing US policy.

His description does not establish that retaliation will succeed. Higher prices can generate pressure, but they can also deepen resentment or be redirected toward a convenient foreign target. A policy built around consumer pain depends on voters correctly identifying who initiated the conflict—precisely what careless framing makes harder.

The personality story is too small

The article foregrounds trade expert Ed Gresser’s view that Trump appears to harbor a personal animus toward Canada. Gresser also says he does not understand the reason. That establishes an observation about Trump’s rhetoric, not its motive.

Calling the conduct “weird” turns an exercise of state power into a psychological mystery. Trump’s references to Canada as the “51st state,” paired with tariffs against a deeply integrated trading partner, have political consequences whether the impetus is personal hostility, bargaining theater, or something else the reporting cannot establish.

The relevant fact is not that presidential behavior seems puzzling. It is that US institutions permit one administration’s antagonism to disrupt supply chains and force a neighboring country to reconsider decades of economic and defense policy. Personality may explain style. Power explains impact.

Dependence was a policy choice

Abelson does not absolve Canada’s political establishment. He argues that successive governments allowed the country to become too reliant on the US market and on disproportionate American funding for continental defense. Discussions about diversification continued for decades without eliminating that exposure.

Carney’s outreach therefore represents less a novel awakening than a delayed response to a known vulnerability. AlterNet’s headline promises a plan to insulate Canada, but the interview supplies a direction rather than an operational blueprint: diversify export markets, pursue selected international agreements, and strengthen strategic sovereignty.

That gap matters. “Resilience” is easy language for governments to adopt; reorganizing trade, industrial capacity, and defense commitments is expensive and politically contested. Without named policies, budgets, benchmarks, or completed agreements, insulation remains an ambition rather than a reported accomplishment.

The cost of unreliable power

The larger pattern is the conversion of economic interdependence into political leverage. A superpower can treat a close trading relationship as a pressure point; the smaller country must then spend money, diplomatic attention, and years of policy work reducing its exposure.

Canada’s answer is not to wait for a more courteous American president. Abelson’s analysis is that the underlying risk now extends beyond Trump: even Biden’s domestic purchasing doctrine reminded Ottawa that US governments will privilege US interests when they choose.

That is the durable consequence of Trump’s trade war. Trust destroyed by executive action cannot be restored by tone alone. Once an ally concludes that American policy is volatile enough to require structural protection, diversification becomes national risk management—and the United States loses influence that intimidation cannot easily recover.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘A wake-up call’: How Canada plans to insulate itself from volatile US politics

item.title: Trump’s attacks threaten to backfire in new fight to oust Fed's Lisa Cook
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s effort to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook may be undermined by his own statements. Trump called Cook “dishonest” but also complained that she is “an automatic no vote” against the lower interest rates he wants, tying his campaign against her to a policy dispute rather than merely to the mortgage allegations cited against her.

The Supreme Court stopped Trump’s initial attempt to dismiss Cook in June because she had not received an opportunity to respond, while leaving open another attempt following due process. The administration then created a committee of Trump appointees and scheduled a closed-door hearing for Nov. 5. Cook denied wrongdoing, had not been criminally charged, and, through attorney Abbe Lowell, questioned the committee’s objectivity and fitness.

The allegations originated with federal housing director Bill Pulte and concern whether Cook improperly identified two properties as primary residences on mortgage applications. According to the report, Cook’s lawyers said a scheduling conflict would prevent her from attending the planned hearing. The White House described the proceeding as fair and open; legal scholars quoted in the reporting questioned whether its outcome had effectively been predetermined.

The president supplied the pretext problem

Trump holds the decisive institutional power in this story. He wants to remove a Federal Reserve governor, selected the officials who will assess her case, and publicly announced both his judgment of Cook’s character and his frustration with her interest-rate position.

That matters because the committee is supposed to evaluate whether the allegations justify removal—not ratify the president’s monetary-policy preferences. Trump’s remark about Cook being an “automatic no vote” exposes an interest separate from the alleged mortgage conduct: he wants a more compliant Federal Reserve.

That does not establish that the allegations are false or prove how the committee will rule. It does establish a conflict between the administration’s claim of neutral adjudication and the president’s stated desire to eliminate a dissenting vote.

A hearing is not independence

The committee consists of National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas, all chosen by Trump. AlterNet reports that Hassett and Sonderling have aligned with Trump’s demand for lower rates, while Hassett has called the allegations serious and urged Cook to take leave.

The Supreme Court’s due-process requirement created an obstacle for the administration. The administration answered with a procedure under its own control. Columbia Law professor Kathryn Judge told The New York Times that the process looked like a series of hurdles surrounding an outcome that may already have been chosen. University of Pennsylvania professor Peter Conti-Brown called the arrangement “quasi judges in a quasi-judicial process” and characterized it as pretext.

The White House disputes that assessment. But “in-person hearing” is a description of format, not proof of impartiality. A closed-door session conducted by presidential appointees does not become independent merely because the administration labels it fair.

The weaker actor is made to carry the burden

The framing invites Cook to prove that she deserves a fair hearing from officials serving the president seeking her removal. That reverses the relevant burden. Cook must answer the allegations, but the administration must justify using state power through a credible process.

She has denied wrongdoing and, as the report notes, faced no criminal charges at that point. Those facts do not exonerate her, but they sharply limit what can honestly be claimed. Allegations can warrant investigation without becoming a ready-made basis for dismissal.

Focusing narrowly on whether Cook attends the Nov. 5 session risks misdirecting attention toward the weaker party’s procedural choices. Her scheduling conflict may affect the hearing, but it does not resolve the central institutional question: whether a committee assembled by Trump can impartially decide a case whose desired result he has already advertised.

Control is the larger prize

The consequence reaches beyond one governor’s tenure. Federal Reserve independence depends partly on insulating monetary-policy decisions from a president’s demand for immediate political obedience. If disagreement over interest rates can be paired with unresolved allegations and processed through an administration-designed tribunal, statutory independence becomes easier to circumvent.

The larger pattern is institutional capture through procedural formality. An executive encounters a legal constraint, constructs a process that minimally satisfies it, and places loyal appointees in the seats of judgment. The paperwork may change; the underlying concentration of power does not.

This case therefore turns on more than whether Lisa Cook completed mortgage documents properly. It tests whether due process will constrain presidential power or merely furnish that power with a cleaner script.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s attacks threaten to backfire in new fight to oust Fed’s Lisa Cook

item.title: The beginning of the end of the 'religious right’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Texas Democratic Senate candidate and seminarian James Talarico could weaken the religious right’s political authority by challenging it on Christian grounds. Appearing on Jimmy Kimmel’s show, Talarico called a religion that excuses cruelty through personal faith “an abomination” and “a cancer on the body of Christ,” then contrasted Republican policies on immigration, poverty, food assistance and Medicaid with Jesus’s teachings.

The article reports that Talarico was leading Republican opponent Ken Paxton by four points in a Times poll, though that snapshot does not establish an election outcome. It also cites Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick’s response that Talarico was “too radical for Texas” after Talarico said Christians cannot reject asylum seekers at the southern border.

AlterNet presents this exchange as evidence that Donald Trump’s conduct has created room for a Christian movement opposed to Republican rule. That possibility remains an argument, not an established beginning of the religious right’s end.

Power is more than scriptural authority

The religious right is not merely a congregation with questionable theology. As AlterNet notes, white evangelicals spent decades taking power within the Republican Party, while religious conservatives came to control Texas. Their influence rests on elections, party machinery and officeholders empowered to shape immigration policy, health coverage, food assistance and abortion law.

Talarico may possess theological credibility, but Republicans hold much of the institutional machinery he is criticizing. A compelling reading of Matthew does not enact legislation. Senators, governors, legislators and party leaders do that. Treating the conflict primarily as a contest over who interprets Christianity correctly risks obscuring the coercive power attached to one interpretation.

Patrick revealed the contradiction

Patrick’s statement did more than criticize a rival. By branding Talarico’s appeal to welcome asylum seekers as radical, the lieutenant governor placed a policy boundary above the religious obligation Talarico invoked.

That is politically revealing because Patrick publicly describes himself, as quoted by AlterNet, as “Christian first.” Talarico’s argument forces officials making that claim to reconcile it with the material consequences of their decisions. The question is no longer what faith they profess but what their power produces.

This is why “show me what you do” matters. It denies politicians the refuge of private belief when their public acts deprive other people of protection or aid.

The article mistakes vulnerability for collapse

AlterNet is strongest when it identifies the religious right’s exposed flank: its leaders claim moral authority while supporting policies Talarico argues are incompatible with the Gospels. The article is weaker when it leaps from that contradiction to “game over.”

No evidence presented here shows white evangelical control of Republican politics collapsing, much less ending. One candidate’s television appearance, one poll lead and one clumsy attack from Patrick demonstrate an opening, not a realignment. Institutions can survive hypocrisy when they continue delivering power, judges, legislation and partisan identity to their supporters.

The headline’s promised ending is therefore unproven. What the reporting establishes is a challenge to the religious right’s monopoly on Christian political language.

Theology can expose policy choices

Talarico’s intervention is potent because it removes the camouflage of abstraction. Cuts to food assistance become a decision about whether hungry people eat. Loss of Medicaid becomes a decision about whether sick people receive care. Deportation becomes state power exercised against immigrants and their families.

His argument also contests a familiar misdirection: presenting suffering as an unfortunate byproduct of neutral policy rather than the foreseeable result of choices made by identifiable officials. The Senate does not accidentally reduce benefits or authorize enforcement. Officeholders vote, administer and justify.

Still, theological criticism cannot substitute for political accountability. The decisive test is whether moral language changes votes, coalitions and governing power—not whether it wins a televised exchange.

The larger breach

The larger pattern is a struggle over who gets to convert religious identity into political legitimacy. For decades, the faction described by AlterNet treated conservative Christianity as nearly synonymous with Republican politics. Talarico is attacking that arrangement from inside the faith rather than asking voters to set faith aside.

That could matter even without ending the religious right. Once professed belief is measured against the treatment of immigrants, poor people, sick people and outcasts, religious branding becomes harder to use as a blanket absolution for state-inflicted harm.

The systemic issue is not whether one politician can reclaim Christianity for liberal policy. It is whether any moral vocabulary will be allowed to conceal the chain of responsibility between officials, their decisions and the people who bear the consequences.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The beginning of the end of the ‘religious right’

item.title: Morning Joe lampoons Trump and GOP for 'flailing desperately’
item.description:
What happened

MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” argued that House Speaker Mike Johnson and the Republican Party were “flailing desperately” because they could not credibly separate voter anger over the cost of living from Republican control of Washington. AlterNet reports that, with 20 days remaining before the Nov. 3 election, Johnson insisted Republicans were “on offense” even as he campaigned in reliably Republican Texas and struggled to explain why the governing party was not responsible for the economy.

Joe Scarborough accused Johnson of lying when the speaker said public frustration was unrelated to Republican policies. Scarborough blamed tariffs and the war for higher prices, while Willie Geist specifically described the war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as policy choices that raised oil and gas costs. The article attributes those causal claims to the hosts; it does not independently substantiate them.

The program also mocked Donald Trump’s continued attempt to blame Joe Biden and highlighted Republican culture-war rhetoric about masculinity. AlterNet further cites Axios reporting that Texas redistricting, once expected to help Republicans win at least 18 seats, appeared more likely to yield roughly five.

Power cannot plead helplessness

Republicans, as described in the report, control the House, Senate and White House. That is the central fact Johnson’s answer tried to evade. A governing party controls legislation, executive policy and much of the national agenda. It cannot plausibly campaign as an innocent spectator to conditions produced under its own authority.

Johnson’s claim that economic dissatisfaction was “not related to the Republicans in office” was not an explanation. It was an attempt to sever power from accountability. The CBS interviewer exposed the contradiction with one elementary question: How can the party running Washington disclaim responsibility for Washington’s results?

These were choices

The “Morning Joe” argument is strongest when it identifies decisions rather than moods. Tariffs are government policy. War is government policy. Redistricting is an exercise of state power. None is an atmospheric event that simply happened to Republican leaders.

The report does not provide enough evidence to independently calculate how much each policy contributed to particular price increases. But Johnson’s blanket denial is broader still: it asks voters to believe that Republican governance has no meaningful connection to the economy it governs. That is not economic analysis. It is political insulation.

The decoys are weaker targets

When material conditions become politically damaging, culture-war spectacle offers an escape hatch. The reported pivot from food and fuel prices to arguments about who counts as a “real man” shifts attention away from officials who set policy and toward people whose identities can be turned into campaign props.

That is classic scapegoating architecture: powerful officials make consequential choices, then public debate is redirected toward the social legitimacy of people with far less institutional power. Scarborough’s remark about Representative James Talarico’s sexuality underscores the point, although the article’s identification of Talarico as a Republican appears internally questionable and should not be treated as established from this text alone.

Gerrymandering meets its limits

Texas Republicans used legislative power to redraw districts and redistribute Democratic voters into more Republican-leaning territory. According to the figures AlterNet attributes to Axios, the anticipated gain then shrank from at least 18 seats to something closer to five.

Even engineered maps cannot guarantee political consent. Redistricting may alter the terrain, but it cannot erase anger over household costs or make an incumbent party look like an insurgency. Johnson’s Texas tour reveals the weakness behind the “on offense” slogan: power had already been used to shape the electorate, yet the party still found itself defending supposedly safe ground.

The governing-party alibi

The larger pattern is rule without ownership. Leaders claim credit for authority, legislative majorities and electoral victories, then describe damaging consequences as somebody else’s inheritance. When that fails, they substitute identity conflict for material explanation.

The misdirection matters because it obscures the only useful chain of accountability: who held power, what they chose, and what followed. A political system cannot discipline bad governance when officials are permitted to wield institutions aggressively and then campaign as if no one was in charge.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Morning Joe lampoons Trump and GOP for ‘flailing desperately’

item.title: Retired general predicts Trump’s firing-squad fantasy will implode
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump is reconsidering having Nidal Malik Hasan executed by firing squad after learning that Hasan, now 60, is paralyzed from the chest down and uses a wheelchair. Citing CBS News and a discussion on The Bulwark’s “Command Post” podcast, the report says the physical reality of the proposed execution may not produce the spectacle Trump expected.

Retired Gen. Mark Hertling and former prosecutor Margaret Donovan said the proposal would also create serious logistical, regulatory and ethical problems for the Army. Military executions are ordinarily conducted at Fort Leavenworth, not Fort Hood, and no serving personnel have experience carrying out a firing-squad execution. They also warned that the spectacle could aid Hasan’s desired portrayal of himself as a religious martyr and inflict moral injury on the service members ordered to participate.

The power belongs to the president

Hasan has no institutional control over the proposed execution. The decisive power sits with Trump and the military officials responsible for implementing any lawful order. The soldiers who might be assigned to fire the rifles would carry the psychological burden, but they would not be the architects of the event.

That distinction matters because spectacle can blur the chain of responsibility. A firing squad visually centers the people holding the weapons. Politically, however, the relevant decision is made far above them: whether the state should arrange this particular method of killing, at this particular location, under these particular conditions.

Governance reduced to stagecraft

According to the account presented by AlterNet, Trump’s hesitation arose after he learned that Hasan could not stand before the squad. If accurate, that suggests the wheelchair changed the envisioned image before it changed the underlying policy judgment.

That is not serious executive deliberation. It is governance organized around a scene: the condemned man, the rifles, the military backdrop and the president’s preferred posture of command. Army regulations, facilities, training requirements and the welfare of participating personnel become production complications.

Donovan’s question—whether the expense and logistical burden are justified for something functioning as theater—identifies the political failure precisely. The military is an institution with legal duties and human members, not a collection of props available to complete a president’s historical reenactment.

Cruelty does not become strength on camera

Hertling’s description strips away the sanitizing language. Hasan would reportedly be shot while seated in a wheelchair. The ammunition under discussion could produce extreme bodily destruction. The personnel ordered to carry out the execution could suffer lasting moral injury.

None of that determines the separate legal question of Hasan’s punishment. It does expose what the firing-squad proposal demands beyond punishment: a deliberately visible performance of state violence.

The foreseeable consequence is not merely revulsion. Hertling and Donovan warned that execution by spectacle could strengthen the martyr narrative Hasan reportedly seeks and make him more useful to extremist recruitment. A performance advertised as dominance could therefore hand propaganda material to the ideology it is supposed to defeat.

The framing lets the fantasy lead

The weakest element of the coverage is its emphasis on whether Trump’s “fantasy” will implode. That framing still grants him the central dramatic role: the strongman conceives a spectacle, then discovers that reality may spoil it.

The more consequential story is institutional. Who inside the government is expected to translate presidential fixation into plans? Who can refuse to treat soldiers as execution scenery? Who calculates the costs, applies Army Regulation 190-55 and accounts for the psychological consequences?

Calling the problem a logistical nightmare risks understating it. Logistics are not an accidental obstacle here. They are the institutional reality that presidential spectacle tries to subordinate.

The state as a personal theater

Donovan connected the firing-squad proposal to Trump’s broader fascination with World War II imagery, including his reported preference for “Golden Fleet” ships styled after an earlier era rather than designs developed through decades of military planning. The pattern is rule by symbol: select an image of past power, demand that contemporary institutions reproduce it and treat technical expertise as an impediment.

But the postwar achievement was not an aesthetic. As Donovan noted, leaders responded to mass destruction by constructing rules, treaties and agreements meant to restrain its recurrence. Appropriating the era’s imagery while disregarding that institutional lesson turns history into costume.

The systemic danger is a government trained to satisfy one leader’s appetite for spectacle. When officials begin evaluating punishment, military design and personnel deployment according to their value as presidential imagery, public institutions cease to serve coherent policy. They become a stage—and everyone below the person giving direction absorbs the cost.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Retired general predicts Trump’s firing-squad fantasy will implode

item.title: Military outraged and 'scrambling' to deal with Trump's new religion rules
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing an MS NOW report published Wednesday, says Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth created a Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs while the Defense Department reduced its list of recognized religious affiliations from 211 to 31. Personnel were told to select from the revised list by Friday.

A May Pentagon memo obtained by MS NOW reportedly removed 180 affiliations. Only nine of the remaining options were described as non-Christian. Air Force official Richard Anderson said the change would improve demographic data for chaplain services while respecting individual convictions.

Six current and former military personnel and chaplains interviewed by MS NOW disputed that explanation. An anonymous former chaplain described the policy as a push toward Christian identity, while a longtime Pentagon civilian called it a violation of law and policy. Those are their assessments; the reporting presented no court ruling establishing that the changes are unlawful.

The power is at the Pentagon

The decisive actors are not troops struggling with a form. Hegseth created the new office, and Pentagon leadership narrowed the official religious categories. Service members received the deadline and the diminished menu; they did not design either.

That hierarchy matters. In the military, an administrative classification issued from above is not a casual invitation. Leadership controls personnel systems, chaplain resources and the terms under which religious identity becomes legible to the institution. Calling the resulting turmoil “scrambling” describes the reaction while obscuring the command decision that produced it.

Inclusion by subtraction

The official rationale is that fewer categories will produce better data and more tailored support. On the facts reported, that claim demands scrutiny: eliminating 85 percent of recognized affiliations makes the data less specific for people whose faiths disappeared from the list.

A system does not protect individual conviction merely by declaring that it does. If dozens of distinct affiliations are compressed or erased while Christian choices dominate the remaining categories, the burden falls disproportionately on those outside that majority. They must accept an inaccurate label, retreat into a residual category if one exists, or become administratively invisible.

Bureaucracy can enforce hierarchy

The policy does not need to order conversion to alter the religious balance of institutional life. Classification determines what the Pentagon formally sees, counts and plans for. Narrow the categories, and minority faiths can appear smaller, less distinct and less entitled to tailored support.

MS NOW’s interviewees interpret that structure as Christian nationalism. The available reporting does not establish Hegseth’s motive as fact, but it does document an outcome consistent with their concern: a defense bureaucracy newly organized around “spiritual readiness” while recognizing far fewer non-Christian identities.

The framing lets authority disappear

The headline emphasis on an “outraged” military risks turning a command policy into a workplace dispute. The central conflict is not that some personnel dislike a new form. It is that political appointees used institutional authority to redefine which religious identities the armed forces will officially recognize.

The word “rules” can also make the change sound neutral and procedural. But procedures distribute recognition. Here, the reported numbers show who gains prominence and who loses specificity. The Pentagon’s explanation deserves attribution, not automatic acceptance—especially when the mechanism contradicts its promise of tailored support.

Administrative erasure is political power

This episode illustrates a broader method of governance: impose an ideological hierarchy through databases, offices and deadlines, then describe the result as efficiency or readiness. The language is managerial; the consequence is political.

Religious freedom is not preserved when the state narrows the identities it is willing to see and calls the narrowing inclusion. Whatever Hegseth’s unproven personal intent, the reported policy places Pentagon power behind a Christian-heavy classification system and makes service members absorb the cost. That is not confusion inside the ranks. It is an institutional choice imposed on them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Military outraged and ‘scrambling’ to deal with Trump’s new religion rules

item.title: ​MS Now supercut catches Trump Team in massive lie about gas prices
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that an MS NOW supercut showed President Donald Trump and senior administration officials repeatedly predicting that gasoline prices would soon fall, only for those forecasts to fail. With the midterm elections reportedly 20 days away, anchor Katy Tur said gas had remained above $4 a gallon for 158 consecutive days. The segment establishes that the promises were wrong; it does not establish that officials knowingly lied.

Tur also cited Bloomberg reporting about traders who allegedly made billions from bets placed roughly 15 minutes before Trump called off an attack on Iran—a decision expected to affect oil prices and markets. According to Tur’s account, Commodity Futures Trading Commission staff were later told to retract a referral concerning possible insider trading. The supplied reporting does not identify the traders, prove they had inside information, or establish that administration officials participated in the trades.

Power made the promises

These were not predictions from spectators. Trump controls major foreign-policy decisions, while the energy and treasury secretaries hold offices capable of shaping energy policy, market expectations, and the government’s public account of economic conditions.

That institutional power makes their assurances consequential. Chris Wright described elevated prices as a matter of weeks, not months. Scott Bessent forecast $3 gasoline between June 20 and September 20. Trump promised prices would be “much lower” before the midterms. They attached the authority of the presidency to claims that events subsequently contradicted.

A failed forecast is not automatically a lie

AlterNet’s headline calls the statements a “massive lie,” but the evidence presented shows failed predictions, not demonstrated knowledge of falsity. That distinction matters. Scathing analysis does not excuse careless accusation.

The defensible indictment is still severe: officials spoke with confidence they had not earned, offered voters precise relief on a politically useful timetable, and were not held to the uncertainty their own power could not eliminate. Whether that was deception, wishful thinking, or political salesmanship is unresolved by the supplied reporting. The public consequence is the same: authoritative assurances proved unreliable while motorists continued paying the reported price.

The graver allegation concerns oversight

The trading episode raises a different question because it involves potential access to a market-moving presidential decision and an alleged retreat by regulators. If CFTC staff were ordered to retract an insider-trading referral, the relevant power lies with agency leadership—not with anonymous traders alone.

But Tur’s broader suggestion that the administration was either ignoring misconduct or helping profit from foreign policy outruns what this account proves. The reporting supports scrutiny of who ordered the referral withdrawn, under what authority, and for what stated reason. It does not establish complicity, corruption, or the traders’ guilt.

Accountability cannot survive insinuation

The story’s strongest political meaning is not that every bad forecast proves a conspiracy. It is that executive power can generate confident promises, move markets through military decisions, and influence whether suspicious activity receives investigation.

Conflating those facts into one sweeping accusation weakens the case. The systemic failure is more concrete: powerful officials can sell certainty without bearing its cost, while politically appointed regulators may control whether questions touching that same administration advance at all. When prediction, presidential discretion, and enforcement authority sit inside one political structure, accountability depends on evidence—and on institutions willing to pursue it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ​MS Now supercut catches Trump Team in massive lie about gas prices

item.title: Trump crows about Social Security boost —but there's a catch
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration presented a 3.6 percent Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans as an improvement in financial stability. The catch is that the increase reflects higher prices rather than a discretionary benefit expansion: prices were reportedly 3.7 percent above their year-earlier level.

Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O’Malley told AlterNet that the adjustment would not preserve retirees’ purchasing power, citing food costs and Medicare copays. He also argued that Social Security’s longer-term financing problem could be eased by applying the payroll tax more fully to high earners.

An inflation adjustment is not a gift

The administration did not create a 3.6 percent windfall. According to O’Malley’s account, the increase follows an inflation-linked formula and arrives after the costs it is meant to offset have already risen.

Calling that adjustment a “boost” converts partial compensation for lost purchasing power into presidential generosity. A benefit can rise in nominal dollars while recipients become less able to afford necessities. The administration’s statement foregrounds the larger check; AlterNet’s figures indicate that prices rose slightly faster.

Who holds the power

Social Security recipients do not control the inflation measure, the timing of the adjustment, Medicare charges, or the amount of earnings subject to Social Security taxes. Federal officials and lawmakers control those policy choices. Retirees absorb their consequences.

Commissioner Frank Bisignano’s statement supplied the administration’s favorable framing. But the article does not quote Trump personally, despite a headline attributing the boasting to him. That is imprecise political packaging: the reporting establishes an administration claim, not a presidential remark.

The convenient missing context

The central misdirection is the treatment of an automatic response to rising costs as an affirmative achievement. It asks readers to credit the officeholder for the adjustment without dwelling on whether the adjustment restores what inflation took.

O’Malley, meanwhile, blamed part of the recent pressure on prices on the “Iran War.” AlterNet presents that causal claim without evidence in the supplied report. It should remain attributed analysis, not established fact. His broader point is better grounded by the article’s own numbers: a 3.6 percent adjustment does not fully match a reported 3.7 percent annual price increase.

Solvency is a distributional choice

O’Malley argues that affluent earners are resisting higher Social Security taxes and that taxing earnings above the reported $184,500 threshold more fully could extend the program’s solvency. He predicts broad support for requiring the wealthiest Americans to pay the same rate as other workers, though the article provides no polling to establish that prediction.

The political conflict is therefore not simply whether Social Security can be “saved.” It is who will bear the cost: beneficiaries through weaker purchasing power and possible benefit restructuring, or high earners through a broader taxable earnings base. Describing that conflict as a technical solvency puzzle obscures the actors with authority to choose.

The larger pattern

This is a familiar governing maneuver: relabel damage control as progress, advertise the nominal number, and leave the diminished purchasing power in the fine print. The weaker actors—elderly and disabled beneficiaries—are then expected to treat incomplete protection from rising costs as benevolence.

The systemic error is not confusion about arithmetic. It is political communication that detaches a benefit increase from the price increases that caused it, while the more consequential distributional decision—whether wealthy earners should contribute more—remains unresolved.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump crows about Social Security boost —but there’s a catch

item.title: Warning Trump is accelerating a American 'intellectual crisis': report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that columnist Ian Dunt described newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s first, 14-minute briefing as evidence of a broader American “intellectual crisis.” His argument rests on her reliance on prepared text, vague pro-Trump language and failure to answer whether the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Zacharia said she would have to get back to the questioner.

According to AlterNet, critics including The View hosts and Jimmy Kimmel questioned Zacharia’s qualifications and vetting. Dunt connected her apparent lack of preparation to an administration in which expertise may be losing ground to personal relationships and political favoritism. The report does not establish how Zacharia was selected or document the hiring process.

The power is above the podium

The press secretary holds a prominent position, but the decisive institutional power belongs to the president and the officials who choose White House personnel, determine access and control what information may be disclosed. Zacharia’s performance is therefore not merely an individual test. It reflects choices made by the administration that installed her and set the conditions under which she speaks.

That distinction matters because ridicule aimed exclusively at the spokesperson can obscure the chain of authority. If an administration appoints an unprepared representative, the failure belongs first to those empowered to assess qualifications and make the appointment. AlterNet raises that possibility but supplies no evidence identifying the decision-makers beyond the administration itself.

Access is the larger instrument

The more consequential allegation in the report concerns the White House press system. AlterNet says the Associated Press was barred for refusing to comply with Trump’s rules and that established outlets were replaced by approved “new media” organizations whose coverage aligned more closely with him.

If that account is accurate, the political function is clear even without assigning an unproven motive: officials are exercising control over access while surrounding themselves with friendlier questioners. A briefing room structured to reduce adversarial scrutiny weakens one of the few immediate checks on executive messaging. Zacharia’s inability to answer even within that favorable environment makes the staffing question sharper, but the access regime is the greater exercise of power.

Mockery misdirects the scrutiny

Dunt’s criticism of Zacharia’s hair, makeup and supposed resemblance to other women in Trump’s orbit contributes little to evaluating government competence. Appearance is not evidence of qualification, favoritism or intellectual capacity. It shifts attention from verifiable conduct—what she knew, what she answered and who appointed her—to gendered aesthetic judgment.

The useful criticism is narrower and stronger: the president’s spokesperson reportedly could not answer a consequential foreign-policy question. Even that fact has limits. One deferred answer does not prove incapacity by itself, and AlterNet does not say whether the administration later supplied the information. The case for institutional failure must rest on documented patterns, not cosmetic contempt.

Competence can be made optional

The article’s central concern is not that one official had a poor debut. It is that a political organization may treat loyalty, familiarity or message discipline as more valuable than subject knowledge. AlterNet presents that as Dunt’s conclusion, not as a demonstrated account of Zacharia’s appointment.

Still, the structure described in the report shows how standards can erode without any formal abolition of them. Leadership selects the personnel. Leadership controls access. Friendly media reduce pressure. Vague answers carry fewer immediate costs. Under those conditions, expertise becomes easier to disregard because the institution has weakened the mechanisms that expose its absence.

The system rewards the vacancy

An intellectual crisis in government is not established by a spokesperson reading from notes or stumbling over a question. It emerges when powerful officials make competence unnecessary and accountability avoidable.

The most revealing feature of this story is therefore not Zacharia’s briefing style. It is the reported combination of opaque hiring, restricted press access and preferential treatment for sympathetic outlets. Fixating on one woman’s presentation turns an institutional arrangement into celebrity mockery. The harder conclusion is that executive power can manufacture an environment in which weak performance is protected—and then leave the public arguing about the performer instead of the people who built the stage.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Warning Trump is accelerating a American ‘intellectual crisis’: report

item.title: War veteran details Trump official's embarrassing Biblical blunders
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth repeatedly used biblical passages to cast American military service and national purpose in sacred terms. Citing Paul D. Miller of Georgetown University, the article identifies the central blunder as Hegseth’s removal of verses from their original context—equating service members with the prophet Isaiah and treating the United States as though it were God’s covenant nation.

Miller argues that Hegseth turned passages from Isaiah, Psalms, and Ephesians into patriotic slogans during a military speech and recruitment campaign. AlterNet also recounts a separate speech in which Hegseth adapted dialogue from Pulp Fiction—loosely associated with Ezekiel 25:17—as though it were Scripture. The supplied reporting describes Miller as an international-affairs professor and military-ethics scholar, but does not substantiate the headline’s characterization of him as a war veteran.

The office matters more than the errors

The embarrassing part is not merely that a senior official mangled the Bible. The defense secretary controls a vast military bureaucracy and speaks with the authority of the executive branch. When he presents military missions through a Christian script, the practical issue is not theological literacy. It is the use of government power to privilege one religious vocabulary and wrap state violence in divine approval.

Hegseth reportedly described physical war as part of a spiritual battle and invoked the “Armor of God” while addressing the work of the Defense Department. That collapses distinctions a civilian-led military needs: between policy and revelation, national interest and divine command, public service and religious mission.

Scripture as state branding

Miller’s criticism is precise: Hegseth’s quotations do not humble or judge the nation; they sacralize it. Scripture becomes stage dressing for recruitment, hierarchy, combat, and obedience.

That use is politically convenient. A policy argument can be questioned. A strategic decision can be judged by evidence, law, cost, and results. But once officials imply that the nation’s battles participate in God’s battle, dissent is easier to portray as weakness, disloyalty, or spiritual failure. The reporting does not establish that Hegseth consciously designed that effect. His rhetoric nevertheless creates it.

The spectacle misdirects

AlterNet frames the story around “Biblical blunders,” inviting readers to laugh at ignorance and hypocrisy. The errors deserve scrutiny, especially the cinematic pseudo-Scripture. But ridicule can shrink a structural abuse into a personality flaw.

The consequential actor is not a confused congregant. It is the defense secretary. The consequential choice is not misremembering a verse. It is using the institutional platform of the Pentagon to fuse Christianity, American nationalism, and military force. Focusing on whether Hegseth passes a Bible quiz risks diverting attention from what his rhetoric authorizes.

Exclusion follows sanctification

The same official who reportedly invoked sacred language also promised a military with “no fatties,” “no trannies,” “no beardos,” “no weirdos,” “no wimps,” and “no radicals.” That list is not theology. It is a political sorting mechanism: define the ideal warrior narrowly, mark disfavored people as contamination, and present exclusion as institutional restoration.

Biblical imagery supplies grandeur to that project. It turns a program of discipline and exclusion into a story about righteousness. The foreseeable consequence is a military culture in which favored identities are associated with strength and divine purpose while targeted groups are cast as evidence of decline.

The larger pattern

Christian nationalism does not require sophisticated Christianity. It requires symbols that can convert political authority into moral authority. In this account, Scripture is valuable to Hegseth precisely because fragments of it can be detached from history, theology, and restraint, then redeployed as patriotic certification.

That is the systemic error exposed here. Coverage fixated on hypocrisy asks whether the official understands the text. The harder political question is what happens when an official with command authority uses that text to sanctify the nation, militarize faith, and make exclusion sound holy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: War veteran details Trump official’s embarrassing Biblical blunders

item.title: Republicans throw in the towel already on getting anything done this year
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Politico, reports that Republican lawmakers had largely deferred plans for an ambitious post-midterm legislative session. With only 24 legislative days available, GOP members expected must-pass bills, possible leadership contests, uncertain election results and poor attendance to consume the remaining calendar.

Georgia Rep. Austin Scott said attendance was already a problem and questioned who would return to Washington after the election. Congress still faced government funding beyond December 11 and the annual Pentagon policy bill, while farm, transportation and surveillance authorizations carried partisan disputes that could stall them.

The report did not describe a formal Republican decision to abandon all legislation. It documented lawmakers lowering expectations, postponing priorities and openly questioning whether members would show up. Retiring North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis also suggested that a Democratic House victory would further diminish Republicans’ incentive to legislate during the lame-duck session.

Power without purpose

Republicans held the congressional leadership positions identified in the report: Mike Johnson was House speaker, and John Thune was Senate majority leader. That is institutional power—the authority to set agendas, schedule votes, negotiate bills and require members to confront deadlines.

The obstacle described here was not simply “a foul national mood.” It was a governing party anticipating that its own lawmakers might skip work, its policy disputes might consume the available time and its leaders might turn inward after an electoral loss. Those are choices and incentives inside the Republican conference, not weather conditions imposed on Congress.

Absence as agency

Scott’s question—who will show up after the election—exposes the most revealing failure. Members of Congress are not volunteers deciding whether another shift is worth the trouble. Attendance determines whether the institution can use the power voters assigned it.

Calling the agenda “deferred” softens that agency. Bills do not defer themselves. Leaders postpone them; committees fail to advance them; members decline compromises; legislators stay away. The reporting supports uncertainty about which measures would fail, but it clearly identifies Republican doubts about doing the work at all.

The lame-duck excuse

Tillis asked why Republicans would act if Democrats won the House. That reasoning treats legislation as valuable only when the governing party can retain political control over the result. Yet a changed House majority would not erase the authority or obligations of the sitting Congress during its remaining term.

The election therefore becomes an excuse in either direction. An uncertain result supposedly prevents preparation; a loss supposedly removes the incentive to govern; leadership contests then consume the time left. Political transition is presented as an external disruption even when party officials choose to prioritize internal position-hunting over public business.

Who absorbs the failure

The immediate consequences would not fall chiefly on the lawmakers engaged in leadership maneuvering. A government-funding deadline carries risks for federal operations. Delayed farm and transportation legislation can prolong uncertainty in programs Congress is responsible for maintaining. Surveillance authorization raises consequential questions that deserve actual debate, not neglect followed by deadline-driven action.

The article’s broad “throwing in the towel” frame captures the surrender but blurs the chain of command. Republican leaders controlled the agenda described in the report, Republican members supplied—or withheld—the attendance, and internal Republican calculations threatened to consume the calendar. The weaker actors are the people and institutions forced to live with whatever rushed bills, temporary extensions or unresolved obligations result.

A legislature organized around control

The larger pattern is a governing party treating legislative power less as a means to govern than as an asset whose value depends on retaining it. When electoral advantage fades, so does the stated appetite for using the authority already in hand.

That is institutional decay expressed through ordinary incentives: absenteeism, deferred decisions, compressed deadlines and leadership intrigue. No conspiracy is required. A Congress can incapacitate itself when those with the power to act decide that governing without assured partisan reward is barely worth showing up for.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republicans throw in the towel already on getting anything done this year

item.title: Trumper tears apart president's 'imbecilic' Russia deal
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative writer Andrew McCarthy, a three-time Donald Trump voter, condemned Trump’s diesel agreement with Vladimir Putin as an attempt to address high fuel prices that McCarthy attributes to Trump’s own policies. McCarthy argued that the deal gives Putin relief without requiring concessions, even as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.

According to McCarthy, the agreement also makes little economic sense: the United States produces about 5 million barrels of diesel a day, consumes fewer than 4 million and is already the world’s leading diesel exporter, while Russia’s export capacity has deteriorated. He predicted that the deal would not lower prices.

McCarthy further alleged that the arrangement belongs to a broader pattern of conflicts involving Trump donors, associates and business partners. AlterNet does not independently establish corruption or provide Trump’s response; it reports McCarthy’s accusation and his conclusion that Trump is abusing presidential power.

The power is in the White House

The decisive actor here is not Putin, American consumers or an unruly market. It is Trump, wielding executive authority over foreign relations, sanctions and trade. McCarthy’s account describes a president using that authority to create the problem, advertise himself as its solution and enlist a hostile foreign power in the sales pitch.

That structure matters more than the spectacle of a loyal conservative finally losing patience. Trump’s voter is not the institutional protagonist. Trump is. The agreement exists because the president’s administration chose to pursue it, and any sanctions relief or commercial opening would flow from powers controlled by that administration.

A cure for a self-inflicted wound

McCarthy’s central indictment is unusually direct: Trump is trying to reduce prices raised by policies Trump imposed. The continuing trade conflict with Canada, instability linked by McCarthy to an unauthorized war against Iran, and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea are not atmospheric conditions. They are policy decisions and foreseeable geopolitical consequences.

The diesel deal then becomes political laundering. Instead of reversing damaging choices, the administration can stage another transaction and call it relief. The public is asked to judge the attempted repair without examining who broke the machinery.

The Putin bargain

On the facts presented, Russia is an implausible rescuer. The United States already produces more diesel than it consumes, while McCarthy says Russia’s energy sector has deteriorated enough that it imported diesel from South Korea during the summer. A deal with Moscow therefore requires an explanation stronger than scarcity, and AlterNet’s report supplies none from the administration.

It does supply a stark imbalance: McCarthy says Putin receives a benefit without making concessions while Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians continue. If that description is accurate, Trump is not extracting peace through leverage. He is weakening leverage while receiving no reported change in Russian conduct.

Corruption alleged, accountability missing

McCarthy connects the diesel agreement to a separate prospective multibillion-dollar transaction involving Lukoil assets and possible sanctions waivers. Citing an October New York Times report, he says Trump associates Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiated it and that potential beneficiaries reportedly include donor Todd Boehly—who gave $2 million to Trump political causes—and executives with business ties to Trump, Kushner and Witkoff.

Those details raise an obvious conflict-of-interest question, but they do not by themselves prove corruption or a statutory offense. McCarthy calls the motive corruption; AlterNet presents that judgment without establishing it independently. The stronger supported point is institutional: presidential power over sanctions and foreign policy is reportedly intersecting with the financial interests of politically connected people. That demands scrutiny more rigorous than treating a supporter’s denunciation as the whole story.

The loyalty trap

The headline’s hook is that a “Trumper” attacked Trump. That framing makes dissent inside the coalition seem more important than the exercise of state power. McCarthy’s voting record may demonstrate the depth of his break, but it neither validates nor invalidates his claims.

The larger pattern is a presidency described as generating economic harm, offering a dubious foreign bargain as remediation and potentially opening lucrative channels for connected interests—all while Putin’s conduct remains unchanged. When coverage centers the astonishment of a disappointed loyalist, it turns governance into intramural drama. The consequential question is not why one Trump voter finally objected. It is why executive power can be deployed through opaque deals whose public rationale appears so thin and whose beneficiaries may be so close to the people arranging them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trumper tears apart president’s ‘imbecilic’ Russia deal

item.title: The toxic link between Trump's corruption and your paycheck
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that household costs are being driven upward by policies adopted under President Donald Trump while wealthy donors, politically connected companies, and members of Trump’s family benefit from exemptions, contracts, and tax cuts. It points to higher fuel costs during the reported Iran war, tariffs on consumer and building goods, support for artificial intelligence infrastructure, and healthcare cuts accompanying tax reductions.

The article reports that SpaceX raised certain Pentagon connection fees, Trump-family-backed investment companies obtained substantial defense contracts and options, and favored industries received tariff exemptions after executives or owners supported Trump or Republicans. It also cites estimates that tariffs increased annual household costs by $1,100 and added $10,900 to the cost of constructing a new single-family home.

AlterNet presents those relationships as corruption. But the article does not establish a specific quid pro quo for each contract or exemption, and some of its economic claims—particularly that AI borrowing and the Iran war drove mortgage rates above 7 percent—are asserted more strongly than the evidence described supports. Its central, better-grounded point is narrower: officials control policies with enormous distributional consequences while major beneficiaries finance the political coalition exercising that power.

Power sets the price

Consumers do not decide tariff schedules, military commitments, contract awards, tax rates, or Medicaid funding. The administration and Congress do. Companies can lobby, donate, and position themselves for advantage, but elected officials convert that influence into enforceable policy.

That distinction matters because “affordability” is often discussed as if prices emerged from weather. Here, government choices reportedly increased costs for fuel, imported goods, construction materials, electricity, mortgages, and healthcare. The burden then moved downward: companies protected margins, asset owners collected returns, and households absorbed the bill.

Access becomes an asset

The reported sequence surrounding tariff exemptions is politically damning even where it falls short of proving bribery. Tim Cook donated $1 million to Trump’s inauguration and Apple later received exemptions covering major product categories. Elon Musk spent heavily to support Trump and Republicans; Tesla received an electronics exemption, while SpaceX benefited from defense spending. Republican donors behind Reyes Holdings also secured an exemption for material used in plastic bottles.

Those facts warrant scrutiny, not automatic criminal conclusions. AlterNet weakens its case when it treats proximity as completed proof of a payoff. The stronger indictment is institutional: discretionary carve-outs give a president something valuable to grant, and concentrated political spending gives corporations privileged access to the official holding that power. A system need not produce a written invoice for influence to produce dependence, favoritism, and public distrust.

The weak carry the blame

Political coverage routinely tells people that healthcare is expensive, housing is scarce, or interest rates are high without naming the officials who made the relevant choices. That framing shifts attention toward consumers, immigrants, workers, or an abstract “economy”—actors with far less control than the government officials writing tax law and trade policy.

AlterNet correctly redirects attention upward, but it sometimes replaces economic analysis with a single sweeping theory. Tariffs directly raise import costs; their effects can be estimated. The path from AI-sector borrowing or war spending to a particular mortgage rate is far more complex. An argument about concentrated power does not need inflated certainty. Overstatement gives beneficiaries an easy way to dismiss the documented conflicts along with the speculative causal claims.

Oversight was a choice

The article identifies the machinery capable of constraining abuse: inspectors general, ethics enforcement, campaign-finance rules, an independent civil service, and the Federal Election Commission. These institutions are not decorative. They determine whether contracts receive scrutiny, conflicts become visible, and discretionary power carries consequences.

Congressional Democrats’ demand for a Pentagon inspector-general investigation into contracts involving Trump-family-backed firms is therefore only a beginning. An investigation request is not evidence of wrongdoing, and oversight conducted only after politically connected businesses profit is remedial, not preventive. Congress controls appropriations, disclosure requirements, enforcement powers, and the legal structure that permits wealthy interests to purchase extraordinary political access.

Corruption is an economic policy

The larger pattern is not simply that rich donors may receive favors. It is that public power can be organized to privatize benefits and distribute costs: contracts for connected firms, exemptions for influential corporations, tax reductions for wealthy backers, and higher everyday expenses or weaker services for everyone else.

That is why affordability cannot be separated from institutional design. When officials possess broad discretionary authority, donors can invest in access, and watchdogs lack independence, a paycheck becomes the final collection point for decisions made far above the worker receiving it. The clearest consequence is not merely scandal. It is a political economy in which influence buys insulation and ordinary households pay retail.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The toxic link between Trump’s corruption and your paycheck

item.title: Opposing Supreme Court justices join forces to call out 'absurdity’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch criticized the government’s prosecution of Jesús Herrera-Salazar, a Mexican national convicted twice under the federal illegal-reentry law. Sotomayor called the result a “constitutional absurdity,” warning that the appellate court’s reasoning could permit repeated, potentially limitless prosecutions for being “found in” the United States.

Herrera-Salazar was found in Texas in 2020, imprisoned, and then placed under supervision that required him to remain in the United States. After authorities found him in Oklahoma, the government prosecuted and convicted him again for illegal reentry. The Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal because he had already been deported; Sotomayor and Gorsuch agreed with that procedural outcome while questioning how the second conviction could be reconciled with the Double Jeopardy Clause.

The government built the trap

The central actor was not an immigrant somehow creating a constitutional puzzle. The government controlled Herrera-Salazar’s custody, imposed the supervision conditions that kept him in the country, and brought the second prosecution.

That sequence matters. The state allegedly treated his continued presence as a new crime even though its own supervision order required that presence. Whatever legal theory supported the conviction, the reported facts expose an extreme imbalance of agency: the government set the conditions and then exercised prosecutorial power against the person bound by them.

A warning without a remedy

The justices’ statement identifies a serious problem but provides Herrera-Salazar no relief. The Court declined review because his deportation made this case an unsuitable vehicle, leaving the disputed conviction and the appellate reasoning undisturbed.

That is institutionally tidy and materially hollow. A constitutional protection has little force when judges can describe its apparent violation after the affected person has passed beyond the Court’s preferred procedural posture. The statement may guide lower courts in a future case, but Herrera-Salazar absorbed the prison sentence, second conviction, and deportation in this one.

The “unlikely allies” distraction

AlterNet emphasizes the supposedly surprising partnership between a liberal justice and a conservative one. That framing converts a coercive prosecution into a story about Supreme Court personalities.

The relevant fact is not that Sotomayor and Gorsuch can occasionally agree. It is that federal authorities obtained a second conviction under circumstances both justices found constitutionally alarming, while the judiciary ultimately supplied criticism rather than correction. Treating cross-ideological agreement as the hook makes institutional collegiality more important than the person subjected to the institution’s power.

The article’s detour into an unrelated death-penalty petition and a 2021 appearance about misinformation compounds that weakness. Those details establish a pattern of public statements, not an explanation for how the government secured this result.

Rights deferred are power preserved

Sotomayor’s warning points beyond one prosecution. If being “found in” the country can repeatedly restart criminal exposure, the government gains the capacity to turn continued presence into a renewable offense. On the reasoning she criticized, the constitutional limit does not meaningfully restrain the state; it waits for some later defendant to present a cleaner case.

That is the larger pattern: institutions acknowledge possible abuse while allowing procedural rules to protect the outcome already produced. The language of constitutional concern survives. The person subjected to government power bears the consequence. And the system calls the unresolved contradiction a reason to be more careful next time.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Opposing Supreme Court justices join forces to call out ‘absurdity’

item.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from wrecking golf course further
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Judge Ana Reyes temporarily barred the Trump administration from taking further action at East Potomac Park and its golf course after more than 400 trees were removed. According to the report, administration lawyers disclosed the planned work at 4:55 p.m. on the Friday before a holiday weekend; within 24 hours, the trees were gone.

The outlet says Reyes told government lawyers she felt misled after trusting the administration to keep the court informed. Attorney Norm Eisen, whose firm represents challengers in the case, said the litigation also contests the placement of untested East Wing demolition debris at the golf course. The report does not establish that the material contained asbestos or other toxic substances, only that concerns were raised because it allegedly had not been tested.

The restraining order stops additional work for now. AlterNet says the next unresolved question is whether Reyes will hold any administration officials or attorneys in contempt; the report supplies no contempt ruling.

The power was federal

This was not a dispute among equally situated conservationists, golfers and contractors. The executive branch controlled the federal property, the demolition machinery, the timing and the flow of information. Its opponents could petition a court only after officials had created facts on the ground.

That distinction matters because an injunction can halt tomorrow’s cutting but cannot reattach yesterday’s trees. When the government acts faster than judicial review can operate, temporary executive control becomes permanent physical consequence.

The timing did the work

The administration’s reported notice was technically a disclosure. Functionally, a 4:55 p.m. warning before a holiday weekend left almost no practical opportunity for scrutiny before the removal was completed.

The article does not prove why officials chose that timing. It does establish the result: the court received notice, the trees disappeared within a day, and the judge concluded that the trust she had extended was misplaced. Procedure became useful to the administration precisely because it was compressed until intervention was nearly impossible.

The golf-course frame is a diversion

Calling this a fight over golf-course construction reduces an institutional confrontation to a landscaping quarrel. Stephen Miller’s reported contention that federal judges have no place in golf-course construction performs that misdirection directly.

The court’s asserted concern was not whether judges should select turf, trees or course layouts. It was whether federal officials honored judicial demands and gave the court a meaningful chance to act. The weaker parties here are not the officials wielding federal machinery; they are the litigants forced to chase completed government action through a slower legal process.

Restraint without consequence

AlterNet places the episode within what it describes as a broader pattern of noncompliance with court orders in several states and Washington, D.C. That allegation is serious, but this article provides neither the underlying orders nor enough case detail to evaluate each cited instance independently.

The immediate case still exposes the enforcement problem. A court may issue commands, but executive officials determine whether obedience is routine or something judges must extract through emergency hearings and possible contempt proceedings. If violations produce only orders against repeating already completed conduct, institutional defiance can become a calculated advantage.

Government by fait accompli

The larger pattern is rule through irreversible action: disclose late, move quickly and force challengers to litigate over what remains. The public-facing controversy may concern trees, debris or a golf course, but the underlying power struggle concerns whether the executive can outrun legal oversight.

Reyes’s restraining order interrupted that method. Whether it deters its repetition depends on what follows. A judiciary that merely records completed defiance manages the aftermath; one that identifies responsible officials and imposes enforceable consequences can still constrain the power that produced it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from wrecking golf course further

item.title: Trump's new secretary caught in embarrassing flub over claim to be 'lawyer’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Katie Zacharia, President Trump’s new press secretary, repeatedly called herself a lawyer despite searches finding no record that she was licensed to practice law in any state or Washington, D.C. Pepperdine University confirmed that she earned a J.D. in 2011, but a law degree does not by itself make someone a licensed attorney.

Popular Information searched nationwide bar records, while AlterNet separately checked California records under Zacharia’s current and maiden names. Neither found a listing. Zacharia also identified herself as Fix California’s general counsel from January 2024 to March 2025 and continued using that title in social-media biographies into 2026. The reporting does not establish what work she performed, whether she was otherwise authorized to practice, or whether she violated California law.

The unanswered question

The evidence supports a discrepancy, not a conviction. Zacharia publicly said, “I’m a lawyer,” Trump described her as “an attorney,” and her résumé claimed a senior legal title. The available licensing records, as reported, do not substantiate those descriptions.

That demands an explanation from Zacharia and from the institutions that promoted the claim. Whether her conduct met California’s legal definition of advertising or practicing law without authorization remains unresolved. AlterNet correctly notes that the investigation presented no evidence of a criminal violation.

Power signed off on the credential

This is not merely an individual résumé problem. Fix California, founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell, reportedly gave—or at least permitted Zacharia to advertise—the title of general counsel. Trump then repeated the attorney designation when appointing her press secretary. Those are decisions by powerful political actors and organizations, not errors committed by spectators.

The central institutional question is therefore broader than whether Zacharia passed a bar examination: Who verified her qualifications, who approved the title, and who allowed it to circulate? The reporting supplies no answers. That absence does not prove complicity, but it exposes an accountability failure around an appointment whose entire function is communicating official claims to the public.

The “flub” framing is too small

Calling this an embarrassing flub reduces a sustained, documented representation to a momentary verbal mistake. AlterNet’s account describes repeated statements, an employment title, a LinkedIn entry, social-media biographies, and Trump’s own announcement. Whatever ultimately explains the discrepancy, it was not a single slip.

The headline also risks turning the story into personality-driven humiliation when the meaningful issue is institutional validation. Zacharia holds less power than the president who appointed her, but she still has agency over how she describes her credentials. Trump and Fix California, meanwhile, had the power to confer legitimacy on those descriptions and the responsibility to check them.

Credentialing as political theater

A J.D. can supply the prestige of legal expertise without conferring authority to practice law. That distinction matters especially in political communications, where credentials are used to manufacture trust quickly and corrections rarely travel as far as the original claim.

The larger pattern is a political ecosystem in which affiliation can substitute for verification. Titles circulate among allied organizations, media appearances and appointments until repetition itself begins to look like proof. When scrutiny finally arrives, the episode is treated as a gaffe rather than the foreseeable result of institutions that reward assertion and neglect validation.

The system behind the résumé

The unresolved legal question belongs to regulators and evidence the reporting does not provide. The political conclusion is narrower but already visible: a claim to professional authority passed through a conservative organization, public interviews and a presidential appointment without the reported record establishing the credential.

That is how institutional decay often presents itself—not as one spectacular deception, but as a chain of powerful actors declining to perform elementary checks. The individual claim matters. The machinery that authenticated it matters more.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s new secretary caught in embarrassing flub over claim to be ‘lawyer’
