item.title: Latest Trump hire failed a 'make or break' test almost immediately: report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing MS NOW, reports that newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia struggled during her first briefing on Tuesday. In a 14-minute appearance, she reportedly relied heavily on a binder and answered only three questions, all from conservative-leaning outlets. Anonymous White House officials described the performance as poor and questioned whether she could keep the job.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung publicly called the briefing “amazing and effective” and dismissed contrary accounts as uninformed or fabricated. One America News Network host David Pollack likewise labeled the criticism “fake news.” The report does not establish that Zacharia will be fired; it establishes that unnamed officials and a former Trump aide believed her position could quickly become precarious.

The power is above the podium

Zacharia occupied the lectern, but she did not hold the decisive power. The president chose the administration’s spokesperson and could remove her. Senior White House officials controlled the internal verdict, while Cheung controlled the authorized public version.

That distinction matters because the article’s personnel-drama framing risks shrinking an institutional story into a performance review. The consequential question is not whether Zacharia impressed colleagues. It is what the White House expects its press secretary to do: distribute information, dominate reporters, or perform loyalty under pressure.

Failure, as defined by Trump’s operation

The criticism reported by MS NOW was revealingly narrow. Zacharia allegedly looked unprepared, appeared weak and failed to project command. The former aide did not warn that she had misled the public or withheld material information. The stated danger was that she did not look “tough and strong.”

That is a political standard, not a public-service standard. The administration insiders quoted in the report treated press relations as a test of dominance. Even the favorable comparison with predecessor Karoline Leavitt emphasized combative engagement, suggesting that access across the press corps mattered partly as another arena in which to display control.

Friendly questions are still a choice

Taking only three questions, all from conservative-leaning outlets, was not merely an aesthetic problem. If accurately described, it restricted scrutiny while preserving the appearance of a briefing. Zacharia had agency over that conduct, although the reporting does not establish whether she selected those outlets independently or followed instructions.

The article concentrates on her nervous presentation because that is easy to dramatize. The more important institutional fact is that the White House press operation reportedly limited questioning to ideologically friendly media. A shaky delivery may embarrass an administration. Managed access protects it.

The denial machine

Cheung’s response did more than defend a colleague. He declared the performance successful, then suggested that critics were either irrelevant employees or inventions. Pollack supplied the movement-media version by invoking “fake news” and “Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

The reporting supports calling this message discipline, not proving a coordinated deception. But its function is plain: it offers supporters a reason to reject an unfavorable account without examining the conduct described. The dispute becomes a referendum on the critic’s legitimacy rather than a factual question about whom Zacharia called on and how she handled the room.

Disposable messenger, durable system

If Zacharia is replaced, the White House will have changed a performer without changing the power structure. The president remains the principal. Senior officials still define competence as effective advocacy. Friendly media still help convert criticism into evidence of persecution. Anonymous insiders can attack an appointee while avoiding responsibility for the operation that hired and prepared her.

That is the larger pattern: personalized government makes subordinates disposable while insulating the institution’s choices from scrutiny. The press secretary absorbs the ridicule; the administration retains the machinery of selective access, loyalty enforcement and reflexive denial.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Latest Trump hire failed a ‘make or break’ test almost immediately: report

item.title: 'Morning Joe' aghast at Trump's bizarre obsession 'with the male physique’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used an Ohio appearance on Monday night to praise Republican Sen. John Husted’s body, saying he examined Husted “up and down” and commenting on his rear end, hands and jawline.

On Tuesday, MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” panel mocked the remarks. Joe Scarborough described Trump as increasingly preoccupied with muscular men, while Mika Brzezinski said he should “keep his private life private.” Scarborough also argued that such commentary was unlikely to help Husted at a midterm campaign event.

The power behind the spectacle

Trump was not merely an eccentric guest saying something embarrassing. He was the president appearing at a political event for a senator whom Scarborough described as potentially vulnerable. Trump held the institutional power in the room: presidential authority, party dominance and the ability to commandeer the purpose of the event.

Husted’s role, by contrast, was to receive the endorsement and absorb whatever spectacle accompanied it. That imbalance matters more than the panel’s jokes. A president turned a senator’s body into rally material, and the political apparatus around them treated the performance as part of the price of presidential support.

Mockery is not analysis

The “Morning Joe” segment focused heavily on insinuation: Trump notices men’s bodies, therefore the panel invited viewers to laugh at what that might imply about his private life. That framing is cheap and politically evasive. Nothing in AlterNet’s account establishes anything about Trump’s sexuality, and speculation about it explains neither his conduct nor his power.

The relevant issue is not that a man complimented another man’s appearance. It is that the president publicly appraised an ally’s rear end during an event ostensibly intended to advance that ally’s political interests. Turning the episode into a Village People joke replaces scrutiny of degrading presidential behavior with adolescent innuendo.

The senator becomes a prop

Trump’s remarks, as reported, reduced Husted’s political value to a collection of physical attributes: hands, jawline, athleticism and body shape. Husted was present as a senator seeking political reinforcement, but the president recast him as an object in Trump’s performance.

That is a familiar structure of personalized power. Allies are not treated as independent officeholders with constituencies and responsibilities; they become scenery for the dominant figure. Their dignity, message and campaign needs remain subordinate to his appetite for attention.

A media system built for diversion

David French joked that while Trump was rambling about physical characteristics, he was not making bad deals with Russia. The line inadvertently exposes the problem. Presidential spectacle consumes airtime precisely because it is easy to clip, ridicule and circulate. Consequential policy becomes the aside.

AlterNet reproduces that distortion rather than correcting it. The story documents the panel’s laughter more thoroughly than the Ohio event’s political purpose, Husted’s electoral position or any substantive issue before voters. The result is coverage about reactions to a provocation, not reporting that clarifies how presidential power was being used.

The politics of permanent distraction

The larger pattern is not hidden sexuality or harmless eccentricity. It is a political and media arrangement in which presidential self-indulgence displaces public substance, allies submit to humiliation for access, and commentators convert the degradation into entertainment.

Trump generated the spectacle. The event’s political organizers enabled it by placing presidential attention at the center of the campaign. “Morning Joe” then turned it into comic content, and AlterNet packaged the comedy as the story. Each institution followed its incentive; none gave readers much reason to understand what power was doing while everyone laughed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Morning Joe’ aghast at Trump’s bizarre obsession ‘with the male physique’

item.title: Nobel scientist calls Trump 'senile felon' and spots a troubling flaw
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton called President Donald Trump a “corrupt, senile felon” and said Trump understands “almost nothing” about artificial intelligence. In a Guardian interview published Tuesday, Hinton specifically criticized Trump’s demand that AI be called “superintelligence,” a term that already refers to systems exceeding human intelligence.

Hinton also accused Marc Andreessen, Elon Musk and Peter Thiel of rejecting democracy and wanting to control society, with Trump serving as a useful instrument. He argued that allowing technology companies to regulate themselves would be as reckless as letting tobacco companies design their own warnings.

The dispute comes amid industry criticism of Hinton’s warnings. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said Hinton’s estimates lack sufficient scientific evidence; Hinton has previously assigned a 10% to 20% chance of AI causing human extinction in coming decades. That estimate remains a prediction, not an established probability.

The president controls policy, not terminology

Trump holds the relevant institutional power. Hinton can warn, criticize and lend scientific authority to the debate, but the president can shape federal regulation, enforcement and the government’s relationship with technology companies.

That distinction is more important than the insult dominating AlterNet’s framing. Whether Trump is accurately described as senile is not established by the reporting. What the article does establish is that he publicly demanded adherence to his preferred terminology and branded dissenters “THE ENEMY.” That is observable conduct: a political loyalty test imposed on a scientific term.

Renaming AI “superintelligence” does not make existing systems more capable. It does, however, replace technical precision with presidential branding. When political authority demands that expertise conform to its vocabulary, confusion is not merely an accident. The foreseeable result is a public debate organized around obedience rather than evidence.

Billionaires want the referee’s whistle

Hinton’s accusation against Andreessen, Musk and Thiel is sweeping, and AlterNet supplies no detailed evidence for it beyond his remarks. The article therefore cannot establish that the three men share a coordinated plan to control society or are using Trump for that purpose.

But the concrete policy question does not require accepting that allegation. Technology executives and investors stand to gain when government declines to impose safeguards on the systems their companies build, finance or sell. Self-regulation gives the regulated industry power to define acceptable risk, select the evidence that counts and decide how much protection is affordable.

Hinton’s tobacco analogy identifies the structural problem cleanly. A warning designed by the company creating the hazard is constrained by the company’s interest in minimizing friction, liability and lost revenue. In AI policy, concentrated wealth does not merely lobby the referee. It seeks custody of the rulebook.

The personality story obscures the governing choice

AlterNet leads with Hinton’s attack on Trump’s mental acuity, turning a dispute over state power and corporate regulation into a spectacle about one man’s fitness. That framing is politically convenient and analytically weak.

The consequential issue is not whether Trump misunderstands AI because of age, temperament or ignorance. The story provides no basis for diagnosing him. The issue is that his reported position favors industry autonomy while he uses presidential attention to police language. Those are choices with institutional effects, whatever produced them.

Focusing on “senility” also risks misdirecting responsibility. A government does not abandon safeguards through one person’s confusion alone. Officials implement policy, agencies alter enforcement, lawmakers permit gaps and corporate actors press their advantage. Personal incapacity, even if proved, would not absolve the network of powerful people enabling the outcome.

Uncertainty is not permission

Huang’s criticism highlights a legitimate problem: catastrophic-risk estimates must not be presented as settled science. Hinton’s 10% to 20% figure cannot be treated as a measured forecast simply because a Nobel laureate supplied it.

Yet uncertainty cuts in both directions. The absence of a precise probability does not establish safety, especially when developers are building systems whose capabilities and effects may outpace public oversight. The political question is who bears the cost if optimistic industry assumptions fail.

Companies capture the immediate revenue and strategic advantage. Workers, institutions and the broader public would absorb many of the harms. That asymmetry gives industry every incentive to demand proof of danger while requiring far less proof for rapid deployment.

Power thrives behind manufactured confusion

This story reveals a familiar pattern: political leaders reduce a technical question to branding, wealthy beneficiaries present oversight as an obstacle, and coverage elevates the most inflammatory insult above the governing arrangement.

The sharper indictment is not that one president may lack technical understanding. It is that public power can be used to enforce rhetorical loyalty while private power is trusted to supervise itself. That arrangement does not need a secret conspiracy to produce foreseeable harm. It needs only officials willing to surrender judgment and corporations prepared to accept the gift.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Nobel scientist calls Trump ‘senile felon’ and spots a troubling flaw

item.title: String of GOP lawmakers make humiliating Navy mix-up
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that several Republican officials marked the U.S. Navy’s 251st birthday on Tuesday with images of foreign warships. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Rep. Tim Moore used pictures of Indian vessels; Ohio state Rep. Mike Dovilla, a longtime naval intelligence officer, used Russian ships; and Border Patrol official Jeffrey J. Dinise featured a Russian Kirov-class battlecruiser. Wall Street Journal editor Dave Brown identified the errors.

The posts paired patriotic tributes with basic failures of recognition. Kemp and Dovilla were campaigning in reportedly close races, while Moore held a substantial polling lead. The article does not establish who selected the images or whether the officials reviewed them before publication.

AlterNet places the blunders against a more consequential record: unusually long deployments and reported hardship during President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, the transfer of naval assets away from the Pacific, and Trump’s proposals for “Trump-class” battleships and a return to steam-powered systems—ideas the article says experts and critics have called obsolete, inefficient and wasteful.

Patriotism as a content template

The humiliation is not merely that politicians mistook Indian and Russian ships for American ones. It is that the imagery was apparently interchangeable because the Navy itself was incidental. The posts needed gray hulls, flags and ceremonial gratitude. Accuracy was optional.

That is how institutional reverence becomes political branding. The officials claimed identification with military service while publishing material that undercut the competence their messages were designed to project. Dovilla’s mistake is especially damaging because he invoked more than 20 years in naval intelligence as a credential. The reporting does not show that he personally chose the image, but attaching his name to it was still his political decision.

Who actually holds power

These officials are not powerless social-media users. Kemp governs a state, Moore serves in Congress, Dovilla holds state office, and Dinise is a federal official. Their communications carry public authority even when staff members may assemble them.

Trump holds vastly greater power over the Navy than any of them. According to AlterNet, his administration has directed deployments, moved major assets between theaters and promoted costly changes in fleet design and propulsion. Confusing one warship for another is embarrassing. Deploying ships in ways that strain crews or leave a strategic region without an aircraft carrier has material consequences.

The joke obscures the governing record

AlterNet’s framing foregrounds a comic procession of image errors. That is easy political content: ridicule requires little explanation, and the screenshots supply their own punch line. But the article’s later details describe a far more serious failure of stewardship.

The USS Lincoln reportedly remained at sea for a record 265 days amid poor conditions, low morale and attempts by crew members to go overboard. Other vessels reportedly faced food shortages. Moving the USS George Washington from the Pacific to relieve the Lincoln, AlterNet says, left the region without an aircraft carrier as China pressed its interests.

Those outcomes cannot be blamed on careless graphics. They flow from decisions made by civilian leaders with command authority. Fixating on foreign ships in birthday posts risks converting a dispute over military management into a harmless story about Republican incompetence online.

Spectacle over capacity

Trump’s proposed “golden fleet” fits the same pattern at a larger scale: martial aesthetics substituted for operational judgment. The article reports that he promoted “Trump-class” battleships as exceptionally powerful even though experts described battleships as obsolete. His proposed return to steam power likewise drew criticism as inefficient and wasteful.

The evidence presented does not establish why Trump favored those ideas. It does show a governing preference for grandiose symbols while sailors and existing ships reportedly bore the costs of extended deployments. The contrast is between advertised strength and maintained capacity—and only the latter keeps a navy functional.

The systemic error

Political militarism often asks the public to admire armed force without examining how political leaders use it. Ceremonial posts reward the performance of loyalty; deployment choices, procurement schemes and crew conditions demand scrutiny of power.

The foreign-warship blunders expose the emptiness of the performance, but embarrassment is the smallest consequence. The larger pattern is a political class using the Navy as patriotic scenery while the administration controlling it makes decisions that, according to the reporting, exhaust personnel, disrupt strategic coverage and prioritize presidential spectacle over military judgment.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: String of GOP lawmakers make humiliating Navy mix-up

item.title: Trump team blames lost email for ignoring court halt in mind-boggling stunt
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon ordered the Trump administration to stop a $20 million Department of Homeland Security advertising campaign praising President Donald Trump, including an ad titled “God Made Trump.” On Sunday, October 11, 2026, she halted the vendor purchase order, stayed the Office of Management and Budget’s apportionment, and barred DHS from spending congressionally appropriated border-security funds on the campaign.

The order took effect at 6:45 p.m., but the ads continued Sunday night and into early Monday. In a status report, Justice Department lawyers said government counsel emailed the order to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m., but agency counsel did not see that email until Monday morning. DOJ apologized; the reporting does not establish whether the continued broadcasts were intentional or merely the product of a failed response.

AlterNet also cites reports that Trump personally directed his budget director to fund the ads and that Customs and Border Protection leaders did not approve using their budget for them. Those claims were attributed to unnamed people familiar with the matter and federal sources.

The power was at the top

The operative decision was not made by a distracted DHS employee. According to the reporting cited by AlterNet, Trump instructed his budget director to use public money for advertisements glorifying Trump. OMB then apportioned the money, DHS placed the order, and a private vendor distributed the product.

That chain matters. Congress appropriated the funds for border security. Executive officials allegedly redirected $20 million toward presidential self-promotion, while CBP leaders were reportedly left outside the decision. The people controlling the money exercised the power; the administrators whose budgets supplied it absorbed the consequence.

An email is not an explanation

DOJ’s account may explain how agency counsel failed to learn of the order promptly. It does not explain why the administration lacked a working procedure for stopping a nationwide advertising campaign when a federal judge issued an immediate restraining order.

Reducing the episode to an unread email misdirects attention from institutional responsibility to clerical mishap. Government counsel received the order at 6:46 p.m. and did not forward it to agency counsel until 7:58 p.m. The administration then depended on somebody noticing an email to execute a time-sensitive judicial command. Even if no one deliberately defied the court, that is a breakdown created by the government’s own chain of command.

Public money, personal propaganda

The central abuse alleged here is not merely waste. It is the conversion of appropriated public funds into political tribute. An advertisement called “God Made Trump” does not resemble a neutral border-security message; as described, it elevates the officeholder whose administration controlled the spending.

That collapses a distinction essential to public administration: federal agencies serve statutory purposes, not the personal image of the president. When presidential aides can commandeer an agency budget without its operational leadership signing off, appropriation becomes suggestion and administration becomes patronage.

The cost of engineered dysfunction

The continued broadcasts created a second injury after the disputed spending itself. A court issued a specific order, yet the executive branch could not promptly translate that order into action. Whether caused by indifference, incompetence, or inadequate procedure, the foreseeable result was the same: taxpayer-funded praise continued after a judge said it must stop.

Calling this “mind-boggling” risks making it sound mysterious. Nothing about the structure is mysterious. Authority was concentrated above the officials responsible for the affected budget, while accountability dissolved across lawyers, agency counsel, DHS, OMB, and a contractor. Power traveled downward quickly; responsibility traveled nowhere.

A system built to evade ownership

This episode reveals a durable governing pattern: senior officials make the consequential choice, subordinate institutions execute it, and failure is later narrated as an administrative misunderstanding. The unread email becomes the story because it is easier to ridicule than the underlying allocation of power.

The sharper question is why public institutions were organized to obey a reported presidential demand for self-promotional spending more effectively than they obeyed a federal court’s order to stop it. That imbalance is not comic bureaucratic chaos. It is what government looks like when loyalty to the person at the top outruns loyalty to appropriations, procedure, and institutional responsibility.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump team blames lost email for ignoring court halt in mind-boggling stunt

item.title: Fox News not pulling punches as host warns ‘reality’ is ‘not good’ for Trump
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox Business host Stuart Varney warned that energy prices were politically damaging President Donald Trump three weeks before the midterm elections. Diesel was about $6.50 a gallon, gasoline about $4, and oil above $90 a barrel, according to Varney, who said farmers, truckers, and voters were “exasperated.”

Varney said Trump’s proposed purchase of millions of gallons of Russian diesel depended on an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Russia then attacked Ukrainian energy facilities within hours of the ceasefire announcement, leaving both the arrangement and the diesel purchases uncertain. The report also cited attacks on energy infrastructure and transport in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf as additional pressure on prices.

AlterNet further reports that Fox personalities have become more willing to criticize Trump over inflation and affordability. It attributes that shift partly to the network’s legal and financial consequences from broadcasting 2020 election-denial claims and to concern about Republican midterm prospects, though the article does not independently establish Fox executives’ motives.

Power sits in the presidency

Trump is not a spectator watching gasoline signs change. As president, he holds executive authority over sanctions enforcement, foreign-policy negotiations, and the administration’s response to an energy shock. His government chose to pursue Russian diesel while Russia was waging war against Ukraine and supporting Iran, according to the report.

That does not mean a president can command global oil prices. The attacks, wars, supply disruptions, and decisions of foreign governments described by AlterNet constrain American policy. But constraints do not erase agency. Trump’s responsibility lies in the bargain his administration pursued, the contradictions it accepted, and the promises it attached to an outcome Russia could disrupt almost immediately.

A purchase built on conflicting policy

The proposed transaction exposes incoherence rather than control. The United States had recently enacted legislation increasing sanctions on buyers of Russian fuel, yet Trump’s answer to domestic price pressure was reportedly to buy millions of gallons from Russia. The plan would also send revenue to a government attacking an American ally.

That is the governing failure at the center of the story: short-term electoral relief colliding with the administration’s own geopolitical posture. A policy cannot credibly punish Russian energy customers abroad while treating Russian fuel as an emergency political escape hatch at home.

Fox discovers material reality

Fox’s criticism is notable because the network has long supported Trump. But Varney’s formulation—“perception is reality”—still converts governance into optics. Voters seeing prices at gas stations are not suffering from a messaging problem. Farmers and truckers paying roughly $6.50 per gallon for diesel face operating costs with consequences for businesses, freight, and food production.

The network’s emerging candor also appears conditional. In AlterNet’s account, sharper criticism arrived as Trump’s political liabilities grew and after Fox suffered legal and financial repercussions connected to election-denial coverage. The evidence supports describing a change in tone; it does not prove a coordinated institutional break. What it does show is a media apparatus acknowledging hardship once that hardship threatens the electoral coalition it helped sustain.

The misdirection is electoral

The weakest frame in the coverage is that Trump is trapped by crises rather than accountable for his administration’s response to them. Calling him “exasperated” places the president alongside the people paying higher prices, as though both possess comparable power and merely share an unpleasant experience.

They do not. Voters absorb the costs. Trucking companies reportedly go bankrupt. Farmers pay more to operate. The president commands the state’s policy machinery and chooses which foreign governments to bargain with. Treating his predicament primarily as a race against the midterm clock redirects attention from public consequences to Republican survival.

When propaganda meets the price board

This episode illustrates a recurring pattern: allied media can suppress political accountability only until material conditions become too visible to narrate away. A gas-station sign does not respond to partisan reassurance. Neither does a freight bill.

The larger systemic failure is not simply expensive fuel. It is a governing and media structure that treats public pain as politically significant only when it becomes an electoral threat, then describes the resulting crisis as bad luck, poor perception, or presidential frustration. Power makes decisions; everyone else pays for them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox News not pulling punches as host warns ‘reality’ is ‘not good’ for Trump

item.title: 'Worst president': Trump creating a Twilight Zone where 'everyone loses’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative commentator Jonathan V. Last argued Donald Trump may be the “worst president” because his administration’s economic and foreign-policy choices are producing losses for both homeowners and prospective buyers. Last cited a 4 percent drop in pending home sales from August to September—the lowest level since 2014 outside the pandemic—and said average 30-year mortgage rates had risen from 6.6 percent in late August to roughly 7.4 percent.

Last attributed the squeeze to Federal Reserve rate hikes, higher energy costs tied to war with Iran, and Trump’s trade wars. Economists Richard Wolff and Robert J. Shapiro separately told AlterNet that military conflict, tariff pressure, damaged oil infrastructure, and uncertainty about the administration’s next moves could raise costs, provoke resistance abroad, and suppress investment. These are their assessments; the article does not independently establish that each economic change was caused by Trump’s policies.

Power made the choices

Homebuyers did not set foreign policy. Homeowners did not launch trade wars. The Trump administration holds the institutional power described in this story: it can impose tariffs, pursue military escalation, threaten trading partners, and create uncertainty across markets.

The Federal Reserve controls interest-rate policy, so assigning every mortgage-rate increase directly to Trump would be sloppy. But Last’s larger argument concerns the environment in which those decisions occur. Policies that raise energy costs or intensify inflationary pressure can leave the Fed confronting conditions the administration helped create. Responsibility must be divided according to actual authority, not dumped into the foggy category of “the economy.”

A market with no winner

The housing figures illustrate a political failure disguised as a market puzzle. Sellers lose demand and watch the value of their investment come under pressure. Buyers face financing costs high enough to push them out. Lower sales do not automatically restore affordability when borrowing has become markedly more expensive.

That is the “Twilight Zone” Last describes: not a violation of supply and demand, but several policy-driven costs landing at once. The laws of economics remain intact. What fails is the comforting political story that every economic loss must produce an equivalent domestic winner.

Belligerence has a price

Wolff’s account places tariffs and military pressure inside the same governing instinct: coercion followed by surprise when the target resists. He said Canada’s response showed that threatened countries can seek alternatives to capitulation. His description of the June 2025 fighting with Iran and renewed conflict beginning February 28 likewise challenges the premise that superior force guarantees submission.

Shapiro identified the longer tail: risk premiums, tanker-insurance costs, degraded oil infrastructure, constrained supply, and uncertainty that deters investment. Even if those effects cannot be cleanly isolated from every other economic force, they are foreseeable channels through which military escalation reaches household budgets.

The framing lets policy hide

AlterNet organizes the piece around the provocative “worst president” verdict. That label attracts attention, but it is analytically weaker than the evidence beneath it. Presidential rankings are spectacle. Decisions, authorities, and material consequences are politics.

The more useful question is not whether Trump wins a contest for historical disgrace. It is why coverage so often converts government action into economic weather. Rates “rise,” markets are “shocked,” and uncertainty “appears,” while the officials choosing tariffs, confrontation, and war recede from view. Passive framing launders agency.

Losses travel downward

The pattern is familiar: concentrated executive power makes high-risk decisions, while the costs disperse through mortgages, fuel, insurance, investment, and trade. Those consequences arrive as separate household problems, making a political chain of cause and responsibility harder to see.

That fragmentation protects power. A family priced out of a home experiences a personal defeat; a homeowner facing a frozen market sees a financial setback. But when public choices systematically raise costs for both, the result is not an inexplicable malfunction. It is policy transmitting risk downward while the people who exercised the power argue over branding.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Worst president’: Trump creating a Twilight Zone where ‘everyone loses’

item.title: Missing $50 million tracks straight to Mar-a-Lago
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet does not establish that $50 million went to Mar-a-Lago. It reports that federal events connected to the United States’ 250th anniversary cost $128 million, with at least $114 million supplied by taxpayers, while The Wall Street Journal reported that corporate donors contributed at least another $50 million. The article does not provide records showing where those private contributions went.

According to AlterNet, Congress had funded an anniversary celebration a decade earlier, but Donald Trump created a separate, privately organized “Freedom 250” effort. The outlet says contracts were awarded without competitive bidding and that the administration has not disclosed a full donor list, contribution amounts, or the ultimate disposition of the donated money.

The Mar-a-Lago connection in the headline is therefore insinuation, not a documented financial trail. AlterNet says Democrats suspect the money may have become a fund benefiting Trump or his family, but it presents neither proof of that allegation nor evidence that the money reached his Florida property.

The power sits with the administration

The decisive actors are not the corporations writing checks or the public left guessing about the accounting. Institutional power belongs to the administration officials controlling the celebration, the contracts, and the records.

That control creates the central political problem: the same operation soliciting private money for a public commemoration also determines which contractors receive taxpayer funds and what information the public may see. When officials refuse to disclose donors and expenditures, opacity is not some atmospheric failure of government. It is a choice made by people with custody of the records.

Congress also holds power. It appropriated money and possesses oversight authority. If lawmakers do not compel an accounting, they enable secrecy by declining to use the tools attached to their offices.

The unanswered arithmetic

The reported figures demand an audit, not a punchline. If the events cost $128 million and taxpayers supplied at least $114 million, the publicly identified gap between those figures is $14 million. Separately, corporate donors reportedly supplied at least $50 million. Those numbers raise obvious questions about whether donor funds paid expenses outside the stated event total, remained unspent, or were routed elsewhere.

AlterNet does not answer them. More importantly, it does not substantiate the headline’s claim that the money “tracks straight” to Trump’s club. A missing accounting is evidence of failed transparency; it is not, by itself, proof of theft, self-dealing, or a particular destination.

That distinction matters precisely because the underlying conduct warrants scrutiny. Inflating an unsupported conclusion gives officials an easy escape: attack the exaggeration and avoid producing the ledger.

Corporate money buys obscurity

Chevron, United Airlines, and defense contractor RTX are identified as major donors. The article does not establish what any company expected or received in return, so a bribery claim would outrun the evidence. But secret or incomplete donor accounting around a presidentially controlled national celebration creates an influence channel the public cannot evaluate.

The corruption risk lies in the structure: corporations with substantial interests before the federal government can finance an operation associated with the president while the administration withholds the details. Disclosure is what allows citizens to distinguish civic sponsorship from access-seeking. Without it, officials are effectively asking the public to trust the beneficiaries of secrecy.

Secrecy is the systemic failure

The larger pattern is the privatization of public authority without public accountability. A national anniversary becomes a presidential brand vehicle; taxpayer funding and corporate sponsorship become difficult to separate; contracts move without competition; and oversight arrives only after watchdogs uncover fragments of the record.

AlterNet weakens its own case by converting that documented opacity into an unproven Mar-a-Lago trail. The stronger indictment is already available: officials controlling public money and presidential access have reportedly refused to provide a transparent account, while Congress retains the power to force one.

A functioning system would not require speculation about bathroom cash. It would require contracts, donor records, invoices, recipients, balances, and enforceable consequences for withholding them. When those records remain hidden, the scandal is not that outsiders cannot guess where the money went. It is that the people empowered to know have arranged matters so the public does not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Missing $50 million tracks straight to Mar-a-Lago

item.title: Megyn Kelly brutally mocked after doubling down on widely debunked lie
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Megyn Kelly continued pressing claims about James Talarico after the Lindner Center of Hope said he had never been a patient there. Talarico reposted the facility’s statement and said he had never been to Ohio. Kelly nevertheless asked whether he had visited within the previous nine days and whether an operator who allegedly said otherwise had been mistaken.

The allegation rested on a 45-second recording promoted by right-wing commentator Nick Sortor. According to The Bulwark’s account cited by AlterNet, the full six-minute call included repeated statements from the apparent facility employee that no James Talarico appeared in its system. The shorter clip omitted those denials. Journalists and political commentators then mocked Kelly’s refusal to accept the correction.

The power was in the edit

The decisive act was not Kelly’s confused follow-up or the facility’s initial refusal to discuss patients. It was the extraction of a misleading fragment from a longer call.

The caller, identified in the reporting as Amacher, allegedly used false statements to solicit private information. Sortor then circulated only the portion that supported the desired insinuation. The Bulwark’s acquisition of the full recording changed the story because it restored what the edited clip removed: repeated denials that Talarico was in the facility’s system.

That is editorial agency. A clip does not shorten itself, and omitted context does not disappear by accident simply because an audience encounters only the finished product.

Kelly chose amplification over correction

Kelly had the larger platform and therefore the greater power to convert a dubious claim into a public controversy. Once the facility issued an unequivocal denial, she could have corrected the record. Instead, she tried to reopen a question the available evidence had already answered.

Her demand that the employee be allowed to speak publicly also inverted responsibility. A mental-health facility’s confidentiality obligations are not evidence of concealment, and an employee should not have to become a public combatant because political personalities circulated a selectively edited call.

Kelly’s persistence did not uncover a contradiction. It preserved an allegation after its factual basis had collapsed.

Mockery is not the central consequence

AlterNet organizes much of the story around prominent people ridiculing Kelly. The ridicule is understandable, but it is also the least important part.

The meaningful harm falls on the person falsely associated with psychiatric treatment and on the institution dragged into denying a manufactured claim without violating patient privacy. Framing the episode primarily as Kelly getting “brutally mocked” turns an information-abuse operation into celebrity spectacle.

That framing also lets the original propagators remain secondary characters. Embarrassment is temporary. The political utility of smearing someone with an invented mental-health narrative can survive long after the correction.

Stigma became a political weapon

The allegation worked by treating psychiatric care as discrediting information. Even if Talarico had received treatment—which the facility denied—the insinuation depended on audiences viewing mental-health care as proof of incapacity or deception.

That is the uglier power structure beneath the episode: operatives manufacture suspicion, high-reach personalities legitimize it by “asking questions,” and privacy rules prevent institutions from responding with unlimited detail. The target is then expected to disprove an allegation built from selective evidence.

The correction cannot match the smear

This episode reveals a familiar propaganda sequence. Create a sensational allegation, strip away contrary context, exploit institutional restraint, and recast definitive denials as unresolved mystery. When the claim fails, shift attention to the pundit’s humiliation instead of the machinery that produced and distributed the lie.

The systemic error is not public confusion. It is an incentive structure that rewards political media figures for keeping a falsehood alive while forcing everyone else—the target, the institution and actual reporters—to spend time dismantling it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Megyn Kelly brutally mocked after doubling down on widely debunked lie

item.title: Trump DOJ is buckling as caseloads explode while staffing withers
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing The Hill’s review of internal Justice Department metrics, reports that the Trump administration’s immigration policies have sharply increased the department’s legal workload while staffing has fallen. The Civil Division’s Office of Immigration Litigation lost nearly 80 attorneys as its workload rose 63 percent.

The office reportedly shrank from about 320 attorneys at the start of Trump’s second term to 243 by August, while its caseload climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500. Former DOJ official Margy O’Herron attributed the surge partly to historically low asylum approvals and the administration’s decision to deny bond hearings, which generated more habeas petitions from detained migrants.

The pressure could increase further. The DOJ said it filed 40 denaturalization cases from late August through early October, while an anonymous former staffer said attorneys had been given a target of 300. The administration has also fired and replaced immigration judges, including within the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Power created this crisis

This is not an unexplained collision between rising demand and scarce personnel. The administration controls the policies producing the cases, the detention practices provoking legal challenges, and the staffing decisions weakening the offices assigned to defend those policies.

Its choices expanded detention to people whom O’Herron described as longtime residents without criminal histories. Cutting off bond hearings then forced detainees to seek judicial review through habeas petitions. The government created more confinement, restricted an ordinary avenue for challenging it, and produced the litigation that followed.

Cruelty has paperwork

Administrative capacity is often treated as separate from policy, as though staff shortages merely interfere with an otherwise coherent agenda. Here, capacity is part of the political story. Aggressive enforcement generates legal obligations, even when the administration would prefer immigrants to disappear into detention without meaningful resistance.

Each additional case represents more than an inconvenient file. Asylum denials must be defended. Detention must be justified. Attempts to revoke citizenship require litigation. The caseload is the institutional residue of decisions imposed on people with far less power than the officials making them.

The buckling frame misdirects

Saying the DOJ is “buckling” accurately describes strain but obscures agency. The department did not simply encounter a natural disaster of immigration litigation. Trump officials intensified enforcement, reduced avenues for release, pursued more denaturalizations, removed personnel, and remade the immigration adjudication system.

The weaker actors are migrants responding to detention, rejected asylum claims, or threatened loss of citizenship. Their petitions did not originate the crisis. They are attempts to make the government account for its conduct. Treating those cases as the burden reverses the power relationship: the state acts, the targeted person challenges it, and the challenge is blamed for exhausting the state.

Institutional depletion serves executive power

The reporting does not establish that staffing losses were deliberately engineered to obstruct legal review. But the foreseeable effect is clear. Fewer government lawyers facing more cases means less time for careful legal work, more pressure on remaining staff, and greater risk that volume will substitute for judgment.

Firing and replacing immigration judges compounds that danger. An administration that simultaneously changes adjudicators, expands enforcement, and overwhelms the lawyers handling the resulting disputes is not merely managing immigration more aggressively. It is concentrating policy control while degrading the institutions expected to process objections.

Dysfunction as a governing pattern

The larger pattern is government by escalation: impose harsher rules, generate predictable resistance, hollow out the machinery responsible for handling it, and describe the resulting breakdown as an external burden.

That framing protects the officials with authority and shifts attention toward those trapped inside the system. The DOJ’s strain is real, but it is not politically mysterious. It is what happens when executive power treats legal process as an obstacle, human beings as enforcement inventory, and institutional competence as expendable.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump DOJ is buckling as caseloads explode while staffing withers

item.title: Cornered ex-Trump staffer gives bonkers answer to defend president’s lies
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney defended President Donald Trump’s claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to pause attacks on energy infrastructure, even though Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of striking a Ukrainian power plant hours later. On Times Radio, Mulvaney described Trump’s conduct as an attempt to “visualize his way to success”: announce an agreement and hope the declaration helps produce one.

Host Darryl Morris pressed Mulvaney on whether Trump had invented a ceasefire. Mulvaney denied that characterization, suggesting there may have been a “kernel” of an agreement that Trump was trying to push across the finish line. He acknowledged witnessing this practice repeatedly in the White House but declined to judge whether it was a wise way to exercise presidential power.

The report does not independently establish the scope or precise terms of any proposed ceasefire, nor does it resolve whether the reported strike violated them. It does establish Mulvaney’s defense: Trump treats public assertion as a negotiating instrument, even when the asserted result has not been secured.

Power does not run on affirmation

Trump holds the institutional power here. A president’s statements can shape diplomacy, military expectations, markets, alliances, and public understanding. Calling an unsettled negotiation a completed agreement is therefore not ordinary salesmanship. It is an official claim carrying consequences beyond the speaker’s personal credibility.

Mulvaney’s “positive thinking” explanation trivializes that distinction. The relevant question is not whether Trump sincerely believes confident language can create momentum. It is whether the president accurately describes what governments have agreed to while attacks continue and civilians depend on energy infrastructure. Personal conviction cannot substitute for consent from the parties, enforceable terms, or observable compliance.

Mulvaney launders false certainty

Mulvaney does not merely explain Trump’s technique. He sanitizes it. “Optimism,” “enthusiasm,” and “momentum” recast an unsupported declaration as an unconventional management style rather than a failure to distinguish aspiration from fact.

His retreat—“I don’t get to make that call”—is especially revealing. He was invited to assess the conduct, not exercise presidential authority. Refusing to judge while supplying excuses is still a choice: it shields the officeholder and leaves audiences to absorb uncertainty that Trump created.

The tax bill and Trump’s electoral success do not validate claims about a ceasefire. Winning political contests after making bold predictions does not make an international agreement exist. Mulvaney substitutes anecdotes about Trump prevailing for evidence that the governments involved accepted and observed specific terms.

The weaker actors bear the reality

The rhetorical fog benefits the most powerful participant. Trump gets credit for peace before peace has been demonstrated; aides and former aides can later downgrade the claim to a negotiating tactic; Ukrainians remain exposed to the material consequences if attacks continue.

That is the misdirection at the center of the story. The issue is not whether Trump is “rattled,” as Morris speculated, or whether he cares about the midterms, as Mulvaney disputed. Neither claim is established by the reported exchange. Speculation about Trump’s emotional state distracts from the documented institutional failure: the president announced an outcome that the subsequent reported conduct immediately called into question.

Government by retroactive meaning

This style of politics makes official language deliberately elastic. If events match the declaration, the leader claims foresight and success. If they do not, defenders say he was expressing confidence, advancing negotiations, or describing a partial understanding. The statement is treated as authoritative when useful and metaphorical when challenged.

That arrangement destroys accountability without requiring anyone to admit error. The president supplies certainty; loyal interpreters later revise what that certainty supposedly meant. Former officials such as Mulvaney become part of the mechanism, converting a testable claim into a story about personality.

The permission structure

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as interpretation. Powerful officials make claims that exceed the evidence, while their defenders translate those claims into harmless quirks and journalists chase theories about temperament. Responsibility dissolves into psychology.

But the chain of agency is clear. Trump made the reported claim. Mulvaney chose to defend the method instead of demanding factual precision. The presidency magnifies the consequences. When political power can announce success first and renegotiate the meaning later, language stops informing the public and starts insulating the person who controls the microphone.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Cornered ex-Trump staffer gives bonkers answer to defend president’s lies

item.title: Trump retreats on taxpayer-funded ads as DOJ dodges legality questions
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration said it would stop airing a $20 million taxpayer-funded advertising campaign after the Democratic National Committee and Common Cause sued and a judge demanded answers about its legality. A Homeland Security official told the court that the ads would air for the last time on Sunday, but the Justice Department did not answer the lawsuits’ allegations or the judge’s questions about the White House’s role.

According to a Customs and Border Protection official cited in the filing, CBP issued the purchase order on Sept. 20 through a previously awarded agreement with Maryland-based LMD Agency. The money came from a Republican law enacted in 2025 and appropriating funds for border-security activities. The ads appeared on major cable and broadcast networks.

The retreat followed broad public opposition: 86 percent of respondents in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted Sept. 30–Oct. 5 called the use of taxpayer money inappropriate, including 80 percent of Republicans surveyed. The administration reportedly has no plan to reimburse the government. Common Cause argues that ending the broadcasts is insufficient and is seeking to recover funds paid but potentially unspent.

The power was federal

This was not a dispute among comparably situated political participants. The administration controlled the agencies, the appropriation and the machinery used to purchase nationwide airtime. The public supplied the money; executive officials decided how to spend it.

Congressional Republicans enabled that discretion by passing the 2025 funding law. The article does not establish that the statute authorized campaign advertising. It does establish the institutional chain that mattered: lawmakers furnished the funds, CBP issued the purchase order, and the administration defended the result in court.

Withdrawal is not accountability

Stopping the ads after they aired does not answer whether officials lawfully commissioned them. Nor does it recover money already spent or establish limits on repeating the tactic.

The Justice Department’s position, as reported, was procedural evasion: dismiss the case because the challenged conduct was ending. That argument asks the court to treat the expiration of the purchase as a substitute for examining the purchase itself. Common Cause’s response identifies the obvious incentive—officials could run out the clock, cease when judicial review approaches and preserve the benefits of conduct that escapes a ruling.

The missing answers matter

The unresolved issue is not merely whether viewers disliked the commercials. It is who directed their creation, what role the White House played and whether public funds were converted into an electoral advantage. AlterNet reports that the Justice Department declined to address the allegations and ignored questions about White House involvement.

That silence is not proof of illegality or of an undisclosed scheme. It is, however, an exercise of institutional power: the government’s lawyers attempted to end scrutiny without supplying the facts the court requested. The administration announced cessation while resisting adjudication.

Backlash is not the governing check

The poll explains the political pressure, but popularity is a poor substitute for enforceable restraint. Taxpayer-funded political promotion would remain an abuse of public power even if polling found it popular; overwhelming opposition merely made retreat less costly than continued defense.

Framing this chiefly as Trump “waving the white flag” risks converting an accountability dispute into a story about tactical defeat. The weaker actors—the DNC, Common Cause and taxpayers—did not control the money or the agencies. They could only sue after officials had already committed funds and distributed the ads.

A system built for faits accomplis

The larger pattern is government by completed transaction: appropriate broadly, spend quickly, litigate slowly and declare the controversy moot once the benefit has been captured. Courts may eventually reject that maneuver, but delay itself favors the officeholder controlling the state.

Without disclosure, recovery of unused funds and a ruling on the legal boundaries, the lesson for future administrations is corrosively simple. Public money can finance politically useful messaging, and accountability may arrive only after the airtime is gone.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump retreats on taxpayer-funded ads as DOJ dodges legality questions

Backlash is not the governing check

The poll explains the political pressure, but popularity is a poor substitute for enforceable restraint. Taxpayer-funded political promotion would remain an abuse of public power even if polling found it popular; overwhelming opposition merely made retreat less costly than continued defense.

Framing this chiefly as Trump “waving the white flag” risks converting an accountability dispute into a story about tactical defeat. The weaker actors—the DNC, Common Cause and taxpayers—did not control the money or the agencies. They could only sue after officials had already committed funds and distributed the ads.

A system built for faits accomplis

The larger pattern is government by completed transaction: appropriate broadly, spend quickly, litigate slowly and declare the controversy moot once the benefit has been captured. Courts may eventually reject that maneuver, but delay itself favors the officeholder controlling the state.

Without disclosure, recovery of unused funds and a ruling on the legal boundaries, the lesson for future administrations is corrosively simple. Public money can finance politically useful messaging, and accountability may arrive only after the airtime is gone.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump retreats on taxpayer-funded ads as DOJ dodges legality questions

item.title: Trump told them to 'pretend' —now it’s the one thing they are trying to hide
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump has urged Republican voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” during the midterm campaign, while some Republican candidates are trying to make their campaigns look less connected to him. The outlet says a dozen candidates removed references to Trump from campaign websites and cites Susan Collins and John Sununu as declining to campaign with him, while Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers publicly opposed Trump’s tariff conflict with Canada.

Democratic candidates are making the association explicit. In recent debates, Troy Jackson blamed Collins for failing to oppose Trump’s Iran war and tariffs; Jon Ossoff tied Michael Collins to Trump’s agenda; and Abdul El-Sayed called Rogers a Trump “sock puppet.” Those are campaign accusations, and the article does not provide voting records or other evidence sufficient to establish each charge independently.

The story’s answer to what Republicans are trying to hide is their political connection to Trump. AlterNet argues that his weak approval ratings have turned that connection into an electoral liability, even as Trump continues presenting the midterms as a referendum on himself.

Power does not disappear from a website

Trump holds the institutional power that matters here: the presidency, command of executive policy and enormous influence over Republican politics. Candidates can delete his photograph, avoid the word “MAGA” and keep him outside their states. None of that changes who imposed the tariffs they now criticize or who directs the administration they have spent years navigating.

The candidates retain agency too. They decide which policies to support, when to object and whether opposition arrives before a policy causes damage or only after polling makes loyalty expensive. The reporting does not document every candidate’s record, so it cannot prove that each Republican now creating distance enabled every Trump decision. But it does reveal an unmistakable campaign strategy: conceal the association without necessarily accounting for it.

Distance without a reckoning

Rogers’s beer-can denunciation of the tariff conflict is politically useful because it isolates one unpopular consequence while leaving the larger relationship unresolved. Sununu’s spokesman similarly framed Trump’s absence as a commitment to campaigning with New Hampshire figures, not as a substantive break with Trump.

That is not repudiation. It is brand management. These candidates want the freedom to benefit from Trump’s political coalition while denying opponents an easy visual reminder of the bargain. Their problem is not merely that Democrats keep mentioning Trump. It is that Republican control of Congress would affect Trump’s ability to govern, face oversight and withstand impeachment. The connection is institutional, not cosmetic.

The article’s evidence has limits

AlterNet is strongest when it identifies the contradiction between Trump’s demand to become the symbolic ballot choice and Republican candidates’ efforts to reduce his visibility. It is weaker when it treats his approval rating as the established cause of every act of distancing. The article supplies suggestive examples, but not enough candidate-by-candidate evidence to prove motive in every case.

Its account of Trump’s rallies also relies heavily on Robert Reich’s interpretation that Trump is campaigning principally for personal adulation. The reported speeches—about his intelligence, hair, polling, crowds and possible impeachment—support the narrower conclusion that he devotes substantial attention to himself. They do not, by themselves, prove his internal motive.

A party trapped by its own leader

Trump’s reported conduct makes the conflict unusually stark. He asks voters to treat congressional races as votes for him, then reportedly spends campaign appearances discussing himself far more than the candidates whose victories would determine control of Congress. AlterNet also reports that he agreed to have MAGA Inc. pay for self-promotional advertising after bipartisan objections to its taxpayer funding, while declining to commit to reimbursing costs already incurred.

The larger pattern is a governing party trying to separate responsibility from identity. Republican candidates cannot plausibly claim Trump’s coalition when useful, obscure him when costly and then describe the resulting backlash as unfair guilt by association. If they supported his power, declined to restrain it or seek office in order to extend it, the association is not a Democratic trick. It is the political consequence of their own choices.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump told them to ‘pretend’ —now it’s the one thing they are trying to hide

item.title: Trump DOJ is buckling as caseloads explode while staffing withers
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing The Hill’s review of internal Justice Department metrics, reports that the Trump administration’s immigration policies have sharply increased the department’s legal workload while staffing has fallen. The Civil Division’s Office of Immigration Litigation lost nearly 80 attorneys as its workload rose 63 percent.

The office reportedly shrank from about 320 attorneys at the start of Trump’s second term to 243 by August, while its caseload climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500. Former DOJ official Margy O’Herron attributed the surge partly to historically low asylum approvals and the administration’s decision to deny bond hearings, which generated more habeas petitions from detained migrants.

The pressure could increase further. The DOJ said it filed 40 denaturalization cases from late August through early October, while an anonymous former staffer said attorneys had been given a target of 300. The administration has also fired and replaced immigration judges, including within the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Power created this crisis

This is not an unexplained collision between rising demand and scarce personnel. The administration controls the policies producing the cases, the detention practices provoking legal challenges, and the staffing decisions weakening the offices assigned to defend those policies.

Its choices expanded detention to people whom O’Herron described as longtime residents without criminal histories. Cutting off bond hearings then forced detainees to seek judicial review through habeas petitions. The government created more confinement, restricted an ordinary avenue for challenging it, and produced the litigation that followed.

Cruelty has paperwork

Administrative capacity is often treated as separate from policy, as though staff shortages merely interfere with an otherwise coherent agenda. Here, capacity is part of the political story. Aggressive enforcement generates legal obligations, even when the administration would prefer immigrants to disappear into detention without meaningful resistance.

Each additional case represents more than an inconvenient file. Asylum denials must be defended. Detention must be justified. Attempts to revoke citizenship require litigation. The caseload is the institutional residue of decisions imposed on people with far less power than the officials making them.

The buckling frame misdirects

Saying the DOJ is “buckling” accurately describes strain but obscures agency. The department did not simply encounter a natural disaster of immigration litigation. Trump officials intensified enforcement, reduced avenues for release, pursued more denaturalizations, removed personnel, and remade the immigration adjudication system.

The weaker actors are migrants responding to detention, rejected asylum claims, or threatened loss of citizenship. Their petitions did not originate the crisis. They are attempts to make the government account for its conduct. Treating those cases as the burden reverses the power relationship: the state acts, the targeted person challenges it, and the challenge is blamed for exhausting the state.

Institutional depletion serves executive power

The reporting does not establish that staffing losses were deliberately engineered to obstruct legal review. But the foreseeable effect is clear. Fewer government lawyers facing more cases means less time for careful legal work, more pressure on remaining staff, and greater risk that volume will substitute for judgment.

Firing and replacing immigration judges compounds that danger. An administration that simultaneously changes adjudicators, expands enforcement, and overwhelms the lawyers handling the resulting disputes is not merely managing immigration more aggressively. It is concentrating policy control while degrading the institutions expected to process objections.

Dysfunction as a governing pattern

The larger pattern is government by escalation: impose harsher rules, generate predictable resistance, hollow out the machinery responsible for handling it, and describe the resulting breakdown as an external burden.

That framing protects the officials with authority and shifts attention toward those trapped inside the system. The DOJ’s strain is real, but it is not politically mysterious. It is what happens when executive power treats legal process as an obstacle, human beings as enforcement inventory, and institutional competence as expendable.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump DOJ is buckling as caseloads explode while staffing withers

item.title: Missing $50 million tracks straight to Mar-a-Lago
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet does not establish that $50 million went to Mar-a-Lago. It reports that federal events connected to the United States’ 250th anniversary cost $128 million, with at least $114 million supplied by taxpayers, while The Wall Street Journal reported that corporate donors contributed at least another $50 million. The article does not provide records showing where those private contributions went.

According to AlterNet, Congress had funded an anniversary celebration a decade earlier, but Donald Trump created a separate, privately organized “Freedom 250” effort. The outlet says contracts were awarded without competitive bidding and that the administration has not disclosed a full donor list, contribution amounts, or the ultimate disposition of the donated money.

The Mar-a-Lago connection in the headline is therefore insinuation, not a documented financial trail. AlterNet says Democrats suspect the money may have become a fund benefiting Trump or his family, but it presents neither proof of that allegation nor evidence that the money reached his Florida property.

The power sits with the administration

The decisive actors are not the corporations writing checks or the public left guessing about the accounting. Institutional power belongs to the administration officials controlling the celebration, the contracts, and the records.

That control creates the central political problem: the same operation soliciting private money for a public commemoration also determines which contractors receive taxpayer funds and what information the public may see. When officials refuse to disclose donors and expenditures, opacity is not some atmospheric failure of government. It is a choice made by people with custody of the records.

Congress also holds power. It appropriated money and possesses oversight authority. If lawmakers do not compel an accounting, they enable secrecy by declining to use the tools attached to their offices.

The unanswered arithmetic

The reported figures demand an audit, not a punchline. If the events cost $128 million and taxpayers supplied at least $114 million, the publicly identified gap between those figures is $14 million. Separately, corporate donors reportedly supplied at least $50 million. Those numbers raise obvious questions about whether donor funds paid expenses outside the stated event total, remained unspent, or were routed elsewhere.

AlterNet does not answer them. More importantly, it does not substantiate the headline’s claim that the money “tracks straight” to Trump’s club. A missing accounting is evidence of failed transparency; it is not, by itself, proof of theft, self-dealing, or a particular destination.

That distinction matters precisely because the underlying conduct warrants scrutiny. Inflating an unsupported conclusion gives officials an easy escape: attack the exaggeration and avoid producing the ledger.

Corporate money buys obscurity

Chevron, United Airlines, and defense contractor RTX are identified as major donors. The article does not establish what any company expected or received in return, so a bribery claim would outrun the evidence. But secret or incomplete donor accounting around a presidentially controlled national celebration creates an influence channel the public cannot evaluate.

The corruption risk lies in the structure: corporations with substantial interests before the federal government can finance an operation associated with the president while the administration withholds the details. Disclosure is what allows citizens to distinguish civic sponsorship from access-seeking. Without it, officials are effectively asking the public to trust the beneficiaries of secrecy.

Secrecy is the systemic failure

The larger pattern is the privatization of public authority without public accountability. A national anniversary becomes a presidential brand vehicle; taxpayer funding and corporate sponsorship become difficult to separate; contracts move without competition; and oversight arrives only after watchdogs uncover fragments of the record.

AlterNet weakens its own case by converting that documented opacity into an unproven Mar-a-Lago trail. The stronger indictment is already available: officials controlling public money and presidential access have reportedly refused to provide a transparent account, while Congress retains the power to force one.

A functioning system would not require speculation about bathroom cash. It would require contracts, donor records, invoices, recipients, balances, and enforceable consequences for withholding them. When those records remain hidden, the scandal is not that outsiders cannot guess where the money went. It is that the people empowered to know have arranged matters so the public does not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Missing $50 million tracks straight to Mar-a-Lago

item.title: Psychologist flags a tell that 'manic' Trump could be on stimulants
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist John Paul Garrison identified Trump’s repeated lateral jaw movement as a possible sign of stimulant use—but he also said it could reflect medication, impaired motor function, or a neurological condition. The footage does not establish that Trump took stimulants, and Garrison did not claim proof.

Analyzing a Tennessee rally for Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Garrison also pointed to Trump’s unusual mouth movements, closed eyes, agitation, repetition, and increasingly concentrated “wild remarks.” He described Trump as unusually excitable and “almost manic,” while suggesting that applause and encouragement could reinforce poorly inhibited behavior.

Trump told the crowd that he could say “the stupidest things” and still receive applause. The audience responded by laughing and clapping, appearing to demonstrate the unconditional loyalty he had just described.

The headline outruns the evidence

The stimulant suggestion is the weakest part of the story. A jaw movement observed in rally footage cannot establish drug use, and Garrison himself offered several possible explanations. “Could be” is not a diagnosis, much less evidence of what caused the behavior.

Making stimulants the teaser converts uncertainty into insinuation. It invites readers to solve Trump as a medical mystery when the politically consequential conduct is visible without speculation: a president mocked his supporters’ credulity, celebrated their loyalty, and received affirmation in return.

Power is not a symptom

Trump holds presidential authority. Blackburn holds a Senate seat and benefited from his appearance. The crowd supplied applause, but it did not command the executive branch or determine which judgments would become government action.

That distinction matters because personality analysis can conceal agency. Whatever explains Trump’s movements, he chose to campaign for Blackburn and publicly test how openly he could describe his followers’ submission. His allies chose to remain inside a political structure organized around that loyalty.

The audience is the prop, not the engine

Trump’s supporters are easy targets for ridicule, especially when they applaud an insult aimed at them. But treating the crowd as the central problem misdirects attention downward.

The more powerful enablers are political officials and insiders who turn personal loyalty into institutional permission. Garrison warned that affirmation from people around a leader with poor judgment could contribute to worse decisions. The article offers no evidence about what occurred behind closed doors, but the public rally shows the underlying incentive clearly: obedience is rewarded, dissent is absent, and humiliation can be repackaged as intimacy.

Spectacle protects the structure

Speculation about stimulants turns governance into celebrity pathology. It asks what might be happening inside Trump’s body instead of examining what officeholders permit him to do with public power.

The documented behavior is already revealing. Trump framed dominance as humor, announced that the audience would applaud anything, and was proven right in real time. That is not merely a curious psychological episode. It is a political performance in which submission becomes belonging and applause substitutes for accountability.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as personal fascination. Coverage fixates on tics, temperament, and possible impairment because those subjects are vivid and safely speculative. The harder story concerns the people with authority who continue converting Trump’s impulses into political action.

A democracy is not governed by body-language clips. It is governed by officials, parties, advisers, and institutions making choices. When those actors yield judgment to one leader and the press responds by diagnosing his gestures, power escapes scrutiny while spectacle absorbs it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist flags a tell that ‘manic’ Trump could be on stimulants
