item.title: The ruthless lesson Trump learned that explains his entire strategy
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s defining political lesson came from Roy Cohn: deny wrongdoing, counterattack, and generate controversy faster than any single scandal can produce accountability. The result, according to the outlet, is an administration that uses relentless conflict to exhaust the public and crowd consequential decisions out of the news cycle.

The article points to Trump’s promotion of meme coins and access-based clubs, Attorney General Todd Blanche’s categorical defense of the president, and reported concerns about Trump’s schedule and exhaustion. It also cites forecasts of a possible Democratic wave in the November 3 midterms, while acknowledging that polling remains uncertain.

Its most consequential example is the administration’s assault on USAID under Elon Musk. AlterNet cites research estimating that the agency’s health programs saved 90 million lives over two decades and reports warnings that the cuts could contribute to hundreds of thousands of deaths worldwide.

Power hides behind spectacle

Trump holds the presidency. His administration controls executive appointments, federal agencies and the implementation of the budget. Musk’s influence over USAID, as described by AlterNet, therefore did not materialize from personal celebrity alone. It depended on presidential authorization and an executive apparatus willing to carry out the cuts.

That distinction matters because spectacle encourages the public to mistake visibility for power. Late-night posts and daily provocations command attention; administrative control changes institutions. The outrage cycle is not the governing program. It is the environment in which the governing program becomes harder to track.

Loyalty replaces restraint

Blanche’s reported defense—that Trump would never ask him to do anything illegal—does not answer whether an attorney general would refuse such a request. It substitutes confidence in the president for an independent standard of conduct.

That is politically useful evasiveness. The attorney general’s institutional duty cannot rest on the premise that presidential misconduct is inconceivable. When senior officials define ethical limits through personal loyalty, oversight is weakened before any specific order is even issued.

The relevant power structure is plain: Trump selects officials, those officials control federal institutions, and their public assurances help insulate his decisions. Calling this merely “unorthodox” understates the erosion described in the reporting.

Exhaustion is not accountability

AlterNet frames the Cohn method as a psychological tactic: one controversy buries another until memory itself becomes a scarce political resource. But public fatigue does not erase responsibility. It only reduces the time available to assign it.

Coverage can assist that process when it treats every provocation as a separate performance. The audience is invited to debate tone, stamina and campaign optics while policy proceeds through staffing decisions and budget cuts. The weaker actor—the distracted or exhausted public—then appears responsible for failing to keep up, even though the information environment is being shaped by people with vastly greater power.

The article is strongest when it connects the noise to material governance. It is weaker when it leans on predictions of a “blue wave” or reports of erratic scheduling. Electoral speculation and personality surveillance can become another layer of the same distraction.

The body count is the policy story

USAID’s dismantling is not significant because it exposes hypocrisy or violates political custom. Its significance lies in the programs interrupted and the lives placed at risk. The estimate of 90 million lives saved concerns the agency’s work over two decades; the warning of hundreds of thousands of future deaths is a projection, not a completed count. Both figures nevertheless establish the scale at which these decisions operate.

The cuts described by AlterNet were enabled by the administration, not caused by media overload. Distraction may reduce scrutiny, but it does not sign orders, delegate authority or slash budgets. Trump’s administration owns the governing decision. Musk exercised the power it gave him. Compliant officials sustained the structure around them.

The system rewards the flood

The larger pattern is government by saturation: concentrate institutional power, surround its exercise with ceaseless conflict, and rely on the press to chase novelty instead of tracing authority. Each controversy becomes disposable; the changes imposed through federal machinery endure.

An election may reduce the administration’s legislative power, but that possibility does not itself restore accountability. The harder task is refusing the central misdirection—confusing the loudest event with the most important one. Political theater matters here because it obscures who controls the state, who authorized the damage and who will bear consequences long after the performance moves on.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The ruthless lesson Trump learned that explains his entire strategy

item.title: Showdown: Europe could trigger ‘nuclear option’ against Donald Trump
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution on October 9, freezing property and obstructing services and transactions involving the Hague-based court. Unlike earlier sanctions against particular officials and organizations, the new package reportedly threatens salaries, financial transfers, cloud services, insurance and travel. Some services received a 180-day exemption while the administration demands “meaningful progress.”

The immediate dispute concerns ICC investigations involving alleged US abuses in Afghanistan and alleged Israeli war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. The article says the sanctions could severely impede ICC operations because international finance and technology infrastructure remain heavily exposed to US jurisdiction.

European governments, Canada, the United Kingdom and Japan declared support for the ICC’s independence. But the article argues that statements alone will not protect it. The European Union could invoke a blocking statute requiring people and companies under EU jurisdiction to disregard the US sanctions, although the EU had not announced that step when the article was published.

The power is in the plumbing

The central actor is not a vaguely troubled “international community.” It is the US executive, using American control over finance, technology and commercial networks to impose costs on a court the United States does not control.

That power reaches well beyond freezing a prosecutor’s bank account. If service providers, insurers and financial institutions fear punishment for dealing with the ICC, they may withdraw before any enforcement action is taken. The uncertainty is functional: it can isolate the court without Washington having to prohibit every transaction individually.

The administration also controls the clock. A 180-day grace period is presented as relief, but the reported demand for “meaningful progress” turns essential services into leverage. The message is that the court may continue functioning only while reconsidering work that has angered Washington.

Accountability with an exemption clause

The United States has never ratified the Rome Statute and has spent decades shielding its nationals from the ICC’s reach. Congress enacted the American Servicemembers’ Protection Act in 2002, and Washington pursued bilateral agreements designed to prevent US citizens from being surrendered to The Hague.

That history matters because this is not a sudden dispute over flawed procedure. According to the article, US pressure intensified when the court pursued allegations involving CIA torture and, later, Israeli officials’ conduct in Gaza. The consistent principle is exemption for powerful allies and Americans, not equal application of international law.

The allegations remain allegations, and the ICC warrants are not convictions. But sanctions against the institution do not rebut its cases on evidence or law. They exploit superior state power to impair the body authorized to examine them.

Europe’s declaration gap

European states possess agency here. They are ICC members, major economies and hosts or sponsors of institutions that the sanctions may disrupt. Their joint statement defending the court’s independence establishes their position; it does not secure the court’s payroll, vendors or digital infrastructure.

The proposed EU blocking statute would convert rhetorical support into legal conflict with Washington by ordering entities under European jurisdiction not to comply. That would carry economic and diplomatic risks, including possible US countermeasures. Those risks are precisely why the decision matters. Institutional commitments become meaningful when honoring them is costly.

Framing Europe’s response as a coming “showdown” can obscure the actual choice. European governments are not spectators waiting to see whether international law survives. They can accept American coercion, build protections against it or force companies into opposing legal obligations. Inaction would also be a decision.

The misdirection of inevitability

The article is strongest when it identifies the machinery of pressure and weaker when it leans on symbolic contrast. Navi Pillay’s reported Nobel Peace Prize and career may dramatize competing visions of international justice, but prestige cannot process salaries, provide cloud infrastructure or shield contractors from sanctions.

Nor is the court being endangered by abstract “fragility.” Institutions become fragile when powerful governments attack them and nominal supporters decline to absorb the cost of defending them. Describing deliberate sanctions chiefly as another test of a delicate legal order risks laundering agency out of the story.

The pertinent division is not between Trump and an ethereal collection of international values. It is between a US administration deploying concrete coercive authority and allied governments deciding whether their professed legal commitments outweigh the price of resistance.

Rules for the weak, discretion for the strong

International criminal law has always depended on states that can enforce judgments while also possessing the power to evade them. This episode exposes that hierarchy without ceremony: a court may investigate weaker governments with limited geopolitical cost, but scrutiny of the United States or a protected ally can threaten the court’s ability to operate.

The larger pattern is selective legality enforced through infrastructure. Financial dominance becomes jurisdiction; commercial dependence becomes discipline; uncertainty becomes deterrence. Europe’s response will show whether ICC membership imposes obligations on powerful states or merely supplies them with language for condemning crimes committed by governments unable to retaliate.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Showdown: Europe could trigger ‘nuclear option’ against Donald Trump

item.title: Lock him up: Trump's surreal new threat may have earned him an orange outfit
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump said at a Republican rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego as “a very small price to pay,” while predicting that the war would end soon. The article presents the remark as treating two American cities as acceptable losses in a conflict Trump announced on February 28, 2026, without prior congressional authorization or public debate.

The headline’s “orange outfit” refers to the author’s argument that Trump should be imprisoned for treason. But the article identifies no charge, investigation, or legal proceeding arising from the remark. Trump’s precise intended meaning remains disputed: White House communications director Steven Cheung said Trump meant that American cities would have faced threats if Iran’s nuclear program had not been stopped, while California Governor Gavin Newsom and Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond condemned the words as dangerous and unacceptable.

The power belongs to the president

The central fact is not merely that Trump said something grotesque. It is that the president who initiated the reported military campaign publicly described catastrophic retaliation against American cities as a tolerable cost.

Trump holds command authority. Californians do not. Neither Newsom’s denunciation nor Desmond’s objection can undo military decisions already made by the executive branch. Treating the episode principally as another controversy over Trump’s rhetoric risks shrinking a question of war-making power into a dispute about tone.

Congress enabled the vacuum

According to AlterNet, Trump began major combat operations without consulting Congress, allies, or the public and had still offered no consistent objective seven months later. If that account is accurate, the institutional failure extends beyond one man’s volatility.

Congress possesses powers over war authorization, appropriations, oversight, and impeachment. The article provides no evidence that lawmakers used those tools to impose an effective constraint. A legislature that permits an open-ended conflict and responds mainly through partisan commentary is not an innocent spectator. It is surrendering authority while preserving deniability.

The cleanup operation

Cheung’s explanation does not match the language AlterNet quotes. Saying cities might have faced danger is materially different from saying an adversary can “take out” those cities for a “small price.” The White House response therefore functions less as clarification than as an attempt to replace the president’s words with a safer statement he did not make.

That pattern matters. Presidential communications staff can turn incoherence into ambiguity, ambiguity into alleged media distortion, and alleged distortion into another loyalty test. The public is pushed to debate what Trump supposedly intended instead of what the commander in chief actually said while Americans and military personnel faced the consequences of his policy.

The treason claim outruns the evidence

AlterNet is right to center the obscenity of declaring American cities expendable. Its leap to treason and life imprisonment is far less grounded. The supplied reporting establishes an alarming public remark; it does not establish that Trump adhered to an enemy or intentionally gave it aid and comfort.

That overreach weakens the sharper indictment available from the facts. A president need not satisfy the Constitution’s narrow definition of treason to demonstrate reckless judgment, contempt for civilian life, or an inability to state coherent war aims. Turning every abuse into a maximal criminal accusation can obscure the mechanisms that actually sustain it: executive power, congressional passivity, partisan protection, and official spin.

Expendability as government policy

Los Angeles and San Diego were not rhetorical abstractions. AlterNet notes that the San Diego area contains major Navy and Marine Corps installations and supports more than 115,000 active-duty personnel. Dismissing attacks there as a small price converts residents and service members into bargaining chips in a war they did not authorize.

The larger pattern is rule through unilateral escalation followed by institutional evasion. The president acts, Congress declines to restrain him, aides rewrite his language, and critics reach for sensational legal claims because ordinary accountability has failed. The systemic error is not confusion about what Trump meant. It is a political order willing to leave immense war-making power in his hands while arguing over how politely to describe the consequences.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Lock him up: Trump’s surreal new threat may have earned him an orange outfit

item.title: Warning: A cornered Trump is ready to unleash more havoc
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s administration was escalating the use of federal power against perceived enemies as voting began in several states. The article points to reported efforts targeting Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook and former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, sanctions aimed at companies working with the International Criminal Court, and the administration’s defense of an ICE operation in which agents reportedly fired seven rifle rounds and wounded a migrant suspect while a five-year-old was inside the car.

The outlet links those actions to Trump’s assertion that he could “do whatever I want” and portrays the escalation as a response to political weakness before Election Day. It predicts possible interference with voting and certification, but supplies no evidence of an operational plan. Several other serious assertions—including alleged pay-for-access arrangements, Republican candidates’ private assessments and contemplated prosecutions—are presented without enough underlying documentation here to evaluate them independently.

Power is the relevant fact

Trump controls the executive branch. That means access to federal investigators, prosecutors, immigration agents, diplomats and the administrative machinery capable of turning a grievance into an inquiry, sanction or armed encounter.

Cook and Hutchinson do not possess remotely comparable power. Nor do migrants confronted by ICE or international jurists subjected to American sanctions. Treating these episodes as clashes among political adversaries would erase the decisive asymmetry: one participant commands institutions that can impose legal expense, professional damage, physical danger and international isolation.

The central abuse alleged by AlterNet is therefore not that Trump is angry. Presidents are allowed resentments. It is that official authority is reportedly being directed toward the objects of his resentment.

Process can become punishment

An investigation need not produce a conviction to inflict damage. AlterNet reports that a Trump-selected inquiry could revisit mortgage-fraud allegations against Cook after grand juries declined to act, and connects that pressure to her votes against lowering interest rates. The article does not establish that Trump ordered the inquiry because of those votes, so that motive remains its inference. The institutional danger it describes is concrete nonetheless: executive pressure applied to a Federal Reserve official whose decisions displease the president.

The reported pursuit of Hutchinson operates similarly. Legal analysts cited by the outlet reportedly consider a case alleging false congressional testimony weak, but weakness does not eliminate its coercive value. Lawyers cost money. Investigations consume years. Public accusations contaminate reputations. When the state repeatedly reaches for doubtful cases against dissenters, failure in court does not mean the tactic failed.

Misdirection protects the armed institution

The ICE episode shows the crudest version of political misdirection. According to AlterNet, officials answered questions about agents firing seven rounds on a residential street during school pickup by emphasizing the wounded man’s criminal record and attacking New York City’s sanctuary policies.

Neither point answers whether agents’ tactics endangered the child in the vehicle or nearby residents. A suspect’s record does not travel backward through time to justify every method used during an arrest. Blaming municipal immigration policy shifts attention from the actors who carried rifles and chose when to fire them.

That rhetorical substitution matters. It converts scrutiny of state conduct into a referendum on the person subjected to it, ensuring that the institution with guns is treated as background while the weaker actor becomes the entire story.

The case is stronger than the speculation

AlterNet weakens its argument when it leaps from documented or attributed actions to predictions of insurrection, election disruption and presidential psychology. A prediction market is not evidence of a government plan. Falling polls do not prove desperation. Speculation about mental health explains nothing that can be established through decisions and chains of command.

The article does not need those shortcuts. Its strongest evidence concerns observable uses of power: inquiries against disfavored officials and witnesses, sanctions against an international court, pardons for January 6 defendants and an official response that reportedly avoided confronting the danger created by an ICE operation.

Calling every development “havoc” can blur distinctions among them. The sharper indictment asks which official acted, under what authority, against whom, with what procedural safeguards and with what foreseeable cost.

Personalized rule is the pattern

The systemic issue is not volatility but the conversion of public institutions into instruments of personal loyalty. Independent officials become targets, witnesses become prospective defendants, armed agencies evade scrutiny and foreign policy becomes entangled with the president’s resentments.

Institutions do not restrain that pattern merely by existing. Courts can issue rulings, grand juries can reject charges and Congress can hold formal powers, yet executive officials still decide whether to honor those limits or keep searching for another mechanism. The people enabling the outcome are not only the president but every official who converts his grievance into a memorandum, investigation, sanction or public excuse.

That is how personalized government advances: not through confusion, but through identifiable decisions made by people with authority who know that imposing the process may be enough.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Warning: A cornered Trump is ready to unleash more havoc

item.title: Major newspaper demands Trump's impeachment in blistering editorial
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Philadelphia Inquirer’s Editorial Board argued Congress must confront President Donald Trump’s possible impeachment over his administration’s use of the Justice Department. But the supplied reporting never quotes the board explicitly demanding impeachment, so the headline’s stronger claim is not established by the excerpt.

Writing for the board, former U.S. attorney Barbara McQuade accused Trump and his appointees of using federal law enforcement to reward allies and punish adversaries. She cited pardons for more than 1,500 people convicted of crimes related to the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack; the dismissal of bribery charges against then-New York Mayor Eric Adams; prosecutions and investigations involving Trump critics; and an antitrust approval she connected to changes at CBS.

AlterNet says Democratic advisers have discouraged impeachment talk because congressional Republicans would protect Trump regardless of the evidence. The reported dispute, then, is not merely whether grounds exist. It is whether anticipated Republican obstruction should prevent Democrats from invoking a constitutional remedy at all.

Power belongs to the executive

The weaker actors in this story are not the officials, prosecutors, media companies, and political opponents exposed to federal pressure. The president controls the executive branch, appoints Justice Department leadership, exercises the pardon power, and commands an administration capable of turning political preference into legal consequence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche’s reported theory of expansive presidential control matters because institutional capture does not require abolishing the Justice Department. It requires subordinating its judgment to one officeholder. McQuade’s examples allege precisely that pattern: clemency for political allies, favorable treatment for useful figures, and government scrutiny for adversaries.

Personnel made the machinery work

“Trump” cannot become shorthand that erases everyone who enabled the reported conduct. Appointees approved decisions, prosecutors pursued cases, and Republican lawmakers supplied political protection. Presidential power becomes operational through officials willing to treat loyalty as a governing standard.

The resignations described by McQuade expose that agency. Interim U.S. Attorney Danielle Sassoon reportedly called the Adams arrangement a “quid pro quo,” and she and eight other Justice Department lawyers resigned. Whatever the ultimate legal merits of the underlying case, those departures show that compliance was not automatic or unavoidable. Some officials refused; others carried the decision forward.

Futility is a political choice

The Democratic advisers’ reported argument converts Republican subservience into a reason for Democratic silence. That is institutional cowardice dressed as tactical realism. If Republican lawmakers will disregard evidence to shield a president, their expected conduct is not an argument against scrutiny. It is part of the conduct that scrutiny should expose.

Impeachment may fail without sufficient votes. Failure and pointlessness are not the same thing. Congress still possesses investigative authority, subpoena power, public hearings, and the ability to create an official record. Declining to use those powers because accountability may be blocked allows the blockers to dictate whether the alleged abuse is examined at all.

The article overstates its own evidence

AlterNet’s framing is sloppier than the stakes permit. It calls the reported conduct Trump’s “crimes,” describes charges as “baseless,” and announces an impeachment demand without supplying the editorial’s explicit language making that demand. Those may reflect McQuade’s argument or the full editorial, but this excerpt does not independently establish them.

That imprecision creates an avoidable escape route. Officials accused of politicizing law enforcement benefit when criticism outruns its evidence: they can attack the exaggeration and evade the documented decisions. A serious indictment of state power must distinguish convictions from pardons, allegations from proof, prosecutorial decisions from adjudicated wrongdoing, and suspicious sequences from demonstrated exchanges.

The system protects power by lowering expectations

The larger pattern is not simply presidential aggression. It is a political system teaching itself that accountability should be attempted only when success is guaranteed. That rule rewards the faction most willing to obstruct, because its promised obstruction becomes the justification for everyone else’s retreat.

A politicized Justice Department can impose costs long before any conviction: investigations, legal bills, reputational damage, and pressure to accommodate the administration. A compliant Congress then supplies a second layer of protection by refusing to examine how that power is used. The systemic error is circular: executive abuse weakens accountability, legislative cowardice excuses itself by citing that weakness, and the absence of accountability is later treated as evidence that no actionable abuse occurred.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Major newspaper demands Trump’s impeachment in blistering editorial

item.title: The 'broken brain' taboo is finally fading
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that a longstanding media reluctance to discuss Donald Trump’s mental fitness is weakening. It cites a Time interview transcript containing disjointed answers and false claims, New York Times reporter Katie Rogers’s observation that his rally remarks sometimes stop making logical sense, and increasingly direct commentary from figures including Lawrence O’Donnell. None of that establishes a medical diagnosis, and the reporting supplies no clinical evidence of dementia.

The article also links Trump’s rhetoric to presidential power. After former International Criminal Court jurist Navi Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize and joked that she might share it with Trump, the administration announced economic sanctions on the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the court “rogue” and said sanctions would continue until US allies reined it in. AlterNet interprets the timing as retaliation for Pillay’s remark, but the material presented does not establish that motive; Rubio publicly framed the action as opposition to the court.

The broader claim is that political weakness is changing how Trump is covered. AlterNet points to a reported 30 percent approval rating, weaker rally attendance and reporters showing less patience with administration claims. Its answer to the headline’s implied question is therefore limited: the taboo may be fading in elite commentary, but the article does not demonstrate a settled media consensus or prove a neurological condition.

The diagnosis is not the evidence

“Broken brain” is a potent phrase and a poor substitute for substantiation. A transcript can show incoherence, falsehoods and grandiosity. It cannot, by itself, distinguish cognitive impairment from habitual lying, ignorance, improvisation or calculated propaganda.

That distinction matters politically. Speculative diagnosis can turn conduct into pathology and thereby blur agency. Trump said he could do whatever he wanted. His administration imposed sanctions. Rubio defended them and threatened continued pressure on allies. Those are attributable acts by officials wielding state power, not symptoms awaiting remote diagnosis.

Power has names

The president controls an enormous executive apparatus. The secretary of state helps direct foreign policy. US businesses and foreign governments must contend with sanctions whether Trump’s assertions arise from confusion, vanity, strategy or some combination the article cannot establish.

Institutional responsibility extends beyond Trump. Rubio did not merely stand near presidential behavior; according to the account, he supplied its official rationale and articulated the coercive demand. Administration officials who execute presidential decisions retain agency. Treating every abuse as the emanation of one man’s supposedly failing mind lets the machinery carrying it out disappear.

The press discovered what weakness permits

AlterNet’s strongest point is not medical but institutional. Reporters appear more willing to describe incoherence and contradict false claims when Trump’s approval, crowds and political position are reportedly deteriorating. If that pattern holds, it exposes caution masquerading as neutrality.

The relevant facts did not become reportable only when empty seats appeared. A press corps that waits for declining popularity before stating plainly that a claim is false is not exercising restraint; it is calibrating candor to power. Jake Tapper’s challenge to Kevin Hassett and Rogers’s blunt description of Trump’s speech are useful precisely because they abandon euphemism. Their lateness remains part of the story.

The misdirection trap

AlterNet risks reproducing the failure it condemns. By organizing coercive government conduct around an unproven dementia thesis, it shifts attention from accountable choices to a condition it cannot establish. That framing may sound harsher than conventional coverage, but it can be less exact.

The defensible indictment is already severe: a president made grandiose and false assertions, claimed sweeping personal authority, and led an administration using economic power against an international court. The article alleges a retaliatory connection to Pillay’s joke, but its chronology alone does not prove one. Precision requires criticizing the documented coercion without converting inference into fact.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is an accountability system that often measures truth against political strength. Powerful leaders receive euphemism while they appear dominant; blunt description arrives when their leverage declines. Officials who implement policy recede behind speculation about personality, and institutions rename their own timidity as a taboo.

Whether Trump has dementia is unanswered here. What is established by the account is more politically immediate: presidential power was exercised, Rubio publicly enabled and defended that exercise, and parts of the press became more candid only as the political cost of candor appeared to fall. A system that needs weakness before it can describe power accurately is not correcting an error. It is revealing one.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The ‘broken brain’ taboo is finally fading

item.title: Don’t be fooled — Trump’s stock market is a 'lousy' dud: analyst
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the S&P 500 reached a record high, but Bloomberg analyst Jonathan Levin argued that the gain was concentrated in a handful of artificial-intelligence companies, including Meta, Microsoft and Nvidia. His answer to the headline’s implied question is blunt: the market looks strong at the index level while remaining “lousy for most” companies and households.

Levin pointed to five months of declining inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings, weaker consumer spending and falling stocks across consumer, travel, transportation, real-estate and financial sectors. He also cited a Federal Reserve Bank of New York report showing that Americans expected their earnings growth to trail consumer inflation over the following 12 months.

The danger, in Levin’s account, is not confined to wealthy AI speculators. With roughly $23 trillion in assets indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 as of 2025, a reversal in AI stocks could damage retirement accounts, consumption and employment. He did not establish when such a reversal might occur; he warned that the market’s concentration makes the consequences potentially severe.

An index is not an economy

Trump treats stock prices as a verdict on his presidency because the S&P offers a flattering number stripped of distributional context. But an index driven upward by a few enormous companies says little about whether wages cover groceries, fuel and housing. It measures the market value of selected corporations, not the material security of the population.

That distinction is especially important when inflation-adjusted pay has been losing ground. A record index beside shrinking purchasing power is not a paradox. It is evidence that financial performance and household welfare can diverge sharply.

Who holds the power

The institutional power here belongs to the White House, Congress, the Federal Reserve and the financial firms directing vast pools of capital. Households with retirement accounts participate in the market, but they do not set tariffs, fiscal policy, interest rates or the investment fashion concentrating trillions of dollars around AI.

According to Levin, the White House was seeking ways to restore tariffs that the Supreme Court had deemed illegal. If implemented, those measures would be a policy choice with foreseeable price effects—not an economic weather event and not something consumers caused by shopping incorrectly.

The political sales job

The misdirection is to present the market’s headline number as shared prosperity. That lets political leaders claim credit for gains concentrated among a few companies while treating inflation, weak real wages and reduced spending as separate complications.

The story’s own framing occasionally slips into the same trap by calling this “Trump’s stock market.” Presidents influence economic conditions, but they do not personally control equity prices. The sharper charge is narrower: Trump is using a concentrated market rally as political evidence while his administration pursues policies that Levin describes as inflationary.

Risk flows downward

AI investors may capture extraordinary gains while enthusiasm lasts. If sentiment breaks, however, the exposure extends through index funds, retirement plans and an economy partly supported by wealth-driven spending. The people absorbing those losses would include workers who never chose a concentrated bet on AI.

That is the recurring arrangement: upside is described as proof of elite competence, while downside is dispersed through pensions, jobs and household balance sheets. Those with the least control over the wager are still made vulnerable to it.

The systemic error

This episode reveals a political economy organized around legible financial symbols rather than broadly shared security. A rising index becomes propaganda because it is simple, immediate and useful to those in power; declining real earnings require harder questions about who benefits from policy.

The deception does not require falsifying the market high. It requires promoting that true number as an answer to a different question: whether most people are doing well. On the evidence AlterNet presents, it is not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Don’t be fooled — Trump’s stock market is a ‘lousy’ dud: analyst

item.title: ​Trump's 'cringeworthy' YMCA dance linked to Epstein by family insider
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Mary Trump linked one gesture in President Donald Trump’s familiar “YMCA” rally dance—not the dance itself—to a 1992 video showing Trump alongside Jeffrey Epstein. She pointed to Trump biting his lower lip in both clips. The reporting provides no evidence that Epstein inspired or originated the dance, so the headline’s promised “Epstein link” is narrower than advertised.

Mary Trump also interpreted Trump’s repeated leg-tapping as an attempt to restore movement before walking. AlterNet paired that observation with another psychologist’s speculation that changes in Trump’s movement and speech could indicate a stroke, dementia, or another brain injury. The article reports polling showing substantial public concern about Trump’s health and distrust of his administration’s disclosures, but it supplies no diagnosis.

The headline outruns the evidence

The article’s strongest documented point is also its least sensational: Trump displayed an expression similar to one captured while he watched women with Epstein in 1992. That historical footage may be politically revealing because it records the men’s social familiarity. It does not establish that Epstein had anything to do with Trump’s later rally routine.

By converting a repeated facial expression into the “Epstein-linked origins” of the dance, the framing manufactures a cleaner revelation than the reporting delivers. That is not accountability. It is click-driven insinuation, and it gives Trump’s defenders an easy way to dismiss the entire story by attacking its weakest claim.

Medical speculation is not scrutiny

Mary Trump is a psychologist and Trump’s niece, but neither relationship turns a rally clip into a clinical examination. The second psychologist’s interpretation is likewise presented as a possible explanation, not a confirmed finding. Polling can establish that voters perceive decline or distrust official disclosures; it cannot diagnose the president.

There is a legitimate institutional question here: whether the administration is providing accurate information about the health of the person exercising presidential power. AlterNet reports that 61 percent of respondents believed the administration was not being truthful about Trump’s condition and notes an unusual number of hospital checkups in 2025. Those facts support scrutiny of disclosure practices. They do not support converting visible gestures into proof of neurological disease.

Power sits with the presidency

Mary Trump can criticize, psychologists can speculate, and voters can express concern. None of them controls the relevant records or the machinery of disclosure. Trump and his administration hold that power. They decide what medical information is released, how it is characterized, and whether the public receives evidence sufficient to evaluate official assurances.

That asymmetry is the political substance. A president’s health matters because the office commands military force and the executive branch. Yet the article spends more energy interpreting a leg tap and mocking an underbite than examining the officials responsible for credible disclosure.

Spectacle protects the institution

The dance, the facial expression, and the Epstein footage are irresistible fragments of spectacle. They also redirect attention from questions that institutions can answer: What have White House physicians reported? What information has been withheld? Who approved the public account of Trump’s condition? What procedures exist if his capacity becomes impaired?

Ridicule may puncture Trump’s cultivated image, but it is not a substitute for evidence. When coverage treats body-language analysis as the main route to accountability, it allows the administration’s information control to recede into the background.

The systemic error

Political media repeatedly turns secrecy into personality content. Officials withhold or tightly manage consequential information; coverage responds by mining video clips for clues; audiences receive insinuation instead of documentation. The powerful institution escapes sustained examination while commentators debate the meaning of a gesture.

That pattern serves power even when the coverage is hostile to the person holding it. The sharper indictment is not that Trump dances badly or resembles his younger self in an Epstein video. It is that presidential health disclosures depend heavily on an administration policing its own credibility—and this article’s inflated framing obscures that institutional failure instead of exposing it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ​Trump’s ‘cringeworthy’ YMCA dance linked to Epstein by family insider

item.title: ‘No regulation’: Trump officials bypass the public to boost invisible code
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, drawing on KFF Health News’ review of messages, transcripts, and recordings, reports that Trump administration health officials gave technology companies privileged access to shape federal policy for AI health apps while excluding the public from key discussions. An FDA listening session in February included at least 35 industry organizations but appeared on neither the agency’s public calendar nor its regulatory notices.

The effort began in an invitation-only Slack workspace established in August 2025. Its roughly 1,700 participants include major technology companies, startups, investors, and digital-health businesses, while doctors, hospitals, and patient advocates reportedly have little representation. CMS officials promoted a Medicare App Library featuring about two dozen commercial products and discussed reimbursing companies for services such as chatbot advice and wearable-device monitoring.

Companies also sought easier, continuing access to patients’ medical records through the federal exchange framework. CMS official Amy Gleason later described the expansion as accomplished with “no regulation, no rulemaking.” CMS called the project an open, voluntary collaboration, declined to answer several questions about the Slack workspace, and did not disclose all its criteria for selecting promoted apps. The FDA did not comment.

The government built the market

The decisive actors are not patients choosing among neutral options. They are CMS and FDA officials controlling access, reimbursement, regulatory treatment, and the credibility conferred by Medicare’s name.

CMS personnel reportedly told executives that the government’s work could become a “sales engine.” They understood that placement on Medicare.gov would signal trustworthiness to older and disabled people. That is not merely providing information. It is using public authority to acquire customers for private companies—some of whose products remain young, lightly reviewed, or vaguely described.

The administration therefore did more than reduce barriers. It helped create demand, promised distribution, and discussed reimbursement while allowing prospective beneficiaries of those decisions unusually direct influence over the rules.

Access disguised as empowerment

The sales pitch is patient control: people should obtain their records easily and use whatever application they prefer. Easier access can be valuable. But the reporting describes companies seeking a “frictionless pathway” through which one act of consent could enable broad access to sensitive medical information.

Calling that empowerment obscures who gains durable leverage. A patient presses a button once; a company may receive the raw material for continuing analysis, product development, or commercial relationships governed by dense privacy policies. Even one participant in the industry discussion warned that privacy systems must anticipate malicious actors if access expands to thousands of apps.

When b.well CEO Kristen Valdes wrote that the industry should “stop protecting patients from themselves,” she framed safeguards as paternalism. Her later acknowledgment that there will be good and bad apps exposes the flaw: reducing friction does not distinguish between them, and consent alone does not supply technical competence, accountability, or meaningful remedies.

A private advisory system

CMS declared in its code of conduct that the Slack group was not an advisory committee and would not be used to obtain recommendations. Yet KFF Health News found participants discussing policy preferences, building consensus, lobbying officials, and receiving invitations to help shape future FDA guidance.

Former FDA lawyer Joseph Daval said the arrangement resembled a federal advisory committee in important respects. He did not establish that it legally was one, and CMS declined to address questions about its legality. But the political problem does not depend on a final legal classification.

Officials created a channel where industry had sustained access and the public did not. Labeling that channel a “technical collaboration” does not change who was present, who was scarce, or whose commercial interests aligned with the policies under discussion.

Deregulation without accountability

Gleason’s boast about achieving change without regulation or rulemaking is the story’s clearest statement of agency. Formal rulemaking is not pointless paperwork. It creates notice, a public record, opportunities for challenge, and an obligation to answer objections from people who do not have access to the government’s Slack room.

Bypassing that process shifted influence toward companies already equipped with lobbyists, executives, and technical specialists. It also left basic questions unanswered: how applications were selected, what standards they met, who bears liability when advice is wrong, and how patients can understand or revoke access to their records.

American Medical Association CEO John Whyte warned that some tools are not ready, that evidence about their operation is inadequate, and that liability is unclear. Kennedy’s claim that AI is better informed than any doctor does not resolve those deficiencies. It substitutes official enthusiasm for demonstrated reliability.

The systemic error

This is regulatory capture in functional form, even if the reporting does not establish a legal violation: public officials convened a heavily industry-weighted process, offered government promotion and potential reimbursement, and weakened the procedural checks that might slow commercial deployment.

The misdirection is the suggestion that the conflict is between innovative patients and obstructive bureaucracy. The actual contest is over who writes the conditions under which private firms gain access to medical data, public money, and Medicare’s institutional credibility.

“No regulation” does not mean no governing decision was made. It means the decisions migrated into spaces where corporate participants could influence them and the affected public could not watch. The state did not disappear. It used its power to build a market, then declined to exercise that power with comparable rigor on behalf of the people supplying the money, data, and risk.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘No regulation’: Trump officials bypass the public to boost invisible code

item.title: Evangelicals revolt against Trump's 'culture of death’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the National Association of Evangelicals joined the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and other religious groups in condemning Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s reported plan to execute Nidal Malik Hasan publicly by firing squad and livestream it. Hasan was convicted for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13 people and injured 32.

Walter Kim, the evangelical association’s president, affirmed the need for justice but told Religion News Service that broadcasting the execution would turn a grave state responsibility into spectacle and promote a “culture of death.” The reporting describes a planned execution, not a completed one, and does not supply evidence of a broader evangelical break with President Donald Trump.

Power sits with the state

The headline’s “revolt” framing exaggerates the power of the objectors. Religious organizations can condemn the decision, but Trump and Hegseth control the executive institutions involved. Hasan, despite the horror of his crimes, is a prisoner facing the ultimate exercise of state power.

That hierarchy matters. The central political act is not evangelical criticism; it is the administration’s reported decision to transform an execution into public media. Calling the dispute a revolt shifts attention from the officials wielding lethal authority to the constituency objecting after the decision was made.

Punishment becomes content

An execution already demonstrates the state’s power over life and death. Livestreaming it adds another purpose: public consumption. Kim’s objection identifies the distinction precisely. Justice does not require an audience, and punishment does not become more legitimate when packaged as entertainment.

Billy Binion’s description of an administration governing for an “online mob” is commentary, not established motive. But the foreseeable effect is plain: broadcasting a firing squad would invite spectatorship, circulation and political performance. The condemned person’s guilt does not erase the government’s responsibility for what it chooses to make of his death.

The article outruns its evidence

AlterNet calls this an evangelical revolt, but it establishes opposition from a prominent association and other religious groups—not a mass rupture between evangelical voters and Trump. That is meaningful institutional dissent. It is not evidence that the political coalition has broken.

The article also pivots to the removal or early retirement of senior military officers, citing more than 900 years of combined experience and sparse public explanations. Those personnel decisions raise a separate question about military capacity and partisan control, but the reporting does not establish that they caused, enabled or directly relate to the proposed public execution. Placing them together suggests a unified program without supplying the connective evidence.

Cruelty as political theater

The larger pattern is the conversion of government power into spectacle. A public, livestreamed execution would not merely impose a sentence; it would stage state violence for an audience. That choice changes the political meaning of the punishment even if the underlying sentence is lawful.

The resistance described here exposes a limit that some conservative Christians are unwilling to cross: justice may permit severe punishment, but it does not require turning death into content. Whether that objection produces any institutional restraint remains unanswered. The officials control the machinery; the critics, so far, control only their refusal to bless the show.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Evangelicals revolt against Trump’s ‘culture of death’

item.title: Conservative analysts blast 'morons' who put 'economic moron' in the White House
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that The Bulwark editors Jonathan Last and Jasmine M. Green blame the renewed inflation shown in a New York Fed estimate on Donald Trump’s tariffs. They call it “moronic inflation”: price pressure created by a policy Trump openly campaigned on, voters endorsed, and his administration imposed after the earlier inflation surge had subsided.

Last and Green contrast that increase with inflation following the COVID shock, when disrupted supply chains collided with stimulus-supported demand. They argue that supply-chain normalization, central-bank action, and Biden administration fiscal policy helped bring price growth down before Trump’s tariffs raised costs and weakened economic activity in 2025.

Their fury is aimed not only at Trump but at voters who expected tariffs and lower prices simultaneously despite economists’ warnings. The article does not provide the underlying chart’s figures, methodology, or enough evidence to measure how much of the reported increase tariffs caused.

Power made the policy

Trump held the decisive institutional power. Voters selected his program, but voters did not set tariff rates or administer trade policy. The president did.

That distinction matters because contempt for “morons” can become its own form of misdirection. An electorate can authorize destructive policy, but the officeholder converts campaign rhetoric into government action. Trump advertised tariffs; his administration imposed them; businesses and consumers encountered the resulting costs described by the analysts.

The public bears political responsibility for empowering him. It does not bear equal operational responsibility for every executive decision that followed.

The insult obscures the machinery

Last and Green’s anger is understandable, but their diagnosis is politically thin. Calling voters cognitively deficient may describe their exasperation; it does not explain how a plainly inflationary policy was sold as a cure for high prices.

The more useful question is who benefited from collapsing a complicated economic record into a fraudulent intuition: foreigners pay tariffs, therefore Americans win. According to the account presented here, economists warned that tariffs would raise domestic costs. Trump nevertheless paired them with promises of lower prices. That contradiction was not hidden. It was marketed.

Reducing the outcome to mass stupidity lets political leadership, partisan persuasion, and the authority of the presidency recede behind an insult aimed downward.

Confusion was politically useful

The earlier inflation had multiple reported causes: pandemic disruption, constrained supply, and stimulus-supported demand. By the spring of 2024, The Bulwark says consumer-goods price growth had returned to a better-than-normal pace. Yet the political memory of the price surge remained available for exploitation even after its growth rate eased.

That gap between inflation and the price level is fertile territory for demagoguery. Slower inflation does not restore every old price, while broad deflation would carry severe economic costs. A candidate can therefore blame the incumbent for prices that remain high, promise their reversal, and prescribe tariffs that push costs in the opposite direction.

The resulting confusion is not merely a voter defect. It is an asset for anyone with the power and media reach to substitute grievance for arithmetic.

Accountability must point upward

The article is strongest when it names inflation by choice. On its account, this was not an unforeseen pandemic shock or an unavoidable wartime disruption. A candidate proposed tariffs despite warnings about their effects, won the election, and implemented them.

It is weaker when it treats voter contempt as sufficient analysis. Citizens can make disastrous choices, but the hierarchy remains clear: political leaders design the offer, institutions execute it, and the public absorbs the consequences. The president commands the machinery; ordinary voters encounter it at the checkout counter and in a slowing economy.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a recurring transfer of blame from powerful actors to the people living with their decisions. Trump’s policy becomes a story about foolish consumers rather than presidential power. Economic pain becomes evidence of public irrationality rather than the foreseeable consequence of a governing choice.

That framing leaves the political operation intact. Leaders can promise mutually incompatible outcomes, weaponize the damage associated with their predecessors, enact policies experts warned would worsen the problem, and then disappear behind contempt for the electorate.

The failure was democratic, but it was not power-neutral. Voters opened the door. Trump controlled what the government carried through it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Conservative analysts blast ‘morons’ who put ‘economic moron’ in the White House

item.title: The plan to purge Washington of Trump's 'cranks and quacks’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that New Republic writer Jason Linkins wants a future Democratic administration to vet and remove Trump-aligned federal employees who engaged in extremism or tried to undermine democratic government. Drawing on recent reporting, he argues that restoring the agencies would require more than rehiring experienced professionals.

The examples include Justice Department hires accused of serious ethical or legal misconduct, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s declaration that his changes to HHS would outlast him, and what Linkins describes as extremist propaganda from the Department of Homeland Security. He endorses “lustration,” a term Yale Law professor Dina Francesca Haynes uses for removing public servants who support extremism or attacks on democracy.

AlterNet does not describe an official Democratic proposal, identify a participating campaign or present a governing blueprint. The “plan” in the headline is Linkins’s recommendation, not an adopted program.

The headline promises too much

Calling this a plan disguises how preliminary it is. Linkins has supplied an argument and a label. He has not supplied the legal standards, evidentiary rules, appeals process or institutional sponsor that would turn “lustration” into policy.

Those omissions are central. A competent government may discipline misconduct, remove unlawful appointees and screen candidates for relevant qualifications. A political purge based on affiliation or broadly defined beliefs is another matter. Without enforceable distinctions, the proposed cure risks borrowing the patronage logic it claims to reverse.

Trump’s appointees hold the power

The weaker actors here are not the officials running federal departments. Trump controls executive appointments; Kennedy runs HHS; Justice Department leadership determines hiring and enforcement priorities; Homeland Security controls personnel, communications and coercive machinery. These officials possess authority over public money, institutional expertise and, in DHS’s case, armed enforcement.

That hierarchy matters more than Linkins’s catalogue of “cranks and quacks.” Mocking an employee who cannot spell “north” may illustrate incompetence, but it can also shrink a structural assault into a freak show. The consequential decisions are made by leaders who select loyalists, relax professional standards and redirect agencies toward political objectives.

Degradation is a governing method

The reported pattern is not merely that eccentric people entered government. It is that loyalty can displace expertise while institutional leaders claim permanence for the resulting changes. Kennedy’s statement that HHS would never return to its previous form, even if he died that night, presents bureaucratic transformation as an accomplished legacy rather than a temporary personnel choice.

If the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has been hollowed out and filled with ethically compromised hires, the political consequence is larger than embarrassment. A division cannot reliably enforce civil-rights law when professional capacity and ethical standards are subordinated to factional loyalty. Administrative incompetence becomes politically useful when it disables protections that those in power do not value.

Accountability needs rules

Linkins is right to focus on durability: political appointees leave, but damaged hiring systems, lost expertise and embedded personnel can survive an election. He is less persuasive when he substitutes exterminator metaphors for institutional design. “Fumigation” and “taking out the garbage” erase the distinction between documented misconduct and ideological contamination.

A legitimate repair program would start with conduct: unlawful orders, ethical violations, falsified qualifications, abuse of authority and participation in prohibited political activity. It would require evidence and review. Otherwise, “rooting out” becomes an invitation for each administration to define the civil service as enemy territory.

The deeper contamination

The larger pattern is the conversion of public administration into personal rule. Agencies cease to be durable institutions governed by law and become prizes to be staffed, weakened and branded by whoever controls the presidency.

Reversing that project cannot mean installing a more agreeable class of loyalists. It requires rebuilding professional capacity while holding identifiable decision-makers responsible under clear rules. The systemic error is not simply that unqualified people obtained government jobs. It is that powerful officials made qualification secondary to obedience—and that their critics may answer an institutional problem with the seductive language of another purge.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The plan to purge Washington of Trump’s ‘cranks and quacks’

item.title: Trump loses control as Congress questions Pentagon chaos and strategy
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump is losing control of the Pentagon narrative as members of Congress question Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership. But the article does not establish that Trump has lost control of Hegseth. It reports growing congressional criticism while describing Hegseth as pursuing personnel cuts, culture-war policies and force movements whose strategic rationale remains unclear.

The article says Hegseth proposed firing as many as 20 percent of the military’s generals and admirals, promoted stricter fitness and grooming standards, and delivered a speech attacking transgender troops and other disfavored groups. It also reports that the United States removed 12 B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford after a foiled attack and concerns about a possible drone strike, while Trump discussed deploying a third aircraft-carrier group near Iran.

AlterNet further alleges that Hegseth has obscured casualties and weapons depletion, but supplies no supporting documentation in the article. Its claim that he remains in office partly because he will not rule out domestic troop deployments is presented as a widespread belief, not an established fact.

Power remains with the executive

The decisive power here does not belong to the troops Hegseth insults, the officers he may dismiss or the legislators asking questions. It belongs to Trump, who appointed Hegseth and can remove him, and to Hegseth, who directs a vast military bureaucracy unless Congress uses its own powers to impose consequences.

That distinction punctures the headline’s premise. Public questioning is not loss of control. Hearings, criticism and predictions of a future “roasting” are political signals; they are not restraints. If Trump keeps Hegseth in office while his secretary remakes personnel policy and military posture, that may indicate presidential tolerance or approval—not presidential helplessness.

Culture war as command policy

Hegseth’s reported slogan—excluding “fatties,” “trannies,” “beardos,” “weirdos,” “wimps” and “radicals”—does more than advertise vulgarity. It converts personal and ideological contempt into an official theory of military readiness.

The practical questions identified by the article concern exposed bases, weapons consumption, recruitment, command capacity and the strategic purpose of deployments. Hegseth’s answer, as presented here, is spectacle: bodies, grooming, uniforms and enemies within the institution. That redirects scrutiny from whether leadership is making coherent decisions to whether service members conform to a reactionary aesthetic.

Congress has tools, not merely questions

The article depicts bipartisan concern but identifies no completed congressional action compelling disclosure, restricting policy or imposing accountability. That matters. Congress controls appropriations, conducts oversight and can demand testimony. Treating legislators as spectators understates their agency.

The same weakness appears in the article’s fixation on why Trump will not “bring” Hegseth under control. Hegseth is not an independent weather system. Trump selected him, retains him and publicly advances his own escalatory proposals. The stronger question is not why presidential discipline has failed, but what policies the administration is choosing—and why Congress has so far answered those choices mainly with criticism.

The spectacle conceals the structure

AlterNet is strongest when it contrasts theatrical “lethality” with unresolved strategic questions. It is weaker when it substitutes insinuation for evidence. Claims about hidden casualties, depleted weapons and Hegseth’s political usefulness require substantiation that this article does not provide.

The larger pattern is nevertheless visible in the reported conduct: institutional power is exercised through personnel decisions, deployments and exclusionary rules, while public attention is drawn toward provocation and personality. The chaos may be real, but calling it chaos can also obscure responsibility. Decisions were made by officials with authority; foreseeable consequences will fall on service members, civilians and institutions that did not make them.

Disorder can still serve power

An administration does not need orderly management to impose its priorities. It can weaken professional constraints, reward ideological loyalty and turn governance into a sequence of spectacles while remaining firmly in command.

That is the systemic error in framing this primarily as Trump “losing control.” The reporting describes concentrated executive authority accompanied by uncertain strategy and limited congressional resistance. The danger exposed by the story is not simply an unruly defense secretary. It is a political system in which officials can exercise enormous coercive power while confusion about their competence distracts from accountability for their choices.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump loses control as Congress questions Pentagon chaos and strategy

item.title: Trump amplifies furious attack on Nobel Prize winner after humiliating snub
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump responded to the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s selection of South African jurist Navi Pillay for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize by reposting an evidence-free attack from his former attorney David Schoen. Schoen accused Pillay of hostility toward the United States and Israel, celebrating terrorists, and rewarding Hamas; the article says he supplied no evidence for those allegations.

Schoen also denounced a United Nations commission chaired by Pillay that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza—a finding Israel rejects—and argued that Trump deserved the prize for his diplomatic record. Less than two days before Pillay’s selection, Trump had told White House reporters that nobody in the prize’s history deserved it more than he did, while repeating what AlterNet describes as the false claim that he had settled eight wars.

Pillay, a former UN high commissioner for human rights and former international judge, was recognized for work pursuing accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. The prize was scheduled to be presented in Oslo on December 10, 2026.

The power belongs to the president

The decisive political fact is not that Trump wanted an award controlled by an independent Norwegian committee. It is that the president of the United States used his platform to amplify unsupported accusations against the woman who received it.

Pillay won a prize. Trump holds executive power. Treating this primarily as the emotional story of a “snub” risks shrinking a presidential act into celebrity resentment. His disappointment is incidental; his capacity to confer legitimacy and reach on an evidence-free smear is the public issue.

The attack has an author and an amplifier

Schoen wrote the accusations. Trump chose to distribute them after repeatedly promoting his own claim to the prize. Those are separate acts of agency, and neither should disappear behind language suggesting that anger simply erupted.

The reporting establishes no evidence that Pillay celebrated terrorists or rewarded Hamas. It does establish that her record includes adjudicating international crimes and chairing a commission whose Gaza finding Israel rejects. Schoen’s post converts that documented dispute into personal vilification. Trump then elevated the vilification without supplying substantiation.

Accountability becomes disloyalty

The attack’s political logic is more consequential than the prize dispute. Pillay’s cited work concerns legal accountability for state violence. Schoen answered that record by branding her an enemy of America and Israel and stripping her of all credibility.

That maneuver replaces engagement with accusation. A finding need not be rebutted if the person associated with it can instead be cast as hateful, illegitimate, or aligned with terrorism. The article does not establish why Trump amplified the post, but the foreseeable effect is clear: it directs attention away from Pillay’s work and toward inflammatory claims about her allegiance and character.

A grievance machine with state power

Trump’s personal campaign for recognition and his amplification of Schoen’s attack fit a broader pattern visible within the story itself: praise is treated as deserved, independent judgment as humiliation, and the person who benefits from that judgment as a target.

The Nobel Committee did not remove Trump from office or constrain presidential authority. It gave someone else an award. Yet the response reported by AlterNet mobilized the communications power of the presidency against the recipient. That is the systemic error: institutions and coverage can become consumed by the powerful man’s grievance, while the unsupported assault he broadcasts—and the accountability work it attempts to discredit—receives secondary attention.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump amplifies furious attack on Nobel Prize winner after humiliating snub

item.title: GOP insider unloads on Trump official’s 'insecurity and imposter syndrome’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Trump White House communications director Sofia Kinzinger attributed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s reported plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution to “insecurity and imposter syndrome.” That diagnosis is Kinzinger’s opinion, not an established explanation for the decision.

According to the cited CBS report, the military planned to execute Hasan by firing squad on December 3 for the 2009 Fort Hood killings of 13 people. If carried out as described, it would be the military’s first execution of a service member since 1961, its first firing-squad execution since World War II, and the country’s first livestreamed execution.

Hegseth argued that people should understand there are “serious consequences” for such crimes. AlterNet does not establish whether the execution or broadcast ultimately occurred, nor does it identify safeguards restricting access by children.

Power, not psychology

The consequential fact is not Kinzinger’s amateur diagnosis. It is that the defense secretary reportedly chose to turn state killing into distributed spectacle.

Hegseth holds institutional power over a military apparatus capable of carrying out the execution and controlling how the government presents it. Hasan’s conviction and sentence explain why he faced execution; they do not explain why officials reportedly wanted an audience. That additional choice belongs to the officials who made and enabled it.

Reducing that choice to one man’s insecurity risks trivializing the machinery involved. A livestream requires authorization, technical preparation, access rules, and institutional compliance. Whatever Hegseth’s personal disposition, a government institution would have to operationalize the decision.

Deterrence as staging

Hegseth’s stated rationale was deterrence: people should see that grave acts bring grave consequences. But an execution already communicates punishment. Broadcasting it adds exposure, spectacle, and political theater.

AlterNet supplies no evidence that livestreaming executions deters violence. It does supply the warning of human-rights professor Jon Yorke, who questioned whether children could watch and compared the proposal to medieval practice. Those are foreseeable consequences of making an execution remotely accessible, not incidental technical concerns.

The government would not merely be enforcing a sentence. It would be packaging death as a public message and inviting viewers to consume it.

The framing lets the institution escape

Kinzinger’s language gives the story a vivid hook, but it also misdirects attention. “Imposter syndrome” turns an exercise of government power into a personality story. It asks readers to contemplate Hegseth’s inner doubts instead of demanding scrutiny of the authority, procedures, and officials behind the broadcast plan.

AlterNet repeats that frame rather than establishing the decision chain. The article does not say who formally approved the livestream, which military bodies would administer it, who could access it, or what rules governed distribution. Those omissions matter because institutions often evade accountability when coverage collapses policy into one official’s temperament.

Cruelty made administrative

The historical comparison is stark. AlterNet cites the 1936 public hanging of Rainey Bethea, witnessed by a crowd estimated at up to 20,000 amid what contemporary reports described as a carnival atmosphere. A livestream replaces the town square with a screen, but it does not remove the spectacle. It scales it.

That is the larger pattern: coercive power is recast as content, while the officials arranging it call the display seriousness. The danger in that framing is not confusion about punishment. It is the normalization of state violence as performance—authorized at the top, executed by an institution, and sanitized as public education.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP insider unloads on Trump official’s ‘insecurity and imposter syndrome’
