item.title: 5 charts that predict the coming GOP 'bloodbath’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that investor and former journalist Steven Rattner used five economic and political comparisons on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” to argue that Republicans could suffer major losses in the 2026 election. The charts do not actually predict a “bloodbath”: they show conditions Rattner considers as bad as, or worse than, those preceding the Democratic takeover of Congress in 2006.

Rattner compared Donald Trump’s second term with George W. Bush’s second term on inflation-adjusted gasoline prices, real wages, broader economic performance, presidential approval and consumer confidence. According to the figures he presented, gas cost about $4.35 per gallon under Trump versus $3.69 under Bush; Trump’s approval stood at 37 percent versus Bush’s 38 percent near the 2006 election; and consumer confidence was 48, compared with 92 under Bush. Rattner also said wages, job creation, growth and interest rates currently compare unfavorably with the Bush-era measures he selected.

The reporting acknowledges the decisive limitation: turnout has not happened, polling can be wrong, and economic similarities do not determine an election. The charts describe public conditions and attitudes; they do not establish how many seats Republicans will lose, or that they will lose control of either chamber.

The power belongs to the governing party

Republicans hold the relevant institutional power in this comparison. Trump occupies the presidency, while his party’s electoral fate is tied to the material conditions voters experience under its rule. House and Senate candidates may try to localize their races, but the governing party cannot plausibly claim to be a spectator to national economic policy.

That does not mean a president personally sets every price, wage or interest rate. It means the administration and its congressional allies choose policies, set priorities and claim credit for economic performance. Political power carries exposure to consequences as well as access to microphones.

A ledger of failure, not a forecast

Rattner’s comparison is useful as an indictment of Republican vulnerability, but weaker as prediction. The 2006 backlash unfolded amid the Iraq war, Hurricane Katrina, rising deficits and public revulsion toward the Bush administration. Similar approval numbers or household pessimism do not reproduce that political environment.

The headline converts warning signs into destiny. That is campaign-season sensationalism masquerading as measurement. Consumer confidence can reveal widespread distress; it cannot allocate House seats. Gas prices can punish incumbents; they cannot tell us who will vote, where district boundaries will concentrate those votes, or which candidates will survive their own campaigns.

Pain becomes political when power denies it

The sharpest evidence is not the Bush analogy but the reported gap between official stewardship and household experience. Rattner’s figures depict higher prices alongside flat real wages, stagnant job growth and exceptionally weak consumer sentiment. Whatever the eventual ballot result, those conditions describe an electorate being told to assess prosperity while its purchasing power is failing to improve.

That is where governing rhetoric often turns into misdirection. Leaders emphasize aggregate indicators, inherited problems or external forces while families encounter the economy through rent, fuel, food, debt and paychecks. Some causes lie beyond presidential control, but responsibility for the policy response still belongs to officials empowered to act.

The missing agents

AlterNet’s framing also lets Congress recede behind Trump’s name. That obscures the lawmakers who authorize spending, shape taxes, approve or block economic measures and defend the administration’s agenda. If Republicans suffer losses, it will not merely be because voters disliked one president’s numbers. It will also reflect choices made—and alternatives rejected—by a party exercising legislative power.

The weaker actors here are consumers and wage earners. They did not set interest rates or national policy, yet coverage often treats their dissatisfaction as a volatile mood requiring explanation. Rattner’s data suggest something less mysterious: people report economic pessimism when their money buys less and their wages do not compensate.

Accountability is not prophecy

The systemic pattern is familiar. Political coverage prefers the drama of an approaching electoral “bloodbath” to the harder work of tracing who governed, what that government chose and whose living standards absorbed the result. The horse race becomes the story; the exercise of power becomes background scenery.

Republicans may face a severe reckoning in 2026, but these charts cannot promise one. What they can show, if the reported figures hold, is a governing party entering an election under conditions of deep economic dissatisfaction. The consequence remains unsettled. The responsibility for confronting those conditions does not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: 5 charts that predict the coming GOP ‘bloodbath’

item.title: Earthquake as ‘anti-MAGA wave’ rattles deep-red state —and Moms for Liberty
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democrats made significant gains in August local elections in Hamilton and Knox counties, Tennessee, but did not overturn Republican dominance. They flipped three seats across county commissions and school boards, won control of the Knox County school board, and reduced large prior deficits in both county-mayor races to four points.

The gains coincided with sharply higher turnout. East Ridge turnout rose from 9.21% in August 2024 to 28.61%, while Knox County turnout increased from 18.07% in its 2022 countywide races to 33.43%. Democratic organizers credited sustained door-knocking and engagement with voters who had assumed defeat was inevitable.

Several victories came against Republican nominees aligned with Moms for Liberty or the party’s MAGA faction. Democratic commissioner Brandon Huckaby called the result an “anti-MAGA wave,” though the evidence remains suggestive rather than conclusive: Republicans still hold most local seats, and Tennessee’s Republican legislative supermajority remains intact.

Power did not change hands

An electoral swing is not an earthquake merely because it occurred somewhere Republicans usually win. The Tennessee GOP still controls the state government and most of the local offices discussed here. Its institutional power includes the ability to write education law, establish censorship criteria and shape the public services that counties must administer.

That distinction matters. Democrats demonstrated that Republican margins can shrink when neglected voters are contacted and given competitive candidates. They did not dislodge the governing structure responsible for deteriorating infrastructure, affordability pressures or the state’s campaign against disfavored material in public schools.

The story is therefore about vulnerability, not transformation. Republican control has become less electorally effortless in these counties. That is politically meaningful, but it is not the same as losing power.

The culture war had authors

The conflicts over books and student services did not descend on Tennessee as an inexplicable outbreak of polarization. State lawmakers enacted the 2022 content law. Republican school-board members applied it when they initially found that a depiction of rape under slavery made Roots impermissible. Superintendent Jon Rysewyk reversed that decision after national backlash.

Republican officials in Hamilton County also voted to end supplemental mental-health services after objections concerning discussions of identity, sexuality and gender. They later restored the provider, alongside other parental options, following local opposition. Those were decisions made by officials with governing authority, not merely “culture-war stuff” floating above local politics.

Moms for Liberty supplied candidates and pressure from the right, but officeholders and party institutions converted that pressure into policy. Treating the organization as the sole villain would let the officials who held the votes escape responsibility for using them.

Voters rejected candidates, not a faction by plebiscite

The defeats of Moms for Liberty-backed candidates are concrete. Bill Sofield lost the Knox County school-board race to Brandy Jenkins after defeating incumbent Republican Kristi Kristy in the GOP primary. Sheri Super, a leader of the local Moms for Liberty chapter, lost a county-commission race to Huckaby.

Calling those outcomes an “anti-MAGA wave” is a campaign interpretation, not a settled measurement of voter intent. The reporting does not present exit polling establishing why voters chose each candidate. Higher Democratic participation, polarizing Republican nominees, local organizing and broader dissatisfaction may all have contributed.

The stronger conclusion is narrower: Republican primaries elevated candidates further to the right, and general-election voters then rejected some of them. A party that replaces viable incumbents with ideological enforcers creates its own exposure. That is not voter confusion. It is a foreseeable consequence of letting a faction use low-turnout primaries to choose who will govern everyone else.

The red-state label conceals the mechanism

“Tennessee is a red state” describes accumulated election results while hiding how those results are produced. Uncontested seats, low-turnout local elections and Democratic organizational neglect can make Republican control appear more unanimous than it is. In East Ridge, a Democrat contested the commission seat for the first time since 2014; turnout then tripled relative to August 2024, and Josh Wichman won.

That does not prove a latent Democratic majority. Republicans also increased their participation, and both Democratic county-mayor candidates still lost. But it exposes the convenience of treating partisan dominance as an immutable cultural trait. Parties benefit when voters regard the outcome as predetermined: incumbents face less scrutiny, challengers struggle to recruit support, and abstention reproduces the power structure that encouraged it.

Democrats bear agency here as well. Wichman said his district had been neglected by the party. If a political organization fails to contest power and then cites the resulting defeats as evidence that competition is impossible, it is not diagnosing the electorate. It is describing its own retreat.

Dominance survives by looking inevitable

The larger pattern is not yet a partisan realignment. It is the erosion of manufactured inevitability. Competitive campaigns and higher turnout narrowed Republican advantages even where decades of election results had taught Democrats to expect humiliation.

Whether that becomes durable depends on what happens after the surprise. Democrats now holding local seats must govern effectively under institutions still dominated by Republicans. Republicans must decide whether factional purity is worth sacrificing offices—and whether culture-war governance can substitute indefinitely for affordable living, functioning infrastructure and competent public services.

The useful political lesson is less dramatic than an earthquake and more damaging to entrenched power: strongholds are often maintained not by universal consent, but by low participation, weak opposition and the disciplined conversion of narrow electoral victories into broad institutional control. Once those conditions change, the map stops looking like destiny and starts looking like what it always was—a record of who organized, who voted and who was allowed to govern.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Earthquake as ‘anti-MAGA wave’ rattles deep-red state —and Moms for Liberty

item.title: How a 'white vigilante' campaign flipped a major state by 1,800 votes
item.description:
What happened

The supplied AlterNet text does not identify the state, the election, the campaign, the people involved, or evidence that a “white vigilante” effort changed an outcome by 1,800 votes. It consists only of an unexplained list of public figures and political terms.

The headline makes a specific causal claim, but the provided material does not substantiate it. No responsible summary can identify who acted, what happened, when it occurred, or whether 1,800 refers to the final margin, shifted votes, or something else.

Power cannot be inferred

Institutional power depends on concrete facts: which officials controlled election administration, which organization conducted the alleged campaign, and which authorities enabled or challenged it. None are supplied.

Naming a powerful actor without evidence would not expose a power structure. It would manufacture one.

The missing chain of agency

A claim that a campaign “flipped” a state requires a documented chain between conduct and result. The supplied material provides no decisions, communications, vote data, legal findings, or attributed testimony establishing that chain.

It therefore cannot support conclusions about vigilantism, racial intimidation, deliberate suppression, or official complicity—however serious those subjects may be.

A headline is not evidence

The framing offers villains, causation, and a razor-thin result before presenting any verifiable reporting. That is misdirection of its own: it invites readers to substitute political recognition and emotional inference for documented agency.

The unexplained names do not repair that defect. They create association without context.

The systemic error

Political analysis becomes propaganda when certainty outruns evidence. Power should be named aggressively when reporting establishes who exercised it, through which institution, and with what consequence.

Here, the only defensible conclusion is narrower: the supplied text cannot sustain the headline’s story. A publication cannot expose manipulation by asking readers to accept an unsupported narrative.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: How a ‘white vigilante’ campaign flipped a major state by 1,800 votes

item.title: Trump is either 'clinically insane' or trying to sink Republicans: Carville
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democratic strategist James Carville offered two speculative explanations for President Donald Trump’s conduct less than four weeks before Election Day: Trump was either mentally unwell or intentionally making it harder for Republicans to retain control of Congress. Carville supplied no evidence establishing either explanation.

On the Politics War Room podcast, Carville and co-host Al Hunt cited Trump’s claim that inflation was nearly nonexistent, his insults toward Democrats, his suggestion that Iran might bomb Los Angeles and San Diego, and his decision to campaign in Grand Island, Nebraska, instead of Omaha, where Republicans faced a competitive House race. Hunt also raised the possibility that Trump could intimidate voters or interfere with the election, but the article reports this as Hunt’s concern—not an established plan or action.

The false choice

The headline converts Carville’s provocation into a binary that the reporting cannot support. Erratic campaigning does not prove a psychiatric condition, and strategically damaging behavior does not prove a desire to lose. “Clinically insane” is not analysis; it is a diagnosis-shaped insult delivered without clinical evidence.

That framing also obscures more ordinary possibilities: Trump may value personal attention, grievance and loyalty displays more than disciplined party strategy. That is an inference, but it fits the conduct described without pretending speculation has become medical fact.

Where the power sits

Trump is not merely another campaign surrogate. As president and the dominant figure in his party, he can determine what Republican candidates must discuss, defend or evade. Carville’s strongest observation is therefore the least sensational one: Trump “dominates everything.”

Congressional Republicans still have agency. They choose whether to align themselves with his claims, challenge them or accept the political cost of silence. Treating them as helpless victims of Trump’s behavior launders their repeated decisions into unfortunate circumstances.

Spectacle replaces accountability

The mental-health framing misdirects attention from conduct to diagnosis. Whether Trump believes his claims, exaggerates deliberately or speaks impulsively, the political question remains the same: What do officeholders and party institutions do when the president makes assertions contradicted by the figures cited in the report?

Calling him irrational can even soften responsibility. It turns choices and their foreseeable effects into symptoms, while allowing Republican officials who enable or excuse those choices to disappear from view.

The consequences are concrete

Voters confronting higher prices will not experience inflation as nonexistent because a president declares it so. Candidates in competitive districts must then carry the burden of defending rhetoric that conflicts with voters’ daily experience.

Hunt’s concern about possible voter intimidation or election interference is more serious than campaign-location gossip, but AlterNet provides no evidence here that such conduct occurred or was planned. The distinction matters: scrutiny should follow documented actions, not become another vehicle for speculation.

The system rewards the provocation

This story reveals a familiar political-media failure. A powerful leader creates controversy; party officials organize themselves around him; commentators reach for extreme personal explanations; and institutional responsibility recedes behind a headline-ready insult.

The useful question is not whether Trump secretly wants Republicans to lose or satisfies an armchair diagnosis. It is why a governing party permits one man’s grievances and improvisations to command its agenda—and why coverage so often treats that surrender of agency as a personality mystery instead of a political choice.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump is either ‘clinically insane’ or trying to sink Republicans: Carville

item.title: Fox has a new strategy to save the GOP — and Trump is furious
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News has intentionally reduced live coverage of President Donald Trump’s midterm rallies, apparently judging that his speeches no longer attract enough viewers and may hurt Republican candidates. A Fox host, speaking anonymously to CNN, said the decision came “from the top down,” while Fox offered no public explanation.

The retreat follows tension between Trump and the network, including Fox’s removal of Maria Bartiromo after she allegedly shared internal guidance with Trump aide Peter Navarro. That guidance reportedly discouraged Fox Business programs from promoting a Trump speech containing unverified election claims, although Fox News aired the July address.

Trump responded by accusing Fox of ignoring rallies he described as sold out, despite reports of empty seats at some events. The reporting does not establish a formal Fox strategy to “save” the GOP; it establishes an intentional reduction in coverage that Republican insiders interpret as an effort to limit Trump’s electoral drag.

The power sits in the control room

Trump holds presidential power, but Fox controls access to a political audience he has relied upon for more than a decade. Network executives decide whether a rally becomes a national event or merely another speech in a crowded media schedule. Refusing live carriage does not silence the president. It denies him free, uninterrupted distribution to Fox’s viewers.

That choice matters precisely because Fox is not functioning here as a passive observer. The network helped create the political value of Trump’s performances by broadcasting them. Now its leadership can reduce that value by changing the programming. The anonymous host’s account identifies the operative decision-makers: executives above the on-air talent, not disgruntled viewers and not some mysterious shift in the atmosphere.

This is risk management, not a reckoning

Nothing in the reporting suggests that Fox suddenly adopted a principled objection to carrying political propaganda. The explanations offered are brutally commercial and electoral: Trump allegedly “doesn’t rate anymore,” and Republican strategists fear that his unpopularity will damage their midterm candidates.

That distinction is the story. Fox’s reported concern is not chiefly that Trump delivered unverified claims about election vulnerabilities. It is that the audience is less interested and the Republican coalition may pay a price. The network tolerated and amplified Trump when the arrangement produced ratings and political energy. Its retreat, as described here, is an exercise in asset management after the asset depreciated.

The headline overstates the plan

Calling this a strategy to “save the GOP” packages an inference as though Fox had announced a rescue operation. It did not. AlterNet cites anonymous network sourcing about an intentional reduction in coverage, CNN’s interpretation of its political significance, and Republican anxiety about Trump’s effect on the midterms. Those facts support a plausible conclusion that Fox is protecting its audience and Republican prospects. They do not prove a formally declared party-saving strategy.

The framing also risks making Trump’s anger the center of the story. His complaints are evidence that he understands the value of Fox’s distribution. But the consequential act is Fox management’s programming decision. The institution with the broadcast switch exercised its power; Trump’s social-media protest merely revealed the leverage he had lost.

The machine is bigger than its star

The larger pattern is not a clean rupture between a political leader and an independent press. It is a struggle inside a shared political-media system over who still benefits from whom. Trump supplied spectacle and audience loyalty. Fox supplied reach, repetition and legitimacy within conservative politics. That exchange worked until the network reportedly concluded that continuous exposure had become less profitable and potentially more damaging to Republican candidates.

This is how partisan media power protects itself. It does not need to repudiate the politics it helped normalize. It can lower the volume, shorten the segment and move on to a more useful vehicle. The reported sidelining of Trump is therefore less a correction than a reminder: the apparatus that elevated a leader can distance itself when he becomes a liability, while leaving the underlying incentives and political project intact.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox has a new strategy to save the GOP — and Trump is furious

item.title: DOJ makes 'striking admission' as judge corners lawyer on Trump influence
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump White House barred reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico beginning September 19 after President Donald Trump accused the outlets, without publicly cited specifics, of publishing “fake news” that endangered national security. Politico said the Secret Service confiscated a reporter’s credentials, while MS NOW said its journalists were denied access to White House grounds.

The outlets sued on September 21, alleging unconstitutional retaliation, viewpoint discrimination and denial of due process. During a Thursday hearing, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly questioned the absence of a specific emergency or adequate notice. Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik defended presidential discretion and then made the admission highlighted by MS NOW: the president was personally making these decisions, and the judge had little practical control over whether the White House obeyed the law. The district-court case remained unresolved, with any ruling expected to be appealed.

The power is in the White House

The institutional hierarchy is not complicated. Trump decided which news organizations could enter government premises. The Secret Service reportedly enforced that decision. The Justice Department supplied the legal defense.

That matters because the dispute is not an argument among equal participants in a media feud. The president controls access to the White House and commands the executive branch. The excluded journalists possess no corresponding state power. Calling the White House a “sacred place,” as Velchik reportedly did, obscures the relevant fact: it is a public institution, not presidential property.

Retaliation dressed as discretion

The administration offered national security as a justification, but AlterNet reports that it identified no specific reporting that created such a danger. The outlets allege they were punished because Trump disliked their coverage; that claim remained before the court.

The conduct described nevertheless exposes the structure of the decision. A president denounced reporting as false and illegal, ordered disfavored outlets excluded, and left government lawyers to argue that his concern about a particular reporter should be enough. “Discretion” becomes a sterile legal label for a power being used selectively against critics.

Velchik’s assertion that Trump accepts negative coverage when he deserves it supplies no meaningful limit. It places the president in charge of deciding which criticism is legitimate and which journalists may retain access after delivering it.

The misdirection is the accusation

The White House’s rhetoric shifts scrutiny from the official exercising coercive authority to the reporters subjected to it. Unsupported references to “lies” and national security invite the public to debate whether the outlets behaved badly before the government establishes what they supposedly did.

That reversal is politically useful. It treats access as a favor that journalists must earn through acceptable coverage, rather than a government-administered privilege that cannot be withdrawn in retaliation for a viewpoint. It also converts a due-process problem into a personality dispute between Trump and the press.

Judge Kelly’s reported questions cut through that maneuver. If there was no identified emergency and no adequate notice, then the administration’s slogans do not fill the evidentiary gap.

A court order is not self-enforcement

The most consequential statement was not that Trump made the decision; the lawsuit already centers on his conduct. It was the Justice Department’s warning, as characterized in the hearing, that judicial authority may not produce executive compliance.

That does not establish that the White House will defy an eventual order. It does reveal the posture its lawyer presented: precedent is supposedly wrong, presidential discretion should dominate, and the judge’s practical leverage is limited. The department charged with defending federal law was telling a federal court about the boundaries of the court’s power over the president.

The larger system

Press access is the immediate dispute. Executive impunity is the larger pattern.

An administration can impose punishment first, provide no specific public evidence for its stated rationale, and force the targets into prolonged litigation. Even if the outlets ultimately prevail, the exclusion has already operated, the expense has already been imposed and other reporters have already been shown the cost of antagonizing the president.

That is how arbitrary power expands without needing a grand legal doctrine. The executive acts, its enforcement apparatus complies, its lawyers manufacture deference, and the courts are left to decide whether a remedy delivered later can restrain a punishment imposed now.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: DOJ makes ‘striking admission’ as judge corners lawyer on Trump influence

item.title: Trump ambassador faces State Dept probe over 4 AM demands and 'toxic' reign
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Kimberly Guilfoyle, President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, is reportedly the subject of a State Department inspector general inquiry after complaints about her treatment of embassy personnel, travel, gifts and possible ethics violations. Five unnamed sources told the Daily Mail that a formal investigation had begun, but the inspector general’s office would neither confirm nor deny that account. Guilfoyle’s lawyer, Jesse Binnall, said any implication of wrongdoing was unsupported.

The allegations include late-night demands, verbal abuse and punitive staffing decisions. One security officer was reportedly reassigned after failing to answer a 4 a.m. demand for ice in Mykonos; two drivers allegedly lost their positions after Guilfoyle objected to a left turn. Investigators are also reportedly examining private-jet use, gifts, ties to an energy and construction company, and a dispute over renovations to the ambassador’s official residence that allegedly ended with Guilfoyle firing her ethics manager.

The disclosures followed congressional Democrats’ requests for scrutiny. Senator Jeanne Shaheen asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio to investigate allegations that Guilfoyle promoted a foreign company and included registered lobbyist Christos Marafatsos in senior diplomatic meetings. Rubio, visiting Athens for defense and energy talks, did not directly answer questions about Guilfoyle’s conduct.

Power wears diplomatic credentials

The institutional hierarchy is straightforward. An ambassador commands an embassy; drivers, security personnel and career staff operate beneath that authority. If the reported punishments occurred, this was not a personality clash among equals. It was a presidential appointee allegedly using official power against workers whose assignments and careers were vulnerable to her displeasure.

That distinction matters because “toxic workplace” can be a laundering phrase. It makes coercive conduct sound atmospheric, as though everyone merely encountered bad office weather. The allegations describe something more concrete: threats of dismissal, demands at extreme hours and employment consequences tied to personal service or trivial irritation.

The ice cubes are not the point

A 4 a.m. demand for ice is memorable because it is absurd. But absurdity can become misdirection when it reduces a power scandal to celebrity gossip. The consequential allegation is not that an ambassador wanted ice. It is that a security officer was reportedly demoted after failing to satisfy the demand.

Likewise, the alleged dispute over a left turn matters because workers reportedly lost assignments afterward. These incidents, if substantiated, would show public authority being treated as a private instrument of discipline. The spectacle is petty; the power is not.

Ethics oversight meets the chain of command

The most serious questions extend beyond abusive management. The reported inquiry encompasses private travel, gifts, corporate associations and the alleged removal of an ethics manager after a disagreement over financing renovations to Jefferson House. Those claims remain allegations, and the available reporting does not establish misconduct. It does establish why independent scrutiny is necessary.

An ethics officer is supposed to constrain an officeholder, not survive at the officeholder’s pleasure only while offering convenient advice. When a person responsible for compliance can allegedly be removed during the very dispute requiring scrutiny, the institution’s safeguard risks becoming another subordinate position.

Rubio’s silence is an official choice

Guilfoyle may have made or authorized the disputed personnel decisions, but responsibility does not end at the embassy gates. The State Department oversees ambassadors, and Marco Rubio leads it. His refusal to address the allegations during an Athens visit was not evidence that they are true. It was evidence that the department’s political leadership chose not to provide a public accounting when asked.

Congressional Democrats supplied the pressure that reportedly preceded the disclosures. The inspector general, if an inquiry is underway, supplies the investigative mechanism. The secretary supplies—or withholds—the political backing required for oversight to mean more than paperwork.

Patronage makes accountability optional

This story exposes a familiar governing pattern: prominent appointees receive enormous institutional authority, career employees absorb the consequences, and oversight begins only after complaints accumulate and legislators intervene. The powerful actor’s alleged conduct becomes a workplace controversy; the weaker actor’s lost assignment becomes an anecdote.

The systemic error is not merely appointing people accused of treating public institutions as personal estates. It is building accountability around the hope that subordinates will complain loudly enough, journalists will obtain enough leaks, Congress will apply enough pressure and an inspector general will eventually be permitted to establish what happened. By then, the institution has already taught everyone inside it who can issue orders—and who must bear the risk of objecting.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump ambassador faces State Dept probe over 4 AM demands and ‘toxic’ reign

item.title: Fox News claims Biden FBI heavily monitored Trump official Susie Wiles
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News obtained White House-released documents showing the FBI cataloged Susie Wiles’s phone activity from at least February through May 2023 during the federal investigation into Donald Trump’s handling of classified documents and presidential records. The records reportedly identify contacts with at least 21 attorneys, as well as journalists, campaign staff, Trump Organization personnel and Secret Service contacts.

The documents show who contacted whom, when and for how long, but not what was discussed or what investigators intended to prove. The FBI and Justice Department opened the investigation in March 2022 after authorization from FBI Director Christopher Wray and approval from Attorney General Merrick Garland; special counsel Jack Smith assumed oversight after his November 2022 appointment. Wiles, then running Trump’s political operation, was not yet White House chief of staff.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called the monitoring an abuse of government power and accused Smith of spying on political opponents. The reporting presented here does not establish that President Joe Biden ordered, directed or knew about the collection.

Metadata is still state power

A catalog of calls is not a recording of conversations, but it is not trivial. Mapping a political adviser’s contacts can expose the structure of a campaign, its legal coordination, its media relationships and its connections to security personnel. Federal investigators wielded that institutional power through an inquiry approved at the highest named levels of the FBI and Justice Department.

That deserves scrutiny. The relevant questions are whether investigators had lawful authority, what evidence justified collecting the records, how broadly the subpoenas were drawn and what safeguards governed sensitive contacts with lawyers and journalists. The documents, as described, do not answer those questions. Their silence supports investigation, not a predetermined verdict.

“Biden FBI” is a political substitution

The headline framing replaces the officials identified in the reporting with Biden. That is misdirection unless evidence connects him personally to the decision. Wray sought authorization, Garland approved the investigation and Smith later supervised it. Those are the actors the available account names.

Collapsing an entire department into the president’s partisan possession also serves Trump’s preferred theory of government: law enforcement is legitimate when it protects him and “weaponized” when it investigates him. Fox’s framing does not merely describe institutional power. It personalizes that power selectively, turning an evidentiary dispute into an accusation against a political enemy without supplying the missing link.

The White House controls the counternarrative

The current White House released the documents and supplied the language through which allies could present them. Wiles is no longer merely a private citizen whose records were subpoenaed; she is chief of staff to the president whose conduct prompted the underlying investigation. The administration therefore holds enormous power to publicize selected records, define villains and convert investigative procedure into political ammunition.

Bis’s claim that this was “spying on political opponents” goes beyond what the reported documents establish. They show contact mapping, according to Fox, but do not reveal investigators’ purpose or the substance of any calls. Calling the operation disgraceful before those facts are established is advocacy dressed as adjudication.

Accountability requires the missing facts

The strongest criticism of the collection is not that Wiles was politically important. Political status cannot create immunity for people operating near a subject of a federal investigation. Nor can an investigation’s existence prove every surveillance method was proportionate.

The central issue is legal and institutional: what process authorized access, what investigative need justified its breadth, and how protected relationships were handled. Fox’s “sprawling” label describes scale, not legality. The White House’s accusation supplies motive without evidence. AlterNet is right to identify the partisan relitigation, but mockery of Trump allies does not resolve the underlying civil-liberties questions either.

Power rewrites the investigation

This episode shows how control of the executive branch can be used to retry a previous administration’s investigation in public. Records collected under one government become narrative weapons under the next. Officials with present power portray themselves as victims of past power while withholding, at least in the account provided, the facts needed to judge whether that power was abused.

The systemic failure is not simply aggressive federal investigation or partisan media distortion. It is the replacement of standards with factional ownership: subpoenas are tyranny when aimed inward and justice when aimed outward. That arrangement protects neither civil liberties nor impartial enforcement. It protects whichever political machine controls the documents, the podium and the labels.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox News claims Biden FBI heavily monitored Trump official Susie Wiles

item.title: Republicans 'diving out of windows' to avoid Trump: family member
item.description:
What happened

Donald Trump’s niece, psychologist Mary L. Trump, said Republican candidates were “diving out of windows” to avoid appearing with him—her metaphor for distancing themselves from an increasingly unpopular president. AlterNet reported that she pointed to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s absence from a San Antonio event and to a Reuters review finding that candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races had broken with Trump on policy or played down their ties to him.

Abbott attributed his absence to previously scheduled campaign events in multiple cities. Mary Trump interpreted that explanation as an attempt to avoid a politically damaging appearance, but AlterNet supplied no evidence establishing that motive. She also cited leaked audio in which Ken Paxton reportedly said Trump’s push for a midterm convention had not helped him.

The article does not clearly establish the timing of all these events, and its references to Abbott, Paxton, a November 3 election, and a sitting president are insufficiently organized. That confusion matters: political analysis cannot substitute insinuation for a coherent chronology.

Power remained with the party

The actual institutional power belonged to Republican officeholders, candidates, and party organizations deciding where to spend money, which alliances to advertise, and whether to share a stage with Trump. Trump possessed attention, an endorsement operation, and influence over Republican voters. Candidates controlled their own campaign appearances and messaging.

That distinction punctures the article’s preferred spectacle. These Republicans were not helpless people fleeing a force of nature. If they minimized their association with Trump, they made a calculated electoral choice after benefiting from—or at least operating within—the political structure he dominated.

Distance is not dissent

A scheduling conflict may be genuine, evasive, or both. The reporting does not prove which. But the broader Reuters finding described by AlterNet suggests an organized pattern: vulnerable candidates were willing to diverge from Trump publicly when proximity threatened their seats.

That is risk management, not necessarily repudiation. A candidate can omit Trump from campaign materials while preserving the policies, judges, enforcement priorities, and partisan machinery produced under his leadership. Personal distance is cheap when institutional alignment remains intact.

The family feud obscures the machinery

AlterNet builds much of the story around Mary Trump’s ridicule of her uncle and Ken Paxton. Her relationship to Donald Trump supplies access to a recognizable name, not special authority over Abbott’s scheduling decisions or candidates’ private calculations.

The result is misdirection through personality. Jokes about Trump’s clothes, voice, and social-media platform consume space that should have been used to establish dates, offices, electoral conditions, and the concrete stakes of the races. Mockery can describe contempt. It cannot demonstrate causation.

The article also repeats Mary Trump’s characterization of Paxton as corrupt without supplying supporting facts in the excerpt. That allegation required evidence and context, not treatment as a punchline.

Candidates enabled what they later concealed

The larger political pattern is selective ownership. Party actors welcome a powerful figure when his endorsement mobilizes voters, then manufacture distance when his unpopularity threatens them. They seek the benefits of affiliation while treating its costs as somebody else’s contamination.

Trump’s reported insult of Paxton illustrates the imbalance inside that bargain. Even an endorsed ally could be publicly demeaned before receiving praise. Paxton’s reported private complaint about the convention suggests resentment, but not an institutional break. Loyalty remained useful enough to maintain despite humiliation.

The system rewards cosmetic separation

The consequential story is not that Republicans suddenly discovered Trump was “toxic.” It is that electoral pressure encouraged them to alter presentation without requiring an accounting of their decisions. Campaign photographs disappeared; policy alliances could endure.

That is how a party evades responsibility without surrendering power. It turns complicity into a scheduling problem, recasts strategic retreat as personal discomfort, and invites political coverage to follow the stage drama instead of the governing record. The windows were metaphorical. The escape route was branding.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republicans ‘diving out of windows’ to avoid Trump: family member

item.title: The ghost of 1932 — and the reckoning threatening to kill the GOP
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s worsening political position stems not merely from broken promises but from collapsing trust. The outlet cites polls reporting that 70 percent of respondents believed his policies were raising grocery costs, while only 17 percent of U.S. adults approved of his handling of the cost of living.

The article links that distrust to Trump’s conduct during the war with Iran. It reports that he alternately considered and denied considering a diesel-export ban, proposed suspending federal diesel taxes, and repeatedly claimed the war was nearly over as fuel and shipping costs climbed. CNN analyst Harry Enten compared Trump’s standing at this point in his presidency to Herbert Hoover’s, raising the possibility that the damage could spread from Trump to the Republican Party.

AlterNet does not establish that such a partisan collapse will occur. Its comparison with the Republican defeat of 1932 is a warning, not a forecast.

Power has a name

Trump is not a spectator trapped inside a bad economy or an unwanted war. As president, he holds the executive power at the center of both. His administration’s decisions shape military policy, energy markets, federal taxation, and the information the White House gives the public.

Congressional Republicans possess power too. They can investigate, legislate, restrict funding, oppose executive decisions, or refuse to repeat presidential claims. AlterNet instead describes vulnerable Republicans waiting for Trump to relieve the political pressure created by policies they have enabled. Their anxiety is not evidence of powerlessness. It is the electoral cost of submission.

Contradiction as government

The diesel episode is more revealing than a conventional “mixed messaging” story. AlterNet reports that Trump said he was considering an export ban, abandoned it two days later, and then claimed, “We were never going to do it.” Those statements cannot be converted into a coherent policy by adding more context.

This is governance by improvisation followed by denial. Markets, businesses, and households must respond to presidential announcements even when the president later pretends the announcements never mattered. The institutional power remains real; only accountability is treated as optional.

The proposed diesel-tax suspension follows the same pattern. Patrick De Haan of GasBuddy told the outlet that it could increase demand without increasing supply, potentially raising long-term prices. The proposal offers a visible gesture while leaving the reported cause of the shock—the war and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz—untouched.

The cash promise is not relief

Trump’s reported offer of $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans retain Congress is presented as a promise contingent on partisan victory. AlterNet calls it bribery. At minimum, it is an attempt to convert economic distress into electoral leverage without an enacted program, identified funding mechanism, or demonstrated path to payment in the reporting provided.

That distinction matters. People struggling with food, fuel, and housing costs need policy already within the reach of governing institutions. Offering future cash from a rally stage shifts attention from what the administration has done to what voters might receive if they preserve its power.

The misdirection is structural: hardship becomes the voter’s problem to solve by rewarding the officials presiding over it.

The Hoover analogy has limits

The article’s 1932 comparison identifies a genuine political mechanism: a governing party can become inseparable from the consequences of its rule. Hoover’s defeat damaged Republicans far beyond one election, and AlterNet argues that Trump may similarly attach his party’s identity to war, inflation, and institutional incompetence.

But history is not an automatic punishment machine. The article itself notes that Franklin Roosevelt helped discredit Republicans for a generation. Durable realignment required an opposition capable of defining responsibility and offering a governing alternative. A film clip released by the Democratic National Committee may dramatize public anger; it does not by itself organize that anger into power.

Nor does polling make extinction inevitable. Even striking movement among independents measures opinion at a particular time under the pollsters’ stated methods. It does not prove causation or guarantee an electoral result.

A party built around impunity

The larger danger to the GOP is not simply that Trump may be caught lying. It is that the party has organized itself around protecting his freedom to make claims, reverse decisions, and disclaim consequences while retaining presidential authority.

That arrangement works only while enough people accept the separation between power and responsibility. Rising prices and an unresolved war make that separation harder to sustain because the costs arrive in forms propaganda cannot permanently erase: grocery bills, mortgage payments, diesel prices, and shipping charges.

The ghost of 1932 is therefore not a mystical cycle. It is the possibility that voters will identify who governed, who enabled that government, and who asked to be believed after the material evidence had become impossible to ignore.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The ghost of 1932 — and the reckoning threatening to kill the GOP

item.title: End-of-life doula explains why Congress has a major letting-go problem
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Congress’s “letting-go problem” is sustained by the identity incumbents derive from office and by institutions that reward them for staying. Parties prize incumbency, staff careers depend on sitting lawmakers, and constituents may value seniority. In Massachusetts, 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey defeated 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton in the September 1, 2026, Democratic primary by nearly 30 percentage points; 11 octogenarians won congressional primaries that year.

The article, republished from The Conversation and written by management professor and trained end-of-life doula Nancy Forster-Holt, argues that succession should be planned before illness forces it. She contrasts Barbara Boxer’s advance retirement announcement with the crisis-driven exits or absences surrounding Dianne Feinstein, Joe Biden and Kay Granger, while noting current scrutiny of Mitch McConnell’s health and Chuck Grassley’s acknowledgment that dying in office could determine which party selects his successor.

Power does not surrender itself

The problem is not simply that elderly politicians cannot imagine retirement. Congressional office carries votes, committee authority, patronage, publicity and influence over legislation and appointments. The person occupying the seat controls those powers until resignation, defeat or death.

Age alone does not establish incapacity, and the article does not claim that every older lawmaker is unfit. But incumbents are not ordinary employees deciding when to leave a private job. Their refusal to plan can transfer the risks of illness and decline to constituents, colleagues and the functioning of government while preserving their own status for as long as possible.

The enablers have names

Parties keep backing incumbents because incumbency is electorally valuable. Staff members and longtime allies may avoid difficult conversations because their careers, access and shared projects are tied to the officeholder. Voters can reinforce the arrangement by preferring accumulated seniority to an orderly transfer of power.

Those incentives help explain why “not yet” so often survives until choice gives way to emergency. Feinstein’s nearly three-month health-related absence in 2023 left the Senate Judiciary Committee deadlocked on dozens of Biden judicial nominations after Republicans blocked a temporary Democratic replacement and Feinstein declined to resign. That outcome involved identifiable decisions, not an abstract failure to “let go.”

Age is the convenient decoy

Framing this chiefly as a gerontocracy story risks blaming biology for an institutional design that rewards indefinite tenure. Markey’s age did not award him the nomination; Massachusetts Democratic primary voters did. Parties did not merely observe these candidacies; they operated within a system that prizes incumbents’ fundraising, recognition and seniority.

The sharper question is not whether 80 is categorically too old. It is why lawmakers can retain consequential authority without credible succession plans, and why the people surrounding them often remain quiet until a medical or political crisis makes concealment impossible. Personal attachment matters, but institutional permission makes that attachment politically consequential.

Crisis is not succession

Boxer announced her departure early enough for candidates to organize and voters to choose among them. By contrast, Biden withdrew from the 2024 presidential race only after the primary process, following advice from his inner circle to seek reelection. Harris then became the Democratic nominee without participating in those primaries and lost to Donald Trump.

The reporting does not establish that the compressed succession caused that defeat. It does establish that delay deprived Democrats of a normal competitive selection process. When leaders and their entourages postpone transition, the public inherits fewer choices, less preparation and greater dependence on insiders making decisions under pressure.

An institution built around “not yet”

Forster-Holt’s palliative-care analogy is useful because it treats departure as something to prepare for while meaningful choice remains possible. But Congress does not need better therapeutic vocabulary nearly as much as it needs political actors willing to place institutional continuity above an incumbent’s preferences.

The larger pattern is a governing class that treats public office as personal identity while distributing the costs of that attachment to everyone else. The scandal is not that lawmakers grow old. It is that parties, aides and political institutions repeatedly allow foreseeable transitions to become emergencies—and then describe the resulting dysfunction as tragedy rather than the consequence of choices made by people with power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: End-of-life doula explains why Congress has a major letting-go problem

item.title: Eyebrows raised as Trump named 'Admiral' in land-locked red state's navy
item.description:
What happened

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen named President Donald Trump an admiral in the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska during a Monday midterm rally in Grand Island, AlterNet reported. The title is a civic honor with no military authority, duties, pay or privileges.

Pillen presented it after a speech lasting more than 20 minutes, calling the ceremony “one little fun thing.” Nebraska governors have issued such commissions since 1930, and Trump is reportedly at least the sixth president to receive one.

Power was the point

The admiralship is harmless pageantry. The setting was not politically neutral. A sitting governor used his discretionary power at a campaign rally to honor the president headlining it.

Pillen was not conferring command. He was performing loyalty. The joke worked because everyone understood the real hierarchy: the governor supplied the state-sanctioned tribute, while Trump supplied the political gravity around which the event revolved.

Patronage in costume

Nebraska’s imaginary navy began as a mechanism for an acting governor to honor friends. Its comic language still makes that favoritism sound quaint: admirals, tadpoles and goldfish enlisted in a ritual of official affection.

That history does not make Trump’s appointment sinister. It does make its function unusually transparent. Pillen had full discretion and chose to spend a state honor on the country’s most powerful political figure at a partisan rally. The certificate conveyed no legal privilege, but symbolism is itself political currency.

The headline inflates the wrong oddity

The landlocked-state joke is the least revealing part of the story. Nebraska has awarded these titles for nearly a century to presidents, entertainers, athletes and other prominent people. There is no genuine mystery about how a state without an ocean acquired a ceremonial navy.

Focusing on “raised eyebrows” risks turning a public display of political deference into novelty news. The relevant question is not whether Nebraska’s navy has ships. It is why an elected governor used an official civic distinction as part of a rally organized around presidential power.

Soft rituals, hard hierarchy

American political patronage often arrives disguised as humor, tradition or harmless ceremony. That packaging discourages scrutiny: objecting looks humorless, while participating costs the officeholder little and signals allegiance to the intended audience.

No evidence in AlterNet’s report establishes that the award purchased a favor or changed policy. Its significance is more basic. Institutions teach the public whom they consider worthy of recognition, and officials reveal whose approval they value by deciding when and where to bestow it.

The system beneath the spectacle

The larger pattern is the conversion of public office into a stage for political relationship management. The formal power remained with Pillen; the political advantage flowed toward Trump; and an honor issued under gubernatorial authority helped fuse state ceremony with campaign theater.

An imaginary navy cannot command anything. But the official who controls its commissions can still use one to advertise where he stands in a real chain of political power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Eyebrows raised as Trump named ‘Admiral’ in land-locked red state’s navy

item.title: 'Devastating': Glee erupts as Susan Collins' 'road salt' boast blows up in her face
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Susan Collins, during a Tuesday debate in Maine against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, answered a question about President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada by touting her success in getting road salt removed from the tariff list. Jackson replied, “What about everything else? We can’t eat road salt.”

Jackson also linked household affordability to what he called Trump’s “Iran war,” arguing that fewer people would be able to afford to drive. Clips circulated online, where Democratic officials, strategists and liberal commentators praised his retort and mocked Collins’ answer. The reporting does not establish whether the exchange changed any votes.

Power was already in the room

Collins is not an observer pleading for relief. She is a sitting United States senator defending her record. Trump imposed the tariffs at issue. Collins presented one exemption as proof that she had exercised influence successfully.

That makes the unanswered question more important than the celebrated comeback: What did Collins do about the broader policy? Her road-salt example shows access and some leverage. It does not demonstrate that she meaningfully restrained the administration’s wider tariff agenda or protected Mainers from its other costs.

A narrow exception is not a governing record

Politicians routinely market carve-outs as victories because carve-outs let them claim effectiveness without confronting the policy producing the damage. The governing failure becomes background scenery; the exception becomes the headline achievement.

Jackson’s line worked because it exposed that substitution in five words. Road salt matters in Maine, but Collins offered it in response to a question about tariffs on Canada, not a question about winter road maintenance. The mismatch made her answer sound less like evidence of control than an admission of how little control she could claim.

The weaker actor did not create the problem

The viral framing naturally centers Jackson because he delivered the sharp line. But Jackson, as the challenger described by RawStory, did not impose the tariffs. Collins did not originate them either, based on this reporting. Trump holds the executive power behind the tariff policy, while Collins holds legislative power and political influence as an incumbent senator.

Reducing the episode to Jackson “destroying” Collins risks turning a dispute over material policy into campaign-spectacle scoring. The retort identified the inadequacy of Collins’ defense; it did not cause that inadequacy. The governing choices came first.

Virality is not accountability

RawStory’s evidence for “glee” is a collection of approving social-media reactions, largely from Democratic and liberal figures. Those reactions establish that the clip traveled within a partisan media ecosystem. They do not establish broad public opinion or electoral movement.

Claims that the line could sway the election were predictions, not results. Treating applause as consequence flatters the political internet’s preferred fiction: that a devastating post is equivalent to a change in power. It is not. Collins’ record, Trump’s policies and voters’ material conditions will persist after the clip disappears.

The politics of the token concession

This exchange reveals a familiar governing pattern. An administration adopts a broad policy; an allied officeholder secures a limited exemption; the exemption is then advertised as protection from the very policy the officeholder failed to stop.

Jackson’s comeback punctured that sales pitch because it restored scale. A senator’s power should be judged by the harms she prevents, the policies she enables and the interests she chooses to confront—not by one item successfully removed from a list. When government delivers broad costs and officials campaign on narrow escapes, the exemption is not the whole achievement. It is evidence of the larger failure surrounding it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Devastating’: Glee erupts as Susan Collins’ ‘road salt’ boast blows up in her face

item.title: GOP panics as Trump's poorly timed purchases squander $500M war chest: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing The Washington Post, reports that Republican groups entered the final midterm stretch with a large financial advantage but could not identify a race in which that advantage had fundamentally changed the contest. Donald Trump had said his super PACs would spend $400 million to $500 million supporting Republican candidates, yet by the Wednesday covered in the report they had reserved more than $194 million in advertising.

The money arrived late. Trump-controlled super PACs reportedly waited until Labor Day to begin major spending, when airtime was scarcer and more expensive. Because super PACs pay higher television rates than candidates, Republicans also received less advertising for each dollar than Democratic candidates who had raised enough money to buy airtime directly.

The Post illustrated the penalty in Dallas: James Talarico’s Democratic Senate campaign reportedly spent $950,000 to reach the average viewer 10 times, while allies of Republican nominee Ken Paxton spent $4.65 million to reach the average viewer 13 times. An anonymous Republican strategist compared the resulting gains to the incremental movement of trench warfare.

The power sat with Trump

This was not a shortage of Republican money. It was a concentration of money under Trump’s control.

Republican candidates depended heavily on party committees and super PACs rather than building comparable fundraising operations of their own. That gave Trump’s political apparatus enormous leverage over when and where resources moved. Candidates were left counting on a rescue controlled by an organization whose delayed purchases made every television dollar less effective.

The institutional power belonged to the people controlling the war chest. The consequences landed on candidates who did not control it.

Delay was a decision

The report describes the tactical failure clearly: the super PACs waited until Labor Day, missed cheaper advance reservations and then paid premium prices for limited inventory. Whatever the reason for that delay—and the supplied reporting does not establish one—it was not an unavoidable feature of campaign finance.

Trump advertised a vast reserve as proof of political strength. But stored money does not persuade voters, organize volunteers or reserve airtime. A war chest can project dominance while producing little electoral value if its controllers refuse to deploy it when deployment is cheapest and most useful.

That distinction matters. The problem was not that hundreds of millions of dollars mysteriously lost their power. The people directing the funds used that power inefficiently.

“GOP panic” blurs responsibility

The headline turns a hierarchy into a collective emotion: “the GOP” panics, as if every Republican actor shared equal control over the spending schedule. They did not.

Candidates facing expensive races could not compel Trump’s super PACs to purchase ads earlier. Republican strategists could complain anonymously, but the reported structure left Trump’s operation holding the money and determining its timing. Treating the outcome as generalized party anxiety softens the central fact: authority was concentrated, and the resulting failure flowed downward.

Even “squander” should be used carefully. The reporting demonstrates dramatically worse purchasing efficiency, not that the entire promised $400 million to $500 million had already been spent or lost. The documented indictment is narrower and strong enough: more than $194 million in reservations bought under unfavorable conditions after months of reliance on a delayed rescue.

Money cannot repair dependence

The Dallas comparison exposes the cost of outsourcing campaigns to billionaire-scale political vehicles. Talarico’s campaign could obtain discounted candidate rates. Paxton’s allies had to spend nearly five times as much for only 30 percent more exposure to the average viewer, according to the Democratic media buyer cited by the Post.

That is not merely an advertising problem. It is a power problem. Candidates who can raise directly possess more control over timing and receive legally favored rates. Candidates made dependent on outside groups become clients of whoever commands those groups, even when the patron’s decisions weaken them.

Trump’s financial dominance therefore carried its own liability: it centralized Republican resources without guaranteeing competent execution.

The war chest as political theater

This episode reveals a recurring weakness in personalized party machinery. Accumulation is mistaken for organization, promised intervention for actual capacity, and one leader’s control for collective strength.

The reported money still mattered, and the article does not establish the eventual electoral effect of the spending. But it does show how concentrated power evades precise accounting. Trump’s operation controlled the funds and delayed the purchases; candidates absorbed the inflated costs; unnamed strategists narrated the damage as helpless frustration.

A party built around dependence on one political figure does not merely inherit his advantages. It also inherits the timing, judgment and priorities of the apparatus he controls—and discovers, too late, that a rescue fund is only as useful as the decisions behind it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP panics as Trump’s poorly timed purchases squander $500M war chest: report

item.title: A-list movie star targeted by Melania Trump team with 'weird flex' about box office bomb
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Marc Beckman, Melania Trump’s senior adviser and a producer of her documentary, celebrated its per-theater opening performance by claiming it beat Tom Cruise’s Digger by about 67 percent. His comparison relied on a narrow metric: Digger opened in 1,543 more theaters.

The broader figures undercut the boast. According to reports cited by RawStory, Melania opened to just over $7 million and finished with roughly $16.6 million worldwide, while Amazon reportedly spent $75 million on production and marketing. Digger earned $8 million domestically and $20 million worldwide during its opening weekend against a reported $160 million budget.

The documentary also received a reported 9 percent critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes, compared with a 99 percent audience score attributed largely to the first lady’s supporters. Melania Trump has since announced another Amazon Prime Video series about her life, tentatively suggested for November.

The metric is the message

Beckman did not rebut the criticism of Melania or demonstrate commercial success. He selected the denominator that made the project look strongest, then compared it with another expensive disappointment.

That is not evidence that Melania succeeded. It is political communication disguised as box-office analysis: isolate one favorable statistic, remove the financial context, and declare victory. The remarkable part is not the arithmetic. It is the expectation that loyal audiences will accept a curated fragment as the whole record.

Power financed the failure

Tom Cruise is the celebrity target, but he is not the consequential actor in this story. The institutional power sits with the first lady’s political operation and Amazon, which reportedly committed $75 million to the documentary and then remained in business with Melania Trump for a follow-up series.

That relationship matters more than a contest between two poorly performing films. A sitting first lady received an enormous commercial platform for a self-authored image project. Her adviser, who also produced it, then used his political position to market its reception as public affirmation. The roles of subject, political surrogate, producer, and promoter collapse into one influence operation.

Celebrity provides the decoy

The Cruise comparison turns scrutiny away from the question Beckman’s own numbers invite: what did Amazon buy, and why does weak financial and critical performance appear to carry so little consequence?

RawStory’s framing partly follows the bait by emphasizing an A-list star and a “weird flex.” The remark is certainly strained, but weirdness is not the central problem. Treating the episode as celebrity sparring shrinks a story about political access, corporate patronage, and reputation management into entertainment gossip.

Cruise’s reported box-office failure supplies a weaker target against which the Trump team can manufacture relative success. His film’s losses do not improve the documentary’s reported return, reception, or artistic standing.

Loyalty replaces accountability

Beckman previously told Fox News that “everybody embraced” the first lady. The reported figures do not establish anything so sweeping. They show a modest theatrical audience, severe critical rejection, and an unusually large divide between critics and audience reviewers.

That gap cannot by itself prove manipulation or even explain why viewers differed so sharply. But Beckman’s rhetoric reveals the political use of fandom: support from committed admirers is presented as universal approval, while contrary evidence is reduced to something that can be managed through selective metrics.

The durable product is access

The larger pattern is familiar: powerful political figures do not need an uncontested success when aligned institutions keep financing the next vehicle and loyal operatives can redefine the previous result. Failure becomes a branding problem, not a material constraint.

The Cruise boast is therefore less a victory lap than a demonstration of insulation. The documentary could reportedly cost tens of millions, earn far less worldwide, receive brutal reviews, and still lead to another Amazon series. In systems organized around access and political value, the numbers need not justify the project. They merely need to be rearranged until power can call itself popular.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: A-list movie star targeted by Melania Trump team with ‘weird flex’ about box office bomb

item.title: Restaurant meltdown puts Trump’s treasury chief under fire: 'He’s got a temper’
item.description:
What happened

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the official under fire. AlterNet, citing Wall Street Journal reporting, says CodePink activists confronted him over U.S. sanctions at Reveler’s Hour in Washington in December 2025. Bessent allegedly called them “ignorant,” berated the restaurant owner for not removing them and, according to the owner, spat into his own food before leaving.

The restaurant episode fits a broader account from current and former Treasury officials, who described Bessent shouting at senior and junior employees and staff trying to avoid him when angry. At a June Senate hearing, Bessent also acknowledged telling Federal Housing Finance Agency chief Bill Pulte that he would “kick his a——,” while denying that he had threatened to punch him.

The White House defended Bessent’s “professionalism and accountability.” Steve Bannon offered a less sanitized assessment: Bessent, he said, has “a tripwire” and a temper.

The power is at Treasury

The protesters could disrupt a dinner. Bessent controls a department whose sanctions and financial-enforcement machinery can affect governments, companies and populations far beyond that restaurant. That imbalance is the political fact the personality-driven coverage risks obscuring.

The consequential conduct is not that an activist embarrassed a Cabinet secretary in public. It is that a powerful official reportedly responded to opposition by demanding that a business owner remove the people confronting him—and that employees inside his department allegedly organize around avoiding his anger.

Management by intimidation

A Cabinet secretary shouting loudly enough to be heard outside meetings is not merely displaying a colorful temperament. When subordinates must calculate how to evade an angry superior, intimidation becomes part of the institution’s operating structure.

The personnel record makes that structure more serious. The Journal reportedly found that dozens of officials lacking Senate confirmation had left or been dismissed, along with seven Senate-confirmed officials, only one of whom had been replaced. The article does not establish why every departure occurred, but widespread vacancies combined with volatile leadership create an obvious risk: decisions become concentrated around the secretary while institutional expertise and internal resistance diminish.

Accountability turned upside down

The White House’s invocation of “professionalism and accountability” does not answer the reported conduct. It reverses the meaning of those words. The official accused of berating workers and demanding the removal of protesters is presented as the agent of accountability, while the people subject to his authority are reduced to anonymous testimony about surviving his management.

Donald Trump’s joke that Bessent had “created a monster” similarly turns a governing problem into entertainment. The administration is not powerless before Bessent’s behavior. The president appointed him, publicly praised him and, through the White House, defended him. If the reports are accurate, the conduct persists because the institution with the power to impose consequences has chosen endorsement instead.

The convenient spectacle

The restaurant details are vivid, especially the allegation that Bessent spat into his own food. They are also politically convenient. A bizarre scene invites readers to treat the story as gossip about an irascible man rather than scrutiny of how executive power is exercised.

Even Bannon’s description narrows the issue to temperament. A “tripwire” sounds like a personal defect that unpredictably activates. But the reported targets were not peers with equal power: they included restaurant staff, junior employees and officials answerable to Bessent. Anger aimed downward is not politically neutral, whatever its psychological cause.

Power without restraint

This story reveals a familiar governing pattern: aggression is recast as decisiveness, staff depletion as accountability and abusive conduct as personality. The euphemisms protect the officeholder while transferring the practical burden to employees, business owners and anyone challenging policy.

The central question is therefore not whether Scott Bessent has a temper. It is why an administration treats reported intimidation as evidence of strong management—and what happens to a powerful department when loyalty to the person at the top matters more than restraint, expertise or dissent.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Restaurant meltdown puts Trump’s treasury chief under fire: ‘He’s got a temper’
