item.title: Fashion guru exposes damning detail in Trump's 'cheap' rally suit: 'I wonder why’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that menswear writer Derek Guy identified President Donald Trump’s Nebraska rally suit as a Jos. A. Bank garment made overseas, typically in countries including China and Bangladesh. Guy contrasted it with the company’s Joseph Abboud line, which he said is made in the United States, and asked why Trump chose “the cheap import” instead.

Trump wore the suit Tuesday at a rally in Grand Island, where he campaigned for Republican candidates including Sen. Pete Ricketts ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. RawStory presents the choice as conflicting with Trump’s claims that his administration is reviving American business, but the article does not establish why he selected that particular suit.

Power wears the contradiction

The suit matters only because Trump has made domestic production a political test for everyone else. A president can shape tariffs, procurement priorities, trade policy and the terms of his party’s economic message. Workers and consumers then absorb the consequences. His wardrobe is not policy, but it exposes how little personal discipline his rhetoric demands from the person wielding that power.

There is no evidence here that Trump personally inspected the label or knowingly rejected an American-made alternative. That limits what can responsibly be claimed about motive. It does not erase the contradiction between nationalist branding and the reported origin of the product he displayed while campaigning.

The choice was Trump’s

RawStory’s headline turns Guy’s observation into an “exposure,” but the underlying fact is simpler: Trump appeared at his own political rally in an imported suit. The relevant agency belongs to Trump and whoever manages his clothing—not to Bangladesh, China, retailers or consumers navigating the market his policies help structure.

Calling the garment “cheap” adds class signaling without sharpening the political case. Price is not the issue. The issue is that the country’s most powerful advocate of economic nationalism reportedly wore a foreign-made product while asking voters to trust his commitment to American industry.

A label is not an economic record

RawStory gestures toward stalled hiring as if one photographed suit can explain or prove the administration’s economic performance. It cannot. Nor does the article provide enough detail about those economic figures—their period, measure or source—to sustain a broader causal claim.

That weak framing lets the spectacle displace the harder inquiry: which businesses benefited from Trump’s decisions, which workers did not, and whether his administration’s policies produced the domestic revival he advertised. A clothing label can reveal hypocrisy. It cannot substitute for an accounting.

Nationalism for sale

The larger pattern is political branding without reciprocal obligation. Economic nationalism becomes a demand imposed downward: workers are told whom to blame, companies are rewarded for patriotic messaging, and consumers are instructed to treat purchasing as national loyalty. The leader remains free to consume globally while presenting himself as the embodiment of domestic renewal.

That asymmetry is the story. The imported suit is not a scandal in itself. It is a small, unusually legible example of a system in which sacrifice is marketed to the public while consistency remains optional for the people in power.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Fashion guru exposes damning detail in Trump’s ‘cheap’ rally suit: ‘I wonder why’

item.title: 'What the hell?' Shock as USPS gets armed guards from firm accused of human rights abuses
item.description:
What happened

Raw Story reports that the U.S. Postal Service contracted with Prosegur to deploy nearly 1,000 armed security officers at at least 55 postal facilities, authorizing almost 40,000 hours of work each week. The contract’s value was redacted. The startled “what the hell?” came from postal contractor and researcher Claire McKean, reacting to a multinational security conglomerate assuming an armed role inside major public mail facilities.

USPS’s law-enforcement arm, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, said the guards deter people who might harm workers or compromise the mail and denied that the deployment was election-specific. Yet internal communications and job postings reportedly conflict over whether these contractors may detain people, exercise arrest authority, or present themselves as federal law-enforcement officers.

Postal workers and union officials alleged harassment, violence, deficient supervision and retaliation connected to contract guards. Prosegur said it could not find the incidents or complaints described by Raw Story and declined to discuss the USPS account on confidentiality grounds. A 2022 inspector-general report had already found serious deficiencies in oversight of Prosegur’s unarmed personnel, while overseas the company has faced allegations of labor and human-rights abuses and was linked to a price-fixing case in Chile.

The state chose privatized force

The institution holding power here is USPS, acting through the Postal Inspection Service. It selected the contractor, determined where armed guards would operate and withheld the contract price from public view. Prosegur supplies the personnel, but the federal agency created the arrangement and retains responsibility for exposing its workforce to it.

That distinction matters because the story’s most consequential fact is not that a controversial company exists. It is that a public institution chose to purchase coercive power from that company despite documented oversight failures. The 2022 inspector-general report found that 30 percent of reviewed contractors lacked proper security clearances, that USPS inadequately measured Prosegur’s performance and that auditors could not verify required training. Those were warnings about the same basic governance problem now attached to firearms.

The agency’s stated rationale—security and deterrence—does not explain the reported scale or distribution. Postal Police Officers Association executive director Frank Albergo said deployment was based on facility headcount rather than criminal risk. If accurate, USPS is arming facilities according to workforce size without publicly demonstrating the danger those weapons are supposed to address.

Authority without accountability

USPS has produced no coherent public description of what these guards may do. Prosegur advertised positions involving “arrest control,” restraint and detention support. A September 2026 postal memo reportedly called the guards federal law-enforcement officers. Yet an August 2026 employee briefing said they would neither make arrests nor portray themselves as police.

That is not a minor communications defect. An armed person’s authority must be unmistakable to the workers subject to it. Ambiguity over detention and arrest powers expands practical coercion: employees confronting a uniformed guard cannot safely pause the encounter to resolve conflicting memos.

Training sharpens the disparity. Albergo said career postal police receive at least 1,440 hours, while Raw Story cited research finding that armed-guard requirements vary widely by state and average roughly 40 hours. USPS is therefore substituting workers with uncertain authority and uneven training for a specialized federal police workforce, while declining to answer the central question of what powers the substitutes possess.

Workers bear the risk

The article’s weakest framing is its emphasis on shock. Surprise is not the political issue. Control is.

In Charlotte, union president Miriam Bell said a worker reported being shoved and punched by a guard in April 2024, then placed on emergency status that could have led to termination. Bell also said another employee was fired after a guard interpreted a comment about someone grabbing his weapon as an actual intention to do so; the union is contesting that dismissal. These remain attributed allegations, and Prosegur said it found no corresponding incidents or complaints. But USPS’s response, as reported, was not to grant Bell’s request for trained postal police.

The foreseeable imbalance is severe. Contractors carry weapons and exercise authority inside the workplace; employees who challenge their conduct may face discipline from postal management. Whatever the final resolution of the individual allegations, the structure protects the institution and contractor more effectively than it protects the workforce.

The union issue is structural

Bell called the arrangement union busting. The reporting does not establish that as USPS’s proven motive, and Albergo’s accusation that the agency was “in cahoots” with Prosegur is likewise an allegation, not demonstrated collusion.

The underlying incentives nevertheless deserve scrutiny. Career postal police are unionized public employees with standardized training and defined institutional obligations. Contract guards place recruitment, employment and parts of supervision behind a private intermediary. A former Prosegur vice president previously testified during negotiations that the company’s personnel could perform postal-police work apart from making arrests, according to Bjork and Albergo.

USPS has found money for a large contract workforce while maintaining only 11 active bargaining-unit postal police officers across Chicago, Albergo said. One suburban facility was slated to receive 12 armed guards. Even without proof of an anti-union motive, the operational choice weakens public labor and transfers leverage to a corporation whose contract value the public is not permitted to see.

Public power, private insulation

This is a familiar political conversion: government does not eliminate coercive authority; it outsources that authority and obscures responsibility. The agency can call the guards contractors. The contractor can invoke confidentiality. Job postings, internal memos and employee briefings can contradict one another. Workers still confront the gun.

Prosegur’s international record increases the due-diligence burden rather than proving misconduct at USPS facilities. Raw Story cites a Chilean price-fixing penalty and a 2024 recommendation from Norway’s Council on Ethics to exclude the company from investment because of risks tied to serious abuses in Brazil. Those facts should have prompted exceptional transparency and oversight. The reported response was a redacted price, evasive answers about authority and an expansion to dozens of facilities.

The systemic failure is not confusion. It is an accountability design in which authority is dispersed just enough for every powerful institution to disclaim part of the outcome. USPS made the choice. Prosegur profits from it. Armed contractors exercise the resulting power. Postal workers absorb the consequences.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘What the hell?’ Shock as USPS gets armed guards from firm accused of human rights abuses

item.title: Trump's long gaze at Natalie Harp during rally repulses onlookers: 'Disgusting’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump appeared to stare at senior aide Natalie Harp’s legs during a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, held for Sen. Pete Ricketts. The moment came shortly after Trump called Harp “the perfect person.”

The outlet says the clip repulsed several social-media commentators, including activist Derek Cressman, Democratic strategist Mike Nellis, and podcaster Joanne Carducci. Their reactions supply the headline’s “disgusting” verdict; the article offers no comment from Trump or Harp and establishes no further consequence.

Where the power sits

Trump is the president. Harp is his aide. Whatever anyone infers from the footage, that hierarchy matters more than the strangers posting reaction GIFs.

RawStory describes Harp as an unusually attentive subordinate who follows Trump with flattering news printouts and has written him admiring letters. But eccentric devotion does not erase institutional rank. Trump controls access and status inside his operation; Harp does not hold equivalent power over him.

Reaction is not reporting

The article turns a brief visual moment into a procession of disgusted posts. That proves the clip circulated and provoked revulsion among selected critics. It does not establish Trump’s thoughts, Harp’s interpretation, or misconduct beyond the observable gaze.

The framing is weak because it substitutes commentary for development. “Onlookers” sounds broad; the evidence presented is a handful of named social-media reactions. One critic’s insult toward Harp is especially revealing: contempt travels downhill easily, even when the central figure is the president who created the spectacle.

The misdirection

Calling Harp “psycho” shifts attention from the man with presidential authority to the woman working beneath him. RawStory amplifies that insult while offering no evidence that Harp caused the incident described in its headline.

That is a familiar political-media failure: a powerful man behaves conspicuously, and coverage expands the target list to include a less powerful woman near him. Her reported flattery may illuminate how Trump’s information environment operates. It does not make her responsible for where he looked.

The machinery of flattery

The more politically significant detail is not the gaze but Harp’s reported role as a supplier of favorable coverage. A president surrounded by aides who curate praise is being served an information system organized around affirmation.

The article does not establish who designed that system or how it affected any decision. Still, the arrangement it describes raises a sharper institutional question than the viral clip: what reaches presidential attention when proximity is rewarded through flattering printouts and personal devotion?

Spectacle protects the structure

Outrage clips are efficient because they require little investigation and produce immediate engagement. Their political cost is that disgust replaces scrutiny. The audience is invited to recoil at a gesture and ridicule an aide, while the architecture of presidential access remains largely unexamined.

The systemic error is not noticing degrading conduct. It is stopping there. Political coverage should identify the hierarchy, examine who controls information, and trace consequences. Otherwise, the powerful figure remains the center of attention while escaping the more consequential inquiry into how his power is maintained.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s long gaze at Natalie Harp during rally repulses onlookers: ‘Disgusting’

item.title: CBS News forced into embarrassing takedown over disgraced GOP speaker's obituary
item.description:
What happened

CBS News deleted and replaced a social media post announcing former House Speaker Dennis Hastert’s death after criticism that it reduced his criminal case to “violating banking laws” while omitting the sexual abuse those violations concealed. According to RawStory, CBS acknowledged that its original post had “missed the mark.”

The replacement said Hastert had been jailed on charges connected to concealing hush-money payments covering up sexual abuse. But The Daily Beast reported that the obituary itself still foregrounded the banking offense and did not mention his abuse of boys until the end of its second paragraph.

Hastert, Republican House speaker from 1999 to 2007, received a 15-month sentence in 2016 for evading banking regulations while hiding payments to a victim. The statute of limitations prevented child-sex-abuse charges. At sentencing, U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin called him a “serial child molester.” Hastert served 13 months and was released in 2017.

The euphemism protected the powerful

“Banking laws” was legally relevant and morally evasive. It described the mechanism of Hastert’s prosecution while suppressing the conduct that made the case significant.

That distinction matters because Hastert was not merely a private citizen with a financial conviction. He had occupied one of the country’s most powerful elected offices. An obituary that leads with technical charges and delays the underlying abuse turns institutional disgrace into regulatory trivia.

CBS made the framing choice

No vague appeal to editorial confusion can erase agency. CBS News wrote the post, structured the obituary and decided which facts readers would encounter first. After criticism, it changed the social-media language while reportedly leaving the obituary’s minimizing hierarchy largely intact.

The correction therefore addressed the most visible embarrassment without fully confronting the editorial failure. CBS did not lack the central fact: a federal judge had explicitly characterized Hastert’s conduct, and the hush-money scheme existed to conceal abuse. The network initially chose a narrower formulation.

The weaker actors disappeared

The framing shifted attention from abused students to the prominent official who paid to conceal his conduct. That is a familiar inversion: the powerful man’s procedural exposure becomes the story, while the people harmed become delayed context.

The expired statute of limitations also demands precision. Hastert was not convicted of child sexual abuse, and the reporting does not justify saying that he was. But that legal distinction does not require journalism to obscure what Judge Durkin found at sentencing or what the payments were reported to have concealed.

Reputation management as news judgment

RawStory places the episode within turmoil at CBS News following Bari Weiss’s installation as editor-in-chief by David Ellison after Paramount acquired the network. It reports declining ratings, prominent departures and uncertainty around “60 Minutes.” Those claims provide institutional context, but they do not by themselves establish why this obituary was written as it was.

The text does establish something narrower and damning enough: CBS softened the defining scandal of a former speaker’s public record, then revised its presentation only after backlash. Whether that resulted from ideology, incompetence or reflexive deference is not proven here. The effect was the same—elite reputation received more protection than victims received clarity.

The systemic error

Political power persists after office through titles, institutional memory and the conventions used to describe disgraced officials. Hastert’s speakership remained prominent; the abuse was initially omitted from the post and subordinated in the obituary.

That ordering is not neutral. Journalism tells readers what matters through placement as much as wording. When a newsroom foregrounds the technical offense and buries the underlying harm, it launders power through procedure—and calls the resulting distortion an obituary.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: CBS News forced into embarrassing takedown over disgraced GOP speaker’s obituary

item.title: 'All lies!' CBS insider erupts after new boss' town hall rankles network staff
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that a CBS News insider dismissed Skydance CEO David Ellison’s promise to protect newsroom independence as “all lies” during the company’s first town hall after the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger on October 6, 2026. According to media correspondent Justin Baragona, the source cited Ellison’s alleged failure to honor a similar promise after acquiring Paramount.

CNN anchor Anderson Cooper questioned Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz about editorial interference and a plan to cut $6 billion in costs over three years. They said most savings would not come from staffing, while Ellison declared that the company could not “cut” its way to growth. Employees reportedly disagreed over Cooper’s participation: one CBS source viewed it as degrading theater, while another CBS source and a CNN source saw his questioning as a defense of newsroom staff.

Ownership is the power

The decisive power here does not belong to Cooper, anonymous journalists, or even newsroom leadership. It belongs to Ellison and the executives controlling budgets, staffing and the corporate structure surrounding CBS News and CNN.

Editorial independence is fragile when the person promising it also commands the machinery that can quietly restrict it. Owners need not dictate a headline to shape coverage. They can eliminate positions, reorganize desks, select executives, narrow reporting priorities and make costly investigations harder to sustain. A verbal pledge does not counterbalance that authority.

The numbers outrank the reassurance

A plan to remove $6 billion in costs over three years is an institutional decision with editorial consequences, even if executives say most savings will come from somewhere other than staffing. RawStory’s account does not establish how much will come from layoffs or which operations will absorb the cuts. That uncertainty is precisely why Ellison’s reassurance cannot settle the matter.

“You cannot cut your way to growth” sounds less convincing when delivered alongside an enormous cost-cutting target. The meaningful test is not whether executives answer difficult questions smoothly at a town hall. It is where the cuts land, which reporting capacity disappears and who gains greater control after the restructuring.

Cooper became the spectacle

The competing reactions to Cooper risk moving attention away from the people making the decisions. Whether he was compelled to perform corporate legitimacy or chose the role to defend colleagues, he did not set the savings target and cannot guarantee editorial autonomy.

Making the anchor’s participation the controversy turns a question of ownership into a question of personality. Cooper could ask every necessary question and still possess no power to enforce the answers. The town hall offered employees a visible exchange; management retained the authority that matters after the cameras stopped.

Trust requires constraints

The anonymous CBS source’s accusation is serious but remains an attributed judgment, not independently established proof in RawStory’s account. The report provides no detailed evidence about the earlier promise the source says Ellison broke. That limits what can responsibly be concluded about deception.

It does not, however, make skepticism irrational. Corporate promises of independence are structurally weak when their enforcement depends on the restraint of the executive making them. Credibility would require observable limits on interference, transparent accounting of cuts and protections that survive management’s shifting incentives—not applause for a polished answer.

The systemic error

Media consolidation repeatedly asks journalists and audiences to treat concentrated corporate power as harmless until a visible abuse occurs. By then, lost staff, abandoned investigations and altered newsroom priorities may be difficult to reconstruct.

The larger pattern is not confusion about what “editorial independence” means. It is a power arrangement in which owners define the budget, control the hierarchy and then ask employees to trust that those tools will not shape journalism. The argument over whether Cooper “sent a signal” only underscores the imbalance: journalists can send signals; executives can make decisions.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘All lies!’ CBS insider erupts after new boss’ town hall rankles network staff

item.title: Jeanine Pirro ensnared by grand jury misconduct questions amid Reflecting Pool fallout
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that lawyers for three-time Olympian David Hearn asked the Justice and Interior departments’ inspectors general to investigate whether U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office improperly secured a felony indictment over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Prosecutors dropped the case after conceding that a botched coating installation—not Hearn—caused the damage. On October 1, D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed the case with prejudice, preventing prosecutors from reviving it.

According to the lawyers’ letter, the government’s only grand-jury damages witness initially said the pool was already substantially damaged, the same repairs would have been necessary regardless, and he could not quantify any loss caused by Hearn. Recalled 21 minutes later, he said the damage would “definitely” exceed $1,000—the threshold separating a misdemeanor from a felony carrying up to 10 years in prison. The letter asks investigators to determine whether prosecutors recalled him to manufacture an unsupported felony figure.

The letter also alleges that Pirro publicly prejudged Hearn’s guilt, personally questioned a defense expert despite his refusal to discuss the case, and misled the court about when her office learned of widespread installation defects. Pirro’s office did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment. The allegations remain requests for watchdog investigation, not adjudicated findings of professional misconduct.

The power was prosecutorial

Hearn touched a loose piece of coating. Pirro’s office controlled the investigation, the grand-jury presentation, the charge and the threat of a decade in prison. That imbalance is the story’s governing fact.

A prosecutor does not merely participate in such a case. The prosecutor decides which evidence the grand jury hears and whether uncertain damage becomes a misdemeanor allegation, a felony indictment or no charge at all. According to the letter, Pirro’s office possessed a National Park Service assessment on July 1 that attributed no measurable loss to Hearn, then obtained the indictment on July 2 anyway.

The inspector generals’ central task is therefore not to examine some generalized “fallout.” It is to determine what government officials knew, what they presented, and why the decisive damages testimony changed after a 21-minute interruption.

Politics entered through the front door

Pirro announced the indictment at a July 2 press conference, reportedly called the alleged conduct “anarchy” and “criminal behavior,” and said the matter was a priority for both President Donald Trump and herself. Those remarks did more than publicize a prosecution. They placed presidential preference and the U.S. attorney’s reputation alongside the evidence before the case had been tested.

The political pressure later became explicit. After Pirro’s office moved to dismiss, Trump accused her of having “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.” CBS News reported that she then carried a box of case evidence to the White House and presented it to him. Judge Edelman cited the danger that presidential pressure, apparently motivated at least partly by Hearn’s political views, could produce another prosecution for a crime prosecutors had concluded he did not commit.

That sequence exposes a degraded chain of accountability: the president publicly demands severity, the U.S. attorney advertises alignment with that priority, and a defendant’s protection ultimately depends on a judge barring the government from trying again.

“Botched” is too gentle

Calling this merely a failed prosecution would conceal the alleged conduct that requires scrutiny. The lawyers say prosecutors charged Hearn despite evidence of installation defects, elicited the felony-threshold estimate only after recalling a witness, and later gave the court a timeline contradicted by records already in their possession.

Those remain allegations. But they are specific, documented allegations about the manipulation or mishandling of state power—not an innocent disagreement over a difficult fact pattern. The case collapsed because prosecutors acknowledged they could not prove Hearn caused damage at all.

The weaker actor here was not the institution facing embarrassment over a defective pool coating. It was the individual threatened with felony punishment while government officials converted an infrastructure failure into a spectacle of personal criminality.

The convenient scapegoat

The government had a damaged national landmark and a visible person who had touched it. Prosecuting that person offered a politically marketable explanation: disorder came from an alleged offender, not from a failed installation overseen by public authorities.

That framing redirected attention from defective work toward “anarchy.” It also turned uncertainty about causation and cost into prosecutorial leverage. When institutional failure can be repackaged as individual deviance, officials gain a scapegoat while the public loses an honest account of what went wrong.

Punishment before proof

This episode reflects a broader pattern in politicized law enforcement: announce guilt, maximize the charge, force the accused to disprove the government’s story, and describe retreat as weakness once the evidence fails.

The requested watchdog investigation must establish whether professional rules or Justice Department policies were violated. The political lesson is already visible in the reported record. When prosecutors treat presidential approval as a measure of resolve, evidentiary restraint becomes “choking,” dismissal becomes surrender, and the machinery of criminal justice becomes a stage for demonstrating loyalty. The defendant bears the danger; the institution calls the performance enforcement.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Jeanine Pirro ensnared by grand jury misconduct questions amid Reflecting Pool fallout

item.title: CBS News forced into embarrassing takedown over disgraced GOP speaker's obituary
item.description:
What happened

CBS News deleted and replaced a social media post announcing former House Speaker Dennis Hastert’s death after criticism that it reduced his criminal case to “violating banking laws” while omitting the sexual abuse those violations concealed. According to RawStory, CBS acknowledged that its original post had “missed the mark.”

The replacement said Hastert had been jailed on charges connected to concealing hush-money payments covering up sexual abuse. But The Daily Beast reported that the obituary itself still foregrounded the banking offense and did not mention his abuse of boys until the end of its second paragraph.

Hastert, Republican House speaker from 1999 to 2007, received a 15-month sentence in 2016 for evading banking regulations while hiding payments to a victim. The statute of limitations prevented child-sex-abuse charges. At sentencing, U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin called him a “serial child molester.” Hastert served 13 months and was released in 2017.

The euphemism protected the powerful

“Banking laws” was legally relevant and morally evasive. It described the mechanism of Hastert’s prosecution while suppressing the conduct that made the case significant.

That distinction matters because Hastert was not merely a private citizen with a financial conviction. He had occupied one of the country’s most powerful elected offices. An obituary that leads with technical charges and delays the underlying abuse turns institutional disgrace into regulatory trivia.

CBS made the framing choice

No vague appeal to editorial confusion can erase agency. CBS News wrote the post, structured the obituary and decided which facts readers would encounter first. After criticism, it changed the social-media language while reportedly leaving the obituary’s minimizing hierarchy largely intact.

The correction therefore addressed the most visible embarrassment without fully confronting the editorial failure. CBS did not lack the central fact: a federal judge had explicitly characterized Hastert’s conduct, and the hush-money scheme existed to conceal abuse. The network initially chose a narrower formulation.

The weaker actors disappeared

The framing shifted attention from abused students to the prominent official who paid to conceal his conduct. That is a familiar inversion: the powerful man’s procedural exposure becomes the story, while the people harmed become delayed context.

The expired statute of limitations also demands precision. Hastert was not convicted of child sexual abuse, and the reporting does not justify saying that he was. But that legal distinction does not require journalism to obscure what Judge Durkin found at sentencing or what the payments were reported to have concealed.

Reputation management as news judgment

RawStory places the episode within turmoil at CBS News following Bari Weiss’s installation as editor-in-chief by David Ellison after Paramount acquired the network. It reports declining ratings, prominent departures and uncertainty around “60 Minutes.” Those claims provide institutional context, but they do not by themselves establish why this obituary was written as it was.

The text does establish something narrower and damning enough: CBS softened the defining scandal of a former speaker’s public record, then revised its presentation only after backlash. Whether that resulted from ideology, incompetence or reflexive deference is not proven here. The effect was the same—elite reputation received more protection than victims received clarity.

The systemic error

Political power persists after office through titles, institutional memory and the conventions used to describe disgraced officials. Hastert’s speakership remained prominent; the abuse was initially omitted from the post and subordinated in the obituary.

That ordering is not neutral. Journalism tells readers what matters through placement as much as wording. When a newsroom foregrounds the technical offense and buries the underlying harm, it launders power through procedure—and calls the resulting distortion an obituary.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: CBS News forced into embarrassing takedown over disgraced GOP speaker’s obituary

item.title: Trump damns NYT 'to hell' in late-night tantrum over 'doctored' photo of his resort
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump spent Monday night accusing The New York Times of doctoring a photograph of Trump National Doral Miami. He said the image made his property look “shoddy” and posted a brighter picture that he claimed showed the real facade.

But the two images were not the same photograph: they showed different landscaping, fountains, framing, and lighting. The comparison therefore did not establish that the Times altered its image. Newsweek had sought comment from the newspaper and photographer Scott McIntyre.

The photograph accompanied reporting on Trump’s plan to hold the G20 summit at his own private club. According to the account cited by RawStory, Trump made at least $2.2 billion last year, accepted a luxury jet from Qatar that the government then spent hundreds of millions of dollars retrofitting, and obtained relief from back taxes that could exceed $100 million.

The president is not the injured party

The institutional power here belongs to Trump. He is the president, commands the federal executive branch, owns the resort under discussion, and possesses a mass political platform from which to attack the journalists covering him.

Yet his posts recast him as the victim of a photograph. The alleged offense was not a government action against him, a legal judgment, or even a demonstrated falsification. It was an unflattering image of a business he owns.

That inversion matters. Trump’s grievance asks the public to treat scrutiny of presidential self-enrichment as persecution of a private businessman. The presidency and the property are kept rhetorically separate when accountability is at issue, then fused when presidential attention can advertise and defend the property.

A brighter picture is not evidence

Trump’s rebuttal did not answer the underlying reporting. It substituted resort marketing imagery for a news photograph and treated visual polish as proof of journalistic misconduct.

Because the pictures were taken from different perspectives under different conditions, placing them side by side establishes almost nothing about whether either was altered. RawStory’s description identifies visible differences; it does not report evidence that the Times doctored its photograph.

The accusation nevertheless serves a political function. It moves the argument from whether a president should direct an international summit toward his own club to whether the club was photographed attractively enough. A conflict involving public authority and private revenue becomes a dispute over curb appeal.

The missing scandal is organized opposition

Trump’s earlier attempt to place the 2019 G7 summit at Doral collapsed after Republican backlash. RawStory says the reported G20 plan has drawn almost no organized protest.

That contrast exposes the enabling structure. Trump can propose using presidential power to route a major diplomatic event through his own property because the institutions capable of imposing political costs are apparently imposing few. The consequential decision is not merely his proposal. It is also the choice by political allies and organized interests to treat it as tolerable.

Paul Rosenzweig’s observation that Trump has “defined deviancy down” describes the result: conduct becomes normalized not because its character changes, but because repetition exhausts resistance. What once produced intraparty backlash returns in an environment trained to regard each new conflict as background noise.

The outrage is the diversion

The central issue is not whether Doral looks beautiful, shabby, dark, or bright. It is whether the presidency is being used in ways that benefit the president’s private interests.

Trump’s attack supplies an easier spectacle: an angry post, an insult, and an unsupported allegation against the press. Coverage can then revolve around the tantrum while the underlying claims—billions in income, tax relief potentially exceeding $100 million, the Qatari jet and its retrofit costs, and the proposed summit venue—receive less sustained attention.

That is not simple confusion. It is a reliable form of misdirection, whatever Trump’s private motive: attack the messenger, narrow the dispute to an emotionally vivid detail, and force critics to litigate the detail while institutional power operates elsewhere.

Power survives through lowered expectations

The larger pattern is normalization through saturation. A president’s private business interests, foreign gifts, tax treatment, and control over government events should invite concentrated scrutiny from Congress, political allies, and the press. Instead, the story can be displaced by an argument over which photograph makes a resort look nicer.

Authoritarian political habits do not require every accusation to succeed. They benefit when power can generate endless false or unsupported controversies, compel institutions to answer them, and make the underlying abuse seem like merely one more item in the churn.

The systemic failure is therefore larger than Trump’s late-night posts. It is an accountability structure so weakened by repetition and political cowardice that a president can redirect attention from the use of public office toward the lighting on his hotel—and reasonably expect much of the political system to follow.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump damns NYT ‘to hell’ in late-night tantrum over ‘doctored’ photo of his resort

item.title: Impeachment on the table after Trump 'jokes' Iran can bomb LA or San Diego: analysts
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump told a Monday rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego while he defended the costs of war as a small price for national and global safety. The crowd applauded, according to the report.

On Tuesday’s “Morning Joe,” MS NOW hosts rejected efforts to excuse the remark as a joke. Joe Scarborough said comparable comments by another president would produce immediate impeachment demands. The reporting identifies no formal impeachment effort, introduced resolution, or commitment from any member of Congress; “impeachment on the table” describes the hosts’ argument about the response such rhetoric would ordinarily provoke.

The power behind the words

The speaker was not a comedian, pundit, or powerless provocateur. He was the president, entrusted with military authority and the protection of every American city—including cities whose voters may oppose him.

That institutional power is what makes the remark politically significant. A president discussing war costs chose mass destruction in two American cities as his punch line. Whether he intended a literal policy statement is not established here. What is established is that he treated millions of residents as rhetorically expendable while selling the public on the burdens of war.

“Just joking” is the escape hatch

Calling the comment a joke does not explain it. It shields the president from accountability while preserving the political function of the remark: identifying disfavored places as disposable and inviting supporters to enjoy the provocation.

The defense also misdirects scrutiny toward the audience’s interpretation. Americans are asked whether they are too literal, too offended, or insufficiently familiar with Trump’s style. The relevant decision belongs to Trump. He selected Los Angeles and San Diego, named their destruction, and did so from the presidency’s platform.

Impeachment without impeachers

RawStory’s framing overstates what its own account demonstrates. Scarborough argued that such language would trigger impeachment calls under a different president; the article does not report that lawmakers had begun an impeachment proceeding or even issued the call highlighted in the headline.

That distinction matters. Cable-news condemnation is not congressional action. Congress holds the constitutional power to pursue impeachment, and the story offers no evidence that its members used it. Turning a hypothetical comparison into an impending institutional response makes outrage look like accountability when no accountable institution has moved.

Selective belonging

Scarborough’s comparison points to the larger pattern: partisan geography has become a license to rank Americans by political worth. Los Angeles and San Diego are not abstractions. They are populous American communities, yet Trump’s formulation cast their destruction as an acceptable cost in a performance about national safety.

The contradiction is the point. “Keeping our country safe” cannot coherently include shrugging at the annihilation of parts of that country. This rhetoric narrows the nation to the president’s favored constituencies and relegates everyone else to targets, burdens, or props.

The system rewards the provocation

The institutional failure extends beyond one remark. Trump supplies the spectacle, defenders convert it into humor, television converts it into an impeachment debate, and Congress—at least in the reporting provided—remains absent. Each layer displaces attention from the one concrete fact: a sitting president publicly invoked the destruction of American cities while justifying war’s costs.

The systemic lesson is not that every grotesque statement automatically becomes an impeachable offense. It is that concentrated power now travels with a mature machinery for dissolving responsibility. The president provokes, allies minimize, media inflate hypothetical consequences, and the institutions with actual authority avoid appearing in the frame.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Impeachment on the table after Trump ‘jokes’ Iran can bomb LA or San Diego: analysts

item.title: MAGA erupts over 'chilling' FBI surveillance revelation: 'Maybe it's time to start over’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reported on October 6, 2026, that newly released documents showed the FBI monitored Melania and Barron Trump’s travel and tapped Susie Wiles’ phone during special counsel Jack Smith’s investigation into Donald Trump’s handling of classified documents after leaving office. The story does not explain the legal authority, investigative purpose, duration, or scope of those measures.

Prominent Trump allies responded by accusing the Biden administration and Justice Department of political persecution. Senator Mike Lee suggested the FBI might not deserve to survive; Stephen Miller alleged a “seditious conspiracy”; Representative Randy Fine called the episode “1000 times worse than Watergate.” RawStory reports the outrage, but supplies too little underlying evidence to determine whether the surveillance was unlawful, improper, routine, or justified.

Power without proof

The FBI and Justice Department held the coercive institutional power here. They could investigate, obtain records, conduct surveillance and impose costs that private citizens cannot. That authority warrants exacting scrutiny—especially when an investigation reaches a former president’s family and future chief of staff.

But scrutiny requires facts. The report does not establish who authorized each measure, what judicial oversight existed, what investigators sought or whether anyone exceeded lawful authority. Calling the conduct an “abuse of power” before answering those questions is a political verdict masquerading as an evidentiary one.

Outrage as leverage

Trump’s allies are not powerless targets yelling from the margins. Blackburn, Lee and Fine are federal lawmakers. Miller serves in the White House. Wiles is identified as chief of staff. These figures possess legislative, executive and public platforms capable of directing investigations, changing laws and reshaping agencies.

Their language therefore carries consequences. Lee’s suggestion that the FBI be dismantled is not merely emotional commentary; it is pressure from a senator against an institution that investigated his political movement’s leader. Fine’s declaration that Democrats must never again possess such power turns a dispute over investigative conduct into an argument for partisan control of state authority.

The missing standard

The central issue is not whether surveillance feels “chilling.” It is whether investigators had lawful grounds, observed required safeguards and limited their actions to legitimate investigative needs. RawStory provides none of the details necessary to answer those questions.

That evidentiary void benefits the loudest actors. “Weaponization,” “seditious conspiracy” and “Watergate” replace legal standards with escalating slogans. The rhetoric invites readers to treat proximity to Trump as proof of innocence and investigation of his circle as proof of misconduct. Neither conclusion follows from the facts presented.

Accountability or immunity

There are two distinct abuses worth guarding against: law-enforcement power used without proper basis, and political power used to intimidate institutions away from investigating influential people. The supplied reporting establishes neither abuse conclusively. It does, however, document powerful officials demanding institutional destruction and partisan exclusion before the public is given the underlying record.

That is the larger pattern: an unresolved question about government surveillance is converted into a loyalty test. Instead of demanding warrants, authorizations, dates and findings, Trump’s allies demand acceptance of their conclusion—and threaten the investigating institution’s legitimacy if it is not granted. When facts remain thin, concentrated political power does not wait for clarity. It fills the gap with commands.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: MAGA erupts over ‘chilling’ FBI surveillance revelation: ‘Maybe it’s time to start over’

item.title: Trump’s 'largest' jobs project hits embarrassing snag
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump announced on September 28 that construction had already begun on a $15 billion Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa. But Lee County officials said the company had not selected a final site, submitted permits or provided detailed plans, while local records showed no major property acquisition tied to the project that year.

The project remained contingent on state approval and extraordinary public support. After Trump’s announcement, Governor Kim Reynolds called a special legislative session, and Iowa lawmakers approved more than $1.3 billion in public funding and tax savings over ten years. Mesabi’s full application still required approval before Iowa could enter a contract.

Mesabi projected roughly 1,750 permanent jobs, thousands of temporary construction jobs and production beginning in 2030. Those remained company projections. AlterNet also cites CBS News reporting that Mesabi and Essar had previously missed deadlines and employment targets, including a Minnesota steel mill announced in 2008 but never built.

The announcement outran the project

Trump did not merely celebrate a proposal. He said building had started. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick declared the deal finished. The reported facts describe something far less developed: no final site, no permits, no detailed plans and no state contract.

That is not a minor scheduling snag. It is a direct conflict between an Oval Office presentation and the project’s documented status. The White House converted a conditional corporate proposal into a presidential accomplishment before Iowa had completed the decisions necessary to make it real.

Iowa holds the risk

Mesabi may receive the plant and its future revenue. Trump may claim the headline. But Iowa’s government controls the approvals, and Iowa taxpayers were positioned to absorb more than $1.3 billion in subsidies and tax savings over a decade.

Reynolds and the Legislature enabled that transfer. Iowa Economic Development Authority director Debi Durham said the special session would not have been necessary had Mesabi accepted the existing incentive structure. Republican state Sen. Dan Dawson’s objection—that taxpayers did not receive the best deal—cuts through the promotional language: state officials were improving the company’s terms after the president had already pronounced the transaction complete.

Jobs as leverage

The projected jobs supply the political pressure. Once officials attach 1,750 permanent positions and thousands of construction jobs to a proposal, scrutiny of the subsidy can be portrayed as hostility to employment rather than oversight of public money.

But projected employment is not employment, and a proposed 2030 production date is not an operating plant. The company’s reported history of missed deadlines makes those distinctions more important, not less. Public officials chose to advertise the benefits before securing the commitments that might produce them.

The snag is the sales pitch

Calling this an “embarrassing snag” understates what the reporting establishes. The unresolved site, approvals and financing conditions were not obstacles that suddenly appeared after construction began. They were evidence that construction had not begun as Trump claimed.

The weaker framing treats the contradiction as administrative confusion. The stronger, evidence-based conclusion is that the president and commerce secretary presented an unfinished, publicly subsidized negotiation as a completed industrial triumph. Whether that overstatement was intentional is not established by the reporting. Its political function is clear regardless: claim credit immediately, while state institutions and taxpayers confront the uncertainty later.

Government by premature victory

This episode exposes a durable governing pattern: spectacle moves faster than accountability. National officials announce certainty; state lawmakers assemble the subsidy; local authorities discover that the supposedly active project still lacks a site and permits.

The consequence is not confined to an inaccurate boast. Premature declarations distort public debate by making unresolved corporate demands appear inevitable. Once a project is branded historic from the Oval Office, local officials are pressured to validate the announcement with public money. Power writes the headline first. Everyone else is left to negotiate the facts underneath it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘largest’ jobs project hits embarrassing snag

item.title: GOP's panicked 'insurance policy' exposed as Trump's hand-picked candidate flails: report
item.description:
What happened

The reported “insurance policy” is a planned $5 million Republican spending push to defend Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. RawStory, citing Axios, reports that Graham—appointed to succeed her late brother, Lindsey Graham, and endorsed by President Donald Trump—was statistically tied with Democratic challenger Annie Andrews despite the state’s long Republican dominance.

According to the report, most of the money would fund television advertising identifying Andrews as a Democrat. Republican operatives described Graham as lacking an independent constituency, while a debate admission that national security was not her “thing” reinforced concerns about her readiness and support.

RawStory attributes the difficult Republican environment partly to rising costs associated with Trump’s war against Iran. The supplied reporting, however, does not provide evidence establishing how much that issue caused Graham’s polling weakness.

Power chose the candidate

Graham’s candidacy was built from institutional advantages: appointment, a prominent family name, presidential endorsement and now national party money. Voters did not create that arrangement. Republican power brokers did.

That makes the party’s predicament less mysterious than the panic-soaked framing suggests. The same political network that elevated Graham is now preparing to spend millions compensating for its choice. The party is not rescuing an outsider caught in bad circumstances. It is protecting an incumbent produced by appointment and inheritance.

The ad strategy gives away the weakness

The reported plan is not primarily to persuade voters that Graham is capable. It is to “remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat.” That is a strategy of partisan activation: make the opponent’s label carry more weight than the incumbent’s record, preparation or appeal.

In a state where Democrats have not won statewide office in two decades, the label may be powerful. But relying on it also exposes what Republicans apparently cannot rely on: enthusiasm for Graham herself. One operative’s blunt assessment—there is “no Darline Graham voter”—describes a candidate whose political value rests on Trump loyalists and a borrowed surname.

The surname is the asset

Graham reportedly dropped her married name during the campaign to emphasize the family name. That detail matters because it reveals the structure beneath the race: political identity is being assembled through recognition rather than earned through a distinct public profile.

Her reported admission that she was not well informed on national security is especially damaging for a Senate candidate, but it is not the central institutional failure. The deeper failure occurred when party leaders treated lineage and endorsement as sufficient qualifications, then reached for donor money when voters proved less compliant than expected.

The framing hides responsibility

Calling the expenditure an “insurance policy” sanitizes the transaction. Insurance ordinarily protects against an external hazard. Here, Republican institutions are spending $5 million against the foreseeable consequences of their own selection process.

The “flailing candidate” frame also concentrates responsibility on Graham’s performance while letting the people who appointed, endorsed and financed her recede into the background. She has agency over her campaign and statements. But the party has the greater power: it supplied the office, the validation and the rescue package.

Nor does one close polling snapshot prove that South Carolina has undergone a durable political realignment. It shows that, at the time of the reporting, Republicans considered a normally secure seat vulnerable enough to warrant substantial defensive spending.

The system protects its selections

This is how insulated party power reproduces itself. Leaders elevate a familiar name, assume partisan loyalty will finish the job and deploy national money when the candidate cannot generate sufficient support on her own.

The broader pattern is not simply nepotism or one weak campaign. It is an institutional preference for controllable succession over demonstrated political capacity. When that preference creates electoral risk, the party’s response is not accountability. It is advertising—paid for by a political apparatus determined to make voters fear the label opposite its own.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP’s panicked ‘insurance policy’ exposed as Trump’s hand-picked candidate flails: report

item.title: 'Nuts!' Judge hears 'damning' ABC arguments as experts tear into Trump's FCC chair live
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that ABC and Disney asked U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan to block FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s unusually early review of licenses held by eight ABC-owned stations. Carr ordered the April review one day after President Donald Trump urged ABC to fire Jimmy Kimmel. ABC alleges that the administration is targeting constitutionally protected programming it dislikes.

At Tuesday’s hearing in Washington, the government characterized the action as part of an investigation into ABC’s hiring practices and disputed the district court’s authority to intervene. ABC argued that the licensing process was being used as leverage before several licenses were eligible for renewal. Its attorney, Beth Wilkinson, said the pressure had already changed editorial decisions, including keeping political candidates off “The View” since February.

AliKhan questioned both sides and issued no reported ruling. The FCC promised to provide 48 hours’ notice before referring the licenses to a formal hearing.

The power is in the license

ABC is a wealthy corporation, but the relevant power belongs to the federal government. The FCC controls licenses necessary for ABC-owned stations to operate. Carr controls the agency’s review machinery. Trump used the presidency’s platform to call for ABC to lose licenses and to demand action against one of its hosts.

That structure matters more than the government’s insistence that no license has yet been revoked. A regulator does not need to complete a punishment to exercise coercive power. If opening an irregular proceeding forces a broadcaster to reconsider guests and programming, the pressure is already producing results.

The government reportedly conceded that ABC’s broadcasts are protected speech. Its defense therefore rests less on denying the right than on arguing that the court should wait while the agency keeps that right under administrative pressure.

Carr owns the decision

Carr ordered the early review. The administration’s lawyer defended it. Responsibility does not dissolve merely because the FCC has not issued a final revocation order.

The timing and scope described in the lawsuit sharpen ABC’s case: Carr acted after Trump’s demand concerning Kimmel, and the review allegedly included ABC’s decision not to carry a Trump speech live in prime time. Meanwhile, the FCC invoked hiring inquiries and broader “public interest obligations.” These are the government’s stated rationales; whether they are pretexts is a question for the court, not an established fact.

But the inconsistency is material. If the dispute concerns incomplete answers about hiring, the government must explain why Carr reached for a licensing mechanism. If programming decisions are also under examination, the claim that this is merely an employment inquiry becomes harder to sustain.

Procedure becomes the shield

The government reportedly argued that ABC was both too early and in the wrong court: there was no final agency order to challenge, and any eventual licensing decision would belong before an appeals court. That position creates a convenient corridor of unreviewable pressure. Before final action, the broadcaster supposedly lacks a ripe claim. Afterward, the government can insist that only the completed order matters.

This is not a technical side issue. It is the mechanism by which institutional coercion can evade scrutiny. The threatened party must absorb legal expense, uncertainty and editorial chilling while the agency says nothing irreversible has happened.

ABC’s size does not cure the constitutional problem. A powerful corporation can afford more lawyers, but it also controls speech reaching millions of people. Government pressure on that editorial process affects more than Disney’s balance sheet.

The misdirection is “cooperation”

AliKhan reportedly asked whether the FCC might be trying to secure cooperation with its hiring investigation rather than punish ABC’s speech. That distinction deserves scrutiny because “cooperation” can become a euphemism for submission when the request is backed by an unrelated existential power.

The weaker actors here are not the federal officials wielding licensing authority. Nor is the central conflict a personality dispute involving Kimmel, Carr and Trump. The institutional question is whether the government may use regulatory uncertainty to influence lawful editorial choices and then escape review by calling the resulting restraint voluntary.

ABC says it is already making different programming decisions. That allegation has not yet been adjudicated, but it identifies the consequence precisely: censorship need not arrive as a written ban when officials can induce a broadcaster to censor itself.

The systemic error

This dispute reveals a broader pattern of executive power operating through anticipatory obedience. An official signals disapproval, an agency activates a consequential process, and lawyers later separate each step into supposedly innocent fragments. The demand was merely rhetoric. The review is merely administrative. The chilled programming is merely a corporate choice.

Taken together, those fragments describe how coercion can work without a final order. The FCC’s authority supplies the force; procedural delay supplies the insulation; the broadcaster’s self-restraint supplies the result. Whether ABC proves that case remains for the court. The political system’s vulnerability is already visible: regulators can exert their greatest influence before anyone is willing to call the punishment final.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Nuts!’ Judge hears ‘damning’ ABC arguments as experts tear into Trump’s FCC chair live

item.title: The Trump admin just admitted to a massive $28 billion military failure
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a Wednesday address at Quantico to announce an Autonomous Warfare Command and Project Meridian, a 120-day study of future warfare led by Elon Musk, Newt Gingrich and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey. The headline’s supposed “admission” was Hegseth’s acknowledgment that inexpensive, mass-produced weapons can threaten costly military platforms—not an explicit admission that the Pentagon suffered a $28 billion failure.

The article says the United States expended $28.1 billion in sophisticated weapons during conflict with Iran while Iran relied on cheaper drones, proxies and asymmetric tactics. But it does not provide the underlying calculation, define the relevant period or establish that the entire sum was wasted. It also asserts that Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz without supplying supporting detail.

Hegseth said the proposed four-star command would oversee artificial intelligence, robotics, drones and counter-drone systems, with dedicated personnel, budgets and acquisition authority. He set an intended operational date of October 1, 2027, contingent on working with Congress to secure authorizing legislation.

The power belongs to the Pentagon

The decisive actor is not “technology,” the media or some abstract transformation in warfare. It is the defense secretary, backed by the Pentagon’s immense purchasing machinery and subject to Congress’s authority over legislation and funding.

Hegseth is proposing a command designed to accelerate procurement outside traditional routes. That is an institutional choice: concentrate authority, shorten review and buy autonomous systems faster. Whether Congress approves that structure—and what safeguards it imposes—will determine whether the announcement becomes durable policy.

His attack on journalists obscures that chain of responsibility. According to AlterNet, Hegseth accused the press of endangering troops by reporting depleted munitions stockpiles. But reporters do not fire interceptors, set procurement schedules or decide whether inventories are adequate. Pentagon leaders and elected officials do. Treating disclosure as the danger redirects scrutiny from the officials who manage the arsenal to the people describing its condition.

Strategy with a sales department

Project Meridian gives Musk and Luckey influence over recommendations in a market where their companies already hold Pentagon contracts, according to AlterNet. That does not by itself prove that either man will shape recommendations for personal profit. It does create an obvious conflict-of-interest risk: contractors may help define the military requirements that their businesses are positioned to satisfy.

That risk is intensified by the project’s structure. The article reports that private consultants do not face the same oversight and ethics constraints as government officials. A rushed 120-day process could therefore convert vendor preferences into strategic doctrine before Congress or the public can meaningfully examine the assumptions underneath them.

The story weakens its own case by speculating that the appointments are political rewards based on campaign spending and personal relationships. Those facts may justify scrutiny, but they do not establish payback. The stronger indictment requires no mind-reading: Hegseth selected politically connected defense-industry figures to help shape a procurement future in which their companies may compete for enormous public contracts.

Automation does not erase responsibility

“Autonomous warfare” sounds clinical because clinical language makes lethal policy easier to administer. The central issue is not whether drones and artificial intelligence will matter in future conflicts; Hegseth’s memorandum argues that they already do. The issue is who retains control over targeting, what level of human judgment is required and who is accountable when a machine-assisted system kills unlawfully.

AlterNet raises that danger but often substitutes denunciation for documentation. Its claims about deaths attributed to aid cuts, killings at sea and deaths in immigration custody are not sufficiently substantiated within the supplied article to support the sweeping conclusions attached to them. Those assertions should not carry the argument.

The documented proposal is serious enough. A new command with its own budget, manpower and expedited acquisition power could embed autonomous systems across the armed forces before the rules governing their use receive comparable attention. Speed is being treated as strategy; accountability is left as an unspecified later problem.

The spectacle serves the structure

The stage design, biblical references and culture-war taunts were not the material policy. They were the political packaging around it. Hegseth paired attacks on journalists and gender nonconformity with a proposal to reorganize military authority and spending.

That pairing matters because spectacle consumes attention while bureaucracy accumulates power. The insults generate headlines; the command structure, procurement authority and contractor access determine what the government can actually do. A press corps fixated on provocation risks covering the costume while missing the transfer of money and discretion.

The recurring system

AlterNet is right to focus on the contradiction between lamenting costly legacy weapons and empowering defense contractors to help design what replaces them. But calling the speech an admission of a “$28 billion failure” stretches the evidence. Hegseth acknowledged a strategic vulnerability; the article supplies the accusation of failure.

The larger pattern is more concrete and more consequential: officials answer a procurement problem by creating another procurement apparatus, invite interested vendors into strategy formation, demand speed and attack scrutiny as disloyalty. The technology changes—from expensive interceptors to autonomous systems—but the political architecture remains familiar. Public failure becomes the justification for concentrated authority, private opportunity and weaker oversight.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The Trump admin just admitted to a massive $28 billion military failure

item.title: GOP 2028 wannabe becomes 'secret weapon' for floundering midterm candidate
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Politico, reports that Sen. Ted Cruz has become a major behind-the-scenes supporter of Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton in Texas. Cruz has campaigned with Paxton, attacked Democratic nominee James Talarico on his podcast, deployed his super PAC against Talarico, advised Paxton informally and connected him with donors. He also helped arrange outreach to bring Paxton to a U.S. Hispanic Business Council town hall.

The intervention followed Paxton’s primary victory over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, which AlterNet attributes largely to President Donald Trump’s endorsement. The outlet says Paxton’s polling position against Talarico subsequently deteriorated, raising the possibility of a Democratic statewide victory, though the article provides no specific poll figures.

Politico reported that Cruz helped raise $3 million during a post-primary tour and has acted as an intermediary between traditional Republican donors and Paxton’s MAGA coalition. Cruz says his objective is to keep Texas and Congress under Republican control. His involvement could also strengthen his influence in Texas and his position before a possible 2028 presidential campaign.

The power is in the machinery

Paxton may be the nominee, but Cruz controls resources a candidate needs: donors, advertising money, media reach, experienced operatives and access to business groups. His value is not mysterious. It is institutional.

The overlap is extensive. Axiom Strategies has worked with both men. Paxton’s senior adviser Nick Maddux previously worked on Cruz’s campaigns. Longtime Cruz adviser Sam Cooper now serves as a senior strategist for a pro-Paxton PAC. This is not merely one senator offering an endorsement. It is a political network transferring money, personnel and legitimacy to a vulnerable nominee.

Calling Cruz a “secret weapon” turns that machinery into campaign-pageantry intrigue. The consequential fact is that one officeholder can mobilize wealthy donors, a super PAC and a shared consulting class to protect partisan control of a Senate seat.

Cruz made the choice

Cruz stayed out of the bitter Republican primary, then committed himself once Paxton became the nominee. That sequence matters. He avoided choosing between Paxton and Cornyn while Republican voters were deciding, then moved aggressively when party power was at stake.

Cruz stated the calculation openly: elect Paxton rather than Talarico, keep Texas Republican and preserve GOP congressional majorities. His possible 2028 ambitions add another incentive, according to Politico: helping Paxton could make Cruz a stronger Texas power broker, broaden his alliances and raise his national profile.

That does not establish that presidential ambition is Cruz’s sole motive. It does establish that his intervention serves both an immediate institutional objective and a plausible personal one. The beneficiaries are the Republican Party, Paxton’s campaign and Cruz’s political future.

The risk is carefully assigned

An anonymous Republican strategist supplied the cleanest account of the arrangement: success could help Cruz claim a more unified Texas base in 2028, while defeat would be blamed on Paxton. Cruz gets the upside of sponsorship without necessarily absorbing the downside of failure.

That is how political power insulates itself. Operatives describe strategic intervention as loyalty when it succeeds and establish distance from the candidate when it fails. Responsibility becomes adjustable after the result is known.

The article’s horse-race language partly obscures this asymmetry. Paxton is depicted as floundering; Cruz is depicted as gambling. But Cruz’s political network is actively trying to determine the outcome, not merely wagering on it.

Loyalty becomes qualification

AlterNet reports that Trump backed Paxton because he considered him sufficiently loyal. Cruz is now working to consolidate donors and Republican factions behind that choice. The chain of authority is revealing: presidential favor helps select the nominee, then party infrastructure mobilizes to make the selection electorally viable.

The voters remain formally decisive. But the menu presented to them has already been shaped by endorsements, donor access, aligned PAC spending and a professional apparatus shared among powerful Republicans.

This is a recurring feature of personality-centered party politics. Loyalty wins advancement; institutional actors then spend money and credibility converting that loyalty into governing power. Questions about fitness become subordinate to control of the seat.

The system protects itself

The larger story is not that Cruz devised a clever campaign assist. It is that political institutions can close ranks around a weakened nominee because losing power is treated as worse than defending the nominee they have.

Cruz’s intervention exposes the hierarchy clearly. Paxton needs support. Donors possess money. Consultants coordinate the network. Trump helped confer partisan legitimacy. Cruz connects the pieces while accumulating leverage for his own future.

The “secret weapon” framing makes this sound like tactical ingenuity. It is better understood as organized power reproducing itself: insiders move personnel, capital and attention toward the approved candidate, then prepare to distribute credit upward and blame downward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP 2028 wannabe becomes ‘secret weapon’ for floundering midterm candidate
