item.title: Trump DOJ fails to get case dismissed against Stars & Stripes reporters
item.description:
What happened

A federal judge refused the Trump administration’s request to dismiss former Stars and Stripes ombudsman Jacqueline Smith’s lawsuit alleging First Amendment violations, AlterNet reported. Judge Amit Mehta also denied Smith’s request for immediate reinstatement, ruling that she had not shown she was likely to prevail on the merits at that preliminary stage.

The decision followed a September 24, 2026 hearing at which former Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer testified. Lederer separately said at an October event that Pentagon officials had labeled journalists “insubordinate” over work the administration disliked and directed him to issue termination notices. He said he challenged the basis for that directive and believed the proposed discipline denied the journalists’ First Amendment rights.

The ruling settles neither Smith’s claims nor the legality of the Pentagon’s conduct. It leaves the case alive while withholding the immediate remedy she sought.

The power came from the Pentagon

The decisive institutional power here did not belong to the journalists accused of insubordination. It belonged to Pentagon officials who, according to Lederer, could direct a publisher to begin removing employees.

That hierarchy matters. Calling journalists “insubordinate” converts a dispute over protected expression into an employment offense. It allows officials to present censorship as routine personnel management and retaliation as enforcement of workplace discipline.

Lederer’s account also exposes where agency rested. He says he was instructed to serve termination notices, objected to the directive, and questioned its foundation. The journalists were not the actors imposing consequences; they were the people facing them.

A partial ruling is not vindication

The administration did not win dismissal, but Smith did not win reinstatement. Those are distinct legal outcomes, not contradictory ones. Mehta found that the complaint should remain before the court while concluding that Smith had not met the more demanding standard for preliminary injunctive relief.

Any account that reduces this to a clean defeat for one side obscures what the order actually did. The First Amendment questions remain unresolved, and Smith still bears the burden of proving her case. A surviving lawsuit is an opportunity to litigate, not a finding that the alleged violations occurred.

That distinction should not soften the political significance of the reported conduct. A government employer can inflict serious professional and institutional damage long before a court reaches a final judgment.

“Insubordination” does political work

The Pentagon’s reported terminology shifts attention away from the officials who disliked the journalism and toward the supposed misconduct of the journalists themselves. That is classic bureaucratic misdirection: the authority issuing the order disappears behind an accusation that the target failed to obey.

The available reporting does not establish every official’s motive or prove that the term was knowingly chosen as a pretext. It does establish Lederer’s account that the administration disliked particular stories, Pentagon officials invoked insubordination, and he was directed to terminate employees. Those facts are enough to identify the structure at work without inventing intent.

The language also narrows the permissible question. Instead of asking whether officials used government power against disfavored expression, it asks whether employees complied. Power prefers that formulation because obedience is easier to administer than constitutional scrutiny.

Independence without protection is fragile

Stars and Stripes occupies an inherently vulnerable position: journalists are expected to perform an independent function inside an institution built around command authority. If senior officials can answer unwelcome reporting with employment directives, editorial independence survives only at their discretion.

Lederer’s resistance mattered, but the episode also shows the weakness of relying on individual supervisors to absorb institutional pressure. A publisher willing to object can slow an abusive directive. He cannot substitute for enforceable safeguards, judicial remedies, or officials who recognize limits on their own authority.

The denial of immediate reinstatement underscores that imbalance. The government retains its machinery while an individual plaintiff must establish a likelihood of success before obtaining urgent relief. Even when a claim survives, delay itself favors the institution.

The larger pattern is rule by reclassification

Political coercion rarely announces itself in its plainest terms. It arrives as discipline, procedure, restructuring, security, or insubordination. The administrative label makes the exercise of power look neutral while directing scrutiny toward the person being punished.

This case has not produced a final judicial answer. But the reported episode reveals a broader method: officials confronted with unwelcome expression can reclassify it as workplace defiance, impose immediate consequences, and leave the target to pursue a slower constitutional remedy.

The systemic failure is not merely that officials may overreach. It is that government institutions possess ready-made vocabularies and procedures that can turn political displeasure into an employment action while preserving the appearance of ordinary administration.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump DOJ fails to get case dismissed against Stars & Stripes reporters

item.title: Trump plan to buy the election crashes as Republicans set money ablaze
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican campaigns and allied groups spent heavily on Senate television advertising through September 2026 without gaining a comparable advantage in airtime or polling. AdImpact calculated that Republicans spent $563 million across nine battlegrounds, versus Democrats’ $375 million, but their 26 percent broadcast-spending advantage produced only 7 percent more ad airings.

The disparity stems partly from Republicans’ reliance on super PACs, which historically paid more for airtime than candidates entitled to the lowest broadcast rates during the 60 days before a general election. The Supreme Court paused an August 2026 appeals-court ruling against an FCC policy extending cheaper rates to outside groups. That gave PACs access to the discount while the litigation continued, provided they had reserved airtime.

The reporting does not establish that Donald Trump personally devised a plan to “buy the election.” It describes a Republican funding structure involving groups including MAGA, Inc., the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund. Nor does it show that the spending has universally failed: Republican attacks reportedly damaged Democrat Troy Jackson’s favorability in Maine, while a large airtime advantage for Republican John Sununu had not erased Democrat Chris Pappas’s polling lead in New Hampshire.

The money is powerful but inefficient

Republicans possess an enormous financial apparatus, but they have routed much of its money through organizations legally barred from coordinating with candidates. That choice inflated advertising costs and weakened centralized control at the campaign level. Democrats’ advantage was not simply thrift. Their candidates raised more money directly, allowing them to buy airtime at protected rates and decide how to present themselves.

That distinction identifies the real power structure. Wealthy donors and Washington-based organizations can flood a race with messages, yet candidates surrender agency when those organizations dominate spending. Ken Paxton’s reported complaint that Washington operatives controlled his campaign’s issues illustrates the consequence: outside money can support a candidate while reducing that candidate to the face on someone else’s product.

The court changed the market mid-election

The Supreme Court’s September 4 intervention mattered because timing is power. By pausing the appeals-court ruling, the justices allowed super PACs to obtain cheaper rates during the election period even though the underlying dispute remained unresolved. A final decision arriving after voting would not undo the advertising already purchased and broadcast.

That is not procedural background. It is an institutional decision that altered who could buy political attention, at what price, and when. The immediate beneficiaries were outside groups already holding vast sums. The practical result was to let concentrated private money purchase more access to the public airwaves while the courts postponed a definitive judgment.

Advertising cannot repeal material conditions

Bill Scher’s central argument, quoted by AlterNet, is that Republicans are trying to market policies voters associate with shrinking household finances. The reported failure of attack ads to move opinion consistently suggests a limit to paid persuasion: repetition cannot guarantee that voters will abandon their own economic experience.

The attacks also reportedly leaned on transphobia and Islamophobia. Those appeals are not evidence of political confusion; they are choices about whom to target when the governing sales pitch is weak. The strategy asks voters to redirect anger away from material conditions and toward vulnerable groups. Where it fails, the failure is tactical—not evidence that the scapegoating was harmless.

The headline overstates the evidence

Calling this “Trump’s plan” personalizes a machinery the article itself describes as broader and more entrenched. Trump’s MAGA, Inc. is one participant, but Senate and congressional leadership funds, donors, party committees, broadcasters, regulators and courts all exercise distinct forms of power. Compressing that structure into one man’s failed scheme makes the system easier to understand and harder to see.

The claim that Republicans are merely setting money ablaze is also too sweeping. The spending produced limited returns in New Hampshire and apparent damage to Jackson in Maine. It may be inefficient, but inefficiency is not impotence. Hundreds of millions of dollars still buy message saturation, force opponents to spend defensively and determine which prejudices dominate political discussion.

The system rewards organized wealth

The larger pattern is not that money suddenly stopped mattering. It is that money works through institutions: campaign-finance rules, candidate-rate protections, court orders, reservation deadlines and networks of nominally independent groups. Those mechanisms decide whether one dollar buys one advertisement or several—and whether candidates or national organizations control the message.

Republicans’ spending advantage did not automatically manufacture voter consent. But the underlying apparatus remains intact, and the Supreme Court’s intervention made it more efficient at the moment efficiency mattered most. A political machine can waste money, lose races and still possess extraordinary power over what the electorate is forced to hear.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump plan to buy the election crashes as Republicans set money ablaze

item.title: Gasps as 'insane' Trump goads enemy to 'take out' 5M Americans: ‘No words’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump told supporters at a Monday-night rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, calling that a “very small price to pay” while predicting that the war would end soon. The audience cheered.

The two cities have roughly 5.3 million residents combined, according to figures cited by RawStory. San Diego County also contains about 110,000 active-duty service members. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria and California Gov. Gavin Newsom condemned Trump’s remarks as dangerous and incompatible with a president’s duty to protect Americans.

The power is in the presidency

The central fact is not that commentators were shocked. It is that the president—who commands the military and shapes national-security policy—publicly treated attacks on American cities as an acceptable cost of his war.

Trump was not an aggrieved spectator discussing somebody else’s policy. RawStory describes him defending a conflict conducted under his authority while acknowledging higher prices at home. The institutional power, the war policy and the attempt to define its acceptable casualties all converge in the same office.

California as expendable territory

Los Angeles and San Diego are not abstractions in a strategy memo. They are cities whose residents the president is obligated to protect. Yet Trump presented their possible destruction as tolerable and did so before an approving crowd.

The choice of two California cities carries an unmistakable political meaning even if the report does not establish Trump’s motive: Americans living in territory associated with his political opposition were rhetorically separated from the country he claimed to be keeping safe. That is factional governance stripped to its ugliest premise—protection for the favored constituency, disposability for everyone else.

Shock is not an explanation

RawStory builds much of its account around reactions calling Trump “insane,” saying there were “no words,” or insisting the remarks were “not normal.” The outrage is understandable, but the framing is analytically weak.

Calling the statement madness can obscure agency. Trump selected the cities, described their destruction as a small price and then returned to promises of a quick ending. Whatever his state of mind, those were words spoken by the president in defense of his administration’s war. Treating the episode chiefly as another shocking violation of decorum lets political institutions avoid the harder question: what constraints exist when a commander in chief publicly discounts millions of American lives?

The applause matters

The crowd’s cheers do not carry presidential authority, but they reveal how authoritarian political culture is rehearsed. The leader identifies a population as expendable; supporters affirm the designation; the resulting spectacle converts cruelty into proof of loyalty.

That does not make the audience responsible for war policy. It shows how power recruits consent for it. The cruelty is not concealed behind sterile language about collateral damage. It is offered openly as entertainment and accepted as belonging within the movement’s politics.

A government of selective protection

The larger pattern is the conversion of public office into factional protection. A president’s basic obligation applies to Los Angeles and San Diego no less than to the people cheering in Grand Island. Once that obligation becomes conditional on geography or political identity, citizenship itself is being divided into protected and expendable classes.

The decisive failure is therefore institutional, not rhetorical. A political system that processes such remarks as another outrage cycle—clips, condemnations and diagnoses—while leaving the speaker’s immense war-making power untouched has confused recognition with restraint. The scandal is not merely that Trump said it. It is that the presidency gave those words consequence.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Gasps as ‘insane’ Trump goads enemy to ‘take out’ 5M Americans: ‘No words’

item.title: Fresh humiliation for Melania after Trump and Natalie Harp's rally antics: MS NOW
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump brought aide Natalie Harp onstage during a Monday-night rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, to deliver an executive order concerning purchases of tax-free red-dyed diesel. Trump signed it before the crowd, called Harp a “perfect person,” and compared the presentation to “The Price Is Right.”

On Tuesday’s “Morning Joe,” MS NOW co-host Willie Geist recounted the exchange and joked, “A penny for the thoughts of the first lady.” Melania Trump was absent, and the report provides no statement from her. It therefore establishes neither her reaction nor the headline’s claimed “humiliation.”

The spectacle hid the power

Trump held the institutional power in that room. He controlled the rally, chose to feature Harp, signed the executive order and turned an official act into a personalized stage routine.

Harp’s appearance was visually prominent but politically subordinate. She delivered the document; Trump exercised presidential authority. Treating their manner onstage as the main event obscures the actual decision and the office behind it.

Gossip replaced scrutiny

The report supplies almost no explanation of what the order does, who qualifies to buy the fuel tax-free, what revenue or regulatory consequences may follow, or under what authority Trump acted. Instead, it dwells on Harp’s appearance, smile and proximity to the president.

That is not accountability reporting. It is court gossip attached to executive power. A consequential government action becomes scenery for speculation about interpersonal tension.

Melania was made into a story without evidence

Geist’s remark was explicitly a joke. RawStory inflated it into a claim of “fresh humiliation” despite offering no evidence that Melania Trump watched the event, objected to it or felt humiliated by it.

The misdirection is gendered as well as political: two women are cast into an implied rivalry while the man with presidential power becomes the object around whom their supposed feelings revolve. Harp is reduced to a “blonde” aide who “pranced”; Melania is assigned an unreported emotional response. Neither framing explains the exercise of state power.

The systemic error

Political coverage routinely confuses access with agency and embarrassment with consequence. An aide carrying paper appears powerful because she is near the president. An absent spouse becomes news because a panel can speculate about jealousy. Meanwhile, the executive action itself escapes examination.

The larger pattern is an accountability failure: personality theater consumes the space where institutional reporting should be. The defensible story here is that Trump staged an executive signing as rally entertainment and television commentators answered with more entertainment. The alleged humiliation is unsupported; the journalistic humiliation is visible on the page.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Fresh humiliation for Melania after Trump and Natalie Harp’s rally antics: MS NOW

item.title: Trump mangles MAGA gov's name to his face as he racks up string of mental flubs at rally
item.description:
What happened

At an October 6, 2026 rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, President Donald Trump repeatedly stumbled while campaigning for Gov. Jim Pillen and Sen. Pete Ricketts, according to RawStory’s account of reporting by several outlets. Most notably, Trump called “Jim Walz” the “worst governor in history,” apparently combining Pillen’s first name with the surname of Democratic candidate Lynne Walz and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz. He then corrected himself.

Trump also portrayed Lynne Walz as closely related to Tim Walz, although the article says she is married to his third cousin. During the nearly 90-minute appearance, he struggled with the name of the venue’s video screens, acknowledged not knowing what red dye diesel was before signing an order concerning it, and missed the designated stage exit.

The rally came on Nebraska’s first day of early voting. Trump was there to support Republican incumbents, including Ricketts, whom the article describes as facing a close race against independent Dan Osborn.

The president is not a bystander

The institutional power in this story belongs overwhelmingly to Trump. He is not merely an elderly campaign surrogate having an uneven night. He is the president, the person signing executive orders and lending the authority of his office to candidates whose prospects concern his party.

That distinction matters. A verbal lapse by an ordinary speaker is trivia. A pattern of confusion from the official empowered to direct the executive branch is a legitimate question about performance. RawStory’s “mental flubs” framing points toward that question but does not establish a medical explanation, and the reported incidents alone cannot diagnose one.

Cruelty survived the correction

The name mix-up is less revealing than what Trump said once he recovered. He called Lynne Walz a “disaster,” inaccurately suggested a close family connection to Tim Walz, and invoked a “bad bloodline.”

That is not policy criticism. It is an attempt to discredit a candidate through ancestry and association, built on a relationship far more distant than Trump presented. The factual error weakened the premise; it did not interrupt the attack. Confusion and scapegoating operated together, but only one of them was the political message.

The spectacle hides the machinery

A story organized around mangled names, strange words and a missed exit risks reducing presidential power to a compilation of embarrassing clips. The more consequential detail is quieter: Trump reportedly signed an executive order expanding access to red dye diesel shortly after admitting he did not know what it was.

The article supplies too little information to assess that order’s substance or implementation. It does, however, expose a basic accountability problem. When coverage treats ignorance as another comic beat, it can obscure the authority attached to the performance. The signature still carries presidential force whether or not the signer demonstrates command of the subject.

Republican dependence is the real setting

Trump traveled to a reliably Republican state because Republican candidates were struggling, according to the report. That puts the rally’s power structure in plain view: Pillen and Ricketts accepted the assistance of a president whose endorsement remains valuable enough to summon him, even when his appearance generates liabilities of its own.

The party’s candidates and officials are not powerless spectators to Trump’s conduct. They benefit from his coalition, seek his intervention and help preserve his central position. Describing Republicans as merely “baffled” by the strategy understates their agency. Whatever private doubts exist, the public arrangement is continued dependence.

A system trained on the gaffe

Political coverage knows how to process a flub: isolate the clip, invite ridicule and move on. It is less comfortable tracing the chain from presidential ignorance to executive action, from false kinship claims to bloodline rhetoric, or from party anxiety to continued submission.

The systemic error is not that a president misspoke. It is that concentrated power can be exercised amid visible disorder while the press packages the disorder as spectacle and the governing party treats access to the performer as an electoral asset. The laughable moment passes. The authority, the degradation and the incentives that sustain both remain.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump mangles MAGA gov’s name to his face as he racks up string of mental flubs at rally

item.title: 'New nightmare fuel dropped': Frenzy as MIT researcher picks apart Russia's plague story
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that MIT biosecurity researcher Kevin Esvelt argued Russia’s response to the unexplained death of a 28-year-old technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute did not resemble the response to a routine laboratory-acquired plague infection. He cited quarantines across several hospitals, reported involvement by the Federal Security Service, hazmat precautions, and the medical observation of nearly 200 people.

Russian authorities dispute the premise. Rospotrebnadzor said the technician had pneumonia of unknown origin, testing found no microorganisms connected to her work, and no laboratory accident occurred. The World Health Organization said no cause of death had been officially confirmed. Esvelt suggested the measures could indicate an unidentified pathogen or engineered antibiotic resistance, but acknowledged they did not mean a pandemic was coming.

Scientists and physicians urged people to take Esvelt’s analysis seriously. Others escalated conjecture into alarm: activist Drew Pavlou proposed sealing Russia’s borders over what he called a possible escaped pandemic weapon, while environmental advocate Jay C. Ford declared that “new nightmare fuel” had arrived. The reporting establishes an unexplained death and an unusually extensive response—not a weapons program, engineered pathogen, or impending pandemic.

The information imbalance

Russian authorities hold the decisive institutional power here. They control the institute, the investigation, the laboratory records, access to samples, and the public release of findings. If the pathogen has been sequenced, as Esvelt believes it surely has, the Russian state is positioned to disclose that evidence or withhold it.

That imbalance makes skepticism reasonable. An official denial does not explain why nearly 200 people reportedly required observation or why hospitals allegedly imposed quarantines. But opacity creates an evidentiary vacuum, not automatic proof of the most frightening theory available.

The state’s failure to provide a persuasive account is politically consequential because it forces outsiders to reason from security measures rather than laboratory findings. Russia’s institutions created the conditions for suspicion. They did not, on the evidence presented, validate every suspicion that followed.

From expert inference to internet certainty

Esvelt offered a technical inference: the reported response appeared inconsistent with an ordinary plague exposure. He also stated a crucial limit—none of this meant a pandemic was coming.

The reaction economy discarded that limit. Professional endorsements established that Esvelt deserved attention; they did not establish that his hypotheses were correct. Pavlou then converted uncertainty into a “disturbingly high possibility” of an escaped pandemic weapon and proposed closing an entire country’s borders. RawStory supplied no public evidence supporting either the weapon claim or that policy.

This is how speculation hardens without acquiring evidence. Expertise lends credibility to a bounded question. Online amplification strips away the boundaries. A conjecture about what official conduct might imply becomes a story about what supposedly happened.

The headline sells panic

RawStory frames the episode as a “frenzy” and leads readers toward “nightmare fuel.” That choice centers viral reaction rather than the underlying conflict between Russian secrecy and incomplete public evidence.

The article does include the necessary cautions: Russian officials confirmed none of Esvelt’s theories, the WHO had no confirmed cause of death, and RFE/RL reported no public evidence that the laboratory was developing plague as a weapon. Those qualifications substantially weaken the sensational frame.

The misdirection is not primarily blame toward weaker actors. It is attention away from the institution with the evidence and toward spectators with the most clickable reactions. Russia’s lack of transparency deserves scrutiny. Internet panic is not a substitute for that scrutiny.

Secrecy and spectacle feed each other

The larger pattern is a mutually reinforcing failure. A security state withholds enough information to make its assurances unconvincing. Media and online commentators then fill the gap with escalating scenarios that the available facts cannot establish.

Both dynamics concentrate power away from the public. Russian authorities retain control of the underlying evidence, while attention-driven platforms reward whoever offers the most alarming interpretation. The result is not clarity but a market in fear built around facts the responsible institutions have not adequately supplied.

The defensible conclusion is narrower and more serious than the viral one: a laboratory worker died of an officially unexplained illness, authorities reportedly mounted an unusually broad response, and Russia has not publicly provided an account sufficient to resolve the discrepancy. Institutional secrecy made the uncertainty politically significant. Sensational coverage made it less intelligible.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘New nightmare fuel dropped’: Frenzy as MIT researcher picks apart Russia’s plague story

item.title: A world of pain awaits Todd Blanche — and Trump's pardon is useless
item.description:
What happened

Raw Story columnist Jason Miciak argues that Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche could face professional discipline and possible state scrutiny that a presidential pardon would not erase. The concrete exposure described is a June 22, 2025 New York bar complaint signed by 101 former federal and state judges; the article says the 69-page filing alleges abuse of Justice Department power, conflicts involving President Donald Trump, disregard of court orders, and misconduct connected to the Abrego García matter.

Miciak also points to Blanche’s role in offering three prosecutors a return to the Justice Department if they expressed regret after resisting the abandonment of the Eric Adams prosecution; they resigned and denied wrongdoing. The column further reports that Blanche dismantled the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team on April 7, 2025, while holding digital assets, and that on September 30 he announced a Justice Department misconduct complaint against Minnesota federal judges who had criticized the administration’s immigration enforcement and handling of court orders.

The article does not establish that Blanche committed a crime, that disciplinary authorities will sanction him, or that any pardon would be invalid. Its narrower legal point is sound: presidential pardons reach federal criminal liability, not state prosecutions or bar discipline. Its headline’s promised “world of pain,” however, remains speculation.

The power is in the office

Blanche is not merely another lawyer making aggressive arguments for a client. As deputy attorney general, he helps command an institution that can initiate prosecutions, abandon cases, discipline employees, redirect enforcement priorities, and lodge complaints against judges. The relevant imbalance is therefore not Blanche against his critics. It is the Justice Department against prosecutors whose employment it controls, defendants whose liberty it can pursue, and judges subjected to its institutional pressure.

That distinction matters in the Adams episode. According to the column, prosecutors who refused to endorse the department’s course were offered reinstatement on the condition that they express regret and acknowledge wrongdoing. Whether that amounted to criminal coercion would depend on evidence the article does not supply. But the reported demand itself presents an institutional choice: loyalty was treated as something to be extracted through control over public employment.

Enforcement for enemies, discretion for allies

The recurring pattern alleged here is selective institutional aggression. Prosecutors resisting leadership faced administrative consequences. Judges criticizing the administration became targets of a Justice Department misconduct complaint. Meanwhile, crypto enforcement was curtailed and existing investigations and prosecutions involving exchanges were redirected.

That does not by itself prove a criminal scheme or corrupt motive. It does reveal how discretionary power can be arranged: scrutiny travels downward and outward, while restraint protects the priorities established at the top. The danger is not bureaucratic “confusion.” These were reported decisions made by officials with authority to make them.

The potential conflict surrounding Blanche’s digital assets deserves examination, but the column outruns its evidence. It reports holdings valued between $159,000 and $485,000 and transfers valued between $116,000 and $350,000 to adult children and a grandchild. It also asserts that his policy change benefited the crypto market. Those facts may raise recusal and ethics questions; they do not, without more, establish market manipulation under New York law.

The pardon is a distraction

The column spends considerable energy imagining a future challenge to a federal pardon issued as part of an ongoing conspiracy. It concedes that this theory would be a “long shot,” and supplies no pardon, agreement, or evidence of such a bargain. That speculation weakens the stronger argument sitting in plain view.

A president cannot pardon state offenses, and a pardon does not compel a state bar to preserve a lawyer’s license. If New York disciplinary authorities substantiate the former judges’ allegations, professional consequences would arise from their own jurisdiction, not from an exotic attempt to puncture presidential clemency.

The real accountability question is therefore less cinematic: whether state institutions and professional regulators will investigate documented conduct independently and apply ordinary rules to a powerful federal official. Jurisdiction exists. Consequences are not guaranteed.

Accountability has not yet happened

Raw Story presents possible exposure as approaching punishment. Those are not the same thing. A complaint is not a finding, an ethics concern is not a criminal charge, and a theory of coercion or financial misconduct is not proof. The article is strongest when it identifies decisions and weakest when it predicts Blanche’s downfall.

That inflation also misdirects attention. The story is not chiefly about whether one official will someday lose his license or beg for mercy. It is about what Blanche can do now because he holds federal power—and whether institutions outside presidential control will examine that conduct without waiting for a change in political weather.

The system rewards obedience first

The larger pattern is the conversion of public authority into a loyalty mechanism. Officials can use personnel power to punish internal resistance, prosecutorial discretion to privilege leadership’s interests, and disciplinary procedures to answer judicial criticism. Each act can be packaged as management, enforcement policy, or institutional defense. Together, as reported here, they describe a Justice Department in which obedience is treated as the governing virtue.

A future pardon would not repair the damage caused when legal institutions teach their employees that professional duty carries a price and submission carries protection. Nor would belated discipline erase decisions already made under federal authority. The systemic failure occurs long before any pardon: it begins when institutions with the power to impose consequences instead organize themselves around the demands of the person above them.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: A world of pain awaits Todd Blanche — and Trump’s pardon is useless

item.title: Patel's FBI makes 'terrifying' cuts as agency shifts to Trump midterm vows: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, summarizing NPR’s reporting, says FBI counterintelligence staffing has fallen to roughly 50% to 60% of authorized positions in many field offices, with some offices cutting the number of counterintelligence squads in half. Agents and analysts have been redirected toward violent crime, gangs, and immigration—the priorities President Donald Trump emphasizes while campaigning for Republicans in the midterms.

NPR’s anonymous sources attributed the decline not to a single order from FBI Director Kash Patel, but to priorities communicated by bureau leadership and implemented by field-office chiefs. The FBI disputed the account, saying its counterintelligence operation remains robust and that expanded task forces include more than 1,500 personnel from the bureau and partner agencies. NPR said it could not independently verify Patel’s claim that his FBI has arrested more foreign spies than any previous iteration of the bureau.

Power without paperwork

The absence of a signed directive does not mean the absence of a decision. Patel and his leadership team control institutional priorities; special agents in charge decide which vacancies to fill and where new personnel go. According to NPR, those officials have repeatedly assigned resources to crime and immigration while leaving counterintelligence positions empty.

That is how bureaucratic power often works: leaders establish what will be rewarded, subordinates reallocate staff accordingly, and no single document bears responsibility for the cumulative result. Calling this a staffing drift would hide the chain of command. It is a leadership choice implemented through personnel decisions.

Security recast as campaign scenery

The shift aligns FBI resources with Trump’s campaign themes even as he claims an historic reduction in violent crime. RawStory cites a PolitiFact review describing crime and immigration as recurring elements of his midterm campaigning. The tension is plain: the administration is directing federal capacity toward issues useful for political messaging while reportedly weakening teams assigned to foreign espionage threats.

That does not prove agents were moved for electoral purposes. It does show that presidential rhetoric, bureau priorities, and field-office staffing are moving in the same direction. A federal law-enforcement agency is being reshaped around the president’s preferred political terrain.

Expertise treated as disposable

Counterintelligence cannot be rebuilt by swapping names on an organizational chart. NPR reported that more than 1,500 special agents have left since Trump returned to office, leaving the bureau with more than 650 fewer agents than in January 2025. Analysts were also moved from headquarters into field offices and, in many cases, reassigned to violent crime and gang work.

The lost capacity includes experience: recognizing foreign recruitment patterns, interpreting fragmentary evidence, and sustaining labor-intensive surveillance. Bureau leadership also fired personnel who had worked on Iranian threats and on investigations involving Trump, according to NPR. Whatever rationale accompanied those dismissals, removing experienced counterintelligence agents carries an obvious operational cost.

The convenient invisibility of failure

The article’s most important point is also the easiest to evade: counterintelligence failures usually do not announce themselves. A stolen technology, compromised official, or penetrated network may remain undiscovered for years. That allows leadership to advertise arrests and task-force head counts while the actual measure of capacity—whether hostile operations are being detected—remains largely hidden.

The FBI’s response does not resolve the reported discrepancy. A task force containing more than 1,500 federal, state, local, and partner-agency personnel is not necessarily equivalent to fully staffed FBI squads with specialized agents and analysts. Nor does an unverified claim about record spy arrests answer detailed reports of vacancies, reassignments, and lost expertise.

The institution follows the incentive

This is a familiar political pattern: institutional capacity is redirected toward the ruler’s most marketable grievances, while quieter responsibilities are starved because their successes are difficult to display and their failures are slow to surface. The weaker actors here are not the officials choosing assignments. They are the career personnel expected to absorb political priorities and the public left exposed to risks it may never see.

The central issue is not confusion inside the FBI. It is accountable officials exercising discretion, then sheltering behind the diffuse mechanics of bureaucracy. When campaign salience becomes an operating principle for national-security staffing, the damage may remain invisible long enough for those responsible to deny it ever occurred.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Patel’s FBI makes ‘terrifying’ cuts as agency shifts to Trump midterm vows: report

item.title: Trump's monstrous taunt is more than insanity — it's a demand for civil war
item.description:
What happened

RawStory columnist Ray Richmond writes that President Donald Trump told a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego and called that “a very small price to pay.” Richmond interprets the remark as encouragement for Iran to attack millions of Americans in two cities that overwhelmingly reject Trump politically.

The column says the crowd cheered, but it provides no date beyond “last night,” no fuller transcript, no video, and no White House explanation. It also does not establish that Trump specified a nuclear attack; that is Richmond’s interpretation of what “take out” could mean. The quoted language is still grotesque on its face: a president treated the destruction of American cities as an acceptable cost.

The power is presidential

Los Angeles and San Diego did not threaten themselves. California’s voters did not create this spectacle by disliking Trump. The actor with institutional power was the president, speaking from the authority and visibility of an office that commands the military and directs foreign policy.

That distinction matters because Richmond repeatedly shifts from Trump’s conduct to the cultural resentment Californians encounter elsewhere. Regional contempt may help make the remark politically useful, but it did not utter the words. Trump did. The crowd’s reported approval enabled the performance; it did not equal the president’s power to turn dehumanizing rhetoric into government policy.

The cruelty is the message

Calling the loss of two American cities “a very small price” does more than insult California. It sorts Americans into those whose lives merit presidential concern and those whose deaths can be offered as applause material.

The supplied account does not prove Trump intended to order an attack, wanted Iran to launch one, or issued a legally actionable threat. Richmond asserts those conclusions without furnishing evidence beyond the rally remark. The stronger, supportable indictment is already severe: Trump publicly framed mass harm to disfavored cities as tolerable. No diagnosis of “insanity” is needed. That label can obscure agency by recasting a political choice as a medical malfunction.

The framing outruns the evidence

Richmond calls the statement a “terroristic threat,” treasonous, and a demand for civil war. The column does not establish those legal or factual conclusions. It identifies no order, operational plan, direct threat by Trump to deploy force, or appeal for Americans to fight one another.

“Civil war” is therefore an inflated frame. The documented issue is not an announced domestic war but presidential scapegoating: the conversion of partisan geography into a hierarchy of human worth. Overstatement weakens the case by inviting debate over Richmond’s most speculative claims instead of holding Trump to the words actually quoted.

Impunity has institutions

The column points toward Republican allies and the Supreme Court but supplies no specific decision, vote, or act connecting them to this episode. Its broader observation is nevertheless politically relevant: incendiary presidential rhetoric becomes easier when party officials, donors, media surrogates, and audiences impose no meaningful cost.

Responsibility should remain properly ranked. Trump chose the language. The rally audience reportedly rewarded it. Any officials who excuse it would be making their own decision to normalize it. Californians are not responsible for provoking presidential contempt by voting against the president or by living in cities used as conservative symbols.

A country divided into expendable zones

The larger pattern is authoritarian scapegoating stripped to its practical core: define domestic opponents as alien, concentrate resentment on the places where they live, and make their suffering sound inconsequential. The political benefit comes from teaching supporters that government protection is conditional on loyalty.

That is the systemic failure exposed here. The scandal is not that a remark may have “gone too far,” as though politics were governed by an invisible boundary. It is that power tests what institutions and audiences will permit—and, when they permit cruelty toward designated enemies, the next escalation becomes cheaper.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s monstrous taunt is more than insanity — it’s a demand for civil war

item.title: Justice Department twice misspells 'north' as filing goes down in flames
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Justice Department appealed to the conservative 11th Circuit for access to information concerning 2020 election workers in Fulton County, Georgia. The filing misspelled “north” twice, but the substantive failure came earlier: U.S. District Judge William Ray ruled in July that the demand was unreasonable and would not produce information supporting any viable criminal charge.

Ray said the Justice Department may work through grand juries but cannot use that power to obtain private information without a legitimate purpose. The filing also identified several news organizations as having an interest in the appeal, although they were not parties to the case.

The requested information concerns a workforce already exposed to political violence and harassment. Fulton County workers Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss became targets of false election-fraud accusations after the 2020 election. They later won a $148 million jury award against Rudy Giuliani after a judge found him liable for false claims about them. AlterNet reports concern that disclosing workers’ identities could expose others to similar targeting.

The typo is not the scandal

The misspelling supplies an easy joke: a powerful department cannot spell “north” while asking an appellate court to revive a rejected demand. But incompetence in presentation is not the central abuse identified by the district judge.

The serious issue is institutional reach. The Justice Department invoked grand-jury authority to seek private information that Ray concluded had no legitimate prosecutorial destination. Fixing the spelling would not fix that defect. A polished demand unsupported by a viable charge would remain an unsupported demand.

Power belongs to the government

Election workers do not possess subpoena power, federal prosecutors, or an appellate apparatus. The Justice Department does. It chose to pursue the information and then chose to appeal after a federal judge rejected its justification.

That disparity matters because the people whose information is sought belong to a class of public servants already made vulnerable by a political campaign built around Trump’s false claim that he won the 2020 election. The government’s asserted purpose therefore cannot be separated from the foreseeable consequences of disclosure, even though the reporting does not establish that harassment is the department’s intent.

The weaker actors become the suspects

The political inversion is stark. Freeman and Moss were not merely criticized; according to the reporting, Trump allies turned them into characters in a conspiracy theory, supporters went to Freeman’s home, and the two women feared ordinary activities such as grocery shopping. Giuliani’s accusations produced a liability judgment and a nine-figure damages award.

Yet government scrutiny remains trained on the election workforce rather than on the machinery that falsely accused and endangered it. That framing converts victims of election disinformation into objects of renewed investigation while treating the disproven premise behind their persecution as something still entitled to institutional servicing.

A court drew the line

Ray’s ruling located the actual constitutional problem: grand-jury authority is not a general license for the Justice Department to collect private information. His conclusion that the material would not support any viable charge stripped the demand of its prosecutorial pretext.

AlterNet’s focus on the spelling errors risks shrinking that judgment into farce. The filing did not “go down in flames” because government lawyers made embarrassing mistakes on the page. It failed because a judge found the asserted use of federal power unreasonable.

The system rewards the lie

The larger pattern is not simple confusion about a settled election. A false political claim generated threats against individual workers, a successful defamation case, and then further government efforts to obtain information about the same category of people.

Institutions reveal their priorities through whom they burden. Here, private citizens who administered an election face the weight of federal process, while the underlying fantasy continues to dictate where that process is aimed. The typo is evidence of sloppiness. The appeal is evidence of something more consequential: public power being spent to keep a discredited grievance operational.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Justice Department twice misspells ‘north’ as filing goes down in flames

item.title: Trump puts US in rare company with Russia and Belarus before midterms
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration did not invite observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe to monitor the November 3 midterm elections. If that remains unchanged, this would be the first U.S. federal election since 2002—and the first of seven midterm elections during that period—without OSCE observers.

The State Department said the OSCE should devote its limited resources to elections where it could have greater impact. The OSCE called the decision “regrettable” and inconsistent with commitments made by participating countries under the 1990 Copenhagen Document. Human Rights Watch noted that Russia and Belarus have also recently denied OSCE observers access to national elections.

At the same time, the Justice Department said it planned to deploy as many as 1,000 federal monitors to polling places, which AlterNet describes as a record. A UC San Diego survey conducted the month before the report found that 49 percent of respondents expected the midterms to be free and fair, while 23 percent did not and 28 percent were unsure.

The administration made the choice

The relevant institutional power rests with the Trump administration. International observers cannot invite themselves, and election administrators did not collectively abandon the practice. The administration withheld the invitation.

The State Department’s resource argument does not explain why the United States should decide where the OSCE’s resources matter most. Nor does it address the OSCE’s claim that participating states committed themselves to election observation. It substitutes bureaucratic language for a defense of the actual decision: excluding an independent outside assessment after 24 years of accepting one.

Scrutiny on government terms

The contrast with the Justice Department’s proposed operation is the story’s central power dynamic. The administration is rejecting outside monitors while preparing an unprecedented deployment of its own federal monitors.

Those groups do not perform identical functions. OSCE observers assess the electoral process independently; Justice Department personnel enforce federal law under the authority of the executive branch. Presenting the second as a practical replacement for the first would erase the crucial question of control. One provides scrutiny the administration does not direct. The other exercises power through an institution the administration leads.

Distrust is not the cause

The polling numbers describe public uncertainty; they do not explain it. Treating voter distrust as the main political problem would shift attention from officials making consequential choices to citizens reacting to them.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen said the refusal risks undermining confidence in the election system. That is plausible, but “confidence” is too soft a frame by itself. Independent observation is not merely reassurance for nervous voters. It creates a record produced outside the government conducting the election. Removing that layer matters whether public opinion rises, falls, or remains unchanged.

The comparison has limits—and meaning

The United States has not become Russia or Belarus merely because all three governments declined OSCE observation. AlterNet’s comparison establishes a shared act, not identical electoral systems or conditions.

But the shared act is politically revealing. Human Rights Watch’s Philippe Bolopion pointed out that the U.S. government has criticized Russia and other governments for avoiding external scrutiny. An administration cannot credibly present election observation as essential abroad and dispensable at home without exposing the principle as conditional.

Accountability without permission

The larger pattern is institutional power narrowing the forms of oversight it cannot control while expanding the machinery it can. The reporting does not establish why the administration chose that arrangement, and it does not prove planned election misconduct. It establishes something more precise: officials rejected an established channel of independent scrutiny and offered a rationale that never confronted the loss.

That is how accountability is weakened without being formally abolished. No one needs to ban observation everywhere. Those in power can simply decide that outside examination is unnecessary here, this time, for reasons they define themselves.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump puts US in rare company with Russia and Belarus before midterms

item.title: Sheriff investigator exposed for extremist ties in court report
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a newly unsealed, court-appointed monitor’s report found that Stephanie Ameiss, whose firm AZ Truthfinder received a Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office contract for sensitive internal investigations, omitted significant parts of her background from her résumé. Those omissions included six years as lead investigator for Understanding the Threat—classified by the Southern Poverty Law Center as an anti-Muslim hate group—and participation in the Cyber Ninjas review of Maricopa County’s 2020 election results.

According to the reporting, sheriff’s office leaders selected AZ Truthfinder less than 24 hours after reviewing three bids. The firm has received approximately $270,000 from the county since June 2025. The monitor questioned whether meaningful vetting occurred and recommended considering a misconduct investigation. The sheriff’s office said it was reviewing the report and remained committed to complying with federal court orders.

The sheriff’s office held the power

Ameiss submitted an incomplete résumé, but the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office controlled the contract. Its leadership decided how thoroughly to investigate the bidders, how much scrutiny sensitive investigative work required, and whether the disclosed record was sufficient.

That distinction matters. The central institutional failure was not simply that an applicant omitted relevant experience. It was that an agency entrusted with coercive authority and confidential misconduct cases either failed to discover readily consequential information or discovered it and proceeded anyway.

Vetting or permission

The monitor framed the alternatives bluntly: the vetting process was either a sham, or officials found the same material and ignored it. The report does not establish which explanation is correct, so claims of deliberate concealment by the sheriff’s office would outrun the evidence. Neither possibility, however, describes an innocent administrative mix-up.

The speed of the selection—less than a day after the bids were examined—deepens the concern. A contractor assigned cases too conflicted for the sheriff’s own Professional Standards Bureau required more scrutiny, not less. The agency instead created a situation in which the independence of those investigations could reasonably be questioned.

Extremism is relevant experience

Understanding the Threat was not merely a controversial former employer. According to the monitor’s report, it published attacks on Muslims, Black Lives Matter activists, Democrats and others; the Southern Poverty Law Center classified it as a hate group promoting anti-Muslim conspiracy theories and selling training to law enforcement.

Ameiss’s work on the Cyber Ninjas-led election review was also directly relevant. Arizona’s Republican-controlled Senate commissioned that review after Donald Trump lost the state in 2020. Whatever the sheriff’s office ultimately thought of that experience, it belonged in any serious assessment of a bidder seeking authority over sensitive public-integrity investigations.

Treating these omissions as résumé trivia would misdirect attention from the public officials who awarded the contract. The stronger actor was the government agency with the money, investigative authority and duty to vet. Its decisions turned one applicant’s background into an institutional liability.

Oversight exposes the contradiction

Sheriff Jerry Sheridan and Maricopa County have been seeking an end to federal court supervision imposed after a racial-profiling lawsuit. Against that backdrop, this contract is not an isolated embarrassment. It is evidence relevant to whether the office’s internal safeguards deserve confidence without outside scrutiny.

The department’s statement that it remains committed to “full and effective compliance” answers none of the monitor’s concrete concerns. Compliance is not demonstrated by reciting its language. It is demonstrated through defensible decisions, documented vetting and accountability when those systems fail.

The systemic error

Law-enforcement agencies often present contracting and personnel choices as technical administration, safely removed from politics. They are not. Choosing who investigates official misconduct determines which backgrounds are normalized, which conflicts are discounted and whose judgment receives public authority.

The larger pattern is institutional self-policing without credible safeguards. An office already under federal supervision rapidly awarded sensitive work to a firm whose founder had omitted politically and professionally significant affiliations. The monitor’s findings show why oversight persists: power does not become trustworthy merely because the institution holding it declares itself compliant.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Sheriff investigator exposed for extremist ties in court report

item.title: The comet has hit: Former party bigwig on the extinction of the old GOP
item.description:
What happened

Former New Jersey governor and EPA administrator Christine Todd Whitman told AlterNet that the Republican Party she left in 2022 is unlikely to return after Donald Trump leaves its leadership. Her answer to the headline’s extinction metaphor is blunt: the old GOP is gone because, in her assessment, the party has become a “cult” whose positions change with Trump’s commands rather than follow a stable platform.

Whitman contrasted that structure with the Republican tradition she identifies with—balanced budgets, alliances, science, refugee protection and negotiated problem-solving. She argued that public frustration with an unresponsive two-party system created an opening for Trump, while Republican officials surrendered their principles instead of constraining him.

Whitman is now building the Forward Party as an alternative. At the time of the interview, she said it had more than 80 officeholders and candidates for the Senate, House, governorships and other offices. AlterNet did not establish that this effort can displace either major party; it presented Whitman’s account of its organization and ambitions.

Power did not disappear

Calling the Republican Party a cult describes its obedience but can obscure who exercises power. Trump sets the line. Republican officeholders, party organizations and aligned media figures enforce it. Candidates learn that dissent can bring a primary opponent, lost support or political exile.

Those officials are not merely confused followers. They possess votes, offices, budgets and procedural authority. Every time they adopt a new position because Trump demands it, they make a choice about how to use institutional power. Personal domination succeeds because people with formal authority repeatedly convert one man’s preferences into party policy.

The convenient obituary

The “old GOP” deserves less sentimental treatment than AlterNet’s framing gives it. The article presents Whitman’s 1993 campaign as honorable, restrained and focused on taxes, spending and jobs. That may distinguish her rhetoric from Trump’s, but decorum is not a governing philosophy, and civility does not establish that policy consequences were fair.

The sharper point is not that Republicans were once good and then inexplicably became cruel. It is that a party accustomed to hierarchy, elite control and punitive enforcement proved vulnerable to a leader who discarded its euphemisms. Trump did not abolish the machinery of partisan discipline. He captured it and made loyalty to himself its organizing principle.

Frustration is not agency

Whitman says voters were understandably angry because Congress had stopped solving major problems, and that Trump successfully promised to “blow it up.” That explains an opening; it does not transfer responsibility for what followed onto an undifferentiated public.

Citizens cast ballots, but officeholders decide whether to resist abuses, enable them or profit politically from them. Party leaders control endorsements and resources. Legislators exercise public authority. Media institutions decide whom to amplify. Blaming “polarization,” loud voters or generalized frustration can turn a chain of identifiable decisions into political weather.

Whitman herself identifies the coercive mechanism: major parties can withdraw support and sponsor challengers against dissenters. That is organized power, not spontaneous extremism from below.

Centrism is not a substitute for leverage

The Forward Party’s promises—constitutional government, lawful voting access, pluralism and cooperation—describe minimum obligations of public office. Their necessity is an indictment of the existing system, but stating them does not answer how a third party overcomes the institutions that protect the two-party monopoly.

Whitman’s reported roster of candidates and officeholders demonstrates persistence, not yet governing power. The article accepts the “boldly centrist” label too easily and does not test what the party would do when compromise collides with rights, material interests or authoritarian conduct. A safe space for disagreement is useful only if it does not become shelter for officials avoiding consequential choices.

The system rewards surrender

This story is larger than the extinction of a Republican faction. It shows how democratic institutions can remain formally intact while their occupants abandon independent judgment. A party need not publish an authoritarian doctrine when obedience itself supplies the doctrine.

Trump holds the commanding position, but his dominance depends on officials and institutions that still possess agency. The old GOP was not struck by a comet. Its leaders repeatedly traded principle for access, office and protection from their own voters. Extinction is too passive a word for a process carried out through thousands of voluntary acts of surrender.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The comet has hit: Former party bigwig on the extinction of the old GOP

item.title: Trump’s Epstein nightmare getting 'much bigger': analyst
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that political analyst David Rothkopf expects the Jeffrey Epstein controversy to become “much, much bigger” after the midterm elections, particularly if Democrats gain congressional power, call witnesses, or obtain new information. That is Rothkopf’s forecast, not a reported new revelation from the files.

Rothkopf made the argument while discussing President Donald Trump’s response to a separate case involving seven former Cornell University students accused of drugging and sexually assaulting a classmate in 2024. After New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, Trump attacked James and said he felt sorry for those she was investigating because they would not receive fair treatment.

Rothkopf interpreted Trump’s reaction as evidence of sensitivity about Epstein-related allegations and asserted that victims would eventually testify. AlterNet provides no substantiation for that prediction. Authorities have not charged Trump with participating in Epstein’s crimes, and Trump denies wrongdoing.

Power before prediction

The consequential fact here is not an analyst’s prophecy. It is that a sitting president used his platform to disparage a state attorney general and prejudge a criminal investigation in favor of the accused.

James holds prosecutorial authority in the Cornell case because Hochul appointed her after losing confidence in the local district attorney’s handling of it. Trump holds vastly greater political power: the presidency, a national audience, and the capacity to turn a pending prosecution into partisan spectacle. The accused students have not been convicted, but Trump did not merely insist on due process. He declared unfairness before James had produced an outcome.

The Epstein inference outruns the evidence

Rothkopf’s theory is that Trump sympathized with the accused students because their allegations reminded him of accusations associated with Epstein. The article establishes no such causal link. It reports an interpretation of Trump’s behavior, then treats that interpretation as the story’s engine.

That is weak framing. Trump’s attack on James can be analyzed without pretending to know his private trigger: she is a longtime political adversary, she received authority over a politically volatile case, and he publicly sought to discredit her work in advance. Those are documented acts. Converting them into amateur mind-reading makes the strongest evidence easier to dismiss.

Misdirection by sensationalism

The headline promises an expanding nightmare, but the reporting offers a prediction contingent on future elections, possible hearings, potential testimony, and information that may or may not emerge. None of that establishes a new Epstein-related fact about Trump.

This sensationalism misdirects attention from conduct already in view. A president intervened rhetorically on behalf of accused men while attacking the official assigned to investigate their case. Making the episode chiefly about his presumed psychological identification with them shifts scrutiny away from his actual exercise of power.

Victims as campaign material

The story also reports that House Democrats released an advertisement featuring Virginia Giuffre’s family and accusing Republican Rep. Jeff Crank of voting to “cover up” Epstein files. AlterNet does not supply the vote’s details, so the accusation cannot bear more weight than its attribution allows.

Democrats may use committee control to seek records and testimony. That would be an institutional act subject to evidence and public scrutiny. A campaign advertisement is something else: it converts victims’ experiences into electoral leverage. If lawmakers possess oversight power, the test is whether they use it to establish facts—not whether they can manufacture the most damaging association.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a political press drawn toward speculative scandal while concrete abuses of office sit in plain sight. Predictions about devastating future disclosures generate heat; a president delegitimizing a prosecutor before a case proceeds reveals how power works now.

Accountability requires sharper distinctions: accusation from proof, prediction from disclosure, due process from political intimidation, and oversight from campaign branding. When coverage blurs those lines, powerful actors gain an escape route. They can dismiss every documented act as just another piece of partisan insinuation—and the spectacle helps them do it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s Epstein nightmare getting ‘much bigger’: analyst

item.title: CNN analyst unloads damning graph showing futility of Trump’s diesel scheme
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump signed an executive order temporarily waiving penalties for highway use of cheaper red-dyed diesel, but CNN analyst Matt Egan said the measure would provide only modest relief and would not address the forces driving diesel prices. AlterNet reported that diesel averaged about $6.32 a gallon and had risen nearly 80 percent so far that year.

Egan estimated that filling an 18-wheeler cost almost $1,600 and that combined federal and state tax moves could reduce that by roughly $150. He cautioned that it was unclear how much of the savings would reach consumers. The federal taxes were being deferred, not automatically forgiven, although the order directed officials to consider forgiveness.

Several states were reportedly considering their own tax relief. But Egan described the resulting state-by-state patchwork as inadequate for truckers crossing state lines and said federal officials did not expect prices to fall before the midterm elections. AlterNet attributed the broader shortage to limited global refinery capacity, the Russia-Ukraine war and refinery destruction connected to Trump’s war with Iran.

The power sits in Washington

Trump held the institutional power at the center of this story. He could direct federal agencies, alter enforcement and use an executive order to present a rapid response. State governments controlled additional fuel-tax decisions. Truckers, farmers and consumers controlled none of the policies determining whether relief was temporary, fragmented or passed along at all.

That hierarchy matters because the people paying the bills appear mainly as evidence of suffering. A New Jersey trucking-company owner called the measure a late “Band Aid.” Farmers already entitled to use red diesel off-road were reportedly struggling despite that existing advantage. Their hardship supplied the urgency; government officials retained the discretion.

Relief designed around the headline

The order changed a tax penalty at the margin. It did not create refining capacity, repair destroyed facilities or resolve the conflicts AlterNet identified as major causes of the shortage. Even its immediate benefit was uncertain: deferral is not forgiveness, and a nominal tax reduction is not proof that consumers will receive the full savings.

That does not make $150 per fill-up meaningless to a trucking business. It makes the scale of the intervention politically revealing. Against a nearly $1,600 tank and an almost 80 percent annual increase to date, the administration offered limited relief while leaving the underlying price structure intact.

The timing also invited an obvious judgment. AlterNet characterized the order as a pre-election tax holiday, and officials reportedly warned that prices would not fall before the midterms. The action therefore offered Trump a visible response more readily than it offered the public a durable solution.

A patchwork is not a policy

The states considering additional relief included North Dakota, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas and North Carolina. For an industry built around interstate movement, separate state decisions create uneven benefits along routes rather than a coherent national answer.

Calling that confusion would obscure responsibility. Federal and state officials were making discrete policy choices, each limited by jurisdiction and political appetite. The predictable result was fragmentation imposed on workers whose jobs require them to cross those boundaries.

The graph cuts through the staging

The most useful part of Egan’s presentation was not that the graph looked “damning.” It was that the scale exposed the mismatch between the crisis and the response. Diesel increases of about 20 percent in 2021 and 2022 were dwarfed by the nearly 80 percent rise reported for the current year.

AlterNet’s framing is weakest when it treats the chart chiefly as evidence of Republican electoral futility. That redirects attention from governing power to campaign consequence. The central failure is not that the order may be too small to rescue Trump’s party. It is that people moving food and goods were offered uncertain, temporary savings while the administration left the reported causes of the price shock untouched.

Government by political anesthesia

This is a familiar governing pattern: permit a crisis to become punishing, announce narrow relief near an election and market motion as control. The public receives a complicated promise involving waivers, possible forgiveness and inconsistent state participation. The officeholder receives a signing ceremony and a claim of action.

The distinction is not between action and inaction. It is between using power to alter material conditions and using it to manage political exposure. In AlterNet’s account, Trump chose the latter instrument: a small, late intervention whose most reliable product was the appearance of response.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: CNN analyst unloads damning graph showing futility of Trump’s diesel scheme

item.title: New Trump-era movie is mind-bending, pretentious and a total box office bomb
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Digger, a $180 million climate-disaster film starring Tom Cruise, failed at the box office. The film depicts an oilman whose Greenland drilling triggers ecological catastrophe, then reveals that this narrative is a play performed in a future already devastated by those decisions.

The review praises the film’s climate politics, elaborate structure and visual ambition but argues that its slow pace, theatrical excess and fixation on elite depravity blunt its impact. It concludes that The Day After Tomorrow, a commercially successful 2004 disaster film, remains the more effective climate parable.

AlterNet places that comparison in the context of President Donald Trump’s dismissal of human-caused climate change and removal of government scientists, while reporting that his administration is pursuing more extraction in Greenland.

Power is not a personality flaw

The fictional Digger is not dangerous merely because he is arrogant. He owns an oil enterprise, has access to the president and can shape the public account of a worsening disaster. The scientists around him possess expertise but not command. Their warnings become optional because political and economic authority belongs to the men creating the danger.

That is the relevant structure: industry makes the profitable decision, executive power protects it, and experts are permitted to speak only until their knowledge threatens the arrangement. Calling the resulting conduct “ignorance” risks understating what the review itself describes. Once warnings have been delivered repeatedly, continued drilling is a choice made under conditions of knowledge.

The review finds the film’s central evasion

AlterNet’s strongest criticism is not that Digger is pretentious. It is that the film spends more attention examining powerful perpetrators than depicting those forced to absorb the consequences. That imbalance grants elites psychological complexity while the public becomes scenery in its own catastrophe.

The reported scene blaming ordinary people for needing oil exposes the deeper failure. Consumers did not design the energy system, control extraction capital or gain presidential access. Treating dependence as consent transfers responsibility from institutions with decision-making power to people whose daily survival has been organized around decisions they did not make.

Spectacle cannot substitute for political clarity

The film’s nested-play device apparently asks how future societies should remember those who ruined their world. But formal complexity can obscure a simple chain of agency: executives pursued extraction, political leaders enabled them, scientists warned them, and everyone else inherited the damage.

That does not make artistic experimentation illegitimate. It makes clarity politically consequential. A climate film that turns accountable decisions into a maze of perspectives can reproduce the same fog that protects power outside the theater. The issue becomes humanity’s tragedy rather than the foreseeable result of choices made by identifiable institutions.

A box-office bomb has limited reach

AlterNet contrasts Digger with The Day After Tomorrow, citing research that found the older film significantly affected climate-risk perceptions, behavioral intentions and policy priorities among roughly 21 million Americans who saw it theatrically. The review does not establish that simpler storytelling always produces political change, but it does establish the practical problem facing Digger: a message cannot shape a mass audience that largely does not encounter it.

Commercial failure does not disprove the film’s argument. It does, however, expose the weakness of treating a lavish Hollywood production as a substitute for politics. A $180 million warning that cannot hold public attention remains an expensive warning, not an intervention in the institutions authorizing extraction.

The system survives by spreading responsibility downward

The larger pattern is familiar: concentrated power makes the consequential decisions, then responsibility is diluted across “humanity,” consumer appetite and personal hypocrisy. That framing is useful to officeholders and industries because it converts governance into guilt and policy into lifestyle.

AlterNet identifies that evasion inside Digger, even as its review sometimes reduces the problem to whether one climate movie is more entertaining than another. The decisive question is not which film frightens audiences most effectively. It is whether the story names who can authorize harm, who can stop it and who is expected to live with the result.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: New Trump-era movie is mind-bending, pretentious and a total box office bomb
