item.title: Once-safe Republicans are in danger because of a new issue out of left field
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Giffords PAC, the gun-control organization founded by former Rep. Gabby Giffords, launched ads in two Republican-leaning House districts as part of a planned $10 million intervention ahead of the November 2026 midterms. The “new issue” is gun policy, deployed alongside public-safety arguments in races national Democrats have not typically treated as top-tier targets.

According to The Bulwark, the PAC committed $1 million in Michigan’s open 10th District to promote Democratic nominee Christina Hines, emphasizing her record prosecuting gun traffickers, domestic abusers, and murderers. It is also supporting Democrat Leela Gray against Republican Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in Florida with an ad accusing Luna of taking gun-lobby money, weakening gun laws, and voting to cut law-enforcement funding.

The reporting establishes substantial outside spending and an expansion of the electoral map—not that either Republican seat has become endangered. Florida’s race was rated “lean Republican” by the Cook Political Report, but the article supplies no polling, fundraising comparison, or race rating for Michigan showing that the ads have altered either contest.

Money expands the map

The institutional power here belongs first to Congress, where lawmakers decide federal gun policy and law-enforcement funding, and then to the organizations capable of spending millions to shape who controls it. Giffords PAC is using that financial power to contest districts where Democratic campaign institutions have previously lacked the resources to compete seriously.

That is the real development. The PAC is not merely advertising a policy preference; it is deciding that Republican incumbency or recent Republican control should no longer guarantee an uncontested race. A $10 million campaign can force candidates and party committees to spend money defending territory they expected to hold cheaply.

The votes belong to lawmakers

The Florida ad names Luna’s votes and ties them to concrete consequences: easier gun access for criminals and domestic abusers, and reduced law-enforcement funding. Those are the PAC’s claims, quoted by The Bulwark, not independently demonstrated in AlterNet’s account. The article does not identify the bills, appropriations, or vote dates, so the precise record cannot be evaluated from the supplied reporting alone.

Still, the framing correctly locates agency in a legislator’s decisions. If Luna voted for those measures, responsibility belongs to Luna—not to an abstract “gun debate,” partisan polarization, or voter confusion. Campaign money may amplify the record, but it did not cast the votes.

“Out of left field” is misdirection

Gun policy did not materialize from nowhere. The novelty described here is strategic: a well-funded group is carrying the issue into districts that national Democrats have often left beyond the edge of their practical ambitions.

Calling that development “out of left field” converts an institutional choice into a surprise event. Republicans were not suddenly exposed by an unpredictable cultural mood. Giffords PAC selected races, purchased advertising, elevated candidates, and framed legislative records around public safety. Political vulnerability, if it follows, will be the result of organized opposition confronting decisions that previously received less sustained scrutiny.

The headline also outruns the evidence. Spending can place races on the map; it cannot by itself prove that formerly safe Republicans are in danger. Without polling or changed race ratings, “danger” remains a campaign hypothesis dressed as an established condition.

The larger pattern

American election coverage routinely treats the existing battleground map as natural terrain rather than the product of money, recruitment, party priorities, and institutional neglect. A district looks “safe” partly because opponents have decided—or been forced—to spend elsewhere. When an outside group supplies the missing resources, the supposed law of political geography can dissolve quickly.

That is the systemic lesson: electoral safety often means insulation from accountability, not broad public consent. Giffords PAC is testing whether specific gun-policy votes can carry a cost in districts Republicans have grown accustomed to defending lightly. The reporting shows that test beginning. It does not yet show the verdict.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Once-safe Republicans are in danger because of a new issue out of left field

item.title: Expert pulls back curtain on 'where Republicans go to do what voters reject’
item.description:
What happened

The venue Elie Mystal identifies as “where Republicans go to do what voters reject” is the Supreme Court. AlterNet reports that Mystal, writing in The Nation on Monday, argued that Republican-aligned litigants use the Court to pursue outcomes they could not secure through elections, including challenges involving the National Voter Registration Act, Title IX, gun restrictions, protections for runaways, and fossil-fuel regulation.

Those cases had not been decided in the reporting supplied. Mystal was forecasting how the Court’s conservative majority would rule during the coming term, warning that it could invalidate popular laws despite record-low public approval measured by Gallup. He argued that Congress could respond through ordinary legislation by changing the Court’s size, reducing its funding, or limiting its jurisdiction.

Power without an election

The institutional power belongs first to the justices who choose cases, interpret federal law and can nullify decisions made by elected governments. Lifetime tenure insulates them from the voters affected by those decisions. In the cases Mystal describes, Republican-aligned plaintiffs provide the vehicles; the conservative majority holds the authority to deliver the result.

That arrangement converts judicial review into a political bypass. Losing at the ballot box does not necessarily end a campaign against a law. It can redirect the campaign toward a forum where public approval is irrelevant and five justices can override legislative majorities, state policy or local voters.

The architects are not bystanders

The Court did not acquire its current ideological direction by accident. Republican political power placed the conservative majority in position, and aligned litigants now ask that majority to produce outcomes unavailable through ordinary democratic persuasion. The reporting supports describing this as a coordinated institutional strategy, even though it does not establish how the justices will decide the pending cases.

The crucial distinction is between prediction and action. Mystal expects the majority to dismantle protections and restrictions he considers popular; AlterNet does not report that those rulings have already occurred. But the decision to bring these disputes before the Court is itself political agency, not neutral weather.

The convenient blame shift

Mystal says voters must pressure Washington, but that formulation risks placing responsibility on the people with the least direct control. Citizens did not grant themselves jurisdiction, select the cases or cast judicial votes. Elected officials constructed the present Court and retain powers that Mystal says could constrain it.

His sharper point is that the political branches “will never buck” the Court on their own. That is institutional cowardice, not public confusion. If lawmakers possess legislative remedies and refuse to use them, the failure belongs to those lawmakers. Voters can apply pressure; they cannot introduce a bill, schedule a vote or enact jurisdictional limits themselves.

Minority rule by legal process

The larger pattern is minority governance laundering itself through judicial procedure. Policies that cannot command electoral support are repackaged as legal claims and delivered to officials who never face reelection. The language of doctrine can make the result appear detached from politics even when the dispute was selected precisely because ordinary politics produced the wrong answer for its sponsors.

The Court’s insulation is therefore not merely a constitutional feature. It is a political resource. Republican-aligned interests can use that insulation to seek durable victories while elected allies avoid openly voting for the consequences.

The system working as arranged

Mystal’s proposed remedies expose the real structure of responsibility. Congress has tools, the justices have authority, litigants choose their cases, and voters bear the consequences. Treating the conflict as a generalized loss of faith in the Court obscures who can act and who is declining to do so.

The systemic error is not that an unpopular institution has become mysteriously powerful. It is that political actors can transfer contested policy choices to an unaccountable tribunal, accept the resulting benefits and then describe the outcome as law operating above politics. The robe does not erase the power struggle. It conceals who won it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Expert pulls back curtain on ‘where Republicans go to do what voters reject’

item.title: What Tennessee wants to do next to Christa Pike is beyond grim
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Tennessee officials intend to attempt to execute Christa Pike again if she recovers from a coma after two failed lethal-injection attempts. Pike remained hospitalized in critical condition with significant injuries to both arms; the state’s pentobarbital injections reportedly entered her arm tissue rather than her veins.

The execution process lasted more than two hours. Pike’s lawyers sought an emergency stay and later demanded preservation of the state’s records. They said Tennessee knew she had unusually small veins, lacked emergency oxygen nearby and argued that corrections officials had no duty to provide life-saving care.

Prisons chief Frank Strada resigned that Saturday, and Gov. Bill Lee announced an independent investigation. Marsha Blackburn, described by AlterNet as the favored candidate to succeed Lee, said Tennessee should pursue another execution after changing its procedures. Her statement advocates a future course; the authority presently belongs to Lee, corrections officials and the courts.

The state controlled the chamber

Pike committed murder at 18 and was convicted in 1995. That explains her sentence. It does not excuse Tennessee’s conduct while carrying it out.

The state selected the method, assembled the execution team and proceeded despite a known vascular problem. State lawyers opposed intervention while the attempt continued. Every consequential decision inside that chamber belonged to public officials exercising institutional power over a restrained prisoner.

Calling this merely a “botched execution” risks laundering those decisions into mechanical bad luck. The relevant question is not whether the machinery malfunctioned. It is why officials used it under conditions that reportedly made failure foreseeable—and why they now contemplate using it on the same injured person again.

An investigation is not accountability

Lee’s investigation may establish what happened, but announcing a review does not itself assign responsibility. Tennessee had already canceled an execution in 2022 because drugs were not properly tested. AlterNet also reports that another planned execution was abandoned in May after a medical team could not find a usable vein.

That history makes the Pike episode harder to portray as an isolated surprise. The state had prior warning that its execution system could fail at basic procedural and medical tasks. Strada’s resignation removes an administrator; it does not establish whether the policies, staffing or commands that produced the outcome will change.

Blackburn’s promise exceeds her present power

Blackburn does not currently control Tennessee’s execution apparatus. Lee’s administration does. But her pledge matters because it converts reported institutional failure into a campaign posture: adjust the process, then try again on Pike.

That framing treats Pike’s injuries as a technical obstacle to completing state business. It also preempts the central legal and moral issue raised by the failed attempts—whether subjecting one person to repeated, prolonged and reportedly painful efforts to kill her crosses the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.

Confusion is the wrong diagnosis

AlterNet concludes that society is “confused” about who should live and die. The reporting describes something more concrete. Tennessee created a protocol, knew of relevant risks, retained custody of Pike throughout the procedure and, according to her lawyers, denied that it owed her life-saving care when the procedure failed.

The public may be divided over capital punishment. The institutions involved were not confused about their objective. They tried to execute Pike, failed twice and retained the power to determine her treatment, records and possible return to the death chamber.

Cruelty administered as procedure

The larger pattern is how government violence becomes insulated by bureaucracy. Officials divide responsibility among medical contractors, corrections administrators, lawyers, governors and courts until no single actor appears to own the whole result. Yet the prisoner experiences the system as one state, with one overriding power.

A death sentence does not give Tennessee unlimited license over the manner of death. When the state injures a captive during failed attempts and then proposes to resume once doctors have kept her alive, “procedure” becomes a euphemism for repeated state-inflicted harm. The system’s error is not merely that it failed to kill efficiently. It is that institutional power can treat that failure as authorization to begin again.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: What Tennessee wants to do next to Christa Pike is beyond grim

item.title: 'Very Bad': Trump faces stunning rejection from swing-state youth
item.description:
What happened

A new Alliance for Youth Power PAC/YouGov poll found Donald Trump deeply unpopular among Michigan voters ages 18 to 29: 78% viewed him unfavorably and 19% favorably. AlterNet reports that the survey, released Monday less than five weeks before the November election, also showed young voters favoring Democratic candidates by wide margins in Michigan’s statewide races.

Among respondents, 61% planned to vote for Democrat Jocelyn Benson for governor, compared with 26% for Republican John James. In the U.S. Senate race, 66% backed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and 24% backed Republican Mike Rogers. The poll surveyed roughly 400 young voters in each of eight battleground states and carried an estimated five-point margin of error.

A poll is not a verdict

The headline sells a “stunning rejection,” but the reporting establishes a hostile poll result, not an electoral repudiation. Voting intentions among roughly 400 young Michiganders cannot show how many will register, turn out or maintain those preferences through Election Day.

That distinction is especially important here. The poll says 42% of Michigan respondents are newly eligible to vote and another 32% did not vote in an earlier election despite being eligible. Only 37% described themselves as “very prepared” to vote. Democrats have an opportunity, not a delivered constituency.

Trump holds the power

Young voters did not create the economic conditions they are judging. Trump holds presidential power, while Republicans seeking statewide and congressional office are asking voters to extend their party’s authority. The relevant political agency belongs first to officials who govern, set priorities and defend the administration—not to young people reacting to the results.

The survey points to that judgment. Nearly half of respondents placed inflation or cost of living among their three leading concerns. More than 20% named housing and rent, the economy and jobs, or political corruption. YouGov analyst John Ray also reported broad pessimism about respondents’ personal finances compared with the previous year.

Discontent is not Democratic ownership

Dakota Hall of the Alliance for Youth Action warned against reading the margins as proof that Democrats’ work is finished. That is the most politically useful fact in the story. Republican support below 30% across the eight surveyed states may reflect rejection of the governing right, but it does not establish durable loyalty to Democrats.

The secretary of state results make that fragility visible. Democrat Garlin Gilchrist led Republican Anthony Forlini 55% to 25%, yet about one-fifth of respondents were undecided and more than 60% had no opinion of each candidate. A large ballot preference can coexist with weak attachment and limited knowledge.

The framing hides the harder test

Personalizing the findings as Trump’s “very bad” reputation makes an institutional story easier to consume and easier to misunderstand. Trump is central because he is president, but the poll also measures whether Republican candidates will bear the cost of association with his administration and whether Democrats can convert dissatisfaction into participation.

The decisive actors now include campaigns, parties and election institutions with the money, organization and authority to reach inexperienced voters. Treating young people as a demographic wave obscures that turnout is organized through registration, information, persuasion and access. If those systems fail, the polling margin will have described frustration without changing who governs.

Political failure creates openings, not outcomes

The larger pattern is a generation judging government through material insecurity and perceived corruption rather than through party messaging alone. Housing costs, groceries, jobs and personal finances are not branding problems. They are the conditions under which political legitimacy is earned or squandered.

Republicans face a severe warning in this poll because they are tied to the president young respondents overwhelmingly dislike. Democrats face a different test: whether they can offer more than being the available alternative. Power will not shift because a survey found anger. It shifts only if institutions convert that anger into votes—and if the winners then use office to change the conditions that produced it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Very Bad’: Trump faces stunning rejection from swing-state youth

item.title: Conservative claims ‘doomsday’ likely even if Dems crush Trump: 'Staring down the barrel’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Jonathan V. Last, an anti-Trump conservative editor at The Bulwark, warned that even a decisive Democratic midterm victory would not guarantee a Democratic presidential win in 2028. His “doomsday scenario” is that Republican candidates could blame a Democratic-controlled Congress for national problems, present themselves as insurgents and retain the White House.

Last named JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr. and Tucker Carlson as possible candidates who could use that strategy. He also cited a Bulwark focus group in which Michigan Trump voters expressed dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump but did not indicate that they would necessarily vote Democratic. The article did not provide a publication date beyond “Monday,” so its references to an election four weeks away and to November cannot be anchored more precisely.

The headline oversells the warning

“Doomsday” suggests that Last predicted catastrophe even after a Democratic landslide. His actual argument is narrower: congressional victory can produce complacency, and control of Congress can make Democrats a more convenient target in the next presidential campaign.

That is a conventional warning about divided responsibility and electoral volatility, inflated into an apocalyptic teaser. RawStory resolves the tease only after wrapping it in loaded language. The result is political coverage engineered around alarm rather than institutional clarity.

Power would still sit with the presidency

Congressional majorities matter, but Last’s scenario begins with Republicans retaining the executive branch after the midterms. The president would still direct the executive apparatus, dominate the party’s national message and exercise the powers of the office. A Democratic Congress could legislate, investigate and block appointments or bills, depending on its margins, but it would not become the administration.

That distinction is the center of the story. Yet the framing treats Democratic electoral success as the source of a future trap, rather than examining how a Republican administration and its potential successors could evade responsibility for governing failures.

Blame is the political weapon

The prospective Republican candidates Last identifies would have agency. If they blamed Congress for outcomes produced partly or primarily by the executive branch, that would be a campaign choice, not an automatic consequence of divided government.

The Michigan focus-group remark about choosing between “fascists and communists” shows how distorted equivalence can survive disappointment with an incumbent. It does not establish what those voters will do, much less predict the 2028 result. It does show why poor presidential performance does not mechanically transfer support to the opposition: voters interpret events through partisan labels that political actors and media institutions continually reinforce.

Democrats cannot campaign on arithmetic

Last is right about one limited point: winning seats is not the same as building durable political support. A large midterm victory could constrain an administration without persuading voters that Democrats deserve the presidency two years later.

But describing that possibility as a Democratic “trap” obscures responsibility. Democratic leaders would be accountable for how they used congressional power. Republican officeholders and candidates would be accountable for their decisions and claims. Voters would make choices within an information system that often rewards theatrical blame more than accurate attribution.

The system rewards displaced responsibility

The larger pattern is not that victory secretly becomes defeat. It is that American political institutions divide power while campaign messaging aggressively scrambles responsibility. Presidents blame Congress. Legislators blame presidents. Candidates run against an “establishment” their own party controls. Coverage then packages the resulting uncertainty as suspense.

That structure benefits the actors most capable of defining whom the public should blame. The danger Last identifies is therefore less mystical than “doomsday”: institutional power can remain in Republican hands while political responsibility is redirected toward Democrats the moment they acquire enough authority to serve as a target.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Conservative claims ‘doomsday’ likely even if Dems crush Trump: ‘Staring down the barrel’

item.title: Jack Smith's shirt sends Fox News into a frenzy: 'Pretty rich for that guy!’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that conservative podcaster Ben Ferguson called former special counsel Jack Smith’s “No Kings” shirt “pretty rich,” falsely accusing Smith of trying to overturn an election. Smith wore the Bruce Springsteen tour shirt at the Power to the People Fest in Columbia, Maryland, on Saturday.

Fox News host Harris Faulkner introduced the shirt after noting that Smith had testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee the previous Tuesday about his investigations of Donald Trump. Those investigations produced an August 2023 indictment concerning Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

The segment began with warnings about progressive candidates and expanded into complaints about musicians displaying political messages. Ferguson predicted such expression could damage performers’ careers.

The inversion is the point

Smith did not attempt to overturn an election. According to the reporting, he investigated and charged Trump over alleged efforts to overturn one. Ferguson erased that distinction and reassigned the accused conduct to the prosecutor.

That is not substantive criticism of Smith’s legal decisions. It is an inversion of the documented roles: the official who pursued a case becomes the supposed attacker, while the defendant disappears from responsibility. RawStory correctly identifies the claim as false.

Power was hiding in plain sight

Smith was presented as a suspicious political actor because he wore a shirt at a music festival. But he is a former special counsel and, in this episode, a private citizen. Trump is the president. Members of Congress possess oversight authority. Fox News controls a national broadcast platform.

Those disparities vanish inside the segment. Faulkner treated Smith’s leisure time as evidence worth scoffing at, as though congressional testimony placed his clothing and weekend attendance under continuing political supervision. The powerful were cast as aggrieved spectators; the former prosecutor’s T-shirt became the provocation.

A grievance machine needs no coherence

The segment bundled progressive candidates, immigration policy, health care, college funding, Supreme Court changes, climate policy, Palestine advocacy, international law and Smith’s clothing into one warning about national destruction. No demonstrated connection was necessary. Proximity did the work.

The complaint about politics entering concerts was especially hollow. The program objected not to political messaging as such, but to political messaging it opposed. Ferguson delivered an extended ideological lecture while condemning performers for delivering ideological lectures.

Punishment replaces argument

Ferguson’s prediction that political expression could hurt musicians’ careers carried the segment’s practical message: dissent may be met with economic consequences. He framed that prospect as neutral “cause and effect,” obscuring the people and institutions that manufacture backlash.

The same mechanism operated against Smith. Fox News converted an ordinary act of expression into a televised character indictment, then used a false account of his prosecution to justify outrage. The shirt was merely the pretext.

The systemic error

This is how accountability gets neutralized without rebutting evidence. Reverse the roles, portray prosecution as persecution, inflate private expression into scandal and surround the whole exercise with unrelated stories of cultural menace.

The larger pattern is disciplined misdirection. Institutional power becomes invisible, weaker actors are made to answer for symbolic offenses, and a false accusation receives the authority of a national platform. The audience is not asked to assess what happened in the 2020 election case. It is instructed to resent the man who investigated it—and, this time, to resent his shirt.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Jack Smith’s shirt sends Fox News into a frenzy: ‘Pretty rich for that guy!’

item.title: 'Oh, come on!' GOP senator shouted down on 'The View' over Don Jr.'s wedding oligarch
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Thom Tillis defended his vote to confirm Attorney General Todd Blanche after “The View” co-host Ana Navarro challenged Blanche’s refusal to examine reported payments by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev toward Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas. When Tillis called Blanche qualified to give President Donald Trump honest advice, Navarro shouted, “Oh, come on!”

According to the report, ProPublica said Kremlev contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars. Trump later said his son repaid Kremlev, but RawStory says neither the White House nor the Trump Organization had provided evidence. Blanche responded to reporters’ questions by asking what there was to investigate. Tillis maintained that private discussions and Blanche’s work justified his confirmation vote.

The vote was the power

Navarro’s central point was not that Tillis failed to recognize compromised nominees. By his own account, he knew Pete Hegseth and Kristi Noem were unqualified, yet voted to confirm them. He now calls the Hegseth vote the biggest regret of his career while hoping someone else fires the official he helped empower.

That is not helplessness. Senators possess confirmation power precisely so they can stop nominees they consider unfit. Tillis repeatedly chose approval, then repackaged his awareness of the defects as evidence of discernment. Recognition without resistance is not oversight. It is informed enablement.

Blanche’s discretion matters

An attorney general commands investigative machinery that television hosts and retiring senators do not. The relevant issue is therefore not whether Navarro won an argument. It is whether Blanche treated a reported foreign oligarch’s substantial spending on the president’s son as worthy of scrutiny.

The reporting does not establish that the payment was illegal, that Trump Jr. failed to repay it, or that Blanche corruptly suppressed an investigation. It does establish the reported payment, the president’s unsupported repayment claim as described by RawStory, and Blanche’s dismissive response when questioned. Those facts justify questions. Declaring there is apparently nothing to examine prevents answers from emerging.

A transaction dressed as principle

Tillis cited two outcomes to defend Blanche: Jerome Powell remaining on the Federal Reserve Board and Blanche rescinding an order connected to a proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund. RawStory reports that Tillis and Sen. John Cornyn withheld support until Blanche reversed course, although the underlying settlement remained intact and the fund could be revived.

That defense exposes the arrangement. Tillis did not describe an independent attorney general reliably applying neutral standards. He described a nominee whose conduct changed under senatorial pressure and whose confirmation could therefore be justified as a political bargain. “Playing the hand” is an admission that institutional power was traded, not a demonstration that it was responsibly exercised.

The headline’s diversion

The spectacle is Navarro shouting down a senator. The substance is that a senator knowingly supplied confirmation votes to officials he criticized as unqualified or compliant, then invoked limited concessions to excuse the larger transfer of authority.

Focusing on the interruption relocates agency from the officeholder who cast consequential votes to the host who objected loudly. Navarro’s volume did not confirm Blanche, Hegseth, or Noem. Tillis and other senators did. The theatrical confrontation is easier to package than the institutional record, but it is far less important.

Regret after authorization

This story reveals a durable pattern: officials enable presidential power when their votes matter, advertise private misgivings when consequences appear, and later market regret as courage. Tillis’s book tour converts failures of judgment into a narrative of candor while the people he helped install retain public authority.

The system does not fail because senators lack information about the nominees before them. In Tillis’s own telling, he saw the defects. It fails when those entrusted with a veto choose accommodation, preserve a few bargaining victories, and call their subsequent disappointment accountability.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Oh, come on!’ GOP senator shouted down on ‘The View’ over Don Jr.’s wedding oligarch

item.title: Explosive CIA leak raises fears of imminent and ‘total collapse’ of major US ally
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that two unnamed U.S. sources briefed Drop Site News on a classified CIA assessment warning that Israel could face civil war or “total collapse.” The August report, titled “Fracture From Within,” reportedly described several pressures converging ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections. Neither RawStory nor Drop Site News obtained the document itself, and the reporting does not establish that collapse is imminent.

According to Drop Site News, the assessment cited economic strain, record-high military spending, widespread psychological trauma and profound political divisions. It reportedly emphasized resentment over broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men while reservists are repeatedly taken away from their jobs and families.

The assessment came from the CIA’s Red Cell, a unit designed to challenge prevailing intelligence assumptions through alternative analysis. That makes the reported warning a scenario deserving scrutiny, not a public CIA prediction that civil war will occur.

The headline outruns the evidence

“Explosive leak” and “imminent collapse” sell certainty the underlying account does not provide. The report was described by anonymous sources, not published or independently authenticated in the supplied reporting. Its starkest conclusion concerns vulnerability to a triggering event, not proof that national collapse is already underway.

That distinction matters. Intelligence analysis identifies risks under particular conditions. Turning a risk assessment into a countdown substitutes alarm for precision and obscures what the analysts reportedly examined: political decisions that have distributed sacrifice unevenly and allowed accumulated pressures to harden into institutional conflict.

Power created the fracture

Israel’s government and political institutions hold the relevant power. Reservists did not design military-conscription rules, determine state benefits or set record military spending. Ultra-Orthodox citizens did not collectively acquire exemptions by administrative accident. Political leaders maintained an arrangement under which one constituency retained protections while others repeatedly supplied labor, time and personal risk.

The reported resentment is therefore not merely a clash between social groups. It is the consequence of state policy. Describing the divide as one population refusing and another population resenting can misdirect attention downward, toward the people living under the arrangement, instead of upward, toward the officials and governing coalitions capable of changing it.

Exemption is political currency

Drop Site News reports that ultra-Orthodox leaders defend the exemptions as necessary to protect religious life and Torah study, not as opposition to Israel’s wars. That explanation should be represented accurately. It does not erase the state’s role in deciding whose obligations are compulsory and whose are negotiable.

When governments depend on organized constituencies, exceptions become instruments of coalition maintenance. The resulting inequality is then presented as a cultural dispute, as though no institution authored it. The CIA assessment, as described, points instead to a dangerous bargain: political power preserves unequal duties until the burden itself becomes destabilizing.

Crisis language can conceal responsibility

Economic hardship, psychological trauma and military strain are not weather systems. They are conditions shaped by policy, spending priorities and the repeated mobilization of reservists. The supplied reporting does not establish that Israeli leaders intended social fracture, but the consequences described were foreseeable enough to become the subject of a classified assessment.

RawStory’s collapse framing also risks converting governance failures into spectacle. “One spark” invites fixation on the eventual trigger. The more important question is who accumulated the combustible material. A dramatic confrontation may ignite a crisis, but institutions create the conditions in which one confrontation can carry national consequences.

The systemic error

States often treat social cohesion as an inexhaustible resource: demand sacrifice, allocate it unequally, protect politically valuable exemptions and call the resulting anger polarization. Intelligence agencies then arrive late to quantify the instability produced by decisions civilian leaders already made.

The broader pattern is not mysterious collapse from within. It is governing coalitions consuming institutional legitimacy to preserve immediate political arrangements. By the time officials describe the result as a security threat, the unequal distribution of power and obligation has already done much of the damage.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Explosive CIA leak raises fears of imminent and ‘total collapse’ of major US ally

item.title: Trump knows horrors so awful that Republicans commit treason to silence him
item.description:
What happened

RawStory argues that Senate Republicans’ hostile questioning of former special counsel Jack Smith reflected loyalty to Donald Trump and an effort to divert attention from the Epstein files. At a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday, Republican senators Eric Schmitt and John Kennedy attacked Smith’s credibility, while ranking Democrat Dick Durbin welcomed him. Smith answered questions without invoking the Fifth Amendment.

The article says Schmitt tried to connect Smith to Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, whom Smith said he had never met, and invoked allegations about Willis’s relationship with a former colleague. Kennedy asked Smith whether he believed in the Tooth Fairy or Easter Bunny. RawStory presents these exchanges as unserious attempts to discredit the official who investigated efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

But the headline’s promised revelation is absent. The article supplies no evidence that Trump possesses compromising information about Republican lawmakers, that Russian hackers obtained such material, or that Republicans committed treason to keep it secret. Those claims are speculation, not reporting.

The power is in the Senate seats

Smith was the witness, but senators controlled the hearing. They chose the questions, set the frame and used institutional time to turn oversight into political defense work. Their failure to land a coherent accusation does not erase that power; it shows what they elected to do with it.

Schmitt’s reported attempt to drag Willis’s personal controversy into questions about Smith illustrates the mechanism. If no operational connection between them was established, the reference did not illuminate Smith’s conduct. It substituted associative suspicion for evidence.

Kennedy’s fairy-tale questions served the same purpose more crudely. A senator does not need to rebut an investigation when ridicule can signal to partisan audiences that the investigator is beneath serious consideration.

Loyalty does not require a secret dossier

RawStory weakens its strongest case by reaching for blackmail. The documented conduct described in the article is already politically significant: Republican senators used a formal hearing to attack Smith, and the party returned to Trump after some members condemned him following January 6.

Those choices do not require hidden Russian files or unnamed “horrors” to explain them. Electoral dependence, partisan incentives and fear of a primary challenge are visible forms of coercion within a party. The article itself cites Representative Thomas Massie being primaried after angering Trump over the Epstein files. That is concrete political pressure. Blackmail remains conjecture.

Inventing a darker mechanism can perversely absolve the actors involved. If lawmakers are imagined as helpless captives of secret kompromat, their public decisions begin to look forced. The available evidence supports a simpler conclusion: they retained agency and repeatedly exercised it.

The article misdirects its own indictment

The piece correctly directs attention toward officials with institutional authority rather than treating Smith as the author of the spectacle. But its insults and unsupported treason theory blur that accountability.

Calling senators stupid may be emotionally satisfying, yet incompetence is not the central problem. Schmitt and Kennedy reportedly used their offices to replace factual examination with insinuation and mockery. That is a choice about how power should function, not merely a deficit of intelligence.

“Treason” is also a specific and exceptionally serious accusation. RawStory does not establish it. Nor does the article substantiate an Epstein-files coverup involving every Republican lawmaker and the attorney general. A publication attacking propaganda should not imitate its evidentiary shortcuts.

The useful pattern is institutional conversion

The larger pattern is not that Trump must possess a supernatural archive of secrets. It is that party institutions can be converted into personal protection systems through ordinary incentives: nominations, committee influence, audience approval and the punishment of dissent.

Once that conversion occurs, oversight becomes theater. Investigators are placed on trial, unrelated scandals become insinuations, and lawmakers perform disbelief rather than test evidence. The objective effect is to make accountability look inherently partisan and facts permanently contestable.

That pattern is more durable—and more damning—than RawStory’s blackmail fantasy. It requires no hidden mastermind, only officials who discover that serving one political leader is safer for their careers than serving the responsibilities of their offices.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump knows horrors so awful that Republicans commit treason to silence him

item.title: Oblivious Trump is barreling forward with a vow even Republicans despise
item.description:
What happened

RawStory columnist Jason Miciak argues that Donald Trump is pressing ahead with a federally supported AI and data-center expansion despite mounting opposition from voters, including Republicans. The column says local communities are objecting to electricity costs, water use, land consumption, and public subsidies, while GOP candidates are struggling to defend the policy.

Citing Axios, Miciak reports that the Republican National Committee warned Ohio Senate candidate John Husted that Democrats’ attacks on data centers were working. Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown had tied Husted to data-center expansion, tax subsidies, and higher electricity costs; a Fox News poll cited by Axios showed Brown ahead by eight points at that time. The column says Republican House candidates in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and Virginia face similar attacks.

The piece also reports that Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio circulated what has been described as a “survival guide” for candidates. RawStory had not seen that document, so the column’s speculation about its contents is not established. Its broader claim is clearer: Trump’s project has become politically costly for Republicans required to campaign beneath it.

Power sits in Washington and the boardroom

Local residents may object, but they do not control the federal subsidies or the national development agenda. Trump and his administration hold that institutional power. Technology companies and their wealthy investors possess the capital and access needed to turn federal encouragement into construction, electricity demand, water consumption, and land acquisition.

That distinction matters because “AI anxiety” can become a fog that hides responsibility. Artificial intelligence is not independently choosing where data centers are built or who absorbs their costs. Government officials authorize incentives. Companies select sites and pursue expansion. Utilities and regulators determine how infrastructure costs are allocated. Communities encounter the consequences after more powerful actors have made the consequential choices.

Republicans have a policy problem, not a messaging problem

The reported “survival guide” exposes the party’s immediate priority: helping candidates talk around an unpopular project. That is political damage control, not policy reconsideration.

Candidates can invoke competition with China or promise local benefits, but rhetoric does not settle who pays for new electricity capacity, who receives subsidies, or whose water and land are consumed. If Republicans believe the buildout is imposing unacceptable costs, they possess legislative and regulatory tools. If they decline to use them while searching for better slogans, they are enabling the policy they claim to find electorally inconvenient.

The vulnerable candidates are not powerless spectators trapped by Trump’s personality. They are officeholders or would-be officeholders operating within his party. Their predicament is a choice between challenging a national economic project and protecting their standing in a political system organized around loyalty to its leader.

The column outruns its evidence

Miciak is persuasive when he identifies a conflict between concentrated economic power and local costs. He is less careful when he declares overwhelming public opposition, predicts a “blue wave,” or treats several races as evidence of a settled national verdict. The supplied reporting cites one poll, party warnings, campaign advertising, and opposition in several districts. That supports evidence of political vulnerability, not certainty about the midterm result or the scale of national consensus.

The column also bundles distinct concerns—data-center construction, electricity prices, job displacement, financial-market risk, and catastrophic fears about AI—into one political force. Those issues overlap, but they are not interchangeable. Opposition to a subsidized facility does not automatically establish opposition to every use of AI, much less agreement about existential danger.

That exaggeration weakens an argument that does not need it. The documented political fact is already significant: Republicans reportedly believe data-center opposition is effective enough to require a nationwide warning and candidate guidance.

Culture-war misdirection has limits

The sharper political pattern is that material costs are harder to displace with symbolic conflict. A voter facing higher utility expenses or a contested industrial development has a concrete grievance tied to identifiable decisions. Campaign messaging about social enemies cannot make an electricity bill disappear.

That helps explain why this issue can cross partisan lines without producing a coherent bipartisan program. Shared anger is not shared power. Residents can oppose a project for different reasons while federal officials, party leaders, corporations, and investors retain control over financing and development.

The danger for political coverage is to romanticize voter backlash while leaving the machinery untouched. Elections can punish candidates, but punishment alone does not determine subsidy rules, utility-rate structures, water protections, or limits on development.

The system privatizes the gain and disperses the cost

This story is ultimately about how the American state advances large private projects. The promised benefits are national—technological leadership, economic growth, strategic competition—while many burdens are local and specific. The companies gain infrastructure and market position; residents confront demands on power, water, land, and public money.

Republican operatives reportedly understand the electoral liability. Their response, as described, is not to transfer decision-making power to affected communities or establish enforceable protections. It is to teach candidates how to survive association with the policy.

That is the systemic error: concentrated actors make the decision, weaker communities absorb the consequences, and political professionals treat the resulting anger as a communications emergency.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Oblivious Trump is barreling forward with a vow even Republicans despise

item.title: 'Oh my god': Trump's passport redesign sparks rumors 'looks like Claude designed it’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that online critics compared the redesigned U.S. passport to an AI-generated layout because its cover uses a small all-caps “PASSPORT” above an oversized country name—a typographic device associated by commenters with Claude. The reporting provides no evidence that Claude or any other AI system designed the passport.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio unveiled the “Flight of the Eagle” design on September 29, 2026, while launching the AI-powered America.gov. Scheduled for 2028, the 38-page passport will feature a larger gold seal, animated eagle imagery and scenes from U.S. history. Rubio’s presentation also showed Trump in one page image, according to One Mile at a Time, but Trump’s inclusion in the standard passport has not been confirmed.

The state has the power

Internet users supplied the jokes. Rubio and the State Department control the document.

That distinction matters because a passport is not promotional merchandise. It is an instrument through which the government certifies identity and regulates international movement. The consequential decisions concern what imagery appears in it, whose version of national history it presents and whether a sitting president enters that official narrative. The resemblance to an AI design habit is trivia beside that authority.

Branding the nation

Rubio described the redesign as putting “United States of America” where it belongs—“first, right on top”—and called the interior a story of “the greatest nation in the history of the world.” Those remarks frame design choices as a correction to insufficient patriotic emphasis.

The larger seal, more conspicuous gold, presentation box and historical procession turn a functional credential into a prestige object. None of that proves misconduct. It does show an administration using routine state infrastructure to stage its preferred nationalism: louder, grander and less interested in restraint.

The personality question

The most politically significant unresolved detail is Trump’s possible appearance. One displayed image reportedly included him, while The Bulwark previously reported that a commemorative edition would place his portrait before the Declaration of Independence. RawStory says the everyday 2028 passport has not been confirmed to include him.

That uncertainty should not be inflated into fact, but it should not be buried under typography discourse either. Depicting a sitting president inside an ordinary passport would collapse the distance between the country and its temporary officeholder. The question is not whether the portrait looks tasteful. It is whether public authority is being used to place one politician inside the state’s visual definition of America.

The safer distraction

The “Claude eyebrow” framing redirects scrutiny toward the weakest actors in the story: designers, design conventions and social-media spectators. It converts an exercise of institutional power into a debate about whether the cover looks machine-made.

That is politically convenient even if no one engineered the distraction. Aesthetic ridicule is easy to circulate; examining who authorized the imagery and what precedents it creates is harder. RawStory identifies the online reaction clearly, but its headline gives the meme more weight than the state decision behind it.

The systemic error

Modern political branding works by embedding ideology in objects presented as administrative upgrades. A redesigned website, a new application process and a revised passport arrive together as improved public service, while symbolism quietly defines who represents the nation and how citizens are expected to see it.

The larger pattern is not that government design has become embarrassing. It is that personalization and nationalist spectacle can enter ordinary institutions under cover of aesthetics. The jokes target the cover. The power lies with the officials deciding what—and potentially whom—citizens must carry.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Oh my god’: Trump’s passport redesign sparks rumors ‘looks like Claude designed it’

item.title: Surprising twist as Republican's racy ad trashed as 'grotesque' on the right
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that California Republican gubernatorial nominee Steve Hilton released a campaign ad depicting one young woman helping another mark a mail ballot for him while they sit on a bed beneath a Pride flag. Hilton, a former Fox News host endorsed by Donald Trump in April, called the spot provocative and funny before releasing a video saying he regretted the pain it caused.

Christian nationalist pastor Jack Hibbs denounced the ad as “grotesque” and portrayed lesbianism among young women as a sweeping social ill. He nevertheless said he would vote for Hilton. Republican attorney-general candidate Michael Gates also condemned the ad, while a CNN panel concluded that the controversy had succeeded in attracting attention.

The uproar arrived with Hilton trailing Democrat Xavier Becerra 58 percent to 33 percent in a Berkeley IGS/Los Angeles Times poll. The article does not establish that the ad changed those numbers or improved Hilton’s position.

The candidate made the choice

Hilton and his campaign hold agency here. They chose the imagery, approved the message and distributed the advertisement. Its failure was not that viewers somehow misunderstood an innocent appeal. The campaign deliberately used sexual suggestion, queer symbolism and secret ballot-marking as attention devices.

Hilton’s subsequent expression of regret does not erase that sequence. He first defended the ad as funny and provocative, then apologized for its effect. That is political message-testing followed by retreat when the reaction proved costly—not a mystery requiring breathless speculation.

Outrage without accountability

Hibbs’s response exposes the limits of right-wing moral condemnation. He attacked the advertisement, cast the underlying sexuality as a social evil, and then insulated Hilton from electoral consequences. CNN analyst Sara Fischer correctly identified the practical result: Hilton retained the pastor’s vote.

That arrangement gives conservative influencers theatrical distance without requiring them to challenge Republican power. Hibbs can rebuke the packaging while continuing to support the candidate responsible for it. The outrage therefore disciplines campaign aesthetics, not political allegiance.

The weaker actors become props

The young women depicted in the ad have no institutional power. Yet they become the terrain on which politicians and religious figures perform their authority. Hilton’s campaign used implied intimacy to sell a vote; Hibbs answered by stigmatizing lesbianism among young women.

Michael Gates accused the campaign of exploiting young women for political advantage. On the facts RawStory presents, that criticism reaches the central problem more directly than the debate over whether the spot was clever, offensive or effective. The people represented in the advertisement were reduced to instruments in a contest among ambitious men.

Attention is not political strength

The CNN discussion treated universal conversation as evidence that the advertisement “works.” That is the media logic campaigns exploit: provocation produces denunciation, denunciation produces airtime, and airtime is reclassified as success.

But visibility is not persuasion. RawStory’s cited poll placed Hilton 25 percentage points behind Becerra. Without evidence of changed voter support, calling the controversy a win confuses media consumption with political movement. It also rewards campaigns for manufacturing spectacle instead of explaining how they would use state power.

The system rewards the stunt

The larger pattern is an alliance between campaign cynicism and attention-driven coverage. A candidate facing a severe polling deficit releases a calculated provocation. Ideological allies condemn it without withdrawing support. Television analysts then praise its ability to dominate discussion.

Every institution gets something: the campaign gets exposure, religious activists get a culture-war target, and broadcasters get conflict. The public gets little information about governing. That is not accidental confusion. It is a political economy in which spectacle is cheap, accountability is optional, and the people invoked by the spectacle bear the contempt.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Surprising twist as Republican’s racy ad trashed as ‘grotesque’ on the right

item.title: 'The unmanly truth' about Trump revealed
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Paul Waldman, writing for MS NOW, identified the “unmanly truth” as the Trump administration’s failure to deliver the economic security it promised young men and other voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024. Citing the latest federal jobs report, Waldman argued that prices remain burdensome, manufacturing employment is lower than when Trump took office, and the promised factory revival has not materialized.

Waldman also attributed higher gasoline prices to Trump’s war with Iran, with sharper consequences for rural residents who drive farther and often use less fuel-efficient vehicles. Meanwhile, he wrote, employment growth has occurred in fields such as home healthcare and social services—work that clashes with the administration’s preferred image of masculinity. With an election reportedly one month away, Waldman suggested that the gap between Trump’s promises and his record may help explain his poor polling, though the article does not establish that explanation as causal.

The power belongs to the president

Young men may have cast decisive votes, but they do not command federal economic, military, or communications policy. Trump and his administration do. The president made the sweeping promise to reduce prices “starting on Day One,” promoted a restoration of manufacturing employment, and took the military action that Waldman links to higher fuel costs.

That distinction matters because political coverage often treats disappointed constituencies as the central characters after an election. They are not. Voters supplied authority; the administration exercised it. The relevant question is not why young men wanted stable work. It is what Trump did with the power obtained by promising it.

Nostalgia was substituted for policy

The manufacturing vision described here was not merely a jobs proposal. It offered status, identity and social restoration through an economy imagined as physically demanding, male and industrial. But a president cannot recreate a vanished labor market through posture. According to Waldman, the measurable result is fewer manufacturing jobs than when Trump entered office, not the factory boom he advertised.

The growing sectors expose the fraud in the fantasy. Home healthcare and social services meet real needs and provide actual employment, yet Waldman argues that Trump’s gender politics make such work difficult for his movement to celebrate. The administration’s cultural script therefore works against economic adaptation: it tells men to recover dignity through jobs that are not appearing while demeaning the kinds of work that are.

Masculinity is the misdirection

AlterNet’s framing risks turning a governing failure into a psychological story about men. The deeper issue is not that young male voters placed too much emotional weight on Trump. It is that a politician made concrete promises, acquired institutional power and, by Waldman’s account, pursued choices that worsened costs without producing the promised employment gains.

The imagery of testosterone, pickups and “manly” labor is politically relevant because it helped sell the program. But it can also obscure accountability. A worker struggling to afford gasoline is experiencing a material consequence, not a crisis of symbolism. Culture-war masculinity offers an explanation for why the sales pitch resonated; it does not excuse the officials who sold it or replace scrutiny of their decisions.

Grievance cannot provide a paycheck

Waldman describes an administration and allied media ecosystem promoting manhood through bullying, violence and anxiety. His interpretation is sharpest when connected to the economic void beneath that performance. If secure work and affordable necessities remain unavailable, theatrical dominance becomes a cheap substitute for material provision.

The predictable beneficiaries are politicians and influencers who can keep converting insecurity into attention and loyalty. The voter receives an identity to defend while the promised economic transformation fails to arrive. Even the reported disappointment can then be redirected toward vulnerable groups rather than toward the officials controlling policy.

The systemic error

This is a recurring political bargain: concentrated power promises to reverse structural economic change, packages the promise as cultural restoration, and leaves ordinary supporters to absorb the failure privately. When the numbers disappoint, public discussion drifts toward voter psychology—alienation, impatience, masculinity—rather than staying fixed on presidential agency.

The consequential divide is not between masculine and unmasculine work. It is between those who make promises and decisions and those who pay for them. A politics organized around lost status can win power. It cannot manufacture an economy merely by insisting that the past deserves to return.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘The unmanly truth’ about Trump revealed

item.title: 'Not a mentally well man': Experts analyze uncensored Trump interview
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that, in a 75-minute interview with Time, President Donald Trump rejected unfavorable polling, blamed the press for public understanding of his statements, defended “annihilating” Iran as a means of creating peace, and declined to rule out invoking emergency powers around the approaching midterm elections. When asked whether ICE agents would be sent to polling places, he said he had not considered it; when asked about the Insurrection Act, he said he “could use it.”

AlterNet asked psychiatrist Bandy Lee and psychologist Vincent Greenwood to assess the interview. Lee described Trump as “not a mentally well man” and argued that his potential for violence was increasing. Greenwood said Trump’s public record and interview responses displayed traits associated with clinical psychopathy. Those are their professional opinions, not diagnoses established by an examination or legal finding; Greenwood argued that his chosen assessment method does not require a personal interview.

The report says Trump also disputed low approval ratings, offered sweeping claims about his economic record, and became angry that Time’s journalists had not asked sufficiently positive questions. The interview, as presented by AlterNet, left unresolved what Trump would actually do during the midterms.

Power is the relevant diagnosis

The psychiatric commentary is arresting, but the institutional fact is more important: Trump is president. He commands the executive branch and can influence the deployment of federal law-enforcement personnel and the military. His refusal to identify limits on those powers therefore cannot be treated as merely strange or emotionally revealing.

Neither Lee nor Greenwood decides whether ICE appears near polling sites or whether an administration attempts to invoke the Insurrection Act. Trump and the officials empowered to execute his directives do. A fixation on his mental state can obscure that chain of agency, converting a question about government power into a spectacle of individual pathology.

Ambiguity serves the officeholder

“I don’t rule anything out or in” is not a policy announcement. AlterNet’s evidence does not establish that Trump had ordered election-related deployments or decided to invoke emergency authority. It does establish that he declined opportunities to state clear limits.

That ambiguity has political utility regardless of its psychological origin. It warns opponents, encourages loyalists to imagine escalation, and preserves deniability if no action follows. The weaker actors in this story—voters, protesters, journalists and targeted communities—do not create that uncertainty. The president does, while holding powers that can give it material force.

The mental-health frame has limits

AlterNet’s headline directs attention toward whether Trump is “mentally well.” That framing risks medicalizing conduct that is already intelligible in political terms: rejecting adverse evidence, demanding flattering coverage, describing mass destruction as peace and presenting coercive authority as personally discretionary.

A clinical label can also become an alibi. If every abuse of power is explained as illness, then advisers, agency leaders, legislators and judges become background scenery. Yet presidential power is never exercised by one nervous system alone. It moves through institutions staffed by people who can authorize, implement, resist or legitimize it.

The record is serious enough

The article is strongest when it stays with Trump’s words and the authority attached to them. His rhetoric about Iran treats catastrophic violence as a solution. His comments about polling and the press cast unwelcome information as corruption. His answer on emergency powers offers no limiting principle. Those facts require scrutiny without turning expert inference into proven diagnosis or a hypothetical deployment into a completed act.

AlterNet weakens its case when it jumps from the interview to the assertion that Trump is capable of “almost anything” to retain power. The interview supports concern about his stated posture and refusal to impose boundaries on himself. It does not establish every future act the article imagines.

A system built around permission

The larger pattern is not simply an erratic president saying alarming things. It is an executive system in which consequential coercive powers can hinge on a president’s judgment, followed by political and legal institutions deciding whether to cooperate.

Personal instability, if present, would magnify that danger; it would not create the machinery. The decisive question is who grants permission when a president tests the boundary. Authoritarian practice becomes governmental reality through compliance: an aide drafts the order, an agency adopts the rationale, a lawyer supplies the justification, and an official carries it out.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Not a mentally well man’: Experts analyze uncensored Trump interview

item.title: US soldiers wounded in Iran attack speak out after horrific medical treatment by Pentagon
item.description:
What happened

Nine U.S. service members wounded in an Iranian drone strike said Pentagon medical care left them navigating serious injuries largely on their own. According to RawStory’s account of Associated Press reporting, the March 1 strike at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, killed six troops and injured dozens on the second day of the war.

The soldiers described delayed evacuation, inadequate transport, missing combat-wound documentation, outpatient treatment for severe injuries, and long waits for diagnoses or test results. Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón was sent to barracks despite shrapnel damage to an artery supplying his brain; Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom said he waited more than four months for MRI results; and some traumatic brain injuries reportedly went undiagnosed until the soldiers reached Fort Hood.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said one drone “squirted” through U.S. defenses, an account survivors disputed. The Pentagon told the AP that physicians evaluate incoming patients and admit them according to injury severity and standard industry practices. The Army declined to comment while its investigation remained unbriefed to the families of those killed.

The power was never with the wounded

These soldiers could not authorize evacuation, correct military records, assign hospital beds, release test results, or explain the defensive failure. Those powers belonged to the Pentagon, the Army, military medical administrators, and the chain of command.

Yet the burden shifted downward. Ramsbottom said he had to build his own case. Bearman attributed the failure to document the troops as combat-wounded to a coding error. Whatever produced that error, the institution controlled both the classification system and its consequences. Calling the breakdown administrative does not make it neutral; it identifies a bureaucracy whose mistakes are absorbed by injured people rather than by its decision-makers.

A euphemism meets survivor testimony

Hegseth’s description of a drone that “squirted” through defenses compresses a lethal event into the language of an unlucky breach. Survivors told CBS News that portraying the attack as a single drone slipping through was false. The reporting does not establish which account the military’s investigation will ultimately support, but it does establish a direct conflict between the defense secretary’s framing and testimony from people who were there.

That conflict matters because official language allocates responsibility. A freak penetration suggests misfortune. A broader defensive failure would raise harder questions about preparation, command decisions, and the protection promised to troops stationed at Port Shuaiba. The Army’s refusal to discuss its investigation before briefing bereaved families may be procedurally defensible, but it leaves the Pentagon’s public framing with an institutional advantage the wounded soldiers do not possess.

“Industry practices” answer the wrong charge

The Pentagon’s response—that physicians assess patients and admit them according to severity—describes a policy. It does not reconcile that policy with the cases reported: a stroke risk sent to barracks, a soldier with widespread shrapnel injuries transported on a cargo-plane floor, delayed brain-injury diagnoses, and months spent waiting for MRI results.

This is a familiar bureaucratic defense: state the existence of a process instead of accounting for its outcome. The question is not whether admission standards exist. It is why those standards, records, transportation arrangements, and follow-up systems produced what nine soldiers described as abandonment after combat injuries.

The sacred-trust story has an owner

Military rhetoric presents care for wounded troops as a solemn national obligation. Bearman’s statement that this trust was broken exposes the gap between the promise and the machinery responsible for honoring it.

The people with institutional power sent troops into danger, managed the defenses, controlled their evacuation, classified their injuries, and administered their treatment. The wounded then carried the practical consequences when those systems failed. Any framing that turns this into a tale of soldiers struggling through medical confusion obscures the direction of responsibility: the confusion was imposed on them by institutions above them.

War’s costs are managed after the cameras leave

The larger pattern is not merely inadequate care. It is the political management of war’s consequences. Leaders announce operations and offer compact explanations for battlefield failures; injured troops encounter the longer reality through cargo transport, barracks assignments, missing codes, delayed diagnoses, and contested paperwork.

When soldiers still serving in the Army take the unusual step of speaking publicly, their testimony punctures the clean official sequence of deployment, injury, evacuation, and care. The system asks them to accept battlefield risk, then makes some of them prove that the resulting wounds deserve recognition. That is not an unfortunate side story to military policy. It is military policy as experienced by the people with the least power to change it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: US soldiers wounded in Iran attack speak out after horrific medical treatment by Pentagon

item.title: Ken Paxton demanded 'chilling' 28-item list from a small-town pediatrician
item.description:
What happened

According to RawStory, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Consumer Protection Division sent a small central Texas pediatric practice a 28-item demand in December seeking 10 years of vaccine records, internal policies, and details of every benefit received from vaccine manufacturers. The letter instructed the pediatrician, identified only as Rachel, not to disclose the request and said citing the CDC’s childhood vaccination schedule would not adequately answer it.

Rachel reported spending nearly $15,000 on lawyers while retrieving records as minor as receipts for $18 vaccines. She disclosed even a drug representative’s $40 batch of cookies, but Paxton’s office issued further demands and called some responses improper or frivolous. After 20 years treating children in her community, she is reconsidering whether to continue practicing.

Paxton announced the investigation in January as an effort to expose alleged bribery by “Big Pharma and Big Insurance.” He described its targets as Texas’s largest medical providers, but the reporting does not establish why Rachel’s tiny practice was included. His office did not answer the New York Times’ request for an explanation.

The power is not ambiguous

Paxton controls a state enforcement office. Rachel runs a small pediatric practice. One side can compel records, impose legal costs, and threaten further scrutiny; the other must spend money and working hours proving that routine vaccine purchasing was not a conspiracy.

That imbalance is the central fact. The investigation does not need to uncover misconduct to inflict damage. A demand broad enough to reach decade-old receipts and trivial promotional items can punish through compliance alone. Whether or not Paxton’s office ultimately alleges a violation, it has already made ordinary medical practice more expensive and precarious.

An allegation in search of evidence

Paxton publicly framed the probe as a response to providers allegedly being bribed to pressure parents into vaccinating children. But the reported evidence from Rachel’s practice consists of modest discounts for prompt payment and a batch of cookies.

That does not establish bribery. It exposes the distance between the inflammatory public accusation and the mundane transactions captured by the demand. When an attorney general announces a conspiracy first and then deploys state power to search for supporting material, the accusation itself becomes political theater backed by compulsory process.

The confidentiality instruction compounds the pressure. Such language may be standard in an investigation, but here its practical effect was to isolate a small practitioner while the attorney general publicly promoted his own sweeping narrative.

The target is medical independence

Paxton later expanded the investigation to the American Academy of Pediatrics. That occurred after the academy sued the Trump administration and prevailed in a case concerning the cancellation of $12 million in federal grants; a judge ruled that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s department had illegally retaliated against it. The timing does not by itself prove that Paxton’s inquiry was retaliatory, but it makes scrutiny of its purpose unavoidable.

Paxton also said he was working alongside President Trump and Kennedy. That places the probe within a broader political campaign against institutions that defend established vaccination practices, not merely a narrow inquiry into a particular commercial transaction.

Calling this confusion about vaccine incentives would conceal agency. Paxton’s office chose the scope, the targets, and the burden. The foreseeable result is that pediatricians must weigh clinical work against the possibility of costly government investigation.

The public-health cost

Texas kindergarten vaccination rates for measles and polio fell from nearly 97 percent in 2019 to about 93 percent, according to the reporting. Against that backdrop, using state investigative power to portray pediatric vaccination as presumptively suspect carries consequences beyond Rachel’s legal bills.

Rekha Lakshmanan of the Immunization Partnership warned of a chilling effect. Rachel’s reconsideration of her career shows what that effect can look like in practice: fewer clinicians willing to provide care, recommend vaccines, or endure the administrative exposure attached to doing so.

The misdirection is “Big Pharma” rhetoric applied to a small-town doctor. It shifts attention upward toward a familiar corporate villain while state power bears downward on someone with far fewer resources.

Punishment without a verdict

This episode reveals a method of governance in which investigation itself becomes the sanction. Officials can impose cost, fear, and professional attrition without filing a charge or proving misconduct. The weaker target is then forced to rebut a story the government has already broadcast.

That pattern rewards officials twice: they gain publicity from alleging a vast conspiracy and leverage from compelling individuals to search for evidence of it. The institution with coercive authority presents itself as the aggrieved party; the pediatrician buried in demands is cast as a potential threat.

The systemic error is treating such an inquiry as a neutral search for facts while ignoring who selected the premise and who pays for it. Here, Paxton’s office made the decision, wielded the power, and created the burden. The documented consequence is not accountability for corporate corruption. It is a community doctor wondering whether practicing medicine is still worth the punishment.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ken Paxton demanded ‘chilling’ 28-item list from a small-town pediatrician
