item.title: 'It will never exist again': Steve Schmidt spots path to 'break MAGA for all time’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that former Republican operative and anti-Trump activist Steve Schmidt argued on his podcast that voters could “break MAGA” as a nationally viable coalition by defeating Trump-aligned candidates in the November midterm elections. He predicted a sweeping repudiation but offered no polling, electoral analysis, or other evidence in the article to establish that outcome.

Schmidt pointed to reported fractures over President Donald Trump’s decision to wage war against Iran and his dismissal of rising living costs as a “Democratic hoax.” RawStory cites criticism from former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene as evidence of internal strain. Schmidt nevertheless warned that even an electorally defeated MAGA faction could remain large enough to destabilize future elections, particularly by treating defeat as proof of fraud.

Prediction is not a pathway

The headline promises a path to permanent political defeat. What the article delivers is Schmidt saying people should vote Trump’s supporters out of office. That is an electoral objective, not a strategy—and certainly not evidence that MAGA “will never exist again” as a national coalition.

No decisive states, races, constituencies, turnout problems, or institutional mechanisms appear in the reporting. Schmidt’s certainty is therefore rhetoric. A movement organized around grievance and personal loyalty does not disappear merely because an opponent declares its expiration date.

Power still sits inside government

Trump holds presidential power. His administration can direct foreign policy, shape federal enforcement, command public attention, and force elected allies to choose between loyalty and dissent. Critics inside MAGA may expose fractures, but disagreement from prominent supporters is not the same as removing that institutional control.

Voters have agency at the ballot box, while parties, candidates, donors, election officials, courts, and legislatures determine how electoral power is organized and constrained. Reducing all of that to bravery makes for a clean podcast ending, but it conceals the institutions that enabled Trump’s coalition and would survive a midterm defeat.

The article sells confidence it does not substantiate

RawStory adopts Schmidt’s forecast as its central premise without seriously testing it. The phrase “spotted a path” upgrades an exhortation into a discovery. References to “cracks” in MAGA likewise suggest a measurable collapse, although the article supplies only selected disputes and public frustration over living costs.

That framing misdirects attention from the stronger actors. MAGA’s durability is not solely the product of devoted voters. It also depends on officeholders, party organizations, media figures, donors, and institutions willing to convert loyalty to Trump into governing power. Treating the coalition as a mass mood lets those enablers fade conveniently into the background.

Losing is not disappearing

Schmidt’s more defensible point cuts against his grand prediction: a faction can lose an election and retain enough power to obstruct government, intimidate officials, dominate a party, or reject legitimate outcomes. Electoral defeat and political extinction are different claims.

His description of a “Trump or else” message also identifies the authoritarian structure at issue: loyalty is elevated above pluralism, opposition is cast as illegitimate, and defeat is preemptively reframed as theft. Those reported claims deserve scrutiny. Declaring the coalition permanently broken does not answer them.

The system outlives the slogan

The larger pattern is liberal politics mistaking one election for institutional repair. Personalistic movements endure when political parties keep nominating their candidates, media systems reward their provocations, and officials face greater costs for dissent than obedience.

A midterm repudiation could restrict Trump’s governing power. It could not, by itself, erase the machinery that made MAGA electorally potent. RawStory’s framing turns Schmidt’s hope into a supposed roadmap; the actual story is harsher. Elections can remove officeholders, but dismantling an authoritarian political structure requires confronting every institution that continues to finance, amplify, normalize, and enforce it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘It will never exist again’: Steve Schmidt spots path to ‘break MAGA for all time’

item.title: Red state parents lash out at Trump: 'Never had this problem before’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Nebraska family nearly lost childcare because the state took unusually long to renew its subsidy. Parent Josh Wigginton said repeated calls failed, an email to his caseworker bounced back, and the uncertainty threatened a routine that allows both parents to work.

Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services acknowledged temporarily longer processing times across programs, including childcare assistance. Spokesman Jeff Powell attributed the slowdown partly to additional eligibility verification required by legislation Congress approved in July 2025, a signature Trump measure.

The headline overstates the evidence presented. AlterNet identifies one frustrated parent, not a documented revolt by “red state parents,” and Wigginton is not quoted blaming Trump or discussing his vote. The policy connection comes from the state agency; the broader electoral interpretation comes from commentators cited by AlterNet.

Power wrote the rules

The consequential actors are not families navigating unanswered calls. Congress imposed stricter eligibility requirements, Trump made the legislation part of his governing program, and Nebraska’s DHHS administers the resulting verification system.

That chain matters because administrative delay is often described as bureaucratic weather: unfortunate, temporary and nobody’s decision. Here, the agency itself linked longer processing partly to a federal requirement. Verification consumes staff time; families absorb the delay. Political officials created the burden, while applicants bear the risk of losing childcare and, consequently, their ability to work.

Suspicion has a constituency

Moving away from an “honor system” sounds like prudent oversight. But every new proof requirement rests on a political judgment: that preventing allegedly improper access deserves priority even when eligible families wait longer for essential support.

The reporting does not establish how much fraud existed, how much the new process prevents or whether Congress provided enough administrative capacity. Without those facts, officials cannot honestly present stricter verification as cost-free housekeeping. Its visible effect in this story is friction imposed on a family already deemed eligible in prior years.

The article’s own misdirection

AlterNet shifts quickly from one Nebraska household to sweeping claims about rural Trump voters, racism, misogyny and hostility toward democracy. Those quoted analyses may describe findings or arguments from other work, but the article supplies no evidence that Wigginton shares those attitudes—or even that he voted for Trump.

Nebraska’s statewide vote does not reveal an individual family’s ballot or motives. Treating a resident of a Republican-leaning state as an exhibit in a psychological profile substitutes demographic inference for reporting. It also lets the institutional mechanism blur: Congress changed the rules, Trump championed the measure, and administrators are processing the added demands. That is sufficient ground for political scrutiny without inventing a morality play around one parent.

Hardship by design, accountability by anecdote

The larger pattern is a familiar one: elected officials make access to public benefits more cumbersome, agencies call the resulting delays temporary, and households become involuntary buffers for the system. Families must keep working and paying providers while government takes longer to decide whether help will continue.

The political consequence is not confined to disappointed supporters. Eligibility barriers fall on everyone who needs the program, regardless of how they voted. The sharper indictment is therefore institutional: policymakers can impose suspicion at scale while responsibility dissolves into caseworkers, websites and disconnected phone calls. When coverage concentrates on whether voters received an ironic punishment, it turns governance into spectacle and leaves the machinery of harm insufficiently examined.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Red state parents lash out at Trump: ‘Never had this problem before’

item.title: Hasty Trump move during swirling scandal blows up into strategic failure 18 months later
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump’s 51-day bombing campaign against Yemen’s Houthis ended in a hastily accepted truce that failed to eliminate the group and gave it time to rebuild. Trump launched Operation Rough Rider on March 15, 2025, promising complete annihilation; by May, after more than 1,000 strikes and an estimated cost exceeding $1 billion, he declared victory and accepted an Oman-brokered ceasefire.

The Houthis continued attacking during the campaign, according to the report, while the United States lost at least seven MQ-9 drones and two F/A-18s, the latter in accidents at sea. RawStory says the administration had begun seeking an exit within weeks and caught Yemen’s Saudi-backed government by surprise when it ended the operation.

Pentagon spokesperson Kingsley Wilson disputed the account, calling the campaign a decisive success that strengthened freedom of navigation. But RawStory reports that the Houthis subsequently rebuilt, seized the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, renewed Yemen’s civil war and attacked Saudi oil and military infrastructure.

Power chose action over assessment

The institutional power belonged to Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and senior military commanders. Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. reportedly proposed updated assessments of what airstrikes could accomplish before the operation began. Gen. Michael “Erik” Kurilla rejected that caution, and Hegseth backed him.

That was not strategic uncertainty imposed by outsiders. It was a choice by officials with command authority to treat analysis as an obstacle. Trump then supplied the maximalist political promise: the Houthis would be “completely annihilated.” When the campaign failed to produce that result, the administration changed the definition of success instead of meeting its own declared objective.

The sequence matters. The government rushed past assessment, launched an expensive campaign without a clear exit strategy, searched for a way out almost immediately and proclaimed victory when a truce became available. Calling this merely “hasty” risks laundering a chain of decisions into a personality quirk.

The scandal exposed the governing method

The Signal episode was not separate from the campaign’s strategic disorder. Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance and other senior officials discussed the strikes in a group chat that mistakenly included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg. A Pentagon inspector general later found that Hegseth’s sharing of specific pre-strike details created an operational-security risk.

The same leadership that dismissed further assessment also handled sensitive military planning through a compromised commercial chat. These were distinct failures, but they reflected the same contempt for disciplined process: urgency was treated as competence, safeguards as optional and confidence as a substitute for preparation.

No evidence in RawStory establishes that the security lapse caused the campaign’s failure. It does establish that senior officials created an avoidable risk while conducting an operation already lacking a coherent political end state.

Victory was a message, not an outcome

Trump said in May 2025 that the Houthis no longer wanted to fight. The subsequent conduct described by RawStory does not support that declaration. According to the report, the group preserved its power, restored its capabilities and later expanded its regional leverage.

The administration’s withdrawal from sustained engagement sharpened the failure. It left the special-envoy position vacant and cut aid after ending the bombing. Military force was deployed as spectacle, then Yemen was treated as disposable once the White House had a victory line.

Washington’s local partners absorbed the consequences. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government supported the campaign but reportedly received no meaningful warning that it was ending. The United States held the power to begin and terminate the operation; weaker Yemeni actors were left to live inside the strategic vacuum.

The failure belongs at the top

The Houthis plainly exercised agency. Yemeni analyst Nadwa Al-Dawsari told the Washington Post that the group uses negotiations and truces to preserve power, rebuild and prepare for further conflict. But recognizing that strategy does not absolve the officials who reportedly entered a ceasefire without accounting for it.

Nor does the Pentagon’s defense settle the question. A ceasefire may have temporarily reduced direct attacks on U.S. forces, but that is narrower than Trump’s promise of annihilation and difficult to reconcile with RawStory’s account of renewed Houthi power. “Freedom of navigation” cannot function as a retrospective magic phrase that converts an abandoned objective into decisive success.

The central misdirection is the temptation to portray the Houthis’ resurgence as an unforeseeable betrayal of diplomacy. The reporting instead describes warnings ignored, limits unexamined and a truce accepted because the administration wanted an exit.

War by slogan produces defeat by euphemism

This is the larger pattern: leaders use overwhelming American force to advertise resolve, refuse the planning required to translate violence into durable political outcomes, and then rename withdrawal as victory. When the consequences arrive, official messaging narrows the objective until almost any result can be sold as success.

The strategic failure was not that bombing proved insufficiently brutal. It was that the people empowered to define the goal, test the assumptions and plan the aftermath chose proclamation over strategy. The Houthis exploited the opening. Trump’s administration created it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Hasty Trump move during swirling scandal blows up into strategic failure 18 months later

item.title: 'People are freaking out': Fox fumbles for upside to Trump 'crisis’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox Business host Stuart Varney and UBS managing director Jason Katz presented a Treasury-bond sell-off as a “generational opportunity” for investors wealthy enough to endure the economic strain. Katz acknowledged that the price was painful but said conditions were “not as bad” for high earners who could buy bonds and wait.

The segment also described corporate growth as heavily dependent on artificial intelligence. Varney said investors needed to see AI spending improve corporate earnings; Katz replied that they “have to” see it, and Varney conceded that otherwise “we’re in trouble.” AlterNet contrasts that confidence with cited polling showing broad dissatisfaction with Trump’s economic management and substantial opposition to AI data centers.

A crisis for whom?

The segment’s definition of opportunity begins where most people’s purchasing power ends. Falling asset prices can reward investors with spare capital, but that does not make the conditions producing those prices broadly beneficial. It means wealth provides access to the recovery while financial pain forces everyone else to absorb the decline.

This is not merely optimistic market commentary. It is a class filter: the same instability becomes hardship for households living on income and a buying opportunity for households living partly on accumulated wealth. Varney and Katz acknowledged that distinction, then treated the privileged side of it as the useful takeaway.

The power is upstream

Ordinary consumers did not set federal economic policy, determine the government’s borrowing needs or make corporations stake so much anticipated growth on AI. Institutional power belongs to the Trump administration, Congress, financial markets and corporate executives allocating enormous sums toward the technology.

Yet the Fox segment centered the investor’s response rather than the decisions creating the exposure. Katz referred vaguely to economic “headwinds” and declined to detail them because, he said, viewers did not need to be bored. That omission matters. Removing policy choices and corporate bets from the discussion makes instability sound like weather: unpleasant, impersonal and nobody’s responsibility.

Optimism as misdirection

The reporting does not establish that Trump alone caused the Treasury sell-off or every measure of economic weakness, and it would be irresponsible to claim that it does. It does show a friendly television platform converting economic alarm into portfolio advice while declining to examine the forces behind it.

That framing redirects attention from governance to positioning. The question becomes whether affluent viewers can profit from fear, not why confidence has deteriorated, who benefits from current policy or who bears the costs. Harm is not denied; it is repackaged as an entry point.

The AI discussion performs a similar maneuver. Public opposition to data centers is treated as an obstacle to growth, while Trump dismisses opponents as people who want the country to become “backwards and poor.” But if the economy is as dependent on AI gains as the cited analysts suggest, skepticism about that concentration is not backwardness. It is a political response to a development model whose rewards and burdens are distributed by people with far more power than nearby residents.

A brittle political economy

According to the figures AlterNet cites, AI accounts for roughly one-third of US economic growth and one-third of stock-market value. Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce warned that growth increasingly depends on AI gains and the resulting spending by higher-income households. That describes an economy propped up by concentrated assets and concentrated consumption.

Varney’s warning that “we’re in trouble” if AI fails to improve corporate results exposes the weakness beneath the reassurance. The promised upside depends on bond buyers having money to wait, technology companies delivering profits and affluent households continuing to spend. Those are conditions for protecting asset values, not evidence of widely shared security.

The system protects the buyer

The larger pattern is familiar: political and corporate institutions produce or tolerate instability, financial media translates that instability into advice for asset owners, and the public experiencing higher costs is cast as fearful, impatient or hostile to progress.

The crucial divide is not between optimists and pessimists. It is between people empowered to buy during a crisis and people required to live through it. A political economy that calls the first group’s opportunity the country’s good news has already disclosed whose welfare it is organized to protect.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘People are freaking out’: Fox fumbles for upside to Trump ‘crisis’

item.title: Trump's '200 feet' pardon pledge tees up clash as charges eyed for his officials
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump pledged to preemptively pardon anyone who had come “within 200 feet” of the Oval Office before leaving office. The remark covered no precisely identified group, and the reporting does not establish that any pardons had been issued. Democrats were considering whether administration officials’ alleged misuse of authority, including Justice Department actions against Trump’s political opponents, could warrant criminal charges.

Democratic lawmakers were also drafting limits on presidential power ahead of the following month’s congressional elections. Their proposals addressed foreign-government payments, White House renovations, settlements involving a president’s own government, emergency tariffs and other uses of emergency authority. No prosecutions, congressional majority or enactment of those bills was reported as settled.

The power sits in the presidency

The central actor is not some vague class of Washington combatants. Trump held executive authority, directed the administration and possessed the constitutional pardon power. His officials exercised federal power through the Justice Department, immigration enforcement, tariffs and National Guard deployments.

Congress can legislate, investigate and control appropriations, but Democrats’ contemplated response depended on winning elections and passing bills. That is prospective and conditional power. Trump’s authority was immediate.

A pardon pledge is a political instrument

The “200 feet” line substitutes proximity for conduct. It suggests that service near the president, rather than an individualized assessment of an offense, could determine access to clemency. The report does not identify intended recipients or establish that any covered official committed a crime, so criminal guilt cannot be presumed.

But the political meaning is still plain: a sweeping pardon promise can reassure officials that personal loyalty may bring legal protection. Even without a completed pardon, that signal weakens the deterrent effect of future investigation and turns an extraordinary presidential power into a potential shield for an administration’s inner circle.

Accountability is not retaliation

The article frames a looming “clash,” but that language blurs a crucial distinction. Prosecuting political enemies without lawful grounds would be an abuse. Investigating officials based on evidence of specific crimes would be ordinary accountability. Michael Waldman’s warning against Democrats copying Trump’s alleged politicization of the Justice Department is sound, but it should not become a pretext for institutional paralysis.

The standard is neither vengeance nor immunity. It is evidence, applicable law and independent process. Treating every investigation as partisan payback grants executive officials practical impunity whenever their party can describe scrutiny as retaliation.

Reform cannot replace enforcement

Jamie Raskin’s proposed restrictions identify how much governing machinery depends on norms that presidents can stretch until Congress writes explicit prohibitions. The reported proposals target concrete vulnerabilities: undisclosed foreign benefits, self-interested government settlements, unreviewed White House alterations and emergency declarations used to bypass Congress.

Legislation, however, addresses future authority. It does not resolve possible past misconduct. A system that responds to alleged abuses only by refining tomorrow’s rules teaches officials that today’s violations carry no personal consequence.

The systemic error

Trump’s spokesman said established procedures were followed; Heritage Action’s Tiffany Justice dismissed the Democratic proposals as partisan hypocrisy. Those are defenses offered by political allies, not findings that settle the underlying allegations.

The larger pattern is executive power expanding first and legislative safeguards arriving later, if at all. Sweeping clemency rhetoric then raises the cost of accountability, while “clash” coverage recasts the officeholder wielding state power and the lawmakers seeking constraints as equivalent contestants. They are not. The relevant questions are who controlled the machinery, how it was used, and whether institutions can examine that use without confusing lawful scrutiny with political revenge.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s ‘200 feet’ pardon pledge tees up clash as charges eyed for his officials

item.title: Trump explodes at New York Times over ‘empty seats’ at rally: 'Should be arrested’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump demanded the arrest of The New York Times and other media outlets after the newspaper described empty seats in the upper sections of his Ohio rally. Trump disputed that account, claimed the arena was full and said thousands of supporters were turned away.

Trump posted the accusation twice on Truth Social and shared a 27-second video of a line whose time, location and destination were unclear. He also asserted that people in upper sections had moved closer to the floor, but the material described by RawStory did not independently establish either side’s account of attendance.

Trump then claimed he “never” has empty seats and said cinematographers now record his venues. RawStory reported that his next scheduled appearance was a campaign rally in Nebraska that Monday; the article did not provide its outcome.

The president named the punishment

The dispute over attendance is almost beside the point. The person wielding federal executive power responded to unfavorable coverage by saying journalists “should be arrested.” He did not identify a crime, cite evidence of criminal conduct or distinguish an inaccurate report from an illegal act.

That is not merely another complaint about media bias. Politicians can challenge reporting, produce evidence and demand corrections. Trump instead invoked state punishment for speech he called dishonest. The institutional power in this story belongs to the president, not to reporters describing an arena.

The evidence does not match the certainty

Trump offered sweeping declarations—no empty seats now, none for years, none ever—while attaching a short clip that, according to RawStory, supplied little usable context. A line outside does not by itself prove that every seat inside was occupied. Nor does a report of empty upper sections necessarily establish weak overall attendance.

His explanation that attendees “migrate down” could account for visible gaps, but it also concedes the possibility that cameras saw empty seats. The reporting leaves the underlying crowd-size dispute unresolved. What it does establish is that Trump treated contradiction as dishonesty and alleged dishonesty as grounds for arrest.

Spectacle becomes a loyalty test

The insistence on perfect crowds turns a mundane factual question into a test of submission. Attendance cannot merely be large; it must be flawless. Photographic evidence cannot show gaps; any gaps must have an exculpatory explanation. A news organization cannot report what its journalists observed; disagreement becomes a “disservice” to the country.

That rhetoric makes personal image synonymous with national interest. Trump’s prestige becomes the standard of truth, while scrutiny becomes an offense against the state. The likely political function is intimidation: shift attention from whether the claim is accurate to whether the speaker may be punished for making it.

The sharper story is the coercion

RawStory’s “explodes” framing captures the emotional display but risks shrinking the event into another episode of presidential temper. Anger is not the central issue. The consequential act was a president publicly proposing arrest for disfavored reporting without identifying a lawful basis.

Focusing on the rally’s seating chart also invites misdirection. The New York Times has influence, but it does not command prosecutors or federal law enforcement. Trump does. The relevant imbalance is therefore not president versus hostile press as equivalent combatants; it is the holder of executive authority invoking criminal punishment against an institution that published an unwelcome observation.

Authoritarianism often enters through trivia

The larger pattern is the conversion of personal grievance into a theory of government power. A crowd estimate becomes a pretext for declaring journalism criminal. Vanity supplies the trigger, but coercion is the proposed remedy.

Whether seats were empty matters far less than the rule Trump articulated: the president decides what is true, dissent is dishonesty, and dishonesty deserves arrest. That is authoritarian rhetoric in unusually plain form. The absurdity of the underlying dispute does not soften it. It shows how little provocation is required.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump explodes at New York Times over ‘empty seats’ at rally: ‘Should be arrested’

item.title: Rick Wilson exposes the Trump allies desperate for it all to end
item.description:
What happened

According to AlterNet, anti-Trump conservative Rick Wilson said Republican pollster Tony Fabrizio and campaign adviser Chris LaCavita were the Trump allies supposedly desperate for “the mess” to end. Wilson offered no direct statements from either man; he attributed the claim to unnamed Republicans and used the “sweet meteor of death” line as his own characterization.

On Molly Jong-Fast’s “Fast Politics” podcast, Wilson contrasted those campaign professionals with the allies who accompanied President Donald Trump to a recent midterm rally in Dayton, Ohio. He argued that Trump was favoring a personally reassuring inner circle over experienced political operators and questioned whether chief of staff Suzie Wiles still had meaningful control. Jong-Fast and Wilson tied the reported anxiety to worsening Republican polling, but the article supplied neither the underlying numbers nor responses from Fabrizio, LaCavita, Wiles, or the other named officials.

Power belongs to the president

The decisive fact is not that two Republican strategists may be miserable. Trump holds the presidency. He chooses his advisers, determines who receives access and can disregard campaign professionals who deliver unwelcome information.

Wiles may manage staff, and Fabrizio and LaCavita may shape electoral strategy, but their influence remains conditional. If Wilson’s account is accurate, their frustration reflects proximity without command: they can measure political deterioration, yet the president retains the authority to ignore them.

Access is not evidence

The article’s headline promises an exposure of desperate Trump allies. What it actually provides is Wilson relaying what unnamed Republicans allegedly told him about two other people’s state of mind.

That may be informed commentary, but it is not established testimony from Fabrizio or LaCavita. AlterNet turns a secondhand claim and a vivid metaphor into the story’s central revelation without reporting corroboration or seeking the named men’s response. The framing is stronger than the evidence.

The comfort-circle problem

Wilson’s more consequential allegation concerns how Trump organizes power: he says the president is choosing people who make him feel good over operatives with electoral expertise. The listed travelers included close aides, lawyers, elected officials and senior government figures, but the article does not establish why each person traveled or what role each played.

Still, the distinction Wilson draws matters. A presidency structured around personal reassurance makes bad information harder to deliver and loyalty more valuable than competence. The institutional consequence is not merely a weaker campaign. Government officials can become participants in maintaining the president’s preferred political reality rather than advisers responsible for testing it.

Operatives are not bystanders

The “desperate professionals trapped in chaos” framing risks laundering agency. Fabrizio and LaCavita, as described by the article, are not powerless citizens caught beneath an administration. They are experienced Republican operators who chose to work within Trump’s political apparatus and whose expertise helps sustain it.

Private alarm, if it exists, does not erase that role. Nor does anticipating electoral losses amount to opposing the decisions producing them. The story invites sympathy for insiders confronting consequences while leaving largely unexamined how their labor enabled the political structure they now allegedly want to escape.

The system protects its mechanics

This is a recurring pattern in political coverage: elite discomfort becomes the drama, while institutional responsibility fades into the background. Readers are asked to watch advisers wince, whisper and wait for disaster as though they were weather forecasters rather than paid participants.

The larger lesson is not that Trump’s circle may be tired of Trump. It is that political systems routinely grant insiders reputational distance from outcomes they helped make possible. Their unease becomes evidence of wisdom; their continued service becomes a footnote. Power survives partly because its mechanics are permitted to describe themselves as its captives.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Rick Wilson exposes the Trump allies desperate for it all to end

item.title: FBI's last-minute plot to hide Trump-Epstein videos claimed in lawsuit
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the FBI acknowledged possessing nine training videos, totaling about 75 minutes, used to instruct more than 1,000 agents reviewing Jeffrey Epstein investigative files. According to a sworn FBI declaration described by legal analyst Allison Gill, two videos taught agents to flag documents containing specified names—including Donald Trump’s—for supervisory review.

Gill sought the videos and related PowerPoint decks through a December 2025 Freedom of Information Act request. She says the Justice Department later sought delays that would have pushed litigation over the records beyond the 2026 midterm elections. A judge rejected a requested 90-day extension, although the department received an additional week and then filed its declaration shortly before the revised deadline.

The FBI is withholding the videos in full, citing exemptions intended to protect the identities of FBI and Justice Department personnel whose faces or voices appear in them. Gill argues that the timing and the disclosed training instructions explain the government’s resistance. The reporting establishes a disclosure fight and a disputed redaction process; it does not establish that election-related concealment was the FBI’s stated purpose.

The power sits with the record keepers

Gill can request records and challenge the government in court. The FBI and Justice Department possess the records, define their initial search, invoke exemptions and control the pace until a judge intervenes. That is the relevant imbalance.

The agencies reportedly relied on a search performed more than a year earlier for someone else’s case to answer Gill’s request. They also rejected an earlier email on the ground that it improperly expanded the request’s scope. Those procedural choices sound technical, but they determine what the public can see and when it can see it.

This was an organized process

More than 1,000 agents were reportedly assigned to the review, with millions of dollars paid in overtime in March 2025. Training materials specified how documents should be redacted and escalated. This was not a few employees improvising over a disordered archive.

Gill says sources told her agents had to record mentions of Trump by document and page number in a spreadsheet, and AlterNet reports that a whistleblower complaint to Sen. Dick Durbin corroborated that instruction. The disclosed descriptions of two videos provide additional support for the existence of name-based supervisory review. They do not, by themselves, prove that every flagged reference was deleted or hidden improperly. That distinction matters—but so does the documented architecture for singling out politically sensitive material.

Delay is an exercise of power

Gill interprets the Justice Department’s requested extension and last-minute filing as an attempt to postpone disclosure until after the midterms. AlterNet’s framing leans heavily on that interpretation without establishing an explicit electoral directive.

Still, treating the dispute as mere bureaucratic friction would obscure agency. Officials chose to request more time, chose the search they deemed sufficient and chose to withhold the videos wholesale rather than release versions edited to protect employee identities. Even when each move has a legal rationale, their combined effect is foreseeable: politically consequential information remains unavailable while voters are making political judgments.

The redaction regime deserves scrutiny

Congress later required release of the files with victims’ names redacted, according to AlterNet. The earlier FBI review reportedly applied broader rules, including a process that Gill says allowed people to identify themselves as victims. She further claims three prospective co-conspirators were consequently hidden from the files. That serious assertion is attributed to Gill; the article does not independently establish the identities, contemplated charges or legal basis for their treatment.

The stronger, supported point is structural. A secrecy system built to protect victims can also shield officials, employees or investigative subjects if its categories are broad and its decisions remain invisible. “Privacy” is not a self-validating explanation when the agency invoking it also controls the evidence needed to test the claim.

Secrecy compounds itself

This story reveals how institutional concealment can operate without a single dramatic order. Agencies classify the material, design the review, select the search, claim exemptions and ask courts for time. Each step can be presented as routine while the cumulative result protects the institution from timely scrutiny.

The central question is therefore larger than whether Trump’s name appeared in Epstein-related records; a mention alone would establish neither misconduct nor criminality. The political issue is whether federal law-enforcement officials created special handling for information involving a sitting president and then used procedural control to keep the public from examining that handling. When the government’s answer is another delay and another layer of redaction, procedure stops looking neutral. It becomes the means by which power avoids an accounting.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: FBI’s last-minute plot to hide Trump-Epstein videos claimed in lawsuit

item.title: Megapastor Trump ally’s stunning backpedal just exposed 'bad' GOP candidate
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Robert Jeffress, a prominent evangelical pastor and longtime Donald Trump ally, said he would not ostracize congregants who vote for Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico over Republican nominee Ken Paxton in Texas. Jeffress told New York Times columnist David French that he would explain his objections to Talarico but ultimately tell such a congregant to follow their conscience and return to church the next Sunday.

The article presents that tolerance as a notable retreat from Jeffress’s harsher political rhetoric. It attributes Republican unease to Paxton’s scandals and says polls placed Talarico ahead as the 2026 midterms approached. But Jeffress did not endorse Talarico, predict the election, or renounce MAGA politics. His remark established only that voting against Paxton would not, in his view, justify religious exclusion.

The permission structure is cracking

Jeffress has spent years helping turn evangelical authority into political permission: a mechanism for excusing conduct that would ordinarily violate the moral standards pastors claim to enforce. AlterNet recalls his argument that evangelicals could disregard allegations surrounding Trump’s personal conduct because supporting him was politically “pragmatic.”

Now the permission runs in the opposite direction. Jeffress is giving church members room to reject a Trump-endorsed Republican without being treated as apostates. That shift matters because political power in this story does not belong primarily to conflicted congregants. It belongs to party leaders who selected and promoted Paxton, to Trump as the endorser, and to religious figures such as Jeffress who help define which political choices conservative Christians may regard as morally acceptable.

Paxton is the party’s decision

Calling Paxton merely a “bad candidate” risks laundering agency out of the story. According to AlterNet, he won the Republican nomination with Trump’s endorsement despite the scandals weighing on his general-election prospects. Republican voters and institutions produced this candidacy; Democrats did not impose it on them.

The resulting discomfort is therefore not an inexplicable electoral accident. It is the foreseeable cost of a political culture that treats scandal as disqualifying only when convenient. Jeffress’s softened posture does not correct that machinery. It manages the fallout after the machinery delivered a nominee some Republicans may find impossible to defend.

Conscience, selectively restored

Jeffress’s appeal to individual conscience sounds generous only because the political Christianity around him has so often made partisan loyalty a test of faith. “I’ll see you in church next Sunday” is ordinary pastoral conduct presented against an extraordinary backdrop: years of rhetoric that fused religious belonging with support for aggressive Republican power.

The asymmetry is revealing. AlterNet says Jeffress previously dismissed concerns about Trump’s alleged misconduct as secondary to political utility. Faced with Paxton, he now recognizes that a voter might be unable to “overlook” what the article describes only as “the other.” The reporting does not establish precisely which Paxton-related concern Jeffress meant, so it should not be converted into a confession or denunciation. What it does show is that moral discretion becomes available when partisan discipline becomes harder to sustain.

The headline overstates the evidence

Jeffress’s remark does not prove that Texas is turning Democratic, nor does it by itself “expose” Paxton’s quality as a candidate. The polling cited by AlterNet is stronger evidence of electoral weakness than one pastor’s refusal to excommunicate dissenters. Even a polling lead cannot establish the eventual result.

The article also compresses several distinct developments—reported declines in Trump’s evangelical approval, dissatisfaction over deportation and prices, conflict with the pope, war with Iran, economic strain, and Paxton’s candidacy—into a suggestive narrative of collapse. Those claims may describe a broader erosion, but the supplied reporting does not demonstrate how much each factor caused it. Political analysis becomes propaganda when correlation is dressed up as settled causation, even when the conclusion flatters the writer.

A movement meets the cost of its exemptions

The larger pattern is not that one pastor suddenly discovered tolerance. It is that a movement built on moral exemptions eventually produces candidates who expect those exemptions as an entitlement. Trump’s endorsement helped Paxton secure the nomination; religious allies helped normalize the idea that personal scandal could be subordinated to political usefulness. The same system now confronts the electoral consequences of that bargain.

Jeffress’s backpedal is significant because gatekeepers rarely loosen discipline without pressure. But it is not repentance, and it is not institutional reform. It is a limited release valve for voters trapped by choices their own political and religious authorities helped create.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Megapastor Trump ally’s stunning backpedal just exposed ‘bad’ GOP candidate

item.title: Trump judge slams federal agents for falsifying records in stunning rebuke
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that U.S. District Judge Gary Brown found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents wrongfully arrested two people—including a U.S. citizen—and then falsified official records to support claims of mistaken identity. Brown, a Trump appointee in New York, reached that conclusion after examining explanations ICE had repeatedly offered for detentions arising from civil immigration enforcement.

Brown wrote that judges had previously been told detainees were confused with enforcement targets because of similarities in appearance or physical description. His inquiry into these two arrests undermined that justification. The article does not identify the agents involved or describe any disciplinary action against them.

AlterNet also recounts Brown’s March ruling concerning Hester Asaf Garcia Lanza, a Honduran national with Special Immigrant Juvenile status. According to the report, ICE detained him in a sweep, pursued removal despite his legal protections, and imposed unauthorized conditions after a court ordered his release, while the Department of Homeland Security added a substantial fine.

The power was federal

The people arrested did not control the operation, the paperwork or the terms of detention. ICE agents exercised the state’s coercive authority. Agency officials and government lawyers controlled the records and explanations presented to the court. DHS controlled the machinery that could add financial punishment even after a judge determined that Garcia Lanza was lawfully present.

That division of power matters. “Mistaken identity” describes an error without naming its author. Brown’s finding, as reported, was more serious: agents falsified records. One phrase invites sympathy for an administrative mishap; the other identifies official misconduct used to rationalize the seizure of human beings.

An excuse collapses under scrutiny

Brown acknowledged that he had accepted similar explanations in earlier cases based on representations from government counsel and sworn statements by ICE personnel. That admission exposes how institutional credibility can shield abuse. Courts routinely depend on executive agencies to tell the truth. When officials supply false records, they exploit that dependence and make judicial review less capable of protecting the people already in custody.

The reported conduct also strips away the convenient assumption that aggressive immigration enforcement harms only people without legal status. One detainee was a U.S. citizen. Garcia Lanza had a recognized legal status. Sweeps built around speed, physical resemblance and broad operational discretion predictably place lawful residents and citizens within reach of the detention system.

The framing lets the institution hide

AlterNet correctly emphasizes Brown’s rebuke, but its focus on the spectacle of a Trump-appointed judge ruling against the administration risks turning institutional failure into partisan surprise. Judges are not supposed to serve as permanent agents of the presidents who nominate them. A ruling against an administration is not judicial betrayal; it is the baseline expectation of an independent court.

The more consequential fact is that judicial intervention came after arrests, detention, removal proceedings, added conditions and financial pressure. Celebrating the judge can obscure the sequence: executive officials acted first, vulnerable people absorbed the consequences, and a court later imposed limits. The existence of a remedy does not erase the state-inflicted harm required to obtain it.

Cruelty as administration

Brown reportedly described the treatment of Garcia Lanza as “unimaginable cruelty.” The details support a narrower but equally damning conclusion: legal protections did not automatically restrain the enforcement apparatus. Officials allegedly proceeded against Garcia Lanza despite his status, then added burdens after a court ordered his release.

The article does not establish the motives of individual agents or prove a department-wide directive to falsify records. It does establish, through Brown’s findings as reported, that coercive enforcement was paired with false documentation in the cases before him. When an agency can arrest first and explain later, bureaucratic language becomes a form of political cover.

The system rewards the first mover

This is the larger pattern: executive agencies possess immediate power, while courts usually exercise corrective power after the injury begins. The arrest happens before the habeas petition. The confinement happens before the evidentiary inquiry. The person with the least authority must then disprove an official account produced by the institution holding them.

A legal system that eventually detects falsehood is preferable to one that never does. But detection is not prevention, and rebuke is not accountability. Until the officials who order, execute and document wrongful detention face consequences, the government retains a grim advantage: it can impose the punishment first and leave its targets to fight over the explanation afterward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump judge slams federal agents for falsifying records in stunning rebuke

item.title: ‘This is big’: Trump admin deals 'damning' blow to 75-year partnership with rushed retreat
item.description:
What happened

The Trump administration confirmed that all U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford had returned to their home stations in the United States after British authorities investigated a suspected terror plot near the base. RawStory, citing NBC News, characterized the redeployment as rushed and suggested it may have ended a military partnership dating to 1950. The reporting does not establish that the broader partnership was formally terminated.

The security incident prompted evacuations near the British base, and five men were arrested and remained under investigation. The article provides no official statement connecting those arrests to the bomber redeployment or showing that U.S. officials concluded Britain could not protect American personnel.

British journalist Ben Leo nevertheless called the move a “damning indictment” of the alliance. Republican Representative Randy Fine went further, blaming Britain’s Muslim population and declaring the country an unreliable ally, despite the article offering no evidence that religion or immigration drove the administration’s decision.

The power sits in Washington

The decisive actor was the Trump administration, which controlled where the aircraft and personnel were stationed. British residents, British Muslims and the five men under investigation did not possess that authority. Whatever prompted the redeployment, it was an American executive decision with consequences for a longstanding military arrangement.

Yet the administration’s quoted confirmation supplied no reason for the move. That omission matters. When an executive disrupts a strategic deployment without publicly explaining its assessment, speculation fills the vacuum—and political allies can turn an opaque security decision into ideological ammunition.

Speculation became a verdict

Leo’s claim that the United States “likely” believed Britain could not secure the base was explicitly conjecture. RawStory’s framing then stretched a confirmed redeployment into the apparent end of a 75-year partnership, although the evidence presented shows neither a formal rupture nor a permanent withdrawal from military cooperation.

That is weak framing. A consequential operational change deserves scrutiny, but “all bombers left” is not interchangeable with “the alliance ended.” Sensational certainty obscures the questions the administration should answer: who ordered the redeployment, what threat assessment supported it, and whether the move was temporary, precautionary or strategic.

Fine supplied the scapegoat

Fine did not merely criticize British security. He recast an unresolved incident as proof that Britain had “fallen” to Muslims. The article reports that five men were arrested, but it does not identify their religion, establish their guilt or connect Britain’s Muslim population to the withdrawal.

That leap is propaganda by scapegoating: take an unexplained government action, attach it to a minority population and present prejudice as strategic analysis. It also redirects attention away from the officials who actually made the decision. The administration owes an account of its conduct; British Muslims do not owe a collective defense against Fine’s insinuation.

Secrecy rewards demagoguery

The larger pattern is institutional opacity feeding political exploitation. Officials exercise substantial military power, disclose the outcome without the rationale, and leave partisan figures to manufacture a story about national decline and an internal enemy.

Responsible coverage should resist completing that circuit. The established facts support reporting on a rapid bomber redeployment following a serious security incident. They do not yet support declaring a historic alliance dead or treating millions of people as responsible for an unproven plot. When journalism collapses those distinctions, executive power escapes examination while weaker actors inherit the blame.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘This is big’: Trump admin deals ‘damning’ blow to 75-year partnership with rushed retreat

item.title: Lawyer lays out Trump scheme to grab a third term with 'realistic chance' of success
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that attorney and Democratic strategist Dmitri Mehlhorn outlined a possible route for Donald Trump to return to the presidency in 2028 despite the Constitution’s presidential term limit. His scenario begins with the Republican Party nominating Trump and election officials struggling to remove or disqualify him.

Mehlhorn argued on The David Pakman Show that litigation could move too slowly to resolve Trump’s eligibility before the election. He speculated that a Supreme Court deferential to Trump might avoid deciding the dispute by treating it as a political question, leaving the electoral process to continue. No nomination, lawsuit, or court ruling has occurred; this is a forecast about how institutions might respond.

The power is institutional

The decisive actors in this scenario are not ordinary voters confronting a novel constitutional puzzle. They are Republican officials who control their party’s nomination machinery, election administrators who determine ballot access, judges who decide whether and when to intervene, and members of Congress who handle electoral votes.

Mehlhorn’s argument depends first on Republican obedience. If party leaders knowingly nominated a constitutionally ineligible candidate, they would not be confused by an obscure technicality. They would be creating the confrontation and betting that procedural delay, institutional caution, and partisan loyalty could overpower the rule itself.

A loophole made of surrender

The supposed scheme is not a clever textual workaround. RawStory identifies no constitutional provision that affirmatively authorizes a third election. The opening instead comes from enforcement failure: nominate first, litigate afterward, and make every institution fear the consequences of saying no.

That distinction matters. A prohibition becomes fragile when powerful actors can violate it early enough and then portray enforcement as the disruptive act. The party creates the crisis; courts are asked to resolve it under maximum pressure; opponents are blamed for challenging the fait accompli.

Speculation is not a legal outcome

The article’s headline oversells Mehlhorn’s prediction. His “realistic chance” is an assessment, not a demonstrated probability, and the reporting supplies no filed case, controlling ruling, vote count, or established enforcement sequence. Even his account of what five justices might do remains conjecture.

That does not make the scenario irrelevant. It makes precision essential. The reported danger is not that Trump’s eligibility has been judicially accepted. It is that elite compliance and delay could manufacture practical leverage before courts settle the legal question.

The real misdirection

Framing the issue principally as whether the Supreme Court would “step in” risks treating the justices as the sole authors of the outcome. In Mehlhorn’s own sequence, Republican officials would have already chosen to nominate Trump despite the constitutional barrier.

Courts would still bear responsibility for any decision to evade a timely ruling. But judicial passivity would be an enabling act, not the first cause. The first exercise of agency would belong to the party officials who converted Trump’s demand into a nomination and forced every later institution to confront an engineered crisis.

Rules without enforcers

The larger pattern is government by fait accompli. A powerful actor crosses a boundary, allied institutions ratify the move, and adjudicators are urged to avoid intervention because reversal would now be politically explosive.

Constitutional limits do not execute themselves. They depend on officials willing to enforce them before defiance accumulates the machinery of legitimacy. Mehlhorn’s scenario reveals the systemic weakness plainly: when party loyalty rewards the violation and institutional caution punishes the remedy, delay ceases to be neutral procedure. It becomes power.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Lawyer lays out Trump scheme to grab a third term with ‘realistic chance’ of success

item.title: Suspected Trump election interference sparks police raids in Brazil: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Brazil’s Federal Police opened an investigation into possible U.S. interference in Brazil’s presidential election and executed two search-and-seizure warrants in São Paulo on the Friday before the first-round vote. Authorities seized computer equipment and communications while examining a reported Trump administration plan to direct U.S. taxpayer money toward groups opposing alleged “judicial overreach and censorship” in Brazil.

The investigation followed a first round in which Trump-backed far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote, ahead of incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45.1%, sending them to a runoff. The report does not establish that U.S. activity changed the result, nor does it disclose what the raids uncovered.

The Federal Police argued that the reported funding plan was designed to undermine Brazil’s judiciary. RawStory also notes that Trump previously imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in response to the prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and publicly demanded that his trial end.

The power sits in Washington

This is not primarily a story about campaign groups, online agitation, or generalized “foreign influence.” The actor with the greatest institutional power is the U.S. government: it controls diplomatic relations, tariff policy and the proposed distribution of American public money.

Trump’s administration made the relevant choices described in the reporting. It reportedly planned to finance groups attacking Brazil’s judiciary, suspended U.S. consular services in Brazil two days before the vote, and had already used trade policy to punish Brazil over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The Federal Police raids are a response to that power, not its equivalent.

Investigation is not proof

The headline’s implication runs ahead of the evidence presented. Brazilian authorities suspect unlawful interference and are investigating it; the seized material has not yet been reported to prove either an illegal operation or an effect on voting.

Likewise, Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected performance cannot be attributed to U.S. conduct from the facts supplied. An electoral result is not evidence of its own manipulation. The serious claim here rests on the reported funding plan and the surrounding use of state power, not on a convenient inference from vote totals.

Pressure disguised as principle

The Trump administration reportedly framed its intervention as opposition to “judicial overreach and censorship.” That language recasts pressure on another country’s institutions as a defense of liberty while avoiding the central question: why should one government spend public money to organize resistance to another country’s courts during an election involving its favored candidate?

Trump’s earlier tariff decision makes the power relationship harder to obscure. He used a 50% levy to retaliate against Brazil over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and demanded that the proceeding stop. Whatever the legal merits of that prosecution, a foreign president trying to impose economic costs until another sovereign state abandons a case is coercion, not detached concern about due process.

The convenient supporting cast

Benjamin Norton called Flávio Bolsonaro a U.S. “puppet,” but RawStory supplies no evidence establishing that characterization. Including it adds heat while weakening precision. The consequential facts concern official policy: reported funding, diplomatic disruption, tariffs and presidential demands.

Focusing too heavily on ideological labels or provocative commentary can also misdirect responsibility downward. Advocacy groups may have carried out funded work, but the institution capable of supplying the money and applying economic pressure was the Trump administration. Brazilian investigators, meanwhile, are exercising state authority through warrants; their claims also require evidence and scrutiny.

Election influence as foreign policy

The larger pattern is the conversion of state resources into leverage for an aligned political faction abroad. Courts become “censors” when they constrain allies. Tariffs become instruments for contesting prosecutions. Public funds reportedly become support for groups positioned against the institutions conducting those prosecutions.

Whether that pattern amounted to unlawful election interference remains unresolved in the reporting. What is already visible is the hierarchy of power: Washington had money, diplomatic machinery and economic coercion at its disposal; Brazilian institutions were left to determine whether those tools crossed a legal line. Calling the episode a vague controversy would conceal the essential fact that governments make these choices, and weaker actors absorb their consequences.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Suspected Trump election interference sparks police raids in Brazil: report

item.title: Humiliating flaw spotted in Trump's latest AI-generated Greenland threat
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image depicting himself in a snowy landscape with flag-draped penguins as part of his continuing campaign to claim Greenland. Penguins do not live in Greenland’s Arctic environment, and Greenlandic commentator Orla Joelson mocked the geographic error. Trump also posted another synthetic image of himself looming over a village with the caption “Hello, Greenland!”

The posts followed Trump’s signing of a trilateral agreement with Greenland and Denmark at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. According to RawStory, the agreement expanded a 1951 U.S.-Denmark treaty that already provided an American military foothold on the island, falling short of Trump’s earlier insistence on a takeover. The outlet also connects the episode to his reported fascination with AI systems and his attempt to rename AI “Super Intelligence.”

The penguins are not the story

The image is ridiculous, but its zoological failure is politically trivial. The consequential fact is that the president of the United States continues to depict Greenland as an object available for American possession—even after signing an agreement with Greenland and Denmark.

RawStory’s emphasis on an “embarrassing flaw” turns a claim of domination into a geography joke. Penguins provide easy mockery. The harder question is why a president can repeatedly advertise territorial acquisition as personal fantasy while coverage grades the scenery.

Power belongs to the president

Trump is not merely an internet user generating bad images. He holds the institutional power to direct U.S. foreign policy and commands a state that already has a military presence on Greenland under the treaty described by RawStory.

That imbalance matters. Greenlandic critics can ridicule him, but ridicule does not equal leverage. Trump can pair propaganda-like imagery with negotiations and military authority. Treating his posts as eccentric content obscures the machinery behind the performance.

The agreement exposes the gap

The reported trilateral agreement did not deliver the takeover Trump had demanded. It expanded an existing security arrangement. That distinction should be central: Greenland and Denmark participated in an agreement, while Trump’s imagery continued to cast Greenland as something he could claim.

The posts therefore project personal conquest over a negotiated institutional outcome. The reporting does not establish that the images changed policy or coerced the other parties. It does show a president replacing the limits of an actual agreement with synthetic scenes in which his desired hierarchy is already complete.

Artificial intelligence as vanity machinery

RawStory cites a White House insider who told TIME that Trump questioned Elon Musk’s Grok about his presidency and legacy for hours and reportedly relied heavily on it before the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro and his wife. Those claims remain attributed reporting, not independently established facts in the supplied article.

Even so, the public posts demonstrate a narrower and verifiable pattern within RawStory’s account: generative technology gives presidential fantasy an instant visual vocabulary. Its political value is not accuracy. It is the ability to manufacture images of dominance without negotiation, consent, or material reality.

The systemic error

The deepest failure here is not that an image generator misplaced penguins. It is that political coverage can reduce imperial imagery from the holder of immense state power to an online “gaffe.”

Mockery makes Trump look foolish, but it can also make the underlying conduct look harmless. The systemic pattern is familiar: spectacle absorbs attention while power escapes scrutiny. The map error becomes the scandal; the president’s repeated presentation of another people’s territory as his prospective possession becomes background scenery.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Humiliating flaw spotted in Trump’s latest AI-generated Greenland threat

item.title: Democrats vow revenge for Supreme Court shenanigans if they gain majority
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reported that Senate Democrats said they could block any Supreme Court nominee President Donald Trump puts forward if they win the Senate majority in November. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer framed control of the chamber as a way to prevent Trump from appointing more “MAGA justices,” while Sen. Ruben Gallego explicitly endorsed using the blockade Republicans imposed on Barack Obama’s 2016 nominee, Merrick Garland.

The dispute followed Justice Samuel Alito’s disclosure that he considered retiring this year and might reconsider in 2027. Republicans held a 53–47 Senate majority at the time of the report; Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to control hearings and votes. No vacancy had opened, and no nominee had been selected.

The power is the Senate’s

This is not chiefly a quarrel over partisan manners. The Senate majority controls whether a Supreme Court nomination advances at all. Committee leadership can deny a hearing, and floor leadership can deny a vote. That institutional authority—not a nominee’s credentials or a president’s preferences—is the decisive fact.

Republicans demonstrated the mechanism in 2016 when they left Garland’s nomination pending for most of a year. Democrats are now signaling that the rule Republicans established through power may be used against a Republican president. Calling that “revenge” personalizes an institutional struggle and obscures who created the precedent.

The vacancy is still hypothetical

Alito has not announced his retirement. Trump has not named a replacement. Democrats have not won the Senate. The concrete event here is a campaign-season declaration about how senators say they would use power they do not yet possess.

That distinction matters because speculative court vacancies are useful mobilization devices. Sen. Graham warned Republican voters that a Democratic Senate would block an Alito successor. Maine Democratic nominee Troy Jackson invoked Susan Collins’s confirmation votes and the later overturning of Roe v. Wade. Both parties are translating an uncertain vacancy into a present argument about control of the judiciary.

Republican precedent, Democratic choice

Republicans bear responsibility for making prolonged vacancy-by-obstruction an openly usable Senate tactic. But precedent does not erase Democratic agency. If Democrats gain the majority and refuse to consider a nominee, that will be their decision, made with the same procedural power Republicans previously exercised.

Gallego acknowledged the choice plainly: Democrats should do what Mitch McConnell did to them. That is clearer than pretending the Senate remains governed by a neutral confirmation custom. The old norm was not accidentally misplaced. Republican leaders discarded it when doing so served their interests; Democrats are considering whether unilateral restraint would merely reward that success.

Reform or retaliation

Sen. Mazie Hirono floated limiting presidents to two Supreme Court nominations. That proposal addresses the arbitrary role of death, retirement timing, and partisan Senate control in shaping a lifetime-appointed court. But the report supplies no legislative details or path to enactment.

Without structural reform, retaliation becomes the available substitute: each majority blocks when it can, confirms when it can, and describes the resulting escalation as the other party’s misconduct. The consequence is not procedural confusion. It is a judiciary whose composition depends increasingly on synchronized control of the presidency and Senate rather than a stable confirmation process.

The system rewards the first norm-breaker

The larger pattern is institutional asymmetry. One party can break a governing convention, secure durable power from doing so, and then condemn equivalent resistance as illegitimate. Coverage centered on Democratic “revenge” risks accepting that asymmetry by treating the response as the scandal while reducing the original seizure of advantage to background.

The honest account is harsher: Republicans turned Supreme Court vacancies into exercises of raw Senate control, and Democrats are considering operating under that reality. The result is predictable—judicial legitimacy gets consumed by a system that gives political actors enormous power, few enforceable restraints, and every incentive to use both.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Democrats vow revenge for Supreme Court shenanigans if they gain majority

item.title: Trump argument at dog park takes horrifying turn for Marine veteran
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that an April argument over Donald Trump at Centerville Mills Dog Park in Bainbridge, Ohio, ended with Emmanuel “Mike” Mathews shooting David Mattai in the lower back and Mattai firing at least four rounds at Mathews’ departing vehicle. Mathews was not hit; Mattai suffered intestinal damage and a fractured spine, underwent two surgeries, and spent months in rehabilitation.

The confrontation began after Mattai challenged Mathews’ praise of Trump. It escalated through shouting, an insult about Mattai’s mother, and Mattai grabbing Mathews by the hair. Mathews told police that Mattai also head-butted him and that he feared for his life; Mattai denied the head-butt. According to a witness, both men mentioned having guns before Mathews retrieved a .45-caliber handgun and fired first. His next trigger pull did not discharge, after which Mattai retrieved a 9-millimeter pistol and returned fire.

Mathews, 80, pleaded not guilty to second-degree felonious assault and planned to claim self-defense under Ohio’s stand-your-ground law at a February trial. Mattai, 55, was charged with misdemeanor assault and disorderly conduct and faced up to six months in jail. Although Mattai claimed ten years of Marine service, official records cited by The New York Times showed less than one year; he admitted embellishing his record and apologized.

Politics supplied the script, guns supplied the consequence

Trump did not order this confrontation, and a political dispute did not pull either trigger. Two armed men made successive decisions that transformed petty antagonism into gunfire: Mattai initiated physical contact by grabbing Mathews’ hair; Mathews escalated to lethal force; Mattai then fired repeatedly as Mathews drove away.

That sequence matters because “political polarization” is too bloodless a diagnosis. Polarization did not act. Men acted inside a culture that treats political identity as personal combat and carrying a firearm as preparation for its final stage. The result was not metaphorical division. It was a torn intestine, a fractured spine, damaged property, criminal charges and lasting disability.

The state holds the decisive power

The argument belonged to Mattai and Mathews. The authority to define it afterward belongs to police, prosecutors, courts and Ohio law. They will decide whether Mathews’ first shot was felonious assault or legally justified self-defense, and whether the alleged head-butt—disputed by Mattai—can be proved.

Ohio’s stand-your-ground framework therefore sits at the institutional center of the case. Mathews’ lawyer planned to invoke it, but the reporting does not establish that the defense will succeed. What it does establish is that lawmakers have created a legal structure in which a shooter may argue that retreat was unnecessary. That policy choice shapes the stakes long before a jury evaluates the facts.

The headline’s borrowed valor

Calling Mattai a “Marine veteran” is technically rooted in some military service, but it also lends him an aura the underlying reporting complicates. He claimed a decade in the Marines; official records reportedly showed less than a year. He later admitted the embellishment.

That deception is relevant to his credibility. It is not evidence that he deserved to be shot, nor does it resolve whether Mathews acted lawfully. Elevating it into the story’s defining identity risks turning a disputed shooting into a morality play about stolen prestige. The central evidence remains conduct: who touched whom, who displayed or retrieved a weapon, who fired first, and whether the claimed fear met the law’s requirements.

Accountability without a false hero

There is no useful innocent-versus-monster arrangement here. Mattai acknowledged grabbing Mathews by the hair and later fired toward his vehicle. Mathews acknowledged shooting Mattai but claimed he feared for his life. One man’s misconduct does not automatically excuse the other’s escalation, and criminal charges are not convictions.

Nor are the consequences remotely symmetrical. Mattai says he can no longer work as a forklift mechanic and now walks with a limp. His statement that he received his “own life sentence” describes the enduring cost of the shooting, not a judicial finding about blame. Precision requires holding both facts at once: he helped escalate the confrontation, and he sustained catastrophic harm.

A system built to turn grievance into force

The larger pattern is not that political disagreement inevitably produces violence. It is that grievance politics, habitual armed readiness and permissive self-defense law can compress the distance between insult and irreversible injury.

Afterward, Mattai poured out his vodka, removed his political bumper stickers and resolved not to confront strangers over politics. Those are personal responses to institutional conditions he does not control. The durable power remains with legislators who define when lethal force is excusable, prosecutors who choose charges and courts that apply those rules. Treating this merely as two hotheaded partisans losing control would miss the system surrounding them: a political culture that markets enemies, a gun culture that places lethal capacity within reach, and a legal order left to decide—after the body is broken—whether the shooting was permitted.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump argument at dog park takes horrifying turn for Marine veteran
