item.title: The Trump era has weaponized a 40-year power shift
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the Trump era has weaponized a transfer of economic and political power that began in the 1970s and 1980s. Robert Reich identifies the beneficiaries as major corporations, executives, shareholders, financial elites and technology billionaires, whose wealth finances campaign contributions, media ownership, litigation and public-relations campaigns.

Reich ties that power shift to weakened antitrust enforcement, declining private-sector unionization, lower taxes on the extremely wealthy and growing corporate concentration. He describes Trump-era corruption as an intensified expression of that system, not its origin, and argues that reversing it should become central to political debate.

Wealth is the machinery

The article’s essential point is not merely that a few people became exceptionally rich. It is that wealth can be converted into control over the institutions that determine who gets richer next.

Campaign money purchases access. Media ownership shapes the boundaries of acceptable debate. Expensive litigation can exhaust weaker opponents. Lobbying and public relations turn private advantage into official policy and manufactured consensus. The resulting laws, regulations and court decisions can then produce still more concentrated wealth.

That is a feedback loop, not an unfortunate side effect of prosperity.

The decisions had authors

Corporate concentration did not simply “rise.” Governments weakened antitrust enforcement. Legislators changed tax and labor laws. Officials chose which regulations to write, enforce or abandon. Courts issued decisions within that transformed political structure.

Those choices transferred leverage from workers and consumers to employers, owners and investors. Reich’s comparison is stark: more than one-third of private-sector workers were unionized in the 1950s; fewer than 6 percent are now. Whatever else shaped that decline, the legal environment became less favorable to organizing.

Trump did not invent this order. Reich’s charge is that his era made its corruption more blatant. Treating Trump as the sole cause would therefore let the institutions and decision-makers that constructed the system escape scrutiny.

Affordability is the symptom

“Affordability” sounds like a condition without an author: prices are high, wages are strained, choices are limited, and everyone is mysteriously frustrated. Reich instead connects those outcomes to concentrated corporate power and weakened worker power.

That reframing matters. If the problem is reduced to household anxiety, politics offers rebates, slogans and temporary relief. If the problem is institutional control, the relevant questions are who can set prices, suppress competition, resist unions and shape the rules governing taxation and markets.

The weaker actors are consumers and employees. Blaming their spending, expectations or voting temperament would invert the power relationship.

Reform confronts a locked door

Reich points to the Progressive Era and the New Deal as evidence that concentrated power has been challenged before through antitrust action, corporate regulation, progressive taxation and a stronger middle class. But historical precedent is not a mechanism.

The present obstacle is that those with the greatest interest in blocking reform possess extraordinary influence over the government expected to enact it. That is the paradox Reich identifies: public authority is needed to disperse private power, while private power is positioned to constrain public authority.

His exception for the Biden administration’s antitrust record also complicates any claim that the entire political system behaves identically. Institutional choices still matter. So does which officials make them.

The system protects its winners

The larger pattern is a four-decade redistribution of agency. Workers lost bargaining power; consumers lost alternatives; concentrated wealth gained additional routes into government, media and law. Trumpism exploited and intensified that architecture, but focusing only on its crudest operator would mistake the weapon for the arsenal.

The central political conflict is therefore not between abstract “elites” and an equally abstract “people.” It is between identifiable concentrations of institutional power and those required to live under rules they have little capacity to shape. Until coverage names the officials, owners and institutions making those rules, “affordability” will remain a sanitized description of consequences whose causes are political.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The Trump era has weaponized a 40-year power shift

item.title: Trump voter in rural Georgia switches to Democrat over one ‘simple fact’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Laura Leigh Taylor, a 37-year-old farmer in Smithville, Georgia, plans to vote for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff in November after supporting Donald Trump in 2024. The “simple fact” behind her switch is that Democrats have addressed family separation under Trump’s immigration enforcement campaign.

Taylor said she regretted her Trump vote after a friend’s father—whom she described as a hardworking provider—was deported. She supports removing violent criminals but said the administration’s crackdown has gone far beyond that stated target.

A KFF-AP survey of 2,241 registered rural voters found an almost even division over the crackdown’s local effects: roughly one-third called them positive, one-third negative, and three in ten reported no impact. Trump nevertheless retains strong backing among rural MAGA Republicans, half of whom said deportations have not gone far enough.

Power made the policy real

Taylor changed her vote after enforcement stopped being an abstraction. A federal campaign authorized and executed by the Trump administration reached a family in a town of about 600 people. The decisive actor was not that family, and the outcome was not an unfortunate misunderstanding. The administration chose a wide-ranging enforcement policy capable of producing deportations like the one Taylor described.

That distinction matters because immigration politics is routinely narrated through the people with the least institutional power: migrants, workers and separated families. They experience the consequences. Federal officials design, direct and defend the machinery producing them.

The slogan collapsed on contact

Taylor drew a line between deporting violent criminals and removing the father she knew. Her account exposes the political utility of using the most frightening category to sell a much broader crackdown. “Violent criminals” supplies the justification; enforcement reaches beyond that category.

The reporting does not establish the deported man’s legal history or the precise basis for his removal, so it cannot prove that his case contradicted every stated enforcement priority. It does establish that Taylor saw the result as incompatible with what she thought she had supported. The policy’s human scope became visible only when someone familiar was taken.

Rural communities are not props

The poll complicates the convenient fiction of a uniformly restrictionist countryside. About seven in ten respondents said legally present immigrants and temporary or seasonal agricultural workers were at least somewhat important to their local economies. Even 45 percent said the same of immigrants in the country illegally.

That is not merely a cultural disagreement. It is a material contradiction. Political leaders can build support by depicting immigrants as an external burden while rural economies depend on their labor. Farmers recognize that dependence because they encounter it in production, not in campaign imagery.

One defection is not a realignment

AlterNet’s framing turns one voter’s decision into a tempting electoral parable. Taylor’s switch is politically meaningful, but it does not establish a rural collapse in support for Trump’s agenda. The same survey found deep division, while two-thirds of rural MAGA Republicans said his immigration policies had benefited their communities.

The stronger story is not that one anecdote predicts November. It is that support for punitive government can coexist with dependence on the people it targets—and can survive until the punishment acquires a familiar face. The poll measures attitudes, not the cause of those attitudes or the eventual election result.

Cruelty becomes legible locally

Mass enforcement is politically easier to sustain when its targets remain anonymous and its consequences are described as administrative necessity. Smithville stripped away that distance for one voter. A national policy became a missing father, a disrupted family and a changed ballot.

That is the larger pattern: concentrated institutional power imposes the harm, while affected communities are left to discover what the campaign language concealed. Taylor’s reversal matters less as a redemption story than as evidence of how punitive politics operates—first by abstraction, then by force, and only afterward by consequence.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump voter in rural Georgia switches to Democrat over one ‘simple fact’

item.title: Trump mixes up countries in late-night election meltdown
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump confused India with Brazil in a late-night post attacking American elections. He initially attributed Brazil’s roughly 125 million valid first-round presidential votes to India, then deleted the post after Indian news outlets highlighted the error. He later corrected the country but retained the unsupported accusation that delayed U.S. results are “rigged.”

Brazil was headed to a runoff because no candidate received more than 50 percent, according to the report. AlterNet says Trump used Brazil’s faster count to allege corruption in several American jurisdictions, while offering no evidence that their timelines reflect fraud rather than different election laws and counting procedures.

The outlet places the post within Trump’s broader effort to discredit the 2026 election before it occurs. It reports that he has blamed Congress for not passing his “SAVE America Act,” repeated allegations about voting machines and mail ballots, and separately promised voters $5,000 if they elect Republicans—without explaining the proposal’s mechanism or conditions.

The error is not the central offense

Mistaking Brazil for India is an obvious factual failure, especially when the mistaken claim is being offered as proof of systemic corruption. But concentrating on the geographical blunder risks turning a campaign against election legitimacy into a story about an elderly politician’s verbal competence.

Trump corrected the country. He did not retract the fraud allegation. That distinction matters. The disposable detail was the identity of the foreign democracy; the durable message was that unfavorable or slow results in the United States should be presumed corrupt.

The correction therefore repaired the post’s weakest fact while preserving its political function.

Power speaks before the count

Trump is not a powerless commentator speculating from the sidelines. As president, he holds the executive branch and the enormous agenda-setting power of the office. When he declares an election fraudulent before voting occurs, the statement can shape how supporters interpret ordinary administrative delays and any eventual defeat.

The relevant agency is clear. Trump chose to equate different counting timelines with “rigging.” He chose to target Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and other jurisdictions. He chose to repeat claims about mail ballots, machines, and buried evidence without substantiation in the material AlterNet cites.

Congress, meanwhile, did not enact the restrictions he demanded. That is not evidence of electoral vulnerability. It is evidence that the president did not obtain his preferred federal voting rules.

Comparison as misdirection

Brazil’s election administration is not a control experiment for the United States. A raw comparison between reporting speeds says nothing by itself about fraud. Different jurisdictions use different ballots, laws, verification procedures, counting rules, and reporting systems.

Trump’s argument strips away those institutional differences and replaces them with insinuation: fast means honest; slower means corrupt. AlterNet should make this defect more explicit. The country mix-up is clickable, but the false inference is politically consequential.

The framing also redirects scrutiny from the person wielding presidential power toward election workers and heavily populated jurisdictions portrayed as suspicious merely because their lawful counting takes time. Administrative complexity becomes a scapegoat for a claim the president has not proved.

Delegitimization as advance strategy

The larger pattern is preemptive delegitimization. Fraud is asserted before ballots are cast, procedural restrictions are presented as the only protection against theft, and routine counting becomes retroactive evidence of conspiracy.

This structure is politically useful because it resists disproof. A Republican victory can be treated as vindication; a loss can be labeled theft; an incomplete count can be cast as manipulation. The accusation does not describe a verifiable standard. It constructs an excuse in advance.

The reported $5,000 promise adds another layer of transactional politics, although AlterNet provides too little detail to establish what Trump proposed or whether it could be delivered. What the report does establish is the juxtaposition: voters are offered a personal financial benefit for electing Republicans while being told that any system failing to produce the desired outcome is corrupt.

The systemic error

The institutional danger lies less in one deleted mistake than in the conversion of presidential authority into a machine for manufacturing distrust. A false country reference can be corrected in seconds. Suspicion planted by the president is harder to retract, particularly when it is repeated before every relevant fact exists.

Coverage that foregrounds the “meltdown” risks reducing a deliberate political tactic to personal confusion. The sharper account is that Trump used a mistaken example to advance an unsubstantiated claim, corrected the example, and preserved the accusation. The error was factual. The power move was political.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump mixes up countries in late-night election meltdown

item.title: Trump official flips lid over viral Jack Smith clip
item.description:
What happened

According to AlterNet, White House communications director Steven Cheung attacked former special counsel Jack Smith after Smith was photographed wearing a “No Kings” shirt at a Maryland music festival organized by guitarist Tom Morello. Cheung called Smith a partisan operative and accused him of weaponizing the justice system against President Donald Trump.

The outburst followed a congressional hearing in which Sen. Eric Schmitt accused Smith of lying about whether he had visited Atlanta in February 2024. The purported evidence placed Smith at a game involving the Iowa Hawkeyes in Maryland—not the Atlanta Hawks. AlterNet reports that Schmitt had been warned the information supplied by Trump’s Justice Department was unvetted but used it anyway.

The shirt is the diversion

Smith’s concert attire is politically expressive, but it does not validate Cheung’s sweeping allegations about Smith’s prosecutorial conduct. Cheung offered outrage in place of evidence, shifting attention from an accusation against Smith that collapsed under elementary scrutiny.

That distinction matters. A former prosecutor wearing opposition-themed merchandise may invite questions about judgment or political preference. It does not retroactively prove that his official investigations were partisan fraud. Cheung’s post attempts to make the photograph carry an evidentiary weight it cannot bear.

Power manufactured the accusation

The central actors were not confused spectators. Schmitt exercised the authority of a senator during a congressional hearing. The Justice Department controlled the information placed in his hands. Schmitt then used that institutional platform to accuse Smith of perjury despite, according to AlterNet, having been warned that the material had not been vetted.

The error was almost absurdly basic: Hawkeyes became Hawks, Maryland became Atlanta, and attendance at a basketball game became evidence of a prosecutorial conspiracy. But the institutional imbalance is serious. A senator can broadcast an allegation under the prestige of Congress; the target must then disprove a story that should never have survived internal review.

Incompetence does not erase responsibility

Calling this merely a “faux pas” understates what happened. A mistake is discovered during a responsible effort to establish facts. Here, AlterNet’s account describes an official proceeding in which a grave allegation moved forward after an explicit warning about the evidence.

The reporting does not establish whether Schmitt knew the claim was false. It does establish that he lacked a sound basis for presenting it as he did. That is not harmless confusion. It is a decision to impose the reputational cost of an accusation on Smith while treating verification as optional.

Propaganda survives correction

Once the Atlanta claim failed, the political operation did not reconsider its premise. It found a shirt. The argument simply migrated from supposed travel evidence to cultural symbolism, while preserving the same conclusion: Smith was corrupt because Trump’s allies said he was.

This is how propaganda protects itself from falsification. Each failed exhibit is disposable because the accusation, not the evidence, is the product. The concert photograph gives supporters a fresh emotional cue and encourages them to forget that a senator’s earlier case disintegrated on contact with a team name and a map.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of government power into an allegation machine. Officials obtain unvetted material, congressional allies amplify it, and communications staff replace failed claims with personal vilification. The weakness of one accusation does not restrain the next because accuracy is not carrying the political burden; repetition is.

Comic incompetence may limit what such actors can execute effectively, but it does not neutralize the machinery they control. Institutional authority can make even a ridiculous claim costly. When powerful officials face no internal penalty for launching accusations they were warned could be unreliable, error stops functioning as a corrective. It becomes a renewable political resource.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump official flips lid over viral Jack Smith clip

item.title: Neurologist says Trump’s conduct may be more than cognitive decline
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that geriatric neurologist Dr. Germaine Odenheimer said Donald Trump’s conduct may reflect cognitive changes, medication effects, the removal of institutional restraints, or some combination of those factors. She did not diagnose dementia and stressed that Trump’s medications, laboratory results, and cognitive-test results are unknown.

Speaking Monday on Dr. Steven Hassan’s podcast, Odenheimer described Trump’s recent GOP speech in Dallas as long and rambling but said she detected no specific language deficit. Hassan argued that Trump’s behavior appears less restrained because healthier advisers and other “guardrails” no longer constrain him. Both raised concern that Trump might interfere if Democrats won control of Congress, but the article provides no evidence of a particular plan.

Speculation is not a diagnosis

The strongest medical conclusion in the story is that no reliable conclusion can be drawn. Odenheimer identifies several possibilities—neurological change, medication, another medical condition, or simply fewer constraints—but lacks the clinical information required to distinguish among them.

That makes the headline’s medical tease more confident than the reporting underneath it. An expert listing hypotheses is not evidence that any one hypothesis is true. Trump’s repeated falsehoods, rambling remarks, and attacks on fellow Republicans are observable conduct. Their medical cause remains unestablished.

Power does not require impairment

The fixation on cognition risks converting political agency into a diagnostic mystery. A president does not need dementia, medication side effects, or kidney failure to abuse power, spread false claims, or punish rivals. Those actions can also be choices.

Trump holds executive power. The advisers who indulge him, party officials who provide a platform, and institutions that decline to impose consequences exercise agency too. Medical speculation can obscure that structure by relocating responsibility from decisions and enablers to an unknowable condition inside one man’s brain.

The missing guardrails

Hassan says restraints around Trump have been systematically dismantled, while Odenheimer attributes part of the change to the Supreme Court. But AlterNet does not identify the rulings, officials, or mechanisms behind that claim. “The guardrails are gone” describes an outcome without adequately naming who removed them.

Guardrails are not atmospheric conditions. They are laws enforced or ignored, oversight exercised or abandoned, appointments confirmed, rulings issued, and party leaders deciding what conduct they will tolerate. Without that institutional accounting, a structural failure gets reduced to Trump becoming more “unhinged.”

The danger of amateur neurology

The article’s weakest move is treating public behavior as an invitation to reverse-engineer private medical records. Odenheimer appropriately acknowledges the limits: Trump has not been examined by her, essential information is unavailable, and even an unsteady gait can have multiple explanations.

That uncertainty should narrow the story, not furnish it with more conjecture. Suggesting medication as “most likely” without knowing what medication Trump takes gives political commentary the costume of clinical precision. Readers do not need a speculative diagnosis to evaluate documented statements and official acts.

Accountability without an MRI

The larger pattern is a media habit of medicalizing authoritarian-style political conduct when institutional analysis would be more useful. A diagnosis can make deliberate behavior sound involuntary, while talk of vanished guardrails can make institutional surrender sound natural and ownerless.

The relevant questions are concrete: what power is being exercised, who enables it, what restraints remain, and who refuses to use them? Trump’s health may be unknown. The distribution of political responsibility is not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Neurologist says Trump’s conduct may be more than cognitive decline

item.title: Trump begs judge: Delay release of unflattering docs until after election
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that lawyers for Donald Trump’s former co-defendants asked the 11th Circuit to postpone oral argument over the release of special counsel Jack Smith’s Mar-a-Lago report. The argument was scheduled for November 2, 2026; the filing requested a date in or after January 2027, placing it beyond the midterm elections. The stated reason was scheduling conflicts.

The dispute concerns whether potentially damaging details from Smith’s classified-documents investigation may become public. AlterNet links the delay request to earlier rulings by U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, including her dismissal of the criminal case and an order restricting Justice Department disclosures. But the article does not establish that Cannon controls the 11th Circuit’s calendar or that the postponement will be granted.

The power lies with the courts

Trump’s former co-defendants can request delay, but they cannot impose it. The 11th Circuit judges hold the immediate institutional power: they decide whether oral argument remains on November 2 or moves beyond the election.

That distinction matters because AlterNet blurs the appellate proceeding with Cannon’s record in the district court. Her prior rulings are relevant context for how litigation has obstructed disclosure, but they are not proof that she can deliver the requested appellate delay.

Delay has political value

The filing states a conventional procedural justification: counsel have scheduling conflicts. The timing nevertheless carries an obvious foreseeable benefit for Trump. Information withheld until January 2027 cannot shape voters’ judgments before the November 2026 midterms.

The reporting does not prove that electoral advantage was the lawyers’ motive. It does establish that postponement would produce that advantage. Political accountability can be defeated without formally suppressing information forever; disclosure postponed until after voters act is disclosure stripped of much of its consequence.

Cannon’s record is the stronger story

AlterNet recounts a pattern of unusually favorable outcomes for Trump before Cannon. In 2022, she halted the Justice Department’s review and appointed a special master at Trump’s request before an appellate court reversed her for exceeding her authority. In 2024, she dismissed the classified-documents prosecution after finding Smith’s appointment unconstitutional, a ruling the outlet describes as departing from decades of precedent.

The article also reports that a later order limiting public discussion created uncertainty for people asked to provide nonpublic information outside the Justice Department, including to a federal grand jury and their own lawyers. Those concrete exercises of judicial authority matter more than speculation that Cannon will somehow determine the appellate schedule.

The framing outruns the evidence

The headline says Trump “begs” a judge and attributes the request directly to him. The body instead quotes a filing by lawyers for his former co-defendants. It does not show Trump personally making the request, identify Cannon as the official deciding it, or establish that embarrassment was the filing’s purpose.

That is avoidable misdirection. A forceful account does not need inflated agency or a personalized villain narrative. The documented issue is already serious: litigants connected to a sitting president seek a delay that would keep politically consequential records from public view until after an election, and judges possess the authority to grant or deny it.

Procedure can become protection

This story exposes how institutional protection often arrives disguised as calendar management, jurisdictional doctrine, and disclosure rules. Each step can be defended as ordinary legal process. Their cumulative effect may still be extraordinary: evidence concerning the conduct of a powerful official remains unavailable while public accountability has a deadline.

The systemic question is therefore not whether every delay proves a corrupt motive. It is whose interests delay serves, who has authority to authorize it, and whether the courts permit procedural control to become political insulation.

Thanks to Alter Net

item.title: Trump's 'stroke' pathways are now 'crossing the brain': psychologist
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychologist John Garrison interpreted videos of President Donald Trump at a Texas Peterbilt factory, an Oval Office signing and an exchange with reporters as possible evidence of neurological impairment. Garrison said apparent spasms had spread from one side of Trump’s body to the other—what he described as dysfunctional pathways “crossing the brain”—and suggested stroke, brain injury or another neurological condition as possible explanations.

His assessment rested on observed gestures, facial movements, posture and apparent lapses in attention. AlterNet supplied no examination, diagnosis, medical records or response from Trump’s physicians, and Garrison acknowledged that several conditions could explain some of the behavior. The reporting therefore establishes that a psychologist made a grave medical claim from video footage—not that Trump suffered a stroke or has neurological damage.

A diagnosis the evidence cannot carry

The article’s headline converts speculation into apparent revelation. “Stroke pathways” sounds clinical and conclusive; the body offers one psychologist narrating clips. Even Garrison’s language moves among possibilities: stroke, neurodegenerative disease, lesion, brain injury or some other neurological illness. That is not a diagnosis. It is a broad field of conjecture.

AlterNet compounds the problem by presenting interpretations as a sequence of discoveries. A clenched hand becomes involuntary. A facial expression becomes loss of muscular control. A stiff gait becomes possible evidence of a hidden brace. Each observation may justify a question, but the article repeatedly allows the question to borrow the authority of an answer.

The presidency is the relevant institution

Trump holds the institutional power here. If a president cannot reliably perform the office’s duties, the consequences are not private: executive authority, military command and federal administration concentrate enormous discretion in one person. That makes credible evidence about presidential capacity legitimate public business.

But institutional seriousness requires more than remote interpretation. The officials positioned to establish incapacity are the president’s medical team, senior executive officials and, under constitutional procedures, the vice president and Cabinet. The article does not report that any of them made such a finding. Their absence from the evidentiary chain is not a minor omission; it is the central limit on what readers can responsibly conclude.

Spectacle displaces accountability

The weakest actor in this story is not Trump but the audience, asked to inspect gestures frame by frame while the institutions possessing information and authority remain largely outside the frame. That is misdirection through spectacle. It substitutes amateur observation for records, formal evaluation and accountable testimony.

It also offers Trump’s political allies an easy escape hatch. A sensational medical claim can be dismissed without addressing whether the administration provides adequate health disclosures or whether officials would act if a president became impaired. Inflated certainty does not strengthen scrutiny. It gives secrecy a convenient foil.

The systemic error

Presidential systems invite a recurring failure: officials conceal, loyalists reassure, media outlets speculate and the public receives performance analysis instead of verifiable evidence. Power remains protected while uncertainty becomes content.

The political question is not whether one provocative gesture proves brain damage. It does not. The question is why presidential fitness depends so heavily on selective disclosure from the president’s own circle—and why coverage so often replaces scrutiny of that arrangement with diagnosis-by-video. When institutions refuse transparency, speculation rushes into the vacuum. Publishing the speculation as if it closed the case only deepens the failure.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘stroke’ pathways are now ‘crossing the brain’: psychologist

item.title: The strategic reason Trump could decide to walk away
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump could strategically resign before finishing his term to install Vice President JD Vance as president. The article’s central theory is that an early transfer would preserve Trump’s influence over the Justice Department and the broader administration while sparing him political exposure after possible Republican losses in the November 2026 midterms.

The piece also cites reported concerns about Trump’s health, the burdens of office, prospective Democratic investigations, departing staff, looming crises, and the possible loss of a Senate majority able to confirm his judicial nominees. It offers no evidence that Trump has decided to resign, that his family is urging him to do so, or that a resignation plan exists. This is a forecast about incentives, not an established development.

The power is the succession

The article’s strongest point is not its attempt to divine Trump’s state of mind. It is the institutional logic of replacing him with Vance. A resignation would not surrender executive power to an opponent. It would transfer that power to Trump’s chosen vice president, who would inherit the presidency, the executive branch and control over federal law enforcement.

That distinction matters. Leaving office can be an act of strategic preservation when the successor belongs to the same governing project. The relevant question is not whether Trump enjoys presidential ceremony more than golf. It is whether departure could protect his influence more effectively than remaining as a weakened lame duck.

Speculation is not evidence

AlterNet weakens its case by presenting a crowded inventory of conjecture: Trump is exhausted, his family is worried, Melania would welcome an exit, advisers are warning him about future catastrophes, and he may want refuge from investigations. Some of these propositions are attributed to public statements or outside observers. Others are assertions about private preferences that the article does not establish.

That is not a minor flaw. Political analysis becomes unreliable when it substitutes amateur mind-reading for demonstrated conduct. Trump’s documented incentives and constitutional authority are sufficient subjects. Claims about what he, his doctors or his family privately want require evidence the piece does not provide.

Accountability does not disappear

The article suggests resignation could help Trump avoid congressional investigations and hostile disclosures. It could reduce his direct exposure to oversight as president, but it would not erase Congress’s investigative powers or make past conduct unknowable. Nor does the article establish that a Vance administration could lawfully prevent every investigation or consequence.

What resignation could change is the machinery surrounding Trump. A loyal successor would control executive appointments and enforcement priorities. That creates an obvious structural risk: public authority can be used to protect a political network even after its central figure formally leaves office. The person changes; the incentives remain.

The article chases the personality

By concentrating on fatigue, vanity and personal escape routes, the piece partially misdirects attention from the actors who would enable the outcome. Vance would have agency as successor. Republican legislators would decide whether to sustain or withdraw congressional protection. Democratic leaders would decide how aggressively to use oversight. Executive officials would decide whether loyalty to Trump outranks institutional independence.

Trump’s temperament may shape events, but personality is not the whole power structure. Treating politics as a puzzle inside one man’s head lets the surrounding party, appointees and lawmakers fade into scenery. They are not scenery. They are the people whose cooperation turns personal interest into state action.

The system outlives the figure

The larger pattern is succession without rupture. A political project can survive the departure of its leader when loyal personnel retain control of the institutions that investigate wrongdoing, distribute benefits and impose costs.

That is why the resignation theory matters even though AlterNet does not prove it will happen. The consequential issue is not whether Trump walks away. It is whether the governing system around him has been organized so that his exit would amount to continuity with a younger face—and whether institutions capable of imposing accountability choose instead to facilitate the handoff.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The strategic reason Trump could decide to walk away

item.title: 'Whoaaa': News panel astonished as expert shows how Trump voters could hand Dems the House
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that MS NOW elections analyst Kabir Khanna identified voter defection as a possible route to Democratic control of the House. A Wall Street Journal poll found that 11% of Donald Trump’s 2024 voters regretted their choice, while 11% of non-MAGA Republicans said they planned to vote for a Democratic congressional candidate.

Khanna’s model showed that Republicans would retain roughly 230 House seats if 3% of Trump voters and 3% of Kamala Harris voters switched sides. But if even half of the regretful Trump voters backed Democrats, his projection flipped the House; a 10% crossover produced a comfortable Democratic majority.

He cautioned against overreading separate New York Times/Siena polling that showed Democrats ahead in red states. With about 600 respondents in each state and correspondingly wide margins of error, Khanna said even a six-point Democratic result in Texas would not constitute a safe lead.

Power is counted in districts

The panel’s astonishment makes for television, but the consequential fact is less dramatic: control of the House can turn on a relatively small group of voters changing sides. That leverage is amplified because a defection removes a vote from one coalition while adding it to the other.

Republicans also enter the contest with what Khanna called a structural advantage produced by redistricting. Voters may shift, but they do so inside maps drawn through exercises of state power. The electorate supplies the votes; political institutions determine how efficiently those votes become seats.

Regret is not realignment

A voter telling a pollster that they regret supporting Trump is not the same as voting for a Democrat in a midterm. Disapproval can become defection, abstention, reluctant Republican support, or nothing at all. Khanna’s scenarios illustrate what could happen under specified crossover rates; they do not establish that those rates will occur.

The same restraint applies to the finding about non-MAGA Republicans. An expressed plan is evidence of current sentiment, not a completed ballot. Treating it as destiny would turn a useful measurement into campaign mythology.

The spectacle obscures the mechanism

The headline centers the panel’s “whoaaa,” converting electoral arithmetic into a reaction clip. That framing misdirects attention from the institutions and political choices that matter: Republican control benefits from the district structure Khanna described, while Democratic success depends on converting dissatisfaction into votes in the contests where those votes can alter seats.

The surprise also reveals how political coverage often treats voters crossing party lines as an exotic event rather than a predictable consequence of governing. If some Trump voters believe his presidency has diverged from what they expected, their response is not a plot twist. It is political accountability operating through an electoral system whose maps can blunt or magnify it.

A poll is leverage, not power

The people holding institutional power are the officeholders governing now and the state actors who shaped the congressional map. Regretful voters possess potential electoral leverage, but they have not yet exercised it. Democrats likewise gain nothing from favorable hypothetical models unless candidates, organizations, and voters translate discontent into district-level victories.

Khanna’s warning about small state samples is therefore essential. A provocative result can influence fundraising, coverage, and partisan confidence long before it proves durable. Calling Texas a toss-up acknowledges uncertainty; presenting a six-point polling result as a settled transformation would erase it.

The larger error

American political journalism routinely personalizes structural contests. It gives the audience an astonished host, a touchscreen map, and a tantalizing percentage, while the durable machinery—district boundaries, incumbency, party organization, and governing consequences—fades into the background.

The meaningful story is not that television personalities were stunned. It is that Republican control may depend on retaining voters who now report regret, even as the party benefits from a map tilted in its favor. Whether Democrats can exploit that opening remains uncertain. The system will not convert dissatisfaction into accountability automatically; it will process that dissatisfaction through institutions already shaped by those with power.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Whoaaa’: News panel astonished as expert shows how Trump voters could hand Dems the House

item.title: Supreme Court justice sounds the alarm as 'vultures circling' around him: 'Foolhardy’
item.description:
What happened

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito told Fox News Sunday that speculation about his retirement felt like seeing “vultures circling.” According to RawStory’s account of reporting by Politico, the 76-year-old justice also said escalating public rhetoric about the Supreme Court concerned him.

Alito called it “foolhardy” to calculate how many more years he would serve. The political stakes are substantial: if he retires during President Donald Trump’s second term, Trump could nominate a fourth justice to the Supreme Court.

The power is Alito’s

Alito is not a vulnerable bystander surrounded by predators. He holds a lifetime appointment to an institution capable of invalidating laws, reversing constitutional precedents and reshaping rights nationwide. The people speculating about his retirement cannot remove him or compel him to leave.

Alito himself controls the decision described in the article. The Senate and president would control the confirmation process after a vacancy, but whether to create that vacancy is his choice.

A metaphor that reverses the hierarchy

The “vultures” framing turns political observers into aggressors and an enormously powerful justice into their prey. Yet retirement speculation is predictable because Supreme Court succession has become a central instrument of presidential power.

That does not make every criticism of the Court sound or every attack acceptable. But the article supplies no concrete example of threatening rhetoric, no identified speaker and no described consequence. It simply relays Alito’s concern. The result is atmosphere without evidence—and a powerful official’s discomfort presented as the main political injury.

What the speculation is actually about

The calculation surrounding Alito is not personal gossip. It concerns control of a Court whose conservative majority overturned Roe v. Wade in the 2022 Dobbs decision. A strategically timed retirement could allow Trump to replace Alito with a younger justice and extend that ideological control for decades.

RawStory mentions this possibility but organizes the story around Alito’s irritation at being watched. That framing misdirects attention from institutional succession to elite grievance. The consequential question is not whether speculation feels unpleasant to him. It is how an unelected justice’s private timing decision can shape public law long after the officials involved leave office.

Lifetime power, personal discretion

The system gives individual justices extraordinary agency over political succession while pretending the Court floats above politics. Presidents nominate, senators confirm and justices decide when—if ever—to surrender their seats. Each actor can make openly strategic choices while the institution retains the language of neutral continuity.

Alito’s refusal to provide a timetable preserves his leverage. The reporting does not establish his motive or whether he plans to retire. It does establish that uncertainty itself has political value: it keeps the president, the Senate and the public guessing while leaving the decisive choice with Alito.

The recurring institutional error

American judicial politics routinely centers the feelings, reputations and intentions of powerful justices instead of the structure that magnifies their choices. A retirement becomes palace intrigue; criticism becomes hostility; lifetime authority fades into the background.

The larger pattern is an accountability inversion. Those subject to Supreme Court rulings are treated as spectators, while the official who helps determine their rights is portrayed as besieged because they scrutinize his plans. The vultures are not the story. The lifetime seat—and the political power concentrated in the person occupying it—is.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Supreme Court justice sounds the alarm as ‘vultures circling’ around him: ‘Foolhardy’

item.title: Trump's attacks on John Roberts are backfiring to help chief justice: biographer
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump’s attacks on conservative Supreme Court justices may be helping Chief Justice John Roberts protect the court’s appearance of independence, according to CNN Supreme Court analyst and Roberts biographer Joan Biskupic. After Trump told Time he regretted some appointments because the justices had voted against him “too often,” Biskupic argued that his criticism gives them a “badge of honor” against perceptions that they are politically aligned with him.

On CNN’s Inside Politics, Biskupic said Roberts remains strongly conservative and has supported many Trump initiatives, while trying to prevent the court from appearing to “link arms” with the president. RawStory reported that she also cited security concerns arising from presidential criticism and acknowledged that Roberts has not found an effective answer to the court’s reputational decline.

Host Manu Raju pointed to a Gallup poll in which 12% of Americans reported “a great deal” of trust in the judicial branch. The story does not establish that Trump’s attacks have changed any justice’s vote or improved public confidence. Its narrower claim is that the attacks may give Roberts and other conservative justices useful political cover.

Power is not personal loyalty

Trump’s complaint exposes his conception of judicial appointments as transactions. He said he gave the justices “the position of a lifetime,” then faulted them for ruling against him. The institutional power here belongs to the president who selects nominees, the senators who confirm them, and the justices who exercise lifetime authority—not to citizens watching the arrangement from outside.

But a president’s appointment does not create a legal debt. Trump’s language treats adverse rulings as ingratitude, collapsing constitutional office into patronage. That is more revealing than the tactical question of whether his criticism backfires.

Independence as reputation management

Biskupic’s account presents Roberts as trying to preserve distance from Trump while advancing a very conservative jurisprudence and supporting many presidential initiatives. That distinction matters. Institutional independence cannot be measured by whether the president occasionally complains about an outcome.

Trump’s anger supplies Roberts with an image of separation at little apparent cost. The court can deliver much of the substantive agenda the president wants while pointing to scattered conflicts as proof that it belongs to no political project. Criticism from a powerful beneficiary becomes reputational insulation.

The article’s narrow frame

RawStory centers the irony that Trump may be helping a chief justice he attacks. That is a plausible observation, but it risks making Trump’s frustration the main measure of the court. The more consequential questions are what the justices have authorized, who benefits from their rulings, and what constraints they have placed on executive power.

Nor does the cited poll prove that this episode caused the court’s low standing. The 12% figure describes one level of confidence; it does not explain why respondents hold it. Using distrust chiefly as Roberts’s legacy problem turns a public crisis of legitimacy into an elite branding dilemma.

The durable arrangement

The larger pattern is a division between policy and presentation. Political actors secure judges capable of reshaping government for decades. Those judges retain enough formal and occasional practical distance to reject the claim that they are instruments of the politicians who elevated them.

Trump’s attacks may strengthen that arrangement because they confuse personal disobedience with institutional neutrality. A justice need not satisfy Trump in every case to expand conservative power. If presidential abuse helps the court advertise independence while its governing consequences receive less scrutiny, the insult is not accountability. It is camouflage.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s attacks on John Roberts are backfiring to help chief justice: biographer

item.title: MAGA senator flooded with payment requests after Trump blasts phone number online
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump publicly posted what he said was Republican Sen. Tom Cotton’s phone number during a dispute over the Sunshine Protection Act. Cotton opposes making daylight saving time permanent, arguing that Arkansas children would otherwise travel to school in darkness.

After journalist Oriana González identified a Venmo account apparently linked to the same number, people flooded the suspected account with payment requests. Some invoked unfulfilled or proposed $5,000 checks; one reporter referenced the cost of war with Iran. The report does not establish that Cotton controlled the account or suffered any financial loss.

Trump also attacked Cotton’s ego, mocked his standing with Arkansas voters, and pressed him to “take the win” by surrendering his position before the midterms.

The president supplied the target

The payment requests are the spectacle, but presidential retaliation is the political event. Trump used his enormous platform to direct public attention toward the purported private contact information of a senator who resisted him on legislation.

Cotton is hardly powerless: he is a United States senator with a vote Trump wants. But the imbalance inside this confrontation is still obvious. The president commands the executive branch, the party’s dominant political machinery, and an audience capable of turning a posted phone number into immediate harassment. Trump made the decision that enabled what followed.

Policy reduced to obedience

The dispute concerns whether the country should keep daylight saving time year-round. Cotton offered a concrete objection tied to dark winter mornings and school travel. Trump’s reported response did not answer that concern. He framed Cotton’s dissent as ego and demanded compliance so Republicans could claim a “win” before the midterms.

That is governance stripped down to factional discipline. The merits of the bill become secondary; the decisive question is whether a senator will obey the president’s political timetable. A legislative vote is treated not as judgment entrusted to an elected official, but as property owed to the party leader.

The prank is not the power

The Venmo requests make for an irresistible social-media anecdote. They also risk shifting attention from the person who exposed the purported number to the people who exploited it afterward.

Those users chose to pile on, and the requests invoking promised checks or military spending turned the episode into protest theater. But they did not create the confrontation or possess the institutional leverage at its center. Fixating on their mockery would convert presidential pressure into a story about unruly spectators.

RawStory’s framing captures the cascade, but “flooded with payment requests” foregrounds the comic consequence over the governing abuse: a president publicly singled out a member of his own party for refusing to yield a legislative vote.

Discipline by humiliation

Nothing in the report establishes that Trump intended the payment requests or knew a Venmo account might be connected to the number. The evidence supports a narrower and still damning conclusion: he publicly exposed what he presented as Cotton’s contact information while attacking him for dissent.

The foreseeable effect is intimidation. Every other Republican senator can see the price of resistance: personal ridicule from the president, doubts cast on their popularity, and a mass audience pointed in their direction. The immediate target is Cotton; the broader audience is anyone considering an independent vote.

A legislature trained to submit

This episode reveals a political system in which formal power and practical agency increasingly diverge. Senators retain constitutional authority to vote, yet party leaders can make exercising that authority personally costly.

The systemic error is not merely that online crowds behave badly. It is that presidential power can be deployed as a weapon of intraparty enforcement, while coverage is easily captured by the resulting internet circus. The joke travels farther than the coercion, and that imbalance helps coercion become routine.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: MAGA senator flooded with payment requests after Trump blasts phone number online

item.title: ​'You're a liar!' Trump interrupted by protester yelling about sex abuse verdict
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that a protester interrupted President Donald Trump’s rally in Vandalia, Ohio, shouting that Trump was a liar and repeatedly calling him a “rapist” over the E. Jean Carroll case. Video showed the protester being escorted from the arena while Trump paused his speech.

In May 2023, a Manhattan federal jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll and defaming her, awarding $5 million. A second jury later awarded Carroll $83.3 million for further defamation. The first jury did not find rape under New York’s narrow statutory definition, though the judge later said Carroll had proved Trump raped her in the term’s ordinary meaning. Trump denies her allegations and has appealed both verdicts.

The power was onstage

The protester had a voice for a few seconds. Trump had the podium, the arena, the presidential office and a rally organized to influence Senate elections. Security removed the interruption; the event continued.

That distinction matters. This was not a confrontation between equivalent political forces. One person briefly challenged an officeholder commanding an institutionally protected platform. Treating the disruption itself as the central drama risks confusing visibility with power.

A verdict, not merely an accusation

The protester’s wording requires the legal distinction RawStory supplies. But the underlying case cannot honestly be reduced to a heckler’s allegation. Two federal juries imposed civil liability and substantial damages, including $83.3 million for further defamation.

Trump retains the right to appeal, and his denials remain part of the record. Neither fact erases the verdicts. Political coverage routinely lets powerful defendants turn adjudicated findings back into an indefinite dispute, as though repetition of a denial restores the uncertainty that a jury resolved.

The headline shrinks the story

The “you’re a liar” spectacle is easy material: an interruption, a reaction and an ejection. The more consequential story is that a sitting president found civilly liable for sexual abuse and defamation could campaign before supporters while the verdicts were treated as an inconvenient disturbance from the crowd.

That framing redirects attention from the person exercising power to the person removed by security. The protester becomes the event; Trump’s documented legal liability becomes background. This is not fabricated reporting, but it is diminished reporting.

Accountability becomes disruption

Trump’s supporters did not need to rebut the verdicts for the rally to proceed. The structure of the event did the work: the challenger was isolated, escorted out and replaced by the scheduled message. Institutional control converted an attempt at accountability into a temporary breach of order.

That is a familiar political mechanism. Conduct established through formal proceedings is recoded as partisan noise, while the person with the largest platform claims the privilege of moving on. The weaker actor is then scrutinized for tone, terminology and decorum more intensely than the powerful actor is scrutinized for the conduct at issue.

The system protects the microphone

The larger pattern is not that one protester shouted an accusation. It is that legal accountability and political accountability operate on separate tracks—and political power can often insulate itself from the first by dominating the second.

Juries can make findings and impose damages. They cannot force a party, a rally audience or a campaign apparatus to treat those findings as disqualifying. When coverage centers the interruption instead of that insulation, it helps power present accountability as heckling and consequence as somebody else’s bad manners.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ​’You’re a liar!’ Trump interrupted by protester yelling about sex abuse verdict

item.title: 'Grab 'em by the throat!' Fox comics joke about physically beating Dem Senate hopeful
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Fox News host Jimmy Failla aired a Saturday-night segment asking guests whether they would buy Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed expensive liquor or throw him “over the top rope” and beat him. Retired professional wrestler Robert “Sgt. Slaughter” Remus chose the latter, adding that he would first grab El-Sayed by the throat and swing him around. The audience applauded.

Comedian Tom Shillue agreed, joking that he might instead hit El-Sayed with the liquor. RawStory says El-Sayed was narrowly leading Republican Mike Rogers in recent polls and had also been targeted by Republican figures, including President Donald Trump, who used El-Sayed’s wife in a social-media comparison with Melania Trump.

The microphone is power

This was not merely a few performers exchanging ugly jokes. Fox supplied the studio, audience, format, editing process and broadcast platform. Failla designed the choice: reward a political candidate or fantasize about physically assaulting him. Remus and Shillue supplied the answers; the network turned them into programming.

That distribution of responsibility matters. The institutional power belongs to Fox, not to El-Sayed and not to an audience supposedly swept up in spontaneous laughter. The violence-themed premise was built into the segment before anyone delivered a punchline.

A joke with a target

Calling the exchange comedy describes its packaging, not its political function. The target was a named Democratic nominee reportedly leading a Republican opponent. The audience was invited to boo him, and the guests were invited to imagine his beating.

Nothing in the report establishes an actual plan or literal threat against El-Sayed. It does establish something more routine: a media venue converting violence against a political opponent into communal entertainment. The applause is part of the product—a cue that contempt for the target is shared, permissible and pleasurable.

The easy alibi

The professional-wrestling frame gives everyone involved an escape hatch. If challenged, they can point to theatrical convention, comic exaggeration or the game’s absurdity. But Failla’s premise did not use a fictional villain. It attached simulated punishment to an identifiable candidate in an active political contest.

The distinction is not that rhetoric automatically produces violence. The distinction is that influential media institutions decide which people can be depicted as legitimate objects of violence without social cost. Here, Fox made that decision and called it a bit.

Personal degradation as politics

RawStory also places the segment alongside Trump’s post using El-Sayed’s wife to contrast her unfavorably with Melania Trump. These are separate episodes, and the report does not establish coordination. They nevertheless show the same political method: evade the candidate’s program and reduce him and his family to objects of ridicule, hostility and spectacle.

El-Sayed answered Trump with a crude insult of his own, according to the report. That response may deepen the degradation, but it does not erase the imbalance in institutional power. A candidate’s retort is not equivalent to a president directing attention at the candidate’s spouse, nor to a national television network staging applause for fantasies of assault.

The system rewards escalation

The larger pattern is an outrage economy with political utility. Republican figures attack; television personalities intensify the attack; audiences supply approval; and the resulting clip becomes fresh material for another cycle. Responsibility dissolves into “banter” even though each participant made a concrete choice.

The consequence is not confusion but normalization. Political disagreement becomes permission to humiliate spouses, imagine beatings and measure success by audience reaction. Fox did not merely report that climate. In the episode RawStory describes, it manufactured and broadcast it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Grab ‘em by the throat!’ Fox comics joke about physically beating Dem Senate hopeful

item.title: Trump singles out lone protester with baseless accusation: 'How much is she being paid?’
item.description:
What happened

President Donald Trump singled out a woman protesting his Washington construction plans and asked on Truth Social, “How much is she being paid, and by whom?” RawStory reports that he offered no evidence that she—or any other protester—was paid.

Trump shared her image with his millions of followers and claimed she appeared at demonstrations against renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and his proposed D.C. arch. According to the report, Trump has said the arch would also function as a military installation with drones and snipers stationed on its roof and plaza.

RawStory notes that Trump has repeatedly made unsupported claims about paid protesters, beginning at least as early as 2016.

The power is not evenly distributed

This is not a dispute between two comparably situated political participants. One person held a protest sign. The other holds the presidency, controls a vast communications platform and commands the attention of millions.

By publishing the woman’s image alongside an unsupported insinuation, Trump directed presidential visibility at an individual dissenter. The question format does not neutralize the accusation. It circulates the premise—that her protest is purchased—without accepting the burden of proving it.

A smear disguised as curiosity

Trump did not identify a payer, produce financial records or cite an investigation. RawStory’s account provides no evidence for his allegation. “How much?” and “by whom?” manufacture the appearance of an unanswered scandal when the reporting establishes no scandal to answer.

That rhetorical maneuver shifts scrutiny away from the projects themselves. Instead of addressing objections to changes at the Reflecting Pool or to a monumental arch incorporating military infrastructure, Trump recasts opposition as a question of personal authenticity. The protester becomes the story; presidential power over public space recedes from view.

Dissent recast as fraud

Calling protesters paid agitators strips them of political agency. Their stated objections no longer need to be answered because their participation has been preemptively described as transactional.

The predictable consequence is intimidation. A private individual’s image is delivered to a mass political audience under a cloud of suspicion created by the president. The report does not establish what response she received, so claims of specific harassment would go beyond the evidence. But the power asymmetry—and the exposure Trump created—is plain.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of dissent into suspected conspiracy. When a powerful official treats opposition as inherently fake, he does more than insult a critic: he supplies supporters with a rationale for disregarding criticism without examining it.

Coverage should keep responsibility fixed where it belongs. The consequential act was not one woman protesting a federal project. It was the president using his office-amplified platform to circulate an evidence-free accusation against her, while evading the substance of what she opposed.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump singles out lone protester with baseless accusation: ‘How much is she being paid?’

item.title: Trump's dumb misfire shot a gaping hole in his billion-dollar grift
item.description:
What happened

RawStory argues that the “misfire” was a war-driven energy shock that pushed consumers and governments away from oil, undermining the fossil-fuel interests Donald Trump had promised to serve. The article says oil prices had recently eased as Iran allowed tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, while an International Energy Agency report found global oil demand had fallen 2.5 percent that year.

The reported result was faster adoption of alternatives: the IEA expected electric vehicles to reach 29 percent of global car sales that year, compared with 5.8 percent in the United States. RawStory attributes much of that shift to higher fuel prices, though the article does not establish how much was caused by the war rather than policy, technology costs, or existing market trends.

The headline’s “billion-dollar grift” refers to a reported 2024 Mar-a-Lago meeting where Trump asked oil executives for $1 billion while promising to dismantle climate rules. The article says he subsequently eliminated wind, solar, and EV incentives. It does not report that the industry actually provided $1 billion, so the transaction implied by “grift” remains an argument, not an established payment.

The power sits in Washington

Individual drivers do not determine whether the United States builds charging networks, finances rooftop solar, prices carbon pollution, or preserves clean-energy subsidies. Presidents, Congress, regulators, utilities, and financial institutions do.

RawStory identifies the Republican Party and the fossil-fuel industry as the central political alliance. Its concrete charge is that Trump offered regulatory relief while seeking extraordinary financial support from oil executives. That is the relevant power relationship: an officeholder controlling federal policy soliciting money from businesses that stand to profit from those decisions.

The public pays either way

The article’s strongest distinction is between price increases imposed by crisis and those created through taxation. A war-related oil shock sends additional revenue toward producers and petroleum-exporting states. A tax can return revenue to households or finance transit, electric vehicles, and distributed energy.

RawStory cites an International Monetary Fund estimate of $7 trillion annually in worldwide fossil-fuel costs and subsidies, including damage shifted away from producers. Its political point is straightforward: cheap fuel is not truly cheap when illness, climate damage, and military costs are charged to everyone else.

That transfer is policy, not weather. The federal gasoline tax cited by the article has remained at 18.4 cents per gallon since 1993. Keeping visible prices low while socializing less-visible costs protects incumbent industries and disguises who receives the subsidy.

Scarcity is the misdirection

The article’s rooftop-solar example exposes another manufactured limit. Germany used favorable loans, government-backed risk, and feed-in tariffs to spread ownership beyond households able to pay upfront. RawStory reports that more than a million German homes now combine solar panels with battery storage and that solar supplies roughly 14 percent of the country’s electricity.

By contrast, treating household electrification as a boutique consumer choice shifts responsibility downward. Families are told to shop their way out of an energy system designed by lawmakers, utilities, lenders, and corporate incumbents. Affordability is then presented as a personal constraint instead of the predictable result of financing and subsidy decisions.

The article is weaker when it leans on the author’s own well-subsidized home as proof of a national solution. One household demonstrates that incentives can work; it does not establish every cost, grid constraint, or distributional effect of scaling the model.

A backlash can accelerate the transition

RawStory presents the energy shock as an unintended consequence of Trump’s policies: an administration aligned with fossil-fuel producers helped make petroleum dependence more expensive, strengthening the economic case for electrification elsewhere.

That interpretation is plausible within the figures presented, but the causal claim outruns the evidence supplied. Sales percentages and declining oil demand show movement, not a complete explanation for it. The article should distinguish more carefully between an accelerator and a sole cause.

Even with that limitation, the broader pattern is clear. Governments can protect entrenched energy wealth, but they cannot guarantee permanent dependence when the costs of that dependence become immediate. Policy can delay a transition, concentrate its benefits, and leave poorer households trapped with higher bills. It cannot make fossil-fuel volatility disappear.

The system protects ownership, not consumers

This is not fundamentally a story about Trump accidentally teaching the world a lesson. It is about institutions deciding who owns energy infrastructure, who finances the transition, and who absorbs the damage while it is delayed.

The American failure described by RawStory is not a shortage of technology. It is a distribution of political power that rewards fossil-fuel producers, restricts public investment, and leaves clean-energy access dependent on income and geography. When crisis finally changes behavior, the same structure makes ordinary people pay first—and allows the officials who preserved that vulnerability to claim credit when prices retreat.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s dumb misfire shot a gaping hole in his billion-dollar grift

item.title: Cheers as jailed JD Vance heckler said to have ‘just ended JD's presidential ambitions’
item.description:
What happened

A viral heckle did not demonstrably end Vice President JD Vance’s presidential ambitions. RawStory reports that the claim came from AllChronology Media Group after Ben Braver, a Democratic candidate for the Florida House, disrupted a Republican rally in Lakeland, Florida, on Friday, October 2, 2026. Braver sarcastically thanked Vance and President Donald Trump before calling Vance a “pedophile protector” and referring to a promised $5,000 check.

Video cited by RawStory shows attendees shouting at Braver as security removed him and a person who appeared to be a law-enforcement officer threw him onto the pavement. The Florida Times-Union reported that Braver was charged with trespassing and resisting arrest without violence. The supplied reporting does not establish who ordered his removal, whether he remained jailed, or whether the physical force was lawful or necessary.

Social-media commentators praised Braver and condemned his treatment. Some asserted that he appeared compliant, but those judgments are attributed opinions based on the video—not findings by a court or an official investigation.

The power was not in the heckle

Braver had a voice, a candidacy and a momentarily receptive online audience. Vance arrived with the authority of the vice presidency, the protection of rally organizers and security, and access to a venue where dissent could be removed.

Law enforcement held the most immediate coercive power: the ability to put a person on the ground, handcuff him and initiate criminal charges. The decisive political fact is not that Braver embarrassed Vance. It is that Braver’s disruption ended with state-backed force while the rally continued.

Virality is not accountability

The headline’s suggestion that three sentences destroyed Vance’s presidential prospects is unsupported. RawStory identifies no polling, donor reaction, party revolt or campaign consequence. It offers a social-media boast and reactions from sympathetic observers.

That framing substitutes internet applause for evidence. A politician’s ambition is not defeated because a clip produces cheers, just as an arrest is not justified because a crowd produces jeers. Treating virality as power flatters spectators while obscuring the institutions that actually determined the outcome.

Speech and force are separate questions

Braver’s political speech does not automatically settle whether organizers could remove him from the event or whether the trespassing charge was warranted. The reporting does not provide the venue rules, the officers’ account, warnings given before removal or enough legal detail to resolve those questions.

But removal and physical force are also distinct. Even if officials had grounds to eject or arrest Braver, that would not by itself establish a need to throw him onto pavement. The resisting charge was specifically reported as “without violence,” making scrutiny of the force shown on video especially relevant. A charge is an allegation, not proof that Braver resisted or that the officer acted improperly.

The spectacle hides the machinery

RawStory packages the encounter as a triumphant heckler humiliating a powerful politician. That is emotionally satisfying and politically shallow. It shifts attention toward whether Braver became an online hero and away from who controlled the room, authorized the ejection and exercised force.

The larger pattern is familiar: political coverage turns institutional power into personality theater. Officials and security personnel make consequential decisions; audiences are invited to score the clip. The meme declares victory, the candidate faces charges, and the people with coercive authority largely escape examination.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Cheers as jailed JD Vance heckler said to have ‘just ended JD’s presidential ambitions’

item.title: Trump ridiculed on nemesis network as montage of him sleeping plays: 'He is knocked out’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that MS NOW’s “The Weekend” mocked President Donald Trump after he described targets of U.S. strikes on Iran as “drug factories slash nuclear factories.” Jonathan Capehart compared Trump’s shifting explanations for the war to an overstuffed diner menu, while Jacqueline Alemany used the remark to introduce a montage of Trump with his eyes closed at public events.

The images did not establish that Trump was asleep, though Capehart said he was “knocked out.” The segment also showed Secretary of State Marco Rubio denying that he had ever seen Trump fall asleep in meetings. The hosts treated that denial—and the administration’s insistence that Trump does not sleep—as additional material for ridicule.

The consequential statement was not about sleep

Trump’s physical alertness is the flimsiest part of this story. A collection of photographs showing closed eyes cannot establish sleep, incapacity, or anything else about presidential performance. Mockery is not evidence.

The consequential event was a president publicly describing military targets in language so muddled that the distinction between nuclear facilities and drug factories became unclear. If the administration’s justification for striking Iran has changed, as Capehart asserted, that is the issue requiring documentation: what rationale officials gave, when they gave it, and whether the underlying evidence supports it.

Power disappears behind the punchline

Trump holds executive power and publicly described U.S. military action. His administration possesses the intelligence, command authority, and communications machinery relevant to explaining that action. The television hosts possess none of those powers.

Yet the segment converted a question about state violence into personality content. Instead of pressing the administration’s claims about the targets, it pivoted to Trump’s eyelids. That does not shift blame onto weaker political actors so much as drain accountability from the stronger one. The president becomes an object of ridicule rather than the official responsible for defending his government’s decisions.

Rubio answered a safer question

Rubio’s denial addressed whether he had personally witnessed Trump sleeping in meetings. It did not clarify what was struck in Iran, why those sites were selected, or why Trump conflated drugs and nuclear activity in his description.

That is how political communication evades consequence: answer the trivial allegation emphatically while the substantive claim goes untested. The available reporting does not establish that Rubio lied. It does show that the segment gave his denial more attention than the administration’s account of military targets.

Satire without accountability

The hosts correctly recognized that Trump’s explanation sounded incoherent. But recognition is not scrutiny. Calling the rhetoric absurd while leaving its factual basis unexplored turns journalism into reaction footage.

The larger pattern is an opposition media economy that treats presidential spectacle as sufficient political analysis. Trump supplies confusion; television supplies laughter; the machinery of war remains largely outside the frame. When officials exercise lethal institutional power, the central question is not whether they look tired. It is whether their stated justification is coherent, supported, and subject to meaningful challenge.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump ridiculed on nemesis network as montage of him sleeping plays: ‘He is knocked out’
