item.title: Trump's 'explosive diarrhea' problem hands Dems 'bizarre' midterm weapon: analysis
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Guardian columnist Arwa Mahdawi argues Democrats could turn foodborne illness into an effective midterm issue by linking severe outbreaks during President Donald Trump’s second term to his administration’s approach to food-safety regulation. Democrats, including Representative Gabriel Amo and Senator Elizabeth Warren, have already incorporated the outbreaks into their messaging.

Mahdawi cited the largest recorded U.S. cyclosporiasis outbreak, linked to lettuce from Taylor Farms, alongside multistate outbreaks associated with jalapeños and sprouts. RawStory notes that Taylor Farms donated $1 million to MAGA Inc. shortly before the administration postponed a food-safety compliance deadline, but the reporting does not establish that the donation caused the delay or that the delay caused an outbreak. Mahdawi also acknowledged that the number of recalls under Trump has not differed markedly from the Biden years; her argument rests on the scale of the illnesses, not the recall count.

The power is regulatory

The people sickened by contaminated food do not set inspection rules, compliance deadlines, or enforcement priorities. The Trump administration does. Congress controls the legislation, appropriations, and oversight that can constrain it. Food producers control their operations and bear responsibility for meeting applicable safety requirements.

That distribution of power is the political core of the story. Foodborne disease may arrive through lettuce, peppers, or sprouts, but government decides how aggressively hazards are monitored and how quickly companies must comply with safeguards. Postponing a deadline is an exercise of state power, not bureaucratic weather.

A connection is not yet a case

The timing of Taylor Farms’ political contribution and the delayed compliance deadline warrants scrutiny. It does not, on the facts supplied here, prove a bargain, regulatory favoritism, or a causal link to contaminated lettuce. Treating proximity as proof would weaken the stronger argument: officials should explain who requested the delay, who approved it, what evidence supported it, and what risks were considered.

The article’s most consequential detail therefore remains underdeveloped. Campaign money creates access and suspicion; documentary evidence establishes influence. Political journalism should pursue that evidence instead of relying on an insinuation vivid enough to circulate but too incomplete to assign culpability.

The toilet framing is a distraction

Trump’s fixation on toilet flushing supplies an irresistible comic hook, and Mahdawi turns digestive illness into a pointed metaphor. But the joke risks displacing the institutional story. People becoming ill across multiple states is not principally a tale about presidential bathroom rhetoric. It is a question of regulatory capacity, corporate compliance, and congressional accountability.

Calling this a “bizarre” Democratic weapon also subtly misdirects attention toward campaign tactics. Democrats did not create the outbreaks described in the reporting. Their choice is whether to connect public illness to identifiable government decisions with evidence—or merely package suffering as a humiliating slogan.

Accountability requires more than disgust

The strongest midterm case would not claim that every recall proves regulatory failure or that every outbreak began with a White House decision. RawStory’s own account blocks that shortcut: recall totals were reportedly not remarkably different under Biden, and the supplied evidence does not establish what caused each outbreak.

The defensible charge is narrower. An administration postponing a food-safety requirement owes the public a concrete justification, especially amid unusually large illness outbreaks. Members of Congress seeking reelection should answer whether they supported that decision, investigated it, or ignored it. Responsibility attaches to acts and omissions, not to partisan proximity alone.

The systemic error

American political coverage routinely converts administrative power into spectacle. A compliance deadline becomes a toilet joke; an outbreak becomes campaign “messaging”; the officials and companies with decision-making authority recede behind the cleverness of the frame.

That inversion protects power. The systemic question is not whether diarrhea makes potent advertising. It is whether government weakened or delayed safeguards, who benefited, what evidence justified the decision, and who absorbed the risk. Until reporting answers those questions, disgust may win attention, but it will not establish accountability.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s ‘explosive diarrhea’ problem hands Dems ‘bizarre’ midterm weapon: analysis

item.title: The insidious reason people still think Trump is honest: NYT columnist
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie attributes Donald Trump’s perceived honesty to a cultural habit of mistaking openly expressed prejudice for candor. In Bouie’s account, racist statements can make Trump appear truthful to voters who already accept the assumptions behind them.

Bouie based his argument partly on a New York Times focus-group response from “Sebastian,” a 50-year-old white independent and former Trump voter. Sebastian said he viewed Trump as someone who “spoke what was on his mind,” voted for him again largely over economics, and now believes Trump does not appear to be delivering the hoped-for fixes. The article provides no polling figures showing how widespread this reasoning is, so Bouie’s explanation is an interpretation of a political pattern, not a measured account of the electorate.

Prejudice disguised as proof

The crucial substitution is between honesty and inhibition. Saying something bluntly proves only that the speaker said it bluntly. It does not establish that the claim is accurate.

But when a politician voices a voter’s existing resentment, recognition can feel like verification. Trump’s racism, in Bouie’s analysis, supplies that sensation: the voter hears a familiar hierarchy stated without apology and mistakes the absence of restraint for the presence of truth.

That is not merely a failure to check facts. It is a standard of credibility built around emotional permission. The politician is deemed honest because he validates what the audience wants licensed.

Power belongs to the president

The focus-group voter has agency at the ballot box, but he does not hold presidential power. Trump does. He chose the rhetoric, sought the office and now controls the authority attached to it. Treating supporters’ projections as the main event risks shrinking a story about political leadership into a puzzle about voter psychology.

Sebastian’s disappointment also exposes the gap between performance and governance. He expected economic repair and believed Trump might have learned from his first term. According to his own assessment in the focus group, that repair “doesn’t seem to be the case.” The cultivated image of fearless authenticity helped secure power; it did not guarantee competence or results.

The “lovable bigot” alibi

Bouie points to familiar cultural figures such as Archie Bunker and Tony Soprano to explain how audiences can interpret prejudice as rough-edged personality rather than racial animus. That archetype offers an alibi: the speaker may say bigoted things, but supposedly does not “really mean it like that.”

This framing moves scrutiny away from conduct and consequence toward imagined inner softness. People affected by the rhetoric are expected to discount its meaning, while the powerful speaker receives endless interpretive generosity. Harm becomes a personality quirk; objection becomes oversensitivity.

Restraint recast as deception

The same logic punishes politicians who choose their words carefully. Deliberation is coded as concealment, while impulsiveness is marketed as authenticity. Under that standard, factual accuracy matters less than whether a speaker appears unfiltered.

This is fertile ground for propaganda because it makes correction self-defeating. Evidence of falsehood can be dismissed as establishment fussiness, while another offensive statement renews the performance of candor. The politician’s brazenness becomes its own counterfeit credential.

The systemic error

Bouie’s larger point is that Trump can serve as a screen onto which voters project the leader they want: economic fixer, truth-teller or chastened second-term executive. When government collides with that imagined figure, disappointment arrives as surprise rather than as the foreseeable result of judging style as substance.

The deeper political failure is a culture that treats cruelty as authenticity and discipline as deceit. That inversion does more than misread one politician. It rewards leaders for breaking social restraints while relieving them of the harder burden: telling the truth, exercising power responsibly and producing the results they promised.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The insidious reason people still think Trump is honest: NYT columnist

item.title: Rock legend joins in mockery of embarrassed GOP senator as Jack Smith attends concert
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Foo Fighters frontman Dave Grohl mocked Sen. Eric Schmitt’s failed accusation against former special counsel Jack Smith during Saturday night’s Power to the People Festival in Maryland. Grohl wore an Iowa Hawkeyes shirt and dedicated “My Hero” to “my new friend Jack,” who was attending the concert.

At a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing the previous Tuesday, Schmitt accused Smith of perjury over whether Smith attended an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024. The texts Schmitt presented did not establish that claim: Smith had been watching Caitlin Clark and the Iowa Hawkeyes, not attending the Hawks game.

Smith was later photographed at the festival wearing a Bruce Springsteen tour shirt bearing the words “No Kings.” Attendees reportedly sought photographs and exchanged high-fives with him.

The accusation had institutional weight

Schmitt was not merely arguing with Smith. He was a United States senator using a Judiciary Committee hearing, staff preparation and the authority of congressional oversight to accuse a former federal prosecutor of a crime.

That power imbalance matters. Smith had to answer an allegation carrying the prestige of the Senate behind it, while Schmitt controlled the accusation and its staging. The evidence described by RawStory did not support Schmitt’s conclusion.

Certainty replaced verification

“I think you’ve already perjured yourself” was not a cautious request to reconcile conflicting information. It was a criminal accusation delivered before the basic premise had been checked.

The error was not an obscure technicality. Schmitt confused watching an Iowa basketball game with attending an Atlanta basketball game. His staff displayed the messages as proof, converting inadequate preparation into public insinuation. Whether this resulted from carelessness or something worse is not established by the reporting. The foreseeable effect was the same: attach the word “perjury” to Smith and let the spectacle outrun the correction.

Mockery clarified the power structure

Grohl’s shirt worked because it compressed the hearing’s failure into one unmistakable image: Iowa was not Atlanta, and watching a game was not attending one. The joke did not manufacture Schmitt’s embarrassment. Schmitt created it by making a grave allegation on evidence that did not prove what he said it proved.

Still, the concert should not become the center of the story. Celebrity ridicule is satisfying, but it carries no subpoena power and imposes no institutional accountability. Schmitt retained his office after the laughter. Smith received public affection, but affection is not a remedy for reckless congressional accusation.

The spectacle is the method

The larger pattern is accusation-first politics: use an official forum to produce a damaging clip, state suspicion as near-certainty, and leave the factual collapse to arrive later with less force. A Senate hearing becomes content production, while oversight becomes a costume worn by partisan performance.

RawStory’s emphasis on shirts, selfies and social-media mockery risks shrinking that abuse into a culture-war punchline. The consequential event was not that a rock musician embarrassed a senator. It was that a senator used institutional power to allege criminal conduct without evidence sufficient to establish even the underlying event.

Power survives the punchline

Schmitt’s humiliation may be memorable, but memory is not accountability. The structural advantage belongs to officials who can launch allegations from government platforms and rely on weaker actors—witnesses, journalists, artists or online spectators—to perform the correction afterward.

That arrangement rewards recklessness. The accuser receives the hearing, the cameras and the criminal vocabulary. Everyone else gets an Iowa T-shirt and the belated task of restoring reality.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Rock legend joins in mockery of embarrassed GOP senator as Jack Smith attends concert

item.title: Horror as final post of banker who outed Howard Lutnick’s ties to Epstein resurfaces
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Simon Andriesz, a 57-year-old former Cantor Fitzgerald Group employee, was found dead in an apparent suicide after publicly identifying himself as a whistleblower who had reported information about Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Jeffrey Epstein, Cantor Fitzgerald and BGC to the FBI in 2020–21. In his final X post, dated August 9, 2026, Andriesz said retaliation had devastated his family and that he intended to publish more evidence.

According to the report, documents Andriesz uncovered showed business dealings involving Lutnick and Epstein, including a 2018 exchange. The story says Lutnick had to revise earlier statements about his relationship with Epstein, but it also states that Lutnick has neither been charged with a crime nor accused of wrongdoing.

RawStory cites commentators who questioned the apparent-suicide account, including one who wrote, “I don’t buy it.” The article provides no evidence establishing foul play, no official finding contradicting suicide and no demonstrated connection between Andriesz’s death and his disclosures.

Power is not a conspiracy theory

Lutnick’s institutional power is concrete. He is the commerce secretary and previously led the financial firm at the center of Andriesz’s disclosures. Andriesz, by contrast, was a former employee claiming that whistleblowing had wrecked his life. That imbalance matters without inventing a murder plot to make it dramatic.

The documented political question is whether powerful institutions properly examined the information Andriesz supplied. He said he contacted the FBI and financial regulators, and that he later provided evidence to the House Oversight Committee. RawStory says the committee questioned Lutnick behind closed doors. Those institutions possess investigative authority, subpoena power and access to records. The whistleblower did not.

Suspicion is not evidence

The article’s headline and structure turn an unexplained death into insinuation. “Horror,” “chilling” and the reactions of social-media commentators do emotional work that the reported facts cannot. Rep. Thomas Massie’s attention may make the suspicion politically notable, but it does not substantiate it.

This framing is reckless because it invites readers to infer an assassination while preserving a technical escape hatch: the article never quite makes the allegation itself. RawStory launders speculation through quoted reactions, then arranges those reactions around Andriesz’s final post. That is not proof. It is atmosphere posing as investigation.

The retaliation claim deserves scrutiny

Andriesz’s allegation that retaliation followed his disclosures is serious, but the report does not identify who retaliated, what specific acts occurred or what evidence connects them to any named person. It therefore cannot support a finding that Lutnick, Cantor Fitzgerald, BGC or anyone else caused his death—or even that they carried out the alleged retaliation.

That uncertainty should sharpen the reporting agenda, not license fantasy. What complaints did Andriesz file? How did the FBI, regulators and Congress respond? What protections were offered? Which allegations were corroborated, rejected or left unresolved? The institutions holding those answers should not disappear behind a cloud of viral suspicion.

Spectacle protects the powerful

Conspiracy framing can masquerade as hostility toward elites while serving them remarkably well. It shifts attention from records, testimony, regulatory decisions and congressional oversight to a claim that cannot presently be proved. Officials can then dismiss the entire matter as internet fever rather than answer narrower, documented questions.

The larger pattern is institutional evasion reinforced by sensational media. A whistleblower said disclosure brought devastating consequences; agencies and Congress reportedly received his material; a cabinet official revised his account of ties to Epstein. Those are legitimate subjects for scrutiny. RawStory weakens them by making unsupported suspicion the center of gravity. When journalism substitutes ominous suggestion for evidence, power gains an easier defense and the public gets a thriller instead of accountability.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Horror as final post of banker who outed Howard Lutnick’s ties to Epstein resurfaces

item.title: Trump secretly believes he's stupid — and is scared you'll find out: biographer
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff believes President Donald Trump’s deepest insecurity is being seen as unintelligent. Wolff said former Trump adviser Steve Bannon had speculated that Vladimir Putin might possess Trump’s college transcripts, but neither man offered evidence that Putin has them or that the records contain damaging information.

Podcast co-host Joanna Coles noted that Trump’s high school and college transcripts have not become public despite journalists’ efforts to obtain them. Wolff further argued that Trump’s intellectual insecurity explains his selection of officials such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. That, too, is Wolff’s interpretation—not an established account of Trump’s motives.

The White House did not respond to these particular claims in the material AlterNet published. In May, answering a separate allegation about Trump’s mental competence, spokesperson Davis Ingle dismissed the critics as politically motivated and called Trump exceptionally sharp and energetic.

Speculation dressed for impact

The headline promises access to a secret belief inside Trump’s mind. The reporting supplies no such access. It supplies Wolff’s emphatic opinion, Bannon’s conjecture about transcripts, and Coles’s inference that favorable records would have been released.

Those observations may suggest insecurity. They do not establish what Trump privately believes about himself, what his academic records show, or what Putin possesses. The distinction matters because psychological certainty is doing work that evidence cannot.

This is not merely an overheated headline attached to solid reporting. The sensational claim is the reporting’s central mechanism. Trump’s repeated public boasting about his intelligence is relevant conduct; declaring the hidden fear behind it is interpretation.

The power sits in the appointments

The politically consequential question is not whether Trump secretly fears looking stupid. It is how a president uses appointment power.

A president can elevate loyalists, sideline expertise, and place consequential institutions under officials chosen for personal compatibility. Wolff alleges that this is what explains Hegseth’s selection, describing him as unqualified and deferential. AlterNet provides that accusation, but it does not independently demonstrate Trump’s selection criteria or assess Hegseth’s performance.

Still, the institutional stakes are concrete. The presidency controls nominations and executive staffing; appointees exercise public authority. Trump holds that power. Advisers, commentators, and undisclosed transcripts do not.

Putin is a distraction without proof

Invoking Putin turns an argument about presidential judgment into a tantalizing blackmail story. Yet the article offers no evidence that Putin has Trump’s transcripts, knows their contents, or has used them as leverage.

That unsupported possibility directs attention away from conduct visible in public: Trump’s intelligence claims, his personnel choices, and the qualifications of those entrusted with state power. A hypothetical Russian secret is more dramatic than an examination of appointments, but it is also far less grounded.

The weaker actor in this framing is not a particular political faction. It is the public, invited to decode a personality mystery while the presidency’s formal powers remain underexamined.

Personality is not accountability

Reducing governance to one man’s insecurity can accidentally soften responsibility. If poor appointments become symptoms of private fear, deliberate choices start to sound like involuntary psychological reflexes.

Whatever Trump’s motives, he remains responsible for whom he selects and what authority he gives them. Senators who confirm nominees exercise their own power. Senior officials who accept office and carry out policy retain agency. None of that depends on a biographer proving what Trump thinks about his intelligence.

The White House’s response pattern also deserves precise treatment. In the separate May exchange, its spokesperson attacked the credibility and politics of health professionals who questioned Trump’s competence. That response did not resolve the allegations; it redirected attention toward the accusers.

The system prefers palace gossip

This story reveals a recurring failure in political coverage: personality speculation displaces institutional analysis. Secret fears, hidden records, and imagined leverage offer an intimate explanation for government without requiring evidence about how decisions were actually made.

The sharper inquiry is less glamorous. Who received power? Who selected and confirmed them? What qualifications were evaluated? What decisions followed, and who absorbed the consequences?

Wolff’s theory may be true, false, or partly true; AlterNet’s material cannot establish which. The systemic error is treating an unverifiable diagnosis as the key to politics when the public record of power is both more knowable and more important.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump secretly believes he’s stupid — and is scared you’ll find out: biographer

item.title: Trump shocks with admission to medical habit said to be 'putting his life at risk’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump told an October 4, 2026, rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, that he takes a large Bayer aspirin every day despite doctors advising him to use a smaller dose. Trump described the habit as psychologically reassuring, said he did not know whether it worked, and argued that 35 years without an apparent problem justified continuing it.

Journalist and lawyer John Aravosis claimed Trump was endangering himself and his supporters by publicizing the practice. Liberal podcaster Joanne Carducci responded that she favored Trump ignoring his doctors. The report says health experts generally discourage prolonged daily use of high-dose aspirin, but it does not quote a clinician assessing Trump, establish the exact dose—Trump called it “386,” an unexplained figure—or document any supporter copying him.

The power behind the anecdote

Trump holds the institutional power here. He is not merely an eccentric patient discussing a private routine; he is the president speaking to supporters from a rally stage. That position gives an uninformed medical anecdote reach and authority no ordinary patient possesses.

Trump also identified his own agency plainly. Doctors advised a lower dose, and he rejected that advice because his personal history felt more persuasive. The decision described in the report is his. The presidency does not make that reasoning medically sound, but it makes broadcasting it politically consequential.

A headline stronger than the evidence

RawStory’s framing outruns its reporting. The headline says the habit is “putting his life at risk,” yet the article supplies no individualized medical assessment showing that Trump’s particular regimen currently endangers his life. It offers a general warning about prolonged high-dose aspirin use and Aravosis’s conclusion. Those are not the same thing.

The claim that supporters’ lives were put at risk is even less established. Trump’s remarks could encourage imitation; that is a foreseeable concern when a president celebrates disregarding doctors. But RawStory documents neither an instruction to followers nor evidence that anyone acted on it. Possibility is presented as outcome because alarm produces a cleaner headline than uncertainty.

Spectacle displaces scrutiny

The politically important conduct is Trump’s public elevation of instinct over expertise: he admitted uncertainty, invoked longevity as proof, and treated medical advice as something to acknowledge ceremonially before ignoring. That is a recognizable form of authority—confidence substituting for evidence.

Yet the article turns the episode into partisan entertainment. Aravosis calls Trump an idiot; Carducci jokes approvingly about his noncompliance. Neither response clarifies the medical facts. One supplies outrage, the other supplies morbidity disguised as wit, and RawStory packages both as content.

The system rewards degradation

The larger pattern is not simply that a powerful man makes questionable personal choices. It is that presidential speech becomes engagement bait while the institutions covering it abandon proportion. Trump offers boastful anti-expertise; influencers convert it into ridicule; the outlet inflates an inadequately established danger claim.

That cycle leaves readers with heat but little usable knowledge. Trump’s power magnifies careless rhetoric, while political media’s incentive structure magnifies the most sensational interpretation of it. The result is a degraded public sphere in which authority performs certainty, opponents perform contempt, and basic factual distinctions become collateral damage.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump shocks with admission to medical habit said to be ‘putting his life at risk’

item.title: NYT flags crowd 'emptying out' of Trump speech just 45 minutes in
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that attendees began leaving President Donald Trump’s rally in Vandalia, Ohio, about 45 minutes after he started speaking. New York Times reporter Katie Rogers posted video showing people moving toward the exits and partially cleared sections of the high school gym’s upper level, while the floor remained packed.

During the speech, a protester invoked the jury verdict finding Trump liable for sexually abusing E. Jean Carroll and was escorted out. RawStory also cites Jen Psaki’s claim that Trump failed to fill half of a 10,000-seat arena in Mobile, Alabama, the previous night. The article connects those scenes to Republican anxiety about Ohio, where cited polls showed Democrat Sherrod Brown narrowly leading Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

What the footage proves—and does not

The video establishes a limited fact: part of the upper level was emptying while Trump was still speaking. It does not establish total attendance, explain why each person left, or measure Trump’s statewide support. Psaki’s estimate from Alabama is likewise an attributed observation, not an independently documented attendance count in this report.

That distinction matters because crowd imagery is irresistible political bait. Supporters treat packed floors as proof of mass legitimacy; opponents treat visible exits as proof of collapse. Neither inference follows automatically. A rally audience is a staged and self-selected group, not an electorate.

Power is not measured in occupied seats

Trump held the institutional power in the room: the presidency, the podium and the authority around which the event was organized. The departing spectators exercised personal agency, but they did not make the consequential political decisions described by the story. Even the protester was quickly removed while the president continued speaking.

That imbalance is the real scene. A few people could leave or object; Trump retained the microphone and the machinery of office. Turning their movement into the central drama risks mistaking a moment of audience dissatisfaction for an actual transfer of power.

The convenient politics of spectacle

RawStory’s framing invites readers to savor embarrassment: Trump was talking, and some supporters had heard enough. But humiliation is not accountability. Empty balcony seats impose no institutional restraint, reverse no policy and resolve no allegation.

The article’s mention of the Carroll verdict supplies more serious context, yet it appears mainly through the spectacle of an interruption and removal. The result is a familiar inversion: the person naming an adjudicated finding becomes the disruption, while the powerful official continues as the event’s unquestioned center.

Ohio is the consequential story

The cited Senate polling carries more political weight than the crowd video. If Sherrod Brown was narrowly ahead of Jon Husted in surveys at the time of reporting, Ohio was competitive despite Trump having won the state comfortably in 2024. Polls do not predict the final result, but they can affect spending, staffing and party strategy.

The weaker framing substitutes anecdote for structure. Republicans’ concern is not that some rallygoers sought the exits early. It is that control of a Senate seat may be contested in territory the party expected to hold comfortably.

Spectacle conceals the machinery

Modern political coverage repeatedly turns visible enthusiasm into a proxy for durable power. That rewards politicians skilled at producing rallies and outlets skilled at extracting a viral image from them. It also directs attention toward spectators—whether they stay, leave or heckle—rather than toward officeholders, party organizations and the institutions that convert authority into consequences.

The broader pattern is not simply that Trump may be boring part of his audience. It is that coverage can recognize weakening spectacle while still leaving power itself largely unscrutinized. A thinning balcony is a useful observation. Treating it as the political event is misdirection.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: NYT flags crowd ‘emptying out’ of Trump speech just 45 minutes in

item.title: Hegseth's killing fantasy is an admission his treason attacks were dead wrong
item.description:
What happened

RawStory argues that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth undercut his own accusation that media reporting on depleted munitions amounted to treason. In a Wednesday address at Quantico, Hegseth attacked journalists for discussing weapons stockpiles, then cited the vulnerability of costly “legacy platforms” to cheap, mass-produced weapons as justification for creating an Autonomous Warfare Command.

Hegseth said the four-star command would oversee artificial intelligence, robotics, drones, and counter-drone systems, with a target operational date of October 1, 2027, subject to congressional authorization. He also announced Project Meridian, a 120-day study of future warfare led by Elon Musk, Newt Gingrich, and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey.

RawStory contends that the appointments create conflicts because SpaceX and Anduril already hold major Pentagon contracts. The article also condemns Hegseth’s rhetoric about “lethality” and autonomous weapons, although several of its broader allegations are asserted without enough supporting evidence in the supplied text to treat them as established fact.

The contradiction is the story

Hegseth’s memorandum recognized a basic military problem: inexpensive systems produced at scale can exhaust or defeat far costlier weapons. That is substantially the same vulnerability journalists expose when they report that munitions are being consumed faster than they can be replaced.

Calling such reporting treason does not rebut it. It redirects attention from the officials who determine procurement, deployment, and expenditure toward the people describing the consequences. Hegseth holds institutional power over Pentagon policy; reporters do not decide how many interceptors exist or how quickly commanders use them.

The word “treason” is especially revealing here. It converts scrutiny of military management into alleged betrayal while leaving management itself beyond scrutiny. The article is strongest when it identifies that maneuver, not when it substitutes insults for evidence.

Power follows the procurement authority

The proposed command would not merely speculate about future combat. According to RawStory’s account, it would receive personnel, budgets, and acquisition authority designed to accelerate deployment outside traditional channels. That is concentrated bureaucratic power over which technologies are purchased, tested, and placed into military use.

Congress still matters because Hegseth said authorizing legislation would be required. But the executive branch is setting the agenda, defining urgency, and selecting the advisers before lawmakers act. Those choices can narrow the eventual debate: once a weapons program is presented as the necessary answer to an emerging threat, resistance is easily recast as weakness.

Project Meridian compounds the problem. Musk and Luckey are not detached futurists if companies associated with them sell relevant systems to the Pentagon. Their commercial interests do not prove that their recommendations will be corrupt, but they create an obvious need for disclosure, independent evaluation, and enforceable safeguards. The supplied reporting does not establish what ethics rules will apply, so it cannot support the categorical claim that their work “won’t” be properly vetted.

Machines do not erase human agency

“Autonomous warfare” sounds like a technical domain operating beyond politics. It is nothing of the kind. Officials choose the systems, contractors design them, commanders establish their permissible uses, and elected branches decide whether meaningful human control is required.

That chain of responsibility becomes more important as decision-making accelerates. A machine may identify or engage a target, but institutions determine the conditions under which it can do so. Automation can diffuse accountability rhetorically without eliminating it materially.

The central risk described by this story is therefore not a robot independently seizing power. It is powerful officials using technological complexity and wartime urgency to make lethal policy harder to examine and responsibility easier to evade.

The article overreaches where scrutiny should sharpen

RawStory weakens its case by presenting grave peripheral allegations—including claims of mass deaths and murders—as settled facts without supplying the evidence needed to assess them here. Its language about “killer robots” conveys the stakes but also collapses important distinctions among remotely operated, semi-autonomous, and fully autonomous weapons.

Those excesses do not vindicate Hegseth’s attack on the press. They show why precise reporting matters. A serious critique should distinguish documented policy, announced intentions, foreseeable risks, and unproven accusations. Otherwise, officials can use an article’s weakest claims to avoid answering its strongest ones.

The strongest unanswered questions are concrete: What targeting decisions could these systems make? Who would authorize lethal force? What testing, legal review, and congressional oversight would apply? And how would advisers with defense-industry interests be prevented from converting national strategy into a customer acquisition plan?

Militarism protects itself through misdirection

The larger pattern is institutional: leaders who control military policy portray scrutiny as sabotage, invite vendors to help define future needs, and then use the resulting sense of urgency to weaken ordinary restraints. The public is told to fear disclosure while procurement decisions move faster and become less accountable.

Hegseth’s own rationale exposes the trick. If cheap systems can strain expensive arsenals, then stockpile reporting concerns a real strategic weakness—not a betrayal invented by journalists. The responsible response would be to defend procurement choices, explain operational tradeoffs, and submit new weapons authorities to rigorous oversight.

Instead, the critic becomes the enemy and the contractor becomes the strategist. That is how power avoids an accounting: not by answering the charge, but by criminalizing the messenger and outsourcing the future to people positioned to profit from it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Hegseth’s killing fantasy is an admission his treason attacks were dead wrong

item.title: Outrage as MAGA lawmaker openly admits plot to block seating of Dem candidate: 'Shameful’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Rep. Tim Burchett, a Tennessee Republican, confirmed Sunday that he was “100%” planning to try to block Democratic nominee Darializa Avila Chevalier from taking her House seat in January if she wins New York’s 13th Congressional District in November.

According to the New York Post reporting cited by RawStory, Burchett pointed to a since-deleted online joke in which Avila Chevalier referred to using an American flag as a napkin. He characterized that post as “disavowing” the Constitution. The article does not establish what procedure Burchett intends to use, whether other lawmakers support him, or whether his effort could succeed.

The election had not occurred when the story was published. The Post said Republican nominee Jomo M. Williams faced slim odds because of the district’s voting history. First Amendment lawyer Ari Cohn and Tennessee journalist Jamie Satterfield condemned Burchett’s announcement.

The power is in the threat

The operative fact is not that a candidate made a tasteless joke. It is that a sitting member of Congress announced an intention to use institutional power against an opponent who might be chosen by voters.

Burchett is not merely criticizing Avila Chevalier or campaigning for Williams. He is proposing action after the election, contingent on the Democrat winning. That shifts the contest from persuading voters to challenging whether their choice will be honored.

One representative’s declaration is not the same as a completed institutional act. RawStory provides no evidence that Burchett can carry out the plan alone. But an incumbent openly proposing it still matters: congressional office supplies the platform, access and potential leverage that turn partisan resentment into more than online abuse.

The flag is the decoy

Burchett’s stated rationale redirects attention from his proposed conduct to Avila Chevalier’s deleted post. The flag joke may be juvenile or offensive. The reporting does not establish that it constitutes constitutional “disavowal,” much less that it provides a valid basis to reject an election winner.

That framing converts symbolic offense into a pretext for institutional punishment. It asks readers to litigate a napkin joke while the officeholder’s announced response—trying to prevent a duly elected opponent from being seated—escapes equivalent scrutiny.

Cohn’s criticism identifies the contradiction: Burchett invokes constitutional fidelity while proposing to obstruct the consequence of an election. The article is strongest when it presents that conflict plainly. Its detour into Burchett’s earlier Air Force One “ride” controversy adds outrage but little explanatory value.

Agency belongs to the incumbent

Nothing in the reporting suggests confusion about who initiated this. Burchett confirmed the plan himself. Avila Chevalier made the post attributed to her; Burchett chose to treat it as grounds for targeting her possible seating.

That distinction matters because political coverage often lets powerful actors disappear inside words such as “controversy” or “outrage.” The outrage did not create the event. Burchett’s announcement did. Critics reacted to a sitting lawmaker declaring that an electoral victory might not be enough for his opponent to take office.

Nor should Williams or the district’s voters be made responsible for Burchett’s choice. The Republican candidate’s reported weakness explains the stakes, not the decision. The institutional actor is the incumbent congressman proposing intervention after voters act.

Losing becomes disqualification

The larger pattern is the conversion of political defeat into a claim that the winner is unfit to govern. A weak electoral position is answered not with a better candidate or argument, but with a search for some supposed offense that can justify overriding the result.

Here, the alleged disqualification is not misconduct in office or a reported legal barrier. It is an online joke recast as betrayal of the Constitution. That is scapegoating dressed as principle: magnify an opponent’s symbolic transgression, then use it to rationalize a far more consequential exercise of power.

The danger lies in making this logic routine. Elections become provisional whenever officeholders reserve the right to decide that the other side’s winner is too offensive to seat. The ballot still occurs, but incumbents claim a veto over what it means.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Outrage as MAGA lawmaker openly admits plot to block seating of Dem candidate: ‘Shameful’

item.title: 'Weak sauce': Trump roasted for bragging about 'packed house' in high school gym
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump attacked Fox News for failing to highlight what he called a “packed house” at an Ohio rally, claiming that recent events in Ohio, Alabama, Texas, and Oklahoma were sold out. The Ohio event, however, took place in the roughly 5,000-seat gym at Butler High School in Vandalia, near Dayton.

Critics—including Democrats, former supporters, and some Republicans—mocked Trump’s boast and contrasted the small venue with the larger arenas associated with his earlier campaigns. A pro-Trump correspondent defended her account by saying she meant the crowd’s emotional intensity, not its size. RawStory also cites a New York Times reporter’s video showing the upper level emptying about 45 minutes into Trump’s speech; the article does not provide attendance figures sufficient to establish how full the gym remained.

The president chose the stage

Trump was not a powerless candidate denied access to an audience. He was the sitting president, commanding the visibility of the office and a political movement capable of organizing events across several states. His campaign chose the high school gym. Trump then chose to describe the result as evidence of extraordinary demand.

That distinction matters. The mockery focused on whether the crowd was impressive, but the political act was the attempt to define an ordinary campaign event as a triumph—and to treat insufficient celebration from a friendly television network as betrayal.

Fox was assigned a role

Trump’s complaint presumed that Fox News owed him promotional coverage. He did not merely dispute a report; according to RawStory, he rebuked the network for failing to broadcast his preferred image of enthusiasm.

Fox holds substantial media power, but Trump holds institutional power. Casting himself as the victim of Fox’s programming decision reverses that hierarchy. It converts a president’s demand for favorable amplification into a grievance against an allegedly neglectful press.

The crowd argument is a trap

“High school gymnasium” became the punch line because it punctured Trump’s attempt at grandeur. But venue size alone does not prove that his support has collapsed, just as an enthusiastic room does not prove broad popularity. RawStory supplies anecdotes from disaffected supporters and video of people leaving; it does not supply comparative attendance data establishing the sweeping conclusion that Trump is politically “cooked.”

The stronger criticism is narrower and better supported: Trump made claims about overwhelming demand while appearing at a modest venue, and the reporting describes visible departures during his speech. His critics did not need to inflate that contradiction into an electoral forecast.

Spectacle substitutes for evidence

The recurring pattern is the manufacture of political strength through superlatives: sold out, thousands excluded, enthusiasm beyond measure. These claims are difficult to separate from the leader’s need to make every gathering a referendum on his dominance.

The response can become equally shallow when opponents answer propaganda with jokes and vibes. Ridicule may expose the gap between the boast and the room, but it cannot measure public support. When political coverage reduces power to crowd shots, it lets the most theatrical actor choose the test.

Power writes its own scoreboard

The consequential story is not that a president spoke in a school gym. It is that a president demanded that an allied media institution validate his account of the event, then framed its failure to do so as mistreatment.

That is how personality-driven politics protects itself from inconvenient evidence: favorable images become proof, unfavorable images become disloyalty, and institutional power disappears behind performative grievance. The gym was small. The machinery for manufacturing the boast was not.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Weak sauce’: Trump roasted for bragging about ‘packed house’ in high school gym

item.title: 'What the hell?' Trump stuns after being spotted 'slumped over' and 'struggling to walk’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that attorney and political commentator Ben Meiselas reacted to photographs of President Donald Trump returning to Washington, D.C., after a Saturday rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio. Meiselas described Trump as “slumped over” and “struggling to walk,” citing images taken shortly after 11 p.m. that showed Trump with his mouth open and, in another, his head resting on his chest while standing.

At the rally, Trump said he takes a daily high-dose aspirin against his doctor’s advice, praised his own intelligence, and lamented losing his pre-political “simple life.” RawStory also cites medical professionals who previously interpreted other observed symptoms as possible signs of a stroke or focal motor seizures. The article supplies no diagnosis, direct medical examination, or evidence establishing what caused Trump’s appearance in the photographs.

The presidency is the relevant fact

Trump’s condition matters because the president exercises enormous institutional power. The legitimate question is not whether an 80-year-old man looked unflattering after 11 p.m. It is whether he can reliably perform the duties of an office empowered to direct the executive branch and make decisions with immediate national and international consequences.

That question cannot be answered from two photographs. Nor can it be dismissed as celebrity gossip merely because the evidence presented here is weak. Presidential health is public business, but serious scrutiny requires records, examinations, observable patterns, and accountable disclosure—not amateur diagnosis by image caption.

Speculation is not accountability

Meiselas made the decisive interpretive move: the photographs became evidence that Trump was “struggling to walk.” RawStory then surrounded that claim with earlier medical speculation about strokes and seizures. The structure encourages readers to connect those claims without establishing that the photographed moment resulted from either condition.

That is misdirection through insinuation. It substitutes a dramatic visual and third-party interpretation for the harder reporting: what Trump’s physicians have assessed, what information the White House has released, and whether officials responsible for continuity of government have identified any impairment.

Trump’s own disclosure matters more

The clearest health-related fact in the report came from Trump himself: he said he takes a daily high dose of aspirin against his doctor’s advice. That statement does not prove incapacity or explain the photographs. It does show a president publicly describing his rejection of medical guidance.

The political significance lies in the conduct that is actually documented. Trump chose to disclose the practice, and the institutions around him apparently permitted the matter to remain rally material rather than the subject of a clear, authoritative account. Speculative diagnosis can obscure that concrete failure of transparency.

Spectacle protects power

Calling the event a “clown show” may communicate contempt, but contempt is not analysis. Trump remained the president before, during, and after an awkward photograph. Turning the episode into a freak-show montage risks making his age and appearance the story while the machinery of presidential power escapes examination.

The weaker actor here is not Trump. He commands the executive branch and a mass political movement. The people without access to reliable medical information are the public. Coverage that offers ridicule instead of verification does not correct that imbalance; it monetizes it.

A system built for concealment and guessing

The larger pattern is an accountability system that depends heavily on voluntary presidential disclosure, partisan interpretation, and episodic images. When institutions do not produce trustworthy information, political media fills the vacuum with certainty it has not earned.

That arrangement serves powerful officeholders. Allies can dismiss every question as partisan abuse, critics can convert ambiguity into diagnosis, and the underlying issue—whether the public receives adequate evidence about a president’s capacity—remains unresolved. The photographs may show fatigue, illness, or merely an unguarded instant. RawStory does not establish which. The systemic error is treating speculation as a substitute for the transparency that presidential power requires.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘What the hell?’ Trump stuns after being spotted ‘slumped over’ and ‘struggling to walk’

item.title: 'He's a maniac': Psychiatrist catalogs the red flags in Trump's behavior
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychiatrist Dr. Henry Abraham described President Donald Trump as displaying numerous clinical “red flags,” including disrupted sleep, daytime drowsiness, tangential speech, disinhibition, rage, grandiosity, apparent disorientation and declining verbal fluency. Abraham called Trump a “maniac” in reference to what he characterized as manic nighttime behavior, but he did not present that term as a formal diagnosis.

Abraham acknowledged that he had not examined Trump and could not determine the cause of the reported behavior. His assessment relied on public appearances, social-media activity, conversations with unnamed observers and comparisons with Trump’s earlier speech. He said possible explanations range from ordinary aging to serious illness, while emphasizing that the relevant medical records and cognitive-test results have not been released.

The interview followed an open letter reportedly sent to Congress in May by 36 health professionals warning of cognitive decline. AlterNet does not report that Congress ordered an evaluation, obtained additional medical evidence or otherwise acted on that warning.

The diagnosis is not the evidence

The interview’s strongest factual point is also its clearest limitation: conspicuous behavior can justify scrutiny without establishing a psychiatric diagnosis. Abraham repeatedly recognizes that boundary, then strains it by moving from observed conduct to loaded clinical interpretations and speculative causes.

Calling late-night posting “manic behavior” does not establish mania. Public rambling does not by itself establish dementia. Trump’s continued insistence that he won the 2020 election could reflect a fixed false belief, a strategic political lie or some combination the interview cannot resolve. Abraham names those alternatives, but AlterNet packages uncertainty beneath the sensational certainty of “He’s a maniac.”

That framing is weak. It converts a legitimate question about presidential capacity and transparency into a remote diagnostic spectacle. The headline supplies a verdict the evidence does not.

Power does not require a diagnosis

Trump holds the institutional power in this story. Whatever explains his conduct, he occupies the presidency and exercises the authority attached to it. The consequential question is not whether a psychiatrist can assign him a disorder through television footage. It is whether presidential decisions are coherent, lawful and constrained by functioning institutions.

Trump is also responsible for conduct that requires no medical interpretation: insulting people, spreading false claims or publishing grandiose imagery remains conduct he chose or authorized unless evidence shows otherwise. Psychiatric speculation can blur that agency. It risks turning political behavior into symptoms and thereby making deliberate acts appear involuntary.

A diagnosis is not needed to judge an abuse of office, a false statement or a reckless decision. Public actions should be assessed through evidence and consequences, not retrofitted into a medical narrative.

The missing institutional actors

The interview points toward a transparency problem but barely examines the people capable of addressing it. Trump’s medical team controls what it discloses. Senior officials and advisers observe his performance directly. Congress possesses oversight and investigative powers. Those actors have access, authority or both; outside clinicians have neither.

If officials have credible evidence that the president cannot discharge his duties, they bear responsibility for using the constitutional and oversight mechanisms available to them. If they lack that evidence, they should not substitute anonymous impressions and armchair medicine for it. Either way, institutional actors—not a psychiatrist speaking from afar—decide whether concern becomes examination, disclosure or action.

AlterNet instead centers professional alarm while leaving institutional passivity largely uninterrogated. That misdirects attention from officials who can obtain evidence to observers who can only interpret appearances.

Speculation becomes its own distraction

Abraham’s claims about Trump’s inner life are least persuasive when they are most confident. His explanation that Trump dismantles Barack Obama’s legacy because of racism, humiliation and low self-esteem is psychological inference, not an established finding in the reporting. The source supplies no examination, direct admission or documentary evidence proving that chain of motive.

The same problem appears when the interview jumps from observed late-night activity to possibilities involving stimulants, sleep disorders or dementia. Listing hypotheses may illustrate uncertainty, but it can also create insinuation by accumulation. Readers are left with a catalog of alarming possibilities unsupported by the clinical evidence needed to distinguish among them.

This is not rigor sharpened into urgency. It is uncertainty dressed in diagnostic vocabulary.

The system prefers spectacle to accountability

The larger pattern is an accountability system that repeatedly personalizes structural failure. A president’s strange or disturbing behavior becomes a story about his hidden pathology; Congress’s inaction, official secrecy and the incentives of loyal advisers recede from view.

That arrangement serves nearly everyone with power. Officials avoid making documented judgments. Journalists receive provocative copy. Political allies can dismiss the coverage as partisan diagnosis. Opponents can circulate alarming labels without proving the institutional case.

The public is entitled to reliable information about a president’s capacity. It is also entitled to analysis that distinguishes illness from misconduct, symptoms from strategy and speculation from evidence. When coverage collapses those categories, it does not expose the machinery of power. It gives that machinery somewhere else to hide.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘He’s a maniac’: Psychiatrist catalogs the red flags in Trump’s behavior

item.title: 'Kitchen-table economics' just upended a safe Senate seat
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that economic pain from Republican policy has made Kansas’s traditionally safe Senate seat competitive. Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton received endorsements from two former Republican governors, including Mike Hayden, while a leading Republican Senate super PAC reportedly redirected money from North Carolina to defend incumbent Senator Roger Marshall.

The outlet attributes the shift to farm losses and rising costs linked to Trump administration decisions. It reports that retaliatory trade measures reduced demand for Kansas crops, tariffs raised machinery costs, relaxed beef-import restrictions hurt ranchers, and the war in Iran disrupted fertilizer and diesel supplies. AlterNet says roughly 700 Kansas farms closed over the past year, though it provides no sourcing for that estimate in the supplied text.

An AP-NORC poll cited by AlterNet put approval of Trump’s handling of the economy at 26 percent and his handling of living costs at 17 percent. The article presents those numbers, the Republican endorsements, and the super PAC’s spending decision as evidence that economic discontent has destabilized the race—not proof that Hamilton will win.

Power has an address

Farmers did not impose the tariffs, alter import restrictions, or wage the war described in the reporting. The Trump administration made those decisions. Republican senators possessed the institutional power to oppose them, constrain them, or withdraw political support. According to Hayden, Marshall instead repeatedly backed the tariffs and the war despite their effects in Kansas.

That distinction matters. “Kitchen-table economics” can sound like weather: prices rise, income falls, voters become restless. But the account describes government choices moving through supply chains and landing on particular people. Washington exercised power; Kansas farmers absorbed the consequences.

Marshall owns his choice

Marshall is not merely sharing a party label with an unpopular president. The reported indictment is more specific: he supported policies that Hayden says were harming the state Marshall represents.

That is agency, not association. Calling Trump an electoral “albatross” risks making Republican candidates sound like passive victims of someone else’s toxicity. Marshall’s vulnerability, as presented here, follows from his own alignment with decisions that raised costs and weakened markets for his constituents.

The super PAC’s intervention reinforces the point. National Republican operatives are moving resources because they perceive danger in Kansas. Money may protect an incumbent from accountability, but it cannot convert his record into an accident.

The euphemism hides the machinery

“Kitchen-table economics” describes where people feel the damage, not where it originates. It compresses tariffs, war, import policy, congressional obedience, lost markets, and farm closures into a pleasant domestic metaphor.

That framing can also obscure who pays first. A strong stock market may reward people who own substantial financial assets while doing nothing for a farmer facing more expensive equipment, fertilizer, and diesel alongside weaker crop demand. The contradiction is not voter confusion. It is a distribution of gains and losses produced by policy.

AlterNet is strongest when it connects those policies to identifiable actors. It is weaker when it leaps from polling and campaign spending to sweeping claims about what Americans collectively know or why they will vote. Economic approval data show deep dissatisfaction; they do not establish a single cause or forecast an election result.

Pain is not the same as power

The article suggests voters may punish Republicans once material harm becomes personal. Perhaps. But electoral pain does not automatically undo the policies that created it, compensate closed farms, or give producers control over trade and war decisions.

Nor should cross-party endorsements be romanticized. Former Republican governors can confer legitimacy on Hamilton, but they do not hold the seat. Marshall does. The administration directs executive policy. National groups command campaign money. Farmers possess the consequences and, eventually, a ballot.

That imbalance is the political core of the story: those with the least control over federal policy are forced to bear its most immediate costs, while those who enabled it mobilize money to preserve their offices.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is familiar. Leaders impose policies from above, loyal legislators protect them, and public discussion later treats the resulting hardship as an impersonal problem of “the economy.” Responsibility dissolves precisely when consequences become undeniable.

Kansas disrupts that evasion because the chain is unusually concrete: decisions in Washington, retaliation and disruption abroad, higher costs and lost sales at home, then political danger for an incumbent who supported the decisions. The seat has not been won, and the supplied reporting does not establish that it will be. But it does expose the structure clearly: institutional power made the choices, political obedience enabled them, and ordinary people received the bill.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Kitchen-table economics’ just upended a safe Senate seat

item.title: An American school district actually burned this famous book in a furnace
item.description:
What happened

In November 1976, the school board in Drake, North Dakota, unanimously ordered Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five removed from school premises after a parent objected to its profanity. AlterNet reports that officials demanded students surrender their copies, searched the lockers of those who refused, and burned 32 copies in the school furnace.

English teacher Bruce Severy had assigned the anti-war novel to his sophomore literature class. Vonnegut later wrote to the board, defending the book as an appeal for kindness and responsibility and noting that he had fought in World War II against governments that burned books. The board did not reply.

The controversy anticipated later fights over school censorship. In January 2026, according to AlterNet, the ACLU sued on behalf of Vonnegut’s estate after Utah’s “sensitive materials” law provided districts with a mechanism to ban the same novel.

The board held the power

The decisive actors were not offended parents, frightened students, or an abstract “community.” A parent complained; the Drake school board exercised state authority. It voted unanimously, directed school employees to seize the books, and controlled the furnace where they were destroyed.

That distinction matters. Parents may criticize curricula, but only public officials can convert an objection into coercive policy. Describing such episodes chiefly as cultural “backlash” blurs the chain of command. The board made the decision. District officials enforced it. Students bore the intrusion.

Obscenity was the pretext

The stated complaint concerned profanity. The wider record described by AlterNet shows why that explanation is inadequate: Slaughterhouse-Five was also attacked for irreverence toward Christianity and for depicting the American bombing of Dresden without patriotic varnish.

Officials can invoke vulgarity as a content-neutral concern while targeting the ideas carried alongside it. The Supreme Court’s fractured 1982 decision in Board of Education v. Pico recognized the relevant boundary: districts may remove material deemed pervasively vulgar or educationally unsuitable, but not simply because officials oppose its political or partisan ideas.

Drake’s conduct was especially revealing. Searching lockers and feeding books into a furnace was not careful curriculum review. It was a public demonstration that institutional authority could suppress disfavored material and compel student obedience.

Censorship wears parental clothing

“Parental rights” rhetoric shifts attention from government power to the grievance that activates it. The weaker actor appears to be the aggrieved parent; the supposedly defensive institution appears merely responsive. But once officials use that complaint to restrict what every student may read, one household’s preference becomes a public prohibition.

The same mechanism now reaches books about race, gender identity, and LGBTQ+ lives. AlterNet cites PEN America’s count of 2,532 public-school bans in 2021–22, 3,362 in 2022–23, and 10,046 in 2023–24. Those figures describe organized institutional exclusion, not a spontaneous outbreak of individual discomfort.

The targets reveal the project

The Island Trees dispute that produced Pico involved 11 challenged books, seven written by authors from minority ethnic or religious groups. Current campaigns likewise disproportionately reach works by Black and LGBTQ+ authors, including Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye, George M. Johnson’s All Boys Aren’t Blue, and Maia Kobabe’s Gender Queer.

That pattern does not prove an identical motive in every challenge. It does show whose experiences repeatedly become negotiable when political groups pressure school systems. Profanity, sex, and “appropriateness” supply flexible rationales; marginalized perspectives and challenges to national mythology repeatedly disappear from shelves.

The furnace is now a procedure

Drake’s furnace makes the violence of censorship impossible to disguise. Modern systems usually substitute statutes, review panels, removal lists, and administrative compliance. The machinery looks cleaner, but the allocation of power is the same: organized activists generate complaints, lawmakers or school boards authorize suppression, and public employees restrict access.

The larger pattern is not confusion about how to protect children. It is the conversion of ideological demands into state-enforced limits on what children may encounter. Book burning was the crude version. Bureaucratic censorship is the scalable one.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: An American school district actually burned this famous book in a furnace

item.title: Trump reboots his most brazen scandal —and nobody's stopping him this time
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump plans to host the G20 summit at Trump National Doral Miami on December 14–15, 2026, directing world leaders and their entourages to his privately owned resort. Trump abandoned a similar plan for the 2020 G7 summit after Republican opposition, but the new arrangement has reportedly produced little protest.

Citing New York Times reporting, AlterNet describes the Doral decision as one part of a much larger pattern of self-enrichment during Trump’s second term. The cited examples include an estimated $2.2 billion increase in his wealth, acceptance of a luxury jet from Qatar, favorable treatment over potential back taxes, a Trump TV trademark alongside taxpayer-backed promotion, and public money used for Republican campaign advertising. The article does not independently establish each claim.

Gallup polling cited in the story found that 89 percent of American adults considered government corruption widespread, up 10 percentage points from the previous year. That measures public perception, not proof that any particular allegation caused the increase.

The beneficiary holds the power

This is not a conflict between evenly matched interests. Trump is simultaneously president, the official presiding over the summit decision, and the owner of the business positioned to benefit from it. Foreign delegations do not choose the venue on equal terms with the White House. The administration controls the event; Trump’s property receives the prestige, traffic and commercial exposure.

That concentration of public authority and private benefit is the central political fact. “Conflict of interest” almost sounds too mild because it suggests two competing obligations. Here, the person empowered to protect the public interest reportedly selected his own asset as the destination for a major government function.

Normalization is an institutional decision

The contrast with 2019 matters. Then, Republican resistance helped force Trump to abandon the plan. In 2026, according to the reporting, essentially the same maneuver is proceeding with little protest.

That change did not happen because the ethical issue became more complicated. It happened because officials, party leaders and other institutional actors stopped imposing the political cost that once mattered. Silence is not an atmospheric condition. It is the cumulative result of people with authority deciding that confrontation is less useful to them than accommodation.

Paul Rosenzweig’s description of the Doral arrangement as relatively small beside Trump’s other reported conduct captures the mechanism: repeated escalation makes yesterday’s scandal look trivial. But scale does not excuse the clearer offense. It reveals how saturation protects it.

The corruption fog

The article’s strongest point is that abundance can become camouflage. When alleged abuses arrive faster than institutions investigate, explain or punish them, each new case competes with the last one for a shrinking supply of attention.

That dynamic can also misdirect responsibility. Saying that “nobody” is stopping Trump blurs the distinction between people who lack enforcement power and those who possess it but decline to use it. Ordinary Americans can disapprove; Congress, executive-branch officials and governing-party leaders can impose consequences. Treating collective exhaustion as the cause lets powerful enablers disappear into the crowd.

The golf-cheating material is a distraction from that structure. Anecdotes about Trump’s conduct on the course may reinforce a character portrait, but they do not explain how presidential authority can be used to steer an international summit toward presidential property. The scandal is governmental, not sporting.

Disapproval without restraint

The Gallup result shows extraordinary public distrust: 89 percent described government corruption as widespread. Yet perception alone does not restrain an administration. Anger becomes politically harmless when institutions absorb it without changing their conduct.

That is the deeper asymmetry. The public bears the cynicism produced by alleged self-dealing, while officials retain the power to normalize it. The resulting distrust can even benefit those who treat government as private spoils: if corruption is assumed to be universal and unstoppable, specific responsibility dissolves into generalized disgust.

Impunity resets the baseline

The larger pattern is not merely that standards have weakened. Standards are being rewritten through repetition and non-enforcement. A practice that once triggered retreat can become routine when the governing coalition decides there will be no penalty.

Doral is therefore useful precisely because it is easy to understand. Public power reportedly selected the president’s private property, and the resistance that stopped the same arrangement before has largely vanished. The system did not become confused about who benefits. The people positioned to intervene learned to tolerate the benefit—and tolerance, exercised by those with power, is how impunity becomes policy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump reboots his most brazen scandal —and nobody’s stopping him this time

item.title: GOP insider warns Trump economy claims are colliding with voters’ realities
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican strategists are warning President Donald Trump and GOP candidates that claims of a strong economy are colliding with voters’ experience of high grocery, fuel, utility, and housing costs. Consultant Jason Cabel Roe said candidates risk appearing out of touch if they answer affordability concerns with favorable economic statistics.

The warning is supported by declining sentiment measures cited in the report. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index fell 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, while the University of Michigan’s index dropped from 51.7 in August to 48.1 in September—15 percent below its January level.

Republicans continue to promote tax provisions affecting tips, overtime, Social Security, and families. But with November’s midterm elections approaching, AlterNet says GOP candidates are shifting toward the costs voters encounter directly, while Senate Republicans review proposals addressing rising electricity prices.

Power writes the message

The decisive actors are not frustrated consumers or nervous campaign consultants. Trump, congressional Republicans, and the party’s Senate majority hold the institutional power described here. They shape federal tax policy, decide which affordability bills receive attention, and determine whether economic pain produces legislation or merely revised campaign language.

The consultants’ anxiety is therefore revealing but secondary. They are not warning that Republicans lack authority. They are warning that Republicans may pay an electoral price for how they describe conditions produced under their governing watch.

A credibility problem, not a vocabulary problem

The emerging Republican solution is to replace national indicators with language about household expenses. That may be tactically smarter, but it does not itself lower a grocery bill, a utility payment, or diesel prices that the report says exceeded $6 a gallon in some areas during harvest season.

Representative Rob Wittman is right that people do not experience the economy through GDP reports. But his observation also exposes the inadequacy of treating this as a communications failure. If governing officials recognize that costs dominate voters’ lives, their responsibility is to explain what they have done about those costs—and what measurable results followed—not merely to sound more sympathetic while campaigning.

The convenient Biden comparison

Republican strategists reportedly fear repeating Joe Biden’s mistake of emphasizing strong aggregate data while many households felt little improvement. That comparison contains a useful warning, but it also offers Republicans an escape hatch: it recasts the collision between official claims and lived conditions as a familiar messaging blunder inherited from the previous administration.

The underlying political question is sharper. Republicans want credit for job growth, spending, steady unemployment, and favored tax provisions while distancing themselves from the prices voters dislike. A governing party cannot plausibly claim ownership of every favorable indicator and treat every unfavorable one as atmospheric interference.

Voters are not the misdirection

The article generally avoids blaming voters for failing to appreciate economic statistics. Its weaker framing lies in allowing campaign strategy to occupy the center of a story about material pressure. Consumer confidence fell across party, age, and income groups, according to Reuters reporting cited by AlterNet. That is not simply a branding obstacle for Republican candidates.

Nor do lower sentiment figures prove that any single policy caused households’ dissatisfaction. They do establish that upbeat claims are meeting broad skepticism. The relevant consequence is not that voters need better instruction; it is that elected officials must answer for the gap between the benefits they advertise and the costs people continue to bear.

Governing reduced to calibration

This is the larger pattern: parties in power often treat public hardship first as a problem of narrative calibration. Consultants test phrases, candidates change emphasis, and legislative activity intensifies as Election Day approaches. Material conditions become urgent when they threaten incumbents.

Republicans have the power identified in this story, and therefore the burden. If their answer to affordability is substantive, the evidence will be lower costs or greater household security. If their answer is merely to stop mentioning GDP and start mentioning grocery bills, that is not economic governance. It is a campaign learning to describe the damage more fluently.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP insider warns Trump economy claims are colliding with voters’ realities
