item.title: Inside the FBI's biggest nightmare yet
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the FBI is confronting two separate crises: internal turmoil over the removal of two veteran counterterrorism supervisors and a breach exposing tens of thousands of personnel files. Deputy Director Andrew Bailey resigned after the personnel dispute, but the reporting does not establish why he left or whether he opposed the removals.

Michael Burgwald and Courtland Rae were reassigned after challenging an order to investigate harassing calls to conservative podcaster Katie Miller, whose husband, Stephen Miller, is a White House deputy. The agents reportedly concluded that the calls neither met the legal threshold for an FBI investigation nor involved terrorism. CNN, as cited by AlterNet, reported that the White House and senior FBI officials accused the pair of obstructing investigations into serious threats and decided to remove them. Patel, the Millers and the White House denied responsibility or knowledge, while Patel reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with the Washington Field Office’s handling of the matter.

Separately, AlterNet reports that a hacking group called ShinyHunters obtained personally identifiable information about current and former FBI personnel. The group said it sought withdrawal of an FBI advisory targeting it and claimed it never intended to publish the data. The FBI was reportedly still determining how the breach occurred and what information had been taken; the article provides no evidence that the hackers released the broader cache or carried out their stated deadline.

Power chose the priority

The decisive hierarchy is not obscure. Kash Patel leads the FBI. Senior bureau officials control assignments and resources. The White House sits above an executive-branch agency whose leadership serves under the president. Burgwald and Rae could assess whether a complaint met investigative standards, but they could not protect their own positions after reaching an unwelcome conclusion.

That distinction matters because the dispute was not simply an office disagreement. According to the reporting, experienced counterterrorism officials applied a legal threshold and found the Miller complaints insufficient. They were then removed from counterterrorism leadership while politically connected complainants received attention from the bureau’s upper ranks.

The exact official who signed the reassignment order remains disputed. Institutional responsibility does not disappear with a missing signature. Senior leadership reportedly wanted the agents out, the agents lost their posts, and Patel headed the organization in which it happened. A bureaucracy cannot invoke its own chain of command when demanding obedience and then pretend decisions emerge spontaneously when accountability arrives.

A private grievance became a federal priority

Harassment can be serious, and the Millers were entitled to report conduct they regarded as threatening. They were not entitled to have political proximity replace the FBI’s legal standards. The relevant question was whether the reported conduct justified federal investigation and had a terrorism nexus. The supervisors reportedly said it did not.

Their reassignment sends a blunt signal down the hierarchy: professional judgment is tolerated only when it produces the result favored by powerful people. That is how selective enforcement takes root—not necessarily through a written order to persecute enemies, but through punishment that teaches officials which conclusions are safe.

The article also reports earlier resistance from career agents to using bureau resources against critical neighborhood flyers targeting Stephen Miller. If accurate, that episode reinforces the same concern: criticism, protest activity and criminal threats were being pressed into one politically useful category. Erasing those distinctions gives connected officials privileged access to coercive state power.

The accountability gap

AlterNet is strongest when it identifies the collision between political demands and investigative standards. It is weaker when it bundles Bailey’s resignation, the personnel dispute, the cyberattack, staffing reductions and Iranian sanctions evasion into one implied chain of causation without establishing each link.

Bailey’s timing may invite suspicion, but timing is not proof. The article says he clashed with Patel and resigned after the reassignments; it also concedes that his position on those removals is unknown. Likewise, the breach is plainly a grave institutional failure if the reported scope is accurate, but the story does not establish that personnel cuts caused it.

That looseness misdirects attention from the case the evidence can support. The problem does not need speculative connective tissue. FBI leaders reportedly devoted high-level attention to complaints from a White House official’s family, veteran supervisors were displaced after resisting, and responsibility for the decision became something every powerful participant denied possessing. That is already an indictment of governance.

Politicization has an opportunity cost

Every agent redirected toward a politically favored complaint is an agent unavailable for another assignment. AlterNet places that dispute beside reduced counterterrorism capacity, reassignment of personnel to immigration enforcement and a breach potentially valuable to foreign intelligence services. The article does not quantify the operational tradeoffs, but the governing choice is visible: leadership determines which risks receive personnel, urgency and protection.

The breach exposes the consequence of distorted priorities in unusually concrete terms. Current and former agents—and potentially their families—may face danger because sensitive personnel information escaped the bureau’s control. ShinyHunters’ assurance that it did not intend to publish the material is not a security guarantee. Once an outside group possesses the records, the FBI no longer controls their use.

Meanwhile, a Senate Democratic report cited by AlterNet found that 84 percent of 846 sanctioned crypto wallets linked to Iran dealt exclusively or nearly exclusively in U.S.-backed stablecoins. That finding does not prove a particular FBI failure, but it illustrates the scale of work competing for federal attention while leadership becomes absorbed in politically charged personal complaints.

The system protects proximity

The larger pattern is not bureaucratic confusion. It is asymmetry. Politically connected people can push their grievances upward until senior officials respond. Career personnel who insist on evidentiary and jurisdictional limits bear the professional risk. When the result becomes embarrassing, authority fragments into denials.

That structure rewards pliability and punishes restraint. It also leaves the public with the worst combination: an FBI potentially more responsive to presidential allies and less capable of protecting its own personnel. The systemic error is not that nobody knows who has power. It is that those who have it can exercise it through an institution, then hide behind the institution when consequences follow.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Inside the FBI’s biggest nightmare yet

item.title: Psychologist exposes Trump’s 'concerning' new stroke-like symptoms
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that clinical and forensic psychologist John Paul Garrison interpreted Donald Trump’s hand movements during a recent meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly as possible involuntary muscle contractions resembling effects sometimes seen after a stroke. The footage does not establish that Trump suffered a stroke, and the article cites no examination, diagnosis, medical records, or statement from a treating physician.

Garrison also pointed to footage from a later Oval Office event, where he said Trump appeared to struggle with his fingers, kept one hand beneath the Resolute Desk, and had difficulty sustaining attention while others spoke. He suggested that a stroke, a neurodegenerative condition, or another neurological issue could explain the behavior, but did not establish any of those possibilities.

The headline outruns the evidence

No one “exposed” stroke symptoms in the clinical sense. A psychologist watched public footage and offered an interpretation of gestures and attention. AlterNet converted that interpretation into a headline carrying far more certainty than its own reporting supports.

The distinction matters. Observable movements are evidence that movements occurred. They are not evidence of their medical cause. Garrison’s qualifications may inform behavioral analysis, but the article provides no basis for treating a remote reading of video as a neurological assessment.

Power sits with the presidency

Trump holds presidential authority. His health can affect executive decision-making, national security, and the operation of the federal government. That makes reliable disclosure a legitimate public concern, not celebrity gossip.

But the institutional power to produce meaningful evidence rests with Trump, his physicians, and the White House. They can provide examinations, records, and accountable medical statements. Garrison cannot compel disclosure, and viewers cannot diagnose a president from hand movements. The information gap is real; speculation does not close it.

Sensation replaces accountability

The weak framing misdirects attention from what can be demanded of powerful institutions to what strangers can infer from clips. A hidden hand becomes suggestive evidence. A wandering gaze becomes neurological decline. Ambiguous footage is made to carry the weight that documented medical disclosure should bear.

This does not protect Trump from scrutiny. It protects the presidency from rigorous scrutiny by substituting viral interpretation for verifiable facts. The story’s most defensible conclusion is simply that Garrison found the behavior concerning and proposed several possible explanations. AlterNet sells that uncertainty as revelation.

A recurring political pathology

Presidential health reporting repeatedly swings between secrecy and spectacle. Officials control the records; commentators inspect public appearances; publishers reward the most alarming interpretation. The result is an accountability vacuum filled with amateur diagnosis and headlines engineered to harden suspicion into apparent fact.

That pattern serves institutional power. When evidence is withheld or absent, the political press should identify the missing evidence and who can provide it. Turning uncertainty into click-ready certainty lets the people with actual access remain peripheral while a speculative claim becomes the story.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Psychologist exposes Trump’s ‘concerning’ new stroke-like symptoms

item.title: Trump and the death of shame: How America's reality was annihilated today
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Senator Eric Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith, during a Senate hearing, of attending an Atlanta Hawks game to coordinate with Fulton County prosecutors pursuing Donald Trump. The evidence did not show that: Schmitt had confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes. Senator Amy Klobuchar exposed the error during the hearing, while Schmitt declined to concede it.

The failed accusation diverted attention from Smith’s opening statement that his investigation had found “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that Trump committed serious crimes against the United States. That was Smith’s conclusion, not a verdict: the account does not report that a court adjudicated the claim.

AlterNet says Schmitt subsequently appeared on The Charlie Kirk Show and agreed with the host’s assertion that he had caught Smith at an NBA game in Atlanta. Sean Hannity and pro-Trump social-media accounts also presented the exchange as a victory, despite the factual collapse described in the hearing.

The power was in the hearing room

Schmitt was not a confused bystander sharing an unfortunate post. He was a United States senator using an official proceeding, enlarged exhibits and the authority of his office to accuse a former federal prosecutor of political conspiracy.

Smith had institutional power when he served as special counsel. At this hearing, however, Schmitt controlled the accusation, the platform and the spectacle. His allegation was designed to discredit the prosecution itself: if Smith could be cast as part of a secret anti-Trump operation, the evidence against Trump could be dismissed without being confronted.

The mistake matters because the accusation was not peripheral to Schmitt’s performance. It was its foundation. Once Atlanta and Iowa were disentangled, the insinuation underneath the display had no support in the reporting presented here.

A blunder that still did its job

Calling this merely humiliation gives Schmitt too little agency. He selected the material, displayed it and used it to call Smith a “villain” and a “total dirtbag.” When challenged, he became angry rather than acknowledging the error. Later, according to AlterNet, he participated in media coverage that preserved the debunked premise.

The public failure therefore produced a usable political product. The hearing generated video, outrage and a story in which Trump’s prosecution—not Schmitt’s unsupported allegation—remained the supposed scandal. Whether diversion was the original purpose is not established. Its effect was unmistakable: Smith’s grave opening claim was displaced by a confrontation organized around false evidence.

The protection racket is informational

Schmitt’s real insulation did not come from personal shamelessness. It came from institutions willing to manufacture a separate outcome for their audience. AlterNet contrasts the hearing record with friendly coverage that treated Schmitt as though he had put Smith “on the spot.” A podcast exchange repeated the Atlanta claim instead of correcting it.

That apparatus changes the political cost of lying or reckless accusation. A senator does not need to persuade everyone. He needs aligned outlets to supply supporters with footage, affirmation and an alternate conclusion. Accuracy becomes optional because the audience is offered identity protection: admitting the factual error would mean conceding ground to the designated enemy.

Traditional coverage can worsen the distortion when it treats the episode chiefly as a colorful “self-own.” That framing makes the senator’s conduct seem like slapstick rather than an abuse of a congressional forum. The significant fact is not that Schmitt looked foolish. It is that he used public power to advance an allegation that collapsed under elementary scrutiny—and then faced a media system prepared to erase the collapse.

Shame cannot enforce reality

The interview with public-policy professor Don Moynihan centers shame as a neglected governing virtue. But shame works only when exposure produces consequences. Here, exposure and consequence were severed. Schmitt could be corrected in public and vindicated inside the partisan information system before the day was over.

Nor is this simply a problem of citizens becoming confused. Powerful actors create and maintain the confusion. The senator supplies the accusation. Political media recodes failure as triumph. Social-media allies distribute the revised account. The audience receives not an accidental misunderstanding but a coordinated incentive structure in which loyalty outranks correction.

That is the larger pattern: congressional oversight becomes opposition research performed on camera, factual defeat becomes fundraising material, and propaganda provides reputational immunity. The damage is not abstract incivility. It is the destruction of accountability as a practical restraint on officeholders.

The system rewards the accusation

A government cannot deliberate competently when evidence has authority only if it helps the faction presenting it. Hearings then cease to test claims and instead generate clips for information networks that have already chosen the verdict.

Schmitt’s error is revealing because it was so simple and the escape from it so immediate. The Hawkeyes were not the Hawks. The alleged Atlanta meeting was not established. Yet the machinery surrounding the senator could still offer supporters a story of prosecutorial corruption and senatorial triumph.

The systemic failure is therefore larger than one politician’s refusal to admit embarrassment. Institutional power launched a baseless insinuation; partisan media protected its author; and the spectacle displaced scrutiny of the conduct the hearing was ostensibly examining. When political success no longer requires surviving contact with the facts, shame is not dead by accident. It has been made strategically irrelevant.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump and the death of shame: How America’s reality was annihilated today

item.title: Eric Schmitt's bad Jack Smith intel likely came directly from White House: Top GOP senator
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Eric Schmitt presented a false claim during a Tuesday Senate Judiciary Committee hearing: that former special counsel Jack Smith had attended an Atlanta Hawks game in 2024 as cover for a secret meeting with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis. Smith had actually attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland.

An unnamed senior Republican senator told RawStory that the White House probably asked Schmitt to make the attack and likely supplied the material. The outlet did not independently establish that claim, and Schmitt’s office did not respond to its request for comment.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar said Schmitt and his allies continued treating Smith’s sworn denial with suspicion until the location error became clear. Sen. Joni Ernst pointed to an elementary failure to verify the allegation before airing it publicly.

The power behind the allegation

Schmitt held the institutional power in the room. He was not an outsider raising a question without access or authority; he was a United States senator using a Judiciary Committee hearing to accuse a former federal prosecutor of covert political coordination.

The unnamed Republican senator’s account, if accurate, places even greater power behind the episode: the White House may have commissioned the attack and furnished its supposed evidence. RawStory did not prove that connection, so it remains an allegation. But the possibility matters because it would turn Schmitt’s performance from individual recklessness into an attempted executive-branch deployment of congressional oversight against a former prosecutor.

The failure was political, not clerical

Ernst framed the debacle as bad staff work and inadequate verification. That is true at the narrowest level, but it understates the institutional misconduct. A senator did not merely confuse two basketball teams. He used that confusion to construct an accusation of prosecutorial collusion.

The decisive failure occurred before Schmitt spoke: neither he nor his staff apparently tested whether the underlying location was correct. The accusation was ready before the evidence was. Verification became optional because the claim served an established political narrative about Trump’s prosecutions.

Conspiracy as a governing method

Klobuchar identified the deeper mechanism. Smith’s denial under oath did not prompt reconsideration; it was absorbed into the suspicion surrounding him. In that structure, denial becomes evidence of concealment and correction becomes another reason to distrust the accused.

That is how conspiracy politics protects itself from facts. The allegation need not survive scrutiny to do its work. It only needs an official platform, a dramatic presentation and an audience already conditioned to treat prosecutors investigating Trump as illegitimate.

Accountability stops at embarrassment

RawStory emphasizes Schmitt’s humiliation and speculation that the episode could damage his reported prospects as a possible 2028 vice-presidential contender. That framing risks shrinking an abuse of congressional authority into a career mishap.

The relevant consequence is not whether Schmitt’s ambitions suffered. It is that a Senate hearing was used to circulate a serious allegation built on a readily checkable factual error. Political embarrassment is not institutional accountability, especially when the people who supplied, approved or amplified the material remain unidentified.

The system rewards the smear

This episode reveals a durable pattern: powerful officials can convert weak material into official spectacle, then retreat into staff-error explanations when it collapses. The target bears the accusation in public; the accuser bears, at most, a humiliating news cycle.

If the White House supplied the claim, responsibility extends beyond Schmitt. If it did not, Schmitt still chose to present it without adequate verification. Either way, the agency belongs to officials with substantial power—not to confused staffers, partisan audiences or the person forced to deny the allegation under oath.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Eric Schmitt’s bad Jack Smith intel likely came directly from White House: Top GOP senator

item.title: Stammering MAGA commentator slammed on his own show over surging diesel prices
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Fox Business host Larry Kudlow dismissed the inflationary risk posed by diesel prices during his Wednesday program, only for fellow Fox Business personality Dagen McDowell to challenge him. McDowell said diesel costs would flow through goods and services, raising consumer prices in the coming months; she described the issue not as hypothetical, but as a question of how large the increase would be.

Kudlow argued that diesel was primarily a refining problem and emphasized that the United States had plenty of oil. He then returned to speculation that Iran’s government might soon collapse and said he was hearing that many ships were passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The reporting offers no evidence establishing that Iran was about to “dissolve,” that the conflict would soon be resolved, or that shipping conditions justified Kudlow’s economic optimism.

The dodge was the argument

McDowell identified a concrete transmission mechanism: diesel powers the movement and production of goods, so higher fuel costs can spread throughout the economy. Kudlow answered with oil supply, refining constraints and an imagined geopolitical reversal. Those points did not rebut the immediate consumer-price concern.

Calling the problem a “what if” was therefore not analysis. It was a way to downgrade an existing cost into a speculative future possibility. McDowell’s correction stripped away that maneuver: in her account, the uncertainty concerned the magnitude of the effect, not whether diesel costs existed.

Power without accountability

Kudlow is not merely a television pundit. He previously directed the National Economic Council during Donald Trump’s first term, and Fox Business gives him a platform to translate political commitments into economic reassurance. That combination of former institutional authority and current media access matters more than his momentary loss of composure.

McDowell could contradict him on air, but Kudlow still controlled the frame: favorable inflation claims, imminent Iranian collapse and vague reports of shipping traffic. The person raising a direct material consequence had to fight for space inside a narrative built to make that consequence disappear.

Speculation as anesthesia

The Iran prediction did most of the political work. If Iran might collapse within weeks, then present costs could be treated as temporary noise on the road to vindication. But RawStory’s account supplies no basis for that timetable. Kudlow presented a dramatic geopolitical possibility as the answer to a measurable economic problem.

That is not proof that he intended to deceive viewers. It is evidence of a familiar form of partisan commentary: replace an inconvenient condition with an unverifiable forecast, then use the forecast to preserve the preferred economic story. When pressed, Kudlow offered “we’ll see.” Consumers confronting higher prices do not receive the same luxury.

The missing decision-makers

RawStory packages the exchange as a television humiliation, emphasizing that Kudlow was flustered and “shut down.” That framing is satisfying but politically shallow. A stammer is not the issue. The issue is an influential former official minimizing a cost that, according to his own colleague, could reach consumers across the economy.

The segment also leaves the relevant chain of responsibility underdeveloped. Refining capacity, war duration, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and consumer prices are shaped by governments, militaries and corporations with far more power than households buying transported goods. Turning the story into a clash of personalities risks obscuring those actors—and the decisions producing the conditions the hosts were debating.

The reassurance machine

This exchange reveals how political media manages economic pain. Material costs are acknowledged only after they become impossible to ignore; responsibility is scattered among technical constraints and foreign uncertainty; relief is projected onto a favorable future that has not arrived.

The larger pattern is not that one television host lost an argument. It is that elite reassurance remains available even when its premises fail in real time. The powerful speculate. The audience pays the price if the speculation is wrong.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Stammering MAGA commentator slammed on his own show over surging diesel prices

item.title: Republicans squirm over Trump's 'shockingly corrupt' TV ads: 'I hate it’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump narrated three taxpayer-funded television ads resembling campaign material. The latest, aired during major weekend programming, attacks the “deep state,” “globalists,” “communists,” and news media before promising to “liberate America.” Each ad identifies the U.S. government as the payer.

Several Republican senators objected to the financing while stopping short of rejecting the message. Majority Leader John Thune called it “great” but said taxpayers should not fund it; Thom Tillis compared it to Viktor Orbán addressing Hungary and said, “I hate it.” The White House maintains that the videos are legitimate public service announcements and says previous administrations produced similar material.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan attempted Tuesday to pass a resolution barring taxpayer-funded presidential promotional ads. Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis blocked it and defended the ads as protecting American values. Democratic senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy separately requested information about their financing, calling the spending illegal and corrupt. The report does not establish the ads’ cost or conclusively resolve their legality.

Objection without restraint

The institutional power here belongs to the administration spending public money and to the senators capable of restricting that spending. Uneasy quotations do not alter either fact.

Republicans such as Thune separated the propaganda from its financing because that lets them endorse Trump’s enemies list while objecting to the invoice. Others offered even less: Mike Rounds said he would not have done it; Shelley Moore Capito suggested the money could “probably” be better spent. These are expressions of taste masquerading as oversight.

The decision that mattered

Lummis made the consequential Senate decision described in the story. Hassan proposed a resolution; Lummis objected; the objection blocked unanimous consent. Whatever private discomfort other Republicans expressed, their conference produced no restraint in the episode RawStory reports.

That distinction matters. Tillis supplied the sharpest comparison, but he is retiring. Lummis exercised power. Coverage centered on Republicans “squirming” risks treating their embarrassment as the event when the operative result was continued institutional permission.

Public money, partisan enemies

A public service announcement ordinarily communicates information meant to serve the public. According to the reported language, these ads instead divide the country into a virtuous political project and named ideological enemies. Calling that a public service does not neutralize its partisan function.

The White House’s claim that prior administrations made similar material is not, by itself, an answer to whether these particular ads crossed legal or ethical lines. Nor is Steven Cheung’s attack on “Fake News.” Both responses redirect scrutiny away from the relevant questions: which authority approved the spending, how much was spent, and under what legal justification?

Discomfort is not opposition

The story’s weakest frame is its emphasis on Republican unease. Senators who possess legislative and oversight power are not spectators trapped beside an offensive commercial. They can seek records, hold hearings, impose funding restrictions, support resolutions, and force votes.

Their reluctance has a foreseeable consequence: it lowers the political cost of turning government communications into presidential promotion. Murphy’s warning about future presidents is therefore not merely hypothetical. Once lawmakers tolerate public financing for material that resembles a campaign message, they create an incentive for later administrations to test the same boundary.

The system rewards permission

This episode reveals a familiar political arrangement: executive power acts, legislators complain about presentation, and the absence of enforcement becomes the governing rule. The rhetoric of discomfort protects senators from association with the method while leaving the method intact.

The systemic failure is not that Republicans lacked the correct emotional response. It is that most of the objections reported here demanded no institutional consequence. Power is measured by what officials stop, authorize, investigate, or fund—not by how convincingly they squirm afterward.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Republicans squirm over Trump’s ‘shockingly corrupt’ TV ads: ‘I hate it’

item.title: GOP strategist warns 'bottom is dropping out' as Trump faces 'wipeout’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican strategist Matthew Bartlett warned a midterm “wipeout could be coming,” arguing that President Donald Trump has given Republican candidates neither governing results to promote nor an agenda to offer voters. Bartlett said GOP officials fear support could deteriorate further before Election Day.

That warning rests partly on two polls: a Wall Street Journal survey placing Trump’s approval at 37 percent—the poll’s lowest recorded for an incumbent president approaching a midterm since 1990—and a Reuters/Ipsos poll from the previous month putting it at 32 percent. Republicans were also facing competitive Senate races in several states once considered safer, while early voting had already begun in some states.

The White House rejected the claim that Trump was hurting Republican candidates. Spokesperson Davis Ingle called him the party’s leader and strongest campaigner. Trump planned appearances in several states and promised $5,000 payments to every adult citizen if Republicans retained power, but the reporting does not establish that such payments were authorized, funded or likely to occur.

The power belongs to the governing party

Republicans hold the institutional power described here. Trump controls the executive branch, commands the party’s national platform and can deploy the White House’s communications machinery. Republican congressional majorities possess legislative authority. Their predicament is not exclusion from power; it is accountability for how they have used it.

Bartlett’s complaint is revealing because it comes from inside that structure. He is not describing an opposition party obstructed from governing. He is describing incumbents unable to present convincing results or a coherent next-term program. When a governing party reaches the campaign’s final phase with slogans, personal appeals and an enormous conditional cash promise, the deficiency is political substance.

Trump made himself the campaign

The White House’s defense concedes the central problem. Calling Trump the party’s “unmatched motivator” treats his dominance as proof of his usefulness, even as Republican candidates reportedly confront worsening conditions. Leadership and electoral value are not synonyms.

Trump’s decision to remain the party’s central messenger also makes attempts to separate vulnerable candidates from his record less credible. Republicans may distance themselves from his immigration enforcement or the conflict in Iran, but selective disagreement does not erase their participation in a party organized around his authority.

Polls are evidence, not prophecy

The word “wipeout” is a strategist’s warning, not an election result. Approval ratings measure opinion at a particular time; they do not establish how every Senate contest will end. AlterNet’s headline amplifies Bartlett’s most alarming phrase, while the underlying reporting supports a narrower conclusion: Republicans saw serious danger, several races had become competitive, and strategists believed little time remained to reverse the trend.

That distinction matters. Breathless horse-race coverage can turn voters into weather and politicians into helpless observers of a gathering storm. The “bottom” does not simply drop out. Support erodes in response to governance, political choices, material conditions and public judgment.

The convenient search for a scapegoat

Republican anxiety may focus on whether Trump has become a drag, but that framing can misdirect responsibility onto one unpopular figure while minimizing the agency of the party around him. Trump dominates because Republican officials repeatedly accepted, defended or accommodated that dominance. Candidates now trying to create distance are not outsiders to the arrangement; they are its beneficiaries confronting its electoral cost.

The same evasion appears when deliberate campaign choices are described as a vague absence of time. Early voting did not suddenly deprive Republicans of an agenda. The party entered voting without one that its own strategists believed candidates could sell. That is a failure produced by people with power, not a scheduling mishap.

The system protects obedience until it becomes expensive

This story exposes a recurring pattern in personalized political parties: institutional loyalty persists while the leader can deliver power, then becomes alarm when that loyalty threatens incumbents’ careers. The concern reported here is not primarily that executive power became too concentrated or that governing priorities were distorted. It is that the arrangement may now lose elections.

That is the systemic error. A party can surrender program, independence and internal accountability to one leader, then portray the foreseeable consequences as an unexpected collapse. The strategists recognize the danger late because the system rewarded obedience earlier.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP strategist warns ‘bottom is dropping out’ as Trump faces ‘wipeout’

item.title: Nobel economist lays out 'really bad news' for Trump before midterms
item.description:
What happened

Paul Krugman’s “really, really bad news” for Donald Trump and Republicans is the widening gap between the administration’s economic sales pitch and voters’ reported experience one month before the midterms. As AlterNet reports, Krugman pointed to worsening economic sentiment, perceptions of a weaker job market, and a sharp rise in mortgage rates.

In an AP-NORC survey of 2,140 adults conducted Sept. 24–28, 74 percent called the national economy poor and 73 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of it. Fifty-five percent said their local economy was worse than when Trump took office in 2025. Separately, the Conference Board reported declining confidence and deteriorating perceptions of job availability in September, while Freddie Mac put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.28 percent.

Krugman acknowledged that some headline employment measures remained comparatively strong. His argument was narrower: prices, housing costs, and anxiety about finding work were moving against the White House’s claim of a “Golden Age.”

The power belongs to the White House

Trump is not a spectator watching an unfortunate economy arrive. He controls the executive branch and has made economic prosperity central to his political claim. Republicans seeking to retain power benefit from that claim when voters accept it and inherit the consequences when they do not.

That does not mean every price, hiring decision, or mortgage-rate movement originates in the Oval Office. The reporting does not establish such a causal chain. But an administration that claims sweeping credit for prosperity cannot plausibly declare itself powerless when households report deterioration.

Propaganda has met local evidence

The most damaging finding is not merely that voters dislike the national economy. During the Biden administration, Krugman observed, Americans often rated conditions near them more favorably than the national picture. In the September survey, that cushion had eroded: 55 percent said their local economy was worse, while only 20 percent said it was better.

That distinction matters because national economic opinion can be shaped by partisan messaging. Local conditions are harder to dismiss when people encounter them through rent, mortgage quotes, household bills, and job searches. The White House’s “Golden Age” branding asks voters to subordinate those experiences to presidential advertising.

The numbers require discipline

AlterNet’s strongest evidence concerns public judgment, not proof that the economy has collapsed. Polling measures what respondents believe; it does not establish the cause of those beliefs or predict the midterm result. The Conference Board figures likewise describe consumers’ perceptions of job availability, while the article says official employment measures remained relatively strong by historical standards.

That qualification does not rescue the administration’s message. It exposes its dishonesty of scale. An economy can produce respectable aggregate statistics while distributing insecurity through unaffordable credit, stubborn living costs, and fear of unemployment. Declaring victory from the top line is a political choice to discount the conditions people actually have to survive.

Accountability is not misdirection

The article largely identifies the correct center of political responsibility: the president and the party governing with him. It does not redirect anger toward workers, consumers, or some conveniently powerless group. Krugman’s critique targets the White House’s response—insisting on triumph while its own promised beneficiaries report strain.

Still, electoral damage should not be mistaken for economic accountability. A bad poll is a threat to officeholders; a 7.28 percent mortgage rate can shut households out of ownership. The political class tends to recognize material pain most clearly when that pain begins endangering its control of government.

The systemic error

This is the recurring failure of economic politics: institutions treat national indicators as reality and household experience as mood. When the two diverge, those in power often try to correct the public’s perception before confronting the public’s conditions.

Krugman’s warning is therefore larger than a forecast about one midterm. Political authority becomes brittle when leaders demand credit for abstractions and deny responsibility for consequences. The White House can call the moment golden. It cannot compel people paying its price to see the shine.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Nobel economist lays out ‘really bad news’ for Trump before midterms

item.title: GOP congressman in swing district suddenly declares: 'I am an independent’
item.description:
What happened

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick told The Washington Sun that he considers himself “an independent who is registered Republican.” He said he would formally leave the GOP if Pennsylvania allowed independents to participate in party primaries, describing himself as politically “homeless.”

AlterNet reports that Fitzpatrick is defending his seat in Pennsylvania’s competitive 1st Congressional District against Democrat Bob Harvie. Fitzpatrick is spending millions on negative advertising while emphasizing his distance from Republican orthodoxy; Harvie is highlighting his votes for an initial version of Donald Trump’s policy bill and for a procedural delay in releasing the Epstein files.

Fitzpatrick has also broken with Republicans on same-sex marriage, an assault-weapons ban and Joe Biden’s bipartisan infrastructure law. An Inquirer analysis found that he supported Trump’s stated positions about 70% of the time in the current Congress—the lowest rate among House Republicans, but still a substantial majority.

The label is not the power

Fitzpatrick may feel independent, but he occupies office as a Republican. His registration gives him access to the Republican primary, and his seat contributes to the party’s strength in the House. Personal branding does not alter either fact.

The institutional question is not whether Fitzpatrick feels at home. It is which party benefits from his incumbency, which leadership structure his election helps sustain and how he votes when legislation and procedure reach the floor.

Independence has a voting record

Fitzpatrick’s departures from his party are real and politically relevant. Treating them as meaningless would flatten the record for partisan convenience. But a 70% alignment rate also makes “independent” an incomplete description, especially when the disputed votes concern major legislation or control over what the House permits to advance.

Harvie’s argument targets that gap: moderation is being marketed as an identity, while institutional allegiance is expressed through votes. Fitzpatrick’s claim that he removes Trump from his decision-making cannot establish that separation by itself. The measurable evidence is what he supported, opposed or helped delay.

“Homeless” is strategic misdirection

Calling himself politically homeless converts an advantageous choice into a condition imposed on him. Fitzpatrick remains registered as a Republican because Pennsylvania’s closed-primary system makes that useful to his political survival. That is a constraint, but it is also agency.

His declaration that both parties have become “cults” performs a second maneuver. It distributes blame symmetrically while avoiding a direct account of which Republican decisions he enabled and which he resisted. The framing makes the congressman the displaced victim of polarization rather than an officeholder who has repeatedly chosen how to use power inside one party’s coalition.

Moderation as electoral insulation

Fitzpatrick’s unusual support from labor unions and environmental groups shows that his cross-party reputation has material value. In a district Trump lost in 2016, 2020 and 2024, separation from the national Republican brand is not merely philosophical; it is central to retaining office.

That context also sharpens the meaning of his more aggressive campaign. Millions spent attacking Harvie allow Fitzpatrick to run simultaneously as a conciliatory independent and a conventional incumbent willing to define his opponent through negative advertising. The moderate image and the hard-edged campaign are not contradictions. Together, they are a survival strategy.

The system rewards ambiguity

This contest exposes a durable pattern in swing-district politics: parties rely on carefully distanced members to preserve institutional power. Those members receive room to dissent on selected issues, then present the exceptions as proof that party affiliation carries little consequence.

Fitzpatrick’s record may be less reliably Republican than that of every other House Republican, according to the cited analysis. It is still a Republican record produced inside a Republican power structure. The consequential question is not which label feels most authentic to him. It is whether voters judge power by self-description or by the governing coalition their representative helps maintain.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP congressman in swing district suddenly declares: ‘I am an independent’

item.title: What’s really behind the Kennedy Center’s 'collapse’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the Kennedy Center’s reported financial collapse followed President Donald Trump’s takeover, not a preexisting fiscal catastrophe. Citing Washington Post reporting based on 15 years of confidential board records and tax filings, it says the center was solvent before Trump removed professional staff, asserted control over programming, and watched revenue, donations, and bookings fall.

The Post reportedly found that the center then exhausted its available bank borrowing, used donor-restricted funds intended to remain unspent, and wrote off unpaid pledges. Trump claimed the institution had already been losing hundreds of millions of dollars, while his board warned of bankruptcy; AlterNet says that account minimizes the administration’s own decisions, including cutting development staff and spending National Opera endowment money.

The power is not mysterious

The decisive actor was not an amorphous arts audience, disloyal donors, or an institution spontaneously forgetting how to function. Trump took control of the Kennedy Center, displaced its professional management, and imposed political authority over artistic decisions. His board then controlled the institution’s response to the resulting financial pressure.

That is institutional power in its plainest form: the ability to remove personnel, redirect programming, spend protected resources, borrow money, and define the official explanation afterward. Audiences and donors could withdraw support, but they did not control the center. They reacted to decisions made above them.

First capture, then blame

The central misdirection is chronological. Trump described the Kennedy Center as a failing institution he inherited, while the records cited by the Post reportedly place its most severe deterioration after his intervention.

That does not eliminate every earlier financial weakness; AlterNet acknowledges genuine areas of dispute. But it makes the sequence unavoidable. An administration cannot seize managerial control, remove revenue-producing expertise, alienate patrons, exhaust credit, consume restricted funds, and then treat the resulting distress as proof that the institution was doomed before it arrived.

This is blame-first governance: announce failure, impose disruption, and use the disruption as retroactive evidence for the original accusation.

Manufactured necessity

A financial emergency can become political permission. If the Kennedy Center is portrayed as irreparably insolvent, drastic action—including the possible razing described by AlterNet—can be presented as reluctant housekeeping rather than the culmination of choices made by those now declaring the emergency.

The available reporting does not establish that the damage was deliberately engineered to justify destruction. It does establish a more limited and still damning pattern: the people exercising control are blaming conditions that reportedly worsened under their control, while discounting their own role in producing them.

That maneuver converts accountability into inevitability. Management decisions disappear; “collapse” becomes something that merely happened.

The allegation outruns the evidence

AlterNet places the Kennedy Center alongside several episodes in which Trump or his allies advanced accusations that the reporting says were not sustained by evidence. These include demands for a “Grand Conspiracy” prosecution that two prosecutors reportedly declined to pursue, Senator Eric Schmitt’s mistaken insinuation about Jack Smith attending an Atlanta basketball game, and a Federal Reserve watchdog’s finding of no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in the bank’s headquarters renovation.

The cases are distinct, and none proves the others. Their shared political function, as presented by AlterNet, is to make accusation itself do the work: stigmatize the target, authorize intervention, and force everyone else to spend time disproving a premise that was never adequately established.

The Kennedy Center’s books matter precisely because records resist that performance. They assign dates to decline, decisions to officials, and consequences to management.

Ruin as political narrative

The larger pattern is institutional capture followed by historical revision. Professional authority is displaced, political loyalists gain control, operational damage follows, and the new leadership cites that damage as evidence that the institution deserved takeover or demolition.

This is not confusion about who was responsible. It is a struggle over whether responsibility will remain visible. Once chronology is stripped away, power can present its own consequences as inherited facts—and turn preventable damage into an argument for still more power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: What’s really behind the Kennedy Center’s ‘collapse’

item.title: GOP lawmakers exasperated with Trump's 'too little, too late' midterms ploy: Politico
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing Politico, reports that President Donald Trump rolled out major infrastructure proposals in Alaska, Iowa and Alabama shortly before the midterm elections. Republican strategists described the move as “too little, too late” because early voting was already underway, Election Day was four weeks away, and none of the projects was expected to become operational before 2030.

The announcements covered a proposed $50 billion Alaska natural-gas pipeline, a $15 billion Iowa steel plant and a $3.2 billion Alabama bridge project. The projects attracted bipartisan praise, but the reporting did not establish that they would be completed. Republicans also doubted that distant construction plans could overcome immediate economic pressures, including gasoline above $4.40 a gallon and mortgage rates near 7.5 percent.

Politico reported that Democrats had become newly competitive in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas, although Trump carried all three states by double digits in 2024. His average approval rating was reportedly around 37 percent as of the Thursday referenced in the story.

Power announced, not delivered

Trump holds the institutional power in this story. His administration chose when to promote these projects, while Republican candidates were left trying to convert presidential announcements into electoral relief.

That distinction matters. A pipeline projected for 2030 cannot lower today’s fuel bill. A future steel plant cannot refinance today’s mortgage. The former Trump official quoted by Politico identified the gap cleanly: announcements generate headlines, but they do not reduce inflation or fuel prices.

The projects may eventually produce real economic benefits. The reporting does not establish that they will. For the current campaign, their immediate product is publicity.

Republican anger is about timing

The Republican complaint is not that governing by spectacle is irresponsible. It is that the spectacle arrived too late to be politically useful.

Iowa strategist Luke Martz called the projects “fantastic” while warning that Republicans had little time to exploit them. That exposes the governing priority embedded in the reaction: public investment is being evaluated first as campaign material and only second as infrastructure.

Republican lawmakers and strategists have agency here too. They are not powerless observers of Trump’s presidency. Yet the story shows them speaking mainly as frustrated dependents, waiting for the White House to manufacture a favorable news cycle while voters judge conditions they already experience.

The electorate is not a messaging defect

The framing risks turning public dissatisfaction into a communications problem. Republicans need “good news.” Trump needs better timing. Announcements may be “subsumed” by other coverage or “tarnished” by his political brand.

But voters facing high gasoline prices and mortgage rates do not require a more disciplined sales pitch. Their material circumstances are not an obstacle to messaging; they are the political substance.

Calling the maneuver “too little, too late” also softens the central failure. The issue is not merely that Trump waited too long to unveil large projects. It is that his party apparently expected distant, uncertain benefits to outweigh present conditions within weeks.

The brand is the government

Politico’s reference to the “Trump brand” separates image from authority too neatly. Trump is not an outside celebrity contaminating otherwise neutral announcements. He is the president directing the administration’s political presentation.

His reported 37 percent approval rating therefore matters as more than a branding problem. It suggests that attaching his name to prospective investments may not rescue vulnerable Republicans because the public is also judging the governing coalition responsible for current conditions.

The candidates’ predicament follows from their political arrangement: they benefit from Trump’s control of the party when he is popular and inherit the consequences when he is not. Dependence is not exoneration.

Governing as campaign inventory

This episode reveals a system that treats public works as electoral inventory. Projects are announced, priced and geographically targeted; strategists then calculate whether the promised benefits can mature quickly enough to influence ballots.

The harder political question is whether institutions can deliver durable public value independent of one president’s approval rating or one party’s campaign calendar. Here, the reported answer is uncertain. The construction remains prospective, while the electoral marketing is immediate.

That inversion is the systemic error: government capacity becomes a prop for managing political exposure, and when the prop fails, party operatives blame the deadline rather than the decision to substitute promises for results.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP lawmakers exasperated with Trump’s ‘too little, too late’ midterms ploy: Politico

item.title: GOP sources say Trump is 'out of his mind' over his new scheme
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that CNN’s John King said some Trump voters reacted with disbelief to reporting about President Donald Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures. One voter called Trump “out of his mind,” then asked whether the story was legitimate. CNN’s Anderson Cooper cited financial filings that he said show the ventures putting more than $1 billion a year in Trump’s pocket.

King also described a Georgia voter who said she lost about $20,000 after investing in two Trump crypto funds and now plans to vote for the Democratic Senate candidate. He said other past Trump voters believe the president is preoccupied with himself rather than the economic concerns that helped return him to office. The report does not establish how representative these voters are or document a broader Republican revolt.

The power belongs to Trump

The central fact is not that some Republicans are shocked. It is that the president holds federal power while private ventures bearing his political identity allegedly generate extraordinary personal income.

Voters can complain, sell investments, or change their ballots. Trump controls the presidency and chooses whether to maintain financial arrangements that create this conflict. Republican officials and institutions also possess agency: they can investigate, demand disclosure, impose political costs, or continue treating presidential self-enrichment as background noise.

Disbelief is not accountability

The “out of his mind” remark supplies the headline, but astonishment is the least important part of the story. The conduct described did not emerge from nowhere. It operated in public, alongside a media ecosystem that King said often withholds unfavorable or ethically troubling information from Trump’s most loyal supporters.

The voter who immediately wondered whether CNN’s report was “fake news” illustrates the protective function of that ecosystem. Discrediting outside reporting does more than preserve loyalty. It raises the evidentiary threshold for facts harmful to Trump while lowering it for claims that serve him.

Economic grievance meets private gain

Trump reportedly insists inflation is under control and faults his own messaging for public dissatisfaction. Cooper’s response was more concrete: costs remained higher and were rising faster than when Trump took office.

That contrast matters because some swing voters backed Trump to improve their material conditions. If they instead see a president earning enormous sums from crypto ventures while their own costs rise—or, in one reported case, losing $20,000 in Trump-linked funds—the political problem is not inadequate explanation. It is the collision between promised economic stewardship and reported private enrichment.

The framing lets institutions disappear

By centering colorful voter reactions, the coverage risks making the scandal a story about consumer disappointment and electoral mood. That shifts attention downward, toward people with little institutional power, and away from the officials, party leaders, regulators, and congressional majorities capable of imposing consequences.

The stronger question is not whether voters have finally noticed. It is why notice must substitute for enforcement. Elections can punish a party, but they are a blunt and delayed mechanism for addressing conflicts created by a sitting president’s business interests.

Grift as a governing pattern

King said Democrats increasingly use “grift” to describe the issue, although affordability remains voters’ largest concern. Those subjects are not separate. Political power becomes materially legible when the person promising relief appears to profit while supporters absorb higher costs or investment losses.

The systemic failure is the conversion of accountability into polling analysis. A presidency entangled with lucrative private ventures is treated as an intriguing voter-perception problem; party actors are reduced to spectators; and institutional inaction vanishes behind anecdotes about surprise. The public’s reaction matters, but it should not be carrying the entire burden that governing institutions have declined to lift.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP sources say Trump is ‘out of his mind’ over his new scheme

item.title: Trump DHS scrambles to salvage billion-dollar deal after contractor departs in scandal
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing The PunchUp and federal procurement records, reports that the Department of Homeland Security replaced Salus Worldwide Solutions as the contractor running Project Homecoming. DHS awarded Virginia-based Response AI Solutions the program’s next phase—worth up to $2.062 billion over three years—after Secretary Markwayne Mullin reopened the contract to competition. DHS has not publicly explained why Salus lost the work.

Salus had received an initial $915 million contract in May 2025 and another $200 million in June for six additional months. A rival bidder’s lawsuit disclosed that DHS contracting personnel and attorneys had warned of an “appearance of impropriety,” while Salus founder William Walters III has maintained that the competition was fair and his company submitted the best technical proposal at the lowest price.

The company later faced scrutiny over an alleged kickback effort involving former DHS adviser Corey Lewandowski, who is reportedly under federal investigation and whose spokesperson denies wrongdoing. Salus denies illegality. Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson sought a formal investigation after leaked data reportedly indicated that about half the “voluntary” departures credited to Salus involved migrants already in ICE custody.

The buyer held the power

This was never merely a contractor problem. DHS controlled the specifications, the competition, the money, the oversight and the decision to keep paying. Salus could pursue public funds, but federal officials decided whether it received them.

That distinction matters because the department’s own personnel reportedly raised concerns before or during the arrangement. The DHS division overseeing the contract was led by a former Walters colleague who held off-site meetings at Salus offices before the award and congratulated him afterward. Those facts do not by themselves prove corruption, but they make scrutiny predictable—and make DHS responsible for explaining how its safeguards functioned.

The scandal was enabled, not discovered late

Salus lacked prior experience as a lead federal contractor, according to the reporting. A competitor challenged the rapid award. Internal officials flagged appearances. Yet DHS still granted the company $915 million, then supplied another $200 million despite documents suggesting most of the original budget had already been spent with limited results.

Calling the replacement a scramble risks treating the department as a victim of circumstances. The reported record instead shows an institution repeatedly exercising discretion in Salus’s favor before reversing course. Reopening the competition may have limited further exposure, but it does not erase the decisions that created it.

Accountability cannot end with a new vendor

Handing Project Homecoming to Response AI Solutions changes the recipient of the money. It does not establish whether the original procurement was fair, whether performance claims were accurate, or whether political access influenced other DHS awards.

The alleged effort by a Salus representative to arrange kickbacks for Lewandowski remains an allegation. His spokesperson denies wrongdoing, and the reported federal investigation is not a finding of guilt. But DHS’s silence about why Salus lost the contract leaves the public with a multibillion-dollar substitution where an institutional accounting should be.

“Voluntary” is doing political work

The dispute over departure statistics exposes more than questionable contractor performance. If roughly half the departures credited to Salus involved people already in ICE custody, as the leaked data reportedly suggested, then the program’s public description may obscure the coercive power behind its results.

Migrants were the objects of the policy, not the authors of the procurement failure. Focusing primarily on whether they departed “voluntarily” can misdirect attention from officials who designed the metric, approved the claims and paid the contractor. The weaker actors become the spectacle while the powerful actors remain an administrative blur.

A system that converts failure into another contract

This episode reflects a durable governing pattern: officials outsource politically charged state action, contractors collect enormous sums, and responsibility fragments when the arrangement draws scrutiny. The company points to the agency’s selection process. The agency points to procurement machinery. A replacement arrives, and the underlying decisions disappear behind a new corporate name.

The central issue is not that government contracting became messy. It is that DHS reportedly continued committing public money after serious warnings and now offers no public explanation for the contractor’s removal. Without that explanation—and without findings on the allegations—the new award looks less like accountability than institutional damage control.

Thanks to Raw Story

item.title: 'He went full beta': MS NOW hosts single out Hegseth's 'really weird' Pentagon pitch
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a Wednesday “State of the Force” speech to declare that the Pentagon was no longer “woke” or “weak,” while deriding categories of people he considered physically or culturally unacceptable. On Friday, MS NOW’s Joe Scarborough and Willie Geist mocked the presentation as insecure and “really weird,” answering the headline’s teaser by calling Hegseth’s performance “full beta.”

The hosts focused particularly on Hegseth’s repeated interest in testosterone and his aggressive stage manner. Their segment established a spectacle: the official who leads the Defense Department publicly defining military strength through body policing, gender conformity and playground insults.

The power behind the performance

Scarborough’s ridicule is entertaining but politically incomplete. Hegseth is not merely an awkward man broadcasting anxieties beneath an American flag. He is the defense secretary, speaking from the institutional summit of the military bureaucracy to officers and senior Pentagon personnel.

That distinction matters. When a television host obsesses over whether Hegseth looks “alpha” or “beta,” the criticism remains trapped inside Hegseth’s own status hierarchy. The relevant question is not whether he successfully performed masculinity. It is what standards, punishments and command priorities his performance signals to people whose careers are subject to his authority.

Insults as policy language

Hegseth’s rhetoric compressed personnel policy into a list of contemptuous stereotypes. That is not clarity. It is governance by humiliation: define a favored military identity, caricature everyone outside it, and present exclusion as institutional renewal.

The reported remarks do not establish which formal policies will follow. But the foreseeable message is plain. Personnel who do not match Hegseth’s preferred image are being told that the department’s leader treats them as symbols of weakness or disorder. Senior officials do not need to issue a detailed directive for subordinates to understand what conduct and appearance power now rewards.

The masculinity trap

MS NOW correctly identified the insecurity in a powerful official’s fixation on testosterone and toughness. But “beta” mockery reproduces the same premise it attacks: that public authority should be judged through a masculinity ranking.

That framing turns a consequential exercise of institutional power into locker-room criticism. Hegseth’s problem is not that he failed an authenticity test administered by television hosts. It is that he used an official Pentagon address to elevate cultural grievance and personal conformity as measures of military worth.

Who bears the consequences

The immediate targets are weaker than the official naming them: service members and Pentagon personnel whose bodies, identities or appearances fall outside his approved template. They do not control the department’s standards, promotions or disciplinary machinery. Hegseth does.

Treating the episode chiefly as a bizarre personality display misdirects attention from that imbalance. The laughter lands on the secretary’s performance; the institutional pressure lands below him. One is a cable-news moment. The other can shape careers, reporting chains and workplace culture.

Contempt in command

This episode reflects a broader political method: officials convert prejudice into proof of toughness, then use the authority of the state to make personal domination look like administrative reform. The crude language is not separate from the power structure. It advertises which people the hierarchy may safely demean.

Calling the performance weird is accurate but insufficient. The systemic error is treating authoritarian aesthetics as merely embarrassing while overlooking what makes them politically effective: contempt spoken from the top quickly becomes permission throughout the institution.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘He went full beta’: MS NOW hosts single out Hegseth’s ‘really weird’ Pentagon pitch

item.title: 'Clown-show' theory eviscerated by Republicans’ own local news program
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Sen. Eric Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith of coordinating with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, relying on the false claim that Smith attended an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024. Smith denied it, and Schmitt escalated by accusing him of perjury.

The game was actually an Iowa Hawkeyes women’s college basketball game. A local news segment reviewed Fox Sports footage, located Smith in section 109, row 1, and noted that the cited seat does not exist in Atlanta. The program said Schmitt’s office did not respond to its request for an explanation or apology.

The senator held the power

This was not a misunderstanding between equal participants. Schmitt had a Senate hearing, official standing and the practical protection enjoyed by lawmakers questioning witnesses. Smith faced an accusation of a crime carrying potential prison time; Schmitt faced embarrassment for making that accusation from a defective premise.

That imbalance is the story. A senator used institutional authority to transform bad information into a televised allegation of perjury. The hearing supplied the scenery of accountability while insulating the person making the baseless charge from comparable accountability.

Abuse dressed as inquiry

Schmitt did not merely ask Smith to clarify where he had been. According to AlterNet, he called Smith a “dirtbag” and a “villain,” then accused him of lying under oath before establishing the elementary fact at the center of his argument.

Calling this “just asking questions” would conceal agency. Schmitt chose the evidence, presented the display and escalated the accusation. The local broadcast’s fact-check mattered because it restored the sequence that political spectacle tries to erase: allegation first, verification later, consequences unevenly distributed.

The correction cannot match the smear

Conservative podcasters reportedly praised Schmitt for taking Smith down before the claim had survived basic scrutiny. That is how the incentive system works: the accusation becomes instant content, while the correction arrives as cleanup.

The local program punctured the performance with a check simple enough to make the Senate theatrics look especially reckless. But factual collapse does not automatically reverse political impact. Audiences who received the confrontation as proof of corruption may never encounter—or accept—the correction.

The framing is too gentle

Describing the episode primarily as a “flub” understates what the reporting establishes. Confusing two basketball teams was the factual error. Accusing a witness of perjury on that basis was the exercise of power.

The evidence supplied here does not establish why Schmitt relied on the false information. It does establish that he publicly intensified the charge without verifying it and, according to the local station, offered no explanation or apology when asked. Treating that conduct as mere incompetence shifts attention from the consequential decision to the embarrassing mistake beneath it.

Spectacle without liability

This episode reveals a durable political arrangement: officials can use hearings to manufacture prosecutorial drama without accepting prosecutorial standards. The target must answer under oath. The senator can be spectacularly wrong, circulate the accusation through friendly media and retreat behind the procedural fiction of inquiry.

The systemic error is not that one lawmaker missed a shot. It is that institutional power rewards the attempt even when the evidence misses the arena.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Clown-show’ theory eviscerated by Republicans’ own local news program

item.title: 'Something is very wrong': Ex-FBI official tears into Stephen Miller-linked FBI shakeup
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that the FBI demoted two veteran counterterrorism supervisors in its Washington Field Office after a dispute over an investigation into alleged harassing phone calls to Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. The FBI confirmed the personnel moves, but the report does not establish who ordered them or whether formal disciplinary procedures occurred.

Former FBI assistant director Frank Figliuzzi told Jim Acosta that the account appeared irregular. He questioned why counterterrorism officials were handling calls that would ordinarily fall under violent crime and disputed the field office chief’s apparent claim of sole responsibility, arguing that demoting senior executives normally requires headquarters authority and a disciplinary board.

Figliuzzi also discussed the reported ShinyHunters breach of the FBI jobs portal, which The New York Times said exposed sensitive information about agents. He inferred that multiple headquarters databases may have been compromised and said he considered a transparent investigation under FBI Director Kash Patel unlikely. The reporting provides his assessment, not independent confirmation of either claim.

Power is the unanswered question

The central issue is not whether a manager shuffled two employees. It is whether political proximity altered federal law-enforcement priorities and personnel decisions.

Stephen Miller holds White House power. His wife was the reported target of the calls. FBI leadership controls assignments, discipline and investigative resources. The displaced supervisors did not possess comparable institutional leverage, yet they absorbed the concrete consequence.

That hierarchy makes the missing chain of command essential. The field office chief’s acceptance of responsibility does not resolve it. Figliuzzi’s account directly challenges whether that official had the authority to impose the reported demotions at all.

Favoritism without an accounting

No evidence presented here establishes that Stephen Miller ordered the investigation or the personnel actions. Nor does the article establish what the calls contained, what the supervisors disputed or what rationale the FBI gave for removing them.

But those gaps make scrutiny more necessary, not less. The confirmed demotions followed a disagreement involving the spouse of a senior White House official, and the bureau has not supplied enough detail to show that ordinary procedures governed the outcome. Institutional silence leaves the appearance of preferential treatment intact.

The relevant standard is not whether Katie Miller deserved protection from harassment. She did. The question is whether her political connection produced an investigative response—and punishment for internal resistance—that an ordinary person could not command.

The convenient local culprit

The public claim that the field office head acted alone directs attention downward, away from headquarters and political leadership. Figliuzzi says that explanation conflicts with the rules governing senior executives. If his procedural account is correct, the local-responsibility narrative is not merely incomplete; it obscures where authorizing power must have existed.

RawStory identifies the contradiction but cannot resolve it. That limitation matters. The article supports a demand for the decision trail, not a definitive accusation about who intervened.

Still, bureaucracies routinely turn hierarchy into camouflage. Senior officials retain authority while subordinates become the visible authors of controversial acts. Responsibility is dispersed just enough that every powerful participant can point somewhere else.

A bureau that cannot credibly police itself

The reported data breach deepens the institutional problem. Agents’ home addresses, Social Security numbers and sensitive assignments are not trivial administrative records. If the reported exposure is accurate, the FBI failed to protect information capable of endangering its own personnel.

Figliuzzi’s broader-hack theory remains an inference, as does his prediction that Patel would resist transparency. But the personnel controversy shows why credibility matters: an agency asking the public to trust its internal investigation is simultaneously declining to explain an apparently irregular exercise of authority.

Secrecy may protect legitimate investigations. Here, it also protects decision-makers from accountability.

Political access as a governing privilege

The larger pattern is a two-tier state: exceptional attention for people near executive power, opaque consequences for officials who object, and procedural ambiguity used to prevent responsibility from settling anywhere.

That pattern does not require proof of a direct White House order to be politically corrosive. It requires institutions that anticipate the preferences of powerful people and understand that compliance is safer than resistance.

The FBI could dispel that inference by identifying who authorized the demotions, what rules were followed and why counterterrorism resources were assigned to the case. Until it does, “something is very wrong” describes more than a disputed personnel action. It describes a system in which proximity to power appears to determine whose grievance becomes a federal priority—and whose career becomes expendable.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Something is very wrong’: Ex-FBI official tears into Stephen Miller-linked FBI shakeup
