item.title: Busted: GOP candidate's move to blame his staff for stolen valor claims falls apart
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Nevada Republican congressional candidate David Flippo blamed unnamed campaign staffers for falsely claiming he earned a Bronze Star with a valor distinction—an honor he acknowledges he did not receive. That explanation was undermined by photographs, cited from Mother Jones, showing Flippo wearing a cap marked with V-shaped symbols associated with combat-valor citations.

The images reportedly appeared on Flippo’s campaign website and social media from at least August 2023. Mother Jones said he appeared to switch to an unmarked version of the cap around June, though the supplied reporting does not specify the year. Veterans interviewed by the outlet said the earlier markings represented an award Flippo had not earned. Flippo did legitimately receive a Bronze Star for rescuing and treating a burned soldier in Iraq, but without the valor device.

The candidate owned the message

Flippo holds the relevant power here. He is the candidate, the beneficiary of the military biography presented to voters and the person who repeatedly wore the insignia in public-facing campaign photographs.

Blaming anonymous aides might address erroneous website copy if that were the only evidence. It does not explain the hat on Flippo’s own head. Staff did not unknowingly dress him for months, and the campaign’s reported removal of the symbols only sharpens the unanswered question: if they were innocent, why did they disappear?

The reporting does not establish who designed the cap or prove Flippo’s intent. It does establish that his staff-error explanation fails to account for his own conduct.

An earned record was not enough

The most revealing detail is that Flippo already had a legitimate record of service. His Bronze Star citation, as described by RawStory, honored him for pulling a burned soldier to safety and administering first aid. That requires no embellishment.

Yet the political presentation reportedly added symbols associated with a rarer distinction tied to action under enemy fire. The difference is not decorative. It is the difference between describing an award accurately and claiming a level of recognition the military did not confer.

This is how résumé inflation becomes political deception: not through one grand fabrication, but through a small symbol chosen because most voters will absorb its prestige without examining the paperwork.

Anonymous staff as a shield

The staff-blaming frame redirects agency downward. Unnamed aides are convenient because they can absorb fault without answering questions, producing records or explaining why the candidate personally displayed the same false distinction.

That tactic also asks the public to treat a sustained campaign representation as clerical confusion. But RawStory’s account describes repeated claims alongside repeated visual signaling. Even if aides confused two honors, that would not explain why Flippo wore two V-shaped devices or why he later stopped.

The article is right to show the explanation falling apart, but the central issue is larger than a campaign “bust.” A candidate sought credit for the message and then assigned responsibility elsewhere when scrutiny arrived.

Prestige without accountability

Flippo is running for an open seat in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, which has not elected a Democrat since its creation in the 1980s. His campaign therefore operates within an inherited Republican advantage, even as Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson mounts what RawStory describes as a strong challenge.

That institutional setting matters. A favorable district can encourage a candidate to treat accountability as a communications problem rather than an obligation. RawStory also reports that Flippo recently moved into the district, has put nearly $2.5 million into his campaigns, lacks outgoing Representative Mark Amodei’s endorsement and faces an AFL-CIO-backed advertisement featuring local veterans’ criticism.

Those pressures do not prove why the award claim was made. They do explain why biography, military legitimacy and personal wealth have become central instruments in the contest.

The systemic error

Political campaigns manufacture authority from symbols: uniforms, titles, endorsements, money and curated origin stories. When one of those symbols proves false, the machinery immediately searches for someone weaker to blame.

The pattern is straightforward. The candidate receives the prestige; anonymous workers receive the liability. The public gets an “error” in place of an accountable explanation. And an actual act of service is cheapened because political branding demanded a rarer medal than the one honestly earned.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Busted: GOP candidate’s move to blame his staff for stolen valor claims falls apart

item.title: Mockery as GOP airs 'most embarrassing ad' featuring candidate's estranged wife
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that a Republican super PAC aired a 30-second ad featuring Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, the estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, as he campaigns against James Talarico for a Senate seat. The ad, funded by an affiliate of Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund, asks voters to support the Republican ticket without naming Ken Paxton.

That omission became the story. Angela Paxton filed for divorce on “biblical grounds” after her husband began his Senate campaign last year, according to the report. She had also attended his 2023 impeachment trial, where his former chief of staff testified about an alleged extramarital affair.

Democratic politicians, strategists and progressive commentators mocked the spot as awkward and self-defeating. The article supplies their reactions but no polling or other evidence establishing how Texas voters received the ad.

The power behind the pitch

The institutional actor here is not Angela Paxton and certainly not the online critics. It is the Republican campaign apparatus behind the advertisement: a super PAC affiliated with the Senate Leadership Fund, which is tied to the party’s Senate leadership.

That apparatus chose to place an estranged wife inside a message demanding partisan loyalty. Her personal history was not incidental background discovered after production. It was the most foreseeable fact shaping how the advertisement would be understood.

Loyalty without a name

Angela Paxton’s line about the “elephant in the room” appears to acknowledge an obvious problem while refusing to identify it. The ad then substitutes the Republican ticket for the candidate himself.

That is the political function of the spot: to make the party label carry what the candidate’s personal reputation may not. Voters are not offered a defense of Ken Paxton’s conduct, an answer to the allegations aired during his impeachment trial, or even his name. They are asked to treat affiliation as sufficient.

Mockery is not accountability

RawStory frames the episode primarily as an embarrassing campaign mishap, assembling a procession of cutting social-media reactions. Some identify the contradiction clearly. Others merely turn a strained marriage into spectacle.

That framing shrinks a decision by a national Republican political operation into an internet blooper. The consequential question is not whether the ad is humiliating. It is why party leaders apparently believed an appeal from Paxton’s estranged wife could neutralize the very history that made her appearance so conspicuous.

The stronger actor disappears

The coverage’s gravitational center is Angela Paxton: what she said, what she omitted and why her participation looks awkward. Ken Paxton’s conduct remains mostly offstage, even though his candidacy created the need for this exercise.

The available reporting does not establish why Angela Paxton agreed to appear, and speculation about a divorce agreement is only a joke quoted from an online personality. Assigning her an invented motive would repeat the ad’s own misdirection—placing the burden on the estranged spouse while the candidate and the political organization supporting him escape sustained examination.

Partisanship as absolution

The larger pattern is institutional protection through abstraction. When a candidate’s record becomes difficult to defend directly, the party asks voters to stop evaluating the person and start defending the team.

That maneuver does not rebut allegations or resolve contradictions. It attempts to make them politically irrelevant. The embarrassment is secondary. The real disclosure is that a powerful Senate campaign network considered partisan identity a plausible substitute for an accounting.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Mockery as GOP airs ‘most embarrassing ad’ featuring candidate’s estranged wife

item.title: 'All hell broke loose': Expert warns Trump's midterm danger zone comes after voting ends
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that voting-rights journalist Ari Berman believes the likeliest opportunity for Trump administration interference in the midterm elections would come after voting ends, during ballot counting and certification, when close margins could make targeted federal action more consequential.

Appearing on the debut episode of the “Stress Test” podcast, Berman said the Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security, or other agencies could invoke a pretext to intervene. He also stressed that this remains a warning, not an accomplished plan: according to Berman, the Justice Department had lost 25 federal-court attempts to obtain state voter rolls, while proposals to stop mail voting or seize election equipment through emergency powers or martial law were a “huge stretch.”

Berman ultimately predicted that Trump would blame others and move on if Republicans lost. RawStory provides no evidence that federal agencies have decided to manipulate a result, and it does not establish that any post-election intervention will occur.

The power sits in government

The relevant power does not belong to voters accused of fraud, local officials processing ballots, or election workers counting late into the night. It belongs to the president and the federal officials who control agencies capable of opening investigations, demanding records, manufacturing legal conflict, or lending official credibility to allegations about an election.

That distinction matters because “interference” can become a foggy abstraction. Institutions do not mobilize themselves. Officials issue orders, lawyers file claims, and political appointees decide whether the machinery of government will administer an election or place it under suspicion.

Failure is not harmlessness

Berman’s account describes an administration that has so far failed to obtain state voter rolls through federal litigation. That is evidence of institutional resistance, not evidence that the effort was benign. Losing in court does not erase the attempt to expand federal leverage over election administration.

Nor does limited formal authority eliminate political power. A president may lack the lawful capacity to seize ballots yet retain enormous power to pressure allies, amplify accusations, provoke litigation, and turn ordinary counting procedures into evidence of conspiracy for supporters already primed to distrust an unfavorable result.

The pretext is the mechanism

The critical word in Berman’s warning is “pretext.” Close contests naturally involve provisional ballots, recounts, litigation, and delayed certification. Those routine features can be repackaged as proof that something illicit occurred.

That is how misdirection works: scrutiny moves away from powerful officials seeking new authority and toward election workers, state administrators, or voters whose ballots remain to be counted. Deliberate political escalation is then reported as generalized “chaos,” as though disorder simply descended rather than being cultivated by identifiable actors.

Trump’s joking exhortation to “cheat like hell,” as described by RawStory, does not by itself establish an operational plan. But Berman’s characterization of it as projection points to a familiar propaganda tactic: accuse opponents broadly, weaken confidence in advance, and preserve a ready-made explanation for defeat.

The article hedges against itself

RawStory packages Berman’s remarks as a looming “danger zone,” but his own assessment is notably restrained. He says Trump possesses little direct election power, calls the most extreme scenarios implausible, and predicts retreat rather than a successful seizure of the process.

That tension should have been made explicit. The reporting supports concern about where pressure might be applied; it does not support certainty that a coordinated federal intervention is coming. Sensational framing blurs that distinction and risks converting a useful institutional warning into suspense-driven political content.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is not that one politician possesses unlimited control. It is that American election coverage repeatedly treats the post-vote period as political theater instead of an administrative process vulnerable to pressure from officials with unequal power.

The sharper question is therefore not whether “all hell” will mysteriously break loose. It is whether judges, state officials, federal employees, and party leaders will use their authority to enforce lawful procedures—or help convert an electoral loss into an accusation against the system itself.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘All hell broke loose’: Expert warns Trump’s midterm danger zone comes after voting ends

item.title: Katie Britt's husband breaks three-year silence over her viral 'Schmitt face' meme
item.description:
What happened

According to RawStory, Wesley Britt ended a posting silence dating to August 2023 after a reaction shot of his wife, Republican Alabama Sen. Katie Britt, became a meme. He captioned the image as her watching him sleepwalk and eat leftovers; she reposted it with “Nailed it.”

The image came from a Tuesday Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith of perjury after Smith denied attending an Atlanta Hawks game on Feb. 3, 2024. Staff displayed text messages Schmitt presented as proof, but AL.com reported that the hearing later established Smith was actually in Maryland watching Caitlin Clark and the Iowa Hawkeyes.

The face was not the scandal

Britt’s expression circulated because it captured the instant Schmitt’s performance appeared to collapse. But the politically significant act was not a facial reaction. It was a senator using a committee hearing—and the authority, cameras and staff that came with it—to level an allegation of criminal conduct before the underlying facts were secure.

Calling the moment the “Schmitt face” at least points toward its cause. Treating it primarily as Katie Britt’s meme risks turning an abuse of institutional theater into disposable internet comedy.

Power sat behind the microphone

Schmitt held the relevant power. As a senator questioning a witness, he could dictate the exchange, display selected material and attach the word “perjury” to Smith’s testimony in real time. Staffers helped stage the accusation by raising the posterboard.

Smith could deny the premise, but Schmitt controlled the frame. That imbalance matters: an official accusation delivered from a Senate dais carries weight even when later reporting undercuts it. The correction rarely travels with the same force as the charge.

A family joke softened a public failure

Wesley Britt’s post was a harmless joke, and RawStory reports no evidence that either Britt engineered the original confrontation. Yet the joke helped convert a moment of senatorial recklessness into relatable domestic content.

That is how political accountability gets diluted without anyone needing to issue a formal defense. The audience is invited to enjoy the reaction, recognize the movie reference and move on. Schmitt’s unsupported leap from disputed recollection to apparent criminal accusation becomes the setup rather than the subject.

The accusation was built for circulation

The posterboard and the declaration “I think you’ve already perjured yourself” supplied a ready-made clip: simple charge, visible evidence, apparent contradiction. The later factual distinction—that Smith was reportedly watching a different basketball game in another state—made the spectacle look less like disciplined oversight than an accusation launched before verification.

The reporting does not establish whether Schmitt knowingly misrepresented the evidence. It does establish that he made the accusation and that the premise presented during the exchange did not hold. Intent remains uncertain; institutional irresponsibility does not.

Spectacle outruns correction

This episode exposes a durable political incentive. Officials can use public hearings to manufacture prosecutorial-looking moments without bearing a prosecutor’s burden. Platforms then reward the accusation, the reaction shot and the celebrity joke as interchangeable entertainment.

The consequence is larger than one failed gotcha. When institutions package unverified claims as authoritative confrontation, factual correction becomes an afterthought and power escapes inside the meme.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Katie Britt’s husband breaks three-year silence over her viral ‘Schmitt face’ meme

item.title: A 'perfect storm' is blasting the bottom out from under Trump's party
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republicans face unexpectedly weak Senate prospects in five Republican-leaning states. Citing New York Times/Siena polling, it says Donald Trump’s approval across those states stood at 40 percent, with 57 percent viewing him unfavorably—a five-point decline since comparable June polling in four of them. The Times attributed the broader deterioration partly to rising fuel prices and mortgage rates.

The reported contests include Democrat James Talarico leading Republican Ken Paxton by six points in Texas and Democrat Mary Peltola running eight points ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s top-four primary. The polling also found Democratic candidates generally rated more favorably on character, while Republican candidates were more often considered ideologically extreme. These are polling snapshots, not election results, and the article supplies neither field dates nor methodological details.

Where the power sits

The decisive power in this story belongs to the president and the Republican officials and candidates aligned with him—not to gasoline pumps, mortgage contracts or atmospheric conditions. AlterNet says Trump chose the conflict with Iran that it links to higher diesel prices. If that account is accurate, the resulting political damage is not an inexplicable gust of bad luck. It is a foreseeable consequence of an executive decision.

Republican candidates also retain agency over whom they support and what governing record they defend. They benefited from Trump’s coalition when it delivered power. They cannot plausibly recast that same political dependency as weather once his policies and unpopularity become liabilities.

The alibi of the storm

Calling this a “perfect storm” turns accountable choices into natural disaster. Storms have no authors. Wars, partisan alliances and candidate nominations do.

The metaphor also bundles distinct liabilities into one supposedly freak event: economic pressure, Trump’s declining approval, candidate-quality problems and voters’ judgments about character and ideological extremity. That packaging obscures the connecting structure. Republican institutions elevated these officials, accepted their liabilities and tied the party’s fortunes to Trump. The predicament described here is not merely happening to the party; much of it was produced through the party’s own exercise of power.

Candidates are consequences

The Texas polling illustrates the point most clearly. AlterNet emphasizes Paxton’s personal controversies, including infidelity and corruption allegations, alongside impeachment efforts. Those allegations must remain allegations, and polling cannot establish why any individual voter prefers Talarico. But Republican exposure in Texas is not adequately explained by Talarico’s appearance, as the article’s “clean-scrubbed” framing suggests. That trivializes a contest the cited polling itself describes in terms of character and ideology.

Alaska’s unusual ballot structure—and the presence of another candidate named Dan Sullivan—may create uncertainty for the incumbent. Yet that curiosity should not eclipse Peltola’s reported eight-point advantage. Ballot quirks can affect a race; they do not erase voters’ agency or substitute for an account of why an incumbent is vulnerable.

A coalition receiving the bill

The larger pattern is a governing coalition losing insulation from its own decisions. The reported erosion is especially significant because Democrats would need to win at least two states Trump carried by 11 points or more, something the Times says no party has accomplished since 2008. That remains a formidable barrier, regardless of favorable early polling.

But the numbers expose how quickly structural advantages can weaken when presidential conduct, economic consequences and compromised candidates reinforce one another. Republicans are not being “blown out to sea” by fate. According to the reporting, they are confronting voters after choosing the leader, policies and candidates now weighing on them. The storm language is memorable; the chain of responsibility is the actual story.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: A ‘perfect storm’ is blasting the bottom out from under Trump’s party

item.title: Trump’s new MAGA cult videos are part of a much larger propaganda operation
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration placed personality-driven videos praising Donald Trump on national television, including Fox News and CBS. One video pairs repeated images of Trump with the refrain “Love me”; another revives a 2024 campaign message promising a “final battle” against political enemies. CNN reportedly said Trump helped select the material himself.

Citing The New York Times, AlterNet says Trump personally directed his budget director to use Department of Homeland Security money for a $20 million advertising contract. The White House described the videos as patriotic public-service announcements, while Trump argued that promoting his political slogan amounted to promoting “the spirit” of the country. The article cites reporting that administration insiders considered the project “obviously illegal,” but it does not establish that a court or other competent authority ruled the ads unlawful.

AlterNet places the broadcasts within a wider communications system spanning rallies, fundraising emails and aligned right-wing media. It also describes a September 10 convention appearance in Dallas where Trump led supporters through a personal loyalty pledge, encouraged them to vote, repeated unsupported cheating accusations and told nonvoters they would “go to hell.”

The power is governmental

This is not merely a politician buying flattering airtime. The relevant power belongs to the presidency: control over executive agencies, access to public money and the authority to direct senior officials. According to the reporting, Trump exercised that power personally, while his budget director and the Department of Homeland Security supplied the administrative machinery.

That distinction matters. A campaign spends campaign money to persuade voters. A government is supposed to spend public money for public purposes. If the Times account is accurate, the administration used an agency funded by taxpayers to manufacture presidential adulation. The officials who approved, contracted for and distributed the material were not confused spectators. They enabled the outcome.

Patriotism as personal loyalty

The White House’s defense performs the central substitution: praise for Trump becomes love of country, and a partisan slogan becomes civic education. That collapses the nation, the governing party and the president into one object of loyalty.

The Dallas pledge makes the hierarchy unusually explicit. Trump did not ask the crowd to affirm constitutional government or any public principle. He staged a pledge to “the greatest president,” meaning himself, then attached religious punishment to failure to vote. The performance was political mobilization organized around personal submission.

AlterNet calls this cult behavior and cites undue-influence expert Steve Hassan in support. That psychological label remains an interpretation. The observable political conduct needs no diagnosis: a president used ritual, grievance and claimed moral authority to place himself above ordinary democratic allegiance.

The enemies make the leader necessary

The videos do more than flatter Trump. They divide the public into followers and enemies: “communists,” Marxists, the “deep state,” the press and a supposedly diseased political class. That language converts political disagreement into contamination and removal.

The repeated promise to defeat or cast out enemies gives the personality campaign its governing purpose. The all-powerful leader requires a permanent siege; the siege, in turn, excuses greater loyalty to the leader. Whether every viewer experiences this as indoctrination cannot be established from the article. But the structure of the message is plain: belonging is conditional, dissent is suspect and national salvation is personalized.

The press shrinks the scandal

AlterNet argues that mainstream coverage concentrated on legality, political norms and electoral effects. The legal question is essential, especially when $20 million in public funds is reportedly involved. But treating the dispute only as a campaign-finance or appropriations puzzle understates what the money purchased.

The deeper issue is institutional capture. Public resources allegedly financed a partisan mythology in which the sitting president embodies the country and his opponents become enemies of it. Networks that carried the material were not exercising presidential power, but they provided distribution. Coverage that reduces the episode to whether the ads technically crossed a statutory line risks hiding the political project in the fine print.

Propaganda becomes infrastructure

The larger pattern is the conversion of government communication into personal rule by image, repetition and enemy designation. Fundraising emails can manipulate supporters; rallies can demand devotion. An executive agency allegedly paying to broadcast the same message is a different order of power because the state itself becomes the amplifier.

That is the systemic failure exposed here. The president reportedly initiated the project, subordinates operationalized it, broadcasters carried it, and much of the political press treated the result as another passing controversy. Propaganda does not need universal belief to succeed. It needs institutions willing to fund it, officials willing to execute it and gatekeepers willing to normalize its presence.

Thanks to Alter Net

item.title: ‘Insecure’ JD Vance targeted by MAGA senator as 2028 contenders trade blows: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz publicly accused each other of positioning for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. After Vance told NBC News that Cruz was “obviously” already running, Cruz told Politico on Saturday that political attacks often come from people who feel “insecure.”

Both men claimed their immediate priority was electing Republicans in the midterms. Cruz cited campaign appearances across several states and planned stops later that month; Vance had campaigned in Texas and Florida and was scheduled to rally in Alaska. Cruz has nevertheless said he could enter the 2028 discussion, while Vance is described as the early favorite. Politico reported that Vance’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to Cruz’s remarks.

Power before policy

This is not a dispute between outsiders competing to be heard. Vance holds the vice presidency. Cruz holds a Senate seat and possesses a national fundraising and campaign network built over years. Both can direct attention, money and party support toward candidates who will owe something to the coalition that elevated them.

Their campaign travel therefore serves two purposes at once: helping Republicans retain congressional power and accumulating endorsements, obligations and visibility for a possible presidential contest. Calling that activity mere midterm assistance strips it of its obvious institutional value.

The denial is the campaign

Vance’s accusation is convenient because it casts Cruz as distracted by ambition while presenting Vance’s own multistate campaigning as selfless party work. Cruz uses the same maneuver in reverse, answering a political charge with amateur psychology and then reciting his service to Republican candidates.

Neither man produced evidence establishing the other’s private motive. But the observable conduct is enough to expose the performance: two nationally prominent officials are publicly policing who may begin the succession struggle, even as both build the relationships that such a struggle requires.

Personality as camouflage

The “insecure” insult supplies an easy headline, but it is the least consequential part of the exchange. Treating the story as a clash of temperaments converts a contest over control of the Republican Party into celebrity gossip.

The material questions are who can convert present office into future dominance, who can claim credit if Republicans hold Congress, and who will emerge with the strongest network after the midterms. Vance begins with the authority and visibility of the vice presidency. Cruz counters with longevity, campaign travel and an explicit refusal to concede that the nomination belongs to Vance.

Loyalty as political currency

Their professed focus on electing Republicans is not separate from personal advancement. It is how advancement is built. Campaigning for candidates creates public proof of loyalty and private stores of political debt. Victory lets the surrogate claim influence; defeat lets him blame insufficient discipline or support.

That structure also rewards ideological conformity. Candidates receiving help from national figures gain incentives to endorse those figures later and to avoid crossing them now. The succession fight can shape congressional behavior years before a presidential primary formally begins.

The system beneath the spat

The larger pattern is a governing party treating public office, congressional elections and presidential positioning as parts of one continuous internal contest. RawStory’s account does not establish that either man has formally begun a 2028 campaign. It does show powerful officials accusing each other of precisely the ambition their own conduct helps cultivate.

The personal jab is political camouflage. The real story is advance competition over the machinery of the party—and the expectation that helping Republicans acquire power now should purchase influence over who inherits it later.

Thanks to Raw Story

item.title: Trump may absolve America's biggest crook — as a favor to his convicted friend
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Donald Trump’s Justice Department is reviewing claims that Watergate prosecutors committed misconduct, though the department told The Wall Street Journal that no formal investigation is underway. The review followed a two-hour Justice Department presentation by former Nixon aide Geoff Shepard, who alleged that special prosecutors secretly met with judges and withheld evidence.

The headline’s suggested favor involves Roger Stone, who worked on Richard Nixon’s campaign and later became a Trump ally. But the article supplies no evidence that Stone requested the review, influenced the department, or is being repaid. Nor has Trump “absolved” Nixon: the reported action is an informal departmental review of allegations against Watergate prosecutors.

The power is at Justice

The decisive actor is not Shepard, an 82-year-old Nixon defender offering a revisionist argument. It is the Justice Department, which granted that argument two hours at headquarters and chose to review it.

That distinction matters. Anyone can try to rehabilitate Nixon. Only an institution backed by federal authority can give the effort official weight. Even without a formal investigation, Justice can transform a partisan grievance into a government matter merely by treating it as worthy of departmental attention.

Revisionism with an official seal

Watergate did not end because prosecutors imposed a fashionable political narrative. As RawStory recounts, the scandal involved the Democratic National Committee burglary, the ensuing cover-up, Nixon’s attempt to stop the pursuit of his White House tapes, an unexplained 18½-minute tape gap, and an 8-0 Supreme Court ruling requiring him to surrender recordings. Republican senators ultimately warned Nixon that the Senate would convict him if he remained in office.

Shepard’s allegations may be examined on their evidence. But “Watergate as Lawfare” does more than allege procedural misconduct: it imports a contemporary political slogan into an extensively documented abuse-of-power scandal. The point is not necessarily to disprove every underlying event. It is to place prosecutors in the dock and recast the powerful official who obstructed scrutiny as the injured party.

The article overreaches too

RawStory is right to focus on institutional degradation, but its headline outruns its own reporting. It presents absolution and a favor to Stone as though they were established developments. The body establishes neither.

That kind of embellishment weakens the stronger indictment already available. Justice officials chose to entertain a Nixon aide’s prosecutorial-misconduct theory while, according to RawStory, career prosecutors were departing and lawyers were resigning in protest over the department’s direction. The documented decision is troubling enough without inventing a hidden transaction.

Rewriting accountability

The larger pattern is the conversion of accountability into persecution. When prosecutions, court orders and congressional pressure constrain presidential power, revisionists rename the constraint “lawfare.” The misconduct of the officeholder then becomes secondary to alleged unfairness by those who investigated it.

That inversion serves present power. A Justice Department willing to reconsider Watergate through the language of presidential victimhood does not need to erase the historical record. It need only teach the public that even the clearest case of executive abuse was really a case of prosecutors going too far.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump may absolve America’s biggest crook — as a favor to his convicted friend

item.title: The ominous 3-word warning everyone missed in the chaotic Jack Smith hearing
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Senate hearing intended to discredit former special counsel Jack Smith instead exposed Republican senators’ factual sloppiness and fixation on defending Donald Trump. Senator Eric Schmitt accused Smith of lying about attending an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024, but the messages Schmitt displayed reportedly placed Smith in College Park, Maryland, for an Iowa–Maryland game—not Atlanta.

Smith testified that his investigation had developed evidence he believed could prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Trump committed serious crimes in attempting to overturn the 2020 election. He also defended obtaining senators’ call metadata as a lawful investigative practice, stressing that the records did not contain call contents.

The headline’s “three-word warning” is not clearly identified in AlterNet’s text. The apparent reference is Smith’s broader warning that the rule of law is usually weakened gradually through attacks on institutions and public servants, followed by his claim that such an effort had occurred “since January 2025.”

Who held the power

The senators questioning Smith held the institutional power in the room. They controlled the hearing, selected its subject and possessed the authority and public platform of Congress. Smith, no longer directing the investigation, could testify and rebut accusations; he could not prosecute, legislate or determine the hearing’s agenda.

That distinction matters because the spectacle invited viewers to treat the senators as aggrieved victims of an overreaching prosecutor. But the senators were exercising state power to interrogate the former official who had investigated Trump. Their complaints concerned investigative scrutiny arising from an alleged attempt to obstruct the lawful transfer of presidential power.

An accusation built backward

Schmitt’s presentation, as AlterNet describes it, was not merely an embarrassing mix-up. He displayed private messages and floated a theory linking Smith to Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, apparently because he believed Smith had been in Atlanta after Willis disclosed her relationship with Nathan Wade.

The geography was wrong, and even the proposed Atlanta trip would not by itself have established a meeting. That is confirmation bias operating through congressional authority: begin with suspicion, hunt for fragments that resemble support, and present the insinuation before establishing the facts.

Calling Smith a “dirtbag” further stripped away the pretense of neutral oversight. Schmitt was not shown testing a supported allegation. He was shown using an official hearing to manufacture one.

The grievance inversion

Republicans also centered the collection of senators’ phone metadata. According to Smith’s testimony, investigators obtained timing and duration records—not call contents—during a complex criminal investigation, and the senators involved were not necessarily targets.

That framing reverses the relevant hierarchy of harm. The central matter was an investigation into an alleged scheme to overturn an election. The hearing redirected attention toward powerful officeholders’ indignation at being touched by ordinary investigative methods.

AlterNet weakens its own case when it speculates about what economically distressed voters must want or believe. No evidence presented in the article establishes how those voters interpreted this hearing. The stronger argument requires no invented electorate: senators used public authority to elevate their personal grievance over scrutiny of presidential conduct.

Protection through spectacle

The hearing’s political function, as reported, was to recast investigation as persecution. Ted Cruz accused Smith of succeeding where Richard Nixon failed by weaponizing the Justice Department against political opponents. Smith countered that Republican officials—including Trump administration officials—had supplied some of the investigation’s strongest testimony.

That answer punctures the preferred story. Evidence does not become partisan merely because it implicates a party leader, and investigators do not create political opponents by examining alleged crimes committed by politicians. Branding accountability as “weaponization” gives officeholders a ready-made excuse to delegitimize any institution capable of constraining them.

The system beneath the fiasco

Schmitt’s bungled accusation was useful theater because it was so visibly incompetent. It was also a distraction from the more consequential fact: members of the Senate used an oversight forum to attack an investigation into an alleged effort to prevent the lawful transfer of power.

The larger pattern is institutional self-protection. Political power scrutinizes the scrutinizer, converts routine investigative contact into elite victimhood and substitutes insinuation for evidence. The danger in that machinery does not depend on every accusation succeeding. Repetition can make accountability appear inherently corrupt—and place anyone enforcing it permanently on trial.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The ominous 3-word warning everyone missed in the chaotic Jack Smith hearing

item.title: Trump's 'beloved' golf getaway a 'ghost town' — and it's all his fault
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Adrian Carrasquillo’s reporting for The Bulwark, says intensified federal immigration enforcement has emptied restaurants and damaged commerce in Doral, Florida, a heavily Venezuelan community that Donald Trump carried by 23 points in the 2024 election.

A worker at El Arepazo estimated business was down 80 percent. The owner of Central Park Food Station reported a 40 percent decline that worsened during the previous month’s surge in ICE activity. Both attributed the losses to residents’ fear of detention and deportation; Carrasquillo reported that employees at several businesses had pending asylum cases.

The power is federal

Doral’s restaurant workers, asylum seekers and small-business owners do not control immigration status, detention policy or ICE operations. The Trump administration does. The immediate political fact is therefore not that a community mysteriously “deteriorated,” but that federal enforcement created fear powerful enough to suppress work, movement and spending.

That distinction matters. “Ghost town” is a description of the result, not an explanation. The mechanism reported here is government power: people stay home because contact with public life may expose them or someone they know to detention and deportation.

Fear is the policy’s reach

Enforcement does not end with the people taken into custody. Its influence travels through households and commercial networks. As one restaurant owner explained, people avoid work, lose income and stop spending. Businesses then discard unsold food and lose revenue.

These are not incidental atmospherics. They are foreseeable consequences when immigration enforcement makes ordinary movement feel dangerous. The state need not close a restaurant directly if its actions frighten away the workers and customers who keep it alive.

Loyalty offers no protection

Doral swung 19 points toward Trump between 2020 and 2024. That electoral support did not give its residents control over the administration’s immigration machinery, nor did it shield local businesses from the consequences of its use.

Trump’s attachment to Doral makes the contrast especially stark. He has celebrated his golf resort there, sought to make it an international diplomatic venue and reportedly borrowed its aesthetic for his second-term Rose Garden renovation. But personal affection for a place is not accountability to the people living around it. A politician can prize a property, a brand and a symbolic landscape while his administration’s policies destabilize the surrounding community.

The framing should name the actor

Calling the damage Trump’s “fault” is directionally clear but institutionally incomplete. The relevant chain runs through presidential authority, administration policy and ICE enforcement. Those are decisions and instruments, not weather.

The weaker framing would cast frightened residents as people who simply stopped participating in the economy. The reporting instead identifies why they withdrew: fear of being detained or deported after people’s status was stripped away, with some workers still pursuing asylum claims. Responsibility belongs upstream, with the officials exercising coercive power—not downstream, with those altering their lives to avoid it.

The systemic error

This episode exposes a recurring political fraud: leaders solicit votes from immigrant communities by promising recognition and security, then wield federal authority in ways that make those same communities economically and socially precarious.

The contradiction is not between Trump’s fondness for Doral and some inexplicable local decline. It is between political branding and material governance. The resort remains useful to the Trump mythos; the people beyond its gates absorb the consequences. In that arrangement, place is cherished as an asset while community is treated as expendable.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘beloved’ golf getaway a ‘ghost town’ — and it’s all his fault

item.title: Former congressman cackles in Scott Jenning’s face
item.description:
What happened

Former South Carolina congressman Bakari Sellers laughed at Republican commentator Scott Jennings on CNN after Jennings blamed weak job growth and declining consumer sentiment largely on economic conditions President Donald Trump inherited from former President Joe Biden. Jennings argued that inflation had mostly normalized but that earlier price increases still shaped voters’ perceptions.

Anderson Cooper replied that Trump was already deep into the second half of his term and noted that Jennings’s defense resembled the Biden administration’s claim that economic conditions were better than voters felt. Sellers said household costs—not favorable indicators—were driving public anger, and pointed to competitive races in Republican strongholds. AlterNet also reported that some Republican candidates, including Leigh Wambsganss and Rep. Byron Donalds, were removing Trump branding from their websites; Wambsganss was reportedly removing the word “Republican” as well.

The people in charge own the result

The laughter supplied the clip, but Cooper’s timeline supplied the relevant fact: according to the report, Trump was no longer at the beginning of his term. A president can inherit economic conditions. A governing party cannot indefinitely treat inheritance as an exemption from accountability.

Republicans held the institutional power at issue. Their administration set federal policy, their candidates sought the benefits of party affiliation, and their media defenders tried to separate public dissatisfaction from the officials currently governing. Biden’s record may help explain how prices reached a given level. It does not erase the decisions made afterward by those empowered to respond.

Jennings recycled the excuse Republicans rejected

Jennings’s argument was not that households were imagining higher prices. It was that inflation had slowed while the accumulated cost increases remained painful. That distinction can be economically coherent. Politically, however, it reproduces the same defense Republicans used against Biden: the indicators are improving, but voters have not recognized it.

Cooper exposed that reversal directly. When Democrats offered this argument, Republicans treated household frustration as decisive evidence of failure. When the same frustration threatened Republicans, Jennings reframed it as a lagging perception caused by the previous administration. The standard changed when power changed hands.

The kitchen table is not a messaging problem

Sellers’s strongest point was not partisan but material. GDP, markets, and inflation rates do not pay a utility bill or fill a prescription. A slower rate of price growth means prices are rising less quickly; it does not restore what households lost in purchasing power.

Calling that gap a communications problem misdirects attention from governing choices to voter comprehension. People deciding which bill to postpone do not need a lecture about aggregate indicators. They need relief. Treating their hardship as a failure to appreciate the data protects officeholders from the consequences of conditions they now have power to address.

The disappearing brand tells the truth

AlterNet’s examples of Republican candidates stripping Trump—and, in Wambsganss’s case, reportedly even the Republican label—from campaign websites matter more than partisan mockery. If those changes were responses to electoral risk, they show politicians seeking distance from a governing brand without surrendering the party machinery, donor networks, or policy coalition attached to it.

That is not accountability. It is reputational laundering: preserve the institutional benefits while hiding the affiliation voters might punish. The candidates’ edits do not establish why particular races became competitive, and Sellers’s remarks do not prove an electoral outcome. But the retreat itself indicates that some Republicans saw their public identification as a liability.

Power changes the alibi

The larger pattern is familiar. Parties campaign by assigning full responsibility to the incumbent, then govern by distributing responsibility backward through time. Economic pain becomes decisive when it can be weaponized and complicated when it must be owned.

The central issue is therefore not whether Sellers laughed at Jennings. It is whether officials and their defenders will name who currently possesses the authority to act. Political accountability collapses when power remains in the present but responsibility is permanently reassigned to the past.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Former congressman cackles in Scott Jenning’s face

item.title: Alabama newspaper shatters Trump’s lies with vicious factcheck
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that AL.com fact-checked remarks President Donald Trump made Friday night in Mobile, Alabama, and found numerous claims false, exaggerated, contradictory, or unsupported. Among them, Trump linked an Interstate 10 bridge groundbreaking to “$3 billion” in administration funding, although AL.com reported that no single grant or appropriation of that size existed. The project’s largest federal grant—$550 million—came through legislation signed by former President Joe Biden, while much of its financing is a repayable federal loan backed by toll revenue.

AL.com also reported that Trump misstated former NFL player Wesley Britt’s career length, promised a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” that would require congressional approval, and claimed sole credit for crime reductions that began during the Biden administration. It rated his blanket-amnesty claims false and found that his asserted $21 trillion in investment included commitments and projects that had not yet occurred.

Most immediately relevant to voters’ daily lives, Trump said his administration had done “nothing but bring prices down.” AL.com reported instead that consumer prices had risen about 4.7 percent since he returned to office, gasoline prices were more than 40 percent above their January 2025 level amid disruptions tied to the Iran conflict, and diesel prices had reached record highs the previous month.

The power belongs to the president

The central actor is not a confused spectator struggling to interpret complicated statistics. Trump is the president, speaking from the country’s most powerful office to supporters at a friendly venue. His words can set legislative priorities, move markets, define Republican campaign messaging, and turn proposed benefits into political leverage.

That matters especially for the “Trump Dividend.” According to the reporting, sending every adult citizen $5,000 would require Congress to act, and some Republicans had already raised objections involving debt, inflation, and legality. Trump nevertheless presented a conditional legislative proposal as a personal reward voters could unlock by keeping Republicans in power. The institutional authority belongs to Congress; the political branding assigns the money to Trump.

Credit is claimed, costs are displaced

The bridge story shows how political appropriation works. A president attaches his name to a visible groundbreaking while the less photogenic facts—the Biden-era grant, the repayable loan, toll revenue, and an unfunded second phase—are pushed outside the frame.

Trump did help advance the project and permit the first phase to begin, according to AL.com. That is the defensible claim. Inflating that role into $3 billion in administration funding converts partial involvement into ownership while obscuring who authorized the largest grant and who will ultimately repay much of the financing.

The same pattern appears in the investment figure. Announced plans, multiyear commitments, and future projects are counted as though promised capital were already deployed. The headline number absorbs uncertainty; Trump takes immediate credit for outcomes that may remain years away or never fully materialize.

The timeline is the target

Crime declined, but AL.com reported that the decline began in 2022 under Biden. Trump’s rhetoric strips away that chronology and presents a continuing trend as his own singular achievement. The statistical distortion is not merely an argument over percentages. It erases the period in which the change began so that causation can be reassigned to the current president.

His immigration claims perform a related trick through scale. AL.com and PolitiFact found no evidence that the Biden administration gave blanket amnesty to everyone who entered unlawfully, while estimates of the undocumented population were between 11 million and 12 million—not the 25 million Trump invoked. An unsupported figure supplies the sense of invasion; the false amnesty claim supplies a culprit.

The correction cannot match the spectacle

AlterNet frames AL.com’s fact-check as a “vicious” takedown, but that language mistakes rebuttal for power. The newspaper can document discrepancies after the rally. It cannot recreate the president’s platform, compel him to correct the record, or ensure that the correction reaches the audience that heard the original claims.

The imbalance is structural. Trump can compress federal financing, economic trends, immigration policy, and hypothetical legislation into memorable declarations. Journalists must then unpack appropriations, loan terms, timelines, legal authority, and statistical baselines. The fabrication or exaggeration is portable; the correction arrives burdened with necessary detail.

Calling these statements “freewheeling” risks laundering responsibility through style. The relevant fact is that the president made claims that available evidence did not support, and a local newsroom performed the elementary institutional work of checking them.

A politics of counterfeit ownership

The larger pattern is government recast as a personal franchise. Public infrastructure becomes Trump’s gift. A payment requiring congressional approval becomes a Trump dividend. Crime trends become his achievement. Future investment becomes present accomplishment. Price increases become price reductions by assertion.

This rhetoric does more than decorate a rally. It trains citizens to understand public money, collective institutions, and long-running social trends as possessions of one political leader. The systemic error is not that the facts are difficult. It is that presidential power can manufacture a simpler reality faster than institutions can document the real one—and that much of the political system rewards the claim before anyone has finished checking the ledger.

Thanks to Alter Net

item.title: MAGA darling in swing district gets ominous polling news
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Democratic challenger Cait Conley leads Republican Rep. Mike Lawler 48 percent to 46 percent among likely voters in New York’s 17th Congressional District, with 7 percent undecided. The Emerson College Polling/PIX11 News survey of 400 voters was conducted September 27–29 and carries a credibility interval of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points, so it does not establish a clear leader.

The poll nevertheless contains bad indicators for Lawler: his favorable rating fell from 52 percent in October 2024 to 45 percent, while his unfavorable rating rose from 42 percent to 46 percent. Conley leads by seven points among voters who say they are “very excited” to vote, though 22 percent remain neutral toward her.

Voters ranked the economy first among their concerns at 31 percent. “Threats to democracy” rose from 10 percent in 2024 to 23 percent, while immigration fell from 20 percent to 13 percent. Fifty-two percent disapproved of U.S. military action in Iran, compared with 37 percent who approved.

Lawler owns his record

Lawler holds the seat. Conley does not. That is the basic power relationship obscured whenever a congressional contest is narrated chiefly as ominous “news” happening to an incumbent.

Lawler chose to defend Donald Trump’s policies repeatedly on cable television, according to RawStory. That alliance gave him national standing within the Trump movement, but it also tied his political identity to decisions and consequences beyond the district. He cannot claim the benefits of proximity when it attracts attention and then be treated as a passive casualty when voters sour on the product.

The poll is a warning, not a verdict

A two-point advantage inside a 4.9-point credibility interval is not proof that Conley is winning. RawStory’s dramatic framing runs ahead of what this single survey can establish.

The more consequential evidence is cumulative: Lawler’s favorability deteriorated, highly enthusiastic voters leaned toward Conley, and the district’s issue priorities shifted away from immigration and toward concerns about democratic governance. None of those findings guarantees an electoral outcome. Together, they suggest that the incumbent’s coalition is under pressure on several fronts at once.

The establishment misread

Some senior House Democrats reportedly doubted Lawler could be beaten, while the broader Democratic campaign operation invested heavily in the race. That disagreement exposes a familiar institutional failure: party elders can turn an incumbent’s reputation for durability into a substitute for testing whether that durability still exists.

The campaign apparatus appears to have treated the district’s competitiveness as actionable rather than ceremonial. That matters because candidate quality alone does not overcome incumbency. Money, recruitment and sustained attention determine whether voter dissatisfaction becomes an actual contest or merely an unused opening.

The realignment beneath the horse race

The sharper story is not that a “MAGA darling” received ominous news. It is that an incumbent in a district Kamala Harris carried in 2024 may be confronting the cost of serving two political constituencies: a national Trump-aligned audience and a closely divided electorate at home.

The issue movement is equally revealing. Immigration—the subject Republicans routinely elevate as an organizing threat—declined as a leading concern in this poll, while anxiety about democratic governance more than doubled. The survey cannot explain why voters changed priorities, and it does not prove which candidate benefits from every concern. But it does show that political messaging cannot permanently dictate what voters regard as urgent.

Power eventually acquires a price

Incumbents are often covered as though elections simply descend upon them. They do not. Officeholders use votes, media appearances and alliances to build a record; challengers, parties and voters then decide whether that record will carry a cost.

Lawler still possesses the advantages of office, and Conley’s narrow polling lead remains statistically uncertain. But the systemic lesson is already visible: institutional power breeds assumptions of permanence, while political coverage converts accountability into personal misfortune. The meaningful question is not whether bad polling happened to Lawler. It is whether his exercise of power has made enough voters willing to remove him.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: MAGA darling in swing district gets ominous polling news

item.title: Kennedy Center moves to sell all of its Steinway pianos
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Steinway grand pianos were removed from the Kennedy Center and moved for sale while the building was closed. A Washington Steinway representative said the instruments were being offered at heavy discounts; photographs taken by mover Van Lewis showed the removal, and Kennedy Center harpist Susan Robinson said musicians had noticed the pianos disappearing.

The closure’s duration and legal status remain contested. Director Matt Floca announced one week of closure, then another. The Justice Department told the court the center was not closing permanently and described the work as safety-related renovations. Yet vendors were reportedly being told the building was shuttered, and the Kennedy Center did not answer AlterNet’s questions.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper had already halted the Trump-aligned board’s planned two-year shutdown while litigation proceeds, calling its decision “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” His order permits repairs but requires 30 days’ notice before demolition, new construction, or another major project change. Lawyers challenging the closure said an unauthorized shutdown would violate that order.

Power is not ambiguous

Donald Trump selected the board that took control of the Kennedy Center. That board pursued the extended closure. The administration is directing the renovation policy, and the Justice Department is defending its account in court. These are the actors with institutional authority over the building, its operations, and its contents.

The musicians, performers, movers, and vendors do not control any of those decisions. They are observing the consequences: canceled appearances, displaced instruments, uncertain access, and a cultural institution stripped of the conditions needed to function. Treating their alarm as the central controversy would invert the power structure.

A closure by installments

The administration’s position, as reported, is that the Kennedy Center is undergoing limited safety work rather than being closed in defiance of the court. But the accumulating conduct matters: a proposed two-year shutdown, successive short-term closures, vendors reportedly told the building is shuttered, and performance instruments removed for sale.

The reporting does not establish that every instrument is being liquidated or that the center has permanently closed. It does establish a widening gap between the government’s narrow description and the visible operational reality. A shutdown does not become less consequential because officials announce it one week at a time.

The pianos are evidence, not decoration

The Steinways are not merely expensive objects, though new examples were valued in the story at roughly $187,000 to $246,900 or more. They are working infrastructure. Removing them diminishes the center’s capacity to operate as a performing-arts institution, regardless of whether officials call the process renovation, temporary closure, or something else.

That is why the movement of the pianos carries political weight. Institutions can be hollowed out through administrative acts that sound provisional: relocate the equipment, disperse the professionals, suspend programming, defer reopening. Each step can be described as temporary even as the cumulative damage becomes harder to reverse.

Congress leaves the gate open

Democrats proposed legislation to protect the building, according to AlterNet, but Republican Sen. Mike Lee blocked it, leaving supporters needing 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. That is not procedural weather. It is an exercise of power that prevents Congress from imposing an additional constraint while the administration presses forward.

The court has supplied the clearest existing limit, requiring notice and continued scrutiny. But litigation is a brake, not a management system. Judges can halt an unlawful plan; they cannot make a politically captured board value the institution it governs.

Capture, then depletion

The larger pattern is institutional capture followed by controlled degradation. A handpicked board assumes authority, the president attaches his name to a national cultural institution, performers withdraw, operations contract, and valuable tools leave the building while official explanations remain narrower than the observable disruption.

The unresolved facts still matter: AlterNet did not establish the fate of instruments beyond the Steinways, and the court has not determined that the administration violated its order. But uncertainty at the edges should not obscure the documented structure. Those holding power initiated the shutdown plan, their allies blocked a legislative safeguard, and the institution is losing functional capacity while they insist the public should focus on terminology.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Kennedy Center moves to sell all of its Steinway pianos

item.title: MAGA outraged as it discovers Trump handed $15B Iowa project to Indian company: 'Comical’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump looks on next to a bust of Benjamin Franklin during the announcement of a Minnesota company’s plan to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, from the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 28, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump announced a proposed $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, with the White House claiming it would create 1,750 jobs. The plant is to be built by Mesabi Metallics, a Minnesota-based subsidiary wholly owned by India-based Essar Group.

On September 29, 2026, former Republican representative Marjorie Taylor Greene and Grace Chong of Steve Bannon’s “War Room” attacked the project because Mesabi Metallics has sponsored H-1B workers. They questioned how many of the projected jobs would go to Americans, but the reporting provides no hiring plan or evidence that any particular share has been reserved for visa holders.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The article also notes Mesabi Metallics’ history of bankruptcy, delays, unpaid contractors and disputes with Minnesota officials. It does not establish that Trump “handed” the company a federal contract, subsidy or exclusive benefit; it establishes that he announced and promoted the planned project.

Power belongs to the dealmakers

The decisive actors are not prospective workers, immigrants or social-media commentators. They are the Trump administration, which put presidential authority behind the announcement, and Essar Group’s subsidiary, which would control construction and hiring.

The White House supplied the politically valuable number—1,750 jobs—without the details needed to evaluate it. The article identifies no binding local-hiring commitment, union agreement, wage standard or enforcement mechanism. A projected job count is therefore not proof of who will be hired, what they will earn or whether the positions will materialize.

MAGA finds its scapegoat

Greene and Chong direct their anger toward H-1B workers before RawStory establishes that those workers will dominate—or even substantially staff—the Iowa plant. That is convenient misdirection. Mesabi Metallics’ executives would make hiring decisions, while federal officials set visa rules and any conditions attached to public support.

Foreign workers do not award visas to themselves, design labor policy or choose corporate ownership structures. Treating them as the central threat converts a question about government oversight and corporate power into another immigration grievance.

The record they chose to ignore

The more concrete warning in the reporting is Mesabi Metallics’ reported history of delays, bankruptcy, unpaid contractors and conflict with Minnesota officials. Those facts concern whether the company can deliver the plant and meet its obligations. Yet the right-wing backlash described by RawStory centers instead on nationality and visas.

That choice exposes the limits of “America First” politics. Corporate reliability, contractor payment and enforceable benefits for workers receive less attention than whether management might employ foreigners. The weaker actors become the spectacle; the company’s record becomes background noise.

Branding is not accountability

Greene’s criticism reveals a factional rupture, but not a serious governing program. Calling MAGA “America Last” punctures Trump’s branding while leaving the essential questions unanswered: What public concessions are involved? What guarantees protect Iowa workers? Who bears the cost if the project stalls? The article does not provide those answers.

RawStory’s own framing also overreaches. Its headline says Trump “handed” the project to an Indian company, while the body describes a presidential announcement and corporate construction plan. Without evidence of an award, incentive package or procurement decision, that wording implies a transaction the reporting does not document.

The recurring political bargain

This is the familiar structure of nationalist economic theater: an administration announces an enormous investment and a precise jobs figure; a corporation gains legitimacy; and supporters are invited to celebrate before enforceable terms are visible. When contradictions surface, outrage travels downward toward migrant labor instead of upward toward officials and executives.

The systemic error is not simply hypocrisy over H-1B visas. It is a politics that substitutes ownership labels and worker nationality for scrutiny of contracts, labor standards and corporate performance. That substitution protects institutional power while giving the audience a weaker target to blame.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: MAGA outraged as it discovers Trump handed $15B Iowa project to Indian company: ‘Comical’

item.title: Trump 'starting to unravel' — and only making voters more furious
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s insistence that the economy is strong has collided with intense dissatisfaction among voters in four states he won by double digits in 2024. Navigator Research managing director Melissa Toufanian said polling in Alaska, Ohio, Iowa, and Texas put Trump’s net approval at minus 14 across the four states and underwater in each one.

Toufanian said Trump was 17 points underwater in Iowa, where 60 percent disapproved of his handling of the economy and 50 percent strongly disapproved. She also cited pessimism about his presidency and the war with Iran. The headline’s claim that Trump is “starting to unravel” comes from New Republic podcast host Greg Sargent’s interpretation of those findings—not from a clinical assessment or an established fact.

AlterNet also cites conservative columnist Tim Carney, who argued that Trump is harming farmers’ ability to sell crops and then trying to compensate them with government checks. Meanwhile, Trump has continued promoting polling that depicts sustained support among Republican or MAGA voters.

Power made the damage

Trump holds the presidency. His administration possesses the institutional power to shape the economic and foreign policies provoking the dissatisfaction described in the polling. Farmers and other voters absorbing the consequences do not.

That distinction matters because political coverage often treats economic anger like weather: it arrives, intensifies, and mysteriously damages approval ratings. Carney’s criticism restores the missing chain of agency. The government interferes with people’s livelihoods, then presents compensation as generosity. The check may soften the loss, but it does not erase who imposed it.

Compensation is not control

Carney compares Trump’s approach with a familiar Republican caricature of Democratic governance: eliminate someone’s job, then offer benefits. His point is not simply that the policy is unpopular. It is that financial compensation cannot replace economic control, professional identity, or confidence that a market will remain available.

Trump can place supporters on a stage beside relief checks. He cannot make that ceremony equivalent to an undamaged livelihood. When state power creates the disruption and then purchases visible gratitude from those affected, assistance becomes political theater layered over dependence.

Polling cannot carry the whole argument

The reported numbers are striking, especially the intensity of disapproval in Iowa. But the article pushes beyond what the evidence establishes when it treats polling in four states as proof that groups in Trump’s coalition are broadly “abandoning him” in 2026.

Toufanian herself supplied an important complication: these voters remain distrustful of Democrats. Disapproval of Trump does not automatically become Democratic support, and unfavorable polling does not by itself mean Republican Senate seats will change hands. Sargent called that possibility “really crazy,” which is enthusiasm about an electoral opening, not evidence that the opening will produce a victory.

The “unraveling” frame is also weaker than the underlying story. It personalizes a conflict produced by presidential decisions, reducing policy consequences to speculation about Trump’s condition. The relevant fact is not whether he appears emotionally composed. It is that voters in heavily Republican states reportedly disapprove of how he is using power.

The counter-polling defense

Trump’s promotion of friendlier polling is an attempt to control which measurement counts. AlterNet describes him highlighting figures showing continued backing among Republicans or the MAGA base while the Navigator results show deep dissatisfaction in states central to his return to office.

Those claims are not necessarily contradictory: a president can retain substantial support among committed partisans while losing approval across a broader electorate. Treating favorable subgroup numbers as a complete answer simply narrows the public until only loyalists remain visible.

The governing bargain breaks

The larger pattern is a government creating material disruption, offering compensation, and expecting partisan identity to close the gap between injury and gratitude. That bargain works only while supporters accept political loyalty as a substitute for results.

The reported anger does not prove a realignment, much less a Democratic revival. It shows something more immediate: concentrated presidential power produces identifiable consequences, and even loyal constituencies can recognize when government aid is being used to manage damage that government policy helped create.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump ‘starting to unravel’ — and only making voters more furious

item.title: 'Scrambled the map': Rick Wilson stunned by 'shock story of 2026’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican strategist Rick Wilson called Ohio “one of the shock stories of 2026” after a Marist poll placed Democrats ahead in two major statewide races. Sherrod Brown led appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted 51% to 43% among registered voters, while Amy Acton led Republican Vivek Ramaswamy 50% to 44% in the governor’s race.

The September 24–27 survey of 1,298 registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, also gave Democrats a 50%–47% advantage on the generic congressional ballot. Donald Trump’s approval stood at 42%, while 41% of respondents described their congressional vote mainly as a vote against him and 25% as a vote for him.

Wilson’s remark that the results had “scrambled the map” referred to the possibility that a state Trump carried by roughly 11 points in 2024 could become competitive in 2026 and complicate Republican planning for 2028. The poll is evidence of a competitive moment, not proof that Ohio has permanently “turned blue.”

Power is not a polling lead

Republicans still hold the institutional advantage described in the story. Husted occupies the Senate seat because he was appointed after JD Vance became vice president. Trump can deploy presidential attention on his behalf, including a reported campaign appearance in Vandalia. The GOP is defending an office it already controls in a chamber where a single race could affect the balance of power.

Brown and Acton have polling leads, but neither has governing authority by virtue of those numbers. The distinction matters: Democrats are challengers seeking power, while Republicans possess it and can use incumbency, appointment, national attention, and party infrastructure to retain it.

The appointment voters can revisit

The Senate contest is not simply a referendum on two candidates. Husted reached the Senate through appointment rather than this electorate’s choice, and the special election will determine who serves the remainder of the term. That makes the race a public review of a decision already made within Republican-controlled institutions.

Brown’s position is also more complicated than a comeback narrative. He lost his seat to Bernie Moreno in 2024 and is now seeking a different path back through the vacancy created by Vance’s elevation. The poll suggests he currently benefits from severe Republican weakness among independents, who favored him 58% to 33%. It does not establish that those voters have become Democrats.

Trump is the drag the framing softens

The clearest political signal is not Wilson’s surprise. It is the imbalance between voters mobilized against Trump and those mobilized for him. His 42% approval, combined with 64% disapproval among independents, gives Ohio Republicans a problem created by the leader of their party and inherited by their candidates.

Calling Ohio’s movement a “shock” turns measurable dissatisfaction into a weather event. Republicans chose to bind their electoral identity to Trump. If that attachment now costs them support, especially among independents, the result is not mysterious partisan drift. It is a foreseeable consequence of political ownership.

Economic pain has a beneficiary problem

The poll found that 41% of registered voters said their personal finances had worsened over the previous year, compared with 19% who said they had improved. AlterNet does not establish what caused those conditions, and the survey cannot prove that financial dissatisfaction produced the Democratic leads.

But governing parties are judged under the conditions they preside over. Republicans cannot claim dominant power when it flatters them and plead helplessness when voters assign responsibility. Trump’s planned intervention for Husted underscores the contradiction: the party is relying on the same figure whom a large share of respondents say they are voting against.

The map follows accountability

The larger pattern is not that Ohio has suddenly acquired a new ideological identity. It is that partisan geography becomes unstable when a governing coalition alienates enough voters outside its base. The decisive numbers here are the independent margins, not the color commentators assign to the state.

A single poll cannot predict November, much less 2028. It can expose where power has become vulnerable. Republicans hold the offices, made the appointments, and tied their candidates to Trump. If Ohio becomes competitive, that is not the map scrambling itself. It is voters reconsidering who should control the institutions that govern them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Scrambled the map’: Rick Wilson stunned by ‘shock story of 2026’
