item.title: Fox icon blasts Republican's Jack Smith face-plant: 'Brought this on himself
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith of lying under oath about attending a basketball game on February 3. Schmitt suggested Smith had attended an Atlanta Hawks game and implied the trip connected him to Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis. Smith said he was actually in College Park, Maryland, watching Caitlin Clark and the Iowa Hawkeyes play the Maryland Terrapins.

According to the outlet, footage placed Smith at the Iowa–Maryland women’s game. After initially insisting that Smith had not answered truthfully, Schmitt conceded to TMZ that Smith had been at the Hawkeyes game. Fox Business host Brit Hume said Schmitt had “brought this on himself,” while Schmitt later responded on X with a joke about Smith being a Caitlin Clark fan.

The accusation was the exercise of power

Schmitt was not an internet spectator making a careless guess. He was a United States senator questioning a witness in the Senate Judiciary Committee. That position gave him a microphone, institutional legitimacy and an opportunity to accuse Smith repeatedly of perjury.

The distinction matters. Smith had to answer an allegation delivered under the authority of congressional oversight; Schmitt faced no comparable burden before making it. The senator used the hearing’s investigative posture to turn his own inference into an accusation against someone else.

The evidence did not support the insinuation

AlterNet says Schmitt claimed to possess text messages indicating that Smith attended the Warriors–Hawks game. But the information, as described in the report, concerned Smith being at “a game,” not necessarily an NBA game or a game in Atlanta. Schmitt supplied the unsupported leap.

The larger insinuation was weaker still. Even if Smith had attended a basketball game in Atlanta, the reporting identifies no evidence that doing so would establish coordination with Willis. The geographic suggestion substituted for an evidentiary chain: Atlanta meant Willis, and Willis meant collusion. That is not proof. It is association dressed up as discovery.

Retreat became reframing

Once confronted with footage, Schmitt recast his allegation as a question and said people could decide whether Smith had told the truth. But according to AlterNet’s account, he had not merely asked where Smith was. He had repeatedly invoked perjury and claimed to have caught Smith lying.

That retreat shifts responsibility from the accuser to the audience. Schmitt made the charge; “people” were then invited to adjudicate the doubt he had manufactured. His later joke similarly avoided a direct acknowledgment that the premise of his accusation had collapsed.

The weaker actor was made to carry the burden

The hearing’s framing placed Smith under suspicion while insulating the senator who advanced the faulty claim. Even after Schmitt’s factual premise failed, he cited Smith’s supposed prior untruthfulness to justify continuing distrust. That reasoning is circular: suspicion licenses an accusation, and the accusation’s failure becomes grounds for more suspicion.

Brit Hume’s criticism is notable because it refused that misdirection. Schmitt’s embarrassment was not inflicted by hostile coverage or clever editing. On the facts AlterNet presents, it followed from his own decision to escalate incomplete information into a public allegation of criminal conduct.

Oversight without accountability becomes propaganda

Congressional questioning can expose misconduct, but only if lawmakers treat evidence as a constraint. Here, the institution’s authority was used to generate a dramatic charge first and sort out the basic facts later. The immediate consequence was reputational harm to Smith; the systemic consequence is the degradation of oversight into televised insinuation.

The pattern is broader than one mangled sports reference. A powerful official makes an accusation, preserves it through ambiguity when it fails, and replaces correction with mockery. The error travels under the seal of the Senate. The concession arrives as a punchline. That imbalance is not incidental to the political tactic—it is what makes the tactic useful.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox icon blasts Republican’s Jack Smith face-plant: ‘Brought this on himself

item.title: Republican group with white power ties openly plots infiltration of Florida government
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that the American Restoration Coalition, a network of Florida Republicans using “Heritage American” rhetoric, is recruiting candidates and placing allies in local government. ARC leaders openly described a strategy of winning seats on planning and zoning boards, city councils and state legislatures. Its members helped Marshall Rawson win a Republican primary for a north-central Florida House seat after campaigning for him in July and August.

The network already includes Palm Bay Councilman Chandler Langevin and planning and zoning board member Jonathon Norris, whom Langevin appointed. RawStory connected ARC members to Patriot Front propaganda, Florida Active Clubs and the secretive Avalon Group. The outlet also documented Rawson and Norris at the 2017 Unite the Right rally; Rawson acknowledged attending, while Norris did not respond.

ARC promoted a speech in which Patriot Front leader Thomas Rousseau called for revolution, and its account described Active Club founder Robert Rundo as “a legend.” RawStory further identified photos and videos linking Norris and ARC cofounder Stefan Hartmann to a gym used by Active Club participants and to armed training imagery. Langevin, Hartmann and Norris did not substantively answer the outlet’s questions.

The project is institutional capture

This is not merely a story about offensive social-media activity. ARC’s declared objective is to convert an organized racial movement into government power. Its leaders have identified the offices, recruited personnel, canvassed for a legislative candidate and claimed multiple local victories.

Planning boards and city councils are not decorative posts. They govern land use, development and the distribution of local authority. State legislators write law. ARC understands that durable political power is accumulated through obscure appointments and low-profile elections long before a movement commands national attention.

The people exercising institutional power here are also plainly identifiable. Langevin holds elected office and appointed Norris to Palm Bay’s Planning and Zoning Board. ARC mobilized volunteers for Rawson. Republican primary voters then made Rawson the party’s nominee for the reported House seat. The outcome was enabled through ordinary political machinery, not imposed from outside it.

The euphemism is doing political work

“Heritage American” gives racial exclusion the surface appearance of historical stewardship. ARC’s own communications strip away that ambiguity. Langevin answered a challenge about whether the organization was “pro white” by asking what the critic thought “Heritage American” meant. ARC separately posted that “White South Africans” and “Old stock Europeans” could stay.

That language matters because respectable packaging is part of the strategy. RawStory reports that Patriot Front similarly replaced conspicuous Nazi imagery with Americana after Unite the Right. The doctrine did not become less exclusionary; the branding became more useful to mainstream conservative audiences.

ARC applies the same technique institutionally. Hartmann spoke publicly about defending American institutions while the organization circulated speeches rejecting democratic structure and endorsing revolution. The contradiction is not resolved by choosing the more respectable statement and ignoring the rest of the record. Public constitutional language can function as camouflage when the same network promotes racial hierarchy and a chain-of-command model.

The weaker actors are not the cause

Coverage of extremist organizing often drifts toward spectacle: masked men, gym photographs, rifles, pseudonymous accounts and vicious posts. Those details establish the network’s associations and paramilitary posture, but they can also distract from the mechanism producing actual power.

The central political act was not a man posing at a shooting range. It was an elected councilman appointing an ally to a government board. It was organizers knocking on doors for a candidate. It was a Republican primary converting that mobilization into a nomination.

Nor is this a case of obscure extremists somehow “infiltrating” an unsuspecting political system without assistance. RawStory’s evidence describes participation through appointments, party elections and campaign work. The sharper question is what screening, opposition or accountability existed inside the institutions that admitted them. On the evidence presented, the article does not establish what Florida Republican officials knew or whether party leaders approved ARC’s project. It does establish that the existing political structure gave the network usable routes to office.

Exposure is not accountability

The men profiled by RawStory largely answered scrutiny with silence or abuse. Langevin attacked the reporter’s politics and appearance. Hartmann dismissed the outlet while vacationing in Italy. Rawson denied knowing what the reporter meant when asked whether Norris was the other man who attended Unite the Right with him, then acknowledged that Norris was his friend and ended the call.

Those responses do not rebut the documented photographs, videos, posts or organizational statements. But journalism alone cannot remove an appointee, defeat a nominee or compel a party to enforce boundaries. Disclosure supplies evidence. Institutions decide whether that evidence carries consequences.

The larger pattern is the conversion of white-nationalist organizing from public spectacle into routine administration. After Unite the Right produced violence, prosecutions and reputational damage, parts of the movement changed their presentation and pursued quieter forms of legitimacy: fitness clubs, civic rhetoric, local appointments and Republican primaries. The masks conceal faces; the ballot line confers authority. Systemic failure begins when political institutions treat that progression as an image problem instead of a struggle over who gets to wield the state.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Republican group with white power ties openly plots infiltration of Florida government

item.title: 'Can't walk in a straight line': Fresh concerns about Trump's health after tech meeting
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that video from a White House appearance on September 29, 2026, showed President Donald Trump standing awkwardly and apparently struggling to walk after a luncheon with technology executives. Commentators reviewing the footage said he seemed to drag his right leg and have difficulty walking straight.

The reporting cites social-media speculation about physical injury and cognitive decline but provides no medical assessment establishing either explanation. It places the footage alongside previously observed bruising, swollen ankles, verbal slips, and slurred speech, while noting that the White House has repeatedly dismissed concerns about Trump’s fitness.

Observation is not diagnosis

The video may justify questions. It does not justify a diagnosis.

RawStory’s weakest move is treating commentary from partisan influencers as meaningful evidence of cognitive decline. A peculiar stance or altered gait can have many causes, and none can be established from a short recording. Ben Meiselas can describe what he sees; Brooklyn Dad Defiant cannot convert mockery into neurology.

That framing gives Trump’s defenders an easy escape. They can attack reckless speculation instead of answering the legitimate question: Has the White House provided an adequate, credible account of the president’s health?

The power sits inside the White House

Trump holds the presidency. His aides control access, schedule appearances, release medical information, and decide how concerns are answered. The burden of institutional disclosure therefore belongs to the administration, not to people dissecting video clips online.

The relevant imbalance is not between Trump and his critics. It is between a White House with privileged medical information and a public asked to accept repeated dismissals without the evidence needed to evaluate them. If officials possess a benign explanation, they have the power to provide it. If they decline, speculation is a foreseeable consequence of their information control.

Spectacle displaces scrutiny

The story’s ridicule-heavy framing misdirects attention from powerful officials toward a president’s body as entertainment. Jokes about “dangling legs” generate engagement, but they establish nothing about his capacity to govern.

They also blur separate questions: whether Trump displayed an unusual gait, whether he has a physical condition, whether he has cognitive impairment, and whether any condition affects his official duties. Collapsing those questions may intensify suspicion, but it weakens accountability by replacing demands for records and precise answers with viral amateur diagnosis.

Proximity is political power

The setting matters. Trump had just met at the White House with executives from Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, and SpaceX—companies positioned near immense economic, technological, and governmental power. Yet the coverage turns those relationships into scenery while making an unexplained movement the central drama.

That is a familiar distortion in political journalism: visible irregularity overwhelms less visible access. The public gets frame-by-frame analysis of a leg while elite executives receive direct presidential proximity. One subject is easy to mock; the other requires reporting on influence, commitments, and decisions.

The systemic error

Presidential health is a legitimate matter of public concern because the office concentrates extraordinary authority in one person. But seriousness requires evidence proportional to the claim. RawStory documents footage that raised questions; it does not establish cognitive decline or identify the cause of Trump’s apparent difficulty walking.

The larger pattern is an accountability system caught between secrecy and spectacle. The administration can restrict meaningful information, partisan commentators can fill the vacuum with certainty they have not earned, and publishers can package that certainty as concern. The result is abundant attention with little verified knowledge—the ideal environment for those already holding power.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Can’t walk in a straight line’: Fresh concerns about Trump’s health after tech meeting

item.title: Schmitt's monstrous gaffe may have just cost his aide a White House job
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Politico, reports that Ethan Harper, general counsel to Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, was expected to leave the senator’s office on Friday and join the White House Staff Secretary’s office the following week. After a Tuesday Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, however, three anonymous sources said the move was in doubt. Neither outlet established that the job had been formally withdrawn.

At the hearing, Schmitt tried to connect former special counsel Jack Smith with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis by claiming Smith had attended an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024. Smith denied it. Schmitt accused him of perjury before the premise collapsed: the evidence concerned an Iowa Hawkeyes women’s college basketball game, not the Atlanta Hawks.

Harper stood behind Schmitt displaying a board of text-message screenshots, but Politico reported no evidence that Harper was responsible for the error. The White House declined to comment; Schmitt’s office and Harper did not immediately provide responses.

The senator held the power

Schmitt controlled the hearing time, delivered the accusation and invoked the grave charge of perjury. Smith was the witness compelled to answer. Harper held the visual aid, but Schmitt held the office, the microphone and the institutional authority behind the attack.

That hierarchy matters because the apparent employment consequence may fall on the aide whose visible role made him convenient to blame. Politico’s reporting does not establish who researched the allegation, approved the board or failed to verify the teams. It does establish who publicly converted that defective work into an accusation: Schmitt.

An accusation built before the facts

This was not merely a verbal slip. Schmitt arrived with posters and a theory intended to suggest coordination between prosecutors investigating Donald Trump. The display gave the performance the appearance of documented proof. The documentation did not prove the central claim.

When Smith denied attending the Hawks game, Schmitt escalated to accusing him of lying under oath. Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s response—that Schmitt should get his facts together before hurling insults—identified the basic failure. The accusation came first; factual control came later.

Accountability flowing downhill

Harper’s prospective White House role involved managing documents and materials sent to the president, while his work for Schmitt included interviewing judicial candidates. Accuracy is plainly relevant to such responsibilities. But the available reporting does not show that Harper created or approved the false claim, so treating his stalled transfer as a clean act of accountability would outrun the evidence.

What the episode does show is a familiar distribution of risk. Senior officials receive the cameras and political benefit from an aggressive attack. Staff members perform the supporting labor and may absorb the professional damage when the attack disintegrates. Institutional power protects the person who chose to speak while exposing the person standing behind him.

The framing softens the offense

Calling this a “gaffe” understates what happened. Confusing two basketball teams was the factual blunder. Accusing a witness of perjury on the strength of that confusion was Schmitt’s decision.

The distinction is political, not semantic. “Gaffe” language turns an abuse of senatorial authority into personal embarrassment. The substantive problem was that a senator used a congressional hearing to advance an unsupported insinuation about prosecutorial coordination and escalated a disputed premise into an allegation of criminal conduct.

Spectacle without responsibility

The larger pattern is investigative theater designed to produce a damaging clip rather than establish a fact. Visual aids supply certainty, confrontation supplies drama, and the correction arrives only after the allegation has been broadcast.

When that machinery fails, responsibility can be displaced onto anonymous staff work, faulty preparation or generalized confusion. But institutions do not make accusations by themselves. Schmitt made this one. Unless consequences reach the official who exercised the power, the system teaches politicians that reckless allegations are cheap—and teaches their aides that accuracy matters most when someone more powerful needs a scapegoat.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Schmitt’s monstrous gaffe may have just cost his aide a White House job

item.title: ‘Does not exist’: Trump’s sweeping Time interview claims get brutally fact-checked
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Time fact-checked 12 claims President Donald Trump made during a Sept. 28 White House interview. Trump said he won 86% of the popular vote in 2024. He actually received 49.8%, against Kamala Harris’s 48.3%; the figure 86 referred to his Electoral College margin, 312 votes to 226.

Trump also claimed 99% popularity in Israel and 107 million views for a September Republican midterm-convention speech. Time found no poll showing 99% approval, citing instead a 2026 Pew survey in which 66% of Israelis expressed confidence in him. Nielsen data cited by Time showed his Fox News speech averaging 2.5 million viewers, while NBC said the NFL season opener averaged 25.1 million.

Power without accuracy

These are not marginal errors from a powerless spectator. They are claims made by the president from the White House, backed by the government’s communications apparatus and amplified by partisan media. Trump possesses the institutional power; Time’s fact-checkers possess only the capacity to annotate what that power broadcasts.

The disparities are not subtle. A plurality became 86%. Sixty-six percent became 99%. An average audience of 2.5 million became 107 million. Whatever produced each assertion, the political effect is consistent: Trump appears more electorally dominant, internationally adored and culturally commanding than the reported evidence supports.

The numbers serve the ruler

Each inflation turns a measurable result into a story of near-total acclamation. That matters because claims of overwhelming support do more than flatter Trump. They portray disagreement as marginal and opposition as illegitimate—a rhetorical advantage for an officeholder who already commands the executive branch.

The available reporting establishes false or unsupported claims, not Trump’s private intent. But motive is unnecessary to identify the function. Repeatedly replacing ordinary majorities and limited audiences with fantasies of unanimity conditions followers to treat the leader’s assertions as more authoritative than election returns, polling or ratings.

Fact-checking’s narrow repair

Time did necessary work: it named the relevant categories, supplied the figures and showed where Trump conflated or inflated them. Yet fact-checking can also shrink a political problem into a clerical one. Calling the popular-vote claim a conflation describes the numerical mechanism without confronting the power relationship.

Trump created the falsehoods. Media institutions then spent time reconstructing reality claim by claim. That arrangement gives the president the initiative and makes correction permanently reactive. The lie travels as political identity; the correction arrives as homework.

The spectacle of dominance

The recurring subject is not policy but supremacy: the biggest mandate, nearly universal foreign approval, an audience larger than professional football’s. These claims manufacture the appearance that Trump does not merely govern but eclipses ordinary comparison.

RawStory’s “brutally fact-checked” framing adds its own layer of spectacle. The brutality here was arithmetic. Presenting correction as a dramatic takedown risks making the fact-checker’s tone the story when the consequential fact is simpler: a sitting president used his office to circulate claims contradicted by basic public measurements.

A system built for repetition

The larger pattern is an asymmetry between political power and factual accountability. A president can generate a dozen dubious claims in one interview; journalists must investigate each separately, while supporters can dismiss the entire correction as hostile media.

That is not public confusion distributed evenly among competing actors. It is a powerful official making specific claims and institutions with less coercive authority trying to contain the damage afterward. When fabricated dominance becomes routine political communication, the systemic failure is not merely that false numbers are spoken. It is that power can keep forcing reality to defend itself.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Does not exist’: Trump’s sweeping Time interview claims get brutally fact-checked

item.title: Trump TV viewer numbers have plummeted to a 'genuinely embarrassing' level: analyst
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that the White House’s “Trump TV” stream, launched after President Donald Trump barred Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House over what he called “fake news,” has attracted strikingly small audiences. According to a Daily Beast analysis cited by RawStory, viewership opened as high as 8,500 but later fell to 91 people at 2 a.m. Eastern.

The stream runs continuously on the White House’s YouTube account and reportedly consists largely of old speeches and appearances. RawStory also notes that an accidental Instagram broadcast by former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt drew more than 1,000 viewers, while a separate pedicure livestream attracted more than 2,000.

The reporting does not provide average viewership, comparable overnight figures, or enough time-series data to measure the channel’s overall audience. It establishes a dismal snapshot, not a complete ratings analysis.

The power is the exclusion

The 91 viewers are amusing. They are not the politically important number.

The consequential act was Trump’s decision to exclude three news organizations from White House access. The presidency controls credentials, briefings and proximity to officials. Reporters and viewers do not possess comparable institutional leverage. Whatever the administration’s complaint about coverage, it used government-controlled access as punishment and then promoted its own channel as a substitute.

That is the power structure: the White House restricts independent intermediaries while presenting official material as the replacement. Whether the replacement succeeds as entertainment does not reduce the significance of the restriction.

A ratings joke obscures the decision

RawStory frames the episode primarily as personal humiliation for a president associated with television ratings. The comparisons—to Air Force One capacity, White House staffing and unrelated livestreams—make the channel look ridiculous. They do little to explain what the government did.

This is misdirection through mockery. The story’s weaker actor is not Trump TV’s tiny audience; it is the press corps whose access depends on decisions made by the institution it covers. Viewers rejecting stale programming did not impose the information restrictions. Trump did.

A failed propaganda product is still a propaganda product. Its immediate audience size tells us about its appeal, not about the legitimacy or consequences of the government sidelining independent scrutiny.

Official content is not reporting

Old speeches and presidential appearances offer controlled images, selected messages and no necessary mechanism for challenge. Calling that stream an “information” service blurs the distinction between access to government messaging and journalism about government conduct.

That distinction is precisely what the ban makes politically relevant. Independent outlets can question claims, pursue contradictions and report facts the administration would prefer not to emphasize. A White House feed exists to transmit the White House’s choices. It cannot replace adversarial reporting because it is the object of that reporting.

The reported audience collapse suggests even committed supporters may not find an endless official loop compelling. It does not show that the attempt to narrow the information environment was harmless.

Failure can still normalize control

The larger pattern is an administration using access as leverage, labeling disfavored coverage “fake news,” and offering state-produced communication as the approved alternative. The channel’s poor performance may expose the weakness of the spectacle, but ridicule alone leaves that structure intact.

The systemic error is treating authoritarian media management as a ratings flop. Trump TV can fail commercially while the underlying practice succeeds politically: punish scrutiny, privilege official narration and train coverage to focus on the ruler’s embarrassment instead of the institution’s exercise of power.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump TV viewer numbers have plummeted to a ‘genuinely embarrassing’ level: analyst

item.title: Trump ridiculed for trying to ‘rewrite history’ with war story: ‘All you can do is laugh’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump claimed on October 1, 2026, that he had always said eliminating Iran’s nuclear threat would take four to six weeks—and that he had instead done it “in one night.” CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale disputed that account, saying Trump’s March remarks described the expected duration of the Iran war generally, not a separate timetable for neutralizing a nuclear threat.

Critics accused Trump of revising his earlier statements after the fact. Former Republican representative Joe Walsh called him a habitual liar, while MeidasTouch said the war had already lasted seven months. The article does not independently establish that Iran’s nuclear threat was eliminated in one night; it reports Trump’s assertion and the immediate challenges to it.

The president owns the claim

The institutional power here belongs to Trump. He is not a commentator fumbling with an old prediction. He is the president describing a war, its purpose, and its supposed success.

That position gives his language material force. Presidential claims shape what agencies defend, what allies must interpret, and what the public is asked to accept about military operations. Trump chose to redefine his original timeline and declare a decisive accomplishment. The responsibility for that account is his.

A retrofit disguised as foresight

According to Dale’s comparison, Trump’s March statements forecast that the war would last six weeks or less. His later post narrowed that forecast retroactively: the timeline supposedly referred only to removing the nuclear threat, while the remaining months became maintenance.

That is not a minor clarification if the original remarks made no such distinction. It is a convenient reconstruction that turns an apparently missed prediction into a completed promise. The measurable claim—how long the war would last—is replaced by a vaguer one about an allegedly extinguished threat.

Ridicule is not accountability

RawStory organizes the dispute around mockery: Trump was “ridiculed,” Walsh denounced him, and Andrew Egger said laughter was the only response. Those reactions convey disbelief, but they also shrink a presidential war narrative into another episode of online spectacle.

The central issue is not that Trump said something laughable. It is that the president asserted an unverified military success while altering the meaning of his earlier public statements. Treating that primarily as material for ridicule misdirects attention from the institution capable of producing evidence—and from its failure, in this account, to supply any.

The missing burden of proof

Trump’s formulation is politically useful because “the Iran nuclear threat” is not defined in the report. No benchmark is given for what was destroyed, disabled, delayed, or verified. “The rest of the time” can therefore absorb every complication without falsifying the victory claim.

RawStory provides criticism of Trump’s wording, not evidence resolving the underlying military question. That distinction matters. Dale’s fact-check, as described, supports the charge that Trump changed his account of the timeline. It does not by itself establish the condition of Iran’s nuclear capabilities.

Power rewrites the metric

The larger pattern is executive self-exoneration through moving definitions. A prediction about a war’s duration becomes a prediction about one objective. A prolonged conflict becomes proof that an instant victory is merely being preserved. Failure is not acknowledged; the measurement is changed.

Political coverage fails when it treats that maneuver as personality content. The consequential fact is that the official with the greatest power over the war also claims the authority to redefine what success meant, when it occurred, and why the fighting continued. Laughter may register the absurdity. It does nothing to constrain the power behind it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump ridiculed for trying to ‘rewrite history’ with war story: ‘All you can do is laugh’

item.title: Trump was stupid to put his signature on this lie — it will blow up in his face
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that the Trump White House planned to mail roughly one million ACA marketplace customers $500 checks bearing Donald Trump’s signature, accompanied by a letter claiming the Biden administration had overcharged them and withheld the money. Trump repeated that accusation in a video, but the article says the administration supplied no supporting accounting.

The outlet cites KFF’s Larry Levitt, who said the surplus likely originated during Trump’s first term, when his administration collected more in marketplace user fees than it spent while limiting enrollment advertising and assistance. RawStory also reports that Biden later reduced those fees. The supposed “Biden overcharge,” then, is the lie Trump put his name on; the claim that it will backfire is the columnist’s prediction, not a reported outcome.

The checks were reportedly aimed at ACA customers in 30 states shortly before the November 3 election. RawStory connects the payments to Trump’s September 9 promise of future $5,000 checks if voters kept Republicans in control of Congress, but it provides no published program accounting establishing how recipients or payment amounts were selected.

The power is in the allocation

The recipients did not create this arrangement. The executive branch controlled the accumulated federal money, devised the payment program, selected its presentation and attached the president’s name and political accusation.

That is the central power relationship. A president can turn public administration into personal promotion because officials under his authority control the machinery: the database, the checks, the letter and the timing. Taxpayers supply the money; the White House supplies the branding.

Calling the checks a bribe goes beyond what the article legally establishes. But the reported design plainly creates a political benefit: conspicuous cash, delivered near an election, carrying the president’s signature and a message blaming his predecessor. Without the missing accounting, the administration has not shown why direct $500 payments were the necessary policy remedy.

The letter launders responsibility

The administration’s story shifts attention from decisions made under Trump. According to the KFF account cited by RawStory, the surplus accumulated because his first administration did not spend money intended to advertise ACA coverage and help people enroll. The same reporting says Biden reduced the relevant user fees.

If that account is accurate, Trump is claiming credit for returning money generated by his own administration’s underspending while assigning fault to Biden. That is not bureaucratic confusion. It is a specific, unsupported accusation embedded in an official communication.

The stronger indictment is administrative dishonesty, not the article’s florid speculation about electoral catastrophe. A government capable of explaining the source, legal authority and formula for a million payments has no legitimate excuse for withholding that accounting while distributing a politically useful narrative.

A refund designed as a spectacle

RawStory notes that $500 exceeds what any individual recipient could have paid in excess fees. That weakens the White House’s description of the payment as a straightforward reimbursement. A genuine fee correction would ordinarily connect what was collected to what is returned—or reduce the fee prospectively.

Instead, the reported program produces a round number, a presidential signature and an election-season event. It converts an obscure pool of public money into a personalized gift. The material benefit may be real, but the ownership claim is false: Trump is not giving recipients his money.

The article’s most important unanswered question is therefore not whether recipients should accept the checks. It is why public funds were distributed through a formula the administration had not disclosed, under a factual claim it had not substantiated.

The weaker actors are not the cause

ACA customers are the targets of this messaging precisely because they have less institutional leverage. RawStory describes them as people buying coverage through the federal exchange, including farmers, small-business owners, hourly workers and early retirees. They bear premium increases; they do not set federal fees, subsidy policy or insurer rates.

The article reports that enhanced ACA subsidies expired under Republican legislation and that about three million people subsequently dropped coverage. Those former customers would receive nothing under a program limited to current enrollees. The government’s payment spectacle thus excludes people who could no longer afford to remain inside the system.

RawStory sometimes buries this serious power analysis beneath insults and unsupported claims about private motives. That excess makes the argument easier to dismiss. The documented contrast is damning enough: federal policymakers altered the affordability structure, then presented a small payment to selected remaining customers as presidential generosity.

Government as campaign property

The larger pattern is the conversion of public authority into personal political capital. The executive controls resources, a president places his name on their distribution, and official messaging tells recipients whom to thank and whom to blame. Missing documentation is not a side issue; it is what prevents the public from distinguishing sound administration from election-timed patronage.

This system works by erasing the chain of ownership. Public money becomes the leader’s gift. Administrative choices become somebody else’s fault. Citizens confronting higher costs are recast as grateful beneficiaries of a politician’s signature.

The likely political consequence cannot be known from the reporting. But the institutional consequence is already visible in the program as described: policy becomes branding, accountability becomes accusation, and the state is made to advertise the person temporarily controlling it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump was stupid to put his signature on this lie — it will blow up in his face

item.title: 'Then do it': Ultra far-right Republican calls out Trump team ineptitude
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that James Fishback, a far-right Republican who lost Florida’s 2026 gubernatorial primary to Byron Donalds, mocked the Trump administration for failing to act on its own hostility toward H-1B visas. After Vice President JD Vance called the program “completely broken” and suggested abolishing it, Fishback replied on X: “Then do it. What are you waiting for?”

H-1B visas provide temporary work authorization to foreign professionals in specialized occupations and are widely used by technology companies. During his campaign, Fishback demanded that 1,900 Florida employers fire H-1B workers and hire Floridians instead, threatening businesses with what he called the “ultimate wrath” of state government.

AlterNet does not report a new administration decision on the program. The event is a dispute over action: Vance denounced the system, while Fishback accused the administration of substituting rhetoric for policy.

The power is in the administration

Fishback currently holds no public office. His leverage is ideological and rhetorical, not institutional. The officials with actual power are Vance, President Trump, and an administration capable of proposing legislation, changing executive policy within legal limits, and directing immigration enforcement.

That distinction matters because Fishback’s post is less an act of opposition than an attempt to enforce discipline from the administration’s right. He is demanding that officials convert a shared political target into government action.

Workers become the target

Vance framed H-1B hiring through a hypothetical in which a lower-paid foreign accountant replaces an American worker. AlterNet’s report does not establish how representative that example is, nor does it provide evidence that abolishing the entire program would restore particular jobs or raise wages.

Fishback goes further. His threat against Florida employers casts foreign employees—not the companies making hiring and wage decisions—as disposable intruders. Employers control recruitment, compensation, and staffing. Migrant workers do not design the visa system or set corporate labor policy. Yet Fishback’s proposed punishment begins with firing them.

Enforcement as spectacle

The phrase “ultimate wrath of the state” reveals the political appeal. Fishback did not merely advocate different visa rules; he advertised state retaliation against businesses that employed legally authorized workers.

The underlying labor question—who suppresses wages, who profits, and which rules permit abuse—gets displaced by a spectacle of expulsion. That is scapegoating with an administrative costume: concentrate public anger on workers with less political power while leaving corporate control of employment largely intact.

The article’s framing falls short

AlterNet correctly identifies Fishback’s complaint as an attack on the administration’s failure to move quickly. But describing the exchange chiefly as “ineptitude” risks accepting Fishback’s premise. The reported facts do not establish bureaucratic incompetence. They establish a gap between Vance’s rhetoric and government action.

That gap could reflect legal constraints, political disagreement, competing business interests, or simple inaction; the article does not determine which. Calling it ineptitude turns an unresolved policy choice into a management failure and makes faster coercion sound like competence.

The radical flank sets the clock

This episode shows how authoritarian policy pressure can operate without electoral success. A defeated candidate can still police the governing coalition by treating denunciation as insufficient and delay as betrayal. The demand is always for quicker punishment, broader executive force, and fewer distinctions between regulating employers and purging workers.

Fishback’s post is therefore not important because he controls the state. It is important because he is telling those who do control it what increasingly counts as proof of loyalty: not merely attacking immigrants in speeches, but making identifiable people bear the consequences.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Then do it’: Ultra far-right Republican calls out Trump team ineptitude

item.title: Sheepish MAGA lawmaker flees show after devastating blunder
item.description:
What happened

Sen. Eric Schmitt withdrew from a planned C-SPAN appearance with Sen. Chris Coons one day after his attempt to accuse former special counsel Jack Smith of lying collapsed during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, according to AlterNet’s account of Mediaite’s reporting.

Schmitt claimed Smith attended an Atlanta Hawks game on Feb. 3, 2024, and used that claim to imply Smith was in Georgia coordinating with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis. Smith denied attending the game. He later said he had watched Caitlin Clark play in an Iowa-Maryland women’s college basketball game, leading Sen. Amy Klobuchar to point out that Schmitt had apparently confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes.

MS NOW anchor Michael Steele subsequently reported that Republican committee staff had warned Schmitt that the material was “unvetted,” but that Schmitt used it anyway. The reporting does not establish why Schmitt canceled the C-SPAN appearance. It also says a planned White House job for Schmitt aide Ethan Harper was in doubt after the hearing, citing three unnamed people familiar with the plans.

The senator had the power

This was not an innocent mix-up between two similarly named teams. Schmitt held the microphone, the Senate office and the institutional authority to question a witness under the threat implicit in congressional proceedings. Smith was required to answer an accusation Schmitt presented in public as grounds for declaring, “I think you’ve already perjured yourself.”

That imbalance matters. A senator can turn sloppy opposition research into an official spectacle. The target must rebut it immediately, while the accusation acquires the visual authority of a hearing room, a poster board and a government title.

The failure was Schmitt’s

If Steele’s reporting is accurate, Schmitt was warned that his material had not been vetted. He nevertheless treated it as sufficiently reliable to accuse Smith of a crime. That makes “blunder” an inadequate description. The error may have been factual, but the decision was institutional: Schmitt chose accusation before verification.

His staff may have assembled the material, but Schmitt delivered it and escalated it. Any consequences for an aide’s White House prospects would preserve a familiar hierarchy of accountability: subordinates absorb professional damage while the officeholder who wielded the allegation keeps the seat.

The insinuation came first

The basketball confusion was not incidental. It was the factual hinge supporting a larger insinuation that Smith had traveled to Georgia to coordinate with Willis against Donald Trump. Once the hinge broke, so did the insinuation.

Calling the episode a “gotcha” gone wrong risks making it sound like failed television banter. It was an attempt to use congressional power to manufacture suspicion around separate prosecutions. The method depends on speed: state the implication confidently, force a denial, and trust that partisan audiences will remember the accusation longer than the correction.

Retreat is not accountability

Schmitt’s withdrawal from the program spared him an immediate encounter with sustained questioning, but the reporting does not prove that embarrassment caused his decision. What it does show is that he was scheduled to appear, suffered a conspicuous factual collapse and pulled out the following day.

That sequence illustrates how political officials can exercise power publicly and evade scrutiny afterward. A witness cannot simply disappear when a senator levels an allegation. The senator, by contrast, can decline the next interview and let surrogates minimize the episode.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is an accountability system calibrated backward. A powerful official can convert unverified material into an accusation carrying the prestige of the Senate, while correction depends on another senator recognizing a sports-team mix-up in real time.

The scandal is not merely that Schmitt confused the Hawkeyes with the Hawks. It is that the institution made his certainty more consequential than his accuracy. When congressional oversight becomes a stage for allegations that staff reportedly warned were unvetted, the mistake is not confined to one humiliating exchange. It becomes a governing technique: insinuate under official authority, retreat when exposed, and leave everyone else to clean up the record.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Sheepish MAGA lawmaker flees show after devastating blunder

item.title: 'Can’t find a silver lining': Trump leaves GOP with nowhere to turn
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s low approval ratings were weighing heavily on Republican candidates in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign. Polls cited in the report placed his approval between 32 and 38 percent, gave Democrats an eight- or nine-point advantage in congressional preferences, and showed especially weak public confidence in his handling of affordability.

Republican candidates had responded by emphasizing local issues and their own records, particularly as voters faced cost-of-living pressures, tariffs and higher fuel prices amid the continuing war with Iran. Trump complicated that strategy at the GOP convention in Dallas by telling Republicans to campaign as though he were on the ballot.

The polling did not settle individual races: district lines, candidate quality, turnout and late shifts could still alter the outcome. But analysts told the i Paper that Republicans had little favorable terrain left, while Washington Post polling analysis found GOP candidates running about four points ahead of Trump on average.

The power sits in the White House

The central actor is not an abstract Republican “brand.” It is the president, who holds executive power, dominates his party and is directing its candidates to bind their fortunes to his.

That matters because the pressures identified in the reporting are tied to governing: affordability, tariffs and war are not campaign aesthetics. They concern decisions made or sustained by institutions under presidential and congressional control. Republican candidates may prefer to discuss local records, but voters are entitled to judge the governing coalition by what it governs.

Distance without dissent

The four-point gap between Republican candidates and Trump suggests that some voters distinguish between the president and individual nominees. It also reveals the party’s preferred escape route: tactical separation without a substantive break.

Candidates can change the subject, foreground constituent service or omit Trump from an advertisement. None of that establishes opposition to his policies or independence from his leadership. Unless they identify which decisions they reject and what they would change, “local focus” is less a governing position than a method of avoiding accountability.

Trump closes the exit

Trump’s instruction to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” removes some of the ambiguity Republicans might otherwise exploit. He is asking candidates to nationalize their races around a president whom the cited surveys show most voters disapprove of.

That demand reflects the party’s power structure. Competitive-state candidates have electoral reasons to create distance, but Trump has the institutional platform and partisan authority to insist on loyalty. Their dilemma was not imposed by Democrats, the press or confused voters. It arose from the leader Republicans empowered demanding political identification with his record.

Polling is evidence, not destiny

The article is strongest when it presents specific measures and weakest when its language approaches inevitability. National approval and generic congressional ballots describe a hostile environment; they do not allocate seats. The report itself acknowledges the variables that can disrupt a national projection.

Nor does the evidence show that Republicans literally had “nowhere to turn.” It shows that their available options were politically costly: defend an unpopular president, separate themselves from him, or try to redirect attention. Calling that predicament a lack of choices risks disguising agency. Republican candidates still had choices; what they lacked was a painless one.

The system protects loyalty until it becomes liability

This is the recurring pattern of a leader-centered party. Officials gain influence by attaching themselves to the president, then discover that the attachment cannot be switched off when his standing deteriorates. Loyalty functions as an asset during internal contests and as a liability before a broader electorate.

The consequence is larger than one difficult midterm. When a party makes personal allegiance more important than policy independence, its candidates lose the ability to respond credibly to public dissatisfaction. The polling may move, and individual Republicans may outperform Trump. But the structural failure remains: a governing party that surrendered its internal agency cannot convincingly rediscover it only when voters begin imposing a price.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Can’t find a silver lining’: Trump leaves GOP with nowhere to turn

item.title: 'Make sure Republicans win': Tumult at DOJ as top-down orders rattle investigators
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, summarizing reporting by The Atlantic, says the Trump White House has pressed FBI and Justice Department leaders to pursue indictments connected to President Donald Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election. More than 40 current and former officials, FBI employees, and congressional staffers described demands relayed as coming from the White House, while FBI Director Kash Patel reportedly pushed investigators to “look harder” after their work failed to produce the anticipated cases.

One Justice Department official said that after asking about rules designed to insulate elections from political interference, the official was told, “There are no rules. Just make sure Republicans win.” A department spokesperson denied that this was ever DOJ guidance, and the White House denied dictating whom the department investigates or charges.

The reported pressure had not produced the promised 2020-election arrests. Prosecutors and Trump-aligned lawyers left the effort amid disputes over demands for indictments before the November election, while agents sought outside legal advice. About 260 FBI employees were diverted for two weeks to examine Fulton County ballot data, an effort the reporting says found nothing substantive.

The power runs downward

The institutional hierarchy is not ambiguous. Trump controls the executive branch. The White House directs administration policy. Patel leads the FBI. Prosecutors, analysts, and rank-and-file agents work beneath them.

That matters because this is not principally a story about unsettled employees or bureaucratic “tumult.” The agitation is the consequence, not the cause. The central allegation is that political leaders pushed federal law enforcement to validate the president’s preferred account of an election, then demanded more searching when investigators failed to find supporting evidence.

Patel has acknowledged receiving directions from Trump, Stephen Miller, and other White House officials, according to the reporting. Receiving direction is not itself improper; law-enforcement leaders operate within the executive branch. The critical question is whether those directions concern legitimate priorities or predetermined prosecutorial outcomes. The reported demands for arrests and pre-election charges place that distinction under severe strain.

An investigation in search of a case

Proper investigations begin with evidence and proceed toward conclusions. The process described here appears inverted: leaders announced that arrests were coming, assigned investigators to revisit material, and pressed for charges on an electoral timetable.

Patel’s public prediction that arrests were “coming soon” is especially revealing. It placed the prestige of the FBI director—and the political expectations of the president—behind a result investigators had not delivered. Once leadership commits publicly to prosecution, every failure to find evidence can be treated as insufficient effort instead of a substantive answer.

The Fulton County operation shows the institutional cost. Hundreds of employees were pulled from other duties, two analysts who questioned the process were escorted out, and the review reportedly produced nothing substantive. The government spent investigative capacity trying to manufacture confirmation for a claim rather than allowing the evidence to determine the outcome.

Resistance is not accountability

Departures and internal objections demonstrate that some officials recognized legal or professional danger. They do not establish that the system successfully checked the pressure.

Joe diGenova resigned from overseeing the “grand conspiracy” investigation, Kurt Olsen left, prosecutors departed after reported clashes with leadership, and FBI co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey also exited. Sources said Bailey raised legal objections, though he called that account “absolutely false.” Those distinctions matter. What remains clear is that personnel resistance has largely taken the form of departure, private alarm, or seeking outside counsel.

That is institutional attrition, not institutional control. When experienced officials leave while the people issuing the demands retain authority, resistance can remove obstacles without changing the policy. Fear of being fired or forced into participation is evidence of a chain of command functioning through coercive pressure, even where no indictment has yet resulted.

The misdirection toward optics

The Republican staffer quoted in the reporting worried that sending FBI agents to polling places or seizing ballots would be disastrous for Republican candidates in vulnerable races. That concern exposes a narrower calculation than the conduct warrants.

The primary problem would not be bad midterm optics. It would be the use—or attempted use—of federal police power around elections for partisan advantage. Framing the danger as electoral backlash converts an abuse-of-power question into campaign strategy.

Patel’s refusal under oath to rule out placing FBI personnel at polling sites deepens that concern. He said he did not know that it could not legally be done, while the reporting notes a federal prohibition on armed federal agents at polling places. The relevant standard is not whether a maneuver helps or hurts Republicans. It is whether officials are using federal authority lawfully, based on evidence, and without intimidating voters.

The larger machinery

This episode reveals how partisan government power can operate without securing its ultimate objective. No reported 2020-election indictments had materialized, but employees were diverted, analysts were removed, officials departed, legal boundaries were tested, and agents came to dread Election Day.

That is already a consequence. Political capture does not begin only when prosecutors file a baseless charge. It begins when leaders make loyalty to a desired conclusion part of the investigative process, when an absence of evidence becomes an order to search again, and when career employees must choose between professional judgment and institutional survival.

The denials from DOJ, the White House, and the FBI deserve attribution, but they do not answer the detailed conduct reported. Nor does Patel’s flippant response about a “gold-plated jet ski” address The Atlantic’s questions. Mockery is not a rebuttal. It is a refusal to account for how federal law-enforcement power is being directed—and whose political interests that direction serves.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Make sure Republicans win’: Tumult at DOJ as top-down orders rattle investigators

item.title: 'Decay and oligarchy': Retired Air Force officer blasts Pentagon's billionaire takeover
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth selected SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich for Project Meridian, a four-month initiative intended to shape the Pentagon’s view of future warfare. Musk and Luckey lead companies with billions of dollars in active Pentagon contracts.

Nine current and former officials reportedly raised conflict-of-interest concerns, warning that the executives could influence decisions that generate more business for their own firms. The Pentagon disclosed little beyond a four-paragraph memo, and the extent of the commission’s authority remained unclear.

Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Wes Bryant, who previously led Pentagon civilian-harm assessments, called the arrangement evidence of “decay and oligarchy.” His accusation is the headline’s answer: billionaires are gaining government influence while retaining enormous financial interests in the policies they may help shape.

The Pentagon made this choice

The institutional power belongs to Hegseth and the Defense Department. Musk and Luckey did not appoint themselves. Pentagon leadership invited contractors inside a strategic process governing the department that buys their products.

That distinction matters because “billionaire takeover” can obscure the mechanism. This is not merely private wealth overpowering a helpless state. It is public officials choosing to share state authority with vendors whose fortunes may benefit from the resulting priorities.

Conflict is built into the design

The concern is not that successful defense executives possess relevant technical knowledge. The concern is that Project Meridian, as described, places two major contractors in a position to help define what capabilities the Pentagon should pursue without a publicly explained process for managing their commercial interests.

A contractor who helps establish the “trajectory of warfare” can potentially influence which technologies appear indispensable, which threats receive emphasis, and which procurement paths become politically urgent. RawStory does not establish that Musk or Luckey has steered contracts to his own company through this project. It does establish a structure in which strategic advice and private financial interest overlap.

Secrecy protects the arrangement

The Pentagon’s sparse disclosure is not a minor communications failure. A four-paragraph memo and sweeping language about technological “dominance” do not tell the public what access the participants will receive, what decisions they may affect, how conflicts will be handled, or whether their recommendations will be published.

That absence shifts the burden backward. Officials create an arrangement carrying obvious self-dealing risks, then leave outsiders unable to measure its reach. The uncertainty does not prove misconduct. It does show institutional indifference to preventing it—or even making prevention visible.

The framing lets government hide

RawStory foregrounds the billionaires, but the decisive actor is the government that empowered them. Treating the story chiefly as Musk and Luckey seizing influence risks turning an official delegation of authority into a tale of entrepreneurial aggression.

The weaker actors are career officials and the public, neither of whom appears to have meaningful control over the commission’s design. The politically useful misdirection is to personalize the problem around notorious wealthy men while allowing the Pentagon officials who opened the door to fade into the background.

Oligarchy is an administrative practice

Bryant’s language is severe, but the reported structure gives it substance. Oligarchy does not require billionaires formally replacing government. It can operate through appointments, advisory panels, opaque mandates, and procurement systems that allow public strategy and private profit to reinforce each other.

Project Meridian reveals a broader pattern: concentrated wealth becomes a credential for exercising public power, while government officials retain just enough formal authority to disclaim responsibility for the influence they granted. The scandal is not simply that defense contractors may shape military policy. It is that the Pentagon reportedly designed a process in which they can do so while the rules, safeguards, and consequences remain largely hidden.

Thanks to Raw Story

item.title: Ridicule as Ken Paxton's 'silly' campaign ad backfires: ‘Voters aren't stupid’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton released an ad on October 2, 2026, acknowledging that groceries, rent, and insurance “keep climbing,” then blaming “liberal politicians” for worsening the strain. The ad features Paxton’s daughter, Mattie Hayworth, presenting him as the politician who will fight back.

Critics pointed to the obvious problem: Republicans held the White House and both chambers of Congress, while their party had controlled every Texas statewide elected office since 1999 and the Texas House since 2003. Paxton nevertheless singled out Democratic rival James Talarico, accusing him of making it harder for Texans to get ahead.

CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale also noted that the ad contradicts President Donald Trump’s claim that prices were falling rapidly. The reported “backfire” was the ensuing online ridicule, not evidence that the ad changed voters’ opinions or altered the race.

Power has a mailing address

The ad speaks as though “liberal politicians” govern Texas from an undisclosed bunker. They do not. Republicans have controlled the state’s principal institutions for decades. At the federal level, their party controlled the elected branches identified in the report when Paxton released the ad.

That does not prove Republican officials caused every price increase. Inflation, rent, insurance, and grocery costs do not share one cause or one policymaker. But anyone assigning political responsibility must begin with the officials empowered to tax, regulate, appropriate, and govern. Paxton’s message instead makes authority disappear precisely where his party holds it.

The candidate posing as the opposition

Paxton does not merely belong to the governing party. He has been a statewide officeholder within the political order his advertisement carefully avoids naming. Yet the ad casts him as an outsider arriving to confront conditions produced under institutions his party runs.

His daughter’s role softens the delivery, but it does not repair the argument. “They” remain conveniently vague: powerful enough to raise the cost of living across Texas, yet somehow untouched by three decades of Republican electoral control. The ambiguity is functional. It lets Paxton claim the posture of resistance without accounting for the record of government.

A contradiction inside the party line

The advertisement creates another problem for Republicans: it concedes that families are still being squeezed. Dale identified the conflict with Trump’s assertion that prices were already dropping rapidly.

Paxton’s solution is not to reconcile those competing claims. It is to acknowledge pain locally while redirecting responsibility toward Democrats. That is less an economic explanation than a messaging maneuver: validate what voters can see, preserve the party’s innocence, and nominate an enemy.

Ridicule is not accountability

RawStory frames the episode as an ad that “backfires,” but the evidence presented establishes online criticism, not electoral damage. Posts from journalists, a Democratic representative, and a political commentator show that the contradiction was noticed. They do not establish what Texas voters believed or how the campaign was affected.

That distinction matters. Calling a campaign message ridiculous can expose its incoherence, but it does not neutralize it. Repetition, partisan loyalty, and unequal access to political attention can keep a weak claim useful long after critics have dismantled it.

Government without responsibility

The larger pattern is rule without ownership. A dominant party claims credit when conditions improve, invents obstructive enemies when they worsen, and campaigns against the consequences surrounding its own tenure.

Paxton’s ad offers no demonstrated chain connecting Talarico or unnamed liberals to the listed costs. It offers a simpler bargain: accept that life is more expensive, then blame actors with less institutional power. The misdirection is the point. It converts a governing record into a grievance and asks voters to return power to the people insisting they never truly had it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ridicule as Ken Paxton’s ‘silly’ campaign ad backfires: ‘Voters aren’t stupid’

item.title: 'MAGA morons' and 'insanity': Retiring GOP senator unleashes ruthless Trump onslaught
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that retiring North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis used an excerpt from his forthcoming book to attack Donald Trump’s advisers and supporters as “MAGA morons,” “sycophants” and drivers of what he predicts will be severe Republican defeats in 2026 and beyond. The excerpt was supplied by publisher HarperCollins ahead of the book’s scheduled Oct. 6 release.

Tillis singles out Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Stephen Miller, Laura Loomer, Steve Bannon, Mike Waltz and Matt Gaetz, while calling Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents “thugs.” He recounts watching Republican senators treat Hegseth’s confirmation hearing like a “pep rally” and says that spectacle convinced him how Trump’s second term would operate.

Tillis insists he has no personal grievance against Trump, although RawStory notes that he announced his retirement one day after drawing the president’s anger. His central warning is that Republicans surrendered their judgment to Trump and will face an electoral reckoning followed by even greater internal chaos.

Power did not belong to the hecklers

The vulgar insults are the excerpt’s marketable feature, but they are not its most revealing detail. Trump held the presidency. Senators held confirmation power. Administration officials received authority over the military, immigration enforcement and foreign policy. Online loyalists could create pressure, but elected Republicans decided whether that pressure would govern them.

Tillis describes Republican senators praising Hegseth instead of scrutinizing him. That is not merely a story about an unruly political base. It is a story about officeholders choosing submission while possessing the constitutional authority to say no.

Courage, outsourced until retirement

Tillis’s phrase “courage outsourcing” lands harder on his own institution than on MAGA celebrities. His account depicts lawmakers who recognized serious concerns yet allowed activists and Trump to define the permissible outcome.

But Tillis is publishing this indictment as he prepares to leave the Senate. RawStory’s excerpt does not establish how he acted in every dispute he now describes, so it cannot support a complete judgment of his record. It does establish the political timing: his bluntest account arrives after he has abandoned another campaign and lost much of the leverage that makes dissent consequential.

Retirement can liberate honesty. It can also expose how thoroughly self-preservation disciplined that honesty while power was still at stake.

The insults obscure the mechanism

Calling people morons, loons and bootlickers may be satisfying, but stupidity is an inadequate explanation for institutional surrender. The mechanism Tillis describes is organized coercion: Trump attacks dissenters, his base punishes them, and Republican officials learn that advancement depends on compliance.

That distinction matters. “Insanity” makes the outcome sound irrational and atmospheric. The conduct described here has a structure. Loyalty is rewarded, scrutiny is stigmatized and senators convert political fear into official consent. Whatever the private doubts, the public result is governance by deference.

The forecast is not absolution

Tillis predicts an electoral “bloodbath” for Republicans in November 2026 and further damage in 2028. That remains his forecast, not an established result. Even if voters eventually punish the party, an election loss would not erase the decisions made before it.

Nor does anticipating disaster amount to preventing it. Politicians routinely recast themselves as prophets once they are no longer willing or able to restrain the system they served. The relevant question is not who saw the wreckage coming. It is who possessed authority before impact and what they did with it.

The system rewards late truth

This episode reveals a durable pattern: party institutions suppress dissent when it could alter events, then package that dissent as candor when it can no longer impose an institutional cost. The departing senator receives attention for saying plainly what serving officials still avoid, while those officials retain power by continuing to avoid it.

The central failure is therefore not that Trump’s movement contains abrasive personalities or reckless rhetoric. It is that Republican senators, by Tillis’s own account, permitted loyalty politics to replace judgment inside institutions designed to constrain executive power. The insults name the cast. The surrender explains the story.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘MAGA morons’ and ‘insanity’: Retiring GOP senator unleashes ruthless Trump onslaught

item.title: ‘People are scared': Trump's loyal friend watches his famed restaurant go empty
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing The Bulwark, reports that El Arepazo in Doral, Florida, has lost roughly 80% of its business as immigrants frightened by the Trump administration’s enforcement campaign stay home. An employee said prepared specials sometimes spoil because customers do not come. Owner Maximo Alvarez had welcomed Donald Trump to the restaurant seven months earlier and pledged his loyalty.

The Bulwark described the formerly lively Venezuelan and South Florida gathering place as subdued and nearly empty. Its reporter attributed the decline to fear of detention and deportation among immigrants who lost legal protections, compounded by families’ financial strain. The article does not specify which protections were revoked, how many residents were affected, or provide business records independently substantiating the employee’s estimate.

Doral voted for Trump by 23 points in 2024, according to the reporting. Meanwhile, Trump border czar Tom Homan promised more enforcement at Trump’s golf club, saying, “Wait until you see what we do next year.”

Power does not reward loyalty

Trump’s administration holds the institutional power here. It sets enforcement priorities, determines how aggressively federal agents pursue immigrants and shapes the conditions under which residents decide whether leaving home is worth the risk. Alvarez’s access to Trump offered visibility, not authority.

That distinction is the story. Alvarez publicly offered personal loyalty to a president. But immigration enforcement is not a reciprocal friendship; it is state power applied to categories of people. A restaurant owner’s allegiance cannot shield a customer base whose legal security and freedom of movement depend on federal decisions.

Fear is an economic policy

The empty tables are not merely a change in consumer sentiment. According to the reporting, customers are staying away because they fear detention and deportation. That fear changes where people travel, work and spend money. It leaves food unsold, workers with fewer hours and businesses without revenue.

Homan’s promise of still more enforcement matters because it reinforces the calculation keeping people indoors. The foreseeable reach extends beyond those directly detained. Enforcement becomes ambient pressure on families, neighborhoods and local commerce.

The voter-blame trap

Doral’s 23-point margin for Trump is politically relevant, but it can also become a cheap device for treating suffering as electoral comeuppance. A city’s vote is an aggregate. It does not establish how frightened immigrants voted, whether they could vote, or whether every harmed worker and customer supported the policy.

The people making federal policy are not interchangeable with everyone experiencing its consequences. Turning the story into “Trump voters got what they chose” would misdirect responsibility downward—from officials wielding coercive power to a heterogeneous community living under it.

A weak frame around a hard fact

The irony of a loyal Trump supporter watching his restaurant empty is vivid, but personality-driven framing narrows the political meaning. The central fact is not that loyalty “didn’t get him too far.” It is that federal enforcement can reorganize daily life across an immigrant community, including institutions whose owners believed proximity to power might matter.

The reported 80% decline remains one employee’s estimate, and the article supplies no broader economic data. That limitation should constrain the scale of the claim, not obscure the mechanism described: fear suppresses public life, and businesses dependent on that public life absorb the damage.

The system beneath the spectacle

Authoritarian politics often advertises control through highly visible punishment while distributing the consequences far beyond its formal targets. Here, the reporting depicts a community withdrawing from restaurants and public spaces while an administration official promises escalation from the comfort of the president’s golf club.

That is the larger pattern: officials exercise power, communities absorb the risk, and coverage gravitates toward the supporter’s surprise. The empty restaurant is not primarily a morality play about misplaced loyalty. It is evidence of how coercive policy travels—through legal status, household finances, neighborhood routines and finally the silence of a room where people have become too frightened to gather.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘People are scared’: Trump’s loyal friend watches his famed restaurant go empty
