item.title: Trump served warning he's making the same mistake that doomed his predecessor — only worse
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that former Biden White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre warned President Donald Trump is repeating the Biden administration’s failure to address voters’ economic experience—and worsening it by openly dismissing affordability concerns. In a New York Times op-ed, she argued that Trump’s confrontational communication style is losing its force as prices remain politically salient.

Jean-Pierre acknowledged that the Biden administration’s emphasis on job creation, wage growth and low unemployment did not overcome public frustration with inflation. She also conceded that her responses about Biden’s age sometimes intensified doubts rather than resolving them. Turning to Trump, she cited his description of “affordability” as a “fake word,” his defense of higher gas prices as a cost of his war aims, and questions about his conduct and medical disclosures.

She further asserted that inflation was higher than when Trump returned to office, the bond market had been unsettled and the Federal Reserve had recently raised interest rates. RawStory presents those claims through Jean-Pierre’s argument; it does not independently substantiate them in the supplied report.

Power is not messaging

Jean-Pierre’s central diagnosis is useful but incomplete. Presidents command executive authority, appoint senior officials, shape fiscal priorities and exercise enormous influence over public debate. Their communications teams choose how to sell those decisions, but the underlying consequences do not originate at the podium.

The Biden administration’s problem was not merely that its evidence “didn’t land.” Its preferred indicators did not settle whether households could comfortably pay for food, fuel and housing. Trump’s problem, as Jean-Pierre describes it, is sharper still: he is not simply failing to translate policy into relatable language. He is treating people’s stated economic distress as a branding obstacle.

Contempt is a governing signal

Calling affordability fake does more than produce poor optics. It tells the public which experience the president considers worthy of recognition. A government that answers material anxiety with semantic dismissal is revealing its hierarchy of concern.

Trump’s remark that higher gas prices are “a very inexpensive price to pay” for his war aims makes that hierarchy more explicit. The president defines the objective; households absorb the cost. Whether those aims justify the burden is a policy question. Pretending the burden is trivial is an exercise of power by someone insulated from it.

The convenient communications alibi

Political coverage often reduces governing failure to a messaging error because that framing is comfortable for everyone near power. Advisers merely chose the wrong words. Reporters merely documented a communications struggle. Presidents remain surrounded by abstractions while weaker actors—the inattentive voter, the fragmented audience, the difficult media environment—quietly inherit blame for refusing to understand.

Jean-Pierre partly reproduces that pattern when describing Biden’s record as evidence the public failed to see. Her admission that the administration did not adjust is candid, but it still centers persuasion rather than asking whether its chosen measurements adequately captured people’s conditions.

Scrutiny without equivalence

Jean-Pierre is also right to connect credibility about the economy with credibility about presidential fitness. Her acknowledgment that White House answers about Biden’s age sometimes fueled concern identifies an institutional choice: officials tried to contain a politically damaging issue and failed.

That history does not excuse evasiveness from Trump’s White House about medical information or public episodes that invite questions about his condition. Equal scrutiny is warranted; false equivalence is not. The relevant facts are what each president did, what aides disclosed, and how institutions responded—not whether one administration’s failure grants the next permission to repeat it.

The system rewards denial

The broader pattern is a presidency increasingly treated as a contest in narrative management rather than an office accountable for material results. Economic indicators become shields, public hardship becomes a perception problem, and presidential conduct becomes a problem for staff to explain away.

But communication cannot indefinitely overrule experience. Jean-Pierre’s warning matters because she has seen this failure from inside the institution: once an administration begins arguing with conditions people encounter every day, its formidable communications machinery becomes evidence of estrangement rather than competence. Trump’s version, on her account, adds open contempt to that estrangement—and asks repetition, spectacle and executive stature to carry the difference.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump served warning he’s making the same mistake that doomed his predecessor — only worse

item.title: Humiliated Republican pulls plug on interview as embarrassing new details trickle out
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing the Daily Beast, reports that Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt withdrew from a scheduled C-SPAN appearance one day after his questioning of former special counsel Jack Smith unraveled during a Senate hearing. Host Dasha Burns disclosed the cancellation but did not report Schmitt’s reason, so the claim that embarrassment drove his decision remains an inference, not an established fact.

At Tuesday’s hearing, Schmitt tried to connect Smith to the Atlanta investigation of President Donald Trump by asking about a February 3, 2024 basketball game between the Golden State Warriors and Atlanta Hawks. Smith had attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland instead. Schmitt later told CNN that his team had information Smith attended “a basketball game” and inferred Atlanta because only one NBA game was scheduled that night.

Power without preparation

Schmitt was not an ordinary citizen making a bad guess. He was a United States senator using a public hearing—and the authority, staff and visibility attached to that office—to insinuate misconduct by a former federal prosecutor.

That institutional imbalance matters. Smith had to answer a premise Schmitt’s office apparently had not adequately verified. The senator could launch the insinuation in public; the target bore the immediate burden of disproving it. A collapsed accusation does not erase the advantage enjoyed by the official who introduced it.

The insinuation was the instrument

The question’s political value depended on association: Smith, Atlanta, Fani Willis and the Trump prosecution placed inside the same frame. Schmitt did not establish that connection. His own explanation shows that his office moved from unspecified information about “a basketball game” to a particular NBA game—and then presented that inference in a Senate hearing.

RawStory characterizes the exchange as an attempt to bait Smith into perjury, but the supplied reporting does not establish Schmitt’s intent that conclusively. What it does establish is reckless evidentiary practice: a senator used an unverified deduction to construct a damaging public suggestion.

The cancellation is not the scandal

The headline centers Schmitt’s humiliation and his abandoned television appearance. That is the least politically important part of the episode. Burns reported when he withdrew, not why. Treating the cancellation as proof of shame substitutes personality drama for institutional scrutiny.

The consequential question is how a senator’s staff converted thin information into an accusation-ready premise. Schmitt’s CNN defense did not answer that question. It merely described the faulty chain of reasoning.

Accountability as spectacle

The hearing demonstrates how oversight can be degraded into opposition research performed in public. A question need not prove anything to circulate a desired association; it only needs cameras, an official setting and a target forced to respond.

When the premise collapses, coverage often turns the failure into comedy. Mockery may be deserved, but it is not accountability. The systemic problem is that powerful officials can spend institutional credibility on poorly supported insinuations, then allow the news cycle to recast the abuse as an embarrassing viral moment. The joke fades. The machinery that produced it remains.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Humiliated Republican pulls plug on interview as embarrassing new details trickle out

item.title: Exposing the ‘overcharge’ lie: The origin of Trump’s new $500 bribe
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the White House planned to mail roughly one million people $500 checks bearing Donald Trump’s signature, accompanied by a letter claiming the Biden administration had “massively overcharged” users of the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace and retained the money. The administration had not published an accounting supporting that explanation, according to the article.

The report cites KFF health-policy expert Larry Levitt, who said the surplus most likely originated during Trump’s first term, when marketplace fees exceeded spending partly because his administration withheld money for enrollment advertising and assistance. Biden later lowered those fees. The New York Times also reportedly found that $500 exceeded what any recipient could personally have overpaid.

AlterNet argues that the checks, directed to ACA customers in 30 states shortly before the November 3 election, were meant to lend credibility to Trump’s September 9 promise of future $5,000 payments if voters kept Republicans in control of Congress. The available reporting establishes the payment program and its political presentation, but not the administration’s unpublished accounting or the article’s characterization of the checks as an illegal bribe.

The power behind the check

The recipients did not create this arrangement. The White House controlled the money, the explanation attached to it, the presidential signature placed on it, and the timing of its delivery. Trump and his administration therefore held the institutional power and made the relevant decisions.

That distinction matters because the transaction was packaged as restitution. Restitution ordinarily connects a documented overcharge to the amount returned. Here, according to the reporting, the administration disclosed no such calculation, while the flat $500 payment exceeded any recipient’s purported excess contribution. The check looked less like precise reimbursement than a politically branded distribution of public money.

The signature is not decoration. It encourages recipients to treat federal funds as a personal gift from the president. Taxpayer money becomes presidential largesse; an administrative payment becomes campaign-adjacent theater.

The invented culprit

The accompanying story supplied a convenient villain: Biden supposedly knew about the surplus and kept it. But the article reports no evidence offered by Trump or the White House for that claim. The account attributed to Levitt points instead toward excess collections and underspending during Trump’s first administration.

That is more than ordinary partisan spin. It reverses agency. Money allegedly left unused because Trump’s administration curtailed efforts helping people enroll in health coverage is presented as money rescued from Biden’s misconduct. A policy choice that made coverage harder to obtain is laundered into proof of Trump’s generosity.

If the money truly represented an overcharge, lowering the marketplace fee would address the mechanism prospectively. Mailing a conspicuous check creates a different benefit: a memorable payment attached to one politician’s name. The administration’s chosen remedy serves political attribution better than administrative coherence.

The harm hidden by the refund

AlterNet reports that enhanced ACA subsidies expired under legislation Trump signed to finance tax cuts, driving annual insurance costs up by thousands of dollars for some families. It says roughly three million people then dropped coverage. Those former customers would receive none of these checks because they were no longer enrolled.

That is the central misdirection. The spectacle focuses attention on $500 returned to selected current customers while pushing the larger loss of affordable coverage out of frame. The people most damaged by rising premiums are not merely undercompensated; those who left the market are excluded altogether.

The payment also targets a population with an obvious reason to feel financial pressure: people buying their own insurance, including farmers, small-business owners, hourly workers and early retirees. The reporting does not establish each recipient’s income or voting intention. It does establish that the administration chose a financially exposed constituency and delivered money under Trump’s signature shortly before an election.

Government as personal patronage

Trump’s September 9 pitch made the political logic unusually plain: elect Republican congressional majorities and families would later receive $5,000. Whether that larger payment would ever materialize remained only a promise at the time of the report. The immediate $500 checks gave the promise a tangible prop.

This is how patronage corrodes public accountability without requiring a secret exchange. Officials first impose or permit material hardship, then return a fraction of public money with the leader’s name attached, while assigning responsibility for the hardship to an opponent. Citizens are repositioned as grateful clients rather than owners of the funds and beneficiaries of public programs.

Calling the episode mere “confusion” would conceal the choices involved. The White House chose the claim about Biden, the fixed payment, the signature and the timing. Even without a published accounting or a legal finding of election bribery, those observed decisions support a clear conclusion: the program was designed to produce political credit for Trump.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of government from an institution into a loyalty machine. Policy distributes losses broadly and quietly; political branding returns a smaller benefit loudly and selectively. The official who controls the machinery then claims personal generosity and directs anger elsewhere.

That structure rewards leaders for creating dependency, obscuring causation and treating public resources as instruments of personal power. The crucial question is not whether a recipient should cash the check. It is who raised the costs, who controlled the surplus, who selected the recipients and who wrote the accompanying fiction. Follow those decisions, and the supposed gift becomes what the branding was meant to hide: the public receiving a fraction of its own money from the officials who control the terms.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Exposing the ‘overcharge’ lie: The origin of Trump’s new $500 bribe

item.title: Conservative icon calls for 'carnage' against Trump's GOP
item.description:
What happened

George F. Will’s call for “carnage” was a demand for sweeping Republican defeats in the November midterms. AlterNet reports that the conservative columnist argued most congressional Republicans had surrendered their independence to President Donald Trump and should be punished electorally for abandoning their role as a check on executive power.

Will urged voters to target lawmakers who enabled Trump, citing trade policy, immigration restrictions, the war with Iran, and anger over gasoline, diesel, and fertilizer prices. He suggested Republican losses from Alaska and Iowa to Texas and Ohio could force the party to reconsider its submission to the president.

His proposed purge was selective. Will endorsed the survival of Maine Senator Susan Collins, praising her handling of Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation, and Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who campaigns as a Trump supporter while differing with him on some issues. The election outcomes were not provided in the reporting.

Congress chose submission

Trump holds executive power, but the institutional failure described here belongs equally to Republican lawmakers. They possess votes, investigative authority, control over legislation, and the capacity to resist presidential decisions. According to Will’s account, they chose political survival instead.

That distinction matters. Congress was not merely overwhelmed by a dominant president. Its Republican members repeatedly accepted their own irrelevance because independence carried electoral risk. Their weakness was cultivated, rewarded, and renewed through individual decisions.

The selective reckoning

Will’s exceptions expose the limits of his indictment. Collins is spared partly because she supported Kavanaugh’s confirmation after reviewing his record and the sexual-assault allegations against him. Rogers is spared despite advertising his support for Trump.

The standard is therefore not a clean rejection of presidential domination. It is a plea to preserve selected Republicans whom Will considers sufficiently serious or useful. The party may be “smashed to atoms,” but familiar conservative priorities and favored personnel remain protected.

That is less a revolution than an attempt at internal discipline.

Where blame belongs

The strongest part of Will’s argument is his refusal to make Trump the sole explanation for Republican conduct. A president can demand loyalty; legislators decide whether to provide it. Concentrating every criticism on the executive lets members of Congress pose as spectators to decisions they enabled.

AlterNet’s framing risks turning the story into spectacle by emphasizing a conservative icon’s call for “carnage.” The consequential claim is not that George Will used violent imagery for electoral losses. It is that lawmakers with constitutional power traded it for continued office.

Defeat as institutional medicine

Will treats electoral punishment as the mechanism capable of changing that calculation. His logic is blunt: if surrender carries no cost, surrender becomes the party’s operating model. Republican defeats would matter not as symbolic condemnation but as evidence that obedience to a president can end careers rather than preserve them.

Whether losses would actually restore congressional independence remains unproven. Parties often respond to defeat by intensifying factional loyalty or blaming disfavored candidates. But Will correctly identifies the incentive structure: lawmakers rarely recover principles that voters consistently allow them to discard.

The architecture of abdication

This story reveals a broader pattern of executive expansion built through legislative consent. Presidential power grows not only when presidents seize authority, but when lawmakers find it safer to stop exercising their own.

The resulting system preserves the appearance of separate branches while draining one of them of agency. Elections then become less a contest over policy than a judgment on whether representatives performed the job they already possessed the power to do. Will’s case is ultimately that Republican legislators made themselves politically irrelevant. The sharper conclusion is that irrelevance was their strategy—and only a material penalty can make it unattractive.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Conservative icon calls for ‘carnage’ against Trump’s GOP

item.title: Shock poll just put one of GOP’s must-win states in play
item.description:
What happened

A Broward County poll did not, by itself, put Florida in play. AlterNet reports that a Bendixen & Amandi International survey found Democrat David Jolly leading Republican Byron Donalds 52 percent to 26 percent in the heavily Democratic county. The Sun Sentinel reported the results; no statewide findings were provided.

The result matters because Jolly’s 26-point margin exceeds Kamala Harris’s roughly 17-point Broward margin in the 2024 presidential election. Separately, the Cook Political Report moved the governor’s race from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican,” citing a tightening contest.

The poll also found narrow Broward support for Amendment 3. The proposal would increase Florida’s homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. It requires 60 percent statewide support in November.

A county is not a state

The headline inflates a favorable local result into a statewide shock. Broward was already expected to support Jolly, and the article supplies no statewide poll showing him ahead—or even tied. A strong Democratic margin there is necessary for a competitive campaign, but it does not establish that Jolly can overcome Republicans’ statewide voter-registration advantage.

The more consequential evidence is Cook’s ratings change. Even that means the race is leaning Republican, not that Florida has suddenly become Democratic terrain. “In play” is defensible as a description of increased competitiveness; presenting one county survey as the event that produced it is political clickbait substituting suspense for scale.

The power remains with Republicans

Republicans hold the structural advantage described in the reporting. Donalds has substantial financial backing, a statewide registration edge behind him and a campaign built around succeeding Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Jolly has a large lead in one Democratic county and a more competitive race than Republicans may have expected.

Those are not equivalent forms of power. One side has the stronger statewide electoral infrastructure; the other has evidence that its required coalition may be forming. Treating Democratic strength in Broward as the decisive development risks mistaking a prerequisite for an accomplishment.

Tax relief, with the bill concealed

Amendment 3 exposes the sharper governing choice. Donalds supports a major expansion of the homestead exemption, arguing that property-tax bills have nearly doubled while household budgets have not. Jolly opposes the proposal because reducing the taxable base could deprive counties of revenue used for public services; he favors more targeted assistance, including help for first-time buyers.

Calling the amendment “relief” describes what eligible homeowners would retain but not what local governments could lose or how they might respond. The political sales pitch isolates the tax cut from its institutional consequences. Counties still have obligations after revenue disappears. The reporting does not quantify the expected loss or identify which services would be affected, so stronger claims would outrun the evidence. But the governing question is plain: who absorbs the cost of the exemption?

The conversion narrative is not the contest

Jolly’s departure from the Republican Party and eventual move to the Democrats is campaign biography, not an explanation of the race. Centering his partisan conversion can turn a contest over state power, taxation and local services into a personality story about ideological migration.

Donalds and Jolly are seeking authority over Florida’s executive branch. Their relevant distinction is not simply which political label each has worn. It is what each would do with that authority—and, in the case of Amendment 3, which institutions and residents would bear the consequences of the policy each supports.

The system behind the surprise

Florida appears “shocking” only if political coverage treats recent Republican dominance as a permanent law rather than an electoral advantage that candidates must continually defend. The Broward poll shows a Democrat running strongly where a Democrat must run strongly. Cook’s shift suggests the broader contest has tightened. Neither fact settles the statewide outcome.

The larger pattern is the conversion of ordinary electoral movement into spectacle while durable power receives less scrutiny. Poll margins generate the drama; registration, money, governing authority and the distributional effects of policy determine what victory would mean. The first tells readers whether a race is interesting. The second tells them who can act, who pays and what changes afterward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Shock poll just put one of GOP’s must-win states in play

item.title: Trump's 'inexplicable' charm offensive toward his own enemies leaves GOP reeling
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing The Hill, reports that President Donald Trump’s friendly meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unsettled Republicans four weeks before the midterm elections. Trump welcomed Xi to the White House shortly after U.S. officials said China had helped Iran target American troops, prompting Republican senators Roger Wicker and John Kennedy to criticize or caution against the outreach.

Trump also praised Mamdani after months of attacking him, calling the democratic socialist mayor “a very rational person” and saying he would cheer for him to improve New York. Asked whether Mamdani was a “jihadist,” as outgoing Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik had called him, Trump said no.

An unnamed Republican strategist described the shift as “inexplicable,” arguing that cordial treatment of two figures portrayed as enemies could depress Republican enthusiasm before the election. The reporting does not establish that Trump’s conduct has actually reduced turnout or cost Republicans congressional support; it documents Republican fear that it might.

The power belongs to Trump

The bewildered-strategist framing obscures the simplest explanation: Trump can change the party’s enemies because he commands the party’s political center. Republican lawmakers and operatives may dislike the reversal, but they are reacting to it, not controlling it.

Wicker can say Xi should never have received the invitation. Kennedy can warn that Beijing remains untrustworthy. Neither senator made the decision. Trump did. The same hierarchy governs the Mamdani meeting: Republicans spent months intensifying Trump’s attacks, only to discover that their designated villain could be rehabilitated the moment Trump found praise more useful.

Yesterday’s menace, today’s guest

The Mamdani episode exposes how disposable Republican threat language has become. Stefanik used “jihadist,” a smear designed to place a Muslim political opponent outside legitimate civic life. Trump discarded it with a single word after meeting the man it targeted.

That reversal does not erase the earlier attacks. It reveals their function. If Mamdani can move from supposed menace to “very rational person” without any reported ideological conversion, then the fevered language was never a stable assessment. It was political equipment: useful for mobilization until the party’s dominant figure chose another posture.

Xi presents a different and more consequential case. U.S. officials had reportedly linked China to Iranian targeting of American troops, yet Trump supplied the ceremonial legitimacy of a White House welcome. Republican objections may be substantive, electoral, or both. But the contradiction belongs to the president who authorized the reception, not to voters who fail to decode his shifting signals.

The base is treated as equipment

The unnamed strategist’s complaint is revealing. The concern is not principally that Trump’s policy is incoherent or that Republican descriptions of Mamdani were reckless. It is that the party had cultivated hostility toward Xi and Mamdani to produce votes, and Trump may have interrupted the emotional machinery four weeks before an election.

That is an admission about how the coalition is managed. Enemies are selected, simplified and repeated until outrage becomes a turnout strategy. When Trump suddenly offers warmth, Republican operatives call it inexplicable because they are counting on supporters to retain the hostility he taught them.

The insult is directed downward. Party leaders manufacture absolutist narratives, reverse them without explanation, and then worry that voters might become insufficiently energized. The base is expected to experience every new position as conviction and every contradiction as strategy.

Confusion is not the central story

RawStory’s “charm offensive” framing risks turning an exercise of presidential power into a personality puzzle. The consequential questions are not whether Trump has become unusually charming or whether Republicans understand him. They are what he chose to authorize, what his allies previously told voters, and how little power those allies possess to enforce their own rhetoric.

The reported congressional anxiety also should not be mistaken for resistance. The senators quoted objected to or qualified Trump’s outreach, while the strategist worried about electoral consequences. The article supplies no evidence that Republican officials imposed a cost, changed policy or withdrew support. Their discomfort demonstrates dependence more clearly than independence.

A coalition built on permission

This episode reveals a party in which hostility is centrally licensed. Trump can elevate an adversary, withdraw a slur or welcome a foreign leader, and Republicans must rapidly reconcile the new posture with yesterday’s claims.

That system produces more than hypocrisy. It makes policy contingent on one leader’s shifting permissions and turns propaganda into a renewable resource. The villains can change overnight; the institutional hierarchy does not. Republicans are reeling because Trump reminded them that even their outrage belongs to him.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s ‘inexplicable’ charm offensive toward his own enemies leaves GOP reeling

item.title: This hissy fit exposes what Trump fears most
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Donald Trump objected to CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters having White House access, saying, “I don’t want them in my office” and “I don’t want them here.” The “hissy fit” in the headline refers to that reaction; the article interprets it as fear of sustained, adversarial scrutiny.

According to the outlet, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, blocked the administration’s press ban after finding that it likely violated constitutional protections because the affected reporters lost access without notice or an opportunity to respond. The outlets asked Kelly to preserve their passes while he considers a final ruling, arguing that the White House would otherwise restore the complete ban immediately.

RawStory also reports that Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the restrictions by characterizing the targeted coverage as misinformation and a national-security problem. The article rejects that rationale and presents the fight as part of Trump’s broader practice of punishing news organizations that refuse his preferred language or challenge his claims.

Power wears the credential

The decisive power here does not belong to individual reporters standing behind a rope line. It belongs to the president and the officials who control physical access to the White House and Air Force One. They can turn credentials—supposedly an administrative mechanism—into leverage over which institutions may question the government at close range.

The administration made the exclusionary decision. The affected outlets challenged it. Kelly imposed a judicial obstacle. Any framing that reduces this conflict to Trump’s temper obscures that chain of authority. The complaint may sound petulant, but it accompanies an attempt to use state-controlled access against disfavored coverage.

Retaliation dressed as security

Blanche’s reported justification performs the central misdirection. It recasts the government as the vulnerable party and critical reporting as the danger. Under that logic, officials may define unfavorable coverage as “misinformation,” call its consequences a national-security concern, and then present exclusion as protection rather than punishment.

The reporting supplied here does not independently establish whether the disputed coverage was false or whether any concrete security harm occurred. It does establish that Blanche invoked national security while defending the ban. Without specific evidence connecting particular reporting to an identifiable threat, that argument functions as an assertion of executive authority, not a demonstrated necessity.

The court identified the process

Kelly’s reported ruling matters because it strips away some of the administration’s rhetoric. The immediate legal issue was not whether Trump enjoyed the reporters’ work. It was whether the government could revoke access without notice or an opportunity to contest the decision. Kelly concluded that the ban probably violated constitutional rights.

That distinction is more useful than RawStory’s insistence that “probably” should be “definitely.” Courts use provisional language when ruling at a preliminary stage. The important fact is that a federal judge found the constitutional claim strong enough to block the administration’s action while the case continued.

The press cannot outsource courage

RawStory is right to identify institutional weakness in a press corps that depends on access controlled by the people it covers. But its argument sometimes substitutes insults and sweeping declarations for evidence. Calling every adverse story “the truth” does not establish accuracy, just as an administration calling coverage “fake news” does not establish falsity.

The sharper indictment is structural. When news organizations treat access as indispensable, the government gains bargaining power over their conduct. Reporters may soften questions, decline to support targeted colleagues, or accept official premises to preserve proximity. The New York Times’ reported description of a continued boycott as “untenable” illustrates the trap: solidarity becomes costly precisely because access has been made scarce.

The larger machinery

This episode reveals a familiar authoritarian method without requiring speculation about Trump’s private fears. An executive identifies hostile scrutiny, converts discretionary access into punishment, and supplies a public-interest justification for retaliation. Weaker actors are then blamed for the conflict: reporters are described as dishonest, disruptive, or dangerous, while the officials wielding government power pose as victims.

The systemic error is treating this as a personality dispute between an irritable president and an unruly press corps. It is an institutional contest over whether the government may condition proximity to power on deference. Trump’s words expose hostility to scrutiny; the ban shows the machinery available to act on it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: This hissy fit exposes what Trump fears most

item.title: Scott Jennings warns Trump 'tsunami' of investigations could be coming
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that CNN commentator Scott Jennings warned Donald Trump and his associates to expect a “tsunami” of congressional investigations if Republicans lose either chamber in November. His warning came during a discussion of a promotion promising leading holders of Trump’s memecoin access to a Nov. 22 dinner at Trump National near Washington, with VIP treatment and Trump-branded gold watches for the highest-ranked investors.

Jennings said he lacked enough information to defend the arrangement and merely assumed White House lawyers had reviewed Trump’s private business activity. He nevertheless called the use of a sitting president’s name in a venture where investors “could get hurt” troubling. AlterNet reports that the coin plunged in value while Trump reportedly earned more than $600 million from it; Senate Democrats called the latest promotion another Trump “grift.” Organizers said attendees would not receive private meetings with Trump and could not give him gifts.

The presidency is the product

This is not principally a story about cryptocurrency volatility. It is about presidential power being used to increase the appeal of a private financial venture bearing the president’s identity.

The dinner contest makes the hierarchy plain: investors compete by acquiring and holding more of the asset, while proximity to a sitting president functions as the prize. Even without a private meet-and-greet, the advertised setting and political celebrity give the promotion value unavailable to an ordinary memecoin operator.

Trump holds the institutional power. The buyers assume the financial risk. That imbalance matters more than the promotional fine print.

Jennings warns the seller

Jennings framed congressional scrutiny as the danger Trump must prepare to survive. His advice was to document everything, anticipate investigations and be ready for transparency “when that day comes.”

That formulation reverses the proper order of concern. The immediate issue described by the reporting is that people may lose money in a president-branded venture while Trump reportedly profits. Yet the warning is directed upward, toward protecting the powerful actor from future investigators, rather than outward, toward protecting buyers exposed to the scheme.

Jennings did acknowledge that people could be hurt. But his primary prescription was compliance preparation. Political accountability became a weather event—a “tsunami”—instead of a foreseeable institutional response to conduct Congress may have reason to examine.

Oversight should not depend on an election

Jennings’s warning also exposes a structural failure: meaningful investigation may depend on which party controls Congress after November.

Republican control, in this account, is treated as insulation. A Democratic takeover would activate scrutiny. That is not neutral oversight; it is partisan contingency governing whether a president’s private financial arrangements receive sustained examination.

The article does not establish that any law was broken, and Jennings did not claim one was. But Congress does not need a criminal conviction before asking whether presidential status is enriching a private venture, who is financing it and what access those financial relationships appear to purchase.

The soft language protects hard power

Calling the arrangement merely “uncomfortable” shrinks a question of public power into a matter of personal taste. Assuming unnamed White House lawyers handled it properly substitutes faith in internal review for evidence.

The organizers’ assurances address narrow optics: no private meeting and no gifts accepted. They do not answer the central question raised by the promotion—whether access to a presidential venue and association with the president are being used to stimulate demand for an asset tied to his financial interests.

That is the misdirection at work. Attention shifts from the officeholder monetizing his political identity to the investors who might make poor choices, and from present accountability to hypothetical investigations after an electoral change.

A system of optional accountability

The larger pattern is not confusion. It is an accountability system designed to become energetic only when partisan control changes hands.

A president can attach his name and political aura to a speculative product; allies can treat legal vetting as sufficient; congressional scrutiny can remain conditional; and commentators can describe investigation as the looming hazard. Every institution then discusses the risk surrounding the transaction without squarely confronting who possesses the power to create it.

The scandal is not simply that investors may get burned. It is that presidential influence can be converted into private commercial leverage while oversight waits for permission from the next election.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Scott Jennings warns Trump ‘tsunami’ of investigations could be coming

item.title: 'Bunch of political losers' threaten GOP hold on Alaska
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins emerged from Alaska’s August open primary as the strongest candidate for governor, while Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson, and Treg Taylor all advanced to the November ranked-choice election. The fractured Republican field gives Kreiss-Tomkins a plausible route to becoming Alaska’s first elected Democratic governor since Tony Knowles won reelection in 1998.

A bipartisan AARP survey cited by AlterNet put Kreiss-Tomkins at 40 percent in first preferences and the three Republicans at a combined 41 percent. Its ranked-choice simulation had him defeating Wilson, the leading Republican, by 10 points. Wilson asked Bronson and Taylor to withdraw; both refused. Bronson argued that Republicans can still prevail if conservative voters rank every GOP candidate.

The election follows Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s two terms in a state Donald Trump carried by 13 points in 2024. Kreiss-Tomkins has emphasized education, living costs, and direct outreach to remote communities. The reported polling suggests a competitive race, not an established November result.

The power is still Republican

Republicans hold the structural advantage. Alaska’s recent presidential vote, Dunleavy’s incumbency, and the GOP candidates’ combined first-preference support all point to an electorate where the party begins with more raw strength than any single rival.

What Republicans lack is not power but coordination. Their predicament was created by three candidates independently choosing to remain on the ballot. Wilson tried to consolidate the field around herself; Bronson and Taylor declined to surrender their candidacies. Calling them “political losers,” as longtime Alaska political observer Larry Persily did, is a judgment about their electoral records or prospects—not an explanation of the institutional forces shaping the contest.

Ranked choice is not the culprit

The easiest Republican excuse is the voting system. But ranked-choice voting does not force GOP voters to divide irreversibly among Wilson, Bronson, and Taylor. It allows them to rank all three.

That means the decisive question is whether Republican candidates and party networks can persuade their voters to use the ballot effectively. Bronson’s strategy depends on precisely that. If Republicans fail, responsibility belongs first to the candidates who stayed in and to a party unable to coordinate its own coalition—not to voters, procedural complexity, or the Democrat who assembled broader support.

The Democrat built an opening

Kreiss-Tomkins did not merely wait for Republicans to trip over one another. AlterNet reports that he traveled hundreds of miles by boat along the Yukon River and visited villages candidates commonly bypass. He centered education and everyday costs, while fellow Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed him.

That contrast matters. Democrats consolidated; Republicans did not. One campaign invested in neglected voters while three others competed for overlapping support. The Republican field may still overcome that dysfunction, but its predicament is self-authored.

A dividend cannot substitute for governing

The Permanent Fund Dividend exposes the material stakes beneath the campaign arithmetic. AlterNet reports that the 2026 payment was set at $1,000 plus $200 in energy relief and that voters were dissatisfied with the amount.

The dividend is not political decoration. It is household income in an expensive state, and anger over it can puncture partisan loyalty. Kreiss-Tomkins’s focus on daily costs recognizes that elections are shaped not only by ideological identity but by whether governing institutions deliver tangible security.

The larger error

The story is tempting to frame as an amusing Republican personality clash. That understates it. A dominant party can possess nearly every structural advantage and still endanger its hold on office through factional ambition, weak coordination, and complacency toward material grievances.

Kreiss-Tomkins’s opportunity is therefore neither a mysterious upset nor proof that Alaska has already realigned. It is the foreseeable consequence of one coalition organizing while the more powerful coalition assumes partisan habit will rescue it from its own decisions.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Bunch of political losers’ threaten GOP hold on Alaska

item.title: Panic as Pentagon quietly moves to expand Trump's 'nuclear options’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s under secretary for policy, told the Senate Armed Services Committee during a closed Sept. 17 hearing that the Defense Department was conducting a classified review of U.S. nuclear-employment guidance “with the goal of increasing options available to the president.” The president is Donald Trump. The report does not establish that Trump ordered the review, approved a new policy, or decided to use nuclear weapons.

Colby said nuclear weapons would be considered only in “extreme circumstances” and attributed the review to a changing global nuclear landscape. Independent journalist Ken Klippenstein argued that expanding presidential options is especially dangerous after what he described as the administration’s war with Iran earlier in 2026. RawStory cites alarmed reactions from journalist Mehdi Hasan, historian Alexander Howlett and professor Ambereen Dadabhoy, but reports no completed policy change or operational decision.

Power sits inside the review

The decisive actor is not the academics reacting online. It is the executive branch’s national-security apparatus, which writes classified guidance governing the circumstances under which a president may consider nuclear use. Colby’s description matters because “more options” is not an abstract debating exercise. It means officials are examining how to widen the menu presented to the one office empowered to authorize nuclear employment.

The Pentagon can package that expansion as technical planning. Classification keeps the underlying scenarios, thresholds and proposed changes beyond meaningful public scrutiny. The result is a profound imbalance: officials deliberate over civilization-scale violence inside secure rooms while the public receives a phrase from closed testimony.

An option is not an order

RawStory’s framing risks outrunning its evidence. The article establishes a classified review intended to increase presidential options. It does not establish that new guidance has been adopted, that nuclear deployment against Iran is under consideration, or that the administration believes an atomic strike would deliver victory. Howlett criticized that idea as a myth, but the report does not show that Pentagon officials advanced it.

That distinction does not make the review harmless. It identifies the danger accurately. Nuclear policy can become more permissive before any launch order exists, through revisions that make previously unthinkable choices appear administratively available. Inflating what has already happened only gives officials an easy rebuttal while obscuring the consequential work they acknowledged doing.

The spectacle of reaction

The headline’s “panic” relocates attention from state power to public emotion. Hasan’s fury and the academics’ alarm are reactions; they neither created the review nor control its outcome. Making those reactions the spectacle can reduce a substantive policy disclosure to another episode of partisan outrage.

Klippenstein also accused mainstream outlets of ignoring the testimony while concentrating on an FBI data breach. RawStory supplies his criticism but no systematic evidence establishing the scope or motive of that alleged neglect. Still, the contrast identifies a familiar media incentive: institutional drama with immediate victims is easier to package than classified policy machinery whose consequences are uncertain but potentially irreversible.

Secrecy expands presidential power

The larger pattern is executive authority growing through obscure procedure. A closed hearing, a classified review and the antiseptic language of “options” allow officials to alter the boundaries of catastrophic force without first defending the details in public.

The immediate fact is limited but severe: the Pentagon acknowledged work aimed at increasing the nuclear choices available to Trump. Whether those choices become policy remains unreported. That uncertainty is not a reason for melodrama, but it is no excuse for complacency. When institutions conceal the substance and coverage centers the people expressing alarm, power disappears from the frame precisely while it is being enlarged.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Panic as Pentagon quietly moves to expand Trump’s ‘nuclear options’

item.title: 'Cowardly' MAGA candidate derided after 'pathetic' campaign move: 'Embarrassing’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Arizona Republican state Rep. Alexander Kolodin removed Donald Trump’s endorsement from the front page of his campaign website while running for secretary of state. A Trump quote displayed there on July 19—calling Kolodin an attorney and “a patriot”—was gone by September 22, replaced by “Protect every vote.”

Democratic state Rep. Oscar De Los Santos called the change cowardly, while journalist Brahm Resnik documented it and other critics mocked Kolodin online. The report does not establish why Kolodin changed the page, and it includes no response from him. It places the move alongside allegations that Florida candidate Byron Donalds and several other Republicans have similarly removed Trump references from campaign materials.

The candidate made the choice

Kolodin holds the relevant agency here. His campaign controls the website, chose to feature Trump’s endorsement and later chose not to feature it. The available evidence establishes a deliberate change in presentation, though not the campaign’s reason for making it.

That distinction matters. Kolodin has not, based on this reporting, renounced Trump or explained a political disagreement. He has merely stopped advertising the endorsement so prominently. The record therefore supports a conclusion about strategic omission, not ideological conversion.

Power without accountability

Trump’s endorsement carried enough value for Kolodin to showcase it when his campaign considered the association useful. Removing it later does not erase that alliance; it changes what voters encounter first.

This is a familiar form of political insulation: accept the benefits of affiliation inside the party, then soften the branding before a broader electorate. The candidate retains the endorsement while attempting to control its visibility. Voters are offered a cleaner slogan—“Protect every vote”—without an explanation of what changed or why.

Mockery obscures the substance

RawStory builds much of its piece around insults from Kolodin’s opponents: “pathetic,” “cowardly,” “embarrassing,” and “Trump stank.” It also revives a 2020 traffic-stop anecdote about an alcoholic beverage found near the scene. That material supplies ridicule, not political understanding.

The consequential question is not whether Kolodin can be humiliated online. It is whether a candidate for statewide office believes voters should evaluate the alliances he cultivated. By centering taunts, the article turns an accountability issue into social-media theater and gives the campaign an easier grievance to answer than the website change itself.

A politics of reversible branding

The broader pattern alleged in the report—Republican candidates benefiting from Trump’s support and later reducing his visibility—shows how party loyalty can become selectively legible. The affiliation remains available for one audience and obscured for another.

That is not confusion. It is message management. The systemic failure comes when coverage fixates on who delivered the sharpest insult instead of documenting how candidates repackage their political commitments without accounting for them. Power survives that bargain; only the branding changes.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Cowardly’ MAGA candidate derided after ‘pathetic’ campaign move: ‘Embarrassing’

item.title: Trump singles out MAGA senator in late-night attack: 'People are sick and tired’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump used a late-night Truth Social post to blame Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas for blocking the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. Trump said Cotton was holding up the bill “for reasons unknown” and declared that people were tired of changing their clocks twice a year.

The measure had passed the House but remained stalled in the Senate. Trump issued his demand after senators had already left for a recess lasting until after the midterm elections, so his post could not produce the immediate Senate action he requested.

Trump also claimed that permanent daylight saving time would improve health, safety, family life and several industries. RawStory reports those claims but supplies no supporting studies or response from Cotton explaining his position.

Power sits in the Senate

The Senate has the institutional power to advance or bury the legislation. Its procedures, agenda and leadership determine whether the House-passed bill receives consideration. Cotton may possess enough influence to impede it, but Trump’s post alone does not establish how he did so or whether he was solely responsible.

That missing mechanism matters. Reducing Senate inaction to one obstructionist senator turns an institutional outcome into a personality dispute. It leaves leadership decisions, procedural barriers and the conduct of other senators largely outside the frame.

Trump chose a target

Trump did not explain Cotton’s objection. He attached Cotton’s name to public frustration and described the reason for the delay as unknown. That is political pressure, not an account of the legislative process.

The asymmetry is clear: the president commands a national platform and can direct supporters’ anger toward an individual lawmaker. Cotton is hardly powerless—he is a senator—but Trump’s framing still substitutes denunciation for evidence. If Cotton blocked the bill, readers need to know what action he took. RawStory does not provide that detail.

A slogan in place of evidence

Trump presented a sweeping catalogue of promised benefits, ranging from fewer murders and traffic deaths to lower cardiac risk and energy bills. The breadth of the list creates an impression of settled authority, but the report neither identifies the studies Trump invoked nor evaluates whether they support permanent daylight saving time specifically.

That distinction is essential. Evidence that changing clocks causes disruption would not, by itself, establish that permanent daylight saving time is preferable to permanent standard time. Trump’s post compresses those separate questions into one politically convenient conclusion.

Manufactured urgency

The timing exposes the performance. Trump demanded immediate action after the Senate had already recessed. Whatever his preference on clock policy, the reported intervention arrived when senators could not deliver the result he publicly demanded.

That allows a familiar maneuver: issue an impossible deadline, identify a culprit and claim alignment with an exhausted public. Legislative strategy disappears. The spectacle of command replaces the work required to move a bill.

The system behind the scapegoat

This episode shows how institutional failure is repackaged as personal drama. A stalled bill involving the House, Senate procedure and legislative leadership becomes a feud between two Republicans, while unsupported policy claims pass through as a list of supposed facts.

The result is political misdirection with a practical consequence: readers learn whom Trump wants blamed, but not who controlled the schedule, what Cotton actually did, or why the Senate failed to act. When coverage adopts that frame, power escapes scrutiny precisely by pointing at a target.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump singles out MAGA senator in late-night attack: ‘People are sick and tired’

item.title: Trash talk bomb set to detonate as Karoline Leavitt settles White House grudges
item.description:
What happened

RawStory columnist Jason Miciak says former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is shopping a book containing behind-the-scenes details from her tenure in the Trump administration. Citing a Page Six report based on unnamed sources, he predicts that Leavitt will settle grudges and expose damaging internal conflict.

The reporting establishes no book deal, publication date, specific revelation, quoted passage, or confirmed target of Leavitt’s alleged grievances. It also provides no evidence that she resigned because she objected to lying or believed the administration was collapsing; Miciak presents those possibilities as speculation.

A bomb made of conjecture

The promised “explosion” exists almost entirely in the columnist’s imagination. Miciak reasons that publishers demand palace intrigue, press secretaries hear sensitive information, and Leavitt must have accumulated resentments. From those premises, he constructs a prospective scandal without identifying its substance.

That is not an account of what Leavitt knows. It is a sales pitch for disclosures she may never make. RawStory’s framing converts an anonymously sourced publishing rumor into suspense while leaving the central question—what she will actually reveal—unanswered.

Where the power sits

The relevant institution is the presidency, and the dominant actor described here is Donald Trump. A White House press secretary possesses access and influence, but serves an administration whose senior officials set policy, control information, and decide what the public is told.

Miciak recognizes that communications staff can be excluded from consequential decisions, sometimes to preserve deniability. But the column then shifts attention from presidential power to Leavitt’s personality, ambitions, competence, marriage, appearance, and imagined payday. The machinery of government becomes scenery for a personality feud.

Gossip as misdirection

The column’s personal contempt is not evidence. References to Leavitt becoming pregnant by “a rich guy,” her “mean-girl disposition,” and her appearance do nothing to establish what happened inside the White House. They replace scrutiny of official conduct with gendered derision.

Leavitt’s record as press secretary can be assessed through her public statements and documented decisions. This article does not do that. Nor does it identify a lie she refused to tell, a cover-up she witnessed, or a mistake she blamed on someone else. It speculates about each, then invites readers to enjoy the anticipated retaliation.

Accountability sold as entertainment

If Leavitt possesses evidence of misconduct, the political question is not whether it can earn a seven-figure advance. It is what officials did, who authorized it, who concealed it, and what consequences followed. None of those questions can be answered from the material presented.

A tell-all may eventually supply evidence. Until then, describing prospective gossip as a detonating “bomb” rewards insiders for withholding information until it becomes commercially valuable. Public service is reduced to access, access to grievance, and grievance to intellectual property.

The systemic error

This is how political coverage launders uncertainty into drama. Powerful institutions disappear behind court intrigue; unnamed sources generate anticipation; an official’s possible disclosures become more important than the conduct those disclosures might document.

The larger pattern is an accountability culture built around spectacle rather than proof. It asks who will betray whom, not who exercised state power and with what result. When reporting cannot yet answer that harder question, the honest conclusion is simple: a book is reportedly being marketed, and the supposed political bomb has not been identified.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trash talk bomb set to detonate as Karoline Leavitt settles White House grudges

item.title: 'Hurting': Elon Musk breaks up with girlfriend as she leaks texts about White House dinner
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that tech executive Shivon Zilis said Elon Musk abruptly ended their romantic relationship, leaving her “hurting,” after he unfollowed her on X. Zilis, the mother of four of Musk’s children, disclosed the split in a Friday post and shared a screenshot she presented as a private exchange with a contact saved as “E.” Musk’s representatives did not immediately respond to People’s request for comment.

In the exchange, the contact said a White House state dinner honoring Chinese President Xi Jinping allowed significant others and that he would have invited Zilis had he known. Musk reportedly attended that dinner with more than 130 guests. The screenshot establishes neither why the relationship ended nor whether sharing it caused the breakup; the article’s headline implies a connection the reporting does not demonstrate.

Zilis said Musk gave her no warning and expressed hope that they could remain friends and co-parents. The article supplements her account with biographical details and mocking reactions from political commentators, but provides no statement from Musk explaining his decision.

The power is not evenly distributed

This is not merely celebrity heartbreak between interchangeable parties. Musk controls immense wealth, major companies, a mass-communications platform, and access to elite political settings. Zilis has her own executive status, but the relationship described in the reporting still places Musk at the center of a much larger apparatus of money, visibility, and influence.

That imbalance matters. He could end the relationship without explanation and remain institutionally insulated. She could make her pain public, but disclosure is not equivalent power. It is one of the few forms of leverage available to someone whose private life intersects with a man capable of turning a platform gesture—an unfollow—into international news.

The headline invents a cause

RawStory frames the episode as a breakup occurring “as” Zilis leaked texts about a White House dinner. That construction invites readers to infer retaliation: she exposed the message, so he left her. But the chronology presented does not establish that. Her post announced the breakup and included the screenshot; nothing in the reporting shows Musk ended the relationship because she published it.

That is tabloid misdirection masquerading as explanation. It substitutes insinuation for evidence while leaving the actual decision opaque. The only supported account of the breakup comes from Zilis, who said it happened suddenly and without warning.

Government access becomes gossip scenery

The politically significant detail is not that a text mentioned dinner etiquette. It is that Musk occupied a seat at a White House state dinner honoring Xi alongside more than 130 guests. Such access reflects proximity to state power, yet the article reduces it to relationship intrigue: who might have received the invitation, and why she did not.

That framing trivializes elite access instead of examining it. The reporting provides no evidence that Musk’s attendance produced improper influence, so corruption cannot responsibly be alleged. But treating entry into a consequential diplomatic setting as romantic décor avoids the more useful question: what political standing makes a corporate billionaire a recurring participant in spaces ordinary citizens cannot approach?

The dynasty obscures the institution

The article closes with jokes about “traditional family values” and a “principal breeder.” Those remarks point toward genuine hypocrisy in political cultures that preach rigid family norms while excusing powerful men from them. But they also turn Zilis and other women into props in a spectacle organized around Musk.

The larger pattern is an attention system that personalizes power. It chronicles the billionaire’s relationships, children, posts, and emotional mythology while giving less scrutiny to the institutions that amplify him. Musk’s private conduct attracts clicks; his structural position deserves examination. When political reporting chooses gossip over governance, powerful people do not disappear from view. They become more visible and less accountable.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Hurting’: Elon Musk breaks up with girlfriend as she leaks texts about White House dinner

item.title: Trump bid to ‘censor’ survivors backfires as thousands flock to see Epstein ties: analysis
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that thousands of people visited Miles Taylor’s traveling “Trump-Epstein Bookmobile,” a converted taco truck displaying Epstein-related files released by the Justice Department. Taylor argues that the turnout backfired on President Donald Trump by amplifying material his administration had sought to keep from public view.

According to RawStory, the White House urged selected Republican lawmakers to withdraw support from the Epstein Files Transparency Act, although Trump ultimately signed it. The outlet also reports that three Epstein survivors were removed from Trump’s midterm convention after a journalist accompanying them questioned a Republican congressional candidate about Epstein.

The released files reportedly mention Trump more than 3,000 times. That figure alone does not establish criminal conduct or complicity, and RawStory does not report such a finding. The story instead concerns political efforts to control access, attention, and questioning around the records.

Power was never in the parking lot

The survivors did not control the Justice Department, the convention, or the legislative pressure campaign. Trump held presidential authority. His administration controlled the department responsible for releasing the records, while the White House had access to Republican lawmakers whose votes could determine whether disclosure became mandatory.

That hierarchy matters more than Taylor’s spectacle. A mobile archive can attract attention, but it cannot compel production of government records. Congress created that obligation through legislation. The administration reportedly tried to prevent Congress from doing so, then complied after Trump signed the resulting law.

The decisions have names

RawStory describes several distinct acts: the White House lobbied lawmakers to reverse their support; officials held meetings about blocking disclosure; convention personnel expelled survivors and their journalistic companion after an Epstein question; and Trump eventually approved the disclosure mandate.

Calling this merely an awkward communications problem would erase agency. Officials made choices about access and exposure. Taylor calls those choices “censorship.” The reporting supports a narrower conclusion: people exercising institutional or organizational authority attempted to restrict disclosure, political support for disclosure, or questioning at a party event.

Attention is not evidence

The article’s headline trades partly on insinuation. A person’s name appearing thousands of times in a large document collection is not, by itself, proof of wrongdoing. Taylor’s claim about Trump’s friendship with Epstein is presented as Taylor’s characterization, not as a conclusion independently established by the article.

That distinction should not become an excuse for suppression. It is the reason disclosure and careful reporting matter. Authorities should release records because the public deserves evidence, not because every reference supplies a verdict. Transparency permits scrutiny; it does not abolish standards of proof.

The attempted diversion of blame

The weakest framing would cast this as a clash between Trump and noisy activists. The consequential conflict was between executive power and public access to government-held information. Survivors and visitors did not create the records, command the DOJ, pressure Republican legislators, or control admission to the convention.

RawStory also cites a Data for Progress survey finding that a majority believed the war against Iran was launched partly to distract from the Epstein scandal. That poll records public suspicion; it does not establish presidential motive or causation. Treating the suspicion as proof would reproduce the same evidentiary sloppiness that secrecy encourages.

Secrecy manufactures its own audience

The broader pattern is familiar: powerful institutions restrict information, then portray the resulting public suspicion as irrational fixation. But secrecy is not neutral. It concentrates interpretive power in the same offices deciding what the public may see.

The bookmobile’s appeal reflects that institutional failure. People are lining up in parking lots because formal channels had to be forced open by legislation. The political consequence is larger than one traveling exhibit: when those with custody of public records resist disclosure, they turn transparency from routine governance into an oppositional act—and ensure that every attempt at control becomes part of the story.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump bid to ‘censor’ survivors backfires as thousands flock to see Epstein ties: analysis

item.title: 'Triage begins': Panicked Republicans launch 'rescue mission' to save MAGA senator
item.description:
What happened

Senate Republicans’ leading super PAC began a costly effort to protect Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, shifting seven figures into his reelection race while canceling its remaining North Carolina reservations, including $18 million in final-month television advertising, RawStory reported. The retreat makes North Carolina’s open Republican-held seat harder to defend and signals that party strategists consider Marshall unexpectedly vulnerable.

The evidence is suggestive, not conclusive. Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton’s campaign cited two polls showing him ahead, while Democratic pollster John Anzalone circulated an unattributed survey placing Hamilton at 47%, Marshall at 43%, and third candidate David Graham at 5%. The Cook Political Report moved Kansas from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” and Republican campaign chief Tim Scott acknowledged that the state was more competitive than he wanted while predicting a Marshall victory.

Marshall, an incumbent closely aligned with President Donald Trump, has already received campaign help from Vice President JD Vance. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and Trump carried the state by 16 percentage points two years earlier.

The money identifies the emergency

The decisive actor here is not a pundit declaring that “triage” has begun. It is the Senate Leadership Fund, an organization with the institutional power to redirect millions of dollars across the national map. Its spending decisions determine which Republican candidates receive protection and which are left with fewer resources.

That does not prove Marshall will lose. It does establish that Republican strategists see enough danger in Kansas to sacrifice planned support in North Carolina. Public assurances from Scott and mockery from Marshall’s adviser cannot erase the allocation. Campaign professionals may spin; budgets disclose priorities.

One rescue creates another exposure

Republicans hold 53 Senate seats and, according to Semafor’s arithmetic, can lose no more than three while retaining control. That makes every unexpected defensive contest expensive twice over: money spent rescuing Marshall cannot defend the seat being vacated by North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis.

This is the structural consequence of a widening map. A party built around comfortably holding Kansas now has to purchase insurance there, reducing its capacity elsewhere. Hamilton does not need Kansas to become broadly Democratic. He needs this race to become competitive enough that Republican institutions keep draining resources into it.

Panic is a headline, vulnerability is a fact

RawStory’s “panicked Republicans” framing goes beyond what the reporting establishes. The article documents a major resource shift, worsening race ratings and Republican reinforcement. It does not provide internal communications proving panic, nor does the unattributed poll deserve the authority of verified public evidence.

But rejecting the melodrama should not obscure the underlying development. “Rescue mission” is a Democratic strategist’s description; the spending move is the material fact. Republican leaders are treating a deep-red incumbent as someone who cannot safely be left to his own campaign.

The distraction beneath the insults

Vance told rallygoers to support Marshall and send “the crazy people” packing. That language substitutes social contempt for an account of Marshall’s record or the reasons voters may be reconsidering him. It turns political competition into a contest between legitimate insiders and supposedly deranged outsiders.

The stronger misdirection, however, would be to make Democratic optimism the story. Hamilton’s campaign memo, partisan posts and favorable polls are claims about momentum. The Republican super PAC’s withdrawal from North Carolina is an exercise of power with national consequences. The institution controlling the money made the consequential choice.

A shrinking margin exposes the machine

Safe seats are political assets because they allow parties to concentrate money elsewhere. When an incumbent turns one of those assets into a liability, the damage travels beyond state lines. Marshall’s vulnerability, if Republican spending accurately reflects it, is not merely a Kansas problem; it reshapes the party’s defense of Senate control.

The larger pattern is a governing coalition forced to spend more of its power preserving itself. Its leaders can dismiss challengers, promise victory and deploy national surrogates. They still have to decide where the money goes. In this case, their decision says that holding Kansas now costs them ground in North Carolina.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Triage begins’: Panicked Republicans launch ‘rescue mission’ to save MAGA senator

item.title: ‘Out of control’: Jared Kushner lashes out at ‘deeply misleading’ CNN report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Jared Kushner attacked a CNN investigation on Friday, October 2, 2026, calling it “deeply misleading” and saying years of ignoring allegedly false coverage were over. CNN had reported that Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, is the largest shareholder in Israel’s Phoenix Financial, which invests in companies supplying the Israeli military.

CNN found no indication that Kushner’s diplomatic work directly affected those investments. Kushner said he does not decide what Phoenix buys or sells and that Affinity invested before Donald Trump returned to office. The reporting therefore establishes overlapping diplomatic and financial interests—not that Kushner used diplomacy to enrich those investments.

Power without a government title

Kushner’s authority does not depend on holding formal office. According to RawStory, he has acted as an unofficial Middle East envoy while remaining outside the administration. That arrangement gives a presidential relative access and influence without the ordinary clarity that comes with a defined public position.

This is the central power question. Kushner can participate in diplomacy touching a region where his firm has substantial financial exposure, yet his defense emphasizes distance from Phoenix’s individual investment decisions. That may answer a narrow allegation of direct control. It does not resolve the broader problem created when private capital and unofficial state influence occupy the same political terrain.

A rebuttal stronger than the allegation

Kushner presents CNN as suggesting that his diplomatic work benefited investments in Israeli defense suppliers. But the network, by RawStory’s account, expressly said it found no evidence that his diplomatic actions directly affected those investments.

That caveat matters. CNN’s evidence supports scrutiny of a possible conflict or alignment of interests, not a finding of intervention for profit. Any headline implying a proven causal link would outrun the reported facts.

Kushner’s response performs the reverse distortion: it treats the absence of proof of direct influence as though it eliminates the legitimate concern. It does not. A conflict question can exist without evidence of a corrupt transaction, particularly when public influence and private holdings converge.

The convenient argument over media conduct

RawStory frames the episode as Kushner “lashing out” in an “unusual public rant.” That captures the spectacle but risks shrinking an institutional issue into a personality dispute between an aggrieved investor and a provocative network.

The stronger question is not whether Kushner sounded angry or whether CNN’s headline was maximally careful. It is why a presidential family member can exercise reported diplomatic influence while his investment firm holds a major stake in a financial institution exposed to the same region. Focusing on tone allows every participant to evade the harder structure: CNN can defend its caveat, Kushner can denounce its framing, and the informal concentration of political and financial power remains intact.

Accountability by personal discretion

Kushner said he would release facts and supporting information “when the truth matters” and let people judge. That is not institutional accountability. It is selective disclosure controlled by the person facing scrutiny.

The public should not have to depend on an unofficial envoy’s judgment about when his financial relationships deserve explanation. Informal power produces precisely this weakness: fewer settled boundaries, less automatic disclosure, and more room for the powerful actor to define which questions are legitimate.

The system behind the quarrel

This story does not establish that Kushner shaped diplomacy to benefit Affinity Partners. It establishes something politically significant on its own: private investment and public influence have been allowed to overlap closely enough that the conflict question is unavoidable, while the available reporting does not prove direct abuse.

That ambiguity serves concentrated power. The press can overstate implications, the subject can use that overstatement to dismiss broader scrutiny, and the underlying arrangement survives. The systemic error is not merely a disputed headline. It is a political order that permits unofficial authority, family access, and regional financial interests to coexist—and then treats demands for a clean accounting as a media controversy.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Out of control’: Jared Kushner lashes out at ‘deeply misleading’ CNN report
