item.title: DNC strategist cleans former Trump official’s clock to his face
item.description:
What happened

On CNN’s Thursday News Central, Democratic National Committee strategist Sawyer Hackett disputed former Trump administration official Matt Mowers’s claim that the economy under President Donald Trump presented a “mixed picture.” AlterNet reports that Hackett argued inflation was higher than when Joe Biden left office, while the job market had slowed, the economy had contracted, and consumer confidence had deteriorated. Anchor Brianna Keilar backed Hackett’s narrower comparison on inflation.

The exchange followed a clip in which Trump said his administration was running the country well but doing “an extremely poor job” promoting its record. Mowers cited record stock-market levels, a five-year-low poverty rate, and low unemployment. Hackett countered that Trump’s problem was not communication but economic performance. The segment ended in disagreement, not an adjudicated statistical analysis.

The power is not on the panel

AlterNet packages the encounter as Hackett “cleaning” Mowers’s clock. That describes television performance, not political power. Hackett can rebut Republican claims; Mowers can defend them. Neither was making economic policy from a CNN studio.

Trump holds the institutional power identified in this story. His administration makes decisions that affect employment, prices, growth, and public confidence. When Trump says the central failure is promotion, he shifts attention from material conditions to messaging—as though mortgage rates above 7 percent and inflation at 3 percent, figures Keilar cited, could be repaired by better advertising.

A slogan is not an economic record

Mowers’s defense relied on selective indicators: stocks, poverty, and unemployment. Hackett relied on others: inflation, economic contraction, labor-market weakness, and consumer confidence. A serious account would define the periods, measures, and data behind each claim.

AlterNet does not do that work. It declares a winner. Even Hackett’s reference to a “current 12-point low” in consumer confidence is reproduced without identifying the index, survey, or comparison period. The article’s preferred argument may be stronger, but applause-line framing is not verification.

The misdirection is the spectacle

The weakest part of the coverage is its conversion of economic accountability into partisan combat. “Who humiliated whom?” is easier television—and easier aggregation—than “Which administration decisions produced which consequences?”

That framing benefits the people with power. Trump’s assertion that the country is doing well becomes one side of a lively exchange rather than a claim requiring disciplined scrutiny. Mowers’s interruptions become proof of defeat rather than an occasion to test his statistics. Viewers are offered a verbal knockout while the governing record remains only partially examined.

Politics by promotion

Trump’s remark reveals the larger pattern: political failure is recast as a sales problem. If voters are unhappy, the administration supposedly needs sharper promotion, not different policy. Their experience becomes a misunderstanding to be corrected.

The press can reinforce that evasion when it grades partisan surrogates on performance instead of tracing authority, decisions, and consequences. Hackett may have won the exchange AlterNet describes. But the consequential contest is not between two commentators. It is between a government’s claims and the conditions people live under—and that contest cannot be settled by declaring who landed the better line.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: DNC strategist cleans former Trump official’s clock to his face

item.title: 'Bizarre' clapping incident shows loyalists 'afraid' of Trump: NYT analysis
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that during a Thursday executive-order signing, President Donald Trump’s Cabinet members and other allies applauded for an unusually long time. New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie interpreted the scene as evidence that Trump’s subordinates were afraid to be the first person to stop.

Bouie compared the social dynamic—not the consequences—to accounts of officials applauding Joseph Stalin. He argued that Trump demands praise, holds grudges and punishes perceived disloyalty, while explicitly noting that Trump’s aides do not face imprisonment or execution.

Bouie also speculated about how Trump might react if Democrats won sweeping electoral victories, mentioning further escalation in Iran and additional damage in Washington as possible outcomes. AlterNet supplies no evidence that either action was planned, and the excerpt does not identify the polls, their dates or the election cycle behind Bouie’s projected Democratic gains.

The applause came from power

These were not powerless spectators trapped in a hostile crowd. They were Cabinet officials and political loyalists occupying the executive branch’s commanding heights. Whatever private anxiety may have shaped their behavior, they possessed institutional authority that ordinary Americans do not.

Calling them merely “afraid” risks laundering submission into victimhood. Trump signed the order, but the officials around him chose to furnish the ceremony with prolonged adulation. They helped turn a government proceeding into a display of personal allegiance.

Fear does not erase agency

Bouie’s interpretation is plausible, but the clip alone cannot establish what each person feared or intended. The observable conduct is narrower and still damning: senior officials publicly participated in an extended ritual of approval around the president.

The distinction matters. Fear can explain obedience without absolving it. Officials who anticipate humiliation, dismissal or retaliation may have strong incentives to flatter the person controlling their careers. They also retain responsibility for using public office to reinforce that system. Institutional cowardice is not the absence of power; it is power surrendered upward and exercised downward.

The analogy outruns the evidence

The Stalin comparison clarifies the mechanism of competitive obedience: nobody wants to become conspicuous by stopping first. Bouie properly acknowledged the enormous difference in stakes. Trump’s aides were not facing a gulag or execution.

That limit should govern the analysis. The reporting supports scrutiny of court politics, sycophancy and fear of presidential retaliation. It does not establish Stalinist terror, diagnose Trump’s psychology or prove how he would respond to an electoral defeat. Historical analogy is useful when it identifies a structure; it becomes propaganda when resemblance substitutes for evidence.

Speculation displaces accountability

The article’s weakest turn is its leap from visible applause to hypothetical electoral catastrophe and possible military escalation. Bouie cited generic-ballot margins of 15 points or more and translated them into roughly 260 House seats, 55 or 56 Senate seats and 30 governorships for Democrats. The excerpt provides too little polling context to assess that projection.

The Iran and Washington scenarios are likewise questions, not reported plans. Framing them as products of anticipated “narcissistic injury” makes an inferred personality the engine of events while pushing institutions out of view. Wars, executive abuses and attacks on federal governance require officials, legal rationalizations, appropriations, enforcement and compliance. A president’s impulses matter because other powerful people convert them into state action.

The system rewards the loyalists

The larger pattern is not that one volatile leader has frightened an otherwise healthy government. It is that ambitious officials can gain access and retain authority by performing devotion, while their offices give that devotion material consequences.

The clapping matters less as amateur psychology than as a public demonstration of hierarchy. Trump occupied the center; senior officials signaled that approval should continue until someone else accepted the risk of ending it. Authoritarian political culture grows through precisely that distribution of agency: power concentrated at the top, responsibility diffused among subordinates, and cowardice repackaged as helplessness.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Bizarre’ clapping incident shows loyalists ‘afraid’ of Trump: NYT analysis

item.title: Hegseth to announce new purge at Pentagon as war drags on: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to announce a 20 percent reduction in positions reserved for generals and admirals, doubling the 10 percent overall reduction he ordered in May 2025. Pentagon officials told The Wall Street Journal that the armed services would have until Jan. 1, 2027, to complete the new cuts.

Hegseth is expected to announce the plan during a “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, as the war with Iran enters its seventh month. He has described the senior ranks as bloated and the reductions as an effort to remove redundant command structures, while denying that they are intended to punish senior officers.

The report does not establish that particular officers will be fired, nor does it identify which commands would disappear. It describes a planned reduction in designated senior positions. The word “purge” in RawStory’s headline therefore goes beyond what the reported details prove.

The power sits with Hegseth

This is not an institutional mystery or a dispute among equal factions. Hegseth issued the earlier reduction order, is directing the new one and controls how the Pentagon presents it. Military leaders have been told to carry out the reductions; they are not the political authors of the policy.

That distinction matters because bureaucratic language can make an imposed decision sound self-executing. “Streamlining” does not abolish commands by natural law. Civilian leadership chooses which positions count as redundant, which responsibilities are consolidated and which officers lose influence as a result.

A rationale without a demonstrated case

Hegseth’s slogan—more generals do not necessarily produce more success—is unobjectionable in the abstract. It is not evidence that this particular reduction is strategically sound.

The article reports that there were 809 active-duty generals and admirals as of Sept. 30, 2023, below the statutory maximum of 857. That figure neither proves that the senior ranks were efficiently organized nor establishes that a 20 percent cut is warranted. Without the affected commands, operational analysis or criteria for elimination, the public is being given a percentage and a posture in place of a demonstrated military case.

Grooming as political theater

The staging makes the administration’s priorities unusually plain. Commanders were asked to nominate attendees who satisfy strict waist-to-height standards and have “impeccable” grooming. Those selected would receive a Pentagon tour and an opportunity to work out with Hegseth.

This follows his previous Quantico appearance, where he demanded “no more beardos” or “fat generals.” Physical readiness can be a legitimate military concern. Curating an audience around appearance while unveiling consequential command changes turns that concern into spectacle: visible bodily conformity becomes a proxy for institutional competence.

The misdirection is not toward some weaker group blamed for the policy. It is from the policy itself. The immaculate audience, workout and insults aimed at supposedly unfit officers offer an easily understood morality play while the harder questions—what expertise disappears, what oversight weakens and how wartime command will be affected—remain unanswered in the reporting.

War raises the stakes

According to RawStory, the announcement comes during the seventh month of the war with Iran, with no end reported in sight. That context makes reductions in senior command structure more consequential, not automatically more suspect. Wartime does not make every headquarters position indispensable, but it does increase the burden on the official ordering the cuts to explain their operational logic.

Calling the plan a purge may be rhetorically satisfying, but the available evidence does not establish political retaliation. Calling it mere streamlining would be equally credulous. The established fact is that Hegseth is using his institutional authority to reduce senior positions while supplying the public with broad assertions rather than the details needed to judge the consequences.

Management by spectacle

The larger pattern is governance through symbolic discipline. Leaders identify an institution as bloated, attach the diagnosis to culturally charged images of softness or disorder, and then treat numerical cuts as proof of strength. The performance makes scrutiny seem like resistance to reform.

Real accountability runs in the opposite direction. The official wielding power must identify the problem, show how the chosen remedy addresses it and accept responsibility for the results. Here, Hegseth owns the decision. Until the Pentagon discloses what will be cut and why, the uniforms, grooming standards and workout are not evidence of military reform. They are stage dressing around an exercise of power whose operational consequences remain undisclosed.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Hegseth to announce new purge at Pentagon as war drags on: report

item.title: GOP senators are plotting Hegseth's doom — but it's really Trump they're coming for
item.description:
What happened

RawStory columnist Jason Miciak argues that Republican senators’ complaints about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are an indirect challenge to President Donald Trump. But the column does not establish that senators are “plotting” Hegseth’s removal or using him as a proxy to target Trump. It offers two critical Senate quotations—one from an unnamed source—and interprets their tone as evidence of a broader revolt.

The reported objections concern the handling of the Iran war, the removal of officers from promotion lists, the firing of generals and admirals, and Hegseth’s request for a $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget plus $88 billion connected to the war and additional weapons. The unnamed source said senators feared the war’s apparently haphazard execution would damage Republican candidates in the fall elections.

Miciak also reports that Hegseth faced eight prospective articles of impeachment associated with Rep. Thomas Massie, while Trump continued to support him. The column predicts that electoral losses, military casualties or renewed escalation could turn Republican frustration into action, but it provides no named senator pledging to remove Hegseth and no evidence that conviction—or a campaign against Trump—was underway.

Power sits above the proxy

Hegseth commands the Defense Department, but Trump holds the greater institutional power described here. He selected Hegseth, continues to back him and, under the column’s account, controls whether the administration intensifies the war. Senators control confirmation, appropriations, oversight and any eventual impeachment trial. House members control whether impeachment advances.

That division matters because Hegseth is not an autonomous accident. If his personnel decisions, spending demands and management of the war reflect administration policy, then concentrating blame on the secretary can obscure presidential responsibility. Republican lawmakers also possess tools to resist. Complaining privately while continuing to fund, defend or tolerate the policy is not resistance; it is participation with reservations.

The evidence does not support the headline

The column’s strongest factual material shows Republican unease with Hegseth’s conduct and its electoral cost. Its central claim—that senators are really “coming for” Trump—is an inference built largely from tone, analogy and hypothetical future events.

That gap should not be disguised as inside knowledge. The unnamed source explicitly discussed the war and the midterms, not a plan to confront Trump. The other quoted senator objected to personnel removals. Neither quotation establishes an organized effort against Hegseth, much less a staged assault on the president.

The framing converts ordinary congressional self-preservation into a dramatic conspiracy. A simpler reading fits the evidence better: senators fear that visible disorder, higher prices and an unpopular war could cost them power. That may eventually produce a break with the administration. RawStory had not shown that it already had.

Accountability delayed is protection

The senators’ reported concern arrived after Hegseth’s confirmation and after the administration had begun removing senior officers. If lawmakers considered him unqualified or regarded those decisions as reckless, they were not powerless observers. The Senate had an opportunity to deny him authority, and Congress retained leverage through money and oversight.

Their quoted anxiety centers partly on electoral consequences. That exposes the governing incentive: tolerate dangerous conduct while it remains politically affordable, then discover institutional standards when the polling turns. The weaker actors—the dismissed officers, deployed service members and civilians paying the economic price—bear consequences before senators decide whether accountability is convenient.

The system rewards disposable loyalists

Hegseth may function as a shield, but not necessarily in the elaborate way the column proposes. Presidents benefit when failure can be assigned to a subordinate, while legislators benefit when they can condemn that subordinate without confronting the leader or policies they enabled.

That is the larger pattern: concentrated executive power paired with conditional legislative courage. Congress delegates, confirms and funds; officials execute; lawmakers complain anonymously when the damage threatens their seats. The public is then offered a personnel drama instead of an accounting of decisions.

Whether Hegseth falls is less important than whether the policies, spending and chains of responsibility change. Removing one loyalist while preserving the machinery that empowered him would not be a reckoning. It would be the system protecting itself by sacrificing its most convenient proxy.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senators are plotting Hegseth’s doom — but it’s really Trump they’re coming for

item.title: Secret recording catches Ken Paxton privately trashing Trump’s convention: NYT
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton privately said Donald Trump’s two-day midterm convention in Dallas hurt Republican polling. Asked at a Washington fundraiser whether Trump was “a little bit of a drag,” Paxton replied that “everybody’s numbers dropped” after the convention and that the situation was “not good.”

The New York Times obtained audio reportedly recorded by a fundraiser attendee who opposes Paxton. Two other attendees corroborated the conversation, according to the Times, while a third confirmed Paxton was present. Paxton adviser Nick Maddux called the report “manipulated nonsense” and said the campaign’s latest poll had Paxton leading Democratic state Rep. James Talarico by three points.

The private diagnosis

Paxton’s reported assessment matters because it strips away the campaign performance. In public, his adviser promises that Paxton will campaign alongside Trump. In private, Paxton reportedly described Trump’s convention as an electoral liability.

That is not proof of a personal break with Trump, nor does the reporting establish what caused any polling movement. It does show a candidate privately attributing weakened numbers to the party’s dominant figure while his campaign publicly dismisses the disclosure.

Power sets the script

Trump holds the greater power in this relationship. He commanded both days of the Dallas event, and Paxton’s campaign still advertises proximity to him even after Paxton reportedly complained about the political cost.

Paxton, meanwhile, is hardly powerless. He is Texas attorney general and a Senate candidate backed by substantial campaign spending in a state where Democrats have not won statewide office in more than three decades. But within Republican politics, his room to criticize Trump openly appears narrower than his freedom to blame him behind closed doors.

Denial without rebuttal

Maddux attacked the Times report as manipulation, but the response quoted by RawStory does not explain what was manipulated or directly deny that Paxton made the remarks. Instead, it changes the subject: an internal poll shows a three-point lead, the campaign says its numbers have improved, and Paxton expects to appear with Trump.

Those claims may be true, but they do not resolve the reported contradiction. A favorable private poll does not disprove Paxton’s statement that the convention hurt Republican numbers. Calling reporting “nonsense” is not a factual rebuttal when the campaign leaves the central quotation standing.

Loyalty as political discipline

The larger pattern is a party in which strategic judgment must often be expressed privately while loyalty is performed publicly. Paxton can reportedly recognize that Trump may be damaging Republican candidates, yet his campaign still treats association with Trump as mandatory.

That arrangement protects the leader from internal accountability and pushes the cost downward. Candidates absorb the electoral risk, donors finance the response, and advisers deny the visible tension. The powerful figure keeps the stage; everyone else is expected to explain the numbers without naming the source of the problem.

The system behind the leak

The recording exposes more than hypocrisy. It shows how concentrated political power degrades honest decision-making inside a party. When candidates believe candor carries a higher price than strategic failure, criticism migrates to private rooms and emerges only through leaks.

Whether Paxton is actually trailing Talarico cannot be settled from the competing polling claims in this report. What the episode does establish is the political structure around that uncertainty: Paxton reportedly blamed Trump in private, his adviser defended Trump-aligned campaigning in public, and the campaign answered an authenticated account with denunciation rather than a specific rebuttal. That is how personal dominance turns ordinary electoral analysis into forbidden speech.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Secret recording catches Ken Paxton privately trashing Trump’s convention: NYT

item.title: She left the ER after a 4-hour wait — they billed her anyway
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Autumn Daniels was billed $410 by Carle Foundation Hospital in Urbana, Illinois, after an April emergency-room visit in which staff registered her, checked her vital signs and sent her to the waiting room. Daniels, suffering a severe migraine and vomiting repeatedly, left after four hours without seeing a doctor or receiving treatment. She obtained care at another hospital after waiting about 90 minutes.

Carle classified the encounter as an “Emergency Room Level 1” visit. Daniels’ state-employee health plan denied the claim because it excludes claims associated with leaving against medical advice, leaving her responsible for the charge. Carle upheld the bill, while Daniels paid $25 and applied for financial assistance. She may appeal the insurer’s denial.

The precise basis for the $410 remains unclear. Daniels said Carle did not provide the itemized bill she requested. The American Medical Association told KFF Health News that triage alone cannot be billed under the evaluation-and-management code listed, while suggesting the hospital may have combined a provider charge with a facility fee. Carle declined to discuss the case despite Daniels’ privacy waiver.

The hospital holds the power

Daniels did not set the wait, define what counted as care or assign the billing code. Carle did. It controlled access to treatment, documented the encounter, priced the alleged service and then declared its own charge “accurate and fully supported.”

That is institutional power in its most mundane and effective form: one party writes the record, interprets the record and demands payment from the person least equipped to challenge it. Carle’s explanation that it must maintain staff, space and equipment may describe hospital overhead. It does not explain why that overhead became a $410 individual charge labeled with a code used for professional evaluation and management.

The insurer completes the trap

HealthLink did not create Carle’s bill, but its coverage rule transferred the dispute directly to Daniels. The hospital allegedly provided too little care to satisfy her needs, yet the insurer treated her departure as a reason not to pay.

Calling this “leaving against medical advice” obscures the reported sequence. Daniels said she waited four hours without seeing a physician and left to seek treatment elsewhere. The article does not report that a clinician advised her to remain or explained the medical risks of departing. HealthLink’s statement identifies a contractual category, not evidence that Daniels rejected actual medical advice.

Her available remedy is an appeal—the familiar administrative burden imposed after institutions have already made their decisions. Carle bills; HealthLink denies; Daniels must supply the labor required to challenge both.

Transparency after the fact is not consent

Carle told Daniels that, effective March 1, 2026, emergency-department visits could generate charges once registration or nursing assessment began, even without direct provider care. Daniels said that during a similar visit in 2025, hospital staff assured her she would not be billed if she left, and she was not. Carle did not answer why its policy changed.

A rule disclosed only when a patient disputes a bill is not meaningful price transparency. A person arriving with piercing pain and repeated vomiting is in no position to negotiate the definition or price of “care.” The hospital possesses the policy, the coding expertise and the leverage; the patient receives the terms after the charge appears.

Carle’s claim that it supports transparency is especially weak beside its refusal to explain Daniels’ case to reporters despite her authorization and her account that it never supplied the requested itemization.

The framing shifts responsibility downward

The practical advice offered by the underlying KFF Health News report—ask about billing policies, monitor insurance portals, request records and file appeals—may help patients survive the system. But it also shows how thoroughly responsibility has been pushed onto sick people.

Daniels was expected to investigate hospital billing rules while seeking urgent care, anticipate an insurer’s interpretation of her departure, preserve paperwork and navigate an appeal. Neither institution is described as having to reconcile the central contradiction: a hospital charged for an emergency visit that did not deliver treatment, and an insurer denied coverage because the patient eventually went somewhere that would.

The weaker actor becomes the case manager for failures she did not create.

A system that monetizes nonservice

This episode reveals a broader political structure built around private administrative authority. Hospitals can convert access, assessment and overhead into opaque charges. Insurers can use contractual classifications to refuse those charges. Patients remain liable until they successfully penetrate systems designed and controlled by the institutions seeking payment.

The result is more than an aggravating bill. It is a deterrent attached to emergency care: seek help and risk being charged even when help never arrives; leave to obtain treatment elsewhere and risk being classified as noncompliant. The system preserves revenue and denial authority on both sides while assigning uncertainty, paperwork and debt to the patient.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: She left the ER after a 4-hour wait — they billed her anyway

item.title: GOP senator shocks with 'remarkable break from Trump': 'Maybe we're doing something wrong’
item.description:
What happened

Sen. Jim Justice urged the Trump administration to reconsider immigration sweeps that remove long-established community members, telling Politico on Tuesday that officials should admit when enforcement has gone wrong and adjust. RawStory reports that Politico journalist Rachel Shin described his remarks as “a remarkable break” from the administration.

Justice’s criticism followed complaints that ICE operations in Texas, Kansas, and Oklahoma were disrupting cattle supply chains and costing producers millions of dollars. Other Republicans had also objected to aspects of enforcement, while the administration reversed an instruction—later characterized as a “miscommunication”—that reportedly told ICE officers to stop arresting immigrants without criminal records.

Justice then retreated. The Trump-endorsed senator declared his complete support for the president’s immigration strategy, accused others of twisting his words, and praised the administration’s record.

Power set the policy

The decisive power here rests with the Trump administration, which determines ICE’s enforcement priorities. Ranchers, immigrant communities, and individual senators can protest the consequences, but administration officials control whom agents are directed to arrest.

Calling the disputed instruction a “miscommunication” obscures that chain of command. Whatever produced the temporary restriction, someone authorized it, communicated it to officers, and then reversed it. Administrative fog is not an explanation for the policy choice that remained in force.

Sympathy arrived with the invoice

Justice acknowledged the human reality of agents taking away people who had lived in a neighborhood for 15 years. But the political pressure described in the reporting came after cattle producers complained about lost money and disrupted supply chains.

That distinction matters. Long-standing community ties apparently did not generate sufficient Republican resistance on their own. Economic damage to an influential industry did. The objection became politically legible when aggressive enforcement imposed costs on producers with access to senators and congressional committees.

The retreat reveals the constraint

Justice briefly named the administration’s capacity for error. Then he issued a statement denying any meaningful break, offering unqualified support for Trump’s strategy and redirecting attention to President Joe Biden.

That is not a policy clarification. It is a demonstration of where authority lies inside the party. Justice could describe harmful consequences, but he would not sustain criticism that might make the president responsible for them. His retreat left the affected communities and businesses in the same position while protecting his standing with Trump.

The headline overstates the rebellion

Treating Justice’s remark as a shocking rupture mistakes discomfort for opposition. He neither announced legislation nor described oversight measures, funding conditions, or another institutional step to restrain ICE. The reporting establishes criticism followed by capitulation.

The stronger story is not that a loyal senator rebelled. It is that even a billionaire former governor with a Senate seat and industry connections quickly narrowed his objection once it could be read as a challenge to Trump.

The system absorbs dissent

This episode shows how a governing coalition can preserve a punitive policy while accommodating complaints rhetorically. Officials call reversals confusion, lawmakers express concern about implementation, and responsibility dissolves before reaching the people with power to change the orders.

The result is a durable political arrangement: enforcement remains aggressive, business losses are treated as an operational problem, human disruption becomes background detail, and dissenting Republicans reaffirm loyalty before their criticism can acquire consequences.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senator shocks with ‘remarkable break from Trump’: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong’

item.title: 'Desperate' Republicans in 'panic mode' as new attack line fails: report
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that prominent Republicans are calling Democratic candidates “weird,” reviving an insult Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz used against Donald Trump, JD Vance and other Republicans during the 2024 campaign. Sen. Tim Scott used it at a Republican convention in Dallas, Vance directed it at Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Trump has applied it to Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, and the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA, Inc. featured it in an ad against Talarico.

The report says Republicans adopted the attack amid low approval ratings for Trump, persistent inflation, gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and a war in Iran that had lasted more than seven months. Republican strategist Mike Madrid and unnamed or Democratic-aligned sources characterized the tactic as desperation or panic. Republican committee spokespeople defended it, while former Harris campaign pollster Geoff Garin said the same insult performed poorly in that campaign’s internal polling.

The people with power chose the distraction

This is not merely a collection of candidates reaching for the same lazy adjective. The president, the vice president, a senator, the Republican National Committee, the National Republican Senatorial Committee and a well-funded super PAC possess the institutional power to set the party’s message. They are choosing personal ridicule.

That choice matters because these actors are not spectators trapped beneath economic conditions or war. They control the White House, shape federal policy and command a national political apparatus. When they replace an account of their governing record with playground contempt, the evasion comes from the people most responsible for explaining what government is doing.

“Weird” is an alibi, not an argument

The attack supplies no information about El-Sayed or Talarico’s policies, qualifications or conduct. Its function is to make the target socially suspect without having to establish wrongdoing. Vance’s additional description of El-Sayed as “evil” escalates the accusation while remaining just as empty in the reporting presented.

That is the misdirection: voters are invited to judge whether Democratic candidates feel culturally normal while the party controlling the presidency avoids a substantive defense of conditions RawStory identifies as politically damaging. Prices and war require explanations. “Weird” requires only repetition.

The panic claim outruns the evidence

RawStory’s framing is stronger than its proof. “Panic mode” comes from an unnamed Democratic operative, while “desperate” is Madrid’s political assessment. Those comments support an interpretation of Republican anxiety; they do not independently establish the party’s internal state.

The article also provides no approval figure, polling date or electoral forecast demonstrating that Republican midterm chances are “drooping.” Even the insult’s supposed failure is complicated by Garin’s statement that it also tested poorly when Democrats used it. The defensible conclusion is narrower: Republican leaders are repeating an apparently weak attack while declining to show that voters respond to it.

The machinery of empty politics

The most revealing response came from RNC press secretary Natalie Baldassarre, who said no study was needed. That is political messaging severed from evidence by declaration. The party does not need to know whether the line persuades voters because the line also serves another purpose: feeding partisan media, disciplining supporters and keeping attention on identity rather than performance.

The larger pattern is familiar. Institutions with power reduce governing disputes to social revulsion, then treat repetition as proof. The consequence is not merely a worse campaign slogan. It is an electorate offered insults where accountability should be—and a governing party attempting to turn its opponents’ alleged strangeness into cover for its own record.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Desperate’ Republicans in ‘panic mode’ as new attack line fails: report

item.title: GOP senator's lawsuit accuses Jack Smith of mocking 'Trump's complexion’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Marsha Blackburn sued former special counsel Jack Smith in federal court in Tennessee, seeking $1 in nominal damages and the return of phone records obtained during Smith’s investigation. The complaint alleges that a May 2023 subpoena to Verizon for Blackburn’s call logs around the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack violated her constitutional rights by preventing her from invoking the Speech or Debate Clause.

The lawsuit also claims the investigation’s codename, “Arctic Frost,” referred to a type of orange and was chosen to mock Donald Trump’s complexion. According to RawStory, the complaint provides no source for that assertion, does not identify who selected the name, and acknowledges that the FBI opened the investigation before Smith became special counsel in November 2022.

Smith has defended the subpoenas as part of an effort to determine whether Trump called members of Congress to delay certification of the 2020 election. Blackburn’s complaint argues instead that Smith lacked lawful authority because the Senate did not confirm him and alleges that her political support for Trump influenced the decision to obtain her records.

The serious question buried underneath

The subpoena raises a legitimate constitutional dispute. Blackburn argues that prosecutors obtained a senator’s records without telling the judge they belonged to a lawmaker and secured nondisclosure that prevented her from challenging the demand under legislative-immunity protections. Those claims deserve adjudication, not dismissal by association with the lawsuit’s weaker flourishes.

The institutional power at issue belonged to the Justice Department and the special counsel’s office. Prosecutors sought the records; a Justice Department official approved the subpoenas after assessing litigation risk; and a court apparently authorized secrecy around the request. Blackburn was not powerless—she was a sitting senator with access to Congress, lawyers, publicity, and federal court—but she lacked notice while the records were being collected.

That is the actual conflict: how far executive-branch investigators may reach into congressional communications while investigating an attempt to obstruct the transfer of presidential power. It is consequential enough without decorative claims about color jokes.

The orange diversion

The complexion allegation is unsupported in the reporting. The complaint cites no source, identifies no decision-maker and supplies no evidence that “Arctic Frost” was chosen to ridicule Trump. Its own chronology weakens any attempt to pin the name on Smith personally because the FBI opened the investigation before his appointment.

This is misdirection by insinuation. A dispute over subpoenas, secrecy and legislative privilege becomes a story about personal humiliation inflicted on Trump. The rhetorical maneuver shifts attention from evidence and legal authority to grievance: investigators are recast not merely as officials whose conduct may be challenged, but as sneering persecutors.

RawStory’s framing appropriately exposes the evidentiary hole, but the headline-friendly complexion claim still does political work simply by circulating. An allegation does not need support to dominate attention; it needs novelty, resentment and a famous target.

Accountability turned backward

Republican senators had spent two years promising revelations about Smith, yet the hearing described by Politico produced insults and a conspicuous factual collapse. Sen. Eric Schmitt suggested Smith had secretly attended an Atlanta Hawks game amid scrutiny of Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis. Smith explained that the messages concerned Caitlin Clark and an Iowa-Maryland women’s basketball game. Schmitt also called him a “dirtbag.”

The people wielding institutional power in that hearing were senators using compulsory oversight, public proceedings and the authority of Congress. Schmitt chose accusation before verification. Sen. Amy Klobuchar corrected him in real time, while Sen. Josh Hawley later indicated that the congressional investigation had effectively exhausted itself.

Oversight is supposed to expose government misconduct. Here, it also became a platform for manufacturing suspicion around the investigator himself. When the promised scandal fails to appear, the accusation becomes the product.

A lawsuit built for politics

Blackburn’s request for one dollar signals that the case is not principally about financial compensation. It seeks a judicial declaration, the return of records and a vehicle for arguing that Smith operated without lawful appointment. The complaint further invokes an 1871 civil-rights law by characterizing him as a private citizen and links the subpoena’s timing to Blackburn’s April 2023 endorsement of Trump.

Those are legal claims, not established facts. The reported chronology alone does not prove that prosecutors targeted Blackburn because of her endorsement, and the appointment theory remains the lawsuit’s argument rather than a settled conclusion.

But the political design is clear from the filing’s structure: combine a substantial separation-of-powers question with an unsupported insult allegation and a broader narrative of partisan persecution. The soundest issue lends credibility to the weakest one; the weakest one captures the audience.

Grievance as an instrument of power

The larger pattern is not confusion. It is the conversion of investigative scrutiny into counter-accusation against investigators, reinforced through congressional hearings, litigation and sensational claims that require less proof than the conduct being investigated.

That strategy obscures the original reason the records were sought: prosecutors said they were examining whether Trump contacted members of Congress to delay certification of the 2020 election. Blackburn is entitled to contest how the government pursued that evidence. She is not entitled to have an unsupported theory about a codename treated as fact.

Institutional accountability fails when officials use their power to replace questions of authority, evidence and constitutional limits with a spectacle of personal victimhood. The result is not greater scrutiny of government. It is scrutiny stripped of standards, deployed as retaliation and packaged as oversight.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senator’s lawsuit accuses Jack Smith of mocking ‘Trump’s complexion’

item.title: Stop telling me to 'find joy' while the GOP is wrecking America
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet columnist D. Earl Stephens rejects the claim that Democrats need to project more “joy” to reconnect with voters. His response was prompted by PBS NewsHour co-host Geoff Bennett’s interview with Fox News commentator Jessica Tarlov, who argued that Democrats need sustained engagement with conservative audiences, more cultural connection, and leadership that includes joy.

Tarlov did not tell frightened voters simply to cheer up. She made an electoral argument: appearing on Fox News, attending events such as “College GameDay,” and entering voters’ cultural worlds can strengthen political persuasion. She also warned that favorable midterm polling might reflect rejection of Republicans rather than genuine confidence in Democrats.

Stephens answers that demand with a catalogue of Republican actions and alleged harms, from attempts to overturn the 2020 election to attacks on rights, public programs, environmental protections, and free speech. Some accusations in the column are stated without supporting evidence, but its central objection is clear: requiring an upbeat performance from people confronting material losses mistakes political presentation for political power.

Joy is not the disputed policy

Tarlov’s diagnosis is narrower and more serious than Stephens sometimes allows. She is talking about persuasion: relationships, cultural fluency, and the failure of Democratic politicians to inhabit spaces where persuadable voters actually live. Those are legitimate concerns. Political communication cannot consist solely of reciting dangers to people who have stopped listening.

But “joy” is the weakest part of that prescription because it converts a strategic failure by party institutions into an emotional deficiency among their voters. Democratic leaders control campaign budgets, candidate recruitment, messaging, media appearances, and legislative priorities. Ordinary liberals do not. If the party lacks cultural reach, the responsibility belongs first to the professionals paid to build it—not to citizens insufficiently delighted by the conditions those professionals failed to prevent.

Power belongs to institutions

The people with actual power in this account are officeholders, party leaders, media executives, legislators, and wealthy interests capable of shaping policy and public attention. Fox News commands an enormous platform. Republican officials exercise governmental authority. Democratic officials decide how to use the offices and resources they possess.

Stephens is strongest when he refuses to let mood obscure that hierarchy. The expiration of the expanded Child Tax Credit, for example, was not caused by liberal dourness. The events after the 2020 election were not a failure of cultural connection. According to the column, Trump resisted the result and sought to alter vote totals; his supporters then attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021. Whatever value optimism has as campaign branding, it does not explain institutional decisions or erase their consequences.

The burden gets pushed downward

The familiar maneuver is to discuss politics as a problem of voter temperament. Democrats scold. Liberals lack joy. Activists sound alarmed. The people reacting to policy are placed under examination, while the people making policy recede into the background.

That is misdirection. It is easier to coach anxious citizens on tone than to confront why Democratic victories have not secured the rights and protections those citizens expected. It is easier to prescribe football appearances than to explain how a party will wield power. Cultural presence may open a conversation, but it cannot substitute for a credible account of who will materially benefit from governing decisions.

Stephens commits some misdirection of his own. His sweeping language—calling Republicans “terrorists,” describing environmental damage as intentional poisoning, and attributing policy to billionaire “owners”—often outruns the evidence supplied in the column. Fury does not relieve a writer of the duty to distinguish documented conduct from inference. Precision makes an indictment harder to evade; exaggeration gives its targets an escape hatch.

Aesthetic politics protects failure

The larger pattern is the conversion of governance into performance criticism. When policy produces fear or anger, commentators ask whether the opposition looks pleasant enough. When a party cannot retain trust, consultants diagnose insufficient relatability. Institutional failure is repackaged as a branding problem.

That framing is useful to nearly everyone already holding power. Republican officials face less scrutiny for the decisions Stephens condemns. Democratic leaders can blame voters’ attitudes instead of their own record and strategy. Media organizations receive another personality dispute to stage. The audience is left arguing over whether alarm should smile.

Joy can sustain political movements, and Tarlov is right that persuasion requires human connection. But joy is neither a governing program nor an alibi. The systemic error is asking citizens to improve the emotional packaging of politics while powerful institutions continue deciding whose rights, security, and material needs are negotiable.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Stop telling me to ‘find joy’ while the GOP is wrecking America

item.title: Kennedy Center 'in free fall' as Trump allies max out credit and spend opera funds: WaPo
item.description:
What happened

RawStory, citing The Washington Post’s review of confidential board documents and tax filings, reports that the Kennedy Center’s Trump-appointed leadership exhausted its $21 million bank credit line, depleted much of its debt reserve and withdrew $10 million from the Washington National Opera’s $10.3 million endowment. Arts-management professor Karen Gahl-Mills described the institution as appearing to be “in free fall.”

Ticket revenue fell 15 percent and donations nearly 25 percent in the fiscal year ending September 2025. The center expected ticket income to decline by more than two-thirds this year, while gifts in early 2026 were reportedly down about 40 percent from the previous quarter. It also wrote off $48 million, mostly in pledges it no longer expects supporters to honor.

The Justice Department told an appeals court on Monday that the center could pay its bills only because of $17 million raised by President Donald Trump and that the money was being spent quickly. The Kennedy Center declined the Post’s questions and had not released its audited 2025 financial statements, which normally appear by March.

The takeover has owners

This is not an institution mysteriously losing altitude. Trump took control, installed new leadership and attached his political project to the center’s governance. That leadership then made the consequential choices: doubling the credit line, borrowing all of it, drawing down reserves, taking nearly the opera’s entire endowment and shrinking the fundraising staff from 94 people to 16.

Those decisions belong to people with institutional authority. Patrons who stopped buying tickets or fulfilling pledges affected revenue, but they did not control the balance sheet. They did not authorize borrowing or decide that restricted cultural assets should become emergency operating cash.

A rescue from a crisis of their making

Trump has claimed that the Kennedy Center was losing hundreds of millions of dollars when he took over. Experts consulted by the Post said the previous leadership instead left a complicated but comparatively stable organization.

That contrast matters because the administration’s preferred narrative casts Trump as rescuer while its appointees preside over accelerating financial distress. The $17.5 million raised through the rebranded Trump Kennedy Center Foundation may temporarily cover bills, but unnamed donors and emergency fundraising do not erase the management choices that made such support necessary.

Calling that money a rescue without naming the preceding depletion reverses cause and effect. Political control creates the crisis; politically branded fundraising then becomes evidence of indispensable leadership.

The board’s silence is governance

Gahl-Mills asked where the trustees were. The reported figures make that more than a rhetorical question. A board exists to supervise executives, protect institutional assets and demand credible financial disclosure. When leadership exhausts available credit, consumes reserves and taps an endowment on this scale, absent oversight becomes an enabling condition.

The missing audited statements deepen the problem. Their absence does not by itself establish wrongdoing, but it deprives donors, artists and the public of the ordinary accounting needed to evaluate an institution already showing obvious signs of distress. The center’s refusal to answer the Post compounds that opacity.

Culture as collateral

The transfer of $10 million from the opera’s $10.3 million endowment is the clearest expression of the power structure. Money intended to sustain one artistic institution was treated as a reservoir for leadership’s broader cash emergency. The opera has since severed ties with the Kennedy Center, and the parties dispute who owes whom money.

That is the consequence of politicized institutional control in material form: artistic programs lose autonomy, donor commitments become uncertain, and long-term assets are consumed to cover immediate obligations. The damage is not an abstract quarrel over prestige. It is reduced financial capacity, fractured partnerships and fewer resources available for the work the institution exists to support.

Capture, depletion, rebranding

The larger pattern is familiar. Political leaders seize an institution, discredit its previous stewardship, install loyal management and then present emergency patronage as proof that only the new regime can keep the doors open. Accountability is displaced by branding; structural damage is narrated as inherited failure.

The Kennedy Center’s reported condition is therefore not merely an arts-management story. It is a case study in institutional capture: authority concentrated at the top, oversight rendered ineffectual, reserves converted into operating cash and responsibility redirected toward audiences and donors reacting to choices they did not make. The people with the least control are left to absorb the consequences of decisions made by those with the most.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Kennedy Center ‘in free fall’ as Trump allies max out credit and spend opera funds: WaPo

item.title: This scumbag's shame shows how low the GOP has plunged
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Eric Schmitt used a Senate Judiciary hearing to call former special counsel Jack Smith a “total dirtbag,” a “villain,” and an alleged perjurer. Schmitt presented messages that he said showed Smith traveling to Atlanta to coordinate with local prosecutors, but the purported evidence confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes; according to the outlet, Smith had attended a college basketball game in Maryland.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar said Schmitt should apologize. He later refused during an appearance on The Charlie Kirk Show. RawStory places the episode alongside other recent cases of lawmakers publicly cursing at witnesses, reporters and constituents, arguing that conduct which once provoked institutional backlash has become routine.

Power behind the insult

Schmitt was not a heckler outside the building. He was a United States senator using a Judiciary Committee hearing, with its authority and public reach, to accuse a former federal prosecutor of misconduct.

That distinction matters. The central failure was not vulgarity. It was a powerful official converting an evidentiary mistake into a public allegation of collusion and perjury. The insult helped sell the charge, but the institutional setting gave it weight.

The evidence collapsed; the accusation remained

Once Schmitt’s mascot mix-up was exposed, the responsible act would have been to withdraw the allegation and correct the record. His reported refusal to apologize preserved the attack after its stated foundation had failed.

That is how political disinformation often survives correction: the dramatic accusation receives the hearing, the poster board and the epithet; the factual collapse becomes a punchline. Smith remains associated with wrongdoing in the audience’s memory even though the episode, as RawStory describes it, did not establish the alleged Atlanta coordination.

Vulgarity is the camouflage

RawStory emphasizes the Republican Party’s descent into routine profanity, citing episodes involving Reps. Lauren Boebert, Nancy Mace and Derrick Van Orden, as well as Sens. Bernie Moreno, Markwayne Mullin and John Kennedy. It also notes that Democratic Rep. Mark Pocan frequently used the same expletive on social media.

But a profanity count can flatten the political stakes. Cursing online is not equivalent to using congressional authority to brand a witness a criminal on defective evidence. Treating every obscenity as interchangeable misdirects attention from who holds power, where the statement was made and what official accusation it was meant to advance.

Contempt as political method

The pattern described here is larger than deteriorating manners. Insults replace substantiation, humiliation replaces examination, and refusal to correct an error becomes proof of partisan loyalty. The objective may be inferred from the conduct even when motive cannot be established: dominate the proceeding, discredit the target and ensure that accountability looks like surrender.

RawStory also cites Schmitt’s earlier declaration that America belongs to “us,” not “them,” and notes that the Missouri NAACP characterized his 2022 campaign advertising as racist. Those facts do not prove precisely whom Schmitt meant by “them,” despite the article’s confident interpretation. They do show a recurring politics organized around an entitled in-group and a suspect out-group.

The institutional collapse

In 1998, House Republican leaders blocked Democratic efforts to discipline Rep. Dan Burton after he called President Bill Clinton a “scumbag,” but the insult still generated a serious backlash. The contrast is not evidence of a more virtuous past; it shows that institutions once recognized reputational costs they now barely attempt to impose.

The deeper decay is therefore not that politicians discovered profanity. It is that legislative power can be used to broadcast an unsupported accusation, the factual premise can disintegrate, and the official responsible can simply refuse repair. The obscenity is memorable. The impunity is systemic.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: This scumbag’s shame shows how low the GOP has plunged

item.title: Jack Smith waving 'proverbial finger' at MAGA could spur 'severe consequences': analyst
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that former special counsel Jack Smith told a Senate panel on Tuesday that his investigation had developed what he described as proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Donald Trump committed serious crimes against the United States. Smith said he would make the same prosecutorial decision regardless of a former president’s party. His statement was not a conviction, and the article does not report any new prosecution or legal penalty.

The “severe consequences” in the headline refer to Salon writer Troy Farah’s warning about consequences for Americans if Trump and his allies succeed in recasting investigations of Trump as partisan persecution while Trump’s Justice Department pursues investigations Farah characterized as politically motivated. Farah argued that Smith’s public refusal to accept the MAGA narrative matters as the midterms approach and Trump continues falsely claiming he won the 2020 election.

The hearing also exposed the quality of the Republican counterattack. Senator Eric Schmitt tried to use Smith’s attendance at a basketball game as evidence of illicit coordination with Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis. According to RawStory, Schmitt cited an Atlanta Hawks game, but Smith had actually attended an Iowa Hawkeyes away game in Maryland.

Power is not evenly distributed

Smith was defending a completed prosecutorial judgment before senators. Trump, by contrast, holds the presidency and controls the executive branch. Republican senators possess subpoena power, a national platform, and the institutional means to turn insinuation into an official spectacle.

That imbalance is the story. Smith can explain what his investigation concluded. Trump and his congressional allies can use state power and legislative theater to discredit the investigation, pressure its participants, and establish retaliation as ordinary governance. Treating this as a feud between equally situated political camps obscures who can actually impose consequences.

The accusation replaces the evidence

Schmitt’s basketball-game gambit was not merely an embarrassing factual error. It showed how the hearing’s attack on Smith operated: begin with the desired allegation, then search for a detail that can be made to resemble support.

The mistake matters because insinuations launched from a Senate dais acquire authority before they acquire evidence. Even after collapse, they can circulate as fragments of a persecution narrative. The correction rarely travels with the accusation, and the official setting lends flimsy material an institutional costume.

Victimhood as governing strategy

Republicans described Trump’s criminal cases as political “witch hunts,” according to RawStory. That framing shifts attention away from the conduct investigators examined and toward Trump’s claimed victimization. It also places prosecutors in a rigged position: defending their work becomes further “proof” that they are partisan actors.

Farah’s argument is strongest here. A president can benefit politically from portraying scrutiny of himself as illegitimate while his own administration directs investigations at adversaries. RawStory presents that contrast sharply, though its broad characterization of those investigations as politically motivated is asserted rather than demonstrated through specific cases in this article.

Accountability is not a taunt

Calling Smith’s testimony a “proverbial finger” to MAGA may be satisfying copy, but it shrinks an institutional conflict into attitude and spectacle. Smith’s relevant act was not defiance for its own sake. It was his willingness to state publicly what his investigation concluded and to defend the standard he says he applied.

The sharper question is whether evidence can survive a political machine organized to make every adverse finding look corrupt. Smith’s declaration carries rhetorical force, but it does not itself create legal accountability. The article’s language of “consequences” risks blurring reputational embarrassment, electoral narrative, and actual institutional sanction.

The system rewards the smear

This episode reveals a durable political method: officeholders use institutional authority to manufacture doubt about institutional findings, then cite that doubt as evidence that the findings lack legitimacy. A failed ambush is still useful if it feeds the larger story that investigators, prosecutors, and political opponents belong to one illicit conspiracy.

The immediate farce was a senator confusing basketball games. The systemic error is more serious: powerful officials can make reckless allegations at low cost while the people they target must answer each one with precision. When fabrication is cheap and correction is laborious, the political advantage belongs to those willing to poison the record faster than anyone can repair it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Jack Smith waving ‘proverbial finger’ at MAGA could spur ‘severe consequences’: analyst

item.title: Republican sounds off on Pete Hegseth's latest military downsizing plans: 'Indefensible’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Rep. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican and retired Air Force brigadier general, called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s handling of senior military officers “indefensible.” On CNN, Bacon cited the firing or stalled promotions of 80 generals and admirals and said he had heard concerns from active-duty personnel.

Hegseth also plans to reduce positions reserved for generals and admirals by 20%, with the cuts expected to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. Bacon conceded that the Pentagon may be overstaffed but argued that an indiscriminate reduction could weaken military representation and leadership.

The power belongs to Hegseth

Bacon can object, but Hegseth controls the department executing these personnel decisions. That distinction matters. This is not a dispute between two equally situated Republicans. One holds a committee seat and a television microphone; the other directs the institution deciding which senior officers remain, advance or disappear from the command structure.

Bacon’s acknowledgment that Hegseth may have legal authority does not settle whether that authority is being used competently. Power can be lawful and still be reckless. “The secretary can do it” is a description of capacity, not a defense of judgment.

Downsizing is not a strategy

A 20% target offers the appearance of rigor because it comes with a number. But RawStory’s account supplies no mission analysis showing why one-fifth is the correct reduction, which commands can absorb it or how the Pentagon will preserve specialized leadership.

Bacon’s objection is therefore more substantial than reflexive institutional resistance. He is challenging the use of a quota where a strategy should be. If the Pentagon is overstaffed, officials should identify redundant functions and explain the operational tradeoffs. A cleaver applied across senior ranks is management theater unless the department can connect each cut to military requirements.

The headline understates the dispute

Calling this merely “downsizing” narrows the controversy to bureaucratic efficiency. Bacon’s criticism also concerns officers already fired and promotions reportedly withheld. Those actions affect careers, command continuity and the willingness of officers to offer unwelcome professional advice.

The reporting does not establish Hegseth’s motives, and it does not identify the affected officers or the reasons for each decision. Any claim that this is a purge would therefore exceed the evidence provided. But the unanswered questions are central, not incidental: who was removed, whose promotion was blocked, under what criteria, and with what operational consequence?

Congress cannot outsource accountability

Bacon says the policy is morally wrong, unwise and harmful. As a member of the House Armed Services Committee, however, he belongs to an institution with oversight power. Public criticism is useful, but it is not a substitute for demanding records, criteria and testimony.

That is the larger pattern: lawmakers denounce executive conduct as indefensible while leaving the machinery of defense to the executive branch. When congressional oversight stops at televised objection, unilateral personnel policy acquires the force of an accomplished fact.

Arbitrary power wears an efficiency badge

The systemic danger is not reducing a particular number of senior officers. Large institutions can become top-heavy, and staffing should be scrutinized. The danger is treating an unexplained numerical target as proof of reform while obscuring who chose the target, how individual decisions were made and what capabilities may be lost.

Institutional damage rarely announces itself as such. It arrives labeled streamlining, modernization or disruption. The test is whether officials can show disciplined criteria and accept scrutiny. On the evidence RawStory presents, Bacon has identified the harm; neither the Pentagon’s rationale nor Congress’s response has yet supplied the accountability.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Republican sounds off on Pete Hegseth’s latest military downsizing plans: ‘Indefensible’

item.title: Jim Acosta thinks GOP’s Schmitt should be 'hiding in a cave today’
item.description:
What happened

Jim Acosta said Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri should be “hiding in a cave” after Schmitt’s conspiracy theory involving former special counsel Jack Smith and Atlanta reportedly collapsed during a televised exchange on Tuesday. AlterNet does not explain what Schmitt alleged or what evidence disproved it, so the precise substance of that failure cannot be established from this account.

Acosta called the episode an extraordinary political blunder and accused conservative media figures of trying to rehabilitate Schmitt’s claim afterward. He argued that the spectacle distracted from Smith’s presentation concerning Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. The article attributes to Smith the position that Trump committed prosecutable crimes; it does not provide Smith’s evidence or detail the proceeding in which he spoke.

The senator had the power

Schmitt was not a confused bystander wandering through an information silo. He was a United States senator using national television to advance a prepared accusation. That office supplies authority, attention, staff and a presumption of relevance unavailable to the ordinary people later described as “trapped” inside partisan media.

The immediate failure therefore belongs first to Schmitt. Whatever role conservative outlets played afterward, he chose to deploy the claim. AlterNet’s lack of detail prevents judging its full content, but not identifying the institutional imbalance: an elected official manufactured the spectacle, while the audience was treated as the explanation for it.

The humiliation is secondary

Acosta’s mockery is understandable, but embarrassment is a weak form of accountability. A senator can endure ridicule, retreat into friendly media and continue exercising exactly the same power the next morning. Calling the episode an “epic fail” risks converting political misconduct into entertainment with a short shelf life.

The more consequential question is why a demonstrably failed argument carries so little professional cost. Schmitt’s allies reportedly tried to recast it as reasonable within 24 hours. That is not merely an audience misunderstanding something. It is an organized political-media apparatus insulating a powerful participant from correction.

The bubble has gatekeepers

“Information bubble” can become evasive language when it makes propaganda sound atmospheric—something that simply forms around people. AlterNet’s account names actors who allegedly sustained the distortion: Schmitt, conservative influencers and programs such as The Charlie Kirk Show. They possess agency. They decide what to repeat, omit or invert.

The weaker actors are the consumers whose confusion is emphasized. Blaming their entrapment obscures the people with platforms and incentives who stock the silo. The audience may accept falsehoods, but officeholders and media operators give those falsehoods institutional reach and political utility.

Spectacle displaced consequence

Acosta’s strongest point was that Schmitt’s performance overshadowed Smith’s claims about Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election and the failure to hold him criminally accountable. Yet even that argument requires precision. The supplied report says Smith believed Trump could have been convicted but for Supreme Court intervention; it does not establish that Trump otherwise would now be imprisoned.

The distinction matters because accountability did not disappear through abstraction. Prosecutors made choices, courts issued rulings and political institutions produced an outcome in which the underlying allegations never reached a completed federal trial. Schmitt’s televised failure was memorable partly because it offered a comic substitute for confronting that institutional result.

The system rewards the rake

This episode reveals a durable pattern: powerful officials can launch weak accusations, allied media can repair the narrative, and broader coverage can fixate on the resulting humiliation instead of the machinery that made it useful. The false claim gets airtime, its collapse becomes content, and the officeholder retains power.

The joke is therefore not the corrective. It is another stage of the same spectacle. A political system that substitutes viral embarrassment for material accountability does not punish propaganda; it turns propaganda’s failure into the next profitable distraction.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Jim Acosta thinks GOP’s Schmitt should be ‘hiding in a cave today’

item.title: Pete Hegseth ridiculed over bizarre video featuring troops exercising: ‘This is insane’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reposted a 36-second official video on September 30, 2026, showing service members running and exercising outside the Pentagon under the slogan “This is War.” Hegseth had appeared earlier that morning wearing a shirt bearing the same phrase.

Veterans, former Pentagon personnel, journalists and political strategists mocked the production online. Iraq War veteran Allison Jaslow rejected its central claim—“This is not war, actually”—while retired Army aviator Crispin Burke questioned whether the drone filming near posted “No Drone” signs was operating in restricted Washington-area airspace. The article does not establish whether any aviation rule was violated.

Power staged as fitness

This was not merely an awkward workout video posted by an overeager influencer. The defense secretary amplified material from an official government account. The institutional power belongs to Hegseth and the department he leads: they control military communications, command structures and the public presentation of the armed forces.

That distinction matters because the ridicule can make the episode look smaller than it is. The spectacle was ridiculous, but it was also official. Government resources and military personnel were used to package routine exercise as martial propaganda.

War reduced to branding

The slogan converts war from a political decision with human consequences into an apparel line and a montage. Running around Pentagon grounds becomes evidence of combat readiness; a gray shirt becomes a declaration of national purpose.

Jaslow’s response punctured that substitution with the authority of experience. War is not choreography outside an office complex. Calling the display “war” strips the word of its dead, wounded, displaced and permanently altered lives. It sells aggression as personal discipline while erasing who pays when officials turn martial posturing into policy.

The joke conceals the decision

RawStory organizes the episode largely through mockery: confused reactions, sarcastic questions and declarations that the country looks ridiculous. Those reactions are understandable, but they risk misdirecting attention toward the video’s absurdity rather than the official choices behind it.

The relevant question is not whether online observers found the production embarrassing. It is why the defense secretary and an official response operation considered militarized branding an appropriate use of their platforms. The service members shown are the weaker actors in that arrangement. Hegseth and the officials controlling the account chose the message and gave it institutional weight.

A costume of seriousness

Political power often uses spectacle to imitate competence. Here, physical exertion supplies the image of toughness, editing supplies urgency, and the word “war” supplies stakes the footage itself does not contain.

The result is propaganda in its cheapest form: not a documented argument about military policy, readiness or national security, but an aesthetic claim that officials should be trusted because they look aggressive. The possible drone issue, raised but not resolved in the reporting, adds an especially revealing irony: a production meant to project discipline prompted questions about whether its own staging respected the rules surrounding the Pentagon.

Militarism without accountability

The larger pattern is the conversion of public institutions into stages for the personal branding of powerful officials. When war becomes a slogan, scrutiny of actual decisions—deployment, procurement, command responsibility and the use of force—gives way to judging whether the performance looked sufficiently tough.

Mockery can expose the fraud, but it cannot be the endpoint. The systemic error is allowing officials with immense coercive authority to substitute martial theater for an account of what they are doing with that authority. A government that markets war as a workout is not explaining military power. It is training the public to consume that power as content.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Pete Hegseth ridiculed over bizarre video featuring troops exercising: ‘This is insane’
