item.title: 'Radioactive' Trump pummeling GOP's midterm chances with surprise move: Maddow
item.description:
What happened

Rachel Maddow argued on NBC’s “Late Night” that Donald Trump’s unpopularity is damaging Republicans’ midterm prospects because GOP candidates remain publicly aligned with him instead of distancing themselves. RawStory, citing The Daily Beast’s account of the Tuesday-night interview, reported that Maddow described Trump as “radioactive” and said his approval rating was in the low 30 percent range.

Maddow attributed part of that political weakness to Trump’s effort to accelerate deportations involving people in the country both legally and illegally. She said the policy had broken trust with Latino voters who shifted heavily toward Trump in the 2024 election. The article supplies no polling methodology, specific midterm races, candidate statements, or evidence that Trump expressly ordered Republicans not to criticize him.

Power runs through Trump

Trump holds the institutional power in this story: the presidency, control over executive immigration policy, and enormous influence inside the Republican Party. Republican candidates may possess individual agency, but their apparent reluctance to separate themselves from him reflects the party structure they helped build.

That distinction matters. Trump’s political dominance is not an inexplicable weather system descending on helpless candidates. Republican officials repeatedly chose alignment as the price of standing within the party. Now that alignment constrains their ability to present themselves as independent when presidential approval becomes an electoral liability.

Loyalty is a choice

RawStory’s framing turns an absence into a “surprise move”: Trump apparently has not given Republicans permission to criticize him. But the report does not establish that he issued any directive at all. Maddow’s point is an inference about his political character and the GOP’s behavior, not a documented campaign order.

The more revealing fact is that Republican candidates seemingly require such permission. Politicians seeking power are responsible for the positions they endorse and the coalitions they maintain. Describing them as trapped by Trump risks laundering strategic submission into mere campaign difficulty.

The policy has consequences

The deportation push is not simply another item depressing a president’s approval rating. According to Maddow, it reaches people in the country legally as well as illegally and has damaged trust among Latino voters who moved toward Trump in 2024. That is a policy consequence before it is an electoral one.

Reducing those voters to a bloc that may punish Republicans also narrows the story. Executive power determines who faces removal, insecurity, or disrupted legal expectations. Midterm backlash, if it materializes, would be a consequence of those decisions—not the primary harm.

Polling is not a verdict

The article leans heavily on dramatic language while providing little supporting detail. “Historically unprecedented hate” is Maddow’s characterization; RawStory offers no underlying survey, comparison period, or evidence establishing that claim. A low approval rating can signal grave political weakness, but it does not by itself prove why voters disapprove or predict control of Congress.

The headline likewise claims Trump is “pummeling” Republican chances, yet the article identifies no race in which his conduct changed the result or any forecast measuring the damage. The argument may be plausible, but the reporting presented here does not demonstrate it.

The party built its own constraint

The larger pattern is a party surrendering independent judgment to a dominant leader and then discovering that personal loyalty creates collective exposure. Trump exercises presidential and partisan power; Republican officeholders decide whether to reinforce it. Neither side is merely confused about the arrangement.

The sharpest political lesson is therefore not that an unpopular president failed to rescue his candidates. It is that those candidates accepted dependence on him when it offered power. If that dependence now carries an electoral cost, it belongs to the officials who sustained the system as well as the president at its center.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Radioactive’ Trump pummeling GOP’s midterm chances with surprise move: Maddow

item.title: We already know who will win the midterms: expert
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet’s headline overstates the evidence: no one already knows who will win the 2026 midterms. Henry Olsen of the Ethics and Public Policy Center wrote in The Washington Post that his model, based on generic congressional-ballot polling and the previous three midterms, projected Democrats winning between 225 and 232 of the House’s 435 seats. That is a forecast, not a result.

Polling analyst Kyle Kondik told AlterNet that President Donald Trump’s weak approval rating, economic dissatisfaction, foreign-policy concerns, and the governing party’s usual midterm disadvantage could cost Republicans congressional seats. Separately, Common Cause policy director Susannah Goodman said the Trump administration was trying to assemble state voter records in a federal database; she reported that several states withheld unredacted records and that Common Cause and its partners had intervened in roughly 17 cases.

A projection is not foreknowledge

Olsen’s calculation identifies the political environment confronting Republicans. It does not settle individual races, turnout, candidate quality, district-level variation, or events between the polling period and Election Day. His range also depends on the assumption that recent relationships between generic-ballot polling and House outcomes remain predictive.

AlterNet converts that conditional analysis into certainty because certainty attracts attention. The underlying reporting supports a narrower conclusion: Democrats appeared favored to win a House majority under Olsen’s model. Declaring the winner in advance replaces analysis with salesmanship.

Power sits with the administration

The most consequential actor in the story is not a polling expert or an opposition voter. It is the federal administration seeking state voter-roll data, including personal identifying information. States control election administration, but the presidency commands agencies, lawyers, enforcement authority, and a national platform capable of pressuring those states.

Goodman described resistance through refusals and legal intervention. Those defenses matter, but they do not equal the executive branch’s institutional reach. The relevant power relationship is an administration demanding sensitive election data and states and civic groups attempting to limit that demand.

The article outruns its evidence

AlterNet repeatedly describes Trump as trying to “rig,” “steal,” or manipulate the elections by obtaining voter rolls and purging likely Democratic voters. But the supplied reporting does not establish that claimed purpose. Goodman documents an effort to centralize voter data and resistance to sharing unredacted personal information; she does not, in the quoted material, provide evidence of an implemented partisan purge.

That distinction is not a concession to euphemism. It is what separates a documented abuse of power from an allegation about intended abuse. The administration’s demand warrants scrutiny on privacy, legal authority, voter eligibility, and potential disenfranchisement. AlterNet weakens that scrutiny when it presents its inference as an already proven plan.

The opposition is not the governing power

The story’s clearest misdirection is subtler: it casts Democrats’ “primary challenge” as warding off Trump, as though protecting election administration were principally a campaign obligation. Democratic officials, litigants, and advocacy groups can resist. But lawful limits must be enforced by courts, state election officials, legislatures, inspectors general, and career administrators.

When institutions shift that burden onto the opposition party, executive overreach becomes another electoral tactic to counter rather than an exercise of state power to investigate and constrain. The weaker actor is told to defend the system while the stronger actor’s authority remains the background condition.

Forecasts cannot substitute for safeguards

This episode exposes two failures that feed each other. Political media treats a polling model as a verdict, then treats an allegation of election interference as established fact. One manufactures confidence about the outcome; the other blurs precisely what government officials have done, what they may be positioned to do, and what remains unproven.

The systemic issue is not whether one pundit can call the House correctly. It is whether institutions controlling election data are subject to enforceable limits—and whether reporting can describe those power struggles without turning prediction into knowledge or suspicion into fact.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: We already know who will win the midterms: expert

item.title: MAGA melts down as Trump rival gets Nobel Peace Prize buzz
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that speculation about Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney receiving a Nobel Peace Prize nomination drew criticism from Fox News host Laura Ingraham and political commentator Ari Goldkind. Ingraham argued that Carney was being celebrated for confronting President Donald Trump despite Canada’s economic strain; Goldkind likewise dismissed the idea. The reporting does not establish that Carney was nominated, shortlisted, or likely to win.

The speculation arose amid a tariff conflict in which the United States imposed duties as high as 50 percent on billions of dollars’ worth of Canadian goods and Canada retaliated. Trump urged Canadian leaders to “fall in line” and warned of consequences “far WORSE” than the existing tariffs. AlterNet says the Nobel committee’s deliberations and shortlist remained secret.

Carney’s profile had risen after a World Economic Forum speech urging middle powers to cooperate rather than submit to larger states. Commentators praised that foreign-policy framework, while two Canadian political scientists predicted that a Carney victory could anger Trump and further strain bilateral relations. Those predictions remained hypothetical.

The headline outruns the evidence

“MAGA melts down” is packaging, not a demonstrated political event. AlterNet supplies two hostile reactions, only one of them clearly tied in the article to Trump’s media apparatus. That supports a story about criticism; it does not establish a movement-wide convulsion.

The distinction matters because inflated framing weakens an otherwise revealing episode. The real story is not that some pundits posted angrily about an unconfirmed prize prospect. It is that defending Canadian autonomy against American economic pressure has become grounds for attack within Trump-aligned media.

Power is not evenly distributed

Trump controls the executive machinery of the United States, whose government imposed the tariffs described in the report. Carney leads the smaller country absorbing that pressure and authorizing retaliation. Whatever one thinks of Carney’s economic record, these are not equivalent positions in a personality feud.

Trump’s instruction that Canadian leaders “fall in line” makes the hierarchy explicit. The dispute concerns whether a powerful state may use market access to discipline a neighboring government. Carney’s refusal is a response to that coercive leverage, not the source of it.

The pundits reverse responsibility

Ingraham’s formulation turns resistance into provocation: Carney supposedly “picked a fight with Trump.” But AlterNet’s own account identifies the US tariffs and Trump’s warning of worse consequences as the operative exercises of power. Blaming Carney for the confrontation shifts responsibility from the government applying pressure to the government declining submission.

That reversal is a standard function of partisan propaganda. The stronger actor’s aggression becomes background scenery; the weaker actor’s refusal becomes the disruptive act. Economic pain inside Canada can then be cited against Carney without asking who imposed the tariffs or what political concessions they were meant to extract.

Prestige as presidential property

The Nobel speculation carries extra weight because AlterNet reports that Trump has repeatedly said he deserves the prize. A hypothetical Carney nomination therefore becomes more than foreign-policy gossip: it challenges a political culture organized around Trump’s demand for personal recognition.

But the article should not confuse the symbolism with an actual contest. No nomination or shortlist placement is established here. The grounded conclusion is narrower: even unsupported speculation was enough to trigger efforts to discredit Carney and redefine resistance to US pressure as irrational hostility toward Trump.

The larger system

This episode shows how coercion acquires a public-relations shield. Government power imposes material costs; aligned media personalities recast the target’s resistance as needless antagonism; attention then drifts toward awards, personalities, and online outrage instead of the decision that created the conflict.

The prize chatter may vanish because it was never more than speculation. The political pattern will remain: powerful institutions act, weaker parties are blamed for reacting, and propaganda launders domination into a complaint about insufficient deference.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: MAGA melts down as Trump rival gets Nobel Peace Prize buzz

item.title: GOP’s Jack Smith 'face plant' blew up Republican midterm chances: insider
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican Senator Eric Schmitt tried to accuse former Special Counsel Jack Smith of perjury during a Wednesday Senate hearing, only to reveal that his supposed evidence concerned the wrong basketball game. Schmitt claimed text messages placed Smith at an Atlanta Hawks game with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis on February 3, 2024; the messages reportedly referred instead to the University of Iowa Hawkeyes.

According to conservative commentator Charlie Sykes, the failed confrontation exposed Republican incompetence and the party’s continuing devotion to President Donald Trump. He argued that the spectacle would damage Republicans shortly before the midterms. The reporting provides no polling or electoral evidence establishing that the hearing actually changed the party’s midterm prospects.

The power was behind the dais

Smith was the witness, but Senate Republicans controlled the confrontation. They had the institutional platform, the prepared accusation and the ability to turn a congressional hearing into televised political theater.

Schmitt exercised that power recklessly. Before resolving the basic facts, he displayed the messages on a poster, suggested Smith had already committed perjury and called him a “dirtbag.” Senator John Kennedy helped present the exhibit. This was not a misunderstanding between equal participants; it was an attempted public prosecution conducted by senators who had not adequately checked their evidence.

An accusation built for television

The hearing, as described, was designed to recast investigations of Trump as partisan wrongdoing by investigators. That project required Smith to become the suspect and Republican senators to become the arbiters of legitimacy.

The factual collapse matters because the accusation came before the verification. Schmitt’s confidence, insult and visual prop supplied the performance of guilt; the evidence was expected to catch up. It did not. Institutional authority was used to manufacture a damaging moment, and elementary scrutiny dismantled it almost immediately.

The frame outran the evidence

AlterNet’s headline adopts Sykes’ political conclusion more firmly than the article supports. His argument that the episode harmed Republican midterm chances is plausible commentary, not a demonstrated electoral result. One disastrous hearing does not, by itself, establish changed votes or “blown” chances.

That exaggeration is unnecessary. The documented failure is serious enough: senators used a formal hearing to level a perjury accusation based on a mix-up between a professional team in Atlanta and a college team in Iowa. Inflating that into a settled forecast repeats the same underlying error—substituting a satisfying narrative for evidence.

Loyalty as legislative purpose

Sykes identifies the larger political priority: defending Trump by discrediting those who investigated him. The hearing apparently produced no substantiated perjury case. Instead, it showed Republican senators spending public authority on a retaliatory narrative whose centerpiece could not survive basic fact-checking.

The consequence extends beyond embarrassment. Congressional oversight loses force when lawmakers treat accusation as proof and hearings as content production. Every failed stunt teaches political operatives that the institution can be used for smears first, with correction arriving only after the spectacle has done its work.

The system rewards the attempted hit

This episode reveals a political structure in which the people wielding coercive institutional power can pose as victims while placing investigators on trial. The misdirection runs downward: scrutiny of Trump becomes alleged persecution by prosecutors, and a senator’s evidentiary failure becomes merely a comic mishap.

It was more than a gaffe. It was oversight hollowed out into partisan enforcement—public power deployed to punish an adversary, with accuracy treated as optional. The electoral effect remains unproven. The institutional damage was visible on the poster board.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP’s Jack Smith ‘face plant’ blew up Republican midterm chances: insider

item.title: Trump AG blows his top denying reality about his own department
item.description:
What happened

At a Wednesday press conference, Blanche repeatedly denied that Justice Department attorney Kurt Olsen had resigned or left his investigation. According to AlterNet, Blanche said Olsen remained employed “exactly where he was before” and blamed inaccurate media reporting for the dispute.

A reporter had asked about reports that Olsen and Joe diGenova had departed a Florida-based investigation involving President Donald Trump. Blanche said prosecutors routinely leave but insisted that this account was false and that the investigation remained well staffed. The material supplied by AlterNet does not independently establish Olsen’s employment status beyond Blanche’s denial and the earlier reports.

AlterNet also cites February reporting by Politico that Olsen received highly classified material despite lacking a security clearance or intelligence experience. A CIA spokesperson told Politico that Trump had asked Olsen to examine intelligence concerning the 2020 election and that the agency was providing the access needed for that work.

Power sits above the personnel dispute

The important issue is not whether Blanche sounded angry. It is that the president reportedly directed an intelligence agency to accommodate a political ally seeking material about an election Trump lost.

Olsen’s formal job status matters, but it is secondary to the institutional arrangement Politico described. The president possessed the authority to request access. The CIA acted on that request. Olsen benefited from it despite the reported absence of the usual clearance and relevant experience. That chain of power is more consequential than the press-conference performance.

The denial answers less than it appears to

Blanche gave a categorical answer about resignation and employment. He did not, in the quoted exchange, resolve the larger questions: whether Olsen had stopped working on the investigation, why reports of his departure emerged, what access he retained, or whether clearance problems affected his role.

Calling the reports “fake news” converted a testable personnel question into an accusation against the press. That is misdirection, even if Blanche’s narrow employment claim was accurate. Government officials control the authoritative records; reporters do not. Scolding journalists for asking about contradictory accounts uses that information imbalance as a weapon.

Access is the real privilege

Politico’s reported description of Olsen repeatedly calling Trump when he encountered obstacles points to the relevant hierarchy. If accurate, Olsen did not need conventional intelligence credentials because he had something more valuable: direct access to the president.

That does not prove the classified material was mishandled or that a law was broken. It does show how personal sponsorship can override ordinary institutional resistance. A system built around rules becomes discretionary when proximity to the executive determines who receives exceptional access.

The framing shrinks the scandal

AlterNet’s “blew his top” framing reduces the episode to temperament. Blanche’s frustration is visible in the quoted remarks, but anger is not the central abuse of power described here. The stronger story is the government’s refusal to provide a clear account of an unusually empowered political loyalist.

The article also states as fact that Olsen helped Trump “steal” the 2020 election and participate in an “insurrection,” but the supplied text does not establish those claims or specify Olsen’s conduct. Those assertions require evidence and attribution. Careless certainty weakens scrutiny by giving officials an easy complaint about the coverage while the documented questions about access and authority remain unanswered.

Loyalty becomes an unofficial credential

This episode reveals a familiar governing pattern: formal qualifications and ordinary safeguards lose force when presidential favor supplies a parallel authorization system. Institutional power remains concentrated at the top, while accountability is diverted toward reporters trying to determine who still holds a government role.

The systemic error is not confusion. It is an arrangement in which officials can grant exceptional access through personal sponsorship, disclose little about the decision, and then treat demands for clarity as the offense.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump AG blows his top denying reality about his own department

item.title: Byron Donalds rages at 'fad' taking over his home state: 'We know how this works’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Republican Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds dismissed solar power as a “fad” at a campaign event in Daytona Beach Shores, arguing that it consumes land and cannot provide consistent electricity after dark. He promoted small modular nuclear reactors as a steadier alternative. His Democratic opponent, David Jolly, said solar should be part of Florida’s future.

The industry’s own plans contradict Donalds’ framing. Florida Power & Light, Duke Energy Florida and Tampa Electric all expect solar generation or capacity to grow, while representatives for those utilities told the Florida Phoenix that small modular reactors are not yet commercially viable or cost-effective. Florida currently generates about 8% of its electricity from renewable sources, mostly solar, and nearly 75% from natural gas.

A federal policy decision is already constraining that expansion: President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax legislation eliminated solar credits. FPL’s latest plan still projects solar supplying 26% of its energy by 2035, but that projection is 30% below its previous plan—a reduction the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy attributes to the expiring credits.

The power behind the grid

Donalds does not control Florida’s electric system merely by campaigning against solar. The immediate institutional power lies with state regulators, legislators, utilities and the federal government that sets tax policy. Those actors decide which projects receive approval, financing and favorable rules.

The utilities’ investment plans are especially revealing. They are not environmental manifestos. They are capital-allocation decisions by companies responsible for supplying electricity. FPL delivered 11% of its energy from solar in 2025; Duke plans 900 megawatts of additional solar capacity by 2027; Tampa Electric expected solar’s share to reach about 17% the following year. Donalds calls a technology a fad while the companies building Florida’s grid treat it as infrastructure.

A solution that does not yet exist at scale

Small modular nuclear reactors may eventually become useful. The reporting does not establish that they are ready to meet Florida’s present needs. FPL said they are neither commercially available at scale nor cost-effective. Duke described advanced nuclear power as a longer-term option, and Tampa Electric said the technology is not commercially viable.

Donalds is therefore contrasting operating solar projects with an aspirational nuclear technology. That is not a serious comparison of available capacity, cost and deployment schedules. It allows him to attack what can be built now by invoking what might become practical later.

Even Florida’s government has not established the case he implies. A legislatively ordered feasibility report recommended more study, while a bill authorizing regulation of advanced reactors passed the state House unanimously but stalled in the Senate. The reactor pitch is a political preference, not an implementation plan.

The misdirection

The weakest part of the framing is its treatment of solar’s limitations as if they settle the question. Solar does not generate at night; no one quoted in the reporting disputes that. But the relevant policy question is how solar operates within a diversified grid—not whether it can single-handedly supply every hour of electricity.

Donalds also directs attention toward solar arrays occupying land while leaving Florida’s overwhelming dependence on natural gas largely unscrutinized. Natural gas supplies nearly three-quarters of the state’s generation. Solar supplies a small fraction. Presenting the smaller source as the pressing reliability problem obscures where the system’s actual concentration lies.

His claim that electricity use is greatest at night is also presented without supporting demand data in the supplied reporting. The article should have tested that assertion rather than merely carrying it. Political rhetoric becomes misinformation by default when journalists quote a technical claim but do not establish whether it is true.

Policy creates the outcome

The clearest exercise of power in this story was not a campaign remark. Congress and the Trump administration removed federal solar incentives, and Florida industry groups warned that the change could devastate the state’s solar business. SACE links that federal action to FPL’s reduced solar projection.

That sequence matters: political officials weaken the economics of an energy source, then allies describe its position as proof of technological inadequacy. The resulting slowdown can be portrayed as the market speaking even when policy helped manufacture it.

Jolly’s alternative deserves scrutiny too. “Soft mandates” and incentives are instruments, not an energy strategy by themselves. But his basic premise—that solar can occupy a growing place in Florida’s mix—is supported by the utilities’ published plans in a way Donalds’ near-term nuclear prescription is not.

The larger pattern

This is how reactionary energy politics protects an incumbent system: ridicule the expanding technology, exaggerate one limitation, ignore the policy decisions suppressing it and substitute a favored technology that cannot yet be deployed economically at scale.

The consequence is not merely a distorted campaign debate. Florida could remain more dependent on natural gas while viable solar development slows and promised reactors remain on the horizon. Institutional power would have preserved the existing arrangement, while voters were invited to blame the alternative it obstructed.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Byron Donalds rages at ‘fad’ taking over his home state: ‘We know how this works’

item.title: Strategists demand answers from Scott Jennings on 'the corpse of McConnell’
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Republican strategists Sarah Longwell, Jonathan V. Last, and Tim Miller challenged pundit and former McConnell staffer Scott Jennings’s claim that he had a substantive conversation with Sen. Mitch McConnell about foreign policy. Citing videos of McConnell using a wheelchair and appearing to struggle to communicate, Longwell questioned whether the conversation occurred as Jennings described it. The article supplies no response from Jennings and does not establish whether his account was false.

McConnell fell at his Washington home on June 14. According to AlterNet, verified emergency-dispatch audio initially described an unconscious person and later referenced cardiac arrest and CPR. McConnell’s account was that he fell and was briefly unconscious but suffered none of several serious conditions, including a heart attack or stroke; he said he later developed mild pneumonia. After 92 days in hospitals, rehabilitation, and home care, he returned to the Senate on Sept. 14.

Miller also said McConnell cast the deciding vote in a 50–49 vote that Miller characterized as an “anti-Iran war vote.” AlterNet does not identify the measure, explain its effect, or provide enough detail to assess that characterization.

Power behind the curtain

The central issue is not whether McConnell looked sufficiently vigorous on camera. It is whether a sitting senator could understand legislation, exercise independent judgment, and communicate a decision while his vote continued to carry federal power.

McConnell’s office, Senate Republican leaders, and the people presenting accounts of his condition held the relevant information. Jennings held no Senate authority in this episode, but his claimed access could lend credibility to assurances that McConnell remained capable of doing the job. If those assurances were misleading, the problem would be institutional image management, not mere pundit embarrassment.

The unanswered factual question

Longwell’s suspicion is understandable, but suspicion is not proof. Public videos cannot establish everything that happened in a private conversation, and AlterNet offers no transcript, contemporaneous notes, medical assessment, or direct questioning of Jennings.

That missing work matters. The article calls Jennings’s account a lie through Last’s quoted remark, yet it does not demonstrate that conclusion. A sharp allegation does not substitute for verification—especially when the allegation concerns a senator’s capacity and the credibility of people speaking around him.

Cruel language, convenient distraction

Miller’s phrase “the corpse of Mitch McConnell” is dehumanizing and analytically cheap. It turns a legitimate question about representation and institutional control into ridicule of an elderly man’s visible impairment. Longwell’s reference to the “live body” of Sen. John Fetterman extends the same degradation.

That language also misdirects attention. McConnell’s frailty did not schedule the vote, control Senate procedure, issue public assurances, or determine what information voters received. Those actions belonged to living officials, staff members, and political operatives with agency. Mocking a disabled body allows the surrounding institution to disappear.

Accountability without spectacle

The proper questions are concrete: What information did Senate leadership have about McConnell’s functional capacity? What accommodations or safeguards were used? Did McConnell understand the measure Miller referenced? What exactly did Jennings observe, and how did he substantiate his description of their conversation?

AlterNet does not answer those questions. Its framing generates confrontation around Jennings while leaving the officials with actual institutional authority largely unexamined. The result is accusation without a sufficiently developed record and outrage aimed below the level where decisions were made.

The system protects the seat

This episode reveals how political institutions treat officeholders as votes first and people second. When control is narrow, party leaders have powerful incentives to preserve the appearance that every seat remains operational. Health disclosures become strategic communications, while outsiders are asked to infer capacity from fragments of video and statements by loyal associates.

That is the larger failure: a system in which the public receives curated assurances, commentators answer opacity with grotesque mockery, and Senate power continues without transparent standards for determining whether a member can exercise it. The spectacle centers the body. The institution escapes scrutiny.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Strategists demand answers from Scott Jennings on ‘the corpse of McConnell’

item.title: Fox News hands Trump brutal reality check on his biggest economic problem
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News polling gave President Donald Trump a blunt political warning: voters view the cost of living as the country’s leading problem and largely disapprove of his economic performance. In the September 11–14 survey of 1,211 registered voters, 34 percent named living costs as the most important issue, while 63 percent said the Trump administration had made the economy worse. Trump received 24 percent approval on inflation and 39 percent overall approval.

Household costs dominated the findings: 62 percent called grocery prices a major problem, 61 percent said the same about gasoline, 54 percent about housing and 52 percent about health care. AlterNet also cites a Reuters/Ipsos survey of 1,277 adults in which Trump’s overall approval was 32 percent and 17 percent approved of his handling of living costs; its reported margin of error was 3 percentage points.

The political pressure coincided with weak economic sentiment. The Conference Board said consumer confidence fell to 81.9 in September, its lowest level in roughly 12½ years. Reuters attributed the decline to concerns about employment, prices and borrowing costs. AlterNet also reports that the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate exceeded 7 percent in September and that single-family home prices were 2.6 percent higher in July than a year earlier.

The podium comes with ownership

Trump used anger over inflation and prices during the 2024 campaign. Now he controls the presidency, the administration’s economic agenda and the country’s most powerful political platform. He cannot plausibly retain ownership of the grievance while assigning ownership of the outcome elsewhere.

That does not mean a poll proves the administration caused every grocery bill, mortgage rate or housing increase. It does mean voters judge presidents by material conditions, and presidential power carries responsibility for policy choices and priorities. The White House may not set every price, but it decides what problems receive action, what tradeoffs are imposed and what story the government tells about the results.

Attention is not relief

Lee Hartley Carter’s formulation—that Trump must persuade Americans he is paying attention—reveals the limits of professional political advice. People confronting expensive food, fuel, housing and medical care do not primarily suffer from insufficient presidential empathy. They suffer from bills they must pay.

Treating affordability as a communications problem shifts scrutiny away from governing decisions and toward presentation. A better speech can alter a news cycle. It cannot lower a mortgage payment. Political spectacle is useful precisely because it invites voters to evaluate performance by attention captured rather than conditions changed.

Fox is protecting the signal

The significance of the Fox polling is not that a conservative institution suddenly became an adversary of Trump. It is that an outlet aligned with his political audience cannot make the affordability problem disappear without sacrificing the credibility of its own data.

Calling the result a “reality check” also softens what the numbers represent. Trump is not merely being informed of an inconvenient issue. His administration is being judged by voters who report sustained pressure across several basic necessities. The warning is aimed at the White House, but the hardship belongs to households.

What the framing cannot establish

AlterNet assembles damaging polling and economic indicators, but it does not identify which Trump administration policies produced the reported conditions or how much responsibility belongs to earlier decisions, Congress, the Federal Reserve or private market actors. Forceful analysis cannot substitute for missing causal evidence.

The defensible conclusion is narrower and still politically severe: Trump campaigned on economic pain, now holds executive power, and is receiving exceptionally poor assessments of his handling of that pain. The polling establishes public judgment, not a complete economic autopsy.

The politics of permanent grievance

This is the recurring bargain of grievance politics: convert hardship into authority, then treat continued hardship as a messaging obstacle. The public is asked to reward recognition of its anger even when the institution empowered to respond has not convinced voters that conditions are improving.

The larger pattern is a transfer of accountability downward. Households absorb the costs; strategists debate tone; media outlets package deteriorating confidence as a campaign challenge. But institutional power remains at the top. Once grievance wins the presidency, failure to relieve it is no longer merely somebody else’s indictment.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox News hands Trump brutal reality check on his biggest economic problem

item.title: Paxton privately trashed Trump’s midterm convention: leaked audio
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Ken Paxton privately said Donald Trump’s September Republican convention in Dallas hurt GOP candidates rather than helping them. In leaked audio from a Washington fundraiser the following Thursday, Paxton said his numbers—and those of other Republicans—dropped after the roughly $50 million event.

The New York Times obtained the recording from an attendee who strongly opposes Paxton and reported corroborating details from three people familiar with the gathering. Paxton adviser Nick Maddux called the audio “fake” and “manipulated,” arguing that Paxton’s polling had improved since early September and that he remained aligned with Trump.

The power runs through Trump

This was not merely a disappointing campaign event. It was an expensive demonstration of who controls the Republican Party’s political machinery: Trump occupied the closing spotlight, elevated favored candidates and intervened for Paxton over Senator John Cornyn.

That power explains why Paxton’s reported criticism surfaced privately before a room of roughly a dozen people, while his public operation rushed to reaffirm loyalty. A candidate who believes the party’s dominant figure is hurting him still has reason to appear beside that figure. Trump’s institutional leverage matters more than Paxton’s private assessment.

Loyalty has a public price

The convention reportedly cost Republicans about $50 million without producing the promised polling improvement. Paxton’s alleged remarks go further: he said the event coincided with declining numbers.

That does not prove the convention caused the decline. Nor does the article provide the underlying polling needed to evaluate either Paxton’s reported assessment or Maddux’s rebuttal. But the exchange exposes the governing campaign incentive: inconvenient performance data must compete with the political necessity of flattering the person who controls endorsements, attention and access.

Denial replaces an explanation

Maddux did not merely dispute Paxton’s interpretation of the numbers. He attacked the recording as fabricated or manipulated, even as the Times reported that other attendees confirmed the question and recalled Paxton’s response.

The article does not establish whether the audio was technically altered, and Maddux’s denial must remain a denial rather than a resolved fact. Still, his response supplied no technical evidence described by AlterNet. It redirected attention from the convention’s reported failure to the supposed misconduct of the messenger—the standard refuge of a political operation that cannot safely debate the substance.

The humiliation is part of the hierarchy

Trump’s support for Paxton has not prevented him from publicly insulting Paxton’s appearance and speaking ability. His praise came wrapped in degradation: Paxton could be celebrated as an attorney general while being reminded that his standing depended on Trump’s judgment.

That dynamic is political discipline disguised as banter. Trump grants legitimacy; the recipient absorbs the insult and remains grateful. Paxton’s campaign response preserved that arrangement by promising he would close the race “alongside President Trump,” regardless of what Paxton reportedly said when he thought the audience was private.

A party trapped by its patron

The larger pattern is not hypocrisy for its own sake. It is dependence. Republicans reportedly spent tens of millions staging a spectacle around one man, then faced evidence that the spectacle may not have helped—and may have hurt—the candidates it was supposed to promote.

When authority is personalized, failure does not weaken the leader first. It pressures subordinates to deny what they saw, attack whoever disclosed it and renew their allegiance. The convention’s political return remains disputed. The hierarchy it displayed does not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Paxton privately trashed Trump’s midterm convention: leaked audio

item.title: Trump plan to make burgers cheaper backfires spectacularly in MAGA country
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump administration expanded the amount of imported lean beef eligible for lower tariffs by 300,000 metric tons—about 661 million pounds—to restrain ground-beef prices. The White House said domestic supply could not meet demand at reasonable prices after ground beef cost about 8 percent more in August than a year earlier.

Purdue economists estimated the imports could reduce wholesale prices by no more than 1.41 percent. Using earlier USDA research on how little wholesale relief reaches shoppers, Vox calculated a best-case retail reduction of roughly 0.27 percent, or about two cents per pound.

Ranchers say the imports will weaken demand for domestic cattle, particularly older cows whose lean meat competes with imported trimmings. Republican senators and cattle groups are resisting the policy as producers also face reduced exports, higher fuel and fertilizer costs, and labor disruptions attributed by industry groups to recent ICE activity.

Power sits in Washington

Ranchers did not create this conflict. The Trump administration changed the tariff treatment, just as federal trade disputes and immigration enforcement were already shaping their costs, markets, and workforce.

That is the institutional hierarchy: the White House can alter import competition, pursue trade fights, and deploy immigration enforcement. Producers absorb the combined consequences. Their political loyalty does not give them control over any of those levers.

Pennies for consumers, pressure for producers

The policy’s promised consumer benefit is vanishingly small. A best-case reduction of two cents per pound is not meaningful grocery relief, particularly after an 8 percent annual price increase.

For cattle producers, however, the signal matters beyond one shipment quota. Ranchers depend on stronger periods in a cyclical market to survive later downturns and rebuild depleted herds. If every price increase prompts more imports, the government suppresses the returns needed to expand domestic supply—the very shortage the White House cited to justify intervention.

The administration manufactured the squeeze

The import decision cannot be isolated from the administration’s other policies. According to Vox, U.S. beef exports fell 12 percent in 2025 amid trade disputes with China. Cattle organizations in Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas said ICE activity kept workers home, delaying shipments and causing losses.

The reporting does not establish that these policies were designed to damage ranchers. It does establish a pattern of federal actions imposing multiple pressures on the same industry, followed by a narrowly targeted price measure that asks producers to absorb still more pain for negligible consumer relief.

The framing obscures responsibility

Calling this a policy that “backfired” suggests an unfortunate accident. The foreseeable distribution of costs was built into the decision: imported lean beef competes with domestic cattle, while only a fraction of wholesale price reductions reaches shoppers.

Nor is this merely a quarrel between consumers seeking cheap hamburgers and ranchers protecting profits. Consumers receive pennies; producers face intervention in the market that determines whether their operations remain viable. The central failure belongs to officials offering a visible gesture in place of an affordability policy.

Loyalty is not leverage

Republicans are contesting unusually close Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, and Nebraska despite Trump’s decisive 2024 margins in those states. That electoral pressure explains why Republican senators are suddenly emphasizing cattle-market cycles and warning their own president against depressing prices.

The larger pattern is transactional politics stripped of its sales pitch. A governing coalition can praise rural producers as cultural symbols while treating their livelihoods as adjustable inputs. When trade policy, immigration enforcement, and tariff policy converge on the same communities, partisan identification offers no protection. Institutional power remains with the officials making the decisions; everyone else is left competing over who must pay for them.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump plan to make burgers cheaper backfires spectacularly in MAGA country

item.title: Trump proves a 50-year-old theory about 'stupid people' wrecking society
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that New Republic writer Ross Rosenfield used Italian historian Carlo Cipolla’s 1976 theory of human stupidity to interpret Donald Trump’s administration. Rosenfield argues that Cipolla’s warning becomes especially relevant when people who harm others without benefiting themselves acquire control over armies, monetary policy, media influence, and regulatory institutions.

Rosenfield points to the administration’s conduct involving Iran, public health, artificial intelligence, and cryptocurrency, alongside Republican attitudes about January 6 and the 2020 election. His conclusion is cautious: the United States may be entering the institutional decline Cipolla described, but the eventual extent of that decline remains unknown.

Power Is the Material Fact

The useful part of Cipolla’s framework is not the insult. It is the recognition that destructive behavior changes scale when backed by the state.

Trump does not merely hold foolish opinions. As president, he directs an administration with military, regulatory, financial, and communications power. An inept private citizen can cause limited damage. An inept health secretary, in Rosenfield’s account, can weaken protections affecting millions. Institutional authority turns bad judgment into public policy.

“Stupidity” Hides Agency

The article’s central framing is also its central weakness. Calling political actors stupid can disguise decisions as cognitive accidents. It shifts attention from who appointed officials, who supports the administration, who weakens oversight, and who benefits from deregulation or public confusion.

Cipolla distinguishes “stupid” actors from “bandits” who profit while harming others. But political systems routinely join the two: powerful officials can produce reckless outcomes while industries gain from weakened regulation. The reporting mentions that possibility without examining which interests benefit from the administration’s approach to AI, cryptocurrency, health policy, or war.

The Republican Party Is an Enabler

Rosenfield cites polling in which only 20 percent of Republicans described January 6 as a violent insurrection, while 71 percent denied that Joe Biden won the 2020 election. Those figures do not establish why respondents hold those views, but they show that the problem described here is larger than one officeholder.

Trump possesses executive power, yet a political party sustains that power by validating his account of reality. Treating this as a mass outbreak of stupidity lets party officials, media figures, and institutional allies fade into the crowd. Their choices deserve individual scrutiny because organized denial is politically more consequential than private ignorance.

The Consequences Are Institutional

The foreseeable damage is not simply that government makes embarrassing mistakes. It is that institutions meant to constrain error become instruments for spreading it. Regulatory neglect exposes the public to risks; distorted historical narratives protect those responsible for political violence; military misjudgment places lives under decisions the public cannot easily reverse.

Rosenfield says it may be too early to know whether the United States is on Cipolla’s path of decline. That uncertainty is warranted. But uncertainty about the final destination does not erase the conduct already described or the officials empowered to carry it out.

A System Built to Amplify Failure

The larger pattern is a political order that concentrates enormous power while encouraging everyone to discuss its use as personality. “Stupidity” supplies a memorable label, but it is not an adequate theory of responsibility.

Systems fail when powerful people make damaging decisions, aligned institutions enable them, and public language converts agency into bewilderment. The scandal is not that destructive actors exist. It is that parties, offices, and industries can place state machinery in their hands—and then invite the country to mistake the result for mere confusion.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump proves a 50-year-old theory about ‘stupid people’ wrecking society

item.title: Trump in 'emergency' mode as leaks reveal scramble to fix dire issue
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet, citing the Financial Times, reports that President Donald Trump and administration officials entered “emergency talks” over sharply rising diesel prices while the U.S. war with Iran continued. The administration considered restricting diesel exports, including a possible ban, but the White House said Trump was still evaluating options and had made no decision.

According to people familiar with the discussions, White House staff opposed an export ban, and oil companies warned Trump that it could disrupt global supplies while raising prices in U.S. regions dependent on imported fuel. Despite those warnings, he was reportedly still considering the measure.

Republican Rep. Tim Burchett said rising fuel prices could cost his party in the November midterms. His explanation was unusually direct: Republicans hold power, so voters are likely to hold them responsible.

Power is not a mystery

The central fact is not that Washington is “scrambling.” It is that Trump holds the decision-making power. Advisers can object, companies can lobby and foreign leaders can warn, but the policy reportedly remains in play because the president may want “to do something big.”

That distinction matters. Institutional disagreement does not diffuse responsibility. If Trump imposes an export ban after being warned that it could backfire, the consequences will not belong to an abstract “White House” or an unruly market. They will follow from his decision.

A crisis meeting is not a solution

“Emergency” language makes the administration sound like a rescue crew arriving at an external disaster. The reporting instead places the diesel spike amid Trump’s continuing war with Iran and describes officials debating a measure experts expect could worsen supply problems.

The proposed ban also displays the political seduction of visible action. Restricting exports looks forceful and is easy to announce. But the reported warnings are concrete: it may fail to reduce American prices, disrupt international supply and raise costs in parts of the United States that import fuel. Spectacle cannot substitute for a policy mechanism that works.

The leak exposes the governing structure

The leaked deliberations depict staff resistance without staff control. Officials are reportedly “thoroughly opposed,” yet the proposal survives because the decisive question is what Trump wants.

Oil companies appear to have more practical influence than the president’s own staff, at least insofar as they managed to warn him about regional price increases. That is not evidence of benevolence; it reveals an administration in which access and persuasion matter, but authority remains concentrated in one person’s appetite for a dramatic move.

Republicans cannot outsource responsibility

Burchett’s remark cuts through the usual partisan misdirection. Whether Republicans believe they “deserve” blame is politically secondary. They control the government, and their president is directing both the war policy surrounding the crisis and the response under consideration.

Consumers and businesses would bear the consequences through transportation costs and higher prices across fuel-dependent supply chains. Political leaders often describe those effects as market pain, as though no official made choices upstream. Burchett acknowledged the simpler reality: governing power carries ownership.

The pattern is decision first, fallout later

This story reveals a recurring model of personalized government: create or intensify instability, confront the predictable domestic costs, then reach for a conspicuous intervention despite warnings that it may make matters worse.

The danger in that model is not mere confusion. It is the separation of political theater from material consequence. Trump gets the dramatic announcement; staff members get plausible deniability through leaks; industry gets private access; and households, truckers and businesses get the bill.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump in ‘emergency’ mode as leaks reveal scramble to fix dire issue

item.title: What Trump truly fears when he lashes out at the Supreme Court
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Atlantic writer Adam Serwer identifies Trump’s fear as the possibility that public criticism can influence Supreme Court justices. Serwer argues that Trump projects this fear when he attributes rulings against him to pressure from the “Radical Left,” then attacks the Court himself in hopes of shaping its next decision.

During his 2024 campaign, Trump suggested that criticizing Supreme Court rulings should bring “very serious fines and beyond that.” After a majority of the justices rejected his effort to restrict voting by mail in the midterms, however, he publicly disparaged them as “a shell of their original selves.”

Serwer notes that Trump had also recently lost high-profile disputes involving tariffs and birthright citizenship. But he argues that the Court has otherwise repeatedly expanded Trump’s power or endorsed outcomes he favored, including presidential immunity and greater presidential control over nominally independent agencies.

Power, not principle

Trump’s contradiction is not difficult to decode. Criticism is intolerable when directed at judges delivering outcomes he wants and legitimate when those judges resist him. The operating principle is permission: allies may exercise power; opponents should be punished for using the same tools.

That matters because a president commands institutional power unavailable to ordinary Court critics. He appoints justices, directs the executive branch and possesses an immense political platform. His denunciations are therefore not merely commentary from another dissatisfied litigant. They tell judges selected under his authority that favorable rulings are expected and deviation will be treated as betrayal.

The appointment as obligation

Trump’s complaint that the justices were not the people he “interviewed to serve” strips away the customary fiction that judicial selection is detached from anticipated results. Presidents have always chosen nominees partly for their legal commitments. Trump’s formulation goes further: the appointment resembles a personal transaction, with continued loyalty as the expected return.

The justices still possess independent authority and made the reported decision themselves. Nothing in the account establishes that Trump’s criticism changed a vote. But his language reveals how he understands the relationship: judicial independence is acceptable only until it frustrates presidential will.

The convenient referee

“Playing the ref” was Trump’s accusation when other people criticized the Court. His own response shows that he was not defending judicial insulation from political pressure. He was arguing for a monopoly on that pressure.

The misdirection lies in presenting weaker actors’ criticism as coercion while minimizing the leverage of the presidency. Protesters, advocates and voters can speak. A president can nominate judges, enforce judgments, shape the federal government and mobilize a party against officials who displease him. Treating those forms of influence as interchangeable launders power out of the story.

A Court that is never loyal enough

Serwer’s sharper point is that Trump’s anger followed isolated defeats from a Court that, in his assessment, has often produced outcomes advantageous to Trump. The grievance is therefore not evidence of sustained judicial opposition. It is evidence that substantial institutional accommodation does not satisfy a leader who treats every adverse ruling as illegitimate pressure or personal disloyalty.

That pattern converts independent institutions into conditional allies. Compliance becomes normal and resistance becomes scandal. Each favorable decision resets the baseline; each unfavorable one triggers another demand for submission.

The system beneath the outburst

The larger danger in this episode is not hypocrisy by itself. Hypocrisy is merely the visible residue of a power theory: law protects the leader’s freedom of action while restricting everyone else’s.

AlterNet’s account shows a president attacking judicial criticism when it threatened useful rulings, then deploying criticism when the Court blocked him. The systemic failure begins when institutions and political coverage treat that asymmetry as inconsistency rather than hierarchy. Trump is not confused about who should be allowed to pressure the Court. His position, as described here, is brutally coherent: power should answer to him, and dissent should carry consequences.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: What Trump truly fears when he lashes out at the Supreme Court

item.title: MAGA senator throws tantrum after epic gaffe in Jack Smith hearing: ‘Quote me on it!’
item.description:
What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Eric Schmitt used a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing to accuse former special counsel Jack Smith of meeting Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis at an Atlanta basketball game in early 2024. Smith said he attended a game in Maryland, not Georgia, undermining the premise of Schmitt’s accusation.

After the hearing, reporters repeatedly asked whether Schmitt had gotten his information wrong. He did not identify evidence placing Smith at the Atlanta game. Instead, he repeated that Smith denied being there, accused him of lying in the past, called him a “total dirtbag,” and invoked Smith’s prosecution of President Donald Trump.

The accusation was the exercise of power

Schmitt was not a spectator making a sloppy argument online. He was a United States senator using a Judiciary Committee hearing to suggest that a former federal prosecutor may have lied under oath.

That institutional setting matters. A senator can place an insinuation into the congressional record, wrap it in the authority of oversight, and generate material for partisan media. Smith could answer the question, but Schmitt controlled the accusation and its staging.

When the premise failed, Schmitt changed the subject

The reporting does not establish that Smith attended a game in Atlanta or met Willis there. Confronted with that failure, Schmitt did not supply better evidence or retract the allegation. He attacked Smith’s character and cited Smith’s attempt to prosecute Trump.

That is not a factual defense of the original claim. It is a substitution: if the audience already regards Smith as an enemy, Schmitt no longer needs to prove where Smith was. Hostility becomes a stand-in for evidence.

Reporters exposed the dodge

The hallway questioning correctly centered the decisive issue: Was Schmitt’s information wrong? His refusal to answer was more revealing than the insult that produced the headline.

Calling the exchange a “tantrum” risks making temperament the story. The more consequential conduct was Schmitt’s use of official proceedings to advance a claim that, according to RawStory’s account, collapsed under a basic geographic distinction—and his unwillingness to correct it afterward.

Loyalty outranked oversight

Schmitt’s reference to Smith trying to jail the president supplied the political logic. He presented Smith’s prosecution of Trump as grounds for contempt, not as a reason to examine the record with greater care.

The hearing therefore functioned less as oversight than as partisan defense work. Schmitt used Senate authority to discredit an investigator associated with criminal cases against Trump, then treated the target’s supposed villainy as permission to disregard the evidentiary failure.

The systemic error is consequence-free accusation

This episode reveals a durable propaganda method: make the allegation through an institution, retreat into abuse when challenged, and rely on partisan identity to preserve the intended impression. The correction travels as detail; the accusation travels as narrative.

The immediate consequence is not merely embarrassment for one senator. It is the degradation of congressional oversight into content production, where officials can spend institutional credibility on claims they will not defend—and where accountability consists of reporters asking the right question while the officeholder simply refuses to answer it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: MAGA senator throws tantrum after epic gaffe in Jack Smith hearing: ‘Quote me on it!’

item.title: Road trip uncovers voter outrage that could 'blow up' Trump and the GOP
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that an NBC News road trip along Interstate 80 in August found widespread voter anger that could damage President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections. Voters cited higher prices, rising interest rates, foreign wars, job anxiety tied to artificial intelligence, and collapsing confidence in federal officials.

The reporting identified vulnerable Republican-held House seats in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Iowa, plus an open Iowa Senate seat. Some incumbents face additional liabilities: New Jersey Rep. Tom Kean’s weeks-long unexplained absence from Congress and abuse allegations made by Ohio Rep. Max Miller’s wife, which Miller has denied. Iowa farmers, meanwhile, described pressure from Trump’s trade policies and disrupted commodity markets.

The quoted voters did not uniformly embrace Democrats. Some expressed indiscriminate hostility toward Washington, while one Republican voter who rejected Miller remained unsure whether she would support his Democratic opponent. The trip therefore found conditions that could “blow up” the governing party—not proof that they will.

Power has a party

The phrase “anger at Washington” blurs the central fact: Trump and congressional Republicans hold the governing power voters are positioned to punish. They shape trade policy, deportation policy, foreign-policy choices, and the legislative agenda. Their incumbents are not spectators trapped inside a sour national mood.

That distinction matters because generalized contempt protects officeholders from accountability. If every politician is equally guilty, the officials currently making decisions can present their consequences as another inexplicable failure of “the system.”

Democrats still have agency where they hold office and must persuade voters that they offer more than opposition. But the midterm danger described here attaches primarily to the party exercising federal power.

Material pain defeats branding

The most damaging testimony came from a three-time Trump voter in Pennsylvania who said everything had become more expensive and blamed Americans’ costs on war. Whether his causal judgment is economically complete is less important politically than what it reveals: partisan loyalty is colliding with household experience.

The same collision appears in Iowa. Farmers are not encountering trade policy as campaign theater; AlterNet’s account says they are facing more expensive operations and disrupted commodity markets. A tariff can be marketed as strength in Washington and experienced as a bill in farm country.

That is the vulnerability beneath Republican messaging. Cultural allegiance can keep voters inside a coalition for years, but it cannot make their expenses disappear.

Scandal meets institutional permission

Kean and Miller illustrate a separate failure of representation. Kean reportedly left constituents uninformed for weeks about an absence connected to mental-health issues. The legitimate privacy surrounding health does not erase an elected official’s obligation to account for an extended inability to serve.

Miller continued seeking reelection after his wife accused him of domestic abuse, including violence involving their two-year-old daughter. Those remain allegations, not adjudicated facts, and Miller has denied them. But Republican institutions still made a consequential choice by leaving voters to absorb the political and ethical risk of his candidacy.

The article is strongest when it names these concrete liabilities. It is weaker when it folds them into a generic “tough atmosphere,” as though candidate conduct were weather rather than the product of decisions by officeholders and the party structures supporting them.

Anger is not realignment

The evidence does not establish a Democratic wave. It shows an opening. Disgust with a Republican incumbent does not automatically produce a Democratic vote, and fury at federal officials can become abstention, anti-incumbent voting, or renewed support for familiar partisan identities.

That uncertainty is precisely why Democrats cannot rely on revulsion alone. They must connect Republican decisions to tangible consequences and present a credible alternative. Otherwise, diffuse anger may punish a few incumbents without changing the structure that produced it.

The system’s favorite disguise

The larger pattern is organized power disappearing behind public frustration. Policies have authors. Candidates have enablers. Governing parties make choices, then benefit when coverage translates those choices into a mysterious national “mood.”

NBC’s road trip, as summarized by AlterNet, supplies useful evidence of political erosion but not a forecast. Its deeper lesson is that voters are tracing at least some material harm back toward those in office. The decisive contest is whether that chain of responsibility remains visible—or is buried again beneath the safer fiction that everyone in Washington somehow did it together.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Road trip uncovers voter outrage that could ‘blow up’ Trump and the GOP

item.title: Trump's 'human printer' and the twisted magic of the MAGA cocoon
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Natalie Harp, President Donald Trump’s personal aide and so-called “human printer,” helps manage the information placed before him: flattering coverage, social-media material and other content aligned with his preferences. According to CNN’s reporting as quoted by AlterNet, Harp showed Trump media clips before he barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on September 19, 2026; a Politico graphic reportedly helped anger him and inform that decision.

A federal judge temporarily ordered the administration to restore the outlets’ credentials. The administration initially resisted, eventually complied, and then—according to AlterNet—again denied CNN and MS NOW access when Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived for a state dinner. Trump did not publicly identify a specific report that prompted the original ban.

AlterNet also describes Harp as a conduit for material Trump posts online, including AI-generated fantasies and racist content. The “MAGA cocoon” is therefore not merely personal devotion around a president. It is an information system in which loyal attendants select what reaches a powerful officeholder and help transmit his preferred version of reality back to the public.

The president holds the power

Harp may curate the feed, but Trump controls the presidency. He decided to punish news organizations, and his administration enforced that decision. Any framing that turns the episode into a profile of an eccentric aide risks relocating responsibility from the officeholder with constitutional authority to the subordinate carrying a laptop.

The institutional actors matter too. White House personnel confiscated credentials and denied access. They did not need to share Trump’s grievance to make it consequential; they only needed to execute it. Harp’s proximity may have helped trigger the response, but proximity is not presidential power.

The court order exposed the machinery

The administration’s conduct after judicial intervention is more revealing than the reported moment of irritation. AlterNet says officials initially refused to restore access, complied only after the outlets returned to court, and later excluded two of them from another event despite the order.

That sequence describes institutional defiance, not confusion. A president’s anger became an administrative sanction, and government employees carried it forward until legal pressure forced a partial retreat. The foreseeable consequence is a press corps made to understand that unfavorable coverage can bring exclusion—and that even judicial relief may require repeated enforcement.

The courtier story is a distraction

The fascination with Harp’s letters, personal-care bag and behavior around Trump offers an easy spectacle. It also invites the public to treat governance as palace gossip: the strange assistant, the peculiar devotion, the whispered relationship. That emphasis makes the aide look like the author of the danger when the machinery belongs to the president and the executive branch.

Her role is politically significant, but not because she is uniquely bizarre. It matters because an administration reportedly permits a personal loyalist to filter information, reinforce grievance and supply material for presidential broadcasting. The operative failure is structural: access appears to be rewarded by emotional service to the leader, while contrary information can become grounds for retaliation.

Propaganda as a feedback loop

AlterNet’s strongest point is that Harp reportedly works in both directions. She brings Trump content that flatters or agitates him, then helps circulate material reflecting his fixations. That arrangement can create a closed loop: curated information produces presidential reaction, and presidential reaction becomes content presented to supporters as political reality.

The article cites polling showing extraordinary loyalty among particular Republican and MAGA constituencies, but those results do not establish that Harp caused that attachment or that every supporter relates to Trump identically. They do show why the loop has political value. A highly committed audience gives the administration an incentive to keep grievance vivid, enemies visible and presidential infallibility intact.

Calling this merely a “cocoon” understates its reach. A private bubble becomes a public instrument when its occupant controls federal agencies, White House access and the country’s most powerful communications platform.

Personal rule needs enablers

The larger pattern is government reorganized around one leader’s emotional demands. Courtiers supply affirmation. Officials convert displeasure into state action. Supporters receive the resulting grievance as proof of persecution. Courts may intervene, but enforcement becomes another contest with an administration willing to test the boundary.

Ridiculing Harp obscures that chain of agency. She reportedly fed the system; Trump made the decision; administration personnel implemented it; news organizations bore the penalty; and the court had to compel compliance. The systemic error is not that a president has an unusually devoted aide. It is that personal resentment can travel through loyal intermediaries and emerge as government policy.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s ‘human printer’ and the twisted magic of the MAGA cocoon

item.title: Trump baffles with 'tremendous' claim after existential warning about AI
item.description:
President Donald Trump speaking during a press conference with AI leaders. (Screengrab via CNN)

What happened

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that artificial intelligence should be subject to “tremendous self-regulation,” while also claiming that the Justice Department and FBI already provide some form of regulation. RawStory reported that he made the remarks after a White House summit with technology executives, when asked whether government guardrails were necessary.

Days earlier, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates had told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that government oversight was necessary and warned that AI could “cause a billion deaths.” Trump did not address that scenario directly. Instead, he praised a group including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos as extraordinarily capable and celebrated their work.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power without a policy

The federal government holds the power to impose enforceable rules. Trump held the presidency and therefore substantial influence over whether executive agencies would develop, apply, or advocate such safeguards. The executives in the room controlled companies with immense capital and technological reach, but they were also the prospective subjects of regulation.

Trump’s answer blurred those distinct roles. The Justice Department and FBI enforce laws and investigate crimes; invoking them did not explain what AI standards existed, what conduct they covered, or how catastrophic risks would be prevented. Calling that arrangement “automatic” regulation substituted institutional names for an actual policy.

The regulated become the regulators

Self-regulation places the central judgment in the hands of companies whose incentives include expansion, market dominance, and speed. It asks those building and commercializing the technology to decide which constraints should slow them down.

The problem is structural, not a referendum on whether Musk, Zuckerberg, Bezos, or their peers are “brilliant.” Technical accomplishment does not eliminate conflicts of interest. Praise for executives answers a different question from the one reporters asked: not whether these men are talented, but whether the public should depend on their voluntary restraint.

Praise as misdirection

The most revealing move was the pivot from risk to prestige. Confronted with a question about enforceable guardrails, Trump praised the people who would face those guardrails. That framing recasts oversight as a matter of confidence in exceptional individuals rather than a question of public authority and accountability.

RawStory’s emphasis on Trump appearing “unfazed” captures the contrast with Gates’s warning, but bafflement is not the core issue. The statement’s political meaning is clearer than its policy content: governmental responsibility was displaced onto private actors while government agencies were cited vaguely enough to suggest that protection already existed.

Catastrophic stakes, voluntary limits

Gates’s billion-death scenario was his warning, not an established forecast in the reporting. But even as a hypothetical, it exposes the inadequacy of Trump’s response. Risks described as potentially catastrophic cannot coherently be met with admiration for the industry and an undefined appeal to self-policing.

This is a recurring pattern of concentrated power: corporations retain operational control, political leaders decline to specify binding limits, and the public is told that elite competence will substitute for enforceable accountability. If harm follows, responsibility becomes easy to scatter among developers, users, agencies, and an allegedly unpredictable technology.

The system behind the shrug

The deeper failure is not that Trump sounded confused. It is that his answer treated public protection as optional while preserving maximum discretion for powerful private institutions.

When government officials answer demands for rules by praising the regulated, they are making a political choice even if they never articulate a policy. The state keeps its enforcement vocabulary, industry keeps its freedom of action, and everyone outside the room inherits the consequences.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump baffles with ‘tremendous’ claim after existential warning about AI
