item.title: 'Hell of a closing message': Mike Johnson's live TV promise leaves onlookers aghast
item.description:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) gives remarks to the media following a vote in the House of Representatives at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 1, 2026. REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz

What happened

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Tuesday on CNBC that Republicans would spend the next two years doing “exactly what we have been doing already” if they retained their House majority. He credited Republican policy with high stock indexes, stronger-than-expected job numbers and an Atlanta Fed projection of 5.1 percent third-quarter economic growth.

RawStory reported that Johnson was preparing a six-week campaign tour across 22 states while Republicans faced deteriorating House prospects. The outlet cited a Cook Political Report assessment shifting 15 races toward Democrats, alongside polling aggregates showing national Republican favorability below 39 percent.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Democratic Rep. Sean Casten and several online commentators portrayed Johnson’s promise as an indictment of Republican governance, citing higher prices, congressional inaction and deference to President Donald Trump. Those descriptions are their characterizations; the article does not independently establish several of their more serious allegations.

The power belongs to the speaker

Johnson is not merely another campaign surrogate defending a record. As House speaker, he controls substantial institutional machinery: what reaches the floor, when members vote and whether the chamber seriously scrutinizes the executive branch.

That makes his pledge unusually revealing. “More of the same” is not an abstract ideological slogan coming from a powerless critic. It is a promise from the official positioned to decide whether the House legislates, conducts oversight or organizes itself around protecting a president from politically inconvenient votes.

The record is being laundered through indicators

Johnson’s argument substitutes selected economic measurements for a full accounting of Republican rule. Stock indexes, one set of job figures and a quarterly growth projection may describe economic conditions, but they do not establish that House Republicans produced them. A projection is not a completed result, and correlation is not legislative authorship.

The rhetorical trick is straightforward: claim ownership of favorable numbers while treating public anger over costs as irrelevant to the verdict. Johnson calls the conditions intentional when they help his case, but the reporting offers no comparable explanation of who bears responsibility for the policies and disruptions his critics blame for higher prices.

Congress cannot campaign as a bystander

The weakest responses quoted by RawStory reduce Johnson’s statement to a marketing blunder. That framing is too shallow. The problem is not that the speaker selected an ineffective closing message. It is that he described continuity as success without supplying a concrete account of what the House actually delivered or what its next majority would do.

Republican control of the chamber is an exercise of power, not a spectator role in Trump’s presidency. If the House avoids oversight, hearings or votes because they might inconvenience the president, that is not confusion or mere laziness. It is an institutional choice. The article quotes critics alleging precisely that pattern, though it provides no legislative tally sufficient to prove each accusation.

The backlash needs evidence, too

Casten’s sweeping charge about protecting predators, facilitating extrajudicial killings and enriching Trump is politically explosive, but RawStory does not substantiate those allegations within this article. Publishing the attack alongside several social-media reactions creates heat without doing the harder work of tracing particular decisions, votes or failures of oversight.

That omission weakens an otherwise legitimate line of inquiry. Johnson’s authority can be examined through documented House conduct. When coverage relies instead on aghast posts, it lets the speaker dismiss criticism as partisan outrage and leaves readers without the institutional evidence needed to judge the record.

The governing pattern

The larger pattern is a congressional leadership that seeks credit for every favorable condition while blurring responsibility for every damaging one. Power is asserted when economic numbers rise and disguised when governing choices impose costs or shield the executive.

Johnson’s promise matters because continuity under his speakership would mean continuity in who sets the House agenda and whose interests that agenda serves. Treating the remark as merely embarrassing misses the political substance: a powerful official openly asked voters to ratify the existing arrangement, while the coverage spent more time cataloguing disbelief than auditing what that arrangement has done.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Hell of a closing message’: Mike Johnson’s live TV promise leaves onlookers aghast

item.title: Trump voters spill why they're ditching Republicans: 'Washington is full of criminals’
item.description:
A supporter of Republican presidential nominee and former U.S. President Donald Trump holds a MAGA hat during a rally at Gaylord Rockies Resort and Convention Center in Aurora, Colorado, U.S., October 11, 2024. REUTERS/Isaiah J. Downing

What happened

RawStory reports that a Michigan focus group of 2024 Trump voters who now disapprove of his performance found several participants considering Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. They described Republican nominee Mike Rogers as an establishment figure and viewed attacks connecting El-Sayed to another person’s remarks as unfair or unpersuasive.

One participant welcomed El-Sayed’s primary victory over an opponent reportedly backed by about $30 million from AIPAC, citing concern about outside money and foreign influence. Others rejected a Rogers advertisement linking El-Sayed to podcaster Hasan Piker’s statement that America “deserved 9/11,” noting that El-Sayed did not make the remark and had distanced himself from it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory also cites New York Times/Siena College polling showing El-Sayed supported by 8 percent of 2024 Trump voters—more crossover support than comparable Democratic Senate candidates in New Hampshire and Maine. A focus group cannot establish how Michigan will vote, and the article does not show that these opinions represent Trump voters generally.

Who holds the power

The participants may cast ballots, but the institutional power in this story belongs to campaigns, parties, major political spenders, and the organizations that select and distribute campaign messages. Rogers’s campaign had the capacity to turn Piker’s words into an attack on El-Sayed. AIPAC, according to the reporting, had roughly $30 million behind El-Sayed’s primary opponent. Those are not merely competing opinions. They are organized attempts to define the choices voters are allowed to see.

El-Sayed’s limited power here comes from refusing the assigned role. He distanced himself from Piker’s remark, while voters in the group declined to hold him responsible for words he did not say. That basic distinction became politically meaningful because campaign advertising so often depends on erasing it.

Guilt by association fails

The Rogers attack substituted proximity for responsibility: a podcaster said something inflammatory, so the Democratic candidate was made to carry it. Valerie, one participant, recognized the trick immediately. The attack did not expose El-Sayed’s conduct; it advertised the campaign’s willingness to manufacture culpability.

RawStory frames this partly as evidence for a Democratic strategy of answering “soft on crime” attacks with Republican corruption. But the focus-group comments establish dissatisfaction with Washington and skepticism toward the advertisement, not that a particular Democratic counterattack caused either response. The article overstates the strategic vindication.

The deeper failure belongs to a political class that treats voters as containers for pretested anxieties. Invoke 9/11, attach the opponent’s name, and assume the emotional charge will survive the missing evidence. In this group, it did not.

Anti-establishment politics has no fixed owner

These voters are not moving neatly from one ideology to another. They are applying an anti-establishment test that Trump once benefited from and Rogers, in their view, fails. Cory translated “America First” into opposition to AIPAC spending. Jade treated Rogers’s FBI background as a liability amid distrust surrounding the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case. Tamara dismissed crime messaging against the backdrop of what she called criminality throughout Washington.

Their reasoning may be inconsistent, imprecise or driven by separate grievances. It is still politically consequential. Party strategists routinely mistake coalition membership for ideological obedience. The result is brittle politics: once a candidate no longer embodies the rebellion voters thought they purchased, some will shop for another vehicle.

Tucker Carlson’s reported description of El-Sayed’s campaign as “literally Trumpian” reinforces that point. “Trumpian” here functions less as a policy category than as a claim to outsider authenticity.

Distrust is being redirected

The danger for Republicans in this account is not that former Trump voters have suddenly embraced Democratic institutions. It is that the party’s own language of betrayal, corruption and elite capture can be turned against its candidates. Rogers’s résumé, party label and attack advertising do not neutralize that suspicion; for these participants, they intensify it.

That does not automatically benefit Democrats. A politics built on generalized distrust can migrate again just as quickly. El-Sayed’s apparent opening depends on being perceived as independent of the same machinery voters despise. If party institutions and large donors absorb him into conventional politics, the distinction could collapse.

The system manufactures its own backlash

This story reveals a recurring error in establishment politics: powerful institutions deploy money and associative smears, then describe voters’ refusal to comply as ideological unpredictability. The voters are “messy” only from the perspective of strategists who assumed partisan identity would override judgment about who actually said what and whose interests a candidate appears to serve.

The consequential divide here is not simply Republican against Democrat. It is between institutions trying to assign guilt and credibility from above, and voters deciding those institutions have forfeited that authority. When campaigns replace evidence with contamination tactics, they do more than weaken one advertisement. They deepen the distrust that anti-establishment candidates—sincere or otherwise—are built to exploit.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump voters spill why they’re ditching Republicans: ‘Washington is full of criminals’

item.title: 'His fault': Trump 'robs GOP of chance' to go on offense in swing states
item.description:
President Donald Trump gestures at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, April 29, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

Donald Trump is the “biggest culprit,” according to an anonymous Republican source quoted by Politico and relayed by AlterNet. The source blamed the political damage on Trump’s trade war and Iran war, saying both had hurt farmers and rural communities. Another GOP source said bluntly: “It’s his fault.” The reporting does not independently establish how much either policy caused Republicans’ electoral problems.

Politico reported Tuesday that Trump was expected to spend the following month campaigning in Alabama, Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas—states Republicans would ordinarily expect to hold—rather than concentrating on traditional swing states. Party strategists hoped his appearances would mobilize supporters who often stay home when he is not on the ballot.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Republicans were reportedly particularly worried about weak candidates in Ohio and Alaska. Despite favorable House maps and a large financial advantage, party insiders feared they could lose control of Congress. One donor described political “fires” everywhere, while a White House-connected source rated the danger in Alaska and Ohio at 10 out of 10.

The power is in the White House

Trump is not a bystander being unfairly saddled with responsibility for somebody else’s campaign. He is the president, the Republican Party’s central political figure and, according to the reporting, the person whose presence the party believes is necessary to activate a substantial part of its electorate.

That dependence gives him extraordinary power over Republican strategy. His time determines which races receive attention. His political brand shapes turnout. His administration’s decisions supply Democrats with material to use against Republican candidates.

Calling his campaign schedule “defense” describes the immediate tactic but obscures the institutional structure. Republicans have built a party whose voters, candidates and campaign apparatus revolve around one officeholder. Now presidential resources must be spent maintaining territory the party once treated as secure.

These are not random fires

The “fires everywhere” metaphor makes the Republican predicament sound like a series of spontaneous emergencies. Politico’s reported details point instead to connected political choices: candidate quality, reliance on Trump-specific voters and policies that one Republican source said damaged farmers and rural residents.

The evidence supplied does not prove that Trump’s trade and Iran policies caused the party’s entire decline. But the allegation comes from inside the Republican coalition, not from a Democratic attack line. It describes a governing agenda producing costs among voters whom Republicans assumed were safely theirs.

Trump’s planned travel therefore represents more than an inconvenient allocation problem. If the reporting is accurate, presidential campaigning is being used to contain the electoral consequences of Republican governance and Republican candidate selection.

The party enabled its own dependency

Republican officials chose to organize around voters whose participation may depend on Trump personally appearing on the ballot or campaign trail. That may help when he is running. In a midterm, it becomes a structural liability: candidates inherit his record without automatically inheriting his turnout.

The party also selected—or accepted—candidates its own operatives now describe as inadequate. One source singled out Ohio Republican Jon Husted as unpersuasive; another blamed poor candidate quality more broadly. Trump may be the largest figure in this system, but party officials, donors and primary voters helped construct it.

Their complaints arrive anonymously, which lets insiders acknowledge the damage without publicly challenging the leader around whom they built their power. That is not accountability. It is private recognition paired with public submission.

The framing shrinks the consequence

To say Trump “robs” Republicans of opportunities in swing states casts the problem as a scheduling loss: every day spent in Alaska is a day unavailable elsewhere. That is true within the campaign logic described by Politico, but it is politically shallow.

The more consequential story is that Republicans may need a sitting president to rescue candidates in conservative strongholds despite gerrymandered maps and a major cash advantage. Those are substantial institutional protections. If they are insufficient, the problem is not merely that Trump has too many stops to make.

Nor are voters simply obstacles on a campaign map. Farmers and rural residents experiencing the effects attributed to Trump’s policies have agency. Their potential rejection of Republican candidates would be a political response to material consequences, not merely another “fire” for the president to extinguish.

A party built around one man cannot distribute responsibility

The larger pattern is a governing party attempting to separate its candidates from the consequences of the power it exercises. When policies are popular, Republicans present them as Trump’s achievements. When those policies become liabilities, insiders describe an unfortunate landscape that forces him to play defense.

But the same concentration of authority that gives Trump credit also makes efforts to treat him as incidental untenable. Republican leaders empowered him, candidates tied themselves to him, and the party conditioned its electorate around him. The reported result is a brittle coalition with money, favorable maps and presidential power, yet still scrambling to defend territory it once took for granted.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘His fault’: Trump ‘robs GOP of chance’ to go on offense in swing states

item.title: Scott Jennings cornered on CNN over Trump's 'communist' political ads: 'What is this?’
item.description:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings on CNN’s “The Arena.” (CNN screenshot)

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump played a leading role in creating two overtly political videos produced by the White House communications office and labeled “paid for by the U.S. Government.” The ads promoted Republicans ahead of the midterms; legal experts cited by the outlet said they clearly violated federal law.

On CNN, conservative strategist Scott Jennings defended the videos as public-service announcements, while conceding that campaign material may have been reused. Asked what public service they provided, he recast Trump’s attacks on “communism” as the message. CNN host Kaitlan Collins and Democratic strategist Ashley Allison challenged that explanation, pointing respectively to Trump’s reception of Chinese leader Xi Jinping and to the administration’s exclusion of disfavored press.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power behind the ads

The decisive actor was not Jennings, and the important event was not his failed television defense. The president reportedly helped shape the ads. The White House communications office produced them. Federal money paid for them. That is the power structure: an incumbent administration using public resources to manufacture electoral messaging for the party it leads.

Jennings had no authority over that machinery. His function was reputational cleanup—offering viewers a softer label for conduct attributed to the White House. Calling partisan advertising a public-service announcement does not change who commissioned it, who benefited or who paid.

Euphemism as permission

“Public service announcement” is not an explanation here. It is an attempt to move the dispute from the government’s conduct to the audience’s vocabulary. Collins exposed the weakness by asking what service the videos actually provided. The reported answer amounted to this: warning voters about “communism” justified the expenditure.

That defense collapses government communication into partisan mobilization. If electing Republicans becomes a public service merely because the president supplies an ideological insult, then virtually any campaign advertisement can be charged to the public. The euphemism is consequential because it normalizes the underlying appropriation instead of contesting the reported facts.

The decoy argument

The segment’s theatrical question was whether Jennings had been “cornered.” That is television’s preferred scale: the clash, the laugh, the awkward pivot. But the institutional question is whether the White House used taxpayer-funded communications to advance Republican electoral interests and, as the cited experts concluded, violated federal law.

Focusing on whether a surrogate performed badly misdirects attention toward the weaker actor in the room. Jennings did not control the Treasury or the White House production apparatus. Trump and his administration reportedly controlled the decision. The pundit’s embarrassment is incidental; executive misuse of public resources is the material issue.

Anticommunism without principle

Jennings’s invocation of “communism” did not answer the funding question. It substituted ideological branding for a defense of government conduct. Collins’s reference to Trump welcoming Xi Jinping underscored the selectivity: the label was deployed against domestic opponents while practical engagement with China’s leader proceeded on different terms.

Allison’s broader point was sharper. Taxpayer-funded personal promotion and exclusion of hostile press are exercises of state power, not evidence against an opponent’s ideology. Her comparison was political rhetoric, not proof that the administration is communist. But it exposed how the accusation functions: as a distraction from specific conduct by the people currently controlling government institutions.

The system behind the spectacle

This story reveals a familiar cycle. Officials use public machinery for partisan advantage; allies rename the conduct; cable television stages the renaming as a debate; and the enforcement question recedes behind the performance. Even a forceful rebuttal can leave that structure intact if the story ends with a surrogate losing an argument.

The central consequence is not hypocrisy. It is the erosion of the boundary between state communication and party propaganda. When those holding executive power can treat the federal government as an incumbent campaign asset, language becomes the first enforcement mechanism to fail. Calling the product a public service does not make it one. It merely tests whether institutions—and journalists—will accept the label instead of following the money and naming the decision-makers.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Scott Jennings cornered on CNN over Trump’s ‘communist’ political ads: ‘What is this?’

item.title: Trump just revealed his midterm strategy hinges on a 'monumental scandal': report
item.description:
US President Donald Trump looks on as he attends the Presidents Cup golf tournament at Medinah Country Club, in Medinah Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

President Donald Trump’s reported midterm strategy is to promote corporate investment announcements as evidence that his administration created jobs. RawStory, citing The New York Times, reported that Trump announced Monday in the Oval Office that Mesabi Metallic plans to build a large steel mill in Iowa as part of an $18 billion investment. Trump said the project probably would not have proceeded under a “less friendly” administration.

The “monumental scandal” was not the mill itself, but the financial relationships surrounding it. According to the reporting, Mesabi Metallic previously paid Trump associate Jason Miller $240,000 a year to lobby, while Miller also received about $150,000 annually under a lobbying contract with the Indian government to attract the company’s business. Public Citizen co-president Robert Weissman called that arrangement scandalous. The article does not establish that the contracts were illegal, that Trump directed them, or that they caused the Iowa investment.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds praised the proposed mill as transformative for the state and region. The reporting provided no job count, construction timetable, or evidence that the announced investment had already produced jobs.

Power owns the announcement

Trump controls the presidential platform and can place a private company’s proposal inside a White House political narrative. Mesabi Metallic controls whether the project is financed, built and operated. Reynolds can confer state-level legitimacy and potentially shape whatever public support follows.

Workers and voters control none of those decisions. Yet they are positioned as the grateful audience for benefits that remain prospective. That is the core power arrangement: public officials collect immediate political credit while the corporation retains control over delivery.

A promise is not a payroll

The framing converts an announced investment into a story about jobs already “created.” Those are not interchangeable facts. An $18 billion figure may sound concrete, but without a disclosed schedule, employment estimate or completed facility, it describes a plan rather than an economic result.

That distinction matters because political credit arrives at the press conference; accountability arrives years later, if at all. The administration gets the image of industrial revival before workers receive a paycheck.

The conflict question cannot be waved away

Miller’s reported contracts create an obvious influence question: how did a Trump associate come to be paid by both the company and the Indian government in connection with attracting that company’s business? The supplied reporting does not prove a corrupt exchange, so it cannot support declaring one.

But lack of proven criminality is not the same as lack of public concern. When access, lobbying money and presidential promotion converge around a politically valuable announcement, scrutiny is the minimum institutional response. Weissman’s remark identifies the normalization problem: relationships that would ordinarily trigger sustained examination risk becoming background noise.

Voters are not the responsible party

RawStory’s suggestion that these deals could help Republicans where voters are tiring of Trump places too much narrative weight on voter sentiment and too little on the officials manufacturing the sales pitch. Voters did not arrange the lobbying contracts, select the Oval Office backdrop or describe a proposed mill as proof of completed job creation.

The relevant agency belongs to Trump, his administration, the company and political allies such as Reynolds. Treating the episode chiefly as a question of whether skeptical voters can be won back obscures how institutional power turns private investment plans into publicly subsidized campaign material.

Government as political branding

The larger pattern is the conversion of governance into promotional theater: announce a large number, attach it to presidential favor, and bank the electoral benefit before the promised outcome can be measured. Corporate access becomes evidence of economic leadership; unresolved influence questions become incidental.

That system rewards spectacle over verification. The people with the most power define the success metric, claim victory at announcement and leave workers and communities holding the risk if the project delivers less than advertised.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump just revealed his midterm strategy hinges on a ‘monumental scandal’: report

item.title: Trump admin silent as American teen jailed and beaten without charge by US ally: report
item.description:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio looks on ahead of expected trilateral signing event with US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, regarding a deal on Greenland’s security, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

What happened

RawStory, citing Zeteo, reports that Abdalkareem Issa Ahmed Safi, an American teenager with Texas ties, remained imprisoned by Israel without charge or trial as of Tuesday. Israeli officers reportedly seized him from his West Bank home in late June, days before his 18th birthday, and placed him in administrative detention, which can be renewed indefinitely.

Safi’s father said a U.S. Embassy official told him his son reported being beaten on his first day in custody. He also fears Safi has scabies, based on information from a released prisoner. The White House, State Department, and U.S. Embassy in Israel did not respond to Zeteo’s requests for comment.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Zeteo identified two other young Americans in Israeli prisons. Sama Safi, 20, denies Israeli allegations connecting her to a student organization allegedly affiliated with a terrorist group; the report says she remained imprisoned after nearly 16 weeks with inadequate food and medical care. Adam Karakrah, 16, was also reportedly detained, and his sister said Israeli officers dismissed documents proving his U.S. citizenship.

The power is not ambiguous

Israel holds the immediate coercive power: its officers conducted the arrests, its authorities control the prisons, and its administrative-detention system permits imprisonment without a criminal charge or trial. Abdalkareem Safi and his family have none of those institutional tools. They cannot compel disclosure, demand a public accounting, or determine when the detention ends.

The United States holds a different kind of power. It can press an ally for information, publicly object to the reported treatment of an American citizen, and make diplomatic support contingent on answers. According to the reporting, the Trump administration did not even provide a public response when asked about Safi.

That silence does not establish what officials did privately or why they declined to comment. It does establish what they withheld publicly: an explanation of whether they were challenging Israel’s conduct or seeking safeguards for a detained American teenager.

Silence is an official choice

Government nonresponse is often reported as an absence, as though nobody quite remembered to speak. But three institutions—the White House, the State Department, and the embassy—were asked for comment. Each possessed authority unavailable to the imprisoned teenagers and their families. None supplied an answer for publication.

The central political fact is therefore not merely that a citizen lacked protection. It is that the agencies responsible for American diplomacy declined to account publicly for their response while an allied government held him without charge.

That choice also protects the stronger party from scrutiny. The family must produce testimony, medical fears, citizenship records, and pleas for information. The governments exercising power are permitted to offer nothing.

Citizenship has a hierarchy

American citizenship is routinely presented as a guarantee that the government will defend its nationals abroad. This reporting depicts something more conditional. Karakrah’s sister said officers threw his passport and birth certificate back at her. Safi’s citizenship, meanwhile, produced no public intervention from the administration agencies Zeteo contacted.

The story does not establish that U.S. officials caused these detentions. It shows that citizenship alone did not secure transparency, charges, a trial, or a visible diplomatic defense. For Palestinian Americans caught inside Israel’s detention system, the passport appears to carry less political force than Washington’s relationship with the government holding them.

That is not bureaucratic confusion. It is an asymmetry in whose vulnerability commands institutional urgency.

The framing can hide responsibility

Calling this primarily a story about administration “silence” risks making the failure sound atmospheric. Israel allegedly detained Safi, held him without charge, and subjected him to conditions his family fears are harming his health. U.S. officials then declined to explain their response. Those are separate exercises of power, and both require named responsibility.

The allegations concerning Sama Safi require the same precision. Israeli authorities eventually accused her of involvement with a student organization they allege is linked to a terrorist group; she denies it. Reporting that allegation does not justify treating prolonged imprisonment, deficient medical access, or detention without timely formal charges as administrative background.

The weaker actors here are not the governments facing questions. They are the young detainees and relatives forced to navigate secrecy while officials control the information, the legal process, and the timetable.

Alliance as insulation

The larger pattern is how an alliance can become insulation from accountability. One government uses detention powers that deny ordinary due-process protections; the other, according to the reporting, refuses to say publicly what it is doing about an imprisoned citizen who reported abuse.

Administrative detention places the burden on the captive to endure confinement without confronting a charge in court. Diplomatic silence reproduces that imbalance at another level: families must prove why officials should care, while the institutions capable of acting need not explain themselves.

A government’s priorities are clearest where its power is available but its accountability disappears. Here, the reported result is stark: Israeli authorities retain custody, American officials retain their silence, and teenagers bear the consequences.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump admin silent as American teen jailed and beaten without charge by US ally: report

item.title: Jack Smith cracks down as MAGA senator attacks wife: 'Not going to speak about my family’
item.description:
Jack Smith, former special counsel at the Justice Department, attends a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing at Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., US, September 29, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith refused three times to discuss his wife’s political views during a September 29, 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, asked whether Smith had been disappointed by Donald Trump’s 2016 victory, then questioned whether Smith’s wife supported Barack and Michelle Obama and had made a favorable documentary about the former first lady.

Smith said he would not speak about his family and repeatedly offered to answer questions about his work as special counsel. That work included leading the Justice Department investigation into Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents. The reported exchange ended without Kennedy establishing that Smith’s wife’s views influenced any investigative decision.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The senator held the power

Kennedy was not an aggrieved bystander searching for answers. He was a senator using an official Judiciary Committee hearing, with its institutional authority and public audience, to interrogate a former prosecutor about his spouse.

Smith could refuse the premise, but Kennedy controlled the questioning. He chose to spend that power on a family member’s presumed politics instead of identifying a decision by Smith, examining the evidence behind it, or testing whether Justice Department rules had been violated.

Guilt by marriage

Kennedy’s questions substituted association for proof. A spouse’s documentary work and political sympathies do not establish misconduct by a special counsel. If Kennedy possessed evidence connecting those views to Smith’s handling of the Trump investigations, RawStory’s account does not report him presenting it.

The tactic is politically useful precisely because it avoids that burden. It places the target inside a web of supposedly suspicious relationships and invites the audience to infer corruption from proximity. The insinuation does the work that evidence cannot—or, in this exchange, did not.

The hearing became the weapon

The institutional question should have been whether Smith exercised prosecutorial authority improperly. Kennedy instead tried to make Smith’s family a proxy defendant.

That maneuver also shifts scrutiny away from the conduct Smith investigated. Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents becomes background noise while the prosecutor’s household becomes the controversy. This is not substantive oversight. It is a reframing operation conducted under the seal of congressional authority.

A boundary is not a crackdown

RawStory’s framing casts Smith’s repeated refusal as a dramatic “crackdown” and Kennedy’s questioning as an attack. The exchange was sharper and more consequential than ordinary disagreement, but the tabloid packaging risks obscuring the actual power relationship.

Smith did not wield state power against Kennedy. He set a boundary and redirected the senator toward his official record. Kennedy was the government official with the microphone, the committee platform, and the ability to decide what the hearing would examine. Calling Smith’s refusal the dominant act mistakes resistance to misuse of power for power itself.

The broader pattern

This episode illustrates how congressional oversight can be converted into partisan insinuation without formally abandoning the language of inquiry. A senator need not prove that an investigation was compromised if he can suggest that the investigator’s spouse belonged to the wrong cultural or political circle.

The consequence reaches beyond one hearing. Public servants and their families are warned that professional decisions may bring ideological inspection of the household, while officials evade the harder work of demonstrating actual wrongdoing. Accountability collapses into guilt by association, and institutional power supplies the camera, the setting, and the legitimacy for the smear.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Jack Smith cracks down as MAGA senator attacks wife: ‘Not going to speak about my family’

item.title: Trump is stopping you from getting richer: A renowned economist explains
item.description:
REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz

What happened

AlterNet’s answer is that President Donald Trump is reducing Americans’ chances of becoming richer by weakening the institutions that support long-term growth. Economist Justin Wolfers pointed to erratic tariffs, favoritism, attacks on democratic accountability, tax cuts favoring wealthy people, and spending cuts affecting poorer people. He argued that the damage may emerge over decades rather than in current economic statistics.

Wolfers specifically rejected the interviewer’s claim that Trump is “keeping Americans poor.” His narrower conclusion was that Americans may inherit fewer jobs, inventions, and economic opportunities than they otherwise would. He also described Trump’s tariff regime as incoherent and said presidential control over exemptions can encourage businesses to seek political favor instead of competing through better products and lower prices.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Wolfers called the “One Big Beautiful Bill” the largest single redistribution from poor to rich in American history, crediting analyst Brendan Duke for the initial analysis. AlterNet’s interview, however, does not provide the underlying estimates or a comparison with other legislation, so readers are given Wolfers’s conclusion rather than enough evidence to independently assess its scale.

The headline outruns the evidence

“Trump is stopping you from getting richer” is a cleaner accusation than the interview supports. Wolfers did not claim that every American would lose wealth, nor that current statistics show economic collapse. He described a counterfactual: future prosperity may be lower than it could have been.

That distinction matters. Lost potential is real, but it is difficult to see precisely because the missing factory, invention, wage gain, or competitor never appears in the data. AlterNet turns that careful argument into a personalized certainty. The stronger formulation attracts attention; the economist’s qualified formulation carries the actual analytical weight.

Power sits in the exemption

Trump holds the institutional power at issue. Congress can write tax and spending law, but the presidency controls major parts of trade policy and the administration’s enforcement machinery. According to Wolfers, Trump’s shifting tariffs and ability to grant exceptions give the White House leverage over companies, industries, and trading partners.

That is not a free market. It is discretionary government power presented under the branding of economic nationalism. When corporate success may depend on access, flattery, or an exemption, executives have an incentive to cultivate the president rather than improve products. Wolfers uses Apple CEO Tim Cook as his illustration, though the interview does not establish that Apple displaced any specific innovation project with political lobbying. The broader incentive structure is the stronger point.

Redistribution is a decision

Tax cuts for wealthy people and reductions in programs serving people with fewer resources do not simply “happen” to produce inequality. Legislators pass them, presidents sign them, and administrations implement them. Calling the result an economic transformation can obscure the chain of agency.

Wolfers describes the legislation as an “anti-Robin Hood” measure because it combines benefits concentrated among the wealthy with large spending cuts affecting poorer Americans. If that distribution is accurate, the inequality is not an accidental side effect. It is embedded in who receives public support and who is required to absorb the losses.

The interview’s weakness is evidentiary: it asserts historic scale without showing the figures. “No one has disproved me” is not a substitute for presenting the calculation. A forceful indictment still needs the receipts.

Incompetence is not the whole story

Wolfers criticizes the administration’s weak preparation and constantly changing tariff policy. That may explain some damaging execution, but “incompetence” can also misdirect attention from the people exercising power. An unpredictable system may be economically irrational while remaining politically useful to the official who controls relief from it.

The reporting supports the existence of volatility and presidential discretion. It does not establish the motive behind every change or exemption. But the foreseeable consequence is clear: uncertainty punishes businesses without privileged access and increases the value of proximity to the White House. Whatever the intent, concentrated discretion creates fertile ground for crony capitalism.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of economic policy from general rules into personalized permission. Tariffs, exemptions, tax advantages, and spending cuts determine who pays, who receives protection, and who must petition the government for relief. The governing question shifts from whether an enterprise serves the public efficiently to whether it can satisfy the official controlling the gate.

That is how institutional damage suppresses prosperity without producing an immediate statistical crater. The public sees an economy still operating; favored actors learn where power has moved. By the time lost competition and foregone investment become visible, the political hierarchy that caused them may already have hardened into the economic order.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump is stopping you from getting richer: A renowned economist explains

item.title: GOP insiders warn Trump going to snap and chase revenge: ex-staffer
item.description:
President Donald Trump looks on as he exits Air Force One on his arrival at Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, January 31, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

AlterNet reports that former Trump administration official Miles Taylor predicts President Donald Trump will respond to expected Republican losses in the November midterms by pursuing revenge and creating political turmoil. The election has not happened, and the article provides no result; “Trump going to snap” is Taylor’s forecast, not an established event.

Taylor cited former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, who said Trump does not care whether Republicans retain Congress and could use defeat to portray himself as a victim. Reporters Brian Karem and Jim Acosta likewise predicted increasingly erratic conduct, attributing the danger partly to aides unwilling to restrain him.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet also relayed Grisham’s allegation that taxpayer-funded advertisements promoted Trump rather than Republican candidates and did so in defiance of federal law. The article does not identify the statute, document an official finding, or report Trump’s response, so the claimed illegality remains unsubstantiated within the supplied reporting.

The forecast is not the fact

The story’s central weakness is grammatical as much as evidentiary: speculation repeatedly hardens into apparent certainty. Republican defeat is presumed. Trump’s reaction is foretold. Motive is assigned through former officials and journalists who know his conduct but cannot know an election result or presidential response that has not occurred.

Their warnings may be informed. They are still warnings. AlterNet should distinguish documented preparation from predictions based on temperament. The article identifies no revenge order, operational plan, target list, or specific post-election action. “Havoc” and “pure hell” convey alarm without defining what institutions or people would face what conduct.

Power sits in the presidency

The meaningful issue is not whether Trump might become emotionally unstable. He holds presidential authority. A hostile Congress could constrain legislation and conduct oversight, but it would not erase executive control over agencies, appointments, enforcement priorities, public communications, or the machinery available to punish perceived enemies.

That is why staff resistance matters. Acosta’s allegation that aides placate Trump instead of challenging him describes institutional surrender, not merely a difficult workplace. Presidential power becomes more dangerous when advisers treat obedience as their job and restraint as somebody else’s responsibility.

Republicans enabled this dependency

Grisham’s account portrays Republican candidates as weaker actors tethered to a leader who may value personal grievance above their electoral survival. But the party is not an innocent bystander. It invested authority in Trump, organized itself around his image, and left its candidates dependent on his attention.

If he promotes himself with resources that could assist them, the problem is larger than personal vanity. It exposes a party structure in which collective goals remain subordinate to one officeholder’s political brand. Trump has agency over that choice; Republican officials have agency over the arrangement that makes it decisive.

Psychology obscures accountability

Words such as “snap,” “unhinged,” and “spoiled brat” personalize what is fundamentally an institutional question. They invite readers to watch Trump’s mood when they should watch decisions: who receives orders, who executes them, who supplies legal rationales, and who refuses oversight.

This framing also gives future enablers an alibi. If harmful conduct is presented as an eruption of temperament, officials can later describe themselves as witnesses to chaos rather than participants who carried out identifiable acts. Volatility may explain behavior. It does not dissolve responsibility.

The system rewards anticipatory obedience

The larger pattern is a presidency organized around personal loyalty, surrounded—according to the people quoted—by officials unlikely to impose meaningful resistance. The decisive danger in that structure is not one predicted outburst after one hypothetical defeat. It is the number of empowered people prepared to convert grievance into government action.

AlterNet’s reporting points toward that structure but retreats into dramatic prophecy. The sharper story is already visible: concentrated executive power, a party dependent on one leader, and aides accused of choosing accommodation over restraint. Elections may change the pressure on that system. They do not determine whether its officials possess agency.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: GOP insiders warn Trump going to snap and chase revenge: ex-staffer

item.title: 'MAGA cult' dying as Trump 'superfans' call for impeachment
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media aboard Air Force One, en route to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S., following a two-day visit to Ireland, September 13, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

What happened

AlterNet reports that several prominent Trump loyalists have broken with President Donald Trump over his war with Iran, economic turmoil, and his administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein. Former rally regular Trisha Hope told Politico that if Republicans lose the November midterms and Trump is impeached again, she would support that impeachment in Congress.

Another former “Front Row Joe,” Rick Frazier, cited the Epstein crimes and support for the military-industrial complex in leaving the movement. Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in 2024, also criticized Trump’s supporters and said Trump had not delivered as he expected on “draining the swamp.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The electoral consequences remain uncertain. AlterNet cites a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll finding that 45 percent of voters identified voting against Trump as their largest midterm motivation, while relaying the Guardian’s assessment that Democrats could retake the House and flip the Senate. Neither defections by several high-profile supporters nor one poll establishes that the broader MAGA coalition is collapsing.

The power is still in the White House

The former superfans have voices, audiences, and symbolic value. They do not command the military, control executive records, or determine what the administration discloses. Trump does.

That distinction matters because the “MAGA cult” framing makes supporter disillusionment the main event. It is politically interesting, but institutionally secondary. The consequential story is what a president did with state power—and whether Congress will constrain him—not whether rally regulars finally became disappointed customers.

Loyalty met its limits

Hope and Frazier did not abandon Trump over an abstract dispute about tone. According to the reporting, they identified war and the handling of Epstein-related records as breaking points. Rogan’s complaint was similarly tied to failed expectations about entrenched power.

Their reversals expose the transactional core beneath claims of unconditional loyalty. Trump’s appeal promised that concentrated personal authority would be used against corrupt institutions and foreign entanglements. When supporters perceive that authority serving those same systems, the contradiction becomes harder to package as strategy.

But belated recognition is not accountability. These supporters helped build the political permission structure around Trump. Their defections may weaken it; they do not erase their role in sustaining it.

Impeachment is not a fan referendum

Hope’s willingness to walk congressional halls in support of impeachment is a striking reversal, not an impeachment proceeding. Congress holds that power. A House majority must approve articles of impeachment, and the Senate determines whether to convict and remove.

The article’s emphasis on superfans risks turning constitutional accountability into another measure of movement mood. Legislators do not need permission from former rally loyalists to investigate presidential conduct. If evidence warrants action, congressional hesitation remains Congress’s decision.

“Crumbling” outruns the evidence

The reporting establishes visible defections and substantial anti-Trump motivation among surveyed voters. It does not establish that MAGA is dying, that Democrats will win either chamber, or that Trump would be impeached after a Republican midterm defeat.

Calling a movement a cult may describe its leader worship, but declaring the cult dead because several adherents walked away is premature. Personality-driven movements can survive disappointment by redirecting blame, inventing betrayal narratives, or narrowing the definition of a true believer.

The sharper conclusion is less comforting: Trump’s coalition is showing fractures, while the machinery that gave him presidential power remains intact.

The system waits for permission

This story reveals a recurring failure in American politics: institutions often treat elite or voter disillusionment as the prerequisite for exercising powers they already possess. Congress watches polls. Influencers revise their brands. Loyalists announce that the latest breach has finally crossed their personal line.

Meanwhile, presidential decisions produce consequences regardless of whether the fan base applauds. The meaningful test is not whether MAGA celebrities feel betrayed. It is whether institutions with actual authority investigate, disclose, legislate, and impose consequences—or continue outsourcing responsibility to the mood of the crowd.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘MAGA cult’ dying as Trump ‘superfans’ call for impeachment

item.title: Late-night report sends Trump into a social media death spiral
item.description:
REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used Truth Social to deny an Axios report that his administration was open to easing sanctions and unlocking frozen Iranian assets if Tehran took concrete steps concerning its nuclear program. Axios attributed that account to anonymous U.S. officials; Trump called it fabricated, demanded a retraction, and said he had offered Iran nothing.

The denial followed Trump’s public rejection of an Iranian peace proposal three days earlier and came amid a broader stream of attacks on news outlets and public figures, including MS NOW and Bill Maher. AlterNet also places the episode within a larger dispute over White House access: Trump had attempted to exclude journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico before a federal judge temporarily restored their credentials.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Major networks—including NBC, ABC, CBS, and Fox News—then suspended participation in the White House television pool in solidarity with the targeted outlets. AlterNet says that response reduced network carriage of Trump’s formal appearances, though the article supplies no audience data measuring the effect.

The power is in the presidency

Axios may publish anonymous claims, and television networks may decide what to broadcast. Neither possesses the coercive authority at the center of this story. Trump does.

The president controls the executive branch, directs foreign policy, influences sanctions policy, and oversees an administration that regulates journalists’ physical access to the White House. That disparity matters. A presidential demand that a publication retract an unfavorable report is not merely another participant objecting to coverage; it comes from an office capable of withholding access and imposing institutional costs.

A denial is not a refutation

Trump’s categorical denial creates a factual conflict with Axios’s anonymously sourced account. The reporting provided here does not resolve that conflict, and AlterNet cannot convert Axios’s unnamed officials into independent proof simply by repeating them.

But Trump’s response also does not disprove the report. Calling journalism a “hoax” and invoking “Trump Derangement Syndrome” replaces evidence with delegitimization. It directs attention away from the substantive question—what terms the administration was considering with Iran—and toward the president’s preferred question: whether hostile media should be treated as inherently fraudulent.

Access became leverage

The clearest exercise of power was not the posting spree. It was the attempt to remove journalists from White House grounds. According to AlterNet, a federal judge temporarily reversed that action, while major networks answered by withdrawing from pool duties.

That sequence reveals the institutional stakes beneath the spectacle. The administration allegedly used access rules against disfavored outlets; the court imposed a temporary constraint; news organizations used their collective distribution power in response. Trump’s suggestion that the Brady briefing room could become a swimming pool may sound absurd, but it also trivializes the press infrastructure his office was trying to control.

The framing mistakes fury for the story

AlterNet’s “death spiral” framing turns an institutional conflict into a personality show. The volume of Trump’s posts may be vivid, but agitation is not the politically important fact. Presidential power does not diminish because its holder communicates erratically.

This fixation can become its own misdirection. It encourages readers to study Trump’s temperament while the administration contests which journalists may enter government space and which accounts of foreign policy receive legitimacy. The weaker actors here are individual reporters whose access can be revoked. Treating the episode chiefly as a meltdown makes the powerful man the spectacle and the exercise of power the subplot.

The systemic error

The recurring pattern is governance through antagonism: unfavorable reporting is branded pathological, access becomes a pressure point, and the resulting fight is packaged as entertainment. Institutions then respond with the tools available to them—litigation, solidarity, and control over distribution.

Those responses may impose costs, but they do not erase the underlying imbalance. A press corps can decline to carry a president’s remarks; it cannot set sanctions policy or command the executive branch. Political coverage fails when it counts insults and diagnoses moods instead of tracing authority. The consequential question is not how angry the president appeared. It is how presidential power was used, who constrained it, and what remains possible when attention moves on.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Late-night report sends Trump into a social media death spiral

item.title: GOP senator silenced as he sneers at Jack Smith: 'You make me want to throw up’
item.description:
Jack Smith, former special counsel at the Justice Department, arrives to testify before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing at Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., US, September 29, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. Dick Durbin cut off Sen. John Kennedy during a Tuesday hearing after Kennedy repeatedly interrupted former special prosecutor Jack Smith and told him, “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.”

Kennedy alleged that President Biden or White House staff had directed Attorney General Merrick Garland to prosecute Donald Trump. Smith said he had no knowledge of that and tried to explain his role, but Kennedy interrupted him with questions about the tooth fairy and Easter Bunny. Durbin intervened, calling the hearing constitutionally and historically important and insisting that Smith be allowed to finish his answers.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power behind the performance

Kennedy was not a powerless critic confronting an official who could ignore him. He was a senator using the authority and visibility of a congressional hearing to accuse, interrupt, and demean a witness.

Durbin also held institutional power within the proceeding, and he exercised it by stopping the barrage and enforcing the basic condition required for testimony: the witness must be permitted to answer. That intervention matters because hearing rules are meaningless when those empowered to enforce them choose spectacle over evidence.

An allegation without support

Kennedy’s central insinuation was that Biden or his staff ordered Garland to prosecute Trump. The reporting provides no evidence for that assertion, and Smith explicitly said he did not know whether it was true.

Instead of developing the claim through documents, testimony, or a coherent chain of responsibility, Kennedy smothered Smith’s response with ridicule. The childish questions were not evidence. They were a device for making an unsupported premise feel established by preventing the witness from contesting it in complete sentences.

Contempt as misdirection

The sneer at Smith supplied the emotional conclusion that Kennedy’s questioning had failed to prove. Disgust replaced substantiation; interruption replaced examination.

This is how a hearing can be converted from an instrument of oversight into a propaganda stage. The senator’s conduct becomes the event, while the unsupported allegation lingers beneath it. RawStory’s framing emphasizes that Kennedy was “silenced,” but Durbin did not suppress an evidentiary argument described in the report. He stopped a powerful official from denying a witness the ability to answer.

The institutional test

Durbin’s intervention was necessary, but it also exposed how little separates formal accountability from televised abuse: one presiding official’s willingness to enforce procedure.

The larger pattern is congressional power used to manufacture suspicion rather than establish facts. An accusation is announced, the answer is obstructed, and humiliation fills the resulting void. When institutions tolerate that method, hearings cease to clarify responsibility. They become machinery for laundering insinuation into political belief.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senator silenced as he sneers at Jack Smith: ‘You make me want to throw up’

item.title: 'My God': Karoline Leavitt shamed after major math goof blows up 'lunatic' attack
item.description:
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, U.S., September 10, 2026. REUTERS/Callaghan O’Hare

What happened

RawStory reports that former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Fox News host Sean Hannity on Monday night that Democratic candidates “do 360s” on policy after campaigning as moderates. Her intended accusation was apparently that they reverse course, but a 360-degree turn ends where it began; a 180-degree turn describes a reversal.

The headline’s “My God” refers to former math teacher Hemant Mehta’s reaction on X. Other commentators also mocked Leavitt’s mistake, while Czech journalist Vojtěch Gibiš cited earlier remarks in which she used percentages in ways he portrayed as mathematically incoherent.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The report does not examine which Democratic candidates Leavitt meant, what policies supposedly changed, or whether her underlying accusation was accurate.

The power behind the mistake

Leavitt was not making an idle geometrical error in private. A former White House spokesperson was appearing on one of the country’s most influential conservative television programs to characterize an entire party’s candidates as dishonest extremists.

Her institutional power came from access: a national platform, the authority conferred by a former senior government role, and a sympathetic venue for delivering a sweeping partisan charge. Hannity’s audience received the accusation without the report identifying any evidence offered for it.

The insult was the point

The wrong number was embarrassing, but it was not the politically important part of the sentence. Leavitt moved from an unsupported generalization about campaigning to calling elected Democrats “radical extreme liberal lunatics.” That language does not clarify a policy dispute. It reduces political opponents to a contemptible category.

Whether the phrase was careless or calculated cannot be established from the report. Its function is nevertheless visible: it replaces names, decisions, and evidence with mass denunciation. No reader can test a claim broad enough to cover “every single policy position.”

A correction that evades the claim

RawStory’s framing turns the episode into a math dunk. Critics get to call Leavitt an idiot; Leavitt’s substantive allegation escapes serious examination.

That is misdirection of a different kind. The weaker target is her vocabulary, not the propaganda technique embedded in the remark. Correcting 360 to 180 would make the sentence geometrically coherent while leaving it politically vacant. Which candidates changed which positions? When? What did they campaign on, and how did they govern? The article supplies none of that.

Accountability reduced to ridicule

Mockery can puncture manufactured authority, especially when a professional communicator repeatedly mangles elementary percentages or directions. But ridicule is not accountability. It can even flatter the political operator by recasting a baseless attack as nothing more than a funny verbal stumble.

The consequence is a familiar media transaction: Fox supplies the accusation, social media supplies the jeering, and an aggregation outlet packages the collision. The public gets spectacle while the original claim remains neither demonstrated nor dismantled.

The systemic error

Political coverage often treats the most clickable defect as the most consequential one. Here, the arithmetic error is vivid; the unsubstantiated collective smear is routine. That hierarchy rewards the very tactic Leavitt used.

The larger pattern is an information system better equipped to adjudicate a turn of phrase than a deployment of power. A former government spokesperson can use national television to substitute contempt for evidence, and the corrective press may answer with a punchline. The math gets checked. The politics does not.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘My God’: Karoline Leavitt shamed after major math goof blows up ‘lunatic’ attack

item.title: 'It's his fault': GOP operatives in frenzy as calamity forces Trump to deep red states
item.description:
US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after exiting Air Force One as he returns from Medinah, Illinois, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory, citing Politico, reports that President Donald Trump was scheduled to campaign in heavily Republican states because GOP candidates there were struggling. The reported itinerary included Alabama, Oklahoma and Ohio, while Republican concern was especially acute in Alaska, where incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan trailed Democrat Mary Peltola by roughly eight points in a nonpartisan primary.

Republican operatives blamed Trump’s political liabilities, including the reported effects of his trade war and the Iran war on farmers and rural voters. One operative called Trump “the biggest culprit” and said plainly: “It’s his fault.” A former Trump official tied the expanding battlefield to 18 months of poor economic developments.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Vice President JD Vance was also campaigning in states Republicans would ordinarily expect to hold, including Texas, Florida, Kansas and Iowa. The result, according to the operatives quoted, was a party forced to defend an unusually broad map despite a cash advantage and a House map shaped by gerrymandering.

Trump built the liability

The central fact is not that Trump must visit red states. It is why Republican professionals reportedly believe those visits are necessary: decisions made by his administration have imposed political costs on the constituencies most essential to Republican power.

Farmers and rural voters are not weather systems. If they are reacting against trade and war policies, their discontent follows decisions made by the president and his administration. Describing the resulting electoral damage as “fires everywhere” turns accountable governance into a natural disaster. The operative who said “It’s his fault” supplied the cleaner analysis.

The party’s defenses are failing

Republicans entered these contests with structural protection. The article cites both a substantial financial advantage and a gerrymandered House map. Those are not incidental campaign assets. They are mechanisms of institutional power designed to make Republican control more resilient than public sentiment alone would permit.

Yet party officials reportedly fear those advantages may not be sufficient. That does not prove Democrats will win either chamber, and primary results do not settle a general election. It does show the scale of Republican anxiety: states Trump won comfortably in 2024 are consuming resources that could otherwise be directed toward competitive territory.

A rescue tour cannot repair policy

Trump and Vance can mobilize loyal voters, but campaign appearances cannot erase the material effects Republicans themselves attribute to administration policy. Sending the president to Alaska or the vice president to Kansas may improve turnout. It does not reverse economic damage or make an unimpressive nominee compelling.

There is also an obvious contradiction in deploying Trump as the remedy for weakness that Republican operatives blame on Trump. His hold over the party makes him its most valuable turnout instrument and, according to the reporting, its principal electoral burden. Republican candidates remain dependent on the same political figure they cannot safely separate from.

Panic is not accountability

The anonymous quotations reveal fear of losing power, not a reconsideration of how that power was used. The complaints center on the expanding map, strained campaign schedules and dwindling opportunities to attack Democrats elsewhere. The harm matters inside this account because it may cost Republicans seats.

That is the deeper institutional failure. Party operatives can identify the decision-maker when electoral consequences arrive, but the machinery around him apparently offered no effective restraint when the decisions were being made. Their candor comes late and mostly without names.

The cost of personal rule

A party organized around one leader eventually inherits his liabilities along with his voters. Candidate quality, local conditions and election mechanics still matter, but the structure described here leaves Republicans with little room to maneuver: Trump defines the agenda, produces the backlash and then becomes the indispensable figure sent to contain it.

The broader pattern is a governing coalition treating policy consequences as a campaign-management problem. When power is centralized and internal dissent is weak, correction comes only after voters impose costs. By then, the party is not governing differently. It is dispatching its leaders across supposedly safe territory to defend what their own decisions put at risk.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘It’s his fault’: GOP operatives in frenzy as calamity forces Trump to deep red states

item.title: Natalie Harp's first devotion wasn't Trump — it was a hellfire pastor who helped him win
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive assistant Natalie Harp listens as Trump speaks during a meeting with travel executives in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

RawStory reports that Natalie Harp, now a close White House aide to President Donald Trump, began attending megachurch pastor David Jeremiah’s sermons around age 13. Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, described Jeremiah’s church as wealthy, Republican-financed and doctrinally rigid. The reporting establishes her long exposure to Jeremiah’s ministry, but it does not establish that he personally caused her later devotion to Trump.

The article also examines Jeremiah’s role in a June 21, 2016 meeting between Trump and roughly 1,000 pastors in New York City. Religion professor J. Derrick Lemons argues that vetted questions—including Jeremiah’s question about Israel—helped evangelical leaders reconcile Trump’s personal history with their political objectives and then sell his candidacy to their congregations.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory further recounts a former ministry executive’s allegation that Turning Point bought about $250,000 of Jeremiah’s books to boost bestseller rankings. The former executive called the practice deceptive and unethical; Jeremiah defended marketing his books without confirming or denying the specific allegation.

The power was in the pulpit

Harp is the article’s connective tissue, but Jeremiah and the assembled evangelical leaders held the relevant institutional power. They controlled churches, media platforms, schools and trusted religious networks capable of reaching millions. Trump’s campaign possessed electoral ambition; these pastors possessed access to a bloc of voters he needed.

The 2016 meeting mattered because it offered something more valuable than a formal endorsement: moral clearance. According to Lemons, the questions were vetted by Trump, and the obvious conflicts between his biography and the pastors’ professed standards were excluded. The pastors were not hapless believers confused by an unconventional candidate. They participated in a controlled presentation that made support for him easier to justify.

The decision was accommodation

Jeremiah had agency. He reportedly joined a meeting structured to protect Trump from difficult questions and asked one that allowed the candidate to give an uncomplicated assurance of support for Israel. Whatever Jeremiah’s later discomfort with Trump, that does not erase his role at the moment when evangelical hesitation carried political leverage.

The key choice was not whether pastors loved every aspect of Trump. It was whether they would apply their stated moral standards when doing so imposed a political cost. The account presented here indicates that influential pastors instead helped convert a liability into permission.

Harp is not the institution

The article’s emphasis on Harp’s adolescent religious formation risks shrinking a political operation into a personality profile. Her conduct around Trump—carrying his printouts, writing effusive letters and remaining constantly near him—is striking. But her proximity is not the source of the machinery described in the story.

Focusing on one unusually devoted aide can misdirect attention from the institutions that trained audiences to accept obedience as conviction. Harp did not convene the pastors, vet their questions or command a media ministry earning a reported $65 million to $100 million annually. The powerful actors were the men with pulpits, money, broadcasting reach and electoral access.

Marketing dressed as discernment

Lemons compared the pastors’ operation to multilevel marketing: influential leaders accepted the product, then promoted it through their own networks. That description exposes the political mechanism. Authority flowed downward while accountability disappeared upward. Congregants heard reassurance from trusted pastors; the candidate received support without submitting to the scrutiny those pastors could have imposed.

The book-buying allegation points to a parallel structure, though it remains an allegation attributed to former chief financial officer George Hale. In both accounts, reputation is not merely earned in public view; it is manufactured through institutions capable of making popularity appear organic. Bestseller status creates authority. Pastoral approval creates legitimacy. Scale then disguises the decisions that produced it.

The system rewards the conversion brokers

The broader pattern is not that religious voters were duped by a single sermon or that Harp’s childhood church mechanically determined her politics. The evidence does not support either claim. It shows something more concrete: political candidates can overcome moral liabilities when institutional gatekeepers recast compromise as principle and distribute that permission through trusted networks.

That is the systemic error. Coverage becomes fascinated with the conspicuous devotee while the brokers of legitimacy recede into the background. Harp may embody the result, but the consequential power belonged to the institutions that made political submission marketable as religious judgment.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Natalie Harp’s first devotion wasn’t Trump — it was a hellfire pastor who helped him win
