item.title: Sarah Sanders incenses right-wing as welfare attack ad backfires: 'Hating young white men’
item.description:
Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, US Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr Mehmet Oz stand behind US President Donald J. Trump as he makes an announcement on healthcare in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 18, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

What happened

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders promoted what she called a “welfare-to-work requirement” in a September 28, 2026 campaign video depicting “Brad,” a fictional young white man, as an idle benefits recipient. Sanders said young, healthy people receiving government assistance should work, attend school, or volunteer. RawStory did not provide the policy’s legal details, the programs affected, or evidence that people matching the ad’s caricature constitute a significant share of recipients.

The ad angered several right-wing commentators—not because it stigmatized people who need assistance, but because its designated freeloader was white. The Daily Wire’s Matt Walsh said a stereotypically Black female character would be more “accurate.” Others called the video anti-white or accused Republicans of “hating young white men.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

BlazeTV host Auron MacIntyre wrote that young white men might seek “none-political” solutions that others “really won’t like.” RawStory described the remark as appearing to suggest possible violence; the wording is ominous but ambiguous and should not be strengthened into an explicit threat.

The governor holds the power

Sanders is the actor with institutional authority. She announced the requirement, attached the governor’s office to it, and used a campaign-style advertisement to define who supposedly deserves public help. “Brad” has no agency because he does not exist. Actual assistance recipients were given no voice in RawStory’s account.

That distinction matters. The backlash is a dispute among influential conservatives over the preferred racial target of welfare resentment. It does not change who can alter eligibility rules or impose new administrative burdens. Sanders can wield state power; the commentators can pressure her over how that power is marketed.

A stereotype built to carry policy

The advertisement substitutes a snack-covered gamer for a documented explanation of the policy. It tells taxpayers that their money supports people who “choose not to work,” but the reporting supplies no data establishing the scale of that conduct, the affected benefits, or the barriers facing recipients.

That is political misdirection by design, whatever Sanders’s private motive may be. A fictional loafer turns questions about eligibility standards, enforcement and access into disgust toward an invented individual. The government’s decision disappears behind a morality play about personal failure.

The backlash exposes the bargain

Walsh’s complaint makes the underlying politics unusually plain. He did not reject racialized welfare propaganda; he objected that Sanders assigned the villain’s role to the wrong race. His proposed substitute relied openly on a stereotype of a Black woman.

Partridge, Fishback and MacIntyre likewise shifted attention away from the governor’s use of benefits policy and toward the supposed victimization of white men. Their grievance was representational: state-backed contempt was acceptable, but its target required protection. The weaker actor—an imagined recipient—became the battlefield on which competing factions negotiated who may be publicly humiliated.

Cruelty with a casting dispute

RawStory frames the episode chiefly as an advertisement that “backfired.” That captures the intramural outrage but understates the political structure. The central event is not that conservative influencers became angry. It is that a governor promoted an eligibility restriction through an unsupported caricature of welfare recipients, followed by critics demanding a more explicitly racial scapegoat.

This is a recurring machinery of punitive politics: officials present reduced access or added conditions as discipline for an undeserving figure, while media allies argue over the figure’s identity. The policy escapes scrutiny because the spectacle consumes the discussion.

The system needs a disposable villain

The larger pattern is not ideological confusion. It is a hierarchy of deservingness enforced through government and sold through stigma. Sanders’s ad divides workers from recipients; her critics attempt to redraw that division along racial and gender lines.

Either way, people with the least institutional power are made responsible for decisions taken above them. The governor supplies the rule. Influencers police the scapegoat. The fictional villain absorbs the anger. And the material question—who loses assistance, under what conditions, and with what consequences—remains unanswered.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Sarah Sanders incenses right-wing as welfare attack ad backfires: ‘Hating young white men’

item.title: This mystery has MAGA women punching themselves hard in the face
item.description:
A “MAGA Mom” hat lies on the ground as Kristi Noem testifies before a House committee. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

What happened

RawStory’s column argues that the supposed “mystery” is why some women embrace MAGA politics and “trad wife” ideology despite the restrictions those movements may impose on women. But the piece never establishes an answer. Its author points to conservative religious upbringing, patriarchal expectations and group conformity, while openly acknowledging that she does not understand these women’s choices.

The column contrasts politically vocal liberal Gen X women with younger conservative influencers. Its main example is Julia Kate, identified only by that name, who reportedly argued in a Jubilee Media debate that women should marry young and have at least 10 children. RawStory provides no broader evidence showing how common those views are among Republican women or trad-wife influencers.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power is not an aesthetic

The article’s strongest underlying point is obscured by its fixation on generational personas. Gray hair, tattoos, prairie dresses and social-media cadence do not determine who holds institutional power. Legislatures, courts, executives, parties and well-funded political organizations do.

Women who promote submission or prolific childbearing may help market a political program, but they do not necessarily control it. The consequential decisions are made by officials who write laws, judges who interpret them, donors who finance campaigns and party organizations that turn religious doctrine into public policy. Treating an influencer as the central antagonist mistakes a salesperson for the governing apparatus.

The punching metaphor misdirects blame

Describing Republican women as punching themselves in the face reduces politics to individual irrationality. Some voters may support policies that ultimately constrain them, but that observation does not explain how political power manufactures consent, rewards conformity or narrows the choices available.

It also shifts attention downward. Mocking women for accepting subordination is easier than examining the institutions that benefit from their compliance. The women repeating the message have agency and deserve scrutiny. But the men and organizations capable of converting that message into law possess greater power and therefore greater responsibility.

Speculation is not an explanation

RawStory attributes conservative women’s views largely to Christian patriarchy and “cult-like” socialization. That may be the author’s interpretation, but the article supplies no interviews, research or evidence establishing why the women in question hold their beliefs. It does not examine material incentives, community status, media ecosystems, partisan identity or the authority structures surrounding them.

That evidentiary gap matters. Declaring that conservative women cannot think for themselves reproduces a familiar paternalism: women’s political choices count as authentic when they are approved and as brainwashing when they are not. A serious critique can condemn an ideology of female submission without erasing the agency of women who promote it.

Ragebait is not reporting

The column identifies Jubilee Media as a producer of ragebait, then adopts the same economy of attention. Julia Kate’s voice, facial expression and clothing receive more scrutiny than any institution capable of enforcing the politics she advocates. The spectacle supplies a villain who is easy to ridicule and difficult to place in any meaningful hierarchy of power.

RawStory’s framing is therefore weaker than its subject. It gestures toward reproductive autonomy and political equality, but offers no specific policy decision, legislative action or measurable consequence. The result is cultural combat presented as structural analysis.

The system prefers a caricature

The larger pattern is not simply that some women support a movement hostile to feminist goals. It is that political media repeatedly substitutes conspicuous minor figures for the officials, funders and institutions with actual authority. A viral influencer becomes the face of a system she did not build and may not control.

That substitution protects power. Readers are invited to despise a woman on camera while the machinery of governance recedes from view. The useful question is not why a stranger online appears eager to surrender her autonomy. It is who gains enforceable authority from that message, who supplies the money and law behind it, and who bears the consequences when private doctrine becomes public rule.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: This mystery has MAGA women punching themselves hard in the face

item.title: 'This is what you like!' Fury after Sean Hannity backpedals defense of Jack Smith attack
item.description:
Television presenter Sean Hannity speaks during the funeral service for late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC) at Washington National Cathedral in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 28, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

What happened

RawStory reports that Fox News host Sean Hannity deleted an X post praising Sen. Eric Schmitt for putting former special counsel Jack Smith “on the spot” during a Tuesday hearing. Schmitt had suggested that Smith attended a professional basketball game in Atlanta and somehow coordinated with former Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis over her prosecution of Donald Trump.

Later in the hearing, Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar said Smith had instead attended a women’s college basketball game in Maryland against the University of Iowa that night. Hannity removed his post after fuller footage circulated, but he did not publicly acknowledge the error in the material RawStory describes. Commentator Brian Beutler preserved a screenshot and criticized Hannity and Schmitt; other journalists likewise mocked the unsupported “gotcha.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The accusation came from power

Schmitt was not a spectator repeating stray internet gossip. He was a United States senator using a formal hearing to advance an allegation against a former federal prosecutor. That office supplies a microphone, an audience and the appearance of investigative legitimacy.

The exchange described by RawStory offers no evidence connecting Smith to Willis. The reported correction instead directly contradicts the premise that placed him in Atlanta. An insinuation delivered from a Senate dais does not become substantial merely because a senator phrases it as a question.

Hannity amplified, then erased

Hannity exercised a different kind of institutional power: the ability to package a senator’s insinuation for a large partisan audience. His caption supplied the desired interpretation before viewers encountered the underlying facts. Schmitt had supposedly cornered Smith; the clip was presented as the proof.

Deleting the post limited further exposure, but deletion without a visible correction leaves the original propaganda mechanism intact. The audience receives the accusation with fanfare and the collapse, if it notices at all, through critics elsewhere. RawStory’s account does not establish why Hannity declined to explain the deletion. It does establish the asymmetry: promotion was public; accountability was absent.

The correction is not the scandal’s whole shape

The easy version of this story is that Hannity and Schmitt embarrassed themselves. That framing is satisfying and insufficient. It turns an abuse of institutional attention into a failed performance.

The consequential act was not getting a sports venue wrong. It was using that false premise to suggest improper coordination in prosecutions involving Trump. The location claim mattered because it was the bridge to the insinuation. Once that bridge collapsed, so did the reported basis for the attack.

Misdirection as method

The target of scrutiny was made to answer an allegation whose factual premise, according to the later exchange, was false. Meanwhile, the officials and media figures spreading it faced no comparable burden before publication or amplification.

RawStory centers the fury after Hannity’s deletion, but online outrage is secondary. The power lies with the senator who can manufacture suspicion under the authority of a hearing and the broadcaster who can circulate the most useful fragment. Critics can document the maneuver; they cannot give the correction the same reach or institutional weight.

The durable system

This episode reveals a political-media system in which insinuation is cheap, correction is fragmented and reputational penalties are optional. A senator can convert a faulty claim into official spectacle. A television host can turn that spectacle into partisan content. When contrary facts emerge, the post can simply disappear.

That is not public accountability functioning imperfectly. It is an information structure that rewards the accusation at every stage and treats the correction as disposable cleanup. The error fades; the suspicion it was designed to plant remains.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘This is what you like!’ Fury after Sean Hannity backpedals defense of Jack Smith attack

item.title: Supreme Court hands Trump a major victory in stunning reversal
item.description:
U.S. Supreme Court justices pose for their group portrait at the Supreme Court in Washington, U.S., October 7, 2022. Seated (L-R): Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice John G. Roberts, Jr., Samuel A. Alito, Jr. and Elena Kagan. Standing (L-R): Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Ketanji Brown Jackson. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo

What happened

The Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration, for the time being, to resume rapidly deporting immigrants to countries other than their own. RawStory reported that the destinations could include Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Honduras and the Central African Republic, despite allegations of human rights abuses in some receiving countries.

Legal reporter Chris Geidner said the Court’s Democratic appointees dissented and that arguments in the case were scheduled for December. The New York Times specifically reported that deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea have faced police beatings. The supplied reporting does not explain the legal basis for the Court’s reversal or identify which people would be deported.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power belongs to the government

The immigrants targeted by this policy do not control the destination, the timetable or the machinery carrying them there. The Trump administration does. It chose to pursue third-country deportations, and the Supreme Court removed the immediate judicial obstacle to resuming them.

That division of power matters. Describing this chiefly as a “victory” turns government authority over human bodies into political scorekeeping. The concrete result is that the executive branch can again send people to countries that are not their own while the underlying litigation remains unresolved.

Permission before judgment

The Court did not need to settle the full case to change conditions on the ground. Its interim decision gave the administration operational freedom before the reported December arguments.

That sequence favors the institution capable of acting fastest and most coercively. Deportation is not an abstract legal position that can simply be restored if challengers later prevail. Once a person has been transported beyond the country’s jurisdiction, exposure to detention or abuse may be immediate and difficult to remedy.

The euphemism does political work

“Third-country deportation” sounds procedural. The policy described here is far more severe: the government may remove immigrants to nations other than their own, including a country where deportees reportedly have been beaten by police.

The framing risks converting foreseeable human consequences into background detail beneath the spectacle of Trump winning and the Court reversing course. Immigrants become objects moved through a contest between powerful institutions, while the people choosing the policy and authorizing its resumption remain insulated by legal terminology.

Accountability runs upward

Responsibility does not rest with the deportees, nor can it be dissolved into institutional confusion. The administration sought the authority to resume these removals. The Supreme Court granted temporary permission over dissent. Each institution exercised distinct power, and each decision produced a foreseeable consequence.

The reporting does not establish what administration officials intended beyond carrying out the policy, or how the Court’s majority justified its action. Those omissions limit any claim about motive. They do not obscure agency: officials asked to deport people to third countries, and the Court allowed them to proceed.

Coercion moves faster than review

This episode exposes a broader political pattern: executive action can become reality while courts postpone final judgment. Legal review then trails behind state power, even when the alleged risks include police violence abroad.

For those exercising authority, the case continues toward argument. For those subjected to that authority, the consequence may arrive first. A system that permits potentially irreversible punishment before resolving whether it is lawful does not merely manage uncertainty. It assigns the cost of that uncertainty to the people with the least power to survive it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Supreme Court hands Trump a major victory in stunning reversal

item.title: The fatal mistake that just blew up a decades-old Republican strategy
item.description:
REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

The “fatal mistake,” according to AlterNet, was one of timing: Republican officials backed policies and crises, then reversed themselves so quickly that voters could see the contradiction. The clearest example is Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who supported President Donald Trump’s war with Iran before releasing an advertisement urging Trump to end it as fuel prices rose.

AlterNet reports similar retreats by Republican House candidates Ashley Hinson, Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, while Representative Maria Elvira Salazar criticized the administration’s immigration enforcement. It also cites a New York Times/Siena poll in which 50 percent of registered voters trusted Democrats more than Republicans to handle foreign wars. The article argues that these episodes have exposed a decades-old strategy: enable damage, disown responsibility and campaign as the remedy.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The piece extends that argument to immigration panics, tax cuts, deregulation, union power, social spending and tariffs. Some of its most serious assertions—including that Republicans intentionally encouraged migration through “open border” rhetoric—are presented as the author’s interpretation, not independently established findings.

Power made the damage possible

The officials changing their language are not spectators. They possess votes, platforms and access to the president. Hinson had voted repeatedly to support the war before advertising her desire for a quick conclusion. Nunn and Miller-Meeks discovered limits on presidential war-making only after supporting the administration whose power they were supposed to constrain.

That distinction matters. A voter reacting to expensive gasoline has limited agency over a military campaign. A member of Congress can authorize, fund or restrict it. Treating both as people merely caught in an unfortunate situation launders the lawmaker’s decision through the public’s pain.

Rogers’s reversal is especially revealing because the policy did not change between endorsement and retreat; its political cost did. His advertisement asks voters to notice the consequence while forgetting his support for the choice that produced it.

Accountability becomes branding

The pattern AlterNet identifies is less “break government” than convert governing failure into campaign inventory. Republicans retain institutional power when authorizing war, cutting benefits or blocking legislation. Once consequences arrive, they reappear as critics of the conditions their power helped create.

That maneuver depends on separating verbs from nouns. Wars simply “drag on.” Prices “rise.” Border legislation “fails.” Benefits “disappear.” The grammatical fog erases who voted, who ordered, who blocked and who benefited.

The article is strongest when it restores those verbs. Trump wanted the bipartisan border bill stopped, the piece reports, because immigration remained electorally useful. Republican lawmakers then killed legislation they had demanded. Whatever one thinks of the bill, that sequence is not confusion. It is a political choice to preserve an issue rather than enact the proposed response.

The weaker actor gets the blame

Fear campaigns work by directing scrutiny downward. Migrants, benefit recipients and workers become the visible objects of resentment, while presidents, legislators, donors and corporate beneficiaries recede from view.

AlterNet’s claim that Republican “open border” language functioned as advertising for smugglers is an inference, and the article does not supply enough evidence to establish coordinated intent or measure its effect on migration. But it documents a long list of Republican officials repeatedly describing Democratic policy as an invitation. Politicians cannot broadcast that message for electoral advantage and then pretend their rhetoric exists only inside American television studios.

The same inversion appears in economic policy. The article says Republicans froze the federal minimum wage at $7.25 while campaigning on affordability, and cites Congressional Budget Office findings that their spending legislation shifted resources away from lower-income households while increasing them at the top. The people absorbing the loss are then offered as proof that government—not the officials allocating its benefits—is the problem.

The reversal exposes the machinery

Political hypocrisy is ordinary. What makes these reversals consequential is their speed and proximity to the original decisions. Voters do not need a forty-five-year ideological history when the endorsement and denial occupy the same election cycle.

That is why the Iran example carries more force than the article’s sweeping claims about every Republican strategy since Reagan. The causal chain is compact: officials supported presidential action, costs became politically dangerous, and some of those officials repositioned themselves as restraints on the president. The record is recent enough that branding struggles to overwrite it.

Even Marjorie Taylor Greene’s criticism of renewed caravan panic, as AlterNet describes it, punctures the performance from inside the political coalition that previously used it. The point is not that one former participant has become a reliable critic. It is that a familiar scare loses potency when its production process becomes visible.

The system rewards manufactured rescue

The larger pattern is government used twice: first to distribute risk and reward through war powers, tax policy, enforcement and social spending; then as a stage on which the officials responsible perform outrage at the results.

This strategy survives when coverage treats reversals as tactical moderation rather than evidence of prior agency. A politician who votes for an outcome and later objects to its consequences has not merely “shifted.” He is asking the public to sever policy from authorship.

The mistake AlterNet describes was allowing too little time for that severance. The promised rescuers were still holding the tools, the damage was still fresh, and their fingerprints had not yet faded.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The fatal mistake that just blew up a decades-old Republican strategy

item.title: 'We had been conned': Heartland voters are having a change of heart
item.description:
(REUTERS)

What happened

AlterNet published commentary by Ben Palen, a fifth-generation farmer and agriculture consultant, who says several farmers he spoke with recently—including some who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 and as early as 2016—now believe they “had been conned.” Palen describes their change of heart as a response to what they see as national moral decline, damaged international trust, reckless spending and threats to agricultural markets.

The piece does not identify the farmers, quantify how many changed their views or establish that Heartland voters broadly are shifting. It reports Palen’s conversations and interpretation, not polling or a documented regional trend. Its strongest supportable claim is narrower than the headline: some Trump-supporting farmers known to the author now regret their votes.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power is not a mood

The farmers may have changed their minds, but they did not hold the institutional power described here. The president and the people empowered to execute his agenda did. Voters granted authority; officeholders decided how to use it.

Palen correctly places responsibility on Trump and those aiding his administration, but offers few concrete policies, orders or legislative decisions by which readers can measure that responsibility. Condemnation without an institutional accounting leaves power strangely abstract: the country is “adrift,” trust has vanished and morality has collapsed, yet the machinery producing those outcomes remains mostly unnamed.

The headline outruns the evidence

“Heartland voters” is a sweeping political category. A number of private conversations cannot establish that this electorate is undergoing a durable realignment. The article supplies no sample, geography beyond Palen’s ties to Kansas and Colorado, or evidence showing how widespread the regret is.

That weakness matters because conversion stories are irresistible political content. They reassure opponents that consequences are finally changing minds while sparing publishers the harder work of demonstrating whether those changed minds are numerous enough to alter power. Anecdote can reveal disillusionment. It cannot measure it.

Regret does not erase agency

Calling voters “conned” captures their sense of betrayal, but it can also soften their responsibility. Trump was not an unknown candidate in 2024. According to Palen, some of these farmers had supported him repeatedly since 2016. Their present regret is politically relevant, but it does not turn years of voluntary support into something that merely happened to them.

The sharper question is not whether decent people can be deceived. They can. It is why warnings, prior conduct and foreseeable consequences failed to outweigh partisan loyalty or promised advantage. Without that examination, the language of victimhood becomes another form of misdirection—away from the choices that enabled those now exercising power.

Nostalgia is not an analysis

Palen contrasts the present with an earlier era when leaders supposedly operated, for the most part, under a moral code and bipartisan duty. His own list—wars, contempt for human life, racial and religious discrimination, fascism and money’s corruption of politics—undercuts that comforting history.

The Trump era may expose a harsher and more shameless exercise of power, but it did not invent institutional cruelty, elite impunity or political exclusion. Treating the past as morally intact obscures the systems that made the present possible. Bob Dole-era civility did not eliminate those systems; often, it gave them respectable manners.

The systemic error

The story’s real significance is not that a few farmers regret a vote. It is that American political coverage repeatedly mistakes personal revelation for structural change. Remorse becomes the plot, while the officials wielding state power, the allies enabling them and the institutions declining to restrain them receive less scrutiny.

A democracy cannot run on redemption narratives. Changed minds matter only when they become changed political behavior, organized opposition or institutional consequences. Until then, “we were conned” is an admission—not an accountability mechanism.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘We had been conned’: Heartland voters are having a change of heart

item.title: Jim Jordan 'will fail miserably': Legal expert wrecks GOP’s Jack Smith ploy
item.description:
Former Special Counsel Jack Smith raises his hand to swear in, before the House Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., January 22, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

CNN legal analyst and former federal prosecutor Ankush Khardori said Rep. Jim Jordan’s attempt to build a criminal case against former special counsel Jack Smith “will fail miserably.” According to AlterNet, Khardori said Smith truthfully answered questions about one method of obtaining communications; he was not asked to disclose that investigators had separately acquired White House communications from the National Archives.

AlterNet reports that Republicans accused Smith of concealing surveillance of GOP lawmakers after learning his investigation obtained call records involving Donald Trump and members of Congress. But the material at issue, Khardori said, was not taken from lawmakers or their devices. Smith, scheduled to testify again on Capitol Hill on a Tuesday the article does not date, maintained that he had testified truthfully and rejected threats of prosecution.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Khardori predicted that a case based on Jordan’s allegation might not survive a grand jury and, even if indicted, could be dismissed by a judge. Republican strategist Ashley Davis separately suggested that the dispute was personal and unlikely to command much attention from Republican voters.

The power belongs to the investigators of the investigator

Jordan holds congressional authority to convene hearings, issue demands and turn insinuation into televised spectacle. The Justice Department holds the far more consequential power to investigate and prosecute. Khardori said Attorney General Todd Blanche and the department appeared eager to investigate Smith.

Smith is no longer exercising the authority of special counsel in this account. He is the target of officials who can repeatedly summon him, scrutinize his testimony and threaten criminal exposure. Treating this as a balanced quarrel between two angry men would conceal the institutional asymmetry.

The accusation depends on collapsing distinctions

The Republican case described by AlterNet substitutes omission for perjury and White House records for surveillance of lawmakers. Those distinctions are not technical clutter. They are the substance of the allegation.

According to Khardori, Smith answered the question he was asked about a particular acquisition method. Republicans are angry that he did not volunteer information about a separate route through the National Archives. If that account is accurate, Jordan’s theory requires audiences to treat a truthful but narrower answer as a criminal lie.

The same distortion operates in the “spying” frame. Communications involving lawmakers are not automatically records seized from lawmakers. Presenting archived White House material as evidence that investigators targeted congressional devices redirects attention from what investigators obtained to the politically useful identity of some people appearing in it.

Oversight becomes retaliation theater

Congressional oversight can expose official abuse. Here, the evidence presented by AlterNet instead describes an effort to manufacture prosecutorial suspicion around Smith’s testimony, despite a former federal prosecutor’s assessment that the legal theory is exceptionally weak.

That weakness does not make the exercise harmless. A hearing can punish without producing a conviction. It consumes the target’s time, supplies partisan media with accusation-shaped content and warns other prosecutors that investigating a powerful political figure may bring years of personal exposure. The process itself becomes the sanction.

Smith’s decision to testify rather than invoke the Fifth Amendment does not prove every contested point. It does, however, undercut the image of a witness hiding from scrutiny. AlterNet says this would be his third congressional appearance.

The missing story is institutional choice

Khardori pointed to another matter the Senate Judiciary Committee might examine: a reported major hack involving FBI agents’ information. AlterNet provides no further details, so no broader conclusion about that incident is warranted. The comparison still identifies a question of priorities.

Committee attention is finite. Choosing to revisit a tenuous accusation against the prosecutor who pursued Trump is an exercise of power, not an accidental distraction. The spectacle tells the public which conduct receives relentless scrutiny and which problems can wait.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of oversight into protection for the politically powerful. Investigators examine a president; allied lawmakers then examine the investigators. Legal distinctions are blurred, archived records become “spying,” and an answer deemed truthful by a former prosecutor becomes the basis for threats of prosecution.

The immediate objective need not be a viable criminal case. Repetition can do the political work: discredit the investigation, burden its personnel and make future officials calculate the personal cost of acting against the party controlling Congress or the executive branch. An allegation that “will fail miserably” in court can still succeed as institutional intimidation.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Jim Jordan ‘will fail miserably’: Legal expert wrecks GOP’s Jack Smith ploy

item.title: Fox host declares Trump can’t fix his 'big problem' — and the GOP will pay
item.description:
US President Donald Trump attends National Design Studio launch event for America.gov, a new AI-powered government website, at the Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., US, September 29, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox Business host Stuart Varney identified President Donald Trump’s central political liability five weeks before the midterms: the war with Iran was raising energy costs and worsening an affordability problem the administration could not quickly repair. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said diesel prices were weighing on races across the Midwest, while polling cited by Newsweek showed Trump underwater in nine of the 10 largest agricultural states.

Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender also acknowledged that a Treasury bond-buyback program had not lowered interest rates. Mortgage rates had risen above 7 percent, and he said meaningful improvement depended on ending the war and restraining the budget deficit—neither a plausible short-term remedy in Varney’s assessment.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The decisions belong to Washington

The actors with institutional power are not motorists, farmers, homebuyers, or vaguely defined “markets.” They are the president directing foreign policy, the administration managing fiscal policy, and the congressional majority controlling legislation and spending.

Varney’s phrase—“a big problem”—softens that chain of responsibility. According to the account he presented, the war is driving defense and energy costs higher while federal debt is amplifying bond-market anxiety. These are not disconnected economic weather events. They are consequences attached to government choices.

Affordability is the consequence, not the cause

Republican leaders describe “affordability” as an electoral issue because that is safer than describing the policies making daily life more expensive. Diesel prices matter across agricultural states because fuel costs run through farming, freight, and household budgets. Higher Treasury yields matter because they raise borrowing costs for mortgages, businesses, and the federal government.

Calling this an affordability problem risks reversing cause and effect. Voters did not manufacture the administration’s predicament by noticing higher prices. The predicament is that federal policy produced—or, in the bond market’s case, reportedly intensified—costs that voters cannot avoid.

The rescue failed its public test

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the bond-buyback effort successful. Faulkender conceded that it did not bring rates down, then defended it through less visible benefits. Varney supplied the obvious political verdict: voters measure economic management by material results.

That exchange exposes a familiar governing maneuver. Officials redefine success around the mechanics of an intervention after its stated economic pain remains. A program may improve market functioning without lowering rates, but that distinction does not erase 7-percent-plus mortgages. If the administration claims credit for technical stabilization, it also owns the limits of that stabilization.

Fox notices when power becomes expensive

The significance of Varney’s criticism is not that a television host discovered economic hardship. It is that a reliably Republican media venue recognized the hardship as a threat to Republican control.

The people paying more for fuel and credit appear primarily as the mechanism through which the GOP might lose seats. That framing turns public harm into campaign analytics. It asks whether Republicans can survive the consequences before asking why those with power imposed or failed to contain them.

Accountability arrives as a polling problem

This story reveals a broader pattern: governing decisions remain abstract until their costs threaten the governing party. War becomes “affordability.” Debt becomes “bond-market stress.” Failed relief becomes an argument over intangible success. Responsibility dissolves into technical language until polling reconnects policy to its authors.

The GOP’s danger, as presented here, is not mysterious. The administration exercised power; households absorbed the costs; Republican candidates inherited the backlash. What cannot be fixed in five weeks is not merely a messaging problem. It is the political bill for decisions already made.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fox host declares Trump can’t fix his ‘big problem’ — and the GOP will pay

item.title: Revealed: WSJ tracks down where Trump’s ad money came from
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One as he departs for a state visit to Britain, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S., September 16, 2025. REUTERS Kevin Lamarque

What happened

AlterNet reports that taxpayer money for President Donald Trump’s television advertisements came from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, using funds Congress provided to the Department of Homeland Security through the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill Act.” The Wall Street Journal traced the funding to CBP through unnamed people familiar with the matter.

According to the Journal, one advertisement was almost identical to a video Trump posted during the 2024 campaign. CNN reported that Trump personally helped create the government-funded ads. By Sunday evening, iSpot estimated nearly 90 national-network airings costing $337,000, while AdImpact counted 2,311 local airings backed by an estimated $1.4 million.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The White House called the commercials educational and patriotic. DHS declined to comment. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin requested an investigation, Public Citizen sued to remove the ads, and Democracy Forward filed a public-records request.

Congress supplied the machinery

Congress holds the power of the purse, and it gave DHS the enormous funding pool from which this spending reportedly came. CBP then supplied the public money, while the president allegedly participated personally in producing the message.

That chain matters. This was not campaign spending accidentally charged to the wrong account. The reported structure ran through institutions empowered to control borders, enforce immigration law and spend federal appropriations. Public authority provided the money and distribution; Trump’s political messaging supplied the substance.

Public service or political promotion

CBP routinely advertises to prospective migrants and undocumented immigrants. That precedent does not settle whether these commercials served the same operational purpose. A government message that closely reproduces a candidate’s campaign material raises a different question: whether an agency communication budget was used to amplify a politician’s personal brand.

The White House’s defense avoids that distinction. Calling an advertisement “patriotic” says nothing about whether taxpayers should finance it, whether its content advances a defined agency mission, or why it reportedly mirrors campaign propaganda. Patriotism is being offered as an exemption from scrutiny.

The power is in the classification

The administration can call the spots public-service announcements because it controls the executive agencies producing them. Critics must then sue, investigate or request records after the money has been committed and the message broadcast thousands of times.

That is the asymmetry. The government acts immediately; oversight arrives later. Even if a court or investigation ultimately finds wrongdoing, the purchased exposure cannot be recalled. The political benefit, if that is what the ads delivered, has already been distributed at public expense.

A pattern of self-advertisement

The controversy follows an earlier DHS campaign featuring then-Secretary Kristi Noem in assorted costumes. AlterNet reports that a company connected to Noem received $200 million for that campaign. Noem testified that Trump approved the expenditure; Trump said he did not.

Those conflicting accounts remain unresolved in the supplied reporting, but they expose an accountability system built for evasion. Senior officials can publicly promote themselves through agency spending, then dispute who authorized it when Congress asks questions. Institutional responsibility dissolves precisely where institutional power is most concentrated.

The state as a political asset

The central issue is larger than whether a particular commercial crossed a legal line—a question the reporting does not resolve. It is whether executive officials can convert government communications into incumbent publicity while forcing watchdogs to prove, after the fact, that the message was political.

That model turns public administration into a personal media apparatus. Congress supplies the money, agencies provide the nominal purpose, and political leaders receive the exposure. The misdirection lies in debating whether the ads sound sufficiently “patriotic” while ignoring the decisive question: who controlled the funds, who shaped the message, and who benefited from taxpayers being made to broadcast it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Revealed: WSJ tracks down where Trump’s ad money came from

item.title: Republican calls out Trump’s weaponization of DOJ in live Senate hearing
item.description:
U.S. Senator Thom Tillis (R-NC) attends a Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee hearing on the Financial Stability Oversight Council’s annual report February 5, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

AlterNet reports that Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican not seeking reelection, used part of a Tuesday Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with former special counsel Jack Smith to criticize President Donald Trump’s targeting of former FBI Director James Comey. Tillis said “8647” was not a sound basis for pursuing Comey or subjecting him to a “perp walk,” though the report does not explain that reference or detail the underlying action against Comey.

Tillis also criticized partisan claims of “vindictive prosecution” and asked who was responsible for the events that forced senators into a secure location while attackers damaged the Capitol and injured more than 100 police officers. Smith defended his investigations but said his refusal to litigate them publicly had allowed false claims about his team and cases to spread unanswered.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power is not evenly distributed

Tillis presented vindictive prosecution as a temptation shared across party lines. That framing obscures the decisive distinction: the president controls the executive branch, while the Justice Department possesses investigative and prosecutorial power. Critics, former officials and political opponents do not wield equivalent authority merely because everyone can accuse everyone else of misconduct.

If federal law enforcement was improperly directed against Comey, responsibility rests with the officials who initiated, approved or enabled that action. A lecture about how “we” behave spreads accountability across the Senate while leaving the people holding executive power conveniently indistinct.

Candor after the cost disappears

Tillis’s criticism matters because it came from within Trump’s party. Its force is also limited by its timing. A senator leaving electoral politics faces fewer consequences for contradicting a president who dominates Republican incentives.

That does not make the objection insincere. It exposes the structure surrounding it. When forthright criticism becomes safest only after reelection is no longer at stake, institutional cowardice has already done its work. The system rewards silence when intervention could matter and permits candor when the political price has fallen.

The false symmetry trap

Tillis correctly identified the danger of prosecutors being treated as instruments of partisan revenge. But his “right and righteous” formulation reduces a question of state power to a problem of mutual self-regard.

The relevant inquiry is not which faction feels morally superior. It is who commanded an institution, what officials authorized, what legal basis they offered and what consequences followed. Treating those questions as another episode of partisan hypocrisy lets powerful actors hide inside a generalized complaint about political temperature.

Silence is not neutrality

Smith said traditional prosecutorial restraint left his team unable to answer claims he described as patently untrue. His proposed lesson—that prosecutors need some way to communicate without compromising fair-trial rights—identifies a genuine institutional weakness.

Courtroom discipline cannot substitute for public accountability when political actors conduct a continuous propaganda campaign outside the courtroom. But prosecutors cannot repair public trust through messaging alone. They need transparent legal reasoning, consistent standards and institutions willing to defend legitimate work before intimidation and repetition turn unsupported claims into accepted partisan fact.

The systemic error

This episode reveals a familiar cycle: concentrated power is softened into shared dysfunction, officials object only after their personal risk declines, and institutional restraint is exploited by actors unconstrained by it.

The central failure is not excessive incivility. It is the refusal to assign responsibility according to actual authority. Until political coverage distinguishes between those exercising coercive state power and those merely commenting on it, accountability will keep dissolving into atmosphere—and the officials making consequential decisions will remain protected by the fiction that everyone is equally responsible.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Republican calls out Trump’s weaponization of DOJ in live Senate hearing

item.title: 'This is bad': Enormous blunder spotted in Trump's 'taxpayer-funded' ad
item.description:
Donald Trump in taxpayer-funded ad (MS NOW screenshot)

What happened

RawStory reports that a U.S. government-funded advertisement featuring President Donald Trump declared, “This is the final battle,” promoted his record, and ended with the disclaimer “Paid for by the US Government.” On Monday, an MS NOW “Morning Joe” panel argued that the ad used public money for political self-promotion while inadvertently highlighting promises they said Trump had not fulfilled.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy told CBS the ad was “probably illegal” and said public money should not be spent to promote an officeholder. Joe Scarborough characterized the spending as “stealing taxpayer dollars,” while he and Jonathan Lemire argued that the ad’s references to foreign wars and prices reminded viewers of Trump’s failures rather than his claimed achievements.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The report does not identify which agency commissioned the ad, who approved it, how much it cost, where it ran, or what law it might violate. It also provides criticism from television commentators, not a legal finding or evidence establishing that Trump personally authorized the expenditure.

The power sits behind the disclaimer

The crucial words are not Trump’s apocalyptic slogan. They are “Paid for by the US Government.” An administration controls agencies, communications machinery, and access to appropriated funds. Taxpayers finance that machinery; they do not authorize its conversion into personal campaign theater.

But RawStory leaves the chain of command blank. Without naming the agency, appropriation, approving official, or production process, the article cannot tell readers who exercised that power. Trump is the beneficiary and centerpiece. The actual decision-maker remains unidentified.

That omission matters because government propaganda is not produced by weather. Someone requested it, someone approved it, and someone determined that public resources could carry a message centered on the president’s political persona. Accountability begins with those names.

A legal question reduced to television reaction

Kennedy’s criticism is politically significant because it came from a Republican senator, but “probably illegal” is not a legal analysis. The report cites no statute, inspector-general review, ethics determination, or court ruling.

Scarborough’s claim that taxpayer money was being stolen is similarly presented as commentary, not an established finding. The defensible conclusion is narrower and still serious: the advertisement carried a government-funding disclaimer and appeared to promote Trump personally. Whether that crossed a legal boundary is unresolved in the reporting.

By building the story around a panel’s verdict, RawStory substitutes outrage for documentation. The sharper investigation would follow the money and authority: which office paid, under what program, after whose approval, and subject to what restrictions.

The blunder framing lets power escape

Calling the advertisement a “massive misstep” treats the central problem as poor messaging. Scarborough and Lemire argued that references to wars and prices reminded viewers of promises they believe Trump failed to keep. That may explain why the ad was politically ineffective. It does not explain why the government was paying to burnish the president’s image.

A blunder is accidental self-injury. Publicly financed leader promotion is an institutional choice, even when it backfires. Focusing on whether the ad helps Republicans redirects attention from the officials who authorized it to the consultants who apparently failed to make it persuasive.

The weaker actor here is the taxpayer, who has no operational control over the communications apparatus bearing the government’s name. The powerful actors are those inside the executive branch who can commission, approve, and distribute such material. The article identifies the first group’s money but not the second group’s responsibility.

Propaganda does not become harmless when it is clumsy

“This is the final battle” casts ordinary political struggle as existential conflict and places the president at its center. In a government-funded message, that framing collapses the distinction between the state, the administration, and one politician’s political identity.

The larger pattern is the personalization of public institutions: government resources become scenery for the leader, official communication becomes self-promotion, and accountability becomes a debate over optics. Critics then ask whether the message will hurt the ruling party instead of first establishing who used state power, by what authority, and at what public cost.

RawStory identifies a legitimate warning sign but stops at the spectacle. The systemic error is not that propaganda can be badly written. It is that institutional power can be converted into personal promotion while coverage fixates on whether the conversion was electorally competent.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘This is bad’: Enormous blunder spotted in Trump’s ‘taxpayer-funded’ ad

item.title: Alina Habba's new husband made fortune in controversial deals tied to romantic partners
item.description:
Alina Habba, Counselor to U.S. President Donald Trump, announces to reporters that Trump has appointed her to serve as interim U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey, at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., March 24, 2025. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

RawStory reports that former New Jersey U.S. Attorney Alina Habba married Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon at New York City’s Waldorf Astoria after a relationship of several months. The article links Mildon’s companies to major government-backed construction ventures in Congo and Venezuela, but it does not establish that his romantic partners obtained those contracts for him.

Mildon’s Milvest reportedly secured roughly $1 billion in Congolese construction contracts after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan introduced him to Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi. Projects later faced allegations involving mismanaged funds and improper import exemptions; Mildon denied the latter accusation, while former Congolese finance minister Nicolas Kazadi denied wrongdoing. Mildon subsequently received a reported $67 million contract to build a drone base.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Middle East Eye also reported that, after Mildon’s 2024 divorce, he dated the daughter of Venezuelan admiral Remigio Ceballos. In 2025, Mildon’s Vencement announced a profit-sharing agreement with Venezuela to revive 10 state-owned cement factories. Mildon denied allegations that the company owed contractors money and blamed extreme cement markups on resale markets the government had failed to control.

Where the power sits

The decisive actors here are not the women Mildon married or dated. They are presidents, ministers, state companies and procurement authorities capable of arranging introductions, granting exemptions and awarding enormous contracts.

The clearest reported connection is political rather than romantic: Erdoğan introduced Mildon to Tshisekedi, and Mildon’s company subsequently obtained extensive Congolese work. That sequence warrants scrutiny, but it does not by itself prove favoritism or illegality. The unanswered questions concern tender procedures, contract terms, oversight and public value—the machinery through which government power becomes private revenue.

In Venezuela, the same principle applies. A profit-sharing deal involving public factories necessarily depends on state authority. If contractors went unpaid or cement reached consumers at grossly inflated prices, responsibility must be traced through company accounts, distribution systems and government enforcement. A businessman’s dating history cannot substitute for that reporting.

A headline outrunning its evidence

RawStory’s framing claims a fortune built through controversial deals “tied to romantic partners.” The reporting supplies proximity and chronology, not a demonstrated causal chain. One former wife’s father had a company associated with an Erdoğan-requested mosque project. Another former partner was the daughter of a Maduro-aligned admiral. Those facts may justify further investigation, but they do not establish that either woman delivered contracts or that Mildon’s wealth came through them.

That gap matters. Turning women into narrative conduits between powerful men gives the story a tabloid charge while allowing the institutions that actually control public money to fade into the scenery. It also risks converting association into evidence: politically connected relatives become insinuations of misconduct without documentation showing what they did.

Habba is context, not proof

Habba’s own political position makes the marriage newsworthy. She represented Donald Trump in his civil fraud case and later resigned as New Jersey’s U.S. attorney after, according to RawStory, her appointment was found improper. Her proximity to presidential power deserves rigorous scrutiny—particularly if it intersects with Mildon’s business interests.

But the article reports no contract, intervention or policy decision involving Habba on Mildon’s behalf. A large diamond, an expensive handbag and the timing of her divorce are celebrity details, not evidence of public corruption. Treating them as substitutes for financial records or official acts weakens the case for accountability.

Access is the system

The larger pattern is access capitalism: private firms pursue public fortunes through relationships with officials who control introductions, contracts and regulatory privileges. That system thrives when scrutiny stops at personal intrigue.

Serious political reporting would follow the money through procurement records, beneficial ownership, exemption decisions, project performance and payments. Romantic genealogy may point reporters toward a network, but it cannot prove how that network operated. When coverage foregrounds marriages and ex-girlfriends while leaving state decision-making largely unexplained, power receives camouflage disguised as scandal.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Alina Habba’s new husband made fortune in controversial deals tied to romantic partners

item.title: 'Dangerous strategy': GOP pollster says Trump's latest move could backfire
item.description:
REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican pollster Frank Luntz called Donald Trump’s effort to make congressional elections a referendum on himself a “very dangerous strategy.” Luntz told CNN that Trump could energize loyal supporters who otherwise might stay home, but weaker support for Trump could instead reinforce the turnout advantage Luntz currently sees for Democrats.

Luntz pointed to Republican vulnerabilities in Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Ohio, arguing that low participation among Trump voters could produce Democratic upsets. He identified Latino voters, male union voters and voters under 30 as important blocs after their movement toward Republicans in 2024, while contending that anger over affordability and the war in Iran could complicate GOP efforts to retain the House and Senate.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power belongs to Trump

The central fact is not that Republican voters are difficult to motivate. It is that Republican candidates remain dependent on one politician’s ability to lend them purpose.

Trump is attempting to substitute personal allegiance for the normal incentives of a congressional election. When he appears on the ballot, Luntz says, his voters participate. When he does not, some disappear. The party’s response is therefore to simulate his presence—to make every Republican contest another test of loyalty to Trump.

That gives Trump enormous power over candidates without guaranteeing that he can transfer his coalition to them. They inherit his demands, liabilities and policy record while hoping to borrow his turnout operation.

Mobilization cannot erase consequences

Luntz’s warning is framed as campaign strategy, but the voter shifts described by AlterNet concern governing outcomes. Latino voters are said to have moved away from Trump as his deportation program became different from what they believed he had promised. Other voters want tangible results on prices and the war in Iran.

Those are not messaging glitches. They are judgments about the exercise of power.

Treating the problem primarily as whether Trump can “excite” his base turns accountability into a technical question of turnout. It invites Republicans to solve dissatisfaction through intensified partisan identification instead of addressing the decisions producing it.

The article’s muddled forecast

AlterNet’s framing is needlessly confusing. It says Democrats are expected to regain control of Congress “if” Trump persuades loyalists to support Republicans, even though that persuasion is presented as the GOP’s route to avoiding defeat. The article also moves between a Democratic advantage, possible Democratic upsets and an unspecified expected blowout without clearly defining the forecast behind any of them.

Luntz’s narrower argument is more coherent: Democrats currently appear to hold a turnout advantage of a couple of points; Trump may narrow it by mobilizing his supporters; and making the election about a weakened Trump could also repel or fail to recover voters Republicans need.

The uncertainty matters. A pollster’s turnout assessment is not an election result, and the reporting supplies no figures showing the size of the alleged movement among the demographic groups it names.

A party trapped inside one man’s coalition

The larger pattern is institutional surrender disguised as electoral realism. Republican candidates have helped build a party whose voters may respond more reliably to Trump than to the party, Congress or the candidates themselves. Now those candidates must invoke him even where his support may be eroding.

If Republicans retain both chambers, Luntz says Trump will demonstrate his political power. If they lose because his voters stay home or defect, the same dependence will have exposed the party’s weakness. Either outcome reveals the structure: congressional Republicans have tied their fortunes to Trump’s personal coalition, then called the resulting vulnerability a turnout problem.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Dangerous strategy’: GOP pollster says Trump’s latest move could backfire

item.title: 95 pages of chaos: The White House rules that nearly tanked the election
item.description:
REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

AlterNet, drawing on ProPublica’s reporting, says the Trump White House pursued mail-voting restrictions that could have disrupted the 2026 midterms before the Supreme Court blocked the final executive order on Sept. 14. An earlier proposal would have required ballots to travel exclusively by certified mail, forcing voters to be present and sign for delivery. The administration abandoned that plan after fierce Postal Service objections that it could not be executed.

The March order instead directed postal workers to compare ballot mailings with state voter lists and reject ballots—or potentially entire batches—for mismatches and other defects. A 95-page implementation rule was issued Aug. 21, less than a month before the first ballots were due to be mailed. Postal officials reportedly considered the rushed system untested, error-prone and likely to disenfranchise eligible voters.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The White House denied improper interference and described the measures as safeguards. Postal officials nevertheless prepared to comply while the agency’s bipartisan governing board remained publicly silent, reportedly fearing retaliation and expecting courts to intervene.

The power came from the White House

This was not administrative confusion bubbling up from postal workers. Trump issued the order. A White House team that included special presidential assistant J. Brian Sikma developed the policy. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick advised on it and received an implementation role despite having no formal authority over the Postal Service.

The order attempted to convert a delivery agency into an election gatekeeper. Postal workers would no longer merely transport ballots; they could determine whether voters received them. According to one former official, the White House insisted that a single mismatch could stop an entire mailing—meaning four defective records in a batch of one million could delay ballots for the other 999,996 voters.

That design placed the consequences of White House policy in the hands of frontline employees while keeping the political decision at a safer distance. If eligible voters lost access to ballots, the visible failure would occur at a postal facility. The authority producing that failure would remain in Washington.

“Security” was the misdirection

The administration presented the order as protection against fraud and noncitizen voting. But the reporting supplies no evidence of a mail-voting problem proportionate to the intervention. Independent audits generally found the system reliable, even though ballots were sometimes lost or delayed. Postal officials had already proposed practical improvements: standardized envelopes, scannable barcodes and recognizable markings.

The White House took those operational recommendations and attached punitive consequences to them. A barcode intended to help workers identify election mail became a possible basis for rejecting it. A voter list became a mechanism for blocking delivery. A modernization proposal became an exclusion system.

Calling that “commonsense” does not resolve the central contradiction. A security measure that predictably prevents qualified voters from receiving ballots—because of stale records, technical defects or errors elsewhere in a giant mailing—does not merely authenticate participation. It conditions participation on a hurried federal matching system that career officials reportedly believed could not be made reliable in time.

Institutional independence without resistance

The Postal Service’s governing structure is supposed to insulate it from partisan control. In this case, that protection proved fragile. Board members reportedly feared Trump might try to remove them, particularly after a June 2026 Supreme Court ruling expanded presidential removal power over leaders of agencies traditionally treated as independent.

Their response was silence. Postmaster General David Steiner, appointed at Trump’s behest in 2025, ordered implementation work to proceed and left the dispute to the courts. Career officials tried to narrow the damage, but the White House counsel rejected their less restrictive approach as insufficient.

The union president, Jonathan Smith, called reliance on judicial rescue a “dangerous calculation.” The criticism is deserved. Courts can block unlawful policy, but they cannot substitute for officials exercising the authority already entrusted to them. An institution that preserves itself by declining to defend its function has protected its officeholders, not its mandate.

Chaos can be an instrument

The reporting does not independently establish the administration’s motive, and the White House denied that the certified-mail proposal was abandoned because it was unworkable. But the foreseeable effects were explicit: millions of identity checks, higher local costs, compressed deadlines, unresolved privacy problems and possible rejection of enormous ballot batches over isolated discrepancies.

That matters because administrative chaos is not politically neutral. When rules become difficult to understand, systems are deployed without testing and valid ballots are delayed alongside defective records, the burden falls on voters least equipped to navigate the disruption. The resulting failures can then be cited as evidence that mail voting itself is unreliable.

That is the larger pattern: use unsupported claims of electoral corruption to justify federal intervention, force neutral administrators into partisan enforcement roles, and let the resulting dysfunction undermine confidence in the system being “secured.” The Supreme Court prevented this version from taking effect. It did not remove the political machinery that produced 95 pages of planned disorder—or the institutional fear that allowed the machinery to run until a court switched it off.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: 95 pages of chaos: The White House rules that nearly tanked the election

item.title: Trump TV flops as Karoline Leavitt accidentally steals the show
item.description:
REUTERS/Daniel Heuer

What happened

AlterNet reports that the White House’s 24-hour “Trump TV” livestream lost nearly all of its launch audience, while former press secretary Karoline Leavitt accidentally drew far more viewers by starting an Instagram Live from bed. Citing The Daily Beast, AlterNet says the official stream fell as low as 187 concurrent viewers, compared with 1,157 for Leavitt’s brief, silent broadcast. She ended it immediately and later said she had gone live while trying to edit a reel.

The channel launched September 21 with about 8,500 viewers and subsequently fell below 1,000 at times, according to figures attributed to The Daily Beast. The White House distributes the continuous feed through its website and YouTube channel, filling it with administration speeches, announcements, and promotional clips.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet links the project to Trump’s exclusion of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House access and the subsequent withdrawal of NBC, ABC, CBS, and Fox News from pooled television coverage. It also reports that Trump’s private company, DTTM Operations LLC, applied on September 24 for a federal trademark on the name “TRUMP TV.”

The joke obscures the decision

The accidental livestream is irresistible clickbait: an administration surrogate unintentionally outdrawing the president’s official channel without even speaking. But audience humiliation is not the politically important fact.

Trump exercised presidential authority to exclude news organizations and take their press passes. The White House then built a continuous distribution system for administration-produced material. The relevant question is not whether the stream is entertaining. It is whether executive power is being used to replace scrutiny with controlled presentation.

Calling the project a “flop” measures the least consequential thing about it. Propaganda does not become harmless because its first broadcast attracts only a few hundred people.

Power belongs to the White House

The institutional imbalance is stark. News organizations can object, withdraw from pooled coverage, and report the conflict. The White House controls access to officials, events, and government information. Trump made the exclusionary decision; his administration created the alternative channel.

That distinction matters because coverage centered on ratings can misdirect attention toward viewers, platforms, or the media organizations that suspended participation. None of them holds the presidency’s gatekeeping authority. The administration chose to restrict access and then offered its own edited output as a substitute.

The reported sequence does not establish that every item on the channel is false. It establishes something more basic: the people exercising government power also control what appears on this feed, while independent questioning and verification occur elsewhere.

Public office, private mark

The trademark application raises a separate conflict that low viewership cannot explain away. AlterNet reports that DTTM Operations LLC—a private Trump company—sought ownership of the “TRUMP TV” name days after the White House launched a channel under that branding.

A filing is not proof that public resources were unlawfully converted into private property, and the reporting supplies no adjudication of that question. But the arrangement plainly warrants scrutiny: a government communications project promotes a name that the president’s company is simultaneously attempting to claim as a private trademark.

That is the recurring Trump-era collapse of boundaries in miniature. Presidential office, personal brand, campaign-style messaging, and private commercial interests are placed beside one another until the public is expected to treat their convergence as routine.

Access is the real currency

The channel’s small audience may limit its immediate reach, but the larger strategy does not depend on building a successful television network. Government-produced clips can be excerpted, reposted, and circulated through other channels. More importantly, restricting press access changes the conditions under which information is gathered before any video reaches an audience.

Independent journalism is not valuable because reporters possess better cameras. It is valuable because they can ask questions the government did not script, compare official claims with evidence, and report facts officials would prefer to omit. A White House feed performs none of those functions merely by operating around the clock.

The administration’s material may be evidence of what officials want the public to see. It is not an independent account of what the government is doing.

The systemic error

This story reveals how spectacle can conceal a transfer of power. The comic comparison—187 viewers for Trump’s channel, 1,157 for Leavitt’s mistake—turns an access fight into a popularity contest. That framing makes the administration look foolish while leaving its institutional maneuver insufficiently examined.

The deeper pattern is executive control presented as media innovation: punish disfavored outlets, narrow independent access, produce an official substitute, and blur the government project with the president’s private brand. The ratings may be dismal. The assertion of power is not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump TV flops as Karoline Leavitt accidentally steals the show
