item.title: 'Scumbags!' Eagles fans unleash profane takedown of DHS after using player footage in ad
item.description:
U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin testifies during a U.S. House of Representatives panel hearing on immigration enforcement funding and other Homeland Security budget priorities, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S. June 3, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

The Department of Homeland Security used footage of former Philadelphia Eagles player Brian Dawkins in a charged social-media post about reports of an approaching migrant caravan. RawStory reports that the post declared “our time has come,” prompting the NFL to request its removal.

Eagles fans and other commenters denounced the use of the footage and urged the team and league to respond. The reporting does not establish who inside DHS approved the post, whether the Eagles or Dawkins authorized it, or whether DHS ultimately removed it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power belongs to DHS

The angry fans are the headline, but they are not the powerful actors. DHS is a federal department with enforcement authority over immigration. It chose to wrap that authority in the emotional language and imagery of professional football.

That distinction matters. Fans supplied backlash; government officials supplied the propaganda. Treating the episode chiefly as a profane online quarrel shrinks an exercise of state messaging into a culture-war spectacle.

Borrowed glory, redirected at migrants

The post appears designed to transfer the drama of athletic combat onto immigration enforcement. Dawkins’s image supplied the heroic spectacle; reports of migrants supplied the adversary.

The article does not establish the caravan’s size, location, composition, or legal circumstances. Yet DHS’s language cast its approach as a moment for confrontation. That is political misdirection: complex questions about human beings and government power are converted into a team-versus-enemy narrative.

The NFL had leverage

The NFL’s takedown request was more consequential than any insult in the replies. The league controls valuable footage and therefore had institutional leverage against its use. RawStory does not report the legal basis for the request or its outcome, but the intervention challenged DHS’s attempt to conscript the league’s imagery into federal messaging.

The Eagles and Dawkins, meanwhile, are central to the symbolism but absent from the reported response. Calls for them to condemn the post reflect a real question: whether institutions whose cultural authority is appropriated by government will defend the boundary or quietly benefit from ambiguity.

The outrage is not the story

RawStory foregrounded fans calling DHS officials “scumbags.” That captures anger but obscures agency. The essential event was not that citizens swore at a department. It was that a department with coercive power used sports footage to dramatize migrants as an approaching opponent.

This is how authoritarian-style propaganda becomes ordinary: state power borrows familiar entertainment, strips vulnerable people of context, and presents enforcement as a righteous contest. The spectacle encourages audiences to choose a jersey before asking what the government is doing.

A government dressed as a franchise

DHS did not need Eagles footage to communicate policy or public-safety information. Its use served a political aesthetic—heroic defenders, looming outsiders, and an appointed hour of action.

That pattern replaces accountable government with branding. Officials become warriors, enforcement becomes entertainment, and migrants become narrative equipment. The institutional danger lies beyond one deleted—or undeleted—post: agencies with immense power learn that spectacle can conceal the people, decisions, and consequences underneath it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Scumbags!’ Eagles fans unleash profane takedown of DHS after using player footage in ad

item.title: Kash Patel spotted partying with suspected Russian 'double agent’
item.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel and country music artist Alexis Wilkins arrive for UFC Freedom 250 in Washington, D.C., U.S., June 14, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

RawStory reports that FBI Director Kash Patel appeared in a photograph from a New York wedding alongside Ali Abdelaziz, an MMA manager whom the FBI reportedly stopped using as an informant in 2008 after suspecting he was acting as a double agent. The photograph establishes that they attended the same event and posed together; it does not establish a personal relationship, access to classified information, or misconduct by Patel.

Nevada federal prosecutor Sigal Chattah posted the photograph early Sunday. RawStory says a court ruled last year that Chattah was serving unlawfully as Nevada’s U.S. attorney and that an appeals court upheld that ruling last month. The outlet also notes scrutiny of prosecutorial decisions by her office and attributes violently anti-Palestinian statements to her.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power in the room

The central figure is not Abdelaziz. It is Patel, the sitting director of the FBI. He commands an institution responsible for counterintelligence investigations, informant handling and decisions about who presents a national-security concern.

Chattah also exercises federal prosecutorial power despite the reported rulings against the legality of her tenure. A politically connected wedding guest occupies no comparable institutional position. Coverage that turns the photograph into a rogue’s-gallery spectacle risks obscuring the officials whose authority makes the gathering politically significant.

A photograph is not a case

Patel’s presence beside a former informant once suspected by the FBI deserves scrutiny because of Patel’s office. But proximity in a group photograph is not evidence that Patel “forgave” a counterintelligence concern, shared information or intervened on Abdelaziz’s behalf. RawStory supplies none of that.

The suspicion against Abdelaziz must also remain a suspicion. The article reports that the FBI dropped him as an informant in 2008; it does not report a charge or finding that he was a double agent. Suggestive captions and sarcastic social-media commentary cannot substitute for evidence.

The stronger institutional question

The more concrete issue is Chattah’s continued proximity to federal power after courts reportedly found her service unlawful. That is not atmospheric intrigue. It concerns whether appointment rules and judicial decisions impose meaningful limits on an administration’s control of law enforcement.

Her reported rhetoric about Palestinians matters for the same reason. Someone wielding prosecutorial discretion reportedly described an entire population—including children—in exterminatory terms. The relevant question is not whether such language is impolite. It is what safeguards remain when an official with coercive authority embraces collective dehumanization.

Spectacle as misdirection

RawStory builds its piece around the sensational phrase “suspected Russian double agent,” then relies heavily on journalists’ social-media reactions. That framing generates heat while leaving the consequential questions underdeveloped: Why does Chattah remain institutionally empowered? What access, if any, did Abdelaziz have to Patel? Were FBI security protocols implicated? The reporting does not answer them.

The result is insinuation where documentation is thin and relative quiet where the institutional record is stronger. That is a familiar failure in political coverage: weaker actors become the lurid hook while officeholders’ actual authority recedes into scenery.

The system behind the photograph

Elite social events matter because they display access, not because every shared frame proves conspiracy. Their political meaning lies in who can move casually through the same private spaces while holding public power, surviving adverse court rulings or carrying unresolved security concerns.

The systemic problem is not established by one wedding photograph. It is revealed by the gap between spectacle and accountability: officials exercise immense discretion, courts identify apparent legal defects, inflammatory conduct accumulates—and coverage still gravitates toward the most cinematic insinuation instead of tracing who retains power and why.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Kash Patel spotted partying with suspected Russian ‘double agent’

item.title: 'Good grief': Golfer ridiculed after giving Trump 'all the credit' for comeback win
item.description:
US President Donald Trump pats Wyndham Clark’s girlfriend Emily Tanner on the shoulder as he joins members of the US Team during the trophy ceremony at the Presidents Cup golf tournament at Medinah Country Club in Medinah, Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that U.S. Presidents Cup captain Brandt Snedeker credited President Donald Trump after the American team erased a three-point final-round deficit and won the tournament on September 27, 2026. Trump attended the final round, but the report identifies no action by him that materially produced the team’s eight singles victories.

Snedeker said Trump had predicted he would bring the players energy and that he had promised Trump “all the credit” if the United States won. RawStory then highlighted three hostile social-media reactions, including criticism from an ESPN writer and an inflammatory accusation from a Canadian radio personality.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Credit without evidence

The athletes produced the comeback. Snedeker chose to transfer rhetorical ownership of their performance to the president.

Nothing in the reporting establishes that Trump devised strategy, coached players or changed the competition’s outcome. The only mechanism offered is “energy,” an elastic explanation that converts attendance into achievement. Snedeker’s remark may have been flattery, humor or sincere admiration; RawStory does not establish which. It does establish that he publicly made Trump the symbolic author of work performed by others.

Power courts applause

Trump already held the only governmental power in this story. Snedeker held authority over the team and control over his own post-match message. The golfers held agency on the course. Online critics controlled none of those institutions.

That distinction matters because the episode was not primarily about powerless posters being mean to a golfer. It was about a prominent sports official using a victory ceremony to elevate a sitting president. Political power did not need to issue an order. A prestigious figure volunteered the tribute.

Outrage as camouflage

RawStory framed the incident around Snedeker being “brutally ridiculed,” then supplied a handful of posts as evidence. That construction makes the backlash the event and the presidential glorification merely its trigger.

The framing is weak. One critic’s inflammatory attack deserved careful attribution, not deployment as outrage bait. More importantly, collecting insults avoids the substantive question: why was a team’s historic comeback repackaged as personal credit for a politician whose reported contribution was showing up?

The loyalty economy

Public flattery is politically useful even when it carries no formal policy consequence. It teaches audiences to associate collective accomplishment with the leader and to treat proximity to power as causation.

Snedeker’s statement fits that pattern precisely: many people performed; one powerful man received the credit. The absurdity is not that Trump accepted praise in the account—RawStory does not report his response—but that an intermediary offered him ownership without evidence that he earned it.

The systemic error

This is how leader-centered politics spreads beyond government. Institutions with their own achievements, labor and expertise begin narrating success through the presence of the president. Voluntary deference does work that coercion never had to do.

RawStory noticed the spectacle but buried its political meaning beneath a compilation of jeers. The sharper story is not that critics groaned. It is that power attracted unearned credit, a captain supplied it, and the press treated the resulting social-media scuffle as more significant than the ritual itself.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Good grief’: Golfer ridiculed after giving Trump ‘all the credit’ for comeback win

item.title: Hot mic catches despondent Trump in plea to staffers: 'I'd like to go home’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump talks to members of the US Team during the trophy ceremony after the US team won the Presidents Cup golf tournament at Medinah Country Club, in Medinah Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump was caught on a live microphone saying, “I’d like to go home,” after the U.S. team’s 17–13 Presidents Cup victory at Medinah Country Club outside Chicago. The remark came after Trump posed with the trophy and congratulated team captain Brandt Snedeker; players then moved away, though the reporting does not establish that they did so because of Trump’s comment.

Earlier Sunday, Trump addressed spectators at the first tee, mocked anticipated media coverage of his reception, and kept his remarks brief. A heckler shouted a profane accusation, while hundreds of protesters gathered outside the club; police separated some protesters and Trump supporters. Trump returned to the White House after 9:30 p.m., called the outing a “tremendous day,” and declined questions.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The headline oversells the evidence

“Despondent” is an interpretation, not an established fact. The recording apparently captures Trump saying he wanted to leave. It does not establish his emotional state, and the article supplies no evidence that the players’ movement was a reaction to the remark.

That inflation turns an ordinary scrap of overheard speech into a miniature psychological drama. The Pink song, the awkward staging and an online critic’s joke make the clip entertaining. They do not make the speculation more reliable.

Power is hiding outside the frame

Trump was not merely another uncomfortable guest. He attended as president, surrounded by heightened security, received the microphone from the PGA Tour’s chief executive and occupied the ceremonial center of an international sporting event. Those are visible expressions of institutional power.

The decisive actors here were the event organizers and security authorities: one gave Trump a prestigious platform; the others managed the disruption surrounding his presence. The players did not control the presidential office, the security perimeter or the public stage. Treating their body language as the central political fact shifts attention from the institutions that accommodated presidential power to people standing near it.

Spectacle replaces scrutiny

The article devotes more energy to an ambiguous mutter than to Trump declining questions after returning to the White House. That is the more consequential act. A president’s access to ceremonial attention is guaranteed by office; journalists’ access to answers is not.

The framing also invites readers into the same media game Trump invoked from the tee: reception, optics, humiliation and partisan comparison. His “fake news” complaint anticipates hostile coverage, while the coverage obliges with a headline stronger than its evidence. The result is mutually reinforcing spectacle, not accountability.

The systemic error

Personality coverage is cheap because it converts power into content. A president becomes a mood to diagnose, a clip to replay or a social-media punchline. Institutions disappear, decisions blur, and accountability is replaced by amateur theater criticism.

The political meaning is not that Trump wanted to go home. It is that presidential power could command a sporting stage, a major security response and extensive coverage—while the resulting story centered on an unverifiable emotion. When journalism magnifies the trivial and softens the structural, it does not expose power. It helps power waste everyone’s attention.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Hot mic catches despondent Trump in plea to staffers: ‘I’d like to go home’

item.title: This fix will stop Trump's wave of destruction — by obliterating him
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: The demolition of the East Wing of the White House, the location of U.S. President Donald Trump’s proposed ballroom is seen from an elevated position on the North side of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., October 23, 2025. REUTERS/ Andrew Leyden/File Photo

What happened

RawStory columnist Ray Richmond argues that Donald Trump’s presidencies have damaged a sweeping range of American institutions, norms and public expectations. He begins with the Kennedy Center, portraying its decline as part of Trump’s broader drive to erase established legacies and replace them with his own brand.

Richmond then lists institutions and principles he says Trump has “destroyed,” from federal agencies and scientific research to alliances, civil rights and the peaceful transfer of power. He ultimately qualifies that claim: democracy, science, education, journalism and the rule of law remain intact, though under severe pressure.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

His proposed remedy is electoral, not literal obliteration. Writing less than six weeks before the midterms, Richmond urges voters to begin reversing Trump’s agenda in November. The article does not specify particular races, policies or institutional reforms that would accomplish that.

Power is more than one man

The presidency commands agencies, appointments, enforcement priorities and immense agenda-setting power. Trump therefore bears responsibility for decisions made through his administration. But the column’s fixation on one man obscures the machinery that converts presidential preference into state action.

Congress funds and authorizes. Courts permit or restrain. Cabinet officials issue orders. Agency leaders carry them out. Political allies defend them, and organized interests benefit from them. Trump may dominate this coalition, but he does not operate it alone. Turning institutional capture into a story of singular personality lets every willing enabler fade into the scenery.

A catalogue is not a case

The column repeatedly substitutes the word “destroyed” for evidence. It names the FBI, IRS, FDA, CDC, EPA, State Department, Supreme Court and many other bodies without identifying the relevant decision, date, legal mechanism or measurable result.

That excess weakens the indictment. If everything has already been destroyed, readers cannot distinguish an abolished program from a weakened norm, a partisan ruling from an incapacitated court, or declining trust from institutional collapse. Richmond himself concedes that several foundations of public life remain “essentially intact.” That admission is important, but it exposes how carelessly the central verb has been used.

Personal pathology hides institutional agency

Richmond frames the Kennedy Center dispute and the broader governing project chiefly through Trump’s vanity, hostility and appetite for self-glorification. Those character judgments may express the columnist’s interpretation, but the article supplies little concrete reporting to establish motive. It asserts that Trump intended to raze the venue and rebuild it under his own name without documenting the decision or identifying evidence for that plan.

More importantly, psychologizing power can misdirect blame. Institutions are not dismantled by temperament alone. They are weakened through budgets, appointments, regulations, executive directives, legislation, judicial permission and bureaucratic compliance. A serious account would identify the people who selected those tools and the officials who agreed to wield them.

Voting is necessary, not self-executing

The column’s answer is November. Elections can alter who controls Congress and constrain an administration, but “vote” is not an institutional repair manual. It does not explain which appropriations should be restored, which authorities should be narrowed, which watchdogs need protection or which forms of executive discretion created the vulnerability.

Richmond’s strongest observation is that constitutional government depends on restraint, independence and enforceable limits. Yet voluntary restraint is precisely the wrong safeguard against officials who reject restraint. Durable limits require statutes, oversight, transparency, independent enforcement and officials prepared to impose consequences.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is not that one president possesses supernatural powers of demolition. It is that American government leaves critical protections dependent on norms, fragmented oversight and the courage of people whose careers may benefit from surrender.

Personalizing the damage makes for a furious column, but it produces an incomplete politics. The relevant question is not merely what Trump wanted. It is who gave him the authority, who enabled its use, who declined to resist and which structural failures will remain available to the next president who finds them useful.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: This fix will stop Trump’s wave of destruction — by obliterating him

item.title: Trump's 'roughshod' remarks prompt stark warning from editor: 'Hardly out of character’
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer arrive by helicopter at Trump International Golf Links, in Aberdeen, Scotland, Britain, July 28, 2025. Jane Barlow/Pool via REUTERS

What happened

RawStory reports that Donald Trump disclosed details about five men arrested near RAF Fairford before British authorities had publicly described their suspected intentions. Trump said the men had been investigated “for a long time” and were looking to do “big damage” to the British airbase; UK officials had announced arrests on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act and explosives offenses but had not confirmed those particulars.

James Ball, political editor of The New World, argued that the remarks raise doubts about whether Britain can trust the U.S. president with sensitive intelligence. He said the immediate episode would “almost certainly prove to be harmless,” while warning that a future disclosure might not be.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power sits in Washington

The five arrested men are suspects, not convicted terrorists, and the reporting does not establish whether RAF Fairford was definitively their target. Yet they are not the central institutional actors in this story. British investigators control the operation; the U.S. president commands an allied intelligence partner with privileged access to closely held information.

That asymmetry matters. A suspect can threaten one investigation. A president who discusses undisclosed operational details can affect intelligence sharing across governments. Trump’s office gives an impulsive remark consequences far beyond the press scrum in which it was made.

Trump chose disclosure

RawStory does not establish exactly how Trump learned the details or whether they were classified. It does establish that he publicly asserted facts British authorities had withheld. That was his decision, not an administrative accident and not a vague failure by “the allies.”

Trump also praised British police. But praise does not neutralize disclosure. Commending an operation while getting ahead of the officials responsible for it still overrides their judgment about what the public—and potentially other interested parties—should know.

The spectacle displaces the investigation

The framing risks turning this into another story about Trump’s unruly personality: he “runs roughshod,” cannot keep quiet and likes to show off. Ball grounds that characterization in what he describes as a recurring pattern, but personality is not the whole political issue.

The more important fact is structural. The president can impose his appetite for public performance on agencies and allies that must absorb the risk. British investigators exercised restraint; Trump did not. The institutionally weaker actors then inherit the operational uncertainty while the most powerful actor faces little immediate constraint.

Allies pay for presidential indiscipline

The foreseeable consequence is not merely embarrassment. If British officials cannot rely on presidential discretion, they must decide whether to share less, share later or accept a greater chance of premature exposure. Any of those choices can make joint security work harder.

The reporting does not show that Trump’s remarks damaged this investigation. Ball explicitly expects that they probably did not. The warning concerns the repeated gamble: sensitive cooperation cannot safely depend on the hope that every unauthorized disclosure happens to be harmless.

A system built on unenforceable trust

This episode exposes a recurring weakness in executive power. Intelligence alliances depend on discretion, but the safeguards become thin when the person at the top treats privileged knowledge as material for public display.

Calling that “out of character” would make it an aberration. Ball’s point is the opposite: the conduct fits a pattern he has observed across Trump’s two terms. The systemic error is allowing consequential restraint to rest on personal discipline when the office supplies extraordinary access, broad latitude and few immediate penalties for breaking an ally’s confidence.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s ‘roughshod’ remarks prompt stark warning from editor: ‘Hardly out of character’

item.title: Trump willing to make stunning concession to Iran amid 'flexible' talks: report
item.description:
US President Donald Trump walks after exiting Air Force One at Chicago O’Hare International Airport, in Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump is again willing to consider sanctions relief and the unfreezing of Iranian funds in exchange for substantial limits on Iran’s nuclear program. Unnamed U.S. officials told Axios that indirect talks through Qatari and Pakistani mediators were expected in New York and described Iran as flexible on nuclear issues.

The reported position reverses Trump’s August statement that his administration was not seeking to extend a June interim agreement containing similar economic concessions. It also resembles the basic exchange underpinning the Iran nuclear deal Trump abandoned during his first term. The reporting establishes another negotiating pivot, not a completed agreement; it does not specify the exact restrictions Iran might accept or the relief Washington might provide.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power sits in Washington

Iran can negotiate, refuse, or make counteroffers. But the institutional power described here belongs to the Trump administration, which controls whether the United States lifts its sanctions and releases restricted funds.

Calling those steps a “stunning concession” obscures that imbalance. Washington imposed the restrictions and can remove them. Iran is not being handed an inexplicable gift; it is being offered relief from American economic pressure in return for nuclear commitments. That is negotiation, even when Trump does it.

Trump destroyed the precedent

The central contradiction is not between toughness and weakness. It is between Trump’s demolition of an existing sanctions-for-nuclear-limits framework and his reported willingness to bargain on substantially similar terms now.

Trump chose to abandon the Obama-era agreement. According to RawStory, he later entertained broad relief in June, withdrew that position after renewed hostilities in July, rejected an extension in August, and has now moved toward it again. Those were presidential decisions, not diplomatic weather. Describing them merely as flexibility launders executive volatility into strategy.

Spectacle replaces accountability

The article’s emphasis on a “major concession” risks accepting the political branding that made ordinary diplomacy appear humiliating when another administration practiced it. Sanctions relief was portrayed as disqualifying appeasement under Obama; under Trump, the same instrument can be presented as proof of transactional boldness.

That framing shifts attention away from the consequential question: what did destroying the earlier framework accomplish, and what costs followed from having to reconstruct its basic logic later? The supplied reporting does not answer that question. It does, however, show how personality-driven coverage can turn policy repetition into presidential reinvention.

A system built around reversals

The negotiators, mediators, and Iranian officials have agency, but they do not control the American policy swings described here. Trump does. Anonymous officials may project optimism, yet they cannot convert a recurring presidential change of position into a durable commitment.

The larger pattern is a foreign-policy system in which agreements are treated as extensions of presidential identity rather than instruments of state. One president’s deal is destroyed because it bears his name; its mechanisms are later revived without acknowledging the damage caused by abandoning them. The result is not principled flexibility. It is concentrated power with weak institutional memory, leaving other countries to negotiate not only with the United States, but with the possibility that its commitments will expire whenever its leader’s story about himself changes.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump willing to make stunning concession to Iran amid ‘flexible’ talks: report

item.title: The untold origins of Trump's plan to sharply restrict mail-in voting
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Judge Amy Coney Barrett after she was sworn in as an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, U.S. October 26, 2020. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst/File Photo

What happened

RawStory, citing ProPublica’s reporting, says the Trump White House considered requiring every mail ballot to travel by certified mail—a system that would have required voters to be home to sign for delivery. The administration abandoned that proposal after fierce Postal Service objections that it could not be executed, then issued a March 2026 order imposing other sweeping restrictions without meaningfully involving the agency expected to carry them out.

The order directed postal workers to match ballots against state voter lists and reject mailings over problems including outdated information or unreadable barcodes. According to a former official, the White House insisted that even one mismatch could stop an entire batch. Postal officials rushed out a 95-page implementation rule on Aug. 21, less than a month before the first ballots were due to be mailed.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The Supreme Court blocked the order on Sept. 14. The reporting says postal governors had avoided confronting the administration because they feared removal, while Postmaster General David Steiner ordered preparations to proceed and left the dispute to the courts. The White House denied improper interference and described the measures as election safeguards.

The power was in the White House

This was not a misunderstanding among election administrators. The president issued the order. A White House team that included special presidential assistant J. Brian Sikma helped develop it. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick participated in an advisory and coordinating role, then received implementation authority despite having no formal control over the Postal Service.

The administration attempted to convert a delivery agency into an eligibility checkpoint. Postal employees ordinarily transport election mail; they do not decide who receives a ballot. The order would have forced them into that decision while making access depend on hastily assembled databases, newly approved envelopes and an untested tracking system.

The mismatch between authority and expertise was the point of failure. Career postal officials knew the operational limits. The White House excluded them from crucial discussions, surprised the agency’s own lawyers with the final order and rejected an implementation proposal intended to keep postal workers from screening ballots.

Security was the pretext

The administration presented its intervention as a response to fraud. But the article supplies no evidence of widespread mail-voting fraud. It instead notes that independent audits found a system used for nearly one-third of ballots in the 2022 and 2024 elections generally worked reliably, despite occasional losses and delays.

Postal officials already had practical remedies for those failures: standardized envelopes, scannable barcodes and recognizable markings. A bipartisan bill incorporating those recommendations stalled in the Senate in 2024. Those measures were designed to help mail move accurately. The White House took pieces of that operational advice and attached punitive rules capable of withholding ballots from eligible voters.

That distinction matters. Improving mail identification is administration. Rejecting an entire mailing because one record fails to match is collective disenfranchisement disguised as quality control. The reporting does not establish how many voters would ultimately have lost access, because the order was blocked. It does establish a mechanism built to make minor data defects consequential on a massive scale.

Institutional independence without resistance

The Postal Service’s bipartisan Board of Governors possessed institutional authority, but fear narrowed its willingness to use it. According to people familiar with the board’s concerns, governors worried that a direct challenge could prompt Trump to try to fire them, particularly after a June 2026 Supreme Court decision expanded presidential removal power over leaders of many nominally independent agencies.

So the board stayed quiet and gambled that judges would intervene. The gamble succeeded this time. That does not make it responsible governance. Postal union president Jonathan Smith called reliance on the courts a dangerous calculation and accused agency leadership of lacking courage and integrity.

Career employees tried to reduce the damage from inside, including by proposing that voter lists be collected without using them to block ballot distribution. Their proposal was rejected as insufficient. This is how institutional submission becomes procedural: leaders preserve their positions, workers quietly blunt the directive, and everyone waits for another institution to accept the political risk.

Chaos had a constituency

Smith argued that the goal was to create chaos and doubt around mail voting. That remains his assessment, not a fact independently established by the reporting. The foreseeable effects, however, are difficult to sanitize: millions of identity checks under the certified-mail proposal; higher costs for local governments; possible rejection of entire ballot batches; and a rushed system that a whistleblower described as untested and error-prone.

The article’s central power story is therefore clearer than its language of “concerns” and “surprise” sometimes allows. The White House chose the policy, excluded relevant expertise and demanded a more aggressive screening regime when postal officials offered a narrower alternative. The weaker actors—voters, local election offices and frontline postal workers—would have absorbed the failures.

Calling that confusion would misdirect responsibility. The uncertainty concerned how the machinery could possibly work. Responsibility for ordering that machinery into existence was not uncertain.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is rule by administrative sabotage: take a functioning public system, invoke an unsupported crisis, impose duties outside the institution’s competence, and treat the resulting disruption as proof that the system was defective all along.

Courts can stop an order after lawsuits are filed. They cannot supply courage to officials who possess authority but decline to exercise it. Nor can judicial intervention erase the lesson delivered to future administrations: nominally independent institutions may bend long before they are formally captured.

The order failed because litigation interrupted it, not because the executive branch respected legal boundaries or postal leadership firmly defended its mandate. A system that depends on last-minute rescue has not neutralized the abuse of power. It has merely survived one attempt.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: The untold origins of Trump’s plan to sharply restrict mail-in voting

item.title: Trump’s economic blueprint backfires as inflation climbs: WSJ
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing at the White House, on the one-year mark into his second term in office, in Washington, D.C., U.S., January 20, 2026. REUTERS Nathan Howard

What happened

AlterNet, citing The Wall Street Journal, reports that key parts of President Donald Trump’s economic program produced the opposite of his promised result: inflation rose, the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above its Inauguration Day level, and consumer borrowing remained expensive. The reported drivers included tariffs, tax cuts and new spending without the promised fiscal restraint, immigration restrictions that reduced labor-force growth, and higher energy prices during the prolonged conflict with Iran.

The Labor Department reported that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in August and 3.4% over the preceding year. Gasoline increased 3.9% that month and accounted for more than one-third of the monthly rise. The Federal Reserve subsequently raised its benchmark rate by a quarter-point to a 3.75%–4% target range—its first increase since 2023—and indicated another increase was possible before year-end if inflation remained high.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump continued demanding a federal funds rate of 1%. Economists interviewed by Reuters warned that such a sharp cut could increase inflation expectations, weaken the dollar, and drive longer-term Treasury yields higher—the reverse of the cheaper credit Trump says he wants.

The power belongs to the White House

This was not an economy merely happening to Trump. The administration controlled the policies the reporting identifies as new sources of price pressure. It imposed tariffs that increased import costs, restricted immigration in ways the Journal said slowed labor-force growth, and failed to deliver the fiscal restraint its own strategy required.

Outside forces mattered, particularly higher energy costs associated with the Iran conflict. So did continued consumer spending and business investment. But those qualifications do not erase presidential agency. The White House chose policies that added inflationary pressure while promising they would reduce prices and borrowing costs.

The contradiction was built in

Trump’s blueprint asked financial markets to believe in discipline while the government pursued tax cuts and additional spending. Jessica Riedl, a former Republican Senate aide, called the resulting inflation problems “entirely predictable.” The central failure was therefore not obscure technical confusion. The program contained conflicting demands from the beginning.

Tariffs make imported goods more expensive. A smaller labor-force growth rate can constrain productive capacity. Fiscal expansion can sustain demand. Pressuring the Fed for dramatically lower rates while inflation remains elevated adds another inflationary signal. Labeling all of this an unfortunate “backfire” risks making a policy collision sound accidental.

The Fed cannot repeal arithmetic

The administration wanted borrowing costs to fall without first resolving the pressures keeping inflation high. But the Federal Reserve’s institutional mandate does not include validating a president’s sales pitch. With economic growth still supported by consumption and business investment, policymakers reported no need to cut rates to rescue demand. Persistent inflation instead pushed them toward tightening.

Trump’s demand for a 1% federal funds rate treats the central bank as an instrument of political convenience. The Reuters economists’ warning exposes the flaw: forcing short-term rates down does not guarantee cheaper long-term borrowing. If markets expect more inflation or a weaker dollar, Treasury yields—and therefore mortgages, car loans, and other credit costs—can rise.

The public absorbs the failure

The administration can argue with the Fed, but households still receive the bills. Higher gasoline prices consume income immediately. Elevated Treasury yields feed into expensive mortgages and other loans. Tariffs transfer part of the administration’s trade strategy into the prices paid by importers, businesses, and consumers.

That distribution of consequences matters. The officials making the decisions can blame monetary policy or external shocks; borrowers cannot negotiate with the interest rate on that basis. Political control remains concentrated at the top, while the costs are dispersed across millions of household budgets.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is government by promise first and mechanism second. The White House advertised lower prices, cheaper money, tax cuts, tariffs, restricted labor supply, new spending, and pressure for easy monetary policy as though these choices carried no tensions or tradeoffs.

When the promised outcome failed to appear, the institutional pressure shifted toward the Federal Reserve—the actor expected to contain the inflation that other policies helped intensify. That is the misdirection: executive decisions create or worsen the constraint, then the institution responding to that constraint is cast as the obstacle. The economic damage is real, but the political maneuver is just as important: power claims credit for every favorable number and assigns responsibility elsewhere when its own program collides with reality.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s economic blueprint backfires as inflation climbs: WSJ

item.title: Trump's rural base is angry, exhausted and ready to sit this one out
item.description:
Photo: The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith’s America Project, Library of Congress

What happened

AlterNet reports that Bulwark publisher and pollster Sarah Longwell believes Republican turnout could weaken in November because some GOP voters in her focus groups are angry about “the war” and gasoline prices. Rather than vote Democratic, she said, these dissatisfied Republicans may stay home—an “undertow” that could help produce Democratic gains.

At a Sunday event in Dayton, Ohio, former Republican strategist Tim Miller identified Iowa and Kansas as long-shot Democratic opportunities, while arguing that Republicans could protect their rural advantage through attack ads. Longwell added that Republican candidates were distancing themselves from Donald Trump on war and deportation policy, though the article names neither the candidates nor the specific contests.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The reporting does not establish that Trump’s rural base broadly intends to sit out. It presents Longwell’s interpretation of unspecified focus groups and political forecasts from two Bulwark figures. No sample sizes, dates, polling results, or representative interviews with rural voters are supplied.

Power belongs to the governing party

The strongest political point here is not that rural voters are moody. It is that Republicans built a party whose electoral machinery depends heavily on Trump’s personal ability to mobilize supporters. Longwell’s question—what remains when he is not on the ballot—goes directly to the institutional weakness beneath that arrangement.

Republican officeholders and strategists are not powerless observers of voter frustration. They choose the party’s candidates, messages, legislative priorities, and loyalty tests. If the coalition lacks a durable agenda beyond Trump, that is an organizational decision made by people who hold party offices, raise money, approve advertising, and govern.

Discontent is not defection

Longwell’s “undertow” theory draws an important distinction: refusing to vote is not the same as changing political allegiance. A Republican who stays home because of war or fuel prices has not necessarily embraced Democratic policy. Depressed turnout can alter an election without producing any broader ideological realignment.

That makes talk of a “blue wave” potentially misleading. A victory created partly by Republican abstention would still transfer institutional power, but it would not prove that Democrats had built lasting support in rural communities. Electoral arithmetic can punish a governing coalition while leaving the deeper partisan structure largely intact.

The headline outruns the evidence

AlterNet converts a focus-group observation into a sweeping claim about Trump’s rural base. The article provides no basis for measuring how widespread the reported anger is, whether it is concentrated in particular states, or how reliably it predicts turnout. It also slides between Republicans generally and rural Republicans specifically without establishing that they are politically interchangeable.

That framing misdirects attention from identifiable decision-makers toward an amorphous bloc of “angry” voters. The consequential actors are Republican leaders who tied their party to one politician, candidates now deciding whether to distance themselves from his policies, and campaign professionals preparing to compensate with negative advertising. Rural voters are not merely an emotional weather system rolling over those choices.

Attack ads fill the policy vacuum

Miller’s Iowa scenario is blunt: if rural economic dissatisfaction threatens Republican control, portray the Democrat as a liberal extremist. That is not an answer to food or fuel costs. It is an attempt to make cultural fear more electorally powerful than material frustration.

The strategy reveals the incentive structure. When a party cannot rely on enthusiasm for its program, it can still mobilize voters against a caricature of the opposition. The article treats this largely as campaign calculation, but the political consequence is larger: economic pain becomes raw material for partisan targeting while responsibility for governing decisions disappears behind an advertising label.

A coalition built around one man

The broader pattern is a party that accumulated institutional power while weakening its independent political identity. Kevin McCarthy’s reported description of Trump as a “turnout machine” captures the bargain: personal loyalty can energize occasional voters, but it leaves candidates exposed when the personality is absent or unpopular.

If Republicans lose ground, the cause will not simply be an exhausted rural electorate. It will also be the choices of party leaders who substituted personal mobilization and enemy construction for a durable governing coalition. The available reporting does not prove a rural revolt. It does show why a party organized around one man may discover that it has built dependence, not strength.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump’s rural base is angry, exhausted and ready to sit this one out

item.title: Legal scholar makes the case to indict Trump for war crimes
item.description:
President Donald Trump with members of the military at Dover Air Force Base in Dover, Delaware, March 7, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

AlterNet reports that Pace University law professor and former New York anti-corruption prosecutor Bennett L. Gershman argued in a Hill op-ed that President Donald Trump and members of his administration should face International Criminal Court prosecution for alleged war crimes. Gershman centered his case on the February 28, 2026, U.S. bombing of a girls’ school in Minab, Iran, which killed 157 people.

According to Gershman, a U.N. Human Rights Council report found “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States committed war crimes. He said photographs and satellite imagery showed the site was a functioning school with children present, and that the report identified its courtyard as the intended point of impact rather than describing the deaths as collateral damage from an errant strike.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Gershman also cited deadly U.S. boat strikes in Caribbean and Pacific waters and the invasion of Venezuela, but AlterNet provides few supporting details about those allegations. His argument is a demand for indictment, not an account of charges already filed or a judgment establishing criminal liability.

The power to choose a target

The decisive actors were not the children at the school, Iranian officials, or an abstraction called “war.” Gershman’s account assigns agency to Trump, who launched the war, and to the administration and military apparatus that selected, approved, and attacked the target.

That distinction matters because the language surrounding airstrikes routinely launders decisions into events. Buildings are “hit.” Civilians “die.” Intelligence “fails.” The chain of command disappears into grammar.

If the U.N. findings are as Gershman describes them, the central fact is not merely that a military operation produced a terrible outcome. It is that visible evidence of a school and children allegedly existed before an attack whose intended impact point was the courtyard. That raises a direct question about who authorized the strike and on what claimed legal and factual basis.

“Tragedy” is not an explanation

Gershman identifies the institutional habit that shields state violence: scrutiny fades when the evidence is technical, dispersed and controlled by the government that used the weapons. Targeting records, munition data and post-strike assessments determine whether the public sees a crime, an error or nothing at all.

Calling such an episode a “war tragedy” can therefore misdirect attention from powerful decision-makers toward the supposed fog of conflict. Fog is not agency. If officials chose the target despite evidence that it was a girls’ school, confusion would be an inadequate description. But AlterNet’s account does not supply the underlying targeting records, so intent beyond the reported finding about the point of impact remains a matter requiring evidence and adjudication.

Impunity speaks in public

Gershman placed the bombing beside Trump’s later U.N. address, where the president threatened to “annihilate” Iran, celebrated strength and invoked the spoils of victory. Those remarks do not by themselves prove criminal responsibility for a particular strike. They do, however, show the governing posture Gershman is challenging: force presented as its own justification and dominance treated as a substitute for law.

The institutional imbalance is stark. A president commands military power, controls substantial information about its use and can publicly glorify coercion. The dead have no comparable machinery. Their families depend on investigators, courts and journalists willing to reconstruct decisions that the state can obscure behind classification and euphemism.

A case requires more than outrage

AlterNet’s framing is strongest when it identifies the school bombing as the core allegation. It is weaker when it rapidly adds boat strikes and the Venezuela invasion without giving readers enough evidence to assess those claims. A catalogue of alleged abuses is not a substitute for establishing command responsibility, jurisdiction and the facts of each incident.

That gap matters precisely because the accusation is grave. War-crimes accountability should not rest on rhetorical accumulation. It requires identifying the order, the target assessment, the officials involved, the applicable law and the evidence connecting individual defendants to the alleged crime. Gershman is making the case for that process; the article does not establish that the process has produced an indictment.

The architecture of selective accountability

The larger pattern is not simply that powerful states commit violence. It is that they retain extraordinary influence over whether their violence is investigated, named and punished. International law is most vulnerable when its application depends on the cooperation of the institutions and leaders it is supposed to constrain.

Gershman’s argument tests whether legal accountability follows evidence or geopolitical rank. If allegations involving a deliberately targeted school can be absorbed into a news cycle while officials boast of domination, the impunity is institutional, not accidental. The operative hierarchy becomes clear: weaker actors are subjected to law, while the powerful are permitted to describe their own conduct.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Legal scholar makes the case to indict Trump for war crimes

item.title: Trump biographer spills uncomfortable truth about Melania’s White House life
item.description:
U.S. first lady Melania Trump visits the Smithsonian’s National Museum Of Asian Art in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. Finn Gomez/Pool via REUTERS

What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff argues Melania Trump has turned her limited public presence as first lady into a lucrative media product. In a Monday column, he characterized her official work as largely performative and said forthcoming media projects monetize the mystery surrounding her life rather than document a substantial public role.

Wolff also contends that journalists rarely probe her residence, marriage, relationships, or announced initiatives because scrutiny can bring letters from her lawyers. AlterNet does not independently establish those claims, detail the reported payments, or prove that any organization she announced was fictitious. The article presents Wolff’s interpretation amid a threatened defamation suit, not a settled account of Melania Trump’s conduct.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The office is the asset

A first lady is not elected and holds no formal governing authority. But the position supplies public resources, ceremonial legitimacy, extraordinary access, and a guaranteed audience. That makes the central question less about whether Melania Trump performs traditional first-lady duties and more about how proximity to presidential power is converted into private value.

Wolff’s claim is that the scarcity itself has become marketable: absence produces intrigue, intrigue produces content, and the White House supplies the branding. If his account is accurate, withdrawal from public responsibility is not merely a personal preference. It becomes part of the commercial product.

Power without accountability

Donald Trump holds the institutional power in this arrangement. The presidency creates the platform, and the first lady’s status derives from it. Melania Trump retains agency over how she uses that status, while media companies decide whether to pay for access to her image and story.

AlterNet says Wolff specifically points to Amazon and Jeff Bezos, alleging that an unusually large payment reflects Bezos’s interest in favorable relations with the White House. The article supplies no evidence establishing that motive, so it should not be treated as fact. What it does establish is the political vulnerability: when a company controlled by someone with business interests before the federal government buys prestige content from the president’s spouse, the transaction deserves scrutiny beyond entertainment coverage.

Lawyers and the scrutiny gap

According to Wolff, the threat of legal action helps explain why reporters avoid basic questions about Melania Trump’s life and official activity. A lawyer’s letter does not prove wrongdoing, nor does it invalidate legitimate reporting. But legal pressure can raise the price of inquiry, especially for smaller outlets and individual journalists.

That imbalance matters. A first family has money, access, attorneys, and the authority conferred by the presidency. Reporters must absorb the financial risk of testing disputed claims. When coverage retreats into gossip about personality and mystique, the more consequential questions—public resources, commercial arrangements, access, and conflicts—remain conveniently underexamined.

The convenient misdirection

AlterNet’s article partly reproduces the weakness it describes. It centers a biographer “dragging” the first lady and spends considerable space on her supposed emptiness. That framing invites readers to judge whether Melania Trump is interesting, industrious, independent, or cynical. None of those judgments reaches the institutional issue.

The stronger question is who profits from proximity to executive power and what safeguards apply. Treating the story as a clash between a caustic biographer and an elusive celebrity spouse shifts attention away from the president, the corporations purchasing the product, and the press institutions deciding how aggressively to examine those relationships.

Government as a licensing brand

The larger pattern is the conversion of public office into private intellectual property. Official status generates attention; controlled access creates scarcity; corporate money turns that scarcity into content. Traditional first-lady advocacy was never democratically accountable, but commercialization makes the conflict sharper: the public supplies the prominence while private parties capture the revenue.

Wolff’s harshest conclusions remain allegations and interpretations, not findings established by AlterNet’s reporting. Yet the structural concern does not depend on accepting every insult. When the presidency functions as a family brand, spectacle becomes a shield: coverage debates the performance while the monetization of political access proceeds behind it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump biographer spills uncomfortable truth about Melania’s White House life

item.title: Trump has finally united Americans with one simple word
item.description:
REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

The word is “corruption.” AlterNet argues that Donald Trump has helped unite Americans around it: cited polls found overwhelming majorities across party lines describing corruption as endemic or systemic, while separate surveys showed substantial concern about Trump’s use of presidential power for personal profit.

The outlet cites an August Reuters/Ipsos poll in which nearly 70% said Trump uses presidential power “inappropriately” for personal gain, a UMass-Amherst poll in which 53% called the presidency the federal government’s most corrupt element, and an Economist/YouGov poll in which respondents most frequently chose “corrupt” to describe him. AlterNet contends that Democrats could benefit in the midterms but warns that doing so credibly would require reforms within their own ranks.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power has an address

General disgust with “Washington” can obscure responsibility. The presidency commands executive agencies, controls appointments and grants extraordinary access to state power. Congress, meanwhile, can investigate, legislate and impose financial-disclosure rules. These institutions are not spectators to corruption; they determine whether conflicts are exposed, constrained or normalized.

The polling described by AlterNet matters because respondents were not merely blaming an abstract government. In the cited UMass-Amherst survey, a majority identified the presidency as its most corrupt component. That finding directs scrutiny toward the office with the greatest concentration of individual federal power—and toward Trump’s reported use of that office.

Consensus is not accountability

A public can overwhelmingly perceive corruption while institutions continue permitting it. Ninety-seven percent calling corruption systemic, as reported in separate UMass-Amherst and Brennan Center surveys, does not itself produce an investigation, a prohibition or a penalty.

The decisive actors remain officeholders. Republicans surrounding Trump have the power to scrutinize his conduct or shield it. Democrats have the power to pursue enforceable reforms or reduce corruption to campaign language. Voters can change congressional control, but elected officials write the rules and decide whether oversight has consequences.

The bipartisan escape hatch

AlterNet acknowledges misconduct across party lines, then argues that Trump-era Republican conduct is unusually brazen and disproportionate. That distinction is essential. “Both parties” can be technically accurate and politically deceptive when it collapses differences in scale, proximity to power and institutional response.

Democratic stock trading is therefore neither irrelevant nor an excuse to blur responsibility. It is a test. A party asking voters to punish Republican corruption cannot preserve profitable conflicts for its own members without weakening both its case and any reform it claims to support.

Investigation is not conviction

AlterNet points to California Representative Robert Garcia’s promise that a Democratic House would investigate what he calls the “Trump crime family.” That is a partisan characterization and a proposed investigation, not a finding of criminal guilt.

The necessary distinction does not require timidity. Congress can examine financial relationships, conflicts of interest and uses of presidential authority without pretending the outcome is already established. Oversight becomes credible through evidence, public findings and rules that apply beyond one target—not through slogans that outrun the record.

Corruption thrives on abstraction

The larger pattern is institutional evasion. Political coverage often treats corruption as atmospheric decay: everyone smells it, nobody caused it, and responsibility dissolves into public cynicism. But corruption is not weather. It consists of identifiable decisions by people who possess power, assisted by officials who decline to restrain them.

AlterNet’s strongest point is not that Trump accidentally restored civic consciousness. It is that reported conduct associated with the country’s most powerful office has made corruption harder to discuss as a vague national defect. The remaining question is whether Congress will impose durable constraints—or merely convert public anger into another election-season asset.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump has finally united Americans with one simple word

item.title: ‘In all my years’: Crowd erupts as John Fetterman blurts out stunning ‘Freudian slip’
item.description:
U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) looks on as U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul (R-KY) presides over a vote whether to hold Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), in contempt for having invoked the Fifth Amendment in response to questions about the government’s COVID-19 pandemic response during a July 29 hearing, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 6, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that Sen. John Fetterman mistakenly called himself a “lifelong Republican” during a September 27, 2026 appearance at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin. CBS News moderator Major Garrett immediately corrected him, and Fetterman laughed before clarifying that he is a lifelong Democrat.

The mistake came after an audience member asked why Fetterman had not become an independent amid accusations that he had moved right and embraced President Donald Trump. Commentators including Don Winslow and former Democratic congressional nominee Russell Foster treated the remark as revealing, while Fetterman and Garrett predicted—correctly, given the ensuing coverage—that the clip would circulate widely.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory situates the episode within Fetterman’s clashes with fellow Democrats over Israel, the Iran war and border security. It also reports that he appeared by video at a Republican midterm convention that month and pledged to work with Trump to protect Pennsylvania’s steel industry.

The slip is not the evidence

Calling the mistake a “Freudian slip” gives a few mangled words more analytical weight than they can bear. The reporting establishes that Fetterman said “Republican,” was corrected and then said he meant “Democrat.” It does not establish whether the error exposed a hidden political identity.

The stronger evidence is his public conduct: the positions he has taken, the alliances he has advertised and the party events he has joined. Those are decisions, not verbal accidents. Winslow and Foster may regard the mistake as confirmation, but their interpretations remain interpretations.

Fetterman holds the power

The audience could laugh and jeer. Online commentators could produce cutting posts. Neither group controls a Senate vote.

Fetterman does. He holds federal office, possesses a platform unavailable to ordinary critics and can lend Democratic legitimacy to Trump-backed policies or Republican political events while retaining the institutional advantages of Democratic membership. The consequential question is not what label briefly escaped his mouth. It is how he uses the authority Pennsylvania voters gave him.

The clip provides an escape hatch

RawStory’s framing turns a dispute over power into a spectacle about authenticity. Was the senator’s mistake secretly truthful? Was it uniquely revealing? Those questions are irresistible online because they require no sustained examination of legislation, coalition-building or material consequences.

That misdirection also benefits the officeholder. A senator can laugh off a gaffe. It is harder to laugh off a record. Garrett’s invitation for the internet to “spin wildly” accurately described the media cycle, but it also helped substitute virality for scrutiny.

Party identity without accountability

The episode points to a broader weakness in party-based political coverage: affiliation is often treated as ideology, even when an official’s choices strain the label. Fetterman’s critics are responding not merely to branding but, according to RawStory, to his positions on several major issues and his appearance at a GOP convention.

That does not make every accusation against him self-proving, nor does one appearance erase his Democratic affiliation. It does show why arguments over whether he should “become an independent” can obscure the operative arrangement. He can remain inside the Democratic Party while choosing when to support Trump and when to invoke bipartisanship.

The system prefers symbolism

The larger pattern is a political press that often makes personality the story when institutional behavior is available for examination. A verbal slip becomes a referendum on a senator’s soul; his exercise of power becomes background context.

That ordering is backward. Fetterman’s accidental word choice may be comic, awkward or politically useful to his critics. His deliberate decisions are what carry consequences. When coverage elevates the clip above the record, it does not expose power. It gives power somewhere to hide.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘In all my years’: Crowd erupts as John Fetterman blurts out stunning ‘Freudian slip’

item.title: Trump caught with mouth 'agape' due to Natalie Harp distraction during game
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump and his executive assistant Natalie Harp exit Marine One at the Ellipse near the White House, in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 16, 2026. REUTERS/Annabelle Gordon

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump briefly looked away from the Tennessee–Texas football game at Neyland Stadium on Saturday to view a laptop held up by aide Natalie Harp. Photographs from Reuters, AFP and Getty Images show Trump leaning across Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty as Harp pointed toward the screen. The reporting does not establish what Trump was shown.

According to reports cited by RawStory, Harp supplies Trump with news coverage and social-media posts and publishes Truth Social messages he dictates. Trump left the Knoxville game at halftime. Videos shared online appeared to show some fans booing when he appeared on the stadium screen, though RawStory does not establish the scale of that reaction.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The screen is not the story

The photograph is political candy: Trump and Hagerty with their mouths supposedly “agape,” staring at an unidentified screen. But a facial expression proves nothing, and the contents of the laptop remain unknown. The headline turns an unexplained moment into a teasing spectacle.

That framing is weak. The consequential issue is not that a president was distracted during a football game. It is that an aide reportedly occupies a privileged position between the president and the information he receives.

Access is power

Trump holds the institutional power. Harp does not make presidential decisions merely because she handles articles, posts and dictated messages. But proximity to presidential attention can still confer substantial influence, especially when an aide reportedly selects material to place directly before him.

Calling Harp a “human printer” trivializes that function. If the cited accounts are accurate, she helps manage both inputs and outputs: what Trump sees and what appears under his name online. That is not clerical work in any meaningful political sense. It is access management inside the presidency.

The blame belongs upward

The article gestures toward concern that Harp may control too much of Trump’s information flow. That risks misdirecting responsibility toward the subordinate. Trump chose this arrangement and remains responsible for the information habits surrounding his office.

An aide can curate coverage only because the president permits, rewards or requests it. The central agency therefore belongs to Trump, not to the staffer holding the laptop. Portraying him as passively captured by an aide’s flattering material would obscure the power hierarchy.

Spectacle crowds out scrutiny

The coverage offers several irresistible diversions: an open mouth, alleged boos, an early departure and even a warning that presidential movements might disrupt team headsets. These details generate attention without establishing much about governance.

The sourced reporting about Harp’s role matters more. A presidency whose public communication may pass through a highly trusted personal aide raises concrete questions about recordkeeping, accountability and the concentration of informal influence. RawStory supplies no evidence that Harp distorted a specific decision, so stronger claims would be speculation. But the structure itself deserves more scrutiny than the stadium reaction shot.

The systemic error

Political journalism routinely mistakes visible oddity for usable evidence. It fixates on the embarrassing image while leaving the governing arrangement in soft focus.

The larger pattern is a personalization of state power: consequential access organized through loyalty, proximity and one person’s media appetite. The laptop’s contents are unknown. The hierarchy is not. Trump possesses the authority, Trump chose the people around him, and Trump bears responsibility for how presidential attention is managed.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump caught with mouth ‘agape’ due to Natalie Harp distraction during game

item.title: Collapse: Grim conservative media trend proves Trump is losing his grip
item.description:
REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

AlterNet columnist Robert Reich argues that Donald Trump’s political position was weakening five weeks before the midterm elections. He cites September polling showing Trump at 37 percent approval and Republican confidence in the economy falling from more than 70 percent in January to 29 percent. He also points to Republican candidates distancing themselves from Trump on tariffs, beef imports and the war against Iran.

Reich’s most novel evidence is a decline in Trump’s presence on conservative podcasts: mentions per hour had fallen nearly 70 percent from their pre-2024-election peak, while monthly mentions had dropped 30 percent since the United States launched the war in late February. That shows reduced attention in one segment of conservative media. It does not, by itself, prove that Trump had lost control of the Republican Party or its institutions.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Reich remains “nauseously optimistic,” warning that right-wing billionaires were financing Republican campaigns while the administration could use federal power to disrupt elections. He cites the Supreme Court’s removal of restrictions on a Trump-backed federal voter database and the administration’s refusal, as reported, to rule out deploying ICE agents at polling places.

Attention is not authority

The headline turns a media metric into a declaration of political collapse. That is stronger than the evidence supports. Podcast hosts mentioning Trump less often may reflect audience fatigue, strategic avoidance or changing news priorities. The reporting does not establish which explanation is correct.

Nor does candidate discomfort equal rebellion. Senators Susan Collins, Roger Marshall and Pete Ricketts questioned policies affecting constituencies essential to their reelection campaigns. Seven House Republicans voted to require congressional authorization for hostilities against Iran. These are meaningful fractures, but they remain selective acts of self-preservation—not evidence that Republicans have withdrawn their broader support from Trump.

The power is still institutional

Trump’s real power does not depend on how often podcasters say his name. It rests in the presidency, control of the executive branch and the Republican officials willing to sustain his agenda. Congress holds war-making and oversight powers, but those powers matter only when legislators use them consistently rather than briefly defecting under electoral pressure.

The Supreme Court’s reported intervention on the federal voter database is more consequential than a fading podcast count. So is the administration’s refusal to exclude ICE activity at polling places. Reich does not establish that agents were deployed or that interference occurred. He does identify where the capacity for coercion resides: inside federal institutions, not among ordinary voters being urged to canvass harder.

Retreat without accountability

Republican candidates are not powerless bystanders discovering that Trump’s policies have unfortunate side effects. They are officeholders seeking renewed authority after their party enabled the administration. Distancing themselves when tariffs threaten aircraft production, ranchers or small businesses does not erase that relationship.

Coverage that emphasizes their “unease” risks laundering agency. The relevant question is not whether individual Republicans feel nervous. It is whether they will use their votes, committee powers and public offices to constrain the policies they now find electorally inconvenient. Anxiety is not opposition, and rhetorical distance imposes no institutional cost.

Money changes the battlefield

Reich correctly shifts attention from polling momentum to material power: billionaire-funded advertising can shape races even when the president is unpopular. Wealthy donors do not need to rehabilitate Trump personally if they can preserve Republican control through candidate-specific spending and attacks on Democrats.

But the column compresses several distinct dangers—campaign spending, alleged falsehoods in advertising, election administration and possible federal intimidation—into one surge of alarm. The sharper analysis is that these mechanisms operate differently and require different evidence. Money amplifies propaganda; government controls enforcement machinery; courts determine which restraints remain in place. Treating them as one generalized menace can obscure who is responsible for each decision.

The system behind the mood

The larger pattern is not a collapsing personality cult. It is a governing coalition learning when to mute its leader without surrendering the power accumulated around him. Conservative media can reduce Trump’s visibility, vulnerable Republicans can criticize discrete policies, and donors can redirect attention toward individual races—all while the institutional project continues.

Polls and podcast counts measure public mood. Courts, executive agencies, congressional votes and concentrated wealth determine what that mood can change. A movement does not lose its grip merely because its central figure becomes less marketable. The decisive test is whether the officials and financiers who converted his popularity into power stop protecting the machinery. Reich’s evidence shows strain. It does not yet show that break.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Collapse: Grim conservative media trend proves Trump is losing his grip
