item.title: Trump White House diet spurs blunt warning by ex-GOP White House doc: 'Will raise BP’
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick react during a cabinet meeting in the Cabinet Room at the White House, in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 27, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

What happened

RawStory reports that cardiologist Jonathan Reiner warned that a meat-heavy diet can work against statin treatment and that sauerkraut’s sodium content can raise blood pressure. Responding on September 27, 2026, to commentary about Trump administration officials reportedly following a “living diet,” Reiner said President Donald Trump should take nutritional advice from his doctor rather than Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The report does not establish that Trump follows this diet. Law professor Dorit Reiss explicitly doubted that he does. It identifies Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Vice President JD Vance and Kennedy as reported adherents, while noting that Trump has taken a statin for years.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The headline outruns the evidence

The supposed “Trump White House diet” is doing too much work. The reporting links several administration officials to the regimen but supplies no evidence that the president adopted it, received dietary instructions from Kennedy or disregarded medical advice.

Reiner’s warning is straightforward medical commentary. RawStory turns it into a Trump-health teaser, using the president’s age, medication and familiar eating habits to imply a conflict that the article cannot confirm. That is not accountability reporting. It is speculation arranged around a recognizable name.

Where the power actually sits

The politically relevant actor is not Trump the prospective sauerkraut eater. It is Kennedy, who controls the Department of Health and Human Services and has placed diet at the center of his “Make America Healthy Again” agenda.

Personal eccentricity becomes politically consequential when an official with authority over federal health policy elevates it into a governing framework. Kennedy’s institutional position gives him influence over agencies, priorities and public messaging. Trump supplied that power by making him HHS secretary. Whether Trump copies his menu is far less important than whether the department converts Kennedy’s preferences into policy.

Spectacle substitutes for scrutiny

The article offers cabinet dining habits as a proxy for examining the administration’s health agenda. That is an easy trade: meat, sauerkraut and Trump’s ketchup invite clicks, while departmental decisions require evidence and sustained scrutiny.

The framing also risks misdirecting responsibility toward individual consumers. People choosing a fashionable diet do not wield the same power as the official promoting health doctrine from the federal government’s top health post—or the president who placed him there. The chain of authority is clear even where the chain of dietary influence is not.

The governing pattern

Modern political coverage repeatedly shrinks institutional power into lifestyle spectacle. An administration’s ideology becomes a cabinet fad; an agency chief becomes a colorful personality; policy consequences disappear behind jokes about what powerful people eat.

The systemic error is not covering an influential official’s health claims. It is treating the most trivial possible consequence—what might be on the president’s plate—as the center of the story. The real question is what Kennedy’s ideas do once backed by federal authority. RawStory’s report never gets there.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump White House diet spurs blunt warning by ex-GOP White House doc: ‘Will raise BP’

item.title: 'They're just stealing your money': Fury as Trump drops another 'absolutely demented' ad
item.description:
Sep 27, 2026; Medinah, Illinois, USA; President Donald Trump addresses the gallery during the final round of the Presidents Cup. Mandatory Credit: Jerod Ringwald-Imagn Images

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump’s administration released a black-and-white advertisement on September 27, 2026, using footage and rhetoric from his 2024 campaign. Trump speaks of a “final battle” to purge enemies from government and confront the media; the closing screen identifies the ad as paid for by the U.S. government.

The administration released it roughly five weeks before the midterm elections and only days after another disputed government-funded Trump advertisement, according to RawStory. Journalists and an immigration lawyer condemned the new ad as campaign propaganda financed by taxpayers, with some alleging the expenditure was illegal. The report does not establish the ad’s cost, where it aired, which agency authorized it, what appropriation funded it, or whether any authority has found the spending unlawful.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power is inside the executive branch

The decisive actor is not the collection of critics quoted from X. It is the administration controlling the government personnel, money, and communications machinery used to produce or distribute the advertisement.

Trump supplies the message and political persona. His administration supplies the institutional conversion: campaign imagery becomes government speech, and government resources become a vehicle for promoting the president’s political narrative. Taxpayers have no comparable power over that transaction at the moment it occurs.

Propaganda with an official receipt

The most consequential detail is not that the advertisement looks “demented” or resembles a horror film. Those descriptions turn an exercise of state power into an argument about taste.

The closing government-funding notice raises the real question: why is public money carrying rhetoric associated with Trump’s electoral campaign shortly before a federal election? Calling the press “fake news” and promising to purge vaguely defined enemies may be familiar Trump material, but government sponsorship changes its political function. It places the authority and resources of the state behind a leader’s factional message.

Outrage is not accountability

RawStory documents anger but leaves the machinery largely concealed. Readers are given posts from journalists and a lawyer, yet not the name of the agency that approved the ad, the official who signed off, the funding source, the distribution plan, or the legal rationale.

That is a serious reporting weakness. One critic alleges illegality, but the article supplies no statute, ruling, or official review supporting that conclusion. The allegation matters; it is not a finding. Without following the authorization chain, coverage risks substituting social-media fury for institutional scrutiny.

The enemy list does political work

The advertisement’s language divides the country between Trump’s supporters and a collection of internal enemies: the “deep state,” “warmongers,” and the press. The categories are broad enough to absorb civil servants, policy opponents, journalists, or anyone else the administration chooses to place inside them.

The reported language therefore does more than advertise policy. It frames government as a weapon to be reclaimed from illegitimate occupants and used in a final confrontation. RawStory does not establish what concrete actions would follow, but the political structure is clear: loyalty is presented as public virtue, opposition as contamination, and institutional restraint as enemy control.

When government becomes campaign property

The larger pattern is the erosion of the boundary between governing and campaigning. An incumbent administration possesses public funds, official platforms, staff, and the symbolic authority of the presidency. Using those assets to circulate campaign-era messaging gives the officeholder an advantage that opponents and ordinary citizens cannot reproduce.

The scandal is not merely that taxpayers may have financed an ugly advertisement. It is that public institutions can be treated as the incumbent’s political property while coverage stops at reactions. The unanswered questions—who authorized it, under what authority, for how much, and through which channels—are where responsibility lives.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘They’re just stealing your money’: Fury as Trump drops another ‘absolutely demented’ ad

item.title: 'Danger for Trump': Maggie Haberman spills convos with 'freaked out' Republicans
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) listens as U.S. Representative Carlos Gimenez (R-FL) addresses reporters, on the day of a House Republican Conference meeting on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on July 14, 2026. REUTERS/Ken Cedeno

What happened

RawStory reports that New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman told the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin that Republicans she speaks with expect serious losses in November. She quoted a former Trump voter in Miami who called President Donald Trump “a real disappointment” and “just another politician.” Haberman argued that this disillusionment is the political danger: Trump sold himself as an exception to ordinary politics, but some voters now see continuity and failure.

Haberman said Trump had failed to deliver on three defining promises: lowering prices, rejecting “forever wars,” and draining the swamp. RawStory also cites Republican strategist Karl Rove warning against centering Trump in the midterms, an unnamed House Republican predicting crushing losses, and Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds reducing references to Trump’s endorsement on his campaign website—an account Trump denied as a “Fake Story.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Republicans own the record

The institutional power here belongs to Trump and the Republican Party. They cannot plausibly campaign as spectators to the conditions voters judge them on. Trump made the promises, Republican candidates attached themselves to his political brand, and the party now faces the consequences of governing under it.

The unnamed lawmakers expressing panic are not powerless witnesses. They are members of the coalition that enabled Trump’s agenda and benefited from his support. Their fear concerns electoral punishment, not a newly discovered lack of agency.

The product has become the liability

Haberman’s quoted voter identifies the deepest breach: Trump’s claim to be fundamentally different has collided with the perception that he is “just another politician.” For a conventional candidate, disappointment can be survivable. For a movement built around one man’s supposed singularity, ordinariness is corrosive.

The reported gap between promise and result matters more than the mythology. Trump promised lower prices, retreat from protracted wars, and an assault on entrenched power. According to Haberman’s account, Republicans now fear voters can see that those pledges were not fulfilled. A political identity built on personal dominance cannot easily transfer responsibility elsewhere when the promised outcomes fail to arrive.

Panic is not accountability

Republican alarm should not be mistaken for repudiation. Rove’s concern, as reported, is that putting Trump at the center of the midterms is strategically damaging. Candidates creating distance are managing exposure. Neither response establishes opposition to the decisions that produced the liability.

That distinction is essential. Political coverage often treats private anxiety and tactical separation as evidence of an internal break. But fear of losing office is not the same as resistance while power is being exercised. These Republicans appear “freaked out” because the arrangement may now cost them, not because the article shows them challenging it when challenge carried a price.

The framing lets the party hide

RawStory packages the story around Haberman “spilling” private conversations, turning institutional failure into insider suspense. The stronger story is already visible: Republican officials helped construct a party centered on Trump, and some are now trying to protect themselves from the electoral consequences of that choice.

Anonymous predictions such as “We’re going to get crushed” offer drama without accountability. The lawmaker receives the benefit of appearing perceptive while avoiding responsibility for the party’s record. That is not revelation. It is a controlled leak from someone seeking distance without paying for dissent.

A party cannot outsource consequence

The larger pattern is familiar: leaders embrace centralized personal power when it mobilizes voters, then rediscover institutional separation when the leader becomes unpopular. Endorsements disappear from websites. Strategists recommend changing the subject. Unnamed officials brief reporters about catastrophe.

But the record remains collective. Trump supplied the promises and commands the party’s political center; Republican officials amplified him, enabled his agenda, and tied their fortunes to his authority. If voters punish that arrangement in November, the result will not be an inexplicable backlash against nervous bystanders. It will be accountability reaching the people who helped build the thing they now fear.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Danger for Trump’: Maggie Haberman spills convos with ‘freaked out’ Republicans

item.title: Kash Patel confuses with stunningly bizarre boast: 'Someone get this man a plaque’
item.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2025. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

RawStory reports that FBI Director Kash Patel posted a campaign-style infographic on September 27, 2026, boasting that he had made 101 calls to “foreign partners” during his first 18 months in office. Commentators noted that this amounted to roughly 1.3 calls per week. Progressive writer Alex Cole supplied the headline’s punch line: “Somebody get this man a commemorative plaque.”

The outlet places the post amid calls for Patel’s resignation and scrutiny of his conduct. It cites FBI records reportedly showing attention to online critics, allegations that he used government resources for trips connected to his girlfriend Alexis Wilkins, and criticism of his handling of Epstein-related files. RawStory also reports allegations involving FBI protection and transportation for Wilkins and a friend, as well as Patel’s firing of an FBI veteran he accused of leaking information about his travel.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power disguised as performance

The number of calls is not a meaningful measure of FBI leadership. It reveals nothing about the substance of those conversations, the decisions they produced, or whether they advanced legitimate law-enforcement objectives. Patel offered activity as achievement and branding as accountability.

That distinction matters because he does not occupy a ceremonial job. The FBI director controls an institution with enormous investigative, surveillance, personnel, and security powers. A self-congratulatory graphic about telephone use trivializes the standard by which that power should be judged.

The jokes are not the story

The ridicule is justified, but it can also shrink the scandal. Mocking Patel for celebrating basic office work is easier than examining what he allegedly did with public aircraft, armed personnel, disciplinary authority, and internal records.

The central issue is not that Patel’s boast was embarrassing. It is that an official facing serious questions about his stewardship answered with public relations theater. Counting phone calls directs attention toward a harmless metric and away from allegations involving state resources and retaliation against an employee accused of exposing controversial travel.

Accountability requires evidence

RawStory’s article bundles several allegations together but supplies limited underlying detail about most of them. Claims that Patel used an FBI jet to attend Wilkins’s performances, assigned a SWAT team to protect her, or had agents transport her reportedly intoxicated friend require documentary evidence, dates, costs, authorization records, and Patel’s response. The article does not establish those allegations merely by repeating them.

That evidentiary gap does not excuse institutional silence. It identifies where scrutiny belongs: official travel logs, protection decisions, personnel records, applicable FBI policies, and the authority under which resources were deployed. Sarcasm cannot substitute for that accounting.

The institution behind the man

Patel made the boast, and according to the reporting, he made or enabled the disputed personnel and resource decisions. But senior officials rarely act without subordinates approving logistics, processing expenses, accepting assignments, or declining to challenge dubious orders.

That is the larger power structure: a director can turn personal priorities into institutional action because the bureaucracy beneath him translates preference into policy. If safeguards exist only until the boss applies pressure, they are not safeguards. They are etiquette.

Propaganda by measurement

The infographic reflects a broader political habit: choose a number that sounds productive, detach it from any useful benchmark, and present it as proof of competence. The metric is designed to preempt judgment, not enable it.

Patel’s critics treated the graphic as an absurdity. More precisely, it is an attempt to define accountability downward. When powerful officials advertise routine motions while withholding the information needed to assess consequential decisions, the comedy serves the same function as the graphic: it risks making institutional failure look merely ridiculous.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Kash Patel confuses with stunningly bizarre boast: ‘Someone get this man a plaque’

item.title: Celebration erupts as heckler hits Trump where it hurts during golf cup: 'You are my hero’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump speaks during the Presidents Cup at the Medinah Country Club, in Medinah, Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that an attendee at the Presidents Cup in Medinah, Illinois, appeared to shout a profanity-laced accusation at President Donald Trump during his Sunday remarks. The words are not independently established in the report; several online commentators interpreted the heckler as calling Trump a “pedophile,” and some in the crowd cheered.

Former Trump supporter and right-wing influencer Breck Worsham circulated a clip and called the unidentified heckler her “hero.” RawStory connects the outburst to criticism of the administration’s handling of Jeffrey Epstein-related files, which it says were released only after Trump unsuccessfully sought to block legislation compelling disclosure.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The interruption did not turn the event against Trump. He subsequently received louder cheers and chants of “four more years.”

The headline outruns the evidence

The report does not establish that the insult “hit Trump where it hurts.” It supplies no response from Trump, no evidence that he understood the words, and no measurable political consequence. His appearance was not derailed; the crowd soon resumed celebrating him.

That framing converts an ambiguous interruption into a satisfying story of humiliation. It is engagement bait masquerading as political consequence. A heckle can expose public anger, but virality is not accountability.

Power was never in the gallery

Trump held the institutional power in this scene: the presidency, control over the executive branch, and a prestigious public platform. The anonymous attendee had a voice for a few seconds. Worsham had an audience large enough to amplify it. Neither controlled the government’s handling of records, enforcement decisions, or disclosure policy.

The consequential conduct identified by RawStory is not the insult. It is the administration’s handling of Epstein-related files and Trump’s reported attempt to stop legislation requiring their release. That is where agency belongs—on the officials who possessed authority over government information and on the lawmakers capable of compelling disclosure.

An accusation is not an argument

The reported epithet is a grave accusation, not evidence. RawStory does not substantiate it, and its uncertainty about the audio matters. Political commentary should not turn a crowd’s interpretation into a verified statement, much less a proven fact.

The earlier phrase “pedophile protector,” attributed to a Michigan autoworker, at least points toward an identifiable dispute: whether the administration resisted transparency around the Epstein records. Even then, the defensible scrutiny concerns documented decisions and obstruction claims—not guilt inferred from association or shouted labels.

Spectacle displaces accountability

The article devotes its emotional center to the heckler, the cheer, and Worsham’s approving post. That choice makes a powerless spectator the protagonist while reducing an exercise of presidential power to background context.

This is a familiar failure in political coverage. Institutions become scenery; confrontation becomes substance. Readers are invited to savor a moment of embarrassment instead of examining who controlled the files, what disclosure was resisted, and what the eventual release contained. The stronger story is harder and less instantly gratifying because it requires tracing authority rather than replaying a clip.

The system rewards catharsis

The episode shows how easily politics becomes a market for symbolic victories. A president can leave with his office, platform, and supportive crowd intact while opponents celebrate a few seconds of heckling as a wound.

That is not a transfer of power. It is catharsis packaged as consequence. When coverage inflates ridicule and compresses institutional conduct, officials escape sustained scrutiny while spectators are handed the illusion that humiliation itself is accountability.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Celebration erupts as heckler hits Trump where it hurts during golf cup: ‘You are my hero’

item.title: The Trump White House 'sycophancy Olympics' and their bizarre 'living diet’
item.description:
(Official White House Photo by Molly Riley)

What happened

AlterNet reports that New York Times contributing writer Molly Jong-Fast described Donald Trump’s White House as a “sycophancy Olympics,” where officials compete through imitation and televised praise. The “living diet” in the headline refers to a reportedly shared regimen of meat and sauerkraut followed by several senior administration figures, including JD Vance, Howard Lutnick, Sean Duffy, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Jong-Fast also reported that Trump considered candidates’ cable-news performances when selecting officials and that, once appointed, their standing appeared to depend on flattering him and performing effectively on television. She argued that Democrats could constrain him through the midterms, Republicans could resist out of self-preservation, and the cabinet could theoretically invoke the 25th Amendment.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The clique controls the state

The high-school analogy is vivid, but it risks shrinking a structure of government into a personality drama. Trump is not merely the dominant member of a social circle. He is the president, with the institutional power to select senior officials and shape the incentives under which they serve.

That distinction matters. Matching shoes, shared diets, curated praise, and copied behavior are not politically important because they are embarrassing. They matter because they reportedly signal that proximity to power depends on personal conformity. The consequence is not just an absurd workplace culture. It is an administration in which officials may learn that loyalty displays are safer than unwelcome advice.

Appointment is the first act of control

If television “sizzle reels” influenced Trump’s personnel decisions as Jong-Fast reports, the central failure began before any televised cabinet flattery. Trump chose the criteria. He had the authority to reward spectacle over qualification and personal reassurance over independent judgment.

The officials who accepted those terms retain agency. They are not powerless students trapped at the wrong lunch table. They hold some of the country’s most consequential offices. When cabinet members praise the president publicly or imitate his preferences, they help sustain the system that elevated them.

Flattery is not governance

The story’s strongest evidence concerns an incentive structure: officials allegedly gain favor by delivering positive coverage, favorable polling, polished television appearances, and praise. That structure can filter information before it reaches the person with the most power.

The reporting does not establish that every official has abandoned substantive advice, nor does it document a particular policy failure caused by this culture. But the foreseeable risk is plain. A government organized around pleasing its leader makes candor professionally dangerous. Information becomes tribute, and public meetings become loyalty demonstrations instead of venues for accountability.

The metaphor misdirects blame

Calling Trump a “mean girl” makes the conduct recognizable, but it also makes it smaller. Teenage bullies do not appoint cabinet secretaries. Their admirers do not administer federal departments. Their classmates do not possess constitutional authority.

The framing also lets senior officials masquerade as victims of peer pressure. They are enabled actors with offices, platforms, and choices. Congressional Republicans likewise have agency; Jong-Fast’s suggestion that they might resist only when self-preservation requires it describes political calculation, not helplessness.

Personal rule needs institutional help

The larger pattern is the conversion of public office into a court organized around one person’s approval. The eccentricities are merely the visible uniform. The political substance is a hierarchy in which access, status, and perhaps continued influence are reportedly tied to performance of loyalty.

Such arrangements do not persist through one leader’s vanity alone. They require appointees willing to flatter, aides willing to curate reality, and legislators willing to postpone resistance until their own positions are endangered. The systemic error is treating those enablers as scenery when they are part of the machinery.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The Trump White House ‘sycophancy Olympics’ and their bizarre ‘living diet’

item.title: ‘Gobsmackingly bananas’ El Niño shatters global records
item.description:
NASA / VIIRS data courtesy of NOAA.

What happened

AlterNet, republishing Grist, reported that a developing El Niño had pushed temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region of the Pacific to 3.11 degrees Celsius above normal, surpassing the peak recorded in November 2015. Forecast models cited in the article put the chance of the event remaining “very strong” through the end of that year at 90 percent.

The report said the naturally occurring shift in Pacific winds and water was intensifying extreme weather against a background of rapid, fossil-fuel-driven warming. Scientists warned of consequences for public health, agriculture, hydropower and severe weather; one study projected as many as 451,000 heat-related deaths worldwide by the following February. The article also said California had declared a statewide emergency, but did not identify the issuing authority or provide the declaration’s date.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The atmosphere is not the decision-maker

El Niño redistributes heat. It does not approve drilling permits, finance fossil-fuel expansion or decide how much protection heat-exposed workers receive. The institutional power in this story belongs to governments, energy companies, financial institutions and regulators whose decisions determine emissions and preparedness.

The reporting acknowledges that fossil-fuel combustion supplies the warming backdrop, but its fascination with “super,” “Godzilla” and “gobsmackingly bananas” risks turning a political crisis into a vocabulary problem. The Pacific did not create the underlying vulnerability. Powerful institutions did—and continue to decide whether it deepens.

Spectacle can obscure responsibility

The argument over terminology is not meaningless. Officials must communicate danger without minimizing it or numbing the public through endless escalation. But a long discussion about whether “super El Niño” is scientifically respectable directs attention toward messengers while leaving decision-makers largely unnamed.

That is the central weakness in the framing. The article gives scientists names, measurements and quotations, yet identifies no government or corporate actor responsible for continuing the fossil-fuel dependence it invokes. Causation becomes atmospheric; agency disappears.

Disaster is administered politically

A forecast does not determine who dies. Heat protections, resilient electrical grids, public-health capacity, crop support and emergency planning shape the consequences. The projected death toll cited by the report was a study’s estimate, not a recorded outcome, but its scale makes the political stakes plain.

Those with the least institutional power are most likely to absorb failures made elsewhere. Workers cannot individually legislate heat standards. Farmers cannot stabilize global weather systems. Households cannot substitute personal preparedness for functioning infrastructure. Shifting the burden onto “awareness” would disguise a chain of public and private decisions as individual vulnerability.

Records are becoming alibis

Repeatedly calling each event unprecedented can make escalation sound unforeseeable. The reporting establishes the opposite: scientists were measuring the anomaly, modeling its persistence and warning about foreseeable effects. Uncertainty remained about the exact distribution and severity of those effects, not about the existence of serious risk.

The larger pattern is institutional delay followed by emergency management. Governments tolerate the conditions that magnify danger, then present declarations and disaster response as evidence of leadership. Preparation matters, but preparation without mitigation is management of a worsening baseline.

The system behind the weather

The useful political question is not whether “super” is dramatic enough. It is who can reduce the danger, who chooses not to use that power, and who pays for the choice.

El Niño is a natural phenomenon. A fossil-fueled climate, uneven protection and recurring institutional unpreparedness are not. Treating their combined damage as an astonishing act of nature launders political agency out of the story—and lets the institutions shaping the future pose as spectators to it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Gobsmackingly bananas’ El Niño shatters global records

item.title: ICE agents 'shocked and frustrated' after being told to 'scale back' in internal memo
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: Federal agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conduct an immigration enforcement operation in Pine Grove, Minnesota, U.S., January 28, 2026. REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton/File Photo

What happened

RawStory reports that ICE officers nationwide received verbal instructions over the weekend to temporarily stop arresting undocumented immigrants unless they had criminal convictions or pending charges. Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin said agents were “shocked and frustrated” by that direction, though none of his sources identified who issued it.

Melugin reported that the Trump administration quickly characterized the order as an erroneous “miscommunication” about prioritizing people deemed the “worst first.” Trump told him that anyone in the country illegally remained eligible for arrest and deportation. New guidance reversed the restriction that same night, allowing ICE to continue arresting people without criminal records, including those encountered as “collaterals.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

DHS publicly denied that anyone had been excluded from enforcement. The episode occurred as Republican lawmakers Maria Elvira Salazar and Roger Marshall criticized aspects of the administration’s immigration crackdown ahead of the midterm elections.

Power remained at the top

ICE agents did not determine the policy. Executive officials did. Whatever the unidentified origin of the first instruction, the administration had the institutional power to narrow arrests, reverse course, and direct field offices accordingly. It used that power within hours.

The operative decision was the reversal: ICE would continue arresting undocumented people without criminal records. Trump confirmed that position, DHS amplified it, and the agency transmitted replacement guidance. The government’s enforcement reach—not agents’ disappointment—is the central fact.

The mystery obscures the decision

The reporting cannot establish who initiated the temporary restriction. That is a legitimate unanswered question. But treating the entire episode as an inexplicable mix-up gives administrative fog more importance than the policy the administration ultimately affirmed.

“Miscommunication” is not an explanation. It identifies no official, decision-making chain, or accountability mechanism. DHS’s blanket denial likewise does not resolve Melugin’s report that field offices actually received both the original instruction and its reversal. The contradiction belongs to the administration that produced those messages, not to immigrants subject to them.

Agents are not the injured party

Centering officers who felt “shocked and frustrated” redirects sympathy toward armed federal personnel whose preferred enforcement latitude was briefly constrained. Their frustration may be real, but it is not the primary consequence of the policy.

The people bearing the state’s coercive power are undocumented immigrants without criminal records who remain eligible for arrest, including people swept up as collateral encounters. The reversal clarified that lacking a criminal record does not shield them from detention and deportation efforts.

Enforcement meets electoral pressure

The timing exposes a political tension inside the governing coalition. Some Republican lawmakers were criticizing the crackdown, while ICE personnel reportedly resisted even a temporary limitation on whom they could arrest.

The administration’s response was not a documented retreat from broad enforcement. It was rapid reassurance to agents and supporters that the target pool remained expansive. The available reporting does not establish why the first instruction was issued, but it does establish which position survived once political pressure reached the White House.

Ambiguity can still serve power

This episode reflects a familiar structure: opaque commands move downward, consequences fall on people with little institutional leverage, and responsibility dissolves upward into claims of confusion. The bureaucracy’s uncertainty does not reduce its coercive capacity.

The larger pattern is government by maximal authority and minimal accountability. Officials preserve broad enforcement discretion while declining to explain how a nationwide directive appeared, who authorized it, or why it required reversal. The machinery remains powerful precisely where its authorship becomes evasive.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ICE agents ‘shocked and frustrated’ after being told to ‘scale back’ in internal memo

item.title: Ex-GOP lawmaker says Republicans now resigned to hospice: 'Make the patient comfortable’
item.description:
U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy (R-LA) listens to an aide during a Senate Finance Committee hearing on health care costs on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., November 19, 2025. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

Former Republican Rep. Barbara Comstock told MS NOW that Republicans had effectively stopped trying to improve their November prospects and were instead attempting to “make the patient comfortable.” She called a GOP pollster’s prediction of Senate gains “delusional” and blamed Donald Trump for damaging Republican candidates over the summer.

Comstock cited the unpopular Iran war, high gasoline and beef prices, rising interest rates, and what she described as Trump’s failure to spend campaign money. She said Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins was trailing by double digits in Georgia and interpreted Trump’s planned October 2 rally in heavily Republican Alabama as political triage rather than an effort to compete elsewhere. RawStory did not provide the underlying polling, spending figures, or the Axios and Politico reports needed to assess those claims independently.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power is not the patient

The hospice metaphor turns the Republican Party into a passive body suffering an unexplained illness. Comstock’s own account describes something more concrete: the party’s dominant figure made choices that damaged its candidates, while Republican leaders failed to prevent or counter them.

Trump holds the power in this telling. He commands the attention, campaign money, and loyalty that shape Republican strategy. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and party donors possess institutional leverage of their own, but the reported response is not an organized break with Trump. It is resignation.

The enablers knew the prognosis

The unnamed operative’s remark matters because it suggests professionals inside the party understood the weakness of the campaign. Yet recognition without resistance is not helplessness. It is an institutional decision to manage expected losses while preserving the hierarchy that produced them.

Republican donors reportedly challenged an optimistic pollster, but donor irritation is not accountability. If party officials continue directing resources and appearances around Trump after concluding that he is hurting their candidates, they are enabling the outcome they privately lament.

A metaphor that conceals responsibility

“Make the patient comfortable” is memorable precisely because it removes the agents. Patients do not choose their disease. Political parties choose leaders, strategies, spending priorities, candidates, and messages.

Comstock partly punctures that misdirection by naming Trump. But her framing still casts Republicans as casualties of his summer rather than participants in a system built around submission to him. The weaker actors here are individual candidates tethered to a national brand they do not control. The party officials with the power to loosen that tether instead appear to be preparing explanations for defeat.

Material pain, strategic failure

Comstock’s list—war, gasoline, interest rates, and “$7 beef”—connects electoral danger to costs and policies voters experience directly. RawStory supplies no evidence establishing how much each issue affected Republican support, so her causal argument remains political analysis, not a demonstrated finding.

Even so, the strategic problem is plain within her account. A governing movement cannot indefinitely replace material results with loyalty performances. Sending Trump to Alabama may energize supporters there, but Comstock interprets the choice as sheltering him in friendly territory while more competitive races deteriorate.

The system protects its center

This is not merely a story about bleak polling. It is a portrait of a party whose internal incentives punish confrontation with its most powerful figure more reliably than voters punish failure.

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice disguised as inevitability. Leaders identify the source of their predicament, preserve his authority, and then describe the consequences as terminal decline. Hospice language makes surrender sound clinical. In politics, it is still a choice.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ex-GOP lawmaker says Republicans now resigned to hospice: ‘Make the patient comfortable’

item.title: Locals evacuated as 'major incident' unfolds near US military 'hub': report
item.description:
B‑1B Lancer bomber at the RAF Fairford airbase, which hosts US Air Force personnel, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, September 27, 2026. According to the police, security measures were increased around the air base after police arrested several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. REUTERS/Toby Shepheard TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY

What happened

RawStory reported that residents of Whelford, near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, were evacuated on September 27, 2026, after police declared a “major incident.” Several people were arrested on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act, and a bomb squad was dispatched. The reporting does not establish what explosives were found, what the suspects allegedly intended, or whether RAF Fairford was their target.

RAF Fairford is a British base used by the United States and described by ABC News as a hub for American operations against Iran. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss the incident’s specifics, while British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said emergency and specialist teams were handling it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory also cited a former CIA officer’s observation that counterterrorism officials were following events closely and recalled an earlier Iranian warning that American use of the base could make it a “legitimate target.” None of the reporting presented evidence connecting Iran, terrorism, or that warning to the arrests.

Power sits above the village

The institutional power here belongs to the British government, which controls the territory and authorizes the base’s use, and to the United States military, which conducts operations from it. The evacuated residents did not decide that a Gloucestershire airfield would support military action involving Iran. They nevertheless absorbed the immediate disruption and possible danger.

That is the political structure surrounding the police operation: strategic decisions are made by governments and military commands, while nearby civilians inherit the exposure. Calling RAF Fairford merely a “hub” launders that arrangement into logistical jargon. A base used for operations against another state is not politically neutral infrastructure.

Arrests are not an explanation

Police apparently had enough cause to make arrests under the Explosives Act and evacuate residents. That establishes a serious law-enforcement response, not the suspects’ guilt, their purpose, or an international plot.

The distinction matters because the article assembles suggestive fragments faster than the known facts can support them: explosives arrests, a U.S.-used air base, counterterrorism attention and an Iranian warning. The juxtaposition encourages readers to infer a connection the reporting never demonstrates.

The headline manufactures suspense

The scare framing does more work than the evidence. Quotation marks around “major incident,” references to a military “hub,” and a former intelligence official saying his professional world is watching create an atmosphere of imminent geopolitical revelation. But the central unanswered question remains elementary: what happened?

RawStory could report the evacuation, arrests and official uncertainty without constructing an implied Iranian or terrorist narrative around them. Instead, the article shifts attention from what authorities know to what readers might fear. That is not clarification. It is speculation by arrangement.

Officials control the facts

British emergency services acted, police arrested suspects, and military officials withheld operational detail. Some secrecy may be justified during an active investigation, but it also leaves institutions controlling both the site and the public account.

Streeting’s reassurance praised the machinery of response without explaining the underlying event. The U.S. Air Force offered similarly polished language about vigilance and safety. Residents received evacuation orders; the public received institutional confidence. Neither statement resolved the factual gaps.

Militarized policy becomes civilian risk

The larger pattern is not proven Iranian involvement. It is the conversion of civilian places into the perimeter of foreign policy. Governments choose where military power is projected from, adversaries issue warnings in response, security agencies prepare for retaliation, and local communities live inside the resulting risk map.

Coverage should trace that chain of authority without turning unproven associations into a culprit. Until investigators establish who possessed what, for what purpose, the responsible conclusion is narrow: there was a serious explosives-related police operation near a strategically important base. The broader political fact is firmer: those who authorize military operations command the strategy, while people with no control over it are ordered from their homes when the consequences approach.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Locals evacuated as ‘major incident’ unfolds near US military ‘hub’: report

item.title: Ex-MAGA insider exposes GOP scheme to 'scare you into voting': 'Nothing else is working’
item.description:
REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

RawStory reports that former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene accused Republicans of using reports of a migrant caravan to frighten voters before the 2026 midterms because “nothing else is working.” Her September 27 post responded to activist Anthony Aguero’s claim that more than 400 migrants, predominantly Honduran, had entered Mexico and were heading toward the United States.

Neither Aguero nor Greene supplied evidence establishing who organized the migrants’ movement or proving a coordinated GOP scheme. The article connects Greene’s allegation to Donald Trump’s pre-election warnings about a caravan in 2018, when he called migration an “invasion” and deployed troops before Republicans lost the House.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory also reports disorder within the administration’s current immigration policy: ICE officers were reportedly instructed to stop arresting immigrants without criminal records, after which the administration called the order a “miscommunication” and reversed it. Some electorally vulnerable Republicans, including Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, have criticized Trump’s crackdown.

The power is still inside the government

Greene is no longer a member of Congress. She can accuse, speculate and attract attention, but she cannot issue ICE directives, deploy troops or determine federal immigration policy. Those powers belong to the Trump administration, executive agencies and the congressional majority responsible for oversight and legislation.

That distinction matters because the story’s most consequential fact is not Greene’s commentary. It is that federal immigration enforcement reportedly changed direction and then changed back after the administration dismissed the original order as a misunderstanding. The people exposed to arrest live with the consequences of that institutional instability; the officials producing it retain the power.

An allegation is not an exposé

The headline calls Greene an insider who “exposes” a scheme. The reporting establishes something narrower: a former Trump ally publicly alleged that Republicans were exploiting the caravan story for electoral fear. It does not establish that party officials arranged the migrants’ movement, coordinated Aguero’s post or deliberately timed the caravan.

Calling this an exposé upgrades partisan suspicion into demonstrated fact. Greene may recognize a familiar Republican campaign tactic, especially after Trump’s 2018 caravan rhetoric, but recognition is not proof of a specific operation. RawStory’s framing gives her claim more evidentiary weight than its own article supports.

Fear is the durable political product

The absence of proof for Greene’s theory does not erase the documented pattern the article identifies. In 2018, Trump described a northbound caravan as an “invasion” and sent troops to the border in the weeks before the midterms. That episode shows how migration can be converted from a policy question into an emergency spectacle.

The political advantage lies in collapsing distinct people and circumstances into a single approaching menace. Once that frame is accepted, executive escalation can be marketed as protection, administrative inconsistency can be buried under alarm, and criticism can be treated as weakness. The caravan becomes useful as an image regardless of whether it changes the underlying conditions at the border.

The scapegoats have the least agency

Migrants walking through Mexico do not control Republican campaign strategy, federal enforcement priorities or the administration’s public messaging. Yet they become the visible object onto which political failure is projected.

That is the central misdirection. Officials with authority over immigration policy can present themselves as besieged responders while people with almost no institutional power are cast as the source of national disorder. Even Greene’s critique remains trapped inside that spectacle: the argument is over why the caravan is being discussed, while the migrants themselves are reduced to campaign material.

Manufactured urgency hides governing failure

The larger pattern is not proven secret coordination; it is a political system that rewards officials for producing fear faster than they produce coherent policy. Republicans can invoke border chaos, reverse enforcement instructions and blame “miscommunication,” all while preserving the posture that only they can control the crisis.

RawStory weakens its own case by selling Greene’s accusation as an exposure. The stronger, supportable indictment is already in the reporting: powerful officials repeatedly turn migration into an electoral emergency, while administrative confusion and policy consequences fall on people who possess neither the microphone nor the machinery of the state.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ex-MAGA insider exposes GOP scheme to ‘scare you into voting’: ‘Nothing else is working’

item.title: Republican senator reveals Trump's 'colossal mistake' that could upend the midterms
item.description:
U.S. Senator Thom Tillis (R-NC) speaks to reporters in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump saying he may temporarily drop the nomination of Todd Blanche to be U.S. attorney general, as he arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 30, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

What happened

The “colossal mistake,” according to Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, was President Donald Trump’s decision to support Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. Tillis told CNN’s Jake Tapper on September 27, 2026, that Paxton’s candidacy could force Republicans to spend heavily defending the Texas Senate seat against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico.

RawStory reports that Tillis, who is not seeking reelection, argued that Cornyn’s fundraising strength would have made the race less expensive for Republicans. KVUE reported that Paxton was not leading Talarico in any public poll, while Texas PAC had reserved roughly $117 million in advertising to support Paxton.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power behind the mistake

Trump held the decisive institutional leverage identified in this story: presidential influence over Republican voters and candidates. He used it against an incumbent senator from his own party and in favor of Paxton.

Tillis’s complaint is therefore not about an electoral accident. It is about a choice made by the party’s dominant figure—and the financial consequences now falling on the broader Republican apparatus.

Loyalty has a price tag

Cornyn’s value, in Tillis’s account, was brutally practical. He could raise money, defend the seat and leave Republican resources available for races elsewhere. Paxton, by contrast, requires an extraordinary advertising commitment while failing, according to the cited polling, to establish a public lead over Talarico.

That makes the reported $117 million more than campaign spending. It is the cost of a political system in which loyalty to Trump can outweigh incumbency, fundraising capacity and strategic efficiency.

Tillis narrows the indictment

Tillis calls Trump’s intervention a mistake because it may hurt Republicans in the midterms. That framing is revealingly narrow. It measures leadership by whether the party can repair the damage with enough money—not by whether the intervention served voters or produced a more capable nominee.

The article largely accepts that electoral-accounting frame. “Paxton has his challenges,” Tillis said, but the reporting does not specify them. Readers are left with the financial burden as the central problem, while the substantive differences between Paxton, Cornyn and Talarico remain mostly outside the frame.

The weaker actors get the bill

Talarico did not create the Republican Party’s predicament. Nor did outside circumstances mysteriously make Texas expensive. Trump backed Paxton, Republican voters produced the outcome Tillis now condemns, and allied donors are preparing to finance the consequences.

Calling the situation an upset risk can obscure that chain of agency. The weaker actor—the Democratic challenger—is treated as the danger, while the powerful actor who reshaped the contest is treated as having committed a tactical error.

A party organized around one man

The larger pattern is a party surrendering institutional judgment to personal authority, then asking donors and candidates elsewhere to absorb the cost. Tillis is willing to criticize the decision once the price becomes visible, but his objection remains managerial: Trump may have made winning harder.

That is the systemic failure. A leader exercises power, party officials accommodate it, and only afterward do they describe the predictable consequences as an unfortunate miscalculation. The money can conceal the weakness for a while. It cannot convert submission into strategy.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Republican senator reveals Trump’s ‘colossal mistake’ that could upend the midterms

item.title: Ex-CIA official warns Trump risking 'mass casualty event' by playing 'very dangerous game’
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump looks at media members after returning to the White House from Scotland, Britain, in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 29, 2025. REUTERS/Umit Bektas

What happened

RawStory reports that former senior CIA officer Marc Polymeropoulos warned that the Trump administration’s reassignment of federal law-enforcement resources from counterterrorism to immigration enforcement could increase the risk of a mass-casualty attack. His warning responded to ProPublica’s finding that the Justice Department dropped 23,000 criminal cases during the first six months of Trump’s second term, including hundreds involving terrorism, drugs and white-collar crime, while prosecuting 32,000 new immigration cases.

Polymeropoulos, who retired from the CIA in 2019, argued that finite personnel make the tradeoff unavoidable: when agents and prosecutors are redirected, counterterrorism receives less attention. He did not identify a specific imminent plot, and the reporting does not establish that an attack will occur.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

RawStory also describes disorder inside the immigration push. ICE officers were reportedly instructed to stop arresting immigrants without criminal records, only for the administration to call the directive a “miscommunication” and reverse it hours later.

The administration chose the priority

Institutional power rests with the administration and Justice Department leadership. FBI, DEA and other federal personnel did not spontaneously abandon existing caseloads. Political officials set immigration enforcement as the dominant priority and moved agents and prosecutors accordingly.

That distinction matters because “finite resources” can sound like a natural constraint rather than a political choice. Scarcity does not determine which work gets neglected. Leadership does. The reported numbers describe an administration reallocating state capacity toward its deportation program while allowing thousands of other federal cases to fall away.

Enforcement as political spectacle

The shift reveals what the administration values: immigration enforcement is not merely one responsibility among many but a governing showcase powerful enough to displace counterterrorism, narcotics and financial-crime work.

The weekend reversal reported by Fox News makes the structure clearer. An apparent limit on arrests of immigrants without criminal records survived only hours before being repudiated as a “miscommunication.” Whatever produced the initial instruction, the reversal showed that restraint lacked durable authority. The deportation campaign did not.

A warning is not a prediction

The headline’s “mass casualty event” language is Polymeropoulos’s warning about risk, not evidence that such an event is imminent or inevitable. RawStory correctly identifies him as a former official and outspoken Trump critic, but the political significance of his argument rests on the resource allocation he cites, not on his résumé or opposition to Trump.

Reducing his claim to partisan alarm would misdirect attention from the officials who control staffing and prosecutorial priorities. At the same time, treating his scenario as a forecast would overstate the evidence. The grounded charge is narrower and still severe: the administration knowingly prioritized one enforcement campaign despite warnings that other federal protections would receive less attention.

The cost is displaced and delayed

The immediate political benefit of aggressive immigration enforcement is visible: arrests, operations and deportation statistics can be displayed as proof of executive resolve. The costs of abandoned investigations are harder to see because they often appear later—or remain unknowable.

That asymmetry rewards reckless governance. Officials receive credit for the activity they stage while the public absorbs the risk created by work that no longer gets done. If a neglected investigation eventually ends in preventable harm, the staffing decision that preceded it will be old news. Power depends on that lag.

Governing by fixation

This is a broader pattern of executive government organized around a political obsession. Agencies with multiple public-safety duties are bent toward the priority most useful to the administration’s identity, while foregone work is treated as an administrative footnote.

The central issue is not whether Polymeropoulos can predict catastrophe. He cannot, and the article supplies no proof of one. It is that federal leaders control where investigative capacity goes, chose to concentrate it on immigration, and thereby accepted reduced attention elsewhere. Calling the resulting disorder a “miscommunication” cannot erase the chain of command—or the consequences of its choices.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ex-CIA official warns Trump risking ‘mass casualty event’ by playing ‘very dangerous game’

item.title: Trump reveals constant violent thoughts in call with Axios: ‘I'm always thinking about it’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump attends the Presidents Cup at the Medinah Country Club, in Medinah, Illinois, US, September 27, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

What happened

RawStory reports that President Donald Trump told Axios he was “always thinking about” resuming strikes against Iran after rejecting Iran’s latest proposal to end the war. He also predicted further negotiations that week but said Iran had “overplayed their hand,” signaling little expectation of an immediate agreement.

The report places that remark alongside Trump’s public suggestion at the United Nations that the United States might “annihilate” the Iranian government, as well as Wall Street Journal reporting that he told aides he expected bombing to resume after the midterms. Experts cited in the coverage said his apparent strategy of imposing economic pain to gain negotiating leverage could backfire with deadly consequences.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power is in the presidency

The consequential fact is not that Trump has violent “thoughts.” It is that the president has the institutional power to reject terms, order military action and shape whether negotiations proceed under diplomacy or bombardment.

Trump made the decision identified in the report: he rejected Iran’s proposal. He then kept renewed strikes explicitly under consideration while publicly discounting the likelihood of a near-term agreement. The article does not establish which advisers, legislators or officials enabled that course, so responsibility beyond the president cannot be assigned from this reporting alone.

A headline that shrinks the story

RawStory’s framing turns a question about possible military escalation into a revelation about Trump’s supposedly “constant violent thoughts.” That is sharper than the evidence supports. “I am always thinking about it” referred specifically to whether he was considering renewed strikes, not to violence in general.

That exaggeration also misdirects attention. The scandal is not an unusual psychological fixation inferred from six words. It is a governing decision: the person commanding American military power is publicly treating further bombing as an active option after rejecting a proposed settlement.

Negotiation under coercion

Trump’s language presents talks and threatened destruction as compatible instruments. More negotiations may occur, but his public posture tells Iran that diplomacy is taking place under the prospect of renewed attack and severe economic pressure.

Experts cited by the reporting describe the apparent objective as extracting concessions through economic harm. That strategy makes civilians bear foreseeable costs for decisions made by governments. The article does not prove Trump’s private motive, but his stated willingness to consider more strikes and his dismissal of Iran’s position make coercion central to the reported approach.

Escalation as political management

The reported timing matters. According to The Wall Street Journal account cited by RawStory, Trump told aides he expected bombing to resume after the midterms. If accurate, that links military timing to the domestic political calendar. The reporting does not establish why he selected that timetable, but it raises an obvious question the article leaves largely unexplored: whether electoral considerations are influencing when force is used.

The larger pattern is executive power packaged as personal temperament. Coverage fixates on Trump’s provocative phrasing because spectacle is easy to publish. But missiles are not launched by rhetoric alone. They are launched through institutions placed at the president’s disposal.

The system behind the threat

Personal volatility can matter, but reducing foreign policy to one man’s violent language lets the machinery of coercion disappear. The central political fact is that decisions capable of producing mass death can be discussed as tactical leverage, timed around politics and reported as personality drama.

That framing protects the system by sensationalizing its operator. Trump supplies the threats and, according to the report, made the decisive rejection. Yet the deeper failure is an arrangement in which catastrophic force can remain a live negotiating tool while public scrutiny settles for decoding the president’s state of mind.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump reveals constant violent thoughts in call with Axios: ‘I’m always thinking about it’

item.title: Eyes roll as musician and noncitizen Nicki Minaj urges Americans to ‘vote red’
item.description:
Nicki Minaj Anton Oparin / (Shutterstock.com)

What happened

RawStory reports that musician Nicki Minaj urged Americans to “vote red” during a Saturday Fox News interview with Lara Trump. Minaj briefly laughed and offered a joking “nah,” but Trump embraced the endorsement and called it a sales pitch to American voters.

Minaj also encouraged viewers to research local candidates before voting. According to the report, she cannot currently vote because she is not a U.S. citizen; although she has claimed she received a Trump Gold Card, she said her citizenship paperwork was still being finalized.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power was in the broadcast

Minaj supplied the celebrity endorsement, but Fox News and Lara Trump controlled the political use made of it. Trump immediately converted an ambiguous, jokingly qualified remark into a clean partisan appeal. The network provided the audience and the legitimacy. Minaj’s citizenship status did not prevent her from expressing a political view, and it did not diminish the platform’s power to circulate that view.

The relevant institutional story is therefore not that a noncitizen spoke about an election. It is that a major political media platform turned celebrity access into partisan messaging.

A weak frame aimed downward

RawStory’s headline centers eye-rolling over Minaj’s inability to vote. That is a cheap substitute for examining the people and institutions that can shape elections: party operatives, broadcasters, candidates and wealthy political patrons.

Noncitizens are allowed to hold opinions and encourage lawful voters to act. Minaj’s lack of a ballot may make the endorsement ironic, but it does not make her the principal power holder. Treating citizenship as the decisive rebuttal also echoes a familiar political misdirection: scrutinize the immigrant’s standing while giving the powerful host and network supporting roles.

Guilt by family association

The report then pivots to the criminal histories of Minaj’s husband and brother. Their convictions are serious: RawStory cites reporting that Kenneth Petty was convicted of attempted rape and later pleaded guilty to manslaughter, while Jelani Maraj was convicted of sexually assaulting an 11-year-old girl. But those facts do not establish anything about the merits of Minaj’s electoral message.

Introducing relatives’ crimes as partisan evidence is guilt by association. Quoting an activist who uses those convictions to declare that Minaj belongs with the MAGA movement does not repair the logic; it merely outsources the smear. If the argument against Republican candidates depends on crimes committed by a celebrity supporter’s relatives, the coverage has abandoned institutional accountability for social-media contempt.

The transaction deserves scrutiny

The more politically consequential detail is Minaj’s claim that she received a Trump Gold Card while still finalizing citizenship paperwork. RawStory describes the initiative as offering a pathway to citizenship for $1 million, but the article does not establish the terms of Minaj’s purported gift, who provided it or whether it changed her legal status.

That unresolved relationship—celebrity endorsement beside claimed access to a costly immigration pathway—warrants careful reporting. The supplied account does not prove a quid pro quo, and it would be irresponsible to allege one. It does, however, raise a sharper question than whether Minaj can vote: how political leaders distribute access, prestige and immigration benefits around influential supporters.

Outrage is not accountability

This episode shows how partisan media and reactive coverage can reinforce each other. One side packages celebrity speech as voter persuasion; the other answers with mockery about immigration status and attacks involving family members. The institutions exercising power escape sustained examination.

The consequence is coverage that personalizes politics precisely where it should follow authority. Lara Trump made the endorsement useful. Fox News amplified it. The reported Gold Card claim raises unanswered questions about elite access. Those are matters of agency and power. Everything else is spectacle arranged around them.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Eyes roll as musician and noncitizen Nicki Minaj urges Americans to ‘vote red’

item.title: Trump faces legal reckoning as desperate plea for love breaks federal law
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks at a ceremony held to dedicate a 4-mile stretch of road from West Palm Beach Airport to his Mar-a-Lago estate as ‘President Donald J. Trump Boulevard’, at the Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, U.S., January 16, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

What happened

RawStory columnist Sabrina Haake reports that U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House on September 24 to restore CNN, MSN, and Politico’s access for 14 days. Kelly found that the outlets met the demanding standard for a temporary restraining order and rejected the Justice Department’s national-security rationale as an after-the-fact justification, noting that the administration originally blamed unfavorable coverage.

Haake also describes a government-funded, pro-Trump video aired by Fox News featuring presidential imagery, military aircraft, policy boasts, a choir repeating “Love me,” and praise from Dana White. She argues that the ad violates the Hatch Act and federal appropriations restrictions on partisan propaganda. The column, however, identifies no court ruling or enforcement finding establishing that conclusion, so the promised “legal reckoning” remains speculation rather than a reported proceeding.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

During the access dispute, several news organizations reportedly curtailed pooled coverage and stopped publishing new Trump images. The White House responded with a curated YouTube livestream that, according to the audience figures cited by Haake, attracted only a few thousand viewers and later fewer than 500 live viewers.

The power belongs to the White House

The banned outlets did not control access to the presidency. The White House did. It used that institutional authority to punish organizations after coverage Trump characterized as negative, according to Kelly’s account of the administration’s stated rationale.

That distinction matters because “a dispute between Trump and the media” would falsely flatten the power relationship. News organizations can criticize an administration. An administration can deploy government machinery to restrict access, marshal Justice Department lawyers and spend public money. Only one side possessed state power.

Kelly’s order temporarily checked that power; it did not erase the decision that made judicial intervention necessary. Nor does his appointment by Trump make speculation about partisan motives evidence. The relevant fact is simpler: a federal judge ruled that the outlets had cleared the high threshold for emergency relief.

National security as a retrofit

The Justice Department claimed that reporting about an East Wing bunker, White House ballroom funding and munitions stockpiles threatened national security or spread falsehoods. Kelly reportedly found that explanation inconsistent with the reason initially given for the ban: hostile coverage.

That sequence exposes the central misdirection. The administration’s own explanation pointed toward retaliation, while its lawyers later supplied a more institutionally respectable vocabulary. “National security” can identify a genuine concern. Here, according to the ruling as described, it functioned as a post hoc defense for excluding disfavored journalists.

The targets were not officials who made policy or controlled classified information. They were outlets reporting on the government. Redirecting scrutiny toward them recasts executive retaliation as media misconduct and asks the public to treat criticism of power as the danger.

Propaganda is not a legal finding

The government-funded video deserves scrutiny because its reported content appears designed to glorify one political leader, not explain a public program. Presidential montage, military symbolism, policy promotion and personal testimonials form a recognizable propaganda package. The repeated plea to “Love me” only makes the purpose unusually unsubtle.

But Haake overstates the established legal record. Calling the video “obviously illegal” does not make it so, and the column does not provide the appropriation, production records, responsible officials, legal analysis or adjudication needed to prove a violation. Its Hatch Act argument is asserted more confidently than it is demonstrated.

The sharper indictment is therefore institutional rather than judicial: federal resources were reportedly used to broadcast personalized political promotion, while the administration was simultaneously trying to control which independent journalists could enter the White House. That combination—restrict adversarial coverage, manufacture favorable coverage—is the consequential fact pattern.

The press cannot outsource its agency

The solidarity campaign showed that major outlets retain leverage when they use it collectively. Reduced pooled coverage deprived the White House of the attention it routinely converts into political power, and the administration’s replacement stream reportedly failed to reproduce that audience.

Haake weakens her own analysis by treating diminished coverage partly as comic relief and by speculating that Kelly might have delayed ruling to help Republican candidates. Neither exhaustion with Trump nor guesses about a judge’s partisan calculations should obscure the principle at stake. Government cannot be allowed to condition press access on favorable treatment merely because silence would be more pleasant—or electorally convenient.

Media companies are not powerless spectators here. They choose whether to reward retaliation with saturation coverage, whether to maintain collective resistance and whether to confront official claims with evidence. Their incentives may favor spectacle, but those incentives remain choices.

The systemic error

The broader pattern is an executive branch attempting to make access conditional, recasting criticism as a security offense and using public communications to elevate the president personally. The court order interrupted one part of that machinery. It did not resolve the incentives behind it.

The deeper failure arrives when each abuse is isolated: the access ban as a press quarrel, the legal justification as routine advocacy, the promotional video as merely embarrassing, and media compliance as inevitable. Taken together, they describe a struggle over who controls the public record. Power seeks immunity from scrutiny; propaganda supplies the flattering substitute; institutions decide whether either effort succeeds.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump faces legal reckoning as desperate plea for love breaks federal law
