item.title: Karoline Leavitt infuriates MAGA TV host with 'immature' Trump 'gossip': 'Breach of trust’
item.description:
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt reacts while she takes questions from the media during a press briefing at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., February 10, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY

What happened

RawStory reports that former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt publicly recounted a private lunch at which President Donald Trump allegedly told British Prime Minister Keir Starmer that his policies were “extremely stupid,” urged him to close Britain’s borders and deport people, and claimed the British public hated what Starmer was doing. Leavitt shared the account during an appearance with Sean Hannity, who had asked about Trump’s candor with foreign leaders.

The encounter apparently occurred at Chequers during Trump’s September 2025 state visit to the United Kingdom. Leavitt could not initially remember whether the lunch took place at Windsor Castle or Starmer’s residence. Newsmax host Greg Kelly condemned her disclosure as gossip and a breach of trust, arguing that it was especially damaging amid the 2026 midterm campaign. RawStory does not report responses from Trump or Starmer, so Leavitt’s account remains attributed to her.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Where the power sits

Trump held presidential power in the encounter Leavitt described. Starmer held the authority of a prime minister hosting a foreign head of state. Leavitt, then the White House press secretary, occupied a privileged position near both leaders and later controlled whether their private exchange became public.

That hierarchy matters more than the personalities. A president addressing an allied prime minister in his own country is not merely displaying bluntness. He is using the status of the American presidency to press another government on immigration policy. Leavitt’s retelling then turns that exercise of power into entertainment for a friendly media audience.

Candor as political merchandise

Hannity’s question supplied the desired premise: Trump is “brutally honest” with world leaders. Leavitt answered with a story designed to validate it. The substance—one national leader reportedly berating another over domestic policy—became evidence of toughness.

That conversion is central to the propaganda style. Diplomacy is stripped of strategy, negotiation and consequence, then repackaged as dominance theater. The measure of presidential strength becomes whether Trump can insult another leader at lunch, while the actual effect on policy or the bilateral relationship goes unexamined.

Kelly protects the machinery

Kelly’s outrage is revealing because it targets the disclosure, not the reported conduct. He objected that Leavitt had exposed a private meeting and might create political trouble during “midterm madness.” His complaint was about message discipline: useful theater had escaped its controlled setting and become a potential liability.

Calling Leavitt immature also shifts attention toward the weaker actor. She chose to publicize the exchange and can be criticized for that decision. But she did not hold presidential authority or make the reported demands. Kelly’s framing protects the principal by disciplining the former subordinate who described him.

A trust argument with selective boundaries

Kelly invoked trust owed to “the President” and “the Nation” as though those interests were interchangeable. They are not. Confidential diplomacy can serve the country, but secrecy can also protect officials from scrutiny. The article provides no basis for concluding that this disclosure caused concrete diplomatic harm. Kelly’s claim of a national breach therefore goes beyond what RawStory establishes.

What the reporting does establish is a conflict inside pro-Trump media over who may circulate presidential bravado and when. Leavitt treated access as social currency. Kelly treated access as something to guard when disclosure might interfere with electoral messaging. Neither response centers the public’s interest in understanding how presidential power is exercised abroad.

The system behind the gossip

The larger pattern is an ecosystem that markets proximity to power while demanding loyalty to it. Insiders monetize anecdotes. Friendly hosts turn governance into personality content. Enforcers condemn disclosure when the same material stops flattering the leader and starts exposing the operation.

That is why reducing this episode to gossip misses the point. The consequential act was not merely Leavitt talking. It was a political-media apparatus converting an alleged diplomatic confrontation into partisan spectacle, then policing its own member when the spectacle threatened to become evidence.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Karoline Leavitt infuriates MAGA TV host with ‘immature’ Trump ‘gossip’: ‘Breach of trust’

item.title: Melania's white-hot hatred for Trump seared through this unguarded photo
item.description:
US President Donald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. REUTERS/MIKE SEGAR

What happened

RawStory argues that a photograph taken during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 24, 2026 White House visit revealed Melania Trump’s “white-hot hatred” for Donald Trump. It does not. The image reportedly shows Donald and Melania Trump appearing distant after a military demonstration, but a still photograph cannot establish either person’s feelings or the state of their marriage.

The article also cites Donald Trump’s reported net approval rating of minus 26 in YouGov polling and describes his September 23 welcome for Xi at Joint Base Andrews. It supplements that account with allegations from former aide Stephanie Winston Wolkoff’s 2020 book about Melania Trump’s delayed move to Washington, renovations to the White House residence, and an effort dubbed “Operation Block Ivanka.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The headline outruns the evidence

RawStory resolves its teaser with an insinuation, not a fact. Body language in one photograph may suggest discomfort or distance. It cannot prove hatred, much less its temperature.

The article compounds that weakness with speculation about divorce, physical intimacy, and Melania Trump’s motives. Rumors remain rumors. An author’s contempt does not convert them into reporting.

Power is not a marriage plot

Donald Trump held the institutional power in this story: the presidency, control of the executive branch, and authority over the ceremonial machinery surrounding Xi’s state visit. Melania Trump possessed status, access, and the public platform of the first lady, but the source identifies no government decision she made during the visit.

Turning the event into marital voyeurism misdirects attention from the people exercising state power. Whatever passed between the Trumps in an unguarded moment mattered less politically than how the president used the White House, the military display, and a diplomatic encounter with China’s leader.

Association is not evidence of conspiracy

RawStory calls Melania Trump a “willing co-conspirator” living from “grifted billions,” but the supplied article establishes neither a conspiracy nor the provenance of those billions. Those are grave claims presented without supporting evidence in the text.

A defensible criticism is narrower. Melania Trump voluntarily occupied a prestigious public role and benefited from its privileges. Her reported indifference does not make her powerless, but neither does it prove participation in every alleged abuse attributed to her husband.

Scorn replaces accountability

The article spends more energy mocking clothing, decorations, fear, marriage, and personal misery than documenting consequential decisions. Even its discussion of Trump’s approval rating is imprecise: a minus-26 figure is described as the lowest “approval rating,” though the wording appears to refer to a net rating, and the supplied text gives no field dates, population, sample, or comparison series.

This is not merely a tonal problem. Personal ridicule can make powerful officials look ridiculous while leaving their power insufficiently examined. It offers emotional satisfaction where scrutiny should identify authority, decisions, beneficiaries, and measurable consequences.

The systemic error

Political coverage fails when it substitutes a speculative domestic melodrama for an account of institutional conduct. The powerful become characters in a grotesque reality show; readers are invited to decode facial expressions while executive power operates outside the frame.

The larger pattern is the conversion of politics into contempt-driven entertainment. RawStory may be justified in scrutinizing the Trumps’ conduct, but this article repeatedly claims more than its evidence supports. Accountability requires sharper distinctions: between appearance and fact, influence and authority, association and complicity. Without them, outrage becomes another form of misdirection.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Melania’s white-hot hatred for Trump seared through this unguarded photo

item.title: 'You have no shame': Conservative fury hits Trump official over lavish party video
item.description:
“Dan Scavino” by Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 2.0

What happened

RawStory reports that White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino posted a video depicting himself in a tuxedo, holding champagne and riding a gilded luggage cart through an ornate, confetti-covered room. Donald Trump briefly appears. Critics described the clip as AI-generated, but the reporting does not independently establish that.

The post drew condemnation from conservatives and others who contrasted its display of luxury with Americans struggling to pay for groceries, gasoline, housing and air conditioning during the Iran war. Former Trump ally Carrie Prejean Boller declared “MAGA is dead,” while Meghan McCain, Jonah Goldberg, Sarah Longwell and several other commentators attacked the post as callous and politically disastrous. RawStory places the backlash amid Republican anxiety about the midterms and reports that Trump’s approval rating had reached a career low.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power is inside the frame

Scavino is not a random influencer committing a branding mistake. He is a deputy White House chief of staff and runs the Presidential Personnel Office, giving him proximity to the president and influence over who enters the administration. The spectacle therefore matters because an official with institutional power chose to publish it.

The critics can ridicule the video, but Scavino holds the office. The people invoked in their complaints—those unable to afford food, fuel, cooling or housing—hold neither his platform nor his appointment authority. Treating the episode merely as offensive content would obscure that imbalance.

Contempt as political communication

Whether the scene was synthetic or staged is secondary. Scavino selected the image: champagne, formalwear, gilded surroundings and access to the president. During a period of reported economic strain and war-related pressure, that choice communicates insulation from consequences.

The reporting does not establish Scavino’s motive, so it cannot prove that he intended to taunt struggling households. But contempt does not need to be formally announced to become the foreseeable effect. Powerful officials who turn proximity to government into aristocratic content are showing the public what status looks like inside their political order.

The conservative objection has limits

Several attacks focused on timing and electoral damage. Goldberg sarcastically called it useful midterm messaging; Longwell compared it to imperial decadence. That criticism identifies the optics while leaving the machinery largely untouched.

The revealing complaint is not simply that governing elites appear indifferent to hardship. It is that Scavino displayed that indifference too plainly when Republicans already fear voters’ judgment. Political consultants call this a messaging failure because acknowledging it as a governing failure would require asking what the administration has done with its power.

Outrage cannot transfer responsibility

McCain’s story about a friend unable to afford air conditioning and Boller’s inventory of household costs give the backlash human stakes. But economic pain is not caused by an offensive video, and the people suffering it did not create this controversy. Scavino made the decision to post; the White House supplied the status that made the post politically consequential.

RawStory’s reliance on social-media reactions risks turning a question of official conduct into a compilation of disgust. View counts and cutting replies measure attention, not accountability. The essential fact is simpler: a senior government official used his public platform to circulate an image of elite indulgence while the administration faced criticism over conditions beyond that protected circle.

The spectacle is the structure

This episode reveals a familiar hierarchy. Officials exercise power, package access as entertainment and then watch commentators debate whether the display was tasteful. Material hardship becomes scenery in an argument about political branding.

The scandal is not that the governing class momentarily forgot how its celebration might look. It is that power can present itself as a private party inside the “People’s House,” while those outside are reduced to props in somebody else’s midterm strategy.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘You have no shame’: Conservative fury hits Trump official over lavish party video

item.title: Biographer: Foreign dictators play Trump 'like A fiddle' exploiting weakness
item.description:
REUTERS/Evan Vucci

What happened

Biographer Michael Wolff told The Daily Beast’s Joanna Coles that foreign leaders can exploit President Donald Trump through flattery because Trump refuses detailed briefings and enters high-stakes meetings without mastering the issues. Wolff’s “like a fiddle” assessment is his interpretation: he said foreign counterparts see a president from whom they can extract concessions, even calling Trump a “buffoon.”

AlterNet connected that criticism to Trump’s recent summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. According to the outlet, the meeting produced a two-month extension of an existing trade deal and lower tariffs on roughly $30 billion in goods. The White House also claimed Chinese commitments involving two fentanyl precursor chemicals, American agricultural products, Boeing aircraft and access for U.S. beef facilities.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The report said the summit produced no movement on Taiwan, artificial intelligence or Iran. It described Trump’s public activities with Xi as emphasizing construction, the military and a National Archives visit, while the administration faced a much broader diplomatic agenda.

The power is presidential

The central fact is not that aides struggle to hold Trump’s attention. It is that Trump possesses the institutional authority to set tariffs, direct foreign policy and speak for the United States while, according to Wolff, refusing the preparation needed to exercise that power competently.

That distinction matters. Staff members can compress briefing books into two points, but they cannot make the president absorb them. Foreign leaders can flatter him, but they did not give him this authority. Voters elected Trump, and the political apparatus surrounding him continues to convert his preferences into state action.

Ignorance is a choice

AlterNet’s framing sometimes drifts toward incapacity: staff must “untangle” problems and somehow make a difficult workload comprehensible. Wolff’s account is sharper. He alleges refusal—Trump “adamantly” does not do the work—not mere difficulty processing information.

If that account is accurate, treating the problem as an eccentric learning style misdirects responsibility. A president who declines preparation before consequential negotiations is making a governing decision. The predictable consequence is that policy becomes vulnerable to vanity, improvisation and whatever fragments advisers can place before him.

The aides are enablers, not safeguards

The White House staff described here has adapted the presidency to Trump rather than requiring Trump to meet the presidency’s demands. Reducing complex negotiations to one or two points may be operationally necessary, but it also normalizes the underlying refusal.

Wolff identifies the rationalization: Trump was elected twice, so insiders conclude that he “must know what he’s doing.” Electoral victory proves political effectiveness, not policy competence. Using the vote as an alibi allows officials to avoid confronting the risk they are managing—and helps conceal how much governing authority is being exercised through accommodation.

The scoreboard is incomplete

The announced trade extension, tariff reductions and claimed Chinese commitments are tangible outcomes. They do not, by themselves, establish Wolff’s broader contention that Xi manipulated Trump or that the United States “gave away the store.” AlterNet supplies no negotiating baseline, enforcement terms or evidence showing what China extracted in exchange.

That evidentiary gap weakens the article. The absence of movement on Taiwan, AI and Iran may show limited results, but it does not prove exploitation. A serious indictment of presidential vulnerability requires more than a biographer’s assessment paired with an inconclusive summit ledger.

Government by managed vanity

The larger pattern is an executive branch reorganized around one officeholder’s aversion to information. Subordinates simplify, foreign governments study his preferences, and public presentation competes with policy substance. The spectacle is not separate from governance; it shapes the conditions under which governing decisions are made.

The systemic failure is therefore larger than an allegedly inattentive president. It includes officials who accommodate the behavior, allies who excuse it as political instinct and coverage that personalizes an institutional breakdown as a colorful contest between a vain leader and clever foreigners. When enormous public power is filtered through flattery and abbreviated briefings, the consequences belong first to the people wielding and enabling that power—not to those skilled enough to notice the weakness.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Biographer: Foreign dictators play Trump ‘like A fiddle’ exploiting weakness

item.title: Parallel reality: Trump's plot to airbrush history weeks before the election
item.description:
REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s social media account posted an AI-generated image of Xi Jinping’s arrival at Joint Base Andrews on a Thursday shortly before an election. The image showed Trump saluting beside Xi as a bomber passed overhead, but omitted Melania Trump and Xi’s wife, Peng Liyuan, both of whom appeared in video of the actual event.

Online speculation claimed Trump aide Natalie Harp had erased Melania and inserted herself. Fact-checkers identified the remaining blonde woman as chief of protocol Monica Crowley, who posted her own photographs from the tarmac, although journalist Aaron Rupar argued that her face appeared altered to resemble Harp. The White House offered no explanation, and the reporting does not establish who created or edited the image.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The power to manufacture the record

The consequential actor here is not whichever staffer may have operated an image generator. It is the president and the White House communications apparatus distributing a synthetic version of an official diplomatic event.

That distinction matters. A random user posting a fake picture creates internet debris. A president’s account posting one uses institutional prestige to blur the boundary between documentation and propaganda. The image was not merely polished; it removed two people who were demonstrably present and replaced an ordinary arrival ceremony with heroic spectacle.

The missing women are not the main trick

The Harp-versus-Melania intrigue is irresistible gossip, but it also misdirects attention toward personalities with less power. AlterNet cannot establish that Harp made the image, inserted herself, or ordered anyone removed. Building the analysis around that theory would turn uncertainty into accusation.

What the evidence does support is narrower and more important: Trump’s account circulated an invented scene that elevated Trump while deleting inconvenient reality. Fixating on which woman the altered face resembles reduces an official act of image manipulation to palace drama.

Propaganda without accountability

The White House’s silence preserves useful ambiguity. Officials need not defend the alterations, disclose who produced them, or explain why synthetic imagery was presented alongside a real diplomatic event. The administration receives the spectacle while responsibility dissolves into speculation about staffers and software.

Calling this “confusion” would conceal the decision that actually occurred. Someone created or selected the image, and Trump’s account published it. The unknowns concern authorship and intent, not whether the public was shown a fabricated record.

Politics as synthetic heroism

The bomber, the salute and the vanished spouses all push the same visual argument: politics is not a collective or diplomatic process but a stage for one dominant man. AI makes that kind of self-mythology cheap, immediate and difficult to police at the speed of an election campaign.

The larger pattern is the conversion of public communication from persuasion into reality management. The objective need not be to make every viewer believe every pixel. Repeated synthetic imagery can make factual precision feel beside the point, leaving supporters with the intended impression and everyone else arguing over forensic details.

The systemic error

The danger in this episode lies less in one clumsy image than in the institutional permission surrounding it. A White House can distribute fabricated political theater, decline to explain it and rely on the controversy itself to carry the desired portrait of presidential power.

When official channels treat the historical record as editable campaign material, the lie does not have to be convincing. It only has to be useful—and consequence-free for the people powerful enough to publish it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Parallel reality: Trump’s plot to airbrush history weeks before the election

item.title: Liberal Supreme Court Justices reveal unexpected shift behind closed doors
item.description:
(REUTERs)

What happened

AlterNet reports that Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson see a limited improvement in how the Supreme Court handles emergency appeals: more justices are publicly explaining fast-track decisions instead of issuing consequential orders without reasoning. Jackson called that shift “good and positive” because lower courts and the public need guidance to understand and apply the Court’s decisions.

The change concerns process, not outcomes. The article says the Court’s conservative majority has repeatedly sided with the Trump administration in emergency cases, including a ruling permitting the administration to cut National Institutes of Health funding. In dissent, Jackson accused the majority of changing its rules to produce administration-friendly results.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet also recounts Kagan’s criticism of political rhetoric intended to intimidate judges. She distinguished legitimate criticism from intimidation and connected such rhetoric to threats against justices.

The power remains with the majority

Kagan and Jackson can dissent, speak publicly and expose inconsistencies. They cannot make five votes appear. The Court’s conservative bloc retains the institutional power to decide emergency applications, determine how much reasoning to disclose and shape the instructions lower courts must follow.

That makes the reported shift real but narrow. Written explanations improve transparency; they do not redistribute authority or reverse the decisions already benefiting the administration. The same majority that controls the outcome also controls how fully it accounts for that outcome.

Explanation is not accountability

AlterNet’s framing risks making a procedural concession sound like a substantive retreat. A majority that explains why it grants extraordinary relief is more legible than one that offers silence. It is not necessarily more restrained, consistent or accountable.

The central question is what the explanations reveal. If the Court applies stable principles across cases, written opinions help establish law. If it changes standards according to which party seeks relief, more prose merely documents the inconsistency. Jackson’s “Calvinball” criticism alleges precisely that deeper failure: not an absence of words, but an absence of fixed rules.

Emergency procedure becomes governing power

The administration’s repeated emergency appeals place major policy disputes on an accelerated track. According to the reporting, the NIH funding case reached a result allowing Trump to act unilaterally while the liberal justices objected to the majority’s reasoning.

That procedure matters because speed favors the actor already holding executive power. An emergency order can permit government action before ordinary litigation fully tests its legality. Even when temporary in form, such permission can produce immediate institutional and material consequences. Funding can stop; programs can be disrupted; lower courts can be left reconstructing doctrine from abbreviated instructions.

The weaker actors are not the cause

The story should not be reduced to liberal justices finally persuading conservative colleagues to communicate better. Kagan and Jackson did not create the underlying problem. Lower courts and the public did not misunderstand sufficiently clear rulings. The majority chose when to provide reasons, while the Trump administration chose to press emergency appeals seeking rapid permission for executive action.

Nor should intimidation be blurred into generic political “tension.” Kagan’s distinction is useful: criticism challenges judicial conduct; intimidation attempts to influence judges through fear. AlterNet reports her warning that political figures and their followers have used language she viewed as intimidating and that justices have faced real threats. The article does not establish who made those threats or prove that particular rhetoric caused them, so the connection should not be overstated. But the institutional consequence is plain: judges are operating amid pressure that extends beyond legal argument.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is rule by exception. Executive officials seek rapid clearance, the Supreme Court majority supplies it through an emergency process, and dissenters are left to explain why the governing standards appear unstable. Public reasoning may make that system easier to inspect, but inspection is not correction.

A court does not earn legitimacy merely by attaching explanations to exercises of power. Legitimacy depends on whether its rules constrain allies as well as opponents. If outcomes dictate doctrine rather than doctrine constraining outcomes, the problem is not a shadow over the docket. It is the use of judicial authority to make political preference look like law.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Liberal Supreme Court Justices reveal unexpected shift behind closed doors

item.title: Democrat casts tie-breaking vote that could have ended Trump's Iran war
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump in Dearborn, Michigan, January 13, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

Congress Chose Deference, and Fetterman Supplied the Decisive Vote

A War Without Authorization

The Senate’s 50–49 vote against House Concurrent Resolution 89 preserved President Donald Trump’s ability to continue U.S. hostilities against Iran without a declaration of war or specific congressional authorization. Sen. John Fetterman joined Republicans to produce the decisive margin; Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, an opponent of the war-powers policy at issue, was the only senator recorded as not voting.

The Power Congress Refused to Use

The institutional question was not whether American forces could defend themselves. The resolution expressly preserved responses to imminent attacks, defensive deployments, intelligence activities, and protection for U.S. forces, diplomatic facilities, and allies.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The question was whether a president may continue an offensive military operation without Congress authorizing it. Congress has the power to impose that boundary. A Senate majority did not exercise it.

Fetterman’s position is explicit: lawmakers should not constrain Trump while the military pursues the objectives of “Epic Fury.” That reverses the constitutional logic of war powers. Military objectives become the justification for continued hostilities, while authorization is postponed until those objectives are achieved—or indefinitely.

Fetterman Made a Choice

Calling this merely “supporting the troops” obscures the decision. The troops did not determine whether Congress would enforce an authorization requirement. Senators did.

Fetterman chose executive discretion over a congressional limit. His vote also spared Vice President JD Vance from potentially breaking a 50–50 tie on a war the reporting says he disagrees with. Whatever Vance might have done remains unknowable because Fetterman ensured he did not have to do it.

That is agency, not confusion.

One Absence Also Mattered

The backlash centered on Fetterman because he cast the vote that created the 50–49 result. But Alsobrooks’s absence was consequential too. According to the reporting, she had attended an earlier Capitol Hill vote and had consistently supported Senate measures requiring withdrawal from unauthorized hostilities with Iran. Had she voted in accordance with that record, the count would have been tied.

The article provides no reason for her absence, so motive cannot responsibly be assigned. Consequence can: the absence removed a vote against continued unauthorized hostilities and helped keep Vance away from the deciding chair.

Propaganda Replaced the Actual Dispute

A Republican commentator celebrated Fetterman by claiming that opposition amounted to being an “IRGC apologist.” That is textbook scapegoating. The resolution did not require sympathy for Iran’s government, prohibit defense against imminent attack, or abandon American personnel. It required specific congressional authorization for hostilities.

Collapsing oversight into allegiance to an enemy is propaganda designed to make the exercise of legislative power appear disloyal. It converts a dispute over who may authorize war into a loyalty test administered on the president’s terms.

War by Institutional Surrender

The larger pattern is not simply presidential expansion. Executive war-making grows because legislators repeatedly decline to bear responsibility for stopping it.

A president commands the operation. Congress possesses the authority to authorize or constrain it. Yet lawmakers can evade ownership by invoking troops already deployed, objectives already announced, or enemies too objectionable to defend procedurally. The result is a self-reinforcing transfer of power: unilateral action creates military facts, and those facts become the excuse for congressional submission.

Fetterman’s vote did not merely support one operation. It endorsed the machinery that allows presidents to wage war first and treat legislative consent as optional afterward.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Democrat casts tie-breaking vote that could have ended Trump’s Iran war

item.title: DOJ zeroes in on Epstein shell company where survivors say he abused them during jail term
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: U.S. financier Jeffrey Epstein appears in a photograph taken for the New York State Division of Criminal Justice Services’ sex offender registry March 28, 2017 and obtained by Reuters July 10, 2019. New York State Division of Criminal Justice Services/Handout via REUTERS.

Epstein’s “Fake Office” Was an Institutional Accommodation

The Jail Sentence With an Exit Door

CNN’s reporting describes an investigation that, if confirmed, reaches beyond Jeffrey Epstein’s already-established crimes and toward the professional machinery around him. According to a person interviewed by investigators, officials from multiple federal agencies are examining Epstein’s longtime lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn, gathering records and asking about the Florida Science Foundation—a nonprofit that survivors say Epstein used to abuse them while on work release. The Justice Department has not confirmed the investigation. Indyke and Kahn deny knowing about or participating in Epstein’s sex trafficking.

Power Made the Arrangement Possible

The central fact is not that Epstein found a clever loophole. It is that institutions gave him one.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The Florida Science Foundation was incorporated in November 2007. Survivors and former associates later told Congress that its Palm Beach office allowed Epstein to leave jail under work-release terms, escorted by sheriff’s deputies who were paid to accompany him. A former assistant described it as essentially a “fake office.”

Epstein could create a shell organization. He could not grant himself work release, authorize official escorts or convert incarceration into supervised access to a private workplace. Government authorities held that power. The reporting does not identify every official who approved or maintained the arrangement, so individual responsibility cannot be assigned from this account alone. But the structure is unmistakable: state power turned a nominal punishment into an accommodation.

Professionals Were Not Peripheral

The scrutiny of Indyke and Kahn matters because lawyers and accountants do not merely stand near wealth. They build and maintain the entities through which wealth operates.

That does not establish criminal responsibility. Both men have repeatedly denied knowledge of Epstein’s trafficking, and no charge is reported here. But their institutional position is precisely why investigators’ reported interest is consequential. Shell companies, trusts, checks and legal instruments are not background paperwork when an enterprise depends on controlled money, property and access. They are part of the operating environment.

As co-executors of Epstein’s estate, Indyke and Kahn also could potentially receive millions of dollars from his trust—an arrangement survivors have challenged as a conflict of interest. Whether that arrangement is legally improper is not established by the reporting. Politically, however, it exposes a familiar hierarchy: the professionals closest to a disgraced fortune may remain positioned to administer and profit from it, while survivors must fight for standing against the structure those professionals oversee.

“Who Knew?” Is Too Narrow

Public discussion of Epstein’s circle repeatedly collapses accountability into one question: who knew the full extent of the crimes?

That standard is conveniently maximal. It allows every intermediary to argue that unless prosecutors can prove comprehensive knowledge of trafficking, there is nothing meaningful to examine. But institutions also depend on narrower acts: forming entities, processing payments, controlling estates, approving release conditions and supplying official personnel.

Those acts do not prove knowledge of abuse. They do show where investigative attention belongs. The relevant question is not only whether an adviser knew everything. It is also what each powerful actor did, what authority each institution exercised, and what those decisions made possible.

Accountability Arrived at the Bottom

According to the article, Ghislaine Maxwell remains the only person prosecuted in the United States in connection with Epstein’s operation. Survivors’ advocates have called that record unacceptable.

The weakness of the usual framing is that it treats this outcome as a mystery—as though accountability simply failed to materialize. But prosecution is an institutional decision, and the long delay in examining alleged enablers has consequences. Witnesses age. Records become harder to recover. Memories degrade. Estates and professional arrangements continue operating. The absence of charges against others may reflect insufficient admissible evidence; it does not erase the need to examine why a criminal operation surrounded by money, employees, advisers and government accommodations produced so little legal accountability.

A System Built to Isolate the Monster

The politically useful version of the Epstein story casts him as an aberration: one monstrous man who deceived everyone around him. That narrative concentrates evil in a dead offender and disperses responsibility across a fog of supposedly peripheral institutions.

The reported investigation may test that insulation, but its existence and scope remain unconfirmed by the Justice Department. What the underlying account already reveals is more concrete. Epstein’s privilege was not merely personal. It was translated into corporate forms, estate authority, work-release access and paid official escort.

Systems protect themselves by treating each enabling decision as too technical, too limited or too innocent to matter. The result is organized impunity without any institution having to admit that it organized it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: DOJ zeroes in on Epstein shell company where survivors say he abused them during jail term

item.title: 'This is evil': Christians say Tim Tebow's favorite wealth seminar buried them in debt
item.description:
JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA-APRIL 14: Professional Football Player Tim Tebow at the Tim Tebow Foundation Celebrity Golf Classic on April 14, 2012 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo credit: Rob Wilson / Shutterstock)

The Celebrity Halo Is Part of the Sales Machine

Worship, Wealth, and the Upsell

Mother Jones reports that Life Surge stages roughly 30 events a year combining Christian worship, celebrity speakers, and promises of financial transformation. Low-cost admission leads to the real product: investing courses priced from about $10,000 to $40,000. Hundreds of attendees have complained to regulators, the Better Business Bureau, and online that the pitch was coercive; Life Surge denies wrongdoing and says enrollment is voluntary.

Who Holds the Power

The customers do not control this encounter. Life Surge controls the stage, the sales process, the counselors, the financing pathway, and the information available at the moment of purchase. Attendees are asked to make five-figure decisions inside an atmosphere engineered around religious trust and celebrity authority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The company says representatives are not trained to push people into unaffordable debt and notes that financing comes from third parties. But outsourcing the loan does not equalize the transaction. Life Surge receives the enrollment; the customer retains the liability.

Even the reported disclaimer illustrates the imbalance. Attendees were technically warned that they could lose money, but Mother Jones says the warning appeared too briefly and in text too small to read easily. A disclosure that cannot be meaningfully absorbed functions less as informed consent than as institutional insulation.

Tebow’s Trust Has Economic Value

Tim Tebow is not merely decorative. His reputation helps establish the moral credibility of the room. One complainant explicitly wrote that Christians such as Tebow made her trust the program that cost her money.

Life Surge says headline speakers are not asked to promote the paid classes. Yet in a 2023 recording obtained by Mother Jones, Tebow addressed people who had apparently enrolled and encouraged them to “follow through on that commitment” and “finish strong.” That is encouragement to proceed, whatever contractual distinction the company draws around the word “promote.”

Tebow did not respond to Mother Jones. The outlet estimated that he could earn $2 million to $4 million from Life Surge appearances this year, based on a speakers’ bureau estimate and a schedule of 20 events. That figure is an estimate, not disclosed compensation. The underlying power relationship is still clear: celebrity confidence is monetized immediately, while customers bear the long-term consequences.

“Voluntary” Is a Convenient Evasion

Calling enrollment voluntary strips the sales environment from the decision. Attendees told Mother Jones that counselors pressed them to enroll immediately and denied them time to go home and pray. If accurate, that tactic weaponized the very faith the event claimed to honor: scripture built trust, while urgency prevented reflection.

The reported consequences were not abstract. An Indiana couple bought a $20,000 package, then borrowed roughly $40,000 on promotional credit cards to invest. They made nothing in the market, according to the report, and later faced rates around 29 percent. Another attendee said she borrowed against her home for a $13,000 real-estate course and was still repaying it.

Life Surge denies directing customers to assume debt they cannot afford. That denial must be preserved. So must the material reality: the company collected course fees, lenders held the debt, and customers absorbed the losses.

Respectability Launders Risk

Mother Jones also traced several Life Surge executives to Online Trading Academy, which settled an FTC lawsuit alleging deceptive earnings claims. The settlement included consumer-debt forgiveness and a $362 million judgment, most of it suspended. None of the Life Surge executives was named in that complaint, so their previous employment does not establish misconduct at Life Surge.

It does, however, make scrutiny more necessary—not less. High-priced financial education marketed through emotional spectacle demands rigorous disclosure and independent evidence of outcomes. Celebrity testimony and religious language provide neither. They provide social permission to stop asking.

The System Sells Faith and Assigns the Losses Downward

This story reveals a familiar structure: powerful institutions convert communal trust into private revenue, then describe the resulting transactions as isolated personal choices. The organization designs the funnel. The celebrity supplies legitimacy. The lender supplies leverage. The customer is left carrying the debt.

That is the political meaning of the arrangement. Risk moves downward; money and plausible deniability move upward. “Kingdom impact” dresses wealth acquisition in moral purpose, but the reported machinery is brutally ordinary: authority sells aspiration, intermediaries collect their cut, and the least powerful participant is told that signing was a free choice.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘This is evil’: Christians say Tim Tebow’s favorite wealth seminar buried them in debt

item.title: Trump has dirt on this senator — and he'll rain hell on her if she steps out of line
item.description:
President Donald Trump speaks to the media as he leaves after a Team USA reception hosting athletes who competed for Team USA at the 2026 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games in Milano Cortina, Italy, in the East Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 6, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

Susan Collins’s “Concern” Is a Political Asset, Not a Check on Power

The Performance of Dissent

The article’s strongest evidence is not its speculation about secret leverage or personal enrichment. It is the public record it cites: Senator Susan Collins repeatedly voices reservations about Republican power, then supplies votes that help that power operate. In 2025, according to the cited CQ Roll Call analysis, she voted with Donald Trump’s stated positions 94.6% of the time. She also supported Russell Vought and Tulsi Gabbard for powerful administration posts and says she does not regret voting to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.

That gap between language and action is the story. “Concern” lets Collins advertise independence without consistently imposing consequences on the officials and policies she claims to question.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The Senator Has the Power

Collins is not a spectator trapped behind a commentary desk. She is a senator with confirmation votes, appropriations authority and the institutional standing to withhold support.

That distinction matters because political coverage often treats her statements as events in themselves. But disapproval is not a meaningful restraint when followed by the vote the administration needs. The decisive act is the confirmation, appropriation or procedural choice—not the carefully calibrated sentence issued before it.

The weaker actors in this arrangement are not senators enduring uncomfortable questions. They are the people who live under decisions senators had the power to block.

Moderation as Branding

Collins’s political value comes partly from being presented as a “pro-choice moderate” willing to depart from her party. Yet the votes cited in the article show how that reputation can serve Republican power even when she does not exercise it against Republican priorities.

Her Kavanaugh vote is the clearest example offered. Collins later told the Portland Press Herald that she did not regret the vote, and an audio recording obtained by The New York Times reportedly captured her saying she would vote for him again. Whatever reservations surrounded the confirmation, her institutional decision was unambiguous.

Calling that posture moderation confuses presentation with outcome. A senator can sound conflicted while acting reliably.

Allegations Are Not Proof—and Speculation Is Not Analysis

The article cites ProPublica reporting about an alleged illegal $150,000 contribution involving defense contractor Navatek and a pro-Collins super PAC, alongside federal contracts Collins helped secure. Collins denies wrongdoing. Those are serious reported allegations, but the supplied material does not establish bribery, guilt or a corrupt exchange.

The article weakens its own case when it leaps from those allegations to an unsupported theory that Trump holds Collins in a “blackmail situation.” It also invites suspicion from an asserted increase in her net worth without establishing that her assets resulted from official misconduct. Questions about campaign money, contracting and financial disclosure deserve evidence, not insinuation dressed as certainty.

There is no need to invent a hidden mechanism when the visible one is already politically consequential: Collins chooses how she votes.

The Misdirection Protects the System

Personal attacks on Collins’s courage may be satisfying, but they can obscure the machinery that gives her conduct force. Senate rules, committee authority and the confirmation process convert individual votes into durable government power. Party leaders benefit when a senator can reassure skeptical voters with dissenting rhetoric while still advancing the party’s agenda.

The relevant question is therefore not whether Collins secretly cares. The supplied evidence cannot answer that. The question is what her decisions enabled. On the examples presented, her votes helped place Vought and Gabbard in powerful offices and Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court. Those outcomes are concrete; speculation about her private motives is not.

Concern Without Consequence

The larger pattern is institutionalized symbolic dissent. Officials preserve reputations for independence through tone, hesitation and public discomfort, while their formal actions continue to support the governing project.

That arrangement distributes responsibility away from the people who possess it. Policy becomes something that simply happened; confirmation becomes an unfortunate development; a decisive senator becomes an anxious observer. The language of concern is useful precisely because it softens accountability. Power should be measured at the moment it is exercised—and Susan Collins’s record, as presented here, lies in her votes.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump has dirt on this senator — and he’ll rain hell on her if she steps out of line

item.title: 'A Communism of Pelf': How Trump betrayed American workers
item.description:
REUTERS/Evan Vucci

The Tariff Bill Comes Due at the Checkout Counter

The Power Sits in the White House

Donald Trump’s tariff policy is often packaged as economic nationalism on behalf of workers. The AlterNet interview instead describes a system in which the president imposes trade barriers, businesses absorb the initial costs, and consumers ultimately pay higher prices—while factories dependent on imported components face higher production costs and greater insecurity.

That chain of responsibility matters. Canada and Europe did not make the United States tax its own imports. Workers did not design the policy. The administration did. Calling the resulting price increases an unfortunate side effect obscures the central fact: the government chose an instrument whose costs could predictably travel through employers to households.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Workers Supply the Branding, Not the Policy

The political sales pitch promised to restore domestic industry. According to historian Elizabeth McKillen, the results described in the interview cut against that promise: factory employment declined, while integrated industries such as automobile manufacturing were disrupted because American production relies on foreign inputs and cross-border supply chains.

The worker serves as the tariff’s mascot but not its governing constituency. McKillen argues that labor should participate directly in trade negotiations, with enforceable protections on both sides of an agreement. By her account, that is not how Trump’s tariff strategy operates. Presidential discretion substitutes for democratic bargaining, and workers are left to absorb consequences they did not negotiate.

This is the misdirection at the heart of the policy. Economic pain is blamed on foreign countries even when the immediate charge is imposed by the United States and paid first by American importers. Nationalist rhetoric converts a domestic policy choice into an external grievance.

Protection Without Labor Power Is a Fraud

Tariffs cannot be assessed separately from the institutions that determine whether workers can claim any resulting gains. McKillen points to Trump’s firing of a National Labor Relations Board member and the board’s resulting lack of a quorum. She also characterizes his treatment of federal workers as union busting.

Those decisions expose the hierarchy behind the rhetoric. A government supposedly protecting workers through trade policy was, in McKillen’s account, simultaneously weakening mechanisms through which workers exercise power at work. Higher barriers to imported goods do not compensate for impaired collective bargaining rights. They can raise prices without raising wages, increasing corporate leverage rather than worker security.

Protectionism can be targeted, reciprocal and negotiated. McKillen explicitly rejects the claim that every tariff is indefensible. But protection without labor participation is not a workers’ program. It is executive economic management conducted in workers’ name.

Discretion Creates a Market for Favor

The interview raises a more serious allegation: that tariff exemptions and advantages may favor industries close to Trump. The interviewer characterizes that arrangement as corrupt, while McKillen agrees that tariffs lend themselves to presidential corruption and alleges that Trump has profited enormously from holding office. The article does not provide transaction-level evidence establishing particular favors, so those claims should remain identified as allegations and interpretation, not proven findings.

The structural danger is visible even without overstating the evidence. Broad presidential discretion over who receives protection, relief or punishment gives businesses an incentive to cultivate political access. Policy becomes less predictable through public rules and more dependent on proximity to the officeholder. That is the useful meaning behind Grover Cleveland’s phrase “communism of pelf”: losses are distributed downward while politically allocated benefits collect near power.

Bullying Is Not Economic Strategy

McKillen distinguishes American influence from simple coercion. Postwar cooperation was never altruistic; the United States supported international institutions and foreign recovery partly because American prosperity depended on functioning overseas markets. Trump’s approach, in her analysis, retains the desire for dominance while rejecting the reciprocal arrangements that made that influence durable.

The consequences extend beyond offended allies. Unpredictable tariffs make long-term decisions harder for manufacturers, workers and trading partners. Attacking tightly integrated partners such as Canada does not disentangle the American economy from theirs. It injects political volatility into relationships on which American production already depends.

The System Protects Authority, Not Workers

This story reveals a familiar political operation: concentrate decision-making at the top, weaken organized labor, impose diffuse costs on the public and describe the entire arrangement as protection from foreigners. The nationalism supplies the scapegoat. Presidential discretion supplies the patronage mechanism. Workers supply both the justification and the money.

The relevant divide is not free trade versus tariffs in the abstract. It is between trade policy negotiated with accountable rules and worker power, and trade policy wielded as a personal instrument of executive authority. The former can distribute bargaining power. The latter distributes favors—and sends everyone else the bill.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘A Communism of Pelf’: How Trump betrayed American workers

item.title: Trump suffers major court loss in late-night ruling from judge he appointed
item.description:
Donald Trump looks on in the Oval Office. REUTERS/Ken Cedeno/File Photo

The White House Does Not Own the Press Room

Exclusion Was the Policy

President Donald Trump’s White House revoked the hard passes of reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. Just after midnight on the Thursday described by The Washington Post, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily restored their access for 14 days while the outlets’ broader constitutional challenge proceeds.

This was not a misunderstanding between officials and journalists. The administration exercised federal power to remove disfavored news organizations from the building, then defended that decision in court.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power Sat With the White House

The reporters did not control access, credentials, security procedures, or the machinery enforcing their exclusion. The White House did. Treating this as a generic “legal fight” risks flattening the power relationship: one side reported on the government; the other used government authority to restrict where those reporters could work.

Kelly, whom Trump appointed, found the outlets had shown a “high likelihood of success” on their due-process claim. His ruling did not finally decide the case or establish that every allegation in the lawsuit was correct. It did recognize that revoking an asserted constitutionally protected interest without notice and an opportunity to be heard likely crossed a constitutional line.

“National Security” as an Unanswered Accusation

The administration accused the outlets of “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods” and publishing classified information, invoking national security to justify the ban. In the reporting provided, however, no specific falsehood, publication, or demonstrated security harm is identified.

That gap matters. “National security” can describe a genuine danger, but here it also functioned as a sweeping accusation attached to an access penalty. The administration’s stated claims should not be treated as established facts merely because officials supplied them in litigation.

The sequence is concrete: punishment came first; the opportunity to contest it did not.

Due Process Is the Minimum, Not the Victory Lap

The outlets’ attorney called the order a vindication of press freedom, due process, and the rule of law. The relief is nevertheless temporary, and Kelly’s reported finding centered on the likely success of the due-process claim. The broader First Amendment challenge remains unresolved.

That distinction prevents a preliminary order from becoming a comforting conclusion. The reporters regained access because a court intervened after the executive branch had already revoked it. A constitutional safeguard that operates only after exclusion still leaves officials able to impose immediate costs on targeted institutions.

Retaliatory Power Does Not Need to Be Permanent

A press-access ban need not survive indefinitely to produce consequences. It can disrupt reporting, raise legal costs, warn other organizations that access is conditional, and force newsrooms to choose between aggressive coverage and proximity to power.

The supplied reporting does not establish the administration’s private motive, so retaliation cannot be declared as a proven fact. But the observable structure is unmistakable: the White House singled out three outlets, removed their credentials, and justified the action with broad allegations that the account does not substantiate. Those are conditions under which intimidation can operate even if a court later reverses the penalty.

The Systemic Error Is Executive Permission

The deeper danger lies in treating White House access as a personal favor dispensed by the president rather than an administrative power constrained by law. When access becomes a reward for acceptable coverage, press management turns into political discipline.

Kelly’s order imposed a temporary limit, not a permanent cure. The larger pattern is an executive branch testing whether accusation alone can support exclusion—and institutions being forced to spend time and money proving that government power still requires process.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump suffers major court loss in late-night ruling from judge he appointed

item.title: 'Trouble for the GOP' as 'key part of Trump's base appears to be cooling on him': analyst
item.description:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) speaks to the media outside of his office on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz

Rural America Wasn’t Betrayed by Abstraction. It Was Hit by Policy.

The Warning Inside the Poll

An Associated Press-KFF poll of more than 2,000 rural voters, conducted over two weeks beginning in mid-August, found that only about 4 in 10 approved of President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy. Roughly half said the economy was worse than when Trump returned to office, while groceries, gasoline, and healthcare ranked among their leading concerns. Trump’s overall approval among these voters stood at 48%.

Republicans Hold the Power

The central political fact is not that rural voters may stay home in November. It is that Trump and the Republican Party control the decisions now testing their loyalty.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Nearly 7 in 10 rural voters backed Trump in both 2020 and 2024, according to the reporting. That support helped construct the governing coalition responsible for current federal policy. Treating rural disaffection as an electoral mood swing reverses the chain of responsibility: voters are reacting to power, not exercising it.

Material Pain Has Authors

MS NOW analyst Zeeshan Aleem attributed rural economic damage to several Trump administration choices: importing hundreds of thousands of tons of ground beef in August, pursuing a trade war with China that he said cost agriculture billions in sales, and policies associated with rising diesel and fertilizer costs. The article says the beef decision angered cattle ranchers and that cash-strapped farmers faced surging input expenses.

Those claims are the article’s account, not independent proof of every causal link. But the political structure is clear even without overstating causation. Import rules, tariffs, and war policy are government decisions. Their costs do not descend on farms like weather. Officials choose them, and producers absorb the consequences.

The Horse-Race Frame Lets Power Escape

The article presents the development primarily as “trouble for the GOP.” That framing is too weak.

Lost votes are a consequence for politicians. Higher operating costs, diminished export sales, and difficulty paying for food, fuel, and healthcare are consequences for rural households. Converting those conditions into campaign arithmetic makes Republican vulnerability the main drama and rural hardship merely the mechanism producing it.

Even the language of Trump “taking his base for granted” softens what the reporting describes. The issue is not insufficient courtship. It is a governing coalition imposing policies that its own supporters say are leaving them worse off.

Loyalty Is Not Economic Protection

Republican strength in rural America has encouraged a dangerous political assumption: cultural identification can indefinitely substitute for material delivery. The poll suggests limits to that bargain, but it does not establish how respondents will vote or whether dissatisfaction will determine any race.

What it does reveal is a fracture between partisan loyalty and lived economics. Rural voters can support a leader overwhelmingly and still face policy choices that raise their costs or weaken their markets. Political allegiance does not confer leverage when party leaders believe the constituency has nowhere else to go.

The System Rewards Neglect Until It Doesn’t

Rural voters constitute about one-fifth of the electorate, and small shifts could matter in competitive races in states such as Maine, Michigan, and Ohio. But the larger pattern is not simply that Republicans risk losing a dependable bloc.

American political coverage routinely notices neglected constituencies only when their suffering becomes electorally actionable. That habit protects institutions from scrutiny: policy damage becomes “discontent,” decision-makers become campaign strategists, and citizens become turnout variables. The sharper account begins where the horse race ends—with who exercised power, which choices carried costs, and why those expected to bear them were treated as politically captive.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: ‘Trouble for the GOP’ as ‘key part of Trump’s base appears to be cooling on him’: analyst

item.title: GOP senators sprint off when asked for verdict on Mitch McConnell's first week: 'Oh man’
item.description:
U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell (R-KY), sitting with Senator John Hoeven (R-ND), votes “aye” as he participates in a Senate Agriculture Committee meeting on whether to vote the farm bill out of committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

The Senate’s Standard for Representation: A Body in the Room

A Vote Without Accountability

Raw Story’s account of Sen. Mitch McConnell’s September 2026 return raises a narrow but serious question: whether he could independently perform his duties after reportedly falling at home on June 14 and remaining hospitalized until August. The article says McConnell appeared for four votes beginning Sept. 14, spoke little in public, and initially cast one vote incorrectly before changing it after colleagues approached him. Republican senators responded not with evidence clarifying his condition, but with evasion, reassurance, and a strikingly diminished definition of representation.

Who Actually Holds the Power

McConnell holds the office. His Republican colleagues hold the immediate power to determine whether his conduct receives scrutiny inside their caucus. Senate officials and aides control access around him. Kentucky voters, meanwhile, cannot directly compel an examination, an interview, or a demonstration that their senator is independently making decisions.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That hierarchy matters. Sen. Deb Fischer did not merely defend a colleague’s privacy. She argued that McConnell’s presence and recorded vote were sufficient: “He was here for our Farm Bill vote, and he voted.” Asked whether he should demonstrate that he could answer questions, she replied, “I don’t think he needs to.”

That is an institutional claim disguised as personal loyalty. It says the public is entitled to a senator’s vote but not necessarily to evidence that the senator understands, chooses, and can explain it.

Confusion Is Not Reassurance

On Sept. 15, McConnell initially voted “no,” then changed his vote to “aye” after Republican colleagues, including Sen. John Boozman, spoke to him. Raw Story reported that the measure passed 12–11 and that his original vote would have reversed the result.

Sen. John Hoeven, who was among those speaking to McConnell, said McConnell had been correct and that Hoeven himself had mistaken the final-passage vote for a procedural one. That explanation must be preserved: the episode does not, by itself, establish that McConnell lacked capacity or that colleagues dictated his vote.

But it also does not settle the underlying concern. The public record described here remains ambiguous, while the senators offering reassurance resisted the most obvious way to resolve that ambiguity: sustained, unscripted engagement from McConnell himself. Hoeven said reporters could talk to him, even though Raw Story reported that previous attempts had been ignored or blocked by aides.

The Caucus Closes Ranks

The Republican response was not a coherent factual defense. Fischer bristled. Sen. Rand Paul avoided the question. Sen. Roger Wicker offered “He’s a great guy” before elevator doors closed. Hoeven promised access the reporting says had repeatedly failed to materialize.

None of those responses addresses capacity. Character testimony is irrelevant. Physical attendance is incomplete evidence. A colleague’s confidence cannot substitute for public demonstration when that colleague’s vote can determine legislation.

This is institutional cowardice in its most ordinary form: powerful officials declining to ask a necessary question because an honest answer could disrupt their coalition. The reporting does not establish what McConnell’s medical condition was in September 2026. It does establish that his colleagues treated requests for clarity as an inconvenience rather than a legitimate demand for accountability.

The Misdirection Toward Spectacle

The weakest part of the surrounding debate is its fixation on whether McConnell looked “vacant” or spoke loudly enough in a particular clip. Appearance is not proof of incapacity, and armchair diagnosis is not accountability.

The relevant issue is functional and political: Could McConnell independently understand the matters before him, decide how to vote, communicate that decision, and represent Kentucky? Republican senators redirected that question toward attendance, personality, and loyalty. “He’s always been that way,” Hoeven said of McConnell’s limited hallway conversation. That framing converts a question about present capacity into a harmless matter of temperament.

It also leaves weaker actors carrying the burden. Reporters must chase elevators. Voters must infer competence from fragments of video. Colleagues with direct access provide assurances while withholding the evidence that might make those assurances credible.

An Institution Protecting Its Arithmetic

The larger pattern is not simply that aging politicians remain in office. It is that political institutions often value a dependable seat more than transparent representation. A senator can become, in the eyes of the caucus, less a public official than a unit of legislative arithmetic.

Raw Story’s reporting does not prove that McConnell was unable to serve. It reveals something the available evidence supports more clearly: Republican senators were unwilling to establish publicly that he could. Their standard was reduced to presence, a murmur, and a counted vote.

When a party treats accountability as optional so long as the vote arrives, representation becomes incidental. The institution keeps functioning—but increasingly for itself.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senators sprint off when asked for verdict on Mitch McConnell’s first week: ‘Oh man’

item.title: Republicans are sweating a Senate seat they didn't expect was at risk: WSJ
item.description:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) and Senate Republican leaders speak with reporters following the Republican weekly policy lunch on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

Nebraska Republicans Found a Race They Cannot Buy Quietly

A Safe Seat Starts Looking Expensive

The reporting describes a Republican-aligned super PAC reserving more airtime than any other advertiser in Nebraska’s Senate race, while Republican Sen. John Kennedy traveled to campaign alongside incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts. Their target is Dan Osborn, an industrial mechanic running as an independent with the Democratic Party’s endorsement. The money and reinforcements do not establish that Osborn will win. They establish that Republicans no longer consider ignoring him a safe strategy.

Power Is Not Evenly Distributed

Ricketts is not merely one candidate trading arguments with another. He is an incumbent senator and former governor whose family fortune came from TD Ameritrade and whose family controls the Chicago Cubs. He has the support of national Republican political machinery and a super PAC capable of dominating the race’s advertising.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Osborn has a different asset: evidence that Nebraska’s usual partisan arithmetic is not absolute. In 2024, with no Democrat in the race, he finished within seven percentage points of the winner. In the previous Senate contest, the Democratic nominee had lost by nearly 40 points. Democrats have again stepped aside, allowing Osborn to compete without splitting the opposition vote.

That contrast explains the spending more clearly than campaign rhetoric does. A candidate outside the customary party structure came close enough to make entrenched power purchase insurance.

The Outsider Has Given Them Ammunition

Republicans did not invent Osborn’s recorded remarks. According to reporting cited in the article, he said some Trump supporters in a small Nebraska town backed the president because they wanted to feel like winners “because their lives probably suck.” Other recordings captured him describing the border wall as “a symbol of racism” and discussing the share of Republican voters he believes he needs.

Osborn has not disputed the recordings. He told CNN he “would apologize to those people that might be offended” and said he had been trying to explain the appeal of outsider candidates.

The contemptuous phrasing was his decision, and it handed opponents a useful weapon. Criticizing the attack campaign does not require pretending its raw material was fabricated. A candidate asking working-class Republicans to cross party lines cannot casually reduce some of them to damaged people seeking emotional compensation and expect the remark to remain politically weightless.

The Disguise Argument Protects the Duopoly

Republicans are using the tapes to portray Osborn as a Democrat concealed beneath an independent label. The state Democratic Party’s endorsement and decision not to field its own candidate give that argument factual material, as do Osborn’s reported comments about the border wall.

But the accusation also serves a larger purpose: it denies voters the possibility that political identity might exist outside party ownership. Under this logic, an independent who receives Democratic support is not an independent making a coalition; he is a fraud. The major parties may absorb donors, activists and interest groups by the thousands, but a candidate who assembles support across existing lines is treated as counterfeit.

That framing is convenient for institutions built to make every viable candidacy pass through one of two gates.

Class Is the Contest Republicans Cannot Avoid

Osborn’s campaign is presenting the race as an industrial mechanic against a wealthy former governor from a nationally prominent family. That contrast does not prove which candidate would govern better, and biography is not a substitute for policy. It does, however, expose why the race has become troublesome for Republicans.

The party’s normal advantage in Nebraska may be vulnerable when partisan loyalty collides with resentment of concentrated wealth and professional political power. The article attributes the more favorable climate partly to voter unease with President Donald Trump and the GOP. The scale of Republican intervention suggests party actors take that possibility seriously, even if it does not tell us how widespread the unease is or determine the election’s outcome.

When Dominance Requires Reinforcements

The larger pattern is not that money guarantees victory or that an independent label guarantees independence. It is that entrenched parties reveal their anxieties through resource allocation. Republicans hold the incumbent, the state’s usual partisan advantage and access to major outside spending. Yet they are treating Osborn as a threat worth saturating the airwaves against.

The misdirection is to make the story primarily about whether Osborn is secretly a Democrat. The more consequential fact is that Nebraska’s political establishment is mobilizing institutional and financial power against a candidate who demonstrated that the state’s voters cannot be treated as permanently assigned property. Osborn’s own words may help that establishment contain him. The expensive containment effort shows why it believes containment is necessary.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Republicans are sweating a Senate seat they didn’t expect was at risk: WSJ
