item.title: NYT issues warning as Trump 'sycophants' prop up 'flailing presidency’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping after watching a military demonstration from a balcony of the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

The Low-Expectations Presidency Is an Institutional Choice

A Summit Reduced to Damage Control

The account describes a U.S.–China summit for which the New York Times editorial board set a remarkable objective: President Donald Trump should leave without making matters worse. It portrays a presidency driven by personal advantage, flattery, and status rather than a coherent strategy for climate change, artificial intelligence, or disrupted Middle Eastern shipping.

That is enough context. The political question is why the most powerful office in the American system has been reduced, in this framing, to a hazard others must contain.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The Power Sits in the White House

Trump is not a bystander trapped inside diplomatic disorder. As president, he commands the executive branch and possesses enormous authority over foreign policy. According to the Times board, he has used that authority erratically and in pursuit of personal interests, weakening American influence and making negotiations harder.

That assignment of responsibility matters. “Flailing” can sound like mere incompetence—an unfortunate lack of coordination. But the conduct alleged by the board is more specific: Trump rejects climate policy, opposes AI regulation, prizes praise from authoritarians, and runs an administration without a coherent approach to major international problems. Those are choices and governing priorities, not atmospheric confusion.

The Editorial Board Lowers the Bar

The Times reportedly warns against granting Trump “the benefit of low expectations,” then adopts precisely that standard by defining success as the absence of additional damage. Its criticism is severe, but its institutional imagination remains cramped.

A president portrayed as repeatedly subordinating national interests to personal ones is not adequately judged by whether he survives a summit without a fresh disaster. That measure converts presidential misconduct into a performance-management problem. The public is invited to hope for restraint while the institutions surrounding the presidency escape serious examination.

Xi Is Not the Alibi

The account also describes Xi Jinping as an authoritarian and difficult negotiating partner. That is relevant to the diplomatic setting, but it does not distribute American responsibility evenly between Washington and Beijing.

Xi controls China’s decisions. Trump controls the direction of the U.S. executive branch. China’s interests and authoritarian system may constrain cooperation, but they do not explain why the American administration allegedly arrived without a coherent strategy. Treating two powerful leaders as matching obstacles can blur the distinction between an external adversary’s conduct and a U.S. president’s use of powers entrusted to him.

The Reporting Has Its Own Gaps

The supplied account contains an unresolved chronology: it says the column appeared Thursday, that Xi arrived Tuesday, and that a state dinner “will” occur Wednesday. Without dates or the original editorial, that sequence cannot be treated as reliable current reporting. It also asserts that Trump destabilized the Middle East “with the Iran war” without supplying dates, decisions, or attribution sufficient to assess that claim.

Those weaknesses do not erase the central power analysis, but they limit what can responsibly be concluded. A scathing argument still requires a stable timeline and evidence proportionate to its claims.

Systemic Failure Wears a Presidential Face

The larger pattern is not simply that one president behaves unpredictably. It is that American institutions can recognize executive conduct as dangerous to national interests while responding with lowered expectations, ceremonial diplomacy, and appeals that the damage remain manageable.

That is institutional cowardice in its most polished form: describe the concentration of power accurately, document its misuse, and then treat endurance as the available remedy. A political system reveals itself not only through the leader it empowers, but through the standards its gatekeepers abandon once confronting that power becomes inconvenient.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: NYT issues warning as Trump ‘sycophants’ prop up ‘flailing presidency’

item.title: 'Crotch harness' in the Capital: How Trump just weaponized the Smithsonian
item.description:
(Chip Somodevilla/Shutterstock.com)

The Smithsonian’s Real Offense Is Refusing a Sanitized America

A Museum Under Financial Siege

The fight over the Smithsonian is not an abstract dispute among historians. The Trump administration holds the executive branch, congressional Republicans control hearings and appropriations pressure, and the Smithsonian depends on the federal government for 62% of its funding—more than $1 billion annually. That is the power structure: an institution formally independent of the president but financially exposed to officials demanding ideological compliance.

President Donald Trump initiated the federal campaign with a March 2025 executive order condemning the Smithsonian’s supposed “divisive, race-centered ideology.” His administration followed with a White House report, an order for warning signs outside the National Museum of American History, and a demand that exhibits be rewritten in “unifying” language. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum then told the Smithsonian’s governing board that federal agencies could not continue supporting the institution under its existing leadership.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Calling this a debate over historical balance obscures what happened. The administration attached reputational attacks and an implicit funding threat to its preferred account of American history.

A Weak Exhibit Becomes a Useful Weapon

The administration did identify a legitimate curatorial failure. “The Electric Dr. Franklin” exhibit said Benjamin Franklin might have used enslaved people in electrical experiments while acknowledging that the evidence could not establish who assisted him. That possibility may warrant investigation, but presenting an eye-catching conjecture in an exhibition risks giving speculation the authority of institutional fact.

The White House turned that weakness into a license to prosecute the museum’s entire intellectual direction. Its report paired the Franklin language with decontextualized provocations: a child’s diary, an artifact from an exhibit on gay history and material from a staff-training document. Republican committee members then displayed the sexual artifact and demanded binary answers about its suitability for children.

This was not a serious evaluation of how an artifact functioned within an exhibit. It was culture-war staging: select the most inflammatory objects, strip away context and force museum leadership to defend itself before cameras.

“Unity” Means Government Control

The demand for a “basic consensus view” of national history sounds moderate only until the government claims the authority to define that consensus. American history contains slavery, dispossession, war, civil-rights struggles, technological achievement and democratic aspiration. Any “unifying” account must decide whose injuries can be softened so that somebody else can feel affirmed.

Former Smithsonian regent Garret Graves offered the conservative version plainly: the country committed “grave sins,” but remains “a net victory for the world.” That is a political judgment, not neutral history. It may belong in public argument, but federal officials cannot honestly impose it while accusing curators of ideology.

The reported pressure reveals the administration’s operative definition of bias: sustained attention to exclusion is political, while national celebration is merely factual. The distinction is false. Both involve selection, emphasis and interpretation.

Institutional Drift Made the Target Easier

The museum’s own failures matter because they created openings for coercion. For decades, it struggled to construct a coherent account of the country. A 2002 commission criticized its lack of organizational clarity and substantive balance. Later directors divided its holdings into thematic exhibits, but the resulting museum could still feel fragmented and disorienting.

After 2020, Smithsonian leaders explicitly elevated race, identity, inclusion and “critical conversations” as institutional priorities. The Biden White House encouraged some of that direction, including temporary displays recognizing heritage months. Conservatives on the governing board warned that the institution was becoming identified with one political camp.

Those choices deserve scrutiny. A publicly funded museum should distinguish documented history from speculation, explain its interpretive standards and avoid substituting activist vocabulary for argument. But administrative drift does not transfer curatorial authority to the White House. Institutional weakness explains vulnerability; it does not justify political capture.

Independence Without Protection Is a Fiction

The Smithsonian’s governing structure supposedly insulates it from presidential command. That protection proved thin. Trump publicly claimed to fire National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet despite lacking the authority to remove her. She left anyway, reportedly hoping to spare the institution. Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch later announced his departure, saying the experience had been stressful.

That is how coercion works even when formal authority is absent. Officials create personal costs, threaten institutional resources and demonstrate that resistance will prolong the punishment. The target then makes a nominally voluntary decision under conditions created by those officials.

Congressional spectacle reinforces the pressure. The hearings described in the reporting were not designed to resolve the museum’s longstanding problems of chronology, interpretation or architecture. They converted curatorial disputes into loyalty tests and treated cultural discomfort as evidence of institutional misconduct.

The State Wants a More Obedient Past

The larger pattern is not that historical institutions became political only after 2020. Museums have always made political choices about what to collect, display and omit. The change is that federal power is now being used openly to discipline those choices while calling the resulting intervention “accuracy.”

The Smithsonian should answer for unsupported conjecture and incoherent presentation. But those correctable failures are being used to rationalize something more consequential: executive officials and congressional allies leveraging money, hearings and public intimidation to narrow the range of history a national institution may present.

A government that orders warning signs outside a museum is not removing politics from history. It is marking independent interpretation as suspect—and teaching every federally dependent institution that survival may require a more obedient version of the past.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘Crotch harness’ in the Capital: How Trump just weaponized the Smithsonian

item.title: Trump goes ballistic in late-night post over Lincoln assassination site
item.description:
REUTERS/Evan Vucci

The Presidency as a Branding Opportunity

A Disputed Plan, Not an Established Fact

MS NOW reported that Trump administration officials circulated ideas for putting President Donald Trump’s name on federal sites, including Ford’s Theatre. Trump denied the report as a “ridiculous lie,” while the White House and Interior Department called it false. The supplied reporting offers no documents, named sources, or independently verified deliberations, so the Ford’s Theatre proposal remains an allegation—not a confirmed administration plan.

Power Sits in the White House

The institutional imbalance is unmistakable. Trump controls the executive branch; his appointees influence federal property, cultural institutions, and access to the presidency. The news organizations he attacks possess no comparable state power.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That distinction matters because the article’s weakest framing treats the dispute as another combustible clash between Trump and the press. It is not an encounter between equals. A president denouncing unfavorable reporting from the machinery of the presidency is exercising power against institutions that scrutinize it.

The Law Is the Obstacle

The reported rationale for considering Ford’s Theatre was bureaucratic convenience: officials allegedly believed it would be easier to rebrand than other prominent sites. Yet the article also says federal law protects the theater’s name and that changing it would probably require congressional action.

That contradiction should restrain sensationalism. Staff discussion, if it occurred, would expose an appetite for personalizing public property. It would not prove that a renaming was legally viable or imminent. The article blurs those categories because scandal travels faster when speculation is presented as a near-completed scheme.

Public Institutions Are Not Presidential Merchandise

The larger pattern described by the reporting is more consequential than the disputed Ford’s Theatre claim. Trump’s name has reportedly been considered for Pennsylvania Station, Dulles International Airport and the U.S. Institute of Peace, while allies allegedly discussed a stadium and “Lake America.” The article also describes an existing legal fight over his name on the Kennedy Center.

These institutions are not trophies distributed by presidential favor. Attaching a sitting president’s identity to civic infrastructure converts public stewardship into personal promotion. When loyalists generate such proposals, they help collapse the distinction between the state and the individual temporarily directing it.

The Ford’s Theatre allegation is especially grotesque in implication, but the reporting does not establish who proposed it, who approved it, or whether Trump knew of it before publication. Those evidentiary gaps cannot be repaired with contemptuous adjectives.

Denial Is Not Accountability

Trump’s response attacked the report as a hoax designed to demean him. The White House and Interior Department issued categorical denials. Those statements matter, but denunciation is not transparency.

The administration could identify whether any rebranding list existed, who participated in relevant discussions, and what records were created. According to the supplied article, it did not provide that detail. Conversely, the outlets advancing the allegation bear responsibility for showing enough evidence to justify it. Anonymous sourcing may sometimes be necessary, but inflammatory claims demand unusually clear substantiation.

The article also says Trump recently tried to exclude MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House before a federal judge blocked the move. If accurately characterized, that episode concerns the use of presidential access as leverage against disfavored press organizations. Folding it into a “leaks scandal,” however, risks obscuring the concrete issue: who wielded government authority, and against whom.

The State Is Not a Monument to Its Occupant

The systemic issue is not whether one lurid renaming proposal can be proven from this thin account. It is the political culture in which officials and allies reportedly treat national institutions as surfaces for presidential branding, while the president treats hostile coverage as an offense to be punished or delegitimized.

That culture rewards personal loyalty over institutional restraint. It encourages subordinates to anticipate a leader’s vanity and turns public assets into instruments of factional tribute. The press should expose that pattern—but it weakens the case when it substitutes explosive framing for disclosed evidence. Power deserves scrutiny precise enough to survive the denials it predictably provokes.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump goes ballistic in late-night post over Lincoln assassination site

item.title: Republican demands answers after Trump taps Secret Service funds for ballroom
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: U..S. President Donald Trump speaks at the site of ongoing construction of the planned White House ballroom in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 19, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque/File Photo

A Presidential Ballroom Built on an Unanswered Transfer of Power

The Money Moved

The reporting describes a White House construction project expected to cost roughly $927 million, encompassing a ballroom and bunker-related security upgrades after President Donald Trump demolished the East Wing in late 2025. After a proposed $1 billion congressional allocation was removed, the administration reportedly redirected Secret Service funding instead. The article gives conflicting figures—approximately $351.6 million, $415 million, and “at least $396 million” redirected in June 2026 from a $1.17 billion appropriation—making a full accounting essential rather than optional.

The President Had the Power; Congress Did Not Make This Choice

Congress did not approve the ballroom appropriation described here. According to the reporting, the House added $1 billion to a budget bill, but that money was ultimately removed. The decisive action came afterward: Trump reclassified the project as a “military center” connected to White House national security, and Secret Service money was shifted into White House security upgrades.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That sequence matters. Calling a desired building a security facility does not answer who authorized the transfer, what legal authority supported it, or why an agency already reporting resource concerns could afford to lose the money. The label supplies a justification. It does not supply accountability.

The Office of Management and Budget may also hold critical answers. Sen. Maggie Hassan’s letter asks whether OMB gave the Secret Service advance notice or a rationale and seeks its correspondence with the agency and other White House offices. Until those records are produced, the reporting does not establish exactly who approved each transfer or whether Secret Service officials objected.

“Donations” Became an Agency’s Problem

Trump said donations would fully fund the project. According to the article, fundraising fell short, and the administration then pursued public money. When Congress did not provide the proposed amount, funds appropriated to the Secret Service were reportedly redirected.

That is not a story about a construction budget unexpectedly becoming complicated. It is a story about executive power converting a presidential priority into an agency expense after the promised financing proved insufficient. The political trick is familiar: describe an elective project as indispensable, attach it to “national security,” and force the public to debate implementation while the foundational decision escapes scrutiny.

The relevant question is not whether a secure White House needs renovations. It is why this particular structure, at this particular scale, acquired priority over money assigned to an agency with existing protective and financial-crime responsibilities.

The Real Costs May Be Elsewhere

The Secret Service does more than guard presidents. Hassan’s questions identify the potential institutional tradeoffs: terminated or disrupted investigations, reduced personnel or hours in financial-crimes work, and effects on state, local, federal, and foreign partners.

The article does not establish that those harms occurred. Hassan is asking whether they did. But that uncertainty indicts the opacity surrounding the transfer, not the legitimacy of the inquiry. If hundreds of millions of dollars can leave an agency without a public account of which operations will shrink, the administration has concealed the policy choice inside bookkeeping.

Every redirected dollar has an opportunity cost. A ballroom described as security infrastructure does not erase that cost; it merely makes the Secret Service absorb it.

Oversight Reduced to Asking for Receipts

Hassan is demanding a budget accounting, operational-impact assessment, advance-notice history, rationale, and internal correspondence. These are basic records needed to determine what the administration did. Yet Congress appears here not as the institution controlling the purse, but as an investigator trying to reconstruct an executive decision after the money moved.

That imbalance is the larger scandal. The administration reportedly failed to obtain the requested appropriation through legislation, then achieved part of its objective through an agency transfer. Congressional dysfunction did not authorize that maneuver, but it weakened the institution most capable of stopping or exposing it.

The article’s own inconsistent totals reinforce the problem. Whether the amount was $351.6 million, $396 million, or $415 million is not a trivial discrepancy when the money came from an agency appropriation. Without itemized records, even the scale of the diversion remains contested.

The Architecture of Executive Impunity

This is larger than a ballroom. It shows how presidential preferences can be laundered through the language of security, financed through obscure transfers, and presented to Congress as a completed administrative fact.

The power lies with the officials who ordered and approved the redirection. The consequences may fall on Secret Service personnel, financial-crime investigations, partner agencies, and taxpayers who were initially told private donations would cover the project. Focusing only on whether the building is extravagant misses the institutional offense: an executive priority reportedly bypassed a failed funding route and reached into another public function instead.

The structure rising at the White House is therefore also a monument to weakened control of public money. Its most revealing feature is not the ballroom’s size. It is how little those exercising the power have yet been required to explain.

Thanks to Alter Net

item.title: Ex-senator's jilted lover broke into her home and smashed up $200K of property: police
item.description:
U.S. Senator Kyrsten Sinema speaking with attendees at the 2019 Legislative Forecast Luncheon hosted by the Arizona Chamber of Commerce & Industry at the Arizona Biltmore in Phoenix, Arizona. (Gage Skidmore/Flickr)

A Felony Case Turned Into a Morality Play About Kyrsten Sinema

The Alleged Crime Is the Story

Maricopa County sheriff’s deputies allege that Matthew Ammel entered former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s Cave Creek home on August 30, pressured her to post a video on X, and threatened to destroy a painting if she refused. After she did refuse, deputies say, he damaged artwork and other property valued at more than $200,000. Ammel has been charged with class 4 felony criminal damage. Those are allegations, not a conviction.

That account describes alleged coercion followed by extensive destruction. Yet the coverage packages it as an “ex-lover” spectacle, surrounding the criminal case with an affair lawsuit, Sinema’s career, her spending, and a worker’s observations about a new wall. The result is less clarity about power than a tabloid inventory of her private life.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power Changes With the Setting

Sinema once possessed the institutional power of a United States senator. She no longer holds that office, but she retains advantages unavailable to most people facing an alleged intrusion: a high-value property, surveillance footage, prior professional security, access to law enforcement, and a position at the global law and lobbying firm Hogan Lovells.

None of that transfers responsibility for Ammel’s alleged conduct onto her. Institutional privilege can shape how quickly a victim is heard and protected; it does not make coercion or property destruction less serious. Political analysis becomes dishonest when it treats a powerful person’s resources as evidence that harm against that person is trivial—or deserved.

The Headline Makes Intimacy Do the Blaming

Calling Ammel Sinema’s “ex-lover and former bodyguard” supplies relevant history, particularly because he reportedly served on her security detail in 2024. But making the former relationship the dominant frame invites readers to interpret the alleged break-in as romantic fallout rather than an exercise of control.

The reported demand that Sinema publish a video is especially important. If prosecutors establish that account, the alleged conduct was not merely vandalism. It involved an attempt to compel another person’s public speech through threatened destruction. The political significance lies there: access gained through intimacy or security work can become leverage, and private coercion can be staged for a public platform.

Mental Health Is Not a Verdict

The article notes that Ammel had been held at a mental health facility under a court order permitting involuntary evaluation and that a deputy described him as combative outside his initial court appearance. Those facts may matter to the legal proceedings. They do not establish why the alleged incident occurred, prove incapacity, or erase agency.

Loose reporting often uses mental-health references as a ready-made explanation when the evidence establishes only evaluation or treatment. That framing can turn specific alleged decisions—entering a home, issuing a demand, destroying property—into atmospheric “instability.” The court must determine criminal responsibility. Journalism should not substitute insinuation for that work.

The Legal System, Not the Gossip Cycle, Holds Authority

Ammel was arrested on September 18, charged, released with electronic monitoring, and was awaiting another court date at the time described. Sinema reportedly supplied texts, recordings, and surveillance footage used to identify him. Prosecutors, defense counsel, and the court now hold the relevant institutional authority.

The separate lawsuit brought by Ammel’s former wife under North Carolina’s so-called “homewrecker” law does not establish the criminal allegations. A federal judge’s decision allowing that civil case to proceed resolves neither Ammel’s guilt nor the truth of every claim surrounding the relationship. Combining the proceedings may generate scandal, but it muddies distinct facts, legal standards, and responsibilities.

Scandal Is a System for Losing the Plot

The larger pattern is familiar: when alleged coercion occurs around a famous woman, coverage expands her biography until her choices compete with the accused person’s alleged actions. The affair, the house, the paintings, the campaign money, and the wall become one lurid collage. Responsibility dissolves into character judgment.

Sinema’s record in office is open to severe political criticism. But accountability requires precision. Her former power does not excuse Ammel’s alleged conduct, and his mental-health evaluation does not prove its cause. A political press that cannot separate a public figure’s record from an alleged crime against her is not exposing power. It is monetizing confusion.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Ex-senator’s jilted lover broke into her home and smashed up $200K of property: police

item.title: Trump labeled 'weird' as Xi delivers blunt warning right to his face
item.description:
REUTERS/Evan Vucci

The Presidency Is Not a Courtship Ritual

A Summit Framed as Submission

At a White House meeting reported only as occurring “Thursday,” Xi Jinping invoked the “Thucydides trap,” while President Donald Trump received him with unusually elaborate ceremony. Commentators Phillips P. O’Brien and Michael McFaul interpreted Xi’s reference as depicting China as ascendant and the United States as declining. Their interpretation is not proof that Xi intended an insult, but the surrounding spectacle made the charge politically potent.

Trump Controlled the American Stage

Xi controls China’s conduct and rhetoric. Trump controlled how the American presidency received him.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

According to The Atlantic, Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews to greet Xi—an honor American presidents rarely extend—and later planned a state dinner. The military display included national anthems, a cannon salute, and B-1 bombers. The Atlantic also reported that Xi had not offered comparable hospitality when Trump visited Beijing.

This was not diplomatic weather that descended on Washington. Trump chose the reception. Whatever concessions or strategic benefits he expected are absent from the reporting, leaving the visible imbalance as the event’s clearest political fact.

The Insult Story Is the Distraction

The weakest part of the coverage is its fixation on whether Xi “insulted” Trump. “Thucydides trap” describes the danger of conflict when a rising power challenges an established one. O’Brien and McFaul read Xi’s usage as a declaration of American decline, but the phrase itself does not conclusively establish that intent.

That ambiguity is precisely why the insult framing is convenient. It turns a question of presidential judgment into a question of personal humiliation. The consequential issue is not whether Trump should have produced a sharper facial expression. It is why he deployed the symbols of American power so lavishly without any reported evidence of reciprocal treatment.

Ceremony Is an Exercise of Power

Protocol is political communication. Who travels, who waits, who receives honors, and who reciprocates all establish hierarchy before negotiations produce a single public result.

A president can decide that exceptional ceremony serves a strategic purpose. But then the administration bears responsibility for identifying that purpose and demonstrating what the country received in return. Without that accounting, pageantry becomes a substitute for policy—a presidential production in which access to grandeur is granted immediately while any national benefit remains unspecified.

Critics who describe Trump as merely dazzled by Xi risk obscuring this agency. Trump was not a bystander at his own reception. He held the institutional power to set the terms and chose the display.

Flattery Is Not Statecraft

The reporting reveals a recurring failure in political coverage: treating presidential conduct as temperament rather than governance. Trump’s expressions, his apparent deference, and even his reaction to the cannon are less important than his use of the office’s machinery.

When a president turns diplomatic protocol into conspicuous personal attention, the cost is not simply embarrassment. It weakens the distinction between courting a leader and advancing a country’s interests. It also gives the visiting government a valuable image: its leader receiving exceptional honors at the center of American power.

That consequence does not require proving Trump’s private motives or Xi’s alleged insult. It follows from the observable imbalance described in the reporting.

The Office Cannot Explain Itself

This episode is larger than one literary reference or one awkward welcome. It shows how easily institutions can be diminished when coverage centers the president’s wounded dignity instead of his discretionary power.

Xi supplied an ambiguous historical analogy. Commentators supplied the insult. Trump supplied the extraordinary reception. Of those actions, only one was performed with the authority and resources of the American presidency. The central political question is therefore not whether Trump recognized a slight. It is why he made the office perform deference—and what, if anything, the United States obtained for it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Trump labeled ‘weird’ as Xi delivers blunt warning right to his face

item.title: Frustrated GOP senators sending Trump's Pentagon pointed message: report
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump listens as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks during a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Thurmont, Maryland, U.S., July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Heuer/File Photo

The Pentagon’s Accountability Vacuum Is a Choice

A Standoff With Names Attached

Federal News Network reports that Alex Velez-Green and Austin Dahmer, nominated by President Donald Trump in June 2025 for senior Pentagon policy posts, remain unconfirmed after testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee that November. Committee Democrats do not support them, enough Republicans are withholding support to deny a majority, and Chairman Roger Wicker has declined to schedule votes, according to two unnamed sources. The reported dispute centers on lawmakers’ complaints that Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby’s office withholds information and communicates poorly with Congress.

Republicans Hold the Decisive Power

This is not a procedural mystery. Republicans control enough of the confirmation machinery to determine whether the nominations advance, but some are reportedly using inaction to express dissatisfaction with Colby. Wicker controls the committee schedule. Senators control their votes. Trump controls whether the White House continues backing nominees who cannot secure a committee majority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

No senator has reportedly placed a formal hold. That distinction matters because it exposes a quieter method of exercising power: refusing to assemble the votes, refusing to schedule the vote, and refusing to publicly claim responsibility for either decision.

The Nominees Are Leverage, Not Outsiders

Velez-Green and Dahmer are not merely bystanders stranded outside the Pentagon. Both already work inside Colby’s policy operation. Velez-Green serves as his chief of staff and was, according to the report, the principal architect of the 2026 National Defense Strategy. Dahmer is performing the duties of a deputy assistant secretary.

The Senate is therefore withholding titles while much of the underlying work continues. That weakens the confirmation process without necessarily removing the officials from influence. It creates the appearance of resistance while preserving an arrangement in which personnel who lack Senate confirmation can still help shape policy.

Congress Is Complaining About Its Own Weakness

Lawmakers from both parties have reportedly complained for months that Colby’s office does not adequately communicate or share information with Congress. Those concerns have intensified during continuing U.S. military operations against Iran.

If those complaints are accurate, the central issue is not bruised senatorial pride. It is whether Congress can perform oversight while military policy is being developed and executed. Yet the reported response is indirect: stall subordinate nominees rather than force a public accounting from the official whose conduct prompted the dispute.

That is institutional cowardice disguised as leverage. A confirmation bottleneck may inconvenience Colby, but it does not establish what information was withheld, compel its production, or tell the public how congressional oversight has been obstructed.

Ambiguity Protects Everyone in Charge

The article’s language of a “holdup” risks making deliberate institutional choices sound like administrative weather. Votes do not simply fail to occur. According to the reporting, Republican reluctance has denied the nominees sufficient support, while Wicker has chosen not to put the question before the committee.

The silence completes the structure. Wicker’s office and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. The Pentagon offered only that it looked forward to working with lawmakers. Each institution retains power; none publicly explains how it intends to use it.

Government by Unresolved Conflict

The immediate consequence is a Pentagon increasingly reliant on less-senior personnel, which the report says can slow decisions. The larger consequence is more revealing: formal offices remain vacant while acting or subordinate officials continue operating, congressional grievances remain opaque, and accountability dissolves into an indefinite personnel dispute.

This is how institutional power evades scrutiny without formally surrendering anything. The executive branch keeps its policy apparatus functioning. Senators signal displeasure without recording decisive votes. Committee leadership prevents a public reckoning. The vacancies are real, but so is the convenience of leaving responsibility vacant with them.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Frustrated GOP senators sending Trump’s Pentagon pointed message: report

item.title: There are 'tapes of Donald Trump': Russia expert unloads explosive claim
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump gestures as he holds a press conference with Russian President Vladimir Putin following their meeting to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. REUTERS/Jeenah Moon REFILE - QUALITY REPEAT REFILE - CORRECTING “PUTING” TO “PUTIN”

Speculation Is Not an Explanation for Presidential Power

The Claim Is Not the Evidence

The Daily Beast reports author Luke Harding’s allegation that President Donald Trump appeases Russian President Vladimir Putin because Trump fears compromising surveillance material. Harding grounds the possibility in his own account of FSB intrusion while he was a Moscow correspondent in 2007. But the reporting provides no evidence that such recordings of Trump exist. Harding’s experience establishes a Russian intelligence method—not its use against this president.

Trump Has the Power

The fixation on hypothetical “dirt” misdirects attention from the institutionally decisive fact: Trump is president. He possesses extensive authority over American foreign policy. Whatever pressures or preferences shape his conduct, the resulting decisions belong to him and his administration.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Explaining that conduct primarily through fear risks turning the most powerful official in the United States into a captive spectator. He is not one. If his policies benefit Putin, the relevant political questions concern what Trump chose, who implemented those choices, and which officials or legislators declined to restrain them.

Putin’s Apparatus Benefits From the Mystery

Harding’s account depicts Russian security services using surveillance and intimidation to unsettle a foreign correspondent and his family. That is concrete conduct attributed to a powerful state apparatus. His extrapolation to Trump is explicitly speculation.

The distinction matters because unsupported kompromat theories can inflate the Kremlin into an all-explaining force. Putin does not need a secret tape to benefit from favorable American policy. Nor does Russian interference in the 2020 election—attributed in the article to U.S. intelligence officials—prove that Putin controls Trump personally. Election interference and alleged personal leverage are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

A Stack of Warnings Is Not an Argument

The article moves from Harding’s theory to Thomas Wright’s discussion of revisionist powers, then to Joseph Bosco’s prediction that failures involving Ukraine and Taiwan could precipitate American decline and wider conflict. These views share a broad anxiety, but the reporting does not establish a factual chain connecting them.

That structure creates gravity through accumulation: surveillance, Russia, China, Ukraine, Taiwan, global conflict. What it does not supply is a precise account of which Trump decisions empowered which government, through what mechanism, and with what demonstrated consequence. The framing is weak because it substitutes ominous adjacency for analysis.

Accountability Does Not Require Kompromat

Trump’s foreign policy can be judged from identifiable decisions and their effects. If those decisions appease Putin or weaken constraints on Russia, responsibility does not depend on proving a hidden motive. If officials enable those decisions, their agency should be named as well.

The larger pattern is political journalism’s recurring preference for secret explanations over visible power. A speculative tape is more dramatic than presidential authority, bureaucratic compliance, and institutional cowardice. It is also less useful. The system does not need a hidden controller to produce damaging policy; it needs powerful actors who choose it and institutions that permit them to proceed.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: There are ‘tapes of Donald Trump’: Russia expert unloads explosive claim

item.title: Trump's DOJ torpedoes his Kennedy Center demolition threat in new court filing
item.description:
Fencing is erected outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, a day after the Kennedy Center Board voted to close the center for repairs, in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Jessica Koscielniak

A Public Institution Held Hostage to a President’s Name

The Filing Undercuts the Threat

A Justice Department status report filed in federal court describes a Kennedy Center with serious safety problems: falling ceiling material, water near electrical equipment, debris on machinery, and concerns about theater rigging. Those facts support an emergency closure. They do not, according to the reporting, support President Donald Trump’s warning that the building may be “ripped down” unless his name is engraved on it.

That distinction is the political story. The administration’s court filing presents an infrastructure problem. Trump presents a loyalty test.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The Power Is Not With the Plaster

The storms, deteriorating building systems, and reported fall of roughly 150 pounds of ceiling plaster from about 60 feet created an immediate public-safety issue. But weather did not vote for a $250 million renovation plan. Ceiling panels did not make the venue’s future contingent on presidential recognition.

The institutional actors did. The Kennedy Center board, described as stacked with Trump appointees, approved the longer closure. Trump then announced that reconstruction and renovation would not proceed unless a court ruled in his favor. Whatever the ultimate legal or engineering outcome, the leverage is plain: the president and his appointees control the decisions that determine whether a temporary safety response becomes a prolonged shutdown.

Maintenance Becomes Personal Leverage

Trump’s own statement strips away the pretense that this is merely prudent facilities management. He tied renovation to the outcome of litigation after previously linking the building’s survival to the placement of his name on it.

The filing does not establish that the center must be demolished. It also sets no reopening date and acknowledges that temporary safeguards would not resolve deeper deterioration. That uncertainty gives those controlling the institution room to maneuver. It does not prove a plan to destroy or permanently abandon the center. It does show how an unresolved capital project can be converted into leverage for a president’s personal branding dispute.

The Weak Framing Is “Contradiction”

Calling the Justice Department filing a contradiction is accurate but insufficient. It makes the episode sound like inconsistent messaging: one branch of the administration says repairs may permit reopening, while the president says demolition is possible.

The sharper point is that official evidence is being forced to coexist with presidential coercion. Government lawyers must describe conditions that can survive scrutiny in court. Trump can publicly inflate those conditions into an ultimatum. The gap between the two is not confusion. It is the difference between an evidentiary record and a political threat.

The Challenge Comes From Outside the Command Structure

Representative Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member, is challenging the closure, arguing that it conflicts with an existing order from U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper and may conceal a permanent move. The reporting does not establish that allegation, and Beatty’s attorneys had not responded to the outlet’s request for comment.

But the power imbalance is already visible. Beatty can litigate and object. Trump’s appointees can vote. The president can declare that renovation will stop. Treating those positions as equivalent “sides” would erase who possesses operational authority and who is trying to constrain it.

Public Property, Personalized Rule

The broader pattern is the conversion of public institutions into instruments of personal recognition. A cultural landmark needs engineering assessments, transparent budgeting, lawful governance, and a repair plan proportionate to documented hazards. Instead, its future has been publicly entangled with whether it bears the sitting president’s name.

That is more than vanity. It is a model of personalized government: institutional power is exercised as though public assets were bargaining chips belonging to the officeholder. The hazards in the Kennedy Center may be physical. The political decay lies in making their remedy conditional on tribute.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump’s DOJ torpedoes his Kennedy Center demolition threat in new court filing

item.title: Stark warning issued to DOJ lawyers: Your future career is 'in jeopardy’
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump listens to reporters at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 8, 2026. REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz/File Photo

A Court Order Is Not a White House Suggestion

The Order, Then the Refusal

In the early hours of Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the restoration of White House credentials to reporters who had been banned. By Thursday morning, according to the reporting, the Secret Service still refused to return the passes despite repeated attempts by at least one correspondent to enter. Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico sought an emergency hearing.

That is the necessary context. The political issue is what happens when the executive branch treats compliance with a court order as negotiable.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power Was Never in the Reporters’ Hands

The excluded journalists did not control access to the White House. The administration did. Its security apparatus physically held the credentials and controlled the gates.

That distinction matters because coverage of press-access disputes can collapse into a story about aggrieved reporters fighting for workplace privileges. But the institutional question is larger: the White House exercised government power to exclude news organizations, and a federal judge ordered that exclusion reversed. The reporters could ask, litigate, and return to the gate. Only executive-branch officials could restore their access.

The weaker actors were forced to seek another hearing simply to obtain what the court had already ordered.

“Sloppy” Is Not an Explanation

CNN legal analyst Elie Honig initially identified two possibilities: administrative failure or intentional defiance. As the denial continued, he said intent became more likely. That is an inference, not an established fact, and the reporting provides no administration explanation from the emergency hearing.

But “sloppy and unintentional” should not become a rhetorical shelter. When officials retain the power to comply, know that a binding order exists, and continue imposing the prohibited result, procedural fog benefits the officials—not the people locked outside.

The article’s framing partly recognizes this, but still lingers over whether the refusal counts as “breaking the law.” The immediate legal reality described by Honig is less mysterious: unless an appellate court stays or reverses the ruling, disagreement does not suspend it.

Appeal Is a Remedy, Not a Permission Slip

The administration had a lawful route available. It could appeal Judge Kelly’s ruling and ask the D.C. Circuit to undo it. What it could not lawfully do, under Honig’s account, was behave as though the appeal had already succeeded.

That separation is fundamental. Courts do not constrain executive power if executive officials may postpone obedience until they feel satisfied with a ruling. An order that operates only at the government’s convenience is not a check on power. It is advice.

The continuing denial also shifted costs outward. Journalists lost access. Their employers had to mobilize lawyers. The court had to convene another proceeding. Executive noncompliance—whether ultimately shown to be deliberate or merely negligent—made everyone else spend time and resources enforcing an obligation that already existed.

The Government’s Lawyers Face the Next Test

Honig’s warning to Justice Department lawyers exposed another layer of institutional power. Government attorneys appearing at the emergency hearing would have to explain what happened without misleading the court or participating in willful defiance. He noted that the consequences could extend beyond contempt to professional discipline.

That is where institutional cowardice often becomes operational: not only in the original decision, but in the willingness of subordinates and lawyers to rationalize it afterward. The reporting does not establish that any attorney lied or enabled defiance. It does show why candor at the hearing mattered. The legal system depends on officials refusing to convert political loyalty into professional misconduct.

Delay Is Its Own Form of Power

This episode reveals a recurring advantage of executive authority: even when challengers win, the government can continue producing consequences while compliance is disputed, processed, or delayed. A reporter denied entry that morning cannot retroactively cover what happened inside. Temporary exclusion can achieve a practical result even if a court later confirms that it should not have occurred.

That is the systemic error. Institutions often measure accountability by the final ruling while ignoring the power exercised before enforcement arrives. The decisive question is not merely whether a judge issued an order. It is whether officials obeyed it when it mattered—and who paid the price while they did not.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Stark warning issued to DOJ lawyers: Your future career is ‘in jeopardy’

item.title: Stolen valor scandal rocks Trump-endorsed Republican as party sweats over Nevada seat
item.description:
Nevada candidate David Flippo (image via campaign website).

Valor by Press Release

The Claim Was False

David Flippo, the Republican nominee for Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, repeatedly claimed that his 2004 Bronze Star included a valor citation. Reporting cited by the article says it did not. The claim appeared first in a campaign announcement video and later in fundraising appeals. Flippo’s campaign apologized but blamed staff.

The Candidate Owns the Campaign

Staff may have produced the materials, but the military record belonged to Flippo. So did the campaign built around it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

A valor device is not decorative punctuation. It distinguishes a Bronze Star awarded for meritorious service from one recognizing bravery while engaged with the enemy. The distinction was central to the prestige Flippo’s campaign invoked. Assigning responsibility to unnamed staff does not explain how a specific and consequential falsehood about the candidate’s own biography survived across years and formats.

The available reporting does not establish who first inserted the claim or whether Flippo personally approved each use. It does establish something simpler: his campaign repeatedly circulated it, and its response shifted responsibility downward.

Safe Seats Weaken Accountability

Flippo won a 13-candidate primary for a district Republicans have held since its creation in 1983. That structural advantage matters more than the campaign’s apology.

In a competitive district, a credibility scandal can threaten a candidacy. In a heavily protected seat, party affiliation may insulate the nominee from consequences that would otherwise follow. The institution with practical leverage is therefore the Republican Party: donors, officials and organizations can withhold money, endorsements and support. The article reports one notable fracture—outgoing Republican Rep. Mark Amodei declined to endorse Flippo—but does not establish how the broader party will respond.

The question is not whether party leaders feel embarrassed. It is whether they treat factual honesty as a qualification for power when enforcing that standard could cost them something.

The Staffing Excuse Is Political Misdirection

Blaming staff turns an accountability problem into a clerical problem. It asks the public to focus on campaign workflow instead of the candidate who benefited from the embellished credential.

That defense may describe how the false language entered campaign materials; the reporting provided does not resolve that question. But even if a staffer wrote every word, the institutional failure remains at the top. Campaigns exist to convert a candidate’s biography into authority. Candidates cannot plausibly claim the benefits of that machinery while assigning its failures exclusively to subordinates.

This is how responsibility disappears in professional politics: credit travels upward, blame travels down.

Military Service as Borrowed Authority

The disputed claim was useful because military valor carries political weight. A candidate invoking combat bravery is not merely adding a résumé line; he is borrowing the moral authority attached to danger, sacrifice and service.

The article places Flippo alongside other politicians accused of overstating military records. That comparison suggests a recurring incentive: military credentials can be converted into electoral legitimacy, while verification often arrives only after the claim has circulated. The result is not just reputational inflation. It cheapens the distinction earned by service members whose awards actually carry the valor device.

The System Rewards the Claim Before Testing It

The larger pattern is an accountability structure built backward. Campaign assertions are distributed immediately through videos and fundraising appeals; scrutiny comes later. By then, the claim has already performed its political function.

Flippo’s case shows how protected districts and partisan incentives can turn truthfulness from a requirement into an optional concern. The false credential is important. More revealing is the machinery around it: a campaign that published it repeatedly, a nominee who benefited, an apology that displaced responsibility and a party apparatus whose meaningful response remained uncertain in the reporting. When electoral power is secure, accountability becomes something institutions can praise without imposing.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Stolen valor scandal rocks Trump-endorsed Republican as party sweats over Nevada seat

item.title: Fundamentalist legal group dives into church fight with Native Americans
item.description:
An evangelical megachurch in 2019 (Wikimedia Creative Commons)

Religious Liberty Is Not a License to Override Tribal Authority

The Dispute Beneath the Slogan

Foundations for Nations came under pressure after Pastor Sarah Lucas urged Native congregants to renounce Northern Arapaho traditions. The Food Bank of Wyoming subsequently ended its partnership with the church, according to Lucas, after receiving a complaint that her message was discriminatory. Liberty Counsel then filed a discrimination complaint for the church and challenged the Northern Arapaho Business Council’s response.

Power Is Split, Not Absent

The Northern Arapaho Business Council holds governmental authority on tribal lands. But the church reportedly owns private fee-simple property, and the council acknowledged in an August 31 resolution that it does not regulate activities on that property. The same resolution said neither the church nor any individual had been formally designated a “bad man.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That distinction matters. Some tribal members called for using treaty provisions to remove the church, and the council initially told church officials to leave. Yet the reporting does not establish that the council ultimately asserted legal power over the church’s private parcel.

The Food Bank of Wyoming holds a different kind of power: control over its partnerships and resources. Whether ending this particular relationship violated discrimination law is the subject of the church’s complaint, not a settled fact.

Liberty Counsel Changes the Balance

Liberty Counsel is not merely defending an isolated congregation. The Florida-based legal organization is providing free representation, filing complaints with state and federal agencies, and asserting that the church needs no tribal authorization to conduct religious activity on its property.

That intervention shifts the conflict. A tribal government and Native community confronting a religious message hostile to their traditions now face an experienced ideological litigation group capable of turning local resistance into an expensive constitutional dispute.

Calling that arrangement a simple free-speech battle erases the unequal legal machinery now in motion. The church has acquired institutional reinforcement far beyond the reservation. The people targeted by its sermon have not been shown to possess comparable resources.

“Religious Freedom” Conceals the Direction of Pressure

Liberty Counsel’s framing centers the church as the injured party. That framing pushes the sermon itself—and the community against which it was directed—to the margins.

The reported message did not merely present Christian doctrine. It urged Native congregants to abandon Northern Arapaho traditions. The predictable consequence is conflict with a community whose cultural practices were placed in opposition to the pastor’s religion.

The evidence does not establish that Lucas intended a broader campaign of cultural suppression. It does establish the direction of the demand: Native people were told to renounce their traditions, while the institution delivering that demand now portrays resistance as discrimination against itself.

The Reporting Needs a Firmer Distinction

The story’s language risks collapsing political rejection, community outrage, loss of a food-bank partnership, and legal eviction into one generalized claim that the church is being forced out.

Those are not interchangeable consequences. The council’s August 31 resolution expressly disclaimed regulatory authority over the church’s private property and denied making a “bad men” designation. Meanwhile, the legality of the food bank’s decision remained contested through an administrative complaint.

Blurring those facts strengthens Liberty Counsel’s preferred narrative: that an embattled church faces coordinated government persecution. The reporting supports a serious dispute, but not that complete story.

A Familiar Conversion of Power Into Victimhood

The larger pattern is institutional inversion. A church challenges Indigenous traditions; community members object; a national legal organization arrives; and the institution with outside counsel recasts itself as the vulnerable dissenter.

The Northern Arapaho council’s authority is real, but the reported resolution also shows its limits. Liberty Counsel’s power lies elsewhere: litigation, federal and state complaint systems, and a political vocabulary that treats consequences imposed on religious organizations as presumptively suspect while treating pressure on Native culture as background.

That is the systemic maneuver. The actor demanding cultural surrender becomes the victim, the community resisting that demand becomes the aggressor, and legal firepower sanitizes the reversal as a neutral defense of liberty.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Fundamentalist legal group dives into church fight with Native Americans

item.title: New signs Trump struggles with 'dementia' or stroke unmasked by expert
item.description:
(REUTERS)

The Presidency Is Not a Remote Diagnosis

Speculation Is Not Accountability

A psychologist, John Garrison, interprets videos of President Donald Trump wincing at a flyover, wearing a heavy coat and gloves, looking downward while walking, bumping into Melania Trump, breathing heavily, and struggling to maintain eye contact as possible signs of dementia, stroke, or another neurological illness. Garrison acknowledges that some observations—such as apparent sensitivity to cold—are not diagnostic in isolation. The reporting supplies no examination, medical records, formal diagnosis, or response from Trump’s physicians.

That distinction is not a courtesy. It is the boundary between observable conduct and medical speculation. A grimace is not a brain scan. Clothing is not a clinical test. Edited footage cannot establish dementia merely because a commentator assembles several ambiguous moments into a pattern.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The President Holds the Power

The relevant institutional fact is not that commentators are worried. It is that the president exercises executive power while outsiders are left interpreting video clips.

Trump, his physicians, and the officials around him possess—or control access to—the information that could clarify his fitness for office. Garrison and Mary Trump do not. Mary Trump’s account of Alzheimer’s in the family and her perception of similarities between Donald Trump and Fred Trump may explain her concern, but family history and resemblance are not diagnoses.

If a president’s health materially affects his ability to govern, the power to document, disclose, evaluate, or obscure that condition is concentrated inside the presidency. A story focused primarily on a psychologist’s frame-by-frame interpretation shifts attention away from those institutional actors and toward evidence that cannot settle the question.

Diagnosis by Montage Is Weak Framing

The article treats contrast as clinical evidence: Trump once appeared to enjoy a flyover but later winced at one; Xi Jinping reportedly showed no comparable reaction; Trump looked overdressed for a reported 65-degree day. These details may justify questions. They do not establish the answers Garrison proposes.

Context could matter: proximity to the aircraft, volume, fatigue, weather conditions, pain, medication, respiratory illness, or countless other factors absent from the account. That does not prove Trump was healthy. It proves the footage is medically indeterminate.

Presenting a list of ambiguous behaviors beside the names of serious diseases gives conjecture the appearance of accumulated proof. The repeated qualifiers do not fully cure that framing. “Could indicate” can become a vehicle for insinuation when the audience is given no clinical evidence capable of distinguishing one explanation from another.

Spectacle Protects the Institution

The fixation on whether Trump looked startled or walked straight converts presidential fitness into content: clips, reaction shots, amateur symptom inventories, and confident narration. It is politically useful theater because it creates alarm without imposing responsibility on anyone empowered to provide reliable information.

The weaker actors in this structure are viewers and outside commentators. They can scrutinize pixels, but they cannot order an evaluation or compel disclosure. The stronger actors are the president and the officials responsible for representing his condition accurately. Coverage that centers speculation allows those power relationships to disappear behind a debate over body language.

That is the misdirection. The public question is not whether one psychologist can diagnose neurological disease through video. He cannot establish such a diagnosis from the evidence described. The question is what credible mechanisms exist to assess a president’s capacity—and whether the people controlling those mechanisms provide trustworthy evidence.

A System Built for Rumor

When institutions offer insufficient verifiable information about a powerful official’s health, speculation fills the vacuum. But speculation does not correct opacity. It often reinforces it by giving officials an easy target: they can dismiss overreaching claims while avoiding the narrower demand for credible disclosure.

The larger pattern is an accountability system degraded into competing performances. Presidential aides control access. Commentators infer disease from gestures. Publishers turn those inferences into political drama. The public receives certainty from neither side.

A functioning system would not require citizens to decide whether a coat, a wince, or a misstep proves neurological decline. It would produce reliable evidence tied to the responsibilities of office. Until then, remote diagnosis remains a distraction from the institution that actually holds the information—and the power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: New signs Trump struggles with ‘dementia’ or stroke unmasked by expert

item.title: The only way to fix Trump's mayhem
item.description:
(REUTERS)

The System Did Not Fail Alone

A Reform List Built Around Power

Robert Reich’s proposal, circulated as an appeal for candidates seeking election on November 3, presents ten reforms meant to constrain presidential abuse and unblock progressive policy. The list ranges from Supreme Court term limits and restored voting protections to wealth taxation, campaign-finance reform, limits on media consolidation, and restrictions on political interference in prosecutions.

Its central insight is sound: removing one officeholder does not dismantle the machinery that made the damage possible. But describing the resulting disorder as “mayhem Trump and his regime have created” leaves too much of that machinery politically anonymous.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump Had Power Because Institutions Supplied It

The presidency holds enormous institutional power over prosecutions, pardons, federal spending, appointments, and executive administration. Reich correctly identifies those pressure points. His proposed restraints are acknowledgments that presidential misconduct is not merely a matter of temperament; it becomes consequential when law and institutional practice leave room for it.

But Trump did not design every vulnerability named here. Congress controls appropriations and writes federal law. States draw congressional districts and administer elections. Supreme Court justices exercise power under lifetime appointments. Wealthy donors and corporate media owners operate through legal structures that government has chosen to preserve.

Trump exploited concentrated authority. Other institutions created, tolerated, or declined to close the openings. Any diagnosis that names the exploiter but softens the role of the enablers is incomplete.

“Abuse” Is Not a Mysterious Force

The list sometimes treats institutional failure as though it were a technical defect awaiting repair. It is also a distribution of power that benefits identifiable actors.

Gerrymandered districts protect politicians from voters. Large donors gain access and influence from privately financed elections. Owners gain leverage when media holdings become more concentrated. Fortunes preserved through stepped-up basis remain with heirs rather than being taxed on unrealized capital gains. None of these arrangements persists because Washington has overlooked a maintenance request.

They persist because people with power profit from them, while the people bearing the consequences usually have less control over legislation, litigation, and political spending.

The “Prerequisite” Claim Hides Political Choices

Reich calls all ten proposals structural prerequisites for enacting good policy. That framing is too neat. Supreme Court tenure, electoral rules, campaign financing, and voting protections plainly shape who governs and what government can do. But a wealth tax is itself a major distributive policy, not merely scaffolding for some later agenda. Restrictions on media ownership are likewise substantive choices about markets and control.

Bundling everything under “reform” can obscure the conflict at the heart of the program. These proposals would not simply make government work better. They would reduce the advantages enjoyed by incumbents, concentrated wealth, dominant media owners, and officials who benefit from weak restraints. That is why passage would be contested.

The source also says these reforms “must be passed by Congress,” while proposing a constitutional amendment or an interstate compact for the popular vote. The contradiction matters. Congress is powerful, but it is not the sole institution capable of delivering every item on the list.

A Checklist Cannot Replace a Theory of Enforcement

Several proposals name a prohibition without explaining who would enforce it. A president would be barred from influencing prosecutions. A president would be held in contempt for impounding appropriated funds. Pardons and commutations would face congressional review.

Those phrases identify real concentrations of authority, but a rule is only as durable as the institution willing and able to impose consequences. “Congressional review” could mean scrutiny without restraint. A contempt finding could become symbolism if enforcement remains uncertain. Conflict-of-interest rules can be written broadly and applied timidly.

Institutional cowardice does not disappear when a statute is enacted. If legislators, prosecutors, judges, or regulators refuse to confront powerful officials, formal safeguards become decorative.

The Systemic Error Is Organized Permission

The larger pattern is not that one president discovered a perfectly healthy government and broke it. It is that American institutions distribute extraordinary power, surround portions of it with weak or politically dependent restraints, and then pretend character will supply the missing safeguards.

Reich is right that opposition to Trump is not a governing program. The harder conclusion is that reform requires confronting every institution and constituency that converts concentrated power into protected advantage. The problem is not mayhem without an author. It is organized permission: authority granted, constraints weakened, enforcement deferred, and responsibility dispersed until no one powerful has to admit choosing the outcome.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: The only way to fix Trump’s mayhem

item.title: Bible verse trips up Tommy Tuberville — as he compares himself to America's poorest
item.description:
U.S. Senator Tommy Tuberville (R-AL) leaves a bipartisan luncheon, weeks into the continuing U.S. government shutdown on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., October 23, 2025. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

Tommy Tuberville Is Not in the Same Boat

A Senator Meets “the Least of These”

When a reporter asked Sen. Tommy Tuberville about the Republican administration’s cancellation of roughly 750,000 Affordable Care Act enrollments, the Alabama Republican did not recognize a reference to “the least of these” from Matthew 25. He nevertheless defended the cancellations, replying, “good job,” and invoking fraud.

That exchange matters less as a Bible quiz than as a display of political priorities. Tuberville regularly advertises his Christian faith and condemns America’s supposed moral decline. When confronted with a central Christian teaching about obligations to poor, sick and hungry people, however, he moved quickly past the principle and endorsed the exercise of state power against people receiving health coverage.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Power Is Doing the Punishing

“We’re all getting punished,” Tuberville said. “We’re all in the same boat.”

They are not. Tuberville is a United States senator. Members of Congress receive substantial taxpayer support for their health insurance, and rank-and-file House members earn $174,000 annually. Meanwhile, more than 16 percent of residents in Tuberville’s home state of Alabama live below the federal poverty line.

The relevant divide is not between equally burdened citizens. It is between federal officials who control health policy and people whose coverage those officials can cancel or obstruct. Tuberville did not merely observe that process. He publicly approved it.

“Fraud” Does the Political Work

Vice President JD Vance and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz said the canceled enrollments included people who did not know they were enrolled, people with employer coverage and people earning more than 400 percent of the federal poverty level. Vance estimated savings of $2.2 billion.

But the administration reportedly did not provide details about who lost coverage or how those people were notified, and health-policy experts questioned its account of the scale of fraud. Another 419,000 marketplace enrollees faced additional verification, while new agents and brokers were suspended for six months.

Those gaps matter. “Fraud” is an accusation, not a substitute for disclosed evidence or competent administration. The reporting does not establish that every canceled enrollment was fraudulent, nor does it establish that the affected people themselves committed fraud. Yet the label allows officials to present mass cancellation first and individual circumstances second.

The Article Finds a Gaffe and Misses the Machinery

The spectacle of a self-described Christian politician failing to recognize scripture is irresistible. It is also the least consequential part of the story.

The sharper issue is that executive officials canceled coverage on a large scale while withholding basic details about the affected population and notification process. A senator from one of the country’s poorest states then endorsed the action without asking who had been harmed, whether the cancellations were accurate or how mistakes would be repaired.

Reducing that record to Tuberville being “puzzled” risks turning institutional indifference into personal embarrassment. The failure here is not theological trivia. It is political judgment backed by federal power.

Moral Language for the Powerful, Suspicion for the Poor

Tuberville’s rhetoric illustrates a durable arrangement: morality is invoked to police the culture, while austerity is invoked to police access to public benefits. The powerful announce virtue. The vulnerable receive verification demands, suspensions and canceled coverage.

The available reporting does not prove that officials intended to strip eligible people of insurance. It does show that Tuberville celebrated the cancellations despite unanswered questions about their scope and administration. His “same boat” claim then erased the material difference between the official praising the policy and the people exposed to its consequences.

That is the larger systemic error. Political leaders use the language of shared sacrifice after making decisions whose risks they do not share. The boat is common only in the rhetoric. The lifeboats remain reserved for those holding office.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Bible verse trips up Tommy Tuberville — as he compares himself to America’s poorest
