item.title: MAGA rages at Catholic bishop who condemned Republican's racist post
item.description:
Bo French, candidate for the Texas Railroad Commission, in Grapevine, Texas, U.S. March 27, 2026. REUTERS/Callaghan O’Hare

The Racism Was Plain. The Republican Evasion Was the Strategy.

The Picture Was the Point

On September 13, Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, posted a photograph of Indian American University of Texas fans celebrating a football victory and portrayed their presence as evidence of a worsening “problem.” Fort Worth Bishop Michael Olson called the message “racist and sinful,” while some MAGA figures defended French and attacked Olson. French did not apologize and, according to Olson’s account, used the backlash to raise money.

Immigration Was the Alibi

French’s post did not establish that anyone pictured was an immigrant, much less that any person lacked legal status. As Olson observed, the photograph revealed only that the fans had “a different complexion.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That makes Jack Posobiec’s defense—an argument about a nation’s right to regulate immigration—a diversion. French had supplied no immigration facts to debate. The defense retroactively assigned foreignness to people based on appearance, then pretended the dispute concerned border policy.

This is how racial exclusion acquires bureaucratic camouflage. First, nonwhite Americans are depicted as evidence of demographic decline. Then defenders replace the actual conduct with a more respectable argument about immigration levels. The prejudice remains; only its label changes.

The Nominee Has Agency

French was not a bystander caught in an ambiguous controversy. He selected the image, described the people in it as a problem and, according to Olson, refused to apologize before fundraising from the uproar.

The predictable consequences were not abstract. The people pictured were treated as presumptively alien to an American university, an American sport and American public life. No evidence about their citizenship mattered because the insinuation worked through complexion alone.

Calling this a “debate among Republicans” risks laundering a clear sequence of decisions into factional noise. French acted. His defenders supplied excuses. Other Republicans, according to Democratic insider Christopher Hale, withheld a defense of the post while continuing to support French’s candidacy. Disapproval without political consequence is not accountability. It is reputation management.

Power Speaks Through Endorsement

Karl Rove said he would vote for the Democratic nominee. Donald Trump responded by attacking Rove as a “RINO.” That exchange clarifies the enforcement mechanism inside the party: the punishable offense was not French’s racial targeting but Rove’s refusal to support the nominee responsible for it.

Trump’s intervention shifted attention from the substance of French’s post to partisan loyalty. The message was straightforward: a Republican who withdraws electoral support risks expulsion from the movement’s definition of a “real” Republican. French, meanwhile, remained inside the boundary.

The institutional power here belongs to the candidate, the party figures who can validate or isolate him and the voters and officials positioned to impose consequences. It does not belong to the students used as visual material for a political message, nor to the bishop being denounced for identifying what the message did.

The Bishop Became the Defendant

Olson condemned the rhetoric in three sentences. His critics answered by calling him an apostate, accusing him of siding with “wolves” and, in one reply cited by Hale, declaring that “Racism is not sin.”

That response was an attempt to reverse the moral burden. French’s treatment of brown students became secondary; Olson’s refusal to bless it became the alleged betrayal. The target of scrutiny moved from a candidate seeking public office to a cleric stating that skin color does not disqualify people from American belonging.

Olson did not retreat. In an interview published later, he repeated his criticism and described the photograph as an object of political exploitation. His persistence matters because institutional cowardice often arrives dressed as caution: a vague lament about tone, followed by continued support for the person who created the offense.

Silence Is Part of the Coalition

Hale contrasted Olson’s response with what he described as a week of silence from Texas Governor Greg Abbott. The supplied reporting does not establish Abbott’s reasons, but the political effect of such silence is visible: French retained support while his critics absorbed the attacks.

This episode exposes a broader structure. Racial scapegoating does not require every party official to defend every racist statement. It requires only that enough powerful actors preserve the offender’s political viability, redirect the argument toward immigration or party loyalty, and leave the targeted people to prove they belong.

The system does not malfunction when explicit exclusion produces fundraising, loyalty tests and continued institutional support. It is revealing what it rewards.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: MAGA rages at Catholic bishop who condemned Republican’s racist post

item.title: Profane MAGA eruption as Trump hoodwinked by 'on the spot' Mamdani midterm gambit
item.description:
US President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speak to reporters during a press conference following their meeting at Gracie Mansion in New York City, US, September 21, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Andrew Hoffstetter

The Scapegoat Shook Hands With the Man Who Needed Him

A Campaign Villain, Briefly Humanized

POLITICO’s Playbook reported that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani invited President Donald Trump, on the spot, to join his Gracie Mansion news conference. Trump accepted and publicly said Mamdani had “great potential.” The exchange infuriated Laura Loomer and other Trump allies because Republicans had spent the run-up to the election presenting the democratic socialist mayor as evidence of a supposed Democratic march toward communism.

That anger exposes the political function Mamdani was expected to perform. He was not merely an opposing officeholder. He had been cast as a campaign prop: a simplified enemy Republicans could attach to every Democratic candidate.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump Broke the Script

Trump held the decisive power in this episode. He could accept or reject Mamdani’s invitation, and he chose to appear beside him. He then offered praise that directly conflicted with the Republican campaign’s preferred caricature.

Mamdani exercised tactical agency, too. He created the moment and then called on MS NOW, CNN, and POLITICO—the three outlets Playbook said Trump had barred from the White House the previous week. On the mayor’s ground, Trump participated in a press event that restored access to reporters his administration had excluded.

This was not ideological conversion. It was a demonstration of how quickly a propaganda line can weaken when its designated monster appears as a governing counterpart rather than an abstraction.

Loomer’s Outrage Reveals the Machinery

Loomer called Mamdani a “communist jihadist,” pairing incompatible political and religious labels into one inflammatory slur. Its purpose was not description. It collapsed socialism, communism, Islam, political opposition, and supposed disloyalty into a single object of suspicion.

Her complaint was revealingly practical: how could Trump motivate voters against Mamdani and his allies after publicly praising him? The problem, in other words, was not a policy concession documented by the reporting. It was that Trump disrupted the emotional discipline of his own coalition.

Loomer described herself as demoralized, but she was not the principal target of harm. Mamdani was the official being branded “anti-American” and turned into a religiously charged enemy. Treating Loomer’s fury as the central injury risks misdirecting attention from the scapegoating strategy she was defending.

The Contradiction Belongs to Republicans

Republican strategist Barrett Marson told Playbook that Trump’s message and the party’s message did not “jibe.” Former New York lieutenant governor Betsy McCaughey likewise called Trump’s conduct a mistake. Their concern was electoral coherence: Republicans wanted to make socialism or communism the campaign’s dominant menace, while their leader publicly treated Mamdani as someone capable of succeeding.

Trump had already asked supporters at the Republican National Committee’s Sept. 9 convention to “pretend that I am on the ballot.” That demand makes the contradiction harder to quarantine. A party organized around one leader cannot easily insist that voters treat his judgment as supreme while disregarding it whenever he improvises past the campaign script.

A Politics Dependent on Permanent Enemies

The episode reveals a coalition whose mobilization strategy depends on maintaining enemies in a state of absolute menace. Normal political contact becomes betrayal because normality punctures the fantasy.

The larger systemic error is not merely inconsistency. It is a political structure that substitutes stigmatized personalities for arguments about power, policy, and consequences. Mamdani was supposed to embody an existential danger; Trump briefly treated him as a mayor. The resulting panic showed how much Republican messaging depended on voters never seeing the difference.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Profane MAGA eruption as Trump hoodwinked by ‘on the spot’ Mamdani midterm gambit

item.title: Trump melts down after midnight over 'sleazebags' and 'totally disloyal Judge’
item.description:
Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office at the White House. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

Loyalty Tests at the Courthouse Door

The Power Is in the White House

Donald Trump holds the institutional power in this story. According to the report, his White House barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, prompting a lawsuit seeking renewed access. Shortly after midnight following his Tuesday appearance before the United Nations General Assembly, Trump attacked CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, denounced the affected outlets, and branded the judge assigned to the case “totally disloyal.”

The relevant conflict is not between a president and journalists of comparable strength. It is between an administration controlling access to the executive branch and news organizations challenging that control in federal court.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Exclusion Was a Decision

The outlets did not wander into a misunderstanding. They were reportedly banned. That distinction matters because political coverage often lets official action dissolve into euphemisms such as “controversy” or “feud.”

The administration exercised its authority to exclude reporters. The affected organizations responded through the courts. Trump then used the presidency’s public platform to insult one journalist and disparage the judge positioned to review the dispute. Those are identifiable decisions by powerful actors, not ambient hostility surrounding an unfortunate disagreement.

A Journalist Becomes the Decoy

Trump’s fixation on Collins redirects attention from the government’s conduct to a reporter’s presence at the United Nations. His complaint—why was she there if CNN supposedly would not cover him?—does not resolve whether the White House may restrict access as reported. It turns institutional scrutiny into a personality drama.

Calling Collins “unhappy,” “sick,” “treasonous,” and “demented” supplies supporters with an enemy while avoiding the substantive question before the court. The insult campaign is not evidence about the legality or justification of the ban. It is an effort to make the journalist’s character, rather than executive power, the object of judgment.

“Disloyal” Means Uncontrolled

The attack on U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly exposes the more consequential demand. Trump appointed Kelly, yet described him as “disloyal.” The report also notes that Kelly ruled against the White House in a similar 2018 case involving CNN correspondent Jim Acosta.

Judicial appointment does not create a personal debt to the president who made it. Trump’s language nevertheless frames an adverse ruling as betrayal. That is a loyalty test imposed on an institution whose function requires independence from the executive. The implication is plain even if the pending case’s outcome cannot be assumed: a judge is treated as legitimate only when his decisions serve the president’s interests.

Abuse as Spectacle

The sneering language is easy to package as another episode in Trump’s long-running combat with the press. That framing is inadequate. The insults accompany the use of government access as leverage and a public attack on the judge reviewing that use of power.

The larger pattern is authoritarian in method: exercise state power against disfavored media, personalize the dispute, label scrutiny treasonous, and portray independent adjudication as disloyalty. The available reporting does not establish the president’s private motive or predict how Kelly will rule. It does establish the public sequence and the hierarchy within it.

The Systemic Error

The danger in personality-driven coverage is that it turns coercive institutional behavior into content about Trump’s temperament. The midnight tirade becomes the story; the machinery behind it becomes scenery.

But the machinery is the story. The executive branch controls access. News organizations must litigate to contest exclusion. A federal judge then faces public denunciation from the president for alleged disloyalty before the reported dispute is resolved. When political power demands personal obedience from both the press and the bench, the insults are not a sideshow. They are the enforcement language of the system Trump is trying to impose.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Trump melts down after midnight over ‘sleazebags’ and ‘totally disloyal Judge’

item.title: FBI blindsided as hackers claim to steal data on 'all employees': 'This is extremely bad’
item.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

The FBI’s Security Claims Collide With Its Own Exposure

A Breach Claim With Real Evidence—and Major Unknowns

ShinyHunters told 404 Media that it stole personal information covering every FBI employee and applicant, including addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and, in some cases, details about spouses. The group supplied a purported 5,000-person sample; 404 Media and Reuters found that some entries matched outside records. But reporters could not determine where the data originated or confirm the group’s claim that it penetrated FBI systems and extracted two to three terabytes. That distinction matters: there is evidence that at least some personal data is genuine, not proof of every claim the hackers made.

The People at Risk Are Not Abstractions

The immediate power here belongs to whoever possesses the records. Home addresses and family information can turn a bureaucratic directory into a map for intimidation. According to 404 Media, criminals in the same ecosystem have previously used stolen phone records to track and harass agents investigating them. The outlet also identified potential value for foreign intelligence services studying the bureau’s personnel and operations.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

This is not merely “data exposure,” the antiseptic phrase institutions use when they want human danger to sound like an IT ticket. If the file is as extensive as alleged, employees, applicants and spouses could face consequences from a security failure they neither authorized nor controlled.

ShinyHunters Is Performing Power

The group’s defacement of the FBI jobs website was political theater with a specific target: the bureau’s claim to technological authority. By copying the FBI’s website-seizure language, the hackers attempted to reverse the symbolism of enforcement. Their representative also framed the operation as retaliation after the FBI publicized the group’s methods in May and advised victims not to pay.

That explanation remains the group’s claim, not an established motive. Its denial of financial motivation deserves no automatic credibility, particularly from an operation associated with demands for payment. Calling the contemplated pressure “coercion” instead of extortion does not clarify what ShinyHunters intends to do with the data. It advertises leverage while withholding the terms.

Institutional Silence Is Not an Answer

The FBI did not immediately respond to 404 Media, while its jobs site and Special Agent Applicant Portal were reported unavailable. BleepingComputer later described the outage as maintenance. None of that establishes how the data was obtained, whether internal systems were breached or whether the attackers exploited PeopleSoft and reached Amazon Web Services GovCloud as alleged.

But uncertainty about the intrusion does not erase institutional responsibility. The FBI controls its systems, its vendors and the conditions under which applicants surrender sensitive information. It therefore owes affected people a precise accounting: what records were held, which systems were touched, who was exposed and what protection is being offered. A maintenance notice cannot perform that function.

Congress Was Already Warned About Capacity

The political context sharpens the stakes. At a September 2025 Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Sen. Dick Durbin said information received by his office indicated that cuts would reduce the FBI cyber division’s personnel by half. FBI Director Kash Patel answered by pointing to increased arrests and convictions under the Trump administration.

That response, as reported, did not address whether the bureau retained enough specialists to defend its own infrastructure and sensitive personnel records. Enforcement statistics are not a substitute for defensive capacity. Arresting more suspects cannot retroactively secure a spouse’s address once it has entered criminal markets.

The reporting does not establish that staffing cuts caused this incident, and the origin of the data remains unresolved. It does establish a serious mismatch in the public argument: lawmakers raised a warning about cyber personnel, while the bureau’s director answered with a different metric.

Security Theater Cannot Secure an Institution

The larger pattern is institutional misdirection through measurement. Officials confronted with questions about capacity often cite visible outputs—arrests, convictions, takedowns—because those numbers project force. Defensive work is harder to stage. Its success usually looks like nothing happening.

Now a criminal group is exploiting that gap, using partially validated personal data and an unverified account of a sweeping intrusion to humiliate the country’s premier federal law-enforcement agency. ShinyHunters may be exaggerating its access; the available reporting cannot settle that question. But the exposure already demonstrates the consequence of treating cybersecurity as branding and enforcement theater while leaving basic questions about staffing, systems and accountability unanswered.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: FBI blindsided as hackers claim to steal data on ‘all employees’: ‘This is extremely bad’

item.title: GOP senator demands probe into Don Jr in move 'very likely to upset Trump': report
item.description:
FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump and his son Donald Trump Jr. arrive at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 3, 2026. REUTERS/Annabelle Gordon/File Photo

The Senate’s Two-Tier Standard for Presidential Families

A Letter About Power

Sen. John Curtis has asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden over their foreign business relationships. His letter cites reporting about significant gifts, cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals and defense-sector investments involving Trump Jr., warning that such ties could create expectations of favorable treatment or national-security vulnerabilities. Those concerns are allegations and risks identified in the letter, not established findings.

Hunter Biden as Political Cover

Including Hunter Biden gives Curtis’s request a bipartisan silhouette, but not a neutral political meaning.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Donald Trump is the sitting president in the events described. His eldest son is reportedly pursuing ventures involving foreign money, foreign officials and industries affected by federal power. That is the immediate institutional conflict. Hunter Biden’s past dealings may merit scrutiny on their own terms, but pairing the two men allows Republicans to discuss access to the current presidency without focusing exclusively on the family that currently possesses it.

The weaker actor becomes camouflage for the stronger one.

Access Is the Asset

The central issue is not whether Donald Trump Jr. holds office. It is whether proximity to a president can be converted into private opportunity—and whether foreign interests might reasonably believe that money, gifts or business relationships purchase access.

Curtis’s letter reportedly points to a lavish Bahamas wedding said to have been financed by a Russian oligarch linked to Vladimir Putin. That report does not by itself establish a corrupt exchange. It does, however, illustrate the vulnerability Curtis identifies: presidential relatives can receive extraordinary benefits from people whose interests may intersect with American policy, while remaining outside many of the formal restraints imposed on government officials.

The commodity is not a job title. It is the family name.

The Majority That Can Refuse to Know

Punchbowl News assessed the request as having “next to zero chance” of advancing under the Republican Senate majority. That is where responsibility lies.

Curtis can request subpoenas, but the committee majority controls whether his concerns become an investigation or remain a letter. If Republican senators decline to examine reported foreign access to the sitting president’s family, they are not powerless observers. They are using institutional power to prevent institutional scrutiny.

The article’s emphasis on Curtis “breaking” with Trump risks turning oversight into palace drama. Whether the president feels offended is politically revealing but constitutionally trivial. The consequential question is whether senators will protect the public interest when doing so might provoke their party’s leader.

A Boundary Enforced Through Fear

Punchbowl reports that Trump considers questions about his family out of bounds. That position seeks a striking privilege: presidential relatives may conduct international business, but Congress must treat examination of those dealings as a personal attack.

The foreseeable effect is impunity without any need for an explicit order. Senators understand that investigation could trigger presidential retaliation. Committee leaders can therefore bury the request while presenting inaction as procedure, scheduling or insufficient support. Institutional cowardice rarely announces itself. It hides in jurisdiction, discretion and votes that never happen.

Oversight as Partisan Property

This episode exposes a durable corruption of congressional oversight: investigations are often treated not as safeguards against conflicts of interest, but as weapons a majority may deploy against opponents and withhold from allies.

Curtis’s letter tests whether one standard can apply to politically connected relatives across administrations. The likely answer, according to the reporting, is that the Republican majority will not permit the test. That is the larger systemic failure. A legislature that investigates only the families of presidents from the other party is not policing influence. It is protecting its own side’s access to it.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP senator demands probe into Don Jr in move ‘very likely to upset Trump’: report

item.title: Former Trump advisor drops a bomb on the president's endgame
item.description:
REUTERS/Marco Bello

“Mistakes Were Made” Is How Power Escapes Judgment

The Alibi of Good Intentions

An AlterNet interview with Anthony Scaramucci presents his book All the Wrong Moves as an explanation for Donald Trump’s rise: trade policy, unpaid wars, financial bailouts, housing policy, and weak Democratic candidates alienated working-class voters and created an opening for right-wing populism. That systemic account has value. Its central weakness is the insistence that these were largely bipartisan mistakes made by well-meaning people.

“Mistakes were made” is not analysis. It is an alibi written in the passive voice.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Trade agreements were negotiated. Wars were authorized. Tax constraints were discarded. Banks were rescued. Risky lending was encouraged and expanded. Political leaders made those choices, while powerful institutions collected the benefits and less powerful people absorbed the damage. Good intentions may explain some decisions; they do not erase agency or distribute responsibility equally.

Trump Had Enablers, Not Weather

Scaramucci correctly locates institutional power among Republican officials who could have acted against Trump and chose not to. He argues that congressional Republicans declined to remove Trump after his second impeachment because they feared losing primaries to candidates backed by Trump’s voters. That is not confusion inside a “Potomac bubble.” It is political calculation.

The distinction matters. Officials with impeachment votes, Senate seats, committee authority, and party machinery were not helpless bystanders. According to Scaramucci’s account, they placed their careers and personal power first. Calling them cowardly captures the moral failure, but the institutional failure is more precise: they possessed constitutional power and withheld it because accountability threatened their positions.

That is how an individual’s dominance becomes a party structure. Personal fear is converted into votes, nominations, silence, and continued access to office.

Bipartisanship Can Blur Unequal Responsibility

The book’s bipartisan framework also risks flattening different decisions into a single national accident. Scaramucci faults Democratic economic policy, Republican wars, Wall Street bailouts, and failures by both parties. Some of those choices may share assumptions or consequences. They do not therefore carry identical authorship, purpose, or responsibility.

His discussion of housing illustrates the problem. He describes the Clinton administration’s effort to expand homeownership as an early contributor to subprime instability, later amplified under George W. Bush. But the interview does not establish that broader access to mortgages, by itself, caused the housing crisis. Nor does it trace the separate authority of lenders, regulators, securitizers, or investors. Turning the story into a morality tale about excessive homeownership risks shifting attention toward financially vulnerable borrowers rather than the institutions that designed, sold, and profited from risky credit.

Systemic analysis should identify every relevant decision-maker. Otherwise “the system” becomes another passive construction—an immense machine apparently operated by no one.

Intolerance Is Political Fuel, Not Background Noise

Scaramucci retreats from an earlier claim that racism, xenophobia, and anti-LGBTQ hostility were not central to Trump’s rise. Based on his conversations with Trump supporters, he now says intolerance has become more pronounced, including anti-trans and anti-immigrant sentiment. He does not offer the granular polling he says would be needed to measure its electoral weight, so the interview cannot establish how many voters were primarily motivated by prejudice.

It does establish something narrower and politically important: economic alienation and organized intolerance are not competing explanations. A movement can exploit material grievance while directing anger toward immigrants, transgender people, Black people, or other politically weaker groups. Economic injury supplies resentment; political actors decide where to aim it.

The powerful beneficiaries of trade policy, war spending, and financial rescue are difficult targets. Marginalized people are easier ones. Any account that emphasizes working-class abandonment while treating scapegoating as incidental misses how elite power protects itself.

Euphemism Protects the Audience—and Power

The interview’s discussion of Gaza exposes another form of misdirection. Scaramucci calls the situation a humanitarian crisis and says Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu influenced Trump’s decision to strike Iran, while explicitly assigning the final responsibility for that reported decision to Trump. That is the correct allocation of formal power: influence is not command, and the American president owns an American military decision.

But Scaramucci also explains that he avoids the word “genocide” because it would polarize listeners and create professional consequences. The interviewer uses that term and alleges that Netanyahu prolonged the war for personal legal reasons; those are the interviewer’s claims, not facts established by the interview. Scaramucci does not adopt them.

His rhetorical caution nevertheless reveals how elite discourse works. Language is selected partly for its factual defensibility, but also for its compatibility with institutions, employers, governments, and audiences. Scaramucci recounts that his podcast partner retracted her use of “genocide” after the Israeli government complained to the BBC. The interview provides only his account of that episode, but the political mechanism he describes is clear: access and professional exposure narrow the vocabulary through which state violence can be discussed.

The System Fails Through Decisions

The larger pattern is not simply that American leaders made errors and voters punished them. It is that institutions repeatedly insulated powerful decision-makers from the consequences of their choices, then offered weaker actors as explanations for the resulting disorder.

Borrowers become the housing problem. Disaffected voters become the entire explanation for Trump. Polarization becomes the reason to avoid contested language. “Both sides” becomes a solvent that dissolves names, votes, offices, and chains of command.

Trump’s rise may be a consequence of institutional failure, as Scaramucci argues. But consequences do not govern by themselves. Officeholders enable them, parties normalize them, donors finance them, and media institutions decide which descriptions remain professionally acceptable. A system is not an alternative to individual responsibility. It is the durable arrangement through which powerful individuals exercise responsibility—and evade it.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: Former Trump advisor drops a bomb on the president’s endgame

item.title: Two-time Trump voter snaps at president after UN visit: 'He's blown it!’
item.description:
Tom Guilfoyle interviewed on MS NOW (Screenshot)

A Few Angry New Yorkers Are Not a Foreign Policy Analysis

The Power Is in Washington

Donald Trump holds presidential power. He—not the voters interviewed on a New York street—can direct US foreign policy, manage alliances, represent the country at the United Nations, and decide how his administration engages Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

That distinction matters because MS NOW’s segment substitutes public reaction for scrutiny of presidential conduct. The report describes Trump’s UN appearance as “belligerent” and mentions plans to honor Xi, but supplies no details about the remarks, the planned reception, or the policy decisions involved. Without that evidence, the segment cannot establish what Trump did, why it matters, or what consequences may follow.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

Reaction Is Easier Than Accountability

The article offers three opinions: Danielle Trietman said the country was making “idiot choices”; Julia Polisoto said the United States was not viewed pleasantly; and former Trump voter Tom Guilfoyle said Trump had “blown it completely” and damaged allied trust.

Those statements document dissatisfaction among three New Yorkers. They do not measure international opinion, demonstrate that allies have withdrawn trust, or establish how any diplomatic relationship has changed. Guilfoyle’s voting history gives his criticism narrative punch, but it does not turn his assessment into evidence.

The Convert Becomes the Story

Political coverage loves the disillusioned supporter because personal betrayal is vivid and inexpensive. A former Trump voter expressing fury creates an emotional arc without requiring the reporting to examine institutions, policy, or measurable consequences.

That framing also shifts attention toward voters: Are they embarrassed? Do they regret their choices? Will they finally reconsider? But voters do not conduct diplomacy. The president and his administration do. When coverage centers spectators rather than decision-makers, responsibility becomes a mood circulating through the electorate instead of power exercised from the executive branch.

Labels Cannot Replace Reporting

Calling an appearance “belligerent” is an editorial judgment. The article provides no quoted UN remarks or described conduct that would allow readers to evaluate that label. Likewise, the reference to plans to “fete” Xi Jinping carries an insinuation of indulgence without explaining what was planned or how it departed from ordinary diplomacy.

A sharper article would identify the relevant words, commitments, reversals, or concessions and then trace who authorized them. Here, loaded description does the work that evidence should have done. That is weak framing, even when the underlying criticism may prove justified.

Spectacle Protects the Decision-Makers

The larger pattern is political journalism organized around spectacle: provocative presidential imagery, sharply edited voter reactions, and a redemption narrative starring the repentant supporter. The format produces heat while leaving the machinery of power largely untouched.

The systemic error is not that ordinary people have opinions. It is that coverage treats those opinions as a substitute for examining presidential agency. If an administration has damaged alliances or granted Xi Jinping unusual political deference, the relevant story lies in documented decisions and their consequences—not in three sidewalk interviews selected to express national humiliation.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: Two-time Trump voter snaps at president after UN visit: ‘He’s blown it!’

item.title: GOP gets fresh dose of bad news as forecaster downgrades party's chances in key races
item.description:
exas Governor Greg Abbott speaks to reporters after casting his early vote in the state’s primary runoff election at a polling station in Austin, Texas, U.S. May 18, 2026. REUTERS/Joel Angel Juarez

Republican Power Is Becoming Its Own Opposition

The Forecast Is Not the Result

Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted several 2026 race ratings toward Democrats: Michigan’s Senate contest now leans Democratic; Iowa’s is a toss-up; Republican advantages narrowed in Kansas, Texas, Florida, Ohio, Nevada, and two House districts. These are forecasts, not votes, but the movement is notably broad—and much of it is occurring where Republicans built durable institutional control.

This Is an Incumbent-Party Problem

The relevant power structure is not mysterious. Republicans hold the long-term governing advantage in the red states highlighted by the ratings changes. They have selected the candidates, shaped policy, defended the president, and—in Texas’ newly created 9th District—designed the electoral terrain itself.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

That matters because coverage built around “bad news” can make political deterioration sound like weather. It is not. Kondik identifies concrete liabilities: the president’s economic credibility has collapsed in the electorate, according to his assessment, while the strike on Iran has become unpopular enough that Republican Senate candidates Mike Rogers in Michigan and Ashley Hinson in Iowa are calling for the president to end the war.

Those liabilities follow governing decisions. Voters did not spontaneously become “exhausted.” Republican leadership accumulated the record producing that exhaustion.

Distance Without Independence

Rogers and Hinson are now trying to separate themselves from the president’s war policy. That may be electorally rational, but it exposes the party’s predicament: Republican candidates want the advantages of party alignment without full ownership of the administration’s consequences.

Calling for an end to the war does not establish who supported the strike, who resisted it, or what either candidate did before public opinion shifted; the reporting does not provide that record. But the timing described by Kondik reveals the incentive. The policy has become costly enough that prominent Republicans believe visible distance is safer than loyalty.

That is not ideological transformation. On the evidence provided, it is political damage control.

Gerrymandering Cannot Eliminate Accountability

Texas’ new 9th District was designed through a Republican gerrymander to function as a safe seat, according to the report. Yet Crystal Ball now rates it only “Likely Republican.”

The seat still favors the GOP, and a forecast downgrade is not proof the gerrymander has failed. But the change exposes the limit of structural manipulation. Mapmakers can dilute opposition and engineer advantages; they cannot guarantee that national conditions will remain favorable. When even a purpose-built district becomes less secure, the problem is larger than one weak candidate.

Republican officials used institutional power to reduce electoral risk. The emerging risk is that their governing record may be outrunning those protections.

The Easy Misdirection Is Candidate Blame

Crystal Ball argues that Abdul El-Sayed may underperform what another Democrat could achieve in Michigan, even as polling cited in the article places him ahead, including a Suffolk University survey showing 47% to 40%. That tension is politically useful: it distinguishes Democratic strength from any assumption that every Democratic nominee is equally strong.

But excessive attention to candidate quality can obscure the larger movement. The revisions extend across Senate, gubernatorial, and House races in multiple states. The common denominator is not El-Sayed, Mariannette Miller-Meeks, María Elvira Salazar, or any single campaign. It is a national Republican governing brand becoming harder to carry.

The weaker framing treats each endangered Republican as an isolated electoral curiosity. The stronger one asks why incumbency, engineered districts, and years of state-level dominance are no longer providing the expected insulation.

Power Eventually Produces a Record

Kondik compares the emerging environment with 2018 and asks why 2026 should not be as bad—or worse—for Republicans, given the president’s damaged economic credibility and the unpopularity of the Iran strike. That remains an analyst’s judgment, not an established election outcome.

The systemic lesson is firmer. A party can use incumbency, redistricting, and geographic advantage to entrench itself, but entrenchment also clarifies responsibility. When one coalition has held power for years, “exhaustion” is not an inexplicable public mood. It is an assessment of who governed, what they chose, and what those choices produced.

The map is shifting because structural power can delay accountability. It cannot permanently erase authorship.

Thanks to Raw Story

Source: GOP gets fresh dose of bad news as forecaster downgrades party’s chances in key races

item.title: 'We drank the Kool-Aid': MAGA voters are sick of 'big liar' Trump
item.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump reacts on stage at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, U.S., September 9, 2026. REUTERS/Callaghan O’Hare

The Exit From MAGA Is Not Yet a Transfer of Power

Disillusionment Without Defection

The reporting describes three former Trump supporters—Ryan Wagner, Kalkaska Mayor Jeff Sieting, and Paul Carroll—who say Trump’s claims and decisions have broken their trust. Wagner cited Trump’s statements about food prices and an unnamed war; Sieting pointed to Trump’s response to the Epstein files and a reported promise of $5,000 if voters kept Republicans in power after the midterms; Carroll blamed the war and rising diesel prices. All three said they did not plan to vote.

Trump Made the Promises

The relevant power does not belong to disappointed voters. It belongs to President Donald Trump and the Republican officials who sustain his governing majority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

The men quoted were consumers of political promises, not authors of policy. Trump chose what to claim about prices, the war, and the strait Wagner referenced. According to the reporting, he also urged the public to “move on” from the Epstein files and tied a promised payment to continued Republican control. The article does not establish the full context or implementation status of that proposal, but Sieting understood it as an attempted political inducement—and called it insulting.

That distinction matters. The story is not fundamentally about voters suddenly discovering dishonesty. It is about a president exercising institutional and rhetorical power while former supporters conclude that what he says no longer matches what they can observe.

The Convenient Redemption Story

Coverage of disillusioned MAGA voters can quietly shift attention from the powerful to the persuaded. “They finally realized” is an emotionally satisfying storyline because it turns politics into a personal awakening: belief, betrayal, remorse.

But remorse is not accountability. Wagner taking down his flag does not constrain presidential power. Sieting turning off Fox News does not reverse a policy. Carroll feeling cheated does not alter the decisions he condemns.

The reporting also offers no basis for treating these three men as representative of MAGA voters nationally. Their testimony establishes their own estrangement, not a measurable collapse of Trump’s coalition. Presenting anecdotal disgust as an electoral wave would merely replace one comforting narrative with another.

Abstention Protects the Machine

Each man says he may answer betrayal by withholding his vote. That could hurt Republican candidates if repeated widely, but it is not the same as transferring power to an opposition capable of checking Trump.

Nonparticipation leaves every other vote carrying more weight. It also allows former supporters to reject the product without choosing who should control the institution that produced it. Sieting predicted a Democratic sweep, but the reporting supplies no polling or electoral evidence supporting that forecast.

The political consequence therefore remains uncertain. Disgust can fracture a coalition. It can also dissipate into private withdrawal while party officials, donors, media allies, and reliable voters keep the governing apparatus intact.

Fox News Was Part of the Bargain

Sieting’s rejection of Fox News exposes another layer of power. He said the network’s portrayal of New York no longer matched what he regarded as reality. His complaint suggests that his political break was not confined to one politician; it extended to the media system through which Republican claims reached him.

Yet the article’s focus on individual believers risks obscuring that system. Political messaging is not simply emitted by Trump and received by isolated voters. It is repeated, normalized, and defended by institutions with far greater reach than any one disillusioned mayor or former supporter.

The evidence here does not establish coordinated deception. It does show a former loyalist concluding that both the politician and a favored media outlet had forfeited credibility. That is a failure of an information structure, not merely a voter’s error in judgment.

A Coalition Can Lose Faith and Keep Power

The larger pattern is brutally simple: recognizing manipulation after power has been delivered does not undo the delivery.

Trump holds the presidency described in the report. Republicans seek to preserve their congressional power. Their former supporters now describe themselves as lied to, insulted, and sold something different from what they received. But unless that recognition changes who governs, it remains politically incomplete.

A governing movement does not need every believer to remain enchanted. It needs enough loyal voters, enough institutional enablers, and enough disillusioned opponents to stay home. The system can survive a crisis of faith. What threatens its control is not private regret, but an organized transfer of power.

Thanks to Alter Net

Source: ‘We drank the Kool-Aid’: MAGA voters are sick of ‘big liar’ Trump

item.title: Florida Republican switches sides to oppose Trump and causes MAGA meltdown
item.description:
US President Donald Trump during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

The Culture War Is a Collection Agency for Failed Government

A Voter Names the Material Crisis

Florida Republican Robbie Smither said Tuesday that he planned to vote for Democratic candidates in November after 41 years of supporting Republicans. His stated reasons were concrete: mortgage payments, homeowners insurance, food, education, therapy for his autistic son, and repeated gasoline fill-ups. The response from prominent MAGA voices was not a governing argument. It was an attempt to replace those concerns with fantasies about Democrats “transing” children.

The People With Power Chose the Distraction

Smither’s family does not control federal policy, Republican campaign strategy, or the political identity candidates construct around Donald Trump. Trump holds presidential power. Candidates such as Byron Donalds and Mike Beltran decide what they emphasize while seeking office. Influential allies such as former Representative Matt Gaetz decide how they defend that political project.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:☕ Buy us a coffee

According to Smither, Beltran made Trump his identity in the race instead of presenting the “principled conservative independence” Smither had valued. That is not an accident committed by powerless voters. It is a campaign choice: substitute loyalty to the party’s dominant figure for an account of how public power would address household costs.

The Scapegoat Cannot Pay the Mortgage

Gaetz’s response—“the Democrats want to trans your kids”—was propaganda in its most functional form. It identified no proposal by David Jolly, Gwen Graham, or Representative Castro. Smither explicitly said he knew of no logical evidence that any of them wanted to do what Gaetz alleged.

The claim’s political purpose is visible even without inferring Gaetz’s private intent: it redirects attention from institutions capable of affecting insurance, education, health care, and household finances toward a stigmatized group that does not set those policies. The weaker target becomes the menace; the powerful officeholder escapes examination.

MAGA Offered Mythology Instead of Government

Other MAGA accounts reportedly answered Smither with claims about a proposed $5,000 “dividend” check, a hypothetical Iranian nuclear attack on the Strait of Hormuz, and “trans illegals.” The article provides no evidence establishing those claims. What it does establish is the pattern of response: when a voter described immediate financial strain, Trump’s defenders supplied an unverified future payment, a counterfactual war scenario, and another culture-war slogan.

This is not confusion about what Smither said. He listed the bills. His respondents changed the subject.

The Article’s Real Conflict Is Accountability

The story is framed around a Republican defection and MAGA anger, but the consequential struggle is over what counts as politically admissible evidence. Smither points to his family’s lived costs and asks candidates to address them. Trump-aligned figures answer that loyalty should instead be organized around fear of transgender people, immigrants, and imagined catastrophes.

Even Smither’s protest leaves an important limit intact: the reporting presents one voter’s account of worsening finances, not proof that Trump caused each expense. But political accountability does not require pretending presidents control every price. It requires judging whether officials use their power to confront material problems—or use spectacle to avoid explaining their record and priorities.

Scapegoating Is a Governing Strategy

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice reinforced by authoritarian-style propaganda. Candidates subordinate their identities to a dominant leader, allies convert policy criticism into tribal betrayal, and vulnerable people are deployed as threats whenever material conditions become difficult to defend.

Smither’s break matters because it exposes the bargain beneath the rhetoric. MAGA asks voters to treat cultural enemies as compensation for insecure lives. But a scapegoat cannot fund therapy, lower an insurance premium, improve a school, or keep a family ahead of its next bill. The people seeking power can act on those conditions. Their decision to talk about almost anything else is itself the political story.
